Stack vs Heap at a Glance

Interviewers often open with "where does this variable live?". The JVM gives each thread its own stack of frames. A frame holds the method's local variables, its parameters and its operand stack. All objects live on the shared heap, and the garbage collector manages it.

StackHeap
HoldsPrimitive locals, references, method framesObjects, arrays, instance fields
ScopeOne per threadShared by all threads
LifetimePopped when the method returnsUntil unreachable, then collected by GC
Size flag-Xss-Xms / -Xmx
FailureStackOverflowError (deep or infinite recursion)OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Thread-safetyLocals are confined to their threadShared objects need synchronization
void place() {
    int qty = 3;                  // primitive: in place()'s stack frame
    Order o = new Order(qty);     // reference 'o' on the stack, Order object on the heap
    o.items = new ArrayList<>();  // the list is on the heap, referenced from the Order
}   // frame popped: 'o' is gone, so the Order becomes unreachable and eligible for GC
💡 With escape analysis, the JIT can avoid allocating an object that never escapes a method by turning it into scalar locals. That is an optimization, though. The language model is still "objects live on the heap".

Interview Questions — Core Java

JDK vs JRE vs JVM?
  • JVM: the abstract machine that runs bytecode. It's platform-specific, and that's what makes Java "write once, run anywhere".
  • JRE: the JVM plus the core libraries, i.e. what you need to run Java.
  • JDK: the JRE plus development tools (javac, jar, jdb, jshell), i.e. what you need to develop Java. (Since Java 11 there's no separate JRE download.)
What are the four pillars of OOP?
  • Encapsulation: keep data private and expose it through methods (getters and setters, validation).
  • Inheritance: an IS-A relationship (extends) used to reuse code. Java supports only single inheritance of classes.
  • Polymorphism: compile-time (method overloading) and runtime (method overriding, resolved by dynamic dispatch).
  • Abstraction: hide the implementation and show only the essentials, using abstract classes and interfaces.
Difference between == and equals()? What is the hashCode contract?

== compares references for objects (and values for primitives). equals() compares logical content, when the class overrides it.

Contract: if a.equals(b), then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(). The reverse isn't required, because collisions are allowed. Always override both together, or HashMap and HashSet will break: an equal key ends up in a different bucket and lookups miss it.

@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
  if (this == o) return true;
  if (!(o instanceof Emp e)) return false;
  return id == e.id && Objects.equals(name, e.name);
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return Objects.hash(id, name); }
Why is String immutable? What is the String pool?

A String can't change once it's created. That gives you:

  1. A safe String Constant Pool: literals are shared across the app.
  2. Security: values like file paths, URLs and DB credentials can't be changed after they're checked.
  3. Thread-safety without synchronization.
  4. A cached hashCode, which makes Strings good HashMap keys.
String a = "hi";            // pool
String b = "hi";            // same pool object → a == b is true
String c = new String("hi"); // new heap object → a == c is false
c.intern() == a;            // true
String vs StringBuilder vs StringBuffer?
StringStringBuilderStringBuffer
MutableNoYesYes
Thread-safeYes (immutable)NoYes (synchronized)
SpeedSlow for concatenation in loopsFastestSlower
final vs finally vs finalize?
  • final: a variable can't be reassigned, a method can't be overridden, a class can't be extended.
  • finally: a block that always runs after try/catch (unless System.exit is called or the JVM crashes). Used for cleanup.
  • finalize(): called by the GC before collecting an object. Deprecated since Java 9. Use try-with-resources or Cleaner instead.
Checked vs unchecked exceptions? Show the hierarchy.
Throwable
 ├── Error (OutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError) – don't catch
 └── Exception
      ├── IOException, SQLException …      → CHECKED (must handle/declare)
      └── RuntimeException                  → UNCHECKED
           ├── NullPointerException
           ├── IllegalArgumentException
           └── ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException

Checked exceptions are verified at compile time. Unchecked exceptions usually mean a programming bug. Spring's @Transactional rolls back on unchecked exceptions by default.

OverloadingOverriding
Same method name, different parametersSame signature in a subclass
Compile-time (static) polymorphismRuntime (dynamic) polymorphism
Return type can differSame return type or a covariant one
Can be in the same classNeeds inheritance; can't override static, final or private methods
Any access modifierCan't reduce visibility or throw broader checked exceptions
Abstract class vs Interface (Java 8+)?
Abstract classInterface
Can have state (instance fields) and constructorsOnly public static final constants
A class can extend only oneA class can implement many
Any access modifiersMethods are public by default; default, static (Java 8) and private (Java 9) methods allowed

How does HashMap work internally?
  1. put(k,v) calls k.hashCode() and spreads the bits (h ^ (h >>> 16)).
  2. The index is (n-1) & hash, which is why the capacity is always a power of 2.
  3. If the bucket is empty, a new Node is stored there. Otherwise the existing nodes are compared with equals(): a match replaces the value, no match appends a node.
  4. When a 9th node is added to a bucket that already holds 8, the list is converted to a Red-Black tree if capacity is at least 64; below 64 the table resizes instead (Java 8). It converts back to a list at 6.
  5. When size exceeds capacity × load factor (0.75), the table doubles in size and entries are redistributed.

💡 Keys should be immutable. If a key's hashCode changes while it's in the map, you can't find the entry again.

HashMap vs Hashtable vs ConcurrentHashMap vs synchronizedMap?
  • HashMap: not synchronized; allows one null key and many null values.
  • Hashtable: legacy; every method is synchronized (one lock for the whole table); no nulls.
  • Collections.synchronizedMap: a wrapper with a single lock.
  • ConcurrentHashMap: Java 8+ uses CAS plus synchronized on the bucket's first node, so reads don't lock. No null keys or values. Its iterators are fail-safe (weakly consistent). It provides atomic computeIfAbsent and merge.
ArrayList vs LinkedList?

ArrayList is backed by a dynamic array: O(1) random access, it grows by 1.5×, and inserting in the middle is O(n). LinkedList is a doubly linked list: O(n) access, O(1) insert or remove at the ends or at an iterator position, and it uses more memory per node. ArrayList is the better choice in almost every case, partly because it's cache-friendly.

Fail-fast vs fail-safe iterators?

Fail-fast iterators (ArrayList, HashMap) throw ConcurrentModificationException if the collection is structurally modified during iteration. They detect this with a modCount check. Use iterator.remove() or removeIf() instead.
Fail-safe iterators (CopyOnWriteArrayList, ConcurrentHashMap) work on a snapshot or are weakly consistent, so they never throw.

Comparable vs Comparator?

Comparable (compareTo) is the class's natural ordering and lives inside the class. Comparator (compare) is an external ordering, and you can have many of them.

list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Emp::getDept)
                    .thenComparing(Emp::getSalary, Comparator.reverseOrder()));
Main Java 8 features?
  • Lambda expressions and functional interfaces (Predicate, Function, Consumer, Supplier, BiFunction)
  • Stream API
  • Method references (String::toUpperCase)
  • Optional
  • Default and static methods in interfaces
  • New Date/Time API (LocalDate, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTime)
  • CompletableFuture, Nashorn (removed later)
Stream API: intermediate vs terminal operations; map vs flatMap? (with examples)

Intermediate operations are lazy and return a Stream: filter, map, flatMap, sorted, distinct, limit, peek. Terminal operations trigger the pipeline: collect, forEach, reduce, count, findFirst, anyMatch. Nothing runs until a terminal operation is called.

// group employees by dept, average salary
Map<String, Double> avg = emps.stream()
   .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Emp::getDept, Collectors.averagingDouble(Emp::getSalary)));

// second highest salary
Optional<Double> second = emps.stream().map(Emp::getSalary).distinct()
   .sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).skip(1).findFirst();

// flatMap: List<List<Integer>> → List<Integer>
List<Integer> flat = nested.stream().flatMap(List::stream).toList();

// frequency of each char
Map<Character, Long> freq = "banana".chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
   .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(), Collectors.counting()));

map transforms each element into exactly one element. flatMap transforms each element into a stream and flattens the results.

What is a functional interface? Can it have default methods?

An interface with exactly one abstract method (SAM). @FunctionalInterface is optional but makes the compiler enforce it. It can also have any number of default and static methods. Examples: Runnable, Callable, Comparator.

Optional — why and how?

Avoids NPEs by modeling "might be absent" explicitly. Use it as a return type, not for fields or parameters.

String city = repo.findById(id)
    .map(User::getAddress).map(Address::getCity)
    .orElse("Unknown");          // orElseGet(supplier), orElseThrow()
Runnable vs Callable; Thread vs ExecutorService?

Runnable.run() returns nothing and can't throw checked exceptions. Callable.call() returns a value through a Future and can throw.

Prefer ExecutorService (a thread pool) over creating Threads yourself. It reuses threads, lets you bound concurrency, and manages lifecycle.

ExecutorService ex = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4);
Future<Integer> f = ex.submit(() -> compute());
Integer r = f.get();   // blocks
ex.shutdown();

CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> fetchUser())
   .thenApply(User::getName)
   .thenCombine(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(this::fetchOrders), (n, o) -> n + o.size())
   .exceptionally(err -> "fallback");
synchronized vs volatile vs Atomic vs Lock?
  • volatile: guarantees visibility (a write happens-before every later read of that variable, enforced with memory barriers). It does not make operations atomic: count++ is still unsafe.
  • synchronized: gives both mutual exclusion and visibility. It's reentrant and uses the intrinsic monitor lock.
  • AtomicInteger etc.: lock-free CAS for single variables.
  • ReentrantLock: like synchronized but adds tryLock, timeouts, fairness, interruptible locking, and multiple Conditions. You must call unlock() in finally.
What is deadlock? How to prevent it?

Two or more threads each hold a lock and wait for a lock the other holds, so none can proceed. The four Coffman conditions are mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. Prevent it by always acquiring locks in the same order, using tryLock with a timeout, keeping locks small, and avoiding nested locks. Use a thread dump (jstack) to detect it.

wait() vs sleep()?

wait() is an Object method. It must be called inside synchronized, it releases the lock, and it's woken by notify or notifyAll. sleep() is a Thread static method. It keeps the lock, can be called anywhere, and wakes after a fixed time.

How does Garbage Collection work? Name the collectors.

The GC finds objects that can't be reached from GC roots (stack locals, static fields, active threads, JNI refs), then marks, sweeps and compacts. Collection is generational: minor GCs in Young, major GCs in Old.
Collectors: Serial, Parallel (throughput), G1 (default since Java 9; region-based, predictable pauses), ZGC (sub-millisecond pauses) and Shenandoah (pauses of a few milliseconds), both for large heaps. System.gc() is only a request.

Can Java have memory leaks? Give examples.

Yes: objects that are still reachable but no longer needed. Examples: static collections that keep growing, unclosed resources, listeners that are never deregistered, ThreadLocal in thread pools that's never removed, inner classes holding a reference to the outer class, and mutable HashMap keys. Diagnose with a heap dump in Eclipse MAT or VisualVM.

How to create an immutable class?
  1. Declare the class final.
  2. Make all fields private final.
  3. Don't provide setters.
  4. Initialize everything in the constructor and deep-copy mutable inputs.
  5. Return copies (or unmodifiable views) of mutable fields from getters.

Since Java 16, record gives you shallow immutability for free.

Write a thread-safe Singleton.
// Double-checked locking
public final class Config {
  private static volatile Config instance;
  private Config() {}
  public static Config get() {
    if (instance == null) {
      synchronized (Config.class) {
        if (instance == null) instance = new Config();
      }
    }
    return instance;
  }
}
// Best: Bill Pugh holder or enum
public enum Registry { INSTANCE; }

An enum singleton is also safe against reflection and serialization attacks.

Serialization; what does transient do?

Serialization turns an object into a byte stream (implements Serializable, ObjectOutputStream). transient fields are skipped and get their default value back on deserialization. Declare a serialVersionUID to control version compatibility. Static fields aren't serialized.

Java 11 → 17 → 21 features you should know?
  • Java 10/11: var, String methods (isBlank, lines, strip, repeat), HttpClient, Files.readString.
  • Java 14–17: switch expressions, records, text blocks """, pattern matching for instanceof, sealed classes, helpful NPE messages.
  • Java 21 (LTS): virtual threads (Project Loom), pattern matching for switch, record patterns, sequenced collections (getFirst(), reversed()).
record Point(int x, int y) {}
sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square {}
String d = switch (shape) {
  case Circle c -> "r=" + c.r();
  case Square s -> "side=" + s.side();
};
try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) { ex.submit(task); }
What are the SOLID principles?
  • Single Responsibility: a class should have one reason to change.
  • Open/Closed: open for extension, closed for modification.
  • Liskov Substitution: a subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is.
  • Interface Segregation: prefer small, focused interfaces.
  • Dependency Inversion: depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. This is what Spring DI is built on.
Common design patterns asked in Java interviews?
  • Creational: Singleton, Factory, Abstract Factory, Builder (Lombok @Builder), Prototype.
  • Structural: Adapter, Decorator (Java IO streams), Proxy (Spring AOP), Facade.
  • Behavioral: Strategy (Comparator), Observer (event listeners), Template Method (JdbcTemplate), Chain of Responsibility (servlet filters), Command.
Pass-by-value or pass-by-reference?

Java is always pass-by-value. For objects, the value being copied is the reference. A method can change the object's state through that copy, but reassigning the parameter has no effect on the caller.

What does the static keyword mean on a variable, method, block and nested class?

static means the member belongs to the class, not to an instance.

  • Variable: one copy shared by all instances, stored with the class.
  • Method: called without an object. It has no this, so it cannot touch instance members directly. Static methods are hidden, not overridden.
  • Block: runs once, when the class is initialized.
  • Nested class: holds no reference to an outer instance.

💡 Mutable static state is shared across all threads and requests, so it is a common cause of concurrency bugs and memory leaks.

Explain the four access modifiers.
ModifierClassPackageSubclass (other package)Everywhere
privateYesNoNoNo
(default, package-private)YesYesNoNo
protectedYesYesYes, through inheritanceNo
publicYesYesYesYes

A top-level class can only be public or package-private. Start with the most restrictive modifier that works. With JPMS modules, even a public type is visible outside its module only if its package is exports-ed.

What is the class-loader delegation model, and why does it exist?

When a class loader is asked for a class, it first delegates to its parent: Application → Platform → Bootstrap. It loads the class itself only if the parent cannot find it. This means core classes such as java.lang.String always come from the bootstrap loader, so application code cannot replace them, and every class is loaded only once per loader. A class's identity is its name plus its defining loader. That is why the same class loaded by two loaders can produce ClassCastException: X cannot be cast to X in app servers and with hot reload.

What is the JIT compiler, and why can Java be as fast as C++ for long-running services?

The JVM first interprets bytecode while it profiles the code. Hot methods are compiled to native code by C1 (fast compile, light optimization) and then by C2 (aggressive optimization). This is called tiered compilation. Because the JIT works from runtime profiles, it can inline virtual calls, remove unneeded locks, use escape analysis and unroll loops. A static compiler cannot always do this. The cost is warm-up: the first requests are slower. For startup-sensitive workloads such as serverless, options include CDS/AOT caches or GraalVM native images.

What are wrapper classes and autoboxing? What is the Integer cache?

Each primitive type has a wrapper class (int→Integer, and so on). Wrappers are needed for generics and collections, and they can be null. Autoboxing converts a primitive to its wrapper automatically (Integer.valueOf). Unboxing goes the other way (intValue()), and it throws NPE on null. Integer.valueOf caches values from -128 to 127, so == between two boxed 127s is true and between two 128s is false. Always compare wrappers with equals.

Integer a = 127, b = 127;   // a == b → true (cached)
Integer c = 128, d = 128;   // c == d → false (two objects)
c.equals(d);                // true
What is a record, and when should you not use one?

A record (Java 16) is a transparent, shallowly immutable data carrier. From its components, the compiler generates a canonical constructor, accessors, equals, hashCode and toString. Use records for DTOs, value objects, map keys and API responses.

public record Money(BigDecimal amount, String currency) {
    public Money { Objects.requireNonNull(amount); }   // compact constructor for validation
}

Do not use a record when you need mutable state, inheritance (records are implicitly final and cannot extend a class), or a JPA entity, which needs a no-arg constructor, mutability and proxies. Records work well as JPA projections and @Embeddable values.

Virtual threads vs platform threads: what changed in Java 21?

A platform thread wraps an OS thread. It is expensive (around 1 MB of stack, kernel scheduling), so apps pool a few hundred of them. A virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM onto a small pool of carrier threads. When it blocks on I/O, it unmounts, which frees the carrier, so you can run millions of them. Use them for blocking, I/O-bound code in the thread-per-request style: Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor(), or spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true in Spring Boot 3.2+.

  • Do not pool them. Create one per task.
  • They do not speed up CPU-bound work.
  • Be careful with ThreadLocal-heavy code and with limited downstream resources such as DB connection pools.
  • In Java 21, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier. JDK 24 (JEP 491) largely removed that limitation.
Marker interface vs annotation: which should you use?

A marker interface, such as Serializable or Cloneable, has no methods. It defines a type, so the compiler can enforce it, for example void save(Serializable s). An annotation, such as @Entity or @Transactional, carries metadata that frameworks read through reflection. It can have attributes and can be applied to methods, fields and parameters as well as types. Use a marker interface when you want compile-time type checking. Use an annotation for framework metadata or for anything that is not a class.

Java Language Basics Foundation

The language itself, from the toolchain to primitive types, operators, control flow, arrays, methods and initialization order. These topics look easy, but they produce most of the tricky output-prediction questions in interviews.

JDK, JRE, JVM and the Toolchain

Java source code is not compiled straight to machine code. javac turns it into bytecode, an instruction set for a virtual processor. The JVM (Java Virtual Machine) then runs that bytecode on the real machine. Bytecode is the same on every platform and each operating system has its own JVM, which is how a .class file built on Windows runs on Linux. So Java programs are portable, while the JVM itself is platform-specific.

PartContainsYou need it to
JVMClass loader, bytecode verifier, interpreter, JIT compilers, garbage collectorsExecute bytecode
JREJVM + standard class libraries (java.base and others)Run applications
JDKJRE + tools: javac, jar, javap, jshell, jlink, jdeps, jcmd, jstackDevelop applications

Oracle stopped shipping a separate JRE with Java 11. The replacement is jlink, which builds a trimmed runtime containing only the modules your application uses. Some other distributions, such as Eclipse Temurin, still publish JRE packages. Java itself is a specification, and OpenJDK is the reference open-source implementation. Oracle JDK, Temurin, Corretto and others are builds of it.

Compile and run

// src/com/shop/Hello.java
package com.shop;
public class Hello {
    public static void main(String[] args) {
        System.out.println("Hi " + args.length);
    }
}
javac -d out src/com/shop/Hello.java    # writes out/com/shop/Hello.class
java -cp out com.shop.Hello a b         # fully qualified CLASS name, no .class
java src/com/shop/Hello.java a b        # single-file launch, compiles in memory (Java 11+)
javap -c -cp out com.shop.Hello         # disassemble the bytecode

java Hello.class is a classic mistake: the launcher takes a class name, not a file name, so it looks for a class called class in a package called Hello and fails. Since Java 22 the source launcher can also run a program spread over several .java files.

A class file records the version that produced it. Java 8 is major version 52, 11 is 55, 17 is 61, 21 is 65 and 25 is 69. Running a class on an older JVM gives UnsupportedClassVersionError. To target an older release, use javac --release 17, which also checks that you only use APIs available in that release.

The main Method and Program Structure

The launcher needs one known entry point. Traditionally that is public static void main(String[] args): public so the launcher can reach it, static so no object is needed first, void because exit status goes through System.exit(n), and String[] for command-line arguments.

DeclarationJava 21 (no preview)Java 25
public static void main(String[] a)RunsRuns
public static void main(String... a)Runs (varargs is an array)Runs
static public final synchronized void main(final String[] a)Runs (order and extra modifiers are fine)Runs
static void main(String[] a) (not public)Error: main method not foundRuns
public void main(String[] a) (instance)Error: main method is not staticRuns; the launcher creates the object first
void main() (no parameter)Compiler accepts it as an ordinary method; launcher errorRuns
public static int main(String[] a)Error: must return voidError
public static void main(String a)Error: main method not foundError

Java 25 (JEP 512) finalized compact source files and instance main methods, after previews from Java 21 onward. A file may contain methods and fields with no class around them, and the compiler wraps them in an implicit final class named after the file. A compact source file automatically imports everything exported by the java.base module, so List and Map work without imports. The new class java.lang.IO offers IO.println and IO.readln.

// Hello.java, Java 25: no class declaration, run with: java Hello.java
void main() {
    var name = IO.readln("Name? ");
    IO.println("Hi " + name + ", " + List.of(1, 2).size());
}

With instance main, the launcher prefers a method with a String[] parameter over a no-argument one, and a non-static main requires a non-private no-argument constructor. A private main is never selected.

Rules of a source file

  • Order: optional package, then imports, then type declarations.
  • At most one public top-level type per file, and the file must be named after it. Any number of package-private types can sit alongside it, and each compiles to its own .class.
  • main may be overloaded (only the proper signature is the entry point), inherited from a parent class, and declared in an interface, enum or record. All of those ran on Java 21.

Packages, Imports and the Classpath

A package is a namespace and an access boundary. com.shop.Hello is the class's real name, and the standard class loader expects it at com/shop/Hello.class under a classpath root.

import is a compile-time naming shortcut. It loads nothing and adds nothing to the class file, which stores fully qualified names regardless, so import java.util.* has no runtime cost. It also does not pull in subpackages: java.util.* does not include java.util.function.Function. java.lang and your own package are visible without importing.

  • Static import: import static java.lang.Math.*; lets you write max(1, 2) and PI.
  • Name conflict: with import java.util.*; import java.sql.*;, using plain Date is a compile error (ambiguous reference). An explicit import java.util.Date; beats the wildcards. Two explicit imports of the same simple name are an error, so write the other one fully qualified.
  • Module imports (Java 25, JEP 511): import module java.base; imports all packages a module exports.

The classpath is the ordered list of directories and jars where the application class loader looks for classes. It defaults to the current directory, and -cp replaces the default. The separator is ; on Windows and : on Linux and macOS. lib/* matches the jar files directly in lib, without recursing. The first match wins, which is why two versions of one library on the classpath cause confusing failures. With java -jar app.jar, the -cp option is ignored and the jar manifest (Main-Class, Class-Path) is used instead.

Interview: ClassNotFoundException means code asked for a class by name at runtime, for example Class.forName, and it was not found. NoClassDefFoundError means a class that existed at compile time is missing or failed to initialize at runtime. The second usually points to a broken classpath or to a static initializer that threw.

Identifiers may start with a letter, _ or $, may contain digits after the first character, and are case-sensitive. The compiler uses $ in generated names such as Outer$Inner, so avoid it. Frameworks rely on the getter conventions: Jackson, Spring and JSP EL all find properties through getX and isX.

Primitive Types

Java has eight primitive types. They hold the value directly rather than a reference to an object, and they exist because arithmetic on raw values is far cheaper than on heap objects. Sizes are fixed by the language, not by the platform as they are in C.

TypeBitsRangeField defaultNotes
byte8-128 to 1270Binary data, I/O buffers
short16-32,768 to 32,7670Rarely used
int32-2,147,483,648 to 2,147,483,6470Default integer type
long64-9,223,372,036,854,775,808 to 9,223,372,036,854,775,8070LSuffix L
float32About ±3.4E38, 6-7 significant digits0.0fSuffix f
double64About ±1.8E308, 15-16 significant digits0.0Default decimal type
char160 to 65,535 (unsigned)'\u0000'One UTF-16 code unit
booleanNot specifiedtrue, falsefalseNot convertible to or from numbers

Signed integer types use two's complement: the negative of x is ~x + 1, and the top bit acts as the sign. That is why the negative range is one larger than the positive range, which is the root of the Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) trap below.

Defaults apply to fields and array elements only. A local variable has no default, and using one before it is definitely assigned is a compile error. The compiler tracks every path: int v; if (cond) v = 1; print(v); fails, while adding an else v = 2; compiles.

Literals

int dec = 1_000_000;      // underscores between digits only (Java 7+)
int hex = 0x1F;           // 31
int bin = 0b101;          // 5 (Java 7+)
int oct = 010;            // 8, a leading zero means OCTAL
int neg = 0xFFFFFFFF;     // -1, hex literals may set the sign bit
long big = 3_000_000_000L;// without L: compile error "integer number too large"
float f = 1.5f;           // 1.5 alone is a double: compile error "lossy conversion"
double d = 1e3;           // 1000.0
double h = 0x1p3;         // 8.0, hexadecimal floating point
char c1 = 'A', c2 = 'A', c3 = 65;   // all the same char
String tb = """
    text block""";        // Java 15+

Unicode escapes are translated before the compiler even tokenizes the file. So // \u000a System.out.println("ran"); really does print, because \u000a becomes a newline that ends the comment. This is a favourite trick question.

Conversions: Widening, Narrowing, Casting

Widening moves to a type that can represent the whole range, and it happens implicitly: byte → short → int → long → float → double, and char → int. Note that byte and short do not widen to char, or the reverse, because char is unsigned.

Widening does not always preserve the value. int → float and long → double keep the magnitude but can lose low digits:

int big = 123456789;
float f = big;                 // implicit, compiles, no warning
System.out.println((int) f);   // 123456792
long lb = 9007199254740993L;   // 2^53 + 1
System.out.println((long) (double) lb);  // 9007199254740992

Narrowing requires a cast. Integer narrowing keeps only the low bits and reinterprets them. Floating-point to integer narrowing truncates toward zero and saturates at the limits rather than wrapping:

ExpressionResultWhy
(byte) 200-56200 is 1100 1000; top bit set means negative
(byte) 30044300 mod 256
(short) 70000446470000 mod 65536
(int) 3.99 / (int) -3.993 / -3Truncates toward zero, does not round
(int) 1e202147483647Saturates at int max
(int) Double.NaN0NaN converts to zero
(int) (char) -165535All 16 bits set, unsigned

Numeric promotion

Before arithmetic, operands are promoted. Anything smaller than int becomes int. If either operand is double the result is double, otherwise float, otherwise long, otherwise int. So byte + byte is an int, and b = b + 1 does not compile.

Implicit narrowing of constants

A compile-time constant of type byte, short, char or int may be assigned to a narrower one of those types if the value fits. This is why byte b = 10; compiles even though 10 is an int.

final int k = 10;
byte a = k;        // OK: constant, fits
int v = 10;
byte c = v;        // ERROR: not a constant
final int w = 200;
byte d = w;        // ERROR: does not fit
char e = 'a' + 1;  // OK: constant 98
char x = 'a';
char y = x + 1;    // ERROR: x is not constant, result is int
Byte boxed = 1;    // OK
Long wrong = 1;    // ERROR: int cannot be converted to Long
Double dbl = 1;    // ERROR: same reason

The rule covers assignment only. A call takesByte(10) does not compile without a cast.

Integer Overflow

Integer arithmetic silently wraps around. No exception is thrown, because checking every addition would be slow and the wrap is well defined by two's complement.

Integer.MAX_VALUE + 1        // -2147483648
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)  // -2147483648, still negative
-Integer.MIN_VALUE           // -2147483648
Integer.MIN_VALUE / -1       // -2147483648, no exception
long a = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000;    // 500654080: multiplied as int, THEN widened
long b = 24L * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000;   // 86400000000: first operand forces long

The long a line is the classic bug: the assignment target does not influence how the right side is computed. Use the exact methods when overflow must not pass silently: Math.addExact, subtractExact, multiplyExact, negateExact and toIntExact all throw ArithmeticException("integer overflow"). A real-world case is (low + high) / 2 in binary search, which overflows on huge arrays. The fix is (low + high) >>> 1 or low + (high - low) / 2.

Floating Point and BigDecimal

float and double follow IEEE 754: a sign, an exponent and a binary fraction. Numbers such as 0.1 have no finite binary form, just as 1/3 has no finite decimal form, so the stored value is the nearest representable one. Printing shows the shortest decimal that uniquely identifies the value, which hides the error until it accumulates.

0.1 + 0.2             // 0.30000000000000004
0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3      // false
0.1f == 0.1           // false: the float is widened, and differs from the double
0.5f == 0.5           // true: 0.5 is exact in binary
double s = 0; for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) s += 0.1;   // 0.9999999999999999
Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-9   // compare with a tolerance, never ==

Special values

ExpressionResultRemember
1 / 0, 1 % 0ArithmeticExceptionInteger division only
1.0 / 0InfinityNo exception for floating point
0.0 / 0, 1.0 % 0, Math.sqrt(-1)NaNNot a Number
Double.NaN == Double.NaNfalseUse Double.isNaN(x)
Double.valueOf(NaN).equals(NaN)trueequals differs from == so collections work
0.0 == -0.0trueYet Double.valueOf(0.0).equals(-0.0) is false
Double.compare(0.0, -0.0)1Total ordering, and NaN sorts last
Double.MIN_VALUE4.9E-324Smallest positive value, not the most negative. Use -Double.MAX_VALUE

Java 17 (JEP 306) made all floating-point evaluation strict, so strictfp no longer has any effect and javac warns about it.

BigDecimal

BigDecimal stores an arbitrary-precision integer (the unscaled value) and a scale: 2.50 is unscaled 250 with scale 2. Because it counts in decimal, 0.1 is exact. It is immutable, so every operation returns a new object, and it is much slower than double. Use it for money and anywhere a decimal value must be exact.

new BigDecimal(0.1)      // 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625
new BigDecimal("0.1")    // 0.1, always construct from a String
BigDecimal.valueOf(0.1)  // 0.1, uses Double.toString, also safe

new BigDecimal("1.10").multiply(new BigDecimal("2.5"))   // 2.750, scales add
new BigDecimal("2.0").equals(new BigDecimal("2.00"))     // false, scale differs
new BigDecimal("2.0").compareTo(new BigDecimal("2.00"))  // 0, numerically equal

BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal(3));
// ArithmeticException: Non-terminating decimal expansion; no exact representable decimal result.
BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal(3), 4, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);   // 0.3333
BigDecimal.ONE.divide(new BigDecimal(3), MathContext.DECIMAL32);     // 0.3333333

new BigDecimal("2.345").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);  // 2.34
new BigDecimal("2.355").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);  // 2.36
new BigDecimal("2.345").setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP);    // 2.35
new BigDecimal("100").stripTrailingZeros();                   // 1E+2
new BigDecimal("100").stripTrailingZeros().toPlainString();   // 100
Gotcha: Because equals and hashCode include the scale, a HashSet holding 1.0 and 1.00 has size 2, while a TreeSet, which uses compareTo, has size 1. Always compare money with compareTo. HALF_EVEN ("banker's rounding") rounds ties to the even neighbour, which avoids the upward bias of always rounding ties up. In JPA, map money to DECIMAL(19,4) or similar, never to FLOAT.

BigInteger is the arbitrary-size integer counterpart. Another option for money is a long holding the smallest unit (cents), which is fast and exact for simple sums.

char and Unicode

A char is a 16-bit unsigned number holding one UTF-16 code unit. It behaves as a number in arithmetic, and it only prints as a character when its static type is char.

char c = 'A'; c++;         // 'B': ++ keeps the type
'a' + 'b'                  // 195: both promoted to int
(char) ('a' + 1)           // 'b'
"" + 'a' + 'b'             // "ab": string concatenation, left to right
'a' + 'b' + ""             // "195"
'7' - '0'                  // 7, the standard digit conversion
Character.getNumericValue('7')  // 7

Unicode has more than 65,536 characters. A character above U+FFFF, such as most emoji, needs two char values called a surrogate pair, so one char is not always one character. "😀".length() is 2, while codePointCount gives 1. The Strings & Text section covers this in depth.

Wrapper Classes, Autoboxing and the Integer Cache

Each primitive has an object form: Byte, Short, Integer, Long, Float, Double, Character, Boolean. Wrappers exist because generics and collections work only with references, and because a wrapper can be null, which expresses "no value" (a nullable database column, say). All are immutable, and the numeric ones extend Number.

Autoboxing (Java 5) is compiler sugar: Integer x = 5 compiles to Integer.valueOf(5), and int y = x compiles to x.intValue(). That second call is why unboxing null throws NullPointerException.

valueOf returns cached objects for small values to save allocation. new Integer(5) always made a new object, and those constructors are deprecated for removal.

WrapperCached by valueOf
ByteAll values
Short, Long-128 to 127
Integer-128 to 127 by default; the upper bound can be raised with -XX:AutoBoxCacheMax=N
Character0 to 127
BooleanTRUE and FALSE
Float, DoubleNone
Integer a = 127, b = 127;  a == b        // true: same cached object
Integer c = 128, d = 128;  c == d        // false: two objects
c.equals(d)                              // true
Integer e = 1000; int f = 1000; e == f   // true: unboxes, compares numbers
Long l = 127L;  l.equals(127)            // false: 127 boxes to Integer
                l.equals(127L)           // true
Double x = 1.0, y = 1.0;  x == y         // false: no cache
Gotcha: The cache is exactly why this bug survives testing: order.getId() == other.getId() on Long IDs passes with small test data and fails in production once IDs exceed 127. Other traps with boxing:
  • int v = map.get("missing"); throws NPE on unboxing.
  • On a List<Integer>, list.remove(1) removes index 1, and list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1)) removes the value.
  • A Long sum in a hot loop allocates on nearly every iteration.

Useful static methods: Integer.parseInt("ff", 16) gives 255; Integer.toBinaryString(10) gives 1010; Integer.toHexString(-1) gives ffffffff; Integer.bitCount(255) gives 8; and Integer.compare(a, b) is the safe alternative to the overflow-prone a - b in comparators. parseInt returns int, valueOf returns Integer, and both throw NumberFormatException on bad input, including null.

Operators and Precedence

Precedence (high to low)OperatorsAssociativity
Postfixx++ x--Left
Unary++x --x +x -x ~ !, castRight
Multiplicative* / %Left
Additive+ -Left
Shift<< >> >>>Left
Relational< > <= >= instanceofLeft
Equality== !=Left
Bitwise AND, XOR, OR& then ^ then |Left
Logical AND, OR&& then ||Left
Ternary? :Right
Assignment= += -= *= /= %= &= |= ^= <<= >>= >>>=Right

Two different ideas get confused here. Precedence decides how an expression is grouped. Evaluation order decides when operands run, and Java guarantees it is left to right: the left operand is fully evaluated before the right one. This holds even when precedence groups the right side first.

Traps from the table: shifts bind looser than addition, so 8 >> 1 + 1 is 2, and & binds looser than ==, so flags & 1 == 0 does not compile for an int. Write (flags & 1) == 0. Integer division truncates toward zero, so 5 / 2 * 2.0 is 4.0 while 5 / 2.0 * 2 is 5.0. The sign of % follows the dividend: -7 / 2 is -3, -7 % 2 is -1 and 7 % -2 is 1. Math.floorMod(-7, 2) gives 1 and Math.floorDiv(-7, 2) gives -4. For that reason n % 2 == 1 misses negative odd numbers; test n % 2 != 0.

Bitwise Operators and Shifts

OperatorMeaningExampleResult
&AND5 & 31
|OR5 | 37
^XOR5 ^ 36
~NOT~5-6 (always -x - 1)
<<Left shift, multiplies by 2 per step1 << 31-2147483648
>>Arithmetic right shift, keeps the sign-8 >> 1-4
>>>Logical right shift, fills with zeros-8 >>> 12147483644

The shift distance is masked. For an int only the low 5 bits count, and for a long the low 6 bits. So 1 << 32 is 1, 1 << 33 is 2, 1L << 64 is 1, and 1 << -1 equals 1 << 31.

Shifts promote first. A byte becomes an int, with sign extension, before the shift:

byte b = -1;
b >>> 4                // 268435455: sign-extended to 0xFFFFFFFF first
(b & 0xFF) >>> 4      // 15: mask to treat the byte as unsigned
b >>>= 4;              // b is still -1: result is cast back to byte

Common uses are flags (flags |= MASK, flags &= ~MASK, (flags & MASK) != 0), and a few idioms worth memorizing:

n & 1                      // 1 if odd, also correct for negative numbers
n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0  // true if n is a power of two
n & -n                     // lowest set bit: 12 & -12 is 4
n & (n - 1)                // clears the lowest set bit, used to count bits
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;    // swap, a curiosity, breaks if both name the same slot
(n - 1) & hash             // HashMap bucket index for power-of-two n

Short-Circuit Logic

&& and || skip the right operand when the left already decides the answer. That is what makes s != null && s.length() > 0 safe. With boolean operands, & and | give the same logical result but always evaluate both sides. Use them only when the right side's effect must happen, which is rare.

f() && t()   // calls f only
f() &  t()   // calls both
t() || f()   // calls t only
t() |  f()   // calls both

Increment Traps and Compound Assignment

x++ yields the old value, then increments. ++x increments, then yields the new value. The trap is that the side effect happens while the expression is being evaluated, not at the end of the statement as many people assume. Bytecode makes this concrete. int i = 5; i = i++; compiles to:

iconst_5
istore_0        // i = 5
iload_0         // push the OLD value (5) on the operand stack
iinc 0, 1       // the local becomes 6
istore_0        // store the pushed 5 back: i is 5 again

To work out any such expression, go left to right, tracking the variable and each operand's value:

CodeTraceResult
i=5; j = i++ + ++i;5 (i=6) + 7 (i=7)j=12, i=7
i=5; j = i++ * 2 + ++i;5*2 (i=6) + 7j=17
i=1; i += i++;Left i saved as 1, then 1 (i=2), sum storedi=2
i=1; i = i++ + i++;1 + 2, stored lasti=3
i=2; i = i++ + i-- - --i;2 + 3 - 1i=4
q=10; q += q++ + ++q;10 + (10 + 12)q=32
y=1; y = y+++y;Tokens: y++ + y, so 1 + 2y=3
b=5; b += b *= 2;Left b saved as 5, then 5 + 10b=15
k=0; a[k] = k = 2;Array index evaluated first, so a[0]a[0] is 2
k=0; a[k++] = k;Index 0, then k is 1, right side is 1a[0] is 1

The hidden cast

E1 op= E2 is defined as E1 = (T)((E1) op (E2)), where T is the type of E1 and E1 is evaluated once. The compiler inserts a narrowing cast without warning:

byte b = 10;  b += 120;     // -126, wraps silently
int i = 10;   i *= 2.5;     // 25
int w = 10;   w -= 0.5;     // 9: 10 - 0.5 = 9.5, truncated
int z = 5;    z /= 2.0;     // 2
short s = 1;  s += 70000;   // 4465
char c = 'a'; c += 1;       // 'b'
int a = 2;    a *= 3 + 4;   // 14: the right side is computed first

The Ternary Operator's Type Rules

The type of c ? a : b is computed from both branches, so the branch not taken can still change the result.

System.out.println(true ? 1 : 2.0);        // 1.0: int promoted to double
Object o = true ? Integer.valueOf(1) : Double.valueOf(2);  // 1.0, unboxes and promotes!
char x = 'X'; int i = 0;
System.out.println(true ? x : 0);          // X: constant 0 fits char, result is char
System.out.println(false ? i : x);         // 88: i is not constant, result is int
Integer n = null;
int r = true ? n : 0;                      // NPE: n is unboxed
Integer q = false ? 1 : n;                 // NPE too: type is int because of the literal 1

That last line surprises people because the target is Integer. One int branch and one Integer branch give type int, so the Integer gets unboxed. Use if/else when a branch can be null.

Control Flow

if requires a boolean; unlike C, if (x) on an int does not compile. That also blocks the if (a = 1) typo, except with boolean variables, where if (flag = true) compiles and is always true.

Loops: for, enhanced for, while and do-while, which always runs once. The enhanced for over an array compiles to an index loop, and over an Iterable it compiles to an Iterator loop. Two consequences follow. The loop variable is a copy, so assigning it changes nothing in the collection. And removing from the collection inside the loop usually throws ConcurrentModificationException.

int[] a = {1, 2, 3};
for (int v : a) v *= 2;          // a is unchanged
for (int i = 0, j = 10; i < j; i += 3, j -= 3) ...   // several loop variables are fine
int i = 0;
do { System.out.print(i); } while (i++ < 2);    // 012
i = 0;
while (i++ < 3);                                // i is 4: the failing test still increments

Unreachable code

The compiler rejects statements it can prove never run, but it does not treat if specially. That exception allows conditional compilation with a constant flag.

while (true) { } int v = 1;   // ERROR: unreachable statement
for (;;) { } int v = 1;       // ERROR
while (false) { v = 1; }      // ERROR
return; int v = 1;            // ERROR
if (false) { v = 1; }         // compiles

Labeled break and continue

A plain break leaves only the innermost loop or switch. A label lets you exit or continue an outer one, which avoids boolean flags. A label can also sit on a plain block for break, but continue needs a loop. There is no goto.

outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j == 1) continue outer;
        if (i == 2) break outer;
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}
// prints: 00 10

switch: Classic, Arrow, Expression, Pattern

Classic switch jumps to the matching label and falls through into later cases until a break. Labels must be compile-time constants and unique. The selector may be byte, short, char, int, their wrappers, an enum or a String (Java 7). It may not be long, float, double or boolean, because switch compiles to jump tables indexed by 32-bit integers. The position of default does not change matching, but fall-through still follows source order:

static String sw(int d) {
    String r = "";
    switch (d) {
        case 1: r += "one ";
        case 2: r += "two "; break;
        default: r += "many ";
        case 3: r += "three ";
    }
    return r;
}
// sw(1) "one two "   sw(2) "two "   sw(3) "three "   sw(9) "many three "

Arrow form and switch expressions (Java 14)

An arrow case has no fall-through. It accepts several labels, and the switch can produce a value. A switch expression must be exhaustive, so default is needed unless the compiler can prove coverage (an enum or sealed type). yield returns a value from a block. It is needed because return would leave the enclosing method. You cannot mix -> and : within one switch.

String kind = switch (day) {
    case 1, 7 -> "weekend";
    case 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 -> {
        String t = "week";
        yield t + "day";
    }
    default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException("day " + day);
};
int y = switch ("b") {      // colon form still falls through, even as an expression
    case "a": yield 1;
    case "b": System.out.print("fall ");
    case "c": yield 3;
    default:  yield 4;
};                          // prints "fall ", y is 3

Pattern matching for switch (Java 21)

The selector can be any reference type, and cases test the type, optionally with a when guard and record deconstruction. Cases are tried top to bottom.

static String describe(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case null -> "null!";
        case Integer i when i > 10 -> "big " + i;
        case Integer i -> "small " + i;
        case String s when s.isEmpty() -> "empty";
        case String s -> "str " + s;
        case int[] a -> "arr " + a.length;
        default -> "other";
    };
}
  • null: without a case null, a null selector throws NPE, in every form of switch. case null, default -> combines both.
  • Dominance: a general pattern before a specific one is a compile error ("this case label is dominated by a preceding case label"). A guarded case before an unguarded one of the same type is fine.
  • Exhaustiveness: a pattern switch must cover all inputs, even as a statement, so a switch on Object needs default.

Primitive type patterns are still a preview feature in Java 25 (JEP 507), so do not rely on them.

How it compiles

tableswitch is an array of jump targets, O(1), used for dense values. lookupswitch is a sorted key list searched in O(log n), used for sparse values. javap confirms it: cases 1, 2, 3 produce a tableswitch, and cases 1, 1000 a lookupswitch. A String switch compiles to a lookupswitch on hashCode(), an equals() check to handle collisions, then a second switch on the resulting index. That is also why switching on a null string throws NPE: the generated code calls hashCode() on it.

Arrays

An array is a fixed-length heap object. Its class is created by the JVM ([I for int[], [Ljava.lang.String; for String[], [[I for int[][]), and its superclass is Object. Elements sit in contiguous memory with a default value, so index access is a simple address calculation and is O(1). Every access is bounds-checked. length is a final field, not a method.

int[] a = new int[3];                // {0, 0, 0}
int[] b = {1, 2, 3};
int[] c = new int[]{1, 2, 3};        // needed when not in a declaration
int[] e = new int[2]{1, 2};          // ERROR: size and initializer together
int d[] = {1}, n = 2;                // n is a plain int
int[] p = {1}, q[] = {{2}};          // q is an int[][]
new int[-1];                         // NegativeArraySizeException at runtime
new int[0];                          // valid, length 0, handy as an empty result

Multidimensional and jagged arrays

Java has no true 2D array. An int[][] is an array of references to int[] objects, so rows can differ in length and are not guaranteed to be adjacent in memory. Iterating row by row is cache-friendly; column by column on a large matrix is noticeably slower.

int[][] grid = new int[2][3];       // 2 rows of 3
int[][] jag = new int[2][];         // rows are null until assigned
jag[0] = new int[3];
jag[1] = new int[]{7};
int[][] tri = {{1, 2}, {3}};
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(tri).startsWith("[[I@"));  // true: prints row references
System.out.println(Arrays.deepToString(tri));                 // [[1, 2], [3]]

Copying

MethodNotes
a.clone()Same type, shallow. For int[][] the rows stay shared
Arrays.copyOf(a, n)Truncates or pads with defaults. copyOf({1,3,5}, 5) gives [1, 3, 5, 0, 0]
Arrays.copyOfRange(a, from, to)to is exclusive
System.arraycopy(src, sp, dst, dp, len)Fastest, and handles overlapping regions correctly: arraycopy(a,0,a,1,4) on 1,2,3,4,5 gives 1,1,2,3,4
int[][] m = {{1, 2}, {3}};
int[][] cl = m.clone();
cl[0][0] = 99;
System.out.println(m[0][0]);   // 99, the inner array is shared

The Arrays utility

CallWhat it does
Arrays.sortPrimitives: dual-pivot quicksort (stability is meaningless for primitives). Objects: TimSort, stable, O(n log n)
Arrays.binarySearch(a, key)Needs sorted input. Returns the index, or -(insertionPoint) - 1. Searching 4 in {1,3,5} gives -3
Arrays.equals, deepEqualsBy content. a.equals(b) on arrays is reference identity
Arrays.hashCode, deepHashCodeContent hash, needed when a class has array fields
Arrays.fill, setAllBulk set, with a value or a function of the index
Arrays.mismatch, compareFirst differing index and lexicographic comparison (Java 9)
Arrays.streamStream, with a primitive stream for int[]
Arrays.asListFixed-size List view over the array
Gotcha: Arrays.asList returns java.util.Arrays$ArrayList, a private class and not java.util.ArrayList. It is a view: set writes through to the array, and add or remove throw UnsupportedOperationException. Also, Arrays.asList(new int[]{1, 2}).size() is 1, because generics cannot hold int and the whole array becomes the single element. With Integer[] the size is 2.

Array covariance

Arrays are covariant: String[] is a subtype of Object[]. Early Java needed this so methods like Arrays.sort(Object[]) could work before generics existed. The cost is a runtime check on every store into a reference array:

Object[] objs = new String[1];
objs[0] = 1;     // compiles; throws java.lang.ArrayStoreException: java.lang.Integer

Generics chose the opposite design: List<String> is not a List<Object>, so the error appears at compile time. Generics are also erased at runtime while arrays need their element type for that store check, which is why new List<String>[3] is a compile error ("generic array creation"). new List<?>[3] is allowed.

Methods, Var-args and Pass-by-Value

A method's signature is its name plus parameter types. Return type, modifiers, parameter names and throws are not part of it, so two methods differing only in return type do not compile. A method call pushes a stack frame holding parameters, locals and an operand stack, and the frame is discarded on return.

Var-args

void f(int... x) is compiled as void f(int[] x) with a flag. The caller's arguments are packed into a new array. It must be the last parameter, there can be only one, and you cannot also declare f(int[]) in the same class.

static int va(int... x) { return x == null ? -1 : x.length; }
va()                     // 0, an empty array, not null
va(1, 2)                 // 2
va(new int[]{1, 2, 3})   // 3, passed as is
va((int[]) null)         // -1, null really is passed

static String vs(String a, Object... r) { return r == null ? "null" : "" + r.length; }
vs("a")                          // 0
vs("a", (Object) null)           // 1, one null element
vs("a", (Object[]) null)         // "null"
vs("a", new Object[]{1, 2})      // 2
vs("a", new int[]{1, 2})         // 1: an int[] is one Object
vs("a", new String[]{"x", "y"})  // 2: a String[] is an Object[]

Overload selection tries var-args last, which is covered next. With generic var-args the compiler warns about heap pollution, and @SafeVarargs is the author's promise that the method does not misuse the array.

How an overload is chosen for primitives

The compiler searches in three phases and stops at the first phase that finds a match: first exact or widening, then boxing and unboxing, then var-args. Widening beats boxing, and boxing beats var-args.

static void m(int x)      { print("int"); }
static void m(long x)     { print("long"); }
static void m(Integer x)  { print("Integer"); }
static void m(Object x)   { print("Object"); }
static void m(int... x)   { print("varargs"); }

byte b = 1; m(b);             // int: widening beats boxing
char c = 'a'; m(c);           // int
m(1L);                        // long
m(Integer.valueOf(1));        // Integer
m(1.0f);                      // Object: boxes to Float, Float is an Object
m(Long.valueOf(1));           // Object
m();                          // varargs
m(1, 2);                      // varargs

Pass-by-value

Java always copies the argument. For a reference variable the copied value is the reference, so caller and method point to the same object but through separate variables. Mutating the object is visible to the caller; reassigning the parameter is not.

static void change(StringBuilder s) {
    s.append("x");                 // mutates the shared object
    s = new StringBuilder("new");  // only the local copy now points elsewhere
    s.append("y");
}
StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder("a");
change(sb);
System.out.println(sb);    // ax

A swap(Integer a, Integer b) method cannot work, while swap(int[] a) that exchanges elements can, because the array object is shared.

Recursion

A recursive method calls itself, with a base case that stops it. Each call takes a stack frame. Too many give StackOverflowError, an Error, not an Exception. Java does not perform tail-call elimination, so writing the call last does not help. The thread stack size is set with -Xss, and a Thread constructor can request a size for one thread.

static int fact(int n) { return n <= 1 ? 1 : n * fact(n - 1); }
fact(5)    // 120
fact(13)   // 1932053504, already overflowed (correct is 6227020800)
fact(17)   // -288522240, overflow can go negative

// Naive Fibonacci makes O(2^n) calls; memoize to get O(n)
static long fib(int n, long[] memo) {
    if (n < 2) return n;
    if (memo[n] != 0) return memo[n];
    return memo[n] = fib(n - 1, memo) + fib(n - 2, memo);
}

Convert to a loop, with an explicit ArrayDeque as the stack if needed, when depth depends on input size.

static, final and Instance Members

A static member belongs to the class, and there is one copy per loaded class. An instance member belongs to each object. Instance methods receive a hidden this argument; static methods do not, which is why a static method cannot touch instance fields without an object ("non-static variable cannot be referenced from a static context"). Calling a static method through a reference compiles to a class call, so the reference is not even dereferenced:

Foo foo = null;
foo.hi();      // runs fine if hi() is static: no NPE

final means "assigned once", and its meaning depends on the target:

OnEffect
Local or parameterCannot be reassigned. Can be assigned later if exactly once
Instance fieldMust be set by the end of every constructor (at the declaration, in an initializer block or in the constructor). A field without an initializer is a blank final
Static fieldMust be set at the declaration or in a static block
ReferenceThe reference is fixed, the object is not: final int[] a = {1}; a[0] = 2; compiles
MethodCannot be overridden
ClassCannot be extended: String, Integer

Effectively final (Java 8): a local that is never reassigned, even without the keyword. Lambdas and anonymous classes may capture only final or effectively final locals, because they capture a copy of the value, and letting the variable change would make the copy silently stale.

Gotcha: A static final field initialized with a constant expression is a compile-time constant, and javac copies its value into every class that uses it. If a library changes VERSION = 1 to 2 and you only replace its jar, your compiled classes keep using 1 until recompiled. Reading such a constant also does not trigger class initialization.

Initialization Order

Initialization has two separate phases. Class initialization runs once, the first time a class is actively used. Instance initialization runs for every new. Within each phase, field initializers and initializer blocks run in source order. javac effectively copies instance initializer code into each constructor that calls super(...), straight after that call.

  1. Parent static fields and blocks, in source order.
  2. Child static fields and blocks, in source order. Steps 1 and 2 occur once.
  3. Memory is allocated and zeroed, so every field holds its default.
  4. Parent instance fields and blocks, then the parent constructor body.
  5. Child instance fields and blocks, then the child constructor body.
class Parent {
    static int ps = log("Parent static field");
    int pi = log("Parent instance field");
    static { log("Parent static block"); }
    { log("Parent instance block"); }
    Parent() { log("Parent constructor"); show(); }
    void show() { System.out.println("  Parent.show"); }
}
class Child extends Parent {
    static int cs = log("Child static field");
    int ci = log("Child instance field");
    String name = "child";
    static { log("Child static block"); }
    { log("Child instance block"); }
    Child() { super(); log("Child constructor"); }
    @Override void show() { System.out.println("  Child.show name=" + name); }
}
new Child();
// Parent static field
// Parent static block
// Child static field
// Child static block
// Parent instance field
// Parent instance block
// Parent constructor
//   Child.show name=null       <-- overridden method runs before Child's fields are set
// Child instance field
// Child instance block
// Child constructor

A second new Child() repeats everything from "Parent instance field" onward.

What triggers class initialization

Triggers are new, calling a static method, reading or writing a non-constant static field, initializing a subclass, reflection such as Class.forName, and being the main class. Not triggers:

class A { static int v = 7; static final int K = 5; static final Integer BOXED = 6;
          static { System.out.println("A init"); } }
class B extends A { static { System.out.println("B init"); } }

System.out.println(B.K);     // 5, and nothing initialized: K is inlined at compile time
A[] arr = new A[1];          // creating an array does not initialize A
System.out.println(B.BOXED); // prints "A init" then 6. Integer is not a constant type,
                             // and only the DECLARING class A is initialized, never B

Static initialization order bug

class Cnt {
    static Cnt inst = new Cnt();  // runs first: a and b become 1
    static int a;                 // no initializer: stays 1
    static int b = 0;             // runs next: resets b to 0
    Cnt() { a++; b++; }
}
System.out.println(Cnt.a + " " + Cnt.b);   // 1 0

Forward references behave similarly. static int a = b; static int b = 1; is a compile error ("illegal forward reference"), but going through a method or this.b compiles and quietly reads the default value 0. Class initialization is thread-safe: the JVM holds an initialization lock, which the lazy-holder singleton relies on. If a static initializer throws, you get ExceptionInInitializerError, and any later use of that class gives NoClassDefFoundError.

var, Keywords and Scope

var (Java 10) is local variable type inference. The compiler determines the static type from the initializer and the bytecode is identical to writing the type. It is not dynamic typing: the type is fixed forever.

var list = new ArrayList<Map<String, Integer>>();   // ArrayList<Map<String,Integer>>
for (var e : map.entrySet()) { }                    // fine
try (var in = Files.newInputStream(p)) { }          // fine
var x;                 // ERROR: no initializer
var n = null;          // ERROR: nothing to infer from
var a = {1, 2};        // ERROR: array initializer needs an explicit type
var f = () -> 1;       // ERROR: lambda needs a target type
class T { var v = 1; } // ERROR: not allowed on fields, parameters or return types
int var = 1;           // OK: var is a reserved type name, not a keyword
var o = new Object() { int hidden = 42; };  o.hidden;  // works: infers the anonymous type

A subtle cost: var list = new ArrayList<String>() infers ArrayList, not List, and var x = new ArrayList<>() infers ArrayList<Object>. Use var when the type is obvious from the right side.

Keywords

Java SE has 51 reserved keywords, including the two unused ones goto and const, and _ (reserved since Java 9, and usable as an unnamed variable or pattern since Java 22). true, false and null are literals, not keywords, though they cannot be identifiers either. Contextual keywords are special only in certain positions and can still name a variable: var, yield, record, sealed, non-sealed, permits, when, module, exports, requires and others. This let Java add features without breaking old code.

Scope, lifetime and shadowing

VariableScopeLifetimeDefault
Local, parameterDeclaring blockUntil the block endsNone
Instance fieldClassUntil the object is collectedYes
Static fieldClassUntil the class is unloadedYes

A local may shadow a field, which is why constructors write this.name = name. A local may not shadow another local of an enclosing block, including lambda parameters: with int ex in scope, ex -> ex does not compile. Sequential blocks are independent, so for (int i...) {} int i = 2; is fine.

Input, Math, Random and Command-Line Arguments

Reading input

Scanner sc = new Scanner(System.in);
int n = sc.nextInt();
String rest = sc.nextLine();    // TRAP: reads what is left of the number's line
String line = sc.nextLine();
// input "42\nhello world\n" gives n=42, rest="", line="hello world"

nextInt consumes only the digits, leaving the newline behind, and the next nextLine reads up to it. Either call an extra nextLine(), or read whole lines and parse. Scanner uses regular expressions internally and is slow on large inputs. BufferedReader.readLine() is much faster. Closing a Scanner also closes System.in, and it cannot be reopened.

System.console() gives a Console, whose readPassword returns a char[] and hides typing. It can return null when input is redirected or in many IDEs (it did on Java 21 with piped input), so check it.

Command-line arguments

args holds what follows the class name, and args[0] is the first argument, not the program name as in C. With no arguments the array is empty, never null. Everything arrives as a String, so numbers need Integer.parseInt. Quotes group spaces at the shell level: java App "a b" c gives two arguments. Options before the class name go to the JVM: java -Dmode=prod App sets a system property read by System.getProperty("mode").

Math

CallResultNote
Math.round(2.5) / round(-2.5)3 / -2Adds 0.5 and floors; returns long for double and int for float
Math.rint(2.5) / rint(3.5)2.0 / 4.0Ties go to even, returns double
Math.ceil(-0.5) / floor(-0.5)-0.0 / -1.0Return double
(int) Math.ceil(7 / 2)3Integer division happened first. Use 7 / 2.0 for 4
Math.max(1, 2.0)2.0Promoted to the double overload
Math.pow(2, 10)1024.0Always double
Math.hypot(3, 4), cbrt(27)5.0, 3.0
Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE)-2147483648Use absExact (Java 15) to get an exception
Math.clamp(15L, 0, 10)10Java 21

Random numbers

ClassThread behaviourUse for
java.util.RandomSafe, but threads contend on an atomic seedReproducible results: the same seed gives the same sequence
ThreadLocalRandom.current()One generator per threadGeneral concurrent use. Never store the instance across threads
SecureRandomSafe, slowerTokens, passwords, keys
Math.random()Shared internal RandomQuick double in [0.0, 1.0)
RandomGenerator (Java 17)Depends on the algorithmCommon interface, choose algorithms by name

Random is a linear congruential generator with a 48-bit state, so an attacker can recover the state from a few outputs. Never use it for security. r.nextInt(100) gives 0 to 99, and r.nextInt(5, 10) gives 5 to 9 (Java 17). (int) (Math.random() * n) gives 0 to n-1; the parentheses matter, because (int) Math.random() * n is always 0.

null Handling

null is a literal meaning "this reference points at nothing". It has no type of its own and can be assigned to any reference type. Calling a member through it throws NullPointerException. Since Java 14 (on by default from 15), helpful NPE messages say exactly what was null: Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "<local65>" is null. Compile with -g and the message shows the real variable name instead of a local slot number.

String s = null;
s + "x"                         // "nullx": concatenation handles null
s instanceof String             // false, no NPE
null == null                    // true
"x".equals(s)                   // false: constant first avoids NPE
Objects.equals(s, null)         // true, null-safe on both sides
Objects.requireNonNull(s, "s"); // fail fast, with a message
Objects.requireNonNullElse(s, "def")  // "def" (Java 9)
Objects.toString(s, "d")        // "d"
String.valueOf((Object) null)   // "null"
String.valueOf((char[]) null)   // NPE: a different overload
System.out.println(null);       // ERROR: ambiguous, println(char[]) vs println(String)
System.out.println((Object) null);  // null

Design practices: return empty collections rather than null; use Optional for return values that may be absent; validate at public boundaries with Objects.requireNonNull; and consider nullness annotations with a static checker in larger projects.

The assert Statement

assert condition; or assert condition : message; checks an internal invariant. Assertions are disabled by default. You enable them with java -ea (or -ea:com.shop... for one package). When they are disabled, the expression is not evaluated at all, so it must never have side effects. When an assertion fails, it throws AssertionError, which is an Error rather than an exception.

private int split(int[] a, int lo, int hi) {
    assert lo <= hi : "lo=" + lo + " hi=" + hi;   // a developer's sanity check
    ...
}

assert list.remove(x);   // BUG: with -ea off, the remove never happens

public void transfer(BigDecimal amt) {
    if (amt.signum() <= 0)                        // public argument check: always on
        throw new IllegalArgumentException("amount must be positive");
}

Use assert for things that "cannot happen" in private code. Do not use it to validate public API arguments or user input, because production normally runs without -ea. JUnit's assertEquals and similar methods are a different thing: they are ordinary method calls and are always active.

Unsigned Values and Rounding-Up Division

Java has no unsigned int or long. (char is the only unsigned primitive.) The wrapper classes provide unsigned operations on the same bits, which you need for binary protocols, checksums and hashes:

byte b = (byte) 0xF0;
int u = Byte.toUnsignedInt(b);                 // 240 (same as b & 0xFF)
int x = -1;
Integer.toUnsignedString(x);                   // "4294967295"
Integer.toUnsignedLong(x);                     // 4294967295L
Integer.divideUnsigned(x, 2);                  // 2147483647
Integer.compareUnsigned(-1, 1);                // > 0: -1 is the largest unsigned value
Integer.parseUnsignedInt("4294967295");        // -1 (same bits)

// Ceiling division: pages needed for 101 items at 10 per page
int pages = (items + size - 1) / size;          // classic idiom, positives only, can overflow
int pages2 = Math.ceilDiv(items, size);         // Java 18+, correct for negatives too

Interview Questions — Java Language Basics

Is Java compiled or interpreted? Why is it called platform independent?

Both. javac compiles source into bytecode. The JVM then interprets that bytecode and JIT-compiles hot code to native machine code at runtime. The bytecode is the same everywhere, and each OS and CPU has its own JVM, so the same .class file runs on all of them. The JVM is platform-dependent; the bytecode is not. Portability can still break through native libraries, hard-coded file paths or a default charset assumption.

Walk through what happens when you run java com.shop.Hello.
  1. The OS starts the JVM, which reads its options and sets up memory.
  2. The launcher asks the application class loader for com.shop.Hello. Loading is delegated upward (bootstrap, platform, application), and the class file is found on the classpath.
  3. Linking: bytecode is verified, static fields get memory and default values, and symbolic references are resolved, usually lazily.
  4. The launcher looks up main. If it is missing, it prints an error, and the static initializer never runs. (A class with only a static { } block printed just the error on Java 21.)
  5. Initialization: parent static initializers run first, then the class's own.
  6. main runs on the main thread, first interpreted, then JIT-compiled where hot.
  7. The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads end or when System.exit is called.
Why is main public static void? Can it be overloaded, final, or in an interface?

Before Java 25: public so the launcher can access it, static so no instance is needed, and void because exit codes use System.exit. It can be overloaded, but only the standard form is the entry point. It can be final or synchronized, written with String..., inherited from a parent class, and placed in an interface, enum or record. Java 25 relaxes this: main may be non-public, an instance method, and parameterless (JEP 512). The return type must still be void.

Can a Java program run without a main method?

Before Java 7 a static block could run first and then call System.exit. Since Java 7 the launcher checks for main first, so that trick fails with "Main method not found". Environments where another program is the entry point are different: a servlet container or JUnit calls your code, but they have their own main. In Java 25 the method can be a simple void main(), but a main method is still required.

Can one source file have several classes? What does javac produce?

Yes. It may have any number of top-level types, but at most one public one, and the file must be named after it. javac writes a separate .class for each type, including Outer$Inner.class and Outer$1.class for nested and anonymous classes. Top-level classes can only be public or package-private; private, protected and static are compile errors there.

Does import java.util.* slow a program down or load all classes?

No. Imports exist only during compilation, as shorthand for names. The class file holds fully qualified names, and classes load lazily on first use. Compile time rises very slightly. Teams prefer explicit imports for readability and to avoid conflicts, such as Date in both java.util and java.sql, not for performance.

What are the default values? Why does int x; x++; fail while a field compiles?

Fields and array elements get zero-like defaults (0, 0.0, false, '\u0000', null) because the JVM zeroes heap memory when allocating. Locals live in stack frames, which are not cleared for speed. The language requires definite assignment instead: the compiler proves every path assigns the local before reading it, which turns a class of bugs into compile errors.

What is the size of a boolean?

The language specifies only the values, not a size. The JVM spec has no dedicated boolean arithmetic instructions: locals and stack values are handled as int, and boolean arrays use byte-sized instructions, so HotSpot uses one byte per element. Fields typically take one byte too. For a million flags, BitSet uses far less memory than boolean[].

Output? System.out.println((byte) 200); System.out.println((int) 3.99); System.out.println((int) Double.NaN); System.out.println((int) 1e20);
-56
3
0
2147483647

Integer narrowing keeps the low 8 bits: 200 is 1100 1000, and with the top bit as a sign that is -56. Floating to integer truncates toward zero, turns NaN into 0, and clamps out-of-range values to the limits.

Why does byte b = 10; b = b + 1; fail but b += 1; and b++; compile?

b + 1 is an int by numeric promotion, and assigning int to byte needs a cast because b is not a constant. b += 1 is defined as b = (byte)(b + 1), with the cast built in, and b++ behaves the same. Neither detects overflow, so byte b = 127; b++; gives -128.

Which of these compile? float f = 1.5; long l = 3000000000; Long w = 1; Byte b = 1; char c = -1; short s = 'a';
  • float f = 1.5; no: a decimal literal is a double. Write 1.5f.
  • long l = 3000000000; no: the literal itself is an int that is too large, so it needs L.
  • Long w = 1; no: an int can box only to Integer, and Integer is not a Long.
  • Byte b = 1; yes: constant narrowing followed by boxing is specifically allowed.
  • char c = -1; no: -1 is outside char's range.
  • short s = 'a'; yes: a constant that fits. With a non-constant char variable it fails.
Output? long a = 24 * 60 * 60 * 1000 * 1000; System.out.println(a);

500654080. All operands are int, so the product overflows before widening to long. The fix is to make the first operand long: 24L * 60 * ... gives 86400000000. In practice use Duration.ofDays(1).toMillis() and Math.multiplyExact.

Why is Math.abs(Integer.MIN_VALUE) negative? Where does this cause real bugs?

The range is -231 to 231-1, so +231 does not exist. Negating MIN_VALUE overflows back to itself. The usual bug is Math.abs(key.hashCode()) % buckets producing a negative index. Some strings do hash to exactly MIN_VALUE: "polygenelubricants" is the famous one. Use Math.floorMod(hash, buckets) or (hash & 0x7fffffff) % buckets.

Why is 0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3? Does float behave differently?

0.1 and 0.2 have infinite binary expansions, so each is stored rounded. Their rounded sum is 0.30000000000000004, while the literal 0.3 rounds to a different double. float has the same limitation at lower precision, and the errors happen to cancel in print: 0.1f + 0.2f displays 0.3, which is luck. Compare with a tolerance, or use BigDecimal for exact decimal values.

What does 1/0, 1.0/0, 0.0/0 and 1%0 give?

1/0 and 1%0 throw ArithmeticException: / by zero, because integers have no value to represent the result. 1.0/0 gives Infinity and 0.0/0 gives NaN, because IEEE 754 defines those values. Floating-point arithmetic never throws.

How would you handle money in Java? Show the mistakes to avoid.
  • Do not use double: rounding errors accumulate and totals stop matching.
  • Use BigDecimal built from a String, or long minor units such as cents. new BigDecimal(0.1) captures the binary error.
  • Choose a rounding mode and scale explicitly, as an accounting decision. divide without one throws on non-terminating results such as 1/3.
  • Compare with compareTo, because equals says 2.0 and 2.00 differ.
  • Store as a SQL DECIMAL, and keep the currency beside the amount.
  • Allocate carefully: splitting 100.00 among 3 gives 33.33 three times, which loses a cent. Assign the remainder explicitly.
Math.round(2.5), Math.round(-2.5), Math.rint(2.5)?

3, -2 and 2.0. Math.round rounds ties toward positive infinity, as if by floor(x + 0.5), so -2.5 goes to -2, not -3. rint rounds ties to the even neighbour and returns a double.

Output of these Integer comparisons, and why?
Integer a = 127, b = 127;
Integer c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);       // true
System.out.println(c == d);       // false
System.out.println(c.equals(d));  // true
Long l = 127L;
System.out.println(l.equals(127));  // false

Autoboxing calls Integer.valueOf, which returns cached objects for -128 to 127, so == on references sees the same object. 128 is outside the cache, so two objects exist. Long.equals first checks the argument is a Long, and 127 boxes to Integer. Rule: never use == on wrappers. The cache's upper bound can be raised by a JVM option, so behaviour at 128 is not even guaranteed.

int or Integer for a field in an entity or DTO?

Use int where a value is mandatory and always present, such as a counter. Use Integer or Long where absent is meaningful: a nullable column, an optional JSON field, or a generated ID. With a primitive, a missing value silently becomes 0, which you cannot distinguish from a real 0. JPA also treats a null ID as "new entity", which is why entity IDs are usually Long. The cost of wrappers is memory, unboxing NPEs, and the == trap.

Why can this line throw NPE: Integer r = flag ? 1 : map.get("k");?

One branch is int and the other Integer, so the ternary's type is int. When flag is false and the map has no key, null gets unboxed before the assignment. Fix it with if/else, or make both branches Integer: flag ? Integer.valueOf(1) : map.get("k").

Output? char x = 'X'; int i = 0; print(true ? x : 0); print(false ? i : x); print(true ? 1 : 2.0);
X
88
1.0

When one branch is char and the other is an int constant that fits in char, the result is char. A non-constant int variable forces promotion to int, so 'X' prints as 88. In the third, int and double give double.

Output? System.out.println('a' + 'b'); System.out.println("" + 'a' + 'b'); System.out.println('a' + 1); System.out.println((char) ('a' + 1));
195
ab
98
b

char values promote to int under + unless a String is already on the left. + is left-associative, so the type at each step decides.
