Why does int i = 5; i = i++; leave i at 5? Answer at bytecode level.

Bytecode from javac: iload_0 pushes 5, iinc updates the local to 6, and istore_0 writes the pushed 5 back. The right side computes its value before the assignment, and the increment finishes inside the right side. Plain i++; as a statement is the correct way.

Output? int i = 5; int j = i++ + ++i; int k = 10; k += k++ + ++k;

j is 12 and i is 7: the operands are 5 (i becomes 6), then 7. k is 32. The compound assignment saves the left value 10 first, then evaluates 10 + 12, and stores 10 + 22. Java evaluates left to right, so this is defined behaviour, unlike the same expression in C. Do not write it in real code.

Output? System.out.println(1 << 32); System.out.println(1L << 32); System.out.println(-1 >>> 28); System.out.println(-1 >> 28);
1
4294967296
15
-1

An int shift uses only the low 5 bits of the distance, so 32 acts as 0, while long uses 6 bits. >>> fills with zeros, leaving 4 set bits. >> copies the sign bit, so -1 stays -1.

What is the difference between & and &&?

&& works only on booleans and short-circuits. & on booleans always evaluates both sides, and on integers it is bitwise AND. obj != null & obj.isOk() throws NPE when obj is null. Note that & and | are precedence-lower than ==, so bit tests need parentheses.

Check whether a number is a power of two, odd, and count its set bits, without loops over digits.
boolean pow2 = n > 0 && (n & (n - 1)) == 0;  // one set bit only
boolean odd = (n & 1) != 0;                  // also right for negatives
int bits = Integer.bitCount(n);
// by hand (Kernighan): each step clears the lowest set bit
int c = 0;
while (n != 0) { n &= n - 1; c++; }
How do you swap two ints without a temporary? Should you?
a = a + b; b = a - b; a = a - b;   // works even with overflow, thanks to wrap-around
a ^= b; b ^= a; a ^= b;            // XOR version
a = (b + (b = a)) - b;             // obfuscated, relies on left-to-right order

Either breaks if both are the same array slot, for example arr[i] and arr[j] with i == j: XOR zeroes it. A temporary is clearer, and the JIT produces code at least as good. Say that in the interview.

What is switch fall-through? Output of switch (2) { case 1: print("a"); case 2: print("b"); case 3: print("c"); break; default: print("d"); }?

bc. Execution jumps to the matching label and continues through later labels until a break. Fall-through is occasionally intentional, but it is a common source of bugs, which is why the arrow form has none.

Why can you not switch on a long? How does a String switch work?

The JVM switch instructions, tableswitch and lookupswitch, take 32-bit int keys. A String switch is compiled to a lookupswitch on hashCode(), followed by equals() to rule out collisions, which then sets a temporary index, followed by a second switch on that index. "Aa" and "BB" share a hash code and can both be cases without problem. A null string throws NPE at the hashCode() call. Java 21 adds case null.

yield vs return? Arrow vs colon?

yield supplies the value of the enclosing switch expression. return would leave the method, and is not allowed inside a switch expression. Arrow cases run just one expression, block or throw, with no fall-through. Colon cases keep fall-through, even in a switch expression. You choose per switch, and cannot mix them.

Does this compile? switch (o) { case Object p -> ...; case String s -> ...; }

No. case String s can never match, so javac reports "this case label is dominated by a preceding case label". Order from most specific to most general. A guarded pattern does not dominate: case Integer i when i > 0 before case Integer i is valid.

Output? Nested loops with continue outer and break outer.
outer:
for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    for (int j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
        if (j == 1) continue outer;
        if (i == 2) break outer;
        System.out.print(i + "" + j + " ");
    }
}

00 10. For i=0 it prints 00, then j=1 continues the outer loop. i=1 is the same. At i=2, j=0 hits break outer.

Are arrays objects? Where do they live? Why does a.length have no parentheses while s.length() does?

Yes. Even int[] extends Object, lives on the heap, and has a header containing the length. The length is read with the dedicated arraylength instruction, which the language presents as a final field. String.length() is an ordinary method. Arrays override clone to be public, and do not override equals, hashCode or toString, which is why printing one gives [I@1b6d3586-style text.

What does cloning a 2D array do? How do you deep-copy one?

clone() copies only the outer array of references, so rows remain shared. Deep copy each row:

int[][] copy = new int[m.length][];
for (int i = 0; i < m.length; i++) copy[i] = m[i].clone();
// or
int[][] copy2 = Arrays.stream(m).map(int[]::clone).toArray(int[][]::new);
Explain ArrayStoreException. Why are generics invariant when arrays are covariant?

Object[] o = new String[1]; o[0] = 1; compiles because String[] is an Object[], and fails at runtime because every array knows its element type and checks each store. Arrays need that check; generics are erased, so they cannot check at runtime. Making List<String> a subtype of List<Object> would allow heap corruption with no error, so generics are invariant, with wildcards (? extends T) for safe read-only covariance.

Which output? vs("a", (Object) null), vs("a", (Object[]) null), vs("a", new int[]{1, 2}), for String vs(String a, Object... r) returning r's length or "null".

1, null, 1. Casting to Object means one element which is null, so the compiler wraps it in an array. Casting to Object[] passes the array parameter directly, as null. An int[] is not an Object[], so it becomes a single element. A String[] would be spread, with its length used.

Why does a long overload beat Integer for an int argument?

Overload resolution runs three phases and stops at the first that yields a candidate: (1) subtyping and primitive widening, (2) boxing and unboxing, (3) var-args. long is reached in phase 1, Integer only in phase 2. The reason is backward compatibility: code written before Java 5 had to keep calling the same methods once boxing arrived.

Is Java pass-by-reference for objects? Prove it either way.

No, it is pass-by-value, and a reference value gets copied. Proof: reassigning a parameter inside a method never changes the caller's variable, and a swap(a, b) on two objects has no effect. In true pass-by-reference (C++ int&) it would. People get confused because mutation through the copied reference is visible to the caller. This matters in practice for String and wrappers: a method cannot "return through" an immutable parameter.

When is recursion a bad choice in Java? What is the depth limit?

There is no fixed limit; depth depends on stack size (-Xss) and frame size, and JIT-compiled frames differ from interpreted ones, so the depth varies from run to run. Typical defaults allow thousands to tens of thousands of simple frames. Avoid recursion when depth grows with input, such as walking a long linked list or a user-supplied JSON tree. Java does no tail-call optimization, so rewrite it as a loop, use an explicit stack, or at least enforce a depth limit. Catching StackOverflowError is not a design.

Print the order of execution for parent and child static blocks, instance blocks and constructors.

Parent statics, child statics (both once per class load), then for each object: parent fields and instance blocks, parent constructor, child fields and instance blocks, child constructor. Fields and blocks within a class run in source order. The important trap: a parent constructor calling an overridden method runs the child's version while child fields still hold defaults, so it printed name=null in the example above.

Output? Why is Cnt.b 0 while Cnt.a is 1?
class Cnt {
    static Cnt inst = new Cnt();
    static int a;
    static int b = 0;
    Cnt() { a++; b++; }
}

Statics first hold defaults (0). Initializers then run top to bottom. new Cnt() sets both to 1. a has no initializer, so it stays 1. b = 0 runs afterward and resets it. This pattern appears in real code when a singleton field is declared above the statics its constructor uses.

Does reading Child.parentStaticField initialize Child?

No, only the class that declares the field is initialized. Reading a compile-time constant initializes neither, since the value was inlined, and creating new A[1] does not initialize A. All verified: in the example above, B.BOXED prints "A init" but never "B init".

Can a constructor be static or final? What is an instance initializer block for?

Neither. A constructor is not inherited, so final has no meaning, and it always works on a new instance, so static has none either; both are compile errors. Instance initializer blocks hold code shared by all constructors, and are required in anonymous classes, which cannot declare constructors. In practice a private init method or constructor chaining with this(...) reads better. A void T() method named after its class compiles, and is just an ordinary method. It is a known trick question.

What does final guarantee for a reference? Can a final field be set without a value at declaration?

It guarantees the variable keeps pointing to the same object. It does not freeze the object: final List<String> l can still be added to. A blank final can be set in an instance initializer or constructor, and must be assigned exactly once on every constructor path. A blank static final is set in a static block. Final fields also give a concurrency guarantee: a correctly constructed object's final fields are visible to other threads without synchronization.

Is var dynamic typing? Name places it cannot be used.

No. The type is inferred once, at compile time, and cannot change. var is not allowed on fields, method parameters, return types, or catch parameters, nor without an initializer, with null, with an array initializer, or with a lambda or method reference. It is allowed in local declarations, for loops, try-with-resources, and implicitly typed lambda parameters since Java 11, so you can attach annotations: (@NonNull var x) -> x.

Are goto, const, true, null and var keywords?

goto and const are reserved keywords with no meaning, kept so that nobody uses them and to give better errors. true, false and null are literals, and also unusable as identifiers. var, yield and record are contextual: int var = 1; and int record = 1; compile, but a class cannot be named var since Java 10.

A unit test passes with IDs 1 to 100 but production says two equal orders are different. Where do you look?

First suspect == on Long or Integer: identical values share a cached object only up to 127. Replace with equals or Objects.equals, or compare unboxed values. Also check equals between Long and Integer (always false), for example comparing an API-parsed Integer with a DB Long. Add a Sonar or Error Prone rule for reference equality on boxed types, and test with values above 127.

Output? Foo foo = null; System.out.println(foo.hi()); where hi is static.

It prints the method's result with no NPE. javac resolves a static call from the declared type, and the bytecode is invokestatic, which ignores the reference. The same applies to static fields. It is legal but misleading, and compilers warn about it.

Why does System.out.println(null) not compile, when m(null) works with m(Object) and m(String)?

null fits any reference parameter. With Object and String, String is more specific, so it wins. println has both println(char[]) and println(String), which are unrelated types, so neither is more specific: "reference to println is ambiguous". Casting (Object) null or (String) null resolves it.

Does this comment execute? // \u000a System.out.println("hi");

Yes, it prints hi. Unicode escapes are processed in the first step of lexing, before comments are recognized, so \u000a is a real newline and the rest of the line is code. For the same reason a \u000a inside a string literal is a compile error. Verified on Java 21.

What is wrong with this for-each? for (Integer x : list) if (x == 2) list.remove(x);

Normally it throws ConcurrentModificationException, because the hidden iterator detects the structural change on the next next(). With [1, 2, 3] it surprisingly does not throw and prints [1, 3]: after removing the second-to-last element, hasNext() compares cursor 2 with the new size 2 and stops, so the check never runs. Use list.removeIf(x -> x == 2) or an explicit iterator's remove().

Scanner reads a number, then an empty line appears instead of the name. Why?

nextInt() stops right after the digits and leaves the line terminator in the buffer. nextLine() then returns the empty remainder of that line. Consume it with one extra nextLine(), or read everything with nextLine() and call Integer.parseInt(line.trim()). The second handles bad input more cleanly too.

Random vs ThreadLocalRandom vs SecureRandom: which do you pick?
  • Random: seedable, so use it when you need repeatable sequences, such as tests or simulations. Shared across threads it suffers from contention.
  • ThreadLocalRandom.current(): the default for general concurrent server code, such as retry jitter.
  • SecureRandom: anything an attacker must not predict, such as session IDs, reset tokens or salts.
How do you avoid NullPointerExceptions in a large codebase?
  • Make invalid states impossible: require non-null constructor arguments with Objects.requireNonNull, so failures appear at the source rather than far away.
  • Return empty collections and Optional, not null.
  • Prefer constant-first comparison ("x".equals(s)) and Objects.equals.
  • Watch hidden unboxing: ternaries, map.get, method parameters of type int.
  • Validate at the edges with Bean Validation, and map nullable DB columns to wrappers deliberately.
  • Use a nullness checker (for example JSpecify annotations with NullAway) in CI.
  • Do not catch NPE as control flow.
Is Java a purely object-oriented language?

No. Java has primitive types (int, double, and so on) that are not objects, and static members that belong to no object. Smalltalk, by contrast, treats everything as an object. The primitives exist for performance. Wrappers and autoboxing let them take part in object APIs such as collections and generics. 💡 Project Valhalla (value classes) aims to narrow this gap, but it is not part of the Java 21 LTS.

Should you use assert to validate method arguments?

Not for public methods. Assertions are off unless the JVM runs with -ea, so a check that protects data or security would silently disappear in production. For public arguments, throw IllegalArgumentException, NullPointerException (through Objects.requireNonNull) or IllegalStateException, or use Bean Validation in Spring. assert is for internal invariants in private code, for example "this branch is unreachable" or "the array is sorted here". Never put a side effect inside an assert.

What do transient, volatile, native, synchronized and strictfp mean?
  • transient (field): skipped by Java serialization. Jackson will not use the field directly, but a public getter is still serialized unless MapperFeature.PROPAGATE_TRANSIENT_MARKER is on, so use @JsonIgnore. For JPA, the explicit form is @Transient.
  • volatile (field): reads and writes go to main memory and are ordered (happens-before), so other threads see changes. It gives visibility, not atomicity: count++ is still unsafe.
  • native (method): the body is implemented in C or C++ through JNI, for example Object.hashCode.
  • synchronized (method or block): mutual exclusion on a monitor, plus visibility.
  • strictfp: obsolete. Since Java 17 (JEP 306), all floating-point math is strict, so the keyword has no effect.
How do you read an unsigned byte from a byte[] (for example, a file header)?

A byte is signed (-128 to 127), so (byte) 0xFF reads back as -1, and widening to int sign-extends it. Mask it with b & 0xFF, or use Byte.toUnsignedInt(b), to get 0 to 255. For multi-byte values, combine the masked bytes with shifts, or use ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes).order(ByteOrder.BIG_ENDIAN).getInt(). For 32-bit unsigned values, store them in a long using Integer.toUnsignedLong.

How do you compute "pages needed" (rounding up) with integer division?

Integer division truncates toward zero, so 101 / 10 is 10. Use (n + size - 1) / size for non-negative values. Be aware that n + size - 1 can overflow near Integer.MAX_VALUE. Since Java 18, Math.ceilDiv(n, size) handles this correctly, and Math.floorDiv is its counterpart. Avoid (int) Math.ceil(n / size): the division has already truncated before ceil runs. Math.ceil((double) n / size) works, but it goes through floating point.

OOP in Java Foundation

How objects are built and laid out in memory, how method calls are resolved, the exact rules of overloading and overriding, and the language features that model data: interfaces, nested classes, enums, records, sealed types and pattern matching. Includes the Object contract, cloning, immutability and singletons.

Classes, Objects and Object Creation

A class is a type: it describes state (fields) and behaviour (methods). An object is an instance of it on the heap. A variable never contains an object; it contains a reference, which is a value that locates the object. Emp a = new Emp(); Emp b = a; creates one object and two references.

What new Emp("Ann") does

  1. Class check: if Emp is not yet loaded and initialized, the JVM does that first, parents first.
  2. Allocation: the size is known from the class. Usually each thread bumps a pointer inside its own TLAB (thread-local allocation buffer), a private chunk of Eden, so allocation needs no lock and is very cheap.
  3. Zeroing: the memory is cleared, which gives fields their default values.
  4. Header: the object header is written.
  5. Constructor: bytecode invokespecial <init> runs the chain: super(...), field initializers and instance blocks, then the constructor body.
  6. The reference is returned.

In bytecode that is new, dup, invokespecial. Without safe publication, another thread can see the reference before the constructor finishes, which is why double-checked locking needs volatile.

Memory layout

On 64-bit HotSpot with default settings and a heap under about 32 GB, an object has a 12-byte header: an 8-byte mark word (identity hash, GC age, lock state) and a 4-byte compressed class pointer. Arrays add a 4-byte length. Fields follow, and the JVM reorders them to reduce gaps, then rounds the object up to a multiple of 8 bytes. So new Object() takes 16 bytes. Java 25 adds optional compact object headers (JEP 519, -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders), which shrink the header to 8 bytes.

Tools: JOL (Java Object Layout) prints real layouts. Escape analysis can remove an allocation entirely when the JIT proves that an object does not leave a method. HotSpot does this through scalar replacement, splitting the object into local values; it does not "allocate on the stack" as is often said.

Constructors

A constructor initializes a new object. It has the class's name and no return type, is not inherited, and is not a member in the usual sense, so it cannot be overridden. It can be overloaded and can have any access level.

  • Default constructor: the compiler adds a no-argument one, with the class's access level, only if you declare no constructor at all.
  • Implicit super: if a constructor does not start with this(...) or super(...), the compiler inserts super(). If the parent has no accessible no-argument constructor, that is a compile error. This is the usual reason for "constructor T in class T cannot be applied to given types".
  • Chaining: this(...) calls another constructor of the same class, and super(...) calls the parent's. Up to Java 24, one of them must be the first statement, and you can only have one. Recursive chains are a compile error.
  • Flexible constructor bodies (Java 25, JEP 513): statements may come before super(...), for example to validate arguments. They cannot use this to read fields or call instance methods, but they may assign fields of the class being constructed.
class Account {
    private final String id;
    private final long balance;
    Account(String id) { this(id, 0); }           // chain to the main constructor
    Account(String id, long balance) {
        super();                                  // implicit if omitted
        this.id = Objects.requireNonNull(id);
        this.balance = balance;
    }
}

class T { int a = 1; { a = 2; } T() { this(5); a *= 2; } T(int x) { a += x; } }
new T().a;    // 14: initializers run once, in the constructor calling super():
              // a=1, a=2, a+=5 gives 7, then a*=2 gives 14
Gotcha: Never call an overridable method from a constructor. The parent constructor runs first, so the override sees uninitialized child fields: 
abstract class Shape {
    Shape() { System.out.println("area=" + area()); }
    abstract double area();
}
class Circle extends Shape {
    double r = 2;
    Circle() { super(); System.out.println("r=" + r); }
    double area() { return r * r; }
}
new Circle();   // area=0.0   then   r=2.0
Since Java 21, javac -Xlint:this-escape warns about such cases.

A private constructor prevents outside instantiation (singletons, factory-only classes, utility classes). It also prevents subclassing, except by classes nested in the same top-level class.

Access Modifiers

ModifierSame classSame packageSubclass, other packageEverywhere
privateYesNoNoNo
(package-private, no keyword)YesYesNoNo
protectedYesYesYes, with the rule belowNo
publicYesYesYesYes
  • Top-level types can only be public or package-private. Nested types can use all four.
  • private works at top-level class granularity: a nested class and its outer class can read each other's private members. Java 11 nestmates (JEP 181) made that a JVM-level concept, removing the old synthetic accessor methods.
  • The protected rule: code in a subclass in another package can reach a protected member only through a reference of its own type or a subclass. Inside class T extends ArrayList<String> in another package, this.removeRange(0, 1) compiles, and otherArrayList.removeRange(0, 1) does not. That is also why new Object().clone() fails to compile outside java.lang.
  • With the module system, even public is visible to other modules only if the package is exported.

The Four Pillars, Applied

The overview section defines them. Here is what each does for you in practice.

Encapsulation is about protecting invariants, not about getters. A class with private fields and a public setter for each is not encapsulated in any useful way. Compare:

class Account {                         // state changes only through rules
    private long balanceCents;
    void withdraw(long cents) {
        if (cents <= 0 || cents > balanceCents) throw new IllegalArgumentException();
        balanceCents -= cents;
    }
    long balanceCents() { return balanceCents; }
}

Encapsulation lets you change the representation without breaking callers, and gives one place for validation.

Inheritance gives an IS-A relationship and shares code. A class extends one class, since multiple class inheritance raises the ambiguity of two parents' state and methods. It inherits accessible members but not constructors, and private fields exist in the object but are not accessible by name. All classes end at Object. The test for correct use is the Liskov Substitution Principle: code using the parent must keep working with any subclass. Square extends Rectangle fails it, because setting a square's width also changes its height, which breaks code that assumes they vary independently.

Polymorphism means one call, many behaviours. Compile-time polymorphism is overloading. Runtime polymorphism is overriding. There is also parametric polymorphism, which is generics. Polymorphism replaces type-checking conditionals:

interface Discount { BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal price); }
// New discount types are added as classes; this code never changes:
BigDecimal total = discount.apply(price);

Abstraction exposes what a thing does and hides how it does it. Abstract classes and interfaces are tools for it, but so is any well-chosen method. List is an abstraction; ArrayList is a detail. Interviewers often ask how abstraction differs from encapsulation: abstraction decides what to show, a design-level concern, while encapsulation decides how to protect it, an implementation-level concern.

Overloading vs Overriding: The Full Rules

The key idea: overloading is decided by the compiler from static types; overriding is decided by the JVM from the object's runtime class.

Overriding rules

AspectRuleVerified compiler behaviour
SignatureSame name and parameter types (after erasure)@Override makes a mismatch a compile error
Return typeSame, or a subtype for references (covariant return, Java 5). Primitives must match exactlylong overriding int: "return type long is not compatible with int"
AccessSame or wider"attempting to assign weaker access privileges"
Checked exceptionsSame, narrower, or none. Never new or broader"overridden method does not throw java.lang.Exception"
Unchecked exceptionsAnyAllowed
final methodCannot be overridden"overridden method is final"
static methodCan only be hidden, by another static methodInstance over static: "overridden method is static". Static over instance: "overriding method is static"
private methodNot inherited; a same-named method is unrelatedNo error, and no polymorphism
ConstructorNever overridden
Package-private methodOverridden only by a subclass in the same packageA different-package subclass creates a new method

The access and exception rules both enforce substitutability: a caller holding a parent reference must not be surprised by a less-visible method or an undeclared checked exception.

A method that widens access and calls super is fine. Covariant returns work through a generated bridge method. For class Ch extends Pa { @Override Ch self() }, reflection on Ch shows two methods: Ch self() and a synthetic Pa self() with the bridge flag, which forwards to the real one. JVM method identity includes the return type, which is why a bridge is needed. Generic overrides use the same mechanism.

Hiding: fields and static methods are not polymorphic

class Base {
    String name = "base";
    static String sm() { return "Base.sm"; }
    String im() { return "Base.im"; }
    String getName() { return name; }
    private String pv() { return "Base.pv"; }
    String callPv() { return pv(); }
}
class Sub extends Base {
    String name = "sub";
    static String sm() { return "Sub.sm"; }
    @Override String im() { return "Sub.im"; }
    private String pv() { return "Sub.pv"; }
}
Base b = new Sub();
b.name          // base      field: chosen by the static type
((Sub) b).name  // sub
b.sm()          // Base.sm   static: chosen by the static type
b.im()          // Sub.im    instance: chosen by the runtime class
b.getName()     // base      Base's code reads Base's field
b.callPv()      // Base.pv   private methods do not participate

A Sub object has two name fields. Only instance methods dispatch dynamically.

Overload resolution order

  1. Collect methods with the right name that are accessible and have a compatible argument count.
  2. Phase 1: matches using subtyping and primitive widening only.
  3. Phase 2: if none, allow boxing and unboxing.
  4. Phase 3: if none, allow var-args.
  5. If a phase finds several, choose the most specific: one whose parameters could all be passed to the other. If none is most specific, the call is ambiguous.
static String n(Object o) { return "Object"; }
static String n(CharSequence s) { return "CharSequence"; }
static String n(String s) { return "String"; }
n(null)                  // String: the most specific
n((Object) "s")          // Object: the STATIC type decides
n(new StringBuilder())   // CharSequence

void g(String s) { } void g(Integer s) { }
g(null);                 // ERROR: ambiguous, the types are unrelated

void w(long a, int b) { } void w(int a, long b) { }
w(1, 1);                 // ERROR: each is better for one argument

void v(int a, int... b) { } void v(int... a) { }
v(1);                    // ERROR: ambiguous

void u(int... a) { } void u(long... a) { }
u();                     // OK: int is more specific than long

static String bx(long x)     { return "long"; }
static String bx(Integer x)  { return "Integer"; }
static String bx(Object x)   { return "Object"; }
static String bx(int... x)   { return "int..."; }
bx(1)                    // long
bx((short) 1)            // long
bx(Integer.valueOf(1))   // Integer
bx(1.0)                  // Object
bx()                     // int...

Overloading and overriding combined

This is the hardest common question. The compiler first selects a signature using only the static type. The JVM then selects the implementation of that signature using the runtime class.

class An { } class Dg extends An { }
class V1 { String who(An a) { return "V1.An"; } }
class V2 extends V1 {
    @Override String who(An a) { return "V2.An"; }
    String who(Dg d) { return "V2.Dg"; }     // an overload, not an override
}
V1 v = new V2();
v.who(new Dg());        // V2.An
((V2) v).who(new Dg()); // V2.Dg

V1 has only who(An), so the compiler fixes that signature for the first call, and at runtime V2's override of it runs. Java is single-dispatch: only the receiver is dynamic, never the argument. The Visitor pattern exists to simulate double dispatch, and pattern-matching switch is the modern alternative.

Dynamic Dispatch, vtables, and Binding

BindingDecidedApplies to
Static (early)Compile timestatic, private, final methods, constructors, super.x(), field access, and overload selection
Dynamic (late)Run timeOverridable instance methods
BytecodeUsed forLookup
invokestaticStatic methodsFixed target
invokespecialConstructors, super.m()Fixed target
invokevirtualClass-typed instance callsvtable slot, or a fixed target for final and private methods
invokeinterfaceInterface-typed callsSearch the class's itable
invokedynamicLambdas, string concatenation, record methods, pattern switchCall site linked by a bootstrap method on first run

In the javap output, a call to a private method in the same class shows invokevirtual: since Java 11 javac no longer needs invokespecial there. The target is still fixed, because private methods cannot be overridden.

The vtable is per class, not per object: an array of method pointers, where a subclass copies the parent's table, overwrites overridden entries and appends new ones. Since the slot number is the same across the hierarchy, a call is just a few memory reads. Interfaces cannot use a fixed slot because a class can implement any number of them in any order, so itables need a search, which is why invokeinterface is a bit slower when interpreted.

The JIT removes most of this cost. It uses class hierarchy analysis: if only one implementation is loaded, it calls directly and inlines, guarded so it can deoptimize if another class loads later. It also uses runtime type profiles: a monomorphic call site (one receiver type seen) or a bimorphic site (two) can be inlined with a type guard, while a megamorphic site (many types) falls back to a table lookup. The advice "avoid interfaces because virtual calls are slow" is usually wrong.

Abstract Classes and Interfaces

An abstract class is a partly implemented class. It cannot be instantiated, can have constructors (they run from subclass constructors), instance fields and any access level, and need not have an abstract method. abstract cannot combine with final, private or static on a method, since each prevents overriding.

An interface is a contract a class promises to fulfil, without state.

MemberSinceImplicit modifiersNotes
Abstract method1.0public abstract
Constant1.0public static finalMust be initialized. Not an instance field
default method8publicLets an interface evolve without breaking implementers. Cannot override equals, hashCode or toString
static method8publicNot inherited: call A.s(). Neither T.s() nor this.s() compiles in an implementer
private method9Shared helper for default methods. Can be static
Nested types1.1public static

Interfaces cannot have constructors, instance fields, protected members or final methods. Implementation methods must be declared public, since narrowing is not allowed.

The diamond problem and how Java resolves it

With multiple inheritance, if B and C both inherit from A and D extends both, which version does D get? Java avoids the state version: only single class inheritance, and interfaces have no instance fields. Default methods bring the behaviour version back, so there are fixed rules:

  1. Class wins: a method from a class or superclass beats any default.
  2. Most specific interface wins: if I3 extends I1, then I3's default beats I1's.
  3. Otherwise you must override, or the class does not compile, and you can pick with Interface.super.method().
interface I1 { default String hi() { return "I1"; } }
interface I2 { default String hi() { return "I2"; } }
class Both implements I1, I2 {      // required, or "inherits unrelated defaults"
    public String hi() { return I1.super.hi() + "+" + I2.super.hi(); }   // I1+I2
}
interface I3 extends I1 { default String hi() { return "I3"; } }
class Dm implements I1, I3 { }      // hi() is I3
class SupCl { public String hi() { return "class"; } }
class Cw extends SupCl implements I1 { }   // hi() is class

If one interface has a default and an unrelated one has the same method as abstract, the class must also override it.

Which to choose

Use an interface whenUse an abstract class when
Unrelated classes share a capability (Comparable, Closeable)Closely related classes share code and state
You want multiple types on one classYou need constructors, protected helpers or instance fields
You expect many implementations, including test fakes and proxies (JDK dynamic proxies need interfaces)You want a Template Method: a fixed algorithm with overridable steps

The two combine well: an interface as the public type and an abstract skeletal class as an optional base, like List and AbstractList.

Marker and functional interfaces

A marker interface has no methods. It tags a type: Serializable allows serialization, Cloneable switches on Object.clone, and RandomAccess tells algorithms that indexed access is fast. Annotations are the modern alternative when you need metadata, but a marker is a real type, so misuse can be caught at compile time.

A functional interface has exactly one abstract method, and it is the target type of a lambda. Abstract methods that match public Object methods do not count: Comparator declares equals and is still functional. The overview section covers the basics, and the Java 8 material covers usage.

Composition, Inheritance and Object Relationships

Inheritance is the tightest coupling in Java: a subclass depends on the parent's implementation details, not only on its public behaviour. This is the fragile base class problem, shown here with a real result:

class CountingSet<E> extends HashSet<E> {
    private int added = 0;
    @Override public boolean add(E e) { added++; return super.add(e); }
    @Override public boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) {
        added += c.size();
        return super.addAll(c);
    }
    int added() { return added; }
}
var s = new CountingSet<String>();
s.addAll(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
s.added();   // 6, not 3: HashSet.addAll internally calls add()

Removing the counting from addAll would work only until the JDK changes how addAll is written. The composition version depends only on the Set contract:

class CountingSet2<E> {
    private final Set<E> inner;                 // HAS-A
    private int added = 0;
    CountingSet2(Set<E> inner) { this.inner = inner; }
    boolean add(E e) { added++; return inner.add(e); }
    boolean addAll(Collection<? extends E> c) { added += c.size(); return inner.addAll(c); }
    int added() { return added; }
}
// addAll of 3 elements: added() is 3

Composition also lets you swap the part at runtime, works with final classes, and is easy to mock. Use inheritance only for true IS-A, ideally when you control both classes or the parent is designed for extension. Modern frameworks follow this: Spring favours injecting collaborators over base classes.

RelationshipMeaningLifetimeExample
AssociationObject uses or knows anotherIndependentTeacher and Student
Aggregation (weak HAS-A)Whole refers to parts that can exist aloneParts outlive the wholeTeam and Player
Composition (strong HAS-A)Whole owns its partsParts die with the wholeOrder and OrderLine
Inheritance (IS-A)Subtype relationshipOne objectDog and Animal
DependencyTemporary use, such as a method parameterDuration of a callService using a Formatter

Java syntax does not distinguish these: all are fields. The difference is who creates the part and who else refers to it. In JPA, composition maps to cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true on the owning side.

Coupling and cohesion

Cohesion measures how strongly the contents of a class belong together. A UserService that also formats PDFs and sends email has low cohesion. Coupling measures how much a class depends on the details of others. The aim is high cohesion and low coupling, so a change stays local.

class ReportTight { private final SmtpMailer m = new SmtpMailer("smtp.acme.com"); }  // tight
class ReportLoose {
    private final Notifier n;                    // an interface, injected
    ReportLoose(Notifier n) { this.n = n; }      // testable with a fake; Spring wires it
}

Signs of tight coupling: new of concrete collaborators, long call chains such as a.getB().getC().save() (Law of Demeter), instanceof ladders, and shared mutable statics.

Nested Classes

KindDeclaredOuter instance?Access to localsTypical use
Static nestedMember, staticNon/aBuilders, Map.Entry-like helpers
InnerMember, not staticYes, hidden referencen/aIterators over the outer object
LocalInside a methodIf in an instance methodEffectively final onlyA helper with a name, used once
AnonymousIn an expressionIf in an instance contextEffectively final onlyOne-off implementation with state or several methods
class Out {
    private int v = 1;
    class In {
        int v = 2;
        String s() { int v = 3; return v + " " + this.v + " " + Out.this.v; }
    }
    static class SN { }
}
Out o = new Out();
Out.In in = o.new In();      // needs an outer instance
in.s();                      // "3 2 1"
new Out.SN();                // does not

javac compiles an inner class to Out$In.class with a hidden Out field set through the constructor. This has a real cost: an inner or anonymous instance keeps its outer object reachable, which leaks memory when the inner object outlives it (a listener or a task in a queue), and serializing the inner object tries to serialize the outer one too. Default to static nested unless you need the outer instance.

Since Java 16 (JEP 395), inner classes can declare static members, and records, enums and interfaces can be declared locally. Those local forms are implicitly static and cannot capture locals. Local classes themselves cannot be declared static.

Lambda vs anonymous class: in an anonymous class, this is the anonymous object and it may declare fields and several methods; each creation site compiles to a class file. A lambda has no this of its own, so this means the enclosing object. It needs a functional interface and compiles to invokedynamic with no extra class file.

class Anon {
    String n = "outer";
    Runnable a() { return new Runnable() {
        String n = "anon";
        public void run() { print(this.n); print(Anon.this.n); }   // anon, outer
    }; }
    Runnable l() { return () -> print(this.n); }                   // outer
}

Enums in Depth

An enum is a class with a fixed set of instances. Before Java 5 people used int constants, which give no type safety, no namespace, and print as bare numbers. An enum solves all three.

enum Level { LOW, MID, HIGH }
// javac generates roughly this:
final class Level extends java.lang.Enum<Level> {
    public static final Level LOW = new Level("LOW", 0);
    public static final Level MID = new Level("MID", 1);
    public static final Level HIGH = new Level("HIGH", 2);
    private static final Level[] $VALUES = {LOW, MID, HIGH};
    private Level(String name, int ordinal) { super(name, ordinal); }
    public static Level[] values() { return $VALUES.clone(); }
    public static Level valueOf(String s) { ... }
}

What follows from that:

  • Constants are created in a static initializer, so creation is thread-safe and each exists once per class loader. Comparing with == is correct, and it is null-safe, unlike equals on a null.
  • Constructors are implicitly private (public is a compile error), and new is forbidden.
  • An enum cannot extends anything, since it already extends Enum, but it can implement interfaces. It cannot be extended either.
  • equals and hashCode in Enum are final and identity-based. compareTo uses ordinal order. clone throws.
  • values() returns a fresh copy of the array on each call. Cache it if called in a hot path.
  • valueOf("x") throws IllegalArgumentException: No enum constant ..., and valueOf(null) throws NPE.
  • Serialization writes only the name, and reflection is refused: Cannot reflectively create enum objects.

Fields, methods and constant-specific bodies

enum Op {
    ADD("+") { int apply(int a, int b) { return a + b; } },
    MUL("*") { int apply(int a, int b) { return a * b; } };   // ; needed before members

    final String symbol;
    Op(String symbol) { this.symbol = symbol; }
    abstract int apply(int a, int b);
}
Op.ADD.apply(2, 3);           // 5
Op.ADD.getClass();            // class Op$1: an anonymous subclass
Op.ADD.getDeclaringClass();   // class Op: use this for the enum type

This is the Strategy pattern built into a type, and it removes switch statements that must be updated for each new constant. An enum with constant bodies is not final; since Java 17 it is implicitly sealed, permitting those anonymous bodies. A simple enum is final.

Static fields and constructors

Constants are created first, in declaration order, so an enum constructor cannot read a non-constant static field of the same enum: static int c; E() { c++; } fails with "illegal reference to static field from initializer". For a lookup table, fill it in a static block, which runs after all constants exist:

enum Level {
    LOW, MID, HIGH;
    private static final Map<String, Level> BY_NAME = new HashMap<>();
    static { for (Level l : values()) BY_NAME.put(l.name().toLowerCase(), l); }
    static Level parse(String s) { return BY_NAME.get(s); }
    Level next() { return values()[(ordinal() + 1) % values().length]; }
}

EnumSet and EnumMap

Prefer these over HashSet and HashMap with enum keys. EnumSet stores a bit vector, one bit per constant: a single long in RegularEnumSet for up to 64 constants, and a long[] in JumboEnumSet beyond that. It is created through factories only. EnumMap is an array indexed by ordinal. Both keep declaration order and do no hashing. Neither is synchronized, and EnumMap refuses null keys.

EnumSet<Level> s = EnumSet.of(Level.HIGH, Level.LOW);  // [LOW, HIGH], declaration order
EnumSet.complementOf(s);                               // [MID]
EnumSet.range(Level.LOW, Level.MID);                   // [LOW, MID]
EnumMap<Level, String> m = new EnumMap<>(Level.class);
Gotcha: Never persist ordinal(). Inserting a constant in the middle silently renumbers everything. With JPA, always use @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING); ORDINAL is the default, and a known source of corrupted data. A renamed constant breaks string storage too, so for stable external values give the enum an explicit code field and map it with an AttributeConverter. Also, the hash code of an enum varies per JVM run, so HashMap iteration order with enum keys is not stable.

Records in Depth

A record (final in Java 16) is a transparent carrier for immutable data. You declare the components, and the compiler provides the rest.

record Pt(int x, int y) {
    Pt {                                     // compact canonical constructor
        if (x < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("neg");
    }                                        // fields are assigned at the end
    Pt(int v) { this(v, v); }                // others must delegate to canonical
    static Pt origin() { return new Pt(0, 0); }
    int sum() { return x + y; }
}
var p = new Pt(1, 2);
p            // Pt[x=1, y=2]
p.x()        // 1, an accessor named after the component, not getX()
p.equals(new Pt(1, 2))   // true

The compiler generates private final fields, a public canonical constructor, public accessors, and equals, hashCode and toString. Those three are implemented through invokedynamic and java.lang.runtime.ObjectMethods, not as generated source-style code.

AllowedNot allowed (compile error)
Static fields and methods, instance methodsExtra instance fields ("field declaration must be static")
Implementing interfacesextends; the superclass is always java.lang.Record
Generics, nesting, local recordsBeing extended: records are implicitly final
Replacing an accessor (must be public)abstract; instance initializer blocks
Assigning parameters in a compact constructorAssigning this.x in a compact constructor

Edge cases

Immutability is shallow. The field cannot be reassigned, but a mutable component can still change. Fix it in the compact constructor:

record Bag(List<String> items) { }
var src = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a"));
Bag bag = new Bag(src);
src.add("b");
bag;     // Bag[items=[a, b]]: changed from outside

record SafeBag(List<String> items) {
    SafeBag { items = List.copyOf(items); }  // reassign the parameter
}

Equality rules: reference components use Objects.equals, primitives use ==, except float and double, which use compare. So a record with NaN equals itself, and records with 0.0 and -0.0 are not equal. Array components compare by identity, which is rarely what you want: two records with separate but identical arrays are unequal.

Reflection: record fields really are final. Field.setInt throws IllegalAccessException even after setAccessible(true). Deserialization always goes through the canonical constructor, so validation cannot be bypassed.

Interview: Records suit DTOs, API responses, query projections, value objects, map keys and configuration (@ConfigurationProperties binds to them). Jackson handles them since 2.12. They cannot be JPA entities, because entities need a no-argument constructor, mutable state and non-final classes for proxies. Hibernate 6.2+ can map them as embeddables. A record is not "a class with less typing": it declares that the state is the API, which is why its accessors, equality and deconstruction are all derived from the components.

Sealed Classes

A sealed type (final in Java 17) restricts which types may extend it. It sits between final (no subclasses) and open (anyone). This lets you model a closed set of alternatives, called a sum type, and lets the compiler check that all cases are handled.

public sealed interface Payment permits Card, Cash, Transfer { }
public record Card(String number) implements Payment { }
public record Cash(int amount) implements Payment { }
public non-sealed class Transfer implements Payment { }   // reopens this branch
  • Each permitted subclass must directly extend the sealed type and state one of final, sealed or non-sealed. Otherwise: "sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected". Records and enums are already final.
  • Permitted subclasses must be in the same module, or in the same package if the code is in the unnamed module.
  • permits may be left out if all subclasses are in the same file.
  • A sealed class with no subclasses is an error.
  • Reflection: isSealed() and getPermittedSubclasses().

Sealing differs from package-private access: the type stays public to use while being closed to extend.

Pattern Matching

A pattern tests a value and, on success, binds variables. It replaces the test, cast and extract sequence.

FeatureFinal in
Type patterns with instanceofJava 16
Pattern matching for switch, when guardsJava 21
Record patterns (deconstruction)Java 21
Unnamed variables and patterns (_)Java 22

instanceof patterns and flow scoping

The binding variable exists exactly where the compiler can prove the match succeeded:

if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 3) { ... }   // s is usable after &&
if (o instanceof String s || s.isEmpty()) { }          // ERROR: s may not be bound
if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;
s.length();                                            // in scope: the early return proves it

null instanceof X is always false, so no null check is needed. An incompatible test such as Integer i; i instanceof String is a compile error rather than false.

Record patterns and exhaustive switch

sealed interface Expr permits Num, Add, Mul { }
record Num(int v) implements Expr { }
record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { }
record Mul(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr { }

static int eval(Expr e) {
    return switch (e) {                               // no default needed
        case Num n -> n.v();
        case Add(Expr l, Expr r) -> eval(l) + eval(r);
        case Mul(Num(var a), Num(var b)) -> a * b;    // nested deconstruction
        case Mul m -> eval(m.l()) * eval(m.r());
    };
}
eval(new Add(new Num(2), new Mul(new Num(3), new Num(4))));   // 14

Omitting a default is a feature. Add a new permitted type and every such switch fails to compile, which points you to all the places to update. With a default, the new case would be silently handled wrongly. If a class changes after compilation so that a case is missing at runtime, the switch throws MatchException.

Record patterns read components through the accessors. A nested record pattern, or a type pattern narrower than the component type, does not match a null component. A var pattern, or a type pattern covering the whole component type, does.

This style is data-oriented programming: records for data, sealed types for alternatives, and pattern matching for operations. Compared with virtual methods, it is easy to add operations but harder to add types; that is the classic expression problem. Use polymorphism when the type set is open, and patterns when it is closed.

The Object Class

Every class ultimately extends Object. Interfaces do not extend it, but expose its public methods implicitly.

MethodDefault behaviourOverride?
equals(Object)Reference identityFor value classes
hashCode()Identity hashAlways with equals
toString()getClass().getName() + "@" + Integer.toHexString(hashCode())Almost always
getClass()Runtime class. final, nativeCannot
clone()protected, shallow copy if CloneableRarely
wait() ×3, notify(), notifyAll()Monitor coordination. finalCannot
finalize()Nothing. Deprecated for removalNever

The monitor methods are on Object because every object can be locked. The identity hash is generated lazily on first request and stored in the object header. It is not a memory address, since the GC moves objects and the hash must stay stable.

Generics are erased at runtime: new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass() == new ArrayList<String>().getClass() is true.

equals and hashCode

The overview gives the basic rule. Here is the whole contract, for non-null references:

PropertyMeaning
Reflexivex.equals(x) is true
Symmetricx.equals(y) matches y.equals(x)
TransitiveIf x.equals(y) and y.equals(z), then x.equals(z)
ConsistentRepeated calls agree while the fields used do not change
Non-nullx.equals(null) is false, and no exception
hashCodeEqual objects have equal hash codes; stable while fields do not change. Unequal objects may collide

A complete, correct class

final class Employee {
    private final long id;
    private final String name;
    private final List<String> roles;

    Employee(long id, String name, List<String> roles) {
        this.id = id;
        this.name = Objects.requireNonNull(name);
        this.roles = List.copyOf(roles);
    }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        if (this == o) return true;                       // fast path
        if (o == null || getClass() != o.getClass()) return false;
        Employee e = (Employee) o;
        return id == e.id && name.equals(e.name) && roles.equals(e.roles);
    }
    @Override public int hashCode() {
        int r = Long.hashCode(id);
        r = 31 * r + name.hashCode();
        r = 31 * r + roles.hashCode();
        return r;
    }
    @Override public String toString() { return "Employee{id=" + id + ", name=" + name + "}"; }
}

31 is the conventional multiplier: it is an odd prime, and 31 * x equals (x << 5) - x. Objects.hash(id, name) is shorter but boxes and allocates a var-args array, which matters in hot code. It computes the same formula as Arrays.hashCode: Objects.hash(1, 2) and List.of(1, 2).hashCode() are both 994. Use Double.compare for double fields, and Arrays.equals and Arrays.hashCode for arrays.

getClass vs instanceof

With instanceof, a subclass that adds a field to equals breaks symmetry:

class P {
    final int x;
    P(int x) { this.x = x; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof P q && q.x == x; }
    @Override public int hashCode() { return x; }
}
class CP extends P {
    final String c;
    CP(int x, String c) { super(x); this.c = c; }
    @Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
        return o instanceof CP q && super.equals(o) && q.c.equals(c);
    }
}
P p = new P(1); CP cp = new CP(1, "red");
p.equals(cp);   // true
cp.equals(p);   // false: symmetry is broken

There is no way to add a value component in a subclass and keep the contract with instanceof. getClass() keeps symmetry but means a subclass is never equal to its parent, which breaks proxies such as Hibernate's. instanceof is right when the class is final or equals itself is final, and is the norm in JDK interfaces: List.equals compares any two lists. If you need both, use composition rather than extending.

Pitfalls, each verified

// 1. Overriding equals without hashCode
class NoHash { int v; ... equals only ... }
set.add(new NoHash(1)); set.add(new NoHash(1));
set.size();   // 2, though the objects are equal: different buckets

// 2. Overloading instead of overriding
class Wrong {
    int v;
    public boolean equals(Wrong w) { return w.v == v; }   // parameter should be Object
    @Override public int hashCode() { return v; }
}
new Wrong(1).equals(new Wrong(1));          // true: picks the overload
Object o = new Wrong(1);
o.equals(new Wrong(1));                     // false: Object.equals
// Set size is 2, since HashSet calls equals(Object). @Override would have caught it.

// 3. Mutating a key after insertion
Mut k = new Mut(1); set.add(k); k.v = 2;
set.contains(k);            // false: lookup uses the new hash, wrong bucket
set.contains(new Mut(1));   // false: right bucket, but equals fails
set.add(k); set.size();     // 2: the same object is in the set twice
Gotcha: JPA entities are the hardest case. An ID-based hashCode changes when the ID is generated at persist, so an entity vanishes from a HashSet. Hibernate proxies make getClass() unreliable. Common solutions: use a natural business key, or use the ID in equals with null handling and a constant class-based hashCode. Avoid Lombok @Data on entities: it includes all fields, so lazy associations load and bidirectional links recurse forever. Include only stable fields, and read them through getters so proxies work.

toString

The default is useless in logs (P@ff). A good toString shows identifying state and is safe to call. Avoid printing passwords or tokens, avoid lazy JPA associations (extra queries or LazyInitializationException), and watch for cycles in bidirectional object graphs, which overflow the stack. Record toString also prints every component, so exclude sensitive values by overriding it. String concatenation and String.valueOf call it automatically and handle null.

clone, Shallow and Deep Copies

Object.clone() is a protected native method. If the class implements the marker interface Cloneable, it makes a field-by-field copy without calling a constructor; otherwise it throws CloneNotSupportedException. Note the odd design: Cloneable has no clone method, it changes the behaviour of a protected method in Object.

class Emp implements Cloneable {
    String n; Addr a; int[] sc = {1, 2};
    @Override public Emp clone() {                       // public, covariant, no checked throw
        try { return (Emp) super.clone(); }
        catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
}
Emp e2 = e1.clone();
e2.n = "b";         // e1.n unchanged: the reference was copied, then reassigned
e2.a.city = "Y";    // e1.a.city is also Y: shared
e2.sc[0] = 9;       // e1.sc[0] is also 9: shared

A shallow copy copies references, so nested objects are shared. A deep copy recursively copies mutable parts. Problems with clone: it bypasses constructors and their validation, cannot assign final fields in the override, must use super.clone() all the way up, and has a clumsy checked exception.

Prefer a copy constructor or a static factory:

class Address { String city; Address(String c) { city = c; } Address(Address o) { this(o.city); } }
class Person {
    String name; Address addr;
    Person(String n, Address a) { name = n; addr = a; }
    Person(Person o) { this(o.name, new Address(o.addr)); }     // deep where it matters
}
Person b = new Person(a);
b.addr.city = "B";     // a.addr.city is unchanged

Arrays are the exception where clone() is the right tool. For large object graphs, a mapping library or serialization round trip works, but it is slow. Immutable objects need no copying at all.

finalize Deprecation and Cleaner

finalize() was meant to let objects release native resources before collection. It failed because timing is unknown and may never happen; an exception inside it is swallowed; it slows allocation and GC, since finalizable objects survive an extra cycle; and it allows resurrection, where this gets stored somewhere and a dead object lives again. It also enables finalizer attacks on partially constructed objects. Deprecated in Java 9, it has been deprecated for removal since Java 18 (JEP 421), which also added --finalization=disabled.

The primary way to release resources is try-with-resources with AutoCloseable. java.lang.ref.Cleaner (Java 9) is only a safety net for users who forget to close:

class Resource implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();
    static class State implements Runnable {   // static: must not reference Resource
        public void run() { /* free the native handle */ }
    }
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new State());
    @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }  // runs at most once
}

The state class must not hold a reference to the object, or the object stays reachable and is never cleaned. That is why it is a static nested class and not a lambda capturing this. A Cleaner uses phantom references and its own thread.

Immutable Classes

The overview lists the steps. The reasons matter as much: an immutable object is automatically thread-safe, a safe map key, freely shareable and cacheable, and always in a valid state. Costs are extra allocation per change, which is fine for most code. The sharp edge is mutable components.

public final class Booking {                         // final: no mutable subclass
    private final Date start;                        // Date is mutable
    private final List<String> tags;

    public Booking(Date start, List<String> tags) {
        this.start = new Date(start.getTime());      // copy IN
        this.tags = List.copyOf(tags);               // immutable copy
    }
    public Date start() { return new Date(start.getTime()); }   // copy OUT
    public List<String> tags() { return tags; }
    public Booking withTag(String t) {               // "wither" returns a new object
        var n = new ArrayList<>(tags);
        n.add(t);
        return new Booking(start, n);
    }
}
  • Copy before validating. Otherwise another thread can change the argument between check and copy (a TOCTOU attack).
  • Collections.unmodifiableList(x) is a view: changes to x still show through. List.copyOf is a real copy, and rejects nulls. Elements themselves must be immutable too.
  • Do not let this escape from the constructor, such as by registering a listener. Final-field safety is only guaranteed once construction finishes.
  • Making the class final is one option; a private constructor with static factories is another, used by java.time.
  • Prefer LocalDate and Instant, which are immutable, over Date. Then no copies are needed.

instanceof, Upcasting and Downcasting

Upcasting (child to parent) is implicit and always safe. The object is unchanged, only the view is narrower. Downcasting needs an explicit cast and is checked at runtime with the checkcast instruction.

Ani a = new Cat();           // upcast
a.speak();                   // Cat's override
a.meow();                    // ERROR: Ani has no meow
((Cat) a).meow();            // downcast, OK at runtime
Ani d = new Dog();
Cat c = (Cat) d;             // compiles; ClassCastException at runtime
if (d instanceof Cat k) k.meow();     // safe form

The compiler rejects casts that can never succeed:

CastResultWhy
(String) integerVarCompile errorUnrelated classes
(String) objectVarRuntime checkCould be a String
(Runnable) arrayListVarCompiles, CCE at runtimeA subclass of ArrayList might implement Runnable
(Runnable) integerVarCompile errorInteger is final, so no such subclass can exist

Repeated instanceof ladders usually indicate a missing polymorphic method, or a case for a sealed hierarchy with a pattern switch.

this and super

this is the current object: disambiguates fields from parameters, passes the object as an argument, returns it for fluent chains, and calls another constructor with this(...). It is not available in a static context.
super accesses the parent's implementation: super.method(), hidden fields with super.x, and the parent constructor with super(...). There is no super.super: skipping a parent would break its encapsulation.

A super.method() call is statically bound, compiled to invokespecial. A fluent builder with inheritance needs return this with a self-typed generic to keep the subclass type.

Singleton Variants

A singleton restricts a class to one instance per class loader. The overview shows double-checked locking and the enum. Here is the whole set with their failure modes.

VariantLazyThread-safeReflection-safeSerialization-safe
Eager static finalNoYesNoNeeds readResolve
Lazy, unsynchronizedYesNoNoNeeds readResolve
synchronized getterYesYes, with a lock on every callNoNeeds readResolve
Double-checked lockingYesYes, needs volatileNoNeeds readResolve
Holder classYesYes, by class initializationNoNeeds readResolve
EnumOn first use of the enumYesYesYes
// Eager
final class Eager {
    private static final Eager I = new Eager();
    private Eager() { }
    static Eager get() { return I; }
}
// Holder: Holder is initialized only when get() first touches it
final class Lazy {
    private Lazy() { }
    private static class Holder { static final Lazy I = new Lazy(); }
    static Lazy get() { return Holder.I; }
}
// Enum
enum Config { INSTANCE; int size() { return 8; } }

Why DCL needs volatile: instance = new Config() is three steps: allocate, construct, assign. Without volatile, the assignment may be reordered before construction, so a second thread sees non-null at the unsynchronized check and uses a half-built object.

How singletons get broken (verified)

// Reflection
Constructor<S1> c = S1.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
c.setAccessible(true);
c.newInstance() == S1.get();      // false: a second instance
// A guard in the constructor that throws if I != null helps, but is not bulletproof.
// Enum: IllegalArgumentException: Cannot reflectively create enum objects

// Serialization
copy(Brk.I) == Brk.I;             // false: deserialization makes a new object
// Fix:
private Object readResolve() { return I; }
copy(Fix.I) == Fix.I;             // true
copy(Config.INSTANCE) == Config.INSTANCE;   // true for enums

Other ways to get two instances are clone(), if a parent is Cloneable, and multiple class loaders: each loader gets its own copy of the class and its statics, as happens with several web apps in a container.

Singletons are global state: they hide dependencies and make tests hard to isolate. A Spring singleton is different: it means one bean instance per ApplicationContext, created by the container, and the class itself is a normal class that can be instantiated in tests. That is usually the better design.

Static Factory Methods vs Constructors

A static factory is a static method that returns an instance, for example List.of, Integer.valueOf, LocalDate.of, Optional.empty or EnumSet.noneOf. Compared with a constructor, it:

  • has a name that explains intent: Money.ofCents(150) vs Money.parse("1.50"), where two constructors with the same parameter types would clash;
  • does not have to create a new object: it can cache or reuse instances (Integer.valueOf, Boolean.valueOf);
  • can return a subtype or a hidden implementation: List.of returns internal immutable classes, and EnumSet picks RegularEnumSet or JumboEnumSet;
  • can validate first or return Optional.

The downsides are that classes with only private constructors cannot be subclassed, and factories are less obvious in Javadoc. The usual names are of, from, valueOf, getInstance, newInstance, create and parse.

public final class Email {
    private final String value;
    private Email(String v) { this.value = v; }

    public static Email of(String raw) {                       // validates, normalizes
        String v = raw.strip().toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT);
        if (!v.contains("@")) throw new IllegalArgumentException("bad email");
        return new Email(v);
    }
    public static Optional<Email> tryParse(String raw) {      // no exception for expected failure
        try { return Optional.of(of(raw)); } catch (IllegalArgumentException e) { return Optional.empty(); }
    }
}

Anemic vs Rich Domain Model (Tell, Don't Ask)

In an anemic model, entities are just getters and setters, and all rules live in services: if (order.getStatus() == NEW) order.setStatus(PAID). The invariants are spread across many places, and any caller can put the object into an invalid state. In a rich model, the object guards its own state. Callers tell it what to do instead of asking for its data and deciding themselves.

// Ask (anemic): every caller re-implements the rule
if (order.getStatus() == Status.NEW && order.getTotal().signum() > 0) {
    order.setStatus(Status.PAID);
    order.setPaidAt(Instant.now());
}

// Tell (rich): one place enforces the invariant
public void markPaid(Clock clock) {
    if (status != Status.NEW) throw new IllegalStateException("Order " + id + " is " + status);
    this.status = Status.PAID;
    this.paidAt = Instant.now(clock);
}

In Spring applications, a pragmatic split works well. Behaviour that depends only on the entity's own state goes on the entity, such as state transitions and total calculation. Orchestration goes in the service: transactions, repositories, calls to other systems and events.

Interview Questions — OOP in Java

What is the difference between a class, an object and a reference?

A class is the definition, loaded once by a class loader. An object is an instance on the heap with its own field values. A reference is a value held in a variable that locates an object. Variables never hold objects, so assigning one to another copies the reference, and == compares references. Two objects can be equal in content but different in identity.

What happens in memory on Emp e = new Emp("Ann");?

If needed, Emp and its parents are loaded and initialized. Space is allocated, usually by a pointer bump in the thread's TLAB in Eden. The memory is zeroed, the header is written, and the constructor chain runs: Object up top first, then each class's field initializers, instance blocks and constructor body. The reference is stored in local variable e, which sits in the current stack frame. The literal "Ann" is a pooled String object referenced from the field.

How much memory does new Object() take? What about a class with one int, and one with an int and a long?

On typical 64-bit HotSpot with compressed class pointers: new Object() is 16 bytes (12-byte header plus 4 padding). A class with one int is also 16, since the int fills the padding. int plus long is 24: header 12, int 4, long 8. These are implementation details, not guarantees. JOL gives exact numbers, and Java 25's optional compact headers change them. This is why an Integer[] costs much more than an int[].

Does Java always call a constructor when creating an object?

No. clone() copies without calling one. Java deserialization skips constructors of Serializable classes, calling only the no-argument constructor of the first non-serializable parent. Records are the exception: they always go through the canonical constructor. Internal tools such as Objenesis also bypass constructors. This is why validation in constructors can be bypassed by old-style deserialization.

Why does this fail to compile? class T { T(int a) { } } class U extends T { }

Declaring T(int) removes T's default constructor. U gets a generated U() { super(); }, and there is no T() to call. Fix it by adding a T(), or by giving U a constructor calling super(0). This also matters to JPA and Jackson, which often need a no-argument constructor.

Can you use both this() and super() in one constructor? Can a constructor call an overridable method?

Not both: each must be the first statement up to Java 24, and in Java 25 a constructor still has at most one explicit constructor call. A this(...) chain ends in a constructor that calls super(...). Calling an overridable method compiles but is dangerous: the subclass version runs before subclass fields are initialized. The example above printed area=0.0. Make such methods private, final, or move the call to a factory.

What is the difference between protected and package-private? What is the trap with protected?

Package-private means same package only. protected adds subclasses in other packages. The trap: from another package, a subclass may access the protected member only through its own type, not through a parent-typed reference. Inside class T extends ArrayList<String> in another package, otherList.removeRange(0, 1) fails with "has protected access". Also, protected is often overused: it is part of your public API for anyone who subclasses.

What is the difference between encapsulation and abstraction?

Abstraction is about the interface: which operations are exposed, so the caller thinks in terms of "send payment" rather than HTTP retries. Encapsulation is about protection: internal state can only change through controlled paths, so invariants hold. You can have one without the other: a class with public setters for everything may offer an abstraction yet have no encapsulation. Abstraction is design, and encapsulation is enforcement, typically through access modifiers.

Why does Java not support multiple inheritance of classes? How do you share code across hierarchies?

Two parents would raise questions about duplicate fields, which constructor runs, and which method wins. Java allows a single superclass but multiple interfaces, since interfaces carry no instance state. Default methods add behaviour, with the conflict rules that a class wins, then the most specific interface, and otherwise you must override. To share code otherwise, use composition: hold a helper object and delegate to it.

Is it overriding or hiding? class A { static void f() {} } class B extends A { static void f() {} }

Hiding. Static methods bind at compile time on the declared type, so A x = new B(); x.f(); calls A.f. @Override on it fails. An instance method cannot replace a static one or the reverse; both are compile errors. Fields are also hidden rather than overridden.

Output of the hiding example? Base b = new Sub(); print(b.name); print(b.sm()); print(b.im()); print(b.getName()); print(b.callPv());
base
Base.sm
Sub.im
base
Base.pv

Field access and static calls use the static type Base. Only im() dispatches dynamically. getName() is inherited code that reads Base.name. callPv() calls the private Base.pv, because private methods are not overridden, so Sub.pv is unrelated.

Output? An an = new Dg(); print(h(an)); print(h(new Dg())); with h(An) and h(Dg).

An then Dg. Overloads are chosen at compile time from the declared type of the argument, regardless of the runtime object. Runtime type only matters for the receiver of a call.

Output? V1 v = new V2(); v.who(new Dg()); where V2 overrides who(An) and adds who(Dg).

V2.An. The compiler only looks at V1 and picks who(An), the sole candidate. At runtime the vtable finds V2's override of that signature. who(Dg) is never considered because it is not visible through a V1 reference. Java has single dispatch: the receiver's runtime type matters, the arguments' runtime types do not.

Can an overriding method have a different return type, throw different exceptions, or change access?

Return type: same or a subclass for references, identical for primitives and void. Exceptions: only the same or narrower checked exceptions, or none. Any unchecked ones are fine. Access: same or wider. Note that throws RuntimeException in an override is always allowed, and a method calling through a parent reference must handle the parent's declared checked exceptions even if the override declares none.

How do covariant return types work at the bytecode level?

The JVM identifies a method by name and full descriptor, including return type. So Ch self() does not override Pa self() at JVM level. javac generates a synthetic bridge method Pa self() in Ch that forwards to the new one. Reflection on Ch shows both, with isBridge() true on the generated one. Generics rely on the same trick: compareTo(Emp) gets a bridge compareTo(Object) that casts, which is where a surprise ClassCastException can come from.

Which overload runs for g(null)?

With g(Object) and g(String): String, being more specific. With Object, CharSequence and String: still String. With g(String) and g(Integer): compile error, because neither is a subtype of the other. Resolve with a cast, g((String) null).

Explain how a virtual call is dispatched, and why overriding costs almost nothing.

invokevirtual names a method, which resolves to a vtable index. At runtime the JVM takes the object's class pointer, reads that index, and jumps there. Interface calls search an itable. After warm-up the JIT uses class hierarchy analysis and type profiles to inline calls guarded by a cheap type check. A site that has seen one or two types is typically inlined; a megamorphic site keeps a table lookup. If a newly loaded class invalidates an assumption, the JVM deoptimizes back to the interpreter and recompiles.

Can an abstract class have a constructor? Can it have no abstract methods? Can it implement an interface without implementing the methods?

Yes to all three. The constructor runs through super(...) from subclasses and initializes shared state. An abstract class with no abstract methods simply cannot be instantiated: HttpServlet is an example. An abstract class implementing an interface can leave methods unimplemented for concrete subclasses to complete.

Why were default methods added? What is their danger?

Java 8 needed to add methods such as Collection.stream() to existing interfaces without breaking every implementation. A default method provides a body that implementers inherit. The danger is that a default can conflict with an implementer's assumptions, as with Collection.removeIf and synchronizedCollection-style wrappers that need their own locking, so a default can be silently wrong for an existing class. Default methods add behaviour, and they cannot add state, so they should be built from the other interface methods.

Can an interface default method override toString? Can a class call a static interface method through itself?

Neither. A default overriding an Object method is a compile error ("default method toString in interface T overrides a member of java.lang.Object"), since a class method always wins, so such a default could never run. Static interface methods are not inherited: from an implementer, write A.s(), not T.s() or this.s(). This avoids conflicts when a class implements several interfaces.

Two interfaces have the same default method. What must the class do? What if one is abstract?

In both cases the class must override, or it fails to compile. With two defaults the error is "inherits unrelated defaults". With a default and an abstract, the class is told to implement the abstract method. Inside the override, A.super.hi() selects an interface's version. If the same method is inherited from a class, the class version wins and no override is needed.

Why is Comparator a functional interface although it declares compare and equals?

Abstract methods matching public Object methods do not count, because every implementation inherits them from Object. Comparator therefore has one real abstract method. Its many other methods, such as reversed and thenComparing, are default or static.

When is composition better than inheritance? Give a concrete failure of inheritance.

Default to composition, and use inheritance only for true IS-A when the parent is designed for it. A concrete failure: a HashSet subclass counting additions, overriding add and addAll, reports 6 after adding 3 elements, since addAll internally calls add. The subclass depends on a parent implementation detail. Inheritance also exposes all parent methods, as with Stack extends Vector, which allows insertion in the middle of a stack. Composition with an interface avoids both and allows swapping the implementation in tests.

Association vs aggregation vs composition? Show the difference in code.
class Order {
    private final List<OrderLine> lines = new ArrayList<>(); // composition: created and owned here
    private final Customer customer;                         // aggregation: passed in, outlives us
    Order(Customer c) { customer = c; }
    void print(Printer p) { p.print(this); }                 // dependency: used, not stored
}

The language treats all of them as references, so the difference is ownership and lifetime. For database modelling it decides cascading: order lines are deleted with the order, a customer is not.

Static nested vs inner class? Why can an inner class leak memory?

A static nested class is a normal class scoped inside another, with no outer instance. An inner class has a hidden reference to its enclosing object. If the inner object lives longer than the outer, such as an anonymous listener or a task on a queue, the outer object cannot be collected. Lambdas capture this only if they use it, so they avoid that when they touch no instance members. Default to static.

Can an anonymous class have a constructor? Can it implement two interfaces?

Neither. It has no name, so no constructor can be declared, though arguments can go to the parent's constructor, and an instance initializer block handles setup. It can extend one class or implement one interface. A local class is the alternative when you need more.
