The "double brace initialization" idiom (new ArrayList<>() {{ add(1); }}) creates an anonymous subclass holding the outer reference, so avoid it.

Why must captured local variables be effectively final?

A local variable lives in a stack frame, which may be gone by the time the lambda or inner class runs. So the value is copied into the object. If the variable could then change, the copy and the original would diverge silently, and concurrent code would race. The compiler enforces it instead. Fields are different: the lambda captures this, and reads the field through it.

How are enums implemented? Why is == safe on them?

An enum compiles to a class extending Enum with one public static final instance per constant, created in a static initializer. Since instances are unique per class loader, cannot be created with new or reflection, and deserialize back to the same object by name, reference equality works. == is null-safe and checked at compile time: comparing different enum types is an error, whereas equals would just return false.

Can an enum have a constructor, abstract methods, implement an interface, or extend a class?

Constructor: yes, implicitly private. Abstract methods: yes, with each constant providing a body, which creates an anonymous subclass, so getClass() differs from getDeclaringClass(). Interfaces: yes. Extending a class: no, because it already extends Enum. Enums also cannot be extended by normal classes.

Why can an enum constructor not read a static field of the same enum?

Static initialization runs top to bottom, and constants come first, so a constructor runs before any other static fields are initialized. javac rejects it: "illegal reference to static field from initializer". Compile-time constants are allowed, since they have no runtime initialization. For a lookup map, fill it in a static block, which runs after all constants exist.

Why are EnumSet and EnumMap faster than HashSet and HashMap?

EnumSet is a bit vector, so contains, add and set operations are single bitwise instructions. EnumMap is an array indexed by ordinal(). Neither hashes or handles collisions, memory is minimal, and iteration follows declaration order. EnumSet.of returned java.util.RegularEnumSet for a small enum. A larger enum uses JumboEnumSet. Collections.synchronizedSet is needed for shared mutable use.

Records: what is a compact constructor? How is it different from a canonical one?

A canonical constructor has one parameter per component. A compact one is a shorter form of it, with no parameter list, and the compiler assigns the fields at the end. Use it for validation and normalization by reassigning the parameter: items = List.copyOf(items);. Writing this.items = ... there is an error. Any non-canonical constructor must start by calling another constructor of the record.

Are records truly immutable? Can you use one as a HashMap key, a JPA entity, or a Jackson DTO?

Shallowly immutable: a component List can still change, and that alters hashCode, so copy defensively if using a record as a key. A record with immutable components makes an excellent key. JPA entity: no, entities need a no-argument constructor, mutable fields and subclassable proxies, though records work for projections and, with Hibernate 6.2+, as embeddables. Jackson: yes, since 2.12.

Compare record equality with hand-written equals. What surprises exist?

Both are field-based, and record equality uses all components. Surprises: double and float use Double.compare semantics, so new D(NaN).equals(new D(NaN)) is true and 0.0 differs from -0.0. Arrays compare by reference. And the hashCode algorithm is deliberately unspecified, so do not persist it.

What problem do sealed classes solve? Sealed vs final vs package-private?

They let a library say "these are all the variants" while keeping the type public. final permits no subclasses. Package-private parents hide the type from users, who then cannot name it. Sealed keeps the type usable but closes extension, so the compiler can check exhaustive switches, and a new variant produces compile errors at every switch. Use them for modelling states and results: Payment, Result = Success | Failure, AST nodes.

Why might it be better not to write default in a switch over a sealed type?

Without default, the compiler checks that all permitted types are handled. Adding a new type then breaks compilation at each switch, which is what you want. A default silences that check and sends the new type to a generic path. Without it, the compiler adds a hidden throwing branch in case classes get out of sync at runtime, which produces MatchException.

What is the scope of the binding variable in o instanceof String s?

Flow-sensitive: it is in scope wherever the compiler proves the test was true. So it works after &&, inside the if, and after an if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;. It does not work after || or in the else branch of a positive test. It may shadow a field, but it cannot redeclare an existing local: with a local s, it is a compile error.

Name all methods of Object. Why are wait and notify there and not on Thread?

equals, hashCode, toString, getClass, clone, finalize, notify, notifyAll, and three overloads of wait: 11 non-private methods. Reflection on Java 21 confirms the list. wait and notify are on Object because a thread waits on a monitor, which is owned by an object, not by a thread. Any object can be a lock, so they apply to any object.

If two objects have the same hashCode, are they equal? If equals is true, must hash codes match?

Same hash does not imply equal: "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112. Equal objects must have equal hash codes; that is the contract. Returning a constant such as 1 is legal, but it puts all entries in one bucket and destroys performance. Breaking the contract makes HashMap lookups miss.

What goes wrong if you override only equals? Only hashCode?

Only equals: equal objects get different identity hashes, so a HashSet stores duplicates and map.get(equalKey) misses. Verified: two equal NoHash objects gave a set size of 2. Only hashCode: equal-looking objects land in the same bucket, but equals still uses identity, so they stay separate. List.contains uses only equals, so hash-based and list-based lookups can disagree.

public boolean equals(Employee o) compiles. What is wrong with it?

It overloads rather than overrides equals(Object). Collections call the Object version through Object-typed parameters, so they use identity, while a direct call with an Employee argument uses your method. The same two objects can look equal or unequal depending on the call site. @Override turns this into a compile error.

getClass or instanceof in equals?

instanceof allows subclass instances, which is correct for final classes or when subclasses add no state, and it works with proxies. getClass demands an exact class, keeps symmetry when subclasses add fields, but breaks the Liskov principle and fails with Hibernate proxies. A value class should normally be final, which makes the debate moot. Defining equality for a type family, as List does, means instanceof on the interface with the contract documented.

Should an entity's hashCode include a generated ID? What do you do with JPA entities?

A generated ID is null before persist and set afterward, so a hash based on it changes while the object is in a HashSet, losing the entry. Options: (1) a natural immutable key, such as an ISBN; (2) a UUID assigned at construction; (3) equals on a non-null ID and a hashCode that returns a constant per class, accepting bucket collisions in rare large sets. Use Hibernate.getClass or instanceof so that proxies compare correctly.

Shallow vs deep copy? Why is clone() considered broken?

A shallow copy duplicates the object's fields, so referenced objects are shared. A deep copy also duplicates what they reference. clone() is criticized because Cloneable has no method and merely changes Object.clone's behaviour; it skips constructors; it cannot reset final fields to copies; it throws a checked exception; and it depends on all parents cooperating. Copy constructors and factories avoid every one of these. clone() remains fine for arrays, where int[] even has a public, covariant one.

Why was finalize deprecated, and what replaces it?

It offers no guarantee of when or whether it runs, swallows exceptions, delays collection, permits resurrection, and is a security hole on partially constructed objects. The replacement is deterministic: AutoCloseable with try-with-resources. Cleaner is a backstop for a forgotten close(). It uses phantom references, so the cleaning action cannot reach the object, and must not reference it. Status: deprecated in 9 and for removal since 18.

Is this class immutable? final class H { private final List<String> l; H(List<String> l) { this.l = l; } List<String> l() { return l; } }

No. final only fixes the reference. The caller keeps the original list and can modify it, and the getter hands out the same list. Fix with this.l = List.copyOf(l);, which makes an unmodifiable copy, and the getter is then safe. Collections.unmodifiableList(l) alone is not enough, because the view reflects changes to l. If elements are mutable, they need the same treatment.

Why is String final? What if an immutable class is not final?

A non-final class allows a subclass that adds mutable state or overrides methods to lie. Code receiving a String parameter can trust it because no subclass can exist. Security checks, class loading and the pool all rely on it. Alternatives to final are a private constructor with factories, or sealing.

When does a cast fail at compile time vs at runtime?

Compile time: the types can never be related, such as two unrelated classes, or a final class and an interface it does not implement. Runtime: the cast is possible but the object is the wrong type, giving ClassCastException. A non-final class to an interface compiles, because a subclass could implement it. (Runnable) new ArrayList<String>() compiles and fails at runtime. (Runnable) Integer.valueOf(1) does not compile. The message names both classes and their loaders, which is useful when the same class name is loaded twice.

Which singleton implementation would you choose today, and how would you break the others?

An enum, if the singleton needs no parent class and early-ish creation is fine; a holder class if it must extend something. In an application, let Spring manage one bean instead. Breaking: reflection's setAccessible calls a private constructor; deserialization produces a copy unless there is readResolve; clone copies if available; a separate class loader gets its own statics. Enum defeats reflection and serialization.

Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

The first null check is outside the lock. Without volatile the write to instance can be seen before the object's constructor effects, so a reader skips the lock and gets a partly initialized object. volatile creates a happens-before edge, and forbids that reordering. It requires the Java 5+ memory model. A holder class gives the same laziness with no explicit synchronization.

Spring singleton vs GoF singleton?

GoF: one instance per class loader, enforced by the class itself through a private constructor, accessed by a static method. Spring: one instance per bean definition per ApplicationContext, enforced by the container. The class stays an ordinary class, so tests can create others or inject mocks. You can define two beans of the same class. Spring beans must be stateless or thread-safe, since all threads share them.

Scenario: a processPayment method has a long if (type == CARD) ... else if (type == UPI) .... How would you redesign it?

If new types are added often, by different teams: a PaymentProcessor strategy interface with one implementation per type, and a Map<PaymentType, PaymentProcessor> filled by Spring injection. Adding a type then means adding one class (Open/Closed). If the type set is closed, and operations are added more often: a sealed Payment hierarchy with records, and exhaustive pattern switches so the compiler finds all sites. An enum with constant-specific bodies suits very small behaviour differences. Pick based on which axis changes.

Scenario: a shared base class BaseService has grown to 2,000 lines, and every change breaks some subclass. What do you do?

That is the fragile base class problem. Steps: identify which groups of methods each subclass really uses; extract each group into a small collaborator class with an interface (auditing, validation, mapping); inject those into subclasses via constructors; move subclasses over one at a time, with characterization tests; and finally delete the base class or reduce it to a Template Method that is final except for declared extension points. Result: high cohesion, lower coupling, and collaborators that are testable alone.

A class has private fields with a public getter and setter for each. Is it encapsulated?

Only in form. If every field has a setter, any caller can still put the object into any state, and the representation is still exposed through the API. Real encapsulation means protecting invariants: expose behaviour (withdraw(amount)) rather than raw setters (setBalance), return unmodifiable views or copies of internal collections, validate in constructors, and leave out setters that are not needed. Getters and setters are still fine on DTOs and framework-bound classes, because there they are the point.

What is the "constant interface" anti-pattern?

It means declaring an interface that holds only constants (interface Config { int TIMEOUT = 30; }) and having classes implements it so they can use the names without a prefix. The constants then become part of the class's public type, so every subclass inherits them and you cannot remove them later without breaking compatibility. Put constants in a final class with a private constructor, or in an enum if they form a set, and use import static for short names. In Spring, prefer @ConfigurationProperties for values that change between environments.

Records vs Lombok @Value / @Data: which should you use?
  • record: a language feature with no annotation processor. It is immutable, has component-based equals/hashCode, cannot extend a class, and has no builder. Its accessors are name(), not getName().
  • @Value: similar immutability, but with getX() accessors. It can be combined with @Builder and @With, and it suits classes that need JavaBean naming.
  • @Data: mutable, with setters and all-field equals/hashCode. Never use it on JPA entities.

For new DTOs and value objects on Java 17+, prefer records. Use Lombok when you need builders for many optional fields, JavaBean-style accessors for older libraries, or mutable entities (@Getter/@Setter only).

What does "program to an interface, not an implementation" mean in practice?

Declare variables, fields, parameters and return types with the most abstract type that offers the operations you need: List<Order> orders = new ArrayList<>(), Map rather than HashMap, and PaymentGateway rather than StripeGateway. The implementation can then change without touching callers, tests can pass fakes or mocks, and Spring can inject a proxy (for @Transactional) or another bean. Do not overdo it: an interface with only one implementation that will never change adds ceremony with no benefit, and Spring can proxy classes through CGLIB anyway.

Why might a team prefer static factories over public constructors for value types?

A factory can validate and normalize before the object exists (trimming or lower-casing an email). It can cache common instances (Money.ZERO, or Integer.valueOf for small values). It can return Optional or a subtype. Its name documents the intent (Duration.ofMinutes(5) vs new Duration(300, 0)). With a private constructor, the class controls every instance, which is how java.time and List.of keep their implementation classes hidden and free to change.

Strings & Text Foundation

How String is built, how the pool and concatenation really work, every method you are likely to use, the builders, text blocks, formatting, regular expressions, encodings, and the string coding questions that appear in most interview rounds.

What a String Really Is

java.lang.String is a final class implementing CharSequence, Comparable<String> and Serializable. Since Java 9 its core state looks like this:

public final class String ... {
    private final byte[] value;   // the text
    private final byte coder;     // 0 = LATIN1, 1 = UTF16
    private int hash;             // cached hashCode, 0 until computed
    private boolean hashIsZero;   // true if the real hash happens to be 0
}

Immutability: how and why

A String cannot change after construction, and every "modifying" method returns a new object. Immutability is enforced by three things: the array field is private and final, no method writes to it, and every path in or out copies. new String(char[]) copies the input and toCharArray() returns a copy, so a caller changing the array affects nothing. The class is final so no subclass can break this.

char[] ch = {'a'};
String s = new String(ch);
ch[0] = 'z';
System.out.println(s);       // a

String x = "a";
String y = x;
x += "b";                    // x now refers to a NEW object
System.out.println(y);       // a

The overview lists the reasons: a safe pool, security, thread safety and a cached hash. The security point deserves detail. A method that checks a file path, then opens it, relies on the value not changing in between. With a mutable string, another thread could swap the value after the check. The same is true for class names given to class loaders. For hashing, a HashMap stores each key's hash, and if a key's content could change, the entry would be lost.

Older JDKs allowed mutation through reflection on the private field. Strong encapsulation of java.base (since Java 16-17) now blocks it with InaccessibleObjectException, unless you add --add-opens.

hashCode

// s[0]*31^(n-1) + s[1]*31^(n-2) + ... + s[n-1]
"ab".hashCode()      // 97*31 + 98 = 3105
"".hashCode()        // 0
"Aa".hashCode()      // 2112
"BB".hashCode()      // 2112: collision, so strings built from these pairs all collide
"polygenelubricants".hashCode()   // -2147483648, so Math.abs of it is still negative

The result is cached in hash, and the algorithm is part of the published API, so it can never change. Because collisions are easy to construct, attackers can send many colliding keys. Since Java 8, HashMap turns large buckets into trees, using Comparable on the keys, which limits the damage to O(log n).

The String Pool and intern()

The string pool is a table of canonical String objects. String objects are large in total, and many are duplicates, so literals are shared. When a class uses a literal, the ldc bytecode instruction resolves it the first time it runs: the JVM looks in the pool and either reuses the entry or adds one.

  • Location: PermGen until Java 6. Since Java 7 the String objects are on the normal heap, so they can be collected. The misconception that the pool is "in Metaspace" is wrong.
  • Structure: the StringTable is a native hash table in the JVM holding weak references to heap Strings, so unreferenced entries can be removed. Its size is -XX:StringTableSize, 65536 buckets by default on Java 21. jcmd <pid> VM.stringtable reports on it.
  • Compile-time constants are folded by javac, so "a" + "b" becomes the single literal "ab"; javap shows just ldc "ab". Only literals and final variables initialized with constant expressions count.
String a = "hello";
"hel" + "lo" == a             // true: folded at compile time
final String f = "hel";
f + "lo" == a                 // true: f is a constant variable
String n = "hel";
n + "lo" == a                 // false: computed at runtime
(n + "lo").intern() == a      // true
final String g = compute();   // returns "hel"
g + "lo" == a                 // false: final, but not a constant expression

intern()

s.intern() returns the pooled String equal to s, adding one if absent. Since Java 7 it adds a reference to the existing heap object rather than a copy. This produces a famous result:

String s1 = new String("a") + new String("b");  // "ab" is not in the pool yet
s1.intern();                                    // pool now points at s1 itself
String s2 = "ab";
s1 == s2                                        // true

String s3 = new String("c") + new String("d");
String s4 = "cd";                               // literal is pooled first
s3.intern();                                    // already present, returns the literal
s3 == s4                                        // false

String s5 = new String("ja") + new String("va");
s5.intern() == s5                               // false: the JDK already pooled "java"

Use intern rarely: only for very many duplicates of long-lived values, and measure it, because the table is a native structure with a real lookup cost. A HashMap<String, String> used as a canonicalizer is often better. String deduplication (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication with G1 and some other collectors) is different: the GC makes duplicate Strings share one byte[], and the String objects stay separate, so == stays false.

How many objects are created?

CodeString objects (not counting byte[])
String s = "a";1 in the pool, or 0 if the literal is already pooled
String s = new String("a");2: pooled literal and new heap object. Only 1 if the literal is already pooled
String s = "a" + "b";1: constant-folded, "a" and "b" do not appear in the class file
String t = x + "b"; with x a variable1 new result, plus pooled "b" if not yet there
new String("a") + new String("b")5: "a" and "b" pooled, 2 new copies, 1 result. "ab" does not go in the pool. Before Java 9 a StringBuilder was also created
Interview: Say "up to", and state the assumption. A literal is added when its ldc first executes, not when the line is merely loaded. The JDK itself may already have pooled it during startup, as with "java" above.

==, equals and friends

== compares references. It often "works" in tests because literals are pooled, then fails with runtime strings: from a request, a database or substring. Always use equals. String.equals checks identity first, then type, then coder and bytes, using an optimized JVM intrinsic.

"x".equals(input)                  // constant first, safe if input is null
Objects.equals(a, b)               // null-safe on both
a.equalsIgnoreCase(b)              // false on null, no exception
a.contentEquals(stringBuilder)     // String vs any CharSequence
"a".equals(new StringBuilder("a")) // false: not a String

Some methods return the same object if nothing changes. All of these are true: a.trim() == a, a.strip() == a, a.substring(0) == a, a.toString() == a, a.concat("") == a, a.replace('z', 'y') == a (no z), "java".toLowerCase() == "java", and String.valueOf(a) == a. These are false: "" + a == a, and "hello ".trim() == "hello", since a real change makes a new unpooled string. Do not depend on this: it is an implementation detail.

Compact Strings

Up to Java 8, a String wrapped a char[] using two bytes per character. Heap studies showed that Strings are a large share of heap data and most hold only Latin-1 text, so half that memory was zero bytes. Compact Strings (Java 9, JEP 254) store a byte[]. If all characters fit in Latin-1 (U+0000 to U+00FF), one byte each is used, with coder 0. If even one character does not fit, the whole string uses two bytes each, with coder 1.

public int length() { return value.length >> coder; }   // LATIN1: as is. UTF16: half

Methods branch on coder, for example to StringLatin1 or StringUTF16, and the JIT inlines those paths. The change is invisible to programs: char APIs behave as before. -XX:-CompactStrings turns it off. Latin-1 strings can be up to about 231 chars and UTF-16 ones about half that. A string constant in a class file has a much tighter limit, 65,535 bytes in modified UTF-8, which gives javac's "constant string too long" error.

One older fact to know: before Java 7u6, substring shared the parent's array using offset and count fields, which was fast but could pin a huge parent string in memory. Today it always copies, in O(k) for a substring of length k.

How Concatenation Compiles

Before Java 9, javac turned a + b into a StringBuilder chain. Since Java 9 (JEP 280) it emits invokedynamic. The real strategy is built by java.lang.invoke.StringConcatFactory at runtime, on first use. This means JDK updates can improve existing compiled code without recompiling, and the runtime can size the result exactly up front.

static String c(String a, int b) { return a + "-" + b; }
// javap -c:
aload_0
iload_1
invokedynamic #7,0  // InvokeDynamic #0:makeConcatWithConstants:(Ljava/lang/String;I)Ljava/lang/String;
areturn
// javac -XDstringConcat=inline reproduces the old form: new StringBuilder, append, append, append, toString

The rules for + follow from left associativity: once one side is a String, the rest is concatenation.

1 + 2 + "3"          // "33"
"1" + 2 + 3          // "123"
1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5  // "3345"
'a' + 'b' + "c"      // "195c"
"c" + 'a' + 'b'      // "cab"
"x" + (1 + 1)        // "x2"
1.0 + 1 + "x"        // "2.0x"
null + "a"           // "nulla"; a null String var + null gives "nullnull"
s += "x";            // if s is null: "nullx"
"a".concat(null);    // NullPointerException

Concatenation in loops

Each result += piece copies everything accumulated so far, so building n pieces is O(n²). One line of a + b + c is fine, and more readable than a builder. For loops, use StringBuilder:

StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder(items.size() * 16);  // presize if you can
for (String item : items) sb.append(item).append(',');
String out = sb.toString();

Indexes are zero-based and count char values, not user-visible characters. End indexes are exclusive. Bad indexes throw StringIndexOutOfBoundsException.

Java 21 added indexOf(ch, begin, end), splitWithDelimiters and StringBuilder.repeat.

split traps

The argument is a regular expression, and trailing empty strings are dropped unless the limit is negative.

CallResult
"a,b,,c,,".split(",")[a, b, , c], length 4
"a,b,,c,,".split(",", -1)[a, b, , c, , ]
"a,b,c".split(",", 2)[a, b,c]
"".split(",")Length 1: holds one empty string
",".split(",")Length 0: both pieces are trailing empties
",a".split(",")[, a]: leading empties stay
"a.b".split(".")[]: . matches everything. Use "\\."
"a|b".split("|")[a, |, b]: empty alternatives. Use "\\|"
" a b".split("\\s+")[, a, b]: strip first
"abc".split("")[a, b, c]

Replacement-string trap

In replaceAll, $ and \ in the replacement are special. "cost".replaceAll("cost", "$5") throws IndexOutOfBoundsException: No group 5. When the replacement comes from data, wrap it with Matcher.quoteReplacement, or use plain replace.

Locale trap

toLowerCase() with no argument uses the default locale. In Turkish, "TITLE" lowercases to "tıtle" with a dotless i, and "title" uppercases to "TİTLE". Code that normalizes keys or protocol names then breaks on a Turkish server. Use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for machine text. Case conversion can even change length: "ß".toUpperCase() gives "SS". For sorting human text use Collator, since compareTo orders by UTF-16 value, putting all capitals before lowercase. String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER is the built-in case-blind comparator.

StringBuilder, StringBuffer, StringJoiner

All three exist to avoid the O(n²) of repeated copying. StringBuilder and StringBuffer both extend the package-private AbstractStringBuilder, which holds a byte[] value, a coder and a count. Unlike String, the array usually has spare capacity, so append is amortized O(1).

new StringBuilder().capacity()          // 16
new StringBuilder("hello").capacity()   // 21: length + 16
new StringBuilder(5).capacity()         // 5
var sb = new StringBuilder();           // capacity 16
sb.append("12345678901234567");         // 17 chars: capacity 34 = 16*2 + 2
sb.append("x".repeat(20));              // 37 chars: capacity 70 = 34*2 + 2
new StringBuilder('a').capacity()       // 97! the char widens to the int capacity; length is 0

When an append needs more room, a larger array is allocated and contents copied. Presizing avoids that. A Latin-1 builder inflates to UTF-16 on the first wider character.

OperationEffect
append(x)Overloaded for all types. append((String) null) adds "null"
insert(i, x)O(n): shifts the tail
delete(b, e), deleteCharAt(i)O(n): shifts the tail
replace(b, e, s)Index-based, unlike String.replace
reverse()Keeps surrogate pairs in order. Combining marks are not handled
setCharAt(i, c)O(1)
setLength(n)Truncates, or pads with \0. setLength(0) clears and keeps capacity for reuse
capacity, ensureCapacity, trimToSizeManage the buffer
toString()Copies, so the result is independent of later appends
Gotcha: StringBuilder does not override equals or hashCode, so new StringBuilder("a").equals(new StringBuilder("a")) is false. Compare using sb1.compareTo(sb2) == 0 (Java 11) or contentEquals. Do not use a builder as a map key.
StringBuilderStringBufferStringJoiner
Since51.08
Thread-safeNoYes, each method is synchronizedNo
Use forAlmost everythingLegacy APIs, such as Matcher.appendReplacement before Java 9Delimited text with prefix and suffix

A key point on StringBuffer: only individual calls are atomic. if (buf.length() < 10) buf.append(x); across threads is still a race. Real multi-threaded building is rare anyway, so prefer each thread building its own text.

StringJoiner j = new StringJoiner(", ", "[", "]");
j.setEmptyValue("EMPTY");
j.toString();          // EMPTY
j.add("a").add("b");
j.toString();          // [a, b]
j.merge(new StringJoiner("-", "<", ">").add("1").add("2"));
j.toString();          // [a, b, 1-2]: merged content, without the other's prefix

String.join(",", list);                               // simple form
stream.collect(Collectors.joining(",", "{", "}"));    // from a stream

Text Blocks

Text blocks (Java 15) are multi-line string literals, so embedded JSON, SQL and HTML need no \n or escaped quotes. They produce an ordinary String, identical at runtime, and pooled: """\n a""" == "a" is true. The opening """ must end its line, so """abc""" is a compile error.

The compiler processes a block in three steps:

  1. Line endings are normalized to \n.
  2. Incidental whitespace is removed: it finds the smallest indentation among all non-blank lines plus the closing delimiter's line, removes that from every line, and strips trailing spaces.
  3. Escape sequences are interpreted, which is why \n or \s survive step 2.
String a = """
        Hello
          World
        """;
// "Hello\n  World\n": closing delimiter on its own line adds the last \n

String b = """
        a
      b""";
// "  a\nb": the delimiter on line "b" sets the margin, and there is no final \n

String c = """
        one \
        two
        x
        y\s\s
        q"\""
        """;
// "one two\nx\ny  \nq\"\"\"\n"
// \ at line end joins lines; \s keeps trailing spaces; \""" escapes the delimiter

String json = """
        {"id": %d}
        """.formatted(7).strip();  // {"id": 7}

Moving the closing delimiter left adds indentation to all lines. Moving it right of the content changes nothing, since it is only one more line in the minimum calculation. Runtime helpers: stripIndent() and translateEscapes().

String templates (STR."...") were previewed in Java 21 and 22, then withdrawn in Java 23. They are not part of Java 25, so use formatted, concatenation, or a template engine.

Formatting

String.format, System.out.printf and "...".formatted(...) share java.util.Formatter. A specifier has the form %[argument_index$][flags][width][.precision]conversion.

SpecifierArgumentResult
%5d / %-5d / %05d42[ 42] / [42 ] / [00042]
%,d / %+d1234567 / 421,234,567 / +42
%x / %X / %o255 / 255 / 8ff / FF / 10
%.2f / %8.3f3.141593.14 / [ 3.142]
%08.3f3.141590003.142
%e1234.51.234500e+03
%s / %10s / %-10sAnyUses String.valueOf. Null prints "null"
%.3s"abcdef"abc (precision truncates)
%c / %b'c' / any%b: null is false, non-Boolean non-null is true
%n / %%NonePlatform line end / a percent sign
%2$s %1$s %1$s"a", "b"b a a

Errors are at runtime: String.format("%d", 1.5) throws IllegalFormatConversionException: d != java.lang.Double, and too few arguments gives MissingFormatArgumentException.

Locale matters. %,.2f of 1234.5 gives 1,234.50 under Locale.US and 1.234,50 under Locale.GERMANY. If output is consumed by a machine (CSV, JSON, SQL), pass Locale.ROOT explicitly, or a comma may appear as your decimal point.

DecimalFormat and rounding

var us = DecimalFormatSymbols.getInstance(Locale.US);
new DecimalFormat("#,##0.00", us).format(1234567.891);  // 1,234,567.89
new DecimalFormat("0.000", us).format(3.1);             // 3.100  (0 forces a digit)
new DecimalFormat("#.##", us).format(3.1);              // 3.1    (# drops zeros)
new DecimalFormat("000", us).format(7);                 // 007
new DecimalFormat("0.0%", us).format(0.256);            // 25.6%
Gotcha: The two APIs round differently. Formatter uses HALF_UP: "%.1f" of 0.25 gives 0.3. DecimalFormat defaults to HALF_EVEN: "#.#" of 0.25 gives 0.2. Also, a double is rarely exactly what it displays: 2.355 is really a bit below, so "#.##" gives 2.35. For money, round a BigDecimal and then format. DecimalFormat and SimpleDateFormat are not thread-safe, so do not share them through a static field. DateTimeFormatter is immutable and safe.

MessageFormat uses positional placeholders with locale-aware numbers: MessageFormat.format("{0} has {1} items", "Ann", 3). A single quote is an escape, so a literal apostrophe needs two: "It''s {0}".

Regular Expressions

A regular expression describes a set of strings. java.util.regex compiles a pattern into a node graph, and a backtracking engine walks it against the input.

Pattern p = Pattern.compile("(?<y>\\d{4})-(?<m>\\d{2})-(\\d{2})");   // immutable, thread-safe
Matcher m = p.matcher("from 2025-01-15 to 2026-11-04");             // stateful, one thread
while (m.find()) {
    m.group();        // 2025-01-15
    m.group("y");     // 2025     named group
    m.group(2);       // 01       named groups are numbered too
    m.start();        // 5
    m.end();          // 15       exclusive
    m.groupCount();   // 3        group(0), the whole match, is not counted
}
Tip: Pattern.compile is relatively expensive. Keep the result in a private static final Pattern. String.matches and replaceAll recompile on each call, so avoid them in hot paths. String.split has a fast path for a single non-regex character.

Syntax reference

SyntaxMeaning
.Any char except line terminators (with DOTALL, any)
\d \w \s and \D \W \SDigit, word char, whitespace, and their negations. ASCII by default
[abc] [^abc] [a-z]Character class, negated class, range
^ $ \bStart, end, word boundary (with MULTILINE, ^ and $ apply per line)
* + ? {n,m}Greedy quantifiers
*? +? ??Lazy (reluctant): as few as possible
*+ ++ ?+Possessive: never give back
( ) (?: ) (?<n> )Capturing, non-capturing, named group
\1 \k<n>Backreference: "abab".matches("(ab)\\1") is true
(?= ) (?! )Lookahead, positive and negative
(?<= ) (?<! )Lookbehind
(?> )Atomic group
(?i) (?s) (?m)Inline flags: case-insensitive, dotall, multiline
\XOne grapheme cluster (Java 9)

In a Java literal each backslash is doubled: the regex \d is written "\\d", and a literal backslash is "\\\\". Pattern.quote("a.b") gives \Qa.b\E, which matches the text literally.

matches, find, lookingAt

MethodMatches where"b" on "abc""a" on "abc"
matches()Whole inputfalsefalse
lookingAt()Prefixfalsetrue
find()Anywhere, next match per calltruetrue

Replacing and streaming

"john smith".replaceAll("(\\w+) (\\w+)", "$2 $1");            // smith john
Pattern.compile("(?<k>\\w+)=(?<v>\\w+)").matcher("a=1,b=2")
       .replaceAll("${v}=${k}");                              // 1=a,2=b
Pattern.compile("(\\w)(\\d)").matcher("a1 b2")
       .replaceAll(r -> r.group(2) + r.group(1));             // 1a 2b (Java 9, function form)
"hello world".replaceAll("\\b(\\w)", "<$1>");                 // <h>ello <w>orld
"foobar".replaceAll("foo(?=bar)", "X");                       // Xbar
"price 100".replaceAll("(?<=price )\\d+", "N");               // price N
Pattern.compile("\\d+").matcher("a1b22c333").results()
       .map(MatchResult::group).toList();                     // [1, 22, 333] (Java 9)
Pattern.compile("\\d").asPredicate();                         // find semantics
Pattern.compile("\\d").asMatchPredicate();                    // matches semantics (Java 11)

Backtracking

A greedy quantifier takes as much as it can. If the rest of the pattern then fails, the engine gives back one character at a time and retries. This is backtracking.

// Input: <a><b>
"<.+>"     // greedy: .+ runs to the end, backs off one char, matches <a><b>
"<.+?>"    // lazy: expands one char at a time, matches <a>
"<[^>]+>"  // negated class: no backtracking needed, usually best

"aaa".matches("a*a")    // true: a* gives one back
"aaa".matches("a*+a")   // false: possessive keeps all, nothing is left for the final a

Catastrophic backtracking happens when nested quantifiers let the engine split the input in exponentially many ways, each tried on failure. This is the basis of ReDoS, a denial-of-service attack through a crafted input.

Gotcha: The textbook example (a+)+b does not blow up on modern Java. JDK 9 added memoization for repeated group loops, and on Java 21 it fails on 28 a's in under a millisecond. Interviewers may not know this. The exponential case still exists: a backreference disables the optimization. On one run, (a+)+\1b on a's followed by "!" took 174 ms for 22 a's, 378 ms for 24, 1.7 s for 26 and 8.3 s for 28, which is about double per added character. Polynomial cases such as (.*a){12}b also remain slow. So do not treat user-supplied patterns as safe on any version.

Defences: never run untrusted patterns; limit input length; prefer negated classes ([^,]*) to .*; avoid nested quantifiers over overlapping alternatives; use possessive quantifiers or atomic groups; wrap the input in a CharSequence whose charAt checks a deadline; or use a linear-time engine such as RE2/J.

A separate failure is stack depth: group repetition recurses. "ab".repeat(1000).matches("(a|b)*") threw StackOverflowError on Java 21 at only 2,000 characters. The character-class form [ab]* runs iteratively and handled 100,000 characters with no problem. Prefer classes to alternations of single characters.

Characters, Encodings and Bytes

Text handling goes wrong when these ideas are confused:

TermMeaningExample
Code pointThe number Unicode assigns to a characterU+1F600, 128512
Code unitThe storage unit of an encoding. Java char is one UTF-16 code unit0xD83D
Grapheme clusterWhat a user sees as one charactere + combining accent
EncodingRule for turning code points into bytesUTF-8

The string "café" holds 4 chars, and its size in bytes depends on the encoding:

CharsetBytes for "café"Bytes for U+1F600Notes
UTF-85 (636166c3a9)41 to 4 bytes per code point. ASCII-compatible. The web and Java default
UTF-16BE842 or 4 bytes
UTF-16106Adds a 2-byte byte order mark when encoding
ISO-8859-14Not representable1 byte, covers Western Europe
US-ASCII4, but é becomes ?Not representableSilent data loss: result is "caf?"

Default charset

Before Java 18, getBytes(), new String(bytes) and FileReader used the OS default, so the same code behaved differently on Windows and Linux. Since Java 18 (JEP 400) the default is UTF-8 everywhere. Still, always name the charset in code, as it documents intent. StandardCharsets.UTF_8 also avoids the checked exception of the name-based overload. Source file encoding is a separate thing: use javac -encoding UTF-8 (the default since Java 18).

Mojibake

Mojibake is garbled text from decoding bytes with the wrong charset. UTF-8 bytes read as Latin-1 turn "café" into "cafÃ©":

byte[] b = "café".getBytes(UTF_8);                 // 63 61 66 c3 a9
String bad = new String(b, ISO_8859_1);            // 5 chars: c a f Ã ©
new String(bad.getBytes(ISO_8859_1), UTF_8);       // "café" again: the damage was reversible
new String(new byte[]{(byte) 0xC3}, UTF_8);        // U+FFFD: invalid bytes are silently replaced
StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newDecoder()
    .onMalformedInput(CodingErrorAction.REPORT)
    .decode(ByteBuffer.wrap(bytes));               // throws MalformedInputException instead

Recovery works only if no bytes were lost, and a ? or U+FFFD means data is gone. To diagnose, print hex with HexFormat.of().formatHex(bytes) (Java 17), then check each hop: HTTP Content-Type, JDBC URL, table charset, file reader.

Gotcha: MySQL's utf8 is an alias for a 3-byte form (utf8mb3), so a 4-byte emoji fails or truncates. Use utf8mb4. Column limits and API limits may count bytes, chars or code points, and those differ, so an "SMS is 160 characters" check on length() can be wrong.

Surrogates and code points

Code points above U+FFFF are stored as a surrogate pair of two chars, a high one in D800-DBFF and a low one in DC00-DFFF.

String em = "\uD83D\uDE00";                  // U+1F600, grinning face
em.length()                                  // 2
em.codePointCount(0, em.length())            // 1
em.codePointAt(0)                            // 128512
Character.isSurrogate(em.charAt(0))          // true
Character.charCount(0x1F600)                 // 2
new String(Character.toChars(0x1F600))       // same string
Character.toString(0x41)                     // "A"
em.getBytes(UTF_8).length                    // 4
em.substring(0, 1).getBytes(UTF_8)           // the byte for "?": a lone surrogate is invalid

So char-by-char code is wrong for such text: truncating with substring can cut a pair in half, and swapping chars in a reversal scrambles it. Iterate with s.codePoints(). Even code points are not always "characters":

String composed = "\u00e9", decomposed = "e\u0301";    // both display as é
composed.equals(decomposed)                            // false
decomposed.length()                                    // 2
Normalizer.normalize(decomposed, Normalizer.Form.NFC).equals(composed)  // true

Normalize text before comparing it when it comes from different sources, such as file names from macOS. To count what users see, use \X or java.text.BreakIterator. Base64 is not an encoding of text but of bytes into ASCII: Base64.getEncoder().encodeToString("hi".getBytes(UTF_8)) gives aGk=, and it provides no secrecy.

char[] for Passwords

A String cannot be wiped: it stays in memory until collected, the GC may have copied it around, and literals or interned values live longer still. A heap dump or crash dump then shows the secret in plain text. A char[] can be overwritten right after use, and accidentally printing one shows [C@1b6d3586, not the secret.

char[] pw = System.console().readPassword("Password: ");
try {
    verify(pw);
} finally {
    Arrays.fill(pw, '\0');     // wipe it now, do not wait for GC
}

JDK APIs follow this: Console.readPassword, JPasswordField.getPassword, PBEKeySpec and KeyStore.load all use char[].

Be honest about the limits. The GC may already have copied the array, and in a web app the password arrives inside request-parsing Strings before your code sees it, so char[] reduces the exposure window rather than removing it. Things that matter more: hash with BCrypt or Argon2, never log request bodies, use TLS, restrict access to heap dumps, and load secrets from a vault.

String Coding Questions: Solutions

All of these were compiled and run on Java 21 with the shown results. Unless noted, they assume text where one char is one character, and mention this to your interviewer.

1. Reverse a string

static String reverse(String s) { return new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString(); }

static String reverseManual(String s) {            // two pointers, O(n)
    char[] c = s.toCharArray();
    for (int i = 0, j = c.length - 1; i < j; i++, j--) {
        char t = c[i]; c[i] = c[j]; c[j] = t;
    }
    return new String(c);
}

static String reverseRec(String s) {               // O(n^2), and deep recursion
    return s.isEmpty() ? "" : reverseRec(s.substring(1)) + s.charAt(0);
}
// "hello" gives "olleh" from all three

StringBuilder.reverse keeps surrogate pairs correct. The manual version scrambles them: reversing an emoji gave an unequal string.

2. Palindrome, ignoring case and punctuation

static boolean isPalindrome(String s) {
    int i = 0, j = s.length() - 1;
    while (i < j) {
        while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(i))) i++;
        while (i < j && !Character.isLetterOrDigit(s.charAt(j))) j--;
        if (Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(i++)) != Character.toLowerCase(s.charAt(j--)))
            return false;
    }
    return true;
}
// "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" true    "race a car" false
// O(n) time, O(1) space, no new strings

3. Anagram check

static boolean isAnagram(String a, String b) {     // lowercase a-z, O(n)
    if (a.length() != b.length()) return false;
    int[] count = new int[26];
    for (int i = 0; i < a.length(); i++) {
        count[a.charAt(i) - 'a']++;
        count[b.charAt(i) - 'a']--;
    }
    for (int c : count) if (c != 0) return false;
    return true;
}

static boolean isAnagramAny(String a, String b) {  // any Unicode text
    Map<Integer, Integer> f = new HashMap<>();
    a.codePoints().forEach(c -> f.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum));
    b.codePoints().forEach(c -> f.merge(c, -1, Integer::sum));
    return f.values().stream().allMatch(v -> v == 0);
}
// listen, silent: true    rat, car: false

Sorting both char arrays and comparing is simpler, but O(n log n).

4. First non-repeating character

static int firstUnique(String s) {       // ASCII, O(n), two passes
    int[] f = new int[128];
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) f[s.charAt(i)]++;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) if (f[s.charAt(i)] == 1) return i;
    return -1;
}

static Optional<Character> firstUniqueStream(String s) {
    return s.chars().mapToObj(c -> (char) c)
        .collect(Collectors.groupingBy(Function.identity(),
                 LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.counting()))     // keeps first-seen order
        .entrySet().stream().filter(e -> e.getValue() == 1)
        .map(Map.Entry::getKey).findFirst();
}
// "swiss": index 1, Optional[w]     "aabb": -1

5. Character frequency

static Map<Character, Integer> freq(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> m = new TreeMap<>();     // sorted output
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) m.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);
    return m;
}
// "banana": {a=3, b=1, n=2}

static char mostFrequent(String s) {                 // first to reach the highest count
    int[] f = new int[128];
    char best = s.charAt(0);
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if (++f[c] > f[best]) best = c;
    return best;
}
// "mississippi": s

6. Remove duplicate characters, keeping order

static String removeDup(String s) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    Set<Character> seen = new HashSet<>();
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) if (seen.add(c)) sb.append(c);
    return sb.toString();
}
// "programming": progamin

7. Reverse the words of a sentence

static String reverseWords(String s) {
    String[] w = s.strip().split("\\s+");
    Collections.reverse(Arrays.asList(w));   // the asList view writes through to w
    return String.join(" ", w);
}
// "  the quick  brown fox ": "fox brown quick the"

8. Count words, vowels and consonants

static int countWords(String s) { return s.isBlank() ? 0 : s.strip().split("\\s+").length; }
// "  hello   world ": 2     "   ": 0

static int[] vowels(String s) {
    int v = 0, c = 0;
    for (char ch : s.toLowerCase().toCharArray()) {
        if (!Character.isLetter(ch)) continue;
        if ("aeiou".indexOf(ch) >= 0) v++; else c++;
    }
    return new int[]{v, c};
}
// "Hello World": [3, 7]

9. Longest substring without repeating characters

A sliding window: start jumps past the previous occurrence of a repeated character. The p >= start check ignores occurrences left of the window, which matters for "abba".

static int longestUnique(String s) {
    Map<Character, Integer> last = new HashMap<>();
    int best = 0, start = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
        Integer p = last.put(s.charAt(i), i);
        if (p != null && p >= start) start = p + 1;
        best = Math.max(best, i - start + 1);
    }
    return best;
}
// "abcabcbb": 3     "pwwkew": 3     "abba": 2       O(n)

10. Longest palindromic substring

Expand around each centre, both odd and even. O(n²) time and O(1) space. Manacher's algorithm achieves O(n), but is rarely expected.

static String longestPal(String s) {
    int bs = 0, bl = 0;
    for (int c = 0; c < s.length(); c++) {
        for (int odd = 0; odd < 2; odd++) {
            int l = c, r = c + odd;
            while (l >= 0 && r < s.length() && s.charAt(l) == s.charAt(r)) { l--; r++; }
            if (r - l - 1 > bl) { bl = r - l - 1; bs = l + 1; }
        }
    }
    return s.substring(bs, bs + bl);
}
// "babad": bab     "cbbd": bb

11. Longest common prefix

static String commonPrefix(String... w) {
    if (w.length == 0) return "";
    String p = w[0];
    for (String s : w) while (!s.startsWith(p)) p = p.substring(0, p.length() - 1);
    return p;
}
// flower, flow, flight: fl     a, b: ""

12. Balanced brackets

static boolean balanced(String s) {
    Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();       // Deque, not the legacy Stack
    for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
        switch (c) {
            case '(', '[', '{' -> st.push(c);
            case ')', ']', '}' -> {
                if (st.isEmpty()) return false;
                char o = st.pop();
                if ("([{".indexOf(o) != ")]}".indexOf(c)) return false;
            }
            default -> { }
        }
    }
    return st.isEmpty();
}
// "{[()]}" true     "([)]" false     "((" false

13. Is one string a rotation of another?

static boolean isRotation(String a, String b) {
    return a.length() == b.length() && (a + a).contains(b);
}
// waterbottle, erbottlewat: true     abc, acb: false

14. Run-length compression

static String compress(String s) {
    StringBuilder sb = new StringBuilder();
    for (int i = 0, j; i < s.length(); i = j) {
        j = i;
        while (j < s.length() && s.charAt(j) == s.charAt(i)) j++;
        sb.append(s.charAt(i)).append(j - i);
    }
    return sb.length() < s.length() ? sb.toString() : s;
}
// "aaabbbcc": a3b3c2     "abc": abc (compressed would be longer)

15. String to int without parseInt

The trick is to accumulate as a negative number. The negative range is larger, so -2147483648 parses without overflow. Integer.parseInt uses the same approach.

static int atoi(String s) {
    s = s.strip();
    if (s.isEmpty()) throw new NumberFormatException("empty");
    int i = 0; boolean neg = false;
    if (s.charAt(0) == '-' || s.charAt(0) == '+') { neg = s.charAt(0) == '-'; i = 1; }
    if (i == s.length()) throw new NumberFormatException(s);
    int r = 0;
    for (; i < s.length(); i++) {
        int d = s.charAt(i) - '0';
        if (d < 0 || d > 9) throw new NumberFormatException(s);
        r = Math.subtractExact(Math.multiplyExact(r, 10), d);
    }
    return neg ? r : Math.negateExact(r);
}
// "-123": -123    "+42": 42    "-2147483648": -2147483648
// "2147483648": ArithmeticException: integer overflow     "12x": NumberFormatException

16. All permutations, skipping duplicates

static void perm(String pre, String rest, List<String> out) {
    if (rest.isEmpty()) { out.add(pre); return; }
    for (int i = 0; i < rest.length(); i++) {
        if (i > 0 && rest.indexOf(rest.charAt(i)) < i) continue;   // same char tried already
        perm(pre + rest.charAt(i), rest.substring(0, i) + rest.substring(i + 1), out);
    }
}
// "abc": [abc, acb, bac, bca, cab, cba]     "aab": [aab, aba, baa]      O(n * n!)

17. Group anagrams

static Collection<List<String>> groupAnagrams(List<String> ws) {
    return ws.stream().collect(Collectors.groupingBy(w -> {
        char[] c = w.toCharArray();
        Arrays.sort(c);
        return new String(c);                // sorted letters are the key
    }, LinkedHashMap::new, Collectors.toList())).values();
}
// eat, tea, tan, ate, nat, bat: [[eat, tea, ate], [tan, nat], [bat]]

18. Title case and substring search

static String toTitle(String s) {
    return Arrays.stream(s.strip().split("\\s+"))
        .map(w -> Character.toUpperCase(w.charAt(0)) + w.substring(1).toLowerCase())
        .collect(Collectors.joining(" "));
}
// "hELLO wORLD java": "Hello World Java"

static int strStr(String h, String n) {      // indexOf by hand, O(n*m) worst case
    for (int i = 0; i + n.length() <= h.length(); i++)
        if (h.startsWith(n, i)) return i;
    return -1;
}
// hello, ll: 2     aaa, b: -1

In toTitle, char + String is concatenation, since the right side is a String. For guaranteed linear search, mention KMP.

Strings and Security: Injection, Encoding, Comparison

Many security bugs start as string concatenation. The rule is: never splice untrusted text into another language, whether SQL, HTML, a log line, a URL or a shell command. Use the API that keeps data separate from code.

// SQL injection: concatenation turns data into code
String sql = "SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = '" + email + "'";   // email = "' OR '1'='1"
// Fix: bind parameters (JDBC / JPA / Spring Data)
PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = ?");
ps.setString(1, email);
em.createQuery("select u from User u where u.email = :e", User.class).setParameter("e", email);

// Identifiers (ORDER BY column, table) cannot be bound, so whitelist them
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("name", "created_at", "total");
String col = SORTABLE.contains(sort) ? sort : "created_at";

// Log injection: CR/LF in user input forges fake log lines
log.info("Login failed for {}", user.replaceAll("[\r\n]", "_"));   // or use a JSON log encoder

// URL query parameters
String q = URLEncoder.encode("a b&c", StandardCharsets.UTF_8);   // "a+b%26c" (form encoding)
URI uri = UriComponentsBuilder.fromUriString(base)                // Spring: encodes each part correctly
        .queryParam("q", "a b&c").encode().build().toUri();

// Constant-time comparison for secrets (API keys, HMAC signatures)
boolean ok = MessageDigest.isEqual(expected.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8), given.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
💡 String.equals returns at the first differing character, so the time it takes can reveal how much of a secret token matched. MessageDigest.isEqual takes the same time no matter where the bytes differ.

Interview Questions — Strings & Text

Why is String final? How is immutability actually enforced?

final stops subclasses from overriding methods to break the guarantee, so any String parameter can be trusted. Enforcement: the value array is private and final, no method writes to it after construction, and every path in or out copies it. Being final alone would not be enough: the array contents would still be writable if a reference leaked. final on the field only fixes the reference.

Where is the string pool stored? Can its strings be garbage collected?

The String objects have been on the ordinary heap since Java 7; before that they were in PermGen, which caused OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space with heavy interning. The lookup structure, StringTable, is a native hash table with weak references, so a pooled String with no other references can be collected. Literals stay alive as long as the class that references them, through its resolved constants. The pool is not in Metaspace.

How many objects does String s = new String("hello"); create?

Up to two String objects: the pooled literal "hello", if it is not already pooled, and the new heap String. The new object shares the literal's byte[], so there is one backing array. If the literal is already in the pool, only one is created. new String("...") is almost never needed. It exists mainly for copying, and it was once useful for detaching a substring.

Output? String a = "hello"; String n = "hel"; final String f = "hel"; print(n + "lo" == a); print(f + "lo" == a); print((n + "lo").intern() == a);
false
true
true

n + "lo" is evaluated at runtime and gives a new object. f is a constant variable, so the expression folds to the literal "hello" at compile time. intern() returns the pooled instance. If f were assigned from a method call, it would be final but not constant, and the second line would be false. Verified.

Output? Explain why the two results differ.
String s1 = new String("a") + new String("b");
s1.intern();
String s2 = "ab";
System.out.println(s1 == s2);   // true

String s3 = new String("c") + new String("d");
String s4 = "cd";
s3.intern();
System.out.println(s3 == s4);   // false

The concatenation makes a heap String that is not in the pool. In the first case intern() finds nothing, and since Java 7 it stores a reference to s1 itself, so the literal resolves to s1. On Java 6 the pool got a copy, and the output would be false. In the second case the literal is pooled first, so intern() returns that one, and its result is discarded anyway. Remember that intern() does not modify the string: s3 = s3.intern() is what you would need.

Why does the "java".equals(s) style matter, and when would == on strings appear to work?

Calling equals on a constant avoids an NPE when s is null. == works only when both refer to the same object: literals, constants, or interned values. So tests with hard-coded values pass, while the code fails on data from HTTP, a database or substring, which are new objects. Static analysis such as SonarLint flags it.

What is the output? String a = "Java"; a.concat(" 21"); System.out.println(a);

Java. concat returns a new string that is thrown away. Same for toUpperCase, replace and trim. It is one of the most common bugs for newcomers. a = a.concat(" 21"); fixes it, and IDEs warn about ignored return values.

Output? System.out.println(1 + 2 + "3" + 4 + 5); System.out.println('a' + 'b' + "c"); System.out.println("Java".charAt(0) + "Java".charAt(1));
3345
195c
171

+ goes left to right. Numeric addition happens until a String is involved. The third has no String at all: charAt returns char, so 74 + 97 is the int 171.

What happens with String s = null; s += "x";, and with s.concat("x")?

+= gives "nullx", since concatenation converts null to the text "null". s.concat("x") throws NPE as it is a method call on null. Also "a".concat(null) throws NPE. null + null with literals does not compile, but with two null String variables gives "nullnull".

What did Java 9 change about concatenation? Should you still use StringBuilder?

javac emits invokedynamic to StringConcatFactory rather than a hard-coded builder chain. The JVM generates a strategy on first use, computes the exact length, and avoids the builder's resizing, so a simple a + b + c is at least as fast, and clearer. Use StringBuilder when accumulating across loop iterations or several statements. The compiler optimizes each expression separately, so a loop still gives O(n²).

Why does repeated += in a loop cost O(n²)?

Each iteration allocates a new string and copies the accumulated text. Copy costs add up as 1 + 2 + ... + n, which is about n²/2 characters. That also generates heavy garbage. A StringBuilder appends in amortized O(1) by keeping spare capacity and doubling, so the total is O(n).

What are compact strings? Does charAt become slower?

Since Java 9, Strings store a byte[] and a coder. Latin-1-only text uses one byte per char, otherwise two bytes per char. That cuts memory substantially for typical data, without API changes. charAt has one extra branch on the coder, which the JIT handles well, and in exchange memory is lower, so there is less GC work and better cache use. One non-Latin-1 character makes the entire string two-byte, so the savings depend on your data.

How did substring change over time, and why?

Up to Java 7u5 it shared the parent's char[] with an offset and count: O(1), but a tiny substring of a huge string kept the entire array alive, a well-known memory leak. People worked around it with new String(sub). From 7u6 it copies: O(k), and no leak, and the fields were removed from String.

What is the difference between trim() and strip()? isEmpty() and isBlank()?

trim removes characters up to U+0020, which predates Unicode awareness, so it keeps U+2003 (em space) while removing control characters. strip (Java 11) uses Character.isWhitespace, so " x ".trim().length() is 3 and strip gives 1. isEmpty tests length 0; isBlank also accepts only-whitespace strings.

replace vs replaceAll: which replaces all occurrences?

Both do. The name misleads: replace treats both arguments literally, and replaceAll treats the first as a regex and the second as a replacement template. "a.b.c".replaceAll(".", "-") gives -----. Use replace unless you need a regex. It also avoids compiling a pattern.

What does "a,b,,c,,".split(",").length give? And "".split(",").length?

4 and 1. Trailing empty strings are removed when the limit is 0 (the default), while interior ones remain. An input with no match returns the whole input as one element, so the empty string gives one empty string, even though that looks odd. To keep all columns of a CSV line, use split(",", -1). For real CSV with quoted fields, use a library.

How does compareTo work? Can it return something other than -1, 0, 1?

It returns the difference of the first unequal chars, or of the lengths if one is a prefix of the other. "a".compareTo("A") is 32, and "apple".compareTo("apple pie") is -4. Only the sign is contractually meaningful. So test < 0, never == -1. It orders by UTF-16 code unit, so "Z" sorts before "a". Use Collator for human sorting.

Why can toLowerCase() break a program on some servers?

It uses the default locale. With a Turkish default, "TITLE" becomes "tıtle", with a dotless ı, so "TITLE".toLowerCase().equals("title") is false, and enum lookups or header comparisons fail. Use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for identifiers and protocols, and equalsIgnoreCase for comparison. Length may change as well: "ß" uppercases to "SS".

StringBuilder default capacity? How does it grow? What does new StringBuilder('a') do?

Default capacity is 16, or the length + 16 for a String argument. It grows to about (old × 2) + 2: 16, 34, 70 in the run above. new StringBuilder('a') compiles because char widens to int, picking the capacity constructor: the result is empty with capacity 97. This is a known trap: new StringBuilder('H').append("ello") gives "ello", because the H is lost.

Is StringBuffer ever the right choice?

Rarely. Each method is synchronized, but a sequence of calls is not atomic, so check-then-append remains unsafe, and the order of interleaved appends from threads is usually useless. In practice each thread builds its own text, then shares the immutable result. It remains in legacy APIs. If you ever need a truly shared buffer, use an explicit lock or a queue of strings.

Why does sb1.equals(sb2) return false for equal content? How do you compare?

StringBuilder inherits identity-based equals from Object. Mutable objects make unsafe keys, and a content-based hash would change. Compare using sb1.compareTo(sb2) == 0 (Java 11), sb1.toString().contentEquals(sb2), or "text".contentEquals(sb).

What is the difference between String.join, StringJoiner and Collectors.joining?

String.join covers a delimiter over an array or Iterable. StringJoiner adds a prefix, suffix, an empty value, incremental add, and merge. Collectors.joining is the stream collector built on the same idea. Note that String.join prints nulls as "null", and none of them skips nulls for you.

How does a text block decide its indentation? Output of this one?
String s = """
        a
      b""";

It equals " a\nb". The compiler takes the minimum indentation of non-blank lines, and the closing delimiter's line if it stands alone. Here b has 6 spaces, the minimum, so 6 are removed from both lines. No final newline, because the delimiter is on the same line as b. Trailing spaces are stripped unless written \s, and a backslash at line end joins lines. A text block is an ordinary compile-time String constant, so it is pooled.

String.format vs concatenation vs StringBuilder: when to use each?

Concatenation for simple one-liners. StringBuilder for loops. format or formatted for alignment, padding, number or date formatting, or templates. format is far slower since it parses the format string at runtime, so avoid it on hot paths. For logging, use parameterized messages such as log.debug("id={}", id), which skip formatting if the level is off.

Why might String.format("%.2f", 1.5) produce "1,50"?

Without a locale argument it uses the default FORMAT locale, and many locales use a decimal comma. That breaks CSV exports, generated SQL and JSON built by hand. Pass Locale.ROOT for machine-readable output. Parsing has the same problem in the other direction.

What does "%.2f" give for 0.125 and 0.135? And DecimalFormat("#.#") for 0.25?

0.13, 0.14, and 0.2. Formatter rounds HALF_UP on the exact decimal value of the double. 0.125 is exactly representable, so its tie rounds up. DecimalFormat defaults to HALF_EVEN, so the tie 0.25 goes to the even 0.2. Non-representable values are not ties at all. If rounding rules matter, use BigDecimal with an explicit mode, or call setRoundingMode.

matches() vs find() vs lookingAt()? Why does "hello".matches("ell") return false?

matches needs the entire input to match, acting as if anchored at both ends. find searches for the next occurrence. lookingAt anchors only at the start. "hello".matches("ell") is false, while "hello".matches(".*ell.*") or contains("ell") works. "a\nb".matches("a.b") is also false, unless DOTALL is set.

Is Pattern thread-safe? Is Matcher?

Pattern is immutable, so share it as a static final constant. Matcher holds position and group state, and is not thread-safe, so create one per use with pattern.matcher(input). matcher.reset(newInput) can reuse one in a single thread.

Greedy vs lazy vs possessive quantifiers?

Greedy (.*) takes the maximum and backs off on failure. Lazy (.*?) takes the minimum and expands on failure. Possessive (.*+) takes the maximum and never backs off, so it fails faster but can miss matches: "aaa".matches("a*+a") is false. On <a><b>, <.+> matches the whole text, and <.+?> matches only <a>. A negated class such as <[^>]+> is often better than either.

What is ReDoS? Is (a+)+b dangerous in Java?

ReDoS is a denial of service through an input that makes a backtracking regex take exponential time, tying up a request thread. (a+)+b is the classic example, and it is exponential in many engines, including Java 8. Since JDK 9 the engine memoizes in group loops, and it finished in under 1 ms on Java 21 even for 28 a's. Adding a backreference, (a+)+\1b, restores exponential behaviour: 8 seconds at 28 a's in our run. So the danger is narrower but real. Mitigate with input length limits, no user-supplied patterns, possessive quantifiers, a deadline-checking CharSequence, or RE2/J.

Validate an email address with a regex. What is the right answer in practice?
private static final Pattern EMAIL =
    Pattern.compile("^[\\w.+-]+@[\\w-]+(\\.[\\w-]+)+$");
EMAIL.matcher("user@mail.com").matches();   // true

This accepts typical addresses, but it is not RFC-complete. A full RFC 5322 regex is impractical. In production, do a light format check (Bean Validation's @Email), then send a confirmation message, the only real proof. Avoid over-strict patterns that reject valid addresses, such as ones with a plus sign or a long TLD.

"😀".length() is 2. Why? How do you count characters correctly?

length() counts UTF-16 code units, and U+1F600 is above U+FFFF, so it needs a surrogate pair. codePointCount(0, s.length()) gives 1. Code points are not user-visible characters either: "é" is 2 code points shown as one letter, and some emoji sequences are many code points joined. To count what a user perceives, use the \X regex (2 matches for an accented letter plus an emoji) or BreakIterator.

How many bytes is "café" in UTF-8? What does getBytes() with no argument do?

5: é takes 2 bytes. In ISO-8859-1 it takes 4, and in UTF_16 10, including the byte order mark. getBytes() uses the default charset: UTF-8 since Java 18, and the platform's setting before. On older JDKs, this is a classic cause of "works on Linux, breaks on Windows". Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8.

Users' names show as "Ã©" on the page. How do you debug it?

"Ã©" is the signature of UTF-8 bytes decoded as Latin-1 or Windows-1252. Follow the data: log the hex of the bytes at each hop. Check the browser's request encoding and Content-Type, servlet filter or Spring's CharacterEncodingFilter, the JDBC connection settings, the column charset (utf8mb4), and the response header. Fix the wrong decode where it occurs. If bad data is already stored, it may be repairable with a re-encode as long as no bytes were replaced, but test it, because a double conversion corrupts good rows.

Why is a char[] preferred to a String for passwords? Is it really safer?

A String cannot be cleared, and it stays in memory until GC, possibly longer if pooled, so a heap dump exposes it. A char[] can be zeroed after use, and does not print its content by accident. But it only reduces exposure: GC can leave copies, and frameworks handle passwords as Strings before your code runs. In web apps, focus on TLS, hashing with BCrypt or Argon2, not logging, and protecting dumps.

Is String a good HashMap key? Why? What about StringBuilder or char[]?

Excellent: immutable, so the hash never changes, and it is cached after the first call, so repeated lookups only compute it once. equals is well defined. StringBuilder and char[] use identity hashing, so an equal-content lookup misses, and they are mutable. Convert to String first.

What does switch on a String do for hash collisions such as "Aa" and "BB"?

The compiler generates a lookupswitch on hashCode(), and each hash bucket holds equals checks for all labels with that hash. Both labels work correctly: a collision only adds one extra comparison.

Can you change a String's content through reflection? Would it be safe?

On modern JDKs, not without --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED, since JDK internals are strongly encapsulated (InaccessibleObjectException). Even if opened, it corrupts the program: pooled literals are shared across all classes, the cached hash becomes stale, and the JIT trusts final fields of String. So the answer is "technically possible with explicit opening, and never appropriate".

What is the maximum length of a String? Of a literal?

The API uses int lengths, so the theoretical maximum is about 231-1 chars; UTF-16 content is limited to about half, because the backing byte[] holds two bytes per char. Available heap and the VM's array limit apply. A literal is limited by the class-file format to 65,535 bytes of modified UTF-8, giving a "constant string too long" compile error. Load large text from a resource file.

Scenario: an app holds many duplicate strings and heap usage is high. What are your options?
  1. Take a heap dump, and check duplicates in Eclipse MAT.
  2. Ask whether the data needs to be strings at all: enums, or IDs as long.
  3. Enable -XX:+UseStringDeduplication with G1. It is a one-line change that shares byte[] arrays in the background. It has a small CPU cost.
  4. Canonicalize in code when parsing: a HashMap or bounded cache, or intern for a small, stable value set.
  5. Do not keep substrings of large documents, or keep parsed fields rather than raw JSON.
Scenario: a service spends a lot of CPU in string handling for log lines. What do you look at?

Profile first, for example with Java Flight Recorder or async-profiler. Common causes: building messages when the level is disabled (use {} placeholders rather than +), String.format on hot paths, replaceAll or split with a regex compiled on each call (use a static final Pattern), += in loops, default-size builders that keep resizing, and serializing whole objects into logs. Fix what the profile shows rather than guessing.

Design: how would you safely truncate a user-entered string to fit a 255-byte database column?

Clarify whether the limit is in bytes or chars. For bytes, encode and cut on a character boundary. A UTF-8 cut must not split a multi-byte sequence, and substring must not split a surrogate pair.

static String truncateUtf8(String s, int maxBytes) {
    CharsetEncoder enc = StandardCharsets.UTF_8.newEncoder();
    ByteBuffer out = ByteBuffer.allocate(maxBytes);
    CharBuffer in = CharBuffer.wrap(s);
    enc.encode(in, out, true);        // stops at the last complete character that fits
    return s.substring(0, in.position());
}

The encoder writes only whole characters, so the buffer positions identify a safe cut. For user-facing limits, consider cutting at grapheme boundaries with BreakIterator, so an accent does not get detached.

What is wrong here? for (char c : s.toCharArray()) { if (c == '\uD83D') ... }, and how should text be iterated?

It inspects half a surrogate pair. Any logic on individual char values is wrong for code points beyond the Basic Multilingual Plane. Iterate code points instead:

s.codePoints().forEach(cp -> {
    if (Character.isEmoji(cp)) { ... }   // Java 21
});
What is the time complexity of indexOf, contains, substring, equals and hashCode?

substring is O(k), since it copies. equals is O(n) in the worst case, but returns immediately on identity or a length difference. hashCode is O(n) once, then O(1) from the cache. length and charAt are O(1). indexOf(String) and contains use a simple scan with a JVM intrinsic: O(n × m) worst case, but very fast in practice.

Why is string concatenation in SQL dangerous even if you escape quotes yourself?

Hand-written escaping is fragile. It misses encodings, backslash rules that differ between databases, numeric contexts where there are no quotes (WHERE id = 1 OR 1=1), and second-order injection, where stored data is concatenated later. A bind parameter (? in PreparedStatement, :name in JPQL, or a Spring Data method) sends the value separately from the SQL text, so it can never be parsed as SQL. The database can also cache the plan. Identifiers such as column names in ORDER BY cannot be bound, so check them against a whitelist. Watch for concatenation inside @Query(nativeQuery = true) and createNativeQuery as well.

Is URLEncoder.encode the right way to build a URL?

Only for query parameter values, and even then it applies application/x-www-form-urlencoded rules: a space becomes +, not %20. That is wrong inside a path segment, and some servers do not decode + as a space. Always pass StandardCharsets.UTF_8; the overload with no charset is deprecated. To build a whole URI, use UriComponentsBuilder or UriBuilder in Spring, which encode each component by its own rules. Never encode an entire URL string at once, because that also encodes :, / and ?.

What is log injection, and how do you prevent it?

If user input containing \r\n is logged as it is, an attacker can add fake log lines, such as a forged "admin login succeeded", or break log parsers. If the logs are viewed in a web console, the input can also be a stored XSS payload. To prevent it:

  • use parameterized logging (log.info("x={}", v));
  • strip or encode CR/LF and other control characters, or use structured JSON logging, where the encoder escapes them;
  • never log secrets or full tokens;
  • limit the length of logged values.

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228) was a related, more severe case: user text was interpreted by the logger's lookup feature.

Why compare API keys or HMAC signatures with MessageDigest.isEqual instead of equals?

String.equals and Arrays.equals stop at the first mismatch, so a response is slightly faster when more leading characters are wrong. With many measurements, an attacker can use that timing side channel to recover a secret one byte at a time. MessageDigest.isEqual(byte[], byte[]) compares in time that does not depend on where the bytes differ. Even better, store a hash of API keys rather than the raw keys, and compare the hashes.

A user can choose the sort column through ?sort=name. How do you build the query safely?

Bind parameters cannot replace identifiers, so map the input to a known value. Either check it against a Set or Map of allowed columns with a default, or use an enum. In Spring Data, pass a Sort built from the whitelisted property (Sort.by(...) or Pageable), and keep JpaSort.unsafe for trusted expressions only. Never insert the raw parameter into the query text. Validate the sort direction (ASC/DESC) the same way.

enum SortCol { NAME("name"), CREATED("createdAt");
    final String prop; SortCol(String p) { prop = p; } }
Sort s = Sort.by(SortCol.valueOf(param.toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT)).prop);

Exception Handling Core Java

How Java reports and recovers from failures: the Throwable hierarchy, what the compiler enforces, exactly how try/catch/finally executes, resource cleanup, exception design, what exceptions cost, and how to handle them globally.

What an exception is and why the mechanism exists

An exception is an object that describes an abnormal event. When one is thrown, normal execution stops and the JVM searches the current method for a matching handler. If it finds none, it pops the stack frame and searches the caller, and so on. This process is called stack unwinding. If no handler exists, the thread dies and its uncaught-exception handler runs.

The alternative is return codes, as in C. Return codes have three problems: callers can ignore them, they mix error paths with normal logic, and they use up the return value. Exceptions separate the two paths, cannot be silently dropped without writing code to do so, and carry data: a type, a message, a cause and a stack trace.

Internally, javac writes an exception table for each method. Each row says "for bytecode between offsets X and Y, if an exception of type T occurs, jump to offset H". The try block itself generates no instructions, so entering a try block costs nothing. The table is only consulted when something is thrown. You can see it with javap -c MyClass.

The Throwable hierarchy

Checked, unchecked and Error

"Checked" describes a compile-time rule. The JVM does not care: at the bytecode level, any method can throw anything. The compiler enforces the catch-or-declare rule: if code can throw a checked exception, the method must catch it or list it in throws.

CheckedUnchecked (RuntimeException)Error
ParentException, excluding RuntimeExceptionRuntimeExceptionError
Compiler enforces handlingYesNoNo
Typical meaningA failure outside the program's control that a caller might recover fromA programming bug or broken preconditionThe JVM or runtime environment is in serious trouble
ExamplesIOException, SQLException, InterruptedExceptionNullPointerException, IllegalArgumentExceptionOutOfMemoryError, StackOverflowError
Should you catch it?When you can act on it, otherwise declare or wrap itRarely, usually only at a boundaryAlmost never, except to log and shut down cleanly
Gotcha: The compiler only checks a catch for a checked type if the try body can actually throw it. try { int x = 1; } catch (IOException e) {} fails with "exception IOException is never thrown in body of corresponding try statement". catch (Exception e) compiles there, because Exception also covers unchecked exceptions.

The design debate. Checked exceptions force callers to think about failure, but they also leak implementation details through signatures and do not work well with lambdas.
