Kotlin, Scala and C# have no checked exceptions. Most modern frameworks, including Spring, wrap them into unchecked exceptions: JdbcTemplate turns SQLException into DataAccessException. A reasonable rule from Effective Java: use checked exceptions for recoverable conditions when the caller can realistically do something, and runtime exceptions for programming errors.

try / catch / finally execution

Rules:

  • A try needs at least one catch, a finally, or a resource list.
  • Catch clauses are checked top to bottom, and the first match wins. Only one catch runs.
  • A subclass must appear before its superclass. Otherwise you get "exception IOException has already been caught".
  • finally runs whether the try completes normally, returns, breaks, continues or throws, and whether or not a catch matched.
  • finally does not run if the JVM stops first: System.exit(), Runtime.halt(), a crash, a killed process or power loss. It also does not run while a try block is stuck forever in an infinite loop or a deadlock. Daemon threads are abandoned at JVM exit, so their finally blocks may never run.

How finally is compiled

There is no bytecode instruction for "finally". Modern javac copies the finally code onto each exit path: once after the normal path, once at the end of each catch, and once in a catch-any handler that rethrows. This explains the classic return trap. return x; first copies x into a hidden local variable, then the inlined finally code runs, then the method returns the hidden copy.

The return traps (all verified on Java 21)

static int a() { int x = 1; try { return x; } finally { x = 2; } }
// returns 1: the value was copied before finally ran

static StringBuilder b() {
  StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder("a");
  try { return s; } finally { s.append("b"); }
}
// returns "ab": the reference was copied, but it is the same object

static int c() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
// returns 2: finally's return replaces the pending one

static int d() { try { throw new RuntimeException("x"); } finally { return 3; } }
// returns 3: the exception disappears completely
Gotcha: Never use return, break, continue or throw inside finally. All of them discard a pending exception silently. javac -Xlint:finally warns about this ("finally clause cannot complete normally").

An exception thrown from finally also replaces the original one, and unlike try-with-resources, the original is not attached as suppressed. It is lost:

try {
  try { throw new IllegalStateException("try"); }
  finally { throw new IllegalArgumentException("fin"); }
} catch (RuntimeException r) {
  System.out.println(r.getMessage() + " supp=" + r.getSuppressed().length);
}
// prints: fin supp=0

Multi-catch and precise rethrow (Java 7)

Multi-catch handles several unrelated types with one block, which removes duplication:

try {
  callService();
} catch (TimeoutException | ConnectException e) {
  retry(e);
}
  • The alternatives cannot be related by inheritance. FileNotFoundException | IOException fails with "Alternatives in a multi-catch statement cannot be related by subclassing", because the subclass is redundant.
  • The parameter is implicitly final. You cannot assign to e.
  • The static type of e is the least upper bound of the alternatives (their closest common superclass), so you can only call methods from that type.
  • The compiler generates one handler with multiple exception table rows, so the bytecode is smaller than duplicated catches.

Precise rethrow is the related feature. If a catch parameter is effectively final, the compiler tracks what the try body can actually throw:

void save() throws IOException {         // no "throws Exception" needed
  try {
    write();                             // only throws IOException
  } catch (Exception e) {
    log.warn("failed", e);
    throw e;                             // compiler knows: IOException or unchecked
  }
}

If you reassign e first, this analysis is switched off and you get "unreported exception Exception".

Since Java 22 you can use the unnamed variable _ when the exception object is not needed: catch (NumberFormatException _) { return 0; }.

try-with-resources and suppressed exceptions

Before Java 7, closing a resource correctly took nested try/finally blocks, and a failure in close() could hide the real error. Try-with-resources (TWR) fixes both problems. Any object implementing AutoCloseable can be declared in the parentheses. It is closed automatically, in reverse order of creation.

try (var in = Files.newInputStream(src);
     var out = Files.newOutputStream(dst)) {
  in.transferTo(out);
}                                  // out closes first, then in

Since Java 9 you can also list an existing variable if it is final or effectively final: try (conn) { … }.

What the compiler generates

// try (R r = open()) { body } becomes approximately:
R r = open();
Throwable primary = null;
try {
  body
} catch (Throwable t) {
  primary = t;
  throw t;
} finally {
  if (r != null) {
    if (primary != null) {
      try { r.close(); } catch (Throwable s) { primary.addSuppressed(s); }
    } else {
      r.close();
    }
  }
}

Three consequences follow. A null resource is allowed; close() is simply skipped. If the body throws and close() also throws, the body's exception stays primary and the close failure is attached as suppressed. If only close() throws, its exception propagates normally.

Order of events

Resources close before any catch or finally attached to the same try statement runs:

class R implements AutoCloseable {
  String n;
  R(String n) { this.n = n; System.out.println("open " + n); }
  public void close() {
    System.out.println("close " + n);
    throw new IllegalStateException("close-" + n);
  }
}

try (R a = new R("A"); R b = new R("B")) {
  System.out.println("body");
  throw new RuntimeException("body-ex");
} catch (Exception x) {
  System.out.println("caught " + x.getMessage());
  for (Throwable s : x.getSuppressed())
    System.out.println(" suppressed " + s.getMessage());
} finally {
  System.out.println("finally");
}
open A
open B
body
close B
close A
caught body-ex
 suppressed close-B
 suppressed close-A
finally

If the second resource's constructor throws, the first one is still closed, and the second has nothing to close. If new BufferedReader(new FileReader(f)) is written as one resource and the outer constructor fails, the inner stream leaks. In practice BufferedReader rarely fails, but with a decorator that might, declare each layer as its own resource.

AutoCloseable vs Closeable

AutoCloseable (Java 7)Closeable (Java 5)
Packagejava.langjava.io, extends AutoCloseable
close() throwsExceptionIOException
Idempotent?Recommended, not requiredRequired: a second close must have no effect

When you write your own resource, override close() with the narrowest exception possible, ideally none, so that callers need no catch. Good uses go beyond I/O: a lock wrapper, a span in tracing, or restoring a thread-local value.

Gotcha: Streams from Files.lines(), Files.list() and Files.walk() hold an open file handle, so they must be used in try-with-resources. An ExecutorService is AutoCloseable since Java 19, and its close() waits for submitted tasks.

throw vs throws

throwthrows
What it isA statement that throws one exception object nowA clause in a method signature that declares possible exceptions
WhereInside a method bodyAfter the parameter list
Followed byAn instance: throw new X()One or more class names

Code directly after throw is unreachable and does not compile. throw null; compiles, and at runtime throws NullPointerException. A method may declare throws for something it does not actually throw, which is useful when you want subclasses to be able to throw it.

Custom exceptions

Create one when callers need to react to the condition differently, or when you need to carry structured data. Otherwise reuse a standard type: IllegalArgumentException, IllegalStateException, UnsupportedOperationException, NoSuchElementException.

public class PaymentDeclinedException extends RuntimeException {
  private final String orderId;
  private final String declineCode;

  public PaymentDeclinedException(String orderId, String declineCode, Throwable cause) {
    super("Payment declined for order " + orderId + ": " + declineCode, cause);
    this.orderId = orderId;
    this.declineCode = declineCode;
  }
  public String orderId() { return orderId; }
  public String declineCode() { return declineCode; }
}
  • Name it with the suffix Exception.
  • Always offer a constructor that accepts a cause, so the chain is kept.
  • Keep fields final and immutable. An exception can be logged or read long after it was thrown, and possibly on another thread.
  • Put identifying data in fields as well as the message, so handlers do not have to parse strings.
  • Do not put secrets or personal data in messages, because they end up in logs.
  • A generic class cannot extend Throwable ("a generic class may not extend java.lang.Throwable"). catch needs a runtime type, and generics are erased.
  • Exceptions are Serializable, because Throwable is. Non-serializable fields should be transient if the exception crosses a serialization boundary.

Exception chaining and translation

Each layer should throw exceptions that fit its own abstraction. A service caller should not have to know about SQLException. Exception translation catches the low-level exception and throws a higher-level one. Chaining keeps the original as the cause, so no diagnostic information is lost.

try {
  repository.save(order);
} catch (SQLException e) {
  throw new OrderPersistenceException("Could not save order " + order.id(), e);  // keep e
}
  • Set the cause with a constructor, or with initCause() when a class has no such constructor (some older exceptions).
  • initCause can only be called once. If a cause was already given to a constructor, it throws IllegalStateException: Can't overwrite cause with java.lang.Exception.
  • new RuntimeException(cause) sets the message to cause.toString(), for example java.io.IOException: io.
  • addSuppressed(this) throws IllegalArgumentException: Self-suppression not permitted.
Gotcha: throw new ServiceException(e.getMessage()); looks like chaining but discards the original stack trace. Pass e itself.

Overriding and exceptions

A subclass must be usable wherever its parent is (the Liskov Substitution Principle). A caller holding a Parent reference only handles what Parent.m() declares, so an override cannot add new checked exceptions.

Parent method declaresOverride may declareOverride may not declare
throws IOExceptionNothing, IOException, a subclass such as FileNotFoundException, any unchecked exceptionException, SQLException or any other broader or unrelated checked exception
NothingAny unchecked exceptionAny checked exception

Constructors follow the opposite rule. A constructor is not overridden, and it calls the superclass constructor. If Parent() declares throws IOException, then Child() must declare IOException or a superclass of it, and it may add more. It cannot catch the exception, because super() must be the first statement, or at least outside a try block. Java 25's flexible constructor bodies (JEP 513) let statements appear before super(…), but you still cannot wrap the call in a try.

When a class implements two interfaces with the same method, the implementation can only throw what is allowed by both (the intersection).

Reading a stack trace

java.lang.IllegalStateException: save failed
	at Ex.lvl2(Ex.java:55)
	at Ex.trace(Ex.java:56)
	at Ex.main(Ex.java:60)
Caused by: java.io.IOException: disk full
	at Ex.lvl1(Ex.java:54)
	... 3 more
  • The first line is the exception's type and message. The top frame is where the exception object was created (where fillInStackTrace ran), which is not always where it was thrown.
  • Frames read bottom-up as the call order: main called trace, which called lvl2.
  • Caused by: is the wrapped exception. The root cause is the last "Caused by". Read that first.
  • ... 3 more means the remaining 3 frames are the same as in the enclosing trace, so they are left out. Here they are lvl2, trace and main.
  • Suppressed exceptions appear indented under Suppressed:.

In code: e.getStackTrace() returns a StackTraceElement[]; StackWalker (Java 9) walks the current stack lazily without creating an exception, for example to find the caller.

Common exceptions

ExceptionTypical triggerMessage on Java 21 / notes
NullPointerExceptionCalling a method, reading a field or indexing an array through null; unboxing null; synchronized(null); throw nullHelpful NPE message, see below
ClassCastExceptionA cast to an incompatible type, often after heap pollution from raw typesclass java.lang.String cannot be cast to class java.lang.Integer (…)
NumberFormatExceptionInteger.parseInt("12a"), extends IllegalArgumentExceptionFor input string: "12a". For null: Cannot parse null string
ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsExceptiona[2] on a length-2 arrayIndex 2 out of bounds for length 2
StringIndexOutOfBoundsExceptionBad substring or charAtRange [5, 3) out of bounds for length 3
ArithmeticExceptionInteger division or modulo by zero/ by zero. Floating point gives Infinity or NaN, with no exception
ArrayStoreExceptionStoring the wrong type through a covariant array referencejava.lang.Integer
NegativeArraySizeExceptionnew int[-1]-1
ConcurrentModificationExceptionStructural change during fail-fast iteration, even in a single threadUsually no message; see Collections Deep Dive
UnsupportedOperationExceptionList.of(1).add(2); Arrays.asList(..).add(..)Message is null
NoSuchElementExceptioniterator.next() at the end; Optional.empty().get()No value present for Optional
IllegalArgumentExceptionA bad method argument; Enum.valueOf with an unknown nameNo enum constant java.lang.Thread.State.X
IllegalStateExceptionAn object is in the wrong state for the call; Iterator.remove() twiceMessage depends on the API
IllegalMonitorStateExceptionwait() or notify() without holding the monitorcurrent thread is not owner
IllegalThreadStateExceptionCalling start() twice on one threadExtends IllegalArgumentException
ClassNotFoundException (checked)Class.forName("…") and the class is missing at runtimeA dynamic lookup failed
NoClassDefFoundErrorThe class existed at compile time but cannot be loaded now, or its static initializer failed earlierCould not initialize class X
ExceptionInInitializerErrorAn exception escaped a static initializerWraps the original as its cause
StackOverflowErrorRunaway recursion; a thread stack limit reachedTune with -Xss, but fix the recursion first
InterruptedException (checked)Another thread interrupted a blocking callRestore the flag, see below

Helpful NullPointerException messages (JEP 358)

Added in Java 14 and enabled by default since Java 15. The JVM analyses the bytecode at the failing instruction and describes which expression was null. Before this, the message was simply null, and with a chain like a.b.c.d you could not tell which link failed.

a.b.c                  // Cannot read field "c" because "a.b" is null
s.length()             // Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "s" is null
arr[0] = 1             // Cannot store to int array because "arr" is null
int q = in;            // Cannot invoke "java.lang.Integer.intValue()" because "in" is null
synchronized (s) {}    // Cannot enter synchronized block because "s" is null

Local variable names only appear if the class was compiled with -g (Maven and Gradle do this by default). Without it, the message says "<local1>". Field names and method names always appear. The flag is -XX:±ShowCodeDetailsInExceptionMessages. The text is computed lazily when getMessage() is called, so an NPE you never inspect pays nothing for it. The message only appears for NPEs raised by the JVM, not for ones created with new NullPointerException().

Unboxing is a common hidden source: Integer r = flag ? nullableInteger : 0; throws NPE when flag is true. One branch is int, so the expression's type is int, and the Integer gets unboxed.

OutOfMemoryError variants

The message tells you which memory ran out, and each has a different fix.

MessageMeaningWhere to look
Java heap spaceAn object could not fit on the heapHeap dump (-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError), Eclipse MAT; a leak or too small an -Xmx
GC overhead limit exceededThe collector spends nearly all its time in GC and frees very littleSame as heap space. Classically seen with the Parallel collector
MetaspaceClass metadata space is fullClassloader leaks, heavy runtime class generation; -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize
Compressed class spaceThe compressed class pointer region is full-XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize, same causes as Metaspace
Direct buffer memoryByteBuffer.allocateDirect exceeded its limit-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; Netty and NIO buffers not released
unable to create native threadThe OS refused a new threadUnbounded thread creation, ulimit, container limits. It is not a heap problem
Requested array size exceeds VM limitThe array is larger than the JVM's maximum array lengthnew int[Integer.MAX_VALUE] gives this even with free heap

Exceptions and threads

An exception only unwinds its own thread's stack. It never crosses to another thread by itself.

// Global fallback for threads that die from an uncaught exception
Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler((t, e) ->
    log.error("Uncaught in " + t.getName(), e));

ExecutorService pool = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();

Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("task"); });
// Nothing is printed. The exception is stored in the Future.
f.get();   // java.util.concurrent.ExecutionException: java.lang.RuntimeException: task

pool.execute(() -> { throw new RuntimeException("exec"); });
// Reaches the uncaught-exception handler, and that worker thread dies and is replaced
Gotcha: submit() plus never calling get() means failures vanish silently. This is one of the most common production bugs with thread pools.

CompletableFuture wraps too: join() throws CompletionException, and get() throws ExecutionException. In a dependent stage such as exceptionally, the argument is a CompletionException wrapping the original, so unwrap with getCause().

InterruptedException

Thread interruption is a polite request to stop. When a blocking method throws InterruptedException, it clears the thread's interrupt flag. If you cannot rethrow it, restore the flag so that code higher up can see it:

try {
  queue.take();
} catch (InterruptedException e) {
  Thread.currentThread().interrupt();     // restore the flag
  return;                                 // and stop working
}

Exceptions and lambdas

Standard functional interfaces such as Function declare no checked exceptions, so a lambda calling Files.readString(path) does not compile. Options:

@FunctionalInterface
interface ThrowingFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws Exception; }

static <T, R> Function<T, R> unchecked(ThrowingFunction<T, R> f) {
  return t -> {
    try { return f.apply(t); }
    catch (RuntimeException e) { throw e; }
    catch (Exception e) { throw new RuntimeException(e); }
  };
}

List<String> texts = paths.stream().map(unchecked(Files::readString)).toList();

Use UncheckedIOException for I/O failures. Files.lines() itself uses it when a read fails partway through a stream.

Performance of exceptions

The expensive part of an exception is usually filling in the stack trace at construction: Throwable's constructor calls fillInStackTrace(), a native method that walks the thread's stack. The cost grows with stack depth. Unwinding through many frames at throw time costs extra, particularly because exception paths are rarely optimized by the JIT. A try block with no throw costs essentially nothing.

A rough run on Java 21, throwing through 50 frames, gave about 75 ns for the no-exception path, about 2.5 µs for a throw without a stack trace, and about 6 µs with a stack trace. That was a quick loop rather than a benchmark, so treat it only as a sense of scale; use JMH for real measurement. Exceptions are fine for exceptional events and bad as normal control flow in hot loops.

// A cheap exception: disable the stack trace and suppression
class ControlFlowSignal extends RuntimeException {
  ControlFlowSignal(String msg) {
    super(msg, null, false, false);  // cause, enableSuppression, writableStackTrace
  }
}

Fast throw. After the C2 JIT compiler sees the same implicit exception (NPE, ArithmeticException, ArrayIndexOutOfBounds, ClassCast, ArrayStore) many times at one location, it may switch to a preallocated exception with no stack trace and no message. This is why logs sometimes show java.lang.NullPointerException with nothing else after hours of uptime. Look further back in the logs for the first occurrences, or start the JVM with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow. In a test loop of 2 million NPEs on Java 21, the late exceptions had an empty stack trace and a null message; with that flag, they kept both.

Global handling

Do not write try/catch in every method. Let exceptions propagate to one boundary that knows what to do.

  • Plain threads: Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler, or a per-thread setUncaughtExceptionHandler. Thread pool factories can set this.
  • Servlet: a filter wrapping the chain, or error-page mappings.
  • Spring MVC: @RestControllerAdvice with @ExceptionHandler methods maps exceptions to HTTP responses. Spring 6 added ProblemDetail, which implements the RFC 9457 error format (formerly RFC 7807).
  • Spring transactions: by default @Transactional rolls back on RuntimeException and Error and commits on checked exceptions. Change it with rollbackFor. Catching an exception inside the method also prevents rollback.
  • Kafka, schedulers, messaging: each framework has its own error handler. Unhandled errors there often mean silent retries or a stopped job.
@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
  ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, e.getMessage());
  }
  @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)
  ProblemDetail unexpected(Exception e) {
    log.error("Unhandled", e);                         // full detail goes to logs
    return ProblemDetail.forStatus(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR);  // none to clients
  }
}

Best practices

  • Fail fast. Validate at the start of a method with Objects.requireNonNull(x, "x") or Objects.checkIndex (Java 9), so the error appears near its cause.
  • Catch the most specific type you can handle. Avoid catch (Exception e) except at a boundary, and avoid catch (Throwable t) almost always, as it also catches OutOfMemoryError.
  • Never swallow. An empty catch hides bugs. If ignoring is correct, say why in a comment and name the variable ignored.
  • Log or rethrow, not both. Doing both produces the same stack trace several times per failure. Log once, at the boundary that handles it.
  • Pass the exception as the logger's last argument: log.error("Failed for {}", id, e). log.error(e.getMessage()) loses the stack trace, and e.printStackTrace() bypasses the logging system.
  • Do not use exceptions for flow control. Prefer Optional, a hasNext-style check or a boolean tryX method for expected outcomes.
  • Clean up with try-with-resources, not hand-written finally blocks.
  • Keep state consistent after a failure. Validate before changing anything, or work on a copy (failure atomicity).
  • Write useful messages with the failing values: "Order 42 not found" rather than "Not found".
  • Document with @throws in Javadoc, including important unchecked ones.

Handling Failures in CompletableFuture

An async pipeline passes a failure down the chain, skipping the normal stages, until a recovery stage handles it. There are three operators, and interviewers ask about the differences:

MethodCalled whenCan change the result?Typical use
exceptionally(ex -> v)Only on failureYes: replaces it with a fallback valueFallback or default
handle((v, ex) -> r)AlwaysYes: maps both success and failureConvert to a result object
whenComplete((v, ex) -> {})AlwaysNo: passes the original outcome onLogging, metrics, cleanup
exceptionallyCompose(ex -> cf) (Java 12)Only on failureYes, with another async callFall back to a second service
CompletableFuture<Price> price = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> pricing.fetch(sku), ioPool)          // may throw
        .orTimeout(2, TimeUnit.SECONDS)                         // Java 9: fail with TimeoutException
        .whenComplete((p, ex) -> { if (ex != null) log.warn("pricing failed", ex); })
        .exceptionally(ex -> {
            Throwable cause = (ex instanceof CompletionException ce) ? ce.getCause() : ex;  // unwrap
            if (cause instanceof TimeoutException) return Price.cached(sku);
            throw new CompletionException(cause);                // not recoverable: rethrow
        });

price.join();   // throws unchecked CompletionException
price.get();    // throws checked ExecutionException (getCause() holds the original)
💡 A failed CompletableFuture that nobody calls join/get on, and that has no handler, fails silently. Always end a fire-and-forget chain with whenComplete or exceptionally that logs. Also, cancel(true) does not interrupt the running task.

Errors as Values: Sealed Result Types

Some failures are expected business outcomes, such as "card declined" or "insufficient stock". Modelling them as return values makes the caller handle every case, and the compiler checks this through an exhaustive switch. Keep exceptions for unexpected failures, such as an unreachable database or a bug.

sealed interface PaymentResult permits Approved, Declined, NeedsVerification {}
record Approved(String txId) implements PaymentResult {}
record Declined(String reason) implements PaymentResult {}
record NeedsVerification(URI redirect) implements PaymentResult {}

PaymentResult r = gateway.charge(card, amount);
String msg = switch (r) {                        // no default: adding a new outcome breaks the build
    case Approved a          -> "Paid: " + a.txId();
    case Declined d          -> "Declined: " + d.reason();
    case NeedsVerification v -> "Redirect to " + v.redirect();
};

Retrying Transient Failures

Before retrying, classify the failure. Transient failures (timeouts, connection resets, HTTP 503/429, deadlock or lock-timeout errors) may succeed on a later attempt. Permanent failures (validation errors, 400/404, auth failures, a NullPointerException) will fail every time.

  • Retry only transient failures, and only idempotent operations. Otherwise use an idempotency key, so a retried payment is not charged twice.
  • Use exponential backoff with jitter and a maximum number of attempts. Immediate retries from many clients make an outage worse (a retry storm).
  • Retry at one layer only. If three layers each retry 3 times, you get 27 calls.
  • Combine retries with a timeout and a circuit breaker, for example Resilience4j @Retry/@CircuitBreaker or Spring Retry @Retryable. Keep retries outside the @Transactional boundary, so each attempt runs in a new transaction.

Interview Questions — Exception Handling

What is the difference between Exception and Error? Can you catch an Error?

Both extend Throwable. Exception represents conditions an application might handle. Error represents serious problems in the JVM or environment, such as OutOfMemoryError.

You can technically catch an Error: catch (StackOverflowError e) compiles and works. You usually should not, because the JVM may be in a damaged state. The legitimate uses are logging and clean shutdown at a top-level boundary. Frameworks sometimes catch LinkageError to handle optional dependencies.

Is Throwable checked or unchecked? And Exception?

Both are checked. throw new Exception() and throw new Throwable() must be caught or declared. Only RuntimeException, Error and their subclasses are unchecked.

Does finally always run? Name every case where it does not.

It runs on normal completion, return, break, continue and any exception. It does not run when:

  • System.exit() or Runtime.halt() is called in the try or catch.
  • The JVM crashes, the process is killed with kill -9, or the machine loses power.
  • The try block never ends (an infinite loop or a deadlock).
  • The thread is a daemon thread and the JVM exits while it is in the try block.

Verified: with try { println("before"); System.exit(0); } finally { println("after"); }, only before prints.

Predict the output. 
static int f() {
  int x = 1;
  try { return x; }
  finally { x = 2; }
}
System.out.println(f());

Output: 1. return x saves the value of x into a temporary slot, then finally runs. Changing the local x does not affect the saved copy.

Predict the output. 
static StringBuilder f() {
  StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder("a");
  try { return s; }
  finally { s.append("b"); }
}
System.out.println(f());

Output: ab. The saved value is the reference. Finally mutates the same object. Had finally done s = new StringBuilder("z"), the result would still be a.

Predict the result. 
static int f() {
  try { throw new RuntimeException("x"); }
  finally { return 3; }
}
System.out.println(f());

Output: 3. The exception is discarded with no trace, because a return in finally ends the method normally and drops whatever was pending. This compiles (with a lint warning under -Xlint:finally).

Predict the output. 
StringBuilder s = new StringBuilder();
try {
  s.append("t");
  throw new RuntimeException();
} catch (RuntimeException e) {
  s.append("c");
  try { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
  catch (IllegalStateException ie) { s.append("i"); }
  finally { s.append("f1"); }
} finally {
  s.append("f2");
}
System.out.println(s);

Output: tcif1f2. A try statement can be nested inside a catch block, and it works as usual. The inner finally runs first, then the outer one.

Predict the result. 
static int f() {
  int n = 0;
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try {
      if (i == 1) continue;
      n += 10;
    } finally { n += 1; }
  }
  return n;
}

Returns 23. continue at i = 1 skips n += 10, but finally still runs. Iterations add 11, 1 and 11.

Predict the output. 
static int f() {
  for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) {
    try { throw new RuntimeException(); }
    finally { break; }
  }
  return 7;
}
System.out.println(f());

Output: 7. break in finally abandons the pending exception, the same as return does. No exception reaches the caller.

Will this compile? 
try {
  throw new IOException();
} catch (Exception e) {
} catch (IOException e) {
}

No. error: exception IOException has already been caught. The first catch makes the second unreachable. Swap the order, placing the subclass first.

Will this compile: int b() { try { throw new RuntimeException(); } finally { } int x = 1; }?

No. int x = 1 is an "unreachable statement", because the try statement can never complete normally. The same happens for any code directly after a throw statement.

Explain try-with-resources. In what order are resources closed, and what are suppressed exceptions?

Resources declared in the parentheses must implement AutoCloseable. They are closed automatically in reverse order, before any catch or finally of that statement runs.

If both the body and close() throw, the body's exception propagates, and each close failure is attached using addSuppressed. Read them with getSuppressed(). Before Java 7, hand-written finally blocks would let the close failure replace the real error. Printed stack traces show them under Suppressed:.

What happens if the resource is null, or the second resource's constructor throws?

A null resource is allowed: the body runs and close() is skipped. If the second resource's initializer throws, the body never runs, the first resource is closed, and the exception goes to the catch. Verified output: open A, close A, caught ctor.

Does the resource close before or after catch runs? Why does that matter?

Before. So in a catch block attached to the TWR, the resource is already closed. For example, you cannot call connection.rollback() from that catch, because the connection declared in the same statement is gone. Nest a try inside the body to roll back, or declare the connection in an outer try.

try (Connection c = ds.getConnection()) {
  c.setAutoCommit(false);
  try {
    work(c);
    c.commit();
  } catch (SQLException e) {
    c.rollback();
    throw e;
  }
}
Closeable vs AutoCloseable?

AutoCloseable.close() throws Exception, and its contract only recommends idempotence. Closeable extends it, narrows the exception to IOException, and requires idempotence: a second call must have no effect. TWR accepts both. Choose AutoCloseable for non-I/O resources and narrow the throws clause in your implementation.

What rules apply to multi-catch?

Alternatives must not be subclasses of each other, the parameter is implicitly final, and its type is the least upper bound of the alternatives. Available since Java 7.

Does this compile? What is "precise rethrow"? 
void m() throws IOException {
  try { read(); }                 // read() throws IOException
  catch (Exception e) { throw e; }
}

Yes, since Java 7. If e is effectively final, the compiler rethrows only what the try body can throw: IOException or unchecked exceptions. If you add e = new Exception(); before the throw, the analysis stops and it fails with "unreported exception Exception; must be caught or declared to be thrown".

What are the rules for exceptions when overriding a method?

An override may declare the same checked exceptions, narrower ones, or none. It cannot add new or broader checked exceptions. Any unchecked exception is always allowed. The reason is substitutability: code written against the parent's signature only handles what the parent declared.

Constructors differ. A subclass constructor must declare at least what the super(…) constructor it calls declares, since it cannot catch it, and it can add more.

What is the difference between ClassNotFoundException and NoClassDefFoundError?
ClassNotFoundExceptionNoClassDefFoundError
TypeChecked exceptionError (LinkageError)
WhenExplicit dynamic loading fails: Class.forName, loadClassThe class was there at compile time, but linking it at runtime fails
Common causesA missing driver JAR, a typo in the nameA missing transitive JAR, a version conflict, or a static initializer that failed earlier
Predict what happens when a static initializer throws, and the class is used twice. 
class Boom { static int v = 1 / 0; static void hi() {} }
for (int i = 0; i < 2; i++) {
  try { Boom.hi(); }
  catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println(t); }
}
java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Boom

The first use runs the initializer; the ArithmeticException is wrapped in ExceptionInInitializerError. The class is then permanently marked as erroneous in that class loader, so every later use gets NoClassDefFoundError. This is a classic production trap: the logs are full of NoClassDefFoundError, and the real cause is one line near startup. On recent JDKs the later error's cause points to the original failure.

What does throw null; do?

It compiles, since null can be typed as any reference type, and throws NullPointerException at runtime. Likewise, if a variable of exception type holds null, throw e throws NPE.

Why does this throw NPE? 
Integer nul = null;
boolean flag = true;
Integer r = flag ? nul : 0;

The operands are Integer and int, so numeric promotion makes the whole conditional type int. The compiler unboxes nul with intValue(), then reboxes the result for assignment. Fix: Integer r = flag ? nul : Integer.valueOf(0);. The same trap appears with int total = map.get(key); when the key is missing.

What are helpful NPE messages? When will a name appear as <local1>?

Since Java 15 (by default), the JVM explains which expression was null by analysing the bytecode, such as Cannot read field "c" because "a.b" is null. Local variable names are only available when compiled with -g; otherwise you see "<local1>". Verified: same code without -g printed Cannot invoke "String.length()" because "<local1>" is null.

A production log shows java.lang.NullPointerException with no stack trace. Why?

Most likely the JIT's fast-throw optimization (-XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow, on by default). After an implicit exception has occurred many times at one site, compiled code throws a preallocated instance with no trace. Search earlier in the logs for the first occurrences, which do have traces, or run with -XX:-OmitStackTraceInFastThrow. Another cause: code that logs only e.toString().

Can you recover from StackOverflowError or OutOfMemoryError?

The JVM throws them as ordinary objects, and a catch at a shallow frame works. After a StackOverflowError, unwinding frees the stack, so simple cases can continue. But the failure could have happened anywhere, including in the middle of a class initializer or while holding a half-updated lock-protected state, so data may be inconsistent.

For OutOfMemoryError, a failed huge allocation (a single massive array) is often survivable, but a heap exhausted by a leak is not. Most production systems configure -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError or -XX:+CrashOnOutOfMemoryError plus a heap dump, and let the orchestrator restart the instance.

What is the problem with catching Throwable or Exception?

catch (Exception e) also catches every RuntimeException, so bugs (NPEs) get treated the same as expected failures. It may also hide InterruptedException, losing the interrupt signal. catch (Throwable t) also catches Errors. Both are appropriate only at top-level boundaries: a request handler, a worker loop, a scheduled job.

Why should you restore the interrupt flag after catching InterruptedException?

Throwing InterruptedException clears the flag. If you swallow it, the code above you (a thread pool's worker loop or a shutdown process) cannot see that someone asked this thread to stop, so shutdown hangs. Prefer declaring it. Otherwise call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() and exit promptly. Do not just wrap it in a RuntimeException and forget the flag.

What happens to exceptions in ExecutorService.submit vs execute?

submit captures anything thrown into the returned Future; you see it only as an ExecutionException from get(). If nobody calls get(), it disappears. execute lets it reach the thread's uncaught-exception handler, which prints it by default, and the pool replaces the worker.

Fixes: catch and log inside the task, wrap tasks, or override ThreadPoolExecutor.afterExecute.

How can checked exceptions be used inside a stream lambda?

A lambda can only throw what the functional interface method declares, and Function.apply declares nothing. Options: catch inside the lambda and wrap in an unchecked exception (UncheckedIOException for I/O), use a wrapper helper, or use a plain loop if handling per item matters. Failing one element stops the whole stream, so if you want partial success, return a result object per element.

What is a "sneaky throw"? Is it a good idea?

Because generics are erased and the checked rule exists only in the compiler, you can throw a checked exception without declaring it:

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <E extends Throwable> void sneak(Throwable t) throws E { throw (E) t; }

Main.<RuntimeException>sneak(new IOException("io"));

The cast to E is erased and does nothing, and the compiler believes only a RuntimeException can escape. Lombok's @SneakyThrows does a similar thing. The catch is that callers cannot catch it by name: catch (IOException e) does not compile, because the compiler sees nothing throwing it. Avoid this in shared APIs.

Why does this finally-based cleanup lose the original error, and how do you fix it? 
Reader r = open();
try { r.read(); }
finally { r.close(); }   // close() can throw too

If read() throws and close() throws too, the close exception replaces the read exception, and the real error is lost. Replace this with try-with-resources, which keeps the read exception and attaches the close failure as suppressed.

How expensive are exceptions? When should you disable stack traces?

A try block costs nothing unless something is thrown. A throw costs microseconds, mostly from fillInStackTrace walking the stack, and it scales with depth. Disable with the protected constructor super(msg, null, false, false) for high-frequency signalling exceptions, for example in parsers or protocol code where the stack is useless. Reusing a static preallocated exception is also possible, but the trace would be wrong or empty, and it must be immutable.

In ordinary business code, exceptions on real failures are not a performance concern. Thousands per second on a hot path are.

When should you use a checked vs an unchecked custom exception?

Ask whether the immediate caller can reasonably recover. If yes, and the case is part of the method's contract (insufficient funds, file not present), a checked exception forces it to be handled. If nearly all callers would just wrap or rethrow it, make it unchecked. Most modern enterprise Java uses unchecked exceptions plus a global handler, because checked exceptions pollute every layer's signature and do not work well with lambdas. An alternative is a sealed result type, so that a failed outcome becomes a normal return value.

Why log only once? What goes wrong with log-and-rethrow?

If each layer logs and rethrows, one failure produces several identical stack traces, which inflates log volume and misleads anyone counting errors or alerting on them. Either handle it (and log there) or propagate it (perhaps with added context by wrapping). The boundary handler logs the full chain once.

Design question: how would you structure error handling for a layered REST API?
  1. Define a small hierarchy: a base ApplicationException with an error code, and subclasses for categories such as not found, conflict, validation and upstream failure.
  2. Repositories let Spring translate persistence errors to DataAccessException. Services translate these into domain exceptions only where the meaning changes.
  3. Controllers have no try/catch. One @RestControllerAdvice maps each category to an HTTP status and a ProblemDetail body.
  4. The catch-all handler logs at ERROR with a correlation ID and returns a generic 500. Never leak stack traces or SQL to clients.
  5. Client errors (4xx) are logged at INFO or WARN so that they do not trigger alerts.
  6. Retries apply only to transient failures, with idempotency guaranteed, and transaction rollback is checked: any checked exception needs rollbackFor.
Scenario: a @Transactional method threw an exception but the data was still committed. Why?

Likely causes, most common first:

  1. It was a checked exception. The default rollback rule covers only RuntimeException and Error. Add rollbackFor = Exception.class.
  2. The exception was caught inside the transactional method and not rethrown, so the proxy never saw it.
  3. The method was called via self-invocation (this.save()), bypassing the proxy, so there was no transaction at all.
  4. The method is private or not reachable through the proxy.
Scenario: a scheduled background job silently stopped running after an exception. Why, and how do you fix it?

Scheduled tasks are a classic: ScheduledExecutorService.scheduleAtFixedRate stops all future runs if one run throws, and the exception stays in the returned future. Check whether the task body has a catch-all with logging. In the same way, check any CompletableFuture chain without exceptionally or whenComplete, and submit without get. Add a catch for Exception at the top of the task, log it, and let the schedule continue.

Why can a ConcurrentModificationException happen with just one thread?

The name is misleading. It means a collection was structurally changed during iteration by something other than the iterator. Calling list.remove(x) in a for-each loop over list does this on a single thread. Use removeIf or iterator.remove(). The Collections Deep Dive section explains the modCount mechanism.

What is wrong with this code? 
try {
  process(order);
} catch (Exception e) {
  throw new ServiceException("Failed: " + e.getMessage());
}

It drops the cause, so the original stack trace and exception type are gone. Pass e as the cause. It also catches all exceptions, including programming bugs, and turns them into a generic one. Catch narrower types if the mapping should differ.

What does e.printStackTrace() do wrong in production code?

It writes to System.err, bypassing your logging system: no levels, timestamps, correlation IDs or structured format, and it may not be collected by the log shipper. Use log.error("context", e).

Why can't a generic class extend Throwable, and can a method use throws T?

Catch clauses select a handler at runtime by class. catch (MyEx<String> e) and catch (MyEx<Integer> e) would be the same class after erasure, so the language forbids generic Throwable subclasses. You also cannot catch (T e) for a type variable.

You can use a type variable in a throws clause, as in Optional.orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) throws X. There the compiler knows the actual type at each call site.

What is MatchException?

Added in Java 21 along with pattern matching for switch. It is a RuntimeException thrown when an exhaustive switch over a sealed hierarchy or enum, compiled without a default, meets a case that did not exist at compile time (for example, a new subclass added and compiled separately), or when a record accessor throws during pattern matching. It tells you that the code is out of step, instead of silently doing nothing.

Does a thread's death from an exception affect other threads or the JVM?

No. Only that thread terminates, after its uncaught-exception handler runs. The JVM keeps running while at least one non-daemon thread is alive. If main throws while other non-daemon threads still run, the process keeps going until they finish, and the launcher then exits with code 1 (verified on Java 21: the worker finished its work and the exit code was 1). An exception in any other thread does not change the exit code.

A Spring bean method throws a checked exception it doesn't declare (through a proxy or a sneaky throw). What does the caller see?

With a JDK dynamic proxy, if the invocation handler or interceptor throws a checked exception that the interface method does not declare, the proxy wraps it in java.lang.reflect.UndeclaredThrowableException. The real cause is in getCause(). Reflection works in a similar way: Method.invoke wraps whatever the target method throws in InvocationTargetException. Spring AOP unwraps InvocationTargetException for you. However, if an advice (for example a custom @Around aspect), or a target that sneaky-throws, raises a checked exception that the proxied method does not declare, the caller sees UndeclaredThrowableException. CGLIB proxies behave the same way. Global handlers should therefore unwrap the cause chain instead of matching only the top-level type.

For "not found", should a method return null, return Optional, or throw?
  • Optional: when absence is a normal, expected outcome of a lookup (findByEmail). The caller has to decide what to do. This is the Spring Data convention.
  • Throw: when absence breaks the caller's precondition (getOrder(id) after the id came from a valid link). Throw a domain exception such as OrderNotFoundException and map it to 404 in @RestControllerAdvice.
  • null: avoid it in public APIs. It is acceptable inside private code or performance-critical internals.

A common pattern is repo.findById(id).orElseThrow(() -> new OrderNotFoundException(id)) in the service layer. For collections, return an empty collection, never null or Optional<List>.

What happens if a constructor throws an exception?

The new expression completes abruptly, and the caller gets no reference, so the half-built object becomes garbage. Two problems remain:

  • Resources the constructor already opened (a socket, a file) leak unless the constructor closes them before rethrowing.
  • Escaped this: if the constructor registered this with a listener or a static field before the throw, a partially initialized object is reachable. In the past, a subclass's finalize() could also resurrect such an object (the "finalizer attack").

To defend against this, validate arguments first, before any side effects. Do not publish this from a constructor. Make security-sensitive classes final, or use a static factory that validates before calling a private constructor.

How does structured concurrency (StructuredTaskScope) treat failures in subtasks?

Structured concurrency (a preview API since Java 21, whose shape changed between releases) runs related subtasks inside a scope that cannot outlive the block that opened it. With a "fail on first error" policy, when one subtask throws, the scope cancels the sibling subtasks by interrupting them, and the owner's join step rethrows the failure (wrapped) so it can be handled in one place. With an "any success" policy, the first successful result wins and the remaining subtasks are cancelled. Compared with loose CompletableFutures, this means no orphaned threads keep running after a failure, and thread dumps show the parent-child relationship. Because it is still a preview API, check the exact API for your JDK version.

An @Async method throws. Where does the exception go?

It depends on the return type. If the method returns CompletableFuture or Future, the exception is stored in the future, and the caller sees it on get()/join() or in a recovery stage. If it returns void, there is no caller to receive it, so Spring passes it to an AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler. The default implementation only logs it. Configure your own (by implementing AsyncConfigurer) to add alerting, and remember that @RestControllerAdvice never sees exceptions thrown on another thread.

Generics Core Java

Compile-time type safety for classes and methods: type parameters, bounds, wildcards and PECS, what type erasure really does at runtime, and the traps it leaves behind.

Why generics exist

Before Java 5, collections held plain Object. Every read needed a cast, and a wrong type only failed at runtime, often far from the line that caused it.

List names = new ArrayList();        // Java 1.4 style
names.add("Ana");
names.add(42);                       // compiles
String s = (String) names.get(1);    // ClassCastException at runtime

Generics let a class or method take a type as a parameter. The compiler then checks every use, and inserts the casts for you.

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>();
names.add(42);                       // compile error
String s = names.get(0);             // no cast in source

Three benefits: stronger compile-time checks, no manual casts, and reusable algorithms that work on many types (Collections.sort needs only one implementation).

Terms: in class Box<T>, T is a type parameter. In Box<String>, String is a type argument, and Box<String> is a parameterized type. Box on its own is a raw type. Conventional names: T type, E element, K key, V value, R result, S, U further types.

Generic classes, interfaces and methods

// Generic class
public class Pair<K, V> {
  private final K key;
  private final V value;
  public Pair(K key, V value) { this.key = key; this.value = value; }
  public K key() { return key; }
  public V value() { return value; }
}
// Same idea, shorter (Java 16+)
public record Pair2<K, V>(K key, V value) {}

// Generic interface: implement it with a concrete type, or stay generic
public interface Repository<T, ID> {
  Optional<T> findById(ID id);
  T save(T entity);
}
public class UserRepository implements Repository<User, Long> { … }
public class CrudRepo<T, ID> implements Repository<T, ID> { … }

// Generic method: its own type parameter, declared before the return type
public static <T> List<T> listOf(T a, T b) { return new ArrayList<>(List.of(a, b)); }

List<String> x = listOf("a", "b");                 // T inferred from arguments
List<String> y = Main.<String>listOf("a", "b");    // explicit type witness

A generic method is independent of whether its class is generic. Its type parameter is inferred at every call, which is why static factories work: List.of, Optional.of, Map.entry. A static method cannot use the class's type parameter (there is no instance to supply one), so it must declare its own.

Type inference

  • Diamond new ArrayList<>() (Java 7) infers type arguments from the target. Java 9 allows it with anonymous classes when the inferred type is denotable.
  • Target typing (improved in Java 8) uses the assignment or argument context: List<String> l = Collections.emptyList();.
  • var list = new ArrayList<>(); infers ArrayList<Object>, as there is no target to infer from. add(1) and add("s") both compile. Write new ArrayList<String>() with var.

Invariance: why List<String> is not a List<Object>

Generics are invariant: List<String> and List<Object> have no subtype relationship, even though String is an Object. If assignment were allowed, this would break type safety:

List<String> strings = new ArrayList<>();
List<Object> objects = strings;   // error: incompatible types (imagine it compiled)
objects.add(1);                   // an Integer in a list of strings
String s = strings.get(0);        // would blow up here

Arrays are covariant: String[] is an Object[]. Java pays for that with a runtime check on every array store:

Object[] o = new Integer[1];
o[0] = "s";                 // compiles; ArrayStoreException: java.lang.String

Arrays know their element type at runtime (they are reified). Generics do not, so the only safe design is to reject the assignment at compile time. Subtyping still follows the class itself: ArrayList<String> is a List<String> and a Collection<String>.

Bounded type parameters

A plain T only allows Object methods. A bound restricts which types are accepted, and in exchange unlocks the bound's methods.

static <T extends Number> double total(List<T> list) {
  double sum = 0;
  for (T n : list) sum += n.doubleValue();    // allowed because T is a Number
  return sum;
}

// Multiple bounds: at most one class, and it must be listed first
static <T extends Number & Comparable<T>> T max(T a, T b) {
  return a.compareTo(b) > 0 ? a : b;
}
  • extends means "is or inherits from", for classes and interfaces alike.
  • In multiple bounds, the class goes first. <T extends Comparable<T> & Number> fails with "interface expected here".
  • Type parameters have only upper bounds. <T super Integer> is a syntax error. super is allowed only on wildcards.
  • The erasure of T is its first bound. This matters, see below.

Wildcards

A wildcard (?) means "some specific type that I do not know". It appears in variable, parameter and field types, but never in new ArrayList<?>() or as a class's type parameter. Wildcards restore flexibility on top of invariance.

FormAcceptsRead givesCan add
List<Number>Only List<Number>NumberNumber and subclasses
List<? extends Number>List<Integer>, List<Double>, List<Number>NumberOnly null
List<? super Integer>List<Integer>, List<Number>, List<Object>ObjectInteger and subclasses
List<?>Any listObjectOnly null

Why you cannot add to ? extends Number: the list might really be a List<Double>, so an Integer would corrupt it. The compiler has no idea which subtype it is. Its error names the unknown type: int cannot be converted to CAP#1. CAP#1 is a capture, a fresh name that the compiler gives each wildcard occurrence.

Why reading ? super Integer gives Object: the list could be a List<Object> holding anything. The only thing certain is that an element is an Object.

PECS: Producer Extends, Consumer Super

This is the rule from Effective Java for choosing a wildcard. Look at what the parameter does for your method:

  • It produces values that you read: use ? extends T.
  • It consumes values that you write: use ? super T.
  • Both: use plain T.
// java.util.Collections
public static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src)

List<Number>  dest = new ArrayList<>(List.of(0.0, 0.0));
List<Integer> src  = List.of(1, 2);
Collections.copy(dest, src);          // T = Integer, or T = Number. Either way it fits.

Other examples in the JDK: Stream.map(Function<? super T, ? extends R>) (the function consumes a T and produces an R), Stream.filter(Predicate<? super T>), List.sort(Comparator<? super E>) and Collection.addAll(Collection<? extends E>). Because of ? super, a Comparator<Object> can sort a List<String>.

Tip: Do not use wildcards in return types. They force every caller to deal with them. Wildcards belong on method parameters, where they make an API more accepting.

Wildcard capture

You cannot put back what you read from a List<?>, even the same element: l.set(0, l.get(0)) fails with "Object cannot be converted to CAP#1". A generic helper solves this, because the compiler can capture the wildcard into a named type parameter T:

public static void swap(List<?> list) { swapHelper(list); }

private static <T> void swapHelper(List<T> list) {
  T first = list.get(0);
  list.set(0, list.get(1));
  list.set(1, first);
}

Type erasure

Generics are implemented by type erasure: they exist in the compiler, and are mostly removed from the bytecode. This kept compatibility with pre-Java 5 code: an old compiled class could keep using a generified ArrayList, and there was only one ArrayList.class. C# chose differently: it has reified generics at runtime.

The compiler does four things:

  1. Checks types using the generic information.
  2. Replaces each type parameter by its erasure: its first bound, or Object if unbounded.
  3. Inserts checkcast instructions where a value must be used as its specific type.
  4. Generates bridge methods to preserve polymorphism.
// Source
public class Box<T extends Comparable<T>> {
  private T value;
  public T get() { return value; }
}
Box<String> b = …;
String s = b.get();

// After erasure, conceptually
public class Box {
  private Comparable value;          // first bound, not Object
  public Comparable get() { return value; }
}
Box b = …;
String s = (String) b.get();         // compiler-inserted cast

The cast is at the call site, not inside the collection. That is why heap pollution fails far from its cause.

Common misconception: "generics are completely gone at runtime". Not quite. The declarations stay in the class file in the Signature attribute: class headers, field types, method signatures. Reflection reads them with getGenericSuperclass(), getGenericReturnType() and so on. What is gone is the type argument of an object instance. An ArrayList object does not know that it was created as ArrayList<String>.

Bridge methods

Erasure can break overriding. Node<T>.set(T) erases to set(Object), but a subclass's override is set(String). At JVM level they are different methods, so the override would not actually override. The compiler adds a synthetic bridge method with the erased signature, which casts and delegates.

class Node<T> { T v; void set(T t) { v = t; } T get() { return v; } }

class StringNode extends Node<String> {
  @Override void set(String t) { v = t; }
  @Override String get() { return v; }
}

for (Method m : StringNode.class.getDeclaredMethods())
  System.out.println(m + " bridge=" + m.isBridge());
java.lang.Object StringNode.get() bridge=true
java.lang.String StringNode.get() bridge=false
void StringNode.set(java.lang.String) bridge=false
void StringNode.set(java.lang.Object) bridge=true

The bridge is essentially void set(Object o) { set((String) o); }. If you use a raw Node and call n.set(1), you get a ClassCastException from the bridge. Covariant return types (non-generic ones too) use bridges as well: a class can have two methods differing only by return type at JVM level, even though the Java language forbids writing that. You will see bridge methods in stack traces, and frameworks that scan methods by reflection must filter them with isBridge().

Restrictions, and why each exists

Not allowedjavac saysReasonWorkaround
List<int>unexpected typeT erases to Object, and a primitive is not an ObjectList<Integer>, primitive streams, int[]
new T()unexpected typeThe class is unknown at runtimeSupplier<T> or Class<T>
new T[2]generic array creationAn array must know its runtime element typeArray.newInstance, or an Object[] inside
new List<String>[2]generic array creationThe array's store check could not see StringList<List<String>>
static T fieldnon-static type variable T cannot be referenced from a static contextAll parameterizations share one class and one static fieldGeneric static methods
T.classcannot select from a type variableT is not known at runtimePass a Class<T>
o instanceof T, o instanceof List<String> from ObjectObject cannot be safely cast to TErased, so the check cannot be madeo instanceof List<?>, type.isInstance(o)
class E<T> extends Exceptiona generic class may not extend java.lang.Throwablecatch works by runtime classA non-generic class with a data field
catch (T e)unexpected typeSame reasonCatch the bound and test the class
m(List<String>) and m(List<Integer>)name clash: … have the same erasureThey would become the same JVM methodDifferent method names
Implementing Comparable twice with different argumentsComparable cannot be inherited with different argumentsThe bridge methods would conflictA separate Comparator

Since Java 16, instanceof accepts a parameterized type if the conversion is provably safe. List<String> l = …; l instanceof ArrayList<String> compiles, because if l is an ArrayList at all, its type argument must be String.

Project Valhalla aims to allow primitive-like value types in generics, but that is not part of any released Java version up to 25.

A static field is shared across every parameterization. After new Sp<String>(); new Sp<Integer>();, a static counter incremented in the constructor reads 2.

Reifiable types

A reifiable type keeps all of its type information at runtime. These are: primitives, non-generic classes, raw types, arrays of reifiable types, and unbounded wildcard parameterizations like List<?>. Non-reifiable types lose information: List<String>, List<? extends Number>, T.

Only reifiable types can be used as array element types in new or in instanceof against Object. That is why new List<?>[2] compiles while new List<String>[2] does not.

Generic arrays

If new List<String>[2] were allowed, array covariance would let it be corrupted, with no store check to help. You can still see this with an unchecked creation:

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
List<String>[] lists = new List[2];          // unchecked warning
Object[] objects = lists;
objects[0] = List.of(1);                     // no ArrayStoreException: it is a List
String s = lists[0].get(0);                  // ClassCastException

How ArrayList does it. It holds an Object[] and casts on read, with @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") in an internal method. This is safe because the array never leaves the class.

class Stack<E> {
  private E[] items;
  @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
  Stack(int n) { items = (E[]) new Object[n]; }  // OK while it stays private
  E[] leak() { return items; }                    // dangerous
}
Stack<String> st = new Stack<>(2);
String[] bad = st.leak();    // ClassCastException: Object[] cannot be cast to String[]

Inside the class E[] erases to Object[], so the cast does nothing. At the call site the compiler adds a cast to String[], and the object is really an Object[]. To create a true typed array, pass the class:

@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <T> T[] newArray(Class<T> type, int n) {
  return (T[]) java.lang.reflect.Array.newInstance(type, n);
}
String[] a = newArray(String.class, 2);    // a real String[]

// How the JDK solves the same problem
String[] arr = list.toArray(new String[0]);
String[] arr2 = list.toArray(String[]::new);   // Java 11

Raw types

A raw type is a generic type used with no type arguments. It exists only for compatibility with pre-Java 5 code. Using one turns off generic checking, with only an unchecked warning.

List raw = new ArrayList<String>();
raw.add(1);                 // warning: unchecked call to add(E)

Trap: raw types erase all generic information in that class's members, even parts unrelated to the type parameter:

class Box<T> { List<String> names() { return List.of(); } }

Box b = new Box<Integer>();
for (String s : b.names()) { }    // error: Object cannot be converted to String
List (raw)List<Object>List<?>
MeansGenerics offA list that holds any ObjectA list of some unknown type
Accepts a List<String>Yes, uncheckedNoYes
Can add anythingYes, with a warningYesOnly null
Type safeNoYesYes

Raw types are still legitimate in List.class and in instanceof List.

Heap pollution

Heap pollution is when a variable of a parameterized type refers to an object that is not of that type. It comes from raw types, unchecked casts, or generic varargs. The runtime does not notice it at the moment it occurs.

List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1));
@SuppressWarnings({"unchecked", "rawtypes"})
List<String> s = (List) ints;      // no failure here

Object o = s.get(0);               // works: no cast is needed for Object
String x = s.get(0);               // ClassCastException
s.get(0).length();                 // ClassCastException
System.out.println(s.get(0));      // ClassCastException: resolves to println(String)

The failure appears wherever the compiler inserted a cast, which may be a long way from the actual bug. For debugging, Collections.checkedList wraps a list and checks every insertion at runtime:

List raw = Collections.checkedList(new ArrayList<String>(), String.class);
raw.add(1);
// ClassCastException: Attempt to insert class java.lang.Integer element
//                     into collection with element type class java.lang.String

Varargs and @SafeVarargs

A varargs parameter is an array. So a T... or List<String>... parameter creates a generic array behind the scenes, which is the very thing Java forbids you to write directly. The language permits it with a warning, since it is so useful. javac warns at the declaration ("possible heap pollution") and at call sites.

@SafeVarargs is the author's promise that the method is safe, and it silences the warnings for callers. It is only allowed where the method cannot be overridden: static methods, final instance methods, constructors, and (since Java 9) private instance methods. Otherwise: "Invalid SafeVarargs annotation. Instance method … is neither final nor private."

A method is safe if it does not write to the varargs array and does not let a reference to the array escape. List.of(E...), Arrays.asList and Stream.of are annotated.

static <T> T[] asArray(T... a) { return a; }       // escapes: unsafe
static <T> T[] pick(T a, T b) { return asArray(a, b); }

String[] s = pick("a", "b");
// ClassCastException: [Ljava.lang.Object; cannot be cast to [Ljava.lang.String;

Inside pick, T is unknown, so the compiler creates an Object[] for the varargs. That array then reaches a caller that expected String[].

Type tokens

Because T.class is impossible, APIs take a Class<T> object as a runtime representation of the type: a type token. Class is itself generic: String.class has type Class<String>, and cast() and newInstance-style methods use it to stay type safe.

Typesafe heterogeneous container

A map keyed by the class can hold values of different types while keeping full type safety, because the key's type parameter links to the value. This is the idea behind Spring's ApplicationContext.getBean(Class<T>).

class Favorites {
  private final Map<Class<?>, Object> map = new HashMap<>();
  <T> void put(Class<T> type, T value) { map.put(Objects.requireNonNull(type), type.cast(value)); }
  <T> T get(Class<T> type) { return type.cast(map.get(type)); }
}
Favorites f = new Favorites();
f.put(String.class, "java");
f.put(Integer.class, 42);
String a = f.get(String.class);
int b = f.get(Integer.class);        // java 42

Super type tokens

List<String>.class does not exist. But a subclass records its parent's type arguments in its class file. An anonymous subclass therefore preserves them. Jackson's TypeReference, Gson's TypeToken and Spring's ParameterizedTypeReference all use this trick (Neal Gafter's "super type tokens").

abstract class TypeRef<T> {
  final Type type = ((ParameterizedType) getClass().getGenericSuperclass())
                       .getActualTypeArguments()[0];
}
System.out.println(new TypeRef<List<String>>() {}.type);
// java.util.List<java.lang.String>

// Real uses:
List<User> users = mapper.readValue(json, new TypeReference<List<User>>() {});
restTemplate.exchange(url, GET, null, new ParameterizedTypeReference<List<User>>() {});

The {} matters. It creates an anonymous subclass, which is what makes the type argument available.

Recursive type bounds

A recursive bound uses the type parameter in its own bound, meaning "T can do something with other Ts".

// T must be comparable to itself
static <T extends Comparable<T>> T max(List<T> list) { … }

// More flexible: T may inherit its compareTo from a supertype (PECS: it consumes T)
static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c) { … }

Why ? super T? java.sql.Timestamp extends java.util.Date, which implements Comparable<Date>, not Comparable<Timestamp>. Without ? super, you could not call max on a List<Timestamp>. The same is true of LocalDate, which is Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>.

Enum<E extends Enum<E>> is the famous example. It ensures that compareTo(E) on Color accepts only Color, and that methods such as getDeclaringClass() return a precisely typed value. enum Color compiles to final class Color extends Enum<Color>.

The curiously recurring generic pattern: fluent builders

abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>> {
  String name;
  abstract T self();
  T name(String s) { name = s; return self(); }
}
class CarBuilder extends Builder<CarBuilder> {
  int kids;
  CarBuilder self() { return this; }
  CarBuilder seats(int n) { kids = n; return this; }
}
new CarBuilder().name("x").seats(2);    // name() returns CarBuilder, not Builder

Without this, name() would return the base type, and the chain could not continue with subclass methods. Testcontainers and many builder APIs follow this shape.

The signature of Collections.max

public static <T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>>
    T max(Collection<? extends T> coll)

Why Object &? The erasure uses the first bound. With Object first, the method erases to Object max(Collection), which matches the pre-Java 5 binary signature. Without it, it would erase to Comparable max(Collection) and break old compiled callers. Reflection confirms the runtime return type is java.lang.Object.

Overload resolution is compile-time

Inside a generic method, the compiler picks overloads using the erased bound of T, not the actual argument.

static void p(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
static void p(String o)  { System.out.println("String"); }

static <T> void call(T t) { p(t); }
static <T extends String> void call2(T t) { p(t); }

call("s");     // Object
call2("s");    // String

Generics with modern Java

  • Records can be generic: record Page<T>(List<T> items, int total) {}.
  • Sealed generic hierarchies model results: sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {}.
  • Record patterns (Java 21) infer type arguments: with Page<String> p, the test p instanceof Page(var items, var total) gives items the type List<String>.
  • Lambdas cannot be generic themselves. A functional interface with a generic method has no lambda form, only a method reference.

Reading JDK Signatures

Interviewers often show a real JDK signature and ask why it looks that way. Each wildcard is there so that callers can pass more types:

// Stream<T>
<R> Stream<R> map(Function<? super T, ? extends R> mapper);
//   ? super T   : a Function<Object, ...> can map a Stream<String> (it consumes T)
//   ? extends R : the function may return a subtype of R (it produces R)

// List<E>
void sort(Comparator<? super E> c);      // a Comparator<Number> can sort a List<Integer>

// Collections
static <T> void copy(List<? super T> dest, List<? extends T> src);   // PECS in one line

// Map<K,V>: why Object, not K?
V get(Object key);  boolean containsKey(Object key);  V remove(Object key);
V put(K key, V value);                  // only writes need K, for type safety

Function<Object, String> f = String::valueOf;
Stream.of(1, 2).map(f);                 // compiles thanks to ? super T

A rule of thumb for your own APIs: if a parameter only supplies T values, use ? extends T. If it only receives T values (a consumer, comparator or sink), use ? super T. Return types should be concrete.

Intersection Types

An intersection type A & B means "a value that is both an A and a B". Besides multiple bounds (<T extends Number & Comparable<T>>, where the class must come first), it is used in casts, most often to make a lambda serializable or to give it a marker interface:

Runnable r = (Runnable & Serializable) () -> System.out.println("hi");  // a serializable lambda
Comparator<String> c = (Comparator<String> & Serializable) String::compareTo;

var x = flag ? 1 : "s";   // inferred type is Serializable & Comparable<...> & Constable & ...
// (only var or generic inference can hold such a type; you cannot write it as a variable type)

Only one type in the intersection can be a class, and the others must be interfaces. A lambda target in a cast must still have exactly one abstract method across all the types.

Generic Sealed Hierarchies and Record Patterns

Generics combine well with sealed interfaces and records to build type-safe results and trees. Pattern matching (Java 21) infers type arguments for record patterns:

sealed interface Result<T> permits Ok, Err {}
record Ok<T>(T value) implements Result<T> {}
record Err<T>(String error) implements Result<T> {}

static <T, R> Result<R> map(Result<T> r, Function<? super T, ? extends R> f) {
    return switch (r) {                      // exhaustive: no default needed
        case Ok<T>(var v)  -> new Ok<>(f.apply(v));
        case Err<T>(var e) -> new Err<>(e);
    };
}
Result<Integer> len = map(new Ok<>("hello"), String::length);   // Ok[value=5]

Because of erasure, case Ok<String> o is allowed only when the compiler can prove it is safe from the selector's static type. It cannot test the type argument at runtime.

Interview Questions — Generics

What problem do generics solve?

They move type errors from runtime to compile time, remove manual casts, and allow one algorithm to work across many types. Without them, collections hold Object, and a wrong element appears as a ClassCastException far from the mistake.

What is type erasure? Why did Java choose it?

The compiler checks generic types and then removes them: type parameters become their first bound or Object, casts are inserted at use sites, and bridge methods are added. It was chosen for migration compatibility: libraries could add generics in Java 5 without breaking existing binaries, and generic and non-generic code could interoperate. The cost is that type arguments are not available at runtime.

Predict the output. 
System.out.println(new ArrayList<String>().getClass()
                == new ArrayList<Integer>().getClass());

true. There is a single runtime class, java.util.ArrayList.

Why is List<String> not a subtype of List<Object>, while String[] is a subtype of Object[]?

If the list assignment were legal, you could add an Integer through the List<Object> view and corrupt the list of strings. Arrays allow it (covariance) because they carry their element type at runtime and every store is checked, failing with ArrayStoreException. Erased generics have no such runtime check, so the compiler must reject it. Arrays' covariance is widely seen as a historical design flaw; it existed so that Arrays.sort(Object[]) could work before generics.

Explain PECS with an example.

Producer Extends, Consumer Super. If a parameter gives you values, use ? extends T. If it takes values from you, use ? super T.

static <T> void transfer(Collection<? extends T> from, Collection<? super T> to) {
  for (T item : from) to.add(item);
}
transfer(List.of(1, 2), new ArrayList<Number>());   // T inferred as Integer

With plain Collection<T> for both, you could not copy integers into a list of numbers.

Which lines compile? 
void b(List<? extends Number> l) {
  l.add(1);            // A
  l.add(null);         // B
  Number n = l.get(0); // C
}
void c(List<? super Integer> l) {
  l.add(1);            // D
  Integer i = l.get(0);// E
  Object o = l.get(0); // F
}

A fails. The list might be List<Double>. B works. null is a member of every reference type. C works. D works. Every possible list type can hold an Integer. E fails, because it might be a List<Object>. F works.

List<?> vs List<Object> vs raw List?

List<?> is a list of an unknown specific type: it accepts any list, you can only read Objects and add null, and it stays type safe. List<Object> accepts only a List<Object>, but you can add anything. Raw List disables checks completely. Prefer List<?> when you only need size() or to print elements.

What is a bridge method? Show when one is created.

A synthetic method generated by the compiler to preserve overriding after erasure. In class StringNode extends Node<String> overriding set(String), the parent's erased method is set(Object), so the compiler adds set(Object), which casts to String and calls set(String). It is also produced for covariant returns. Detect it with Method.isBridge() or javap -c. This is why a raw call with a wrong type fails with ClassCastException inside the subclass.

Why does this fail to compile? 
class A {
  void m(List<String> l) {}
  void m(List<Integer> l) {}
}

error: name clash: m(List<Integer>) and m(List<String>) have the same erasure. Both become m(List), and a class cannot have two methods with the same JVM signature. Rename one.

Why does this fail? 
class Par implements Comparable<Par> { public int compareTo(Par p) { return 0; } }
class Ch extends Par implements Comparable<Ch> { }

error: Comparable cannot be inherited with different arguments: <Ch> and <Par>. A class cannot implement a generic interface with two different type arguments, because they share one raw interface, and the bridge methods would conflict. Use a Comparator for Ch.

Can you create a generic array? How does ArrayList store elements?

new T[n] and new List<String>[n] are compile errors, since arrays need their runtime type for store checks. new List<?>[n] is allowed. ArrayList stores an Object[] elementData and casts on read. For a real T[], use Array.newInstance(Class, n). If you do (T[]) new Object[n], never expose the array: an outside caller gets a ClassCastException.

Predict the output. 
List<Integer> ints = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1));
List<String> s = (List) ints;
System.out.println(s.size());
Object o = s.get(0);
System.out.println(o);
String t = s.get(0);
System.out.println(t);

Prints 1, then 1, then throws ClassCastException: class java.lang.Integer cannot be cast to class java.lang.String. The compiler adds a cast only where the String type is needed. Assigning to Object needs no cast, so the pollution stays hidden.

Does System.out.println(s.get(0)) throw for a polluted List<String> holding an Integer?

Yes. The compile-time type is String, so overload resolution chooses println(String), which requires a checkcast. Verified on Java 21. String concatenation "x" + s.get(0) also threw in the same test. If you first assign to Object, no cast happens.

Predict the output.
