static void p(Object o)  { System.out.println("Object"); }
static void p(String o)  { System.out.println("String"); }
static <T> void call(T t) { p(t); }
public static void main(String[] a) { call("s"); }

Object. Overloads are picked at compile time. In call, T is unbounded, and p(Object) is the only applicable choice. With <T extends String>, it prints String.

What is heap pollution? How can it occur, and how do you detect it?

A parameterized variable refers to an object of the wrong actual type. It arises from raw types, unchecked casts, and generic varargs. It does not fail at the pollution point, but at a later compiler-inserted cast. Detect: pay attention to unchecked warnings (build with -Xlint:unchecked, maybe -Werror), and use Collections.checkedList at the boundary with legacy code to catch the insertion.

What does @SafeVarargs do? Where can it be used?

It declares that a generic varargs method does not perform unsafe operations on its array, and it suppresses the warning at call sites. It is not verified by the compiler beyond placement. It is allowed on constructors, static methods, final instance methods, and private instance methods (Java 9+), since these cannot be overridden. A subclass override could otherwise make the promise false.

Predict the result. 
static <T> T[] arr(T... a) { return a; }
static <T> T[] pick(T a, T b) { return arr(a, b); }

String[] s = pick("a", "b");

ClassCastException. In pick the compiler does not know T, so the implicit varargs array is an Object[]. String[] s = … casts it to String[] and fails. Calling arr("a", "b") directly works, since there T is String and a String[] is created.

Can you instantiate T? List the alternatives.

new T() is impossible since T is unknown at runtime. Alternatives:

static <T> T make(Supplier<T> s) { return s.get(); }            // preferred
String x = make(String::new);

static <T> T make(Class<T> c) throws ReflectiveOperationException {
  return c.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
}
Why can't static fields or static methods use the class's type parameter?

Statics belong to the single class, shared across all parameterizations. static T x would have to be both String and Integer. A static method can declare its own type parameter: static <U> Box<U> of(U u). Notice that Box<String>.staticMethod() is not valid syntax.

What is a reifiable type?

A type fully available at runtime: primitives, non-generic types, raw types, List<?>, and arrays of these. Non-reifiable: List<String>, T, List<? extends X>. Array creation needs a reifiable element type.

What is wildcard capture? Why does l.set(0, l.get(0)) fail on a List<?>?

The compiler treats each ? as a fresh unnamed type (CAP#1). l.get(0) returns it as Object, and set requires CAP#1, and Object does not convert to it. A private generic helper <T> void helper(List<T> l) gives the unknown type a name for the method's duration, so the call compiles.

Explain class Enum<E extends Enum<E>>.

It is a recursive bound that forces each enum to be parameterized by itself: Color extends Enum<Color>. So compareTo(E) accepts only the same enum, and EnumSet<E extends Enum<E>> can guarantee that it holds a real enum type. Without it, comparing Color with Size would compile.

Why is T extends Comparable<? super T> preferred over T extends Comparable<T>?

Some classes inherit compareTo from a parent. java.sql.Timestamp is a Comparable<Date>, and LocalDate is a Comparable<ChronoLocalDate>. The stricter bound rejects them. Comparable consumes a T, so by PECS it should use super.

Why does Collections.max declare T extends Object & Comparable<? super T>?

Binary compatibility. The erasure of a type variable is its first bound. Listing Object first keeps the erased return type as Object, the same as before generics, so old compiled code still links. Without it, the method descriptor would return Comparable.

How can you get the generic type at runtime? What does Jackson's TypeReference do?

A value does not know its type arguments, but class declarations retain them in the Signature attribute. new TypeReference<List<User>>() {} creates an anonymous subclass whose declaration says "extends TypeReference<List<User>>". The constructor reads that through getClass().getGenericSuperclass(). Likewise, with reflection you can read a field's declared List<String> using Field.getGenericType().

Is catch (T e) allowed? What about throws T?

catch (T e) is not, since the handler is picked by runtime class. <X extends Throwable> void m() throws X is allowed, and is how Optional.orElseThrow(Supplier<? extends X>) stays checked-aware. An unchecked cast in such a method makes a "sneaky throw" possible; see Exception Handling.

Does overriding work with generics? Will this override? 
class Base<T> { void put(T t) {} }
class Sub extends Base<String> { void put(Object o) {} }

This is a name clash compile error. Sub.put(Object) has the same erasure as Base.put(T), but it does not override put(String), the parameterized form. Write void put(String s), and add @Override always, so the compiler confirms it.

What does this print? Static counter in a generic class. 
class Sp<T> { static int c = 0; Sp() { c++; } }
new Sp<String>();
new Sp<Integer>();
System.out.println(Sp.c);

2. There is one class, so there is one static. C++ templates would produce two separate classes; Java does not.

What does var list = new ArrayList<>(); infer?

ArrayList<Object>. Nothing constrains the diamond. list.add(1); list.add("s"); compiles and prints [1, s], which is probably not what you meant.

What is the difference between a bounded type parameter and a bounded wildcard? When is each right?

<T extends Number> void m(List<T> a, List<T> b) names the type, so it can link parts of the signature: both lists have the same T, and a return value can be T. void m(List<? extends Number> a) is simpler if the type appears only once. Rule: if the type is mentioned once and only used for reading or writing, prefer a wildcard. If two places must agree, use a type parameter. A type parameter can have multiple bounds; a wildcard cannot. A wildcard can have a lower bound; a type parameter cannot.

Is generic code slower? Is there any runtime overhead?

Generics add no runtime types, so there is no per-parameterization code and no template bloat. Costs: a checkcast at reads (cheap, and usually eliminated by the JIT), and boxing, which is the real cost. List<Integer> stores references to heap objects, with worse memory use and cache locality than int[]. Use IntStream and primitive arrays on hot paths.

Write a generic method to find the maximum element of a list.
public static <T extends Comparable<? super T>> T max(Collection<? extends T> c) {
  T best = null;
  for (T t : c) if (best == null || t.compareTo(best) > 0) best = t;
  return best;
}
System.out.println(max(List.of(3, 9, 2)));   // 9

A library version would throw NoSuchElementException on an empty input, or return Optional<T>.

Write a generic, type-safe cache that stores different types per key.
final class Key<T> {
  final String name; final Class<T> type;
  Key(String name, Class<T> type) { this.name = name; this.type = type; }
}
final class TypedCache {
  private final Map<Key<?>, Object> map = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  <T> void put(Key<T> k, T v) { map.put(k, k.type.cast(v)); }
  <T> T get(Key<T> k)         { return k.type.cast(map.get(k)); }
}

The type parameter on Key<T> ties a key to its value type, and Class.cast makes reads safe without unchecked warnings. Here each key's identity is the object; add equals and hashCode if you want keys to compare by name.

What happens with the type parameter in class Box<T extends Comparable<T> & Serializable> after erasure?

T erases to Comparable, the first bound. Where the value is used as Serializable, the compiler adds a cast to it. List the bound you use most first, to reduce casts.

Why can't lambdas implement a generic method's functional interface?

If the single abstract method itself declares a type parameter, as in interface F { <T> T id(T t); }, there is no lambda syntax for type parameters, so a lambda cannot implement it. Method references can: F f = Main::identity;. Generic interfaces like Function<T, R> are fine, as T and R are fixed at the target type.

Design question: how do you design a generic Repository or Service base class in Spring?

Spring Data shows the pattern: interface CrudRepository<T, ID>. A concrete interface UserRepo extends JpaRepository<User, Long> fixes the type arguments in its declaration. Those arguments survive erasure in the class file, so Spring reads them by reflection (ResolvableType) to know the entity class. It also injects by generic type: @Autowired Repository<User, Long> r selects the matching bean.

A custom abstract service: abstract class CrudService<T, ID> with a constructor taking the repository. Avoid deep generic hierarchies; once a signature has three or more type parameters with bounds, composition usually reads better.

Why does List<Number> l = List.of(1, 2.0); compile, while List<Integer> a = List.of(1); List<Number> b = a; does not?

In the first, inference uses the target: E becomes Number, and 1 and 2.0 box and widen to Number. In the second, the list already has a fixed type, and invariance forbids the assignment. List<? extends Number> b = a; works.

What is the output of Comparator.class.getTypeParameters()[0], and how does reflection expose generics?

It prints T. java.lang.reflect.Type is the supertype of Class, ParameterizedType, TypeVariable, WildcardType and GenericArrayType. toGenericString() prints a full signature; Collections.class.getMethod("max", Collection.class).toGenericString() gives public static <T extends java.lang.Object & java.lang.Comparable<? super T>> T java.util.Collections.max(java.util.Collection<? extends T>).

Why is Map.get declared as get(Object key) instead of get(K key)?

A lookup cannot corrupt the map, so there is no type-safety reason to restrict it. The contract is based on equals, and objects of different types can be equal. For example, an ArrayList key can be found with an equal LinkedList. get(Object) also lets code holding a Map<?, V> perform lookups. It also predates generics and stayed this way for compatibility. The downside is that map.get(42) on a Map<String, V> compiles and silently returns null. IDEs and Error Prone flag this as a "suspicious call". The same reasoning applies to contains, remove and indexOf.

Can you write obj instanceof List<String>?

Only when it is provably safe. Since Java 16, instanceof with a parameterized type compiles if the static type of the expression makes the check exact, for example when coll is a Collection<String> and you test coll instanceof List<String> l. If obj is an Object, it is a compile error, because erasure means the JVM can only check List. Use obj instanceof List<?> l and then check or cast the elements one at a time.

What are the naming conventions for type parameters?

Single uppercase letters: T for a type, E for a collection element, K/V for map key and value, R for a result or return, N for a number, S, U and so on for second and third types, and ID is common in Spring Data (CrudRepository<T, ID>). Using single letters keeps type parameters visually distinct from real class names. If a name like Customer were used as a type parameter, it would shadow the real class.

Why should public methods avoid returning wildcard types like List<? extends Number>?

The wildcard passes the restriction on to every caller. They cannot add elements, they have to repeat the wildcard in their own variables, and type inference gets harder. Wildcards belong in parameters, where they make the method more flexible for callers. Return types should be concrete (List<Number>), or a type parameter of the method (<T extends Number> List<T>) when the caller decides the type. A rare exception is deliberately returning a read-only, covariant view.

What is a generic constructor? Does it relate to the class's type parameter?

A constructor can declare its own type parameters, independent of the class's: class Box { <T extends Number> Box(T seed) { ... } }. It is useful when the constructor needs a bound or relationship only during construction, for example <T extends Comparable<T>> Range(T lo, T hi), which stores derived values. A generic class can also have one: new <Integer>Pair<String>(1) is legal syntax, but the explicit form is almost never written because inference handles it. In practice, a static generic factory method is clearer.

Why does Stream.map take Function<? super T, ? extends R> rather than Function<T, R>?

So that more functions are accepted. With ? super T, a function written for a supertype works: a Function<Object, String> such as String::valueOf can map a Stream<Integer>. With ? extends R, a function returning Integer can be used where R is inferred as Number. With an invariant Function<T, R>, those calls would fail to compile even though they are type-safe. This is PECS applied to a function: it consumes T and produces R.

Collections Deep Dive Core Java

Every implementation in the Java Collections Framework, with its data structure, internals and cost: lists, deques, heaps, hash tables, trees, concurrent collections, iterators, sorting and how to choose. The Core Java section has the hierarchy diagram and a summary table; this section explains how each one actually works.

Big-O reference

Big-O describes how cost grows with size n. Amortized O(1) means that an occasional operation is expensive, but the average across many operations is constant, as when a dynamic array resizes.

ArrayList

What it is: a resizable array. It stores references in an Object[] elementData, plus an int size. It implements the marker interface RandomAccess, which tells algorithms such as Collections.binarySearch that index access is fast.

Growth

new ArrayList<>() starts with a shared empty array, using no element storage. The first add allocates capacity 10. When the array is full, a new one is made with oldCapacity + (oldCapacity >> 1), which is 1.5 times, and elements are copied with System.arraycopy.

Capacity observed on Java 21 by reflection:
new ArrayList<>()   : 0, then 10, 15, 22, 33 …
new ArrayList<>(0)  : 0, then 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 9, 13, 19, 28, 42 …

Why 1.5x and not 2x? It wastes less memory, while geometric growth still gives amortized O(1): total copying over n adds is proportional to n. Growing by a fixed amount would make it O(n²). Note that capacity and size differ: new ArrayList<>(100).get(0) throws IndexOutOfBoundsException, as size is still 0.

If you know the size, pre-size with new ArrayList<>(n) or ensureCapacity(n) to avoid repeated copying. trimToSize() releases unused capacity. clear() nulls the elements but keeps the capacity, which can pin memory for a list that was once huge.

remove pitfalls

List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
list.remove(1);                    // remove(int index): removes the value 2
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));   // remove(Object): removes the value 1
System.out.println(list);          // [3, 4]

// Index loop skips elements: everything after a removal shifts left
List<Integer> x = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 1, 2));
for (int i = 0; i < x.size(); i++) if (x.get(i) == 1) x.remove(i);
System.out.println(x);             // [1, 2], the second 1 survived

// Correct and O(n)
x.removeIf(v -> v == 1);

Each single remove shifts the tail, so removing in a loop is O(n²) in the worst case. removeIf and removeAll compact in a single pass.

subList is a view

subList(from, to) returns a view over the same array, not a copy. Changes go both ways, and sub.clear() is the idiom for removing a range.

var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5));
var sub = list.subList(1, 3);
sub.set(0, 99);      // list = [1, 99, 3, 4, 5]
sub.clear();         // list = [1, 4, 5]

list.add(6);         // structural change on the parent
sub.size();          // ConcurrentModificationException

A long-lived small subList also keeps the whole parent reachable. Copy it with new ArrayList<>(sub) if you keep it.

LinkedList

A doubly linked list that implements both List and Deque. Each element has a Node object with item, next and prev; the list keeps first, last and size. get(i) walks from whichever end is nearer.

The misconception: "LinkedList is faster for insertions in the middle." Relinking is O(1), but reaching the position is O(n), and pointer chasing is slow because nodes are scattered in memory. Each element costs an extra node object, typically 24 bytes with compressed references, against 4 bytes for an array slot. ArrayList's System.arraycopy is a fast bulk move. In practice ArrayList wins for nearly all workloads, and ArrayDeque wins for queues. LinkedList only has a real advantage when you already hold a ListIterator at the position, or if you need a list that also acts as a deque and holds nulls.

Vector and Stack

Vector is the original resizable array from Java 1.0. Each method is synchronized. It doubles by default (or grows by capacityIncrement if set). Per-method locking does not make compound actions atomic: if (!v.contains(x)) v.add(x); still races. It is regarded as legacy; use ArrayList, or concurrent collections if you need sharing.

Stack extends Vector, which is a design mistake: it inherits add(int, E) and get(int), so callers can break LIFO. Prefer Deque<E> s = new ArrayDeque<>(). Their iteration orders differ, and this is a good interview trap:

Stack<Integer> st = new Stack<>();       st.push(1); st.push(2); st.push(3);
Deque<Integer> dq = new ArrayDeque<>();  dq.push(1); dq.push(2); dq.push(3);
System.out.println(st);   // [1, 2, 3]   bottom to top
System.out.println(dq);   // [3, 2, 1]   top to bottom

ArrayDeque

A double-ended queue on a circular array: head and tail indexes wrap around the array end, so adding or removing at either end needs no shifting. It is the default choice for both stacks and FIFO queues. It is usually faster than LinkedList since it allocates no node per element and has better cache locality.

It forbids null, because poll() uses null to signal "empty". It has no index access. The default-constructed capacity is 16 elements; it grows as needed, and since Java 9 the capacity no longer has to be a power of two.

PriorityQueue

A binary min-heap stored in an array. A heap is a complete binary tree where each parent is less than or equal to its children. That partial order gives fast access to the smallest element without sorting everything. The default initial capacity is 11. For index i: parent is (i-1)/2, children are 2i+1 and 2i+2.

  • offer: place at the end, then sift up: swap with the parent while smaller. O(log n).
  • poll: take the root, move the last element to the root, then sift down by swapping with the smaller child. O(log n).
  • peek: O(1). remove(Object) and contains: O(n), a linear scan.
  • Building from a collection (heapify): O(n), which beats n offers at O(n log n).
Gotcha: iterating or printing a PriorityQueue is not sorted. Only repeated poll() gives sorted order. Elements that compare as equal come out in no particular order, as it is not stable. To get FIFO among ties, add a sequence number to the comparison. Elements must be Comparable, or you must supply a Comparator; otherwise the second insert throws ClassCastException. Nulls are rejected.
// Max-heap: reverse the comparator
PriorityQueue<Integer> max = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.reverseOrder());

// Smallest deadline first
PriorityQueue<Task> tasks = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparing(Task::deadline));

HashMap internals

The Core Java section outlines the put flow. This is the full mechanism for JDK 8 and later.

Fields

Node<K,V>[] table;        // bucket array, allocated lazily on the first put
int size;                 // number of mappings
int modCount;             // structural change counter, used by iterators
int threshold;            // resize when size exceeds this (capacity * loadFactor)
final float loadFactor;   // 0.75 by default

static class Node<K,V> {  final int hash; final K key; V value; Node<K,V> next; }

Hash spreading

static final int hash(Object key) {
  int h;
  return (key == null) ? 0 : (h = key.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
}
int index = (n - 1) & hash;     // n = table length, always a power of two

The index uses only the low bits of the hash: for a table of 16, only the bottom 4. If two hash codes differ only in high bits, they would always collide. XOR-ing the high 16 bits into the low 16 lets high bits influence the index, at almost no cost.

Without spreading, table of 16:
  hashCode 0x10000 & 15 = 0
  hashCode 0x20000 & 15 = 0       always the same bucket

With spreading:
  0x10000 ^ 0x1 = 0x10001, & 15 = 1
  0x20000 ^ 0x2 = 0x20002, & 15 = 2

Why the capacity is a power of two

  • For n = 2^k, (n-1) is a mask of k one-bits, so hash & (n-1) equals hash mod n, but is computed with one AND rather than a slow division.
  • It always gives a non-negative index. Math.abs(h) % n does not: "polygenelubricants".hashCode() is Integer.MIN_VALUE, and Math.abs of that stays negative.
  • It makes resizing simple: each entry either stays or moves by exactly the old capacity.

If you ask for another size, tableSizeFor rounds up to the next power of two. new HashMap<>(17) gives a table of 32 on the first put (confirmed by reflection).

put walk-through

  1. Compute hash(key).
  2. If the table is null, call resize() to allocate it.
  3. Find the bin: i = (n-1) & hash. If empty, store a new Node.
  4. Otherwise check the first node. A key matches if p.hash == hash && (p.key == key || key.equals(p.key)). Comparing the stored int hash first avoids most equals calls.
  5. If the bin is a tree, call putTreeVal.
  6. Otherwise walk the list. If a key matches, stop; if the end is reached, append at the tail. If the list already held 8 nodes before this append (TREEIFY_THRESHOLD), call treeifyBin.
  7. For an existing key: replace the value, and return the old one. modCount does not change, since replacing is not structural.
  8. For a new key: ++modCount; if ++size > threshold, call resize().

get walk-through

Compute the hash, go to the bin, check the first node, then walk the list or search the tree. null from get is ambiguous in a HashMap: the key may be absent or mapped to null. Use containsKey or getOrDefault. Note that getOrDefault returns null, not the default, for a key that maps to null.

Resize

When size > threshold, the table doubles. With 16 and 0.75, the threshold is 12, so the 13th entry triggers the resize to 32 (confirmed: 12 entries table 16; 13 entries table 32).

Rehashing is not needed, thanks to the stored hash. The new index depends on one extra bit: e.hash & oldCap. If that bit is 0, the entry stays at index j. If it is 1, it moves to j + oldCap. Each bin splits into a "lo" list and a "hi" list, and both keep their relative order.

Treeification

A long bin degrades to O(n). Since Java 8, a long bin can convert to a red-black tree (TreeNode), which gives O(log n) and limits the damage from poor hash functions or deliberate hash-flooding attacks.

  • TREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 8: checked as a new node is appended to a list that already has 8 nodes, so the bin holds 9 when it converts. Verified on Java 21 with keys sharing a hash: in a table of 64, nodes stayed plain through the 8th insert and became TreeNode on the 9th.
  • MIN_TREEIFY_CAPACITY = 64: if the table is smaller, the map resizes instead. Verified: starting from 16 with colliding keys, the 9th insert grew the table to 32, the 10th to 64, and the 11th treeified.
  • UNTREEIFY_THRESHOLD = 6: applied when a resize splits a tree bin. On removal, a bin reverts based on the tree's shape when it becomes too small. The gap between 6 and 8 prevents flapping back and forth.
  • Ordering in the tree: by hash first. For equal hashes, by compareTo if the key class is Comparable; otherwise by a tie-break of class name and identityHashCode. So making keys Comparable helps when many hashes collide.
  • A TreeNode takes about twice the memory of a Node. With a decent hash, bins reaching 8 are extremely rare: the source comments put the probability at about 0.00000006 under random hashes at load factor 0.75.

Load factor and sizing

0.75 is a space and time compromise. A higher value saves memory but gives longer chains. A lower one wastes table slots. To hold n entries without a resize, you need capacity above n / 0.75. new HashMap<>(n) does not mean "room for n entries": it may resize once. Java 19 added HashMap.newHashMap(n) and HashSet.newHashSet(n) for exactly this.

Mutable keys

class Key { int v; Key(int v) { this.v = v; }
  public int hashCode() { return v; }
  public boolean equals(Object o) { return o instanceof Key k && k.v == v; } }

var map = new HashMap<Key, String>();
Key key = new Key(1);
map.put(key, "x");
key.v = 2;                                   // the hash changed after insertion

System.out.println(map.get(key));            // null: it looks in the bin for hash 2
System.out.println(map.get(new Key(1)));     // null: right bin, but equals fails
System.out.println(map.size());              // 1: the entry is stranded and leaks

Use immutable keys: String, Integer, enums, records of immutable values. String also caches its hash. The same applies to sets: adding a list to a HashSet and then adding to the list makes contains return false.

Useful Map methods (Java 8+)

counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);                       // counting
groups.computeIfAbsent(dept, d -> new ArrayList<>()).add(emp);  // multimap
map.getOrDefault(key, 0);
map.putIfAbsent(key, value);
map.compute(key, (k, v) -> v == null ? 1 : v + 1);
map.replaceAll((k, v) -> v * 2);
map.entrySet().removeIf(e -> e.getValue() == 0);
Gotcha: The function passed to computeIfAbsent must not modify the same map. HashMap detects this since Java 9 and throws ConcurrentModificationException; ConcurrentHashMap throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update when it detects the case. Both verified on Java 21.

LinkedHashMap

LinkedHashMap extends HashMap. Its entries extend HashMap.Node with before and after pointers, forming a doubly linked list through all entries. Lookups use the hash table; iteration follows the linked list, so it is O(size), not O(capacity). HashMap calls hooks (afterNodeAccess, afterNodeInsertion, afterNodeRemoval) to keep the list right.

Insertion order is the default. Re-putting an existing key does not change its position: after a, b, a, the order is {a=3, b=2}.

Access order is enabled by the three-argument constructor: new LinkedHashMap<>(16, 0.75f, true). Each get or put moves the entry to the tail, so the head is the least recently used.

LRU cache in eight lines

class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
  private final int capacity;
  LruCache(int capacity) { super(16, 0.75f, true); this.capacity = capacity; }
  @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
    return size() > capacity;
  }
}
var lru = new LruCache<String, Integer>(2);
lru.put("a", 1); lru.put("b", 2);
lru.get("a");                     // a becomes most recently used
lru.put("c", 3);                  // evicts b
System.out.println(lru.keySet()); // [a, c]

removeEldestEntry is called after each insertion. It is not thread-safe. Wrapping in Collections.synchronizedMap works but serializes everything, and even get needs the lock because it changes the list. In access-order mode get is a structural change, so calling get while iterating throws ConcurrentModificationException (verified). In production, use Caffeine, which has better eviction, expiry and concurrency.

TreeMap

A sorted map backed by a red-black tree: a self-balancing binary search tree. It keeps keys sorted by Comparable or a Comparator. All key operations are O(log n).

Red-black rules: every node is red or black; the root is black; a red node has no red child; every path from a node down to a leaf has the same number of black nodes. Together they guarantee that the longest path is at most twice the shortest, so the height is at most about 2 log₂(n+1). After an insert or delete, the tree restores these rules by recolouring and rotating. An insert needs at most 2 rotations, and a delete at most 3.

Why a red-black tree and not AVL? AVL trees are more tightly balanced, so lookups are slightly faster, but updates rebalance more. Red-black does fewer rotations and is a good general purpose compromise.

The comparator defines key identity. equals is never called: two keys are "the same" when compare returns 0. A TreeMap keyed by Comparator.comparing(String::length) treats "aa" and "bb" as one key, and put("bb", 2) overwrites the value while keeping "aa" as key: {aa=2}.

The first put runs compare(key, key), so a null key with natural ordering throws NPE at once, and a non-Comparable key throws ClassCastException. A comparator that accepts null permits null keys.

NavigableMap

var m = new TreeMap<>(Map.of(10, "a", 20, "b", 30, "c"));
m.floorKey(25);      // 20   greatest key <= 25
m.ceilingKey(25);    // 30   smallest key >= 25
m.lowerKey(10);      // null strictly less
m.higherKey(30);     // null strictly greater
m.headMap(20);       // {10=a}          exclusive by default
m.headMap(20, true); // {10=a, 20=b}
m.tailMap(20);       // {20=b, 30=c}    inclusive by default
m.subMap(10, 30);    // {10=a, 20=b}
m.descendingMap();   // {30=c, 20=b, 10=a}
m.firstEntry();      // 10=a
m.pollFirstEntry();  // removes and returns 10=a

Range methods return live views. A later insert in range shows up in the view. Putting a key outside a view's range throws IllegalArgumentException: key out of range. Typical uses: time-ranged lookups, rate tiers, consistent hashing rings (ceilingEntry on a hash ring), leaderboards.

HashSet, LinkedHashSet, TreeSet

Sets are thin wrappers around maps. HashSet holds a HashMap<E, Object>, and each element is a key mapped to one shared dummy value (PRESENT). add returns map.put(e, PRESENT) == null. LinkedHashSet extends HashSet and uses a LinkedHashMap via a package-private constructor. TreeSet wraps a NavigableMap, by default a TreeMap.

So everything about the map applies: HashSet uses hashCode and equals, and TreeSet uses compareTo only. They can disagree:

new HashSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size();  // 2
new TreeSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size();  // 1

BigDecimal.equals compares scale too, but compareTo does not. The docs call such a type's ordering "inconsistent with equals", and a sorted set then breaks the general Set contract. A String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER TreeSet is a deliberate use of this.

EnumMap and EnumSet

When keys are enum constants, the ordinal gives a perfect hash. EnumMap stores values in an array indexed by ordinal(). EnumSet is a bit vector. RegularEnumSet (64 constants or fewer) uses one long, so contains is a bit test and addAll is one OR. JumboEnumSet uses a long[]. There are no constructors; use factories.

EnumSet.of(Day.MON);  EnumSet.range(Day.MON, Day.TUE);  EnumSet.allOf(Day.class);
EnumSet.noneOf(Day.class);  EnumSet.complementOf(set);
Map<Day, Integer> hours = new EnumMap<>(Day.class);

Iteration follows declaration order, not insertion order. put(null, …) throws NPE, though null values are allowed in EnumMap. Iterators are weakly consistent: changing the map during iteration does not throw (verified). Use these rather than HashMap or bit flags when keys are enums.

IdentityHashMap

Compares keys with == and uses System.identityHashCode, deliberately violating the general Map contract. It uses linear probing in one flat array, rather than chains: keys at even slots, values at the next odd slot. On a collision, it tries the next slot.

var m = new IdentityHashMap<String, Integer>();
m.put(new String("a"), 1);
m.put(new String("a"), 2);    // a different object: new entry
m.put("b", 1);
m.put("b", 2);                // the same interned literal: replaces
System.out.println(m.size()); // 3

Uses: object graph traversal (serializers and deep-copy code tracking visited objects, including cycles), and proxies where equals cannot be trusted.

WeakHashMap

Keys are held by weak references: an object reachable only through weak references can be collected. Entry extends WeakReference, and each is registered with a ReferenceQueue. After GC clears a key, the entry appears on the queue, and expungeStaleEntries() removes it during later operations such as get, put and size.

var m = new WeakHashMap<Object, String>();
Object keep = new Object();
m.put(keep, "v");
m.put("literal", "v");       // interned string: strongly reachable forever
m.put(new Object(), "gone"); // no other reference
System.gc();                 // only a hint; loop and sleep in real tests
// size eventually 2 (verified with a retry loop)
Gotcha: Values are held strongly. If a value references its own key, the key stays reachable and the entry is never cleared, which is a memory leak in a class that seems built to prevent them. Fix by wrapping the value in a WeakReference. size() can shrink between two calls with no writes.

Good for associating metadata with objects whose lifetime you do not control. It is not a general cache: entries vanish as soon as the key is unreferenced, regardless of memory pressure. SoftReference-based or Caffeine caches suit that better.

Hashtable

Java 1.0's hash table: every public method is synchronized on the instance. Null keys and values throw NPE. The default capacity is 11, and it grows to 2n + 1, keeping sizes odd. The index is (hash & 0x7FFFFFFF) % table.length, using a real modulo. It has fail-fast iterators, plus legacy Enumerations that are not fail-fast. It remains only for legacy APIs (Properties extends it). For new code use HashMap or ConcurrentHashMap.

ConcurrentHashMap

A hash map safe for concurrent use, in which reads do not block and writes contend only on a small part of the table. Its design changed completely in Java 8.

Java 7Java 8 and later
StructureSegment[], each a small hash table extending ReentrantLockOne Node[] table
Lock granularityOne segment; concurrencyLevel defaulted to 16One bin: CAS for an empty bin, synchronized on the first node otherwise
Long chainsListsTreeified bins (TreeBin)
ResizePer segment, under its lockIncremental: threads help move bins
size()Tried without locks, could lock every segmentSum of baseCount and CounterCells; no locking

Java 8+ put

  1. Reject null key or value. Spread the hash: (h ^ (h >>> 16)) & HASH_BITS, which clears the sign bit, as negative hashes are reserved for special nodes (MOVED = -1, TREEBIN = -2, RESERVED = -3).
  2. If the table is null, initialize it (sizeCtl coordinates which thread does that).
  3. If the bin is empty, CAS (compare-and-swap, an atomic CPU instruction) a new node into it. No lock. On failure, retry.
  4. If the first node's hash is MOVED, a resize is running; help transfer, then retry.
  5. Otherwise synchronized (firstNode), re-check it is still first, then update the list or tree.
  6. Treeify if needed, and update the count with addCount, which may start a resize.

get never locks. Node's val and next are volatile, and table slots are read with volatile semantics. During a resize, a ForwardingNode sends readers to the new table. Writing threads each claim a range of bins to move, so resizing is shared.

Using it correctly

Each method is atomic, but a sequence of methods is not.

// Race: two threads can both read the same value and lose an update
map.put(key, map.getOrDefault(key, 0) + 1);

// Atomic
map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum);
map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new LongAdder()).increment();

// 4 threads, 10000 merges each -> {k=40000} (verified)

Why no null keys or values? In a concurrent map, get(k) == null would be ambiguous, and you could not safely follow it with containsKey, as the map may change in between. Forbidding null means that null always means absent.

size() is an estimate while writes are happening. mappingCount() returns a long and is preferred. Iterators are weakly consistent. Bulk methods forEach, search and reduce take a parallelism threshold. ConcurrentHashMap.newKeySet() gives a concurrent Set. Keep compute* functions short: they run while holding the bin lock.

Other concurrent collections

CopyOnWriteArrayList

Holds a volatile array. Each write takes a lock, copies the entire array, modifies the copy, and swaps the reference. Reads use no lock. Iterators work on the array that existed when they were created (a snapshot), so they never throw CME, never see later changes, and iterator.remove() throws UnsupportedOperationException.

var cow = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2));
for (int x : cow) cow.add(x + 10);   // iterates the snapshot [1, 2]
System.out.println(cow);             // [1, 2, 11, 12]

Writes are O(n), and a burst of n writes costs O(n²) with a lot of garbage. It is meant for read-mostly lists such as event listeners. CopyOnWriteArraySet is built on it, so contains and add are O(n).

ConcurrentSkipListMap and ConcurrentSkipListSet

The concurrent equivalent of TreeMap: sorted, implementing ConcurrentNavigableMap. A skip list is a sorted linked list with extra index levels, where each level skips over roughly half the nodes below it, chosen by random coin flips. A search starts at the top and drops down, giving expected O(log n). There is no ConcurrentTreeMap, because a tree rebalance touches many nodes and is hard to do lock-free; a skip list insert only changes a few local pointers, done by CAS. No nulls. size() is O(n), as it traverses.

ConcurrentLinkedQueue and ConcurrentLinkedDeque

Unbounded, lock-free FIFO queue, using the Michael-Scott algorithm: CAS on head and tail pointers. poll returns null if empty, and never blocks. size() is O(n) and inexact, so use isEmpty(). Choose it for many fast producers and consumers when you do not need blocking or a bound.

BlockingQueue

A thread-safe queue whose operations can wait: put blocks when full, and take blocks when empty. This is the backbone of the producer-consumer pattern and of thread pools.

OperationThrowsReturns special valueBlocksTimes out
Insertadd(e)offer(e)put(e)offer(e, t, unit)
Removeremove()poll()take()poll(t, unit)
Examineelement()peek()n/an/a
ImplementationBounded?InternalsUse
ArrayBlockingQueueYes, fixedCircular array, one ReentrantLock, two Conditions; optional fairnessBackpressure with predictable memory
LinkedBlockingQueueOptional; default Integer.MAX_VALUELinked nodes, two locks (put and take), so producers and consumers rarely contendHigher throughput; unbounded default is a risk
LinkedBlockingDequeOptionalDoubly linked, one lockWork stealing, both-end access
PriorityBlockingQueueNoHeap with one lock; put never blocksPriority work queue
DelayQueueNoHeap of Delayed elements; available only once expiredScheduled retries, expiring entries
SynchronousQueueCapacity zeroDirect handoff: each insert waits for a removeExecutors.newCachedThreadPool
LinkedTransferQueueNoLock-free; transfer() waits until consumedHigh-throughput handoff
BlockingQueue<Integer> q = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(2);
final int POISON = -1;                      // sentinel to end the consumer

Thread producer = new Thread(() -> {
  try {
    for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++) q.put(i);  // blocks while full: backpressure
    q.put(POISON);
  } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
});
Thread consumer = new Thread(() -> {
  try {
    int sum = 0;
    for (int v; (v = q.take()) != POISON; ) sum += v;
    System.out.println("sum " + sum);       // sum 15
  } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
});

With bounded queues, offer returns false when full, add throws IllegalStateException: Queue full, and put waits. On a SynchronousQueue, offer returns false unless a consumer is already waiting, and size() is always 0.

Gotcha: Executors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. If tasks arrive faster than they finish, the queue grows until OutOfMemoryError. In production, build a ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy.

Synchronized wrappers

Collections.synchronizedList/Map/Set put a single lock (the wrapper object) around every method. Iteration is a compound action and must be locked by hand:

List<String> list = Collections.synchronizedList(new ArrayList<>());
synchronized (list) {
  for (String s : list) process(s);
}

Iterators

IteratorListIteratorSpliteratorEnumeration
Since1.21.281.0
DirectionForwardBothForward, splittableForward
Modifyremoveremove, set, addNoneNone
Key methodshasNext, nextprevious, nextIndextryAdvance, trySplit, characteristicshasMoreElements
Used byfor-eachListsStreams, parallel streamsLegacy Vector, Hashtable

The for-each loop is compiler sugar for an Iterator, so any Iterable works in it:

class Range implements Iterable<Integer> {
  final int from, to;
  Range(int f, int t) { from = f; to = t; }
  public Iterator<Integer> iterator() {
    return new Iterator<>() {
      int cur = from;
      public boolean hasNext() { return cur < to; }
      public Integer next() {
        if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
        return cur++;
      }
    };
  }
}
int sum = 0;
for (int x : new Range(1, 4)) sum += x;    // 6

iterator.remove() needs a prior next(), and it can be called once per next(); otherwise IllegalStateException. ListIterator.add inserts before the cursor.

Spliterator ("splittable iterator") is what streams consume. trySplit() hands off a part of the data to another thread. characteristics() reports properties such as SIZED, ORDERED, SORTED and DISTINCT, so a pipeline can skip needless work; for example sorted() on a SORTED source does nothing. An ArrayList spliterator with 8 elements splits into 4 and 4. A LinkedList splits poorly, which is why parallel streams favour arrays.

Fail-fast vs weakly consistent

Each non-concurrent collection has a modCount field, incremented on each structural change: adding or removing elements, not set() or replacing a map value. An iterator copies it to expectedModCount. next() compares them and throws ConcurrentModificationException on a mismatch. The iterator's own remove() resynchronizes the two.

Fail-fastWeakly consistentSnapshot
ExamplesArrayList, HashMap, TreeMapConcurrentHashMap, ConcurrentLinkedQueue, EnumMap, skip listsCopyOnWriteArrayList
Change during iterationThrows CME, best effortNo exception; may or may not see changesNo exception; never sees changes
CostA counter checkTraverses live structureThe copy is paid on write

"Fail-safe" is an informal term, not one used by the Java docs. They say "weakly consistent" and "snapshot". Fail-fast detection is best effort and not synchronized, so never rely on CME for correctness. The hasNext trap: the check is in next(), while hasNext() just tests cursor != size.

var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : list) if (s.equals("b")) list.remove(s);
System.out.println(list);  // [a, c] and no exception!

Removing the second-to-last element makes size 2 while cursor is 2, so hasNext() returns false, the loop exits, and next() never checks. Removing "a" or even "c" throws CME: for "c", cursor 3 differs from size 2, so the loop continues into next().

Comparable and Comparator

compareTo and compare return a negative number, zero or a positive number. They must be anti-symmetric (sign flips when swapped), transitive, and consistent: if a == b then they compare alike against any c. Being consistent with equals is strongly recommended, for sorted collections.

record Emp(String name, String dept, int salary) {}

// Department ascending, then salary descending
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept)
                    .thenComparing(Emp::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()));

// With primitives, avoid boxing
list.sort(Comparator.comparingInt(Emp::salary));

// Nulls
names.sort(Comparator.nullsFirst(Comparator.naturalOrder()));   // [null, a, b]
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder())));

// Map entries
map.entrySet().stream().sorted(Map.Entry.comparingByValue(Comparator.reverseOrder()));

Where reversed() sits matters. It reverses everything chained before it. With data a(x,3), b(y,2), c(x,5):

comparing(dept).thenComparing(salary, reverseOrder())  // [c, a, b]
comparing(dept).reversed().thenComparingInt(salary)    // [b, a, c]  only dept reversed
comparing(dept).thenComparingInt(salary).reversed()    // [b, c, a]  both reversed

Type inference trap: Comparator.comparing(e -> e.dept()).reversed() does not compile, because inference does not flow through the chained call, so the lambda's e is Object. Use a method reference, or write the type: (Emp e) -> e.dept().

Gotcha: Never write (a, b) -> a - b. It overflows: compare(Integer.MIN_VALUE, 1) gives 2147483647, a positive number, so MIN_VALUE sorts as larger. Use Integer.compare(a, b), which gives -1. A broken comparator can make TimSort throw IllegalArgumentException: Comparison method violates its general contract! (reproduced with a random comparator on 2000 elements).

Sorting algorithms

CallAlgorithmStable?TimeExtra space
Arrays.sort(int[]) and other primitivesDual-pivot quicksortNo (irrelevant for primitives)O(n log n)Usually O(log n) stack; may allocate a buffer to merge runs
Arrays.sort(Object[]), List.sort, Collections.sortTimSortYesO(n) best, O(n log n) worstUp to O(n)
Arrays.parallelSortParallel merge on the common ForkJoinPoolYes for objectsO(n log n)O(n)
stream.sorted()Buffers elements and uses the object sortYes for ordered streamsO(n log n)O(n)

Dual-pivot quicksort (Yaroslavskiy, Bentley, Bloch; Java 7) partitions around two pivots into three ranges, which does fewer memory swaps than classic quicksort. Plain quicksort has an O(n²) worst case; since JDK 14 the implementation falls back to heap sort when recursion gets too deep, and it uses insertion sort for tiny ranges.

TimSort (Tim Peters, from Python; in Java since 7) is a hybrid of merge sort and binary insertion sort. It looks for existing sorted runs (reversing strictly descending ones), extends short ones with binary insertion, and merges runs using a stack with balance rules. A "galloping" mode skips ahead when one run keeps winning. Real data often has order in it, so on sorted input it takes only n-1 comparisons.

Why two algorithms? Objects need stability: sorting employees by name and then department should keep names sorted in a department. Comparator calls can also be expensive, and TimSort minimizes them. Primitives have no identity, so stability cannot be observed, and quicksort's cache friendliness and in-place operation win.

Collections.sort(list) delegates to list.sort(null). ArrayList.sort sorts its array in place. The default List.sort, used by LinkedList, copies to an array, sorts, and writes back with a ListIterator.

Collections and Arrays utilities

java.util.Collections

  • sort, reverse, shuffle, swap, rotate
  • max, min, frequency, disjoint
  • binarySearch (the list must be sorted)
  • nCopies(n, x): immutable; one shared element
  • emptyList, singletonList: immutable
  • unmodifiableX, synchronizedX, checkedX: wrappers
  • addAll(c, a, b, c)

java.util.Arrays

  • sort, parallelSort, binarySearch
  • toString, deepToString
  • equals, deepEquals, hashCode
  • copyOf, copyOfRange
  • fill, setAll
  • asList, stream
  • mismatch, compare (Java 9)
int[] a = {1, 3, 5};
Arrays.binarySearch(a, 3);   // 1
Arrays.binarySearch(a, 4);   // -3    -(insertion point) - 1, insertion point 2
Arrays.binarySearch(a, 9);   // -4
new int[]{1}.equals(new int[]{1});          // false: arrays inherit Object.equals
Arrays.equals(new int[]{1}, new int[]{1});  // true
Arrays.deepToString(new int[][]{{1}, {2}}); // [[1], [2]]

A negative binarySearch result encodes where the key would go, which is why it is not simply -1. An unsorted array gives undefined results.

UOE = UnsupportedOperationException. Collectors.toUnmodifiableList() (Java 10) rejects nulls.

var src = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1));
var view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src);
var copy = List.copyOf(src);
src.add(2);
System.out.println(view + " " + copy);     // [1, 2] [1]

String[] arr = {"x", "y"};
List<String> l = Arrays.asList(arr);
l.set(0, "z");                             // arr[0] is now "z"
arr[1] = "w";                              // l is now [z, w]
l.add("q");                                // UnsupportedOperationException

int[] p = {1, 2};
Arrays.asList(p).size();                   // 1: a List<int[]>, generics cannot hold int
Arrays.asList(1, 2).size();                // 2

var imm = List.of(1);
System.out.println(List.copyOf(imm) == imm);  // true: no copy needed
  • Set.of(1, 1) throws IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element: 1. Map.of throws on duplicate keys.
  • Map.of takes up to 10 pairs; use Map.ofEntries(Map.entry(k, v), …) beyond that.
  • Iteration order of Set.of and Map.of is deliberately randomized per JVM run by a salt, so do not rely on it.
  • Internally there are compact classes such as ImmutableCollections.List12 and ListN.
  • All these are shallow: mutable elements can still change.

Sequenced collections (Java 21)

JEP 431 fixed a long-standing gap: there was no common type for "has a defined order", and getting the last element differed per type: list.get(list.size()-1), deque.getLast(), sortedSet.last(), and nothing at all on LinkedHashSet.

interface SequencedCollection<E> extends Collection<E> {
  SequencedCollection<E> reversed();
  void addFirst(E e);  void addLast(E e);
  E getFirst();        E getLast();
  E removeFirst();     E removeLast();
}
// SequencedSet: Set + SequencedCollection, reversed() returns SequencedSet
// SequencedMap: firstEntry, lastEntry, pollFirstEntry, pollLastEntry,
//               putFirst, putLast, reversed, sequencedKeySet/Values/EntrySet

List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet, LinkedHashMap and SortedMap were fitted into this hierarchy. HashSet is not sequenced.

var seq = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
seq.getFirst();                  // 1
var rev = seq.reversed();        // a live view, not a copy
seq.add(4);                      // rev is [4, 3, 2, 1]
rev.addFirst(9);                 // seq is [1, 2, 3, 4, 9]

var set = new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
set.addFirst(3);                 // moves 3: [3, 1, 2]

var map = new LinkedHashMap<String, Integer>();
map.put("a", 1); map.put("b", 2);
map.putFirst("c", 3);            // {c=3, a=1, b=2}

getFirst on an empty list throws NoSuchElementException. A sorted set's position comes from its comparator, so TreeSet.addFirst throws UnsupportedOperationException.

You needUse

Declare variables as interfaces (List<String> x = new ArrayList<>()) unless you need specific methods.

Map Default Methods: Exact Semantics

The Java 8 Map methods look alike but behave differently in two ways that interviewers check: when the value is computed (eagerly or lazily), and what a null result does.

MethodRuns whenValue argumentFunction returns nullReturns
putIfAbsent(k, v)Key absent or mapped to nullEager: v is built even if unusedn/aPrevious value (null if it inserted)
computeIfAbsent(k, f)Key absent or nullLazy: f called only if neededNothing storedCurrent (or new) value
computeIfPresent(k, f)Key present with a non-null valueLazyRemoves the entryNew value or null
compute(k, f)Always; f gets null if absentLazyRemoves the entryNew value or null
merge(k, v, f)Absent: stores v; present: f(old, v)v must be non-nullRemoves the entryNew value or null
cache.putIfAbsent(id, loadFromDb(id));           // BUG: hits the DB on every call
cache.computeIfAbsent(id, this::loadFromDb);     // loads only on a miss

stock.merge(sku, -1, Integer::sum);              // decrement
stock.computeIfPresent(sku, (k, q) -> q <= 1 ? null : q - 1);   // decrement, remove at zero

index.computeIfAbsent(tag, t -> new ArrayList<>()).add(post);   // multimap
// NOT putIfAbsent(tag, new ArrayList<>()).add(post): it returns null the first time, so NPE

Converting Between Arrays, Lists and Primitives

List<String> names = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b"));
String[] arr1 = names.toArray(new String[0]);    // preferred: the JVM sizes it, and it is as fast or faster
String[] arr2 = names.toArray(String[]::new);    // Java 11, same result
Object[] objs = names.toArray();                 // Object[], cannot be cast to String[]

List<String> fixed = Arrays.asList(arr1);        // fixed-size view: set OK, add/remove throw; writes reach arr1
List<String> copy  = List.of(arr1);              // immutable copy, rejects nulls
List<String> mut   = new ArrayList<>(Arrays.asList(arr1));   // independent mutable copy

int[] nums = {3, 1, 2};
List<Integer> boxed = Arrays.stream(nums).boxed().toList();           // int[] to List<Integer>
int[] back = boxed.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();    // List<Integer> to int[]
Integer[] wrappers = boxed.toArray(Integer[]::new);
Set<Integer> set = IntStream.of(nums).boxed().collect(Collectors.toSet());

There is no direct cast between int[] and Integer[], because they are unrelated array types. Every conversion boxes or unboxes each element.

Interview Questions — Collections Deep Dive

How does ArrayList grow? What is the default capacity?

A no-arg ArrayList begins with a shared empty array and allocates 10 slots on the first add. When full, new capacity is old + (old >> 1), or 1.5 times, and elements are copied with System.arraycopy. Observed capacities: 10, 15, 22, 33. Adds are amortized O(1) because the growth is geometric. Pre-size if you know the count.

Predict the output. 
List<Integer> list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3, 4));
list.remove(1);
list.remove(Integer.valueOf(1));
System.out.println(list);

[3, 4]. remove(1) with an int picks remove(int index) and removes the value 2. remove(Integer) picks remove(Object) and removes the value 1. Overload resolution prefers no boxing.

Predict the output. 
var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b", "c"));
for (String s : list) if (s.equals("b")) list.remove(s);
System.out.println(list);

[a, c], with no exception. "b" is second-to-last. After removal, size is 2 and the iterator's cursor is 2, so hasNext() returns false and next(), which contains the modCount check, is never called. Remove "a" or "c" instead, and you get ConcurrentModificationException.

Predict the output. 
Set<Short> set = new HashSet<>();
for (short i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
  set.add(i);
  set.remove(i - 1);
}
System.out.println(set.size());

5. i - 1 is an int, so it boxes to Integer. remove(Object) accepts it, but an Integer never equals a Short, so nothing is removed. The same trap: List<Long>.contains(1) is false, and contains(1L) is true.

What does subList return? What can go wrong?

A view on the parent list. Non-structural and structural changes through the view pass to the parent. A structural change on the parent after creating the view makes later view calls throw ConcurrentModificationException. Retaining a small sublist also keeps the entire parent array alive. Copy it when you need independence.

How do you remove elements from a list while iterating?
list.removeIf(x -> x < 0);                     // best, O(n)

for (Iterator<Integer> it = list.iterator(); it.hasNext(); )
  if (it.next() < 0) it.remove();              // O(n²) for ArrayList

for (int i = list.size() - 1; i >= 0; i--)     // backward index loop
  if (list.get(i) < 0) list.remove(i);

A forward index loop skips the element after each removal, and for-each throws CME.

Why is LinkedList usually slower than ArrayList even for insertions?

Getting to position i takes O(n) pointer hops, each a likely cache miss, since nodes are scattered in memory. ArrayList does an O(n) shift, too, but as one fast bulk memory move in contiguous memory. LinkedList also allocates a node per element, adding GC pressure. LinkedList's O(1) advantage holds only at the ends, where ArrayDeque is better, or when you already have an iterator at the position.

Why should you prefer ArrayDeque over Stack and LinkedList?

Stack extends synchronized Vector, paying for locks you rarely need, and exposes index methods that break LIFO. LinkedList allocates a node per element. ArrayDeque is a circular array with amortized O(1) at both ends and good locality. It forbids nulls, and iterates from the head, so a stack built with push iterates top-first.

How does PriorityQueue work? Is printing it sorted?

It is a binary heap in an array. Parent at (i-1)/2, children at 2i+1 and 2i+2. Add sifts up, and poll moves the last element to the root and sifts down, both O(log n). Printing shows array order, which is not sorted: inserting 5,1,4,2,3 prints [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Only polling returns sorted order: 12345.

Find the K most frequent words.
static List<String> topK(List<String> words, int k) {
  Map<String, Integer> freq = new HashMap<>();
  words.forEach(w -> freq.merge(w, 1, Integer::sum));
  var heap = new PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<String, Integer>>(Map.Entry.comparingByValue());
  for (var e : freq.entrySet()) {
    heap.offer(e);
    if (heap.size() > k) heap.poll();     // evict the smallest
  }
  List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
  while (!heap.isEmpty()) out.add(heap.poll().getKey());
  Collections.reverse(out);
  return out;
}
topK(List.of("a","b","a","c","a","b"), 2);   // [a, b]

O(n log k), and it holds only k entries in the heap. Sorting all entries would be O(n log n). The trick is a min-heap of size k for the largest k.

Why does HashMap XOR the hash with its upper 16 bits?

The index comes from only the low bits (hash & (n-1)). Hash codes that differ only in high bits, such as Floats or shifted keys, would all land in the same bin. h ^ (h >>> 16) mixes the high half into the low half. It is one cheap operation, since tree bins already handle the worst cases.

Why must the table size be a power of two? What happens with new HashMap<>(17)?

So that hash & (n-1) equals a non-negative modulo, using a fast mask, and so that resizing can split each bin by a single bit. The constructor rounds up: 17 gives 32, allocated at the first put. A downside is that weak hash functions are exposed, which is why the bits are spread.

When exactly does a bin treeify? Is it at 8 nodes?

The check fires while appending to a list that already has 8 nodes, so the conversion happens when the 9th node arrives, and only if the table has at least 64 slots. If it is smaller, the map doubles instead. Verified on Java 21 by reflection with keys that have the same hash: from capacity 64, the 9th key created TreeNodes. From capacity 16, the 9th key resized to 32, the 10th to 64, and the 11th treeified.

What happens during resize? Does it recompute hashCode?

No. Each node stores its hash. Doubling adds one index bit. Each bin splits into a lo list staying at j and a hi list moving to j + oldCap, based on hash & oldCap. Relative order is kept. Resizing is O(n), so pre-size large maps. It also never shrinks automatically: removing all entries leaves a big table, and iteration stays proportional to capacity.

Why was HashMap dangerous under concurrency in Java 7, and is it safe in Java 8?

Java 7 used head insertion during transfer, reversing lists. Two threads resizing together could form a circular list, so get hung at 100% CPU. Java 8's tail insertion with lo/hi splitting removes that specific failure, but HashMap is still unsafe: lost updates, wrong size, and corrupted tree bins remain possible. Use ConcurrentHashMap.

Can two unequal objects have the same hashCode? What happens if hashCode returns a constant?

Yes, that is a collision; "Aa" and "BB" both hash to 2112. A constant hashCode is legal and the map still works correctly, but everything lands in one bin: O(n) with a list, O(log n) once it is a tree. If keys are not Comparable, tree lookups may need to search both subtrees, so they degrade further.

What happens if you override equals but not hashCode?

Equal objects get different identity hashes, so they usually go to different bins. map.get(equalKey) returns null, and a HashSet holds duplicates. If you override hashCode only, two objects share a bin but equals (identity) says they differ, so duplicates remain.

Predict the output. 
var set = new HashSet<List<Integer>>();
var list = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1));
set.add(list);
list.add(2);
System.out.println(set.contains(list) + " " + set.size());

false 1. A list's hashCode depends on its elements. After the change, contains looks in a different bin. The element remains in the old bin, unreachable by lookup.

Is get returning null proof that a key is absent? What does {null=2, a=null} teach?

No. HashMap allows one null key (hash 0, bin 0) and null values. So get("a") and get("zz") both return null while containsKey differs. getOrDefault and putIfAbsent treat null values differently from each other too: putIfAbsent replaces a null value, whereas getOrDefault returns the stored null.

How would you implement a HashMap from scratch?
class MyMap<K, V> {
  private static class Entry<K, V> {
    final int hash; final K key; V value; Entry<K, V> next;
    Entry(int h, K k, V v, Entry<K, V> n) { hash = h; key = k; value = v; next = n; }
  }
  @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
  private Entry<K, V>[] table = new Entry[16];
  private int size;

  private static int hash(Object k) {
    int h;
    return k == null ? 0 : (h = k.hashCode()) ^ (h >>> 16);
  }
  V get(K key) {
    int h = hash(key);
    for (var e = table[h & (table.length - 1)]; e != null; e = e.next)
      if (e.hash == h && Objects.equals(e.key, key)) return e.value;
    return null;
  }
  V put(K key, V value) {
    int h = hash(key), i = h & (table.length - 1);
    for (var e = table[i]; e != null; e = e.next)
      if (e.hash == h && Objects.equals(e.key, key)) {
        V old = e.value; e.value = value; return old;
      }
    table[i] = new Entry<>(h, key, value, table[i]);
    if (++size > table.length * 3 / 4) resize();
    return null;
  }
  @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
  private void resize() {
    Entry<K, V>[] old = table;
    table = new Entry[old.length * 2];
    for (var bucket : old)
      for (var e = bucket; e != null; ) {
        var next = e.next;
        int i = e.hash & (table.length - 1);
        e.next = table[i]; table[i] = e;
        e = next;
      }
  }
}

Tested with 100 keys plus a null key. Mention what is left out in an interview: removal, tree bins, tail insertion, thread safety, iteration.

Implement an LRU cache without LinkedHashMap, with O(1) get and put.

A HashMap gives O(1) lookup. A doubly linked list gives O(1) move and eviction. Sentinels remove null checks.

final class LruCache<K, V> {
  private final class Node { K key; V val; Node prev, next;
    Node(K k, V v) { key = k; val = v; } }
  private final Map<K, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
  private final int capacity;
  private final Node head = new Node(null, null), tail = new Node(null, null);

  LruCache(int capacity) {
    this.capacity = capacity;
    head.next = tail; tail.prev = head;
  }
  V get(K key) {
    Node n = map.get(key);
    if (n == null) return null;
    unlink(n); linkFirst(n);
    return n.val;
  }
  void put(K key, V val) {
    Node n = map.get(key);
    if (n != null) { n.val = val; unlink(n); linkFirst(n); return; }
    if (map.size() == capacity) {
      Node lru = tail.prev;
      unlink(lru);
      map.remove(lru.key);
    }
    n = new Node(key, val);
    map.put(key, n);
    linkFirst(n);
  }
  private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
  private void linkFirst(Node n) {
    n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
    head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
  }
}
// capacity 2: put a, put b, get a, put c, then get a / b / c gives 1 null 3
How does LinkedHashMap maintain order? What does accessOrder do?

It extends HashMap, and entries have before and after links. accessOrder=true moves an entry to the tail on get and put. Overriding removeEldestEntry gives eviction. In access order, get counts as a structural change, so for (k : map.keySet()) map.get(k) throws CME.

Does re-inserting a key change LinkedHashMap's insertion order?

No. Put a=1, b=2, a=3 yields {a=3, b=2}. Since Java 21, putLast and putFirst reposition a key explicitly.

How does TreeMap decide keys are equal?

Only by compareTo or compare returning 0. equals and hashCode are unused. With a length comparator, put("aa", 1); put("bb", 2); prints {aa=2}: the original key remains, and the value is replaced.

Predict the sizes. 
new HashSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size();
new TreeSet<>(List.of(new BigDecimal("1.0"), new BigDecimal("1.00"))).size();

2 and 1. BigDecimal.equals considers scale, so the HashSet keeps both. compareTo ignores scale, so the TreeSet sees one value.

What is a red-black tree, and why is it used in TreeMap and HashMap?

A self-balancing BST with colour rules that keep the height at about 2 log₂ n, with few rotations per update. It offers guaranteed O(log n). HashMap uses it for overflowing bins, and TreeMap as its main structure. A plain BST degrades to a linked list on sorted input; red-black trees do not.

Give a use for floorEntry or ceilingEntry.

Tiered pricing: tiers.floorEntry(quantity).getValue() finds the band a quantity falls in. A consistent hash ring: ring.ceilingEntry(hash) finds the next node clockwise, wrapping with firstEntry(). In both, a TreeMap replaces a chain of if-statements or a linear scan.

How is HashSet implemented? Why does add return a boolean?

It wraps a HashMap, using elements as keys and a shared static dummy object as the value. add returns true if map.put returned null, that is, if the key is new. The dummy exists so that put returns non-null for an existing key.

Why use EnumSet instead of HashSet of enum?

It is a bit vector, one long for up to 64 constants. Operations become bit operations, there is no hashing or per-element node, and iteration is in declaration order. It is also more readable than integer flags: EnumSet.of(READ, WRITE).

How does IdentityHashMap differ from HashMap?

It compares keys by reference (==) with System.identityHashCode, and it uses linear probing in a flat array with keys and values in alternate slots. So it violates the Map contract on purpose. Use it for tracking object identity, as in graph copying and cycle detection. Two new String("a") keys are two entries.

When would a WeakHashMap entry never get removed?

When the key stays strongly reachable: a string literal, a key still referenced elsewhere, or a value that references the key. The map holds values strongly, so a value pointing to its key keeps it alive forever. Also, stale entries are purged only when the map is used.

How does ConcurrentHashMap achieve thread safety in Java 8+? How is it different from Java 7?

Java 7 used 16 (by default) Segment locks, each with its own table. Java 8 has one table: reads use volatile access with no lock, empty bins are filled by CAS, and occupied bins are locked with synchronized on the first node. Resize is shared between threads through forwarding nodes. Counting is striped. Long bins become TreeBins.

Is this thread-safe? 
ConcurrentHashMap<String, Integer> m = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
if (!m.containsKey(k)) m.put(k, 1);
else m.put(k, m.get(k) + 1);

No. Each call is atomic, but the sequence is check-then-act. Two threads can read the same value and lose an increment. Use m.merge(k, 1, Integer::sum). For very hot counters, use LongAdder values.

Why doesn't ConcurrentHashMap allow null?

Null would be ambiguous. In a HashMap you can follow a null get with containsKey, but concurrently the state may change between calls. Forbidding it means that get returning null always means "not present at that moment". Doug Lea has also said that nulls in maps invite errors in general.

Is ConcurrentHashMap.size() accurate? Can an iterator miss updates?

While writers are active, it is an estimate. Use it for monitoring, not logic. mappingCount() avoids int overflow. Iterators are weakly consistent: they reflect the state at some point at or after creation, never throw CME, and may or may not show concurrent changes.

Predict the result. 
var m = new ConcurrentHashMap<Integer, Integer>();
m.computeIfAbsent(1, k -> m.computeIfAbsent(1, j -> 2));

On Java 21 it throws IllegalStateException: Recursive update. Older versions could hang (notably Java 8). A mapping function must never update the same map. The HashMap version with an inner put throws ConcurrentModificationException.

Hashtable vs synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap under load?

The first two use one lock for the entire map, so all threads queue up, even for reads. ConcurrentHashMap lets reads run without locks and writers proceed in parallel on different bins, so throughput scales with cores. Atomic compound methods exist on it. A synchronizedMap iteration needs a manual lock for its whole duration; a ConcurrentHashMap iteration needs none.

When is CopyOnWriteArrayList a bad choice?

With frequent writes or large lists: each write copies the whole array, costing O(n) and much garbage. It suits small, read-mostly lists such as listener registrations. Iterators see an old snapshot, which can be stale, and they do not support remove.

Predict the output. 
var cow = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2));
for (int x : cow) cow.add(x + 10);
System.out.println(cow);

[1, 2, 11, 12]. The loop iterates over the array at the moment it began. With a normal ArrayList, this would throw CME. And there is no infinite loop.

Why is there no ConcurrentTreeMap?

A red-black rebalance changes several nodes at once near the root, so it is hard to make non-blocking without a global lock. Skip list updates are local and can be done by CAS. The result, ConcurrentSkipListMap, is sorted and scales well. It uses more memory and has slower constant factors than a TreeMap in single-threaded use.

ArrayBlockingQueue vs LinkedBlockingQueue?

ArrayBlockingQueue is always bounded, preallocates its array, and uses one lock, so puts and takes contend. LinkedBlockingQueue uses two locks, so producers and consumers can run in parallel. It allocates a node per element and is effectively unbounded unless given a capacity. Choose ArrayBlockingQueue for stable memory and strict limits, or LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) for throughput.

What is SynchronousQueue, and why does newCachedThreadPool use it?

It has no storage: an insert waits for a matching remove. A ThreadPoolExecutor adds a new thread only when its queue refuses a task. Since offer fails unless a worker is already waiting, tasks go to an idle worker or else create a thread. This gives instant dispatch but unbounded thread growth under load.

What is the difference between add, offer and put? remove, poll, take?

add and remove throw on failure (IllegalStateException, NoSuchElementException). offer and poll return false or null. put and take block. Only BlockingQueues have put and take.

How is fail-fast implemented? Is CME guaranteed?

Using a modCount incremented on structural changes, and expectedModCount in the iterator, checked in next(). It is not guaranteed: it is unsynchronized, and the docs say it is best effort, for bug detection only. set and replacing a map value do not trigger it. For example, map.put(existingKey, v) during iteration of a HashMap is fine.

What does a ListIterator let you do? Predict the output. 
var li = new ArrayList<>(List.of("a", "b")).listIterator();
li.next();
li.add("x");
li.next();
li.set("B");
while (li.hasPrevious()) System.out.print(li.previous());

Bxa. After next (a), add inserts x before the cursor. The next call returns b, and set replaces it with B. Going backward gives B, x, a.

What is a Spliterator, and why does ArrayList parallelize better than LinkedList?

It is an iterator that can split its source for parallel work, and reports traits such as SIZED and ORDERED. ArrayList's trySplit computes a midpoint in O(1) and gives balanced halves. LinkedList has to walk nodes and copies batches to an array, so splitting is costly and unbalanced.

What is wrong with (a, b) -> a - b as a comparator?

Overflow: Integer.MIN_VALUE - 1 wraps to 2147483647. The result claims MIN_VALUE is greater. It breaks transitivity and can trigger "Comparison method violates its general contract!". Use Integer.compare or Comparator.comparingInt.

Sort employees by dept ascending, salary descending, nulls last. Why might reversed() surprise you?
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(Emp::dept, Comparator.nullsLast(Comparator.naturalOrder()))
                    .thenComparing(Emp::salary, Comparator.reverseOrder()));

reversed() flips the whole comparator built so far. Putting it at the end also reverses dept. Use the two-argument thenComparing for one key. With a lambda before reversed(), the type has to be given explicitly.

Which sort does Java use, and why are there two?

Primitives use dual-pivot quicksort (fast, in place, with stability meaningless). Objects use TimSort (stable, adaptive, fewer comparisons, O(n) on sorted data). parallelSort uses Fork/Join merging.

Arrays.asList vs List.of vs new ArrayList<>(…)?

Arrays.asList: fixed size, set allowed, writes through to the array, allows nulls. List.of: immutable, no nulls, contains(null) throws NPE. new ArrayList<>(…): a fully mutable independent copy. Arrays.asList(int[]) gives a list with a single element, the array itself.

Is Collections.unmodifiableList immutable?

No. It is a read-only view. Anyone with the original reference can change it, and the view shows that. For a true snapshot, use List.copyOf. In a getter, returning an unmodifiable view is a reasonable way to prevent changes while avoiding copying, if the changing visibility is acceptable.

stream.toList() vs collect(Collectors.toList())?

toList() (Java 16) returns an unmodifiable list and allows nulls. Collectors.toList() gives an unspecified mutable list, an ArrayList today. Replacing one by the other can cause UnsupportedOperationException if code later adds to the result.

What did sequenced collections add in Java 21?

Three interfaces: SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap, giving uniform getFirst, getLast, addFirst, addLast, removeFirst, removeLast and reversed. reversed() is a live view. Existing types were adjusted, and LinkedHashSet finally got a way to reach its last element. Sorted collections reject addFirst with UOE. Note that adding reversed and getFirst can conflict with same-named methods in your own List subclasses.

Do these print true? 
new ArrayList<>(List.of(1)).equals(new LinkedList<>(List.of(1)));
new HashSet<>(List.of(1)).equals(new TreeSet<>(List.of(1)));
List.of(1).equals(Set.of(1));

true, true, false. The List contract defines equals by elements in order, regardless of implementation, and Set by elements. A List never equals a Set.

Two Sum: find indexes of two numbers adding up to a target.
static int[] twoSum(int[] nums, int target) {
  Map<Integer, Integer> seen = new HashMap<>();
  for (int i = 0; i < nums.length; i++) {
    Integer j = seen.get(target - nums[i]);
    if (j != null) return new int[]{j, i};
    seen.put(nums[i], i);
  }
  return new int[0];
}
twoSum(new int[]{2, 7, 11, 15}, 9);   // [0, 1]

O(n) time and O(n) space, trading memory for the nested O(n²) search.

Group anagrams.
static Collection<List<String>> group(List<String> words) {
  Map<String, List<String>> m = new LinkedHashMap<>();
  for (String s : words) {
    char[] c = s.toCharArray();
    Arrays.sort(c);
    m.computeIfAbsent(new String(c), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(s);
  }
  return m.values();
}
// eat tea tan ate nat bat -> [[eat, tea, ate], [tan, nat], [bat]]

The sorted letters form the canonical key. Note that a char[] cannot be a key: arrays use identity equals.

First non-repeating character.
static Character firstUnique(String s) {
  Map<Character, Integer> count = new LinkedHashMap<>();
  for (char c : s.toCharArray()) count.merge(c, 1, Integer::sum);
  for (var e : count.entrySet()) if (e.getValue() == 1) return e.getKey();
  return null;
}
firstUnique("swiss");    // w

LinkedHashMap keeps first-seen order, so the second loop finds the earliest.

Check balanced brackets.
static boolean balanced(String s) {
  Deque<Character> st = new ArrayDeque<>();
  for (char c : s.toCharArray()) {
    switch (c) {
      case '(' -> st.push(')');
      case '[' -> st.push(']');
      case '{' -> st.push('}');
      default -> { if (st.isEmpty() || st.pop() != c) return false; }
    }
  }
  return st.isEmpty();
}
balanced("{[()]}");   // true
balanced("(]");       // false
Sliding window maximum in O(n).
static int[] slide(int[] a, int k) {
  int[] r = new int[a.length - k + 1];
  Deque<Integer> d = new ArrayDeque<>();   // indexes, values decreasing
  for (int i = 0; i < a.length; i++) {
    while (!d.isEmpty() && d.peekFirst() <= i - k) d.pollFirst();
    while (!d.isEmpty() && a[d.peekLast()] <= a[i]) d.pollLast();
    d.offerLast(i);
    if (i >= k - 1) r[i - k + 1] = a[d.peekFirst()];
  }
  return r;
}
slide(new int[]{1, 3, -1, -3, 5, 3, 6, 7}, 3);   // [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]

Each index enters and leaves the deque once, so the total work is O(n).

Merge overlapping intervals.
static List<int[]> merge(int[][] in) {
  Arrays.sort(in, Comparator.comparingInt(x -> x[0]));
  List<int[]> out = new ArrayList<>();
  for (int[] c : in) {
    if (out.isEmpty() || out.getLast()[1] < c[0]) out.add(c.clone());
    else out.getLast()[1] = Math.max(out.getLast()[1], c[1]);
  }
  return out;
}
// {1,3},{8,10},{2,6} -> [1,6],[8,10]
Remove duplicates from a list while keeping the order.
new ArrayList<>(new LinkedHashSet<>(List.of(3, 1, 3, 2, 1)));   // [3, 1, 2]
list.stream().distinct().toList();                             // also order-preserving
Scenario: a service's HashMap cache keeps growing and memory rises. How do you diagnose and fix it?
  1. Take a heap dump and check the dominators in Eclipse MAT. An unbounded HashMap shows up with a huge retained size.
  2. Check for keys that never repeat, or mutable keys, which strand entries.
  3. Replace it with a bounded cache: Caffeine with maximumSize and expireAfterWrite, and hit-rate metrics.
  4. If shared between threads, also check for data races on the plain HashMap.
Scenario: you need a thread-safe top-N leaderboard with many score updates and reads of the top entries. What would you use?

Use a ConcurrentHashMap<PlayerId, Score> for current scores, and a ConcurrentSkipListSet<ScoreEntry> sorted by score then ID, so that first() and an iterator give the top N. An update removes the old entry and inserts the new one; lock per player or use compute on the map to keep the two structures in step. ScoreEntry must be immutable, and its comparator must include the ID, or equal scores would collapse. At scale, use a Redis sorted set.

Scenario: 10 million lookups per second by integer ID on a read-only dataset of 5 million entries. Is HashMap right?

HashMap would box every key, add one node per entry, and scatter memory. That costs tens of bytes per entry and many cache misses. Better: if IDs are dense, a plain array indexed by ID. Otherwise a sorted int[] with Arrays.binarySearch, or a primitive open-addressing map from a library such as fastutil. Benchmark with JMH using realistic keys. For reads only, immutability removes any need for synchronization.

putIfAbsent vs computeIfAbsent: which is right for a cache?

computeIfAbsent. putIfAbsent(k, expensive()) evaluates its argument before the call, so the expensive work runs on every hit. computeIfAbsent calls the function only on a miss.
