How do you debug a stream pipeline that gives the wrong result?
  • Use the IDE's stream debugger (IntelliJ "Trace Current Stream Chain"), which shows each element at every stage.
  • Add temporary peek(e -> log.debug("after filter: {}", e)) calls between stages, and remember that laziness and short-circuiting mean some elements never reach later stages.
  • Replace complex lambdas with named methods (.filter(this::isEligible)), so they can be unit-tested and appear clearly in stack traces.
  • Split a long chain into named intermediate variables, or collect to a list at a midpoint while investigating.
Explain currying with an example. Is it common in Java?

Currying turns f(a, b) into a -> (b -> result), for example Function<Integer, Function<Integer, Integer>> add = a -> b -> a + b; add.apply(2).apply(3), which gives 5. Its practical value is partial application: building specialized functions from general ones (discount.apply(0.1) gives a "10% off" function). Full currying is rare in Java because the nested generic types get verbose. The everyday form is a factory method that returns a lambda capturing configuration, such as Comparator.comparing(keyExtractor), Predicate.not(...) or maxLen(20).

When would you define your own functional interface instead of using java.util.function?

Define your own when:

  • you need more than two arguments (there is no TriFunction);
  • the function must throw a checked exception (interface SqlFunction<T, R> { R apply(T t) throws SQLException; });
  • a domain name makes the API clearer (PricingRule, RetryPolicy), possibly with default helper methods.

Annotate it with @FunctionalInterface, so the compiler rejects a second abstract method being added. Otherwise prefer the standard types, including the primitive variants such as IntPredicate, because every developer and library already understands them.

@FunctionalInterface
interface TriFunction<A, B, C, R> {
    R apply(A a, B b, C c);
}
TriFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer, Integer> vol = (l, w, h) -> l * w * h;

Multithreading & Concurrency Core Java

Threads, monitors, the Java Memory Model, locks, atomics, executors, CompletableFuture, virtual threads and the failure modes interviewers ask about, explained from the mechanism up.

Process vs Thread

A process is a running program with its own address space, file handles and at least one thread. A thread is one path of execution inside a process. Threads of the same process share the heap and method area, but each thread has its own stack and program counter. That shared heap is why threads communicate cheaply, and also why they can corrupt each other's data.

AspectProcessThread
MemoryIsolated address spaceShares heap with sibling threads; private stack
Creation costHighLower, but a platform thread still costs an OS thread and a reserved stack (commonly 1 MB on 64-bit, set by -Xss)
Context switchMore expensive: address-space switchCheaper: same address space
CommunicationPipes, sockets, shared memoryShared objects, guarded by synchronization
FailureA crash stays in that processA native crash kills the process; an uncaught Java exception kills only that thread

Concurrency means dealing with many tasks over the same period, possibly by switching between them on one core. Parallelism means running tasks at the same instant on several cores. A web server handling 1,000 slow requests is mainly a concurrency problem. Summing a billion numbers on 8 cores is a parallelism problem.

Almost every bug in this section comes from one of three causes:

  • Atomicity: an operation that looks like one step is really several, and another thread slips in between.
  • Visibility: a write by one thread is not guaranteed to be seen by another without synchronization.
  • Ordering: the compiler, JIT and CPU may reorder operations as long as the current thread can't tell.

Creating Threads

// 1. Runnable passed to Thread: separates the task from the mechanism
Thread t1 = new Thread(() -> System.out.println("hi"), "worker-1");
t1.start();

// 2. Subclass Thread: works, but uses up your single inheritance
class Worker extends Thread { @Override public void run() { /* task */ } }
new Worker().start();

// 3. Callable + FutureTask: a result and checked exceptions without a pool
FutureTask<Integer> task = new FutureTask<>(() -> 6 * 7);
new Thread(task).start();
int answer = task.get();           // blocks until done

// 4. Thread builders (Java 21)
Thread p = Thread.ofPlatform().name("io-", 0).daemon().start(() -> {});
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().name("v-", 0).start(() -> {});

// 5. What production code normally does: hand tasks to an executor
try (ExecutorService pool = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(4)) {
    pool.submit(() -> System.out.println("in a pool"));
}                                  // close() waits for tasks (Java 19+)

Prefer option 5. A raw new Thread per task has no upper bound, no reuse and no handle for the result. Name your threads either way: a thread dump full of Thread-37 tells you nothing.

The Thread API

start() vs run()

start() asks the JVM to create a new thread of execution, which then calls run(). Calling run() directly is an ordinary method call on the current thread. A thread can be started once. Starting it again throws IllegalThreadStateException, even after it finished.

Thread t = new Thread(() -> System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName()), "worker");
t.run();     // prints main
t.start();   // prints worker
t.join();
t.start();   // IllegalThreadStateException

join, sleep, yield

  • t.join() blocks the caller until t ends. When it returns, everything t wrote is visible to the caller. On platform threads it's implemented with wait() on the Thread object, which is one reason not to synchronize on Thread objects yourself. Timed forms exist, including join(Duration) (Java 19).
  • Thread.sleep(ms) pauses the current thread. It keeps every lock it holds. It's a static method: otherThread.sleep(100) compiles, but it sleeps the current thread.
  • Thread.yield() is a hint that the current thread is willing to give up the CPU. The scheduler can ignore it, so correct code never depends on it. Thread.onSpinWait() (Java 9) is the hint for spin loops.

Daemon threads

The JVM exits when only daemon threads remain, without waiting for them. Their finally blocks may never run, so don't let a daemon own work that must complete, such as flushing a file. setDaemon(true) must be called before start(), otherwise it throws IllegalThreadStateException. A new thread inherits the daemon status of its creator. ForkJoinPool workers and all virtual threads are daemon threads, which is why a main that fires CompletableFuture.runAsync and returns can exit before the work finishes.

Priority

Priorities run from 1 to 10, with a default of 5. They are only hints mapped to the OS scheduler, and HotSpot on Linux ignores them under default settings. Never use priority to get correctness. Virtual threads always report 5, and setPriority on them has no effect.

Interruption: the cooperative cancellation protocol

Java has no safe way to kill a thread. Thread.stop() released locks mid-update and left objects corrupted, so it was deprecated long ago and has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20. The replacement is interruption: one thread politely asks another to stop, and the target decides when and how.

Each thread has an interrupt flag. t.interrupt() sets it, and blocked threads may react to it:

What the target is doingWhat interrupt() does
sleep, wait, join, BlockingQueue.take, Lock.lockInterruptibly, Condition.awaitThrows InterruptedException and clears the flag
Blocked on an InterruptibleChannelCloses the channel and throws ClosedByInterruptException; the flag stays set
Blocked in Selector.selectReturns immediately; the flag stays set
Waiting to enter synchronized, or in Lock.lock()Nothing visible. The flag is set and the wait continues
Running ordinary codeOnly sets the flag. The code must check it

Two methods read the flag, and they differ in a way interviewers love. t.isInterrupted() reads it. The static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears the current thread's flag.

public void run() {
    try {
        while (!Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted()) {   // CPU work checks the flag
            Job job = queue.take();                         // blocking call throws
            job.process();
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();                 // restore, then leave
    } finally {
        cleanup();
    }
}
Gotcha: Never write catch (InterruptedException e) {}. The exception cleared the flag, so swallowing it erases the stop request and the code above you never finds out. Either rethrow it, or call Thread.currentThread().interrupt() to put the flag back.

A plain volatile boolean running flag also works for loops, but it can't wake a thread stuck in take(). Interruption can.

Uncaught exceptions

An exception that escapes run() ends that thread only. main and other threads carry on. The JVM calls the thread's UncaughtExceptionHandler, or the default handler set with Thread.setDefaultUncaughtExceptionHandler, which otherwise prints the stack trace to stderr.

Thread Lifecycle in Detail

Thread.State has six values. The Core Java overview has a diagram of them; this table gives the exact transitions, including the two that are often taught wrong.

StateMeaningEntered byLeft by
NEWCreated, not startednew Thread(...)start()
RUNNABLERunning or ready to run. The JVM doesn't separate them. It also covers a thread stuck in a blocking native call such as a socket readstart(), getting the monitor, being unparkedBlocking, waiting or finishing
BLOCKEDWaiting for a monitor only: entering synchronized, or re-entering it after wait()The monitor is held by someone elseAcquiring the monitor
WAITINGWaiting with no timeoutwait(), join(), LockSupport.park(), which includes ReentrantLock.lock()notify, thread end, unpark, interrupt
TIMED_WAITINGWaiting with a timeoutsleep(ms), wait(ms), join(ms), parkNanosTimeout or the same events as WAITING
TERMINATEDrun() finishedNormal return or uncaught exceptionNever
Interview: A thread woken by notify() does not go straight to RUNNABLE. It must take the monitor back first, so it goes WAITING → BLOCKED → RUNNABLE. A test run on Java 21 showed the state as BLOCKED for as long as the notifying thread kept the lock. Second trap: a thread queued on ReentrantLock.lock() shows as WAITING, not BLOCKED, because that lock parks the thread instead of using a monitor.

Race Conditions

A race condition is a bug where the result depends on the timing of threads. Three shapes cover nearly all of them:

  • Read-modify-write: count++ compiles to getfield, iconst_1, iadd, putfield. Two threads can read the same value, and one increment is lost.
  • Check-then-act: if (!map.containsKey(k)) map.put(k, v); or lazy initialization. The check is stale by the time you act.
  • Compound actions on thread-safe objects: each method is safe, but the sequence isn't. if (!list.isEmpty()) list.remove(0); on a synchronizedList can still fail.
int[] plain = {0};
AtomicInteger atomic = new AtomicInteger();
Runnable inc = () -> {
    for (int i = 0; i < 1_000_000; i++) { plain[0]++; atomic.incrementAndGet(); }
};
Thread a = new Thread(inc), b = new Thread(inc);
a.start(); b.start(); a.join(); b.join();
System.out.println(plain[0] + " " + atomic.get());
// atomic is always 2000000. plain is NOT deterministic: one run printed 1557030.

A data race is a narrower, formal term from the Java Memory Model: two threads access the same variable, at least one writes, and no happens-before relation orders them. The two ideas overlap but differ. Using AtomicInteger for get() followed by a separate set(v + 1) has no data race, yet it still has a race condition.

synchronized and Monitors

What it does

Every Java object can act as a monitor: a lock combined with a wait queue. synchronized gives you mutual exclusion and also a visibility guarantee. Releasing a monitor happens-before the next acquire of that same monitor, so the next owner sees everything the previous owner wrote.

Forms and which lock each takes

class Account {
    private static int open;
    private long balance;
    private final Object lock = new Object();

    public synchronized void deposit(long x) { balance += x; }      // locks this
    public static synchronized void opened() { open++; }            // locks Account.class

    public void withdraw(long x) {
        synchronized (lock) { balance -= x; }                       // locks 'lock'
    }
}
  • The instance lock and the class lock are unrelated. A thread in a static synchronized method doesn't block a thread in an instance synchronized method.
  • The two synchronized methods above and the lock block use different locks, so deposit and withdraw do not exclude each other here. All access to one piece of state must use the same lock. That mismatch is deliberate in this example so you can spot it.
  • In bytecode, a block compiles to monitorenter and monitorexit, with an extra exception path so the lock is released on a throw. A synchronized method just has the ACC_SYNCHRONIZED flag.
  • Prefer a private final Object lock to synchronized(this). Outside code can lock your this and interfere.
  • synchronized is not inherited. An override isn't synchronized unless it says so. Constructors can't be synchronized.

Reentrancy

The monitor records its owner and a count. If the owner enters again, the count goes up, and the lock is released when the count returns to zero. Without this, a synchronized method calling another synchronized method on the same object, or calling super.method(), would deadlock on itself. Reentrancy is per thread, not per call.

What not to lock on

  • A non-final field: synchronized (list) { list = new ArrayList<>(); } means two threads may lock two different objects. The lock belongs to the object, not the variable.
  • Boxed values and string literals: Integer.valueOf(1) and "lock" are shared across the whole JVM, so unrelated code ends up with the same lock. synchronized (count) on an Integer that you then change locks a different object each time. javac warns about value-based classes since Java 16.
  • getClass(): a subclass locks a different Class object. Use the literal Foo.class.

The object header and lock states

On 64-bit HotSpot, each object starts with a mark word (64 bits) followed by a class pointer. The mark word stores the identity hash, the GC age and the lock bits. With default compressed class pointers the header is 12 bytes. Compact object headers (JEP 519, a product option in Java 25, off by default) shrink it to 8 bytes.

A monitor isn't allocated for every object. HotSpot uses the cheapest representation that works:

StateWhenHow it works
UnlockedNo ownerLock bits in the mark word say so
Biased (historic)One thread re-locking repeatedlyThe mark word recorded a preferred thread to skip atomic operations. Disabled by default in Java 15 (JEP 374) and later removed. Older material still teaches it as current
Lightweight (thin)Uncontended, or threads taking turnsA CAS on the mark word and no OS involvement. Classic stack-locking pointed the mark word at a lock record on the owner's stack; newer JDKs use a per-thread lock stack instead
Heavyweight (inflated)Real contention, or wait() calledA native ObjectMonitor with owner, recursion count, entry queues and wait set. Waiters spin briefly, then park

The "synchronized is slow" claim is outdated. An uncontended lock is cheap, and the JIT can remove a lock on an object that never escapes the thread (lock elision) or merge adjacent lock regions (lock coarsening). What hurts is contention, not the keyword.

wait, notify and a Correct Producer-Consumer

wait() atomically releases the monitor and suspends the thread until it's notified, then takes the monitor back before returning. notify() moves one arbitrary waiter to the entry set, and notifyAll() moves all of them. The caller must own the monitor, or it gets IllegalMonitorStateException.

Why must you hold the lock? To avoid the lost wakeup. If checking the condition and sleeping were not one atomic step, a producer could add an item and notify in the gap between a consumer's check and its wait. The notification would go nowhere and the consumer would sleep forever.

Why a while loop and not if? After wait() returns, you can't assume the condition holds:

  • Spurious wakeups: the specification lets a thread wake with no notify at all.
  • Stolen conditions: between the notify and regaining the lock, another thread may have taken the item.
  • Mixed waiters: producers and consumers share one wait set, and notifyAll wakes both kinds.
class BoundedQueue {
    private final Deque<Integer> items = new ArrayDeque<>();
    private final int capacity;
    BoundedQueue(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; }

    public synchronized void put(int x) throws InterruptedException {
        while (items.size() == capacity) wait();   // re-check after every wakeup
        items.addLast(x);
        notifyAll();
    }

    public synchronized int take() throws InterruptedException {
        while (items.isEmpty()) wait();
        int v = items.removeFirst();
        notifyAll();
        return v;
    }
}

notify vs notifyAll: with one wait set holding two kinds of waiter, notify() can wake the wrong kind. A consumer finishing a take might wake another consumer instead of a producer, and everyone ends up asleep. Use notifyAll() unless all waiters are interchangeable and exactly one can proceed. The cleaner fix is two Condition objects, shown in the classic problems below. In real code use ArrayBlockingQueue; this one exists to teach the mechanism.

volatile

volatile makes reads and writes of one field visible across threads and restricts reordering around them. It gives no mutual exclusion, so volatile int count; count++ is still a lost-update bug.

class Worker implements Runnable {
    private volatile boolean running = true;
    public void stop() { running = false; }
    public void run() { while (running) doWork(); }
}

Without volatile, the JIT may legally hoist the read out of the loop, turning it into if (running) while (true), and the thread never stops.

How it works: the JIT must not cache the field in a register across accesses or move other memory operations past it in forbidden directions, and it emits memory barriers where the CPU needs them. The common phrase "volatile reads and writes go directly to main memory" is a simplification. CPU caches stay coherent through hardware protocols. The real work is stopping compiler and store-buffer reordering.

  • Reads and writes of long and double: non-volatile 64-bit writes may tear into two 32-bit halves (JLS 17.7). Volatile ones can't. References are always atomic.
  • Piggybacking: everything written before a volatile write becomes visible to a thread that reads that volatile. The example in the next section relies on it.
  • Arrays: volatile int[] a makes the reference volatile, not the elements. Use AtomicIntegerArray.
  • When it's enough: a single writer, or writes that don't depend on the current value, such as flags and publishing an immutable snapshot.

The Java Memory Model and Happens-Before

The Java Memory Model (JMM), defined in JLS chapter 17, says which values a read may return in a multithreaded program. Its key idea is happens-before: if action A happens-before B, then B is guaranteed to see the effects of A. It's a rule about visibility and ordering, not wall-clock time. Two actions with no happens-before relation can be seen in any order, including an order that seems impossible from reading the source.

RuleGuarantee
Program orderEach action in a thread happens-before later actions in that thread
Monitor lockAn unlock happens-before every later lock of that same monitor
VolatileA write happens-before every later read of that same field
Thread startt.start() happens-before every action in t
Thread terminationEvery action in t happens-before another thread seeing t.join() return or isAlive() false
Interruptiont.interrupt() happens-before t detecting the interrupt
FinalizerA constructor's end happens-before the start of the finalizer
TransitivityA hb B and B hb C gives A hb C

java.util.concurrent documents more: putting into a BlockingQueue happens-before the take, submit happens-before the task runs, the task happens-before Future.get returns, and countDown happens-before the matching await returns.

A classic demonstration of reordering. With x and y starting at 0 and no synchronization:

// Thread 1           // Thread 2
x = 1;                y = 1;
r1 = y;               r2 = x;

Reasoning by interleaving says at least one of r1, r2 must be 1. The JMM also allows r1 == 0 && r2 == 0, because each thread's write can sit in a store buffer or be reordered past its read. The result is not deterministic and depends on hardware and timing. Making x and y volatile rules out 0, 0.

Sequential consistency for race-free programs: if a program has no data races, it behaves as if actions ran in one global order. That's the promise you get in exchange for synchronizing correctly.

Since Java 9, VarHandle exposes finer access modes between plain and volatile: opaque, acquire/release and full volatile. Library authors use them. Application code rarely needs to.

Double-Checked Locking: Why volatile Is Required

The Core Java overview gives the code. The question that matters is why it needs volatile. instance = new Config() is roughly three steps: allocate memory, run the constructor, store the reference. Without happens-before, another thread can see the steps out of order, so it may see a non-null reference to an object whose fields aren't initialized yet. The first, unlocked null check then returns that half-built object. A volatile write orders the store after the construction and pairs with the unlocked read.

private static volatile Config instance;

static Config get() {
    Config local = instance;              // one volatile read on the fast path
    if (local == null) {
        synchronized (Config.class) {
            local = instance;
            if (local == null) instance = local = new Config();
        }
    }
    return local;
}

Usually you don't need any of this. The holder idiom gets lazy, thread-safe initialization from the JVM's class initialization lock, with no volatile on the read path:

final class Config {
    private Config() {}
    private static final class Holder { static final Config INSTANCE = new Config(); }
    static Config get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }   // Holder initializes on first use
}

Final Fields and Safe Publication

A final field has its own JMM guarantee. At the end of the constructor the field is "frozen". Any thread that gets a reference to the object after construction sees the correct final values, and everything reachable through them as of the freeze, even if the reference reached it through a data race. That's what makes a properly built immutable object safe to share without locks.

The guarantee is void if this escapes during construction: registering a listener in the constructor, or starting a thread from it, can expose the object before the freeze.

class Bad {
    final int value;
    Bad(EventBus bus) {
        bus.register(this);   // another thread can now see value == 0
        value = 42;
    }
}

Safe publication means making an object visible along with its state. The ways to do it:

  • Initialize it from a static initializer.
  • Store it in a volatile field or an AtomicReference.
  • Store it in a final field of a properly constructed object.
  • Store it in a field guarded by a lock, reading under that lock.
  • Pass it through a thread-safe container such as a concurrent queue or map.

Atomics, CAS, ABA and LongAdder

Compare-and-swap

CAS is a CPU instruction (lock cmpxchg on x86) that says: "if this memory location still holds the value I expect, store the new value, atomically, and tell me if it worked." No thread blocks. If you lose the race, you read again and retry. This is called lock-free programming, and it can't deadlock, because no thread ever holds anything while waiting.

// What AtomicInteger.incrementAndGet effectively does
int prev, next;
do {
    prev = value;                         // volatile read
    next = prev + 1;
} while (!compareAndSet(prev, next));     // retry if another thread got in first
return next;

Atomics have volatile read and write semantics, so they provide happens-before too. Under very heavy contention many CAS attempts fail and burn CPU, and a lock or LongAdder can then do better.

ClassUse
AtomicInteger, AtomicLong, AtomicBooleanCounters, sequence numbers, once-only flags
AtomicReference<V>Swapping an immutable snapshot of state as one unit
AtomicIntegerArray and friendsVolatile semantics per array element
AtomicIntegerFieldUpdaterCAS on a volatile field without an object per instance
AtomicStampedReference, AtomicMarkableReferenceReference plus version or mark, to detect ABA
LongAdder, LongAccumulator, DoubleAdder, DoubleAccumulatorHigh-contention statistics

updateAndGet(fn) and accumulateAndGet(x, fn) run a CAS loop for you. The function can run more than once, so it must have no side effects.

Gotcha: AtomicReference.compareAndSet compares with ==, not equals. With AtomicReference<Integer> r = new AtomicReference<>(1000), the call r.compareAndSet(1000, 1001) returned false when run, because each autobox of 1000 is a separate object. The same code with 100 returned true, because values from -128 to 127 come from the Integer cache.

The ABA problem

CAS checks only that the value is the same, not that it never changed. Thread 1 reads A. Thread 2 changes A to B and back to A. Thread 1's CAS succeeds even though the world changed. On a lock-free stack this can be a real bug: thread 1 plans to set top to A.next, but A was popped, B was popped too, and A was pushed back, so A.next now points at a removed node.

Attach a version so that every change is detectable:

AtomicStampedReference<Node> top = new AtomicStampedReference<>(head, 0);

int[] stamp = new int[1];
Node current = top.get(stamp);                         // reads ref and stamp together
boolean ok = top.compareAndSet(current, current.next,
                               stamp[0], stamp[0] + 1);

Garbage collection removes the C-style variant where memory is freed and reused while someone still holds a pointer. ABA can still happen in Java when objects are recycled or values repeat logically.

LongAdder

When many threads hammer one AtomicLong, they all fight over one cache line and CAS failures pile up. LongAdder, built on the internal Striped64, keeps a base and, once contention appears, an array of Cells. A thread that fails a CAS moves to its own cell, chosen by a per-thread probe value, so threads stop colliding. Cells are padded with @Contended to avoid false sharing.

  • sum() adds base and all cells. It's not an atomic snapshot: updates that happen during the scan may be missed. Fine for metrics, wrong for a sequence or anything like "allocate the next ID".
  • It uses more memory and makes reads slower. It suits many writes and few reads.
  • Stick with AtomicLong when you need incrementAndGet()'s return value or compare-and-set. LongAdder has neither.

Lock, ReentrantLock and Condition

java.util.concurrent.locks.Lock exists because synchronized can't time out, can't be interrupted while waiting, can't be released in a different block from where it was taken, and offers only one wait set per lock.

FeaturesynchronizedReentrantLock
ReleaseAutomaticManual, in finally
Try without blockingNotryLock()
TimeoutNotryLock(time, unit)
Interruptible waitNolockInterruptibly()
FairnessNot offerednew ReentrantLock(true)
Wait queuesOne per monitorAny number of Conditions
InspectionThread.holdsLock(obj)isLocked, getHoldCount, getQueueLength, more
Thread dumpShown as monitorsShown as parked on a synchronizer
private final ReentrantLock lock = new ReentrantLock();

void transfer() {
    lock.lock();          // BEFORE try: if lock() failed, finally must not unlock
    try {
        // critical section
    } finally {
        lock.unlock();
    }
}

boolean tryTransfer() throws InterruptedException {
    if (!lock.tryLock(200, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)) return false;  // gave up, no deadlock
    try { return true; } finally { lock.unlock(); }
}

Calling unlock() without holding the lock throws IllegalMonitorStateException. Each lock() needs one unlock(): after two locks, the first unlock leaves it held.

AbstractQueuedSynchronizer (AQS)

Most of java.util.concurrent is built on AQS: ReentrantLock, Semaphore, CountDownLatch, ReentrantReadWriteLock. It has a volatile int state changed by CAS, and a FIFO queue of waiting threads based on the CLH lock design, parked with LockSupport.park. Each synchronizer only defines what state means. For ReentrantLock it's the hold count, for Semaphore the permits left, for CountDownLatch the remaining count.

Fairness

A non-fair lock (the default) lets an arriving thread barge ahead of the queue if the lock happens to be free. It seems unjust, but it gives better throughput: a running thread can grab the lock now, while waking a parked thread takes time, during which nobody holds the lock. A fair lock hands the lock to the longest waiter. That prevents starvation but costs substantial throughput. Untimed tryLock() barges even on a fair lock; tryLock(0, unit) respects fairness.

Condition

A Condition is a wait set attached to a lock: await() is wait() and signal() is notify(). Because one lock can have several, producers wait on notFull and consumers on notEmpty, and you can wake exactly the right kind of thread. The same while loop rule applies, and await must be called holding the lock. Don't confuse them: condition.wait() compiles, and it uses the Condition object's own monitor, which is a bug.

ReadWriteLock and StampedLock

ReentrantReadWriteLock holds a pair of locks: many readers may hold the read lock at once, while the write lock is exclusive. Its state packs the read count and write count into 16 bits each. It only pays off when reads are frequent, take real time and rarely overlap writes. For a very short critical section its extra bookkeeping can make it slower than a plain lock.

class Cache<K, V> {
    private final Map<K, V> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final ReadWriteLock rw = new ReentrantReadWriteLock();

    V get(K k) {
        rw.readLock().lock();
        try { return map.get(k); } finally { rw.readLock().unlock(); }
    }
    void put(K k, V v) {
        rw.writeLock().lock();
        try { map.put(k, v); } finally { rw.writeLock().unlock(); }
    }
}
  • Upgrading deadlocks: a thread holding the read lock can't take the write lock, because it would wait for all readers, including itself. Run on Java 21, writeLock().tryLock() while holding the read lock returned false; plain lock() would block forever.
  • Downgrading is allowed: take the write lock, take the read lock, release the write lock.

StampedLock (Java 8) adds an optimistic read: take a stamp with no locking at all, read fields into locals, then call validate(stamp). If no writer got in, you're done. Readers never block writers, which suits read-mostly data.

class Point {
    private double x, y;
    private final StampedLock sl = new StampedLock();

    void move(double dx, double dy) {
        long stamp = sl.writeLock();
        try { x += dx; y += dy; } finally { sl.unlockWrite(stamp); }
    }

    double distance() {
        long stamp = sl.tryOptimisticRead();
        double cx = x, cy = y;                 // copy first, use only after validating
        if (!sl.validate(stamp)) {             // a writer interfered: fall back
            stamp = sl.readLock();
            try { cx = x; cy = y; } finally { sl.unlockRead(stamp); }
        }
        return Math.hypot(cx, cy);
    }
}

Limits: StampedLock is not reentrant, has no Condition support and no owner tracking. A second writeLock() from the same thread hangs forever. The try variants return 0 when they fail.

Synchronizers

ClassPurposeReusable?Typical use
SemaphoreN permits limit concurrent accessYesLimit calls to a downstream service
CountDownLatchOne or more threads wait for a count to reach 0NoWait for N services to start
CyclicBarrierN threads wait for each otherYes, resets automaticallyIterative parallel algorithms
PhaserBarrier with dynamic parties and many phasesYesMulti-stage work with a changing team
ExchangerTwo threads swap objects at a meeting pointYesSwapping full and empty buffers
// Semaphore: at most 10 concurrent calls
Semaphore permits = new Semaphore(10);
void call() throws InterruptedException {
    permits.acquire();
    try { remote.invoke(); } finally { permits.release(); }
}

// CountDownLatch: a start gun, and waiting for workers to finish
CountDownLatch start = new CountDownLatch(1), done = new CountDownLatch(4);
for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
    pool.execute(() -> {
        try { start.await(); work(); }
        catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
        finally { done.countDown(); }             // in finally, or a failure hangs await()
    });
}
start.countDown();
done.await(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS);

// CyclicBarrier: the action runs once all parties arrive
CyclicBarrier barrier = new CyclicBarrier(3, () -> mergeResults());
Runnable worker = () -> {
    try { computeChunk(); barrier.await(); }
    catch (InterruptedException | BrokenBarrierException e) { /* stop */ }
};

// Phaser: parties register and deregister over time
Phaser phaser = new Phaser(1);                    // register self
phaser.register();                                // a new party joins
phaser.arriveAndAwaitAdvance();                   // wait for the phase to complete
phaser.arriveAndDeregister();                     // leave; no parties left = terminated

// Exchanger: both threads block until the other arrives
Exchanger<Buffer> ex = new Exchanger<>();
Buffer empty = ex.exchange(fullBuffer);
  • Semaphore has no owner: any thread can call release(), and doing so without an acquire adds a permit. new Semaphore(1) followed by release() reports 2 available permits (verified). A binary semaphore, unlike a lock, isn't reentrant.
  • CountDownLatch: extra countDown() calls at zero do nothing. It can't be reset.
  • CyclicBarrier: if one party is interrupted or times out, the barrier breaks and all the others get BrokenBarrierException. await() returns the arrival index.
  • Latch vs barrier: a latch waits for events and is counted down by anyone. A barrier waits for threads, each of which must arrive.

ThreadLocal and Its Leaks

ThreadLocal gives each thread its own copy of a variable. Common uses are per-thread instances of non-thread-safe objects and passing context such as a user or transaction through a call stack without a parameter. Spring's transaction and security contexts work this way.

How it's stored: the data isn't in the ThreadLocal. Each Thread has a field threadLocals of type ThreadLocalMap, a custom open-addressing hash table. The ThreadLocal object is only the key. Each Entry extends WeakReference<ThreadLocal<?>>: the key is weak, but the value is a strong reference.

Thread ──strong──▶ ThreadLocalMap ──strong──▶ Entry ──strong──▶ value
                                               └──weak───▶ ThreadLocal (key)

The leak: in a thread pool, threads live for as long as the application. If the ThreadLocal key is collected, the entry stays with a null key and its value remains strongly reachable through the thread. Stale entries are only cleaned up opportunistically during later map operations. Static ThreadLocals are worse in a sense, because the key never goes away at all, and every value stays until replaced. In an app server, a value whose class came from a webapp's classloader can pin that classloader across redeploys.

The worse bug is data bleed: the next task on a pooled thread sees the previous task's value. On a single-thread executor, one task did user.set("alice") and the next task's user.get() printed alice. In a web app, that means one user's identity appearing in another user's request.

private static final ThreadLocal<User> CURRENT = new ThreadLocal<>();

void handle(Request req) {
    CURRENT.set(authenticate(req));
    try {
        process(req);
    } finally {
        CURRENT.remove();     // always; set(null) leaves the entry behind
    }
}

// Lazily created per-thread object
private static final ThreadLocal<SimpleDateFormat> FMT =
    ThreadLocal.withInitial(() -> new SimpleDateFormat("yyyy-MM-dd"));

InheritableThreadLocal copies the parent's value to a child thread at creation. A plain ThreadLocal reads null in the child (verified). It's unreliable with pools, because workers are created once, at an unrelated moment. Context must be propagated explicitly there, typically by a task decorator.

ScopedValue

ScopedValue is the modern alternative for passing context down a call stack. It was a preview API from Java 21 and became final in Java 25 (JEP 506). A value is bound for the duration of a call and unbound automatically when the call ends, so there's nothing to remove and nothing to leak. Code below the binding can only read it.

private static final ScopedValue<String> USER = ScopedValue.newInstance();

static String who() { return USER.isBound() ? USER.get() : "nobody"; }

public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println(who());                                   // nobody
    ScopedValue.where(USER, "alice").run(() -> {
        System.out.println(who());                               // alice
        ScopedValue.where(USER, "bob").run(() ->
            System.out.println(who()));                          // bob: nested rebinding
        System.out.println(who());                               // alice again
    });
    System.out.println(who());                                   // nobody
}
ThreadLocalScopedValue
Mutabilityset anywhereImmutable within a binding; rebinding only for a nested scope
LifetimeUntil remove() or thread endThe bounded call
Child threadsInheritable copies per thread, costly in bulkInherited cheaply by structured concurrency subtasks
Fit with virtual threadsWorks, but millions of copies cost real memoryDesigned for it

Executors and ExecutorService

An executor separates what to run from how it runs. Executor has the single method execute(Runnable). ExecutorService adds lifecycle and Futures. ScheduledExecutorService adds timing. ThreadPoolExecutor, ScheduledThreadPoolExecutor and ForkJoinPool are the implementations you'll meet.

Pools exist because creating threads is expensive, and because a bounded pool protects the application: without a limit, a traffic spike creates threads until memory or the OS gives out.

ThreadPoolExecutor Internals

ThreadPoolExecutor pool = new ThreadPoolExecutor(
    4,                                     // corePoolSize
    16,                                    // maximumPoolSize
    60, TimeUnit.SECONDS,                  // keepAliveTime for idle extra threads
    new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1000),        // workQueue: bounded
    Thread.ofPlatform().name("orders-", 0).factory(),   // threadFactory
    new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());         // rejection handler
ParameterMeaning
corePoolSizeThreads kept even when idle, unless allowCoreThreadTimeOut(true). They're created lazily, on demand, unless you call prestartAllCoreThreads()
maximumPoolSizeUpper limit, reached only after the queue is full
keepAliveTimeHow long a surplus idle thread lives
workQueueHolds tasks waiting for a thread
threadFactoryNames, daemon status, uncaught handler
handlerWhat to do when both queue and pool are full

Most people guess the order is core, then max, then queue. It isn't. With 2 core threads, 4 max, a queue of 2 and tasks that block, running this printed:

task 1: pool=1 queue=0     (new core worker)
task 2: pool=2 queue=0     (new core worker)
task 3: pool=2 queue=1     (queued)
task 4: pool=2 queue=2     (queued, queue now full)
task 5: pool=3 queue=2     (extra worker)
task 6: pool=4 queue=2     (extra worker)
task 7: rejected

Notice tasks 5 and 6 run before the queued tasks 3 and 4. A pool isn't strictly first-in, first-out.

How it works inside

  • ctl: a single AtomicInteger packing the run state (high 3 bits) and the worker count (low 29 bits), so both can be read and updated together.
  • Run states: RUNNING → SHUTDOWN (no new tasks, finish the queue) or STOP (drop the queue, interrupt workers) → TIDYING → TERMINATED.
  • Worker: wraps a thread and extends AQS as a simple non-reentrant lock, used to tell busy workers from idle ones when interrupting.
  • runWorker: loops running its first task, then calls getTask(). That's queue.take() for core threads and a timed poll(keepAlive) for surplus ones. A null return ends the worker.
  • Hooks: subclasses can override beforeExecute, afterExecute and terminated for metrics or context.

The queue decides the behaviour

QueueBehaviourConsequence
ArrayBlockingQueueBounded arrayGives real back-pressure. The usual production choice
LinkedBlockingQueue (no argument)Capacity Integer.MAX_VALUEThe queue never fills, so maximumPoolSize is ignored. Tasks can pile up until out of memory
SynchronousQueueZero capacity, a direct hand-offEvery task needs an idle worker or a new thread
PriorityBlockingQueueUnbounded, orderedPriority scheduling; low-priority tasks can starve

Run with core 2, max 10 and an unbounded queue, 100 blocked tasks gave a pool of 2 threads and 98 queued. Max was never used.

Gotcha: new ThreadPoolExecutor(0, 5, 1, SECONDS, new LinkedBlockingQueue<>()) doesn't give five threads. Step 1 never fires with core 0, the queue accepts everything, and an extra check after queuing starts just one worker so the task isn't stranded. Running it with three blocking tasks gave pool size 1 and queue size 2.

Rejection policies

PolicyWhat happensUse when
AbortPolicy (default)Throws RejectedExecutionExceptionThe caller can react, e.g. return HTTP 503
CallerRunsPolicyThe submitting thread runs the task itselfNatural back-pressure: producers slow down. Beware of it blocking a request or event-loop thread
DiscardPolicySilently drops the taskLoss is truly acceptable. At least count them
DiscardOldestPolicyDrops the head of the queue, then retriesOnly the latest data matters, e.g. sensor readings. Don't combine with a priority queue
Custom RejectedExecutionHandlerYour codeLog, record metrics, persist for later

submit after shutdown() is also rejected through the same handler, so it threw RejectedExecutionException with the default policy.

Sizing a pool

  • CPU-bound work: about the number of cores, sometimes plus one. More threads only add context switches.
  • I/O-bound work: Goetz's formula, threads = cores × target utilization × (1 + wait time / compute time). With 8 cores, full utilization and tasks that wait 90 ms for every 10 ms of CPU: 8 × 1 × (1 + 9) = 80.
  • By throughput: Little's law says concurrency = arrival rate × time in system. 200 requests per second at 50 ms each needs about 10 busy threads on average. Add room for spikes.

The formulas give a starting point; load testing gives the answer. The real ceiling is often downstream: 200 threads in front of a database pool of 20 just move the queue. Runtime.availableProcessors() is container-aware in current JDKs, so it respects CPU limits. Keep separate pools for different kinds of work (bulkheads), so slow reports can't use the threads that serve checkout.

The Executors factory pitfalls

FactoryActual configurationRisk
newFixedThreadPool(n)core = max = n, unbounded LinkedBlockingQueueUnlimited queue: out of memory under sustained overload
newSingleThreadExecutor()One thread, unbounded queueSame
newCachedThreadPool()core 0, max Integer.MAX_VALUE, SynchronousQueue, 60 s keep-aliveUnlimited threads under load
newScheduledThreadPool(n)Unbounded delay queueScheduled tasks can accumulate
newWorkStealingPool()A ForkJoinPoolOrder not guaranteed; daemon workers
newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()Not a pool: a new virtual thread per task (Java 21)Concurrency is unbounded, so limit downstream calls yourself

That's why many teams construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly, with a bounded queue and named threads.

Shutting down properly

void stop(ExecutorService pool) {
    pool.shutdown();                                       // no new tasks; queued ones run
    try {
        if (!pool.awaitTermination(30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)) {
            pool.shutdownNow();                            // interrupts; returns queued tasks
            pool.awaitTermination(10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);
        }
    } catch (InterruptedException e) {
        pool.shutdownNow();
        Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
    }
}

Pool threads are non-daemon by default, so forgetting shutdown() keeps the JVM alive. shutdownNow() only interrupts; a task that ignores interruption keeps running. Since Java 19, ExecutorService is AutoCloseable: close() calls shutdown and waits, so it can block for a long time. Spring's @Async and Tomcat pools sit on this same machinery.

Future, Callable and Scheduled Tasks

A Future is a handle on a result that may not exist yet. Callable<V> differs from Runnable by returning a value and allowing checked exceptions.

MethodBehaviour
get()Blocks. Task exceptions come wrapped in ExecutionException
get(time, unit)Throws TimeoutException, and the task keeps running
cancel(true)Stops it if not started; interrupts it if running. Later get() throws CancellationException
isDone()True for normal end, failure and cancellation alike
state(), resultNow(), exceptionNow()Non-blocking inspection (Java 19)

FutureTask is the standard implementation, and it's what submit wraps your task in. That explains the most common silent failure in Java:

pool.execute(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("A"); });
// Escapes the worker: uncaught handler runs, the worker thread dies and is replaced

Future<?> f = pool.submit(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("B"); });
// Captured inside the FutureTask. Nothing is printed. If nobody calls f.get(), it's gone.

Helpers: invokeAll waits for every task. invokeAny returns the first success and cancels the rest. ExecutorCompletionService gives you results in the order they finish instead of the order you submitted them.

ScheduledExecutorService

ScheduledExecutorService ses = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor();
ses.schedule(task, 5, TimeUnit.SECONDS);                    // once
ses.scheduleAtFixedRate(task, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);     // start to start
ses.scheduleWithFixedDelay(task, 0, 10, TimeUnit.SECONDS);  // end to start
  • Fixed rate aims at a steady clock: 0, 10, 20. If a run takes 15 s, the next starts late, right after it. Runs of one task never overlap. Fixed rate can burst to catch up.
  • Fixed delay waits 10 s after each run ends, so it drifts but never bursts.
  • An exception stops the schedule silently. A task that threw on its third run ran exactly 3 times, its future reported done, and get() threw ExecutionException. Wrap periodic task bodies in try/catch.
  • Prefer it to java.util.Timer, which has one thread that dies on any exception, ending all tasks.

ForkJoinPool and Work Stealing

ForkJoinPool is built for tasks that split into smaller tasks. Each worker has its own double-ended queue (deque). A worker pushes and pops its own tasks at the top, in LIFO order, which is cache-friendly because the newest task touches recently used data. An idle worker steals from the base of another worker's deque, in FIFO order. The oldest tasks tend to be the largest, so one steal grabs a lot of work, and thieves and the owner rarely touch the same end.

class SumTask extends RecursiveTask<Long> {
    private static final int THRESHOLD = 1_000;
    private final int[] data; private final int lo, hi;
    SumTask(int[] data, int lo, int hi) { this.data = data; this.lo = lo; this.hi = hi; }

    @Override protected Long compute() {
        if (hi - lo <= THRESHOLD) {
            long sum = 0;
            for (int i = lo; i < hi; i++) sum += data[i];
            return sum;
        }
        int mid = (lo + hi) >>> 1;
        SumTask left = new SumTask(data, lo, mid);
        SumTask right = new SumTask(data, mid, hi);
        left.fork();                            // queue one half
        return right.compute() + left.join();   // do the other half here
    }
}
long total = ForkJoinPool.commonPool().invoke(new SumTask(array, 0, array.length));
  • Use RecursiveTask<V> for a result and RecursiveAction for none.
  • Calling left.fork(); right.fork(); left.join() + right.join() wastes the current thread. Fork one and compute the other. Join the forked task last.
  • join() in a worker isn't idle waiting: the worker helps by running other tasks.
  • The common pool is shared across the JVM. Its parallelism defaults to availableProcessors() - 1 (7 on an 8-core machine, verified), because the calling thread helps. Change it with -Djava.util.concurrent.ForkJoinPool.common.parallelism=N.
  • Don't block in ForkJoin tasks. If you must, use ForkJoinPool.ManagedBlocker, so the pool can compensate with an extra thread.

CompletableFuture

Future makes you block to get a result. CompletableFuture<T> (Java 8) implements both Future and CompletionStage: you describe what happens when a value arrives, composing asynchronous steps without blocking. Internally each future holds its result plus a lock-free stack of dependent Completion objects, which fire when it completes.

Creating

MethodMeaning
supplyAsync(supplier[, executor])Runs a task that returns a value
runAsync(runnable[, executor])Runs a task with no value
completedFuture(v), failedFuture(ex)Already finished (the second is Java 9)
new CompletableFuture<>()Finished by hand with complete(v) or completeExceptionally(ex). This is how you adapt callback APIs. Only the first completion wins

Chaining

MethodInput → outputStream analogue or use
thenApply(fn)T → Umap
thenCompose(fn)T → CompletableFuture<U>, flattenedflatMap: chaining another async call
thenAccept(consumer)T → voidUse the value at the end
thenRun(runnable)() → voidDo something after, ignoring the value
thenCombine(other, fn)(T, U) → VMerge two independent results
thenAcceptBoth, runAfterBothBoth done, no result
applyToEither, acceptEither, runAfterEitherFirst of two to completeHedged requests
allOf(cfs...)All done, CompletableFuture<Void>Fan-in. Gives no results itself; read each with join()
anyOf(cfs...)First done, CompletableFuture<Object>Loses the type. If the first to finish failed, the result fails

Async variants and threads. Each step has an ...Async form, with an optional executor. Without the suffix, the callback runs on whichever thread completes the previous stage, or on the calling thread if that stage is already done. completedFuture(1).thenRun(...) printed main. ...Async without an executor uses the common pool. If its parallelism is below 2, each task gets a new thread instead.

Gotcha: The common pool is small and shared. Blocking I/O on it starves parallel streams and everything else in the JVM. For I/O, always pass your own executor: supplyAsync(this::load, ioPool).

Error handling

MethodRuns onCan change the result?Notes
exceptionally(fn)Failure onlyYes: recover with a valueLike catch
handle((v, ex) -> ...)BothYes: result becomes the return valueLike catch plus a transform
whenComplete((v, ex) -> ...)BothNo: the original result or failure passes throughLike finally, for logging
exceptionallyCompose(fn)Failure onlyYes: recover with another futureJava 12

Which exception type do you see? This surprises people, so here's what ran on Java 21:

supplyAsync(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); })
    .exceptionally(e -> ...)     // e is CompletionException, cause ISE
failedFuture(new IllegalStateException("boom"))
    .exceptionally(e -> ...)     // e is ISE itself, unwrapped
failedFuture(new IllegalStateException("boom"))
    .thenApply(x -> x)
    .exceptionally(e -> ...)     // e is CompletionException: wrapped on the way through

future.join();   // throws CompletionException, cause ISE (unchecked)
future.get();    // throws ExecutionException, cause ISE (checked)

So your handler should unwrap: Throwable cause = (e instanceof CompletionException && e.getCause() != null) ? e.getCause() : e;

Timeouts and cancellation (Java 9+)

  • orTimeout(t, unit) fails the future with TimeoutException (seen wrapped in CompletionException at join).
  • completeOnTimeout(value, t, unit) completes with a default instead.
  • Neither stops the underlying work. It keeps running and using a thread.
  • cancel(true) doesn't interrupt the thread: the mayInterruptIfRunning argument has no effect here. The future just completes with CancellationException, and dependents get a CompletionException with that as its cause.

A realistic composition

ExecutorService io = Executors.newFixedThreadPool(32);

CompletableFuture<Page> page(long userId) {
    CompletableFuture<User> user = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> users.find(userId), io)
        .orTimeout(500, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

    CompletableFuture<List<Order>> orders = user
        .thenCompose(u -> CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> this.orders.of(u), io))
        .exceptionally(ex -> { log.warn("orders down", ex); return List.of(); });

    CompletableFuture<List<Offer>> offers = CompletableFuture
        .supplyAsync(() -> this.offers.all(), io)
        .completeOnTimeout(List.of(), 300, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS);

    return user.thenCombine(orders, Page::new)
               .thenCombine(offers, Page::withOffers);
}

// Collect a list of futures into a future of a list
static <T> CompletableFuture<List<T>> sequence(List<CompletableFuture<T>> fs) {
    return CompletableFuture.allOf(fs.toArray(new CompletableFuture[0]))
        .thenApply(v -> fs.stream().map(CompletableFuture::join).toList());
}

allOf does not fail fast. With one already-failed future and one taking 300 ms, it still waited for the slow one before reporting the failure (verified). For fail-fast behaviour, add a handler to each future that completes a shared result exceptionally, or use structured concurrency.

Other common mistakes: calling join() inside the chain instead of composing, using thenApply with a function that returns a future (you get CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<U>>), and ending a chain without an error handler, which loses failures just as submit does. Since Java 21, plain blocking code on virtual threads is often a simpler alternative for I/O fan-out.

Parallel Streams and the Common Pool

Parallel streams run on the same common pool as CompletableFuture's default async methods, and the calling thread joins in (main was among the threads doing the work when tested). The consequences:

  • One blocking call in a parallel stream ties up shared workers for the entire JVM.
  • Concurrent requests that use parallel streams compete for the same few workers, so "parallel" gives each one less than you think.
  • Running the stream inside your own pool, with customPool.submit(() -> list.parallelStream()...), makes it use that pool. Tested with a pool of 3, only that pool's workers ran it. This is undocumented behaviour, not a contract.

When and whether to use them is covered in the Lambdas, Streams & Optional section.

Virtual Threads (Java 21)

The problem: a platform thread is a thin wrapper over an OS thread, so a typical JVM can afford thousands of them, not millions. In thread-per-request servers, most of a thread's life is spent waiting on I/O while holding that scarce OS thread. Reactive frameworks work around this but give up simple sequential code, stack traces and debugging.

The solution: a virtual thread (JEP 444, final in Java 21) is a java.lang.Thread managed by the JVM rather than the OS. It only needs an OS thread while actually running on the CPU. When it blocks, it steps aside.

How it works

  • Carrier threads: virtual threads are scheduled onto platform threads in a dedicated FIFO ForkJoinPool, separate from the common pool. Its parallelism defaults to the number of processors and can be tuned with -Djdk.virtualThreadScheduler.parallelism.
  • Mounting: to run, a virtual thread is mounted on a carrier, and its frames are lazily copied onto the carrier's stack as needed. Thread.currentThread() still returns the virtual thread.
  • Unmounting: when it reaches a blocking operation in the JDK, such as socket I/O, sleep, BlockingQueue.take or ReentrantLock.lock, the JDK parks it instead of blocking the carrier. A continuation saves its stack frames to the heap, and the carrier picks up another virtual thread. When the operation completes, the virtual thread becomes runnable and can continue on any carrier.
  • Stack: it starts tiny and grows on the heap, instead of reserving a fixed block.
try (var executor = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    List<Future<String>> results = urls.stream()
        .map(url -> executor.submit(() -> http.fetch(url)))     // plain blocking call
        .toList();
    for (Future<String> f : results) process(f.get());
}                                                               // waits for all tasks

Thread.startVirtualThread(() -> handle(request));
Thread t = Thread.ofVirtual().name("v-", 0).unstarted(task);
Platform threadVirtual thread
Backed byOne OS thread for its whole lifeA carrier, only while running
Practical countThousandsMillions
StackFixed reservationGrows on the heap
PoolingYes, they're expensiveNever, create one per task
DaemonConfigurableAlways daemon
Priority1 to 10Always 5
NameGenerated if not setEmpty string unless set
Best forCPU-heavy workMany tasks that mostly wait on I/O

Virtual threads improve throughput, not the speed of a single task. They run the same code at the same speed; there's just far more waiting capacity. CPU-bound work gains nothing, because a virtual thread doing computation occupies a carrier just the same.

Pinning and JEP 491

A virtual thread is pinned when it can't unmount, so a blocking operation blocks its carrier too. If all carriers are pinned, other virtual threads can't run, even though they're ready.

SituationJava 21 to 23Java 24+ (JEP 491)
Blocking inside synchronizedPinnedNot pinned: unmounts, the monitor stays held by the virtual thread
Blocked trying to enter synchronized, or in Object.wait()PinnedNot pinned
Native method or foreign function on the stackPinnedStill pinned
Blocking in a class initializer, or waiting for onePinnedStill pinned

The reason for the old limit: HotSpot tracked monitor ownership by the carrier thread, so a virtual thread had to stay on its carrier while holding a monitor. JEP 491 tracks the virtual thread instead. That's why advice from the Java 21 period to replace synchronized with ReentrantLock is obsolete on Java 24 and later, including Java 25 LTS. On Java 21 LTS, it still applies to synchronized blocks that wrap long I/O.

To find pinning, use the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned. The system property -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads belonged to Java 21 to 23 and was removed in Java 24.

Using them correctly

  • Never pool them. A pool exists to share an expensive resource, and a virtual thread isn't one.
  • Limit what's scarce, not threads. A pool used to throttle database calls by accident. With a virtual thread per task, 100,000 requests can all hit the database. Use a Semaphore or a connection pool as the limit.
  • Watch ThreadLocal use. They work, but a heavy per-thread cache was designed around a few hundred threads. Prefer ScopedValue on Java 25.
  • Spring Boot 3.2+: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs request handling on virtual threads.
  • Thread dumps: jstack doesn't list unmounted virtual threads. Use jcmd <pid> Thread.dump_to_file -format=json dump.json.

Structured Concurrency

Structured concurrency treats a group of related tasks as a single unit, with a scope like a code block: subtasks can't outlive the block that started them. If one fails, the others are cancelled, and if the parent is cancelled, so are they. Compare that with plain submit: if the first task fails, the second keeps running, and nothing links them.

Status: StructuredTaskScope is still a preview API, needing --enable-preview, and its shape has changed between releases. It was first previewed in Java 21 (JEP 453). Java 25 is the fifth preview (JEP 505), which replaced public constructors and subclassing with static open factories and Joiners. It was still in preview in Java 26. Don't confuse it with ScopedValue, which is final.

// Java 25 preview API
Response handle() throws InterruptedException {
    try (var scope = StructuredTaskScope.open()) {          // default: all must succeed
        Subtask<User>  user  = scope.fork(() -> findUser());
        Subtask<Order> order = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrder());
        scope.join();                                       // throws if a subtask failed
        return new Response(user.get(), order.get());
    }                                                       // no subtask outlives the block
}

// Java 21 preview API (a different shape, shown because you may meet it)
try (var scope = new StructuredTaskScope.ShutdownOnFailure()) {
    var user = scope.fork(() -> findUser());
    var order = scope.fork(() -> fetchOrder());
    scope.join().throwIfFailed();
    return new Response(user.get(), order.get());
}

Each fork runs in a new virtual thread by default. Scoped values bound in the parent are visible in the subtasks. Thread dumps show the tree of scopes, which helps a lot with debugging.

Deadlock, Livelock and Starvation

ProblemWhat happensThreads areFix
DeadlockA cycle of threads, each waiting for a lock another holdsBlocked, no CPU useGlobal lock order, timeouts
LivelockThreads keep reacting to each other, and no one progressesBusy, high CPURandomized backoff
StarvationA thread never gets the resource because others keep winningWaiting indefinitelyFair locks, bounded lock holds, separate pools

Prevention

The Core Java overview lists the four Coffman conditions. All four must hold, so prevention means breaking one.

  • Break circular wait with a global lock order. It's the usual fix, and the code is below.
  • Break hold-and-wait or no-preemption with tryLock and a timeout. Release what you hold, back off for a random time, and retry. The randomness avoids a livelock.
  • Hold fewer locks. Don't call unknown code ("alien methods", such as listeners and callbacks) while holding a lock.
  • Avoid sharing altogether, with immutable data or by confining state to one thread.
// Deadlocks: transfer(a, b) and transfer(b, a) lock in opposite orders
void transfer(Account from, Account to, long amount) {
    Account first  = from.id() < to.id() ? from : to;   // same order for every caller
    Account second = first == from ? to : from;
    synchronized (first) {
        synchronized (second) {
            from.debit(amount);
            to.credit(amount);
        }
    }
}

A less obvious kind is thread-starvation deadlock, which involves no locks. If every task in a fixed pool submits a subtask to the same pool and waits on its Future, all threads can end up waiting for queued tasks that no thread is free to run. A single-thread executor does this with just one nested submit. Use separate pools for dependent tasks, or use ForkJoinPool or CompletableFuture composition.

Detection

ThreadMXBean mx = ManagementFactory.getThreadMXBean();
long[] ids = mx.findDeadlockedThreads();                 // null if none
if (ids != null) {
    for (ThreadInfo info : mx.getThreadInfo(ids)) {
        System.out.println(info.getThreadName() + " waits for " + info.getLockName()
                           + " held by " + info.getLockOwnerName());
    }
}

findDeadlockedThreads covers monitors and java.util.concurrent ownable locks. It can't see a cycle formed through wait, semaphores or latches, or a pool deadlock, because those have no owner to follow.

Reading a thread dump

A thread dump is a snapshot of every thread's state and stack. Take one with jstack <pid>, jcmd <pid> Thread.print, or kill -3 <pid> (which writes to the JVM's stdout). Below is trimmed real output from a deliberate deadlock on Java 21:

"worker-1" #21 [25072] daemon prio=5 os_prio=0 cpu=0.00ms elapsed=0.57s nid=25072
           waiting for monitor entry
   java.lang.Thread.State: BLOCKED (on object monitor)
        at Dead.lambda$main$0(Dead.java:4)
        - waiting to lock <0x00000007145e6500> (a java.lang.Object)
        - locked <0x00000007145e64f0> (a java.lang.Object)

Found one Java-level deadlock:
=============================
"worker-1":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x000001aabf38b4e0 (object 0x00000007145e6500, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "worker-2"
"worker-2":
  waiting to lock monitor 0x000001aabf1aee30 (object 0x00000007145e64f0, a java.lang.Object),
  which is held by "worker-1"
What you seeLikely meaning
Many threads BLOCKED on the same addressLock contention. Find the thread with - locked on that address and see what it's doing
WAITING (parking) in ThreadPoolExecutor.getTaskIdle pool workers. Normal
WAITING (parking) on a lock's sync objectQueued on a ReentrantLock
RUNNABLE in socketRead or similar native codeStuck on a remote call. Often a missing timeout
RUNNABLE with high cpu= growing across dumpsA hot loop

Take three dumps a few seconds apart. One dump can't tell a stuck thread from one that happens to be there. To trace high CPU on Linux, run top -H -p <pid> to find the busy OS thread and match its ID to nid in the dump. nid was decimal in the Java 21 output above, while older JDKs print hex, so convert when needed. Java Flight Recorder gives you lock contention over time, which one snapshot can't.

False Sharing

CPUs move memory in cache lines, commonly 64 bytes. If two independent variables happen to sit in one line and two cores write them, each write invalidates the other core's copy. The line bounces between cores, and the threads slow down although they share no data logically. The cost shows up only as lost throughput, with no bug in the results.

class Counters {
    volatile long a;    // thread 1 writes this
    volatile long b;    // thread 2 writes this: likely the same cache line
}

Fixes are to pad the fields apart, to give each thread its own data and merge later, or to use @jdk.internal.vm.annotation.Contended. That annotation is internal: the JDK uses it in Striped64.Cell and Thread, and application classes need --add-exports to compile it and -XX:-RestrictContended for it to take effect. In practice you meet false sharing when benchmarking per-thread counters or arrays of counters. A profiler showing a slowdown as you add threads to what should be independent work is the usual clue.

Designing Thread-Safe Code

Thread safety means a class stays correct when used from several threads, with no extra coordination from callers. Prefer these strategies in order, because each is simpler than the next:

  1. Stateless: no fields, so nothing to protect. A Spring singleton service should look like this.
  2. Immutable: state set once in the constructor. Share freely. The Core Java overview shows how to build one.
  3. Confined: only one thread touches the object. Local variables, a per-request object, or one owner thread fed by a queue.
  4. Delegated: state lives in a thread-safe class, such as an AtomicLong or a concurrent collection.
  5. Guarded: explicit locks, and only with a clear rule for which lock protects what.

A powerful combination of 2 and 4 is an immutable snapshot behind an atomic reference. Readers never lock, and writers replace the whole state:

final class Settings {
    private record State(int timeout, List<String> hosts) {}
    private final AtomicReference<State> state =
        new AtomicReference<>(new State(1000, List.of()));

    int timeout()         { return state.get().timeout(); }
    List<String> hosts()  { return state.get().hosts(); }

    void addHost(String host) {
        state.updateAndGet(s -> {
            var hosts = new ArrayList<>(s.hosts());
            hosts.add(host);
            return new State(s.timeout(), List.copyOf(hosts));
        });
    }
}

Rules that catch most bugs in review:

  • Every field used by more than one thread has a stated guard: final, volatile, atomic, or a named lock. All reads go through it too, not just writes.
  • Two thread-safe calls in a row are not thread-safe. Use atomic operations such as computeIfAbsent, or lock around the pair.
  • Keep critical sections small, and never do I/O inside one if you can help it.
  • Don't return references to mutable internals from guarded code.
  • Prefer high-level tools: BlockingQueue over wait/notify, executors over threads, ConcurrentHashMap over a locked HashMap. The internals of the concurrent collections are covered in the collections section.

Classic Coding Problems

Print odd and even alternately

class OddEven {
    private int n = 1;
    private final int max;
    OddEven(int max) { this.max = max; }

    synchronized void print(int remainder) throws InterruptedException {
        while (true) {
            while (n <= max && n % 2 != remainder) wait();
            if (n > max) { notifyAll(); return; }     // release the other thread too
            System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().getName() + " " + n);
            n++;
            notifyAll();
        }
    }
}
// new Thread(() -> call(oe, 1), "odd"), new Thread(() -> call(oe, 0), "even")
// Output for max 4 is fixed despite threading: odd 1, even 2, odd 3, even 4

The shared counter decides whose turn it is, so the order is deterministic even though scheduling isn't. The easy bug is the end condition: without the notifyAll before returning, the other thread can wait forever.

Bounded buffer with two conditions

class BoundedBuffer<T> {
    private final Object[] items;
    private int head, tail, count;
    private final Lock lock = new ReentrantLock();
    private final Condition notFull = lock.newCondition();
    private final Condition notEmpty = lock.newCondition();

    BoundedBuffer(int capacity) { items = new Object[capacity]; }

    void put(T x) throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == items.length) notFull.await();
            items[tail] = x;
            tail = (tail + 1) % items.length;
            count++;
            notEmpty.signal();                  // only consumers wait here
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }

    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
    T take() throws InterruptedException {
        lock.lockInterruptibly();
        try {
            while (count == 0) notEmpty.await();
            T x = (T) items[head];
            items[head] = null;                 // don't retain the object for GC
            head = (head + 1) % items.length;
            count--;
            notFull.signal();
            return x;
        } finally { lock.unlock(); }
    }
}

Two conditions allow signal() instead of signalAll(), because everyone waiting on a condition is waiting for the same thing. This is essentially how ArrayBlockingQueue works.

Rate limiter

A token bucket allows short bursts up to the capacity, then a steady rate. Refilling lazily on each call avoids a background thread:

final class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double tokensPerNano;
    private double tokens;
    private long lastRefill = System.nanoTime();

    TokenBucket(long capacity, double tokensPerSecond) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.tokensPerNano = tokensPerSecond / 1e9;
        this.tokens = capacity;
    }

    synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = System.nanoTime();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - lastRefill) * tokensPerNano);
        lastRefill = now;
        if (tokens >= 1) { tokens -= 1; return true; }
        return false;
    }
}

A bucket of capacity 5 at 10 tokens per second allowed 5 of 20 instant calls, then about 2 more after 250 ms (timing-dependent). Use System.nanoTime(), not currentTimeMillis(): wall-clock time can jump. A sliding-window log stores recent timestamps in a Deque, removes the expired ones and compares the size to the limit. It's exact but uses memory per request. A fixed window counter is simplest but allows double the limit around a window edge. For one limit per user, keep buckets in a ConcurrentHashMap via computeIfAbsent. Across several instances, the state has to move to shared storage such as Redis.

Dining philosophers

Five philosophers share five forks and each needs two. If everyone takes their left fork first, a circular wait gives deadlock. The standard fix breaks the cycle by making everyone take the lower-numbered fork first:

Object[] forks = new Object[5];
Arrays.setAll(forks, i -> new Object());

Runnable philosopher(int id) {
    int left = id, right = (id + 1) % forks.length;
    Object first = forks[Math.min(left, right)];
    Object second = forks[Math.max(left, right)];    // philosopher 4 reverses direction
    return () -> {
        for (int i = 0; i < 20_000; i++) {
            think();
            synchronized (first) {
                synchronized (second) { eat(); }
            }
        }
    };
}

Run with five threads and 20,000 meals each, this always finished with every count at 20,000. Alternatives: a Semaphore(4) so that at most four sit down at once, or tryLock on both forks with a random backoff.

Print A, B, C in turn with semaphores

Semaphore a = new Semaphore(1), b = new Semaphore(0), c = new Semaphore(0);
Runnable printer(String s, Semaphore mine, Semaphore next, int times) {
    return () -> {
        try {
            for (int i = 0; i < times; i++) {
                mine.acquire();
                System.out.print(s);
                next.release();
            }
        } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); }
    };
}
// Three threads with (A,a,b), (B,b,c), (C,c,a) print ABCABC... in a fixed order

This shows why a semaphore having no owner is useful: one thread acquires and a different thread releases.

Locks Do Not Cross JVMs: Concurrency With Several Instances

synchronized, ReentrantLock, atomics and ConcurrentHashMap only coordinate threads inside one JVM. Once a Spring Boot service runs as 2+ pods, two requests for the same seat, stock item or account can land on different instances, and each local lock is happily acquired. The shared resource is usually the database, so coordinate there:

  • Unique constraint: let the DB reject the duplicate (e.g. one booking per seat per show) and translate DataIntegrityViolationException into a 409.
  • Conditional (atomic) update: UPDATE stock SET qty = qty - 1 WHERE id = ? AND qty > 0, then check the affected row count.
  • Optimistic locking: a JPA @Version column; a concurrent writer gets OptimisticLockException and retries. Best when conflicts are rare.
  • Pessimistic locking: SELECT … FOR UPDATE (@Lock(PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)) inside a short transaction. Best when conflicts are frequent.
  • Distributed lock (Redis, ZooKeeper, a lock table/ShedLock): last resort, needs a lease timeout and a fencing token, because a paused holder can outlive its lease.
@Modifying
@Query("update Product p set p.stock = p.stock - :n where p.id = :id and p.stock >= :n")
int reserve(@Param("id") long id, @Param("n") int n);

// service
if (repo.reserve(id, qty) == 0) throw new OutOfStockException(id);   // safe on any number of pods

Per-Key Locking and Lock Striping

One global lock serialises unrelated work: transferring between accounts A→B should not block C→D. Options, from simplest:

  • Keep the state in a ConcurrentHashMap and mutate with compute/merge: the update for one key is atomic, other keys proceed in parallel. Keep the function short and never touch other keys of the same map inside it.
  • Lock striping: a fixed array of N locks, pick locks[hash(key) % N]. Memory is bounded (no lock per key to clean up), and collisions only cost some contention. ConcurrentHashMap (Java 7) and LongAdder use the same idea.
  • Avoid a Map<Key, Lock> that only grows: it leaks unless entries are removed safely.
final class StripedLocks {
    private final ReentrantLock[] locks;
    StripedLocks(int stripes) {
        locks = new ReentrantLock[stripes];
        for (int i = 0; i < stripes; i++) locks[i] = new ReentrantLock();
    }
    ReentrantLock forKey(Object key) {
        return locks[Math.floorMod(key.hashCode(), locks.length)];
    }
}
// usage
var lock = striped.forKey(accountId);
lock.lock();
try { applyDebit(accountId, amount); } finally { lock.unlock(); }
For two keys (a transfer), acquire both stripes in a fixed order (e.g. by stripe index), and lock once if both keys map to the same stripe, otherwise you reintroduce deadlock.

Amdahl's Law: Why More Threads Stop Helping

If a fraction s of the work is serial (a lock, a single DB row, a shared queue), the maximum speed-up with N threads is 1 / (s + (1 - s) / N). With 10% serial work, even infinite threads give at most 10×; 16 threads give about 6.4×. Past a point, extra threads only add context switches, contention and memory. To scale, shrink the serial part (finer-grained locks, partitioning, batching) rather than adding threads. For I/O-bound work the limit is usually the downstream resource (DB pool size, API rate limit), not the thread count.

Interview Questions — Multithreading & Concurrency

Output? t.run(); t.start(); t.join(); t.start(); where the task prints the thread name and t is named "worker".
main
worker
java.lang.IllegalThreadStateException   (thrown by the second start)

Verified. run() is an ordinary call on the main thread. start() launches the new thread, and join() makes the order fixed. A second start() throws, because a thread can never be restarted, and the state stays TERMINATED.

Output? Current thread interrupts itself, then prints isInterrupted() twice and Thread.interrupted() twice.
Thread.currentThread().interrupt();
System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());   // true
System.out.println(Thread.currentThread().isInterrupted());   // true
System.out.println(Thread.interrupted());                     // true, and clears the flag
System.out.println(Thread.interrupted());                     // false

Verified. isInterrupted() only reads the flag. The static Thread.interrupted() reads and clears it.

A sleeping thread is interrupted. What is the flag inside the catch block? What if the flag was set before sleep() was called?

Inside catch (InterruptedException e), isInterrupted() returns false, because throwing the exception clears the flag (verified). That's why you must restore it with Thread.currentThread().interrupt() if you don't rethrow.

If the flag is already set when sleep is called, it throws immediately without sleeping, with the message sleep interrupted (verified).

Why are wait(), notify() and notifyAll() on Object and not on Thread?

Because a thread waits on a condition guarded by a lock, and in Java any object can be that lock. The wait set belongs to the monitor, and the monitor belongs to the object. A thread doesn't wait for a particular other thread. If these methods were on Thread, one thread would need to know which thread to signal, and any object couldn't serve as a coordination point.

Compare sleep, wait, join, yield and LockSupport.park.
MethodReleases locks?Needs monitor?Woken by
Thread.sleepNoNoTimeout, interrupt
