Object.waitOnly that one monitorYesnotify, timeout, interrupt, spuriously
Thread.joinNo locks of the caller, except the Thread object's monitor internallyNoTarget ends, timeout, interrupt
Thread.yieldNoNoOnly a hint, may continue at once
LockSupport.parkNoNounpark, interrupt (no exception), spuriously

wait only releases the monitor it's called on. Other monitors the thread holds stay held, which is a source of deadlocks with nested locks. unpark grants a single permit, so an unpark before park isn't lost, unlike a notify with no waiter.

A worker thread throws an unchecked exception. What happens to main?

Nothing. Only that thread dies. The exception doesn't propagate across threads. The handler is called with the thread and exception, and main carries on. In a test with a handler that printed a message, the output was bad died: boom and then main still alive. try/catch around t.start() in the parent can't catch it, because the exception happens in a different stack.

When does the JVM exit? What happens if main ends while other threads run?

The JVM exits when all non-daemon threads have finished, or when System.exit or Runtime.halt is called, or on a fatal signal or crash. If main ends while non-daemon threads run, the JVM stays up. main isn't special. Daemon threads are abandoned at exit, without running their finally blocks. Shutdown hooks run on normal exit and on System.exit, but not on halt or kill -9.

What happens when you call obj.wait() or notify() outside synchronized?

Both compile, then throw java.lang.IllegalMonitorStateException: current thread is not owner at runtime (verified). The compiler can't know which monitor you hold. The rule exists to prevent lost wakeups: the condition check and the sleep must be one atomic step, which only the lock gives you.

Can two threads run two different synchronized methods of the same object? What about static and instance?
  • Two synchronized instance methods on the same object: no, they share this.
  • The same methods on different objects: yes, different locks.
  • A synchronized method and a non-synchronized one: yes. synchronized only excludes others that use the same lock.
  • A static synchronized and an instance synchronized method: yes. One locks the Class object and the other locks the instance. If both touch a static field, that's a race.
What does this print? volatile int c; with two threads each doing c++ a million times.

The output is not deterministic. It's usually less than 2,000,000. c++ is a read, an add and a write. volatile makes each read and write visible but doesn't join them into one step, so two threads can read the same value and lose an update. Fix with AtomicInteger, LongAdder or a lock.

Which Thread.State is a thread in when it waits for a ReentrantLock? For a socket read? After notify()?
  • Waiting on ReentrantLock.lock(): WAITING (or TIMED_WAITING for a timed tryLock), because it parks. BLOCKED is reserved for monitors.
  • Blocked in a socket read: RUNNABLE. The JVM doesn't track blocking in native code as a state, so a thread hung on a dead connection looks "running" in a dump.
  • After notify(): BLOCKED until the notifier releases the monitor, then RUNNABLE. Tested on Java 21: WAITING before notify, BLOCKED while main still held the lock.
Why was Thread.stop() removed from use? What replaces it?

stop() threw an asynchronous ThreadDeath at any point in the target's code, which released all its monitors immediately. Objects those monitors protected could be left half-updated, visible to everyone, with no error shown. It was deprecated in Java 1.2 and has thrown UnsupportedOperationException since Java 20. The replacement is interruption, or a volatile flag, where the target stops at a safe point of its own choosing.

Are local variables thread-safe? Is an object referenced by a local variable?

Local primitives and references live on the thread's own stack, so they can't be shared. The object a local refers to is on the heap, and it's confined only if the reference never escapes. If you pass it to another thread, store it in a field or return it to shared code, it's shared. A lambda capturing a local AtomicInteger and running on several threads shares that object, even though the variable is local.

Is a Spring singleton bean thread-safe?

Spring creates one instance and doesn't synchronize access, so it's only as safe as you make it. Every request thread runs through the same object at once. Stateless services are safe, and injected dependencies are fine because they're set once at startup. Danger starts with a mutable field:

@Service
class ReportService {
    private User current;                     // shared across all requests: a bug
    private final SimpleDateFormat f = ...;   // not thread-safe
    private int count;                        // lost updates
}

Use locals, immutable objects, DateTimeFormatter, LongAdder, or a request-scoped bean.

Why does double-checked locking need volatile? Was it always safe with volatile?

Publishing the reference can be reordered with the constructor's writes, so without volatile, the unsynchronized first check can see a non-null reference to an uninitialized object. Volatile adds a happens-before edge from the write to every later read. Before Java 5, it was broken even with volatile, because the old memory model didn't stop ordinary writes moving past volatile ones. JSR-133 in Java 5 fixed that.

Explain happens-before. If A happens-before B, must A run earlier in real time?

Happens-before is a guarantee about visibility: if A happens-before B, then B sees A's effects. It's a partial order built from rules such as program order, monitor unlock to lock, volatile write to read, thread start and join, combined by transitivity.

It doesn't say that A physically executes earlier. The JVM may reorder two statements in the same thread if no one can observe the difference. The reverse also fails: A running earlier in real time, with no happens-before relation, gives no guarantee that B sees A's write.

What can this print? int data; boolean ready; Writer: data = 42; ready = true; Reader: while (!ready); print(data);

The behaviour is not deterministic, since it's a data race. Three outcomes are allowed: it prints 42, it prints 0 (the writes appeared reordered), or it never terminates, because the JIT may hoist ready out of the loop. Making ready volatile guarantees 42 by the chain shown in the happens-before diagram.

Does final make an object thread-safe?

Only partly. A final field guarantees that the reference is set and visible after construction, along with what was reachable through it at that time. It doesn't make the referenced object immutable. final List<String> names = new ArrayList<>() is a fixed reference to a mutable, unsynchronized list. Elements added after construction get no guarantee at all. The class needs all state final and no mutation after construction, and this must not escape during it.

Is iterating a Collections.synchronizedList safe? What's a thread-safe way to do check-then-act on a map?

No. Each call is synchronized, but an iteration is many calls. Another thread's add can trigger ConcurrentModificationException. The documentation requires you to hold the list's lock by hand:

synchronized (list) { for (String s : list) use(s); }

For maps, replace check-then-act with one atomic operation: map.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> load(k)) or map.merge(key, 1, Integer::sum). Separate containsKey and put calls race, even on ConcurrentHashMap.

What is CAS and what are its downsides?

CAS atomically stores a new value only if the location still holds the expected value. Retry loops built on it give lock-free counters and data structures. Threads never block, so there's no deadlock, and a stalled thread can't hold up others.

Downsides:

  • Under heavy contention, repeated failures waste CPU and cause cache-line traffic.
  • The ABA problem.
  • It covers one variable. Several variables must be combined into one immutable object behind an AtomicReference.
  • The update function may run several times, so it must have no side effects.
Output? new AtomicReference<Integer>(100).compareAndSet(100, 101), then the same with 1000 and 1001.

Prints true, then false (verified). AtomicReference compares references. 100 is boxed from the Integer cache, so both boxes are the same object. 1000 is outside the default cache range, so the two boxes differ. Use AtomicInteger for numbers, or keep the exact reference you got from get().

AtomicLong vs LongAdder: which and when?

Use LongAdder for write-heavy statistics under contention, such as request counters. It spreads updates across cells, so threads don't fight over one location. sum() is not a consistent snapshot, and it doesn't return a value on increment.

Use AtomicLong when each update's result matters: ID generation, or CAS decisions like "only increment if below the limit". With low contention, the two perform about the same and AtomicLong uses less memory.

synchronized or ReentrantLock in new code? Why does lock() go before try?

Default to synchronized when it's enough: it's shorter, and you can't forget to release it. Choose ReentrantLock when you need a timeout, interruptible waiting, several conditions, fairness or queue inspection. On Java 21 to 23 only, avoid long blocking inside synchronized with virtual threads, because of pinning.

lock() goes just before try. If it were inside and threw, finally would call unlock() without the lock being held, and that IllegalMonitorStateException would hide the original error.

What's the difference between fair and non-fair locks? Why is non-fair the default?

Fair locks grant access in roughly arrival order. Non-fair locks let an arriving thread take a free lock at once, jumping the queue. Waking a parked thread takes a long time compared with a short critical section. A running thread that barges in and gets out again can complete inside that gap, so non-fair throughput is much better. The risk is that some threads wait a long time. Use fairness only when bounded waiting truly matters, and note that it doesn't guarantee fair OS scheduling.

Output? A thread holding a read lock calls writeLock().tryLock(). Then a thread holding the write lock calls readLock().tryLock().

The first returns false and the second true (verified). Upgrading isn't supported: read holders block writers, including yourself. With plain lock() it would hang forever. Downgrading works, because a writer is exclusive and can safely also take a read lock. After unlocking the write lock, the read count remained 1.

When would you use StampedLock? What are its traps?

Use it for read-mostly data with short reads, where ReentrantReadWriteLock overhead shows up. An optimistic read writes no shared state, so readers scale, and writers aren't blocked by them.

Traps:

  • Not reentrant, so nested acquires deadlock. On a held write lock, tryWriteLock() and tryReadLock() returned 0 when tested.
  • In an optimistic section you must copy to locals, then validate, and only then use the values. Data read before validation can be inconsistent, so don't follow pointers or index arrays based on it.
  • No Conditions, and stamps must be matched to the right unlock method.
Is a Semaphore with one permit the same as a mutex? Output of new Semaphore(1) then release() then availablePermits()?

Prints 2 (verified): permits are just a count, and release doesn't check that you acquired one.

It's not the same as a mutex. A semaphore has no owner, so any thread can release it. It isn't reentrant, so a second acquire by the same thread blocks. That lack of ownership is a feature in signalling between threads, but a mistake in a finally can silently add permits and weaken your limit.

CountDownLatch vs CyclicBarrier vs Phaser?
  • CountDownLatch: one-shot. Waiters wait for N events, which anyone can signal, and the waiters don't have to be the signallers. After zero it's permanently open.
  • CyclicBarrier: reusable. N threads wait for each other, with an optional action when they all arrive. A failure breaks it for everyone.
  • Phaser: a flexible barrier. Parties can register and leave between phases, phases are numbered, and it can be tiered for large groups. When the last party deregisters, it terminates.
Explain the ThreadLocal memory leak. Why is the key weak if the value still leaks?

Values live in a map on the Thread, with a weak reference to the ThreadLocal key and a strong reference to the value. In a pool the thread lives on, so the value lives on until it's removed.

A weak key is a partial defence. If the map held the key strongly, a dropped ThreadLocal could never be collected, as long as the thread lived. With a weak key, the ThreadLocal can be collected, the entry becomes stale, and later get, set and rehash operations can clear stale entries. That cleanup is opportunistic, and it doesn't happen at all if nobody touches the map. So always call remove() in finally.

Output? On a single-thread executor, task 1 sets a ThreadLocal to "alice", and task 2 reads it.

Prints alice (verified). Both tasks ran on the same reused thread, and the value was never removed. In production this leaks one user's context into another's request, which is a security bug and not only a memory one.

What is ScopedValue? Is it final? How does it compare to ThreadLocal?

A way to share an immutable value with everything called within a bounded scope: ScopedValue.where(KEY, value).run(task). It previewed from Java 21 and is final in Java 25 (JEP 506). The binding ends with the call, so there's no remove to forget and no leak. Called code can't change it, so data flow is one-way, and a nested where rebinding only lasts for that inner call. Keep ThreadLocal for real per-thread caching or code that needs to mutate its value. The older signatures such as callWhere differ from the final API, so check which version an example targets.

Core 2, max 4, ArrayBlockingQueue of 2, tasks that never finish quickly. What happens to tasks 1 to 7?

Verified: tasks 1 and 2 start core threads, 3 and 4 go in the queue, 5 and 6 start extra threads (pool size 4), and 7 is rejected with RejectedExecutionException under the default policy. Threads only grow past core after the queue is full. Tasks 5 and 6 begin running before 3 and 4, which still sit in the queue.

Core 10, max 50, with new LinkedBlockingQueue(). How many threads can you get?

Only 10. The queue is effectively unbounded, so offer always succeeds and the "start extra worker" step is never reached. Tested with core 2, max 10: 100 blocked tasks gave 2 threads and 98 queued. The maximumPoolSize setting looks like protection, but it does nothing, and the failure mode becomes a growing queue, rising latency and eventually out-of-memory. Use a bounded queue.

Why is it recommended not to use the Executors factory methods in production?

They hide unbounded resources. newFixedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor have an unbounded queue, so overload becomes a memory problem and queued tasks wait with no limit. newCachedThreadPool has an effectively unlimited thread count, so a burst of slow calls can create thousands of threads. They also give default thread names and offer no rejection path. Construct ThreadPoolExecutor directly, with a bounded queue, a named ThreadFactory and a chosen rejection policy, so that overload behaviour is a decision you made. They're fine for tools and tests with known, small workloads.

execute() vs submit(): how do exceptions differ?

execute takes a Runnable and returns nothing. An exception escapes, reaches the thread's uncaught exception handler and kills that worker, which the pool replaces. submit wraps the task in a FutureTask. The exception is stored and only appears as ExecutionException when someone calls get().

Verified: submit printed nothing until get() threw ExecutionException with cause IllegalStateException: from submit, while execute reached the handler at once. So a submit whose future is ignored fails silently. Catch and log inside the task, or override afterExecute.

shutdown() vs shutdownNow() vs close()?
  • shutdown(): rejects new tasks, finishes queued and running ones, and returns immediately.
  • shutdownNow(): rejects new tasks, removes queued tasks and returns them as a list, and interrupts running workers. Tasks that ignore interruption keep going.
  • awaitTermination: blocks until finished or timeout. It returns false on timeout. It doesn't shut anything down itself.
  • close() (Java 19): shutdown plus waiting, with shutdownNow if the waiting thread is interrupted. Lets you use try-with-resources.
Scenario: an API averages 100 ms per request, with 10 ms CPU and 90 ms waiting on the database, on 8 cores, at 500 requests per second. Size the thread pool.

Little's law: 500 × 0.1 s = 50 concurrent requests on average. Goetz: 8 × (1 + 90/10) = 80 threads at full CPU. Total CPU demand is 500 × 10 ms = 5 cores' worth, so 8 cores are enough.

So start around 60 to 80 threads, with a bounded queue short enough that its wait is acceptable, for example 100 tasks, which adds about 0.2 s of waiting at that rate. Then check the database: if each request holds a connection for most of the 90 ms, you need about 45 connections, so a pool of 10 would be the true bottleneck. Finally, load test and watch p99 latency, because averages hide spikes.

Which rejection policy would you choose for (a) a payment API, (b) a metrics pipeline, (c) a batch importer?
  • (a) Payment API: AbortPolicy. Fail fast, return 503 with Retry-After, and let the client retry. Dropping money events silently is unacceptable, and running on the request thread just hides the overload.
  • (b) Metrics: DiscardPolicy or DiscardOldestPolicy plus a dropped-event counter. Recent data is what matters.
  • (c) Batch importer: CallerRunsPolicy. The reading thread slows down to match the workers, which gives back-pressure for free.
scheduleAtFixedRate vs scheduleWithFixedDelay? What if a run throws?

Fixed rate measures from start to start, and fixed delay measures from the end of one run to the start of the next. If a run overruns the period with fixed rate, the next one starts late. Runs of one task never overlap.

An exception cancels all future runs with no log. Tested with a 10 ms period and a task that throws on run 3: after 200 ms it had run exactly 3 times, isDone() was true, and get() threw ExecutionException. Wrap the body in try/catch for Exception, and log it.

How does ForkJoinPool differ from ThreadPoolExecutor?
ThreadPoolExecutorForkJoinPool
QueueOne shared queueA deque per worker plus submission queues
BalancingWorkers take from the shared queueWork stealing
Best forIndependent tasks, often blockingRecursive, short, non-blocking tasks
Waiting for subtasksA blocked worker is lostjoin() helps by running other tasks
ContentionShared queue is a hot spot with many tiny tasksLow, because mostly local
thenApply vs thenCompose vs thenCombine?
  • thenApply: synchronous transform of a result, T to U. Like map.
  • thenCompose: the function itself returns a future, and it's flattened. Like flatMap. Use it when the next step is async and depends on the previous result.
  • thenCombine: two independent futures merged into one when both finish.
CompletableFuture<CompletableFuture<Integer>> nested = cf.thenApply(x -> asyncCall(x));
CompletableFuture<Integer> flat = cf.thenCompose(x -> asyncCall(x));
Which thread runs the callback in thenApply? In thenApplyAsync?

For thenApply, it depends on timing. If the stage is complete when you attach the callback, the attaching thread runs it. If not, the thread that later completes the stage runs it. completedFuture(1).thenRun(printThreadName) printed main; in a pending chain the same code would run on a pool thread, so don't rely on one or the other.

thenApplyAsync(fn) always submits to the common pool (it printed a ForkJoinPool name) and thenApplyAsync(fn, executor) to that executor. A slow non-async callback can block the thread of the task that completed it, so use the async variant for anything heavy.

exceptionally vs handle vs whenComplete?

exceptionally runs only on failure and returns a replacement value. handle always runs, receives the value and the exception, and its return becomes the new result, so it can recover. whenComplete always runs but can't change the outcome: the original value or exception passes through.

Verified: handle((v, e) -> e == null ? v : -1) gave -1. whenComplete saw the failure, and join() still threw CompletionException. Note that if the whenComplete action itself throws while the stage had succeeded, the result becomes that new exception.

Output? What does the exception handler receive in each of these?
supplyAsync(() -> { throw new ISE("boom"); }).exceptionally(e -> print(e));
failedFuture(new ISE("boom")).exceptionally(e -> print(e));
failedFuture(new ISE("boom")).thenApply(x -> x).exceptionally(e -> print(e));
cf.completeExceptionally(new ISE("boom")); cf.exceptionally(e -> print(e));

Verified on Java 21, in order:

  1. CompletionException wrapping the ISE: exceptions thrown inside async tasks are wrapped.
  2. The plain IllegalStateException: this stage was completed directly with that exception.
  3. CompletionException: it's wrapped when it moves to a dependent stage.
  4. The plain IllegalStateException.

Also join() throws CompletionException, and get() throws ExecutionException. Always unwrap getCause() before checking types.

What does CompletableFuture.allOf(a, b).join() return? Does it stop on the first failure?

It returns null, because it's a CompletableFuture<Void> (verified). Read the values afterward with a.join(), which won't block by then. It doesn't fail fast either: it completes only after all inputs finish, then reports a failure. In a test, a failed future and a 300 ms task together took the full 300 ms.

Does orTimeout or cancel(true) stop a running CompletableFuture task?

No. A CompletableFuture doesn't know which thread is doing its work. cancel just completes it with CancellationException, and mayInterruptIfRunning is ignored. orTimeout completes it with TimeoutException. In both cases the task continues, holding its thread and possibly its side effects. To really stop work, keep the Future from an ExecutorService.submit and call cancel(true) on it, have the task check a flag, or use structured concurrency. Client-level timeouts on the HTTP or JDBC call are also needed, since those are what actually free the thread.

Virtual threads: what are they, and when should you not use them?

JVM-managed threads, final in Java 21. They mount on a small set of carrier platform threads while running and unmount to the heap when blocked, so you can write simple blocking code and still handle a huge number of concurrent tasks.

Avoid them, or get no gain, for:

  • CPU-bound work: use a pool sized to the cores, or parallel streams.
  • Workloads with few concurrent tasks: nothing to gain.
  • Code relying on heavy ThreadLocal caches per thread: memory grows with task count.
  • Java 21 to 23 code with long I/O inside synchronized, including in libraries: pinning, which is fixed in Java 24.
  • Unbounded access to a limited resource: add a semaphore or pool limit.
What is pinning? What did JEP 491 change, and what's left?

Pinning means a virtual thread can't unmount, so when it blocks it holds its carrier too. On Java 21 to 23 this happens while inside synchronized, and during native code. Because the scheduler has few carriers, a handful of pinned threads can stall a whole server. Symptoms include requests hanging while CPU sits idle.

JEP 491 (Java 24) lets virtual threads acquire, hold and release monitors independently of their carrier, so they can unmount inside synchronized and in Object.wait(). Pinning remains for native frames (JNI or foreign function calls on the stack) and class initialization. Detect it with the JFR event jdk.VirtualThreadPinned.

Output? Print isDaemon, getPriority and isVirtual for a virtual thread, then call setDaemon(false) and setPriority(10).
Thread v = Thread.ofVirtual().name("v1").unstarted(task);
System.out.println(v.isDaemon() + " " + v.getPriority() + " " + v.isVirtual());
// true 5 true
v.setDaemon(false);   // IllegalArgumentException: 'false' not legal for virtual threads
v.setPriority(10);    // no effect, getPriority() still 5

Verified on Java 21. Inside the task, Thread.currentThread() printed VirtualThread[#41,v1]/runnable@ForkJoinPool-1-worker-1, which shows the carrier. The number and worker vary per run.

You move to virtual threads and the database pool starts timing out. Why? And should you put virtual threads in a pool to fix it?

The old fixed thread pool was acting as an accidental limit: at most 200 requests could reach the database. With unlimited virtual threads, thousands pile onto a connection pool of 20. Many wait, and they time out.

Don't pool virtual threads. Limit the actual resource: size the connection pool properly and let its queue and timeout do the work, or guard the call with a Semaphore. Decide what to do when overloaded, too, since rejecting early is usually better than queuing without limit.

How is structured concurrency better than CompletableFuture for fan-out, and can you use it in production?

With CompletableFuture, a failing branch doesn't cancel its siblings, cancellation doesn't reach running tasks, and threads have no parent-child relation. Structured concurrency ties subtasks to a scope: on failure the others are cancelled by interruption, the block doesn't exit until they've finished, and you write plain blocking code with ordinary try/catch.

It's still a preview API on Java 25, and it changed form across releases, so production use means enabling preview features and accepting API changes. For stable code today, use CompletableFuture or an executor with explicit cancellation.

A service hangs with low CPU in production. Walk through your diagnosis.
  1. Take three thread dumps a few seconds apart, before restarting anything.
  2. Look for "Found one Java-level deadlock" at the end of the dump.
  3. Look for many threads BLOCKED on one address. Then find who holds it and what it's waiting on.
  4. Look for workers stuck in socketRead, HikariPool.getConnection or similar. Slow downstream calls and exhausted connection pools are the most common real cause, and the fix is usually timeouts.
  5. Check whether all pool threads wait on Future.get for tasks in the same pool (thread-starvation deadlock).
  6. Check GC logs too: long pauses also look like a hang.
  7. On virtual threads, get a dump with jcmd Thread.dump_to_file, and check for pinning on Java 21 to 23.
Show how a single-thread executor can deadlock with no locks.
ExecutorService one = Executors.newSingleThreadExecutor();
Future<String> outer = one.submit(() -> {
    Future<String> inner = one.submit(() -> "inner");   // queued behind this task
    return inner.get();                                  // waits forever
});
outer.get();   // never returns

The only worker is busy waiting for a task that needs that same worker. This is thread-starvation deadlock. findDeadlockedThreads reports nothing, because no lock cycle exists. Avoid waiting on tasks in the same bounded pool. Use a separate pool, or chain with thenCompose.

Livelock vs starvation, with examples?

Livelock: threads are active but make no progress, like two people in a corridor who keep stepping aside the same way. In code, two threads using tryLock on two locks each fail, release and retry in lockstep. Random backoff fixes it.

Starvation: others progress but a thread doesn't. A low-priority task behind a steady flow in a priority queue, a writer behind constant readers, or a reader in a non-fair lock with long holders. Fix with fair policies, aging priorities or separate pools.

What is false sharing and how would you detect it?

Independent variables that share a cache line cause cores to invalidate each other's cache copies on each write. Logically unrelated threads slow each other down, with correct results but poor scaling.

Clues: throughput falling as threads are added to work that shares no data, with counters or per-thread slots in one array or object. Confirm with hardware counters (for example perf c2c on Linux) or by adding padding and measuring with JMH. Fix by separating the data, padding, or per-thread state merged later, which is what LongAdder does.

Design: compute an expensive value once per key, even with many concurrent callers.

Store a future per key, so that later callers wait for the same computation:

class Memoizer<K, V> {
    private final ConcurrentHashMap<K, CompletableFuture<V>> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    private final Function<K, V> loader;
    Memoizer(Function<K, V> loader) { this.loader = loader; }

    V get(K key) {
        CompletableFuture<V> f = cache.computeIfAbsent(key, k ->
            CompletableFuture.supplyAsync(() -> loader.apply(k)));
        f.whenComplete((v, ex) -> { if (ex != null) cache.remove(key, f); });  // retry later
        return f.join();
    }
}

Why a future: putting the computation directly in computeIfAbsent would hold a map bin lock for its whole duration, which blocks unrelated keys. Removing failed futures avoids caching an error forever. Note what's missing for production: size limits and expiry, which is why libraries such as Caffeine exist.

Design: process events concurrently but keep order per customer.

Route events by key to one of N single-threaded lanes, so that the same customer always goes to the same lane. That preserves per-key order while different keys run in parallel:

ExecutorService[] lanes = new ExecutorService[n];   // each a single-thread executor
void dispatch(Event e) {
    int i = Math.floorMod(e.customerId().hashCode(), lanes.length);
    lanes[i].execute(() -> handle(e));
}

Use bounded queues, and decide on overflow behaviour. A slow customer delays others sharing that lane. A plain pool can't do this: two events for one customer could overtake each other. Kafka partitions apply the same idea at the cluster level.

Design: gracefully stop a queue consumer so no accepted message is lost.
  1. Stop accepting new work: close the source or set a flag.
  2. Call pool.shutdown(), so queued tasks still run.
  3. Wait with awaitTermination for a bounded time, shorter than the platform's kill timeout (Kubernetes defaults to 30 s).
  4. If time runs out, call shutdownNow(), and save the returned tasks, or leave them unacknowledged so that the broker redelivers them.
  5. Consumers should end with the interrupt protocol, and acknowledge only after processing finishes.

Run this from a shutdown hook, or let Spring's lifecycle do it (server.shutdown=graceful in Spring Boot). Delivery is usually at-least-once, so handlers must be idempotent.

Why shouldn't you start a thread in a constructor?

It lets this escape before construction finishes. The new thread can see default field values, and final-field guarantees don't apply yet, because the constructor hasn't completed. Subclass constructors won't have run either, so an overridden method called by the thread can act on an uninitialized subclass. Instead, use a private constructor plus a static factory method that creates the object, then starts the thread.

Why is SimpleDateFormat a classic concurrency bug?

It keeps parsing state in a mutable Calendar field. A shared static instance gives wrong dates, or exceptions such as NumberFormatException, under load, usually only in production. Fixes, best first: use the immutable DateTimeFormatter, create a new instance per use, or wrap it in a ThreadLocal.

Your synchronized booking method prevents double bookings locally, but in production with 3 pods two users booked the same seat. Why, and how do you fix it?

A Java lock only protects threads in one JVM; each pod has its own monitor, so both requests entered the critical section. Move the guarantee to the shared store: a unique constraint on (show_id, seat_no), an atomic conditional UPDATE … WHERE status = 'FREE' checking the row count, optimistic locking with @Version, or SELECT … FOR UPDATE. Use a distributed lock only if no DB-level guarantee fits.

💡 Interviewers like hearing "the database is the source of truth for the invariant, so the database should enforce it".
How do you avoid one global lock when updates for different keys are independent?

Lock per key. The easy route is ConcurrentHashMap.compute(key, …), which is atomic per key. For arbitrary critical sections, use lock striping: a fixed array of locks indexed by floorMod(key.hashCode(), n). It bounds memory and avoids the leak of a never-cleaned Map<Key, Lock>. When two keys are needed, lock stripes in a consistent order.

You doubled the thread pool from 50 to 100 and throughput did not improve. Why?

Something serial is the bottleneck (Amdahl's law): a shared lock, a hot DB row, a DB connection pool of 20, a rate-limited downstream API, or CPU saturation. Extra threads just queue on that resource and add context switching and memory. Measure where threads wait (thread dump, JFR lock profiling, pool metrics like Hikari pending connections) and fix the constraint: raise the downstream limit, partition the hot data, batch, or cache.

Which concurrent collection would you pick for: a read-mostly listener list, a shared cache, a sorted concurrent index, a work queue?
  • Read-mostly listeners: CopyOnWriteArrayList (iteration never throws, writes copy the array).
  • Shared cache/map: ConcurrentHashMap (or Caffeine when you need eviction).
  • Sorted concurrent map/set: ConcurrentSkipListMap/Set.
  • Producer–consumer: a bounded ArrayBlockingQueue or LinkedBlockingQueue(capacity) for back-pressure; ConcurrentLinkedQueue if you never need to block.

Avoid Collections.synchronizedX in new code: compound actions and iteration still need external locking.

Is it safe to use @Transactional with a Java lock, e.g. lock, then call a transactional method, then unlock?

Often not. If the lock is acquired inside the transactional method, the unlock happens before the proxy commits, so a second thread can enter and read the old, uncommitted state. The lock must wrap the whole transaction (acquire before the transactional call, release after it returns), and even then it only works on one instance. Prefer a DB-level guarantee (constraint, conditional update, row lock).

File I/O, NIO & Serialization Core Java

Moving data in and out of a program: classic streams and decorators, text encoding, the modern Path and Files APIs, NIO channels, buffers and selectors, Java serialization and its security risks, and network programming up to HttpClient.

The two generations of Java I/O

java.io (1.0)java.nio (1.4) and NIO.2 (7)
AbstractionStream: one byte or char at a timeChannel + Buffer: blocks of data
BlockingAlways blockingNon-blocking available for sockets
DirectionOne way (input or output)Channels may be two-way
FilesFilePath, Files
Best forSimple sequential I/O, easy codeMany connections, large files, advanced file operations

Byte streams vs character streams

All data on disk or a network is bytes. Text only exists after a charset decodes those bytes into characters. Java has two families for this reason.

Byte streamsCharacter streams
Base classesInputStream, OutputStreamReader, Writer
Unit8-bit byte16-bit char
FilesFileInputStream, FileOutputStreamFileReader, FileWriter
MemoryByteArrayInputStreamStringReader, CharArrayReader
BufferedBufferedInputStreamBufferedReader (has readLine)
Use forImages, ZIPs, class files, anything binaryText

Bridges: InputStreamReader turns bytes into chars, and OutputStreamWriter turns chars into bytes, each with a given charset.

Key InputStream details

  • read() returns an int: 0 to 255, or -1 for end of stream. It cannot return byte, or -1 would be indistinguishable from the value 0xFF.
  • read(byte[]) may return fewer bytes than requested. It returns the count actually read. Ignoring that count is a classic bug, particularly on sockets. readNBytes (Java 11) reads exactly n unless the stream ends.
  • readAllBytes() and transferTo(out) (Java 9) remove most hand-written copy loops.
byte[] data = {1, (byte) 0xFF, 2};
var in = new ByteArrayInputStream(data);

byte b; int n = 0;
while ((b = (byte) in.read()) != -1) n++;   // bug: 0xFF casts to -1, stops early
System.out.println(n);                      // 1

in.reset();
int v; n = 0;
while ((v = in.read()) != -1) n++;          // correct: compare the int
System.out.println(n);                      // 3

Decorators and buffering

java.io is built on the Decorator pattern. A decorator wraps a stream, has the same interface, and adds one capability. You stack what you need instead of having a class for every combination.

DecoratorAdds
BufferedInputStream/OutputStream, BufferedReader/WriterAn in-memory buffer (default 8192)
DataInputStream/OutputStreamPrimitives in binary: readInt, writeUTF
ObjectInputStream/OutputStreamObject serialization
PrintStream, PrintWriterprint, printf; never throw IOException
GZIPInputStream, ZipInputStream, CipherInputStreamCompression, encryption
PushbackInputStream, LineNumberReader, SequenceInputStreamUn-read a byte, count lines, join streams

Why buffering matters

An unbuffered FileInputStream.read() makes one operating system call per byte. System calls are expensive, so reading a large file byte by byte is drastically slower than reading through a buffer, which fetches a chunk with one system call and serves bytes from memory.

For writes, buffered data stays in memory until the buffer fills, or until flush() or close(). Verified on Java 21:

var w = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(file));
w.write("hello");
Files.size(path);    // 0: still in the buffer
w.flush();
Files.size(path);    // 5
w.close();
w.write("x");        // IOException: Stream closed

If the process exits with no close, buffered data is simply lost. flush() pushes data to the OS, not necessarily to disk. For a real durability guarantee, use FileChannel.force(true).

Gotcha: PrintWriter and PrintStream swallow IOException. If the disk fills up, your writes silently vanish, and you must call checkError() to find out. Verified with a failing writer: checkError() returned true and nothing was thrown.

Reading and writing text correctly

Prefer the Files helpers. They always state their charset behaviour, and default to UTF-8.

Path p = Path.of("data.txt");

String all = Files.readString(p);                 // Java 11
List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(p);
Files.writeString(p, "text", StandardOpenOption.APPEND);

// Large file: do not load it all into memory. Close the stream!
try (Stream<String> s = Files.lines(p)) {
  long errors = s.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).count();
}

try (BufferedReader r = Files.newBufferedReader(p);
     BufferedWriter w = Files.newBufferedWriter(Path.of("out.txt"))) {
  String line;
  while ((line = r.readLine()) != null) {
    w.write(line.toUpperCase());
    w.newLine();
  }
}
ScannerBufferedReader
PurposeParsing tokens and numbersFast line reading
SpeedSlower, uses regexFaster
ExceptionsSwallows IOException (ioException())Throws IOException
Thread-safeNoYes (synchronized internally)

Character encoding

A character set assigns numbers (code points) to characters; Unicode is the universal one. An encoding turns code points into bytes. UTF-8 uses 1 to 4 bytes per code point, and ASCII stays one byte. Java's String is a sequence of UTF-16 code units, with compact storage since Java 9, which uses one byte per char when all fit in Latin-1 (JEP 254).

String s = "héllo";
s.length();                                 // 5
s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length;       // 6: é takes 2 bytes
s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.ISO_8859_1).length;  // 5
s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_16).length;      // 12: 2-byte BOM + 10

// Mojibake: bytes written as UTF-8, read as ISO-8859-1
new String(s.getBytes(UTF_8), ISO_8859_1).length();   // 6: é became Ã©

// Characters outside the Basic Multilingual Plane use a surrogate pair
String emoji = "😀";
emoji.length();                         // 2
emoji.codePointCount(0, emoji.length()); // 1
emoji.getBytes(UTF_8).length;           // 4

Default charset: since Java 18 (JEP 400), the default is UTF-8 on all platforms. Before that, it came from the OS, so code using new FileReader(f) or getBytes() with no charset could behave differently on Windows and Linux. Always name the charset anyway. FileReader gained a charset constructor in Java 11.

Malformed input

The APIs differ on bad bytes, as verified with the invalid UTF-8 sequence C3 28:

  • Files.readAllLines, Files.newBufferedReader: throw MalformedInputException: Input length = 1.
  • new InputStreamReader(in, UTF_8), new String(bytes, UTF_8): quietly replace it with U+FFFD, the replacement character.

To control this, use a CharsetDecoder with onMalformedInput(CodingErrorAction.REPORT). Java's UTF-8 decoder also does not strip a byte order mark (BOM), so a file saved with one begins with a stray ﻿.

File vs Path

java.io.Filejava.nio.file.Path + Files
Failure reportingdelete(), mkdir() return false, with no reasonSpecific exceptions: NoSuchFileException, AccessDeniedException, DirectoryNotEmptyException
Symbolic linksPoorFull support
AttributesA fewPOSIX, DOS, owner, ACL
Directory walklistFiles() loads everythingLazy Files.list/walk/find
Other file systemsNoPluggable: ZIP, in-memory (FileSystemProvider)
Copy, moverenameTo onlycopy, move, atomic move

Convert with file.toPath() and path.toFile(). A Path is only a name. Creating one does not touch the disk, and the file may not exist.

Path p = Path.of("/home/a/../b/./c.txt");     // Java 11; before that, Paths.get
p.normalize();                  // /home/b/c.txt   text only, no disk access
p.getFileName();                // c.txt
p.getParent();                  // /home/a/../b/.
p.getNameCount();               // 6

Path.of("/a/b").resolve("c/d");         // /a/b/c/d
Path.of("/a/b").resolve("/x");          // /x      absolute argument wins
Path.of("/a/b").resolveSibling("z");    // /a/z
Path.of("/a/b").relativize(Path.of("/a/c/d"));  // ../c/d
Path.of("abc").startsWith("a");         // false: compares whole name elements

Output above is shown with forward slashes, as on Linux; Windows prints backslashes. p.toRealPath() resolves symlinks and needs the file to exist. equals on paths follows the platform: Path.of("a.txt").equals(Path.of("A.txt")) was true on Windows and is false on Linux.

Files API

Files.exists(p);  Files.isDirectory(p);  Files.size(p);
Files.createDirectories(Path.of("a/b/c"));        // no error if it exists
Files.createTempFile("pre", ".tmp");
Files.delete(p);                                  // throws if missing
Files.deleteIfExists(p);                          // returns boolean
Files.copy(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
Files.move(src, dst, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE);
Files.mismatch(a, b);                             // Java 12: -1 if identical

try (Stream<Path> s = Files.list(dir)) { … }      // one level
try (Stream<Path> s = Files.walk(dir)) { … }      // recursive
try (Stream<Path> s = Files.find(dir, 5, (path, attrs) -> attrs.size() > 1_000_000)) { … }

// Delete a tree: children before parents
try (Stream<Path> s = Files.walk(dir)) {
  s.sorted(Comparator.reverseOrder()).forEach(q -> q.toFile().delete());
}

Errors verified on Java 21: Files.delete on a missing file throws NoSuchFileException; on a non-empty folder, DirectoryNotEmptyException; Files.copy onto an existing file, FileAlreadyExistsException. In contrast, file.delete() just returns false.

Atomic file replacement: a crash during Files.writeString(config, …) leaves a partial file. Write to a temporary file in the same directory, then Files.move(tmp, config, ATOMIC_MOVE). A reader sees the old file or the new one, never half.

Check-then-act races: if (Files.exists(p)) Files.delete(p); can fail if something else deletes it in between. Just attempt the operation and handle the exception. This pattern, when it has security consequences, is called TOCTOU (time of check to time of use).

NIO: channels and buffers

A Channel is a connection to a file or socket. A Buffer is a fixed-size block of memory. You read from a channel into a buffer, and write from a buffer to a channel. Working with blocks is much closer to how the OS operates.

Buffer state

A buffer has three numbers: capacity (fixed size), position (next index) and limit (first index that must not be touched).

MethodEffectWhen
flip()limit = position, position = 0After filling, before reading
clear()position = 0, limit = capacity. Data is not erasedReady to fill again
compact()Moves unread data to the front, position after itWhen some data is left, e.g. a partial message
rewind()position = 0, limit unchangedRead the same data again
mark(), reset()Remember and return to a positionTrial parsing

Forgetting flip is the most common NIO bug: position sits at the end, so you read nothing or get BufferUnderflowException. Writing past the limit gives BufferOverflowException.

Heap vs direct buffers

ByteBuffer.allocate(n)ByteBuffer.allocateDirect(n)
MemoryOn the Java heap, backed by a byte[]Native memory, outside the heap; no accessible array
AllocationCheapExpensive, so pool or reuse them
I/OJVM copies via a temporary native bufferThe OS reads and writes it directly
LimitHeap size-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize; exceeding gives OutOfMemoryError: Direct buffer memory

The GC can move heap objects, so native code cannot be handed a heap array directly while the OS uses it. That is why the JVM needs an intermediate copy, and why servers such as Netty use pooled direct buffers.

FileChannel

try (FileChannel in = FileChannel.open(src);
     FileChannel out = FileChannel.open(dst, CREATE, WRITE)) {
  long pos = 0, size = in.size();
  while (pos < size) pos += in.transferTo(pos, size - pos, out);   // may transfer less
}

transferTo can use zero-copy (for example sendfile on Linux): the kernel moves data from the page cache to the socket with no trip through user space. Kafka uses it to serve consumers. FileChannel also offers lock() for file locks held by the whole JVM process, positional reads, and force().

Memory-mapped files

FileChannel.map maps a region of a file into the process's virtual address space, so you access file contents as memory. The OS pages data in on demand and writes dirty pages back on its own.

try (FileChannel ch = FileChannel.open(path, CREATE, READ, WRITE)) {
  MappedByteBuffer mb = ch.map(FileChannel.MapMode.READ_WRITE, 0, 16);
  mb.putInt(0, 42);
  mb.force();                          // flush to storage
  System.out.println(ch.size());       // 16: the file was extended
  System.out.println(mb.getInt(0));    // 42
}
  • Good for huge files with random access, and for sharing data between processes. Reads avoid a copy into user space. Lucene, Kafka index files and many databases use mapping.
  • Size limit: one MappedByteBuffer covers at most 2 GB (IllegalArgumentException: Size exceeds Integer.MAX_VALUE); use several, or the Foreign Function & Memory API (final in Java 22), whose FileChannel.map overload returns a MemorySegment, works beyond this and can be closed deterministically through an Arena.
  • No unmap call: a MappedByteBuffer is released only when garbage collected. On Windows, the file cannot be deleted until then.
  • A page fault blocks the thread, and if another process truncates the file, access can crash with an internal error. Page-ins are not visible as I/O calls.

Selectors: non-blocking network I/O

With blocking I/O, each connection needs a thread sitting in read(). Ten thousand idle connections mean ten thousand platform threads. A Selector lets one thread watch many channels and react only to the ready ones. It wraps OS facilities: epoll on Linux, kqueue on macOS, and an equivalent on Windows.

Selector selector = Selector.open();
ServerSocketChannel server = ServerSocketChannel.open();
server.bind(new InetSocketAddress(8080));
server.configureBlocking(false);                       // must be non-blocking
server.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_ACCEPT);

while (true) {
  selector.select();                                   // blocks until something is ready
  Iterator<SelectionKey> it = selector.selectedKeys().iterator();
  while (it.hasNext()) {
    SelectionKey key = it.next();
    it.remove();                                       // you must remove it yourself
    if (key.isAcceptable()) {
      SocketChannel c = server.accept();
      c.configureBlocking(false);
      c.register(selector, SelectionKey.OP_READ, ByteBuffer.allocate(1024));
    } else if (key.isReadable()) {
      SocketChannel c = (SocketChannel) key.channel();
      ByteBuffer buf = (ByteBuffer) key.attachment();
      if (c.read(buf) == -1) { c.close(); continue; }  // peer closed
      buf.flip();
      while (buf.hasRemaining()) c.write(buf);         // echo back (simplified)
      buf.clear();
    }
  }
}

This echo loop was run on Java 21 with a test client. In real code, a non-blocking write may send only part of the buffer, so you keep the rest and register OP_WRITE. One read also may not be a whole message, which is why you need framing. Long work must not run on the event loop thread.

BIO vs NIO vs AIO vs virtual threads

ModelThreadsCode styleFits
Blocking I/O + platform threadsOne per connectionSimple, sequentialUp to a few thousand connections
NIO + SelectorFew event loopsCallbacks, state machinesMany mostly idle connections, proxies
AIO (NIO.2 asynchronous)OS or thread pool completesCompletion handlers, FutureRarely chosen; Netty dropped its AIO transport
Blocking I/O + virtual threads (Java 21)One cheap virtual thread per connectionSimple, sequentialHigh concurrency without async code

A virtual thread that blocks on a socket is unmounted from its carrier thread, and the JDK waits with its own selector-like poller. So you write blocking code and get NIO-like scaling. NIO remains useful in frameworks and for fine buffer control.

AIO: asynchronous channels

Java 7 added AsynchronousFileChannel and AsynchronousSocketChannel. Unlike a Selector, which tells you a channel is ready, these start an operation and tell you when it has completed, through a Future or a CompletionHandler.

try (var ch = AsynchronousFileChannel.open(path)) {
  ByteBuffer buf = ByteBuffer.allocate(1024);
  Future<Integer> f = ch.read(buf, 0);
  int n = f.get();                         // or pass a CompletionHandler

  ch.read(buf, 0, null, new CompletionHandler<Integer, Void>() {
    public void completed(Integer bytes, Void att) { /* runs on a pool thread */ }
    public void failed(Throwable t, Void att) { log.error("read failed", t); }
  });
}

WatchService

Monitors a directory for changes through OS file notifications, where available (inotify on Linux). Used for hot config reloads and development tools.

Path dir = Path.of("conf");
try (WatchService ws = dir.getFileSystem().newWatchService()) {
  dir.register(ws, ENTRY_CREATE, ENTRY_MODIFY, ENTRY_DELETE);
  while (true) {
    WatchKey key = ws.take();                  // blocks
    for (WatchEvent<?> ev : key.pollEvents()) {
      if (ev.kind() == OVERFLOW) continue;     // events were lost
      Path name = (Path) ev.context();         // relative to dir
      System.out.println(ev.kind() + " " + name);
    }
    if (!key.reset()) break;                   // the directory is gone
  }
}
  • Not recursive. You register each directory yourself.
  • You must call key.reset(), or the key stops delivering events.
  • The context is relative: resolve it against the directory.
  • Editors may trigger multiple events per save, so debounce. Events can also be dropped (OVERFLOW).
  • Where no native support exists, a polling fallback can add delays of seconds. Network drives often do not report changes.

Java serialization

Serialization converts an object graph to bytes; deserialization rebuilds it. A class opts in with the marker interface Serializable, which has no methods. It was designed for RMI and for early persistence. In new code, avoid it: it is fragile and insecure, as explained below. You still need to know it for interviews and legacy systems.

class Child extends Base implements Serializable {
  private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;
  int c = 7;
  transient int t = 8;        // skipped
  static int s = 1;           // not part of the instance, skipped
}

try (var out = new ObjectOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(p))) {
  out.writeObject(child);
}
try (var in = new ObjectInputStream(Files.newInputStream(p))) {
  Child c2 = (Child) in.readObject();
}

What happens on deserialization

The JVM allocates the object without running its constructor, sets fields from the stream, and only runs the no-arg constructor of the first non-serializable superclass. Field initializers do not run either. Verified, with non-serializable Base whose constructor sets b = 9:

c.c = 70; c.b = 50; c.t = 80; Child.s = 2;
serialize, then Child.s = 3; deserialize:

Base()                     // printed: Base's no-arg constructor ran
r.b = 9                    // from Base(), not the 50 that was set
r.c = 70                   // restored
r.t = 0                    // transient gets the default, not the initializer 8
Child.s = 3                // static is not restored
transient String n = "x"   // comes back null
SituationResult
Field's class is not serializableNotSerializableException: java.lang.Object (at write)
Non-serializable parent with no accessible no-arg constructorInvalidClassException: …; no valid constructor (at read)
A superclass is serializableAll subclasses are serializable automatically
Same object written twice in one streamSecond is a back-reference; object identity kept and cycles are handled
Mutate, then write the same object againThe stream repeats the old state, unless you call reset()
Different serialVersionUIDInvalidClassException: local class incompatible
M m = new M();                // v = 1
out.writeObject(m);
m.v = 2;
out.writeObject(m);           // back-reference: reader sees v = 1 again
out.reset();
m.v = 3;
out.writeObject(m);           // written anew
// read back: 1, 1 (same object), 3

serialVersionUID

A long stored in the stream and compared to the local class on read. If you do not declare it, the JVM computes a hash from class details: name, interfaces, fields and methods. Compiler differences or a small change, such as adding a method or a lambda, can alter it and break old data.

With a declared ID, compatible changes work. Compatible: adding a field (default value on old data), removing a field. Incompatible: changing a field's type, moving a class in the hierarchy in certain ways, changing between Serializable and Externalizable.

Customizing

HookPurpose
private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream)Add or transform data. Call defaultWriteObject() first
private void readObject(ObjectInputStream)Rebuild transient state, validate invariants, defensively copy mutable fields
Object writeReplace()Serialize a different object in place of this one
Object readResolve()Replace the deserialized object after reading
readObjectNoData()Stream has no data for this class
ExternalizableThe class takes total control of the format
class Cust implements Serializable {
  transient String secret = "pw";
  private void writeObject(ObjectOutputStream o) throws IOException {
    o.defaultWriteObject();
    o.writeUTF(new StringBuilder(secret).reverse().toString());  // toy "encryption"
  }
  private void readObject(ObjectInputStream i) throws IOException, ClassNotFoundException {
    i.defaultReadObject();
    secret = new StringBuilder(i.readUTF()).reverse().toString();
  }
}

These private methods are found by reflection, so they look like they could never be called.

readResolve and singletons

class Single implements Serializable {
  static final Single I = new Single();
  private Single() {}
  private Object readResolve() { return I; }   // discards the new copy
}
deserialize(serialize(Single.I)) == Single.I;  // true; false without readResolve
deserialize(serialize(En.A)) == En.A;          // true: enums serialize by name

Without readResolve, deserialization makes a second "singleton". Enums are always safe, as the stream stores only the name, and readObject hooks are ignored for them.

Serializable vs Externalizable

SerializableExternalizable
MethodsNone requiredwriteExternal, readExternal
Who writes dataJVM, by reflectionYour code
Constructor on readNot called for serializable classesPublic no-arg constructor is called
transientHonouredIrrelevant: you choose what is written
Field initializers on readSkippedRun, as a normal construction

Verified: an Externalizable class that writes only v, with transient int w = 4 set to 40, comes back with v restored and w = 4, because the constructor ran. Without a public no-arg constructor, it fails: InvalidClassException: …; no valid constructor.

Records

Records (Java 16) serialize by their components, and deserialization goes through the canonical constructor, so validation runs. Hooks such as readObject are ignored. This fixes the classic flaw that deserialization bypasses constructors. Verified: a compact constructor printed on creation and again on deserialization.

Deserialization security

ObjectInputStream.readObject() instantiates whatever classes the stream names, if they are on the classpath, and runs their readObject methods, all before your cast is checked. An attacker who controls the bytes chooses the classes. A gadget chain is a set of ordinary library classes whose readObject, hashCode or similar methods can be combined to reach dangerous code, up to remote code execution. The well-known 2015 case abused Apache Commons Collections, and affected WebLogic, WebSphere, JBoss and Jenkins. ysoserial is a public tool that produces such payloads.

Defences:

  1. Never deserialize untrusted data with native serialization. This is the only real fix.
  2. Use a data format with no code execution: JSON into specific DTOs, Protobuf.
  3. If you cannot avoid it, use ObjectInputFilter (JEP 290, Java 9) with an allow-list ending in !*. Java 17 added filter factories per context (JEP 415).
ObjectInputStream in = new ObjectInputStream(stream);
in.setObjectInputFilter(ObjectInputFilter.Config.createFilter(
    "com.acme.dto.*;java.util.*;maxdepth=5;maxbytes=100000;!*"));
Object o = in.readObject();    // InvalidClassException: filter status: REJECTED
                               // for anything outside the list

A JVM-wide filter can be set by -Djdk.serialFilter=…. The same class of problem applies to JSON libraries with polymorphic typing: never enable Jackson's default typing on untrusted input.

Alternatives

FormatTypeSchemaStrengthWeakness
JSON (Jackson, Gson)TextOptionalReadable, universal, REST defaultLarger, slower, no binary or strong numeric types
ProtobufBinary.proto, requiredCompact, fast, field numbers allow evolution; gRPCNot human-readable, generated code
AvroBinaryRequired, with schema registryStrong schema evolution; common with KafkaNeeds writer's schema to read
KryoBinaryNoneFast in JVM-only systemsJava-centric; do not use on untrusted data
Java serializationBinaryClass itselfBuilt in, handles object graphsInsecure, fragile, Java-only, slow

Properties

Key-value configuration, in simple text files.

Properties p = new Properties();
try (Reader r = Files.newBufferedReader(Path.of("app.properties"))) {
  p.load(r);
}
try (InputStream in = Main.class.getResourceAsStream("/app.properties")) { // on classpath
  p.load(in);
}
String url = p.getProperty("db.url", "jdbc:h2:mem:test");   // with default
  • The separator can be =, : or whitespace. # and ! start comments. A line d e gives key d and value e.
  • load(InputStream) always decodes as ISO-8859-1, so UTF-8 text is garbled unless you use \uXXXX escapes. load(Reader) uses your reader's charset.
  • Properties extends Hashtable<Object, Object>, a known design flaw. put("n", 5) compiles, and then getProperty("n") returns null, since the value is not a String. Use setProperty.
  • new Properties(defaults) chains defaults: getProperty sees them, but get and size do not. Verified: getProperty("a") gave 1, get("a") gave null, size() gave 0.
  • No ordering is retained on store.

ZIP and GZIP

// Create
try (var zip = new ZipOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("t.zip")))) {
  zip.putNextEntry(new ZipEntry("x/a.txt"));
  zip.write("hi".getBytes(UTF_8));
  zip.closeEntry();
}
// Read sequentially
try (var zip = new ZipInputStream(Files.newInputStream(Path.of("t.zip")))) {
  for (ZipEntry e; (e = zip.getNextEntry()) != null; ) {
    System.out.println(e.getName() + " " + new String(zip.readAllBytes(), UTF_8));
  }
}
// Treat a ZIP as a file system: read, add or replace entries using the Files API
try (FileSystem fs = FileSystems.newFileSystem(Path.of("t.zip"))) {
  Files.readString(fs.getPath("x/a.txt"));
  Files.writeString(fs.getPath("y.txt"), "more");
}
// A single compressed stream
try (var gz = new GZIPOutputStream(Files.newOutputStream(Path.of("d.gz")))) { gz.write(bytes); }

ZipFile reads the central directory, so it offers random access. ZipInputStream walks the file and works on any stream. JAR files are ZIP files. GZIP compresses one stream, and .tar.gz is what bundles many files; the JDK has no TAR support.

Gotcha: Zip Slip. An archive entry can be named ../../etc/passwd. Always validate before extracting: Path target = base.resolve(entry.getName()).normalize(); if (!target.startsWith(base)) throw …. Also guard against zip bombs by limiting total extracted bytes and entry count.

Console and standard streams

System.in is an InputStream, while System.out and System.err are PrintStreams. Redirect them with System.setOut.

Console c = System.console();
if (c != null) {
  String user = c.readLine("User: ");
  char[] pw = c.readPassword("Password: ");   // no echo
  try { authenticate(user, pw); }
  finally { Arrays.fill(pw, ' '); }           // wipe it
}

readPassword returns char[], not String, because an array can be overwritten once used, whereas a String stays in memory until collected. System.console() historically returned null when there was no interactive terminal, such as under an IDE, a pipe or a service. From Java 22 it may return an object even when redirected, and Console.isTerminal() tells you which it is. Java 25 also added the java.lang.IO class with simple println and readln methods (JEP 512), aimed at beginners and small programs.

Networking basics

TCP gives a reliable, ordered byte stream over a connection. UDP sends independent datagrams with no guarantee of delivery or order, and less overhead. A socket is one end of a connection, identified by IP address and port.

Blocking TCP server

try (ServerSocket server = new ServerSocket(8080);
     var pool = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {   // Java 21
  while (true) {
    Socket s = server.accept();                   // blocks until a client connects
    pool.submit(() -> handle(s));
  }
}

static void handle(Socket s) {
  try (s;
       var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(s.getInputStream(), UTF_8));
       var out = new PrintWriter(s.getOutputStream(), true, UTF_8)) {
    out.println("echo: " + in.readLine());
  } catch (IOException e) {
    log.warn("client failed", e);
  }
}

// Client
try (Socket s = new Socket("localhost", 8080);
     var out = new PrintWriter(s.getOutputStream(), true, UTF_8);
     var in = new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(s.getInputStream(), UTF_8))) {
  out.println("hi");
  System.out.println(in.readLine());    // echo: hi
}
  • Set timeouts. socket.setSoTimeout(ms) limits a read; connect(addr, ms) limits a connect. Without them, a dead peer can hang a thread forever.
  • TCP has no message boundaries. readLine relies on newlines; for binary protocols, use a length prefix.
  • The true argument of PrintWriter turns on auto-flush for println (not for print). Forgetting to flush is a common "client hangs" bug.
  • Errors: ConnectException: Connection refused (nothing listens), SocketTimeoutException (timed out), SocketException: Connection reset (peer aborted), BindException: Address already in use.

URL, URI and URLConnection

A URI identifies a resource; a URL is a locator, and URL carries network behaviour. Prefer URI. new URL(String) has been deprecated since Java 20: use URI.create(s).toURL().

URI u = URI.create("https://example.com:8443/a/b?q=1#f");
u.getHost(); u.getPort(); u.getPath(); u.getQuery(); u.getFragment();
// example.com  8443  /a/b  q=1  f

URLEncoder.encode("a b&c=d", UTF_8);   // a+b%26c%3Dd   for form or query values
URLDecoder.decode("a%20b+c", UTF_8);   // a b c

Trap: java.net.URL.equals and hashCode may perform a DNS lookup to compare hosts. It is slow, and its result depends on the network. Never use URL as a map key.

HttpClient (Java 11)

The standard client, replacing HttpURLConnection. It supports HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, WebSocket, and synchronous and asynchronous sends. It is immutable and thread-safe, so build one and share it, because each instance holds a connection pool. Since Java 21, it is AutoCloseable.

HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder()
    .version(HttpClient.Version.HTTP_2)
    .connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2))
    .followRedirects(HttpClient.Redirect.NORMAL)
    .build();

HttpRequest get = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.acme.com/users/1"))
    .timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(5))                // request timeout
    .header("Accept", "application/json")
    .GET()
    .build();

// Synchronous
HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(get, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
System.out.println(res.statusCode() + " " + res.body());

// Asynchronous
client.sendAsync(get, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString())
      .thenApply(HttpResponse::body)
      .thenAccept(System.out::println);

// POST
HttpRequest post = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.acme.com/users"))
    .header("Content-Type", "application/json")
    .POST(HttpRequest.BodyPublishers.ofString("{\"name\":\"Ana\"}"))
    .build();

A non-2xx status does not throw. You must check statusCode(). By default it does not follow redirects, and it has no request timeout. version(HTTP_2) is a preference: on a plain-text server, the verified response above was HTTP_1_1.

Java 18 also added a small static file server, jwebserver (JEP 408), for testing. Java 16 added Unix domain sockets to SocketChannel (JEP 380).

UDP

try (DatagramSocket s = new DatagramSocket()) {
  byte[] b = "ping".getBytes(UTF_8);
  s.send(new DatagramPacket(b, b.length, InetAddress.getByName("localhost"), 9999));
}

Checked IOException in Lambdas and Streams

Function, Consumer and friends cannot throw checked exceptions, so paths.map(Files::readString) does not compile. The JDK's own answer is UncheckedIOException: wrap the IOException, then unwrap it at the boundary. Files.lines and BufferedReader.lines() already do this when a read fails mid-stream.

List<String> contents;
try (Stream<Path> files = Files.list(dir)) {
    contents = files.filter(p -> p.toString().endsWith(".txt"))
                    .map(p -> {
                        try { return Files.readString(p); }
                        catch (IOException e) { throw new UncheckedIOException(e); }
                    })
                    .toList();
} catch (UncheckedIOException e) {
    throw e.getCause();             // back to a checked IOException for callers
}

For many paths, a plain for loop is often clearer than a wrapper, and it keeps the checked exception.

File Locking Between Processes

FileChannel.lock() / tryLock() return a FileLock held by the whole JVM, used to coordinate with other processes (e.g. two instances of a batch job on one machine).

  • Locks are per JVM, not per thread: a second lock() on the same file from the same JVM throws OverlappingFileLockException.
  • On many OSes the lock is advisory: a process that does not ask for the lock can still write the file.
  • Locks on network file systems (NFS, SMB) are unreliable. For coordination across machines use the database or a distributed lock.
  • Closing the channel releases the lock, so keep it in try-with-resources.
try (FileChannel ch = FileChannel.open(Path.of("job.lock"),
         StandardOpenOption.CREATE, StandardOpenOption.WRITE);
     FileLock lock = ch.tryLock()) {
    if (lock == null) { log.info("another instance is running"); return; }
    runJob();
}

Streaming Large JSON and CSV

objectMapper.readValue(file, List.class) builds the whole tree in memory. For a multi-GB export, read one record at a time with Jackson's streaming parser (or a MappingIterator), and write with a JsonGenerator. Memory stays constant regardless of file size.

try (JsonParser p = mapper.createParser(Files.newInputStream(path))) {
    if (p.nextToken() != JsonToken.START_ARRAY) throw new IOException("expected array");
    while (p.nextToken() == JsonToken.START_OBJECT) {
        Order o = mapper.readValue(p, Order.class);   // one object at a time
        process(o);
    }
}

For CSV, never line.split(","): quoted fields can contain commas, quotes and newlines. Use a CSV library (Apache Commons CSV, OpenCSV, Jackson CSV), stream rows, and declare the charset (watch for a UTF-8 BOM from Excel exports).

Interview Questions — File I/O, NIO & Serialization

Byte stream vs character stream: when do you use each?

Byte streams handle raw data: images, archives, encrypted content. Character streams handle text, and apply a charset to decode. Using a Reader on binary data corrupts it, because invalid byte sequences get replaced. InputStreamReader is the bridge between the two.

Why does InputStream.read() return int rather than byte?

It must represent 256 byte values plus one "end of stream" signal, which is 257 states. A byte has 256. So it returns 0 to 255, or -1. Casting to byte before comparing makes 0xFF look like end of stream: a loop over {1, 0xFF, 2} stopped after one byte in testing.

What is the Decorator pattern in java.io?

Each wrapper implements the same abstract type and holds an instance of it, adding a feature. new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new GZIPInputStream(new FileInputStream(f)), UTF_8)) stacks four behaviours. Without decorators, you would need a subclass per combination. Closing the outermost closes all.

Why is buffered I/O faster? Does flush guarantee that data is on disk?

A buffer reduces system calls by moving data in blocks. flush only hands bytes to the OS, where they sit in the page cache. Surviving a power failure takes FileChannel.force(true) or FileDescriptor.sync(), and those are slow, so databases group them.

What is the output? 
var w = new BufferedWriter(new FileWriter(f));
w.write("hello");
System.out.println(Files.size(path));
w.close();
System.out.println(Files.size(path));

0, then 5. The data stays in the 8 KB buffer until flushed. close flushes first. Without close, the data would be lost on exit.

Why might a text file look fine on one machine and show garbled characters on another?

The bytes were encoded in one charset and decoded in another. Before Java 18, the default charset depended on the platform, so new FileReader(f) differed between Windows (often windows-1252) and Linux (UTF-8). Fix by always naming the charset. Since Java 18, UTF-8 is the default, which can itself change behaviour for old Windows apps; -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT restores the old behaviour.

Predict the output. 
String s = "héllo";
System.out.println(s.length());
System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8).length);
System.out.println(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_16).length);

5, 6, 12. é takes 2 bytes in UTF-8. Java's UTF_16 encoder writes a 2-byte byte order mark, plus 2 bytes for each of 5 chars.

What does String.length() return for an emoji?

2 for most emoji, since it counts UTF-16 code units, and characters above U+FFFF need a surrogate pair. codePointCount returns 1. For user-visible characters (grapheme clusters, like flags), use BreakIterator. substring can split a pair and corrupt the text.

File vs Path: why was NIO.2 added?

File returns booleans on failure with no reason, handles symlinks poorly, lacks attribute support, and loads whole directories. NIO.2's Path and Files (Java 7) throw precise exceptions, stream directories lazily, offer atomic moves, attributes and file systems beyond the default one, such as inside a ZIP.

Predict the results. 
Path.of("/a/b").resolve("/x");
Path.of("/a/b").relativize(Path.of("/a/c/d"));
Path.of("/home/a/../b/./c.txt").normalize();
Path.of("abc").startsWith("a");

/x (an absolute argument replaces the base), ../c/d, /home/b/c.txt, and false: startsWith compares whole path elements, not string prefixes.

How do you read a 10 GB log file?

Do not use readAllLines or readString: both load everything and cause OOM. Stream line by line:

try (Stream<String> lines = Files.lines(path)) {
  lines.filter(l -> l.contains("ERROR")).forEach(this::handle);
}

Or use BufferedReader.readLine in a loop. For random access in fixed-size records, use a FileChannel or a memory map. Remember try-with-resources, since Files.lines holds a file handle. A very long line is still fully loaded, so that is the limit of this approach.

What is the role of flip, clear, compact and rewind in ByteBuffer?

flip: switch from filling to draining (limit = position; position = 0). clear: reset for filling, without erasing. compact: keep unread data by moving it to the front. rewind: reread the same content. Example from Java 21: after 3 puts, pos=3 lim=8; after flip, pos=0 lim=3; after one get, pos=1; after compact, pos=2 lim=8.

Direct vs heap buffers?

Heap buffers wrap a byte array on the Java heap, and are cheap to allocate. The OS cannot use movable heap memory directly, so the JVM copies through native memory. Direct buffers live off-heap, skip that copy, and cost more to allocate and free. Use direct, pooled, long-lived buffers for heavy socket or file I/O. They do not count toward -Xmx, but have their own limit, and hasArray() is false.

How does a Selector work? Why must you remove keys from selectedKeys?

Channels in non-blocking mode register interest in events. select() blocks until the OS (epoll or similar) reports readiness and adds keys to the selected set. The selector only adds to the set; it never removes. If you do not remove a handled key, the next loop sees it again, and processes a stale event, such as accept() returning null.

Explain BIO, NIO and AIO. How do virtual threads change the choice?

BIO: one blocking thread per connection, simple but limited by platform thread cost. NIO: a few threads multiplex many non-blocking channels, scalable but with complex code. AIO: the kernel or a pool notifies you on completion; rarely used in Java. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, so one thread per connection scales again, with a simple programming model. For many applications, this removes the reason to use reactive code just for scale. Frameworks like Netty still use NIO directly.

What is zero-copy, and how do you do it in Java?

A normal file-to-socket send copies disk to kernel buffer, to user buffer, to socket buffer. FileChannel.transferTo can use sendfile, so the kernel moves data directly, with no user-space copy and less CPU. Kafka relies on this for consumers. It does not apply if data must be modified in user space, such as with TLS (unless kernel TLS is used).

When are memory-mapped files useful, and what are the pitfalls?

For large random-access files, where the OS page cache does the caching, and access looks like arrays. Pitfalls: 2 GB per buffer, no explicit unmap (Windows then blocks deletion), page faults stall a thread with no timeout, and force is needed for durability. Since Java 22, the FFM API's MemorySegment with an Arena removes the size and unmap limits.

What limitations does WatchService have?

Not recursive; you must reset the key; events can be lost (OVERFLOW); multiple events per save; the implementation varies, polling on some platforms; often no support on network file systems. Make the handler idempotent, and rescan on overflow.

What is the purpose of serialVersionUID? What happens if you omit it?

It is the version identifier compared on deserialization. If omitted, the JVM computes it from the class structure, so harmless edits or a different compiler can change it, causing InvalidClassException on existing data. Declare private static final long serialVersionUID = 1L;, and change it only for intentional incompatibility.

Predict the output. Non-serializable parent, serializable child. 
class Base { int b = 5; Base() { System.out.println("Base()"); b = 9; } }
class Child extends Base implements Serializable {
  int c = 7; transient int t = 8; static int s = 1;
  Child() { System.out.println("Child()"); }
}
Child x = new Child();
x.b = 50; x.c = 70; x.t = 80;
byte[] data = serialize(x);
Child r = (Child) deserialize(data);
System.out.println(r.b + " " + r.c + " " + r.t);
Base()
Child()
Base()
9 70 0

new Child() prints both constructors. Deserializing runs only the first non-serializable ancestor's constructor. b is not in the stream, so Base's constructor sets 9. c is restored. t is transient and gets 0: neither the constructor nor the initializer runs for Child.

Are constructors called during deserialization? Do transient final fields work?

Constructors of serializable classes are not called. Only the no-arg constructor of the nearest non-serializable superclass runs. So a transient final field (other than a compile-time constant) comes back as null or zero and cannot be assigned in readObject by normal code. That is one reason to prefer a serialization proxy or records.

How can serialization break a singleton, and how do you stop it?

Deserialization creates a new instance, ignoring the private constructor. Add private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }, and make instance fields transient, or use an enum, which is safe by specification. Verified: without readResolve, the instance differed.

What does the serialization proxy pattern do?

A class's writeReplace returns a small private nested proxy holding the logical state. The proxy's readResolve rebuilds the object through its public constructor or factory, so invariants are checked, and final fields work. The outer class's readObject throws InvalidObjectException, to block forged streams. EnumSet uses it. Records give you the same benefit natively.

Serializable vs Externalizable?

With Serializable, the JVM writes all non-transient fields by reflection, and no constructor of the class runs. With Externalizable, you write and read exactly what you want, and a public no-arg constructor is mandatory, because it runs first. Externalizable gives speed and format control, at the cost of hand-maintained code. Neither fixes the security problem.

Why is Java deserialization dangerous? How do you mitigate it?

Because readObject creates arbitrary classes, and runs their code before the application sees the object. An attacker uses gadget chains in common libraries for remote code execution. Mitigate by not accepting serialized objects from untrusted sources, using JSON or Protobuf, adding ObjectInputFilter allow-lists, and keeping dependencies up to date. Casting the result is no protection, as the damage is already done by then.

What happens with an object written twice to one ObjectOutputStream?

The stream keeps a handle table. The second write stores a back-reference, so identity and cycles are preserved, and later changes to the object are not recorded.
