Tested: writing v=1, changing to 2, and writing again read back 1 and 1, the same object. out.reset() clears the table. This table also retains every object written, so a long-lived stream leaks memory without reset.

How would you version data if you moved away from Java serialization?

Use JSON with tolerant readers (FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES off), and add fields as optional. Or Protobuf or Avro, where each field has a stable number or the schema is registered. Migrate by writing both formats during transition, then reading the new one first, and falling back on the old.

Why can getProperty return null after put("n", 5)?

getProperty only returns String values, and treats anything else as absent. Properties extends Hashtable<Object, Object>, so put accepts an Integer. Always use setProperty. Verified: getProperty("n") printed null while get("n") printed 5. load(InputStream) also assumes ISO-8859-1.

What is Zip Slip?

A path traversal attack during extraction: entry names with ../ write outside the target folder, potentially replacing executables or configs. Resolve and normalize the name, then check target.startsWith(base). Verified: /tmp/out resolved with ../../etc/passwd normalizes to a path that does not start with the base.

How would you replace a file safely so readers never see partial content?

Write to a temp file in the same directory (same file system), force it to disk if durability matters, then call Files.move(tmp, target, ATOMIC_MOVE, REPLACE_EXISTING). Rename is atomic on POSIX file systems. A move across file systems is a copy, which is why ATOMIC_MOVE then fails with AtomicMoveNotSupportedException.

How do you make a Socket read not hang forever?

Use setSoTimeout(ms) for reads, and connect(addr, timeoutMs) for connecting. The read then throws SocketTimeoutException, and the socket stays usable. Verified with ServerSocket.setSoTimeout(50): accept threw SocketTimeoutException: Accept timed out. Without a timeout, a silently dead peer leaves the thread blocked. In HttpClient, set both connect and request timeouts.

Why is one read not one message on a TCP socket?

TCP is a byte stream with no message boundaries. A send may arrive split or merged with others. Define framing: a delimiter like newline, a fixed size, or a length prefix, and loop until the frame is complete. DataInputStream.readFully helps with that.

HttpClient vs HttpURLConnection vs RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient?

HttpURLConnection is the old JDK API: clumsy, no HTTP/2. java.net.http.HttpClient (Java 11) is modern, supports HTTP/2 and async, and has no JSON mapping. In Spring, RestTemplate is the older synchronous client; WebClient is reactive; RestClient (Spring 6.1) is the modern synchronous fluent API. In Spring apps, use RestClient or WebClient, and set timeouts. A client should be a shared bean, to reuse connections.

Does HttpClient.send throw on a 500 response? What are the defaults worth changing?

No. It returns a response with status 500; only transport problems throw (IOException, HttpTimeoutException). Defaults to revisit: no redirects followed, no connect or request timeout. Reuse a single client, as creating many leaks threads and connections until collected.

Why does URL make a bad map key?

URL.equals and hashCode resolve host names, which blocks on DNS, and gives results that vary with the network. Two hosts with one IP compare equal. Use URI, whose equals is purely textual (scheme and host case-insensitive, per its rules).

Why is the password from Console.readPassword a char[]?

Strings are immutable, and may be retained in the heap or string pool, appearing in heap dumps. A char[] can be wiped by your code straight after use. The same applies to JPasswordField.getPassword. Note that System.console() may be null in IDEs or when input is redirected, particularly before Java 22.

Scenario: an app slowly hits "Too many open files". How do you find and fix it?
  1. Confirm it: lsof -p <pid>, group by path or type, and compare to ulimit -n.
  2. Look for unclosed items: Files.lines/Files.list without TWR, responses or sockets not closed, a new HttpClient per request.
  3. Fix with try-with-resources, and share clients.
  4. Only raise the limit after fixing leaks, if real load demands it.
  5. Add a metric for open file descriptors; JVM metrics expose this via Micrometer.
Scenario: upload a 5 GB file through a Spring service. How do you avoid running out of memory?

Do not buffer it in a byte[] or a MultipartFile.getBytes() call. Stream it: read from getInputStream() and use transferTo to a Path or object storage, in fixed-size chunks. Enforce size limits, validate the type, generate server-side names to avoid traversal, and hold no transaction during the copy. For very large files, give clients a pre-signed URL to upload straight to storage, with multipart resume.

Design question: build a simple log tailer that ships new lines from a growing file.
  • Keep the last offset in a state file, so a restart resumes.
  • Open the file with FileChannel or RandomAccessFile, seek to the offset, read until end, and handle a partial last line by waiting for its newline.
  • Use WatchService as a hint, with polling as a fallback, since events can be lost.
  • Detect rotation: file size smaller than the offset, or a changed file key (BasicFileAttributes.fileKey()).
  • Ship in batches, and advance the offset only after success, for at-least-once delivery.
How do you call a method that throws IOException inside a stream's map()?

Catch it inside the lambda and rethrow as UncheckedIOException, then catch that outside the pipeline and unwrap with getCause() if callers expect a checked exception. Alternatives: a small helper/functional interface that throws, or a plain loop. Don't swallow it or wrap it in a bare RuntimeException that loses the type.

A user uploads a file named "../../etc/cron.d/x". How do you store uploads safely?

Never use the client's file name as a path. Generate your own name (e.g. a UUID) and keep the original name only as metadata. If you must use it, take Path.of(name).getFileName(), then base.resolve(it).normalize() and verify startsWith(base). Also check size limits, validate the content type by inspecting bytes rather than trusting the extension or header, and store outside the web root.

What is Base64 and when do you use it? Which encoder?

Base64 turns arbitrary bytes into ASCII text (about 33% larger) so binary data can travel in JSON, headers, URLs or emails. It is encoding, not encryption. java.util.Base64.getEncoder() is the standard alphabet, getUrlEncoder() uses - and _ (used by JWT, often with withoutPadding()), and getMimeEncoder() adds line breaks. For large files use encoder.wrap(outputStream) to stream instead of building a huge string.

How do you parse a 3 GB JSON array without running out of memory?

Use Jackson's streaming API: create a JsonParser, advance to START_ARRAY, then bind each element with mapper.readValue(parser, Item.class) (or readerFor(Item.class).readValues(…) for a MappingIterator) and process it before moving on. Memory is bounded by one record. Combine with batching for DB inserts. Better still, ask producers for NDJSON (one JSON object per line), which is trivially streamable and splittable.

Two instances of a scheduled job run on the same server. How do you make sure only one processes the file?

On one machine, take an exclusive FileChannel.tryLock() on a lock file and exit if it returns null; the OS releases it if the process dies. Remember it is JVM-wide and often advisory. Across several machines this does not work reliably, so use a DB lock row, ShedLock, or move the file atomically to a "processing" folder (ATOMIC_MOVE) so only the instance whose move succeeds owns it.

Date/Time, Annotations & Reflection Core Java

The java.time API and its time zone and DST traps, what annotations are and how they get processed, and the runtime toolkit behind every Java framework: reflection, dynamic proxies, method handles and ServiceLoader, plus Locale basics.

The legacy Date and Calendar problems

You still meet java.util.Date, Calendar and SimpleDateFormat in old code and old libraries. Knowing what is wrong with them explains how java.time was designed.

ProblemDetail
Mutabledate.setTime(…) changes a shared object. A getter returning a Date leaks internal state, so classes need defensive copies
Misleading nameDate is an instant (milliseconds since 1970 UTC), not a date. Its toString prints it in the default zone, making it look zoned
Odd numberingMonth is 0-based (Calendar.JANUARY == 0). new Date(124, 0, 15) means the year 2024: years count from 1900
Lenient by defaultcal.set(2024, 1, 30) (Feb 30) silently becomes March 1. SimpleDateFormat parses 2024-02-31 as March 2
Not thread-safeSimpleDateFormat and Calendar keep working state in fields. Sharing a static formatter corrupts results
No separate conceptsNo type for "just a date", "just a time" or "a duration"
java.sql odditiesjava.sql.Timestamp extends Date but breaks symmetry: date.equals(ts) was true and ts.equals(date) false. java.sql.Date.toInstant() throws UnsupportedOperationException

Java 8 added java.time (JSR 310), led by the author of Joda-Time. All of its main types are immutable and thread-safe, months are 1-based, invalid values throw, and each concept has its own type.

// Legacy interop
Date d = Date.from(instant);
Instant i = date.toInstant();
ZonedDateTime z = gregorianCalendar.toZonedDateTime();
Timestamp ts = Timestamp.valueOf(localDateTime);
LocalDate ld = sqlDate.toLocalDate();           // not toInstant()

Choosing a java.time type

TypeRepresentsExampleUse for
InstantA point on the UTC timeline, in nanoseconds2024-06-15T12:00:00ZTimestamps, logs, event times
LocalDateDate, no time or zone2024-06-15Birthdays, holidays, invoice dates
LocalTimeTime of day09:05Opening hours
LocalDateTimeDate and time, no zone: not a point in time2024-06-15T09:05A wall-clock value; needs a zone to become an instant
ZonedDateTimeDate, time, offset and zone rules2024-06-15T14:00+02:00[Europe/Amsterdam]Calculations in a real location, DST-aware
OffsetDateTimeDate, time and fixed offset2024-06-15T14:00+02:00APIs, ISO 8601 payloads, database values
DurationMachine time: seconds and nanosPT25HTimeouts, elapsed time
PeriodCalendar time: years, months, daysP2M5DAge, subscription length
Year, YearMonth, MonthDayPartial dates2024-02Card expiry, recurring birthdays
ClockSource of current timeClock.systemUTC()Testable code

Working with java.time

LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, Month.MARCH, 15);
d.plusDays(1);                       // returns a new object
d.getMonthValue();                   // 3     getMonth() returns MARCH
d.getDayOfWeek();                    // FRIDAY
d.isLeapYear();  d.lengthOfMonth();
d.atStartOfDay();                    // 2024-03-15T00:00
d.atTime(10, 30);                    // 2024-03-15T10:30
d.datesUntil(end);                   // Stream<LocalDate>, Java 9, end exclusive

d.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastDayOfMonth());             // 2024-03-31
d.with(TemporalAdjusters.firstInMonth(DayOfWeek.MONDAY)); // 2024-03-04
d.with(TemporalAdjusters.next(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY));       // 2024-03-22
d.with(TemporalAdjusters.nextOrSame(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY)); // 2024-03-15

ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b);       // long
a.isBefore(b);  a.isAfter(b);  a.isEqual(b);
Gotcha: java.time objects are immutable, so date.plusDays(1); on its own line does nothing. Assign the result. The same mistake is common with String and BigDecimal.

Month-end arithmetic

LocalDate j = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31);
j.plusMonths(1);                 // 2024-02-29  clamped to the last valid day
j.plusMonths(1).plusMonths(1);   // 2024-03-29  the clamp carries forward
j.plusMonths(2);                 // 2024-03-31
LocalDate.of(2024, 2, 29).plusYears(1);   // 2025-02-28

So adding months is not associative. For a monthly billing date anchored on the 31st, compute from the original date each time (start.plusMonths(n)), not from the previous result.

Duration vs Period

DurationPeriod
MeasuresExact time in seconds and nanosCalendar years, months, days
Works onInstant, LocalTime, LocalDateTime, ZonedDateTimeLocalDate, and adding to zoned or local date-times
A "day" isExactly 24 hoursA calendar day: 23, 24 or 25 hours across DST
PrintPT1H1M1SP2M5D
var a = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);
var b = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 20);
Period.between(a, b);            // P2M5D
Period.between(a, b).getDays();  // 5      only the day component!
ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b);   // 65     total days

Duration.ofHours(25);            // PT25H  never normalized into days
Duration.ofHours(25).toDays();   // 1
Duration.ofHours(25).toHoursPart(); // 1
Period.of(1, 14, 40).normalized();  // P2Y2M40D  days do not roll into months

Duration.between(LocalTime.of(23, 0), LocalTime.of(1, 0));  // PT-22H  negative

Duration.between(a, b);
// UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Seconds
Instant.now().plus(1, ChronoUnit.MONTHS);
// UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Months

Why the errors? A LocalDate has no seconds. An Instant has no calendar, so "one month" is not defined without a zone.

Time zones and DST

An offset is a fixed difference from UTC, such as +02:00. A zone is a region such as Europe/Amsterdam, whose offsets changed through history and change twice a year. ZoneRules hold that data, drawn from the IANA tz database that ships in the JDK. Governments change the rules, so old JVMs can have outdated data; update the JDK or use tzupdater.

In short: offset is a number, and zone is a set of rules. ZoneId.of("IST") and ZoneId.of("EST") threw ZoneRulesException: Unknown time-zone ID on Java 21. Abbreviations are ambiguous, so use region IDs.

Daylight saving transitions

When clocks go forward, a local hour does not exist (a gap). When they go back, a local hour happens twice (an overlap). A LocalDateTime can land on either.

ZoneId ny = ZoneId.of("America/New_York");

// Gap: 02:30 does not exist on 2024-03-10. Shifted forward by the gap's length.
ZonedDateTime.of(LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 10, 2, 30), ny);
// 2024-03-10T03:30-04:00[America/New_York]

// Overlap: 01:30 happens twice on 2024-11-03. The earlier offset is chosen.
var ov = ZonedDateTime.of(LocalDateTime.of(2024, 11, 3, 1, 30), ny);
// 2024-11-03T01:30-04:00[America/New_York]
ov.withLaterOffsetAtOverlap();   // 2024-11-03T01:30-05:00[America/New_York]
ov.plusHours(1);                 // 2024-11-03T01:30-05:00  same wall clock, one hour on!

// A day is not always 24 hours
var b = ZonedDateTime.of(LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 9, 12, 0), ny);
b.plusDays(1);                   // 2024-03-10T12:00-04:00  same wall clock
b.plusHours(24);                 // 2024-03-10T13:00-04:00  exactly 24 hours
b.plus(Period.ofDays(1));        // behaves like plusDays
b.plus(Duration.ofDays(1));      // behaves like plusHours(24)
Duration.between(b, b.plusDays(1));   // PT23H

You can inspect these with zone.getRules().getValidOffsets(localDateTime). It returns an empty list in a gap, one offset normally, and two in an overlap. In Europe/Amsterdam, 2024-03-31T02:30 gives [], and 2024-10-27T02:30 gives [+02:00, +01:00].

Conversions

var z = ZonedDateTime.of(2024, 6, 15, 12, 0, 0, 0, ZoneId.of("UTC"));
z.withZoneSameInstant(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));  // 2024-06-15T17:30+05:30  same moment
z.withZoneSameLocal(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata"));    // 2024-06-15T12:00+05:30  same wall clock

var a = ZonedDateTime.parse("2024-06-15T12:00:00Z");
var b = ZonedDateTime.parse("2024-06-15T17:30:00+05:30");
a.equals(b);        // false: equals compares local time, offset and zone
a.isEqual(b);       // true:  compares the instant

ZoneId.of("UTC").equals(ZoneOffset.UTC) is false, as they are different classes of zone id, though they mean the same offset.

Storage rules

DataStoreWhy
When something happenedInstant, or UTC timestampThe past is fixed; display per user zone
A date with no time, like a birthdayLocalDateConverting to a zone can shift it by a day
A future meeting at 09:00 in AmsterdamLocalDateTime + zone IDIf DST rules change, the meeting stays at 09:00 local, while a stored UTC instant would be wrong
Recurring scheduleLocal time + zone ID + recurrence ruleThe UTC time differs across DST

JDBC 4.2 mapping: LocalDate to DATE, LocalTime to TIME, LocalDateTime to TIMESTAMP, OffsetDateTime to TIMESTAMP WITH TIME ZONE. Read with rs.getObject(col, LocalDate.class). ZonedDateTime and Instant are not required by JDBC, though drivers may handle them. Hibernate 6 maps Instant, and its time zone storage strategy is configurable.

Configuring JSON: Jackson needs the JavaTimeModule for java.time types; Spring Boot registers it automatically and writes ISO 8601 text by default.

Testable time: Clock

Code that calls LocalDate.now() directly depends on the real date, which makes tests flaky. Inject a Clock.

class SubscriptionService {
  private final Clock clock;
  SubscriptionService(Clock clock) { this.clock = clock; }
  boolean expired(LocalDate end) { return LocalDate.now(clock).isAfter(end); }
}

// In a test
Clock fixed = Clock.fixed(Instant.parse("2024-01-01T10:00:00Z"), ZoneOffset.UTC);
new SubscriptionService(fixed).expired(LocalDate.of(2023, 12, 31));   // true

Also, LocalDateTime.now() uses the server's default zone, which may differ between machines. Always pass a zone or a clock.

DateTimeFormatter and parsing

Thread-safe and immutable, so one static final instance is the right pattern, unlike SimpleDateFormat.

static final DateTimeFormatter F = DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu HH:mm");

var t = LocalDateTime.of(2024, 3, 5, 14, 7, 9);
t.format(F);                                                         // 05/03/2024 14:07
t.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("EEE, d MMM uuuu", Locale.US)); // Tue, 5 Mar 2024
LocalDate.parse("05/03/2024", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("dd/MM/uuuu"));

DateTimeFormatter.ISO_LOCAL_DATE;        // 2024-03-05, also what toString prints
DateTimeFormatter.ISO_OFFSET_DATE_TIME;  // 2024-03-05T14:07:09+01:00
DateTimeFormatter.ISO_INSTANT;           // 2024-03-05T13:07:09Z
DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM).withLocale(Locale.GERMANY);  // 05.03.2024
PatternMeaningCommon mistake
yyyy / uuuuYear of era / proleptic yearSTRICT mode needs uuuu
YYYYWeek-based yearGives the wrong year around New Year
MM / mmMonth / minutedd/mm/yyyy prints minutes in the month slot
dd / DDDay of month / day of yearDD gives 65 for March 5, 2024
HH / hh0-23 / 1-12 with ahh without a loses AM/PM
X, Z, VVOffset, offset, zone IDFails on types without a zone

The classic YYYY bug has caused real outages. It uses the week-based year:

var d = LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 30);
d.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd", Locale.US));  // 2025-12-30 (!)
d.format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("yyyy-MM-dd"));             // 2024-12-30

Resolver styles

Style"2023-02-30" with uuuu-MM-dd"2023-02-32"
SMART (default for ofPattern)Clamps to 2023-02-28Throws
STRICTThrows: Invalid date 'FEBRUARY 30'Throws
LENIENTRolls overRolls over

So LocalDate.parse("2023-02-30"), with the built-in ISO formatter which is STRICT, throws, but a pattern of your own accepts it. For validating user input, use .withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT) and uuuu. With yyyy, strict mode fails on a valid date, as year-of-era needs an era: Unable to obtain LocalDate from TemporalAccessor.

Parsing errors

LocalDate.parse("2023-13-01");    // Text '2023-13-01' could not be parsed: Invalid value
                                  //   for MonthOfYear (valid values 1 - 12): 13
LocalDate.parse("2024-1-5");      // could not be parsed at index 5: needs 2-digit fields
LocalDate.parse("15/01/2024");    // could not be parsed at index 0
LocalDateTime.parse("2024-01-15");// could not be parsed at index 10: time missing
LocalDate.of(2023, 2, 29);        // DateTimeException: Invalid date 'February 29' as
                                  //   '2023' is not a leap year
LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1).format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("HH:mm"));
// UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported field: HourOfDay

Pass a Locale when a pattern uses names: text such as MMM and EEE depends on the locale, and parsing "Mar" fails on a machine with a different default.

Annotations

An annotation is structured metadata attached to code. It does nothing by itself. Something has to read it: the compiler, an annotation processor at build time, or a framework by reflection at runtime. It replaced marker interfaces and XML config in most frameworks.

Built-in annotations

AnnotationPurpose
@OverrideCompiler verifies that a method overrides something
@DeprecatedWarns callers; Java 9 added since and forRemoval
@SuppressWarningsSilences a named lint: "unchecked", "rawtypes", "deprecation"
@SafeVarargsPromise of a safe generic varargs method
@FunctionalInterfaceCompiler verifies a single abstract method

Meta-annotations

Annotations placed on annotation declarations.

Meta-annotationEffect
@RetentionHow long it is kept (below)
@TargetWhere it is allowed: TYPE, FIELD, METHOD, PARAMETER, CONSTRUCTOR, LOCAL_VARIABLE, ANNOTATION_TYPE, PACKAGE, TYPE_PARAMETER and TYPE_USE (8), MODULE (9), RECORD_COMPONENT (16). Without it, nearly all declaration contexts are allowed
@DocumentedInclude it in Javadoc
@InheritedSubclasses inherit it from a superclass. Classes only
@RepeatableThe annotation can appear more than once
RetentionIn .class file?Visible by reflection?Examples
SOURCENoNo@Override, @SuppressWarnings, Lombok's @Getter
CLASS (default)YesNoBytecode tools
RUNTIMEYesYes@Autowired, @Entity, @Test
Gotcha: The default retention is CLASS, not RUNTIME. A custom annotation without @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) compiles fine, and then getAnnotation returns null. This is the first thing to check when "my annotation does nothing".

Declaring a custom annotation

Use @interface. Elements look like methods, and may only return primitives, String, Class, enums, other annotations, or one-dimensional arrays of these. Defaults must be compile-time constants, and null is not allowed, so a sentinel such as "" is the convention. An element named value allows the short form @Name("x").

A runtime validator using reflection

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@interface NotBlank { String message() default "must not be blank"; }

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Target(ElementType.FIELD)
@interface Range { int min() default 0; int max() default Integer.MAX_VALUE; }

class User {
  @NotBlank String name;
  @Range(min = 18, max = 120) int age;
  User(String n, int a) { name = n; age = a; }
}

static List<String> validate(Object o) throws IllegalAccessException {
  List<String> errors = new ArrayList<>();
  for (Field f : o.getClass().getDeclaredFields()) {
    f.setAccessible(true);
    Object v = f.get(o);
    NotBlank nb = f.getAnnotation(NotBlank.class);
    if (nb != null && (v == null || v.toString().isBlank()))
      errors.add(f.getName() + " " + nb.message());
    Range r = f.getAnnotation(Range.class);
    if (r != null) {
      int i = (Integer) v;
      if (i < r.min() || i > r.max())
        errors.add(f.getName() + " must be between " + r.min() + " and " + r.max());
    }
  }
  return errors;
}

validate(new User(" ", 10));
// [name must not be blank, age must be between 18 and 120]

This is a tiny version of what Jakarta Bean Validation does. An annotation is a special interface extending java.lang.annotation.Annotation. The object from getAnnotation is a dynamic proxy: Proxy.isProxyClass(ann.getClass()) returned true.

Repeatable annotations

Before Java 8 you needed a wrapper annotation. @Repeatable keeps the wrapper, but hides it: the compiler creates it for you.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Repeatable(Roles.class)
@interface Role { String value(); }

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@interface Roles { Role[] value(); }

@Role("a") @Role("b") class Two {}
@Role("a") class One {}

Two.class.getAnnotation(Role.class);          // null! they are inside @Roles
Two.class.getAnnotation(Roles.class);         // @Roles({@Role("a"), @Role("b")})
Two.class.getAnnotationsByType(Role.class);   // 2 elements: use this one
One.class.getAnnotation(Role.class);          // @Role("a")
One.class.getAnnotationsByType(Role.class);   // 1 element

@Inherited

It works only for class annotations through extends. Verified on Java 21: a subclass inherited an @Inherited annotation, but not a plain one. It is not inherited from interfaces, and an overriding method does not inherit annotations. Spring gets around this with its own search utility, AnnotatedElementUtils and MergedAnnotations, which also supports meta-annotations such as @Service being annotated with @Component.

Annotation processors

A processor is a compiler plugin that runs during javac. It sees source-level program elements, can report errors and warnings, and can generate new files. Generated sources trigger another round. Unlike reflection, it costs nothing at runtime. Uses: MapStruct and Dagger (generated code), Hibernate's JPA static metamodel, Lombok, Spring Boot's configuration metadata.

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.SOURCE) @Target({ElementType.TYPE, ElementType.METHOD})
public @interface Todo { String value(); }

@SupportedAnnotationTypes("Todo")
@SupportedSourceVersion(SourceVersion.RELEASE_21)
public class TodoProcessor extends AbstractProcessor {
  @Override
  public boolean process(Set<? extends TypeElement> annotations, RoundEnvironment env) {
    for (Element e : env.getElementsAnnotatedWith(Todo.class)) {
      String text = e.getAnnotation(Todo.class).value();
      processingEnv.getMessager().printMessage(Diagnostic.Kind.WARNING, "TODO: " + text, e);
    }
    return true;      // claims the annotation
  }
}
$ javac -cp out -processor TodoProcessor -d out2 Use.java
Use.java:1: warning: TODO: split this class
@Todo("split this class") public class Use { }
                                 ^
1 warning

A processor library registers itself in META-INF/services/javax.annotation.processing.Processor. New files are written through processingEnv.getFiler(). The official API can only create new files, not change existing classes. Lombok modifies the compiler's internal syntax tree through non-public APIs, which is why it needs updates for new JDKs. Since JDK 23, javac no longer runs processors discovered implicitly on the class path by default, so builds should configure a processor path or pass -proc:full.

Reflection

Reflection lets a program inspect and use classes, methods and fields at runtime, with names not known at compile time. It is how Spring creates beans, Hibernate fills entities, Jackson binds JSON, and JUnit finds tests.

Getting a Class object

Class<?> a = String.class;                 // literal: does not initialize the class
Class<?> b = "x".getClass();                // from an instance
Class<?> c = Class.forName("java.util.ArrayList");   // by name: initializes it
ClassLoader cl = …; cl.loadClass("X");     // by name: does not initialize it
Class.forName("X", false, cl);             // by name, no initialization

Verified order: a Foo.class literal and loadClass ran no static block, and neither did reading a compile-time constant static final int K = 5, which is inlined. Reading a non-constant static, or calling Class.forName(name), ran it. This is why old JDBC code used Class.forName("com.mysql…Driver"): the static block registered the driver. Since JDBC 4.0, ServiceLoader does this.

Class naming: int[].class.getName() is [I, String[] is [Ljava.lang.String;, and Map.Entry is java.util.Map$Entry by getName, but java.util.Map.Entry by getCanonicalName.

Members: get vs getDeclared

MethodReturns
getFields(), getMethods()Public members, including inherited ones
getDeclaredFields(), getDeclaredMethods()All visibilities, but this class only, nothing inherited
getConstructors() / getDeclaredConstructors()Same split; constructors are never inherited
Class<?> k = Pub.class;
Object o = k.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();    // Class.newInstance() is deprecated
Method m = k.getMethod("up", String.class);             // parameter types identify overloads
m.invoke(o, "x");                                       // "X"
k.getMethod("add", int.class, int.class).invoke(null, 1, 2);   // static: null target

Field f = k.getDeclaredField("c");
f.setAccessible(true);                                  // needed for private
f.set(o, 9);

// Also
Modifier.toString(m.getModifiers());         // "public static"
Point.class.getRecordComponents();           // Java 16
Shape.class.getPermittedSubclasses();        // Java 17
Array.newInstance(String.class, 3);

Failure modes (verified)

ActionException
getMethod on a private methodNoSuchMethodException
Wrong argument typeIllegalArgumentException: argument type mismatch
Wrong target objectIllegalArgumentException: object is not an instance of declaring class
Private field without setAccessibleIllegalAccessException
Invoked method throwsInvocationTargetException, whose getMessage() is null: read getCause()
JDK internalsInaccessibleObjectException

setAccessible, modules and strong encapsulation

setAccessible(true) disables the language's access checks for that one reflected object. Since the module system, it works only if the target's package is open to you. Unnamed-module application classes are open to each other. JDK internals are not: since Java 16 (JEP 396) they are strongly encapsulated by default, and since Java 17 (JEP 403) the --illegal-access escape hatch is gone.

Field f = String.class.getDeclaredField("value");
f.setAccessible(true);
// InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private final byte[]
//   java.lang.String.value accessible: module java.base does not
//   "opens java.lang" to unnamed module

Fix options: --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED as a stop-gap, a library upgrade, or a public API. trySetAccessible() returns false rather than throwing.

Breaking the rules

class Sing { private static final Sing I = new Sing(); private Sing() {} }
var c = Sing.class.getDeclaredConstructor();
c.setAccessible(true);
c.newInstance() != Sing.I;     // true: reflection made a second instance

class Fin {
  private final int x = 1;         // compile-time constant: inlined into x()
  private final Integer y = Integer.valueOf(1);
  private final int z;  Fin() { z = 1; }
  int x() { return x; } int y() { return y; } int z() { return z; }
}
// After setAccessible + field.set(obj, 2) on each:
// x() = 1, y() = 2, z() = 2, and field.get(obj) for x = 2

Writing to x worked, but the method kept the inlined constant. A static final field cannot be set this way (IllegalAccessException: Can not set static final int field…), nor can a record's fields, nor those of a hidden class. Enums cannot be constructed reflectively; Constructor.newInstance refuses them, which is why the enum singleton is safe.

Performance

Reflective calls have overhead: argument arrays and boxing, access checks, and less inlining. Since Java 18 (JEP 416), core reflection is built on method handles. A rough 20-million-call loop on Java 21 measured about 0.2 ns direct, about 3 ns through a non-constant MethodHandle, and about 10 ns through Method.invoke. Treat that as a sense of scale; only JMH gives real numbers, and the direct loop was likely optimized heavily.

Frameworks reduce this by reflecting once at startup and caching Method objects, or by generating bytecode, or generating code at build time (Spring AOT, Micronaut, Quarkus). For GraalVM native images, reflection targets must be declared ahead of time.

Dynamic proxies

java.lang.reflect.Proxy creates, at runtime, a class implementing given interfaces. Each call goes to one InvocationHandler. You can add behaviour around a target without changing it: logging, transactions, caching, retries.

interface Greeter { String hi(String n); }

class Real implements Greeter {
  public String hi(String n) {
    if (n == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("null name");
    return "hi " + n;
  }
}

class LoggingHandler implements InvocationHandler {
  private final Object target;
  LoggingHandler(Object target) { this.target = target; }

  @Override
  public Object invoke(Object proxy, Method m, Object[] args) throws Throwable {
    System.out.println("before " + m.getName());
    try {
      return m.invoke(target, args);
    } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
      throw e.getCause();                       // unwrap, or callers see the wrong type
    } finally {
      System.out.println("after " + m.getName());
    }
  }
}

Greeter g = (Greeter) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    Greeter.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class<?>[]{Greeter.class},
    new LoggingHandler(new Real()));

System.out.println(g.hi("Ana"));
before hi
after hi
hi Ana
  • g instanceof Greeter is true; g instanceof Real is false. The proxy is a sibling of the target, not a subclass.
  • hashCode, equals and toString also go through the handler. Verified: g.hashCode() printed before and after.
  • JDK proxies need interfaces. Passing a class gives IllegalArgumentException: … is not an interface.
  • If a handler throws a checked exception the interface method does not declare, the caller gets UndeclaredThrowableException. This is why you unwrap above.
  • Returning the wrong type gives ClassCastException; returning null for a primitive return type gives NPE.
  • Java 16 added InvocationHandler.invokeDefault for calling default methods.
JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB / ByteBuddy
MechanismNew class implements the interfacesGenerated subclass of the target
NeedsAn interfaceA non-final class, non-final methods
Bean injectable asInterface onlyClass or interface
Used bySpring AOP on interfaces, Spring Data repositories, FeignSpring Boot default (proxyTargetClass=true), Hibernate lazy proxies, Mockito

Why @Transactional fails on self-invocation: the proxy wraps the bean. A call from outside goes through the proxy; this.other() inside the bean goes straight to the target and skips the advice. Fix by moving the method to another bean.

MethodHandles and VarHandles

A MethodHandle (Java 7) is a typed, directly executable reference to a method, constructor or field. It is a lower-level, faster alternative to reflection. Access is checked once, at lookup, using the caller's rights, not at every call. When a handle is in a static final field, the JIT can inline it like a normal call. invokedynamic and lambdas are built on this machinery.

MethodHandles.Lookup lookup = MethodHandles.lookup();

MethodHandle upper = lookup.findVirtual(
    String.class, "toUpperCase", MethodType.methodType(String.class));
String s = (String) upper.invokeExact("abc");        // ABC

MethodHandle concat = lookup.findVirtual(
    String.class, "concat", MethodType.methodType(String.class, String.class));
MethodHandle bound = concat.bindTo("x");             // partial application
String t = (String) bound.invokeExact("y");          // xy

MethodHandle add = lookup.findStatic(
    Calc.class, "add", MethodType.methodType(int.class, int.class, int.class));
int r = (int) add.invokeExact(1, 2);                 // 3
Object bad = add.invokeExact(1, 2);
// WrongMethodTypeException: handle's method type (int,int)int but found (int,int)Object

invokeExact requires the call site's static types to match exactly, including the return type, which is why the cast matters. invoke adapts types, for example boxing, and is more forgiving. To reach private members in another class, use MethodHandles.privateLookupIn(Target.class, lookup).

VarHandle (Java 9) does the same for variables, adding memory-ordered and atomic access (getAcquire, setRelease, compareAndSet), and it replaces most sun.misc.Unsafe field operations.

VarHandle vh = MethodHandles.arrayElementVarHandle(int[].class);
int[] a = {1};
vh.compareAndSet(a, 0, 1, 5);      // true; a[0] is now 5
ReflectionMethodHandle
Access checkAt each call (cached)Once, at lookup
Type handlingObject[] with boxingStrongly typed signature
InliningLimitedExcellent from a static final handle
DiscoveryFull: list all members, annotationsNone: you must know the member
Exception wrappingInvocationTargetExceptionPropagates directly

ServiceLoader

A built-in plug-in mechanism. An API defines an interface (the service), and any JAR can supply an implementation (a provider), with no compile-time link from the consumer. This decouples the two.

// 1. Service interface in the API JAR
public interface PaymentGateway { String name(); }

// 2. Provider JAR: must be a public class with a public no-arg constructor
public class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { … }

// 3a. Class path registration: a file named after the interface
//     META-INF/services/com.acme.PaymentGateway, containing:
com.acme.stripe.StripeGateway

// 3b. Module path registration, in module-info.java
module acme.stripe {
  requires acme.api;
  provides com.acme.PaymentGateway with com.acme.stripe.StripeGateway;
}
module acme.app {
  uses com.acme.PaymentGateway;
}

// 4. Consumer
ServiceLoader<PaymentGateway> loader = ServiceLoader.load(PaymentGateway.class);
for (PaymentGateway g : loader) System.out.println(g.name());
loader.findFirst();
loader.stream().map(ServiceLoader.Provider::type);   // inspect without instantiating

Loading is lazy: providers are created during iteration, and cached by that loader. In the test, stream() listed the type without creating an instance, the first for loop created it, the second reused it, and reload() created a new one. A non-public provider class fails with ServiceConfigurationError … could not be instantiated. On the module path, a provider may instead offer a public static provider() method.

Real uses: JDBC's DriverManager finds drivers this way, SLF4J 2 finds its logging backend, and java.nio.file.spi.FileSystemProvider, Charset providers and annotation processors work similarly. Spring Boot has its own variation: META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports.

Locale and i18n basics

Internationalization (i18n) means designing code so it can adapt to languages and regions. Localization (l10n) is the adaptation itself. Locale is a language plus optional region: nl-NL, pt-BR.

Locale nl = Locale.of("nl", "NL");              // Java 19; constructors are deprecated
Locale br = Locale.forLanguageTag("pt-BR");
nl.toLanguageTag();                             // nl-NL
Locale.getDefault();                            // from the OS or -Duser.language

NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.GERMANY).format(1234.56);         // 1.234,56
NumberFormat.getInstance(Locale.US).format(1234.56);              // 1,234.56
NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.US).format(1234.5);       // $1,234.50
NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(Locale.US).format(0.256);         // 26%
NumberFormat.getCompactNumberInstance(Locale.US,
    NumberFormat.Style.SHORT).format(1200000);                    // 1M, Java 12
String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%.2f", 1234.5);                    // 1234,50

NumberFormat and DecimalFormat are not thread-safe. Currency formatting does not convert amounts, it only formats. Use BigDecimal for money.

Resource bundles

// messages.properties          greeting=Hello {0}
// messages_nl.properties       greeting=Hallo {0}
// messages_de_AT.properties    …

ResourceBundle b = ResourceBundle.getBundle("messages", Locale.of("nl", "NL"));
String text = MessageFormat.format(b.getString("greeting"), "Ana");

Fallback order, for the requested locale nl_NL with default en_US: messages_nl_NL, messages_nl, then the default locale's messages_en_US, messages_en, then the base messages. A missing key throws MissingResourceException. Since Java 9, property bundles are read as UTF-8 (JEP 226).

MessageFormat

MessageFormat.format("Hello {0}, you have {1} items", "Ana", 1234);
// Hello Ana, you have 1,234 items         numbers follow locale formatting
MessageFormat.format("{0,choice,0#no files|1#one file|1<{0} files}", 5);   // 5 files
MessageFormat.format("It's {0}", "x");     // Its {0}   a single quote escapes!
MessageFormat.format("It''s {0}", "x");    // It's x

Traps

  • Turkish I. In Turkish, lowercase of I is dotless ı, and uppercase of i is dotted İ. "TITLE".toLowerCase() on a Turkish-default JVM gives a string that is not equal to "title" (verified with the tr locale), breaking config keys and SQL. For non-user text, use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT).
  • Parsing numbers: Double.parseDouble is locale independent; NumberFormat.parse is not.
  • Sorting: String.compareTo uses UTF-16 values, so Z sorts before a, and accented characters after z. Use Collator.getInstance(locale) for user-visible sorting.
  • CLDR: since Java 9 (JEP 252), locale data defaults to CLDR. Formats changed between Java 8 and 9+, which can break code parsing formatted text.
  • In Spring, MessageSource and LocaleResolver wrap all of this.

Epoch Time and Legacy Interop Cheatsheet

Many APIs (Kafka timestamps, JWT exp, JavaScript Date.now(), Firebase, logs) exchange epoch time: seconds or milliseconds since 1970-01-01T00:00:00Z. An epoch value is always UTC; a zone only matters when you display it.

ConversionCode
Epoch millis to InstantInstant.ofEpochMilli(ms)
Epoch seconds (JWT exp) to InstantInstant.ofEpochSecond(sec)
Instant to millis / secondsi.toEpochMilli() / i.getEpochSecond()
Instant to local date-time for a useri.atZone(ZoneId.of("Asia/Kolkata")).toLocalDateTime()
LocalDate to start-of-day Instantd.atStartOfDay(zone).toInstant()
java.util.Date to/from Instantdate.toInstant() / Date.from(instant)
java.sql.Timestamp to/from LocalDateTimets.toLocalDateTime() / Timestamp.valueOf(ldt)
Classic bug: treating seconds as millis (or vice versa) gives dates in January 1970 or tens of thousands of years in the future. Name fields with their unit, e.g. expiresAtEpochSec.

java.time in JSON and REST APIs

Spring Boot auto-registers Jackson's JavaTimeModule and disables WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS, so java.time types are written as ISO-8601 strings. Recommended contract:

  • Instants (createdAt, events): Instant or OffsetDateTime, serialised like "2025-03-01T10:15:30Z". Unambiguous across clients.
  • Calendar dates (birth date, due date): LocalDate, "2025-03-01". Never send a birth date as an instant, or users in other zones see the previous day.
  • Override the format per field with @JsonFormat(pattern = "dd-MM-yyyy"), or globally with spring.jackson.date-format / a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer. Prefer ISO formats in APIs and format for humans in the UI.
  • Request parameters (?from=2025-03-01) are bound by Spring's conversion service, not Jackson: use @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE) or spring.mvc.format.date.
public record AppointmentDto(
        long id,
        LocalDate visitDate,                 // "2025-03-01"
        Instant createdAt,                   // "2025-03-01T04:45:00Z"
        @JsonFormat(pattern = "HH:mm") LocalTime slot) {}

@GetMapping("/appointments")
List<AppointmentDto> list(@RequestParam @DateTimeFormat(iso = DateTimeFormat.ISO.DATE) LocalDate from) { … }

Interview Questions — Date/Time, Annotations & Reflection

What was wrong with java.util.Date and Calendar?

They are mutable, so not thread-safe, and shared instances can change. Months are 0-based and years in the deprecated constructor are offset by 1900. Date is really an instant with a misleading toString. Invalid values roll over silently. There are no separate types for date-only, time-only or duration values. SimpleDateFormat is not thread-safe.

Why is SimpleDateFormat not thread-safe? How do you fix it in legacy code?

It stores intermediate state in an instance Calendar field during format and parse, so threads overwrite each other, giving wrong dates or exceptions. Reproduced on Java 21: 8 threads sharing one instance gave bad results. Fixes: move to DateTimeFormatter (best), create one per call, use a ThreadLocal, or synchronize.

LocalDateTime vs ZonedDateTime vs OffsetDateTime vs Instant?

LocalDateTime is a wall clock reading with no zone, so it does not name a moment. OffsetDateTime adds a fixed offset and so names a moment. ZonedDateTime adds zone rules, and can do DST-correct arithmetic. Instant is a point on the UTC timeline, with no human fields. Log and store events as Instant; use ZonedDateTime for calculations in a location; use OffsetDateTime in API payloads.

Is LocalDateTime appropriate for an event timestamp?

No. Without a zone, "2024-11-03T01:30" in New York is two different moments, and two servers in different zones produce incomparable values. Use Instant. LocalDateTime fits scheduled local times, along with a stored zone ID.

Predict the output. 
LocalDate j = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 31);
System.out.println(j.plusMonths(1));
System.out.println(j.plusMonths(1).plusMonths(1));
System.out.println(j.plusMonths(2));
2024-02-29
2024-03-29
2024-03-31

The day is clamped to the month's end. The second line starts from Feb 29, so it stays at 29. Date arithmetic with months is not associative.

Predict the output. 
var a = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 15);
var b = LocalDate.of(2024, 3, 20);
System.out.println(Period.between(a, b).getDays());
System.out.println(ChronoUnit.DAYS.between(a, b));

5, then 65. Period is P2M5D, and getDays returns only the days component. ChronoUnit.DAYS gives the total. Mixing them up is a very common bug.

Predict the result. 
LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2024, 1, 1);
d.plusDays(1);
System.out.println(d);

2024-01-01. The object is immutable; the result of plusDays was thrown away.

What is the difference between Duration and Period? When does it matter?

Duration is exact seconds and nanos, and Period is calendar units. Across DST, plus(Period.ofDays(1)) keeps the same wall clock, whereas plus(Duration.ofDays(1)) adds exactly 24 hours. Noon before the US spring change gave 12:00 and 13:00 respectively on the next day. A subscription uses Period; a cache TTL uses Duration.

What does Duration.between(LocalDate, LocalDate) do?

It throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Seconds, as dates have no time component. Use Period.between or ChronoUnit.DAYS.between, or convert with atStartOfDay().

Why can you not do Instant.now().plus(1, ChronoUnit.MONTHS)?

The length of a month depends on the calendar and zone, and Instant has neither. It throws UnsupportedTemporalTypeException: Unsupported unit: Months. Convert first: instant.atZone(zone).plusMonths(1).toInstant().

What happens with 02:30 on a day when the clocks skip from 02:00 to 03:00? And when an hour repeats?

For the gap, ZonedDateTime.of moves the time forward by the gap's length: 03:30-04:00 in New York on 2024-03-10. For the overlap, it keeps the earlier offset by default (summer time), and withLaterOffsetAtOverlap() selects the other. Adding one hour to the first 01:30 yields the second 01:30. If a schedule must not skip or duplicate, check getValidOffsets.

Offset vs time zone?

An offset (+02:00) is a number at one moment. A time zone (Europe/Paris) is a set of rules mapping any instant to an offset, including DST and historic changes. You can compute an offset from a zone and an instant, but not a zone from an offset, because many zones share one offset.

How should dates be stored in a database across time zones?

Past events: UTC timestamp, displayed in the user's zone. Set the JDBC and Hibernate time zone to UTC (hibernate.jdbc.time_zone), so JVM defaults do not alter data. Date-only: DATE with LocalDate. Future local appointments: local date-time plus an IANA zone ID, converting at display time, since zone rules can change. Never store abbreviations such as EST.

What does this print, and why is it a bug? 
LocalDate.of(2024, 12, 30).format(DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("YYYY-MM-dd", Locale.US));

2025-12-30. YYYY is the week-based year, and Dec 30 2024 falls in week 1 of 2025. It usually looks right in testing, and breaks only around New Year. Use uuuu or yyyy. The same goes for mm (minutes) and DD (day of year).

Does this parse? 
LocalDate.parse("2023-02-30");
LocalDate.parse("2023-02-30", DateTimeFormatter.ofPattern("uuuu-MM-dd"));

The first throws DateTimeParseException: … Invalid date 'FEBRUARY 30', because the built-in ISO formatter is STRICT. The second returns 2023-02-28: ofPattern uses SMART, which clamps days 29 to 31 in shorter months. Add .withResolverStyle(ResolverStyle.STRICT) to reject it.

Why is DateTimeFormatter safe to share?

It is immutable, and parse state is created per call. A private static final instance is the normal approach. Methods such as withLocale return new instances.

equals vs isEqual for ZonedDateTime?

equals compares local date-time, offset and zone. isEqual compares the instant. 12:00Z and 17:30+05:30 are the same moment: equals is false, and isEqual is true. compareTo is also not purely instant-based: it returned -1 for these, after comparing the instant then the local fields.

What does LocalDate.of(2024,1,1).compareTo(LocalDate.of(2024,3,1)) return?

-2. It returns the difference of the first differing field, here months. Do not compare it to -1; only the sign is meaningful. Prefer isBefore or isAfter.

How do you make code using now() testable?

Inject a Clock (or InstantSource, Java 17) and call LocalDate.now(clock). Production wires Clock.systemUTC(), and tests use Clock.fixed(…). Mockito's static mocking of LocalDate.now works too, but is a worse design.

How would you calculate someone's age, or the last Friday of a month?
int age = Period.between(birthDate, LocalDate.now(clock)).getYears();
LocalDate lastFriday = date.with(TemporalAdjusters.lastInMonth(DayOfWeek.FRIDAY));
What is an annotation? What makes it "do" something?

Metadata with no behaviour. Effects come from a reader: the compiler (@Override), a processor at build time (Lombok, MapStruct), or runtime reflection (Spring's @Autowired). Technically, it is an interface extending java.lang.annotation.Annotation, and at runtime instances are dynamic proxies.

What are the retention policies? What is the default?

SOURCE: dropped by the compiler. CLASS: in the class file, not visible at runtime; this is the default. RUNTIME: readable by reflection. A framework annotation must be RUNTIME.

My custom annotation returns null from getAnnotation. Why?

Check, in order:

  1. Missing @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME).
  2. It sits on a method of a class, but you are inspecting a proxy or subclass. Spring's CGLIB proxies do not carry method annotations; use AopUtils.getTargetClass or AnnotationUtils.
  3. It is repeated, so the JVM wrapped it in the container. Use getAnnotationsByType.
  4. It is on a superclass, without @Inherited, or on an interface.
What can an annotation element's type be? Can a default be null?

Primitives, String, Class, an enum, another annotation, or a one-dimensional array of those. Defaults must be constants, and cannot be null. Elements cannot have parameters or throws. Annotations cannot extend others or be generic.

Predict what these return. 
@Role("a") @Role("b") class Two {}
Two.class.getAnnotation(Role.class);
Two.class.getAnnotationsByType(Role.class).length;

null and 2. Repeated annotations get wrapped in the container @Roles. getAnnotationsByType looks through the container, and also finds a single use.

Does @Inherited work on interfaces or methods?

No. It works only for annotations on classes, with subclasses via extends. Tested: a class implementing an annotated interface had 0 annotations, and an overriding method had 0.

Annotation processors vs runtime reflection?

Processors run in javac, can generate source files and report compile errors, and add no runtime cost, so startup is faster and they suit native images. They work only with what is known at compile time. Reflection works on anything at runtime, but with a startup cost, errors appearing late, and native-image friction. This is why Micronaut and Spring AOT shift to compile-time generation.

How does Lombok work if processors cannot change classes?

The official API only creates new files. Lombok uses a processor as an entry point, then casts to javac's internal classes and modifies the abstract syntax tree before code generation. It is effectively a compiler hack, so it depends on JDK internals. Since records arrived, many of its uses have gone. With recent JDKs, make sure Lombok is explicitly set as an annotation processor.

getMethods vs getDeclaredMethods?

getMethods: all public methods, inherited included. getDeclaredMethods: all methods declared in this class, of any visibility, with no inherited ones. Order is unspecified. To scan the full hierarchy, loop over getSuperclass(). Bridge and synthetic methods also appear, so filter with isBridge and isSynthetic.

Class.forName vs ClassLoader.loadClass vs .class?

Class.forName(name) loads and initializes (runs static blocks). loadClass and the .class literal load it but do not initialize. Test output confirmed this. Class.forName(name, false, loader) lets you choose. Reading a constant such as static final int K = 5 does not initialize the class either, since the value is inlined.

Can reflection change a private final field? Predict x(). 
class Fin { private final int x = 1; int x() { return x; } }
var f = Fin.class.getDeclaredField("x");
f.setAccessible(true);
var o = new Fin();
f.set(o, 2);
System.out.println(o.x());
System.out.println(f.get(o));

Prints 1, then 2. The set worked, but 1 is a compile-time constant, so the compiler inlined it in x(). For a final field set in a constructor, x() shows 2, though JIT trust of final fields can make this unreliable. static final and record fields refuse this, with IllegalAccessException. Newer JDK work aims to restrict changing finals further, so do not depend on it.

What is InvocationTargetException?

A checked wrapper thrown by Method.invoke and Constructor.newInstance when the called code itself throws. It separates "reflection failed" from "the target failed". getMessage() is null, as verified, so logging only the message hides everything. Use getCause().

Why do you get InaccessibleObjectException after upgrading Java?

Since Java 16 and definitely Java 17, JDK internals are strongly encapsulated. A library calling setAccessible on java.base internals fails. Upgrade the library first, and if needed add a narrow --add-opens java.base/java.util=ALL-UNNAMED, tracked as technical debt.

Can reflection break a singleton? Which singleton resists it?

Yes: setAccessible on a private constructor makes another instance, for a class in your own code. Add a guard in the constructor which throws if the instance exists. An enum singleton is safe: the reflection API refuses to construct enums, and serialization preserves identity.

How does reflection affect performance, and how do frameworks handle that?

A reflective call is typically tens of times slower than a direct one in a tight loop, because of boxing, arrays, and reduced inlining, but that is nanoseconds. The bigger cost is scanning and metadata reading at startup. Frameworks cache Method objects, generate bytecode (Hibernate's ByteBuddy-based accessors) or use build-time generation. Never optimize this without profiling.

Write a dynamic proxy that measures method duration.
@SuppressWarnings("unchecked")
static <T> T timed(T target, Class<T> iface) {
  return (T) Proxy.newProxyInstance(iface.getClassLoader(), new Class<?>[]{iface},
    (proxy, method, args) -> {
      long start = System.nanoTime();
      try {
        return method.invoke(target, args);
      } catch (InvocationTargetException e) {
        throw e.getCause();
      } finally {
        log.info("{} took {} ns", method.getName(), System.nanoTime() - start);
      }
    });
}

Without unwrapping, callers get UndeclaredThrowableException or an InvocationTargetException instead of the real exception.

JDK proxy vs CGLIB? Why can't a final class be proxied by Spring?

JDK proxies implement interfaces. CGLIB generates a subclass and overrides methods. A final class cannot be subclassed, and final methods cannot be overridden: those calls run on the proxy instance with uninitialized state, and without advice. Spring Boot defaults to class-based proxies. Kotlin classes, final by default, need the kotlin-spring plugin.

Why does this.method() skip @Transactional?

The annotation is applied by a proxy outside your object. Internal calls use this, the raw target, so no interceptor runs. Move the method to a separate bean; or inject self lazily; or use TransactionTemplate. The same applies to @Async and @Cacheable.

What is a MethodHandle? How is it different from reflection?

A strongly typed, invocable reference to a member. Access is checked at lookup, and a static final handle inlines like a direct call. It has no discovery ability, so frameworks often use reflection to find a member, then unreflect it to a handle to invoke it quickly. Exceptions pass straight through.

Why does Object r = add.invokeExact(1, 2); fail with WrongMethodTypeException?

invokeExact is signature polymorphic: the compiler records the call's types from the source, including the return type. Here the call site is (int,int)Object, while the handle is (int,int)int. Write int r = (int) add.invokeExact(1, 2); or use invoke.

How does ServiceLoader work? Where is it used?

It reads META-INF/services/<interface> files on the class path, and provides clauses for modules, then lazily instantiates each provider, which must be public with a public no-arg constructor (or a provider() method for modules). Used by JDBC 4 drivers, SLF4J 2, and annotation processors. It allows a plug-in design: adding a JAR adds a feature, with no code change in the consumer.

Why does "TITLE".toLowerCase() sometimes not equal "title"?

It uses the default locale. In Turkish, I lowercases to dotless ı. So use toLowerCase(Locale.ROOT) for keys, protocol values and enum names. Verified with Locale.forLanguageTag("tr"). For case-insensitive comparison, use equalsIgnoreCase.

How does ResourceBundle pick a file? What are the main i18n pitfalls?

It tries the requested locale from most to least specific, then the default locale the same way, then the base bundle. Pitfalls: a server default locale leaking into output; concatenating translated fragments, instead of using full messages with placeholders; a single quote in MessageFormat; plurals needing rules; dates and numbers formatted with a default locale; and assuming that text length is stable in a UI.

Design question: how would you implement a simple dependency injection container?
  1. Scan classes for @Component, using a classpath scanner, or ServiceLoader, or a compile-time index.
  2. Build a definition for each: its class, the constructor annotated @Inject (or the single constructor), and dependencies from getParameterTypes.
  3. Instantiate in dependency order: computeIfAbsent in a singleton map, keeping an "in creation" set to detect cycles.
  4. Inject fields annotated @Inject with setAccessible(true), though constructor injection avoids this.
  5. Wrap beans with a Proxy if methods have advice annotations.
  6. Resolve generics using getGenericParameterTypes, so that Repository<User> selects the right bean.

Discuss trade-offs: startup time from scanning, and the alternative of compile-time generation.

Scenario: scheduled jobs run an hour off after a DST change, and some ran twice. How do you fix it?

Likely causes: the job uses a fixed offset or stores a next run time in UTC computed by adding 24 hours, or the job's cron runs in local time inside the skipped or repeated hour. Fixes: state the zone explicitly (Spring's @Scheduled(cron = "…", zone = "Europe/Amsterdam")); avoid scheduling between 01:00 and 03:00 local time; or run in UTC if the business does not depend on local time. Compute "same time tomorrow" with ZonedDateTime.plusDays. For the duplicates, make jobs idempotent with a run key for the logical date.

Scenario: a startup got slow as the codebase grew, and a profiler shows annotation scanning. What can you do?

Limit component scan paths, and avoid scanning all JARs. Use a compile-time index or Spring AOT processing. Consider class data sharing (AppCDS). Make rarely used beans lazy. Reduce classpath size. For serverless, consider a GraalVM native image, keeping in mind that reflection hints are then required. Measure with Spring Boot's startup actuator endpoint (BufferingApplicationStartup), not by guessing.

How do you measure elapsed time in Java? Why not System.currentTimeMillis() or Instant.now()?

Use System.nanoTime() (or a Stopwatch/Micrometer Timer built on it). It is a monotonic clock: it never jumps backwards. currentTimeMillis() and Instant.now() are wall-clock time and can jump when NTP adjusts the clock, giving negative or wrong durations. nanoTime values are only meaningful as differences within one JVM, never as a timestamp.

long t0 = System.nanoTime();
work();
Duration took = Duration.ofNanos(System.nanoTime() - t0);
Your Angular client sends "2025-03-01T00:00:00.000Z" for a date of birth, and the server stores 28 Feb. What went wrong?

The client serialised a local midnight as an instant (JavaScript Date.toISOString() converts to UTC), so a user east of UTC sends the previous day, and the server converts it again. A date of birth is a calendar date with no zone: send "2025-03-01" and bind it to LocalDate. Reserve Instant/OffsetDateTime for moments in time.

Jackson throws "Java 8 date/time type java.time.LocalDate not supported by default". Why, when Spring Boot works?

A plain new ObjectMapper() does not register JavaTimeModule (jackson-datatype-jsr310). Spring Boot's auto-configured mapper does, so the error usually means code created its own mapper. Inject the Spring-managed ObjectMapper, or call registerModule(new JavaTimeModule()) (or findAndRegisterModules()) and disable WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS.

Where do annotations on a record component end up?

An annotation on a record component is propagated to every element it is applicable to, based on its @Target: the private field, the accessor method, the canonical constructor parameter, and the record component itself (ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT). That is why @NotNull or @JsonProperty on a record component work for validation and Jackson. Read them with getRecordComponents() and component.getAnnotation(…).

A JWT has "exp": 1735689600. How do you check whether it is expired?

JWT times are epoch seconds. Instant exp = Instant.ofEpochSecond(1735689600); then exp.isBefore(clock.instant().minus(skew)) with a small clock-skew allowance (for example 30–60 seconds). Inject a Clock so tests can control "now". Using ofEpochMilli here would put the expiry in January 1970 and reject every token.

JVM Internals & Performance Senior

How a class gets from a file into running machine code, how memory is laid out, how the JIT and the garbage collectors work, and how to diagnose a slow or crashing production JVM. Examples were run on HotSpot 21 unless a newer release is named. This section is the deep follow-up to the JVM overview in Core Java.

Interview: Senior interviewers rarely ask "name the collectors". They ask "the service's p99 went from 80 ms to 900 ms after a release, what do you do?" Learn the mechanisms here, then practise the scenario questions at the end, because they use all of it together.

Bytecode and javap

Bytecode is the instruction set of the JVM, a virtual CPU. javac doesn't produce machine code; it produces a .class file containing bytecode. Each instruction has a one-byte opcode, which is where the name comes from. The JVM is a stack machine: instructions don't name registers, they push values onto an operand stack and pop them off. That makes bytecode compact and independent of any real CPU's registers, which is the basis of "write once, run anywhere". The JVM then runs it with an interpreter and compiles hot parts to native code.

javap is the JDK's class file disassembler. -c prints the bytecode, -p includes private members, and -v prints everything (constant pool, flags, stack limits).

public class Calc {
    static int add(int a, int b) { int c = a + b; return c; }
    int inc(int i) { i = i++; return i; }
    String hello(String n) { return "Hello " + n; }
}
$ javac Calc.java && javap -c -p Calc
  static int add(int, int);
    Code:
       0: iload_0        // push local 0 (a)
       1: iload_1        // push local 1 (b)
       2: iadd           // pop two ints, push their sum
       3: istore_2       // pop into local 2 (c)
       4: iload_2        // push c
       5: ireturn        // return top of stack

  int inc(int);
    Code:
       0: iload_1        // push i (slot 1, because slot 0 is 'this')
       1: iinc  1, 1     // add 1 to local 1 directly, stack unchanged
       4: istore_1       // overwrite local 1 with the OLD value
       5: iload_1
       6: ireturn

  java.lang.String hello(java.lang.String);
    Code:
       0: aload_1
       1: invokedynamic #7,  0  // makeConcatWithConstants:(Ljava/lang/String;)Ljava/lang/String;
       6: areturn

Three things to read off this output. The numbers on the left are byte offsets, not line numbers, which is why they jump. A static method's slot 0 is the first parameter, but an instance method's slot 0 is this. And the inc listing proves why i = i++ leaves i unchanged: the old value is pushed, the local is incremented, then the old value overwrites it.

The prefix letter gives the type: i int, l long, f float, d double, a reference. boolean, byte, char and short are treated as int on the operand stack.

The five invoke instructions

InstructionUsed forHow the target is chosen
invokestaticStatic methodsFixed when resolved
invokespecialConstructors, super.x()Fixed when resolved, no dynamic dispatch
invokevirtualNormal instance methods on a class typeVirtual method table (vtable) of the receiver's runtime class
invokeinterfaceCalls through an interface typeInterface method table (itable) search; a class can implement many interfaces, so a fixed slot isn't possible
invokedynamicLambdas, string concatenation (since 9), records' toString/equals/hashCode, pattern switchThe first execution calls a bootstrap method, which returns a CallSite; later calls go straight to the linked target

invokedynamic exists so the strategy can be decided at run time rather than frozen into the class file. Before Java 9, "Hello " + n compiled to a StringBuilder chain; since JEP 280 it compiles to invokedynamic and StringConcatFactory, so the JDK can improve concatenation without recompiling your code. Lambdas work the same way through LambdaMetafactory, which is why a lambda doesn't produce a separate .class file the way an anonymous class does.

Class file structure

A class file is a strict binary format defined by chapter 4 of the JVM Specification. Its parts, in order:

PartPurpose
Magic numberThe four bytes 0xCAFEBABE identify a class file
Minor and major versionClass file format version. A JVM refuses a class newer than it supports
Constant poolTable of constants: strings, numbers, and symbolic references (class, field and method names as text). Instructions refer to entries by index, such as #7
Access flagspublic, final, abstract, interface, enum and so on
this_class, super_class, interfacesConstant pool indexes for this class and its parents
Fields and methodsEach with name, descriptor (type signature such as (II)I), flags and attributes
AttributesCode (bytecode, max_stack, max_locals, exception table), LineNumberTable, LocalVariableTable, StackMapTable, Signature (generics), BootstrapMethods, ConstantValue
Java release811172125
Class file major version5255616569
  • Why this matters: UnsupportedClassVersionError: ... class file version 65.0, this version of the Java Runtime only recognizes class file versions up to 61.0 means the code was built for 21 and is running on 17. Fix the runtime or compile with --release 17.
  • Limits come from the format: a method's bytecode can't exceed 64 KB (code too large), which generated code sometimes hits. The constant pool holds at most 65,535 entries, and a method has at most 255 parameter slots.
  • Generics: generic types are erased from the bytecode, but they stay in the Signature attribute. That's how frameworks read List<String> from a field declaration by reflection.
  • Debug info: local variable names exist only if compiled with -g. Without them, a helpful NPE message says "<local4>" is null rather than the variable's name.

Class loading in full

Classes aren't all loaded at startup. The JVM loads each one lazily, the first time it's needed. A class goes through three stages: loading, linking (verify, prepare, resolve) and initialization.

The three built-in loaders

LoaderLoadsIn code
BootstrapCore modules such as java.base. Part of the JVM, written in native codeString.class.getClassLoader() returns null
Platform (called Extension before Java 9)Other platform modules such as java.sqlClassLoader.getPlatformClassLoader()
Application (System)Your code: class path and module pathClassLoader.getSystemClassLoader()

Java 9 removed the jre/lib/ext mechanism, and the built-in loaders stopped being URLClassLoader instances. Old code that cast the system loader to URLClassLoader to add JARs throws ClassCastException on 9 and later.

A run on Java 21 printed the following. Note that array classes for primitives report null, and an array of your class reports the element type's loader.

System.out.println(String.class.getClassLoader());                       // null
System.out.println(Init.class.getClassLoader().getClass().getName());    // jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$AppClassLoader
System.out.println(Init.class.getClassLoader().getParent().getClass().getName()); // jdk.internal.loader.ClassLoaders$PlatformClassLoader
System.out.println(Init.class.getClassLoader().getParent().getParent()); // null
System.out.println(java.sql.Connection.class.getClassLoader().getName());// platform
System.out.println(int[].class.getClassLoader());                        // null
System.out.println(Init[].class.getClassLoader().getName());             // app

Parent delegation

Delegation gives two guarantees. Security: core classes come from the trusted loader, and a class in a java. package can't be defined by an application loader at all (SecurityException: Prohibited package name). Consistency: everyone sees one java.lang.Object.

Class identity: same name, different class

At run time a class is identified by the pair (fully qualified name, defining class loader). Load the same file through two loaders and you have two unrelated classes. This run used two URLClassLoaders with a null parent over the same directory:

Class<?> c1 = l1.loadClass("Pl"), c2 = l2.loadClass("Pl");
System.out.println(c1.getName().equals(c2.getName())); // true
System.out.println(c1 == c2);                          // false
Object o = c1.getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance();
System.out.println(c2.isInstance(o));                  // false
c2.cast(o);                                            // ClassCastException: Cannot cast Pl to Pl

The confusing message "Cannot cast Pl to Pl" (or "X cannot be cast to X") in production almost always means two loaders. Spring Boot DevTools' restart loader is a common cause in development.

Custom class loaders

You write one to load classes from somewhere the built-in loaders don't look (a database, the network, encrypted files), to isolate plugins from each other, or to make hot reload possible by throwing away a loader. Override findClass, not loadClass, so that delegation stays intact.

public class DirLoader extends ClassLoader {
    private final Path root;
    public DirLoader(Path root, ClassLoader parent) { super(parent); this.root = root; }

    @Override protected Class<?> findClass(String name) throws ClassNotFoundException {
        Path file = root.resolve(name.replace('.', '/') + ".class");
        try {
            byte[] b = Files.readAllBytes(file);
            return defineClass(name, b, 0, b.length); // bytes become a Class object
        } catch (IOException e) {
            throw new ClassNotFoundException(name, e);
        }
    }
}

Places that deliberately change the normal delegation rule, which are favourite follow-ups:

  • Tomcat gives each web app its own WebappClassLoader, which looks in the app's WEB-INF first (child-first) so two apps can use different library versions. It still delegates java.* and the Servlet API upward.
  • Thread context class loader: core code loaded by bootstrap (such as JDBC's DriverManager or ServiceLoader) must find implementations on the application class path, which a parent can't see. It uses Thread.currentThread().getContextClassLoader().
  • OSGi uses a graph of loaders rather than a tree. Spring Boot's executable JAR uses its own loader to read JARs nested inside BOOT-INF/lib.

Linking

  1. Verification checks that the bytecode is safe: types on the stack match, no stack overflow or underflow, jumps land on valid instructions. Failures give VerifyError. The compiler's StackMapTable makes this fast.
  2. Preparation allocates static fields and sets them to default values (0, false, null). static int x = 5 is 0 at this point. The exception is a compile-time constant (static final int K = 7), which is set here from its ConstantValue attribute.
  3. Resolution turns symbolic references in the constant pool into direct references. HotSpot does this lazily, the first time each instruction runs. That's why a missing method shows up as NoSuchMethodError only when that line executes, not at startup.

Initialization triggers

Initialization runs <clinit>, the method the compiler builds from static field initializers and static {} blocks, in source order. It happens once, under a per-class lock, so a lazy holder singleton is thread-safe without any synchronized of your own. Two classes initializing each other from two threads can deadlock on those locks.

Triggers initialization
  • new
  • Reading or writing a static field that isn't a compile-time constant
  • Calling a static method
  • Class.forName(name)
  • Initializing a subclass (the superclass goes first)
  • The main class at startup
Does not trigger it
  • Reading a compile-time constant (the value is copied into the caller at compile time)
  • Child.parentStaticField (only the declaring class initializes)
  • new Child[3]
  • Child.class
  • loader.loadClass(name)
  • Class.forName(name, false, loader)

Interfaces follow a special rule: initializing a class doesn't initialize its superinterfaces unless the interface declares a default method. The question section below has a run that confirms these rules.

Class unloading

A class can be unloaded only when its defining class loader becomes unreachable, which also requires that no instances of any of its classes and no Class references remain. Unloading happens per loader, never per class, and classes from the bootstrap loader are never unloaded. This explains the classic redeploy leak: one surviving reference to one object from the old web app (a ThreadLocal in a pooled thread, a JDBC driver registered in DriverManager, a shutdown hook) pins its loader, which pins every class it loaded, and Metaspace grows with each redeploy.

The linkage errors compared

ErrorMeaningTypical cause
ClassNotFoundException (checked exception)Code asked for a class by name at run time and no loader found itClass.forName or loadClass with a name missing from the class path, such as a missing JDBC driver
NoClassDefFoundError (Error)The class was present at compile time, and the JVM can't get it nowA JAR missing at run time, or the class's static initializer failed earlier
ExceptionInInitializerErrorA static initializer threwThe first attempt. Later attempts give NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X
NoSuchMethodError, NoSuchFieldErrorClass found, member goneCompiled against one library version, running with another. Check with mvn dependency:tree
IncompatibleClassChangeErrorA class changed shape, such as class to interfaceBinary-incompatible library upgrade
UnsupportedClassVersionErrorClass file newer than the JVMBuilt with a newer JDK
LinkageError: loader constraint violationTwo loaders disagree on which class a shared name meansThe same library in the app and in the server's shared lib
Gotcha: When you see NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class X, don't look for a missing JAR. Scroll up in the log to the first ExceptionInInitializerError, because that one carries the real cause.

Runtime data areas in depth

The Core Java overview shows the map of areas. This part explains what's inside each one.

Stack frames and the operand stack

Each thread has its own stack. Every method call pushes a frame and every return pops one. A frame holds:

  • Local variable array: numbered slots for this, parameters and locals. long and double take two slots.
  • Operand stack: the scratch area that bytecode works on.
  • Frame data: a link to the class's runtime constant pool, the return address, and what's needed to handle exceptions.

The sizes are computed by javac and stored as max_locals and max_stack, so the interpreter knows a frame's size before entering the method. Walking through add(2, 3) from the listing above:

InstructionLocals [a, b, c]Operand stack
start[2, 3, ?]empty
iload_0[2, 3, ?]2
iload_1[2, 3, ?]2, 3
iadd[2, 3, ?]5
istore_2[2, 3, 5]empty
iload_2[2, 3, 5]5
ireturnframe popped, 5 goes on the caller's operand stack

Stack size is set with -Xss, typically 1 MB by default on 64-bit systems. Running out gives StackOverflowError, usually from unbounded recursion. Each platform thread reserves its own stack outside the heap, so 2,000 threads can account for a large part of a process's memory. Reference variables sit in the frame, while the objects they point to are on the heap.

TLAB: why allocation is so cheap

If every new had to synchronize on the shared heap, allocation would be a bottleneck. So each thread gets its own chunk of Eden called a Thread-Local Allocation Buffer. Allocating there is just moving a pointer: check that top + size <= end, then advance top. No lock and no atomic operation, so it takes only a few instructions.

  • When a TLAB fills, the thread gets a new one, which is the slower path using an atomic operation.
  • An object too large for the current TLAB may be allocated directly in Eden.
  • Any leftover space in a retired TLAB is wasted, and the JVM sizes TLABs adaptively to balance this.
  • Allocation is cheap, but its cost shows up later as more frequent GCs. Allocation rate (MB per second) is what drives young GC frequency.

String table

The string table is the structure behind the string pool. It's a native hash table in the JVM that maps string contents to String objects. Since Java 7 the String objects themselves live on the normal heap, so interned strings can be garbage collected. Its bucket count is set by -XX:StringTableSize (65,536 by default on 21). A literal is added lazily, when the ldc instruction that uses it first runs, not when the class loads. That detail explains a famous output question below.

Separate from this is string deduplication (-XX:+UseStringDeduplication). The GC finds distinct String objects with equal contents and makes them share one byte[]. The String objects stay distinct, so == behaviour doesn't change. It began with G1 and was added to other collectors in Java 18.

Code cache

JIT-compiled native code is stored in the code cache, outside the heap. Its size is set by -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize (240 MB by default with tiered compilation). Since Java 9 it's divided into segments for non-method code, profiled code and non-profiled code. If it fills up you get the warning CodeCache is full.
