Compiler has been disabled, and new hot code stays interpreted. The symptom is a slow performance decline with no GC problem. Check with jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache.

Metaspace

Metaspace stores class metadata: method bytecode, constant pools, field and method descriptions. It replaced PermGen in Java 8 and lives in native memory, not the heap.

  • Why PermGen went away: PermGen had a fixed maximum, so apps failed with OutOfMemoryError: PermGen space when the number of classes was hard to predict.
  • Two parts: the class space holds Klass structures reachable through 32-bit compressed class pointers (1 GB reserved by default, set by -XX:CompressedClassSpaceSize). The non-class space holds everything else.
  • Limits: -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize is unlimited by default, so a class loader leak grows until the OS or container stops it. Always set a limit in containers. -XX:MetaspaceSize isn't an initial size; it's the high-water mark at which the first Metaspace-triggered GC happens.
  • Allocation is per loader: each class loader has its own chunks, and they're freed together when the loader dies.
Gotcha: Static fields are not in Metaspace. Since Java 7 in HotSpot they sit on the heap, stored with the class's java.lang.Class mirror object. So are interned strings. Metaspace holds metadata, not your data. Saying "statics are in the method area" is the textbook description of the concept; it isn't where HotSpot puts them.

Everything a Java process uses

AreaLimit flagFailure
Heap-XmxOutOfMemoryError: Java heap space
Metaspace-XX:MaxMetaspaceSizeOutOfMemoryError: Metaspace
Thread stacks-Xss times thread countStackOverflowError, or unable to create native thread
Code cache-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSizeCompiler disabled warning
Direct buffers-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize (defaults to the max heap size)OutOfMemoryError mentioning direct buffer memory
GC structures, JIT memory, native librariesNo single flagProcess killed by the OS or container

Object layout in memory

On 64-bit HotSpot with default settings, every object starts with a header:

  • Mark word: holds the identity hash code once computed, the 4-bit GC age, and lock state. Because age has 4 bits, MaxTenuringThreshold can't exceed 15.
  • Klass pointer: points to the class metadata in Metaspace. This is how the JVM knows an object's type.
  • Padding: objects are aligned to 8 bytes. The JVM reorders fields by size to fill gaps, so declaration order doesn't determine layout.

Sizes measured with Instrumentation.getObjectSize on Java 21. The size is shallow: it doesn't include objects that are referenced.

ObjectBytesWhy
new Object()1612 header + 4 padding
Integer, Boolean1612 + a 4-byte int exactly fills 16; Boolean is 12 + 1 + 3 padding
Long2412 + 4 gap (a long needs 8-byte alignment) + 8
String24Plus its separate byte[]
new byte[0]16Array header only
new int[3]3216 + 12 = 28, rounded to 32
new ArrayList<>()24Plus its backing array once elements are added
new HashMap<>()48Plus table and a node per entry

So List<Integer> with a million elements costs far more than int[1_000_000]: 16 bytes per boxed object plus a 4-byte reference, against 4 bytes per element. Boxing is often the biggest and easiest memory saving in a data-heavy service.

Compressed oops

An oop (ordinary object pointer) is a reference to a heap object. On a 64-bit JVM a raw reference would take 8 bytes. Since objects are 8-byte aligned, the low 3 bits of every address are zero, so the JVM stores address >> 3 in 32 bits and shifts back when using it. That lets 4-byte references address 232 × 8 = 32 GB.

The feature turns off automatically once the heap needs more than that. A check on this JVM confirmed UseCompressedOops is true at -Xmx31g and false at -Xmx40g. The consequence is the classic trap: every reference doubles in size, so a 40 GB heap can hold less live data than a 31 GB heap. Staying just below the limit is a common recommendation. -XX:ObjectAlignmentInBytes=16 stretches the range to 64 GB at the cost of more padding.

Compact object headers: JEP 450 (experimental in Java 24) and JEP 519 (a product feature in Java 25) shrink the header to 8 bytes on 64-bit, enabled with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders. It isn't on by default in 25. Services with many small objects can save a meaningful share of heap.

Interpreter and tiered JIT

Java starts by interpreting bytecode, then compiles what's actually used. Compiling everything up front would make startup slow and would waste time on code that rarely runs. Waiting also has a real benefit: at run time the JVM knows which branches are taken and which classes actually appear, so it can optimize for what the program really does. This is why Java has a warm-up period, and why a service's first requests after a deploy are slower.

LevelRuns asPurpose
0InterpreterStarts immediately, counts calls and loop iterations
1C1, no profilingTrivial methods such as getters, where C2 can't do better
2C1, call and loop counters onlyUsed when the C2 queue is busy
3C1, full profilingThe usual step: receiver types and branch frequencies recorded
4C2Highest optimization, using the profile

A method's counters are compared with thresholds (Tier3InvocationThreshold is 200 and Tier4InvocationThreshold is 5,000 on 21, along with loop-based thresholds). The old -XX:CompileThreshold=10000 applies only when tiered compilation is off. On-Stack Replacement (OSR) handles a method that's called once but loops for a long time: the JVM compiles the method and switches to the compiled version in the middle of the running loop.

Key optimizations

  • Inlining copies a callee's body into the caller. It's the most important optimization, because it removes the call and exposes the code to all the others. Hot methods up to 325 bytes of bytecode (FreqInlineSize) can be inlined, and any method up to 35 bytes (MaxInlineSize). Small methods and getters cost nothing once hot.
  • Devirtualization: a call site that has seen one receiver type is monomorphic, and two is bimorphic; the JIT inlines these behind a cheap type check. With three or more types a site is megamorphic, and it falls back to a real virtual call without inlining. Class Hierarchy Analysis goes further: if only one implementation of a method is loaded, the JIT can call it directly.
  • Escape analysis determines whether an object can be seen outside the method or thread that created it. If not, C2 can apply scalar replacement, breaking the object into its fields so that no heap allocation happens at all, and lock elision, removing synchronized on an object no other thread can reach. HotSpot doesn't do "stack allocation" as such, despite how this is often described.
  • Others: dead code elimination, constant folding, loop unrolling, range-check elimination, loop vectorization, and intrinsics, where the JVM replaces well-known methods like System.arraycopy or Math.sqrt with hand-tuned CPU instructions.
// After inlining, escape analysis can remove this allocation entirely
int lengthSquared(int x, int y) {
    Point p = new Point(x, y);          // p never leaves this method
    return p.x() * p.x() + p.y() * p.y();
}

Deoptimization

C2's speed comes from speculation: it assumes what the profile showed will continue. It leaves an uncommon trap on paths it thinks never happen. When an assumption breaks, such as a never-taken branch being taken or a new subclass being loaded that invalidates a Class Hierarchy Analysis result, the JVM discards that compiled code, rebuilds the interpreter frame, and continues in the interpreter. The method can then be recompiled with the new information. -XX:+PrintCompilation shows this as made not entrant.

This is what's behind a real production pattern: a rarely used code path, or a late-loaded plugin class, suddenly gets exercised and causes a latency blip with no GC activity.

Gotcha: Naive benchmarks lie. The JIT can delete a loop whose result isn't used, and early timings measure the interpreter. Use JMH, the OpenJDK benchmark harness, which handles warm-up, forks, and dead code elimination through Blackhole.
Gotcha: -XX:+OmitStackTraceInFastThrow is on by default. After an implicit exception such as an NPE has been thrown many times at the same hot site, C2 replaces it with a preallocated exception with no stack trace. Logs then show bare java.lang.NullPointerException lines. Look earlier in the log for the first occurrences.

Garbage collection theory

Reachability and GC roots

HotSpot uses tracing: an object is live if it can be reached by following references from a GC root. Everything else is garbage. Reference counting isn't used because it can't reclaim cycles: A pointing to B pointing to A would never reach a count of zero. Tracing handles cycles without any special effort.

GC roots include: local variables and operand stack entries in all thread stacks, static fields (through loaded classes), JNI references, objects used as monitors in synchronized, and classes held by live class loaders.

Being unreachable doesn't require x = null. The JIT knows when a local variable isn't used again and can treat it as dead, even within the method. Assigning null to locals is almost always unnecessary; removing entries from long-lived collections is what matters.

The basic algorithms

AlgorithmHow it worksStrengthWeakness
Mark-sweepMark live objects, add dead space to free listsNo movingFragmentation: free memory exists, but not in one large piece
Mark-compactMark, then slide live objects togetherNo fragmentation, bump allocation afterwardsMoving objects costs time and needs reference updates
CopyingCopy live objects to an empty space, abandon the old oneCost depends only on live data, ideal when most objects dieNeeds spare space to copy into

Generations use the right algorithm for each population. Most objects in Young are dead, so copying is cheap there. Old is mostly live, so collectors use marking and compaction.

The generational hypothesis

The weak generational hypothesis says most objects die young. Request-scoped objects are the obvious example. So the heap is divided: new objects go in Young, and a minor GC copies the few survivors out and treats the whole of Eden as empty afterwards. Each survivor's age increases, and at the tenuring threshold (at most 15) it's promoted to Old.

The thresholds are adaptive. Objects can be promoted early if survivor space overflows. Premature promotion is when medium-lived objects reach Old and then die there, which turns cheap young collections into expensive old ones. It's a common cause of rising GC cost.

Card tables and write barriers

A minor GC wants to scan only Young, but Old objects may point into Young, and those are roots for the minor GC. Scanning all of Old would defeat the purpose. The solution has two parts:

  • Card table: a byte array where each byte represents a 512-byte card of the old generation.
  • Write barrier: a few instructions the JIT adds around every reference store (obj.field = other). They mark the card containing obj as dirty.

At a minor GC, only dirty cards are scanned. G1 extends the idea with a remembered set per region, recording who points into that region, so it can collect any region without scanning the whole heap.

// Conceptually, what a store of a reference compiles to
obj.field = value;
cardTable[address(obj) >> 9] = DIRTY;   // shifted by 9 because 512 = 2^9

A barrier in GC means code injected around reference reads or writes, and has nothing to do with CPU memory barriers. Barriers are the throughput price paid for lower pauses: G1's are heavier than Parallel's, and ZGC and Shenandoah also pay on reads.

Concurrent marking and tri-colour

To mark while the program runs, collectors use three colours: white (not visited), grey (visited, fields not yet scanned), and black (visited and fully scanned). The danger is that the running program moves the only reference to a white object into a black object, which won't be rescanned, and the live object is then freed. Barriers prevent this in one of two ways:

  • Snapshot-at-the-beginning (SATB): before a reference is overwritten, record the old value. Everything live at the start of marking is kept. Used by G1 and Shenandoah.
  • Incremental update: record new references stored into black objects, and rescan them. Used by CMS.

Safepoints and stop-the-world

A stop-the-world (STW) pause suspends all application threads. To do it safely, every thread must be at a safepoint, a point where the JVM knows exactly which stack slots and registers hold references. Threads check a poll at method returns and loop back-edges; when a safepoint is requested, the poll traps and the thread parks. A thread in native code counts as safe, since it can't touch the heap and blocks on return.

GC isn't the only user of safepoints: class redefinition and some diagnostics such as a thread dump need one too.

The time to safepoint is included in the pause felt by your users, and one slow thread delays everybody. A known case is a long counted loop, which the JIT may compile with few polls. HotSpot added loop strip mining to bound this. Measure it with -Xlog:safepoint, which on 21 prints lines such as:

[0.073s][info][safepoint] Safepoint "G1CollectForAllocation", Time since last: 44691700 ns,
    Reaching safepoint: 9200 ns, Cleanup: 18200 ns, At safepoint: 3232900 ns, ...

If "Reaching safepoint" is large, the GC isn't the problem; some thread is slow to arrive. Java 10 added thread-local handshakes, which let the JVM stop threads one at a time, and ZGC relies on them.

Every collector compared

CollectorFlagStatusPauseConcurrent workBest for
Serial-XX:+UseSerialGCAvailableLong relative to heapNone, one GC threadSmall heaps, one CPU, CLI tools, small containers
Parallel-XX:+UseParallelGCAvailable. Default on 8Proportional to heapNone; many GC threads during STWBatch jobs that care about throughput rather than pauses
CMSFlag goneDeprecated in 9, removed in 14Short, with long fallbackMarking and sweepingHistorical. No compaction, so fragmentation caused full GCs
G1-XX:+UseG1GCDefault since 9Target-based, 200 ms defaultMarking; copying is STWGeneral-purpose server apps
ZGC-XX:+UseZGCProduction since 15. Generational added in 21, default mode in 23, sole mode from 24Usually under 1 ms, independent of heap sizeMarking, relocation, reference fixingLow latency, multi-GB to TB heaps
Shenandoah-XX:+UseShenandoahGCProduction since 15. Generational mode experimental in 24, product in 25. Not in Oracle JDK buildsLow milliseconds, independent of heap sizeMarking, evacuation, reference updatingLow latency on OpenJDK builds such as Temurin or Red Hat
Epsilon-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions -XX:+UseEpsilonGCExperimental since 11NoneIt never collectsBenchmarks, very short jobs, measuring allocation

Default selection: the JVM picks G1 on a "server-class" machine, meaning at least 2 CPUs and about 2 GB of memory. Otherwise it picks Serial. Running with -XX:ActiveProcessorCount=1 here selected UseSerialGC. So a pod limited to one CPU silently gets Serial, which regularly surprises people who assumed G1.

Tested on this machine: -XX:+UseShenandoahGC on Oracle JDK 21 fails with Option -XX:+UseShenandoahGC not supported, and -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC fails with Unrecognized VM option.

G1 in detail

G1 works to a pause target, not a guarantee. It predicts how long each region takes, and picks as many as fit. It shrinks the young generation if pauses run long, so setting MaxGCPauseMillis very low gives frequent small collections and lower throughput.

What goes wrong:

  • Humongous allocations: frequently creating huge arrays or strings fragments the regions. Look for Humongous regions in logs. Reuse buffers, or increase -XX:G1HeapRegionSize.
  • Evacuation failure (to-space exhausted): no free regions for survivors, often because of a small heap or late marking.
  • Full GC: G1's last resort. Parallel since Java 10, but still a long STW pause. If you see one, something upstream is wrong.

ZGC and Shenandoah

G1 stops the world to copy objects. ZGC and Shenandoah copy while the program runs, so the pause no longer grows with heap or live set size. The hard problem is that a thread may read a reference to an object that's being moved.

  • ZGC stores metadata in unused bits of the 64-bit pointer (coloured pointers) and uses a load barrier: a check on each reference load. If the pointer's colour shows it's stale, the slow path fixes it, relocating the object if needed. The reference heals itself, so later loads take the fast path. Because metadata lives in the pointer, ZGC doesn't use compressed oops.
  • Shenandoah also moves objects concurrently, using a load reference barrier and forwarding information to find an object's new copy.
  • Generational ZGC (JEP 439, Java 21, enabled with -XX:+UseZGC -XX:+ZGenerational on 21) applies the generational hypothesis, which reduces allocation stalls and CPU cost. It became the default ZGC mode in Java 23 (JEP 474), and the non-generational mode was removed in 24 (JEP 490). On 25 you just use -XX:+UseZGC.

The cost isn't pause time but throughput and memory. Barriers run on application threads, and GC threads compete for CPU. If allocation outpaces collection, threads get an allocation stall, which looks like a pause though it isn't a STW pause. A tiny test with a 128 MB heap on ZGC printed exactly that, which is a good reminder that low-pause collectors need spare heap:

[0.147s][info][gc] Allocation Stall (main) 18.057ms

Reading GC logs

Since Java 9 all JVM logging uses unified logging through -Xlog. The old -XX:+PrintGCDetails and -Xloggc style is gone or mapped to it. A good production setting:

-Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/var/log/app/gc.log:time,uptime,level,tags:filecount=5,filesize=20m

Logging has very little overhead, so keep it on all the time. You can't turn it on after an incident that's already past. Real output from a run with G1, -Xmx128m:

[0.010s][info][gc] Using G1
[0.091s][info][gc] GC(0) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 22M->4M(128M) 2.433ms
[0.099s][info][gc] GC(1) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 33M->10M(128M) 2.933ms
[0.119s][info][gc] GC(2) Pause Young (Normal) (G1 Evacuation Pause) 73M->23M(128M) 4.218ms

Read a line as: at 0.091 s, the first collection, a young pause. Heap use went from 22 MB to 4 MB, total heap 128 MB, and the pause took 2.433 ms. With -Xlog:gc* each GC also shows details:

GC(0) Using 3 workers of 8 for evacuation
GC(0)   Evacuate Collection Set: 1.5ms
GC(0) Eden regions: 23->0(29)
GC(0) Survivor regions: 0->3(3)
GC(0) Old regions: 0->2
GC(0) Humongous regions: 0->0

What to look for:

  • After-GC heap keeps rising across full or mixed cycles: a leak, or a live set too large for the heap.
  • Pause Full at all under G1: investigate the cause in brackets.
  • GC frequency: many young GCs per second means a high allocation rate.
  • Old regions growing quickly after young GCs: premature promotion.
  • User and real time: real much greater than user + sys divided by GC threads means the GC threads weren't getting CPU (CPU throttling, noisy neighbours, swapping).

Paste a log into a tool such as GCViewer or GCeasy to see the trend. A single line doesn't tell you much.

Reference types

A normal reference keeps an object alive. java.lang.ref provides weaker kinds, which let you co-operate with the GC.

TypeCollected whenget()Typical use
StrongNever while reachableIt's the normal variableEverything by default
SoftOnly under memory pressure; all are cleared before an OutOfMemoryErrorObject, or null once clearedMemory-sensitive caches (with care)
WeakAt the next GC that finds no stronger referenceObject, or null once clearedWeakHashMap, ThreadLocal keys, canonicalizing maps
PhantomAfter it's phantom reachable; enqueued for cleanupAlways nullNative resource cleanup through Cleaner
Object o = new Object();
WeakReference<Object> w = new WeakReference<>(o);
System.gc();
System.out.println(w.get() != null);  // true: o still holds it strongly
o = null;
System.gc();
System.out.println(w.get());          // null

ReferenceQueue<Object> q = new ReferenceQueue<>();
Object p = new Object();
PhantomReference<Object> pr = new PhantomReference<>(p, q);
System.out.println(pr.get());         // null, always
p = null;
System.gc();
System.out.println(q.remove(1000) == pr); // true

That output is from a real run on HotSpot's default G1, where System.gc() does a full collection. The specification doesn't promise that System.gc() does anything, and -XX:+DisableExplicitGC turns it off, so don't depend on this in real code.

  • ReferenceQueue: the GC appends a reference object to it after clearing the referent, so your code can remove the matching map entry.
  • Soft reference caches are usually a bad idea. The JVM keeps them based on free heap (-XX:SoftRefLRUPolicyMSPerMB, 1000 ms per free MB), so the heap stays full, GC runs harder, and eviction is unpredictable. Use Caffeine with a maximum size.
  • Cleaner (Java 9) replaces finalizers. finalize() is slow, unordered and unpredictable, can resurrect objects, and is deprecated for removal (JEP 421, Java 18). Prefer try-with-resources, with Cleaner only as a safety net.
public final class NativeBuffer implements AutoCloseable {
    private static final Cleaner CLEANER = Cleaner.create();
    private final Cleaner.Cleanable cleanable;

    public NativeBuffer(long address) {
        // State must not refer to 'this', or the object can never become unreachable
        cleanable = CLEANER.register(this, new State(address));
    }
    @Override public void close() { cleanable.clean(); }  // runs at most once

    private record State(long address) implements Runnable {
        @Override public void run() { /* free the native memory */ }
    }
}

Memory leaks: causes and diagnosis

In Java a leak is memory that's still reachable but will never be used again. The GC is doing its job; your code is still holding the reference.

CauseMechanismFix
Unbounded static map or cacheStatic fields are GC rootsBounded cache with eviction (Caffeine)
ThreadLocal in a poolThe map's key is weak but the value is strong, and pool threads live foreverCall remove() in finally; or a servlet filter or interceptor doing it for you
Listeners never removedThe publisher holds subscribersUnregister on shutdown, or use weak listeners
Non-static inner class or lambdaIt captures the outer instanceUse a static nested class, and don't capture this
Changing a key's hashCodeThe entry can't be found, so can't be removedImmutable keys
Class loader leakOne reference pins all classes after redeployFind the path to GC root of the old loader
Unclosed resourcesConnections, streams and their native buffers persisttry-with-resources
Hibernate first-level cache in a long transactionThe session holds every loaded entityPaginate, and flush() and clear() during batches
Unbounded queue in an executorExecutors.newFixedThreadPool uses an unbounded queue, so slow consumers let tasks pile upA ThreadPoolExecutor with a bounded queue and a rejection policy

Step-by-step diagnosis

  1. Confirm it's a leak. In the GC log, look at heap use right after old collections. A sawtooth with a level floor is healthy. A floor that rises over time suggests a leak.
  2. Capture a heap dump. Configure -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps in advance, or take one with jcmd <pid> GC.heap_dump /tmp/h.hprof. A dump pauses the JVM and has the size of the live heap. Dumps contain real data such as passwords and customer details, so treat them as sensitive.
  3. Open it in Eclipse MAT and start with the Leak Suspects report.
  4. Use the dominator tree to find what retains the most. An object A dominates B if every path to B passes through A, so freeing A frees B. Shallow size is the object itself, and retained size is everything that would be freed along with it.
  5. Use "Path to GC Roots" (excluding weak references) to see exactly who's holding it.
  6. For slow leaks, compare two class histograms over time (jcmd <pid> GC.class_histogram) and see which class count only grows. JFR's Old Object Sample event can also show where long-lived objects were allocated.

OutOfMemoryError variants

The message tells you which memory ran out, so read it before anything else. The ones marked as run were produced on Java 21 here.

MessageMeaningAction
Java heap space (run)An object couldn't be allocated even after GC. A single huge array can cause it tooHeap dump. Leak or undersized heap
GC overhead limit exceededParallel GC: over 98% of time spent in GC while recovering under 2% of the heapSame as heap space. Don't simply disable the check
Requested array size exceeds VM limit (run with new long[Integer.MAX_VALUE])The array is larger than the JVM can ever allocateA size calculation bug, or use a different structure
Metaspace (run)Too much class metadataClass loader leak, or too many generated classes (proxies, Groovy, reflection)
Compressed class space (run)The class part of Metaspace is fullAs above, or raise CompressedClassSpaceSize
Cannot reserve N bytes of direct buffer memory (run; older releases say Direct buffer memory)NIO direct buffers reached the limitNetty, Kafka, NIO usage. Check for buffers not released
unable to create native threadThe OS refused a thread: user limit, cgroup pid limit, or no memory for a stackThread dump to find a thread leak. Check ulimit -u and container pids limit

StackOverflowError is a sibling, not a variant; both extend VirtualMachineError. A container "OOMKilled" (exit code 137) isn't a Java error at all: the kernel killed the process, nothing is logged by the JVM, and there's no heap dump.

Tip: In a service, add -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError. After an OOM a JVM is in an unknown state: some threads died, others continue. It's better to exit, take the heap dump, and let the orchestrator restart.

The jstat -gcutil columns are percentages of survivor spaces, Eden, Old, Metaspace and compressed class space, then counts and seconds for young, full and concurrent GCs. Watching the FGC count rise while O stays near 100 is the classic picture of a dying JVM.

Reading a thread dump: take three dumps a few seconds apart. Threads stuck in the same place are the story. BLOCKED threads waiting for a monitor point to lock contention, and Found one Java-level deadlock is printed for you when there's a deadlock. Many threads in RUNNABLE at SocketInputStream.read mean they're waiting on a slow downstream, because RUNNABLE includes blocking in native I/O.

Interview: "How do I find which thread is using all the CPU?" On Linux, run top -H -p <pid> to find the busy thread ID, convert it to hex, and find the matching nid=0x... in a thread dump. Or use async-profiler, which gives you the answer as a flame graph.

Key JVM flags

Each flag below was confirmed to exist on Java 21 with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal, which also shows the final value of every flag. Defaults are from this run unless noted.

FlagPurpose
-Xms, -XmxInitial and maximum heap. The default maximum is 25% of RAM
-XssStack size per thread
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage, -XX:InitialRAMPercentageHeap as a share of available memory (or container limit)
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize, -XX:MetaspaceSizeMetaspace ceiling, and the first GC trigger
-XX:MaxGCPauseMillisG1 pause target, 200 by default
-XX:InitiatingHeapOccupancyPercentG1: old occupancy that starts marking, 45 initially, adjusted adaptively
-XX:G1HeapRegionSize, -XX:G1ReservePercentRegion size, and space held back for evacuation
-XX:MaxTenuringThresholdMaximum age before promotion, 15 by default
-XX:NewRatio, -XX:SurvivorRatioGeneration sizing. Avoid fixing young size under G1, as it stops G1 adapting
-XX:ParallelGCThreads, -XX:ConcGCThreadsGC thread counts, set from CPU count
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:HeapDumpPathAutomatic heap dump. Should be on everywhere
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError, -XX:+CrashOnOutOfMemoryErrorExit, or crash with a core dump, on the first OOM
-XX:+AlwaysPreTouchTouch all heap pages at start, for steadier latency at the cost of startup time
-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSizeCode cache limit
-XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1C1 only. Quicker startup for short tools; lower peak speed
-XX:MaxDirectMemorySizeNIO direct buffer limit
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summaryEnables native memory reporting with a small overhead
-XX:+UseStringDeduplicationShare byte[] between equal strings during GC

-XX:+DisableExplicitGCIgnore System.gc(). Careful: direct buffer cleanup may rely on it

Tuning methodology

Tuning is measurement, not flag collecting. Most production problems are fixed in application code, and the default G1 is good for most services.

  1. Define the goal in numbers. For example p99 latency under 200 ms at 500 requests per second. Pick your priority among latency, throughput and footprint. You can improve two at the cost of the third.
  2. Measure the baseline under realistic load, with GC logs and JFR on. Get the actual live set size (heap after a full collection), allocation rate and pause distribution.
  3. Fix the application first. Allocation hot spots (JFR or async-profiler), oversized queries returning thousands of rows, boxing, and huge humongous arrays. Reducing allocation helps every collector.
  4. Size the heap. A usual starting point is 3 to 4 times the live set. Set -Xms equal to -Xmx on servers to avoid resize pauses.
  5. Choose a collector by the goal, not fashion. Try ZGC only if pauses are truly the limiting factor.
  6. Change one thing at a time, re-measure, and record the result. Copying a page of flags from a blog is a classic source of outages, since old flags may have become harmful.

Containers

Old JVMs read the host's memory and CPUs, so a pod limited to 1 GB on a 64 GB node would try a 16 GB heap and get killed. Modern JVMs read cgroup limits (-XX:+UseContainerSupport, on by default on Linux since 10 and backported to 8u191). cgroup v2 support came in 15 and was backported to 11.0.16 and 8u372.

# Typical Dockerfile
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75", "-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError",
            "-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError", "-XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  • Prefer percentages to -Xmx so the same image works across memory limits. The default is only 25%, which wastes most of a small container. Commonly 50% to 75% is used.
  • Leave room for non-heap memory: Metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, direct buffers and GC structures. The process size (RSS) exceeds the heap, often by hundreds of megabytes. Use Native Memory Tracking to measure it.
  • OOMKilled (exit 137) with a healthy heap means non-heap memory or too large a heap percentage. There's no Java exception.
  • CPU limits: the JVM sizes GC, JIT and ForkJoinPool.commonPool threads from the limit. A CPU limit of 1 can select the Serial GC. CFS throttling under Kubernetes CPU limits can look exactly like long GC pauses, so compare real time with throttling metrics.
  • Use exec form in ENTRYPOINT, so Java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

CDS and AOT cache

Startup spends much of its time loading, parsing and verifying the same classes on each run. Class Data Sharing (CDS) stores the processed form in an archive file that's mapped into memory, and several JVMs can share it.

ReleaseFeature
10Application CDS (JEP 310) opened to everyone, covering your own classes
12Default CDS archive of JDK classes ships with the JDK (JEP 341)
13Dynamic archive at exit (JEP 350): -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa
19-XX:+AutoCreateSharedArchive creates and refreshes the archive automatically
24AOT cache (JEP 483): classes are also loaded and linked ahead of time
25Simpler commands (JEP 514) and stored method profiles (JEP 515), so less warm-up
# Java 13+: dynamic CDS. Classes must come from JARs
java -XX:ArchiveClassesAtExit=app.jsa -jar app.jar
java -XX:SharedArchiveFile=app.jsa -jar app.jar

# Java 24: training run, create, then production run
java -XX:AOTMode=record -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -jar app.jar
java -XX:AOTMode=create -XX:AOTConfiguration=app.aotconf -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar app.jar
java -XX:AOTCache=app.aot -jar app.jar

# Java 25: the first two steps combined
java -XX:AOTCacheOutput=app.aot -jar app.jar

Limitations: the archive must match the JVM and class path used to create it, or it's ignored. Classes from plain directories aren't archived. Trying that here printed Skipping Gc: Unsupported location. This work comes from Project Leyden, whose goal is better startup and warm-up while keeping the normal JVM. Spring Boot documents CDS and AOT cache setups for its applications.

GraalVM native image

Native image compiles a Java application ahead of time into a standalone executable with no JVM. At build time, a static analysis starting from main finds all reachable code, and only that is compiled. The result runs on a small runtime called Substrate VM.

JVM (JIT)Native image (AOT)
StartupSeconds for a Spring appTens of milliseconds
MemoryHigherMuch lower RSS
Peak throughputExcellent after warm-up, helped by runtime profilingUsually lower without profile-guided optimization
Build timeQuickMinutes, and memory-hungry
Reflection, proxies, resourcesJust workMust be declared in reachability metadata
Dynamic class loadingFully supportedNot supported: closed-world assumption
ToolsFull JVM toolingLimited, though JFR and heap dumps are supported in part

The closed-world assumption means that everything reachable must be known at build time. That clashes with Java's dynamism, so frameworks do extra work. Spring Boot's AOT engine analyses the application context at build time and generates code and hints. With the Spring Boot parent POM, mvn -Pnative native:compile builds it.

It suits serverless functions, CLI tools, and scale-to-zero services. For a long-running, high-throughput service, a tuned JVM usually wins. Between the two sit CDS, the AOT cache and CRaC (saving a warmed-up process and restoring it).

Benchmarking Correctly with JMH

A System.nanoTime() loop around a method measures the interpreter, OSR, dead-code elimination and GC noise rather than your code. JMH (Java Microbenchmark Harness, from OpenJDK) handles warm-up iterations, forking fresh JVMs, and preventing the JIT from deleting unused results.

@BenchmarkMode(Mode.AverageTime)
@OutputTimeUnit(TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS)
@Warmup(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Measurement(iterations = 5, time = 1)
@Fork(2)
@State(Scope.Benchmark)
public class ConcatBench {
    @Param({"10", "1000"}) int n;

    @Benchmark
    public String builder() {
        var sb = new StringBuilder();
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) sb.append(i);
        return sb.toString();               // returning the result defeats dead-code elimination
    }

    @Benchmark
    public void joining(Blackhole bh) {
        bh.consume(IntStream.range(0, n).mapToObj(Integer::toString).collect(Collectors.joining()));
    }
}
  • Return or Blackhole.consume every result, or the JIT may remove the work.
  • Keep inputs in @State fields, not constants, or constant folding computes the answer at compile time.
  • Use @Fork > 0 so profile pollution from other benchmarks does not leak in; add -prof gc to see allocation rate per operation.
  • A microbenchmark answers a narrow question. Validate real impact with a load test and a profiler (JFR, async-profiler) on the service.

Which Tool for Which Symptom

SymptomFirst toolWhat you look for
High CPUtop -H + jcmd <pid> Thread.print, async-profiler/JFRHot threads and methods; GC threads vs application threads
Hang, low CPU3 thread dumps a few seconds apartBLOCKED/WAITING threads on the same lock or pool; deadlock report
Heap growingGC log, jcmd GC.class_histogram, heap dump in MATOld gen after full GC rising; dominator tree
RSS > heap, OOMKilledNative Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary)Metaspace, threads, direct buffers, code cache

Slow startup-Xlog:class+load, Spring startup actuator, JFRClasspath scanning, bean init, missing CDS/AOT cache

Interview Questions — JVM Internals & Performance

What is the difference between the JVM specification and HotSpot?

The JVM Specification defines the class file format, instruction set and required behaviour. It doesn't dictate memory layout or GC. HotSpot is the main implementation, used by OpenJDK and Oracle JDK. Others include OpenJ9 and the GraalVM compiler stack. So "Metaspace", "TLAB" and "G1" are HotSpot details, not language rules. Being able to separate "the spec says" from "HotSpot does" is a good sign in a senior interview.

Why does Java use both an interpreter and a JIT, instead of compiling everything ahead of time?

An interpreter starts immediately. Compiling everything would slow startup and waste effort on rarely run code. The JIT compiles only hot code, and it does this with knowledge unavailable to a static compiler: real branch frequencies and receiver types. It can then apply speculative inlining, with deoptimization to recover if an assumption fails. The cost is warm-up time and extra CPU early in the process's life. AOT approaches such as native image reverse that trade-off.

What does javap -c show and when have you needed it?

It disassembles a class file into bytecode. Uses: seeing how a language feature really compiles (i = i++, try-with-resources, string concat, switch on string), confirming whether a class was built with the expected version (javap -v shows the major version), and checking a library's actual method signature during a NoSuchMethodError.

Output: what does this print? int i = 5; i = i++; System.out.println(i);

It prints 5. The bytecode loads i (5) to the operand stack, increments the local to 6, and stores the value from the stack back into the local, overwriting 6 with 5. See the inc listing above, where istore_1 does this.

Output: predict the initialization order.
public class Init {
  static class Parent {
    static int v = 1; static final int K = 7;
    static { System.out.println("Parent init"); }
  }
  static class Child extends Parent {
    static int w = 2;
    static { System.out.println("Child init"); }
  }
  interface I { int X = print("I init"); default void d() {} }
  interface J { int Y = print("J init"); }
  static class Impl implements I, J {
    static { System.out.println("Impl init"); }
  }
  static int print(String s) { System.out.println(s); return 1; }

  public static void main(String[] args) {
    System.out.println("1:" + Child.K);
    Child[] arr = new Child[3]; System.out.println("2");
    System.out.println("3:" + Child.v);
    System.out.println("4:" + Child.w);
    new Impl(); System.out.println("5");
  }
}
1:7
2
Parent init
3:1
Child init
4:2
I init
Impl init
5

Line by line. Child.K is a compile-time constant, inlined into main, so nothing initializes. Creating an array doesn't initialize the element class. Child.v is declared in Parent, so only Parent initializes. Child.w initializes Child, whose parent is done. new Impl() initializes I because it has a default method, while J has none, so it isn't initialized.

Output: the static singleton counter puzzle. What is printed?
class Single {
    static Single s = new Single();
    static int a;
    static int b = 0;
    Single() { a++; b++; }
}
System.out.println(Single.a + " " + Single.b);

It prints 1 0. During preparation s, a and b are all default values. Initializers then run in source order. First new Single() sets a = 1 and b = 1. a has no initializer, so stays 1. b = 0 then runs and resets it to 0. Moving the s line to the end prints 1 1.

Output: what happens when a static initializer throws, and then the class is used again?
static class Bad { static int x = 1 / 0; }
try { new Bad(); } catch (Throwable t) { System.out.println(t); }
try { new Bad(); } catch (Throwable t) {
    System.out.println(t);
    System.out.println(t.getCause());
}
java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError
java.lang.NoClassDefFoundError: Could not initialize class Init$Bad
java.lang.ExceptionInInitializerError: Exception java.lang.ArithmeticException: / by zero [in thread "main"]

A class that fails initialization stays in an erroneous state for the life of its loader; it isn't retried. On Java 17 and later the second error has a cause pointing to the original failure, as this run on 21 shows. Note that the error is a Throwable but not an Exception, so catch (Exception e) misses it.

Output: Class.forName vs loadClass.
public class L2 {
  static class A { static { System.out.println("A init"); } }
  static class B { static { System.out.println("B init"); } }
  public static void main(String[] x) throws Exception {
    ClassLoader c = L2.class.getClassLoader();
    c.loadClass("L2$A");                System.out.println("loaded");
    Class.forName("L2$A");
    Class.forName("L2$B", false, c);    System.out.println("no init");
    Class<?> k = B.class;               System.out.println(k.getSimpleName());
    Class.forName("L2$B");
  }
}
loaded
A init
no init
B
B init

loadClass loads without initializing. Class.forName(name) initializes. The three-argument form lets you choose. A class literal doesn't initialize either. This is why old JDBC code used Class.forName("com.mysql.jdbc.Driver"): the driver's static block registered it with DriverManager. Since JDBC 4, ServiceLoader finds drivers automatically.

Output: the intern() puzzle.
String s = new String("ja") + new String("va2x");
System.out.println(s.intern() == s);     // true

String t = new String("xy") + new String("z");
String lit = "xyz";
System.out.println(t.intern() == t);     // false
System.out.println(t.intern() == lit);   // true

Concatenation builds a new heap string that isn't in the pool. In the first case "java2x" isn't pooled yet, so intern() adds this same object to the table and returns it. Since Java 7 the table can reference heap strings directly, so no copy is made. In the second case, lit = "xyz" has already run, so the literal is pooled first and intern() returns that other object. Move the lit line below the comparison and the first result flips to true, since literals resolve lazily. Avoid the classic example string "java" for this: the JDK itself may already have interned it.

Output: what are the size and contents of this WeakHashMap after a GC?
Map<Object, String> m = new WeakHashMap<>();
Object k = new Object();
m.put(k, "v");
m.put("lit", "v2");
m.put(new String("tmp"), "v3");
System.out.println(m.size());
k = null;
System.gc();
Thread.sleep(100);
System.out.println(m.size() + " " + m);
3
1 {lit=v2}

The object key lost its strong reference, and new String("tmp") never had one. The key "lit" stays, because a literal in the string table is strongly held by the class's constant pool. That's a trap when testing weak maps with literal strings. Only keys are weak: a value that references its own key keeps the entry alive forever.

Explain the parent delegation model and how to break it, and why you might.

A loader asks its parent first and searches its own locations only if the parent fails. This protects core classes and prevents duplicates. To break it, a loader overrides loadClass and looks locally first. Tomcat does that so each web app can have its own library versions, while still delegating java.* and the Servlet API, since those must be shared. ServiceLoader is the other common exception: bootstrap-loaded code uses the thread context class loader to reach "down" to application classes.

Can I write my own java.lang.String and have it loaded?

No. With delegation the bootstrap loader's version wins, and the class path copy is never used. A custom loader that tries to define it gets SecurityException: Prohibited package name: java.lang. On Java 9 and later a class path copy of a package in java.base is also ignored, because that package belongs to a named module. Only special flags like --patch-module can replace JDK classes.

ClassNotFoundException vs NoClassDefFoundError?

ClassNotFoundException is a checked exception. It's thrown when code explicitly asks to load a class by name and it isn't found. NoClassDefFoundError is an Error: code compiled against a class, and the JVM can't provide it when it's needed. It has two causes: the class file is really missing at run time (for instance a provided dependency that isn't provided), or its static initializer failed earlier. The message Could not initialize class tells you it's the second.

What causes NoSuchMethodError in a Spring Boot app after a dependency upgrade?

A class compiled against library version X, and at run time another version without that method was chosen. Usually Maven's nearest-wins mediation picked an older transitive version. Steps: identify the owning class, find which JAR it came from with -Xlog:class+load or Foo.class.getProtectionDomain().getCodeSource(), run mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=group:artifact, then pin the version in dependencyManagement, or better use a BOM so related libraries move together.

How can a class be unloaded? Why did my Metaspace grow with each redeploy?

Classes unload only when their defining loader becomes unreachable, after no instance or Class reference remains. In a redeploy, the container discards the old loader. If anything outside the app holds an object from it, the loader survives along with all of its classes. Common holders are a ThreadLocal value on a pool thread owned by the container, a driver in DriverManager, a logging framework reference, a timer thread, and a shutdown hook. In a heap dump, find WebappClassLoader instances, look for one marked as stopped, and use Path to GC Roots.

Where are static variables stored? Where is the string pool?

In HotSpot since Java 7, static fields live on the heap, alongside the class's java.lang.Class mirror. The string table is a native structure, but the String objects it refers to have been on the heap since Java 7. Metaspace holds metadata only. Many tutorials still say "statics are in Metaspace", which is a mix-up between the spec's "method area" concept and HotSpot's implementation.

Stack vs heap: what goes where? Does an object ever live on the stack?

Primitive locals and references live in the frame. Objects, including their primitive fields, live on the heap, as do arrays. The language gives no way to request stack allocation. HotSpot's C2 can eliminate an allocation through scalar replacement if escape analysis proves the object doesn't escape, but that isn't a guarantee and it applies only to compiled code.

What is a TLAB and why does it matter?

A Thread-Local Allocation Buffer is a chunk of Eden owned by one thread, so allocation is a pointer bump with no synchronization. That's why Java allocation is often cheaper than malloc. Consequences: many threads can allocate without contention; objects allocated together by one thread sit together in memory, which is good for cache; and short-lived small objects are close to free, though each still adds to GC frequency.

How much memory does an Integer take vs an int? What about a String holding "abc"?

int: 4 bytes. Integer: 16 bytes for the object, plus a 4-byte reference (with compressed oops) to reach it. A String object is 24 bytes, plus its byte[]: 16 byte header + 3 bytes, rounded to 24. So 48 bytes for "abc". Compact strings (Java 9, JEP 254) store Latin-1 text with 1 byte per character; before that it was a char[] with 2 bytes each. A HashMap.Node adds more per entry on top. This is why a million-entry map of small objects can use hundreds of MB.

What are compressed oops, and why is a 40 GB heap possibly worse than a 31 GB heap?

Compressed oops store references in 32 bits, shifted by 3 because objects are 8-byte aligned, which addresses 32 GB. Beyond that limit the JVM switches to 64-bit references. References take 4 extra bytes each, and on a reference-heavy object graph that can consume all the extra capacity, and cache efficiency falls too. Check with -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal | grep UseCompressedOops. Note that UseCompressedClassPointers is a separate feature.

What is the identity hash code, and is it the memory address?

No. Object.hashCode(), if not overridden, generates a number on first call (by default a thread-local random generator) and stores it in the mark word. That storage is why the value stays the same even as the GC moves the object. Moving objects is exactly why it can't be the address. The default toString()'s hex value is this hash, not an address.

Explain tiered compilation, OSR, and how you would see JIT activity.

Code starts in the interpreter (level 0), then C1 with profiling (level 3), and hot code reaches C2 (level 4). OSR switches a long-running loop to compiled code mid-execution. -XX:+PrintCompilation logs each compile, showing the tier, with % marking OSR and made not entrant marking invalidated code. Better tools are JFR compilation events and jcmd <pid> Compiler.codecache. -XX:TieredStopAtLevel=1 forces C1 only, which is handy for short tools.

What is escape analysis? Does it really allocate objects on the stack?

Escape analysis determines how far an object's reference can travel: not at all, through a call as an argument, or globally. In HotSpot's C2, an object that doesn't escape can be scalar-replaced: its fields become plain local values and there's no allocation. Locks on it are also removed. It's not literally stack allocation. It only works after inlining, so a call that isn't inlined can make the object appear to escape. It can be disabled with -XX:-DoEscapeAnalysis to measure its effect.

Why can adding one more interface implementation make hot code slower?

The JIT inlines call sites with one or two observed receiver types. If a third type shows up at a call site, it becomes megamorphic and stops being inlined, losing not just the call but all the optimizations inlining enabled. Loading a second implementation may also invalidate Class Hierarchy Analysis, deoptimizing code that assumed only one. That's the mechanism behind occasional performance surprises from "harmless" abstractions.

What is deoptimization, and when does it happen?

Compiled code is built on assumptions. When one fails, the JVM discards the compiled method and continues in the interpreter, rebuilding the frame. Triggers: reaching an uncommon trap (a branch never seen in profiling), a type check failing at an inlined site, or a newly loaded class invalidating a Class Hierarchy Analysis assumption. It's a normal mechanism. It's a problem only if a method repeatedly compiles and deoptimizes.

How does the GC deal with cycles? Why not use reference counting?

Tracing starts at GC roots, and anything not reached is garbage, whether or not it's in a cycle. Reference counting can't reclaim cycles without extra work, and it adds an atomic counter update to every reference assignment, which is costly under concurrency.

Explain what a minor GC does, step by step.
  1. Allocation fails because Eden is full, so a safepoint is requested.
  2. Roots are found: thread stacks, statics, and dirty cards or remembered sets from Old to Young.
  3. Live objects in Eden and the from-survivor space are copied to the to-survivor space, ages are incremented, and old enough objects are promoted to Old.
  4. References are updated, Eden and the from-space are considered empty, and survivor roles swap.
  5. Threads resume with empty Eden.

Its cost depends on the number of live objects, not on how many died. A larger young generation therefore doesn't necessarily mean longer pauses.

Why do we need card tables?

So a young collection doesn't need to scan all of Old for references into Young. A write barrier marks the card containing any object that has a reference stored into it, and the GC scans only dirty cards. Without this, minor GCs would cost as much as a full scan. G1's remembered sets are the region-based version of the same idea.

What is a safepoint? Why can a pause be long when GC work is short?

A safepoint is a state where all Java threads have stopped at known points, so the JVM can safely examine or change the heap. Threads reach one by checking a poll. If one thread takes a long time, for example in a long counted loop or a page fault, every other thread sits waiting. -Xlog:safepoint prints "Reaching safepoint" separately from "At safepoint". A long first number points at time to safepoint rather than the collector.

Difference between minor GC, major GC, mixed GC and full GC?
  • Minor (young): collects Young.
  • Major: loosely, collecting Old. The term is not precise, so ask which collector is meant.
  • Mixed (G1): Young plus a selection of Old regions.
  • Full: whole heap, usually long STW, a fallback under G1.
G1 vs Parallel vs ZGC: how would you choose?

Parallel: batch and data processing where total throughput counts and pauses of a second or more are fine. G1: the sensible default for services, balancing throughput and pause targets of around 100-200 ms. Generational ZGC: latency-critical services where p99.9 matters, with heaps from a few GB upward, and CPU headroom available. Serial: tiny containers and CLI tools. Measure rather than assume: a low-pause collector with too small a heap stalls allocation and gives worse results than G1.

Why was CMS removed?

CMS never compacted the old generation, so fragmentation eventually forced a long single-threaded full GC. It also had a high maintenance cost, a large tuning surface, and failure modes ("concurrent mode failure"). G1 replaced it for most uses, and it was deprecated in 9 (JEP 291) and removed in 14 (JEP 363).

How can ZGC move objects while threads are running?

A load barrier runs each time a reference is loaded from the heap. ZGC stores metadata bits in the pointer. If the pointer is out of date, the slow path finds the object's new location (or relocates it first), and overwrites the field with the good pointer. Application threads therefore help finish the GC's work. STW phases handle only small tasks such as root scanning preparation, so pause time doesn't scale with heap size.

Is System.gc() ever a good idea? What does it do on G1?

It's only a hint. On G1 it normally runs a full STW collection, unless -XX:+ExplicitGCInvokesConcurrent makes it start a concurrent cycle instead. So calling it in application code tends to create the pauses you're trying to avoid. Legitimate uses are limited to tests and benchmarks. A library that calls it can be found with the GC cause in the log: Pause Full (System.gc()).

Soft vs weak vs phantom references?

Soft: cleared under memory pressure, and all before an OOM. Weak: cleared at the next GC once only weakly reachable. Phantom: get() always returns null; you only learn from a queue that the object is gone, which makes it right for post-mortem cleanup, and it's what Cleaner is built on. WeakHashMap uses weak keys. ThreadLocalMap also has weak keys, with strong values.

Why is finalize() deprecated, and what replaces it?

It has no timing guarantee and might not run at all. It delays reclamation by at least one GC cycle, runs on a limited finalizer thread that can fall behind, has no ordering, allows objects to be resurrected, and adds a cost to allocating such objects. It was deprecated in 9 and deprecated for removal in 18 (JEP 421). Use try-with-resources for deterministic cleanup, and Cleaner as a safety net.

Why is ThreadLocal a classic memory leak in Tomcat?

Each thread has a ThreadLocalMap. Its entries hold the key weakly and the value strongly. Tomcat threads are pooled and live indefinitely, so a value set during a request stays until overwritten, even after the request ends. That leaks data between requests too, which can be a security problem, such as one user's context visible to another. And if the value's class came from a web app's loader, it pins the loader across redeploys. Always call remove() in finally.

Explain shallow vs retained size, and a dominator tree.

Shallow size is the memory of one object alone. Retained size is what would be freed if it were collected: everything reachable only through it. In a dominator tree, a node's children are objects it alone keeps alive. So a HashMap might have a shallow size of 48 bytes and a retained size of 2 GB, and the tree's top entries show where memory really goes.

Scenario: Heap climbs to the limit over two days, then the service dies with an OOM. Walk through it.
  1. Check GC logs: is the post-GC floor rising? That says leak rather than a burst.
  2. Restart to restore service. Make sure HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError is on, with a path on a volume that survives the restart.
  3. Analyze the dump in MAT. Leak Suspects, then dominator tree.
  4. Follow Path to GC Roots to see who holds it, such as a static cache or a queue.
  5. Check the code and recent commits. Reproduce it in a load test.
  6. Fix, then add a metric (cache size, or heap after GC through Micrometer) with an alert.
Scenario: p99 jumped after a release, but CPU and heap look normal. How do you investigate?
  1. Correlate first: compare latency graphs with GC pauses. If GC pauses line up with spikes, look at the GC log. Otherwise leave GC out of it.
  2. Check for lock contention and pool saturation: JFR's JavaMonitorEnter events, thread dumps, HikariCP pending connections.
  3. Check downstream timings using distributed tracing, as a downstream or SQL plan change is a common cause.
  4. Compare with the previous release: flame graphs from async-profiler or JFR show new hot paths. Look for new allocation, logging, or N+1 queries.
  5. Look at safepoint time and deoptimization.

The method: form a hypothesis from data, change one thing, and verify.

Scenario: The container is OOMKilled, but the heap is only 60% used. What's going on?

Heap use doesn't describe the process. The kernel's OOM killer uses the cgroup memory limit against RSS. Causes: too high a MaxRAMPercentage so the committed heap plus non-heap exceeds the limit; thread stacks from many threads; Netty or Kafka direct buffers; Metaspace without a limit; and native allocations from libraries, such as compression. Enable -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary, and use jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary, comparing that with RSS. The difference shows memory outside the JVM's accounting. Then set heap percentage and MaxMetaspaceSize, cap direct memory, and add headroom. Exit code 137 and no Java exception are the giveaways.

Scenario: CPU is at 100% and GC logs show back-to-back full GCs. What now?

This is a "GC death spiral": the live set nearly fills the heap, each collection recovers almost nothing, and the application barely runs. Parallel GC would report GC overhead limit exceeded. Take a heap dump if possible (on an instance you've removed from the load balancer). The immediate relief is more heap or fewer requests. The cause is a leak, an unbounded in-memory result (like loading a whole table), or traffic beyond what the heap can hold. -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError doesn't help until the OOM is actually thrown, so a liveness check that depends on response time helps here.

Scenario: How do you diagnose high CPU on one Java process?

Start with GC: if GC threads are busy, it's memory pressure. Otherwise, use top -H -p <pid> to find hot threads, and match them to nid in jcmd <pid> Thread.print. Take several dumps. A better option is an async-profiler CPU flame graph or a JFR recording. Common causes: an infinite loop (historically HashMap under concurrent modification), regex backtracking, a spinning retry without backoff, and heavy serialization.

Scenario: Startup takes 45 seconds on Kubernetes and pods fail liveness probes. How do you approach this?

Use a startup probe rather than an excessive liveness delay. Then look at why it's slow: a CPU limit during startup is the most common reason, as class loading and JIT are CPU-heavy, so a higher startup CPU allowance helps. Check with -Xlog:class+load and Spring's ApplicationStartup or Actuator's startup endpoint. Options for reducing it: CDS or the AOT cache, lazy initialization where acceptable, fewer auto-configurations, or native image if the trade-offs fit.

What's in your standard production JVM flag set?
-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=70
-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m
-XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError -XX:HeapDumpPath=/dumps
-XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError
-Xlog:gc*,safepoint:file=/logs/gc.log:time,uptime:filecount=5,filesize=20m
-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary

Almost everything else stays at its default until a measurement justifies changing it. Size MaxMetaspaceSize from your own measurements; 256 MB is an example, not a recommendation.

What is CDS, and what's the difference between CDS, the AOT cache and native image?

CDS stores parsed class metadata in a mapped archive, so class loading is faster and memory can be shared. The AOT cache (Java 24 onward) builds on that, and also keeps classes loaded and linked, and from 25 method profiles too, while staying on a normal JVM with JIT and all Java dynamism. Native image compiles to a standalone binary, with no JVM, under a closed-world assumption. In short: CDS and AOT speed up the JVM, while native image replaces it.

What is the closed-world assumption in native image, and how does it affect Spring?

All code that can run must be known at build time, so classes can't be loaded at run time. Reflection, dynamic proxies, resources and serialization must be declared in metadata. Spring normally decides a lot at startup, such as evaluating @Conditional and creating proxies. Spring AOT moves that work to build time and generates source and hints. Consequences: the set of beans and profiles is fixed at build time, so @Profile can't change at run time as it does on the JVM, and libraries without metadata may need hints.

Why is a hand-written timing loop not a valid benchmark? What does JMH fix?

The first iterations run in the interpreter, then C1, then C2, so timings mix compilation stages. The JIT can hoist or delete work whose result is unused, fold constants, and inline differently than in production. GC can pause in the middle. JMH runs warm-up iterations, forks separate JVMs, consumes results via Blackhole, and reports error bars, so you compare steady-state performance.

After each deployment, the first minute of traffic has very high latency, then it settles. Why, and what can you do?

That is JVM warm-up: classes load lazily, code runs interpreted until the JIT compiles hot paths, and caches/connection pools are cold. Mitigations: a readiness probe that only passes after a warm-up routine has exercised the main endpoints; pre-initialised pools (Hikari minimumIdle); CDS or the AOT cache (newer JDKs can also store method profiles) to cut class loading and JIT time; gradual traffic shifting in the rollout; and enough CPU during startup, because CPU limits throttle the JIT compiler threads.

Can you catch OutOfMemoryError? Should you?

You can, because it is a Throwable, but you rarely should. It can be thrown in any allocation, possibly in another thread, leaving shared state half-updated, and the handler itself may fail to allocate. A narrow exception: catching it around one large, isolated allocation (e.g. a huge image buffer) to reject that request. In services, prefer -XX:+ExitOnOutOfMemoryError plus -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError so the orchestrator restarts a clean instance and you keep a dump for analysis.

Java Versions: 8 → 25 Language

What changed in each release that interviewers actually ask about, with code. Code for features up to 21 was compiled and run on Java 21. Features finalized after 21 are noted with the release and JEP (JDK Enhancement Proposal) that finalized them; they couldn't be compiled here.

The release model and LTS

Before Java 9, big releases came every few years and were held up by large features. Java 9 took over three years because of modules. So since 2017, the JDK has a feature release every six months, in March and September, containing whatever is ready. A feature that's not ready waits for the next train.

A Long-Term Support (LTS) release is one that vendors commit to patching for years. LTS is a vendor support decision, not a technical category; the language has no such concept. Other releases get updates for about six months, until the next one replaces them. After 17, the LTS cadence moved from three years to two.

ReleaseGA dateTypeHeadlineClass file

9Sep 2017FeatureModules, JShell, G1 default53
10Mar 2018Featurevar54
11Sep 2018LTSHttpClient, Java EE modules removed55

17Sep 2021LTSSealed classes, strong encapsulation61

Releases keep coming on the same schedule after 25. These are non-LTS, and the two-year cadence points to Java 29 as the next LTS. Check your vendor's roadmap for support dates.

JDK distributions

All major builds come from the OpenJDK source: Oracle JDK, Eclipse Temurin, Amazon Corretto, Azul Zulu, Red Hat build, Microsoft Build of OpenJDK. Differences are mostly licence, support, and a few features. For example, Oracle's builds don't include Shenandoah.

Framework baselines

Spring Boot 3 and 4 require Java 17 or later, and the javax.* to jakarta.* move came with Spring Boot 3. So a Spring Boot 2 on Java 8 service moves to at least 17 as part of any modern upgrade.

Preview, incubator and experimental status

New features can ship before they're finished, so real users can give feedback. The labels mean different things, and interviewers do ask:

StatusApplies toHow to enablePromise
PreviewLanguage and API features, fully implementedjavac --enable-preview --release 21 and java --enable-previewMay change or be withdrawn. Class files are tied to that exact release
IncubatorAPIs in jdk.incubator.* modules--add-modules jdk.incubator.vectorEarlier than preview. Can change a lot. The Vector API has been here for years
ExperimentalJVM features-XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptionsNot production-supported yet
Final (standard)Everything elseNothingPermanent, under Java's compatibility rules

A real case of withdrawal: String Templates were a preview in 21 and 22, then removed in 23 for a redesign. That's why you shouldn't build production code on preview features. Compiling a preview feature without the flag gives an error such as string templates are a preview feature and are disabled by default.

Java 8 (LTS)

Java 8 was the largest language change since generics, bringing functional programming into Java. Lambdas and streams get full treatment in their own section; here's what else was new. Default methods exist so that interfaces could evolve: Collection.stream() could be added without breaking every existing implementation.

// Default-method conflict: the class must resolve it
interface A { default String who() { return "A"; } }
interface B { default String who() { return "B"; } }
class C implements A, B {
    @Override public String who() { return A.super.who(); } // compile error without this override
}

// java.time: immutable and thread-safe, replacing Date and Calendar
LocalDate d = LocalDate.of(2026, 1, 31).plusMonths(1);   // 2026-02-28, adjusted to a valid day
Duration timeout = Duration.ofSeconds(30);               // machine time
Period age = Period.between(birth, LocalDate.now());     // calendar time
ZonedDateTime utc = ZonedDateTime.now(ZoneOffset.UTC);

// Map additions
counts.merge(word, 1, Integer::sum);
groups.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(value);
String v = map.getOrDefault("k", "none");

Also: Optional, CompletableFuture, StringJoiner, Base64, Metaspace replacing PermGen, repeatable annotations, parallel streams, and HashMap's tree buckets.

Java 9

Modules (JPMS) in depth

The Java Platform Module System (Project Jigsaw) added a level above packages. It solves three problems with the class path:

  • No real encapsulation: public meant visible to everyone, so the world came to depend on internals such as sun.misc.Unsafe.
  • No reliable configuration: a missing JAR was found only when a class failed at run time, and with duplicates, the first on the path won.
  • A monolithic JDK: everyone shipped all of it. The JDK is now split into about 70 modules, and jlink can build a smaller runtime.

A module is a set of packages with a descriptor, module-info.java, in the source root.

module com.acme.orders {
    requires java.sql;                      // I depend on this
    requires transitive com.acme.model;     // my users get this too
    requires static lombok;                 // needed at compile time only

    exports com.acme.orders.api;                     // public API for everyone
    exports com.acme.orders.spi to com.acme.plugin;  // qualified: only this module

    opens com.acme.orders.dto to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind; // deep reflection allowed

    uses com.acme.orders.spi.Pricing;                // I look this up with ServiceLoader
    provides com.acme.orders.spi.Pricing
        with com.acme.orders.internal.DefaultPricing; // I implement this
}
DirectiveMeaning
requiresRead another module. java.base is implicit. Missing modules fail at startup, not later
requires transitiveAnyone reading me also reads that module (implied readability). Use it when your API exposes its types
requires staticRequired at compile time, optional at run time
exportsPublic types of a package are accessible at compile time and run time. Non-exported packages are hidden even if the types are public
exports ... toOnly to named modules
opensReflection, including private members, at run time only. Frameworks need this
open moduleAll packages are open for reflection
uses, provides ... withDeclares a ServiceLoader consumer and provider, decoupling the two

Readability and accessibility: to use a type in another module, your module must read it (requires) and the other module must export the package. A two-module test, where com.acme.core exported only its api package, gave this at compile time:

error: package com.acme.core.impl is not visible
  (package com.acme.core.impl is declared in module com.acme.core, which does not export it)

Reflection fails as well. Running Class.forName("com.acme.core.impl.Impl").getDeclaredConstructor().newInstance() gave IllegalAccessException, since the package isn't exported.

javac -d out --module-source-path mods $(find mods -name '*.java')
java --module-path out -m com.acme.app/com.acme.app.Main
jdeps --print-module-deps app.jar        # which JDK modules does it use?
jlink --add-modules java.base,java.sql --output myjre   # custom runtime
java --list-modules

Migration: three kinds of module

KindHow it arisesBehaviour
NamedJAR with module-info.class on the module pathExports only what it declares
AutomaticPlain JAR on the module pathName from the Automatic-Module-Name manifest entry or the file name. Exports everything, reads everything
UnnamedEverything on the class pathReads all modules, exports all, but a named module can't require it

Split packages: two named modules can't contain the same package. That's a common migration blocker. The old class path allowed it silently.

Strong encapsulation of JDK internals: Java 9-15 allowed illegal reflective access with a warning. Java 16 denied it by default (JEP 396). Java 17 removed the --illegal-access switch (JEP 403). So code that reflects into the JDK now fails, even on the class path:

var f = String.class.getDeclaredField("value");
f.setAccessible(true);
// java.lang.reflect.InaccessibleObjectException: Unable to make field private final byte[]
//   java.lang.String.value accessible: module java.base does not "opens java.lang" to unnamed module

$ java --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED Refl    # the escape hatch, runs fine

This is why old versions of Lombok, Mockito, Hibernate, Spring and ByteBuddy break on a new JDK, and why upgrading those libraries is step one in any Java migration. Also useful: --add-exports and --add-reads.

Interview: "Does your Spring Boot app use modules?" Almost certainly not. Most applications still run on the class path, in the unnamed module, because frameworks rely on broad reflection and fat JARs don't fit. But JPMS still affects them, through strong encapsulation of the JDK. Libraries typically publish an Automatic-Module-Name.

Other Java 9 features

// JShell: a REPL for trying code
$ jshell
jshell> "abc".repeat(2)
$1 ==> "abcabc"

// Private interface methods: share code between default methods
interface Report {
    private String header() { return "Report: "; }
    default String title(String t) { return header() + t; }
    private static int helper() { return 1; }
}

// Immutable factory collections
List<Integer> l = List.of(1, 2);
Set<String> s = Set.of("a", "b");
Map<String, Integer> m = Map.of("a", 1, "b", 2);
Map<String, Integer> big = Map.ofEntries(Map.entry("a", 1));

// Stream additions
Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 1).takeWhile(i -> i < 3).toList();  // [1, 2]
Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 1).dropWhile(i -> i < 3).toList();  // [3, 4, 1]
Stream.iterate(1, i -> i < 20, i -> i * 3).toList();      // [1, 3, 9]
Stream.ofNullable(null).count();                          // 0

// Optional additions
Optional.empty().or(() -> Optional.of(2));
opt.ifPresentOrElse(System.out::println, () -> log.warn("none"));
opt.stream();

// try-with-resources on an effectively final variable
BufferedReader r = open();
try (r) { r.readLine(); }

The factory collections' behaviour is a favourite trap. They're immutable and reject nulls, unlike Arrays.asList, and output below is from a real run:

Set.of(1, 1);            // IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element: 1
Map.of("a", 1, "a", 2);  // IllegalArgumentException: duplicate key: a
List.of(1, null);        // NullPointerException
List.of(1).contains(null); // NullPointerException, even for a query
List.of(1).add(2);       // UnsupportedOperationException
Arrays.asList(1, null).contains(null); // true

Iteration order of Set.of and Map.of changes between JVM runs (a per-run salt) on purpose, to stop code depending on it. Other Java 9 changes: G1 is the default GC, compact strings, unified logging (-Xlog), ProcessHandle, VarHandle, Flow (Reactive Streams interfaces), multi-release JARs, and _ stopped being a legal identifier.

Java 10

Local variable type inference (var): the compiler infers the type of a local from its initializer. The variable is still statically typed. var isn't a keyword but a reserved type name, so int var = 2; still compiles, and only a class called var is forbidden.

var map = new HashMap<String, List<Integer>>();  // HashMap<String, List<Integer>>
var list = new ArrayList<>();                    // ArrayList<Object>: diamond has nothing to infer from

// Not allowed:
// var x;                 no initializer
// var n = null;          no type to infer
// var f = () -> 1;       lambda needs a target type
// var a = {1, 2};        array initializer needs a type
// fields, method parameters and return types can't use var

Also new: List.copyOf, Collectors.toUnmodifiableList, Optional.orElseThrow() without arguments, Application CDS, container awareness, and G1 parallel full GC.

List<Integer> src = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2));
List<Integer> copy = List.copyOf(src);                  // a real copy
List<Integer> view = Collections.unmodifiableList(src); // a read-only VIEW
src.add(3);
System.out.println(copy + " " + view);  // [1, 2] [1, 2, 3]
System.out.println(List.copyOf(copy) == copy);  // true: already immutable, so no copy made

Java 11 (LTS)

// String methods
"  ".isBlank();                 // true
"a\nb\r\nc".lines().count();    // 3
"ab".repeat(2);                 // abab
"  a ".strip();            // "a": strip is Unicode-aware, trim only removes chars up to U+0020

// Files
String text = Files.readString(Path.of("a.txt"));
Files.writeString(Path.of("b.txt"), text);

// Standard HTTP client: HTTP/2, sync and async
HttpClient client = HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build();
HttpRequest req = HttpRequest.newBuilder(URI.create("https://api.example.com/x")).GET().build();
HttpResponse<String> res = client.send(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString());
client.sendAsync(req, HttpResponse.BodyHandlers.ofString()).thenApply(HttpResponse::body);

// var in lambda parameters, so that annotations can be attached
BiFunction<Integer, Integer, Integer> add = (@NonNull var a, @NonNull var b) -> a + b;

// Small additions
Optional.empty().isEmpty();
Stream.of("a", "").filter(Predicate.not(String::isEmpty));
String[] arr = list.toArray(String[]::new);

// Run a single source file directly (JEP 330)
$ java Hello.java

Removals that break upgrades from 8 (JEP 320): java.xml.bind (JAXB), java.xml.ws, javax.annotation, java.activation, CORBA, and java.transaction were removed from the JDK. Add them back as explicit dependencies, or you'll see ClassNotFoundException: javax.xml.bind.JAXBContext. Also: ZGC (experimental), Epsilon GC, JFR open-sourced, TLS 1.3, and nest-based access control. Since 11 Oracle's JDK has no separate JRE, and JavaFX is separate too.

Java 12 to 16

Switch expressions (final in 14)

switch became an expression that yields a value. Arrow cases don't fall through. yield returns a value from a block. Over an enum, a switch expression must be exhaustive, and the compiler checks that.

String r = switch (day) {
    case MON, TUE -> "work";
    case SAT, SUN -> {
        String t = "weekend";
        yield t + "!";       // yield, not return
    }
};

Text blocks (final in 15)

A multi-line string starts with """ and a line break. Indentation common to all lines is removed (including the closing delimiter's line), trailing spaces are stripped, and line endings become \n. Two escapes are new: \ at line end joins lines, and \s keeps a space.

String json = """
      {
        "a": 1 \
      ok
      }\tx
      """;
System.out.print(json.replace(" ", "."));
// {
// .."a":.1.ok
// }<TAB>x

String b = """
        one
      two\s
    """;                   // the closing delimiter sets the left margin
System.out.print(b.replace(" ", "."));
// ....one
// ..two.

Records (final in 16)

A record is a transparent carrier for immutable data. The compiler generates a canonical constructor, accessors named x() rather than getX(), and equals, hashCode and toString.

record Point(int x, int y) {
    Point {                              // compact constructor: validates, then fields are assigned
        if (x < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("neg");
    }
    static int created;                  // static fields are allowed
    int sum() { return x + y; }          // methods are allowed
}
System.out.println(new Point(1, 2));                       // Point[x=1, y=2]
System.out.println(new Point(1, 2).equals(new Point(1, 2))); // true
  • Records are implicitly final, extend java.lang.Record, can implement interfaces, and can't have extra instance fields.
  • Immutability is shallow: a record R(List<String> l) still has a mutable list unless you copy it in the compact constructor with List.copyOf.
  • Good for DTOs, value objects, query projections and map keys. Not suitable as JPA entities, because those need a no-arg constructor, mutable state and proxies.
  • Serialization of a record always uses the canonical constructor, which makes it safer than ordinary class deserialization.

Pattern matching for instanceof (final in 16)

if (o instanceof String s && s.length() > 1) {   // no cast needed
    System.out.println(s.length());
}
if (!(o instanceof String s)) return;           // s is in scope after this line
s.isEmpty();

Everything else in 12-16

ReleaseInterview-relevant additions
12Collectors.teeing, String.indent, String.transform, Files.mismatch, compact number format, Shenandoah (experimental), default CDS archive
13Dynamic CDS archives, switch and text block previews
