String tee = Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).collect(Collectors.teeing(
    Collectors.counting(), Collectors.summingInt(i -> i), (n, s) -> s + "/" + n));  // 10/4

Stream.of(1, 2, 3).<Integer>mapMulti((x, sink) -> {
    if (x % 2 == 1) { sink.accept(x); sink.accept(x * 10); }
}).toList();                                   // [1, 10, 3, 30]

NumberFormat.getCompactNumberInstance(Locale.US, NumberFormat.Style.SHORT).format(1200); // 1K
"x".indent(2);                                 // "  x\n"

// Helpful NPE (compiled with -g, to get the variable name)
Point p = null;
p.x();   // Cannot invoke "Point.x()" because "p" is null

CallMutable result?Allows null elements?
collect(Collectors.toList())In practice yes (ArrayList), not guaranteedYes
stream.toList() (16)NoYes (printed [1, null])
collect(Collectors.toUnmodifiableList()) (10)NoNo: NullPointerException

Java 17 (LTS)

Sealed classes

A sealed type lists exactly who may extend it. That sits between final (nobody) and open inheritance (anybody). It models a closed set of variants, and lets the compiler know the set is complete, which is what makes an exhaustive switch without default possible.

sealed interface Shape permits Circle, Square, Tri {}
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {}     // records are implicitly final
record Square(double s) implements Shape {}
final class Tri implements Shape {}

static double area(Shape s) {
    return switch (s) {                         // Java 21 pattern switch; no default needed
        case Circle c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r();
        case Square q -> q.s() * q.s();
        case Tri t -> 0;
    };
}

Rules: each permitted subclass must be final, sealed or non-sealed (which reopens that branch). Permitted subclasses must be in the same package, or the same named module. If they're in the same source file, permits can be left out. The benefit over default: adding a new subtype produces a compile error at every switch, rather than a surprise at run time.

Other Java 17 features

  • Strong encapsulation of JDK internals (JEP 403): see the modules section.
  • RandomGenerator interface (JEP 356), and HexFormat: HexFormat.of().formatHex(new byte[]{10, -1}) gives 0aff.
  • Context-specific deserialization filters (JEP 415).
  • Deprecated for removal: Security Manager (JEP 411) and the Applet API. Removed: RMI Activation, and the experimental AOT and Graal JIT compilers.
  • strictfp behaviour became the only one (JEP 306).

Java 18 to 20

ReleaseFinal featuresPreview or incubator
18UTF-8 by default (JEP 400), jwebserver simple file server (JEP 408), @snippet in Javadoc (JEP 413), core reflection reimplemented with method handles (JEP 416), finalization deprecated for removal (JEP 421)Pattern switch, Vector API, FFM
19Linux/RISC-V portVirtual threads and record patterns previews, structured concurrency incubator
20None of note for interviewsScoped values incubator, further previews

The practical one is UTF-8. Before 18, new FileReader(f) and String.getBytes() used the OS default charset, which differed on Windows, causing encoding bugs. Now the default is UTF-8 everywhere unless you set -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT.

Java 21 (LTS)

Virtual threads (JEP 444)

A platform thread wraps an OS thread, so it's expensive: about 1 MB of stack and a context switch through the kernel. A thread-per-request server is capped at a few thousand. Virtual threads are scheduled by the JVM. A small pool of platform "carrier" threads (a ForkJoinPool) runs them. When a virtual thread blocks on I/O, the JVM unmounts it, saves its stack on the heap, and the carrier runs another. So blocking becomes cheap, and plain blocking code scales like reactive code.

try (var ex = Executors.newVirtualThreadPerTaskExecutor()) {
    for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) ex.submit(() -> callDownstream());
}   // close() waits for tasks

Thread vt = Thread.ofVirtual().name("v1").start(() -> {
    Thread t = Thread.currentThread();
    System.out.println(t.isVirtual() + " " + t.isDaemon() + " " + t.getName()); // true true v1
});
vt.join();                                 // needed: virtual threads are always daemon threads
  • Good for tasks that wait a lot, such as HTTP and database calls. No gain for CPU-bound work.
  • Don't pool them. They're cheap, so create one per task. Limit concurrency with a Semaphore, not a pool size.
  • Pinning: in 21, blocking inside synchronized pins the carrier thread, so it can't run others. ReentrantLock avoids that. JEP 491 in Java 24 removed this limitation for synchronized. Blocking inside native code still pins.
  • ThreadLocal: works, but millions of copies cost memory. Scoped values are the replacement.
  • Priorities and daemon status are fixed: getPriority() always returns 5, and isDaemon() always returns true.
  • Spring Boot: spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true (3.2 or later).

Concurrency details are in the concurrency section. An upstream limit still applies: 10,000 virtual threads hitting a pool of 20 database connections will wait on the pool.

Pattern matching for switch (JEP 441)

static String f(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case null -> "null!";                        // otherwise switch throws NPE
        case Integer i when i > 10 -> "big " + i;    // guard
        case Integer i -> "small " + i;
        case String s when s.isEmpty() -> "empty";
        case String s -> s.toUpperCase();
        case int[] a -> "ints " + a.length;
        default -> "other";
    };
}

Dominance: the compiler rejects a case that can never match. case CharSequence c before case String s is a compile error, as is an unguarded case Integer i before case Integer i when .... Order matters, unlike the old constant switch. A pattern switch must be exhaustive even as a statement.

Record patterns (JEP 440)

A record pattern takes a record apart into its components. Patterns can nest.

record Line(Point a, Point b) {}

if (obj instanceof Point(int x, int y)) { System.out.println(x + y); }

String s = switch (o) {
    case Line(Point(var x, var y), Point b) when x == 0 -> "from-x0 y=" + y + " " + b;
    default -> "other";
};

Sequenced collections (JEP 431)

Before 21, getting the last element was different for each type: list.get(list.size() - 1), deque.getLast(), sortedSet.last(), and nothing at all for LinkedHashSet. New interfaces SequencedCollection, SequencedSet and SequencedMap unify this.

var sl = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
var rev = sl.reversed();       // a live VIEW, not a copy
sl.add(4);
rev.addFirst(9);               // writes through to sl, at its end
System.out.println(sl + " " + rev + " " + sl.getFirst() + " " + sl.getLast());
// [1, 2, 3, 4, 9] [9, 4, 3, 2, 1] 1 9

var m = new LinkedHashMap<String, Integer>();
m.put("a", 1); m.put("b", 2);
m.putFirst("z", 0);
System.out.println(m + " " + m.firstEntry() + " " + m.reversed());
// {z=0, a=1, b=2} z=0 {b=2, a=1, z=0}

new TreeSet<>(List.of(1, 2)).addFirst(1);  // UnsupportedOperationException: position is set by sort order

Other additions in 21: generational ZGC (JEP 439), Math.clamp, StringBuilder.repeat, String.splitWithDelimiters. Previews: String Templates (later removed), unnamed classes, structured concurrency, scoped values.

Java 22 to 25

This code can't run on the Java 21 here. Each item names the release and JEP that finalized it.

Unnamed variables and patterns (final in 22, JEP 456)

_ marks something you must declare but won't use. It documents intent, and it can appear several times.

for (var _ : items) count++;
try { parse(s); } catch (NumberFormatException _) { return 0; }
map.forEach((key, _) -> System.out.println(key));
if (o instanceof Point(int x, _)) use(x);
switch (o) {
    case Line(Point _, Point _) -> "line";
    default -> "other";
}

Foreign Function & Memory API (final in 22, JEP 454)

Calls native code and manages off-heap memory safely, without JNI's hand-written C glue. It's the supported replacement for most sun.misc.Unsafe memory access. Arena controls lifetime, and a MemorySegment is bounds-checked.

Linker linker = Linker.nativeLinker();
MethodHandle strlen = linker.downcallHandle(
    linker.defaultLookup().find("strlen").orElseThrow(),
    FunctionDescriptor.of(ValueLayout.JAVA_LONG, ValueLayout.ADDRESS));

try (Arena arena = Arena.ofConfined()) {
    MemorySegment s = arena.allocateFrom("hello");
    long len = (long) strlen.invokeExact(s);      // 5
}                                                 // memory freed here

Restricted methods produce a warning unless you pass --enable-native-access=ALL-UNNAMED or name your module.

Other Java 22 and 23 changes

  • 22: launching multi-file source programs (JEP 458), so java Main.java compiles other source files as needed. G1 region pinning (JEP 423), which keeps GC running during JNI critical regions.
  • 23: Markdown in documentation comments with /// (JEP 467). Generational ZGC became the default ZGC mode (JEP 474). sun.misc.Unsafe memory-access methods deprecated for removal (JEP 471). String Templates dropped.

Stream gatherers (final in 24, JEP 485)

Collectors let you customize the end of a stream, but custom intermediate operations were impossible, so things like sliding windows needed awkward workarounds. Stream.gather adds an intermediate operation you can define, and java.util.stream.Gatherers provides common ones.

Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).gather(Gatherers.windowFixed(2)).toList();
// [[1, 2], [3, 4], [5]]

Stream.of(1, 2, 3, 4).gather(Gatherers.windowSliding(2)).toList();
// [[1, 2], [2, 3], [3, 4]]

Stream.of(1, 2, 3).gather(Gatherers.scan(() -> 0, Integer::sum)).toList();
// [1, 3, 6]

// Call a service with at most 8 in flight, on virtual threads, keeping stream order
ids.stream().gather(Gatherers.mapConcurrent(8, this::fetch)).toList();

Other Java 24 changes

  • Virtual threads no longer pin in synchronized (JEP 491).
  • Class-File API (JEP 484), a standard way to read and write class files, so frameworks needn't bundle a library that's tied to JDK versions.
  • Ahead-of-Time class loading and linking (JEP 483), the first AOT cache.
  • Security Manager permanently disabled (JEP 486). ZGC's non-generational mode removed (JEP 490).
  • Warnings on use of sun.misc.Unsafe memory access (JEP 498) and on JNI (JEP 472), as the platform moves to integrity by default.

Flexible constructor bodies (final in 25, JEP 513)

Previously super(...) had to be the first statement, so validation meant helper static methods. Now statements may come before it. That code can't read this, but it may assign fields of the class being constructed.

class Employee extends Person {
    private final String dept;

    Employee(String name, int age, String dept) {
        if (age < 18) throw new IllegalArgumentException("too young");  // fail before super()
        this.dept = dept;      // assigned before super(), so a parent constructor calling an
        super(name, age);      // overridden method can't see a null dept
    }
}

Module import declarations (final in 25, JEP 511)

import module java.base;   // every package exported by java.base

class Demo {
    List<Path> paths = new ArrayList<>();
}

It doesn't require your code to be in a module. Ambiguous simple names, such as Date if you import both java.base and java.sql, need an ordinary single-type import to settle them.

Compact source files and instance main (final in 25, JEP 512)

Beginners and small scripts no longer need a class, static or String[] args. A new java.lang.IO class gives simple console I/O, and a compact source file imports java.base automatically.

// Hello.java, run with: java Hello.java
void main() {
    IO.println("Hello");
}

Other Java 25 changes

  • Scoped values (JEP 506, final): immutable per-call context, a cheaper and safer replacement for many ThreadLocals.
  • Compact object headers (JEP 519): 8-byte headers as a product option with -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders.
  • Generational Shenandoah (JEP 521) as a product feature.
  • AOT command-line simplification (JEP 514) and method profiling (JEP 515).
  • Key Derivation Function API (JEP 510).
  • JFR additions: CPU-time profiling (experimental, JEP 509), cooperative sampling (JEP 518), method timing and tracing (JEP 520).
  • 32-bit x86 port removed (JEP 503).
  • Still preview or incubating in 25: structured concurrency, primitive types in patterns, stable values, PEM encodings, Vector API.

Migration: 8 to 17 to 25

  1. Upgrade tools first: Maven, Gradle, compiler plugin, Lombok, Mockito, ByteBuddy, ASM, Jackson and Spring. Old bytecode libraries fail on newer class file versions.
  2. Run jdeps --jdk-internals to find uses of JDK internals, and jdeprscan for deprecated APIs.
  3. Add removed modules back: JAXB and others, as Maven dependencies.
  4. Compile with --release N, which also checks API use, unlike -source and -target.
  5. Fix InaccessibleObjectException by upgrading libraries. Use --add-opens only as a temporary measure.
  6. Check JVM flags: removed GC flags stop the JVM from starting. -XX:+UseConcMarkSweepGC gives Unrecognized VM option, and old GC logging flags were replaced with -Xlog.
  7. Compare performance in load tests, because the default GC moved from Parallel to G1 after Java 8.
  8. Spring Boot 2 to 3: javax.* to jakarta.*, with OpenRewrite recipes to automate it.

Multi-Release JARs

Since Java 9 a library can ship one JAR that works on several Java versions. Classes in the normal root are the baseline; versions under META-INF/versions/N/ override them on Java N and later, and the manifest has Multi-Release: true. Libraries use this to offer a Java 8/11 baseline while using newer APIs (e.g. VarHandle, virtual-thread aware code) when available.

my-lib.jar
 ├─ com/acme/Util.class                    // compiled with --release 11
 └─ META-INF/
     ├─ MANIFEST.MF                         // Multi-Release: true
     └─ versions/21/com/acme/Util.class     // compiled with --release 21, same public API

The public API must be the same in every version; only the implementation differs. Tools like jdeps --multi-release 21 analyse a specific view.

Value-Based Classes and Project Valhalla

Classes such as Integer, Optional, LocalDate and List.of(…) results are documented as value-based: equality via equals only, no reliance on identity. Project Valhalla aims to let such classes become value classes without identity, so the JVM can flatten them in arrays and fields. Preparation already visible in the JDK:

  • The wrapper constructors (new Integer(5)) are deprecated for removal; use valueOf or autoboxing.
  • javac warns (and -XX:DiagnoseSyncOnValueBasedClasses can fail at run time) when you synchronized on a value-based instance.
  • Never use == or identity hash codes on these types.

Value classes are not part of a final Java release as of Java 25; describe them as the direction, not a feature you can use in production.

Interview Questions — Java Versions

What is LTS, and what is the current release cadence?

A feature release ships every six months. Some are chosen for long-term support by vendors: 8, 11, 17, 21 and 25, with a two-year gap since 17. An LTS isn't technically different: it's a promise of security and bug-fix updates for years. A non-LTS release gets updates only until the next one. Most companies deploy LTS releases, though some teams track the latest.

Is Java free? What changed with Oracle?

OpenJDK is open source under GPLv2 with the Classpath Exception. Oracle publishes free OpenJDK builds with short update windows, and its Oracle JDK has its own licence terms, which have changed over time. Most teams use a free vendor distribution with long updates, such as Temurin or Corretto. Say you'd check the current licence for a specific Oracle JDK build rather than quoting terms from memory.

What's the difference between a preview, incubator and experimental feature?

Preview features are complete language or API features you enable with --enable-preview at compile time and run time. Incubator APIs are earlier stage, delivered in jdk.incubator.* modules through --add-modules. Experimental features are JVM capabilities enabled with -XX:+UnlockExperimentalVMOptions. Any of them can change or vanish. String Templates, removed after two previews, is the proof.

What are the goals of JPMS? What does module-info.java contain?

Strong encapsulation, reliable configuration, and a modular JDK. The descriptor names the module and uses requires, exports, opens, uses and provides. The result is that dependencies are checked at startup and a non-exported package is hidden even from reflection, which a plain public can't achieve.

exports vs opens? Why does Jackson or Hibernate need opens?

exports gives access to public types at compile time and run time. opens gives run-time reflection on all members, including private ones, and no compile-time access. Frameworks set private fields reflectively, so their target packages must be opened. Without it, you get InaccessibleObjectException. A DTO package typically has opens com.acme.dto to com.fasterxml.jackson.databind. Hibernate needs the same for entity packages.

requires vs requires transitive vs requires static?

requires: you read it. requires transitive: your readers read it too, needed when your public API uses its types. requires static: needed at compile time, not at run time, such as annotation processors.

What are the unnamed module and automatic modules?

Everything on the class path sits in the unnamed module, which reads all modules and exports everything, but which named modules can't require. A plain JAR on the module path becomes an automatic module, with its name from Automatic-Module-Name or the file name. It reads everything and exports everything, and it's the bridge that lets libraries be migrated gradually.

What is a split package, and why is it a problem?

The same package in two modules. JPMS forbids this because each package must belong to one module for the loader to find classes directly. On the class path it worked silently. A typical case: javax.annotation in both a JDK module and a third-party JAR. Fixes: rename, merge the JARs, or remove the duplicate dependency.

What is jlink, and how does jdeps help?

jlink builds a custom runtime containing only the modules you need, which suits small container images. jdeps analyses JARs: --print-module-deps gives the list of modules for jlink, and --jdk-internals reports use of internal APIs.

Why can private methods exist in interfaces?

Since Java 8 interfaces can contain default methods, which may share logic. Before Java 9, the shared code had to be another default method, making it part of the public API. Private methods keep it internal. They can be instance or static, and they can't be default or abstract.

Output: what does each line do?
Set.of(1, 1);
List.of(1, null);
List.of(1).contains(null);
Arrays.asList(1, null).contains(null);

In order: IllegalArgumentException: duplicate element: 1; NullPointerException; NullPointerException; and it returns true. The List.of family refuses null even in contains, which can surprise you when replacing Arrays.asList.

What's the difference between Collections.unmodifiableList and List.copyOf?

unmodifiableList is a read-only view: changes to the original show through. List.copyOf makes an independent immutable copy, rejects nulls, and returns the same instance if the source is already an immutable list. A run confirmed this: after src.add(3), the copy printed [1, 2] and the view [1, 2, 3].

What is the type of var list = new ArrayList<>();? Is var dynamic typing?

It's ArrayList<Object>, because the diamond has nothing to infer from. So list.add("s"); list.add(1); compiles. var isn't dynamic: the type is fixed at compile time, and the bytecode is identical to the explicit form. It's a reserved type name, so a variable called var is legal.

trim() vs strip()?

trim() removes characters with code at or below U+0020. strip() (Java 11) uses Character.isWhitespace, so it handles Unicode whitespace. "  a ".trim() leaves the em space in place, while strip() returns "a". isBlank() uses the same Unicode definition.

Why did upgrading from 8 to 11 give ClassNotFoundException: javax.xml.bind.JAXBContext?

JEP 320 removed the Java EE and CORBA modules from the JDK in 11. JAXB must now be declared as a dependency: jakarta.xml.bind:jakarta.xml.bind-api and an implementation. The same applies to javax.annotation and JAX-WS.

Switch expression vs old switch statement? yield vs return?

A switch expression produces a value and must be exhaustive. Arrow labels have no fall-through and can list several constants. yield supplies the value from a block. You can't return out of a switch expression, because the enclosing expression needs a value. The old form still exists, and colon labels still fall through, even in an expression.

Output: what is printed, with dots for spaces?
String b = """
        one
      two\s
    """;
System.out.print(b.replace(" ", "."));
....one
..two.

The minimum indentation among the lines, including the closing delimiter's line, is 4. That amount is stripped. one keeps 4 and two keeps 2. \s becomes a space after trailing whitespace is stripped, so it survives. The line ending after the last content line is kept, because the closing delimiter is on its own line.

What does a record give you? What can't it do? Can it be a JPA entity?

It gives a canonical constructor, private final fields, accessors, and equals, hashCode and toString based on all components. It can't extend a class (it extends Record), can't declare extra instance fields, and is final. It can implement interfaces, and have static members and methods. A JPA entity needs a no-arg constructor, is mutable, and can be proxied by subclassing, so a record can't be one. A record works well as a DTO or a query projection, or as an @Embeddable in Hibernate 6.

Is a record immutable?

Only shallowly. The fields are final, but they can refer to mutable objects. Fix it in the compact constructor:

record Team(List<String> names) {
    Team { names = List.copyOf(names); }
}

In a compact constructor, assigning to the parameter name changes what's stored in the field.

Why use sealed classes instead of an enum, or an open class with default?

An enum has a fixed set of instances, each with the same shape. A sealed hierarchy has a fixed set of types, and each can carry different data. Compared with an open hierarchy, the compiler can check that a switch is exhaustive, so adding a subtype creates compile errors exactly where handling is needed. Common use: a Result type with Success and Failure, or domain events.

Output: what does f return for each input?
static String f(Object o) {
    return switch (o) {
        case null -> "null!";
        case Integer i when i > 10 -> "big " + i;
        case Integer i -> "small " + i;
        case String s when s.isEmpty() -> "empty";
        case String s -> s.toUpperCase();
        case int[] a -> "ints " + a.length;
        default -> "other";
    };
}
f(null); f(5); f(50); f(""); f("q"); f(new int[2]); f(1.0);

The run printed null!, small 5, big 50, empty, Q, ints 2, other. Cases are tested from the top, and a guard's failure moves on to the next case. Without case null, the switch throws NullPointerException. Swapping the two Integer cases is a compile error, because the unguarded one dominates.

What are the differences between toList(), Collectors.toList() and toUnmodifiableList()?

See the table above. Stream.toList() is unmodifiable and allows nulls. Collectors.toList() gives a list that's mutable in practice, with no specification guarantee. toUnmodifiableList() is unmodifiable and throws on null. Replacing collect(Collectors.toList()) with toList() is usually fine, but it breaks callers that then modify the list.

What are helpful NullPointerExceptions?

Since JEP 358 (14, default in 15), the JVM analyses the bytecode at the failure site and says exactly what was null, for example Cannot invoke "Point.x()" because "p" is null. It's useful for chained calls like a.b().c().d(). Local variable names appear only if compiled with -g. Otherwise you get "<local13>", which is what plain javac gave in this run.

What changed in Java 18 with charsets, and what can break?

JEP 400 made UTF-8 the default for standard APIs regardless of the OS locale. Code that relied on the platform default to read legacy files, such as Windows-1252 on Windows, can now misread them. Fix: pass the charset explicitly, or use -Dfile.encoding=COMPAT as a stop-gap. Passing a charset explicitly was always the better habit.

Platform thread vs virtual thread? When shouldn't you use virtual threads?

A platform thread maps one-to-one to an OS thread, and is limited by memory and scheduling overhead. A virtual thread is managed by the JVM, costs little, and frees its carrier when it blocks. Don't use them for CPU-bound work, where the number of cores is the limit, nor to pool them, nor where code holds a lock across a blocking call on Java 21 to 23 (pinning). Heavy ThreadLocal use is also a concern. Fairness and throughput depend on downstream limits, so keep semaphores and connection pools.

Output: what does this print?
var sl = new ArrayList<>(List.of(1, 2, 3));
var rev = sl.reversed();
sl.add(4);
rev.addFirst(9);
System.out.println(sl + " " + rev);

It prints [1, 2, 3, 4, 9] [9, 4, 3, 2, 1]. reversed() is a live view: sl.add(4) appears in it, and addFirst on the reverse view adds at the end of the original.

Which collection types implement SequencedCollection? Do HashSet or HashMap?

No, because they've no defined order. List, Deque, LinkedHashSet, SortedSet, LinkedHashMap and SortedMap do. Position-based methods like addFirst throw UnsupportedOperationException on a sorted set, since position comes from the comparator. Adding to the interface hierarchy did produce rare conflicts: a class implementing both List and Deque with differing return types needed a fix.

What are stream gatherers, and how do they differ from collectors?

A collector is a terminal step producing one result. A gatherer (final in Java 24) is an intermediate step: it transforms a stream into a stream, can keep state, can short-circuit, and can emit any number of elements per input. Before that, a fixed window needed a workaround. Gatherers.windowFixed, windowSliding, fold, scan and mapConcurrent are built in, and you can write your own through Gatherer.of or Gatherer.ofSequential.

What does the FFM API replace?

JNI, for calling native libraries, and sun.misc.Unsafe or direct ByteBuffer for off-heap memory. There's no C glue code, memory lifetimes are explicit through Arena, and access is bounds-checked and checked for use-after-close. It was finalized in Java 22. jextract can generate Java bindings from a C header.

What can code before super() do in Java 25, and what can't it do?

With JEP 513, the part before the constructor call (the prologue) can run ordinary statements, validate arguments, and assign fields of the class being constructed. It can't use this, call instance methods, or read instance fields. A useful effect: fields can be set before a superclass constructor calls an overridden method, which removes a long-standing bug source.

What are compact object headers, and should you enable them?

They merge the mark word and class pointer so that headers take 8 bytes rather than 12 on 64-bit HotSpot. JEP 519 made it a product option in 25, off by default. For services with many small objects, this reduces heap use, sometimes also CPU, because more objects fit in cache and GC has less to do. Test on your workload using -XX:+UseCompactObjectHeaders.

Which GC changes happened across versions?
  • 8: Parallel default, Metaspace replaces PermGen.
  • 9: G1 default, CMS deprecated, unified logging.
  • 10: G1 parallel full GC.
  • 11: ZGC and Epsilon experimental.
  • 12: Shenandoah experimental.
  • 14: CMS removed.
  • 15: ZGC and Shenandoah production.
  • 21: generational ZGC.
  • 23: generational is the ZGC default.
  • 24: non-generational ZGC removed.
  • 25: generational Shenandoah a product feature.
Scenario: Your team's Spring Boot 2.7 on Java 8 service must move to a supported stack. How do you plan it?
  1. Audit: dependency report, jdeps --jdk-internals, custom JVM flags.
  2. Move to the last Boot 2.7 with Java 17 first, keeping javax, so one thing changes at a time. Get tests green.
  3. Upgrade to Boot 3.x, migrating javax to jakarta with OpenRewrite, plus Spring Security 6 config and Hibernate 6.
  4. Move on to a current Boot release and an LTS JDK, reading each release's migration guide.
  5. Run load tests to compare GC behaviour and memory. Roll out with a canary.
  6. Only then adopt new features such as records, virtual threads and pattern switch.
Scenario: A library works on 11 but fails on 17 with InaccessibleObjectException. What are your options?

The library reflects into JDK internals, which was allowed until strong encapsulation arrived. First upgrade the library, as that's nearly always fixed. If not possible, add a specific --add-opens java.base/java.lang=ALL-UNNAMED, named to the exact package in the error, and record a ticket to remove it. An executable JAR can also declare Add-Opens in its manifest. Don't try to go back to --illegal-access, which is gone.

Your switch over a sealed interface is exhaustive with no default. Another team adds a new permitted subtype and recompiles only their module. What happens at run time?

Your already-compiled switch meets a type it did not know about, and the compiler-generated default throws MatchException (since Java 21 this also applies to exhaustive enum switch expressions, which previously threw IncompatibleClassChangeError). When you recompile your code, the compiler instead reports the switch as not exhaustive. That is the main benefit of sealed types: adding a case becomes a compile error wherever it is not handled, instead of silently falling into a default.

Why should a team on Java 17 move to Java 21 or 25? Give the short pitch.
  • Virtual threads: high-concurrency blocking code without reactive rewrites (and from Java 24, no pinning on synchronized).
  • Language: record patterns, pattern matching in switch, sequenced collections, unnamed variables; less boilerplate.
  • Runtime: generational ZGC, better G1, faster startup via the AOT cache, compact object headers (25) for lower memory.
  • Support: 21 and 25 are LTS releases, and frameworks (Spring Boot 3.x/4.x) target and test on them.

Risks are mainly in libraries using internals (bytecode tools, Lombok, mocking agents), so upgrade those first and run the full test suite with the new JDK in CI before switching production.

SOLID & Design Patterns Design

The principles behind maintainable object-oriented code, all 23 Gang of Four patterns with Java code and real JDK and Spring examples, the enterprise patterns used in every Spring project, UML basics, and low-level design questions worked through.

Interview: Patterns are a shared vocabulary for known solutions, not goals. Don't list them from memory. For each one be ready to say what problem it solves, what it costs, and where you've seen it. "I'd use Strategy here because the rule varies by country and we add countries often" beats any definition.

SOLID principles

Robert C. Martin grouped five principles for code that's easy to change. They all aim at the same thing: when a requirement changes, as little existing code as possible should have to change with it.

S: Single Responsibility Principle

A class should have one reason to change, meaning it should answer to one kind of stakeholder. It doesn't mean "one method". If accountants and DBAs can both force changes in the same class, those concerns are tangled, and a change for one can break the other.

// Bad: business rule, persistence and formatting change for different reasons
class Invoice {
    BigDecimal total() { /* tax rules */ }
    void saveToDatabase() { /* SQL */ }
    String toPdf() { /* layout */ }
}

// Good: each class has one reason to change
class Invoice { BigDecimal total() { /* tax rules */ } }
interface InvoiceRepository { void save(Invoice invoice); }
class InvoicePdfRenderer { byte[] render(Invoice invoice) { /* layout */ } }

Probe: a Spring UserService with 3,000 lines that handles registration, password reset, reports and billing is the usual real-world violation. Splitting by use case fixes it.

O: Open/Closed Principle

Code should be open for extension but closed for modification: you add behaviour with new code, without editing tested code. In practice, you find the part that varies and put it behind an abstraction.

// Bad: every new customer type edits this method
class Discounts {
    BigDecimal apply(String type, BigDecimal price) {
        return switch (type) {
            case "GOLD" -> price.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.8"));
            case "SILVER" -> price.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.9"));
            default -> price;
        };
    }
}

// Good: a new type is a new class. Nothing existing changes
interface DiscountPolicy {
    boolean supports(String type);
    BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal price);
}
@Component class GoldDiscount implements DiscountPolicy {
    public boolean supports(String t) { return "GOLD".equals(t); }
    public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal p) { return p.multiply(new BigDecimal("0.8")); }
}
@Service class Discounts {
    private final List<DiscountPolicy> policies;     // Spring injects all implementations
    Discounts(List<DiscountPolicy> policies) { this.policies = policies; }
    BigDecimal apply(String type, BigDecimal price) {
        return policies.stream().filter(p -> p.supports(type)).findFirst()
                .map(p -> p.apply(price)).orElse(price);
    }
}

Don't overdo it: a two-branch if that never changes doesn't need an interface. Add the abstraction when the variation actually appears. With a closed set of variants, a sealed type and an exhaustive switch can be better: the compiler then finds every place to update.

L: Liskov Substitution Principle

A subtype must be usable anywhere its base type is expected, without surprising the caller. Formally, a subclass can't strengthen preconditions, weaken postconditions, or break invariants. It concerns behaviour, not just compiling.

// Bad: the classic. A Square is a Rectangle in geometry, but not in behaviour
class Rectangle {
    protected int w, h;
    void setWidth(int w) { this.w = w; }
    void setHeight(int h) { this.h = h; }
    int area() { return w * h; }
}
class Square extends Rectangle {
    @Override void setWidth(int w) { this.w = w; this.h = w; }
    @Override void setHeight(int h) { this.w = h; this.h = h; }
}
void resize(Rectangle r) {
    r.setWidth(5); r.setHeight(4);
    assert r.area() == 20;      // fails for Square: area is 16
}

// Good: no mutable base that promises independent sides
sealed interface Shape permits Rect, Sq { int area(); }
record Rect(int w, int h) implements Shape { public int area() { return w * h; } }
record Sq(int side) implements Shape { public int area() { return side * side; } }

Warning signs: an override that throws UnsupportedOperationException, instanceof checks on subtypes, and empty overrides. The JDK itself bends this rule: List.of(1).add(2) throws, because List marks mutation as "optional".

I: Interface Segregation Principle

Clients shouldn't depend on methods they don't use. A fat interface forces implementers to write stubs, and it recompiles and retests clients for changes that don't concern them.

// Bad
interface Machine { void print(Doc d); void scan(Doc d); void fax(Doc d); }
class BasicPrinter implements Machine {
    public void print(Doc d) { /* ok */ }
    public void scan(Doc d) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }  // also an LSP violation
    public void fax(Doc d) { throw new UnsupportedOperationException(); }
}

// Good
interface Printer { void print(Doc d); }
interface Scanner { void scan(Doc d); }
class BasicPrinter implements Printer { public void print(Doc d) { /* ok */ } }
class OfficeMachine implements Printer, Scanner { /* both */ }

Spring Data shows this well: Repository, CrudRepository, ListCrudRepository, PagingAndSortingRepository are separate, so you can expose only what's needed. Note that JpaRepository exposes everything, including deleteAll.

D: Dependency Inversion Principle

High-level policy shouldn't depend on low-level detail. Both depend on an abstraction, and the abstraction belongs with the high-level code. Dependency Inversion is the principle. Dependency Injection is one technique to achieve it. Inversion of Control is the wider idea that a framework calls your code. These three are often confused.

// Bad: business logic welded to a vendor
class OrderService {
    private final StripeClient stripe = new StripeClient("key");
    void pay(Order o) { stripe.charge(o.total()); }
}

// Good: business logic owns the interface. Infrastructure implements it
interface PaymentGateway { void charge(Money amount); }

@Service class OrderService {
    private final PaymentGateway gateway;
    OrderService(PaymentGateway gateway) { this.gateway = gateway; } // testable with a mock
    void pay(Order o) { gateway.charge(o.total()); }
}
@Component class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { /* adapts StripeClient */ }

DRY, KISS, YAGNI and friends

PrincipleMeaningMisuse to avoid
DRY (Don't Repeat Yourself)Each piece of knowledge has one authoritative placeMerging code that merely looks alike. If two things change for different reasons, shared code couples them. Duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction
KISS (Keep It Simple)Prefer the simplest thing that worksUsing simplicity as an excuse for ignoring real requirements such as concurrency
YAGNI (You Aren't Gonna Need It)Don't build for imagined futuresSkipping cheap good structure, or anything that's costly to retrofit, such as security
Composition over inheritanceBuild behaviour by holding objects rather than extending classesBanning inheritance outright, even for true is-a relationships
Law of DemeterTalk only to direct collaborators: no a.getB().getC().doIt()Applying it to fluent APIs and streams, which return the same kind of thing
High cohesion, low couplingRelated things together; few dependencies between modulesNone. This is the goal all the others serve

UML class relations

A class diagram is the quickest way to sketch a design on a whiteboard. Know the six relations and the difference between aggregation and composition.

RelationMeaningIn Java
DependencyUses temporarilyParameter or local variable
AssociationKnows about, long termA field
AggregationWhole-part, shared lifetime not impliedA field holding an object passed in
CompositionWhole-part, whole owns the part's lifetimeA field created inside. In JPA, orphanRemoval = true
InheritanceIs-aextends
RealizationFulfils a contractimplements

Gang of Four: overview

The 1994 book by Gamma, Helm, Johnson and Vlissides catalogued 23 patterns in three groups. Modern Java made some lighter: a lambda can replace a one-method Strategy or Command class, and enums and sealed types shrink State and Visitor.

GroupConcernPatterns
Creational (5)How objects get createdSingleton, Factory Method, Abstract Factory, Builder, Prototype
Structural (7)How objects are composedAdapter, Bridge, Composite, Decorator, Facade, Flyweight, Proxy
Behavioral (11)How objects interactChain of Responsibility, Command, Interpreter, Iterator, Mediator, Memento, Observer, State, Strategy, Template Method, Visitor

Creational patterns

Singleton

Problem: exactly one instance must exist and be globally reachable, such as a registry.

// 1. Eager: simple and thread-safe, created when the class initializes
public final class Eager {
    private static final Eager INSTANCE = new Eager();
    private Eager() {}
    public static Eager get() { return INSTANCE; }
}

// 2. Holder idiom: lazy and thread-safe, relying on class initialization
public final class Lazy {
    private Lazy() {}
    private static class Holder { static final Lazy INSTANCE = new Lazy(); }
    public static Lazy get() { return Holder.INSTANCE; }
}

// 3. Enum: safe against reflection and serialization
public enum Registry { INSTANCE; public void register(String s) { } }

Double-checked locking is shown in Core Java. volatile is essential there: instance = new Config() is several steps, and without it another thread could see a non-null reference to an object whose constructor hasn't finished.

Ways to break it: reflection calling a private constructor (a test confirmed this returns a second instance); deserialization creating a new object unless readResolve returns the instance; and two class loaders, each with its own copy. Enums block the first two: reflection fails with Cannot reflectively create enum objects.

In the wild: Runtime.getRuntime(). Spring's default bean scope is also called singleton, but it means one per ApplicationContext, not one per JVM.

Pitfalls: global state hides dependencies and makes tests depend on order. In Spring code, write a normal class and let the container manage it. The bean must be stateless or thread-safe, as all requests share it.

Factory Method

Problem: calling code needs an object, but shouldn't name the concrete class. In the GoF form, a superclass defines the workflow, and subclasses decide which product to create.

interface Notification { void send(String msg); }
class Email implements Notification { public void send(String m) { /* SMTP */ } }
class Sms implements Notification { public void send(String m) { /* gateway */ } }

abstract class Notifier {
    protected abstract Notification create();         // the factory method
    public void alert(String msg) {
        Notification n = create();
        n.send("[ALERT] " + msg);
    }
}
class EmailNotifier extends Notifier {
    @Override protected Notification create() { return new Email(); }
}

// Commonly used in practice: a "simple factory", which isn't a GoF pattern
class Notifications {
    static Notification of(String kind) {
        return switch (kind) {
            case "email" -> new Email();
            case "sms" -> new Sms();
            default -> throw new IllegalArgumentException(kind);
        };
    }
}

In the wild: Calendar.getInstance(), NumberFormat.getInstance(), Collection.iterator() (each collection returns its own iterator), Charset.forName. Spring: FactoryBean, @Bean methods.

Pitfalls: a switch-based factory needs editing for each new type. Also, naming: static factory methods such as List.of are a useful idiom from Effective Java, not the GoF pattern.

Abstract Factory

Problem: create families of related objects that must go together, without naming concrete classes. Factory Method creates one product; Abstract Factory creates a matching set.

interface Button { String render(); }
interface Dialog { String render(); }
interface UiFactory { Button button(); Dialog dialog(); }

class DarkFactory implements UiFactory {
    public Button button() { return () -> "dark button"; }
    public Dialog dialog() { return () -> "dark dialog"; }
}
class LightFactory implements UiFactory {
    public Button button() { return () -> "light button"; }
    public Dialog dialog() { return () -> "light dialog"; }
}
class Screen {
    private final Button b; private final Dialog d;
    Screen(UiFactory f) { b = f.button(); d = f.dialog(); }  // never mixes themes
}

In the wild: DocumentBuilderFactory, and a JDBC Connection, which creates statements that belong to one vendor's driver. Spring's BeanFactory is often cited as a generic version.

Pitfalls: adding a new product type (a Menu) changes every factory. Don't use it if there's just one family.

Builder

Problem: an object has many optional parameters. Telescoping constructors are unreadable, and setters leave an object half built and mutable.

public final class HttpCall {
    private final String url; private final String method;
    private final int timeoutMs; private final Map<String, String> headers;

    private HttpCall(Builder b) {
        url = b.url; method = b.method; timeoutMs = b.timeoutMs;
        headers = Map.copyOf(b.headers);
    }
    public static Builder builder(String url) { return new Builder(url); }

    public static final class Builder {
        private final String url;                 // required goes through the constructor
        private String method = "GET";            // defaults for the optional ones
        private int timeoutMs = 3000;
        private final Map<String, String> headers = new HashMap<>();

        private Builder(String url) { this.url = Objects.requireNonNull(url); }
        public Builder method(String m) { method = m; return this; }
        public Builder timeoutMs(int t) { timeoutMs = t; return this; }
        public Builder header(String k, String v) { headers.put(k, v); return this; }
        public HttpCall build() {
            if (timeoutMs <= 0) throw new IllegalStateException("timeout");
            return new HttpCall(this);            // validate once, before the object exists
        }
    }
}
HttpCall c = HttpCall.builder("https://x").method("POST").timeoutMs(500).build();

In the wild: HttpRequest.newBuilder(), Stream.builder(), Locale.Builder, Lombok's @Builder, Spring's UriComponentsBuilder and MockMvcRequestBuilders.

Pitfalls: required fields can be forgotten and only fail at run time, so take them as builder constructor arguments. Lombok's @Builder ignores field initializers unless you add @Builder.Default. For a few fields, a record or constructor is enough.

Prototype

Problem: create new objects by copying an existing configured instance, for instance when construction is expensive, or the concrete type is unknown at the point of copying.

class Template implements Cloneable {
    String name; List<String> tags = new ArrayList<>();

    @Override public Template clone() {
        try {
            Template copy = (Template) super.clone();  // shallow: tags list is shared
            copy.tags = new ArrayList<>(tags);         // deep copy of mutable state
            return copy;
        } catch (CloneNotSupportedException e) { throw new AssertionError(e); }
    }
}

// Usually better: a copy constructor
class Template2 {
    final String name; final List<String> tags;
    Template2(Template2 other) { name = other.name; tags = new ArrayList<>(other.tags); }
}

In the wild: Object.clone(), ArrayList.clone(). Spring's prototype scope shares the name, but it creates a new bean each time rather than copying one.

Pitfalls: clone() is shallow by default, doesn't call constructors, and Cloneable is a badly designed marker interface. Prefer copy constructors, or records with wither methods. A prototype-scoped bean injected into a singleton is created only once, unless you use ObjectProvider or @Lookup.

Structural patterns

Adapter

Problem: an existing class has the wrong interface, and you can't or shouldn't change it. Common at the edge of your system, wrapping third-party SDKs.

// Ours
interface PaymentGateway { void charge(long cents, String currency); }

// Third-party, can't change
class LegacyBank { void makePayment(double amount, String iso) { } }

class LegacyBankAdapter implements PaymentGateway {
    private final LegacyBank bank;
    LegacyBankAdapter(LegacyBank bank) { this.bank = bank; }
    @Override public void charge(long cents, String currency) {
        bank.makePayment(cents / 100.0, currency);    // translate the call and the units
    }
}

In the wild: Arrays.asList (array as a List), InputStreamReader (bytes to chars), and Spring MVC's HandlerAdapter, which lets DispatcherServlet call any kind of handler.

Pitfalls: don't leak the third-party types through the adapter's interface, or you haven't isolated anything.

Bridge

Problem: something varies along two independent dimensions. Inheritance would need a class per combination (EmailUrgentAlert, SmsUrgentAlert...). Bridge splits them into two hierarchies, connected by composition.

interface Channel { void deliver(String text); }                  // implementation hierarchy
class EmailChannel implements Channel { public void deliver(String t) { } }
class SmsChannel implements Channel { public void deliver(String t) { } }

abstract class Alert {                                            // abstraction hierarchy
    protected final Channel channel;                              // the bridge
    Alert(Channel channel) { this.channel = channel; }
    abstract void raise(String msg);
}
class UrgentAlert extends Alert {
    UrgentAlert(Channel c) { super(c); }
    @Override void raise(String msg) { channel.deliver("URGENT: " + msg); }
}
new UrgentAlert(new SmsChannel()).raise("disk full");             // 2 + 2 classes, 4 combinations

In the wild: JDBC (your code uses the abstraction, and each driver is an implementation) and SLF4J (an API with pluggable providers).

Pitfalls: don't apply it when only one dimension actually varies. Bridge is planned up front to let both sides vary; Adapter is fitted afterwards to make two existing things work together.

Composite

Problem: a tree of objects, where clients should treat a single item and a group the same way.

interface Node { long size(); }
record FileNode(long bytes) implements Node {
    public long size() { return bytes; }
}
class Dir implements Node {
    private final List<Node> children = new ArrayList<>();
    Dir add(Node n) { children.add(n); return this; }
    public long size() { return children.stream().mapToLong(Node::size).sum(); }
}
new Dir().add(new FileNode(10)).add(new Dir().add(new FileNode(5))).size(); // 15

In the wild: java.awt.Container, Spring's CompositeCacheManager and HandlerMethodArgumentResolverComposite.

Pitfalls: recursion can overflow on very deep or cyclic trees. Putting add on the shared interface forces leaves to throw.

Decorator

Problem: add behaviour to an object at run time, and combine behaviours freely, without a subclass per combination. A decorator implements the same interface as what it wraps, and delegates.

interface DataSource { String read(); }
class FileSource implements DataSource { public String read() { return "data"; } }

abstract class SourceDecorator implements DataSource {
    protected final DataSource inner;
    SourceDecorator(DataSource inner) { this.inner = inner; }
}
class Upper extends SourceDecorator {
    Upper(DataSource d) { super(d); }
    public String read() { return inner.read().toUpperCase(); }
}
class Bracket extends SourceDecorator {
    Bracket(DataSource d) { super(d); }
    public String read() { return "[" + inner.read() + "]"; }
}
System.out.println(new Upper(new Bracket(new FileSource())).read());  // [DATA]
System.out.println(new Bracket(new Upper(new FileSource())).read());  // [DATA]

In the wild: Java I/O is the textbook case: new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new GZIPInputStream(in))). Also Collections.unmodifiableList, synchronizedList, HttpServletRequestWrapper.

Pitfalls: order matters when decorators interact, such as caching and retry. An equals or identity check against the wrapped object fails. Deep stacks are hard to debug.

Facade

Problem: a subsystem has many moving parts, and most callers want one simple operation.

@Service class CheckoutFacade {
    private final InventoryService inventory;
    private final PaymentService payments;
    private final ShippingService shipping;
    // constructor omitted

    @Transactional
    public OrderId checkout(Cart cart, Card card) {     // one call for the controller
        inventory.reserve(cart);
        payments.charge(card, cart.total());
        return shipping.schedule(cart);
    }
}

In the wild: JdbcTemplate hides connections, statements and exceptions. SLF4J is literally named a "Simple Logging Facade".

Pitfalls: a facade can grow into a god class with all the logic in it. It should coordinate, not contain rules. It simplifies access, and doesn't stop clients from using the subsystem directly, unlike a Mediator.

Flyweight

Problem: huge numbers of similar objects use too much memory. Share the unchanging (intrinsic) state, and pass the varying (extrinsic) state in from outside.

record GlyphStyle(String font, int size) {}                 // intrinsic: shared
class Styles {
    private static final Map<GlyphStyle, GlyphStyle> CACHE = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    static GlyphStyle of(String f, int s) {
        return CACHE.computeIfAbsent(new GlyphStyle(f, s), k -> k);
    }
}
record Glyph(char c, int x, int y, GlyphStyle style) {}     // extrinsic: per character

Integer a = 127, b = 127, c = 128, d = 128;
System.out.println(a == b);     // true: Integer.valueOf cache of -128 to 127
System.out.println(c == d);     // false

In the wild: Integer.valueOf, Boolean.valueOf, the string pool, enum constants.

Pitfalls: shared objects must be immutable. Comparing boxed values with == happens to work inside the cache range and fails outside. An unbounded cache is a memory leak.

Proxy

Problem: control access to an object through a stand-in with the same interface: add lazy loading, security, caching, transactions or remote access.

interface Greeter { String hi(); }
class RealGreeter implements Greeter { public String hi() { return "hi"; } }

// Hand-written proxies repeat; a JDK dynamic proxy is generated at run time
Greeter target = new RealGreeter();
Greeter proxy = (Greeter) Proxy.newProxyInstance(
    Greeter.class.getClassLoader(),
    new Class<?>[] { Greeter.class },
    (p, method, args) -> {
        System.out.println("before " + method.getName());
        Object r = method.invoke(target, args);
        System.out.println("after");
        return r;
    });
System.out.println(proxy.hi());
// before hi
// after
// hi

In the wild: Spring AOP behind @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async; Hibernate lazy-loading proxies; Feign clients; Spring Data repositories, which have no hand-written implementation.

JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB (subclass)
RequiresAn interfaceA non-final class
ResultImplements the interfaceGenerated subclass
Can't interceptNon-interface methodsfinal and private methods
Spring Boot defaultOnly if configuredYes, proxyTargetClass=true

Pitfalls: the proxy wraps the object from outside, so self-invocation bypasses it: this.save() inside the same bean doesn't start the transaction. A Hibernate proxy touched outside a session throws LazyInitializationException.

Proxy vs Decorator: their structure is the same. A proxy controls access and usually manages the target itself. A decorator adds features and gets its target from the caller, and decorators are designed for stacking.

Behavioral patterns

Chain of Responsibility

Problem: a request passes through a series of handlers. Each one may handle it, change it, stop it or pass it on, and the sender doesn't know who handles it.

abstract class Handler {
    private Handler next;
    Handler then(Handler next) { this.next = next; return next; }
    final void handle(Request r) {
        if (process(r) && next != null) next.handle(r);
    }
    protected abstract boolean process(Request r);    // false stops the chain
}
class Auth extends Handler {
    protected boolean process(Request r) { return r.token() != null; }
}
class RateLimit extends Handler {
    protected boolean process(Request r) { return true; }
}
Handler chain = new Auth();
chain.then(new RateLimit());
chain.handle(request);

In the wild: servlet FilterChain, Spring Security's filter chain, Spring MVC's HandlerInterceptor, and java.util.logging parent handlers.

Pitfalls: order is critical (authentication before authorization). A request may fall off the end unhandled. Forgetting chain.doFilter() in a filter silently swallows the request.

Command

Problem: turn a request into an object, so it can be queued, logged, retried or undone. The caller is separated from the code that does the work.

interface Command { void execute(); void undo(); }

class AddText implements Command {
    private final StringBuilder doc; private final String text;
    AddText(StringBuilder doc, String text) { this.doc = doc; this.text = text; }
    public void execute() { doc.append(text); }
    public void undo() { doc.setLength(doc.length() - text.length()); }
}
class Editor {
    private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c) { c.execute(); history.push(c); }
    void undo() { if (!history.isEmpty()) history.pop().undo(); }
}

In the wild: Runnable and Callable submitted to an ExecutorService; messages on a Kafka topic in a CQRS system; Spring Batch steps.

Pitfalls: undo requires the state to restore, so it may need Memento. If there's no undo or queueing, a plain method call or lambda will do.

Interpreter

Problem: evaluate sentences of a small language by representing its grammar as a tree of classes.

interface Expr { int eval(Map<String, Integer> vars); }
record Num(int v) implements Expr { public int eval(Map<String, Integer> m) { return v; } }
record Var(String n) implements Expr { public int eval(Map<String, Integer> m) { return m.get(n); } }
record Add(Expr l, Expr r) implements Expr {
    public int eval(Map<String, Integer> m) { return l.eval(m) + r.eval(m); }
}
int r = new Add(new Num(2), new Var("x")).eval(Map.of("x", 3));   // 5

In the wild: java.util.regex.Pattern, Spring Expression Language (SpEL), Thymeleaf expressions.

Pitfalls: only sensible for simple grammars; beyond that use a parser generator such as ANTLR. Evaluating user input as an expression language is a security risk: SpEL injection has caused remote code execution vulnerabilities.

Iterator

Problem: walk through a collection without exposing how it's stored, and allow several independent traversals.

class Range implements Iterable<Integer> {
    private final int from, to;
    Range(int from, int to) { this.from = from; this.to = to; }
    @Override public Iterator<Integer> iterator() {
        return new Iterator<>() {
            private int cur = from;
            public boolean hasNext() { return cur < to; }
            public Integer next() {
                if (!hasNext()) throw new NoSuchElementException();
                return cur++;
            }
        };
    }
}
for (int i : new Range(1, 4)) System.out.print(i);   // 123

In the wild: java.util.Iterator, the for-each loop, Stream (internal iteration), Spring Data's Page.

Pitfalls: next() must throw NoSuchElementException at the end, not return null. Structural change during fail-fast iteration throws ConcurrentModificationException.

Mediator

Problem: many objects talk to each other directly, creating a web of dependencies. A mediator centralizes that communication, so that each object knows only the mediator.

class ChatRoom {                                // mediator
    private final List<User> users = new ArrayList<>();
    void join(User u) { users.add(u); }
    void send(User from, String msg) {
        users.stream().filter(u -> u != from).forEach(u -> u.receive(msg));
    }
}
class User {
    private final ChatRoom room;
    User(ChatRoom room) { this.room = room; room.join(this); }
    void say(String msg) { room.send(this, msg); }   // never references another User
    void receive(String msg) { System.out.println(msg); }
}

In the wild: an air traffic controller is the classic analogy. Spring's ApplicationEventPublisher and a message broker play this role, as does DispatcherServlet between handlers, resolvers and views. java.util.concurrent.ExecutorService is sometimes cited as well.

Pitfalls: the mediator can turn into a god object. Observer vs Mediator: Observer distributes one-way notifications, and subjects don't know the listeners. A Mediator actively coordinates a conversation between colleagues.

Memento

Problem: save and restore an object's state without exposing its internals.

class Draft {
    private String text = "";
    void write(String s) { text += s; }
    String text() { return text; }

    record Snapshot(String text) {}                 // memento: immutable, opaque to others
    Snapshot save() { return new Snapshot(text); }
    void restore(Snapshot s) { text = s.text(); }
}
Deque<Draft.Snapshot> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); // caretaker: stores, never looks inside
Draft d = new Draft();
d.write("a"); history.push(d.save());
d.write("b");
d.restore(history.pop());
System.out.println(d.text());   // a

In the wild: java.io.Serializable for snapshots, undo stacks in editors, saved checkpoints in Spring Batch's ExecutionContext.

Pitfalls: memory cost with large states, so limit the history. Mementos must be immutable or deep copies.

Observer

Problem: when one object changes, an unknown set of others must react, and the subject shouldn't depend on them.

// Plain Java
class Stock {
    private final List<Consumer<BigDecimal>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();
    void subscribe(Consumer<BigDecimal> l) { listeners.add(l); }
    void setPrice(BigDecimal p) { listeners.forEach(l -> l.accept(p)); }
}

// Spring: decoupled through the application context
public record OrderPlaced(long orderId) {}

@Service class OrderService {
    private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
    OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher events) { this.events = events; }
    @Transactional void place(Order o) {
        /* save */
        events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.id()));
    }
}
@Component class EmailListener {
    @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
    void on(OrderPlaced e) { /* send email only if the transaction committed */ }
}

In the wild: Spring events, PropertyChangeListener, Reactive Streams through Flow and Reactor. java.util.Observable has been deprecated since 9.

Pitfalls: listeners that aren't removed leak memory. Spring's @EventListener runs synchronously in the publisher's thread and transaction by default, so a slow or failing listener affects the publisher. Control flow gets harder to follow.

State

Problem: an object's behaviour depends on its state, and large if or switch blocks repeat across methods. Each state becomes its own class, and the transitions are explicit.

enum OrderState {
    NEW {
        @Override OrderState pay() { return PAID; }
        @Override OrderState cancel() { return CANCELLED; }
    },
    PAID {
        @Override OrderState ship() { return SHIPPED; }
        @Override OrderState cancel() { return CANCELLED; }
    },
    SHIPPED, CANCELLED;

    OrderState pay()    { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + " can't pay"); }
    OrderState ship()   { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + " can't ship"); }
    OrderState cancel() { throw new IllegalStateException(name() + " can't cancel"); }
}
System.out.println(OrderState.NEW.pay().ship());   // SHIPPED
OrderState.SHIPPED.cancel();                       // IllegalStateException: SHIPPED can't cancel

In the wild: order workflows, TCP connections, Spring Statemachine, an ATM (see below).

Pitfalls: state classes for two or three simple states are overkill. State vs Strategy: the same structure, with different intent. Strategy is chosen by the client and doesn't usually change. State changes itself as the object moves through its lifecycle.

Strategy

Problem: several interchangeable algorithms, chosen at run time, kept out of the code that uses them.

interface PaymentStrategy { void pay(BigDecimal amount); }

@Component("card")   class CardPayment implements PaymentStrategy { public void pay(BigDecimal a) { } }
@Component("paypal") class PayPalPayment implements PaymentStrategy { public void pay(BigDecimal a) { } }

@Service class PaymentService {
    private final Map<String, PaymentStrategy> strategies;      // bean name to bean
    PaymentService(Map<String, PaymentStrategy> strategies) { this.strategies = strategies; }

    void pay(String method, BigDecimal amount) {
        PaymentStrategy s = strategies.get(method);
        if (s == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException(method);
        s.pay(amount);
    }
}

// In modern Java, a one-method strategy is simply a lambda
list.sort(Comparator.comparing(String::length));

In the wild: Comparator, RejectedExecutionHandler, Spring's PlatformTransactionManager, AuthenticationProvider and Resource implementations.

Pitfalls: not needed if the algorithm never varies. Exposing strategy details pushes knowledge onto callers.

Template Method

Problem: the steps of an algorithm are fixed, and some vary. A base class holds the skeleton, and subclasses fill in the steps.

abstract class CsvImport {
    public final void run(Path p) throws IOException {         // final: skeleton can't change
        List<String> lines = Files.readAllLines(p);
        for (String l : lines) {
            if (accept(l)) save(parse(l));
        }
    }
    protected boolean accept(String line) { return !line.isBlank(); }  // hook: optional override
    protected abstract Object parse(String line);                      // required step
    protected abstract void save(Object row);
}

In the wild: HttpServlet.service dispatching to doGet, AbstractList, InputStream.read(byte[]) built on read(), and AbstractApplicationContext.refresh(). JdbcTemplate follows the same idea with callbacks rather than subclasses, which is the composition-based form.

Pitfalls: a base class ties you to inheritance. Prefer passing a function if it's only one or two steps. Template Method vs Strategy: Template uses inheritance and varies parts of an algorithm. Strategy uses composition and swaps a whole algorithm.

Visitor

Problem: add new operations to a stable set of classes without changing them. It uses double dispatch: Java picks a method by the receiver's run-time type, but by the argument's compile-time type. accept gets around that by calling back with this, whose static type is exact.

interface Visitor<R> { R visit(Circle c); R visit(Square s); }
interface Shape { <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v); }
record Circle(double r) implements Shape {
    public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}
record Square(double s) implements Shape {
    public <R> R accept(Visitor<R> v) { return v.visit(this); }
}
class AreaVisitor implements Visitor<Double> {
    public Double visit(Circle c) { return Math.PI * c.r() * c.r(); }
    public Double visit(Square s) { return s.s() * s.s(); }
}
Shape sq = new Square(2);
System.out.println(sq.accept(new AreaVisitor()));     // 4.0

// Java 21: a sealed type and pattern switch give the same result with far less code
sealed interface Sh permits Ci, Sq {}
record Ci(double r) implements Sh {}
record Sq(double s) implements Sh {}
static double area(Sh s) {
    return switch (s) { case Ci c -> Math.PI * c.r() * c.r(); case Sq q -> q.s() * q.s(); };
}

In the wild: java.nio.file.FileVisitor with Files.walkFileTree, javax.lang.model element visitors, ASM's ClassVisitor, and Spring's BeanDefinitionVisitor.

Pitfalls: adding a new element type changes every visitor. It suits a stable element set with new operations, and it's the wrong choice for the opposite case.

Enterprise patterns

Layered structure and MVC

MVC separates the Model (data), View (presentation) and Controller (handles input and chooses what to do). Spring MVC applies it with a Front Controller: DispatcherServlet receives every request and delegates. In a REST API the "view" is the JSON produced by a message converter.

Controller      HTTP only: parse, validate, return status. No business rules
   |  DTO
Service         Business rules and transaction boundaries (@Transactional here)
   |  Entity
Repository      Persistence
   |
Database

DTO (Data Transfer Object)

A simple object that carries data across a boundary, shaped for the consumer. It exists so that the API isn't tied to the database schema.

public record UserResponse(long id, String name, String email) {
    static UserResponse from(User u) { return new UserResponse(u.getId(), u.getName(), u.getEmail()); }
}
public record CreateUserRequest(@NotBlank String name, @Email String email) {}
  • Returning entities directly leaks fields such as password hashes, triggers lazy-loading errors or N+1 queries during JSON serialization, and couples clients to your tables.
  • Binding request bodies to entities allows mass assignment: a client sets isAdmin. A request DTO lists only what's allowed.
  • Mapping can be manual, or use MapStruct, which generates code at compile time.

DAO vs Repository

DAORepository
OriginJ2EE core patternsDomain-Driven Design
ViewpointClose to the database: tables, queriesClose to the domain: a collection of aggregates
Typical methodsinsert, update, selectByStatussave, findById, findOverdueOrders
ScopeOften one per tableOne per aggregate root

A repository may use DAOs. In practice, Spring Data's interfaces blur the two.

// DAO with JdbcTemplate
@Repository class UserDao {
    private final JdbcTemplate jdbc;
    UserDao(JdbcTemplate jdbc) { this.jdbc = jdbc; }
    Optional<User> findById(long id) {
        return jdbc.query("select id, name from users where id = ?",
            (rs, n) -> new User(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name")), id).stream().findFirst();
    }
}
// Repository with Spring Data
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByStatusAndCreatedAtBefore(Status status, Instant cutoff);
}

Service Layer

The service layer defines the application's use cases and is where transactions begin. Keep transactions on service methods: one controller action should map to one business operation, committed or rolled back as a whole. Domain rules can live on entities (a rich domain model), with services only coordinating. Services that hold all logic, with entities as plain data, form what Martin Fowler calls an anemic domain model. It's common in Spring, and acceptable for simple CRUD.

Low-level design: how to approach it

  1. Clarify requirements. Who uses it, what are the main operations, how much concurrency, and what's out of scope.
  2. Name the entities from the nouns, and the behaviour from the verbs.
  3. Define relationships and interfaces, finding what will vary. That's where patterns apply.
  4. Write the core code, covering the main flow.
  5. Address edge cases and concurrency: two users taking the last spot, for example.

Parking lot

Requirements: floors with spots of different sizes, entry and exit, tickets, and pricing that varies. The variations are spot allocation and pricing, so both are strategies.

enum Size { MOTORCYCLE, CAR, TRUCK }
record Vehicle(String plate, Size size) {}

class Spot {
    final int id; final Size size;
    private Vehicle parked;
    Spot(int id, Size size) { this.id = id; this.size = size; }
    boolean fits(Vehicle v) { return parked == null && size.ordinal() >= v.size().ordinal(); }
    void park(Vehicle v) { parked = v; }
    void free() { parked = null; }
}
record Ticket(String id, Spot spot, Vehicle vehicle, Instant in) {}

interface PricingStrategy { BigDecimal price(Duration parked, Size size); }
class HourlyPricing implements PricingStrategy {
    public BigDecimal price(Duration d, Size s) {
        long hours = Math.max(1, (d.toMinutes() + 59) / 60);    // round up, minimum one hour
        return BigDecimal.valueOf(hours * (s == Size.TRUCK ? 5L : 2L));
    }
}
class ParkingLot {
    private final List<Spot> spots;
    private final PricingStrategy pricing;
    private final Clock clock;                 // injected so tests control time
    private final Map<String, Ticket> active = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    ParkingLot(List<Spot> spots, PricingStrategy pricing, Clock clock) {
        this.spots = spots; this.pricing = pricing; this.clock = clock;
    }
    synchronized Optional<Ticket> enter(Vehicle v) {   // check and take must be atomic
        return spots.stream().filter(s -> s.fits(v)).findFirst().map(s -> {
            s.park(v);
            Ticket t = new Ticket(UUID.randomUUID().toString(), s, v, clock.instant());
            active.put(t.id(), t);
            return t;
        });
    }
    synchronized BigDecimal exit(String ticketId) {
        Ticket t = active.remove(ticketId);
        if (t == null) throw new IllegalArgumentException("unknown ticket");
        t.spot().free();
        return pricing.price(Duration.between(t.in(), clock.instant()), t.vehicle().size());
    }
}

Follow-ups: finding a spot is O(n), so keep a free-spot queue per size (Map<Size, Deque<Spot>>) for O(1). The single lock limits concurrency, so use one lock per floor or size. In a multi-node system the database enforces it, with a unique constraint or optimistic locking.

LRU cache

Requirement: get and put in O(1), evicting the least recently used entry at capacity. A hash map gives O(1) lookup, and a doubly linked list gives O(1) reordering. The JDK already combines them:

class LruCache<K, V> extends LinkedHashMap<K, V> {
    private final int capacity;
    LruCache(int capacity) {
        super(16, 0.75f, true);            // true: iterate in access order
        this.capacity = capacity;
    }
    @Override protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry<K, V> eldest) {
        return size() > capacity;
    }
}
LruCache<String, Integer> c = new LruCache<>(2);
c.put("a", 1); c.put("b", 2);
c.get("a");                 // a is now most recent
c.put("c", 3);              // evicts b
System.out.println(c);      // {a=1, c=3}

Interviewers usually then ask for it by hand:

class Lru<K, V> {
    private class Node { K key; V val; Node prev, next; }
    private final Map<K, Node> map = new HashMap<>();
    private final Node head = new Node(), tail = new Node();  // sentinels avoid null checks
    private final int capacity;

    Lru(int capacity) { this.capacity = capacity; head.next = tail; tail.prev = head; }

    public synchronized V get(K key) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n == null) return null;
        unlink(n); addFront(n);
        return n.val;
    }
    public synchronized void put(K key, V val) {
        Node n = map.get(key);
        if (n != null) { n.val = val; unlink(n); addFront(n); return; }
        if (map.size() == capacity) {
            Node lru = tail.prev;
            unlink(lru);
            map.remove(lru.key);       // why each Node stores its key
        }
        n = new Node(); n.key = key; n.val = val;
        map.put(key, n); addFront(n);
    }
    private void unlink(Node n) { n.prev.next = n.next; n.next.prev = n.prev; }
    private void addFront(Node n) {
        n.next = head.next; n.prev = head;
        head.next.prev = n; head.next = n;
    }
}

Follow-ups: a read changes the order, so even get needs the lock, and ReadWriteLock doesn't help. For production, use Caffeine, which handles concurrency with far less contention and has a better eviction policy (Window TinyLFU). Thread safety across nodes means a shared store such as Redis.

Rate limiter

AlgorithmIdeaTrade-off
Fixed windowCount per minute, reset at the boundarySimple, but allows double the rate across a boundary
Sliding logKeep the timestamp of each requestAccurate, high memory use
Sliding window counterWeighted mix of current and previous windowsGood accuracy, small memory
Token bucketTokens refill at a steady rate, each request takes oneAllows bursts up to bucket size. The usual choice
Leaky bucketRequests drain at a fixed rateSmooths output, bursts wait or drop
class TokenBucket {
    private final long capacity;
    private final double refillPerNano;
    private final LongSupplier nanoClock;       // injected for testing
    private double tokens;
    private long last;

    TokenBucket(long capacity, double perSecond, LongSupplier nanoClock) {
        this.capacity = capacity;
        this.refillPerNano = perSecond / 1_000_000_000.0;
        this.nanoClock = nanoClock;
        this.tokens = capacity;
        this.last = nanoClock.getAsLong();
    }
    synchronized boolean tryAcquire() {
        long now = nanoClock.getAsLong();
        tokens = Math.min(capacity, tokens + (now - last) * refillPerNano);  // lazy refill
        last = now;
        if (tokens < 1) return false;
        tokens -= 1;
        return true;
    }
}
class RateLimiter {
    private final Map<String, TokenBucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
    boolean allow(String clientId) {
        return buckets.computeIfAbsent(clientId,
            id -> new TokenBucket(10, 5.0, System::nanoTime)).tryAcquire();
    }
}

Follow-ups: lazy refill needs no background thread. The per-client map needs eviction, or it becomes a leak. With several instances, keep the state in Redis, using a Lua script so that the check and decrement are atomic. Return HTTP 429 with Retry-After. Resilience4j and Bucket4j are the libraries to use.

ATM outline

An ATM's behaviour depends on where you are in a session, so State is the central pattern. The cash dispenser is a Chain of Responsibility: 500s, then 200s, then 100s, each passing on the remainder.

Atm --- current: AtmState (Idle, CardInserted, Authenticated, Dispensing)
    --- BankClient (Adapter over the bank network)
    --- CashDispenser (Chain of Responsibility by denomination)

interface AtmState {
    default void insertCard(Atm a, Card c)       { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
    default void enterPin(Atm a, String pin)     { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
    default void withdraw(Atm a, int amount)     { throw new IllegalStateException(); }
    default void eject(Atm a)                    { a.returnCard(); a.setState(new Idle()); }
}
class Idle implements AtmState {
    public void insertCard(Atm a, Card c) { a.setCard(c); a.setState(new CardInserted()); }
}
class CardInserted implements AtmState {
    public void enterPin(Atm a, String pin) {
        if (a.bank().verify(a.card(), pin)) a.setState(new Authenticated());
        else if (a.incrementFailures() >= 3) { a.retainCard(); a.setState(new Idle()); }
    }
}

Key points to raise: withdraw must be atomic and idempotent: the debit and the dispense can't both be assumed to succeed. So use a transaction ID, debit first, and reverse if the hardware fails to dispense. Money uses BigDecimal or integer minor units, never double. Include session timeouts and audit logging.

Layered vs Hexagonal (Ports and Adapters) Architecture

A typical Spring app is layered: controller → service → repository, with each layer depending on the one below. It is simple, but the domain often ends up depending on JPA entities, HTTP DTOs and framework annotations.

Hexagonal (ports and adapters) and Clean Architecture invert that: the domain and use cases sit in the centre with no framework dependencies; they define ports (interfaces) such as LoadPatientPort or PaymentGateway; adapters implement or call them (REST controller, JPA repository, Kafka listener, Stripe client). Dependencies always point inwards (Dependency Inversion applied to the whole app).

LayeredHexagonal / Clean
Domain depends onPersistence layerNothing; infrastructure depends on it
Swap DB / add a Kafka entry pointTouches servicesAdd or replace an adapter
Unit-testing logicMock repositoriesPlain objects plus in-memory port fakes
CostLow, familiarMore interfaces and mapping code
FitsCRUD servicesRich business rules, many integrations
// domain/application (no Spring, no JPA)
public interface PaymentGateway { PaymentResult charge(Money amount, CardToken card); }   // port

public class CheckoutService {                     // use case
    private final PaymentGateway payments;
    private final OrderStore orders;               // another port
    public CheckoutService(PaymentGateway p, OrderStore o) { payments = p; orders = o; }
    public Order checkout(Cart cart, CardToken card) { … }
}

// infrastructure (adapters)
@Component class StripePaymentAdapter implements PaymentGateway { … }
@Repository class JpaOrderStore implements OrderStore { … }
