DDD Building Blocks: Entity, Value Object, Aggregate

  • Entity: has an identity that persists while its attributes change (a Patient with an id). Equality by id.
  • Value Object: defined only by its values, immutable, equality by value (Money(amount, currency), Email, DateRange). It validates itself in the constructor, so invalid states cannot exist. Java records are a natural fit; JPA maps them as @Embeddable.
  • Aggregate: a cluster of entities and value objects changed together under one aggregate root (Order with its OrderLines). Outside code only references the root; invariants ("total ≤ credit limit") are enforced inside it; one transaction modifies one aggregate; other aggregates are referenced by id.
  • Domain service: logic that does not belong to one entity (e.g. transfer between two accounts). Repository: one per aggregate root.
public record Money(BigDecimal amount, Currency currency) {
    public Money {
        Objects.requireNonNull(currency);
        if (amount.signum() < 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("negative amount");
        amount = amount.setScale(currency.getDefaultFractionDigits(), RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN);
    }
    public Money plus(Money o) {
        if (!currency.equals(o.currency)) throw new IllegalArgumentException("currency mismatch");
        return new Money(amount.add(o.amount), currency);
    }
}

Null Object Pattern

Instead of returning null and forcing every caller to check, return an object that implements the interface with harmless "do nothing" behaviour: NoOpNotifier, GuestUser, NoDiscount (a pricing strategy returning 0). Collections.emptyList() is a JDK example. Use Optional when the absence is meaningful to the caller; use a Null Object when callers should simply not care.

interface Discount { BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal price); }
enum NoDiscount implements Discount { INSTANCE; public BigDecimal apply(BigDecimal p) { return p; } }

Discount d = discounts.getOrDefault(code, NoDiscount.INSTANCE);   // no null checks downstream

Interview Questions — SOLID & Design Patterns

Explain the Single Responsibility Principle in a way that isn't "a class does one thing".

A class should have one reason to change: it should serve one actor or stakeholder. Employee.calculatePay() (finance) and Employee.reportHours() (HR) in one class is the known example: a shared helper changed for one team can break the other's numbers. So the test isn't the count of methods, but who could request a change.

Does the Open/Closed Principle mean code can never be edited?

No. Bugs get fixed and code gets refactored. It means that adding a new variant shouldn't require editing stable code. You can't be closed against every change, so you choose where based on what has actually varied. A good answer mentions both sides: abstraction costs indirection, so add it when a second or third variation appears.

Why does Square extends Rectangle violate LSP? How do you recognize violations?

Rectangle's implied contract is that setting width leaves height alone. Square breaks it, so code correct for a Rectangle fails with a Square. Signs of a violation: UnsupportedOperationException in an override, instanceof checks, subclass methods doing nothing, tighter input checks, or exceptions the base doesn't declare. The fix is to separate the types or make them immutable.

Dependency Inversion vs Dependency Injection vs Inversion of Control?

DIP is a design principle: depend on abstractions, with the interface owned by the high-level module. IoC is a broader idea: the framework controls the flow and calls your code. DI is a technique: objects receive dependencies from outside, in Spring through constructor injection. You can do DI and still violate DIP, if you inject a concrete vendor class.

When is duplication better than DRY?

When two pieces of code look alike but represent different knowledge. Merging them couples unrelated changes, and the shared code fills up with flags. Common example: one DTO reused for create, update and response, until each needs different validation. A reasonable rule is to wait until the third occurrence, and to be sure they change together.

Composition vs inheritance: why prefer composition?

Inheritance exposes parent internals, fixes the relationship at compile time, and subclasses can break when the parent changes (the "fragile base class"). The JDK has known mistakes: Stack extends Vector and Properties extends Hashtable. Composition hides internals, allows swapping at run time, and is easy to test with mocks. Use inheritance for a true is-a relationship where LSP holds. In Effective Java, the example is a counting HashSet subclass that double-counts because addAll calls add.

Aggregation vs composition?

Both are whole-part. In aggregation, parts exist independently: a Team and Player. In composition, the whole owns the lifetime: an Order and its OrderLines. In JPA, composition is cascade = ALL, orphanRemoval = true. Aggregation has no cascade delete.

List the ways to implement a Singleton and their trade-offs.
FormLazyThread-safeNote
Eager staticNoYesSimple
synchronized methodYesYesLock on every call
Double-checked lockingYesNeeds volatileVerbose
Holder classYesYesBest general form
EnumNoYesSafe from reflection and serialization. Can't extend a class
Why does double-checked locking need volatile?

Creating an object has three steps: allocate, run the constructor, assign the reference. Without a happens-before relationship, another thread may observe the reference before seeing the writes from the constructor, and use a half-built object. volatile establishes that ordering. The first check runs outside the lock for speed, and the second inside, since another thread may have created it while waiting.

How can a singleton be broken, and how do you protect it?
  • Reflection: setAccessible(true) on the private constructor. Throw from the constructor if an instance exists, or use an enum.
  • Serialization: deserialization creates a new object. Add private Object readResolve() { return INSTANCE; }.
  • Cloning: don't implement Cloneable.
  • Class loaders: each has its own static. There's no code-level fix, so keep it in a shared parent loader.
Is Spring's singleton the same as GoF Singleton? Are singleton beans thread-safe?

No. Spring's is one instance per container and bean name. You can define two beans of the same class. The container, not the class, enforces it, so the class stays testable. Spring doesn't make beans thread-safe. Since all threads share one instance, keep them stateless. Per-request state belongs in method parameters or request scope.

Simple factory, Factory Method and Abstract Factory: what's the difference?

A simple factory is a method containing a switch; it's a useful idiom, not a GoF pattern. Factory Method uses inheritance: a subclass chooses which product is created. Abstract Factory uses composition: an object creates a family of related products. Summary: one class with a switch, one subclass per product, and one factory per family.

Builder vs constructor vs setters? What does Lombok's @Builder not do?

Constructors are good for a few required fields. Setters allow an incomplete mutable object. Builder gives readable, validated, immutable construction with many optional fields. Lombok doesn't enforce required fields at compile time; it doesn't validate unless you add that; and field initializers are ignored without @Builder.Default. Combined with JPA, Lombok's @Builder removes the no-arg constructor unless you add one.

Shallow vs deep copy? Why is clone() discouraged?

A shallow copy shares referenced objects, while a deep copy duplicates them. clone() is awkward: Cloneable has no methods and only switches behaviour on Object.clone; it doesn't call constructors; final fields can't be reassigned; and it throws a checked exception. Effective Java recommends a copy constructor or copy factory.

Output: what does this decorator chain print?
interface S { String r(); }
class Base implements S { public String r() { return "x"; } }
class Trim implements S {
    final S in; Trim(S in) { this.in = in; }
    public String r() { return in.r().substring(1); }
}
class Wrap implements S {
    final S in; Wrap(S in) { this.in = in; }
    public String r() { return "[" + in.r() + "]"; }
}
System.out.println(new Trim(new Wrap(new Base())).r());
System.out.println(new Wrap(new Trim(new Base())).r());

The output is x] then []. The innermost runs first. In the first, Wrap gives [x] and Trim removes the first character. In the second, Trim gives an empty string and Wrap brackets it. Decorator order changes the result.

Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade?
PatternInterfaceIntent
AdapterChanges itMake incompatible things work together
DecoratorSameAdd features, stackable
ProxySameControl access
FacadeNew and simplerHide a subsystem
Why doesn't @Transactional work when called from the same class?

Spring wraps the bean in a proxy, and the transaction logic runs only when a call passes through it. this.save() goes directly to the target. @Cacheable and @Async have the same problem. Fixes: move the method to another bean (the cleanest), inject a TransactionTemplate, or inject a self-reference. Private and final methods can't be intercepted either.

Output: what does this dynamic proxy print?

Using the Proxy example in the Proxy pattern section, the output is:

before hi
after
hi

The handler prints during the call, and println prints the returned value after hi() finishes. Every method on the interface goes through the handler. So do toString, hashCode and equals, which is why calling proxy.toString() inside the handler can cause infinite recursion.

Strategy vs State vs Template Method?

Strategy: the client picks an algorithm through composition, and it rarely changes during a call. State: same structure, but the object moves itself between states and behaviour follows. Template Method: inheritance fixes a skeleton, and subclasses fill in steps. If behaviour is replaced at run time, it's Strategy or State. If only steps vary and it's fixed at class-writing time, it's Template Method.

How do you select a strategy in Spring without a big switch?

Inject Map<String, PaymentStrategy>, keyed by bean name, or inject a List<PaymentStrategy>, where each has a supports(type) method, and build a lookup map in the constructor. Adding a type then only needs a new @Component. Fail clearly when a key isn't found, and add a test that checks every enum value has a strategy.

How does Observer differ from publish-subscribe?

In Observer, a subject knows its observers (as an interface) and calls them directly, usually synchronously in the same process. In pub-sub, a broker sits between them; publishers and subscribers don't know each other and work asynchronously, often across processes, as with Kafka. Spring's event mechanism sits in between: the publisher knows only the event type, and the context routes it.

What can go wrong with Spring @EventListener?

By default it's synchronous, in the publisher's thread and transaction. A listener exception propagates to the publisher and can roll back the transaction. A listener sending an email may do so for a transaction that later rolls back. Use @TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) for side effects, and @Async to decouple timing. Remember that events in memory are lost on a crash, so critical ones need a transactional outbox.

Output: what happens with this state enum?

Using the OrderState code above, OrderState.NEW.pay().ship() prints SHIPPED, since NEW.pay() returns PAID. OrderState.SHIPPED.cancel() uses the enum's default body and throws IllegalStateException: SHIPPED can't cancel. Constants with a body compile to anonymous subclasses, so NEW.getClass() isn't OrderState.class, whereas NEW.getDeclaringClass() is.

What is double dispatch, and how does Visitor achieve it?

Java selects overridden methods by the receiver's run-time type, and overloads by the compile-time type of arguments: single dispatch. Calling visitor.visit(shape) with a Shape variable doesn't pick the Circle overload, and wouldn't even compile here. With shape.accept(visitor), the first dispatch finds Circle.accept, where visit(this) has a static type of Circle, resolving the overload. Java 21's pattern switch on a sealed type reaches the same goal directly.

Which patterns did lambdas make simpler?

Strategy, Command, Template Method (pass a function), Observer (listeners), and simple factories (a Supplier). Map<String, Supplier<Shape>> replaces a switch. A class still makes sense when the object has several methods, its own state, or needs a name, such as a Spring bean with dependencies.

What's an anti-pattern? Name a few you've seen.
  • God class: does everything.
  • Anemic domain model: entities with no behaviour.
  • Service locator: pulling dependencies from a global registry, which hides them.
  • Golden hammer: one tool for every problem.
  • Pattern overuse: a factory for a single implementation.
  • Magic numbers and strings, primitive obsession (a String for an email), and exceptions for control flow.
Why not return JPA entities from controllers?

Sensitive fields can leak. Lazy associations either throw LazyInitializationException or, with open-session-in-view, fire extra queries while serializing. Bidirectional relations cause infinite recursion. And any schema change becomes an API change. DTOs give a stable contract. Reading into a DTO projection also fetches only the columns you need.

DAO vs Repository? Do I need a DAO with Spring Data?

A DAO abstracts data access in storage terms, while a Repository acts like a collection of aggregates in domain terms. With Spring Data the interface is enough for most cases. Use a custom fragment with EntityManager or JdbcTemplate for complex queries or batch work.

Where should @Transactional go, and why not on controllers or repositories?

On service methods, because a business operation is the unit of work. On a controller, it would hold a transaction during HTTP serialization and mix concerns. On separate repository calls, each call commits alone, so a multi-step operation can't roll back together. Keep transactions short: don't call remote APIs inside them, since that holds a connection.

Design an LRU cache. What's the complexity? How do you make it thread-safe?

A HashMap plus a doubly linked list gives O(1) for both operations. See the code above. Each node needs its key, in order to remove the map entry on eviction. Sentinel head and tail nodes remove null edge cases. Since get reorders the list, it's a write, so all access takes one lock. The simplest form is Collections.synchronizedMap(new LruCache<>(n)). For high throughput, use Caffeine. It records reads in buffers and applies them later, avoiding contention on each read.

Output: what does this LinkedHashMap LRU print?

With capacity 2: put a, put b, get a, put c. It prints {a=1, c=3}. get("a") moves a to the most-recent end, so b is the eldest and is removed. Without the true access-order flag, it's insertion order, and the map would be {b=2, c=3}.

Design a rate limiter for a REST API. Which algorithm, and how would it work across servers?

Token bucket per client key, as it allows short bursts while enforcing an average rate. On one instance, an in-memory map with lazy refill works. Across instances, a shared store is needed: Redis with an atomic Lua script that reads, refills and decrements. Decide on failure behaviour if Redis is down: fail open for availability, or fail closed for protection. Put it at the gateway when you can, return 429 with Retry-After, and evict idle clients. Avoid fixed windows if bursts at boundaries matter.

Design a parking lot: which classes, and which patterns?

Classes: ParkingLot, Floor, Spot, Vehicle, Ticket, with Strategy for pricing and for spot allocation. The important part is concurrency: checking a spot and taking it must be atomic. Inject a Clock, which makes pricing tests deterministic. For performance, keep free spots per size in a queue rather than scanning. Say what you'd change with multiple gates and a shared database: a unique constraint or an optimistic version on the spot row.

Design a notification system supporting email, SMS and push, with retries.

NotificationChannel is a Strategy, with one implementation per channel, each an Adapter over a vendor SDK. A NotificationService looks up the channels by user preference. Sending is asynchronous through a queue, as a Command with a retry count. Failures back off exponentially and go to a dead-letter queue. Templates use Builder or Template Method. Idempotency keys stop duplicates on retry. Mentioning a transactional outbox ensures a notification isn't lost if the app crashes after a commit.

Design a Logger class that supports levels and multiple outputs.

Levels use Chain of Responsibility, or a simple threshold. Outputs (console, file, network) are Strategy or Observer: a logger holds a list of appenders. Layout formatting is another Strategy, and async output is a Decorator around an appender, backed by a queue. A logger per name comes from a factory cache (Flyweight). That's how Logback and Log4j2 are organized.

Design an elevator system outline.

Classes: Elevator, Request, Scheduler, Door. State pattern for an elevator's states (moving up, moving down, idle, door open). Strategy for scheduling: nearest car, or SCAN, which continues in one direction and serves requests on the way. A per-elevator pair of TreeSets holds up and down stops. Handle capacity, emergency stop, and concurrent button presses through one event queue per elevator.

You see a 300-line if/else that picks a pricing rule. How would you refactor it safely?
  1. Add characterization tests, to pin current behaviour, including odd cases.
  2. Identify the variation, and define a PricingRule interface.
  3. Move one branch at a time into a class, keeping tests green.
  4. Replace the selection with a registry or injected list.
  5. Delete the old code.

Small commits that can each be reviewed and reverted are the main point. If rules change often and are owned by business users, consider a rules table or engine rather than classes.

What do high cohesion and low coupling mean, and how do you spot violations?

Cohesion: how closely the members of a class or module belong together (a InvoiceCalculator whose methods all work on invoice totals is cohesive). Coupling: how much one module depends on the internals of another. You want high cohesion and low coupling so changes stay local. Warning signs: a class with unrelated method groups or a name like Manager/Utils, a change that ripples across many classes (shotgun surgery), classes reaching through getters into others' data, and circular package dependencies.

What is the Law of Demeter ("tell, don't ask")? Give an example.

A method should talk only to its own fields, parameters and objects it creates, not to "friends of friends". order.getCustomer().getWallet().debit(total) couples the caller to three classes' structure. Better: order.payWith(paymentService) or customer.pay(total), so the object that owns the data makes the decision. Fluent builders and stream chains are not violations, because they return the same kind of object.

Layered vs hexagonal architecture: which would you choose for a new Spring Boot service?

For a mostly CRUD service, layered is fine and cheaper. Choose hexagonal when business rules are complex or you integrate many external systems (payment, messaging, third-party APIs): the domain stays free of framework code, adapters can be swapped (REST and Kafka entry points calling the same use case), and core logic is tested without Spring. A pragmatic middle ground: keep layers, but put interfaces for external systems in the domain package and their implementations in an infrastructure package. ArchUnit tests can enforce the dependency direction.

Entity vs Value Object: how do you decide, and how do you persist a value object with JPA?

Ask "if all attributes are equal, is it the same thing?" Two Money(100, INR) are interchangeable, so it's a value object; two patients with the same name are not, so Patient is an entity. Make value objects immutable and self-validating. Persist them as @Embeddable (Hibernate 6.2+ supports records as embeddables) or with an AttributeConverter for single-column values like Email.

Design a vending machine. Which patterns apply?

Classes: VendingMachine, Inventory (slot → product, count), Product, Coin/Note enums, Transaction. The core is the State pattern: IdleState, HasMoneyState, DispensingState, OutOfStockState, each implementing insertMoney, selectProduct, dispense, refund and rejecting invalid actions. A Strategy computes change (greedy over available denominations, failing if exact change is impossible). Mention edge cases: insufficient funds, sold out after payment (refund), and synchronising state changes if multiple inputs can arrive concurrently.

Design a movie ticket booking system. How do you prevent two users booking the same seat?

Entities: Movie, Theatre, Screen, Show, Seat, ShowSeat (status per show: AVAILABLE, HELD, BOOKED), Booking, Payment. Flow: select seats → hold them for a few minutes → pay → confirm, or release on timeout/failure. Concurrency: make the hold an atomic conditional update (UPDATE show_seat SET status='HELD', held_until=? WHERE show_id=? AND seat_id IN (…) AND status='AVAILABLE') and accept only if all rows were updated, or use optimistic locking with @Version; a unique constraint on (show, seat) for confirmed bookings is the final guard. A scheduled job or TTL (e.g. Redis key expiry) releases expired holds. Patterns: Strategy for pricing (weekday, premium seat), Observer/events for notifications, Factory for payment methods.

Testing: JUnit & Mockito Quality

How to structure a test suite, JUnit's architecture and annotations, Mockito in depth, AssertJ, TDD, Spring Boot's test slices, Testcontainers and coverage. JUnit and Mockito examples were run with JUnit 6.1 and Mockito 5.24 on Java 21. Spring and Testcontainers code wasn't run here; their class names were checked against the published JARs.

The test pyramid

The test pyramid says to have many fast, narrow tests at the bottom and few slow, broad tests at the top. A test's value depends on how much confidence it gives, and its cost depends on how slow and fragile it is.

LevelScopeToolsSpeed
UnitOne class, collaborators replacedJUnit, Mockito, AssertJMilliseconds
SliceOne Spring layer@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTestSeconds
IntegrationSeveral layers with real infrastructure@SpringBootTest, TestcontainersSeconds to minutes
ContractAPI agreement between servicesSpring Cloud Contract, PactSeconds
End-to-endWhole system, through the UI or APIPlaywright, Cypress, RestAssuredMinutes

What a good test looks like

Tests follow Arrange, Act, Assert (or Given, When, Then). Good unit tests are FIRST: Fast, Independent, Repeatable, Self-validating and Timely. Test behaviour through the public API, not implementation, so refactoring doesn't break tests.

@Test
void orderOver100GetsFreeShipping() {
    // Arrange
    Order order = new Order(new BigDecimal("120.00"));
    // Act
    BigDecimal shipping = calculator.shippingFor(order);
    // Assert
    assertThat(shipping).isEqualByComparingTo("0");
}

Test doubles have precise names, though everyone says "mock":

DoubleWhat it doesExample
DummyFills a parameter, never usednull or an unused object
StubReturns canned answerswhen(...).thenReturn(...)
SpyReal object that records callsspy(realObject)
MockPre-programmed, and its interactions are verifiedverify(mock).save(x)
FakeWorking lightweight implementationH2, or an in-memory repository

JUnit architecture

JUnit 4 was one JAR, and IDEs depended on its internals, which made it hard to evolve. JUnit 5 split it into three parts, separating how tests are run from how they're written.

PartRole
JUnit PlatformFoundation for launching test frameworks. IDEs and build tools use its launcher API. Defines the TestEngine API
JUnit JupiterThe programming model (annotations, assertions) and its test engine
JUnit VintageAn engine for running old JUnit 3 and 4 tests. Deprecated in JUnit 6

Because the platform takes any engine, Cucumber, Spock and others run on it as well. JUnit 6 (released September 2025) continues the same Jupiter model with unified version numbers for all parts, and it requires Java 17. For most test code the move from JUnit 5 is a dependency change. Spring Boot 4 uses JUnit 6, and Spring Boot's test starter brings the right version in.

JUnit 4JUnit 5 and 6
@Before, @After@BeforeEach, @AfterEach
@BeforeClass, @AfterClass@BeforeAll, @AfterAll
@Ignore@Disabled
@RunWith, @Rule@ExtendWith, @RegisterExtension
@Test(expected = X.class)assertThrows(X.class, ...)
Tests must be publicPackage-private is fine, and is the convention
Message is the first argumentMessage is the last argument, and can be a Supplier

Lifecycle

By default, JUnit creates a new instance of the test class for every test method, so instance fields can't leak state between tests. A run with two tests and a nested class printed:

class LifeTest {
    int n = 0;
    LifeTest() { System.out.println("ctor"); }
    @BeforeAll static void ba() { System.out.println("beforeAll"); }
    @AfterAll  static void aa() { System.out.println("afterAll"); }
    @BeforeEach void be() { System.out.println("beforeEach n=" + n); n++; }
    @AfterEach  void ae() { System.out.println("afterEach n=" + n); }
    @Test void a() { System.out.println("a"); }
    @Test void b() { System.out.println("b"); }
    @Nested class In {
        @BeforeEach void ibe() { System.out.println("innerBeforeEach"); }
        @Test void c() { System.out.println("c"); }
    }
}
beforeAll
ctor
beforeEach n=0
a
afterEach n=1
ctor
beforeEach n=0
b
afterEach n=1
ctor
beforeEach n=0
innerBeforeEach
c
afterEach n=1
afterAll

n is 0 each time, which proves a fresh instance. For a nested test, the outer @BeforeEach runs first. @BeforeAll must be static, unless the class uses @TestInstance(Lifecycle.PER_CLASS), which shares one instance for all tests. That allows non-static @BeforeAll (useful in @Nested classes), but brings back shared state.

Method order is deterministic but deliberately not obvious. Tests must not depend on it. If order is genuinely needed, as in a step-by-step scenario, use @TestMethodOrder(MethodOrderer.OrderAnnotation.class) with @Order. @Order alone does nothing: JUnit logged Ineffective @Order annotation when this was tried.

Complete annotation reference

AnnotationPurpose
@TestA test method. Must return void
@ParameterizedTestRuns once per set of arguments
@RepeatedTest(n)Runs n times, can take RepetitionInfo
@TestFactoryReturns DynamicTests created at run time
@TestTemplateBase mechanism behind parameterized and repeated tests, for extensions
@BeforeEach, @AfterEach, @BeforeAll, @AfterAllLifecycle callbacks
@NestedNon-static inner class grouping related tests
@DisplayName, @DisplayNameGenerationReadable names, set individually or by a generator
@TagLabel for filtering, such as @Tag("slow")
@DisabledSkip, with a reason
@EnabledOnOs, @DisabledOnOs, @EnabledOnJre, @EnabledForJreRangeConditions on OS and Java version
@EnabledIfEnvironmentVariable, @EnabledIfSystemProperty, @EnabledIfConditions on the environment, or a method
@TimeoutFails if a test or lifecycle method runs too long
@TempDirInjects a temporary directory, deleted afterwards
@TestInstancePer-method or per-class lifecycle
@TestMethodOrder, @TestClassOrder, @OrderExplicit ordering
@ExtendWith, @RegisterExtensionRegister extensions, declaratively or through a field
@AutoCloseCloses a field's resource after the test
@Execution, @ResourceLock, @IsolatedControl parallel execution
@ParameterizedClassRuns a whole test class per set of arguments

Extensions are the replacement for JUnit 4's runners and rules. An extension implements callback interfaces such as BeforeEachCallback or ParameterResolver. That's how MockitoExtension and SpringExtension plug in, and unlike @RunWith, several can be combined on one class.

class TimingExtension implements BeforeEachCallback, AfterEachCallback {
    private static final Namespace NS = Namespace.create(TimingExtension.class);
    @Override public void beforeEach(ExtensionContext c) {
        c.getStore(NS).put("start", System.nanoTime());
    }
    @Override public void afterEach(ExtensionContext c) {
        long ms = (System.nanoTime() - c.getStore(NS).get("start", long.class)) / 1_000_000;
        System.out.println(c.getDisplayName() + " took " + ms + " ms");
    }
}

Assertions and assumptions

assertEquals(expected, actual);           // expected first
assertEquals(0.3, 0.1 + 0.2, 1e-9);       // delta for floating point
assertNotNull(x); assertTrue(c); assertSame(a, b);
assertArrayEquals(new int[]{1}, arr);
assertIterableEquals(List.of(1), set);
assertLinesMatch(List.of("a", "\\d+"), lines);   // regex lines allowed
assertInstanceOf(String.class, o);        // returns the cast value

// Groups: every assertion runs and failures are reported together
assertAll("user",
    () -> assertEquals("Ann", u.name()),
    () -> assertEquals(30, u.age()));

// Exceptions
IllegalStateException e = assertThrows(IllegalStateException.class, () -> svc.run());
assertEquals("boom", e.getMessage());
assertThrowsExactly(IllegalStateException.class, () -> svc.run());  // subclass doesn't pass
assertDoesNotThrow(() -> svc.run());

// Timeouts
assertTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1), () -> svc.run());            // waits for completion
assertTimeoutPreemptively(Duration.ofSeconds(1), () -> svc.run()); // aborts, on another thread

// Assumptions: abort rather than fail when a precondition doesn't hold
assumeTrue(System.getenv("CI") != null);
assumingThat(isLinux, () -> assertEquals(...));
Gotcha: assertTimeoutPreemptively runs the code on a different thread. ThreadLocal-based state, including Spring-managed transactions, won't apply there, and @Transactional test rollback can silently fail.

assertThrows accepts subclasses, and assertThrowsExactly doesn't. It returns the exception so you can inspect it. Keep the lambda to the one call that should throw, or an earlier line might throw the same type and pass the test falsely.

Parameterized tests

One test logic, many inputs. Each input is reported as a separate invocation, so a failure names the case. The sources:

SourceProvides
@ValueSourceOne literal per run: ints, strings, and so on
@NullSource, @EmptySource, @NullAndEmptySourcenull, empty string or collection
@EnumSourceEnum constants, filterable by name
@CsvSource, @CsvFileSourceMultiple columns, inline or from a file
@MethodSourceA static factory method returning a stream of arguments
@FieldSourceA static field
@ArgumentsSourceA custom ArgumentsProvider
@ParameterizedTest(name = "{0} is {1}")
@CsvSource({"1,one", "2,'two, x'", "3,"})
void csv(int a, String b) { System.out.println(a + "=" + b); }
// 1=one
// 2=two, x      quotes protect the comma
// 3=null        an empty unquoted column is null

@ParameterizedTest
@NullAndEmptySource
@ValueSource(strings = {" "})
void rejectsBlank(String s) { assertTrue(s == null || s.isBlank()); }  // null, "", " "

static Stream<Arguments> doubles() {
    return Stream.of(Arguments.of(1, 2), Arguments.of(2, 4));
}
@ParameterizedTest
@MethodSource("doubles")
void doubled(int in, int expected) { assertEquals(expected, in * 2); }

@ParameterizedTest
@EnumSource(value = DayOfWeek.class, names = {"SATURDAY", "SUNDAY"})
void weekend(DayOfWeek d) { assertTrue(isWeekend(d)); }

@TestFactory
Stream<DynamicTest> dynamic() {
    return Stream.of("a", "b").map(s -> dynamicTest("t" + s, () -> assertNotNull(s)));
}

Parameterized tests live in the junit-jupiter-params artifact, which junit-jupiter includes. @MethodSource methods must be static, unless the class uses per-class lifecycle. Note that @BeforeEach runs for each invocation of a parameterized test, but only once around a whole @TestFactory, not per dynamic test.

Mockito

Mockito generates test doubles for your class's collaborators, so a unit test stays isolated from databases and networks. Since Mockito 5 the default inline mock maker uses a Java agent with ByteBuddy to change bytecode, so final classes, final methods and static methods can be mocked with no extra setup. A test with a final class and final method passed.

@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)
class OrderServiceTest {
    @Mock OrderRepository repo;
    @Mock PaymentGateway gateway;
    @InjectMocks OrderService service;       // receives the mocks
    @Captor ArgumentCaptor<Order> captor;

    @Test
    void savesPaidOrder() {
        when(gateway.charge(any())).thenReturn(Receipt.ok());

        service.place(new Cart(new BigDecimal("10")));

        verify(repo).save(captor.capture());
        assertThat(captor.getValue().status()).isEqualTo(Status.PAID);
    }
}

Unstubbed behaviour

A mock's unstubbed methods don't throw; they return an empty default. A run printed null [] Optional.empty 0 false null for a method returning String, List, Optional, int, boolean and String[]. Empty collections, Optional and Stream are returned rather than null. Arrays give null.

Stubbing

when(repo.find(1)).thenReturn("a");
when(repo.find(anyInt())).thenReturn("a", "b");   // a, b, then b forever
when(repo.find(-1)).thenThrow(new IllegalArgumentException());
when(repo.find(anyInt())).thenAnswer(inv -> "id" + inv.getArgument(0));

// void methods can't go inside when(...)
doThrow(new IllegalStateException()).when(list).clear();
doNothing().when(mailer).send(any());
doAnswer(inv -> { System.out.println("arg=" + inv.getArgument(0)); return true; })
    .when(list).add("z");

// BDD style: reads as given/when/then
given(repo.find(1)).willReturn("x");
then(repo).should().find(1);

Argument matchers: any(), anyInt(), eq(x), isNull(), argThat(a -> a.total() > 0). If you use a matcher for one argument, all arguments must be matchers. when(t.f(anyInt(), "x")) threw InvalidUseOfMatchersException in a test. Write eq("x"). Also, any() matches null, whereas any(String.class) doesn't.

Verification

verify(repo).save(order);                // exactly once
verify(repo, times(2)).save(any());
verify(repo, never()).delete(any());
verify(repo, atLeastOnce()).find(1);
verifyNoInteractions(mailer);
verifyNoMoreInteractions(repo);

InOrder o = inOrder(repo, mailer);       // order across mocks
o.verify(repo).save(order);
o.verify(mailer).send(any());

Verify what's a real side effect: a save, a published event, an email. Don't verify stubbed queries. If the code's result depends on the stub, the assertion already proves the call happened. Over-verifying ties tests to the implementation.

ArgumentCaptor

Use it when you need to inspect an object that the code under test created internally.

ArgumentCaptor<String> c = ArgumentCaptor.forClass(String.class);
m.save("a");
m.save("b");
verify(m, times(2)).save(c.capture());
System.out.println(c.getValue() + " " + c.getAllValues());   // b [a, b]

getValue() returns the last value. Avoid using a captor with when(...), which makes tests hard to read. Prefer argThat, or check the captured value in the assert step.

Spy

A spy wraps a real object: methods run for real unless stubbed. The classic trap is that when(spy.method()) calls the real method while setting up the stub.

List<String> sp = spy(new ArrayList<>());

when(sp.get(0)).thenReturn("a");     // IndexOutOfBoundsException: the real get(0) runs

doReturn("a").when(sp).get(0);       // correct: the real method isn't called
System.out.println(sp.get(0) + " " + sp.size());   // a 0

A spy is usually a design smell, since partial mocking implies the class is doing too much. It's reasonable for legacy code.

@InjectMocks

@InjectMocks creates the object under test and tries injection in order: constructor (the biggest one), then setter, then field. If constructor injection is attempted, it doesn't go on to the others. It doesn't report a failure: if no mock matches, the dependency silently stays null or the constructor gets null, and you see an NPE. With a single explicit constructor, you may prefer plain new OrderService(repo, gateway), which fails at compile time when a dependency is added.

Strict stubs

MockitoExtension runs in strict stubs mode by default, which keeps tests clean. Tests of both failures here:

SituationException
A stub is never used by the testUnnecessaryStubbingException
Code under test calls a stubbed method with different argumentsPotentialStubbingProblem: Strict stubbing argument mismatch
when(r.find(1)).thenReturn("x");
new Svc(r).go(2);                // PotentialStubbingProblem, when Svc is in another source file

The argument mismatch is reported only when the call comes from a different source file than the test. If it's in the same file, Mockito assumes it's deliberate, and you get UnnecessaryStubbingException; a test showed exactly that for a nested class. Stubs used only in some tests can be marked lenient().when(...), or set with @MockitoSettings(strictness = Strictness.LENIENT), but first consider moving the stub out of @BeforeEach.

Static mocks and constructor mocks

try (MockedStatic<Svc> ms = mockStatic(Svc.class)) {
    ms.when(Svc::st).thenReturn("fake");
    System.out.println(Svc.st());      // fake
}
System.out.println(Svc.st());          // real: restored when closed

try (MockedConstruction<Client> mc = mockConstruction(Client.class)) {
    new Client();                      // a mock
    assertEquals(1, mc.constructed().size());
}

The static mock applies only to the current thread and only within the block, so always use try-with-resources. If you often need it, it suggests a hidden dependency: inject a Clock rather than mocking LocalDateTime.now(). Don't mock core JDK classes: mockConstruction(ArrayList.class) gave a StackOverflowError here, because the JVM's own machinery uses ArrayList.

On recent JDKs, Mockito prints a warning that it's self-attaching its agent, which future JDKs will stop allowing (JEP 451). The fix is to add Mockito as a -javaagent in the Surefire configuration, as described in Mockito's documentation.

Don't mockWhy, and what instead
Value objects, records, DTOsJust create them
Types you don't own, in depthYou'd encode assumptions about a third-party API. Wrap it in your own adapter and integration-test that
The class under testPartial mocks suggest splitting the class
Everything in a chainRETURNS_DEEP_STUBS usually means a Law of Demeter issue

AssertJ

AssertJ offers fluent assertions, with better failure messages and autocompletion. It's included in spring-boot-starter-test.

assertThat(name).startsWith("he").endsWith("lo");
assertThat(list).hasSize(3).contains(2).doesNotContain(9);
assertThat(list).containsExactly("a", "b");         // exact order
assertThat(list).containsExactlyInAnyOrder("b", "a");
assertThat(users).extracting(User::name).contains("Ann");
assertThat(users).filteredOn(u -> u.age() > 18).hasSize(2);
assertThat(optional).contains(1);
assertThat(price).isEqualByComparingTo("10.00");    // BigDecimal: ignores scale
assertThat(actual).usingRecursiveComparison().ignoringFields("id").isEqualTo(expected);

assertThatThrownBy(() -> { throw new IllegalStateException("boom"); })
    .isInstanceOf(IllegalStateException.class)
    .hasMessageContaining("oo");

SoftAssertions soft = new SoftAssertions();         // collect failures, like assertAll
soft.assertThat(a).isEqualTo(1);
soft.assertThat(b).isEqualTo(2);
soft.assertAll();

If you static-import both Assertions classes with wildcards, an unqualified fail() doesn't compile: reference to fail is ambiguous. Import names individually.

Test-Driven Development

TDD writes the test first, in a short cycle:

  1. Red: write a small failing test for the next behaviour. Confirm that it fails.
  2. Green: write the least code to pass it.
  3. Refactor: clean up with the tests as a safety net.
// Red
@Test void emptyStringIsZero() { assertEquals(0, Calc.add("")); }
// Green
static int add(String s) { return 0; }
// Red: next behaviour drives the design
@Test void singleNumber() { assertEquals(5, Calc.add("5")); }
// Green
static int add(String s) { return s.isEmpty() ? 0 : Integer.parseInt(s); }

Its value is in the design pressure: code that's written to be tested tends to have clear inputs and injected dependencies. Limits: it's less useful for exploratory work and UI layout. BDD (Behaviour-Driven Development) extends it with business-readable scenarios, such as Cucumber's Given, When, Then.

Spring Boot test slices

Starting a full application context is slow. A slice starts only the part of Spring you're testing.

AnnotationLoadsDoesn't load
@WebMvcTestControllers, filters, @ControllerAdvice, converters, Spring Security config, MockMvc@Service, @Repository, @Component
@WebFluxTestWebFlux controllers, WebTestClientServices, repositories
@DataJpaTestEntities, repositories, TestEntityManager, embedded database, transactional testsControllers, services
@JdbcTestJdbcTemplate, a data sourceJPA, web
@DataMongoTest, @DataRedisTestThat store's repositoriesOthers
@JsonTestJackson, JacksonTesterEverything else
@RestClientTestREST clients, MockRestServiceServerOthers
@SpringBootTestThe full contextNothing
Tip: Spring Boot 4 split auto-configuration and test support into modules, with new packages. @WebMvcTest moved to org.springframework.boot.webmvc.test.autoconfigure and @DataJpaTest to org.springframework.boot.data.jpa.test.autoconfigure, confirmed in the 4.0.0 JARs. You also need the matching test modules. @MockBean and @SpyBean are gone in Boot 4: use @MockitoBean and @MockitoSpyBean from Spring Framework 6.2 and later, in org.springframework.test.context.bean.override.mockito.

@WebMvcTest and MockMvc

MockMvc sends requests through the full Spring MVC stack without a real server: dispatching, JSON conversion, validation, exception handlers. So it tests what a plain unit test on the controller can't: the URL mapping, status codes, and the JSON shape.

@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
    @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
    @MockitoBean UserService service;     // the controller's dependency

    @Test
    void returnsUser() throws Exception {
        when(service.find(1L)).thenReturn(new UserResponse(1L, "Ann"));

        mvc.perform(get("/users/1").accept(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON))
           .andExpect(status().isOk())
           .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Ann"));
    }

    @Test
    void rejectsInvalidBody() throws Exception {
        mvc.perform(post("/users").contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON)
                .content("""
                    {"name": ""}
                    """))
           .andExpect(status().isBadRequest());
        verifyNoInteractions(service);
    }
}

With Spring Security on the class path, the filter chain is active, so tests get 401 or 403. Use @WithMockUser from spring-security-test, and .with(csrf()) on POST requests when CSRF protection is on. Spring Framework 6.2 also added MockMvcTester, an AssertJ-style API.

@DataJpaTest

@DataJpaTest
class OrderRepositoryTest {
    @Autowired TestEntityManager em;
    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;

    @Test
    void findsOverdue() {
        em.persistAndFlush(new Order(Status.OPEN, Instant.parse("2026-01-01T00:00:00Z")));
        em.clear();     // so the query hits the DB, not the first-level cache

        assertThat(repo.findByStatus(Status.OPEN)).hasSize(1);
    }
}

Each test runs in a transaction that rolls back at the end. By default the data source is replaced with an embedded database, if one is on the class path. To test on a real database, add @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) with Testcontainers. Forgetting flush and clear is the classic mistake: without them, you may be asserting against Hibernate's cache and the SQL never runs, so constraint errors go unnoticed. What's worth testing here is custom queries, mappings and constraints, not Spring Data's save.

@SpringBootTest

@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class OrderFlowIT { /* MockMvc, or a real HTTP client against the port */ }
webEnvironmentMeaning
MOCK (default)Mock servlet environment, no real port. Use with MockMvc
RANDOM_PORTA real embedded server on a free port
DEFINED_PORTA real server on the configured port
NONENo web environment

Context caching: Spring caches contexts between test classes, keyed by configuration. Each different set of @MockitoBeans, properties or profiles creates a new context, which is the main cause of slow test suites. @DirtiesContext throws one away, and it's expensive. Use a shared base class with one configuration.

Rollback trap: @Transactional on a RANDOM_PORT test doesn't roll back the server's work, because the server handles requests on different threads and in its own transactions. Clean up explicitly. The rollback may also hide bugs, as code that requires a commit, or a lazy load outside a transaction, behaves differently in the test.

Also useful: @ActiveProfiles, @TestPropertySource, @Sql, @TestConfiguration, and @DynamicPropertySource.

Testcontainers

H2 isn't PostgreSQL: its SQL dialect, JSON columns, locking and constraints all differ, so tests can pass on H2 and fail in production. Testcontainers starts real dependencies in throwaway Docker containers from your test code.

@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryIT {

    @Container
    @ServiceConnection            // Spring Boot 3.1+: connection details are wired automatically
    static PostgreSQLContainer postgres = new PostgreSQLContainer("postgres:17-alpine");

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;

    @Test
    void savesAndLoads() { /* real SQL against real PostgreSQL */ }
}

// Before @ServiceConnection, or for custom properties
@DynamicPropertySource
static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
    r.add("spring.datasource.url", postgres::getJdbcUrl);
    r.add("spring.datasource.username", postgres::getUsername);
    r.add("spring.datasource.password", postgres::getPassword);
}

The example uses Testcontainers 2.x. Its artifacts now have a testcontainers- prefix, for example org.testcontainers:testcontainers-postgresql and testcontainers-junit-jupiter. The class org.testcontainers.postgresql.PostgreSQLContainer is non-generic. In 1.x it's org.testcontainers.containers.PostgreSQLContainer<>, which code you'll meet today still uses.

  • A static @Container is shared within a class. An instance field restarts for every test.
  • Share one container across classes using the singleton container pattern: start it in a static block of a base class. Ryuk, a helper container, removes it at the end.
  • It needs a Docker-compatible runtime in CI.
  • Modules exist for Kafka, Redis, MongoDB and others. WireMock fills the same role for external HTTP APIs.

Coverage with JaCoCo

JaCoCo attaches a Java agent that instruments bytecode at class load, records which instructions ran, and produces a report.

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.jacoco</groupId>
  <artifactId>jacoco-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <version>0.8.16</version>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals><goal>prepare-agent</goal></goals>     <!-- sets the argLine property -->
    </execution>
    <execution>
      <id>report</id>
      <phase>verify</phase>
      <goals><goal>report</goal></goals>            <!-- target/site/jacoco -->
    </execution>
    <execution>
      <id>check</id>
      <goals><goal>check</goal></goals>
      <configuration>
        <rules><rule><limits><limit>
          <counter>BRANCH</counter>
          <value>COVEREDRATIO</value>
          <minimum>0.70</minimum>
        </limit></limits></rule></rules>
      </configuration>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>
CounterMeasures
InstructionsBytecode instructions run. Independent of source formatting
BranchesBoth sides of each if and switch
Lines, methods, classesReached at least once
ComplexityCyclomatic complexity covered
Gotcha: If you configure <argLine> in Surefire yourself, you'll overwrite the property JaCoCo set, and coverage shows 0%. Use <argLine>@{argLine} -Xmx1g</argLine>.

Coverage is a negative indicator: low coverage shows what's untested, but high coverage proves nothing. A test without assertions counts fully. Mutation testing (PIT) changes your code, and checks whether a test fails. Surviving mutants reveal weak tests.

WireMock: Testing Calls to External HTTP APIs

Mocking your own RestClient/WebClient wrapper proves nothing about JSON mapping, headers, timeouts or error handling. WireMock starts a real HTTP server with stubbed responses, so the real client code runs end to end. It can also simulate delays and broken connections to test timeouts and retries.

@SpringBootTest
@WireMockTest(httpPort = 8089)          // JUnit 5 extension from wiremock
class LabResultClientTest {

    @DynamicPropertySource
    static void props(DynamicPropertyRegistry r) {
        r.add("lab.base-url", () -> "http://localhost:8089");
    }

    @Autowired LabResultClient client;

    @Test
    void mapsResult() {
        stubFor(get(urlEqualTo("/results/42"))
            .willReturn(okJson("""
                {"id": 42, "status": "FINAL", "value": 5.4}
                """)));

        assertThat(client.fetch(42).status()).isEqualTo("FINAL");
        verify(getRequestedFor(urlEqualTo("/results/42"))
            .withHeader("Authorization", matching("Bearer .*")));
    }

    @Test
    void timesOut() {
        stubFor(get(anyUrl()).willReturn(ok().withFixedDelay(5_000)));
        assertThatThrownBy(() -> client.fetch(1)).isInstanceOf(ResourceAccessException.class);   // RestClient wraps I/O timeouts (needs a read timeout below 5 s)
    }
}

Alternatives: MockRestServiceServer (in-process, only for RestTemplate/RestClient), MockWebServer (OkHttp), or contract tests when you also own the provider.

ArchUnit: Testing the Architecture

Rules like "controllers must not call repositories directly" or "domain must not depend on Spring" erode silently. ArchUnit checks them as ordinary JUnit tests by analysing compiled bytecode.

@AnalyzeClasses(packages = "com.acme.clinic")
class ArchitectureTest {
    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule layers = layeredArchitecture().consideringAllDependencies()
        .layer("Web").definedBy("..web..")
        .layer("Service").definedBy("..service..")
        .layer("Persistence").definedBy("..repository..")
        .whereLayer("Web").mayNotBeAccessedByAnyLayer()
        .whereLayer("Service").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Web")
        .whereLayer("Persistence").mayOnlyBeAccessedByLayers("Service");

    @ArchTest
    static final ArchRule noFieldInjection = noFields().should().beAnnotatedWith(Autowired.class);
}

Readable Tests: Naming, Builders and One Behaviour per Test

  • Name the behaviour, not the method: rejectsAppointmentInThePast() or @DisplayName("rejects an appointment in the past"), rather than testCreate2().
  • One behaviour per test: several assertions are fine if they describe one outcome (use assertAll or AssertJ soft assertions); separate scenarios belong in separate tests.
  • Test data builders / Object Mother: hide irrelevant setup so each test shows only what matters. Defaults are valid; each test overrides what it is about.
  • Avoid logic (loops, ifs) in tests, and avoid sharing mutable fixtures between tests.
class PatientBuilder {
    private String name = "Test Patient";
    private LocalDate dob = LocalDate.of(1990, 1, 1);
    private boolean active = true;
    static PatientBuilder aPatient() { return new PatientBuilder(); }
    PatientBuilder born(LocalDate d) { dob = d; return this; }
    PatientBuilder inactive() { active = false; return this; }
    Patient build() { return new Patient(name, dob, active); }
}

@Test void inactivePatientCannotBook() {
    var p = aPatient().inactive().build();
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> booking.book(p, slot)).isInstanceOf(InactivePatientException.class);
}

Interview Questions — Testing

What is the test pyramid, and when would you deviate from it?

Many unit tests, fewer integration tests, and a few end-to-end tests, since cost and fragility rise as you go up. Deviate when the risk is elsewhere. A thin CRUD service has little logic but a lot of SQL and wiring, so more integration tests with a real database (a shape sometimes called the "testing diamond") find more bugs than many mock-heavy unit tests.

Unit test vs integration test: where's the boundary?

A unit test exercises a unit in isolation, in memory, and doesn't touch I/O. An integration test checks that components work together with real infrastructure: SQL actually runs, JSON actually serializes. A class using a mock repository can pass while the query itself is broken. You need both.

What's the difference between JUnit Platform, Jupiter and Vintage?

Platform launches tests and defines the TestEngine API that IDEs and build tools use. Jupiter is the modern API and its engine. Vintage is an engine for old JUnit 3 and 4 tests. Splitting them means a new framework can run on the same platform, and tools don't depend on test-writing APIs.

What changed in JUnit 6?

It's an evolution of the same Jupiter API rather than a rewrite. All modules now share one version number, the minimum is Java 17, and Vintage is deprecated. Existing Jupiter tests generally keep working after a dependency change. Check the release notes for removed deprecated APIs.

Output: in what order do these callbacks run, and what does n print?

See the LifeTest run in the Lifecycle section. beforeAll runs once; then, for each test, ctor, beforeEach, the test, afterEach; then afterAll once. beforeEach prints n=0 every time, as each test gets a new instance. With @TestInstance(PER_CLASS), one instance is shared, so n would keep growing.

Why does JUnit create a new instance per test method?

To isolate tests: state in instance fields can't leak from one test to another, so tests can run in any order. That's why fields in a test class don't need resetting. Static fields are shared, so avoid mutable statics. A static counter in the constructor counted 24 instances in a run of 25 tests, showing that each test and each parameterized invocation gets its own.

@BeforeEach vs @BeforeAll? Why must @BeforeAll be static?

@BeforeEach runs before each test, on that test's instance. @BeforeAll runs once for the class, before any instance exists, so it has to be static. Under PER_CLASS, an instance exists first, so it needn't be. Use @BeforeAll for expensive shared setup, such as starting a server.

assertThrows vs assertThrowsExactly vs the JUnit 4 expected attribute?

assertThrows passes for the type or any subclass, and returns the exception. assertThrowsExactly needs the exact type: assertThrowsExactly(RuntimeException.class, ...) fails if an IllegalStateException is thrown, as a test run confirmed. JUnit 4's expected covered the whole method, so an exception from the setup lines could pass the test by mistake.

What's the difference between assertAll and consecutive assertions?

Normal assertions stop at the first failure. assertAll runs every one, and reports them together as a MultipleFailuresError. In a run, two failing assertions reported getFailures().size() == 2. It's handy when checking several properties of one result.

Assertion vs assumption?

A failed assertion means the test failed. A failed assumption aborts the test, which shows as skipped: a run displayed Assumption failed: skip. Use assumptions for environment preconditions that don't reflect a bug, such as a required external tool. Too many skipped tests hide problems, so use conditions and tags with care.

How would you test a method with many input combinations?

Use @ParameterizedTest with @CsvSource for readable tables, or @MethodSource for complex objects. Include boundary values, null, empty, and invalid inputs. Use @NullAndEmptySource for strings. Give a name so reports show which case failed. For properties that should hold for all inputs, jqwik offers property-based tests.

Output: what does this @CsvSource pass in?
@CsvSource({"1,one", "2,'two, x'", "3,"})
void csv(int a, String b) { System.out.println(a + "=" + b); }

It prints 1=one, 2=two, x, 3=null. Single quotes protect the comma. An empty unquoted value is null, and an empty quoted value '' would be an empty string.

Mock vs stub vs spy vs fake?

A stub returns canned data. A mock also verifies interactions. A spy wraps a real object and can override parts. A fake is a light working implementation, such as an in-memory repository. Stubs support state verification (checking the result) and mocks support behaviour verification (checking the call). State verification breaks less on refactoring.

What do Mockito mocks return for unstubbed methods?

Defaults: 0 for numbers, false for boolean, null for objects, and empty for collections, Optional and Stream. Arrays return null. That's the behaviour of RETURNS_DEFAULTS. So a forgotten stub can give an NPE far from the mock, in the code under test.

Output: what does this print?
when(m.find(anyInt())).thenReturn("a", "b");
System.out.println(m.find(1) + m.find(1) + m.find(1));

It prints abb. Consecutive values are consumed in order, and the last repeats.

Why does when(spy.get(0)) throw on an empty list? How do you fix it?

Java evaluates the argument of when() first, which calls the real get(0) on the real list, throwing IndexOutOfBoundsException. Use doReturn("a").when(spy).get(0), where when(spy) returns a stubbing proxy, and .get(0) on that isn't real. The same form is used for void methods.

What's the error here? when(t.f(anyInt(), "x")).thenReturn("y");

It throws InvalidUseOfMatchersException. Matchers register state on a stack, and Mockito needs one matcher per argument. Mixing a raw value breaks the count. Use eq("x"). A related error is using a matcher outside when or verify.

any() vs any(String.class)?

any() matches anything, including null. any(String.class) does a type check, and doesn't match null, since Mockito 2. So if the code passes null, the second doesn't match, and the stub isn't applied.

How does @InjectMocks decide how to inject? What are the pitfalls?

It tries the biggest constructor, then setters, then fields, in that order. It stays silent if it can't resolve something. Two mocks of the same type are matched by field name. Since constructor injection is used if possible, adding a new dependency passes null to it, so you get an NPE, not a compile error. Direct new in a setup method is more honest.

What are strict stubs? What is UnnecessaryStubbingException?

Strictness makes Mockito fail tests that have unused stubs (UnnecessaryStubbingException), and report argument mismatches from production code (PotentialStubbingProblem). It's the default with MockitoExtension. It's useful because stale stubs mislead readers. Common cause: shared stubs in @BeforeEach that only some tests use. Fix by moving them, or marking as lenient() if they're truly shared.

How do you test code using LocalDateTime.now() or UUID.randomUUID()?

Best: inject the dependency. Pass a java.time.Clock and use LocalDateTime.now(clock), with Clock.fixed(...) in tests. For IDs, inject a Supplier<UUID>. mockStatic is available for legacy code, but mocking java.time classes is fragile, and core JDK types can break, as the stack overflow with ArrayList showed.

How does Mockito mock final classes and static methods?

The default mock maker before version 5 created subclasses, so it couldn't override final members. The inline mock maker, default since Mockito 5, uses the instrumentation API to rewrite class bytecode, adding interception into the real class, with a per-thread check for active mocks. That's why static mocks are scoped to one thread.

How would you verify an object created inside the method under test?

Use ArgumentCaptor at the mock that receives it, then assert on its fields. If there's no collaborator to capture from, either the behaviour is visible in the return value, which you should test, or the class should get a factory.

How would you test a private method?

You normally don't. Test it through the public method that uses it. If it's complex enough to need its own tests, that's a sign it belongs in its own class with a public API. Reflection tests couple you to implementation details and block refactoring.

How do you test a method that runs asynchronously?

Split the logic into a synchronous method and test that directly. To test the async path, use CompletableFuture.get(timeout), or Awaitility for polling: await().atMost(5, SECONDS).until(...). Never use fixed Thread.sleep, which causes slow and flaky tests. For an @Async method in Spring, a synchronous TaskExecutor in the test config helps too.

What is a flaky test? What causes them, and what do you do about them?

A test that passes and fails with no code change. Causes: time and timing (sleep, midnight, time zones), shared state or data between tests, reliance on order (HashMap iteration), external services, and concurrency. Treat it as a bug. Quarantine it so the main build stays trustworthy, reproduce by running it repeatedly, then fix the cause. Don't just add retries, which train people to ignore failures.

@WebMvcTest vs @SpringBootTest with MockMvc?

@WebMvcTest loads only the web layer, so services must be replaced with @MockitoBean. It starts quickly and tests HTTP concerns. @SpringBootTest plus @AutoConfigureMockMvc loads everything, running through real services to the database: slower, higher confidence. A typical split is mostly slices, with a few full-flow tests.

@Mock vs @MockitoBean (and the old @MockBean)?

@Mock creates a Mockito mock without Spring, for plain unit tests. @MockitoBean puts a mock into the Spring context, replacing the bean of that type. It came with Spring Framework 6.2, and @MockBean was deprecated in Boot 3.4 and removed in Boot 4. Changing the set of mock beans creates a new cached context, so many varied combinations slow the suite.

Why does my @WebMvcTest fail with "No qualifying bean of type UserService"?

The slice doesn't scan @Service beans, so the controller's dependency is missing. Add @MockitoBean UserService. If @SpringBootApplication has extra annotations such as @EnableJpaAuditing, these apply to slices too, and can fail for the same reason. Move them to a separate @Configuration class.

Why might a repository test pass with H2 and fail in production?

Differences in SQL dialect, native queries, JSON and array types, case sensitivity, index and locking behaviour, and migrations written for PostgreSQL or MySQL. Also, Hibernate may generate H2 schema with ddl-auto while production uses Flyway. Use Testcontainers with the same database version and run your real migrations.

In @DataJpaTest, why call flush() and clear()?

Within one transaction, persist may not issue SQL yet, and a read may be served from the persistence context. So constraints wouldn't fire and mappings wouldn't be exercised. flush() sends the SQL, clear() empties the cache, and the following read really hits the database. Since the test rolls back, nothing persists.

Is it a good idea to put @Transactional on tests?

It gives automatic cleanup, but changes what you test. The test's transaction wraps the service's, so REQUIRES_NEW, commit-time constraints, @TransactionalEventListener and lazy-loading failures behave differently. With a real HTTP port, it doesn't roll back the server's work at all. Many teams prefer no test transaction for integration tests, and clean the tables with @Sql or truncation.

How does Spring's test context cache work, and how do you speed up a slow test suite?

The cache key combines configuration classes, profiles, properties, and mock definitions. Identical configurations reuse one context. To speed up: use slices, a shared base class, avoid @DirtiesContext, reduce varied @MockitoBean sets, share containers, and run in parallel where safe (Surefire forks or JUnit parallel execution). Also separate unit tests from integration tests so that feedback comes first.

What's the difference between Surefire and Failsafe?

Surefire runs unit tests in the test phase, matching names like *Test. Failsafe runs integration tests, named *IT, in the integration-test phase, and reports failure in verify, so that post-integration-test cleanup still runs. Run with mvn verify.

What does Testcontainers do, and how do you keep it fast?

It runs real services in Docker for your test's duration, through the Docker API. To keep it fast, use one static container shared by all classes, so startup happens once. Use small images and a pinned version. Clean data between tests instead of restarting the container. Combine with @ServiceConnection to avoid wiring properties by hand.

Is 100% coverage a good goal?

No. It rewards tests of trivial code, and coverage doesn't show that behaviour was checked: a test with no assertions counts. Aim for strong coverage on business logic and branches, and use it to find gaps. A sensible team uses a threshold on new code, reviews test quality, and uses mutation testing on critical parts. Branch coverage says more than line coverage.

Is TDD always worthwhile?

It works well for domain logic, algorithms and bug fixes, where a failing test proves the bug first. It's less suited to exploratory prototypes and UI, or integration with an unknown API, where you learn first and then write tests. A balanced answer describes when you'd use it, not an absolute position.

Scenario: A test passes alone but fails when the whole suite runs. How do you debug it?

It's a test isolation problem. Suspect shared mutable state: static fields, a singleton, database rows left by another test, a cached Spring context altered by a @MockitoBean or a modified bean, or system properties. Bisect: run with the class before it to find the polluter. Check that data is cleaned up. ThreadLocal left set, such as SecurityContextHolder, is also a common cause.

Scenario: You've inherited a legacy class with no tests and static calls. How do you start?
  1. Write characterization tests that pin current behaviour at the highest usable level.
  2. Find a seam: extract a method or wrap static calls behind an interface.
  3. Use mockStatic as a temporary measure.
  4. Refactor in small steps, then replace with focused unit tests.

The aim is to make change safe rather than to reach a number.

Scenario: How would you test a Kafka consumer that writes to a database?

Unit-test the handler's logic with plain objects. Use @SpringBootTest with Testcontainers for Kafka and the database for one realistic flow: publish, then use Awaitility to wait for the row. Cover duplicate delivery (idempotency), poison messages going to the dead-letter topic, and retries. @EmbeddedKafka is a lighter alternative, though it's not the same as a real broker.

How do you test a service that calls a third-party REST API?

Unit-test the business logic with the client interface mocked. Then test the client itself against a WireMock server (or MockRestServiceServer): stub realistic JSON, assert the mapping, verify the request (path, headers, body), and simulate 4xx/5xx, slow responses and connection resets to prove timeouts, retries and error translation. Point the base URL at WireMock with @DynamicPropertySource. Never call the real third-party API in automated tests.

What is ArchUnit and why would you use it?

A library that turns architecture rules into JUnit tests by inspecting bytecode: layer dependencies, no cycles between packages, naming conventions (*Controller only in web), no field injection, domain free of framework imports. It makes code review rules enforceable in CI, which matters most in large or hexagonal codebases.

Your tests have 40 lines of setup each and break whenever a constructor changes. How do you fix that?

Introduce test data builders (or an Object Mother) with valid defaults, so tests set only the fields relevant to the scenario and constructor changes are fixed in one place. Move shared Spring context setup into a common base or @TestConfiguration without breaking context caching, and check whether the class under test simply has too many dependencies, which is a design smell the tests are exposing.

Should a unit test have only one assertion?

The real rule is one behaviour per test. Checking several fields of one result is fine; use assertAll or AssertJ SoftAssertions so you see every failure at once. What to avoid is a test that exercises several scenarios in sequence, because the first failure hides the rest and the name can't describe what broke.

Maven, Gradle & Logging Tooling

How a Java project is built, how dependency conflicts are resolved and fixed, what is inside the JAR you deploy, and how to log properly in production. Dependency resolution examples were run with Maven 3.9 and Gradle 8.10, and logging examples with SLF4J 2 and Logback 1.5.

What a build tool does

A real project needs more than javac: downloading libraries with the right versions, compiling, running tests, packaging, and publishing. Doing that with scripts is fragile. Maven replaces scripts with a declarative project description and a standard project layout: you state what the project is, and conventions define how it's built. Gradle does the same with a programmable build script.

my-app/
  pom.xml
  mvnw, mvnw.cmd, .mvn/wrapper/      Maven wrapper
  src/main/java/                     application code
  src/main/resources/                config, included in the JAR
  src/test/java/                     tests, excluded from the JAR
  src/test/resources/
  target/                            build output, not committed

Maven: the POM and coordinates

The POM (Project Object Model) in pom.xml describes the project. Every artifact is identified by its coordinates, often written groupId:artifactId:version (GAV).

<project xmlns="http://maven.apache.org/POM/4.0.0">
  <modelVersion>4.0.0</modelVersion>

  <parent>                                  <!-- inherit config -->
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-parent</artifactId>
    <version>4.0.0</version>
  </parent>

  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>                <!-- organization, reversed domain -->
  <artifactId>orders</artifactId>            <!-- project name -->
  <version>1.4.0-SNAPSHOT</version>
  <packaging>jar</packaging>                 <!-- jar is the default; also war, pom -->

  <properties>
    <java.version>21</java.version>
    <project.build.sourceEncoding>UTF-8</project.build.sourceEncoding>
  </properties>

  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.postgresql</groupId>
      <artifactId>postgresql</artifactId>
      <scope>runtime</scope>                <!-- version comes from the parent -->
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>

  <build>
    <plugins>
      <plugin>
        <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
        <artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
      </plugin>
    </plugins>
  </build>
</project>

Every POM implicitly inherits from Maven's super POM, which sets the default layout and the Central repository. mvn help:effective-pom shows the final result, with inheritance merged. SNAPSHOT versions are in development and can change, so Maven re-checks for newer ones. Release versions are immutable. Never build a release on a SNAPSHOT dependency, since the same build can give different results next week.

Lifecycle, phases and goals

This is the most frequently confused part of Maven.

  • A lifecycle is a named sequence of phases. There are three: default (build), clean, and site.
  • A phase is a step in a lifecycle, such as test. A phase does nothing itself.
  • A goal is a task provided by a plugin, such as compiler:compile. Goals do the real work.
  • Binding: goals attach to phases, and the packaging type sets the default bindings.
PhaseWhat happens
validateCheck that the POM is correct
process-resourcesCopy src/main/resources to the output
compileCompile main code
test-compileCompile test code
testRun unit tests with Surefire
packageCreate the JAR or WAR
integration-testRun integration tests with Failsafe
verifyCheck results and quality gates
installCopy the artifact to the local repository, for other local projects
deployUpload to a remote repository, for other developers and CI
mvn clean verify                  # the usual CI command
mvn clean                         # lifecycle "clean": delete target/
mvn package -DskipTests           # compile tests but don't run them
mvn package -Dmaven.test.skip=true  # don't even compile tests
mvn test -Dtest=OrderServiceTest#placesOrder
mvn dependency:tree               # a goal called directly, no phase involved
mvn -pl orders-api -am verify     # one module, plus what it depends on
mvn -T 1C verify                  # parallel builds, one thread per core
mvn -U verify                     # force an update of snapshots
mvn -o verify                     # offline

mvn install is often used out of habit. In CI, mvn verify is enough unless another local build needs the artifact from ~/.m2.

Dependency scopes

A scope controls which class paths include a dependency, and whether it passes on to projects that depend on you.

ScopeCompileTestRun timeTransitive?Example
compile (default)YesYesYesYesSpring, Guava
providedYesYesNo: the container supplies itNoServlet API, Lombok
runtimeNoYesYesYesJDBC drivers
testTests onlyYesNoNoJUnit, Mockito
systemLike provided, with a local path. Deprecated, avoid itNone
importOnly in dependencyManagement, for type pom. Imports a BOM's version listSpring Boot BOM

When a dependency is itself pulled in transitively, the two scopes combine. If you depend on A with compile and A depends on B with runtime, you get B with runtime. If your dependency on A is test, then B is test. A provided or test dependency of A doesn't reach you at all.

Why a runtime scope? Your code uses only the JDBC API at compile time, so a runtime scope stops anyone accidentally importing driver-specific classes.

Transitive resolution and nearest-wins

If you depend on A and A depends on B, B is downloaded too. Across a tree, two paths may ask for different versions of one library. Only one can be on the class path. Maven's rule is dependency mediation:

  1. Nearest definition wins: the version closest to your project in the tree is chosen. A direct dependency always wins.
  2. Tie: at equal depth, the one declared first in the POM wins.

Note what this doesn't do: it doesn't choose the highest version. So this can silently downgrade a library. Real output, with a direct commons-lang3:3.9 alongside commons-text:1.10.0, which needs 3.12.0:

$ mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose
demo:p1:jar:1.0
+- org.apache.commons:commons-text:jar:1.10.0:compile
|  \- (org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:jar:3.12.0:compile - omitted for conflict with 3.9)
\- org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:jar:3.9:compile

commons-text was compiled against 3.12.0 and will now run on 3.9. If it calls a method added in between, you get NoSuchMethodError at run time. It's the most common cause of that error in Spring projects. Gradle resolved the identical case to the higher version:

+--- org.apache.commons:commons-text:1.10.0
|    \--- org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:3.12.0
\--- org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:3.9 -> 3.12.0

Controlling dependencies

<!-- Exclude a transitive dependency -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  <exclusions>
    <exclusion>
      <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-tomcat</artifactId>
    </exclusion>
  </exclusions>
</dependency>

<!-- Optional: needed to build me, but users must opt in -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>redis-support</artifactId>
  <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

dependencyManagement and BOMs

<dependencies> adds a dependency. <dependencyManagement> only sets the version to use, in case it appears, and adds nothing to the class path. A parent POM uses it to keep all its modules consistent, and modules then declare a dependency with no version.

A managed version also overrides transitive versions, which beats the nearest-wins rule. With commons-lang3 managed to 3.14.0, this run's tree shows:

demo:p2:jar:1.0
\- org.apache.commons:commons-text:jar:1.10.0:compile
   \- org.apache.commons:commons-lang3:jar:3.14.0:compile

A BOM (Bill of Materials) is a POM holding only a dependencyManagement list of versions known to work together. You import it, and leave versions out of your own dependencies.

<dependencyManagement>
  <dependencies>
    <dependency>
      <groupId>org.springframework.cloud</groupId>
      <artifactId>spring-cloud-dependencies</artifactId>
      <version>${spring-cloud.version}</version>
      <type>pom</type>
      <scope>import</scope>
    </dependency>
  </dependencies>
</dependencyManagement>
Parent POMBOM import
How many?Only oneSeveral
InheritsEverything: properties, plugin config, versionsOnly dependency versions
Typical usespring-boot-starter-parentYour company parent plus spring-boot-dependencies

With the Spring Boot parent, override a version through its property, such as <jackson-bom.version>, rather than adding a version on a single artifact. If your company has its own parent, import spring-boot-dependencies as a BOM instead.

Order matters: if two BOMs manage the same artifact, the first one imported wins, and anything in your own POM's dependencyManagement beats both. Use maven-enforcer-plugin rules such as dependencyConvergence or requireUpperBoundDeps to fail a build on conflicts rather than hope.

Multi-module projects

A multi-module build shares configuration, and builds related components together. The parent has pom packaging and lists modules. The reactor is the Maven component that sorts them by dependency, and builds them in that order.

<!-- parent pom.xml -->
<groupId>com.acme</groupId>
<artifactId>shop</artifactId>
<version>${revision}</version>
<packaging>pom</packaging>
<modules>
  <module>shop-domain</module>
  <module>shop-api</module>
  <module>shop-app</module>
</modules>
<properties><revision>1.0.0-SNAPSHOT</revision></properties>

<!-- shop-app/pom.xml -->
<parent>
  <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
  <artifactId>shop</artifactId>
  <version>${revision}</version>
</parent>
<artifactId>shop-app</artifactId>
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>com.acme</groupId>
    <artifactId>shop-domain</artifactId>
    <version>${project.version}</version>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>

Two different ideas are often confused. Inheritance (<parent>) means a child takes configuration. Aggregation (<modules>) means building them together. The same POM usually does both, but needn't. Module cycles are forbidden. -pl picks modules, -am also builds what they depend on, and -amd builds what depends on them. When using ${revision}, add the flatten-maven-plugin, so that published POMs have real versions.

Plugins

PluginPurpose
maven-compiler-pluginCompiles. Set <release>21</release>. Annotation processors such as Lombok and MapStruct go in annotationProcessorPaths
maven-resources-pluginCopies and optionally filters resources
maven-surefire-pluginUnit tests: *Test, *Tests, Test*
maven-failsafe-pluginIntegration tests: *IT. Must be declared with its goals
maven-jar-pluginBuilds a plain JAR
maven-shade-pluginFat JAR by merging classes, with package relocation
spring-boot-maven-pluginrepackage for the executable JAR, build-image for OCI images, run
maven-enforcer-pluginEnforces rules: Java version, dependency convergence
jacoco-maven-pluginCode coverage
versions-maven-pluginReports available updates
