The default is 30 minutes in Tomcat; <session-timeout> takes minutes and setMaxInactiveInterval takes seconds (30 in web.xml reported 1800 at runtime). The JSESSIONID cookie normally has no max-age, so the browser deletes it when closed, leaving the server copy to expire. In web.xml a timeout of zero or less means the session never times out, and that's a memory leak.

What is session fixation and how do you prevent it?

The attacker gets a valid session ID and tricks the victim into using it, for instance through a ;jsessionid= link. After the victim logs in, that same ID is authenticated and the attacker can use it. Change the ID at login with req.changeSessionId(), which keeps the attributes. Spring Security does this by default. Also disable URL tracking with <tracking-mode>COOKIE</tracking-mode>.

How are cookies and sessions different?

A cookie is a small value stored by the browser (about 4 KB per cookie), visible to the client and sent with each request. A session is data held on the server and found through an ID, usually inside a cookie. Sensitive data belongs in the session, or in a signed or encrypted token if stateless.

Can a filter run without a servlet? What about for a static file?

Yes. The chain always ends at some resource, and for static files that's the container's default servlet, so /* filters run for CSS and images. A filter can also generate the entire response itself and never call the chain.

Why doesn't my filter run on a forward?

A filter's default dispatcher type is REQUEST only. Add it: @WebFilter(urlPatterns = "/*", dispatcherTypes = {DispatcherType.REQUEST, DispatcherType.FORWARD}), or <dispatcher>FORWARD</dispatcher> in the mapping. Be careful to avoid double work: a filter that runs on both will run twice for one user request, and OncePerRequestFilter guards against this.

Why can't you set a response header after chain.doFilter()?

Often the servlet has written enough to flush, or the container has committed the response, so headers have gone. Calls to setHeader on a committed response are silently ignored. Solutions: set the header before the chain, or pass a response wrapper with a buffer so nothing commits until you decide.

How would you compress or modify a response in a filter?

Pass a HttpServletResponseWrapper down the chain. Override getWriter and getOutputStream so that the servlet writes into your stream, a GZIPOutputStream or an in-memory buffer. After the chain returns, finish the stream or transform the buffer and write it to the real response. It's the Decorator pattern. In practice, enable compression in the connector (server.compression.enabled=true) or at the proxy.

How do you log request bodies in a filter without breaking the app?

The body stream can only be read once. Wrap the request in a class that buffers the bytes and returns a fresh ServletInputStream on each getInputStream call, or use Spring's ContentCachingRequestWrapper, which caches as the application reads, so you log after chain.doFilter. Cap the size, skip multipart, and mask passwords.

How can 10,000 clients stay connected to a Tomcat with 200 threads?

The NIO connector separates connections from threads. Idle keep-alive sockets are watched by one Poller using a Selector. A worker is used only while a request is being processed. maxConnections (8192 by default) limits open sockets and maxThreads (200) limits active processing. If all 200 workers are busy, ready sockets wait for a free worker. Blocking calls in your code are what really exhaust the pool.

Tomcat is up but requests hang. How do you diagnose it?
  1. Take a thread dump (jstack, jcmd <pid> Thread.print) and look at the http-nio-*-exec-* threads.
  2. If all are in HikariPool.getConnection, the DB pool is exhausted, probably from a leak or slow queries.
  3. If they're in socket read, a downstream call has no timeout.
  4. If they're BLOCKED on a monitor, there's a contention point such as a synchronized method.
  5. Check the busy-thread count via JMX or Actuator (tomcat.threads.busy).
  6. Fix the cause: timeouts, query tuning, a bulkhead around slow dependencies. Raising maxThreads alone only delays failure.
Does async processing make the request faster?

No, the client waits just as long, and each request has some added overhead. It improves throughput under waiting by releasing the container thread during slow I/O. It helps only if the wait doesn't merely move to another thread: 200 tasks on an executor that blocks 200 threads has saved nothing unless those threads use non-blocking I/O or are virtual threads. For CPU-bound work it gives no benefit.

What's the difference between AsyncContext.complete() and dispatch()?

complete() means the response is finished, so the container commits and ends the request. dispatch() re-enters the container on a container thread with DispatcherType.ASYNC so a servlet or JSP can produce the output. Filters run again if they include ASYNC. Spring MVC uses dispatch() for Callable: the worker gets the result, then a second pass through DispatcherServlet renders it. Calling neither makes the request hang until the timeout.

How do virtual threads change servlet thread safety and pool sizing?

Thread safety is unchanged: the same servlet instance is still shared and fields are still dangerous. Sizing changes: with one cheap virtual thread per request (Java 21+), maxThreads stops being the limit, so the limit moves to other resources such as the DB pool. Concurrency may need explicit limits (a Semaphore) to protect downstream systems. Heavy use of per-thread caches stops making sense. Java 21 pins a virtual thread to its carrier inside synchronized blocks during blocking; Java 24 removed that limitation for most cases.

How do you share data between two servlets?

Pick the narrowest scope. Request attributes when forwarding; session attributes for one user's requests; ServletContext attributes for the whole app on one node; a database or cache for everything across nodes. Query params or cookies are for carrying small data over a redirect.

Can you call one servlet's doGet from another directly?

It's a protected method, and the servlet instance is owned by the container, so direct calls are wrong: you'd bypass filters and any setup. Use a RequestDispatcher, or better, move the shared logic to a plain service class called by both servlets.

How do you deliver a file download from a servlet?
res.setContentType("application/pdf");
res.setHeader("Content-Disposition", "attachment; filename=\"invoice.pdf\"");
res.setContentLengthLong(Files.size(path));
try (OutputStream out = res.getOutputStream()) { Files.copy(path, out); }

It uses getOutputStream because the data is binary, and a stream copy so that the whole file isn't held in memory. The file's path must not come straight from user input. Content-Disposition: inline shows it in the browser instead.

What's a RequestDispatcher, and how do you get a named one?

An object wrapping a target resource that can be forwarded to or included. req.getRequestDispatcher(path) accepts a relative path. ctx.getRequestDispatcher(path) needs a leading /. ctx.getNamedDispatcher("servletName") locates by name. All return null if nothing matches. With a named dispatcher the forward attributes aren't set, because the path doesn't change.

Why is a servlet in a WAR unreachable under WEB-INF, and why is that useful?

The container refuses direct client requests for WEB-INF and META-INF content. But a server-side forward can reach them. So put JSPs in /WEB-INF/views/ and users must go through a controller that does authorisation and loads data, instead of opening the view directly.

Explain the startup of a Spring Boot embedded Tomcat app in servlet terms.
  1. Spring Boot creates the application context, then an embedded Tomcat object through TomcatServletWebServerFactory.
  2. It adds a Context and registers all ServletContextInitializer beans.
  3. DispatcherServletRegistrationBean maps DispatcherServlet to /, and each Filter bean is registered through FilterRegistrationBean or by default adaptation.
  4. Boot's embedded setup doesn't scan for @WebServlet unless you add @ServletComponentScan, and ServletContainerInitializer from the classpath isn't run by default.

So the servlet model is intact, only inverted: the app starts the container, and not the other way around.

A @WebServlet returns 404 after deployment. Checklist?
  • Context path wrong? The URL needs /app/x, not /x, unless deployed as ROOT.
  • Was the class deployed, and is it in WEB-INF/classes?
  • metadata-complete="true" in web.xml turns scanning off.
  • Is it a javax.servlet class on Tomcat 10+? The container won't recognise it, so the annotation is ignored.
  • In Spring Boot, is @ServletComponentScan missing?
  • Did startup fail? Check catalina.out.
Design: how would you implement a rate limiter or request ID in the servlet layer?

Use a filter, since it runs before all servlets, can reject early and can see the raw request. For request ID: read or generate an ID, put it in the MDC (Mapped Diagnostic Context, a logging ThreadLocal), add it to the response header before chain.doFilter, and clear the MDC in finally. For rate limiting: key by authenticated user or a trusted client IP, count in Redis so that all nodes share the limit, and return 429 with Retry-After. Don't call the chain when the limit is hit. Order it after authentication if you key by user, and consider async requests where the MDC doesn't propagate.

What's the difference between a web server, a servlet container, and an application server?

A web server (nginx, Apache httpd) serves static content and proxies. A servlet container (Tomcat, Jetty) runs the servlet, JSP, EL and WebSocket specs. An application server (WildFly, Payara) implements Jakarta EE fully, with CDI, JPA, JMS and JTA. Tomcat also includes an HTTP server, so nginx in front is optional but common for TLS, caching and load balancing.

no-cache vs no-store?

no-store means the response must not be stored anywhere, which is right for sensitive data. no-cache means it may be stored but must be revalidated with the server (via ETag or Last-Modified) before each reuse, so a 304 can save bandwidth. For fingerprinted static files use a long max-age with immutable.

How do ETags and conditional requests work?

The server sends an ETag identifying the version of a resource. The client later sends If-None-Match: "etag"; if the version is unchanged the server returns 304 with no body. For updates, If-Match enables optimistic concurrency: a PUT with a stale ETag gets 412 Precondition Failed.

How does a WebSocket connection start, and how is it different from SSE?

It starts as an HTTP GET with Upgrade: websocket and Sec-WebSocket-Key; the server responds 101 Switching Protocols and the connection becomes a full-duplex message channel. SSE is one-way (server to client) over plain HTTP, with automatic reconnect, and is simpler through proxies. Use WebSockets for chat or collaborative editing, SSE for notifications and progress updates.

Why does getParameter() return null for a PUT with a form body?

The Servlet spec only requires the container to parse application/x-www-form-urlencoded bodies into parameters for POST. For PUT or PATCH, read the body yourself, use JSON, or in Spring add FormContentFilter (enabled by default in Spring Boot), which parses form bodies for PUT, PATCH and DELETE.

Why do non-English characters appear garbled?

The encoding wasn't set at the right time. setCharacterEncoding("UTF-8") must run before any parameter is read, and the response charset must be set before getWriter() is called. Also check the DB connection and column charset (utf8mb4) and the HTML meta charset. Spring Boot sets UTF-8 by default through its encoding filter.

How do you get the real client IP behind a load balancer?

Proxies put the original address in X-Forwarded-For (a comma-separated chain) or the standard Forwarded header. Configure Tomcat's RemoteIpValve or server.forward-headers-strategy=native/framework in Spring Boot with the trusted proxy ranges, so getRemoteAddr(), scheme and HTTPS detection are correct. Never trust the header blindly, because clients can spoof it.

How do you handle a CORS preflight in a servlet filter?

For non-simple requests (JSON body, custom headers like Authorization) the browser first sends OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method. The filter checks the origin against an allowlist, returns Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers and optionally -Max-Age with 200/204, and doesn't pass the preflight to the servlet. With cookies you need Allow-Credentials: true and a specific origin, never *. In Spring Security configure http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) with a CorsConfigurationSource bean so preflights aren't blocked by authentication.

Does HTTP/2 change how you write servlets?

Mostly no: the servlet API is the same, and the container handles multiplexing many streams over one connection, header compression and binary framing. Benefits are fewer connections and no head-of-line blocking at the HTTP level, which reduces the need for tricks like domain sharding and sprite bundling. Server push existed in Servlet 4 but browsers dropped it and it was deprecated, so don't rely on it. HTTP/2 is often terminated at the proxy or load balancer.

JSP View Layer

JavaServer Pages: HTML with Java tags. Under the hood every JSP is compiled into a servlet.

JSP Lifecycle

<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<h2>Welcome, ${user.name}</h2>          <%-- EL --%>
<c:forEach var="o" items="${orders}">
   <c:if test="${o.total > 100}"><b>${o.id}</b></c:if>
</c:forEach>
<jsp:include page="footer.jsp"/>

What JSP Is Today

JSP is now formally Jakarta Server Pages. The related specs are Jakarta Expression Language (EL) and Jakarta Standard Tag Library (JSTL, also called Jakarta Tags). Jakarta EE 11 has Pages 4.0 and EL 6.0, and Tomcat 11 implements them. JSP exists because writing HTML with out.println inside a servlet is unreadable. A JSP inverts this: it's a text file of HTML with small pieces of dynamic code, and a translator turns it into a servlet. New projects rarely choose it, but interviews still ask because many enterprise systems run on it, and because it tests your understanding of servlets.

Gotcha: Tomcat includes JSP and EL but not JSTL. You must add the JSTL API and implementation JARs to the WAR, or <%@ taglib %> fails with "cannot resolve taglib". The test app used jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl-api 3.0 plus the GlassFish implementation. With JSTL 3.0 the URIs are jakarta.tags.core and so on; older JSPs use http://java.sun.com/jsp/jstl/core.

Lifecycle and Translation in Detail

The diagram above shows the phases. Here's what is actually produced. The container's JSP engine (Jasper in Tomcat) is itself a servlet, JspServlet, mapped to *.jsp. It does the following on each request:

  1. Finds the generated class for that JSP.
  2. If there's none, or the .jsp is newer (checked in development mode), translates it into a Java source file. Translation also validates syntax and processes directives and static includes. JSP syntax errors appear here.
  3. Compiles the source. Java errors in scriptlets appear here. Tomcat uses the bundled Eclipse compiler by default, so a JRE is enough.
  4. Loads and instantiates the class, calls jspInit(), then calls _jspService().

Tomcat writes generated files under work/Catalina/<host>/<app>/org/apache/jsp/. Reading one is the fastest way to understand JSP. A hello.jsp becomes roughly this:

// Simplified output of Jasper for hello.jsp
public final class hello_jsp extends org.apache.jasper.runtime.HttpJspBase {
  // <%! declarations %> land here, as members of the class
  int hits = 0;

  public void _jspInit()    { }
  public void _jspDestroy() { }

  public void _jspService(HttpServletRequest request, HttpServletResponse response)
      throws IOException, ServletException {
    final PageContext pageContext;
    HttpSession session = null;
    final ServletContext application;
    final ServletConfig config;
    JspWriter out = null;
    final Object page = this;
    try {
      response.setContentType("text/html;charset=UTF-8");
      pageContext = _jspxFactory.getPageContext(this, request, response, null, true, 8192, true);
      application = pageContext.getServletContext();
      config = pageContext.getServletConfig();
      session = pageContext.getSession();
      out = pageContext.getOut();

      out.write("<h2>Welcome</h2>\n");        // template text
      int local = 0;                                    // <% scriptlet %>
      out.print(hits);                                  // <%= expression %>
    } catch (Throwable t) {
      // clears the buffer if possible, then pageContext.handlePageException(t)
    } finally {
      _jspxFactory.releasePageContext(pageContext);
    }
  }
}

This one listing explains many rules at a glance:

  • Implicit objects are local variables of _jspService. That's why they exist in scriptlets and expressions, but not in declarations (<%! %>), which sit at class level.
  • Scriptlet variables are locals too, so a page has one instance and many threads, just like any servlet, and <%! int hits %> is a shared instance field.
  • You can override jspInit() and jspDestroy() in a declaration, but you can't override _jspService, since the container generates it. The underscore marks it as off-limits.
<%! @Override public void jspInit() { /* e.g. read init params */ }
    @Override public void jspDestroy() { } %>

Precompilation

The first request to each JSP pays for translation and compilation, and a syntax error appears only when someone opens that page. To avoid both, precompile as part of the build with Tomcat's JspC (for example the Jasper Maven plugin) and add the generated servlets to web.xml, or hit the page with ?jsp_precompile=true after deployment. In production, set Jasper's development init param to false so it stops checking files on every request.

Implicit Objects in Detail

ObjectTypeScopeCommon use
requestHttpServletRequestrequestParams, attributes
responseHttpServletResponsepageHeaders, redirects
outJspWriterpageBuffered output
sessionHttpSessionsessionAbsent when session="false"
applicationServletContextapplicationShared attributes
configServletConfigpageInit params of the JSP
pageContextPageContextpageAccess to everything else; attribute lookup in any scope
pageObject (= this)pageRarely used
exceptionThrowablepageOnly when isErrorPage="true"

pageContext is a gateway to the others. pageContext.getAttribute("x", PageContext.SESSION_SCOPE) reads a specific scope, pageContext.findAttribute("x") searches page, request, session, application in order (this is what EL does), and it also has forward() and include().

JspWriter differs from PrintWriter: it has its own buffer, set with <%@ page buffer="16kb" %>, and autoFlush controls what happens when that fills up (flush if true, otherwise an IOException). Its print methods throw IOException, unlike PrintWriter, which hides errors. Setting buffer="none", or writing more than the buffer holds, commits the response early, and after that a forward or error page can't work.

Directives in Detail

Directives are instructions to the translator. They produce no output and act at translation time.

page attributeDefaultEffect
importjava.lang, jakarta.servlet.*, jakarta.servlet.http.*, jakarta.servlet.jsp.*Java imports. The only attribute you may repeat.
contentTypetext/htmlSets the response type and charset
pageEncodingISO-8859-1 (from contentType if given)Encoding of the JSP file itself
sessiontruefalse stops the page creating a session; the session object then doesn't exist
buffer8kbSize of the out buffer, or none
autoFlushtrueFlush when full, or throw if false
errorPagenonePage to forward to on an uncaught exception
isErrorPagefalseEnables the exception object
isELIgnoredfalsetrue prints ${x} literally
trimDirectiveWhitespacesfalseRemoves blank lines left by directives and scriptlets
extendsContainer classSuperclass for the generated servlet; rarely used
isThreadSafetrueDeprecated; relied on the removed SingleThreadModel
errorOnELNotFoundfalsePages 3.1+: an unresolved EL identifier raises an error rather than printing nothing

Settings can apply to groups of pages through web.xml, which beats repeating directives:

<jsp-config>
  <jsp-property-group>
    <url-pattern>*.jsp</url-pattern>
    <page-encoding>UTF-8</page-encoding>
    <scripting-invalid>true</scripting-invalid>        <!-- scriptlets become a compile error -->
    <trim-directive-whitespaces>true</trim-directive-whitespaces>
    <include-prelude>/WEB-INF/jspf/taglibs.jspf</include-prelude>   <!-- added to the top of each page -->
    <include-coda>/WEB-INF/jspf/footer.jspf</include-coda>
  </jsp-property-group>
</jsp-config>

Scripting Elements and Comments

SyntaxNameGoes toNotes
<% code %>ScriptletInside _jspServiceStatements; needs semicolons
<%= expr %>Expressionout.print(expr)No semicolon. Prints the word null for null. Not encoded.
<%! decl %>DeclarationClass bodyFields and methods; implicit objects unavailable
<%-- x --%>JSP commentRemoved at translationNever reaches the client
<!-- x -->HTML commentSent to the browserVisible in page source, and code inside still runs
<%@ page contentType="text/plain" %>
<%! int hits = 0; %>              <%-- one per servlet instance, shared by all users --%>
<% int local = 0; hits++; local++; %>
hits=<%= hits %> local=<%= local %>

Run on Tomcat 11, the first request printed hits=1 local=1 and the second hits=2 local=1. hits persists and is a data race, since hits++ isn't atomic. Don't use it.

Standard Actions

Actions are XML-syntax tags in the jsp: prefix, executed at request time, unlike directives.

ActionPurpose
<jsp:include page="x.jsp" flush="false"/>Runs another resource and inserts its output
<jsp:forward page="x.jsp"/>Same as RequestDispatcher.forward. Output buffered so far is lost, and nothing after it runs.
<jsp:param name="" value=""/>Adds a parameter to an include or forward
<jsp:useBean id="u" class="b.User" scope="session"/>Finds the bean in the scope, or creates and stores it
<jsp:setProperty name="u" property="age" value="30"/>Calls a setter with type conversion. param="n" reads from a request param, and property="*" binds all params with matching names.
<jsp:getProperty name="u" property="name"/>Calls a getter and prints
<jsp:attribute>, <jsp:body>, <jsp:element>, <jsp:text>Build tags and attribute values dynamically
<jsp:doBody/>, <jsp:invoke/>Inside tag files: evaluate the body or a fragment attribute

useBean first looks in the given scope. Only if it finds nothing does it instantiate the class, so the body of <jsp:useBean>...</jsp:useBean> runs only on creation, which makes it suitable for one-time setup. The class needs a public no-arg constructor and must be in a named package. type="..." without class means "the bean must already exist", and missing beans cause an error.

<jsp:useBean id="u" class="b.User" scope="page"/>
<jsp:setProperty name="u" property="name" param="n"/>      <%-- value of ?n= --%>
<jsp:setProperty name="u" property="age" value="30"/>       <%-- String "30" converted to int --%>
<jsp:getProperty name="u" property="name"/> ${u.age}        <%-- ?n=Zed prints Zed 30 --%>

Expression Language (EL) in Depth

EL exists so that a view can read data without Java code. An expression like ${user.address.city} doesn't use reflection directly: it goes through a chain of ELResolvers, each handling one kind of base object. user is first resolved to one of the EL implicit objects, or found with pageContext.findAttribute. Then for each .property, the resolver depends on the object's type:

Base objectWhat x.y or x['y'] means
JavaBeanCalls getY() or isY(). A missing property throws PropertyNotFoundException.
Mapmap.get("y"). A missing key gives null. The key always wins.
Listlist.get(y), with y coerced to an integer. Out of range gives null.
ArraySame as List
nullThe result is null and nothing throws, however long the chain is

. and [] are interchangeable, but you need brackets when the name isn't a valid identifier or comes from a variable: ${header['user-agent']}, ${map[keyVar]}, ${list[0]}.

EL implicit objects

These are separate from the 9 JSP objects. ${request} is not the request; it looks for an attribute with that name. There are 11:

ObjectHoldsExample
pageContextThe PageContext (route to the real request)${pageContext.request.contextPath}
pageScope, requestScope, sessionScope, applicationScopeAttribute maps per scope${sessionScope.cart}
param, paramValuesRequest params: first value / all values${param.id}, ${paramValues.id[1]}
header, headerValuesRequest headers${header['host']}
cookieCookie objects by name${cookie.theme.value}
initParamContext init params${initParam.region}

Operators, with results from Tomcat 11

ExpressionOutputRule
${10/2}5.0/ and div are always floating-point
${7 div 2}3.5
${7 mod 2}, ${10 % 3}1
${1/0}InfinityNo ArithmeticException
${0/0}NaN
${null+1}1null is coerced to 0 in arithmetic
${"1"+"2"}3+ is only arithmetic; strings are coerced to numbers
${'a' += 'b'}ab+= is concatenation (EL 3.0+)
${'a'=="a"}trueSingle or double quotes; == uses value equality, not references
${1 == 1.0}, ${'1' == 1}trueOperands are coerced
${null == 0}, ${"" == null}false
${empty ""}, ${empty null}, ${empty emptyList}trueTrue for null, empty String, array, Map or Collection
${[1,2,3].stream().sum()}6EL 3.0 collection construction and streams
${(x -> x * 2)(4)}8EL 3.0 lambda
\${escaped}${escaped}Backslash escapes EL

Word forms exist because < and && are awkward in XML: eq ne lt gt le ge and or not. Ternary works as usual: ${admin ? 'yes' : 'no'}.

Gotcha: ${list.size} on a java.util.List doesn't work. List has no getSize(), and the list resolver tries to read "size" as an index. On Tomcat 11 it failed with NumberFormatException: For input string: "size". Use ${list.size()} (method calls since EL 2.2) or ${fn:length(list)}. For a Map containing the key size, ${map.size} reads that entry, and ${map.size()} calls the method: the same map printed MS and 2.
Gotcha: EL doesn't escape output. ${html} printed <i>x</i> raw, while <c:out value="${html}"/> and ${fn:escapeXml(html)} printed &lt;i&gt;x&lt;/i&gt;. Printing user data through plain ${} is XSS. It's a key difference from Thymeleaf's th:text, which escapes by default.

${expr} is immediate evaluation. #{expr} is deferred: the expression is passed to a tag to evaluate later, or to set a value, which Jakarta Faces uses. Plain JSPs almost never need it.

JSTL (Jakarta Tags)

JSTL replaces common scriptlet logic with tags. Five libraries exist, and the first three matter.

<%@ taglib prefix="c"   uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="fmt" uri="jakarta.tags.fmt" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="fn"  uri="jakarta.tags.functions" %>
<%-- also jakarta.tags.xml and jakarta.tags.sql --%>

Core

TagPurpose
c:outPrint with XML escaping. default covers null, and escapeXml="false" disables it.
c:set, c:removeSet or remove a scoped variable. scope defaults to page. With target and property it sets a bean or map entry.
c:ifCondition. There is no else.
c:choose, c:when, c:otherwiseif / else-if / else
c:forEachLoop over a collection, array, Map, or a numeric range with begin, end, step
c:forTokensSplit a string by delimiters
c:url, c:paramBuild a URL: adds the context path, URL-encodes params, rewrites the session ID if needed
c:importInclude any URL, including other sites; can capture into a variable
c:redirectSend a redirect
c:catchCatch an exception into a variable
<c:forEach var="x" items="${list}" varStatus="s">
  ${s.index}/${s.count}/${s.first}/${s.last}=${x};
</c:forEach>
<%-- list = [a, b]: 0/1/true/false=a; 1/2/false/true=b; --%>

<c:forEach var="i" begin="1" end="9" step="3">${i} </c:forEach>     <%-- 1 4 7 --%>

<c:forEach var="e" items="${someMap}">${e.key}=${e.value}</c:forEach>  <%-- Map entries --%>

<c:choose>
  <c:when test="${list.size() > 5}">big</c:when>
  <c:otherwise>small</c:otherwise>
</c:choose>

<c:url value="/x" var="u"><c:param name="q" value="a b"/></c:url>
<a href="${u}">link</a>                    <%-- /app/x?q=a+b --%>

<c:catch var="err">${bean.mayThrow()}</c:catch>
<c:if test="${not empty err}">Failed</c:if>

Formatting (fmt)

<fmt:setLocale value="de_DE"/>
<fmt:setBundle basename="messages"/>               <%-- messages_de.properties on the classpath --%>
<fmt:message key="welcome"><fmt:param value="${user.name}"/></fmt:message>
<fmt:formatNumber value="${price}" type="currency"/>
<fmt:formatNumber value="1234.5" pattern="#,##0.00"/>
<fmt:formatDate value="${order.date}" pattern="yyyy-MM-dd"/>     <%-- needs java.util.Date --%>
Gotcha: fmt:formatDate takes a java.util.Date, not a LocalDate, so a modern model needs conversion or a formatted String. fmt:formatNumber depends on a locale: on Tomcat 11 with an Accept-Language: en header the example printed 1,234.50, while a request without that header printed the unformatted 1234.5, because no locale could be chosen. Set one with fmt:setLocale or the jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl.fmt.locale context param.

Functions (fn)

fn:length, fn:contains, fn:containsIgnoreCase, fn:startsWith, fn:endsWith, fn:indexOf, fn:substring, fn:substringBefore, fn:substringAfter, fn:replace, fn:split, fn:join, fn:trim, fn:toUpperCase, fn:toLowerCase, fn:escapeXml.

The sql library runs queries from a JSP. It exists for prototypes and shouldn't be used, because it puts data access in the view.

Custom Tags

When JSTL isn't enough, write your own tag to hide Java from the page. There are three routes.

RouteEffortUse for
Tag file (.tag)A JSP fragment, no Java or TLDReusable markup: cards, form rows
SimpleTagSupport (JSP 2.0+)A Java class and a TLDLogic, new instance per use
Classic TagSupport / BodyTagSupportJava, with a complex lifecycleLegacy code only
// 1. Handler. Must be in a named package: a default-package class gave
//    "cannot be resolved to a type" when the JSP compiled.
package com.acme.tags;
public class HelloTag extends SimpleTagSupport {
  private String who;
  public void setWho(String who) { this.who = who; }     // container calls this for the attribute

  @Override public void doTag() throws JspException, IOException {
    JspWriter out = getJspContext().getOut();
    out.print("Hello " + who + ": ");
    if (getJspBody() != null) {                          // null when the tag has no body
      StringWriter body = new StringWriter();
      getJspBody().invoke(body);                         // evaluate the body, captured
      out.print(body.toString().toUpperCase());
    }
  }
}
<!-- 2. WEB-INF/acme.tld, or META-INF/ in a library JAR -->
<taglib xmlns="https://jakarta.ee/xml/ns/jakartaee" version="3.0">
  <tlib-version>1.0</tlib-version>
  <short-name>acme</short-name>
  <uri>urn:acme</uri>
  <tag>
    <name>hello</name>
    <tag-class>com.acme.tags.HelloTag</tag-class>
    <body-content>scriptless</body-content>      <!-- empty, scriptless or tagdependent -->
    <attribute>
      <name>who</name><required>true</required><rtexprvalue>true</rtexprvalue>
    </attribute>
  </tag>
</taglib>
<%-- 3. Page --%>
<%@ taglib prefix="acme" uri="urn:acme" %>
<acme:hello who="Bob">body ${1+1}</acme:hello>      <%-- Hello Bob: BODY 2 --%>

<%-- Tag file: WEB-INF/tags/badge.tag --%>
<%@ tag body-content="scriptless" %>
<%@ attribute name="label" required="true" %>
<b>${label}:<jsp:doBody/></b>

<%-- Use it, no TLD needed --%>
<%@ taglib prefix="t" tagdir="/WEB-INF/tags" %>
<t:badge label="L">in</t:badge>                    <%-- <b>L:in</b> --%>

The classic lifecycle is setPageContext → setParent → setters → doStartTag → doAfterBody → doEndTag → release, with return codes such as EVAL_BODY_INCLUDE, SKIP_BODY, EVAL_PAGE, SKIP_PAGE. Containers may pool classic tag instances, so state left in a field leaks into the next use. SimpleTag is never pooled: a new instance is made each time. A static Java method can also be exposed as an EL function with a <function> entry in the TLD.

Scopes and Attribute Lifetime

ScopeBacking objectLifetimeSurvives forward?Survives redirect?Thread-safe concern?
pagePageContextThis JSP's executionNoNoNo
requestHttpServletRequestOne requestYesNoNo
sessionHttpSessionOne user, until timeoutYesYesYes
applicationServletContextWeb app lifetimeYesYesYes

The narrowest scope that works is best: session data costs memory for each user. On Tomcat 11, with v set to P, R, S and A in the four scopes, ${v} printed P and ${requestScope.v} printed R. With only request and session set, ${r2} gave the request value. In a page that set a page attribute a and a request attribute b, then used <jsp:include>, the included page printed a=[] b=[rq]: an included JSP is a different page, so it can't see page scope. A static include can, since it's the same servlet.

Gotcha: ${user} searches scopes, so a stray page or request attribute silently shadows the session one. Be explicit (${sessionScope.user}) when the scope matters. Explicit scopes are also slightly faster.

Model 1 vs Model 2 (MVC)

Model 1: the browser requests a JSP directly, and that JSP handles the input, uses beans and renders. Good for tiny pages, but logic spreads through views and navigation is hard-coded in links. Model 2: every request goes to a servlet (controller), which calls services, puts results in request attributes, and forwards to a JSP that only renders.

Model 1Model 2
Entry pointThe JSP itselfA servlet
SeparationMixedController, model and view
TestingHardControllers and services can be tested without a browser
Security checkRepeated per pageCentral
ExampleOld intranet pagesStruts, Spring MVC
@WebServlet("/orders")
public class OrderController extends HttpServlet {
  private final OrderService service = new OrderService();      // stateless, so safe to share

  @Override protected void doGet(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    long customerId = Long.parseLong(req.getParameter("customer"));
    req.setAttribute("orders", service.findByCustomer(customerId));       // the model
    req.getRequestDispatcher("/WEB-INF/views/orders.jsp").forward(req, res);  // the view
  }
  @Override protected void doPost(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res) throws IOException {
    service.create(req.getParameter("item"));
    res.sendRedirect(req.getContextPath() + "/orders?customer=1");        // Post/Redirect/Get
  }
}
<%-- /WEB-INF/views/orders.jsp: no Java, and unreachable by direct URL --%>
<%@ page contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<%@ taglib prefix="c" uri="jakarta.tags.core" %>
<c:choose>
  <c:when test="${empty orders}"><p>No orders</p></c:when>
  <c:otherwise>
    <table>
      <c:forEach var="o" items="${orders}">
        <tr><td>${o.id}</td><td><c:out value="${o.item}"/></td></tr>
      </c:forEach>
    </table>
  </c:otherwise>
</c:choose>

Spring MVC is Model 2 with a single front controller, DispatcherServlet. A controller returns the view name "orders", and a ViewResolver builds the path from spring.mvc.view.prefix=/WEB-INF/views/ and spring.mvc.view.suffix=.jsp, then forwards.

Error Handling in Depth

There are several levels, and the most specific one wins:

  1. <c:catch> or try/catch within the page.
  2. errorPage in the page directive, which beats web.xml.
  3. <error-page> in web.xml, by exception type or status code.
  4. The container's default error page.
<%@ page isErrorPage="true" contentType="text/html;charset=UTF-8" %>
<%-- ep.jsp --%>
<h2>Sorry, that failed</h2>
Status: ${pageContext.errorData.statusCode}          <%-- 500 --%>
URI:    ${pageContext.errorData.requestURI}          <%-- /app/ex.jsp --%>
<%-- Log details on the server; don't print the message to users. --%>

On Tomcat 11, a page throwing RuntimeException("bad") with errorPage="ep.jsp" gave these values, and exception.getMessage() and ${pageContext.exception.message} both returned bad. Translation errors are different: they're not caught by the page's own errorPage, because the page never compiled, so they surface as a 500 through the web.xml or container handler.

Gotcha: error handling needs an uncommitted response. A page with out.flush() followed by <jsp:forward> sent the client a 200 with only the output so far. The buffer also commits once it passes 8 KB, so a failure deep in a long page leaves a half-rendered page with status 200. Load data in the controller, before rendering starts.

Include Types Compared

<%@ include file %><jsp:include page /><c:import url />
WhenTranslation timeRequest timeRequest time
MechanismText is pasted in, one servletRequestDispatcher.includeInclude for local, HTTP fetch for external
TargetFile in the appResource in the appAny URL, even another site
Page-scoped variables sharedYes, including Java localsNoNo
Dynamic pathNo, must be a literalYes, can use ${...}Yes
Can pass paramsNoYes, jsp:paramYes, c:param
PerformanceFastestSlight overheadNetwork cost if remote
Can store outputNoNoYes, var
Set headersYes, it's the same pageNo, ignoredNo

Because static include pastes source, two files that declare the same local fail to compile. <% int a=1; %> plus an include containing <% int a=2; %> gave "Duplicate local variable a". It's conventional to give static fragments a .jspf extension (for taglib declarations or a shared header), and use jsp:include for pieces with their own logic.

JSP vs Thymeleaf

JSPThymeleaf
ExecutionCompiled to a servletParsed and interpreted by a template engine (with a cache)
Needs a servlet containerYes, plus a JSP engineNo, it runs anywhere, even for emails or a unit test
Spring Boot executable JARNot supported; use WAR packagingFully supported
File is valid HTMLNo: tags break in a browserYes: "natural templates" open in a browser
Output escapingOff for ${}; must use c:outOn for th:text; th:utext opts out
Java in the viewPossible with scriptletsNot possible; only expressions (SpEL with Spring)
LayoutsIncludes, tag files, or Tiles/SiteMeshFragments and the Layout dialect
Raw speedVery fast (compiled bytecode)Slower, but usually irrelevant next to DB time
Spring integrationThrough InternalResourceViewResolver and form tagsAuto-configured when the starter is on the classpath
<!-- JSP -->
<c:forEach var="o" items="${orders}">
  <tr><td><c:out value="${o.item}"/></td></tr>
</c:forEach>

<!-- Thymeleaf: "Sample" appears when opened as a plain file -->
<tr th:each="o : ${orders}">
  <td th:text="${o.item}">Sample</td>
</tr>

Running JSP with Spring Boot requires tomcat-embed-jasper, JSTL dependencies, and WAR packaging. Boot's docs list JSP limitations and recommend against JSP where possible. Other server-side options are FreeMarker, Mustache and JTE. Many modern teams render on the client with Angular or React instead, and use the server for a REST API only.

Spring MVC Form Tags in JSP

Legacy Spring MVC apps often render forms with the Spring form tag library, which binds inputs to a model object (the "command" or form-backing object), re-fills values after a validation error, and shows field errors. A view resolver maps a logical view name to the JSP, for example "patient/edit" to /WEB-INF/views/patient/edit.jsp.

<%@ taglib prefix="form" uri="http://www.springframework.org/tags/form" %>
<form:form modelAttribute="patient" action="${pageContext.request.contextPath}/patients" method="post">
  <form:label path="name">Name</form:label>
  <form:input path="name"/>
  <form:errors path="name" cssClass="error"/>
  <form:select path="gender" items="${genders}"/>
  <button type="submit">Save</button>
</form:form>
@PostMapping("/patients")
String save(@Valid @ModelAttribute("patient") PatientForm form, BindingResult result,
            RedirectAttributes ra) {
    if (result.hasErrors()) return "patient/edit";      // same JSP, errors shown by form:errors
    service.save(form);
    ra.addFlashAttribute("msg", "Patient saved");      // survives one redirect
    return "redirect:/patients";                       // Post/Redirect/Get
}

With Spring Security, <form:form> automatically adds the hidden CSRF token field. A plain HTML <form> does not, so you add it yourself.

<form method="post" action="${pageContext.request.contextPath}/logout">
  <input type="hidden" name="${_csrf.parameterName}" value="${_csrf.token}"/>
  <button>Logout</button>
</form>

Interview Questions — JSP

JSP vs Servlet?

A servlet is Java code that writes out HTML, so it's good for controller logic. A JSP is HTML with embedded tags, so it's good for the view. Every JSP is translated into a servlet. JSPs are recompiled automatically when they change.

Name the 9 JSP implicit objects.

request, response, out (JspWriter), session, application (ServletContext), config (ServletConfig), pageContext, page (this), exception (only available in error pages).

What are JSP directives?
  • <%@ page %>: page settings: import, contentType, session, errorPage, isErrorPage, isELIgnored.
  • <%@ include file="" %>: a static include, merged at translation time.
  • <%@ taglib %>: declares a tag library such as JSTL or custom tags.
Include directive vs <jsp:include> action?
<%@ include file %><jsp:include page />
Translation time (static)Request time (dynamic)
Content is merged into a single servletA separate resource is called at runtime
A change to the included file may not be picked upAlways the latest output; can take params
Scripting elements: scriptlet, expression, declaration?

<% code %> is a scriptlet and goes into _jspService. <%= expr %> is an expression and is printed to out. <%! decl %> is a declaration and becomes a class-level field or method. Avoid scriptlets: they mix logic into the view and are hard to maintain. Use EL and JSTL instead.

What are the four JSP scopes?

page (the current JSP) < request (one request, survives a forward) < session (one user) < application (the whole app). EL searches them in that order: ${user}.

What is EL and JSTL?

EL (Expression Language): ${expr} reads beans and scoped attributes, e.g. ${param.id}, ${sessionScope.cart.size()}, and returns null instead of throwing NPEs. JSTL is the standard tag library: core (c:if, c:forEach, c:choose, c:url), fmt (i18n and formatting), functions (fn:length), sql, xml.

How to handle exceptions in JSP?

Set <%@ page errorPage="error.jsp" %> on the page and isErrorPage="true" on error.jsp, which gives it access to exception. Or configure it globally in web.xml with <error-page> by exception type or status code.

Is JSP still used? What replaced it?

It's mostly legacy now. New server-side rendering uses Thymeleaf (the usual choice with Spring Boot, which has no default), FreeMarker, or SPA front ends (Angular, React) talking to REST APIs. Spring Boot's support for JSP with an embedded JAR is limited (you need WAR packaging).

Output: what do two consecutive requests print?
<%! int hits = 0; %><% int local = 0; hits++; local++; %>hits=<%= hits %> local=<%= local %>

hits=1 local=1, then hits=2 local=1 (run on Tomcat 11). The declaration is an instance field of the single generated servlet, so it persists, while the scriptlet variable is a local of _jspService. hits is also unsafe under concurrency, and it resets on recompilation or redeploy.

Why can't you use request or session inside a declaration?

Implicit objects are local variables of _jspService, and a declaration is placed at class level, outside that method. A method declared in <%! %> must receive them as parameters. Only scriptlets and expressions see them directly.

Can you override _jspService()? What about jspInit()?

You can't override _jspService, because the translator generates that method from the page, so writing your own creates a duplicate. jspInit and jspDestroy can be overridden inside a declaration. Use them for one-time setup.

Does a JSP run on every request? Is it recompiled every time?

The compiled servlet runs on every request, but translation happens only the first time or when the file changes. Whether changes are checked depends on Jasper's development and checkInterval settings. Compiled code means it's no slower than a hand-written servlet after the first hit.

Translation-time vs request-time errors?

Translation-time: bad JSP syntax, a missing tag library, a bad directive, an unclosed tag. Compile-time: errors in Java inside scriptlets, or using session when session="false" (Tomcat 11 said "session cannot be resolved"). Request-time: runtime exceptions such as an EL PropertyNotFoundException. The first two return 500 with a JasperException and don't reach the page's errorPage.

What does session="false" do, and when would you use it?

The page no longer creates or touches an HTTP session, and the session implicit object doesn't exist. Use it on public pages such as a landing page, so that crawlers and anonymous visitors don't each cost a session in server memory. Note that it doesn't invalidate an existing session.

What's the output of ${10/2}, ${1/0}, ${"1"+"2"} and ${null+1}?

5.0, Infinity, 3 and 1, verified on Tomcat 11. EL division is floating-point, so dividing by zero doesn't throw. + always means numeric addition, with strings coerced to numbers and null to 0. A non-numeric string in + fails: ${"a"+1} raised NumberFormatException on Tomcat 11. Concatenate with += or by placing expressions side by side.

What does EL print when a value is null, compared with an expression?

EL prints an empty string. A scriptlet expression prints the word null: in a test, <%= request.getAttribute("n") %>|${n}| printed null||. EL also ignores null in a chain: ${nothing.x.y} prints nothing. But an existing bean without the property throws PropertyNotFoundException.

Why doesn't ${request.method} work?

request is a JSP implicit object, not an EL one, so EL looks for an attribute called request, doesn't find it, and prints nothing. Use ${pageContext.request.method}. In the test, ${pageContext.request.contextPath} printed /app and ${pageContext.request.method} printed GET.

What does empty check? How is it different from == null?

empty x is true if x is null, an empty String, or an empty array, Collection or Map. x == null is true only for null: ${"" == null} is false. It's the right check for lists: <c:if test="${not empty orders}">.

How do you access a request parameter, a header and a cookie in EL?

${param.id}, or ${paramValues.id[1]} for a repeated param; ${header['user-agent']}, with brackets because of the hyphen; and ${cookie.theme.value}, because cookie.theme is the Cookie object. ${cookie.theme} alone would print its toString().

c:out vs ${}: when must you use which?

Use <c:out> or fn:escapeXml for any data that a user could have influenced. Plain ${} is fine only for values known to be safe (numbers, your own constants). Otherwise a name of <script>...</script> executes in other users' browsers. Note that it escapes for HTML only. Inside JavaScript or a URL you need encoding for that context (c:url with c:param, or the OWASP Java Encoder).

How do you implement if/else in JSTL?

c:if has no else branch. Use c:choose, c:when, c:otherwise, which works as if / else-if / else, stopping at the first true when. For a one-liner, use a ternary: ${active ? 'On' : 'Off'}.

What's varStatus?

An object that describes the current iteration of c:forEach: index (from 0), count (from 1), first, last, current, plus begin, end and step. It's useful for zebra rows: ${s.count % 2 == 0 ? 'even' : 'odd'}.

What does c:url do that a plain link doesn't?

It prepends the context path to paths beginning with /, URL-encodes c:param values, and adds ;jsessionid= if the client hasn't shown cookie support. In the test, /x with param q="a b" gave /app/x;jsessionid=...?q=a+b on a first request. Without it, moving the app to a different context breaks hard-coded links.

jsp:forward vs response.sendRedirect from a JSP?

Same difference as in servlets. jsp:forward stays on the server, so the request attributes and URL are kept, and buffered output is dropped. It must happen before commit. Page content after it doesn't run, because the generated code returns. sendRedirect makes the browser issue a new request. In a scriptlet, follow it with return; or the rest of the page still executes.

Does the included file get its own scope with jsp:include? Does a param passed by jsp:param stay?

The target gets a new page scope, so page attributes aren't visible there, but it shares the request and session. jsp:param values are added to the request for the duration of the include: ${param.x} worked in the target, and they disappear when control returns. If the same name already exists, the new value takes precedence.

A shared header is changed and included by a static include directive. Will pages show it?

The content was pasted into each page at translation, so each one must be retranslated. Tomcat tracks these dependencies in development mode and recompiles. Other containers or production settings with no checks may keep the old output until redeployed. Runtime includes avoid this.

How do you disable scriptlets across an application?

<scripting-invalid>true</scripting-invalid> inside a jsp-property-group in web.xml, with <url-pattern>*.jsp</url-pattern>. Pages containing scripting elements then fail at translation. That enforces the "no Java in views" rule, so a code review doesn't have to.

Why put JSPs under WEB-INF?

Files under WEB-INF can't be requested from a browser, only reached by a forward. That guarantees the controller runs first, so security checks happen and model data exists. Otherwise a direct hit on orders.jsp renders an empty page or an error.

What are classic tag return values, and how do they control the body?

doStartTag returns EVAL_BODY_INCLUDE (process the body) or SKIP_BODY. doAfterBody returns EVAL_BODY_AGAIN (loop) or SKIP_BODY. doEndTag returns EVAL_PAGE or SKIP_PAGE, the latter stopping the rest of the JSP. BodyTag adds EVAL_BODY_BUFFERED to capture the body. SimpleTag replaced all this with one doTag and getJspBody().invoke().

What's the purpose of a TLD?

A Tag Library Descriptor is an XML file that tells the translator the tag names, handler classes, attributes, and which attributes are required or accept expressions (rtexprvalue). It's used to validate tag usage at translation time. Containers find TLDs under WEB-INF and in META-INF of library JARs, which is why JSTL works with only a URI. Tag files in /WEB-INF/tags need no TLD.

Is a JSP thread-safe?

Exactly as much as a servlet, because it is one. Scriptlet locals and page scope are safe. Declarations (<%! %>), session attributes and application attributes are shared. isThreadSafe="false" is deprecated and was never a true fix. Avoid declaring mutable fields.

How would you handle internationalisation in JSP?

Create messages.properties, messages_de.properties and so on, on the classpath. Load with fmt:setBundle, or set the jakarta.servlet.jsp.jstl.fmt.localizationContext context param. Print text with <fmt:message key="..."/>, and pass arguments using fmt:param. The locale comes from fmt:setLocale or the browser's Accept-Language. Use UTF-8 for pageEncoding, and format numbers and dates with fmt:formatNumber and fmt:formatDate because they differ by locale.

How do you migrate a legacy JSP/Struts app to a modern stack?
  1. Characterise behaviour with end-to-end tests first.
  2. Move logic from scriptlets into services, and add Spring MVC controllers in front, so JSPs become pure views.
  3. Replace views in stages with Thymeleaf, or expose REST endpoints for an Angular or React front end, using a strangler approach where a proxy routes migrated paths to the new app.
  4. Upgrade javax to jakarta together with the Spring Boot upgrade. JSTL URIs and library versions change too.
  5. Decide whether to keep WAR packaging until the last JSP has gone.
A JSP shows raw ${...} text in the browser. Why?

EL is off for that page. Causes: isELIgnored="true"; a matching <el-ignored> in web.xml; or an old web.xml with a Servlet 2.3 DTD, which ignores EL by default. Another case: the file isn't being processed at all, such as a .html file or a static template served by the default servlet.

Why do blank lines appear in generated HTML, and does it matter?

Each directive or scriptlet line leaves its newline in the template text. It's mostly harmless for HTML, but it breaks a page that must output plain JSON or XML starting at the first byte, or a file download. Fix it with trimDirectiveWhitespaces="true", or better, don't produce non-HTML from a JSP. A cause of "getOutputStream() has already been called" is using a JSP for binary output, since the page's out uses the writer.

What does the Spring form tag library give you over plain HTML inputs?

Binding: path="name" reads and writes the property of the modelAttribute object, so values are redisplayed after a validation error; <form:errors> prints BindingResult messages; select/checkbox tags handle selected state; values are HTML-escaped; and with Spring Security the CSRF token is inserted automatically.

Why does a POST from my JSP return 403 after adding Spring Security?

CSRF protection is on by default and the form didn't send the token. Use <form:form>, or add <input type="hidden" name="${_csrf.parameterName}" value="${_csrf.token}"/> to plain forms. For AJAX calls, put the token in a meta tag and send it in the X-CSRF-TOKEN header.

How do you show a "saved successfully" message after a redirect in a JSP app?

Use Post/Redirect/Get with a flash attribute: in the controller call redirectAttributes.addFlashAttribute("msg", "Saved") and return "redirect:/list". Spring stores it in the session for exactly one following request and exposes it as a model attribute, so the JSP prints ${msg} (escaped with c:out). Request attributes wouldn't survive the redirect, and plain session attributes would linger.

How does a controller's return value map to a JSP?

The InternalResourceViewResolver (or Spring Boot's spring.mvc.view.prefix/suffix) turns the logical view name into a path, for example prefix /WEB-INF/views/ + home + .jsp. The DispatcherServlet copies model attributes into request attributes and forwards to that JSP. A redirect: or forward: prefix bypasses the resolver.

JSP vs JSF?

JSP is a template technology that is translated into a servlet and renders whatever the controller prepared. JSF (Jakarta Faces) is a component-based MVC framework with a component tree, lifecycle phases, managed beans and Facelets (XHTML) views; it keeps UI state across requests. JSF is found in older enterprise/Java EE apps; new projects mostly use Thymeleaf or a SPA with REST.

JDBC Database Access

The low-level Java API for talking to relational databases. JPA, Hibernate and JdbcTemplate are all built on it.

String sql = "SELECT id, name, salary FROM employee WHERE dept = ? AND salary > ?";
try (Connection con = dataSource.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
  ps.setString(1, "IT");
  ps.setBigDecimal(2, new BigDecimal("50000"));
  try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
    while (rs.next()) {
      list.add(new Emp(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"), rs.getBigDecimal("salary")));
    }
  }
}

// Transaction + batch
con.setAutoCommit(false);
try (PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO audit(msg) VALUES (?)")) {
  for (String m : msgs) { ps.setString(1, m); ps.addBatch(); }
  ps.executeBatch();
  con.commit();
} catch (SQLException e) { con.rollback(); throw e; }

// Spring JdbcTemplate
List<Emp> emps = jdbcTemplate.query("SELECT * FROM employee WHERE dept = ?",
    (rs, i) -> new Emp(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"), rs.getBigDecimal("salary")), "IT");
Note: behaviour marked "tested" in this section was run against MySQL 8.4 with Connector/J 9.1 and HikariCP 5.1. Other databases and drivers can differ, and the interview answer often turns on that.

Architecture: API, Driver Manager, Driver

JDBC (Java Database Connectivity) separates your code from the database. The JDK ships mostly interfaces (Connection, PreparedStatement, ResultSet), and each vendor ships a driver JAR that implements them. Your code compiles against java.sql and javax.sql, and the actual class behind Connection is, for example, com.mysql.cj.jdbc.ConnectionImpl. That's the Bridge idea: swapping databases means swapping a JAR and a URL (SQL dialects aside).

InterfaceRoleImportant methods
DriverEntry point implemented by a vendorconnect(url, props), acceptsURL
DataSourceFactory for connections, usually pooledgetConnection()
ConnectionA session with the DB; owns the transactionprepareStatement, commit, rollback, setAutoCommit, setSavepoint, isValid, getMetaData
Statement / PreparedStatement / CallableStatementRuns SQLexecuteQuery, executeUpdate, execute, executeBatch
ResultSetCursor over rowsnext, getXxx, wasNull, getMetaData
SQLExceptionChecked error with vendor detailsgetSQLState, getErrorCode, getNextException

JDBC version milestones

JDBCJavaAdded
4.06Driver auto-loading through ServiceLoader; SQLException subclasses
4.17AutoCloseable resources for try-with-resources; getObject(col, Class)
4.28java.time support via setObject/getObject; executeLargeUpdate
4.39Sharding keys; beginRequest / endRequest hints for pools

DriverManager vs DataSource

DriverManager is the original entry point. At first use it finds all drivers listed in META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver on the classpath (this is why Class.forName is no longer needed) and keeps them in a list. getConnection(url) simply asks each driver in turn to connect: a driver returns null for a URL it doesn't recognise. If all do, you get No suitable driver found for jdbc:... with SQLState 08001 (tested). That message usually means a missing JAR or a mistyped URL.

DriverManagerDataSource
Connection costNew TCP socket, TLS and authentication on each callNormally borrowed from a pool
ConfigurationURL and password in codeExternal: Spring config, or JNDI in app servers
SwappableNoYes, inject the interface; test with H2
Limit on connectionsNone, so it can overload the databasePool maximum
Distributed transactionsNoXADataSource variant
Use forSmall tools, scriptsEverything else
// DriverManager: fine for a one-off tool
try (Connection con = DriverManager.getConnection(
        "jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shop?connectionTimeout=3000&socketTimeout=30000", "app", secret)) { ... }

// DataSource: everything else
HikariConfig cfg = new HikariConfig();
cfg.setJdbcUrl("jdbc:mysql://db:3306/shop");
cfg.setUsername("app");
cfg.setPassword(System.getenv("DB_PASSWORD"));
cfg.setMaximumPoolSize(10);
DataSource ds = new HikariDataSource(cfg);
try (Connection con = ds.getConnection()) { ... }   // close() returns it to the pool

The URL format is jdbc:<subprotocol>://host:port/db?options. Set network timeouts: Connector/J's socketTimeout defaults to none, so a dead server can block a thread forever. Spring's DriverManagerDataSource looks like a pool but creates a new connection per call, so don't use it in production.

Statement Types in Depth

MethodUse forReturnsWrong use (tested)
executeQuerySELECTResultSetOn an UPDATE: "Statement.executeQuery() cannot issue statements that do not produce result sets"
executeUpdateINSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DDLint rows, 0 for DDLOn a SELECT: "Can not issue executeUpdate() ... with statements that produce result sets"
executeLargeUpdateSame, for over 2 billion rowslong
executeUnknown SQLtrue if the first result is a ResultSetThen call getResultSet or getUpdateCount (-1 when there's a ResultSet)
executeBatchMany statementsint[]

What "precompiled" really means

A PreparedStatement separates SQL text from data. In the true server-side form, the driver sends the text once (COM_STMT_PREPARE), the server parses it and returns a handle, and later executions send only binary parameters, so data can't change the SQL's structure.

Interview: a common misconception. "PreparedStatement is precompiled on the database" isn't true by default for MySQL. Connector/J's default is useServerPrepStmts=false: the driver escapes the values on the client and sends ordinary SQL text. Tested: Com_stmt_prepare stayed at 0 by default. With useServerPrepStmts=true&cachePrepStmts=true, three executions caused one server prepare. Injection protection holds either way, because the driver treats values as data and escapes them. The speed benefit doesn't hold by default, because the server parses each statement. Oracle and PostgreSQL drivers do use server-side preparation (PostgreSQL after several executions: prepareThreshold, default 5).

What ? can and can't do

A placeholder stands for a value, never for an identifier, keyword or list.

// ⚠ Sorts by a constant string, so no sorting happens and no error is raised (tested)
PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY ?");
ps.setString(1, "id DESC");
// Fix: map allowed input to a fixed column
String column = switch (sortParam) {
  case "name"   -> "name";
  case "salary" -> "salary";
  default       -> "id";
};
String sql = "SELECT id FROM t ORDER BY " + column;   // safe: only our own constants

// ⚠ IN (?) with "1,2" compares id to the string '1,2'.
// MySQL converts that string to 1, so one row came back with no error (tested).
// Fix: generate one placeholder per value
String marks = String.join(",", Collections.nCopies(ids.size(), "?"));
try (PreparedStatement in = con.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM t WHERE id IN (" + marks + ")")) {
  for (int i = 0; i < ids.size(); i++) in.setLong(i + 1, ids.get(i));
  ...
}

// LIKE: the wildcard goes into the value
ps.setString(1, "%" + term + "%");

// NULL: must state the type, and "= ?" with NULL never matches. Use IS NULL.
ps.setNull(2, Types.VARCHAR);

Parameters are numbered from 1. Leaving one unset throws No value specified for parameter 1 (tested).

Useful statement settings

  • setQueryTimeout(seconds): asks the driver to cancel a long query.
  • setMaxRows(n): limits rows returned, but the server may still do the work. Prefer SQL LIMIT.
  • setFetchSize(n): a hint about how many rows to fetch per round trip.
  • getWarnings(): non-fatal messages such as truncation.

ResultSet API

A ResultSet is a cursor that starts before the first row. next() moves forward and returns false after the last row. Reading before calling next() fails with "Before start of result set". Columns are numbered from 1, so getInt(0) fails with "Column Index out of range, 0 < 1." (both tested). Read columns by label for clarity, or by index in hot loops.

SQL typeJava typeGetter
INT, BIGINTint, longgetInt, getLong
DECIMALBigDecimalgetBigDecimal. Never use double for money.
VARCHAR, TEXTStringgetString
BOOLEAN / TINYINT(1)booleangetBoolean
DATELocalDategetObject(c, LocalDate.class)
DATETIMELocalDateTimegetObject(c, LocalDateTime.class)
TIMESTAMPOffsetDateTime or Instant via conversiongetObject(c, OffsetDateTime.class)
BLOB, TEXT largeInputStream, ReadergetBinaryStream, getCharacterStream
Gotcha: NULL in primitive getters. getInt on SQL NULL returns 0. You can tell them apart with wasNull(), called immediately after the getter, or use getObject(col, Integer.class), which returns null. Tested: getInt gave 0, wasNull gave true, getObject gave null. A field with 0 and a field with no value are very different for a salary.

Type, concurrency, holdability

Statement s = con.createStatement(ResultSet.TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE,
                                  ResultSet.CONCUR_UPDATABLE,
                                  ResultSet.HOLD_CURSORS_OVER_COMMIT);
try (ResultSet r = s.executeQuery("SELECT id, name, v FROM jt ORDER BY id")) {  // must select the PK
  r.last();                 // jump to the end
  int rows = r.getRow();    // row number
  r.absolute(1);            // also relative(n), previous(), first(), beforeFirst(), afterLast()
  r.updateInt("v", 777);    // change in the cursor
  r.updateRow();            // sends UPDATE to the DB
  // moveToInsertRow() + updateXxx() + insertRow() and deleteRow() also exist
}
  • Forward-only is the default. previous() there throws "Operation not allowed for a result set of type ResultSet.TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY." (tested).
  • Scroll-insensitive doesn't show later changes by others. Scroll-sensitive would. Connector/J reports that it doesn't support TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE (tested), so always check DatabaseMetaData.supportsResultSetType.
  • Holdability decides whether a cursor survives commit.
  • Running a second query on the same Statement closes the first ResultSet automatically (tested). A common bug is reusing a statement in a nested loop. Each open cursor needs its own statement.

Reading large results without running out of memory

By default Connector/J reads the entire result into the heap before executeQuery returns, so a query for 10 million rows can kill the JVM, whatever setFetchSize(100) says. There are two ways to stream.

ModeHowTrade-off
Row streamingForward-only, read-only, setFetchSize(Integer.MIN_VALUE)Rows arrive one by one. The connection can't run anything else until all rows are read. Tested: a second statement failed with "Streaming result set ... is still active".
Cursor fetchuseCursorFetch=true in the URL plus setFetchSize(1000)Server-side cursor; more round trips, but the server may build a temp table

PostgreSQL needs autocommit off and a positive fetch size. Oracle fetches 10 rows at a time by default. Holding a stream open also holds locks and metadata locks on the server, so process rows fast and keep long-running work out of the loop.

Metadata

Metadata is data about the database or a result. Generic tools (ORMs, migration tools, CSV exporters) rely on it.

// ResultSetMetaData: shape of THIS result
try (ResultSet r = st.executeQuery("SELECT id AS x, name FROM jt")) {
  ResultSetMetaData m = r.getMetaData();
  for (int i = 1; i <= m.getColumnCount(); i++) {
    System.out.println(m.getColumnLabel(i) + " " + m.getColumnName(i) + " "
        + m.getColumnTypeName(i) + " " + m.getColumnClassName(i));
  }   // x id BIGINT java.lang.Long ...
}

// DatabaseMetaData: the DB and its schema
DatabaseMetaData d = con.getMetaData();
d.getDatabaseProductName(); d.getDriverVersion();
d.supportsBatchUpdates();   d.supportsSavepoints();
try (ResultSet t = d.getTables("shop", null, "%", new String[]{"TABLE"})) { ... }
try (ResultSet c = d.getColumns("shop", null, "orders", null)) { ... }
try (ResultSet k = d.getPrimaryKeys("shop", null, "orders")) { ... }
Gotcha: getColumnName is the underlying name and getColumnLabel is the alias. rs.getLong("id") on SELECT id AS x fails with "Column 'id' not found." (tested). Getters match the label. ParameterMetaData does the same job for ? placeholders, but drivers support it unevenly.

Transactions

A connection starts in autocommit mode: each statement is its own transaction. setAutoCommit(false) starts manual mode, where changes stay private until commit(). The transaction belongs to the connection, not to any statement, so all statements in one transaction must use one connection. That's the reason Spring binds the connection to the thread.

public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amt) throws SQLException {
  try (Connection con = ds.getConnection()) {
    con.setAutoCommit(false);
    try (PreparedStatement debit  = con.prepareStatement("UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ? AND bal >= ?");
         PreparedStatement credit = con.prepareStatement("UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + ? WHERE id = ?")) {
      debit.setBigDecimal(1, amt); debit.setLong(2, from); debit.setBigDecimal(3, amt);
      if (debit.executeUpdate() != 1) throw new InsufficientFunds(from);   // an unchecked exception
      credit.setBigDecimal(1, amt); credit.setLong(2, to);
      credit.executeUpdate();
      con.commit();
    } catch (SQLException | RuntimeException e) {
      con.rollback();
      throw e;
    }
  }
}
Gotcha: a catch on a try-with-resources runs after the resources are closed, and the variable is out of scope. So you can't roll back in the catch of the same try that opened the connection. That's why the code above has an inner try. Catch RuntimeException as well, or a non-SQL failure skips the rollback.
  • Closing without commit: the spec leaves it undefined. On MySQL the uncommitted change was rolled back (tested). Oracle's driver commits on close. Always decide explicitly.
  • Pool return: HikariCP rolled back the dirty transaction and restored autoCommit=true (tested). So a forgotten commit disappears silently.
  • Implicit commit: in MySQL, DDL commits the running transaction. After UPDATE; CREATE TABLE; ROLLBACK the update survived (tested).
  • setAutoCommit(true) during an open transaction commits it.

Isolation through JDBC

ConstantValuePrevents
TRANSACTION_NONE0No transactions
TRANSACTION_READ_UNCOMMITTED1Nothing
TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED2Dirty reads. Default on Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server.
TRANSACTION_REPEATABLE_READ4+ non-repeatable reads. Default on MySQL InnoDB (tested: getTransactionIsolation() = 4).
TRANSACTION_SERIALIZABLE8+ phantoms

Set the level before starting work. Changing it mid-transaction is undefined by the spec or rejected by drivers. The MySQL section covers how each level really works.

Savepoints

A savepoint is a marker inside a transaction that lets you undo part of it. Spring's Propagation.NESTED uses them.

con.setAutoCommit(false);
stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE jt SET v=100 WHERE name='a1'");
Savepoint sp = con.setSavepoint("sp1");
stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE jt SET v=200 WHERE name='a2'");
con.rollback(sp);                                   // undoes only a2
stmt.executeUpdate("UPDATE jt SET v=300 WHERE name='a3'");
con.commit();                                       // a1 and a3 kept (tested)
// con.releaseSavepoint(sp) frees it early

Batch Processing

Sending 10,000 inserts separately costs 10,000 network round trips plus 10,000 commits if autocommit is on. Batching groups statements. The two problems are separate: always use one transaction, and enable the driver's batching.

Gotcha: on MySQL, addBatch and executeBatch alone don't reduce round trips. Without the flag, a batch of 5 inserts raised Com_insert by 5. With rewriteBatchedStatements=true, the same batch raised it by 1: the driver merged them into one multi-row INSERT (tested).
// URL: jdbc:mysql://db/shop?rewriteBatchedStatements=true
int n = 0;
con.setAutoCommit(false);
try (PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("INSERT INTO event(type, payload) VALUES (?, ?)")) {
  for (Event e : events) {
    ps.setString(1, e.type());
    ps.setString(2, e.payload());
    ps.addBatch();
    if (++n % 1000 == 0) {       // keep memory and packet size bounded
      ps.executeBatch();
      con.commit();              // optional: shorter locks, but no all-or-nothing
    }
  }
  ps.executeBatch();             // the remainder
  con.commit();
} catch (SQLException e) {
  con.rollback();
  throw e;
}

Reading the result

Value in int[]MeaningTested
0 or moreRows changedDefault: [1, 1, 1, 1, 1]
Statement.SUCCESS_NO_INFO (-2)Succeeded, count unknownWith rewriting: [-2, -2, -2, -2, -2]
Statement.EXECUTE_FAILED (-3)That statement failedIn BatchUpdateException.getUpdateCounts()

Failure behaviour varies by driver. With a duplicate in position 2 of 3 and autocommit on, Connector/J kept going: counts were [1, -3, 1] and rows 1 and 3 were stored (tested, continueBatchOnError defaults to true). Others stop at the first error. Run batches in a transaction and roll back to get all-or-nothing behaviour. The rewrite also respects max_allowed_packet by splitting. With JPA, Hibernate silently disables insert batching for GenerationType.IDENTITY, because it needs each key immediately.

Generated Keys

try (PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(
        "INSERT INTO jt(name, v) VALUES (?, ?)", Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {
  ps.setString(1, "a"); ps.setInt(2, 1);
  ps.executeUpdate();
  try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) {
    if (keys.next()) long id = keys.getLong(1);      // by index: the label is driver-specific
  }
}
// Standard alternative, required by Oracle to name the column:
con.prepareStatement(sql, new String[] { "id" });

Connector/J labels the key column GENERATED_KEY, not id (tested), so read it by index. A batch returned all five keys in order with or without rewriting (tested). PostgreSQL's RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS appends RETURNING *. Without that flag, getGeneratedKeys fails. Avoid a follow-up SELECT MAX(id): it's a race between sessions. In SQL, LAST_INSERT_ID() is safe, as it's per connection, but only on the same connection.

BLOB and CLOB

BLOB holds binary data and CLOB holds characters. MySQL has TINYBLOB (255 B), BLOB (64 KB), MEDIUMBLOB (16 MB), LONGBLOB (4 GB), and the same sizes for TEXT. MySQL has no CLOB keyword, so getClob works on TEXT columns. The key rule is to stream data and not hold it all in a byte[].

// Write
try (PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("UPDATE doc SET body = ?, text = ? WHERE id = ?");
     InputStream in = Files.newInputStream(path);
     Reader text = Files.newBufferedReader(txtPath)) {
  ps.setBinaryStream(1, in, Files.size(path));
  ps.setCharacterStream(2, text);
  ps.setLong(3, id);
  ps.executeUpdate();
}
// Read
try (ResultSet r = ps2.executeQuery()) {
  if (r.next()) {
    try (InputStream in = r.getBinaryStream("body")) {
      Files.copy(in, target, StandardCopyOption.REPLACE_EXISTING);
    }
    Blob b = r.getBlob("body");            // or as an object
    byte[] head = b.getBytes(1, 16);       // positions start at 1
    b.free();                              // release resources
  }
}

Check max_allowed_packet, because a single value can't exceed it (64 MB by default in MySQL 8). Connector/J buffers even "streamed" BLOBs in memory by default. In real systems, keep files in object storage (S3) and just the URL in the database. A large BLOB bloats the buffer pool, backups and replication.

Calling Stored Procedures

// CREATE PROCEDURE cnt(IN p INT, OUT o INT, INOUT io INT)
// BEGIN SELECT COUNT(*) INTO o FROM jt WHERE v >= p; SET io = io * 2;
//       SELECT name FROM jt ORDER BY id LIMIT 1; END
try (CallableStatement cs = con.prepareCall("{call cnt(?, ?, ?)}")) {
  cs.setInt(1, 0);
  cs.registerOutParameter(2, Types.INTEGER);    // before execute
  cs.setInt(3, 21);
  cs.registerOutParameter(3, Types.INTEGER);    // INOUT: set AND register
  boolean hasRs = cs.execute();
  if (hasRs) try (ResultSet r = cs.getResultSet()) {  // read result sets FIRST
    r.next(); r.getString(1);
  }
  int out = cs.getInt(2);                       // then OUT params
  int inout = cs.getInt(3);                     // 42
}
// A function: {? = call tax(?)}
// More than one result set: loop with getMoreResults() and getUpdateCount()

{call ...} is JDBC escape syntax, which the driver translates into native SQL. Similar escapes exist for dates ({d '2026-01-01'}) and functions ({fn NOW()}).

Connection Pooling Internals (HikariCP)

A new MySQL connection means a TCP handshake, usually TLS, authentication and session setup, tens of milliseconds at best. A pool opens connections in advance and lends them out. ds.getConnection() returns a thin proxy around the real one: tested, c.getClass() was HikariProxyConnection and unwrap gave ConnectionImpl. Calling close() on the proxy doesn't close the socket. It marks the entry as available.

What borrow and return do

  1. Borrow: check the calling thread's own recently used entries. Then scan the shared list and claim a free entry with compare-and-swap (no lock). If nothing is free, ask the pool to add a connection if below the maximum, and wait in the handoff queue.
  2. Validate: if the entry has been idle for more than about 500 ms, test it with Connection.isValid(), and discard it if dead.
  3. Return: close() on the proxy rolls back if work is uncommitted, resets changed state (autocommit, isolation, read-only, catalog, network timeout), closes any statements left open, and marks the entry free. Another waiting thread gets it through the handoff.
  4. Housekeeper runs every 30 seconds: it removes idle connections above minimumIdle, tops up the pool, and detects clock jumps. maxLifetime and keepaliveTime tasks are scheduled for each connection, with some random variance so they don't all expire together.

Hikari is fast because of small things: ConcurrentBag avoids a central lock, it uses its own FastList rather than ArrayList for tracking statements, and its proxy classes are generated as simple delegates.

SettingDefaultAdvice
maximumPoolSize10Size to the database's ability, not the thread count
minimumIdleSame as maximumKeep equal for a fixed pool, which Hikari recommends
connectionTimeout30 sTime a thread waits for a connection. Often lowered so requests fail fast.
idleTimeout10 minOnly applies if minimumIdle is below the maximum
maxLifetime30 minSet shorter than any DB or firewall timeout (wait_timeout)
keepaliveTime2 min in HikariCP 6+; 0 (off) in 5.xPings idle connections so that firewalls don't drop them
validationTimeout5 sLimit for a validity test
leakDetectionThreshold0 (off)Logs a stack trace if a connection is held longer than this

How large should the pool be?

Bigger isn't better. A database with 8 cores can run about 8 CPU-bound queries at once, and more connections cause context switching and lock waits, which slow everything. Hikari's docs quote a starting formula from the PostgreSQL project: connections = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count. Queue in the application and keep the pool small. With many app instances, total connections = instances × pool size, and that must stay under max_connections. 20 pods with 20 connections means 400. PgBouncer or ProxySQL can help.

Gotcha: pool-induced deadlock. If each request holds one connection and then needs a second (say REQUIRES_NEW in Spring), then with 10 threads and a pool of 10, every thread holds one and waits for another forever, until timeout. Hikari's docs give a minimum: threads × (connections per task − 1) + 1. Avoid nesting connections.

try-with-resources and Closing

Before Java 7, correct closing took nested finally blocks. Any object implementing AutoCloseable can be declared in the try header. Resources close in reverse order of declaration, even on exception, and before catch or finally run. Tested: open con, ps, rs; body; close rs, ps, con; then the catch block.

try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
  ps.setLong(1, id);                         // parameters must be set between...
  try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {   // ...so the ResultSet needs its own inner try
    ...
  }
}
  • If the body throws and close() also throws, the body's exception propagates and the close failure is attached: e.getSuppressed(). With the old finally approach, the close exception would replace the real one.
  • Closing a Statement closes its ResultSet; closing a Connection should close its statements. Don't rely on this with pools, or with connection wrappers. Hikari does close tracked statements on return.
  • Closing twice is harmless: close() on a closed JDBC object does nothing.

Connection Leaks

A leak is a borrowed connection never returned. Each leak permanently reduces the pool, and after maximumPoolSize leaks every request blocks and then fails. Tested with a pool of 2 and 500 ms timeout: SQLTransientConnectionException: demo - Connection is not available, request timed out after 500ms (total=2, active=2, idle=0, waiting=0). Reading that message tells you most of the diagnosis: active equals total and nothing is idle.

// ⚠ Leak: an exception in query() skips close()
Connection con = ds.getConnection();
