ResultSet rs = con.createStatement().executeQuery(sql);   // also leaks the Statement
List<Row> rows = map(rs);                                 // throws: con is never returned
con.close();

// ⚠ Leak by early return, or by storing a connection in a field
// ⚠ Not a leak but acts like one: @Transactional around a 30-second HTTP call
  1. Set leakDetectionThreshold=20000. Hikari logs "Connection leak detection triggered" with the stack trace of the borrower, so you see the guilty code path. It's only a warning, not a fix, and slow queries can trigger it too.
  2. Check metrics: hikaricp.connections.active, pending, and acquire time through Actuator.
  3. Take a thread dump: threads parked in HikariPool.getConnection show the waiters.
  4. Check the database: SHOW PROCESSLIST displays connections in Sleep state with long Time, or idle in a transaction.

SQLException Handling

AccessorTested: duplicate key on MySQLPortable?
ClassSQLIntegrityConstraintViolationExceptionYes, one of the JDBC 4 subclasses
getSQLState()23000 (integrity violation class)Mostly standard
getErrorCode()1062No, vendor-specific

The subclasses are grouped into SQLTransientException (retry may work: timeout, deadlock rollback), SQLNonTransientException (fix the code or data: syntax, constraint), and SQLRecoverableException (get a new connection). This gives a sound retry policy: retry MySQL deadlocks (1213) and lock wait timeouts (1205), but never a syntax error. Exceptions can also chain, so walk them with getNextException() or a for (Throwable t : sqlEx) loop.

RowSet

A RowSet extends ResultSet with JavaBean behaviour. They're in javax.sql.rowset and rarely seen in new code, but they're a classic interview question.

TypeConnected?Use
JdbcRowSetConnectedA scrollable, updatable wrapper for a ResultSet
CachedRowSetDisconnectedCopies rows to memory and works without a connection; can sync changes
WebRowSetDisconnectedReads and writes XML
FilteredRowSetDisconnectedApplies a filter in memory
JoinRowSetDisconnectedJoins row sets in memory
try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
     PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("SELECT id, name FROM emp ORDER BY id LIMIT 2");
     ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery();
     CachedRowSet crs = RowSetProvider.newFactory().createCachedRowSet()) {
  crs.populate(rs);                    // rows copied into memory
  con.close();                         // connection returned
  while (crs.next()) System.out.println(crs.getString("name"));   // still works (tested)
}

Today people map rows to a List of records instead.

A Complete DAO

DAO (Data Access Object) puts SQL behind one class, so that services don't touch JDBC. This code ran as shown against MySQL through HikariCP. It has one connection per method, parameters, checked exceptions converted to an unchecked type, and a clear transaction boundary.

public record Employee(Long id, String name, String dept, BigDecimal salary) { }

public class DataAccessFailure extends RuntimeException {
  public DataAccessFailure(String msg, Throwable cause) { super(msg, cause); }
}

public class EmployeeDao {
  private static final String COLS = "id, name, dept, salary";      // never SELECT *
  private final DataSource ds;
  public EmployeeDao(DataSource ds) { this.ds = ds; }               // injected, so tests can swap it

  private static Employee map(ResultSet rs) throws SQLException {
    return new Employee(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"),
                        rs.getString("dept"), rs.getBigDecimal("salary"));
  }

  public long insert(Employee e) {
    String sql = "INSERT INTO employee_d (name, dept, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql, Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS)) {
      ps.setString(1, e.name());
      ps.setString(2, e.dept());
      ps.setBigDecimal(3, e.salary());
      ps.executeUpdate();
      try (ResultSet keys = ps.getGeneratedKeys()) {
        if (keys.next()) return keys.getLong(1);
        throw new DataAccessFailure("no generated key", null);
      }
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("insert failed for " + e.name(), ex);
    }
  }

  public Optional<Employee> findById(long id) {
    String sql = "SELECT " + COLS + " FROM employee_d WHERE id = ?";
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
      ps.setLong(1, id);
      try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        return rs.next() ? Optional.of(map(rs)) : Optional.empty();
      }
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("findById failed: " + id, ex);
    }
  }

  public List<Employee> findByDept(String dept, int limit, int offset) {
    String sql = "SELECT " + COLS + " FROM employee_d WHERE dept = ? ORDER BY id LIMIT ? OFFSET ?";
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
      ps.setString(1, dept);
      ps.setInt(2, limit);
      ps.setInt(3, offset);
      try (ResultSet rs = ps.executeQuery()) {
        List<Employee> out = new ArrayList<>();
        while (rs.next()) out.add(map(rs));
        return out;
      }
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("findByDept failed: " + dept, ex);
    }
  }

  public boolean updateSalary(long id, BigDecimal salary) {
    String sql = "UPDATE employee_d SET salary = ? WHERE id = ?";
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
      ps.setBigDecimal(1, salary);
      ps.setLong(2, id);
      return ps.executeUpdate() == 1;
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("updateSalary failed: " + id, ex);
    }
  }

  public boolean delete(long id) {
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement("DELETE FROM employee_d WHERE id = ?")) {
      ps.setLong(1, id);
      return ps.executeUpdate() == 1;
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("delete failed: " + id, ex);
    }
  }

  public int[] insertAll(List<Employee> rows) {               // all-or-nothing batch
    String sql = "INSERT INTO employee_d (name, dept, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?)";
    try (Connection con = ds.getConnection();
         PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(sql)) {
      con.setAutoCommit(false);
      try {
        for (Employee e : rows) {
          ps.setString(1, e.name());
          ps.setString(2, e.dept());
          ps.setBigDecimal(3, e.salary());
          ps.addBatch();
        }
        int[] counts = ps.executeBatch();
        con.commit();
        return counts;
      } catch (SQLException ex) {
        con.rollback();
        throw ex;
      } finally {
        con.setAutoCommit(true);
      }
    } catch (SQLException ex) {
      throw new DataAccessFailure("batch insert failed", ex);
    }
  }
}
Gotcha: updateSalary returning "1 row" needs care. Connector/J reports rows matched by default: an update that sets the same value returned 1 (tested), whereas the MySQL server itself counts rows changed (0). useAffectedRows=true switches to the server's meaning. For optimistic locking, UPDATE ... WHERE version = ? with the default is exactly what you want.

Spring JdbcTemplate

The DAO above is mostly repetition: open, try, close, catch. JdbcTemplate is the Template Method pattern applied to JDBC. It handles the fixed steps, and you supply SQL and row mapping as a callback. The code below ran on Spring Framework 6.2.

JdbcTemplate jt = new JdbcTemplate(dataSource);          // thread-safe: share one instance
RowMapper<Employee> rowMapper = (rs, i) -> new Employee(
    rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("name"), rs.getString("dept"), rs.getBigDecimal("salary"));

List<Employee> it = jt.query("SELECT * FROM employee_d WHERE dept = ?", rowMapper, "IT");
Integer count     = jt.queryForObject("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employee_d", Integer.class);
List<String> names = jt.queryForList("SELECT name FROM employee_d", String.class);
int updated       = jt.update("UPDATE employee_d SET salary = salary + 1 WHERE dept = ?", "IT");

// Generated key
KeyHolder kh = new GeneratedKeyHolder();
jt.update(con -> {
  PreparedStatement ps = con.prepareStatement(
      "INSERT INTO employee_d(name, dept, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?)", Statement.RETURN_GENERATED_KEYS);
  ps.setString(1, "Dee"); ps.setString(2, "IT"); ps.setBigDecimal(3, BigDecimal.ONE);
  return ps;
}, kh);
Number id = kh.getKey();

// Batches
jt.batchUpdate("UPDATE employee_d SET salary = ? WHERE id = ?",
    List.of(new Object[]{BigDecimal.ONE, 2L}, new Object[]{BigDecimal.TEN, 3L}));
int[][] byChunk = jt.batchUpdate("INSERT INTO employee_d(name, dept, salary) VALUES (?, ?, ?)",
    employees, 500,                                       // chunk size
    (ps, e) -> { ps.setString(1, e.name()); ps.setString(2, e.dept()); ps.setBigDecimal(3, e.salary()); });
CallbackCalledUse
RowMapper<T>Once per row; returns an objectAlmost everything
ResultSetExtractor<T>Once, gets the whole ResultSetOne-to-many joins needing grouping
RowCallbackHandlerPer row, returns nothingStreaming rows to a file
BeanPropertyRowMapper, DataClassRowMapperReflection-based mappersColumn first_name to firstName; records
Gotcha: queryForObject expects exactly one row. Zero rows throw EmptyResultDataAccessException and two rows throw IncorrectResultSizeDataAccessException (both tested), which trips people expecting null. Catch the first, or use query(...).stream().findFirst() or JdbcClient's .optional().

How it works with @Transactional

JdbcTemplate doesn't call dataSource.getConnection() directly. It goes through DataSourceUtils.getConnection(ds), which checks TransactionSynchronizationManager (a ThreadLocal map) for a connection bound to this thread. Inside @Transactional, the transaction manager has already fetched one, turned autocommit off, and bound it. So every template call in the method shares it and close is deferred. Outside a transaction, each call gets its own connection with autocommit on. That's why multiple update() calls without @Transactional aren't atomic, and why a new Thread inside a transaction is outside it.

It also translates exceptions. SQLExceptionTranslator uses error codes and SQLState to throw unchecked DataAccessException subclasses. Tested: a duplicate key gave DuplicateKeyException, and a missing table gave BadSqlGrammarException. Service code can then handle failures without database-specific logic.

NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, SimpleJdbcInsert and JdbcClient

? placeholders get unreadable at ten columns, and order mistakes aren't caught by the compiler. NamedParameterJdbcTemplate wraps a JdbcTemplate, parses :name markers into ? (and caches the parse), then delegates.

NamedParameterJdbcTemplate np = new NamedParameterJdbcTemplate(jdbcTemplate);

var params = new MapSqlParameterSource()
    .addValue("dept", "IT")
    .addValue("min", 0);
List<Employee> rows = np.query(
    "SELECT * FROM employee_d WHERE dept = :dept AND salary > :min", params, rowMapper);

// A collection expands to the right number of placeholders: IN (?, ?)
List<String> names = np.queryForList(
    "SELECT name FROM employee_d WHERE id IN (:ids)", Map.of("ids", List.of(2L, 3L)), String.class);

// From an object's getters
np.update("INSERT INTO emp(name, dept) VALUES (:name, :dept)", new BeanPropertySqlParameterSource(bean));

// Batch from a list of beans
np.batchUpdate(sql, SqlParameterSourceUtils.createBatch(beans));

// SimpleJdbcInsert: builds the INSERT from table metadata
Number key = new SimpleJdbcInsert(jdbcTemplate)
    .withTableName("employee_d").usingGeneratedKeyColumns("id")
    .executeAndReturnKey(new MapSqlParameterSource()
        .addValue("name", "Sim").addValue("dept", "Q").addValue("salary", 5));

// JdbcClient (Spring 6.1+): one fluent API over both styles
JdbcClient client = JdbcClient.create(dataSource);
List<Employee> q = client.sql("SELECT * FROM employee_d WHERE dept = :d ORDER BY id")
    .param("d", "Q").query(Employee.class).list();
long n = client.sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employee_d WHERE dept = ?").param("Q").query(Long.class).single();
Optional<String> maybe = client.sql("SELECT name FROM employee_d WHERE id = :id")
    .param("id", -1).query(String.class).optional();     // Optional.empty

JDBC and Virtual Threads (Java 21+)

JDBC is blocking: a thread waits while the database works. Virtual threads make blocking cheap, because a waiting virtual thread unmounts from its carrier platform thread, so a Spring Boot app with spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true can handle many concurrent requests on few OS threads while still using plain JDBC.

  • The pool is still the limit. 10,000 virtual threads still share, for example, 20 Hikari connections; the rest wait in getConnection() up to connectionTimeout. Size the pool for what the database can handle, not for the number of threads, and consider a semaphore or bulkhead in front of hot paths.
  • Pinning: on Java 21–23, blocking inside a synchronized block pins the virtual thread to its carrier. Older JDBC drivers and pools used synchronized heavily; recent driver versions (MySQL Connector/J, PostgreSQL, HikariCP) replaced it with ReentrantLock. Java 24 (JEP 491) removed most monitor pinning. Diagnose with JFR's jdk.VirtualThreadPinned event.
  • Don't cache connections or heavy objects in ThreadLocal per virtual thread; there may be millions of threads.

R2DBC and Spring Data JDBC

OptionModelUse when
JDBC / JdbcTemplate / JdbcClientBlocking, SQL you writeFull SQL control, reports, bulk work
Spring Data JDBCBlocking, simple repositories over aggregates; no lazy loading, no dirty checking, no session cacheDDD-style aggregates, wanting repositories without JPA complexity
JPA / HibernateBlocking, full ORM with persistence contextRich domain models, many relationships
R2DBCNon-blocking, reactive streams (Mono/Flux)Fully reactive WebFlux stack end-to-end

R2DBC is not JDBC: it has its own drivers and API, no JPA, and only helps if the whole request pipeline is reactive. With virtual threads, many teams now get similar scalability with simpler blocking code.

Schema Migrations with Flyway or Liquibase

Database changes should be versioned with the code. Flyway runs ordered SQL scripts (V1__create_patient.sql, V2__add_email.sql) and records them in flyway_schema_history; Liquibase uses changelogs (XML/YAML/SQL) with rollback support. Spring Boot runs either automatically at startup. Rules: never edit an applied migration (checksum fails), keep migrations backward compatible for rolling deploys (add column → deploy code → drop old column later), and set spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate rather than update in production.

-- src/main/resources/db/migration/V3__add_patient_email.sql
ALTER TABLE patient ADD COLUMN email VARCHAR(255) NULL;
CREATE INDEX idx_patient_email ON patient (email);

Interview Questions — JDBC

Steps to connect to a DB using JDBC?
  1. Load the driver. This is automatic since JDBC 4; it used to be Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver").
  2. Get a Connection from DriverManager.getConnection(url, user, pwd) or, better, from a DataSource.
  3. Create a PreparedStatement.
  4. Execute it: executeQuery (SELECT returns a ResultSet), executeUpdate (DML returns a row count), execute (anything).
  5. Process the ResultSet.
  6. Close the resources with try-with-resources.
Statement vs PreparedStatement vs CallableStatement?
StatementPreparedStatementCallableStatement
Static SQL built by string concatenationParameterized with ?; precompiled by the DB when server-side prepare is on (MySQL Connector/J emulates it on the client by default)Calls stored procedures: {call proc(?,?)}
⚠ Open to SQL injection✔ Prevents injection; faster when reusedSupports IN, OUT and INOUT parameters
What is SQL injection and how to prevent it?

The attacker's input becomes part of the SQL: "... WHERE name='" + input + "'" with input ' OR '1'='1. Prevent it with PreparedStatement parameters (or JPA parameters), allow-list validation, least-privilege DB users, and never concatenating user input into ORDER BY or table names.

What is connection pooling? Why HikariCP?

Opening a DB connection is expensive (TCP, authentication). A pool keeps reusable connections open. HikariCP is Spring Boot's default because it's very fast and lightweight. Key settings: maximumPoolSize (often around 10–20; more isn't better), minimumIdle, connectionTimeout, idleTimeout, maxLifetime (shorter than the DB's wait_timeout), leakDetectionThreshold.

How do you manage transactions in JDBC?

Call con.setAutoCommit(false), run the statements, then con.commit(), or con.rollback() in the catch block. Savepoints: con.setSavepoint() and rollback(sp). Isolation: con.setTransactionIsolation(Connection.TRANSACTION_READ_COMMITTED).

What is batch processing in JDBC?

addBatch() followed by executeBatch() groups many statements (a single round trip only if the driver supports it). For MySQL, add rewriteBatchedStatements=true to the URL to turn them into a single multi-row INSERT, which is much faster.

ResultSet types and concurrency?

Types: TYPE_FORWARD_ONLY (default), TYPE_SCROLL_INSENSITIVE, TYPE_SCROLL_SENSITIVE. Concurrency: CONCUR_READ_ONLY, CONCUR_UPDATABLE. For large results, use setFetchSize() to stream rows (with MySQL: Integer.MIN_VALUE or useCursorFetch=true).

JDBC driver types?

Type 1 is the JDBC-ODBC bridge (removed). Type 2 is native-API. Type 3 is network protocol (middleware). Type 4 is a pure Java thin driver that speaks the DB's protocol directly. Almost all modern drivers, including MySQL Connector/J, are Type 4.

JDBC vs JdbcTemplate vs JPA?

Raw JDBC means a lot of boilerplate and checked SQLExceptions. JdbcTemplate handles opening and closing resources, translates exceptions into DataAccessException, and maps rows with RowMapper. Use it for SQL-heavy or reporting code. JPA gives you object mapping, dirty checking and caching, and suits domain-heavy CRUD. Newer options are JdbcClient (Spring 6.1) and jOOQ.

Why was Class.forName("com.mysql.cj.jdbc.Driver") needed, and why not now?

A driver registers itself with DriverManager in a static initialiser, so loading the class was enough. Since JDBC 4, DriverManager uses ServiceLoader to read META-INF/services/java.sql.Driver from each JAR, loading drivers automatically. In some WAR setups class loader visibility still breaks that, and Class.forName works around it. Using a DataSource avoids the matter.

Why doesn't PreparedStatement always prevent SQL injection?

It only protects values bound through setXxx. If you concatenate into the SQL ("... ORDER BY " + input) and then prepare that string, the injection already happened. Placeholders can't stand for table names, columns or sort direction, which leaves concatenation as a temptation there. Use an allow-list that maps input to fixed strings. The same applies to dynamic SQL inside stored procedures and to JPQL string building.

What's the output: ps = "SELECT id FROM t WHERE id IN (?)" with setString(1, "1,2")?

On MySQL, one row: id 1, and no error (tested). The whole string is a single value, and comparing an integer column to '1,2' converts the string to the number 1. You must build one ? per value, or use NamedParameterJdbcTemplate, which expands a collection. For very long lists, use a temporary table or batches of IN clauses.

Are JDBC objects thread-safe? Can I share a Connection?

Don't share one. Even where a driver synchronises internally, a Connection carries one transaction and runs one statement at a time, so two threads' work would mix into one transaction. Statement and ResultSet are not thread-safe. The right design is one connection per unit of work, borrowed from a thread-safe DataSource. JdbcTemplate is safe to share since it has no per-call state.

Why not keep a single Connection in a static field?

All threads would share one transaction and one server thread, so requests would serialise and commits would cross. The DB or a firewall will eventually drop an idle connection, leaving every later call broken. There's no recovery logic. A pool solves all of these.

What's the output: rs.getInt("bonus") when bonus is NULL?

0 (tested). Primitive getters can't represent null. Call rs.wasNull() straight after, or use rs.getObject("bonus", Integer.class), or getBigDecimal, which returns null. In a record with Integer fields, use getObject, since auto-boxing 0 hides the missing value.

What's the difference between execute(), executeQuery() and executeUpdate()?

executeQuery returns a ResultSet and throws for non-SELECT. executeUpdate returns a count and throws if the SQL produces rows. execute runs anything and returns a boolean: true means a ResultSet is ready (getResultSet), false means use getUpdateCount. In a test, execute("SELECT 1") returned true with update count -1, and an UPDATE returned false with count 1. It's for tools running unknown SQL, and procedures returning several results.

Why might an UPDATE return 1 when nothing changed?

Connector/J returns rows found by default, by setting the client "found rows" flag, while MySQL's own default count is rows changed. Setting a column to its current value returned 1 in the test. useAffectedRows=true changes that. This also matters for INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, which reports 1 for an insert and 2 for an update.

How would you load 10 million rows into a table with Java?
  1. Use a PreparedStatement batch with rewriteBatchedStatements=true, flushing every 1,000 to 5,000 rows and committing per chunk so undo logs and locks stay small.
  2. Stream the input; don't load it all into a list.
  3. Keep secondary indexes minimal during the load, or add them afterwards. Foreign key and unique checks cost time.
  4. For maximum speed use LOAD DATA from a file, though it requires configuration.
  5. Make it restartable: record the last committed chunk.
  6. Don't use a single huge transaction: it creates replica lag and a slow rollback on failure.
How would you read and export 10 million rows without running out of memory?

Don't use LIMIT/OFFSET, which gets slower as offset grows. Either stream one query (setFetchSize(Integer.MIN_VALUE) or useCursorFetch=true on MySQL, with a RowCallbackHandler or queryForStream in Spring, closing the stream) and write to the file row by row, or use keyset pagination: WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000. Keyset allows restarts and doesn't hold one connection for hours. For a streaming read, use a replica and set a timeout.

What's the difference between connection pool size and thread pool size?

Threads handle requests; connections are a scarcer resource used for part of each request. If the thread pool (200) is much larger than the connection pool (10), threads queue on getConnection, which is fine provided DB time is short. Set connectionTimeout so they fail fast rather than pile up. A pool as large as the thread pool usually pushes the overload onto the database, which is worse.

Why must maxLifetime be shorter than MySQL's wait_timeout?

The server closes connections idle past wait_timeout (8 hours by default), and firewalls often do so much sooner. If the pool believes a connection is alive, the first use fails with "Communications link failure". Retiring connections earlier, by a margin of at least a few seconds, means Hikari always closes first. keepaliveTime also helps with idle-drop firewalls. A connection in use isn't retired until it's returned.

What happens to session state on a pooled connection?

The physical session lives on, so anything you set without the pool knowing leaks to the next borrower: SET @var, SET time_zone, temp tables, SET sql_mode, and unclosed locks from GET_LOCK. Pools reset only the JDBC-visible properties (autocommit, isolation, read-only, catalog). Use the JDBC setters where they exist, and undo other changes before returning, or set them in connectionInitSql for all connections.

Explain the transaction steps in plain JDBC with an exception after the first update.

With setAutoCommit(false), the first update takes row locks and writes undo records. The exception jumps to catch, rollback() applies undo and releases locks, and the row returns to its original value. Without manual mode, the first update would have committed already, leaving half-finished work. If the catch only handles SQLException, a NullPointerException skips the rollback and it's left to the pool on close.

Does con.rollback() undo everything since the connection opened?

No, only work since the last commit, and it requires autocommit off. Calling it in autocommit mode throws an exception on most drivers. DDL statements in MySQL commit implicitly, so can't be rolled back. Non-transactional engines (MyISAM) and sequences or auto-increment values aren't rolled back: a rolled-back insert left a gap in the ID sequence in a MySQL test.

Batch insert with an error in the middle: what's stored?

It depends. With MySQL Connector/J in autocommit mode, the failing row was skipped and others stored: counts [1, -3, 1] (tested). With continueBatchOnError=false it stops at the first failure. With rewriteBatchedStatements=true the batch is one statement, so one bad row fails the whole chunk. With a transaction and a rollback in the catch, nothing is stored. Always read BatchUpdateException.getUpdateCounts(), and design explicitly.

Statement vs PreparedStatement batch?

Statement.addBatch(sql) can mix different SQL strings, but it still concatenates values. PreparedStatement.addBatch() repeats one SQL with different values. It's safe, and the rewrite optimisation works better on it. For inserts with rewriting, the driver merges VALUES lists. For prepared updates with rewriting, it sends a multi-statement packet.

Which exceptions should a DAO throw?

Generally unchecked ones with a clear message. SQLException leaks implementation detail through every layer, and callers can rarely recover. Keep the cause when wrapping. Convert expected cases into meaningful types, such as a duplicate into EmailAlreadyTaken. With Spring you get DataAccessException by adding @Repository or by using templates. Don't catch and log at every level: you'd get the same error several times.

How would you test JDBC code?

Test real SQL on a real database, because mocks of ResultSet only prove your mock. Use Testcontainers to start the same MySQL version as production. H2 is fast but differs in syntax and locking, so it can pass tests that fail in production. Spring's @JdbcTest slices the context and rolls back after each test. Mock the DAO when testing services.

What's a phantom "Communications link failure" and how do you handle it?

It means that the driver lost the socket: the server restarted, a firewall dropped an idle connection, or a failover happened. Check timeouts first: is maxLifetime under wait_timeout? Is keepaliveTime set? Are connectTimeout and socketTimeout configured? A retry is safe only for idempotent work, as you can't know whether a commit in flight succeeded. For writes, use idempotency keys.

JDBC vs Hibernate: when would you pick plain SQL even in a JPA project?

For bulk operations (a saveAll of a million entities is slow), reporting with window functions and CTEs, and hot paths needing exact SQL. JPA is better for rich aggregates and change tracking. Both can share a transaction in Spring because JpaTransactionManager exposes its connection to JdbcTemplate when the data source is the same. Call EntityManager.flush() first so pending changes reach the DB before your SQL reads them.

Output: what does this print?
Statement s = con.createStatement(); ResultSet r1 = s.executeQuery("SELECT 1"); ResultSet r2 = s.executeQuery("SELECT 2"); System.out.println(r1.isClosed());

true (tested). A statement holds at most one open result by default, so re-executing closes the previous one. Nested loops need separate statements. getMoreResults(Statement.KEEP_CURRENT_RESULT) exists for multiple results from one execution, if the driver supports it.

What's the order of closing, and what if you close the connection first?

The correct order is ResultSet, Statement, Connection, the reverse of opening, and try-with-resources does this automatically. Closing a real connection first invalidates its children, so they fail if used. With a pool, closing the connection returns it, and using an old statement after that is dangerous, since it may touch a connection now lent to someone else. Hikari's proxy protects you by rejecting calls on a closed connection.

How do you implement optimistic locking in plain JDBC?
int n = jt.update("UPDATE product SET stock = ?, version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?",
                  newStock, id, readVersion);
if (n == 0) throw new OptimisticLockException(id);

Read the row with its version, do the work, and let the WHERE clause detect interference. Zero rows means that someone else won, so retry or report it. No locks are held during the work. Use pessimistic locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE in a transaction) when conflicts are frequent.

What's the N+1 problem in JDBC, and how do you fix it?

A loop that runs a query per row: load 100 orders, then a query per order for items, 101 round trips. Fixes: use a JOIN with a ResultSetExtractor that groups rows, or do two queries with WHERE order_id IN (...) and assemble in memory. The second avoids row multiplication when there are several child collections. It's the same problem as in JPA, only more visible.

What's the purpose of ConnectionPoolDataSource and XADataSource?

Both are in javax.sql. ConnectionPoolDataSource is a vendor SPI that hands physical connections to a pool. XADataSource produces connections that can join a distributed transaction (two-phase commit across resources), coordinated by a JTA manager. XA is slow and fragile, so microservices generally use the outbox pattern or sagas.

Design: an audit service must write 5,000 events per second to MySQL. Sketch the JDBC approach.
  1. Don't insert per request. Put events on a bounded in-process queue, or Kafka if loss is unacceptable.
  2. One or a few writer threads drain up to N events or wait T milliseconds, then write a batch with rewriting on, in one transaction.
  3. Keep indexes few, and use a sequential primary key so inserts append to the B+Tree instead of splitting pages.
  4. Partition by date to allow dropping old data instantly.
  5. Handle failure: retry with backoff on deadlocks, then send to a dead-letter store; when the queue fills, apply backpressure or sample.
  6. Give it a separate small pool so that audit writes can't starve user traffic.
Do virtual threads make JDBC faster?

No, each query takes the same time. They increase throughput under concurrency because threads waiting on I/O no longer hold OS threads. The connection pool and the database remain the bottleneck, so a too-small pool now shows up as waits in getConnection(), and a huge pool can overload the DB. 💡 Use recent drivers to avoid synchronized pinning on Java 21.

What is pinning and how does it relate to JDBC drivers?

A virtual thread is pinned when it cannot unmount from its carrier while blocked, notably when blocking inside a synchronized block or native call on Java 21–23. Drivers that guarded socket I/O with synchronized could therefore block carrier threads and kill scalability. Fixes: upgrade the driver and pool, move to Java 24+ where monitors no longer pin in most cases, and check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads (older JDKs) or JFR.

JDBC vs R2DBC?

JDBC is blocking and universal, with mature drivers and full tooling (JPA, Flyway, JdbcTemplate). R2DBC is a non-blocking reactive API returning Publishers, used with Spring WebFlux and Spring Data R2DBC; it has no JPA, fewer features and a harder debugging model. Choose R2DBC only for a fully reactive stack; otherwise JDBC plus virtual threads is simpler.

Spring Data JDBC vs Spring Data JPA?

Spring Data JDBC maps aggregates directly with SQL: loading an aggregate loads it fully, save() writes immediately, and there is no lazy loading, dirty checking, first-level cache or proxy magic. JPA offers more features (lazy associations, caching, JPQL, cascades) at the cost of complexity such as N+1 queries and LazyInitializationException. Spring Data JDBC suits simpler, well-bounded aggregates.

How do you manage schema changes across environments?

With a migration tool like Flyway or Liquibase: versioned scripts in the repo, applied automatically in order and recorded in a history table, so every environment reaches the same schema. Never modify applied scripts, test migrations in CI against a real database (Testcontainers), and design changes in expand/contract steps so old and new app versions work during a rolling deploy.

How do you route read-only queries to a replica?

Mark transactions with @Transactional(readOnly = true), which calls Connection.setReadOnly(true) and lets Hibernate skip dirty checking. A routing DataSource (Spring's AbstractRoutingDataSource, wrapped in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the decision is made after the transaction flags are set) sends read-only transactions to the replica pool and others to the primary. Remember replication lag: read-your-own-writes flows must hit the primary.

MySQL / SQL Database

SQL queries, joins, indexes, normalization, transactions and ACID, isolation, InnoDB, and query tuning.

-- Top-3 salaries per department (window function, MySQL 8)
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk
  FROM employee e
) t WHERE rnk <= 3;

-- 2nd highest salary
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employee);

-- Duplicate emails
SELECT email, COUNT(*) c FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING c > 1;

-- Delete duplicates, keep lowest id
DELETE u1 FROM users u1 JOIN users u2 ON u1.email = u2.email AND u1.id > u2.id;

-- Employees earning more than their manager (self join)
SELECT e.name FROM employee e JOIN employee m ON e.manager_id = m.id WHERE e.salary > m.salary;

-- Department with no employees
SELECT d.name FROM dept d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.id IS NULL;

-- Composite index + EXPLAIN
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_cust_date ON orders(customer_id, created_at);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > '2026-01-01';
Note: every query in this section with a shown result, and every behaviour marked "tested", was run on MySQL 8.4 with the sample data below. EXPLAIN plans depend on data and statistics, so yours may differ in detail.
CREATE TABLE dept (id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL);
CREATE TABLE employee (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY, name VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL, dept_id INT NULL, manager_id INT NULL,
  salary DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, hired DATE NOT NULL,
  FOREIGN KEY (dept_id) REFERENCES dept(id),
  FOREIGN KEY (manager_id) REFERENCES employee(id));
INSERT INTO dept VALUES (1,'IT'),(2,'HR'),(3,'Sales'),(4,'Legal');
INSERT INTO employee VALUES
 (1,'Asha',1,NULL,150000,'2019-01-10'), (2,'Ben',1,1,90000,'2020-03-01'),
 (3,'Chen',1,1,120000,'2021-06-15'),    (4,'Dia',1,2,120000,'2022-02-20'),
 (5,'Eli',2,1,70000,'2020-07-07'),      (6,'Fay',2,5,70000,'2021-01-05'),
 (7,'Gus',3,1,80000,'2023-04-01'),      (8,'Hana',NULL,1,60000,'2024-01-15');

SQL Command Categories

CategoryMeaningStatementsRollback?
DDLData Definition: structureCREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAMENo: implicit commit
DMLData Manipulation: rowsSELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REPLACEYes (InnoDB)
DCLData Control: accessGRANT, REVOKENo: implicit commit
TCLTransaction ControlSTART TRANSACTION, COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINTn/a

Some texts split SELECT out as DQL. "Implicit commit" means that DDL ends any open transaction first: after UPDATE; CREATE TABLE; ROLLBACK the update survived (tested).

-- DDL
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note VARCHAR(100), ALGORITHM=INSTANT;  -- metadata only, 8.0+
ALTER TABLE orders ADD INDEX idx_status (status), ALGORITHM=INPLACE, LOCK=NONE;
-- A type change can't be instant: error 1846, "Need to rebuild the table" (tested)

-- DML variants
INSERT INTO acct VALUES (1, 50) AS new
  ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE bal = acct.bal + new.bal;      -- upsert; the alias form replaces VALUES(), 8.0.19+
REPLACE INTO t(id, email) VALUES (1, 'a');               -- DELETE then INSERT: other columns reset!
INSERT IGNORE INTO t(id, email) VALUES (1, 'zz');        -- duplicate becomes a warning
UPDATE employee e JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id SET e.salary = e.salary * 1.1 WHERE d.name = 'HR';
DELETE FROM log WHERE created < '2025-01-01' ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000;   -- purge in small chunks

-- DCL, with roles (8.0+)
CREATE ROLE 'readonly';
GRANT SELECT ON shop.* TO 'readonly';
CREATE USER 'report'@'%' IDENTIFIED BY '...';
GRANT 'readonly' TO 'report'@'%';
SET DEFAULT ROLE 'readonly' TO 'report'@'%';             -- or the role is inactive at login
REVOKE SELECT ON shop.* FROM 'readonly';

-- TCL
START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - 10 WHERE id = 1;
SAVEPOINT s1;
UPDATE acct SET bal = bal + 10 WHERE id = 2;
ROLLBACK TO s1;
COMMIT;
Gotcha: REPLACE isn't an update. On a row with n=5, note='keep', REPLACE INTO r(id, email) VALUES (1,'a') left n=0, note=NULL (tested), because the old row was deleted. It also fires delete triggers and cascades through foreign keys. Prefer ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE.

Data Types

FamilyTypesNotes
IntegerTINYINT 1B, SMALLINT 2B, MEDIUMINT 3B, INT 4B, BIGINT 8BINT(11)'s number is display width, not size, and it's deprecated. BOOLEAN is TINYINT(1).
Exact decimalDECIMAL(p,s)Exact. Use for money.
ApproximateFLOAT, DOUBLECAST(0.1 AS FLOAT)+CAST(0.2 AS FLOAT) gave 0.30000000447034836 (tested). Literal 0.1+0.2=0.3 is true, as literals are exact.
StringCHAR(n) up to 255 chars, VARCHAR(n) up to 65,535 bytes across the rown is in characters. utf8mb4 uses up to 4 bytes, and it's the default charset in 8.0+. MySQL's utf8 is a 3-byte alias that can't store emoji.
LargeTEXT, BLOB and TINY/MEDIUM/LONG variantsStored off-page, can't be fully indexed (prefix only), and force on-disk temp tables in some cases
Date/timeDATE, TIME, DATETIME, TIMESTAMP, YEARFractions up to 6 digits: DATETIME(3)
OthersENUM, SET, JSON, BIT, BINARY, spatialENUM stores an index, and adding a value in the middle needs a rebuild

Choose the smallest type that fits: smaller rows mean more rows per page, and every secondary index also stores the primary key. A BINARY(16) UUID is half the size of CHAR(36).

Functions worth knowing (tested results)

SELECT 7/2, 7 DIV 2, 7 MOD 2, 1/0;              -- 3.5000  3  1  NULL
SELECT ROUND(2.5), ROUND(-2.5), TRUNCATE(1.99,1); -- 3  -3  1.9   (DECIMAL rounds away from zero)
SELECT LENGTH('é'), CHAR_LENGTH('é');            -- 2  1   (bytes vs characters)
SELECT CONCAT('a', NULL), CONCAT_WS('-','a',NULL,'b'), COALESCE(NULL,2), IFNULL(NULL,3), NULLIF(1,1);
                                                 -- NULL  a-b  2  3  NULL
SELECT DATEDIFF('2026-03-01','2026-02-01');      -- 28
SELECT DATE_ADD('2026-01-31', INTERVAL 1 MONTH); -- 2026-02-28
SELECT LAST_DAY('2026-02-10');                   -- 2026-02-28
SELECT TIMESTAMPDIFF(MONTH,'2026-01-15','2026-03-14');  -- 1
SELECT '5'+3, '5a'+3, 'a'=0;                     -- 8  8  1   (string to number conversion)

Constraints

ConstraintRuleDetails
NOT NULLValue requiredAlso helps the optimizer
UNIQUENo duplicatesMultiple NULLs are allowed: 2 NULLs and a 1 were all inserted (tested)
PRIMARY KEYUnique + not nullDefines the clustered index
FOREIGN KEYMust match a parent rowChild column is indexed automatically; error 1452 when violated (tested)
CHECKCondition must not be falseEnforced since 8.0.16, earlier parsed and ignored. NULL passes, since it's not false (tested). Error 3819.
DEFAULTValue when omittedExpressions allowed since 8.0.13
AUTO_INCREMENTGenerated sequenceNot a constraint strictly, but always on a key

Foreign key actions: ON DELETE / ON UPDATE can be CASCADE, SET NULL, RESTRICT, or NO ACTION (InnoDB treats the last two the same: it checks immediately). FKs give safety but each insert into the child has to check and lock the parent row. Very high-write or sharded systems often drop them and enforce integrity in the application.

Auto-increment gaps are normal. A rolled-back insert still consumes a value (IDs 1 then 3 in a test), so never assume that IDs are continuous. DELETE FROM t keeps the counter and TRUNCATE resets it (next IDs 4 and 1, tested).

Joins with Results

A join combines rows from two tables. The default strategy is nested loop: for each row in the driving table, look up matching rows in the other. An index on the join column of the inner table makes this a quick lookup. Hash join (8.0.18+) builds a hash table on the smaller input and is used when no index helps, replacing the older block nested loop. There's no sort-merge join in MySQL.

-- FULL OUTER JOIN doesn't exist in MySQL: emulate it
SELECT e.name emp, d.name dept FROM employee e LEFT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
UNION
SELECT e.name, d.name FROM employee e RIGHT JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id;
-- 9 rows, including (Hana, NULL) and (NULL, Legal)

-- Self join: a table joined to itself under two aliases
SELECT e.name emp, m.name mgr FROM employee e LEFT JOIN employee m ON m.id = e.manager_id;
-- LEFT, so that Asha (no manager) stays: Asha NULL, Ben Asha, Dia Ben, ...

-- LATERAL (8.0.14+): a derived table that can refer to earlier tables. "Top row per group".
SELECT d.name, x.name, x.salary
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN LATERAL (
  SELECT e.name, e.salary FROM employee e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id
  ORDER BY e.salary DESC, e.id LIMIT 1
) x ON TRUE;
-- IT Asha 150000 | HR Eli 70000 | Sales Gus 80000 | Legal NULL NULL
Gotcha: ON vs WHERE in an outer join. A condition on the right table in ON limits what matches. In WHERE it filters afterwards, and removes the NULL rows, which turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN. 
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM dept d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id AND e.salary > 100000;
-- IT Asha, IT Chen, IT Dia, HR NULL, Sales NULL, Legal NULL   (all depts kept)
SELECT d.name, e.name FROM dept d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id WHERE e.salary > 100000;
-- IT Asha, IT Chen, IT Dia                                    (others lost)

USING(col) is shorthand when the names match. NATURAL JOIN joins on all same-named columns, so adding a column can silently change results. Avoid it: JOIN employee e USING(id) on our tables joined the wrong columns and returned 4 rows rather than 7 (tested). a, b without a condition is a cross join.

Logical Execution Order

SQL is written SELECT ... FROM, but it's evaluated as if in this order. The optimizer may do things differently physically, as long as the result is the same.

That order explains these errors (all tested):

  • WHERE d > 1 using a SELECT alias: error 1054, because WHERE runs before SELECT. MySQL does allow aliases in GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY as an extension to the standard.
  • WHERE COUNT(*) > 1: error 1111, "Invalid use of group function". Groups don't exist yet, so use HAVING.
  • WHERE ROW_NUMBER() OVER (...) = 1: error 3593. Window functions run after HAVING, so wrap them in a derived table or CTE.

GROUP BY, HAVING and Aggregates

SELECT d.name, COUNT(e.id) cnt, COALESCE(SUM(e.salary),0) total, AVG(e.salary) avg_sal
FROM dept d LEFT JOIN employee e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.id, d.name;
-- IT 4 480000 120000 | HR 2 140000 70000 | Sales 1 80000 80000 | Legal 0 0 NULL

SELECT COUNT(*), COUNT(dept_id), COUNT(DISTINCT dept_id) FROM employee;   -- 8  7  3
  • COUNT(*) counts rows, COUNT(col) counts non-NULL values. For Legal, COUNT(*) would give 1 from the NULL-extended row. COUNT(e.id) gives 0.
  • Aggregates ignore NULL: values 10, NULL, 20 give AVG 15, while SUM/COUNT(*) gives 10.
  • On no rows: COUNT returns 0, and SUM, MAX return NULL. With GROUP BY and no rows, you get no rows at all.
  • GROUP BY treats NULLs as one group, and ORDER BY puts NULLs first ascending and last descending in MySQL.
  • HAVING without GROUP BY works, on the single implicit group.
  • ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY is on by default: selecting a column that isn't grouped, aggregated, or functionally dependent gives error 1055. Before 5.7.5 MySQL returned an arbitrary row's value. ANY_VALUE(col) is the explicit opt-out. Grouping by a primary key allows other columns of that table.
SELECT dept_id, COUNT(*) FROM employee WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id WITH ROLLUP;
-- 1 4 | 2 2 | 3 1 | NULL 7   (the last row is the grand total)
SELECT IF(GROUPING(dept_id), 'ALL', dept_id) d, COUNT(*) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id WITH ROLLUP;
-- GROUPING() tells a real NULL group from a super-total: NULL 1 ... ALL 8

SELECT dept_id, GROUP_CONCAT(name ORDER BY name SEPARATOR ', ') FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id;
-- 1  Asha, Ben, Chen, Dia     (truncated at group_concat_max_len, default 1024 bytes)

-- Pivot: rows to columns
SELECT dept_id,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(hired) <= 2020 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) old_hires,
       SUM(CASE WHEN YEAR(hired) >  2020 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) new_hires
FROM employee WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL GROUP BY dept_id;     -- 1 2 2 | 2 1 1 | 3 0 1

NULL: Three-Valued Logic

NULL means "unknown". A comparison with it gives NULL, not false. WHERE keeps only true rows. The table shows real output.

ExpressionResultWhy
NULL = NULLNULLUse IS NULL
NULL <=> NULL1MySQL's null-safe equality
1 + NULLNULLNULL spreads through arithmetic
1 IN (1, NULL)1A match was found
2 IN (1, NULL)NULLNot found, but it might equal the NULL
2 NOT IN (1, NULL)NULLSo it filters the row out!
Gotcha: the NOT IN trap. SELECT name FROM employee WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT manager_id FROM employee) returned no rows (tested), because Asha's manager_id is NULL. Add WHERE manager_id IS NOT NULL to the subquery, or better use NOT EXISTS, which isn't affected. Both return Chen, Dia, Fay, Gus, Hana.

Subqueries

KindReturnsWhereExample
ScalarOne valueAnywhere a value fitsWHERE salary > (SELECT AVG(salary) FROM employee)
RowOne rowRow comparisonWHERE (a, b) = (SELECT x, y ...)
ColumnA listIN, ANY, ALLWHERE dept_id IN (SELECT id ...)
Table (derived)RowsFROM; needs an aliasFROM (SELECT ...) t
CorrelatedAny of thoseRefers to the outer rowWHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id

A correlated subquery logically runs once per outer row, because it depends on it. That's costly without an index on the correlation column.

-- Earning above their own department's average
SELECT e.name, e.salary FROM employee e
WHERE e.salary > (SELECT AVG(x.salary) FROM employee x WHERE x.dept_id = e.dept_id);
-- Asha 150000

-- EXISTS stops at the first match; the select list is ignored
SELECT e.name FROM employee e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee r WHERE r.manager_id = e.id);
-- Chen, Dia, Fay, Gus, Hana: people with no reports
INEXISTSJOIN
MeaningValue in a listRow existsCombine rows
DuplicatesNo duplicates in the outer rowNo duplicatesMultiplies rows if the right side has many matches
NULL in subqueryNOT IN breaksSafeSafe
Can return inner columnsNoNoYes
Performance in 8.0Rewritten as semijoin when possibleSame engine

"JOIN is always faster than a subquery" is outdated. On d.id IN (SELECT dept_id FROM employee), MySQL 8.4 flattened it into a join and EXPLAIN showed FirstMatch(d) (tested), a semijoin strategy that stops at the first match. Restrictions remain: LIMIT in an IN subquery gives error 1235, and a DELETE or UPDATE can't select from the target table directly (error 1093). Wrap it in a derived table instead, as the delete-duplicates example below does.

Common Table Expressions (CTEs)

A CTE (8.0+) is a named temporary result that exists for one statement. It makes multi-step queries readable, can be referenced several times, and is the only way to do recursion.

WITH dept_avg AS (
  SELECT dept_id, AVG(salary) av FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id
)
SELECT e.name, e.salary, a.av
FROM employee e JOIN dept_avg a ON a.dept_id = e.dept_id
WHERE e.salary > a.av;                 -- Asha 150000 120000
CTEDerived tableViewTemp table
LifetimeOne statementOne statementPermanentSession
Referenced twiceYesNo, repeat itYesYes (once per query in some cases)
RecursiveYesNoInside a view definitionNo
IndexesAuto onlyAuto onlyBase tables'You can add them

Recursive CTEs

A recursive CTE has an anchor that gives the starting rows, and a recursive member that joins to the CTE itself. Each iteration works only on rows produced by the previous one, and it stops when no new rows come out.

-- Org chart: walk the tree downward
WITH RECURSIVE org AS (
  SELECT id, name, 0 AS lvl, CAST(name AS CHAR(200)) AS path
  FROM employee WHERE manager_id IS NULL                 -- anchor
  UNION ALL
  SELECT e.id, e.name, o.lvl + 1, CONCAT(o.path, ' > ', e.name)
  FROM employee e JOIN org o ON e.manager_id = o.id      -- recursive member
)
SELECT lvl, path FROM org ORDER BY path;
-- 0 Asha | 1 Asha > Ben | 2 Asha > Ben > Dia | 1 Asha > Chen | 1 Asha > Eli
-- 2 Asha > Eli > Fay | 1 Asha > Gus | 1 Asha > Hana

-- Generate a date series, to fill gaps in a report
WITH RECURSIVE d(dt) AS (
  SELECT DATE '2026-01-01'
  UNION ALL
  SELECT dt + INTERVAL 1 DAY FROM d WHERE dt < '2026-01-05'
)
SELECT dt FROM d;              -- 5 rows: Jan 1 to Jan 5
  • The column types come from the anchor. Without CAST(name AS CHAR(200)), path takes the width of name, and longer values fail or truncate.
  • A runaway query is stopped by cte_max_recursion_depth (default 1000). Counting to 2000 failed: "Recursive query aborted after 1001 iterations" (tested). Raise it per session, or SET_VAR as a hint.
  • A cycle in the data (A manages B, B manages A) never terminates by itself. Track the path and test FIND_IN_SET, or limit the depth.
  • Use UNION rather than UNION ALL in the CTE to remove duplicate rows, which also stops simple cycles.

Window Functions

An aggregate with GROUP BY collapses rows. A window function (8.0+) computes across related rows and keeps every row. The syntax is func() OVER (PARTITION BY ... ORDER BY ... frame): partition picks the group, order sorts it, and the frame picks which rows around the current one to use.

FamilyFunctions
RankingROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, NTILE(n), PERCENT_RANK, CUME_DIST
ValueLAG, LEAD, FIRST_VALUE, LAST_VALUE, NTH_VALUE
AggregateSUM, AVG, COUNT, MIN, MAX with OVER
SELECT name, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) dept_total,
       ROUND(salary / SUM(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id) * 100, 1) pct,
       LAG(salary) OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY hired) prev_hire
FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1 ORDER BY hired;
-- Asha 150000 480000 31.3 NULL
-- Ben   90000 480000 18.8 150000
-- Chen 120000 480000 25.0 90000
-- Dia  120000 480000 25.0 120000

The frame: a classic trap

With ORDER BY and no frame, the default is RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW. RANGE treats rows with the same sort value as peers, so ties share a total. Without ORDER BY, the frame is the whole partition.

SELECT id, salary,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS rng,
       SUM(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) AS rws
FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1;
-- 2   90000   90000   90000
-- 3  120000  330000  210000     (rng includes id 4, a tie)
-- 4  120000  330000  330000
-- 1  150000  480000  480000

SELECT id, salary,
       LAST_VALUE(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary) AS wrong,
       LAST_VALUE(salary) OVER (ORDER BY salary
         ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND UNBOUNDED FOLLOWING) AS right_one
FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1;
-- wrong just shows the current value: 90000, 120000, 120000, 150000
-- right_one: 150000 on every row. The default frame ends at the current row.

Frames can also be sliding: ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW is a moving average. A named window saves repetition: ... OVER w ... WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC).

SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER w rn, RANK() OVER w r, DENSE_RANK() OVER w dr
FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1 WINDOW w AS (ORDER BY salary DESC);
-- 150000 1 1 1 | 120000 2 2 2 | 120000 3 2 2 | 90000 4 4 3

Window functions usually need a sort of the partition, so an index matching (partition, order) can avoid it.

Set Operations

OperatorResultSince
UNIONBoth sets, duplicates removedAlways
UNION ALLBoth sets, keptAlways
INTERSECTOnly rows in both8.0.31
EXCEPTRows in the first but not the second8.0.31
SELECT dept_id FROM employee WHERE salary > 100000
INTERSECT
SELECT dept_id FROM employee WHERE salary < 100000;     -- 1
SELECT id FROM dept EXCEPT SELECT dept_id FROM employee; -- 4

-- ORDER BY and LIMIT per branch need parentheses
(SELECT id FROM dept ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 1)
UNION ALL
(SELECT id FROM dept ORDER BY id LIMIT 1);               -- 4, 1

Column counts must match (error 1222 otherwise), and names come from the first SELECT. Duplicates are compared across the whole row. UNION is left-associative, so in SELECT 1 UNION SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT 1 the result was two rows (tested).

Views

A view is a stored SELECT. It adds no data, but simplifies queries and restricts access (grant on the view, not the base table). MySQL processes a view in one of two ways: MERGE, which inlines the view's SQL into your query, so indexes still work, or TEMPTABLE, which materialises the view's results first. GROUP BY, DISTINCT, aggregates and UNION force TEMPTABLE, which is slower and not updatable. MySQL has no materialized views: build a summary table refreshed by an event or the application.

CREATE VIEW v_it AS
  SELECT id, name, dept_id, salary FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 1
  WITH CHECK OPTION;

UPDATE v_it SET salary = salary * 1.1 WHERE id = 2;   -- updates employee through the view
UPDATE v_it SET dept_id = 2 WHERE id = 2;             -- ERROR 1369: CHECK OPTION failed (tested)
-- A view with GROUP BY: ERROR 1288: not updatable (tested)
-- EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM v_it WHERE id = 2 shows the PRIMARY key: it was merged (tested)

Stored Procedures and Functions

A stored program is SQL plus control flow, stored in the server. Each session parses and caches the routine when it first calls it. Note that MySQL doesn't precompile it to a shared plan, unlike the claim commonly made in interviews. DELIMITER is a client command that stops ; ending the definition early.

DELIMITER //
CREATE PROCEDURE raise_dept(IN p_dept INT, IN p_pct DECIMAL(5,2), OUT p_count INT)
BEGIN
  DECLARE EXIT HANDLER FOR SQLEXCEPTION BEGIN ROLLBACK; RESIGNAL; END;
  START TRANSACTION;
  UPDATE employee SET salary = salary * (1 + p_pct/100) WHERE dept_id = p_dept;
  SET p_count = ROW_COUNT();
  COMMIT;
END//

CREATE FUNCTION tax(p DECIMAL(10,2)) RETURNS DECIMAL(10,2) DETERMINISTIC NO SQL
BEGIN
  RETURN CASE WHEN p > 100000 THEN p * 0.3 ELSE p * 0.2 END;
END//
DELIMITER ;

CALL raise_dept(3, 10, @n);
SELECT @n, tax(200000.00);     -- 1  60000.00
ProcedureFunction
Called withCALLInside SQL expressions
ReturnsOUT params, result setsExactly one value
ParametersIN, OUT, INOUTIN only
TransactionsCan commitCan't commit or roll back
Dynamic SQLYes: PREPARE, EXECUTENo
Used in WHERENoYes, but runs per row and blocks index use

With binary logging on, a function needs DETERMINISTIC, NO SQL or READS SQL DATA to be created without SUPER-level trust. Pros of stored logic: fewer round trips and central data rules. Cons: hard to test, version and debug, ties you to the vendor, and uses DB CPU, the hardest resource to scale. Modern teams keep business logic in services, using procedures only for data-heavy batch work.

Cursors

A cursor iterates a result row by row in a stored program. In MySQL they're read-only, forward-only, and asensitive. Set-based SQL is nearly always faster, so use a cursor only when each row needs procedural logic.

CREATE PROCEDURE cur_demo(OUT p_total DECIMAL(12,2))
BEGIN
  DECLARE done INT DEFAULT 0;
  DECLARE v_sal DECIMAL(10,2);
  DECLARE c CURSOR FOR SELECT salary FROM employee WHERE dept_id = 2;
  DECLARE CONTINUE HANDLER FOR NOT FOUND SET done = 1;     -- declared after the cursor
  SET p_total = 0;
  OPEN c;
  read_loop: LOOP
    FETCH c INTO v_sal;
    IF done THEN LEAVE read_loop; END IF;                  -- check right after FETCH
    SET p_total = p_total + v_sal;
  END LOOP;
  CLOSE c;
END
-- CALL cur_demo(@t); SELECT @t;   gives 140000.00

Triggers and Events

A trigger runs for each affected row, BEFORE or AFTER an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. NEW and OLD hold the row. BEFORE triggers can change NEW or reject the row. MySQL has row-level triggers only, with no statement-level triggers.

CREATE TRIGGER trg BEFORE UPDATE ON employee FOR EACH ROW
BEGIN
  IF NEW.salary < 0 THEN
    SIGNAL SQLSTATE '45000' SET MESSAGE_TEXT = 'negative salary';    -- aborts the statement
  END IF;
  IF NEW.salary <> OLD.salary THEN
    INSERT INTO audit_log(emp_id, old_sal, new_sal) VALUES (OLD.id, OLD.salary, NEW.salary);
  END IF;
END
-- UPDATE employee SET salary = -1 WHERE id = 7;   ERROR 1644: negative salary (tested)
-- The raise_dept call above added one audit row: 7, 80000.00, 88000.00

A trigger runs inside the same transaction, so a failure in it undoes the statement. It can't modify the table it's defined on through another statement, and it doesn't fire for changes made by a foreign key cascade, which often surprises people. Triggers hide logic and add per-row cost. Use them for narrow audit or denormalisation needs.

An event is a scheduled job inside MySQL, run by the event scheduler (event_scheduler=ON by default in 8.0+).

CREATE EVENT purge_audit
  ON SCHEDULE EVERY 1 DAY STARTS '2027-01-01 02:00:00'
  DO DELETE FROM audit_log WHERE at < NOW() - INTERVAL 90 DAY;

It only runs on the node where enabled: on replicas events are disabled by default, and after failover you must enable them. A central scheduler is easier to monitor.

Indexes in Depth

Why a B+Tree

InnoDB stores everything in 16 KB pages (innodb_page_size), because disks and the buffer pool work in blocks. An index has to find a key with as few page reads as possible. A B+Tree is a wide, shallow tree. Internal pages hold only keys and child pointers, so one page fans out to many children. All row data sits in leaf pages, which are linked to each other for range scans.

The sizing maths is a favourite question. A BIGINT key (8 bytes) plus a pointer (6 bytes) is 14 bytes, so one 16 KB internal page holds about 1,170 entries. With 1 KB rows, a leaf holds about 16. A tree of height 3 then addresses 1,170 × 1,170 × 16, about 20 million rows, in 3 page reads, and the top levels are normally cached in memory.

StructureWhy not (for a general index)
HashEquality only; no ranges or ordering. USING HASH is for the MEMORY engine.
Binary / AVL / Red-black treeTwo children per node, so height grows to about 30 for a billion keys, and each level may be a disk read
B-TreeData in internal nodes lowers fan-out, and range scans must walk up and down the tree
B+TreeHigh fan-out, predictable height, and linked leaves for ranges and sorting

Clustered and secondary indexes

In InnoDB the table is the primary key B+Tree: leaves hold the entire row. If there's no primary key, InnoDB uses the first unique NOT NULL index, or else makes a hidden 6-byte GEN_CLUST_INDEX on a row ID. Every other index is secondary: its leaves hold the indexed columns plus the primary key value (not a physical address, so rows can move during page splits without touching secondary indexes).

So the choice of primary key affects the entire table:

  • Sequential key (BIGINT AUTO_INCREMENT): new rows append to the last leaf, so pages fill up and stay compact.
  • Random key (UUID v4): each insert lands in a random page, causing page splits, half-empty pages, poor cache locality, and more I/O. If you need UUIDs, use a time-ordered form (UUID v7), or BINARY(16) with UUID_TO_BIN(uuid, 1), which moves the time bits forward.
  • Short key: its bytes are repeated in every secondary index entry.

In MyISAM there's no clustering. All indexes, including the primary, point to a file offset.

Composite indexes and the leftmost prefix rule

An index on (a, b, c) is sorted like a phone book: by a, then b inside equal a, then c. Values of b alone aren't sorted across the tree, so the index helps only when you start from the left.

Condition on INDEX(a, b, c)Uses the index?
a = 1Yes, column a
a = 1 AND b = 2Yes, a and b
b = 2 AND a = 1Yes: order in WHERE doesn't matter
a = 1 AND b = 2 AND c = 3Yes, all three
b = 2No (possibly a skip scan)
a = 1 AND c = 3a for seeking; c can filter by index condition pushdown
a > 1 AND b = 2a for the range; b can't seek, since a range stops the seek
a = 1 AND b > 2 AND c = 3a and b; c only filters
a = 1 ORDER BY bYes, and no sort is needed
a > 1 ORDER BY bRange on a, then a filesort (tested)
ORDER BY a ASC, b DESCNeeds a mixed index: (a ASC, b DESC) (descending indexes are 8.0+). Otherwise filesort (tested).

Design rule, called ERS: columns tested with Equality first, then the ones used for Range or Sorting. For WHERE status = ? AND created > ? ORDER BY created, use (status, created). The old advice to put the most selective column first is secondary: what matters is that the query can use the columns. Note that (a, b) makes a separate index on (a) redundant.

Covering index

If an index contains every column the query touches, InnoDB doesn't visit the clustered index. Secondary indexes silently contain the primary key too, so INDEX(customer_id, created_at) also covers SELECT id .... Covering turns random row lookups into a sequential leaf scan. EXPLAIN shows Using index. Don't confuse that with Using index condition, which is the pushdown described next.

Index Condition Pushdown (ICP)

Without ICP, the engine fetches each row, then the server applies the rest of WHERE. With ICP (5.6+), conditions on columns that are in the index are evaluated by the engine on index entries before going to the row, so far fewer rows are read. EXPLAIN shows Using index condition.

Index merge

Normally one index is used per table in a query. Index merge uses several and combines the row IDs: union for OR, intersect for AND, and sort_union. It often shows that a composite index is missing.

EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 OR total = 1000.00;
-- type: index_merge   key: idx_cust_date,idx_total
-- Extra: Using sort_union(idx_cust_date,idx_total); Using where         (tested)

Cardinality and selectivity

Cardinality is the estimated number of distinct values (SHOW INDEX). Selectivity is cardinality divided by rows, 1 being unique. On 30,000 rows the test table reported 500 for customer_id, 4 for status. A low-selectivity index is often ignored: if a value matches 25% of rows, reading a quarter of the table through secondary lookups is slower than a scan. status is still useful for a rare value, or as a leading column in a composite. The numbers are estimates from sampled pages, and stale statistics give bad plans: ANALYZE TABLE refreshes them. For skewed columns, ANALYZE TABLE t UPDATE HISTOGRAM ON col stores a value distribution (8.0+).

Other index kinds and features

FeatureExamplePurpose
PrefixINDEX(url(50))Index the first N characters of long strings. Can't cover or sort.
Functional (8.0.13+)INDEX((YEAR(created_at)))Index an expression; the query must use the same expression (tested)
Invisible (8.0+)ALTER TABLE t ALTER INDEX i INVISIBLETest dropping an index safely, since it's kept up to date. Tested: the plan fell back to a full scan.
Descending (8.0+)INDEX(a ASC, b DESC)Mixed-direction sorts. A plain index can also be read backwards (Backward index scan).
Full-textFULLTEXT(title) and MATCH ... AGAINSTWord search
SpatialSPATIAL INDEX(geo)R-tree for geometry
Multi-valued (8.0.17+)On a JSON arrayOne row, many index entries

Each index slows writes, takes memory and disk, and increases lock footprint. Remove unused ones: sys.schema_unused_indexes and sys.schema_redundant_indexes list them.

EXPLAIN

EXPLAIN shows the plan the optimizer chose, without running the query. The test table orders has 30,000 rows and indexes idx_cust_date(customer_id, created_at), idx_status(status), idx_total(total).

ColumnMeaning
id, select_typeWhich SELECT: SIMPLE, PRIMARY, SUBQUERY, DERIVED, UNION
table, partitionsTable, and partitions after pruning
typeAccess method. The most important column.
possible_keys, keyCandidates, and the index chosen
key_lenBytes of the index used. Tells you how many composite columns are in play: 4 for an INT, 9 with a DATETIME added (tested).
refWhat's compared to the index
rows, filteredEstimated rows examined, and % left after conditions
ExtraDetails: see below
type, best to worstMeaningTested example
system / constAt most one row, via PK or uniqueWHERE id = 5
eq_refOne row per driving row, via PK or uniqueJoining on a primary key
refEquality on a non-unique indexWHERE customer_id = 7: 60 rows
rangeIndex rangecustomer_id = 7 AND created_at > ...: 28 rows, key_len 9
indexScan a whole indexCOUNT(*) used the smallest index
ALLFull table scanWHERE created_at > ... alone: about 30,000 rows
ExtraMeaningReaction
Using indexCovering indexGood
Using index conditionPushdownGood
Using whereServer filters rows after the engineFine, but check the row counts
Using filesortA sort outside of index order. May be in memory, despite the name.Add an index that matches, if it's frequent
Using temporaryTemp table for GROUP BY, DISTINCT or UNIONLook for an index; cut row count
Backward index scanIndex read in reverseFine
Select tables optimized awayMIN(id) answered from the indexGreat
Using sort_union(...)Index mergeConsider a composite
Using index for skip scanSkip scan (8.0.13+): jumps across distinct leading valuesGood, if a little unusual
EXPLAIN FORMAT=TREE SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) FROM orders WHERE status='PAID'
GROUP BY customer_id ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;
-- -> Limit: 5 row(s)
--     -> Sort: SUM(total) DESC, limit input to 5 row(s) per chunk
--         -> Table scan on <temporary>
--             -> Aggregate using temporary table
--                 -> Index lookup on orders using idx_status (status='PAID')

EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 7 AND created_at > '2026-01-01';
-- 8.0.18+: RUNS the query, and adds real times and row counts to each step.
-- A large gap between estimated and actual rows means stale or missing statistics.
Gotcha: EXPLAIN ANALYZE really executes the SELECT, and rows in plain EXPLAIN is an estimate. Also, LIMIT isn't taken into account in the rows figure, so LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000 showing 20,020 rows is a real warning, but a plain LIMIT 10 may look worse than it is.

Query Optimisation Playbook

MySQL's optimizer is cost-based: it estimates the I/O and CPU cost of each candidate plan from statistics, and picks the cheapest estimate. It isn't always right, so check rather than assume.

Conditions that stop index use (tested on 30,000 rows)

BadWhyPlanBetter
ABS(customer_id) = 7Function hides the columnALLcustomer_id = 7, or a functional index
YEAR(created_at) = 2026SameNo range on created_atcreated_at >= '2026-01-01' AND created_at < '2027-01-01'
ref = 12345 on VARCHARThe column is converted to a number, as many strings equal 12345ALLref = '12345': ref, 1 row
ref LIKE '%123'No sorted prefix to seekALLLIKE '123%' is a range. For infixes, full-text search.
created_at > ... aloneSkips the leftmost columnALLAn index starting with created_at

The rule is called being sargable (Search ARGument ABLE): leave the column alone on one side of the comparison. Note the opposite direction: comparing an integer column to a string is fine, because the constant is what's converted.

Pagination

-- ⚠ Reads and throws away 20,000 rows: rows = 20020 in EXPLAIN
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000;

-- Keyset pagination: start from the last row seen. Index seek, constant cost.
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > 20000 ORDER BY id LIMIT 20;

-- Multi-column keyset: (created_at, id) makes the order unique. Needs INDEX(created_at, id).
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at < ? OR (created_at = ? AND id < ?)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;

-- Deferred join when you must keep OFFSET: find ids on a small covering index, then fetch
SELECT o.* FROM orders o
JOIN (SELECT id FROM orders ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 20 OFFSET 20000) p ON p.id = o.id;

The expanded OR form gave a range plan in testing. The shorter row form, (created_at, id) < (?, ?), is valid, but got type index: no seek, only a walk from the end of the index. Keyset can't jump to page 500, and that's usually acceptable for infinite scroll or APIs. Rows inserted while paging don't shift pages, unlike OFFSET.

A checklist

  1. Find: turn on slow_query_log with long_query_time (10 s by default, so usually lowered). performance_schema.events_statements_summary_by_digest and sys.statement_analysis rank queries by total time. A 5 ms query run a million times can matter more than one 30 s report.
  2. Understand: EXPLAIN, then EXPLAIN ANALYZE.
  3. Fix the query: list columns, remove needless DISTINCT, avoid functions on columns, push filters down, use UNION ALL where duplicates can't occur.
  4. Fix the index: composite in ERS order; aim for covering on hot paths.
  5. Check join order: the driving table should be the smallest after filtering, and the inner table's join column should be indexed. Both columns must have the same type and collation, or the index is skipped.
  6. Fix the schema: type sizes, a summary table, deliberate denormalisation, partition pruning.
  7. Tune the system: innodb_buffer_pool_size (often 50–70% of RAM on a dedicated host; the default is only 128 MB), read replicas, a cache in front.

Hints exist for when the optimizer is wrong: FORCE INDEX (idx), /*+ INDEX(t idx) */, /*+ JOIN_ORDER(a, b) */. They're a last resort, as they keep forcing the same plan when the data changes. MySQL 8.0 removed the old query cache, because its global lock didn't scale.

Normalization with a Worked Example

Normalization removes redundancy so a fact is stored once. Redundancy causes three anomalies: an update anomaly (changing a customer's city in one row but missing others), an insert anomaly (you can't record a product until someone orders it), and a delete anomaly (deleting the last order loses the customer). The key concept is a functional dependency: X → Y means that X determines Y.

Start with a flat order sheet:

order_idcustomercityzipitemsorder_date
1AshaPune411001Pen x2 @10, Book x1 @502026-01-05
2BenPune411001Pen x1 @102026-01-06

1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups. items holds a list, so split to one row per item. The key becomes (order_id, product).

order_idproductqtypricecustomercityziporder_date
1Pen210AshaPune4110012026-01-05
1Book150AshaPune4110012026-01-05

2NF: no partial dependency. Non-key columns must depend on the whole key. order_id → customer, order_date and product → price use only part of it. Split into orders(order_id, customer, city, zip, order_date), product(product, price), and order_item(order_id, product, qty). A table with a single-column key is automatically in 2NF if it's in 1NF.

3NF: no transitive dependency. In orders, order_id → customer → city, and zip → city. Non-key columns determine others, so split: customer(customer_id, name, zip) and zip(zip, city). Orders keep only customer_id. Practical teams often stop short of a zip table.

BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key. It's stricter than 3NF, and matters when candidate keys overlap. Take enrolment(student, course, instructor), where a student has one instructor per course, and each instructor teaches one course. Candidate keys: (student, course) and (student, instructor). The dependency instructor → course doesn't break 3NF, because course is part of a key, but instructor isn't a key, so it breaks BCNF. Split into teaches(instructor, course) and enrolment(student, instructor). The cost: "one instructor per student per course" can no longer be enforced by a single unique constraint.

Keep in mind: order_item should store the price at order time. It looks like redundancy, but it's a different fact: the product price can change, whereas a past order mustn't. Denormalisation is the deliberate reverse, for read speed: a counter column, or a copied name to avoid a join. You pay with duplicate writes and the risk of drift. 4NF and 5NF handle multi-valued and join dependencies, and come up rarely.

ACID Mapped to InnoDB

Interviewers want the mechanism behind each letter.

PropertyMechanism
AtomicityUndo log: before-images let a rollback reverse changes
ConsistencyThe goal. Constraints, plus the other three properties, and correct application code.
IsolationMVCC for reads, locks for writes
DurabilityRedo log flushed at commit, plus the doublewrite buffer against torn pages

Isolation Levels and Anomalies

AnomalyWhat happens
Dirty readYou read another transaction's uncommitted change, and it then rolls back
Non-repeatable readRe-reading a row gives a different value, because someone committed in between
PhantomRe-running a range query returns more or fewer rows
Lost updateTwo transactions read, then both write. One change vanishes.
Write skewTwo transactions read overlapping data and write different rows, jointly breaking a rule (two doctors both go off call)

Real two-session tests:

-- Non-repeatable read: session B adds 7 and commits between A's two reads
-- READ COMMITTED:   A reads 0, then 7
-- REPEATABLE READ:  A reads 7, then 7      (the snapshot holds)

-- Phantom under REPEATABLE READ: B inserts a row and commits between A's reads
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p;              -- 2
                                     -- B: INSERT ... COMMIT
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p;              -- 2   snapshot read
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p FOR UPDATE;   -- 3   current read: sees the latest committed data
UPDATE p SET n = 1;                  -- affects 3 rows, including B's!
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM p;              -- 3   A's own update makes the row visible

So "REPEATABLE READ prevents phantoms in InnoDB" is only partly true. Plain reads never see them, and next-key locks block inserts into a locked range when you read FOR UPDATE. Mixing snapshot reads with current reads in one transaction can still expose a phantom, as above.

-- Lost update: two sessions, default REPEATABLE READ, both do:
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT n FROM p WHERE id = 1;        -- both read 0
UPDATE p SET n = 0 + 1 WHERE id = 1; -- computed in the app
COMMIT;
-- Final n = 1, not 2 (tested). Isolation didn't help.
-- Fixes: UPDATE p SET n = n + 1           (atomic, reads the latest value)
--        SELECT ... FOR UPDATE            (pessimistic)
--        UPDATE ... WHERE version = ?     (optimistic)

At SERIALIZABLE, InnoDB turns plain SELECTs into shared-locking reads when autocommit is off. This prevents write skew at the cost of concurrency and more deadlocks.

Interview: why is RR the default in MySQL, whereas Oracle and PostgreSQL use READ COMMITTED? History: statement-based replication needed RR for correct replay. With row-based binlogs, the default since 5.7.7, many high-write systems switch to READ COMMITTED, which has fewer gap locks and so fewer deadlocks.

MVCC: How Readers Don't Block Writers

Multi-Version Concurrency Control keeps old versions of each row, so a reader sees a consistent past state without taking locks. Each clustered index record has hidden columns: DB_TRX_ID (the last transaction to change it) and DB_ROLL_PTR (a pointer to the previous version in the undo log). Together they form a version chain.

A read view is a snapshot of transaction state: the IDs active at creation, the lowest of them, and the next ID to be assigned. For a version with transaction ID T:

  1. T is my own ID: visible.
  2. T is below the lowest active ID: committed before the snapshot, so visible.
  3. T is at or above the next ID: started after the snapshot, so invisible.
  4. Otherwise, visible unless T is in the active list.

The only difference between the two main levels is when the read view is created. In READ COMMITTED it's created for each statement. In REPEATABLE READ it's created at the first consistent read and reused. So in RR the snapshot begins at the first SELECT, not at START TRANSACTION, unless you use START TRANSACTION WITH CONSISTENT SNAPSHOT.

Snapshot read vs current read: plain SELECT uses the read view. SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, UPDATE and DELETE read the latest committed version and lock it. That explains the phantom test.

Gotcha: a long-running transaction keeps an old read view, so the purge thread can't discard undo records anyone might need. History grows (SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS shows the "History list length"), and every reader has to walk longer chains. One forgotten open transaction can slow the whole server. Find it with information_schema.innodb_trx.

Undo, Redo and Binlog

Undo logRedo logBinary log
LayerInnoDBInnoDBServer, any engine
HoldsLogical before-imagesPhysical page changesLogical events: row changes or statements
PurposeRollback, MVCCCrash recoveryReplication, point-in-time recovery
WrittenDuring the transactionDuring it, flushed at commitAt commit
RetentionUntil no reader needs itCircular: reused after checkpointBy expiry (binlog_expire_logs_seconds)

Write-ahead logging: changing a data page on disk at each commit would be random I/O. Instead InnoDB changes the page in the buffer pool, leaving it dirty, and appends to the redo log, which is sequential and fast. Commit needs only the log on disk. Background threads flush dirty pages later. After a crash, redo replays what wasn't flushed, and undo rolls back transactions that hadn't committed. A checkpoint marks how far dirty pages have been flushed, and that's how much of the redo log can be reused.

Two-phase commit between redo and binlog

Two logs must agree, or a replica could differ from its source. MySQL uses an internal two-phase commit.

Group commit batches many transactions into one disk flush, which is how this stays fast.

SettingValueEffect
innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit1 (default)Flush redo at every commit: full durability
2Write to OS each commit, fsync once a second: an OS crash can lose about 1 s
0Once a second: a mysqld crash can lose about 1 s
sync_binlog1 (default)fsync the binlog each commit

The defaults are both 1, the "double 1" safe configuration. Other parts: the doublewrite buffer writes each page to a safe area first, because a crash mid-write could tear a 16 KB page, and redo can't fix a torn page. The buffer pool uses an LRU list with a midpoint (old sublist 37% by default), so a table scan can't push out hot pages. On MySQL 8.4, the change buffer (innodb_change_buffering=none) and adaptive hash index are off by default (tested).

Binlog formats: ROW (default) logs changed rows, which is safe for non-deterministic functions, but large for bulk updates. STATEMENT logs SQL text and isn't safe with non-deterministic statements, such as UUID() or LIMIT without ORDER BY. MIXED chooses per statement.

Locks

LevelLockPurpose
ServerMetadata lock (MDL)Protects table structure. A long transaction blocks ALTER, and the waiting ALTER then blocks everyone after it.
TableIntention IS, IX"I hold or want row locks", so a table lock can check quickly
TableAUTO-INCShort-held; mode 2 (default in 8.0+) avoids it for most inserts, so one bulk insert's IDs can interleave
RowShared (S), exclusive (X)FOR SHARE, and FOR UPDATE or DML
RowRecord lockLocks one index entry
RowGap lockLocks the space between entries, to prevent inserts. Gap locks don't conflict with each other.
RowNext-key lockRecord + the gap before it. The default in RR.
RowInsert intentionA gap lock taken by INSERT that waits on existing gap locks

InnoDB locks index entries, not rows. Two facts follow.
