A query that can't use an index scans and locks everything it reads: in a test, UPDATE g SET k=k WHERE v=99 on an unindexed column matched no rows, yet another session's update to an unrelated row timed out with error 1205. And locks on a secondary index also lock the matching clustered record.

Seeing gap locks

CREATE TABLE g(id INT PRIMARY KEY, k INT, v INT, INDEX(k));
INSERT INTO g VALUES (1,10,0),(2,20,0),(3,30,0);

START TRANSACTION;                                 -- REPEATABLE READ
SELECT * FROM g WHERE k = 20 FOR UPDATE;

SELECT INDEX_NAME, LOCK_TYPE, LOCK_MODE, LOCK_DATA FROM performance_schema.data_locks;
-- NULL     TABLE   IX            NULL
-- k        RECORD  X             20, 2     next-key: gap (10, 20] and the record
-- k        RECORD  X,GAP         30, 3     gap (20, 30)
-- PRIMARY  RECORD  X,REC_NOT_GAP 2         the row itself

-- From another session, tested:
-- INSERT k = 15: blocked (error 1205 after timeout)
-- INSERT k = 25: blocked
-- INSERT k = 5:  OK
-- INSERT k = 35: OK

-- Same SELECT under READ COMMITTED:
-- k RECORD X,REC_NOT_GAP 20, 2  and  PRIMARY RECORD X,REC_NOT_GAP 2. No gap locks.
-- INSERT k = 15: OK

Rules of thumb in RR: a range scan takes next-key locks. An exact match on a unique index that finds the row takes only a record lock. If it finds nothing, it takes a gap lock on the gap where the row would be. That last case causes the classic deadlock: two sessions run SELECT ... FOR UPDATE on a missing row (both get the compatible gap lock), then both INSERT, and each waits for the other.

Deadlocks

-- Session A                         -- Session B
START TRANSACTION;                   START TRANSACTION;
UPDATE g SET v=1 WHERE id=1;
                                     UPDATE g SET v=2 WHERE id=2;
UPDATE g SET v=1 WHERE id=2;  -- waits
                                     UPDATE g SET v=2 WHERE id=1;
                                     -- ERROR 1213: Deadlock found (tested)
-- A then completes

A background check finds cycles in the wait-for graph (innodb_deadlock_detect=ON) and rolls back the transaction with the fewest row changes. That victim loses its whole transaction, so the application has to retry it. That's different from a lock wait timeout (1205, innodb_lock_wait_timeout=50 s), which by default rolls back only the statement, leaving the transaction open and locks held. Handle both. Log all deadlocks with innodb_print_all_deadlocks=ON. Reduce them by touching rows in a fixed order, keeping transactions short, indexing, and considering READ COMMITTED.

-- Job queue: workers pick rows without blocking each other (8.0+)
SELECT id FROM job WHERE status = 'NEW' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
SELECT id FROM dept WHERE id = 2 FOR SHARE NOWAIT;      -- errors immediately instead of waiting

InnoDB vs MyISAM in Detail

InnoDBMyISAM
TransactionsYesNo
Lock levelRow, MVCCTable; readers block writers
Foreign keysYesNo
Crash recoveryAutomatic through redoManual REPAIR TABLE; corruption possible
Index structureClustered on PKHeap file + indexes pointing to offsets
CachePages (data + index) in the buffer poolIndex only; data via OS cache
COUNT(*) with no WHEREMust scan an index, since visible rows depend on the transactionInstant: stored row count
Full-textYes, since 5.6Yes
Use todayDefaultLegacy only; system tables moved to InnoDB in 8.0

Other engines: MEMORY (RAM, hash indexes, lost at restart), ARCHIVE, CSV, and MyRocks (LSM-tree in Percona/MariaDB builds, for write-heavy loads).

Replication

Three threads do the work. On the source, a dump thread sends binlog events. On the replica, an I/O receiver thread writes them to the relay log, and applier (SQL) threads replay them. Current MySQL says source and replica rather than master and slave, as in CHANGE REPLICATION SOURCE TO, START REPLICA and SHOW REPLICA STATUS.

ModeSource commit waits forRisk
Asynchronous (default)NothingFailover can lose recent commits; replicas lag
Semi-synchronousAt least one replica has the event in its relay logAdds network latency per commit
Group ReplicationA majority agrees through Paxos-style consensusBasis of InnoDB Cluster; needs primary keys; write conflicts are rejected
  • GTID (Global Transaction ID): each transaction has an ID, source_uuid:sequence, so a replica can find its place on a new source without working out file positions. Not on by default.
  • Replication lag arises from single large transactions, long ALTERs, or a too-slow applier. replica_parallel_workers (default 4) replays in parallel. Monitor Seconds_Behind_Source, or a heartbeat table, which is more reliable.
  • Read-your-writes: after a write to the source, a read from a lagging replica can return old data. Fixes: read from the source right after a write, track a GTID and wait (WAIT_FOR_EXECUTED_GTID_SET), or send a session to the source for a few seconds.
  • A replica isn't a backup: DROP TABLE replicates too. A delayed replica (SOURCE_DELAY) helps with mistakes. Real backups need full dumps (mysqldump, Percona XtraBackup) plus binlogs for point-in-time recovery.

Partitioning

Partitioning splits one logical table into several physical pieces on the same server. The optimizer skips irrelevant partitions (pruning). Its biggest benefit is instant data removal: DROP PARTITION rather than a slow DELETE.

TypeHowUse
RANGEValue rangesDates; rolling retention
LISTExplicit value listsRegions
HASH / KEYModulus of a hashEven spread
RANGE COLUMNSRange over non-integer or multiple columnsDates directly
CREATE TABLE ptest (
  id BIGINT NOT NULL, created DATE NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (id, created)               -- must include the partition column
) PARTITION BY RANGE (YEAR(created)) (
  PARTITION p2025 VALUES LESS THAN (2026),
  PARTITION p2026 VALUES LESS THAN (2027),
  PARTITION pmax  VALUES LESS THAN MAXVALUE
);
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM ptest WHERE created = '2026-05-01';   -- partitions: p2026 (tested)
ALTER TABLE ptest DROP PARTITION p2025;                     -- removes a year at once
  • Every unique key must include all partition columns. PRIMARY KEY(id) gave error 1503 (tested). So global uniqueness of id alone can't be enforced.
  • Foreign keys aren't supported: error 1506 (tested).
  • A query without the partition column searches all partitions, and it's slower than an unpartitioned table with a good index. Partitioning isn't an automatic speed-up.

Sharding

Sharding splits data across separate servers, each with a subset of rows. It's the way to scale writes and storage beyond one machine, and the last resort, because it pushes complexity into everything else. Try indexing, caching, replicas, vertical splitting and archiving first.

PartitioningShardingReplication
ScopeOne serverMany serversMany servers
DataSubset per partitionSubset per shardFull copy each
ScalesMaintenance, some queriesWrites and storageReads, availability
Application changeNoneNeeds routingRead routing
StrategyHowProCon
RangeIDs 1–1M on shard 1Easy range queriesHot newest shard
Hashhash(user_id) % NEven spreadChanging N moves most keys
Consistent hashingKeys and nodes on a ringAdding a node moves a small shareMore complex
DirectoryA lookup table maps tenant to shardFlexible, can move one tenantExtra lookup; a critical dependency

Pick a shard key seen in almost every query (usually tenant or user ID) with high cardinality. Problems that follow: no cross-shard joins, cross-shard transactions need sagas, unique IDs can't use AUTO_INCREMENT (use Snowflake-style IDs), aggregates need scatter-gather, and rebalancing is an operation of its own. Vitess and ProxySQL or ShardingSphere reduce some of this.

JSON Columns

The JSON type (5.7.8+) validates input and stores a binary format that allows quick key lookup. It suits flexible attributes such as product specs. It doesn't suit data you filter, join or constrain constantly: use real columns for those.

CREATE TABLE jdoc (
  id INT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  doc JSON NOT NULL,
  city VARCHAR(50) GENERATED ALWAYS AS (doc->>'$.addr.city') STORED,   -- index JSON through a column
  INDEX idx_city (city),
  INDEX idx_tags ((CAST(doc->'$.tags' AS CHAR(20) ARRAY)))             -- multi-valued index, 8.0.17+
);
INSERT INTO jdoc(doc) VALUES
 ('{"name":"Asha","addr":{"city":"Pune"},"tags":["java","sql"]}'),
 ('{"name":"Ben","addr":{"city":"Delhi"},"tags":["js"]}');

SELECT doc->'$.name', doc->>'$.name', JSON_LENGTH(doc, '$.tags') FROM jdoc;
-- "Asha"  Asha  2                  -> keeps JSON quotes, ->> removes them

SELECT id FROM jdoc WHERE 'java' MEMBER OF (doc->'$.tags');     -- 1, type ref via idx_tags (tested)
SELECT id FROM jdoc WHERE city = 'Pune';                         -- ref via idx_city (tested)
UPDATE jdoc SET doc = JSON_SET(doc, '$.age', 30) WHERE id = 1;   -- partial update where possible

-- Expand an array into rows
SELECT j.id, t.tag FROM jdoc j
JOIN JSON_TABLE(j.doc, '$.tags[*]' COLUMNS (tag VARCHAR(20) PATH '$')) t;
-- 1 java | 1 sql | 2 js

Other functions: JSON_OBJECT, JSON_ARRAY, JSON_ARRAYAGG, JSON_OBJECTAGG, JSON_CONTAINS, JSON_SEARCH, JSON_REMOVE, JSON_MERGE_PATCH. JSON columns can't be indexed directly, have no foreign keys or per-field types, and the key names cost space in every row.

Classic SQL Problems (All Verified)

Nth highest salary

Salaries in descending distinct order are 150000, 120000 (twice), 90000, 80000, 70000 (twice), 60000. The second-highest distinct value is 120000.

-- 1. LIMIT/OFFSET: N-1 rows skipped. DISTINCT handles ties.
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 1;     -- 120000

-- 2. Window function: most flexible
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) r FROM employee
) t WHERE r = 2;                                                                -- 120000

-- 3. Correlated, no LIMIT or window functions: exactly N-1 higher distinct salaries
SELECT DISTINCT e1.salary FROM employee e1
WHERE 1 = (SELECT COUNT(DISTINCT e2.salary) FROM employee e2 WHERE e2.salary > e1.salary);  -- 120000

-- Return NULL, rather than no row, if there's no Nth value: wrap it as a scalar subquery
SELECT (SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employee ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 99) AS nth;  -- NULL

Follow-ups: RANK rather than DENSE_RANK gives a different meaning for ties. Without DISTINCT, LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2 returns the second 120000 row, not the third-highest salary. LIMIT can't take an expression like N-1 outside a prepared statement or routine variable.

Find and delete duplicates

-- users(id, email): (1,a@x) (2,b@x) (3,a@x) (4,c@x) (5,a@x) (6,b@x)
SELECT email, COUNT(*) c FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING c > 1;     -- a@x 3 | b@x 2

-- The extra rows, keeping the lowest id
SELECT id, email FROM (
  SELECT id, email, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) rn FROM users
) t WHERE rn > 1;                                                    -- 3, 5, 6

-- Delete them. The extra derived table is required:
-- DELETE FROM users WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT MIN(id) FROM users GROUP BY email);
-- gives ERROR 1093: can't specify target table for update in FROM clause (tested)
DELETE FROM users WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM (
    SELECT id, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY email ORDER BY id) rn FROM users
  ) t WHERE rn > 1
);                                                                   -- leaves ids 1, 2, 4
ALTER TABLE users ADD UNIQUE (email);                                -- so that it can't recur

Running totals and moving averages

-- sale(day, region, amount)
SELECT day, SUM(amount) daily,
       SUM(SUM(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY day) running,
       AVG(SUM(amount)) OVER (ORDER BY day ROWS BETWEEN 2 PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) mov3
FROM sale GROUP BY day ORDER BY day;
-- 2026-01-01 100 100 100.0000
-- 2026-01-02 250 350 175.0000
-- 2026-01-03 300 650 216.6667
-- 2026-01-05 150 800 233.3333

-- Per group
SELECT day, region, amount,
       SUM(amount) OVER (PARTITION BY region ORDER BY day ROWS UNBOUNDED PRECEDING) r
FROM sale;

-- Without window functions (O(n squared), pre-8.0)
SELECT a.id, a.amount, SUM(b.amount)
FROM sale a JOIN sale b ON b.id <= a.id GROUP BY a.id, a.amount;

The nested SUM(SUM(amount)) looks odd: the inner one is the GROUP BY aggregate, and the outer is the window running over those grouped rows.

Consecutive days (gaps and islands)

The trick: within a consecutive streak, date and row number rise by 1 together, so date - row_number is a constant. It names each island.

dayrow_numberday − rn days
Mar 11Feb 28
Mar 22Feb 28
Mar 33Feb 28
Mar 54Mar 1
Mar 65Mar 1
-- login(user_id, day). Streaks of 3+ days:
SELECT user_id, MIN(day) start_day, MAX(day) end_day, COUNT(*) days
FROM (
  SELECT user_id, day,
         DATE_SUB(day, INTERVAL ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) DAY) AS grp
  FROM login
) t
GROUP BY user_id, grp HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3;
-- 1 2026-03-01 2026-03-03 3
-- 2 2026-03-03 2026-03-06 4

-- Quick check for "at least 4 consecutive days" with LAG:
SELECT DISTINCT user_id FROM (
  SELECT user_id, day, LAG(day, 3) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY day) p FROM login
) t WHERE DATEDIFF(day, p) = 3;                 -- 2

-- Missing ids: gaps. ids are 1 2 3 5 6 9
SELECT id + 1 AS gap_start, nxt - 1 AS gap_end
FROM (SELECT id, LEAD(id) OVER (ORDER BY id) nxt FROM m) t
WHERE nxt > id + 1;                              -- 4 4 | 7 8

If a user can have two rows on a day, use DENSE_RANK or remove duplicates first, or the trick fails.

Employees and managers

-- Earning more than their manager
SELECT e.name, e.salary, m.name, m.salary
FROM employee e JOIN employee m ON m.id = e.manager_id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;                       -- Dia 120000 Ben 90000

-- Everyone with manager's name, including the CEO
SELECT e.name emp, m.name mgr FROM employee e LEFT JOIN employee m ON m.id = e.manager_id;

-- Number of direct reports
SELECT m.name, COUNT(*) reports
FROM employee e JOIN employee m ON m.id = e.manager_id
GROUP BY m.id, m.name ORDER BY reports DESC;     -- Asha 5 | Ben 1 | Eli 1

-- Non-managers
SELECT e.name FROM employee e
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee r WHERE r.manager_id = e.id);

-- Whole chain: the recursive CTE above

Top-N per group

-- Top 2 distinct salaries in each department. Ties are all included.
SELECT name, dept_id, salary, rnk FROM (
  SELECT e.*, DENSE_RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk
  FROM employee e WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
) t WHERE rnk <= 2 ORDER BY dept_id, rnk, name;
-- Asha 1 150000 1 | Chen 1 120000 2 | Dia 1 120000 2 | Eli 2 70000 1 | Fay 2 70000 1 | Gus 3 80000 1

-- Exactly 2 rows per department: ROW_NUMBER, with a tie-breaker for a stable answer
SELECT name, dept_id, salary FROM (
  SELECT e.*, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY dept_id ORDER BY salary DESC, id) rn
  FROM employee e WHERE dept_id IS NOT NULL
) t WHERE rn <= 2 ORDER BY dept_id, rn;
-- Asha, Chen | Eli, Fay | Gus

-- Highest in each department, without window functions
SELECT d.name dept, e.name, e.salary
FROM employee e JOIN dept d ON d.id = e.dept_id
WHERE (e.dept_id, e.salary) IN (SELECT dept_id, MAX(salary) FROM employee GROUP BY dept_id);
-- IT Asha | HR Eli | HR Fay | Sales Gus

Choose by the wording: "top 3 earners" with ties needs RANK/DENSE_RANK, "any 3 rows" needs ROW_NUMBER. An index on (dept_id, salary) supports it.

More patterns interviewers like

-- Median: average the middle one or two rows
WITH o AS (
  SELECT salary, ROW_NUMBER() OVER (ORDER BY salary) rn, COUNT(*) OVER () n FROM employee
)
SELECT AVG(salary) median FROM o WHERE rn IN (FLOOR((n+1)/2), CEIL((n+1)/2));
-- 85000  (sorted: 60 70 70 80 90 120 120 150, the middle two are 80 and 90)

-- Year-on-year change with LAG
SELECT YEAR(created_at) y, SUM(total) rev,
       LAG(SUM(total)) OVER (ORDER BY YEAR(created_at)) prev
FROM orders GROUP BY y;

-- Each category's share of the total
SELECT status, COUNT(*) c, ROUND(100 * COUNT(*) / SUM(COUNT(*)) OVER (), 1) pct
FROM orders GROUP BY status;

-- Swap values with one UPDATE
UPDATE sw SET g = CASE g WHEN 'm' THEN 'f' ELSE 'm' END;

-- First order per customer
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT customer_id, id, created_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at, id) rn
  FROM orders
) t WHERE rn = 1;

-- Departments with no employees
SELECT d.name FROM dept d WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM employee e WHERE e.dept_id = d.id);  -- Legal

Full-Text Search

LIKE '%term%' can't use a B-tree index (leading wildcard) and scans every row. An InnoDB FULLTEXT index builds an inverted index of words, queried with MATCH ... AGAINST, and returns relevance scores.

ALTER TABLE article ADD FULLTEXT INDEX ft_title_body (title, body);

-- natural language mode: ranked by relevance
SELECT id, title, MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('diabetes diet') AS score
FROM article
WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('diabetes diet')
ORDER BY score DESC LIMIT 20;

-- boolean mode: + must, - must not, * prefix, "" phrase
SELECT id FROM article
WHERE MATCH(title, body) AGAINST ('+insulin -pump diab*' IN BOOLEAN MODE);
  • The MATCH column list must match a FULLTEXT index exactly.
  • Short words (below innodb_ft_min_token_size, default 3) and stopwords are ignored; for Chinese/Japanese/Korean use the WITH PARSER ngram parser.
  • For typo tolerance, synonyms, facets or large scale, use Elasticsearch/OpenSearch and keep MySQL as the source of truth.

Generated Columns, Functional Indexes and CHECK

A generated column is computed from other columns: VIRTUAL (computed on read, no storage) or STORED (written to disk). Either can be indexed, which lets you index an expression or a JSON path. MySQL 8.0.13+ also supports functional key parts directly. CHECK constraints are enforced since MySQL 8.0.16; earlier versions parsed and silently ignored them.

CREATE TABLE patient (
  id         BIGINT PRIMARY KEY AUTO_INCREMENT,
  email      VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  birth_date DATE NOT NULL,
  first_name VARCHAR(50), last_name VARCHAR(50),
  full_name  VARCHAR(101) AS (CONCAT(first_name, ' ', last_name)) VIRTUAL,
  CONSTRAINT chk_birth CHECK (birth_date > '1900-01-01'),
  INDEX idx_full_name (full_name),
  INDEX idx_email_lower ((LOWER(email)))      -- functional index: note double parentheses
);
-- uses idx_email_lower only if the query repeats the same expression
SELECT id FROM patient WHERE LOWER(email) = 'a@b.com';

Upsert Variants Compared

StatementOn duplicate keyGotcha
INSERT IGNORESkips the rowAlso downgrades other errors (bad data, truncation) to warnings
REPLACE INTODeletes the old row, inserts the new oneNew auto-increment id, fires DELETE triggers and FK cascades, columns not given reset to defaults
INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATEUpdates chosen columns in placeUsually the right choice; affected rows = 1 (insert), 2 (update), 0 (no change)
INSERT INTO daily_visit (clinic_id, visit_date, cnt)
VALUES (7, CURRENT_DATE, 1) AS new
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE cnt = daily_visit.cnt + new.cnt;   -- row alias form (8.0.19+), replaces VALUES()

Interview Questions — MySQL

What is ACID?
  • Atomicity: all or nothing (undo log).
  • Consistency: constraints hold before and after the transaction.
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions don't interfere (MVCC and locks).
  • Durability: committed data survives a crash (redo log).
Isolation levels and anomalies? MySQL default?
LevelDirty readNon-repeatablePhantom
READ UNCOMMITTED✔✔✔
READ COMMITTED✘✔✔
REPEATABLE READ (InnoDB default)✘✘mostly ✘ (gap locks / MVCC)
SERIALIZABLE✘✘✘
What are indexes? Clustered vs non-clustered?

An index is a B+Tree that speeds up lookups and ordering at the cost of slower writes and extra storage. Clustered (InnoDB's PK): the table rows themselves are stored in PK order, and there's one per table. Secondary (non-clustered): its leaves hold the PK value, so a lookup goes through the clustered index ("bookmark lookup"). A covering index contains every column the query needs, so the table isn't touched at all (EXPLAIN shows "Using index").

When is an index NOT used?

A function on the column (WHERE YEAR(created_at)=2026; use a range instead) · a leading wildcard LIKE '%abc' · implicit type conversion (comparing a string column to a number) · not using the leftmost prefix of a composite index · OR across unindexed columns · low selectivity (the optimizer chooses a full scan) · != or NOT IN, often.

How do you optimize a slow query?
  1. Find it with the slow query log or performance_schema.
  2. Run EXPLAIN / EXPLAIN ANALYZE and check type (ALL is bad; ref, range, const are good), key, rows, and Extra ("Using filesort", "Using temporary").
  3. Add the right composite or covering index.
  4. Select only the columns you need, not SELECT *.
  5. Use keyset pagination instead of a large OFFSET.
  6. Rewrite subqueries as joins, use batching, use a cache.
  7. Look at the schema: data types, normalization or deliberate denormalization, partitioning.
Explain normalization (1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF).
  • 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups.
  • 2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on part of a composite key.
  • 3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-key → non-key).
  • BCNF: every determinant is a candidate key.

Denormalize deliberately for read performance (reporting, caches).

DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?

DELETE: DML, row by row, can have WHERE, can be rolled back, fires triggers. TRUNCATE: DDL, removes all rows quickly, resets AUTO_INCREMENT, causes an implicit commit. DROP: removes the table structure and its data.

WHERE vs HAVING? UNION vs UNION ALL?

WHERE filters rows before grouping. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and can use aggregates. UNION removes duplicates (sorts or hashes, so it's slower). UNION ALL keeps everything and is faster.

InnoDB vs MyISAM?

InnoDB (the default): transactions, row-level locking, foreign keys, MVCC, crash recovery. MyISAM: table-level locks, no transactions or foreign keys. It's legacy.

What is a deadlock in MySQL? How to avoid?

Two transactions each hold a row lock the other needs. InnoDB detects this and rolls one back (error 1213). Avoid it by accessing rows in a consistent order, keeping transactions short, using proper indexes so fewer rows get locked, and retrying on 1213. Inspect with SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS.

Primary key vs Unique key vs Foreign key?

PK: unique, not null, one per table, clustered. Unique: unique values, allows NULLs, you can have many. FK: referential integrity to a parent table, with ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL / RESTRICT.

What are views, stored procedures, triggers?

View: a saved query, used as a virtual table. Stored procedure: SQL logic stored in the DB (MySQL parses it and caches it per session) (CALL proc()). Trigger: runs automatically BEFORE or AFTER an INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE. Modern apps keep business logic in the application layer.

Rank vs Dense_Rank vs Row_Number?

For the values 100, 100, 90: ROW_NUMBER gives 1, 2, 3. RANK gives 1, 1, 3 (leaves a gap). DENSE_RANK gives 1, 1, 2 (no gap).

How does MySQL replication / scaling work?

The source writes changes to the binlog, and replicas read and apply it (asynchronously or semi-synchronously). Use read replicas to scale reads, with routing through ProxySQL or a Spring routing DataSource. To scale writes: sharding (Vitess) or vertical partitioning. For high availability: InnoDB Cluster or Group Replication.

CHAR vs VARCHAR? DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP?

CHAR(n) is fixed-length and padded. VARCHAR(n) is variable-length with a 1–2 byte length prefix. TIMESTAMP is stored in UTC, converted using the session time zone, and limited to 1970–2038. DATETIME stores the value as given, with no time zone conversion, and covers years 1000–9999.

Why does TRUNCATE differ from DELETE without WHERE, internally?

DELETE removes rows one at a time, writing undo and redo, firing triggers and taking row locks. TRUNCATE drops and recreates the table, so it's quick regardless of size, resets AUTO_INCREMENT (next IDs 1 vs 4 in a test), fires no triggers, needs the DROP privilege, and fails if a foreign key from another table references it.

Output: SELECT COUNT(*), SUM(salary), MAX(salary) FROM employee WHERE id < 0?

0, NULL, NULL (tested). An aggregate without GROUP BY always returns one row. Application code that reads SUM into a primitive must handle NULL, or wrap it: COALESCE(SUM(x), 0). Add GROUP BY and the same query returns zero rows.

Output: table n holds 10, NULL, 20. What do AVG(v) and SUM(v)/COUNT(*) return?

15.0000 and 10.0000 (tested). AVG and COUNT(v) skip NULL, whereas COUNT(*) counts 3. Use AVG(COALESCE(v, 0)) if NULL should count as zero.

Why did my LEFT JOIN return the same rows as an INNER JOIN?

A WHERE condition on the right table rejects the NULL-extended rows. Move it to ON. EXPLAIN shows MySQL even rewrites such a join as inner. The exception is WHERE right.id IS NULL, which deliberately keeps only the unmatched rows, the anti-join pattern.

What's the difference between WHERE and ON in an INNER JOIN?

For inner joins, none in results: the optimizer treats them alike. Convention puts join logic in ON and filters in WHERE. For outer joins they differ, as above.

How can a JOIN return more rows than either table?

When the join key isn't unique on both sides, each matching pair gives a row. Two rows with key 1 joined to three rows with key 1 give six. This causes inflated SUMs: joining orders to items and to payments double-counts. Aggregate each child table in a derived table first, then join.

IN vs EXISTS: which is faster?

In MySQL 8 usually neither: both become semijoins and get the same plan. Older advice (EXISTS for a large inner table, IN for small) came from a time when IN ran as a dependent subquery. Choose on semantics: NOT EXISTS is safer than NOT IN due to NULLs. Check EXPLAIN rather than following a rule.

Can you use a column alias in WHERE? In ORDER BY? In GROUP BY?

Not in WHERE (error 1054), because SELECT is evaluated afterwards. MySQL allows it in GROUP BY, HAVING and ORDER BY. The standard allows only ORDER BY, so HAVING c > 1 isn't portable to every database.

How do you find rows in table A that aren't in table B? Give three ways.
SELECT a.* FROM a LEFT JOIN b ON b.id = a.id WHERE b.id IS NULL;
SELECT a.* FROM a WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM b WHERE b.id = a.id);
SELECT id FROM a EXCEPT SELECT id FROM b;      -- 8.0.31+

NOT IN is a fourth, but it returns nothing if the subquery has a NULL. In MySQL 8 the first two typically get the same antijoin plan.

What's a derived table vs a CTE vs a temporary table?

All hold an intermediate result. A derived table is inline in FROM, and a CTE is the same thing with a name that you can reference several times or recursively. Either may be merged into the outer query or materialised. CREATE TEMPORARY TABLE lives for the session, is visible only to it, and can have indexes you choose, which helps a multi-step report. With connection pools, drop it explicitly.

What's a CTE's recursion limit, and how do you prevent infinite recursion?

cte_max_recursion_depth defaults to 1000 and raises error 3636 past it. max_execution_time also limits time. In the query, add a depth column with WHERE lvl < 20, or keep a visited path and stop on repeats. A cycle will otherwise run until the limit stops it.

Why does GROUP BY name fail with error 1055 on code that worked on old MySQL?

ONLY_FULL_GROUP_BY became a default in 5.7.5. The old behaviour returned an arbitrary value for ungrouped columns, which hid bugs. Fix the query with an aggregate, include the column in GROUP BY, or group by the primary key so dependent columns are valid. Don't remove the SQL mode to silence it.

Do NULLs count as duplicates under UNIQUE, DISTINCT and GROUP BY?

They vary. A UNIQUE index allows many NULLs, because NULL isn't equal to NULL. DISTINCT and GROUP BY treat all NULLs as a single value (tested: two NULLs formed one group, and COUNT(DISTINCT v) ignored them). For "only one row may have NULL", use a functional unique index on COALESCE(col, 0).

Why isn't my index being used?
  1. Function, conversion or leading wildcard: not sargable.
  2. Leftmost column missing.
  3. The optimizer estimates a scan is cheaper: low selectivity or a tiny table. That's often correct.
  4. Stale statistics: run ANALYZE TABLE.
  5. Type or collation mismatch in a join: utf8mb4 vs latin1 columns can't use the index directly.
  6. The index is invisible.

Find out with EXPLAIN, and with the optimizer trace: SET optimizer_trace='enabled=on', then read information_schema.OPTIMIZER_TRACE, which shows each plan's cost.

Given WHERE a = ? AND b > ? AND c = ? ORDER BY d, what index do you create?

(a, c, b): equality first, then the range. With a and c fixed, it seeks on all three. After a range, sorted order on d is lost, so d needs a filesort unless you reverse the priority: (a, c, d) reads in order and filters b, which wins when the query has a small LIMIT. Which is best depends on how selective b is. Adding the selected columns makes it covering.

Does a primary key need to be AUTO_INCREMENT? Why not use a UUID?

No, but the choice has a physical cost. A random UUID inserts all over the B+Tree, causing page splits and fragmentation, and its 16 or 36 bytes are copied into each secondary index. Sequential keys append. If IDs must be generated without the DB or not be guessable, use UUID v7 or a Snowflake ID, stored as BINARY(16) or BIGINT. Auto-increment exposes row counts and doesn't work across shards.

Why can adding an index slow the system down?

Every INSERT, DELETE and indexed-column UPDATE must also change the index tree, and each change needs I/O plus redo. Indexes occupy buffer pool memory, evicting data pages. More indexes also mean more lock entries and more deadlock paths, and the optimizer has more plans to evaluate. Add indexes for measured queries and check sys.schema_unused_indexes.

Why might COUNT(*) be slow in InnoDB, and which is faster: COUNT(*), COUNT(1), COUNT(id)?

Different transactions see different numbers of rows under MVCC, so InnoDB can't keep one counter and has to scan an index. The optimizer picks the smallest: EXPLAIN showed idx_total rather than the primary key, since a clustered scan reads full rows. COUNT(*) and COUNT(1) are equivalent. COUNT(col) differs only if the column is nullable. For a dashboard, keep a counter table, or use the approximate value from information_schema.TABLES.

What does key_len tell you?

How many bytes of the index are used, hence how many columns of a composite. With (customer_id INT, created_at DATETIME), a value of 4 means only customer_id, and 9 means both: 4 + 5 for DATETIME (tested). A nullable column adds 1 byte. For VARCHAR, it's the maximum byte length plus 2: VARCHAR(20) in utf8mb4 gave 82.

A query is fast in dev and slow in production. What do you check?
  1. Data volume and distribution: dev has 1,000 rows, so a scan is fine.
  2. Compare EXPLAIN on both, and ANALYZE TABLE.
  3. Parameter values: a common customer vs a rare one.
  4. Lock waits: sys.innodb_lock_waits and performance_schema.data_lock_waits. The query may be blocked rather than slow.
  5. Buffer pool hit rate: cold data needs disk reads.
  6. Concurrency: CPU saturation or a full connection pool.
  7. Replica lag if you read from a replica.
  8. Version and config differences.
An ALTER TABLE has been hanging for 10 minutes and everything else is blocked. Why?

The ALTER needs an exclusive metadata lock, and some open transaction holds a shared one, maybe an idle session that ran a SELECT and never committed. The queued ALTER then blocks all later queries on that table, so one forgotten transaction becomes an outage. Find it: information_schema.innodb_trx and performance_schema.metadata_locks, then kill it. Prevent it by setting a low lock_wait_timeout for DDL. Use ALGORITHM=INSTANT where possible, or online tools (gh-ost, pt-online-schema-change) for large tables.

How do you add a column to a 500-million-row table in production?

In MySQL 8, ADD COLUMN ... ALGORITHM=INSTANT changes only metadata, so it completes at once. For things that can't be instant (index creation uses INPLACE, LOCK=NONE but takes hours; type changes rebuild), use gh-ost or pt-online-schema-change. They copy to a shadow table, keep it in sync, and swap names. Consider replica lag, disk space for double the table, and throttling. Add columns as nullable, backfill in small batches, then add constraints. Deploy code that tolerates both schemas.

How would you delete 100 million old rows from a live table?

Not in one statement: that makes a giant undo log, long locks, replica lag and a very long rollback if it fails. Delete in chunks by primary key range or DELETE ... LIMIT 5000 in a loop, with a pause, each chunk committing, and watch replica lag. If most of the table goes, copy the keepers to a new table and rename. If it's a recurring need, partition by date so that DROP PARTITION does it instantly. InnoDB doesn't return disk space until an OPTIMIZE TABLE rebuild.

Explain "snapshot read" vs "current read" with an example of the difference.

A plain SELECT reads the version visible to the transaction's read view, with no locks. A current read (FOR UPDATE, FOR SHARE, UPDATE, DELETE) sees the newest committed version and locks it. In a REPEATABLE READ test: plain COUNT(*) returned 2, and in the same transaction COUNT(*) ... FOR UPDATE returned 3. That's why you shouldn't SELECT, compute and UPDATE unprotected, as you act on stale data.

Which isolation level would you pick for a payment system?

The level alone doesn't protect the balance: a lost update happens even at RR. Use an atomic conditional update (UPDATE acct SET bal = bal - ? WHERE id = ? AND bal >= ?) and check the row count, or lock rows in a fixed order with FOR UPDATE. READ COMMITTED with those rules gives fewer gap-lock deadlocks. Add idempotency keys, an append-only ledger, and retries on 1213. Reach for SERIALIZABLE only for a small set of write-skew cases.

How can a deadlock occur with a single row or just one statement each?

A statement locks index entries one by one. Two UPDATEs reaching the same rows through different indexes take locks in different orders. Also, two transactions holding S locks on a row that both try to upgrade to X deadlock: a child INSERT takes an S lock on the parent via the foreign key, followed by an UPDATE of the parent. Reading SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS shows the two latest conflicting transactions and their locks.

What's the difference between a deadlock and a lock wait timeout?

A deadlock is a cycle, so waiting can't help. InnoDB detects it instantly and rolls back a victim's whole transaction (error 1213). A lock wait is one transaction blocked by another that may simply be slow. After innodb_lock_wait_timeout (50 s) you get error 1205, and only the statement is rolled back by default, so the transaction stays open with its locks. Roll it back in the catch block. Retry both, with limits.

Does UPDATE ... WHERE id = 5 on a missing row lock anything?

In REPEATABLE READ, yes: a gap lock on the gap where id 5 would go, blocking inserts there. Gap locks from two transactions are compatible, so both proceed, then their INSERTs wait on each other's gap, a deadlock. This is the classic "check then insert" problem. Use a unique constraint with INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE, or READ COMMITTED, where these gap locks don't exist.

What happens physically when you run UPDATE and COMMIT?
  1. Find the page through the index. Load it into the buffer pool if needed.
  2. Lock the record.
  3. Write the old version to undo, update DB_TRX_ID and DB_ROLL_PTR.
  4. Change the page in memory, making it dirty, and add redo records to the log buffer.
  5. On COMMIT: flush redo in PREPARE state, flush the binlog, and mark redo as COMMIT.
  6. Release locks and return.
  7. Later, a background thread flushes the dirty page through the doublewrite buffer, and purge removes old undo.
Why are both the redo log and binlog needed?

They have different jobs. Redo is InnoDB's, physical and circular: it's for crash recovery and can't be replayed elsewhere. The binlog belongs to the server, is logical, and is kept for replication and point-in-time recovery. Historically the binlog came first, at the server layer, and InnoDB brought its own crash-safe log as a plug-in engine.

The server crashes straight after a COMMIT returns. Is the data safe?

With innodb_flush_log_at_trx_commit=1 and sync_binlog=1 (the defaults), yes. The redo and binlog were on disk before COMMIT returned, and recovery replays them. With value 2, an OS crash can lose up to about a second, and with 0 a server crash can. Disks that lie about fsync, or a replica that hadn't received the transaction before failover in async replication, are other routes to losing it.

What's a torn page, and what's the doublewrite buffer for?

A page is 16 KB, but a disk writes in smaller units, so a power cut can leave a page half-written. Redo describes changes to a valid page, so it can't repair one. InnoDB therefore writes pages to the doublewrite area first, syncs, then writes them in place. On recovery, a corrupt page gets restored from the copy.

How do you do point-in-time recovery after a bad DELETE at 14:05?
  1. Restore the last full backup to a separate server.
  2. Find the event's position with mysqlbinlog.
  3. Replay the binlogs from the backup's position up to just before the statement, using --stop-datetime or --stop-position.
  4. Export the lost rows and load them to production.

This needs retained binlogs. With row format, tools can even flash back single events. Practising restores is the only proof that a backup works.

Read replicas are lagging by 30 seconds. Causes and fixes?

Causes: one huge transaction replays as one unit; a long ALTER; a replica with weaker hardware; tables with no primary key under row format, where each event scans the table; or too little applier parallelism. Fixes: split big writes, add primary keys, tune replica_parallel_workers, ensure hardware parity, and move reporting elsewhere. In the application, route read-after-write to the source, and alert on lag.

How does failover work, and what can go wrong?

A tool or InnoDB Cluster detects a failed source, promotes the most up-to-date replica, repoints others (GTIDs make it simple), and switches clients through a proxy (ProxySQL, MySQL Router, or DNS). Problems: lost transactions under async replication; split brain, with two writable sources after a partition, which is why fencing and quorum matter; and events or jobs disabled on the new source. Applications need to retry with fresh connections.

Vertical vs horizontal partitioning?

Vertical: split columns, moving rarely used or large ones, such as a bio TEXT, to a second table, so that the main table stays small and fast. Or split by domain, into separate databases. Horizontal: split rows, in partitions on one server or shards on many. Note the term "vertical scaling" means a bigger machine, and that's different.

When should you NOT use MySQL partitioning?

When queries don't filter on the partition column, as each must then search every partition. When you need foreign keys, or uniqueness on a column other than the partition key. When the goal is just speed: a good index on a billion rows is three to four levels deep, and partitioning often adds little. It's best for time-series retention, and for restricting scans to a recent range.

Design a schema for an e-commerce order system. What are the key decisions?
  • Tables: customer, product, inventory, orders, order_item, payment, order_status_history.
  • order_item snapshots price and name at purchase.
  • Money as DECIMAL or integer minor units, with a currency.
  • Timestamps in UTC.
  • Stock decrement: UPDATE inventory SET qty = qty - ? WHERE sku = ? AND qty >= ?.
  • Indexes: orders(customer_id, created_at) for history, orders(status, created_at) for processing.
  • Don't hard-delete orders; archive by date.
  • Keep idempotency keys on payments.
Design the "top 10 products this hour" feature on a large orders table.

Don't run a GROUP BY over the raw table on each page view. Keep a summary table product_sales_hourly(hour, product_id, qty) with a primary key on those two columns. Update it through INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE qty = qty + ? from an event consumer, or with a scheduled roll-up. Query it with ORDER BY qty DESC LIMIT 10 and cache the result for 30 seconds. For true real-time ranking, use a Redis sorted set. The trade-off is freshness vs load.

How do you implement a job queue in MySQL safely?
START TRANSACTION;
SELECT id FROM job WHERE status='NEW' ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
UPDATE job SET status='RUNNING', worker=? WHERE id IN (...);
COMMIT;

SKIP LOCKED (8.0+) makes workers take different rows without waiting. It needs an index on (status, id), or the scan locks too much. Handle crashes with a lease timestamp, and a sweeper that requeues expired jobs. Delete or archive finished rows so the table stays small.

What is a phantom read, and how can a gap lock prevent it?

A phantom is a new row appearing in a range you already read. Row locks can't stop it, since the row doesn't exist yet. Next-key locks also lock the gaps between index entries, so an insert into a range locked by SELECT ... FOR UPDATE blocks. In the test, k = 20 FOR UPDATE blocked inserts of 15 and 25, but not of 5 or 35. READ COMMITTED removes those gap locks, and the insert of 15 succeeded.

What's the difference between optimistic and pessimistic locking in SQL terms?

Pessimistic: take the lock first with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, and others wait. Good for high contention or short critical sections, but holding it across user think-time is not possible. Optimistic: read a version, then UPDATE ... SET version = version + 1 WHERE id = ? AND version = ?, and retry on 0 rows. Good for low contention and long flows, with no locks held. JPA's @Version does this.

What's the difference between CHAR and VARCHAR storage when it comes to trailing spaces and charset?

In a CHAR column, trailing spaces are stripped on retrieval. VARCHAR keeps them. Comparison depends on the collation: PAD SPACE collations ignore trailing spaces, and the default utf8mb4_0900_ai_ci is NO PAD. It's also case- and accent-insensitive (ai_ci), so 'abc' = 'ABC' is true. A login or unique email check inherits that. Use a binary or _as_cs collation where case matters.

Output: SELECT 1 = '1', 'a' = 0, '5a' + 3?

1, 1, 8 (tested). A string in numeric context is converted using its leading digits, and non-numeric text gives 0. This also explains why WHERE varchar_col = 0 matches all non-numeric strings, a real injection and bug risk. In strict mode these give warnings for SELECT, but errors for INSERT.

What's the best way to store time zones, and DATETIME vs TIMESTAMP in practice?

Store instants in UTC, and convert at display. TIMESTAMP converts from the session's time zone to UTC and back, so it's an instant, but its 2038 limit is a hazard for far-future dates. DATETIME is a wall-clock value with no conversion, up to year 9999. Many teams use DATETIME with UTC by convention, keeping time_zone and the JDBC connectionTimeZone consistent. For a future event such as a meeting, store local time plus the IANA zone, because rules can change.

Why doesn't MySQL use the query cache any more? What should you cache instead?

It was removed in 8.0. Any write to a table invalidated all cached results for that table, and a global mutex limited concurrency on multi-core servers. Caching belongs in the application or Redis, where you control keys and expiry. Use cache-aside, keep TTLs short, and take care with invalidation and stampedes.

How do you check what's running or stuck on the server right now?
  • SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST: sessions, state, time.
  • sys.innodb_lock_waits: who is blocking whom, with a ready KILL statement.
  • information_schema.innodb_trx: open transactions, and how long.
  • SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS: last deadlock, history list length.
  • performance_schema.data_locks: current locks.
  • KILL QUERY id stops a statement, and KILL id ends the connection. Note a rollback may take a while.
Why is LIKE '%term%' slow and what are the alternatives?

A leading wildcard prevents a B-tree range seek, so MySQL scans the whole table or index. Alternatives: a FULLTEXT index with MATCH ... AGAINST for word search, LIKE 'term%' (prefix) which can use an index, or an external search engine such as Elasticsearch for fuzzy matching and relevance tuning.

What is a generated column, and VIRTUAL vs STORED?

It is a column whose value is computed from an expression over other columns in the row. VIRTUAL is computed on read and takes no space (it can still have a secondary index, which stores the values); STORED is computed on write and saved like a normal column. Common uses are indexing a JSON path or a normalised value such as LOWER(email).

How do you index an expression like LOWER(email) or YEAR(created_at)?

Use a functional index (MySQL 8.0.13+): CREATE INDEX idx ON t ((LOWER(email))), or an indexed generated column. The query must use the same expression. For dates it's usually better to rewrite the query as a range, created_at >= '2025-01-01' AND created_at < '2026-01-01', which uses a normal index.

Are CHECK constraints enforced in MySQL?

Since MySQL 8.0.16, yes: a violating INSERT or UPDATE fails with error 3819. Before that they were parsed and silently ignored, so old schemas may contain unenforced checks, and adding enforcement during an upgrade can reveal bad data. They can't reference other tables or use non-deterministic functions like NOW().

INSERT IGNORE vs REPLACE vs ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE?

INSERT IGNORE skips duplicates but also hides other errors as warnings. REPLACE deletes then inserts, which changes the auto-increment id, triggers deletes and cascades, and resets omitted columns. ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE updates the existing row in place and is the usual upsert. All of them depend on a PRIMARY or UNIQUE key and take locks that can cause deadlocks under heavy concurrency.

How do you combine soft deletes with a UNIQUE email constraint?

With a deleted_at column, UNIQUE(email) blocks re-registering a deleted email, and UNIQUE(email, deleted_at) doesn't work for active rows because MySQL allows many NULLs in a unique index. A common fix is a generated column that is the email only for active rows, active_email AS (IF(deleted_at IS NULL, email, NULL)), with a UNIQUE index on it: active emails must be unique, deleted ones are ignored.

JasperReports & Jasper Studio Reporting

JasperReports is the open-source Java library that fills report templates with data and exports pixel-perfect PDF, Excel, HTML and more. Jaspersoft Studio is the visual designer where you build those templates.

@Service
public class ReportService {

    private final Map<String, JasperReport> cache = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();

    private JasperReport compiled(String name) {
        return cache.computeIfAbsent(name, n -> {
            try (InputStream in = new ClassPathResource("reports/" + n + ".jrxml").getInputStream()) {
                return JasperCompileManager.compileReport(in);   // compile once, reuse
            } catch (IOException | JRException e) {
                throw new IllegalStateException("Cannot compile report " + n, e);
            }
        });
    }

    public byte[] invoicePdf(Invoice invoice) throws JRException {
        Map<String, Object> params = new HashMap<>();
        params.put("INVOICE_NO", invoice.getNumber());
        params.put("CUSTOMER", invoice.getCustomerName());

        JRBeanCollectionDataSource lines = new JRBeanCollectionDataSource(invoice.getLines());
        JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(compiled("invoice"), params, lines);
        return JasperExportManager.exportReportToPdf(print);
    }
}

JasperReports Library vs Jaspersoft Studio

  • JasperReports Library: the Java engine (the net.sf.jasperreports artifacts). You embed it in your app to compile, fill and export reports. It has no UI.
  • Jaspersoft Studio: an Eclipse-based desktop designer that replaced the old iReport. You drag fields and bands, configure data adapters, preview with real data and save .jrxml.
  • JasperReports Server: a separate web application for scheduling, a report repository, permissions and dashboards. You do not need it to generate reports from Spring Boot.

Keep the Studio version and the library version compatible. A template saved by a newer Studio may contain elements an older library cannot read. Newer major versions (7.x) also reorganized the project: the JRXML format changed, and exporters and extensions moved into separate modules. Check the migration notes before upgrading.

.jrxml vs .jasper & the Report Lifecycle

.jrxml is the human-readable XML template that you design and keep in version control. .jasper is the compiled, serialized JasperReport object. The lifecycle has three stages:

  • Compile: JasperCompileManager.compileReport(jrxml) → JasperReport. Expressions are compiled into Java (or Groovy) code here. It is expensive, so do it at build time or once at startup and cache the result.
  • Fill: JasperFillManager.fillReport(report, params, dataSource or connection) → JasperPrint, the paginated document in memory.
  • Export: turn the JasperPrint into PDF, XLSX, HTML, CSV, DOCX and so on.
// Load a pre-compiled .jasper file (e.g. produced by a Maven plugin)
JasperReport report;
try (InputStream in = getClass().getResourceAsStream("/reports/invoice.jasper")) {
    report = (JasperReport) JRLoader.loadObject(in);
}

Report Bands

A report is a stack of horizontal bands. The engine prints each band at a specific moment:

  • Title: once, at the very start (logo, report name).
  • Page Header: at the top of every page.
  • Column Header: above the detail rows on every page (table headings).
  • Detail: once per record of the data source.
  • Column Footer / Page Footer: at the bottom of each column or page (page numbers). Last Page Footer replaces the page footer on the final page.
  • Summary: once at the end (grand totals, charts).
  • Group Header / Group Footer: around each group of records, e.g. per department, with subtotals. Sort the data by the group expression first.
  • Background (watermark on every page) and No Data (shown when the data source is empty, if "When No Data" = No Data Section).

Fields, Parameters & Variables

  • Fields $F{name}: columns of the current record. They come from SQL result columns or JavaBean properties, so $F{amount} calls getAmount(). Each field has a declared Java class.
  • Parameters $P{name}: values passed in at fill time through the Map: filters, titles, logo images, subreport objects. Use $P{x} in a SQL query as a bind parameter. $P!{x} substitutes text literally, so whitelist those values. Built-ins include REPORT_CONNECTION, REPORT_LOCALE, REPORT_VIRTUALIZER.
  • Variables $V{name}: calculated values with a calculation (Sum, Count, Average, Highest, Lowest, First, Distinct Count…), a reset type (Report, Page, Column, Group) and an increment type. Built-ins: PAGE_NUMBER, REPORT_COUNT, PAGE_COUNT, <group>_COUNT.
  • Expressions are Java (or Groovy). Text field evaluation time controls when they are computed. "Page X of Y" needs Y with evaluation time Report.
  • $R{key} reads localized text from a resource bundle.
<parameter name="FROM_DATE" class="java.util.Date"/>
<queryString><![CDATA[
  SELECT id, customer, amount FROM invoices WHERE created_at >= $P{FROM_DATE} ORDER BY customer
]]></queryString>
<field name="customer" class="java.lang.String"/>
<field name="amount" class="java.math.BigDecimal"/>
<variable name="TOTAL" class="java.math.BigDecimal" calculation="Sum">
  <variableExpression><![CDATA[$F{amount}]]></variableExpression>
</variable>

Data Sources

  • JDBC connection: the report holds its own SQL query and you pass a java.sql.Connection to fillReport. This is simple and fast for large reports. Take the connection from Spring's DataSource and close it in try-with-resources.
  • JRBeanCollectionDataSource: wraps a Collection of POJOs or DTOs that your service already loaded (JPA, REST, computed data). The SQL stays in your application and is testable, and security rules stay in one place.
  • Others: JRMapCollectionDataSource, JRResultSetDataSource, JSON/XML/CSV data sources, JREmptyDataSource (for a static report with only parameters), or a custom JRDataSource that streams rows with next()/getFieldValue().
try (Connection conn = dataSource.getConnection()) {
    JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(report, params, conn);
}

Subreports & Charts

A subreport is a report embedded inside another one, for master-detail layouts such as an invoice with its lines or a patient with visits. Pass the compiled subreport as a parameter, plus either the connection ($P{REPORT_CONNECTION}) with linking parameters or a nested data source built from a collection field. Data comes back to the master through return values.

<subreport>
  <reportElement x="0" y="0" width="555" height="40"/>
  <dataSourceExpression><![CDATA[
     new net.sf.jasperreports.engine.data.JRBeanCollectionDataSource($F{lines})
  ]]></dataSourceExpression>
  <subreportExpression><![CDATA[$P{LINES_SUBREPORT}]]></subreportExpression>
</subreport>

Charts (bar, line, pie, area, time series…) are rendered by JFreeChart by default. A chart has its own dataset (category, pie, XY, time series) that collects values as records are processed, so it usually goes in the Summary or a group footer. For tables over different data, use a Table component or sub-dataset. Crosstabs give pivot-style summaries.

Exporting to PDF, Excel & HTML

// PDF (simple helper)
byte[] pdf = JasperExportManager.exportReportToPdf(print);

// Excel (XLSX)
JRXlsxExporter xlsx = new JRXlsxExporter();
xlsx.setExporterInput(new SimpleExporterInput(print));
xlsx.setExporterOutput(new SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput(outputStream));
SimpleXlsxReportConfiguration cfg = new SimpleXlsxReportConfiguration();
cfg.setOnePagePerSheet(false);
cfg.setDetectCellType(true);
cfg.setRemoveEmptySpaceBetweenRows(true);
xlsx.setConfiguration(cfg);
xlsx.exportReport();

// HTML
HtmlExporter html = new HtmlExporter();
html.setExporterInput(new SimpleExporterInput(print));
html.setExporterOutput(new SimpleHtmlExporterOutput(outputStream));
html.exportReport();

Other exporters: JRCsvExporter, JRDocxExporter, JRPptxExporter, JRXmlExporter. For Excel, design reports on a clean grid (aligned elements, no overlaps) and fill with the IS_IGNORE_PAGINATION parameter set to true to get one continuous sheet. For PDF, embed fonts through a font extension so non-Latin text and custom fonts render the same on every server.

Generating a PDF from Spring Boot

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/reports")
@RequiredArgsConstructor
public class ReportController {

    private final ReportService reportService;
    private final InvoiceService invoiceService;

    @GetMapping(value = "/invoices/{id}.pdf", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF_VALUE)
    public ResponseEntity<byte[]> invoice(@PathVariable Long id) throws JRException {
        Invoice invoice = invoiceService.findForCurrentUser(id);   // auth check here
        byte[] pdf = reportService.invoicePdf(invoice);

        return ResponseEntity.ok()
            .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION,
                    ContentDisposition.inline().filename("invoice-" + id + ".pdf").build().toString())
            .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
            .body(pdf);
    }
}

Put .jrxml files in src/main/resources/reports. Add the JasperReports dependency, plus the PDF exporter module and font extensions if your version splits them out. Use inline to open the PDF in the browser or attachment to force a download. For very large outputs, stream to response.getOutputStream() instead of building a byte[].

Performance Tips

  • Compile once: precompile .jasper at build time (Maven plugin) or cache the JasperReport. Never compile per request.
  • Push work to the database: filter, sort, aggregate and paginate in SQL, select only the columns you need, and add indexes for report queries.
  • Avoid N+1 subreports: a subreport per detail row runs a query per row. Prefer one joined query with groups, or pre-loaded nested collections.
  • Virtualizer for big reports: pass JRSwapFileVirtualizer or JRFileVirtualizer as REPORT_VIRTUALIZER so filled pages spill to disk instead of causing OutOfMemoryError.
  • Run long reports asynchronously: use a job queue or @Async, store the file and notify the user. Limit concurrent fills with a bounded executor.
  • Keep images small and pass them once as parameters, keep expressions simple, and stream output to the client.

Groups, Print When and Conditional Styles

A group breaks the data on an expression (for example $F{department}) and adds a Group Header and Group Footer band per value. The data must be sorted by the group expression (ORDER BY in the query, or sort fields), or the same group appears several times. Group options: Start on new page, Reprint header on each page, Keep together, Min height to start new page. Variables can reset per group (resetType="Group") to give subtotals.

  • Print When Expression: a Boolean expression on an element or band; it prints only when true, e.g. $F{balance}.compareTo(BigDecimal.ZERO) > 0. "Remove line when blank" collapses the gap.
  • Conditional styles: a style with conditions such as red text when $F{status}.equals("OVERDUE"), or zebra rows with $V{REPORT_COUNT} % 2 == 0. Defined once, reused across fields.
  • Built-in variables: PAGE_NUMBER, REPORT_COUNT, PAGE_COUNT, COLUMN_COUNT, and <group>_COUNT.
<group name="dept">
  <groupExpression><![CDATA[$F{department}]]></groupExpression>
  ...
</group>
<variable name="deptTotal" class="java.math.BigDecimal" resetType="Group" resetGroup="dept" calculation="Sum">
  <variableExpression><![CDATA[$F{amount}]]></variableExpression>
</variable>

Crosstabs and the Table Component

  • Crosstab: a pivot table with row groups, column groups and measures (sum, count, average), e.g. visits by clinic (rows) by month (columns), with automatic totals. It grows in both directions, so place it in Summary or a group footer and plan for wide output.
  • Table component: a grid bound to its own sub-dataset with column headers, detail cells and footers. It replaces many simple subreports, since it runs in the same report with a dataset run (parameters plus a connection or data source expression).

Internationalisation, Images and Barcodes

  • i18n: set a resource bundle on the report (resourceBundle="i18n.labels"), use $R{label.patientName} in text fields, and pass JRParameter.REPORT_LOCALE at fill time; the locale also drives date and number patterns. Use fonts with full glyph coverage (font extensions) for non-Latin scripts.
  • Images: an image element's expression can be a classpath or file path, a URL, an InputStream or a byte[] from a BLOB. In a JAR deployment, pass the logo as a parameter (an InputStream or Image) rather than a file-system path. Mark static images as cached (isUsingCache) to avoid reloading per record.
  • Barcodes and QR codes: the barcode components (Barcode4J and ZXing based for QR) render from an expression such as an order number; they need the corresponding library on the classpath.
Map<String, Object> params = new HashMap<>();
params.put(JRParameter.REPORT_LOCALE, Locale.forLanguageTag("ta-IN"));
params.put("LOGO", getClass().getResourceAsStream("/reports/logo.png"));
JasperPrint print = JasperFillManager.fillReport(compiledReport, params, dataSource);

Scriptlets and Caching Compiled Reports

A scriptlet is a Java class extending JRDefaultScriptlet whose hooks (beforeReportInit, afterDetailEval, afterGroupInit, ...) run during filling, for calculations too complex for expressions. Today, prefer preparing data in the service layer and keeping reports simple. In a web app, compile .jrxml once (at build time or on first use) and cache the JasperReport object; JasperReport is reusable across threads, while each fill creates its own JasperPrint.

Interview Questions — JasperReports & Jasper Studio

What is the difference between JasperReports and Jaspersoft Studio?

JasperReports is the Java library you embed in the application to compile templates, fill them with data and export them. Jaspersoft Studio is the Eclipse-based designer used to build and preview .jrxml templates visually. A separate product, JasperReports Server, adds a web repository and scheduling, but a Spring Boot app only needs the library.

What is the difference between .jrxml and .jasper?

.jrxml is the XML source template, editable and kept in version control. .jasper is the compiled binary JasperReport produced by JasperCompileManager, with expressions already compiled. Loading a .jasper avoids the compile cost at runtime, but it must match the library version, so many teams compile from .jrxml at build time or startup.

Explain the compile → fill → export lifecycle.

Compile turns the jrxml into a JasperReport. Fill combines the report with parameters and a data source or JDBC connection to produce a JasperPrint (the paginated pages in memory). Export renders that JasperPrint to PDF, XLSX, HTML and so on. One JasperPrint can be exported to several formats without filling again.

Name the report bands and when each prints.

Title (once at the start), Page Header (every page), Column Header (above the details on each page), Detail (once per record), Column Footer, Page Footer (every page; Last Page Footer on the final page), Summary (once at the end), plus Group Header/Footer around each group, Background, and No Data. 💡 Put totals in the Summary or group footers and page numbers in the Page Footer.

Fields vs parameters vs variables?

Fields ($F{}) are values from the current record of the data source. Parameters ($P{}) are inputs passed in at fill time, such as filters, titles, images or subreports. Variables ($V{}) are computed during the fill, like sums, counts and averages, with a reset scope of Report, Page or Group, plus built-ins such as PAGE_NUMBER and REPORT_COUNT.

What is the difference between $P{} and $P!{} in a report query?

$P{x} becomes a bind parameter in a prepared statement, which is safe from SQL injection. $P!{x} pastes the text into the SQL before execution, which is useful for a dynamic ORDER BY column or an optional WHERE clause. Because it is not bound, only pass whitelisted values, never raw user input.

JDBC connection vs JRBeanCollectionDataSource — which do you choose?

With a JDBC connection the SQL lives in the report. It is quick for large tabular reports and lets the database do the work, but the query is hidden from application code and tests. With JRBeanCollectionDataSource, your service layer loads DTOs (reusing repositories, security filters and business logic) and the report is only a view. The downside is that the whole collection sits in memory. Many teams use beans for documents (invoices, prescriptions) and JDBC or a streaming custom data source for big listings.

How do subreports work and what are their pitfalls?

A subreport element embeds another compiled report. You pass it via a parameter or expression and give it either the master's connection plus linking parameters or a nested data source, e.g. new JRBeanCollectionDataSource($F{lines}). Results can go back through return values. The main pitfall is performance: a subreport in the Detail band runs per row, which causes N+1 queries. Paths to subreport files also break when you move from Studio to the server, so pass compiled objects as parameters.

How do you show "Page X of Y"?

Use two text fields. The first is "Page " + $V{PAGE_NUMBER} with evaluation time Now. The second is " of " + $V{PAGE_NUMBER} with evaluation time Report, so it is filled in after all pages exist and shows the total. Put both fields in the Page Footer. Jaspersoft Studio's palette also has ready-made "Page X of Y" elements that set this up for you.

How do you generate and return a PDF from a Spring Boot endpoint?

Load or cache the compiled report, build the parameter map and data source, call JasperFillManager.fillReport, then JasperExportManager.exportReportToPdf. Return the bytes with Content-Type: application/pdf and a Content-Disposition of inline or attachment. Check authorization before loading the data. For big files, stream to the response output stream with JRPdfExporter and SimpleOutputStreamExporterOutput.

How do you export to Excel properly?

Use JRXlsxExporter with SimpleXlsxReportConfiguration: detectCellType for real numbers and dates, removeEmptySpaceBetweenRows, and onePagePerSheet(false). Fill with IS_IGNORE_PAGINATION=true so headers do not repeat every page. Lay out elements on a strict grid with no overlaps. Otherwise Excel output ends up with merged or empty cells. 💡 For pure data dumps, a CSV export or Apache POI is often simpler than a designed report.

How do you add a chart to a report?

Drop a chart element (bar, pie, line, time series) into the Summary or a group footer and configure its dataset: series, category and value expressions over fields. The dataset is filled as records are iterated, and the chart is rendered (via JFreeChart) when the band prints. If the chart needs different data than the main report, use a sub-dataset with its own query or data source.

A large report causes OutOfMemoryError. What do you do?

Pass a virtualizer (JRSwapFileVirtualizer/JRFileVirtualizer) in REPORT_VIRTUALIZER so filled pages are written to disk. Use a JDBC or streaming data source instead of loading a huge bean list. Aggregate in SQL, remove per-row subreports, and stream the export instead of building a byte[]. Then run it as an async job with limited concurrency and, if needed, more heap.

Fonts look wrong or characters are missing in the PDF. Why?

The PDF exporter only uses fonts it can find and embed. Server JVMs (especially Docker images) often lack the font that was used in Studio, or the font has no glyphs for the language. Fix it by packaging a font extension JAR (export it from Studio), referencing that font family in the template, and enabling PDF embedding. That gives identical output on every machine and correct Unicode rendering.

How do you improve JasperReports performance in general?

Compile once (build-time .jasper or a cache), optimize and index the SQL, aggregate in the database, avoid subreports inside the Detail band, use virtualizers for huge outputs, keep images small, reuse one JasperPrint for several formats, and generate heavy reports asynchronously with a bounded thread pool so they do not starve request threads.

Why does the same group header appear several times in my report?

Groups break whenever the group expression value changes from one record to the next; they don't sort the data. If the query isn't ordered by the group field, the same department appears in several separate runs. Add ORDER BY department (and nested group fields in order) or define sort fields in the dataset.

How do you show subtotals per group and a grand total?

Create a variable with calculation="Sum", resetType="Group" and resetGroup="dept" and place it in the group footer; create another with resetType="Report" for the Summary band. A variable shown in a group header needs evaluationTime="Group" to display the final value rather than the current running value.

What is a Print When Expression?

A Boolean expression on an element or band that controls whether it is printed, e.g. show a "DISCOUNT" label only when $F{discount} != null, or print a band only on the first page with $V{PAGE_NUMBER} == 1. Combine it with "Remove line when blank" to avoid empty gaps.

How do you highlight overdue rows in red?

Define a style with a conditional style whose condition is $F{dueDate}.before(new java.util.Date()) (or a Boolean field computed in the service) and set the forecolor or backcolor; apply the style to the detail text fields or a background rectangle. Alternating row colours use $V{REPORT_COUNT} % 2 == 0.

When would you use a crosstab instead of a table?

When both rows and columns come from data, i.e. a pivot such as revenue by product (rows) and month (columns), with totals in both directions. A table component has fixed columns defined at design time with rows from a dataset. Crosstabs can grow wide, so consider landscape pages or Excel export.

How do you produce the same report in several languages?

Put labels in resource bundles (labels_en.properties, labels_ta.properties), reference them with $R{key} or str("key"), and pass REPORT_LOCALE when filling. Use locale-aware patterns for dates and numbers, and embed fonts that contain the required glyphs so the PDF renders correctly.

How do you add a logo that works when the app runs from a JAR?

Don't use an absolute file path. Load it from the classpath and pass it as a parameter of type java.io.InputStream or java.awt.Image, then use $P{LOGO} as the image expression. Keep it cached so it isn't re-read for every page.

Why does my Excel export have repeated headers and empty rows?

The layout is page-oriented: page headers and footers repeat for every page and absolute positioning creates spacer rows and merged cells. For data exports, fill with IS_IGNORE_PAGINATION set to true (one long page), use XLSX export settings such as removing empty space between rows, detecting cell types and one-page-per-sheet off, and align elements to a clean column grid. Often a dedicated data-only report or a direct Apache POI/CSV export is better.

Should you compile the .jrxml on every request?

No. Compilation is slow (it generates and compiles expression classes). Compile at build time (the Maven plugin produces .jasper) or compile once at startup and cache the JasperReport object, which is thread-safe to reuse. Each request then only fills and exports.

What are scriptlets, and should you use them?

Scriptlets are Java classes extending JRDefaultScriptlet or JRAbstractScriptlet with callbacks during report filling (before/after report, page, group, detail), able to read and set variables. They help with complex running calculations, but they hide logic inside the report. In modern apps, compute values in the service layer and pass ready data through a bean data source.

IoC/DI, the bean lifecycle, scopes, AOP, transactions, Spring MVC, Security.

Spring MVC — DispatcherServlet Flow

AOP — Proxy Based

AOP termMeaning
AspectA module holding a cross-cutting concern (@Aspect class)
Join pointA point where advice can apply. In Spring that's always a method execution
AdviceThe action to run: @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing, @Around
PointcutAn expression that selects join points, e.g. execution(* com.app.service.*.*(..))

@Service
public class OrderService {
  private final OrderRepository repo;           // constructor injection (recommended)
  private final PaymentClient payment;
  public OrderService(OrderRepository repo, PaymentClient payment) { this.repo = repo; this.payment = payment; }

  @Transactional(propagation = Propagation.REQUIRED, isolation = Isolation.READ_COMMITTED,
                 rollbackFor = Exception.class, timeout = 10)
  public Order place(OrderDto dto) { ... }
}

@Aspect @Component
public class TimingAspect {
  @Around("@annotation(com.app.Timed)")
  public Object time(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp) throws Throwable {
    long t = System.nanoTime();
    try { return pjp.proceed(); }
    finally { log.info("{} took {}µs", pjp.getSignature(), (System.nanoTime() - t) / 1000); }
  }
}

The Container in Depth: BeanFactory, ApplicationContext and refresh()

Inversion of Control means your classes no longer build their collaborators. They declare what they need, and a container reads a description of the application, creates the objects, and connects them. The benefit is practical: a class that receives a PaymentGateway through its constructor can be tested with a fake one, and production can swap implementations without touching that class.

FeatureBeanFactoryApplicationContext
What it isThe core interface: getBean, scope, type lookup. DefaultListableBeanFactory is the real implementationExtends BeanFactory and wraps a DefaultListableBeanFactory
Singleton creationOn first getBeanEagerly during refresh(), so wiring errors fail at startup
BeanPostProcessorMust be registered by handDetected and registered automatically
BeanFactoryPostProcessorMust be invoked by handDetected and invoked automatically
Events, i18n, resources, EnvironmentNoYes: ApplicationEventPublisher, MessageSource, ResourcePatternResolver, EnvironmentCapable
Annotation processingNone by itself. @Autowired does nothing without the post-processorRegistered for you by annotation-based contexts

Common implementations: AnnotationConfigApplicationContext (plain Java config), AnnotationConfigServletWebServerApplicationContext (Boot with an embedded servlet server), GenericApplicationContext (programmatic registration).

What refresh() actually does

Everything in a Spring application happens inside AbstractApplicationContext.refresh(). Knowing the order explains most startup puzzles.

  1. prepareRefresh: record the start time, validate required properties.
  2. obtainFreshBeanFactory and prepareBeanFactory: get the bean factory, register internal beans such as environment, and add ApplicationContextAwareProcessor.
  3. invokeBeanFactoryPostProcessors: this is where your configuration is read. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses @Configuration, @ComponentScan, @Import and @Bean and turns them into bean definitions. No application bean exists yet.
  4. registerBeanPostProcessors: create all BeanPostProcessor beans first, so they can process everything after them.
  5. initMessageSource, initApplicationEventMulticaster.
  6. onRefresh: a hook. Spring Boot creates the embedded web server here.
  7. registerListeners.
  8. finishBeanFactoryInitialization: instantiate every non-lazy singleton. Then SmartInitializingSingleton.afterSingletonsInstantiated() runs.
  9. finishRefresh: start Lifecycle beans and publish ContextRefreshedEvent.

Bean Definitions and Component Scanning

The container works from recipes, not from objects. A BeanDefinition is metadata about one bean: its class or factory method, scope, lazy flag, depends-on names, primary flag, constructor arguments, property values, and init and destroy method names. Bean definitions all exist before any bean is created, which is why a BeanFactoryPostProcessor can rewrite them.

Way to registerUse it forMechanism
@Component and stereotypesYour own classesClassPathBeanDefinitionScanner reads class files with ASM, without loading them, and matches the annotation, including when it is a meta-annotation
@BeanThird-party classes, conditional constructionParsed from a configuration class; the method becomes a factory method
@Import(X.class)Pulling in specific configuration explicitlyX can be a plain class, an ImportSelector, or an ImportBeanDefinitionRegistrar. Most @EnableXxx annotations are a meta-annotated @Import
registerBean(...)Programmatic registrationGenericApplicationContext.registerBean(Foo.class, () -> new Foo())
BeanRegistrar (Framework 7)Programmatic registration with loops and conditionsImplement the interface and @Import it
@Configuration
@ComponentScan(
    basePackages = "com.shop",
    includeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(type = FilterType.ANNOTATION, classes = Plugin.class),
    excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(type = FilterType.REGEX, pattern = "com\\.shop\\.legacy\\..*"))
public class AppConfig { }

Bean names. The default name for a scanned class comes from Introspector.decapitalize: FooBar becomes fooBar, but URLParser stays URLParser because the first two letters are capitals. A @Bean method's name is the method name. If two definitions share a name, Boot fails at startup, because spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding defaults to false.

Gotcha: @Order and @Priority do not control the order in which singletons are created. They sort elements in injected collections and order advice. To force creation order use @DependsOn or a real dependency.

Injection Resolution

For each injection point, DefaultListableBeanFactory.doResolveDependency narrows the candidates in this order:

  1. Find all beans assignable to the type. Generics count, so Repository<Order> does not match a Repository<User> bean.
  2. Drop beans with autowireCandidate=false, and filter by @Qualifier if one is present.
  3. If more than one remains: pick the @Primary one. Otherwise drop @Fallback beans (Framework 6.2). Otherwise take the highest jakarta.annotation.Priority. Otherwise match the parameter or field name against bean names.
  4. Still ambiguous: NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Nothing found and required: NoSuchBeanDefinitionException.
public interface PaymentGateway { }

@Component @Primary class StripeGateway implements PaymentGateway { }
@Component("paypal")  class PaypalGateway implements PaymentGateway { }

// A custom qualifier avoids stringly-typed names
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.PARAMETER, ElementType.TYPE})
@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Qualifier
public @interface Legacy { }

@Service
class CheckoutService {
  CheckoutService(PaymentGateway main,                          // StripeGateway, via @Primary
                  @Qualifier("paypal") PaymentGateway paypal,   // qualifier beats @Primary
                  List<PaymentGateway> all,                     // every bean, sorted by @Order
                  Map<String, PaymentGateway> byName,           // key = bean name, handy for strategies
                  ObjectProvider<FraudCheck> fraud,             // lazy and optional
                  Optional<AuditClient> audit) { }              // optional
}

Optional dependencies can also be written with @Autowired(required = false) or a nullable parameter. Note that @Resource (Jakarta) resolves by name first, then by type, while @Autowired and @Inject resolve by type first.

Circular Dependencies and the Three-Level Cache

A cycle exists when A needs B and B needs A. With constructor injection there is no way out: to call A's constructor you need a finished B, and vice versa. With field or setter injection Spring can hand out a reference to a half-built A, because the object already exists once the constructor has returned. The bookkeeping for that lives in DefaultSingletonBeanRegistry as three maps.

LevelMapHolds
1singletonObjectsFully initialized beans. What getBean normally returns
2earlySingletonObjectsEarly references that have already been handed out, not yet populated
3singletonFactoriesAn ObjectFactory lambda per bean in creation. Calling it produces the early reference

Why three levels and not two? If A will end up behind an AOP proxy, B must receive the proxy, not the raw object. But proxies are normally created at the very end of initialization. Creating a proxy early for every bean would be wasteful, so level 3 stores a factory that calls getEarlyBeanReference on the SmartInstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessors only if a cycle really occurs. AbstractAutoProxyCreator remembers it did this, so it does not wrap the bean a second time at the end. Level 2 then caches the result so the factory runs at most once.

CaseResult
Constructor-only cycleFails: BeanCurrentlyInCreationException
Field or setter cycle, plain SpringWorks
Field or setter cycle, Spring Boot 2.6+Fails unless spring.main.allow-circular-references=true
Prototype beans in a cycleAlways fails: nothing is cached
Cycle with one @Lazy injection pointWorks, even with constructors: a proxy is injected and the real bean is resolved on first call
