Cycle with @Async on a beanCan fail with "has been injected into other beans in its raw version", because that post-processor wraps the bean late and does not take part in early references. Whether it fails depends on creation order, so it can appear after an unrelated change
Interview: A strong answer describes the three maps, says that the third exists to delay proxy creation, and then says the real fix is to remove the cycle by extracting the shared logic into a third class. Setter injection alone does not fix it on Boot 2.6+, which is a common misconception: you also need the property, and turning it on hides a design problem.

Scopes in Depth

A scope decides how many instances exist and how long they live. Singleton beans are stored in the level-1 cache. Prototype beans are built on every lookup and then forgotten: the container does not track them, so @PreDestroy never fires. Web scopes store the instance in the request or session through RequestScope and SessionScope objects that implement the Scope interface.

A singleton is not automatically thread-safe. The container only guarantees one instance; all request threads share it. Keep singletons stateless, or use immutable or concurrent fields.

Injecting a shorter-lived bean into a longer-lived one

Injection happens once, when the singleton is created. So a prototype field in a singleton holds the same instance forever, and a request-scoped bean cannot even be injected at startup, because no request exists. There are four solutions.

@Component @Scope("prototype")
class ReportBuilder { }

// 1. ObjectProvider: the usual choice
@Service class ReportService {
  private final ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders;
  ReportService(ObjectProvider<ReportBuilder> builders) { this.builders = builders; }
  Report run() { return builders.getObject().build(); }          // new instance each call
}

// 2. @Lookup: Spring subclasses the bean with CGLIB and overrides the method
@Service abstract class ReportService2 {
  Report run() { return builder().build(); }
  @Lookup abstract ReportBuilder builder();
}

// 3. Scoped proxy: the field holds a proxy that fetches the real instance per method call
@Component
@Scope(value = "prototype", proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)
class Counter { }

// 4. jakarta.inject.Provider<ReportBuilder>: the same idea as 1, without a Spring import

Request and session scopes usually use option 3, and @RequestScope and @SessionScope set the proxy mode for you:

@Component @RequestScope
class RequestContext { String tenantId; }

@Service class TenantService {
  private final RequestContext ctx;                  // really a proxy, safe in a singleton
  TenantService(RequestContext ctx) { this.ctx = ctx; }
  String tenant() { return ctx.tenantId; }           // BUG: field read on the proxy, always null
}
Gotcha: A scoped proxy forwards method calls only. Reading a field directly, as above, reads the proxy's own empty field. Give the class a getter and call that. Likewise, a @Scope("prototype", TARGET_CLASS) bean creates a new target on each method call, so counter.inc(); counter.get(); operate on two different objects. @Lookup does not work on beans created by a @Bean method, because the container does not control that new. Using a request-scoped bean outside a web request throws IllegalStateException: "No thread-bound request found".

The Full Bean Lifecycle

Two extension points frame the lifecycle, and they are often confused.

BeanFactoryPostProcessorBeanPostProcessor
Works onBean definitions (metadata)Bean instances
RunsOnce, before any normal bean existsAround initialization of every bean
ExamplesConfigurationClassPostProcessor, PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurerAutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, CommonAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator, AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor
CanChange scope, add definitions, replace placeholdersInject, validate, or return a different object such as a proxy

The complete order for one singleton, as the tiny test below prints it:

  1. postProcessBeforeInstantiation (InstantiationAwareBeanPostProcessor): may short-circuit creation.
  2. Constructor or factory method, with constructor injection.
  3. postProcessMergedBeanDefinition: finds @Autowired and @PostConstruct metadata. The level-3 cache entry is added here.
  4. postProcessProperties: field and setter injection, handled by a post-processor rather than core code.
  5. BeanNameAware, BeanClassLoaderAware, BeanFactoryAware.
  6. postProcessBeforeInitialization on all post-processors. ApplicationContextAware and @PostConstruct are themselves implemented here.
  7. InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet().
  8. Custom init-method.
  9. postProcessAfterInitialization: the AOP proxy is created here. The object stored in the container may now be a different one.
  10. After all singletons: SmartInitializingSingleton, then SmartLifecycle.start(), then ContextRefreshedEvent.

On context.close(): ContextClosedEvent, SmartLifecycle.stop() by descending phase, then per bean @PreDestroy, DisposableBean.destroy(), custom destroy method. Singletons are destroyed in reverse dependency order. A @Bean method also infers a public close() or shutdown() as the destroy method; set destroyMethod = "" to turn that off.

// Run against Spring 6.2. Bean: @Bean(initMethod="im", destroyMethod="dm"), with a BeanPostProcessor present
ctor
setter inject
BeanNameAware
BPP before
@PostConstruct
afterPropertiesSet
init-method
BPP after
-- context.close() --
@PreDestroy
DisposableBean.destroy
destroy-method
// A BeanFactoryPostProcessor: make every bean in .batch lazy.
// static is required on the @Bean method, see below
@Bean static BeanFactoryPostProcessor lazyBatch() {
  return factory -> {
    for (String name : factory.getBeanDefinitionNames()) {
      BeanDefinition d = factory.getBeanDefinition(name);
      if (d.getBeanClassName() != null && d.getBeanClassName().contains(".batch.")) d.setLazyInit(true);
    }
  };
}

// A BeanPostProcessor: warn about slow-looking beans, or wrap them
@Component
class StartupAudit implements BeanPostProcessor {
  @Override public Object postProcessAfterInitialization(Object bean, String name) {
    if (bean instanceof Auditable a) return new AuditingDecorator(a);    // may return another object
    return bean;
  }
}
Gotcha:
  • A non-static @Bean method that returns a post-processor forces its @Configuration class to be created too early, so @Autowired and @Value in that class are skipped. Declare these methods static.
  • A bean created to satisfy a BeanPostProcessor is created before the remaining post-processors exist. You see "Bean X is not eligible for getting processed by all BeanPostProcessors", and X may silently lose @Transactional or @Async.
  • In @PostConstruct, this is the raw object: the proxy does not exist yet. A @Transactional method called from there runs with no transaction. Use ApplicationReadyEvent or a separate bean.

@Configuration: Full Mode vs Lite Mode

Inside a @Configuration class, one @Bean method may call another. Without help, that would be an ordinary Java call and would construct a second object. Spring prevents this by replacing the class with a CGLIB subclass at startup. Its BeanMethodInterceptor intercepts each @Bean method: if the bean already exists, the existing one is returned instead of running the method body.

static class Repo { Repo() { System.out.println("Repo created"); } }
static class Svc  { final Repo r; Svc(Repo r) { this.r = r; } }

@Configuration                                  // full mode (proxyBeanMethods = true)
static class Full {
  @Bean Repo repo() { return new Repo(); }
  @Bean Svc a() { return new Svc(repo()); }
  @Bean Svc b() { return new Svc(repo()); }
}
// Prints "Repo created" once. a.r == b.r is true. Class is V$Full$$SpringCGLIB$$0

@Configuration(proxyBeanMethods = false)        // lite mode: identical body
static class Lite { /* same three methods */ }
// Prints "Repo created" three times. a.r == b.r is false
Full (@Configuration)Lite (proxyBeanMethods=false, or @Bean in a @Component)
SubclassCGLIB; the class cannot be final, nor can its @Bean methods beNone; a plain class, can be a final class or a record
Inter-bean method callReturns the managed singletonA plain Java call: a new unmanaged object
Startup and memorySlightly moreSlightly less, friendlier to native images
Correct wiring styleMethod calls workTake dependencies as @Bean method parameters, which also works in full mode

Spring Boot's own auto-configurations use proxyBeanMethods = false and parameter injection. In practice, parameters are the safer habit everywhere.

Conditional Beans and Profiles

@Conditional decides whether a component or @Bean method is registered at all. It runs while configuration is parsed, before any bean exists, so a condition must only look at the environment, class path, and existing definitions.

public class OnLinuxCondition implements Condition {
  @Override public boolean matches(ConditionContext ctx, AnnotatedTypeMetadata md) {
    return ctx.getEnvironment().getProperty("os.name", "").toLowerCase().contains("linux");
  }
}

@Bean @Conditional(OnLinuxCondition.class)
FileWatcher inotifyWatcher() { return new InotifyWatcher(); }

@Profile is just @Conditional(ProfileCondition.class). Spring Boot adds the richer @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, @ConditionalOnProperty and so on, covered in the Boot section. A ConfigurationCondition can additionally say whether it must be evaluated at parse time or at bean-registration time, which matters for conditions that look at other beans.

@Profile("dev")                     // active when dev is active
@Profile({"dev", "test"})           // dev OR test
@Profile("prod & !eu")              // boolean expression: &, |, !
@Profile("default")                 // only when no other profile is active
@ActiveProfiles("test")             // on a test class

Profiles are activated through spring.profiles.active or environment.setActiveProfiles(...) before refresh. With no active profile, the profile named default is used.

Environment, @Value and SpEL

Environment combines two things: the active profiles and an ordered list of property sources. env.getProperty("x") walks that list and returns the first hit. Plain Spring contains system properties and environment variables; @PropertySource adds a file; Boot adds many more.

@Configuration
@PropertySource("classpath:shop.properties")                    // .properties only, YAML needs a custom factory
class ShopConfig {
  @Autowired Environment env;
  @Bean Client client() {
    return new Client(env.getRequiredProperty("shop.url"),      // fails fast if absent
                      env.getProperty("shop.retries", Integer.class, 3));
  }
}

@Value supports two different syntaxes. ${...} is a property placeholder, resolved from the Environment. #{...} is a SpEL expression that is evaluated.

@Value("${app.name}")                       String name;       // required, startup fails if absent
@Value("${app.timeout:5000}")               int timeout;       // default after the colon
@Value("${app.note:#{null}}")               String note;       // default of null
@Value("${app.hosts}")                      List<String> hosts;// a,b,c is split by the ConversionService
@Value("#{systemProperties['user.home']}")  String home;
@Value("#{@pricingRules.discount() * 100}") int pct;           // @name refers to a bean
@Value("#{'${app.hosts}'.split(',')[0]}")   String first;      // SpEL around a placeholder
@Value("classpath:banner.txt")              Resource banner;   // converted to a Resource

Mistakes: @Value on a static field is silently skipped; it works only on Spring-managed beans; a field set this way is still null in the constructor, so prefer constructor parameters.

SpEL (Spring Expression Language) is also the language of @PreAuthorize, @Cacheable(key=...) and @EventListener(condition=...). Useful syntax, each line run against SpelExpressionParser:

ExpressionResultFeature
{1,2,3,4}.?[#this>2][3, 4]Selection (filter)
{'a','bb'}.![length()][1, 2]Projection (map)
null?:'dflt'dfltElvis operator
T(java.lang.Math).max(2,3)3Static access through T()
user?.address?.citynull if any part is nullSafe navigation
Gotcha: ⚠ Never evaluate SpEL built from user input with the default StandardEvaluationContext: T(java.lang.Runtime).getRuntime().exec(...) is remote code execution. If user-supplied expressions are truly needed, use SimpleEvaluationContext, which rejects type references with EL1005E: Type cannot be found.

Application Events

Events decouple the code that causes something from the code that reacts. The publisher does not know the listeners. Internally, ApplicationEventMulticaster finds matching listeners by event type, and by default calls them synchronously, on the publisher's thread, inside the publisher's transaction. So a listener exception propagates to the publisher and can roll it back.

public record OrderPlaced(long orderId, BigDecimal amount) { }     // any object can be an event

@Service class OrderService {
  private final ApplicationEventPublisher events;
  OrderService(ApplicationEventPublisher e) { this.events = e; }
  @Transactional public void place(Order o) {
    repo.save(o);
    events.publishEvent(new OrderPlaced(o.getId(), o.getTotal()));
  }
}

@Component class OrderListeners {
  @EventListener                                       // sync, same transaction
  void audit(OrderPlaced e) { }

  @EventListener(condition = "#e.amount > 1000")        // SpEL filter
  @Order(1)
  void flagLarge(OrderPlaced e) { }

  @EventListener                                       // a non-void return value is published as a new event
  Invoice invoice(OrderPlaced e) { return new Invoice(e.orderId()); }

  @Async @TransactionalEventListener(phase = TransactionPhase.AFTER_COMMIT)
  void sendEmail(OrderPlaced e) { }                    // only if the commit succeeds, on another thread
}

@TransactionalEventListener phases are BEFORE_COMMIT, AFTER_COMMIT (default), AFTER_ROLLBACK and AFTER_COMPLETION. The event is held in a transaction synchronization until the phase is reached.

Gotcha:
  • If no transaction is active, a @TransactionalEventListener silently drops the event, confirmed by a test run. Set fallbackExecution = true if it must still run.
  • In AFTER_COMMIT the transaction is finished but its resources are still bound, so a repo.save() inside the listener is not committed. Use REQUIRES_NEW or @Async for further writes.
  • If the process dies between commit and listener, the event is lost. For guaranteed delivery use a transactional outbox, not in-memory events.

Built-in events: ContextRefreshedEvent, ContextStartedEvent, ContextStoppedEvent, ContextClosedEvent, ServletRequestHandledEvent, plus Boot's application events.

Resource Loading and i18n

Java's URL handles class-path files poorly. Spring's Resource interface gives one abstraction over class path, file system, URL and byte array. Any bean can get one through ResourceLoader or by @Value.

PrefixExampleMeaning
classpath:classpath:db/schema.sqlFirst match on the class path
classpath*:classpath*:META-INF/plugin.xmlAll matches, across every jar
file:file:/etc/app/config.ymlFile system
https:https://example.com/x.jsonURL
noneWEB-INF/x.xmlDepends on the context type
@Service class TemplateLoader {
  private final ResourcePatternResolver resolver;              // ApplicationContext implements it
  TemplateLoader(ResourcePatternResolver r) { this.resolver = r; }

  List<String> load() throws IOException {
    List<String> out = new ArrayList<>();
    for (Resource r : resolver.getResources("classpath*:templates/**/*.txt")) {
      try (InputStream in = r.getInputStream()) {              // not r.getFile()
        out.add(new String(in.readAllBytes(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
      }
    }
    return out;
  }
}
Gotcha: resource.getFile() works in the IDE and throws FileNotFoundException once the app runs from a JAR, because a class-path entry inside a JAR is not a file. Always use getInputStream().

MessageSource resolves localized text: with messages.properties and messages_de.properties on the class path, messageSource.getMessage("order.placed", new Object[]{id}, locale) picks the right file. Boot auto-configures it from spring.messages.basename.

AOP in Depth

Some concerns cut across many classes: logging, transactions, security checks, metrics. Writing them in each method tangles them with business logic. Aspect-Oriented Programming moves them to one place and declares where they apply. Terms not in the table above: the target is the original object, the proxy is the wrapper that callers actually hold, an advisor is Spring's pairing of one pointcut with one advice, and an introduction adds an interface to a proxied bean.

Advice types and order

@Aspect @Component
public class AuditAspect {

  @Pointcut("execution(public * com.shop.service..*(..))")
  void serviceLayer() { }                                   // a reusable named pointcut

  @Before("serviceLayer()")
  public void before(JoinPoint jp) { log.info("enter {}", jp.getSignature()); }

  @AfterReturning(pointcut = "serviceLayer()", returning = "result")
  public void ok(JoinPoint jp, Object result) { }           // cannot replace the return value

  @AfterThrowing(pointcut = "serviceLayer()", throwing = "ex")
  public void failed(JoinPoint jp, RuntimeException ex) { } // cannot swallow the exception

  @After("serviceLayer()")
  public void always(JoinPoint jp) { }                      // like finally

  @Around("@annotation(retry)")                             // binds the annotation to the parameter
  public Object around(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, Retry retry) throws Throwable {
    for (int i = 1; ; i++) {
      try { return pjp.proceed(); }                         // forget this and the method never runs
      catch (IOException e) { if (i == retry.times()) throw e; }
    }
  }
}

@Around is the most powerful: it decides whether to proceed, can change the arguments with proceed(args), can replace the result, and can catch exceptions. It must return the result, or the caller gets null. Prefer the weakest advice that does the job. Output of one aspect with all five advices, on Spring 6.2:

Normal return
around-before
before
method
afterReturning
after
around-after
Method throws
around-before
before
method
afterThrowing
after
around-catch

This order has held since Spring 5.2.7: @AfterReturning and @AfterThrowing run before @After. Older blog posts show the reverse. Between different aspects, @Order decides: the lowest value is the outermost, so it runs first on the way in and last on the way out. Transactional advice has the lowest precedence by default, so it sits closest to the target, and an aspect with an explicit @Order wraps the transaction.

Pointcut syntax

execution( modifiers?  return-type  declaring-type?.method(params)  throws? )

execution(public * *(..))                       // any public method
execution(* com.shop.service.*.*(..))           // any method of a class directly in service
execution(* com.shop.service..*.*(..))          // .. includes sub-packages
execution(* *..*Service.find*(Long, ..))        // find* on *Service, first arg Long
execution(java.util.List com.shop..*(..))       // return type List
DesignatorMatchesExample
executionMethod signatureas above
withinAll methods in a type or packagewithin(com.shop.service..*)
@withinMethods in a type carrying an annotation@within(org.springframework.stereotype.Service)
@annotationMethods carrying an annotation@annotation(com.shop.Timed)
argsRuntime argument types; binds argumentsargs(id, ..)
@argsArgument's class has an annotation@args(com.shop.Sensitive)
this / targetProxy type / target typetarget(com.shop.Auditable)
beanSpring bean name (Spring only)bean(*Service)

Combine with &&, || and !. Static designators (execution, within, bean) are checked once when the proxy is built. args, @args and similar may need a runtime check on every call, so narrow them with within first.

How proxies are built

AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator is a BeanPostProcessor. In postProcessAfterInitialization it finds every advisor whose pointcut matches the bean. If any match, it asks ProxyFactory for a proxy and returns that instead of the bean. On a call, the proxy runs an interceptor chain through ReflectiveMethodInvocation.proceed(), one interceptor per advice, ending at the target.

JDK dynamic proxyCGLIB proxy
Mechanismjava.lang.reflect.Proxy implements the interfacesGenerates a subclass at runtime
NeedsAt least one interfaceA non-final class
Inject asInterface only. Injecting the class fails with BeanNotOfRequiredTypeExceptionClass or interface
Cannot interceptMethods not in the interfacefinal and private methods, and static ones
DefaultPlain Spring, when the bean has an interfaceSpring Boot, always (spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true), and plain Spring when no interface exists

CGLIB instances are created with Objenesis, so the constructor does not run for the proxy, and its fields stay at default values. That creates a nasty case:

@Component class Biz {
  String nf = "field";
  public String nonfin()      { return nf; }
  public final String fin()   { return nf; }
}
// With any aspect matching Biz, on Spring 6.2:
biz.nonfin();   // "field": intercepted, forwarded to the target
biz.fin();      // null: final, so it runs on the PROXY instance, whose field was never set
biz.nf;         // null: field access is never intercepted
Gotcha: No exception warns you. A final method on a proxied bean quietly skips the advice and sees null fields, typically showing up as a confusing NullPointerException on an injected dependency. Kotlin classes are final by default, which is why the kotlin-spring plugin exists.

Self-invocation

The proxy wraps the target; the target does not know about it. A call to this.other() inside the target is a plain Java call that goes straight to the same object.

@Service public class ReportService {
  public void runAll()  { generate(); }              // this.generate(): no proxy, no transaction
  @Transactional public void generate() { }
}

Tested: calling runAll() gives isActualTransactionActive() == false inside generate(), while calling generate() from outside gives true. Fixes, best first:

  1. Move the method to another bean. This usually also improves the design.
  2. Use TransactionTemplate for programmatic control, when the boundary is narrower than the method.
  3. Inject the bean's own proxy: @Autowired @Lazy ReportService self; then call self.generate().
  4. ((ReportService) AopContext.currentProxy()).generate() with @EnableAspectJAutoProxy(exposeProxy = true). Works, but couples code to Spring AOP.
  5. AspectJ weaving (mode = AdviceMode.ASPECTJ), which modifies bytecode rather than using a proxy.
Spring AOPAspectJ
WeavingRuntime proxiesCompile-time, post-compile, or load-time bytecode weaving
Join pointsMethod execution on Spring beansAlso field access, constructors, static methods, call sites
Self-invocationNot interceptedIntercepted
SetupNoneCompiler or Java agent

Spring AOP uses AspectJ's annotations and pointcut parser only, not its weaver. That is why aspectjweaver is on the class path.

Transactions in Depth

A transaction makes several database operations succeed or fail as one unit. Declarative transactions keep the begin, commit and rollback out of business code.

  1. @EnableTransactionManagement (automatic in Boot) registers an advisor whose advice is TransactionInterceptor.
  2. When a call arrives, TransactionAspectSupport.invokeWithinTransaction looks up the attributes. Method annotation beats class annotation, and class beats interface.
  3. PlatformTransactionManager.getTransaction() applies the propagation rule. To start a transaction it takes a connection from the pool and calls setAutoCommit(false).
  4. The connection or EntityManager is bound to the current thread through TransactionSynchronizationManager. Repositories and JdbcTemplate find it there. That is how they join without being passed anything.
  5. On normal return: commit. On exception: completeTransactionAfterThrowing checks rollback rules.

The direct consequence: a transaction belongs to one thread. Work in @Async, parallelStream(), new Thread or CompletableFuture.supplyAsync runs outside the transaction on its own connection. Reactive code cannot use a ThreadLocal, so it uses ReactiveTransactionManager with the Reactor context.

All seven propagation levels

PropagationTransaction existsNone existsUse
REQUIRED (default)Join itStart oneAlmost everything
REQUIRES_NEWSuspend it, start an independent one on a second connectionStart oneAudit rows that must survive a rollback
NESTEDCreate a savepoint; a failure rolls back to itStart oneOptional sub-steps
SUPPORTSJoin itRun withoutRead logic that does not care
NOT_SUPPORTEDSuspend it, run withoutRun withoutSlow non-DB work inside a transactional flow
MANDATORYJoin itThrow IllegalTransactionStateExceptionEnforce "must be called in a transaction"
NEVERThrow an exceptionRun withoutEnforce "must not be in a transaction"

REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED. REQUIRES_NEW commits on its own: if the outer transaction later rolls back, the inner work stays. NESTED lives inside the outer transaction: an outer rollback undoes it too, and it uses the same connection. NESTED needs JDBC savepoints; it works with DataSourceTransactionManager, and JpaTransactionManager has it off by default because a savepoint rollback does not undo the entity state held in the persistence context.

Gotcha: REQUIRES_NEW holds two connections per thread at once. If the pool has 10 connections and 10 threads each hold one while waiting for a second, nothing can proceed: a pool deadlock, which appears as Hikari timeouts under load.

Tested outcomes with H2 and DataSourceTransactionManager:

ScenarioResultRows left
Outer inserts, calls inner REQUIRED that throws; outer catchesUnexpectedRollbackException thrown at outer commitNone
Inner REQUIRES_NEW commits, then outer throwsOuter exceptionnew only
Inner REQUIRES_NEW throws; outer catchesCommitsouter only
Inner NESTED throws; outer catchesCommits, back to savepointouter only
Method throws checked ExceptionException thrown and committedThe insert is kept

The first row deserves attention. Inner joined the same transaction, so when it failed, its interceptor could not roll back alone; it marked the shared transaction rollback-only. Outer swallowed the exception and tried to commit. The manager saw the flag, rolled back, and threw UnexpectedRollbackException, because the caller must not believe it committed. Fix: let the exception propagate, or use NESTED or REQUIRES_NEW if the failure is meant to be tolerated.

Isolation

LevelDirty readNon-repeatable readPhantom read
READ_UNCOMMITTEDPossiblePossiblePossible
READ_COMMITTEDNoPossiblePossible
REPEATABLE_READNoNoPossible by the standard
SERIALIZABLENoNoNo
  • Dirty read: you see another transaction's uncommitted change. Non-repeatable read: reading the same row twice gives different values. Phantom read: re-running a range query returns new rows.
  • Isolation.DEFAULT uses the database's default: READ COMMITTED on PostgreSQL, Oracle and SQL Server, REPEATABLE READ on MySQL InnoDB.
  • Databases differ from the textbook. PostgreSQL's REPEATABLE READ is snapshot isolation, which also prevents phantoms, and its READ UNCOMMITTED behaves as READ COMMITTED.
  • Isolation and timeout are applied only when a transaction starts. A method that joins an existing transaction silently ignores its own isolation, unless you set validateExistingTransaction=true on the manager.
  • Lost updates are not solved by READ COMMITTED. Use optimistic locking (@Version) or SELECT ... FOR UPDATE.

Rollback rules

By default, rollback happens on RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions commit. The reasoning dates from EJB: a checked exception is treated as an expected business outcome.

@Transactional(rollbackFor = Exception.class)                        // also on checked
@Transactional(noRollbackFor = InsufficientStockException.class)     // this one commits
@Transactional(rollbackForClassName = "PaymentException")            // matched by name substring
@Transactional(transactionManager = "reportingTm")                   // with several managers
@Transactional(readOnly = true, timeout = 5)

@EnableTransactionManagement(rollbackOn = RollbackOn.ALL_EXCEPTIONS) // Framework 6.2, global setting

Programmatic transactions

@Service class ImportService {
  private final TransactionTemplate tx;
  ImportService(PlatformTransactionManager tm) {
    this.tx = new TransactionTemplate(tm);
    tx.setPropagationBehavior(TransactionDefinition.PROPAGATION_REQUIRES_NEW);
    tx.setTimeout(30);
  }
  void importAll(List<Batch> batches) {
    for (Batch b : batches) {
      tx.executeWithoutResult(status -> {            // commit per batch, no self-invocation problem
        try { save(b); }
        catch (DuplicateKeyException e) { status.setRollbackOnly(); }
      });
    }
  }
}

// Run something only after a successful commit, from anywhere in the transaction
TransactionSynchronizationManager.registerSynchronization(new TransactionSynchronization() {
  @Override public void afterCommit() { cache.evict(id); }
});

Pitfalls checklist

PitfallWhyFix
Self-invocationSkips the proxySeparate bean or TransactionTemplate
private or final methodCannot be overridden; annotation silently ignored. Since Framework 6.0, protected and package-private methods do work with class-based proxies (tested); public-only is an outdated ruleNon-private, non-final
Checked exceptionCommits by defaultrollbackFor
Catching and swallowingThe interceptor never sees the exceptionRethrow or setRollbackOnly()
Remote call in a transactionHolds a connection during slow I/O; retry and timeout make it worse; the call cannot be rolled backCall outside, or use an outbox
Bean not managednew OrderService() has no proxyInject it
Wrong managerTwo data sources, default manager usedName it in the annotation
Table engineMySQL MyISAM has no transactionsInnoDB
@Transactional on an @Async callerDifferent thread, different transactionPut it on the async method itself
@Retryable inside the transactionA retry reuses a rollback-only transactionRetry advice must wrap the transaction
Timeout assumptionChecked when statements are issued; Java code is not interruptedUse it as a database statement limit

readOnly = true is a hint to the stack. With Hibernate, flushing is off for that session, so dirty checking is skipped and it can drop state snapshots, which saves memory. On the JDBC side, Connection.setReadOnly(true) is called, and drivers or a routing data source can use that to send the query to a replica. It does not by itself guarantee that writes are rejected.

Open Session in View. Boot registers OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor by default (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, with a startup warning). It keeps the EntityManager open during view rendering so that lazy loading "just works" in the controller, at the cost of a connection held longer and hidden queries outside any service. Most production apps turn it off.

Spring MVC Components

DispatcherServlet is a single servlet that receives every request and delegates to strategy beans. Each strategy is an interface, so behaviour can be replaced without touching the servlet.

StrategyJobDefault implementations
HandlerMappingFind the handler plus its interceptors for a requestRequestMappingHandlerMapping, RouterFunctionMapping, SimpleUrlHandlerMapping for static files
HandlerAdapterKnow how to call that kind of handlerRequestMappingHandlerAdapter, HttpRequestHandlerAdapter
HandlerMethodArgumentResolverProduce each method parameter~30 built in: @PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, Pageable...
HandlerMethodReturnValueHandlerHandle what the method returnedRequestResponseBodyMethodProcessor, HttpEntityMethodProcessor, view name handler
HttpMessageConverterConvert between body bytes and objectsJackson JSON, String, ByteArray, Resource, form, XML if present
HandlerExceptionResolverTurn an exception into a responseExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver, DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver
ViewResolverTurn a view name into a viewContentNegotiatingViewResolver, Thymeleaf's resolver
MultipartResolver, LocaleResolverParse uploads, determine localeStandardServletMultipartResolver, AcceptHeaderLocaleResolver

What happens inside the adapter

  1. doDispatch asks the mappings for a HandlerExecutionChain: handler plus interceptors. None found: NoHandlerFoundException or NoResourceFoundException (404).
  2. It runs each interceptor's preHandle. A false return stops the request.
  3. The adapter loops over the parameters. For each, the first resolver with supportsParameter true provides the value. For @RequestBody, the resolver picks a converter from the Content-Type (no match: 415).
  4. The controller method runs.
  5. A return value handler processes the result. For @ResponseBody, ResponseBodyAdvice gets a look, and a converter is chosen from the Accept header (no match: 406). The response is now written, usually committed. Otherwise a ModelAndView goes to the view resolver.
  6. postHandle runs, then rendering, then afterCompletion.

A custom argument resolver

@Target(ElementType.PARAMETER) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface CurrentTenant { }

public class TenantArgumentResolver implements HandlerMethodArgumentResolver {
  @Override public boolean supportsParameter(MethodParameter p) {
    return p.hasParameterAnnotation(CurrentTenant.class) && p.getParameterType() == String.class;
  }
  @Override public Object resolveArgument(MethodParameter p, ModelAndViewContainer mav,
                                          NativeWebRequest req, WebDataBinderFactory f) {
    String t = req.getHeader("X-Tenant");
    if (t == null) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "X-Tenant is required");
    return t;
  }
}

@Configuration
class WebConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  @Override public void addArgumentResolvers(List<HandlerMethodArgumentResolver> list) {
    list.add(new TenantArgumentResolver());
  }
}

@GetMapping("/orders")
List<OrderDto> orders(@CurrentTenant String tenant) { ... }
Gotcha: Adding @EnableWebMvc to a Boot application switches off Boot's MVC auto-configuration. Implement WebMvcConfigurer alone to customize and keep the defaults.

Filters, interceptors and aspects

Servlet FilterHandlerInterceptorAOP advice
Owned byServlet containerSpring MVCSpring container
RunsBefore and after DispatcherServletInside it, around the handlerAround any bean method
SeesRaw request and response; can wrap themRequest, response, chosen handlerMethod arguments and result
Applies toEverything, including static files and unmapped URLsMapped requestsMatching beans
Typical useSecurity, CORS, compression, request logging, tracingLocale, tenant, per-handler auth checks using handler annotationsTransactions, metrics, business rules
public class TimingInterceptor implements HandlerInterceptor {
  @Override public boolean preHandle(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, Object handler) {
    req.setAttribute("start", System.nanoTime());
    if (handler instanceof HandlerMethod hm && hm.hasMethodAnnotation(Internal.class)) {
      res.setStatus(403);
      return false;                     // stops here; controller and postHandle are skipped
    }
    return true;
  }
  @Override public void afterCompletion(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res,
                                        Object handler, Exception ex) {
    long us = (System.nanoTime() - (long) req.getAttribute("start")) / 1000;  // runs even after errors
  }
}
// registry.addInterceptor(new TimingInterceptor()).addPathPatterns("/api/**").excludePathPatterns("/api/public/**");

@Component @Order(Ordered.HIGHEST_PRECEDENCE)
class CorrelationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {     // not run twice on forwards and error dispatch
  @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String id = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Correlation-Id")).orElseGet(() -> UUID.randomUUID().toString());
    MDC.put("cid", id);
    res.setHeader("X-Correlation-Id", id);
    try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.remove("cid"); }
  }
}
Gotcha:
  • postHandle is skipped if the handler throws. Cleanup belongs in afterCompletion.
  • With @ResponseBody, the body is already written by the time postHandle runs, so changing headers there is too late. Use ResponseBodyAdvice or a filter.
  • @ExceptionHandler does not catch exceptions thrown in a filter, because the filter runs outside DispatcherServlet.
  • The request body stream can be read only once. For logging, wrap it with ContentCachingRequestWrapper.

@ControllerAdvice

@ControllerAdvice is a component holding cross-controller @ExceptionHandler, @InitBinder and @ModelAttribute methods. @RestControllerAdvice adds @ResponseBody. Scope it with basePackages, annotations or assignableTypes.

Resolution: ExceptionHandlerExceptionResolver first checks the controller's own @ExceptionHandler methods, then each advice in @Order. In one class, the handler with the closest exception type wins. In a list of advices, the first advice with any match wins, so a catch-all Exception handler in a high-priority advice shadows specific handlers in others. If nothing handles it, ResponseStatusExceptionResolver honours @ResponseStatus, and DefaultHandlerExceptionResolver maps Spring's own exceptions. The rest reaches the container, which forwards to /error.

@RestControllerAdvice(basePackages = "com.shop.api")
public class ApiErrors extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {   // handles standard MVC exceptions as ProblemDetail
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFound.class)
  ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFound ex) {
    ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    p.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.example/problems/order-not-found"));
    p.setProperty("orderId", ex.id());
    return p;
  }
}

@ControllerAdvice
class BodyWrapper implements ResponseBodyAdvice<Object> {           // inspect or change every body
  public boolean supports(MethodParameter m, Class<? extends HttpMessageConverter<?>> c) { return true; }
  public Object beforeBodyWrite(Object body, MethodParameter m, MediaType t,
      Class<? extends HttpMessageConverter<?>> c, ServerHttpRequest req, ServerHttpResponse res) {
    res.getHeaders().add("X-Api-Version", "1");
    return body;
  }
}

Validation

Bean Validation (Jakarta Validation, implemented by Hibernate Validator) puts constraints on classes. Spring triggers it at the boundaries.

public record Address(@NotBlank String city, @Pattern(regexp = "\\d{6}") String pin) { }

public record CreateCustomer(
    @NotBlank @Size(max = 80) String name,
    @Email @NotNull String email,
    @Valid @NotNull Address address,                      // @Valid cascades into the nested object
    @NotEmpty List<@Valid @NotNull Item> items,           // and into list elements
    @Min(18) int age) { }

// Group validation: different rules per operation
public interface OnCreate { }
public record UserDto(@Null(groups = OnCreate.class) Long id, @NotBlank String name) { }
@PostMapping void create(@Validated(OnCreate.class) @RequestBody UserDto dto) { }

// Custom constraint
@Target({ElementType.FIELD, ElementType.RECORD_COMPONENT}) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@Constraint(validatedBy = SkuValidator.class)
public @interface ValidSku {
  String message() default "invalid SKU";
  Class<?>[] groups() default {};
  Class<? extends Payload>[] payload() default {};
}
public class SkuValidator implements ConstraintValidator<ValidSku, String> {
  public boolean isValid(String v, ConstraintValidatorContext c) {
    return v == null || v.matches("[A-Z]{3}-\\d{4}");     // null is @NotNull's job
  }
}
WhereTriggerFailure exception
@RequestBody object@Valid or @Validated on the parameterMethodArgumentNotValidException (400)
Controller parameter constraint (@RequestParam @Min(1) int size)Built in since Framework 6.1HandlerMethodValidationException (400)
Any bean's method@Validated on the class (AOP proxy)ConstraintViolationException, which maps to 500 unless you handle it

@Valid is the Jakarta annotation, and cascades. @Validated is Spring's, and adds groups and class-level method validation.

CORS

The browser's same-origin policy lets a page on https://app.shop.com send a cross-origin request but not read the response unless the server opts in. For anything beyond a "simple" request, the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight. CORS relaxes a browser rule; it is not server-side protection, and curl ignores it entirely.

@Configuration
class CorsConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  @Override public void addCorsMappings(CorsRegistry r) {
    r.addMapping("/api/**")
     .allowedOrigins("https://app.shop.com")
     .allowedMethods("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE")
     .allowedHeaders("*")
     .exposedHeaders("Location", "ETag")
     .allowCredentials(true)
     .maxAge(3600);                     // the browser caches the preflight for an hour
  }
}
// Per controller: @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://app.shop.com")
Gotcha: allowedOrigins("*") with allowCredentials(true) is rejected at startup; use allowedOriginPatterns. With Spring Security, call http.cors(...) so CORS is handled before authentication: a preflight carries no credentials and would otherwise get 401, which the browser reports as a CORS error.

File upload and download

@PostMapping(path = "/documents", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
public ResponseEntity<Void> upload(@RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file,
                                   @RequestPart("meta") @Valid DocMeta meta) throws IOException {
  if (file.isEmpty()) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST, "empty file");
  String safeName = UUID.randomUUID() + ".pdf";            // never trust getOriginalFilename()
  Path target = uploadDir.resolve(safeName).normalize();
  try (InputStream in = file.getInputStream()) {           // validate real content, not Content-Type
    Files.copy(in, target);
  }
  return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/documents/" + safeName)).build();
}

@GetMapping("/documents/{id}")
public ResponseEntity<Resource> download(@PathVariable String id) {
  Resource file = storage.load(id);
  return ResponseEntity.ok()
      .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
      .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION, ContentDisposition.attachment().filename("doc.pdf").build().toString())
      .body(file);
}
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size: 20MB      # default 1MB
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size: 25MB   # default 10MB

Exceeding the limit raises MaxUploadSizeExceededException. A path built from getOriginalFilename() invites path traversal (../../etc/cron.d/x). Large files go to disk in a temp location; for very large ones use direct-to-object-storage presigned URLs. For streaming responses, return StreamingResponseBody.

Asynchronous MVC and path matching

A controller may return Callable, DeferredResult, CompletableFuture, SseEmitter or StreamingResponseBody. The servlet thread is released using Servlet async support, and the response is finished later on another thread. Boot defaults to the PathPattern parser. In Framework 6, trailing-slash matching is off, so /users/ no longer matches /users.

HTTP Clients: RestClient, WebClient, @HttpExchange

ClientModelStatus
RestTemplateBlocking, template methodsMaintenance mode; the Spring team has announced its phase-out starting with the Framework 7 line
RestClientBlocking, fluent (Framework 6.1, Boot 3.2)The default for servlet apps
WebClientNon-blocking, reactive, from spring-webfluxFor WebFlux and for concurrent fan-out
@HttpExchangeDeclarative interface on top of eitherReplaces many uses of Feign
@Configuration
class ClientConfig {
  @Bean RestClient inventoryClient(RestClient.Builder builder) {      // Boot provides a prototype builder
    var factory = new JdkClientHttpRequestFactory(
        HttpClient.newBuilder().connectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2)).build());
    factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(3));
    return builder.baseUrl("https://inventory.internal")
        .requestFactory(factory)
        .defaultHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT, MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
        .requestInterceptor((req, body, exec) -> { req.getHeaders().setBearerAuth(token()); return exec.execute(req, body); })
        .defaultStatusHandler(HttpStatusCode::is5xxServerError, (req, res) -> {
          throw new UpstreamException("inventory: " + res.getStatusCode());
        })
        .build();
  }
}

Stock s = client.get().uri("/stock/{sku}", sku).retrieve().body(Stock.class);

List<Stock> all = client.get().uri("/stock").retrieve().body(new ParameterizedTypeReference<>() { });

ResponseEntity<Void> res = client.post().uri("/reservations")
    .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON).body(reservation)
    .retrieve()
    .onStatus(s -> s.value() == 409, (req, r) -> { throw new OutOfStock(); })
    .toBodilessEntity();

// Declarative client
@HttpExchange("/stock")
public interface StockApi {
  @GetExchange("/{sku}")  Stock get(@PathVariable String sku);
  @PostExchange           void reserve(@RequestBody Reservation r);
}
@Bean StockApi stockApi(RestClient inventoryClient) {
  return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(inventoryClient)).build()
      .createClient(StockApi.class);
}

// WebClient: three calls concurrently, combined when all finish
Mono<Dashboard> d = Mono.zip(
    web.get().uri("/orders").retrieve().bodyToMono(Orders.class),
    web.get().uri("/stock").retrieve().bodyToMono(Stock.class),
    web.get().uri("/news").retrieve().bodyToMono(News.class).onErrorReturn(News.EMPTY)
).map(t -> new Dashboard(t.getT1(), t.getT2(), t.getT3())).timeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));

Framework 7 adds @ImportHttpServices to register groups of @HttpExchange interfaces without the factory boilerplate. Always set timeouts. A client with no read timeout lets one slow dependency consume all threads. retrieve() throws RestClientResponseException on 4xx and 5xx unless you add a status handler.

WebFlux and Reactive Basics

A servlet stack ties up one thread per request. If that thread waits 200 ms on a database, it does nothing meanwhile. Reactive programming replaces waiting with callbacks: a small number of event-loop threads (Netty defaults to one per CPU core) start I/O and move on, then continue when data arrives. It suits many concurrent, I/O-heavy connections.

Reactive Streams is a small spec with four interfaces: Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription and Processor. Its key addition over plain callbacks is backpressure: the subscriber calls subscription.request(n) to say how much it can handle, so a fast source cannot flood a slow consumer. Project Reactor implements it with Mono<T> (0 or 1 element) and Flux<T> (0 to N).

Nothing happens until someone subscribes. Operators only assemble a pipeline. In WebFlux, the framework subscribes to what your controller returns.

Mono<String> m = Mono.fromSupplier(() -> { System.out.println("supplied"); return "v"; })
                     .map(s -> { System.out.println("mapped"); return s; });
System.out.println("assembled");
m.subscribe(System.out::println);
// Output: assembled, supplied, mapped, v (run on Reactor 3.7)

Flux.just(1, 2, 3).flatMap(i -> Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(40L * (4 - i))))
// flatMap: subscribes concurrently, emits as ready: [3, 2, 1]
Flux.just(1, 2, 3).concatMap(i -> Mono.just(i).delayElement(Duration.ofMillis(40L * (4 - i))))
// concatMap: one at a time, keeps order: [1, 2, 3]
OperatorUse
mapSynchronous 1-to-1 transform. Returning null raises NullPointerException into the stream
flatMap / concatMap / flatMapSequentialAsync step: concurrent unordered / sequential / concurrent but ordered
zip, merge, concatCombine pairwise / interleaved / one after another
onErrorResume, onErrorReturn, retryWhenError handling; errors are data signals in the stream
switchIfEmpty, defaultIfEmptyHandle an empty stream. map never runs on an empty Mono
timeout, buffer, window, limitRateTime limit, batching, backpressure shaping
subscribeOn, publishOnWhich scheduler the source / the following operators run on
@RestController
class StockController {
  @GetMapping("/stock/{sku}")
  Mono<ResponseEntity<Stock>> one(@PathVariable String sku) {
    return repo.findBySku(sku)                                  // R2DBC, not JPA
        .map(ResponseEntity::ok)
        .defaultIfEmpty(ResponseEntity.notFound().build());
  }

  @GetMapping(path = "/stock/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
  Flux<Stock> stream() { return updates.asFlux(); }             // server-sent events
}

// Functional style, an alternative to annotations
@Bean RouterFunction<ServerResponse> routes(StockHandler h) {
  return RouterFunctions.route().GET("/v2/stock/{sku}", h::one).build();
}

// If you must call blocking code, move it off the event loop
Mono.fromCallable(() -> legacy.call()).subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic());
Gotcha: ⚠ One blocking call on an event-loop thread (JDBC, Thread.sleep, .block()) stalls every connection served by that thread. BlockHound can detect this in tests. Also, ThreadLocal does not work when one request hops threads: security and tracing data travel in the Reactor Context instead. JPA and JDBC are blocking; a fully reactive stack needs R2DBC or a reactive driver.
Spring MVC + platform threadsSpring MVC + virtual threadsWebFlux
Code styleImperativeImperativeFunctional pipelines
Concurrency limitThread pool (Tomcat 200 by default)Very high; the real limit is downstreamVery high
BackpressureNoneNoneBuilt in
StreamingLimitedLimitedFirst class
DebuggingSimple stack tracesSimple stack tracesFragmented stack traces
JDBC / JPAYesYesNo

Since Java 21, virtual threads give most of the throughput benefit with plain blocking code, so WebFlux is now mainly chosen for streaming, gateways and backpressure, or where a reactive stack already exists. Reactive is not automatically faster: under low concurrency it adds overhead.

Caching

Spring's cache abstraction is, once again, a proxy. @EnableCaching registers CacheInterceptor. Before the method runs it computes a key and looks in a Cache obtained from a CacheManager; on a hit, the method is not called. Caffeine, Redis and others plug in behind the same annotations.

@Service
@CacheConfig(cacheNames = "products")
public class ProductService {

  @Cacheable(key = "#id", unless = "#result == null")
  public Product find(long id) { return repo.findById(id).orElse(null); }

  @Cacheable(cacheNames = "search", key = "#q + ':' + #page",
             condition = "#q.length() > 2",         // checked BEFORE the call, using args
             sync = true)                            // one thread computes a missing key
  public List<Product> search(String q, int page) { ... }

  @CachePut(key = "#result.id")                      // always runs, then updates the cache
  public Product update(Product p) { return repo.save(p); }

  @CacheEvict(key = "#id")
  public void delete(long id) { repo.deleteById(id); }

  @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "search", allEntries = true)
  @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *")
  public void clearSearch() { }

  @Caching(evict = { @CacheEvict(key = "#p.id"), @CacheEvict(cacheNames = "search", allEntries = true) })
  public void reprice(Product p) { ... }
}
spring:
  cache:
    type: caffeine            # or redis
    cache-names: products,search
    caffeine.spec: maximumSize=10000,expireAfterWrite=10m
    redis.time-to-live: 10m
TopicDetail
Default keySimpleKeyGenerator: no args gives SimpleKey.EMPTY, one arg gives that arg, several give a composite. So two methods sharing a cache with the same args collide; the method name is not included
condition vs unlesscondition runs before the method, on arguments. unless runs after and can see #result
TTLThe abstraction has no TTL concept; it is configured on the provider
StampedeMany concurrent misses on one key all hit the DB. sync = true serializes per key
Local vs distributedCaffeine: fastest, per instance, can go stale between instances, stores references. Redis: shared, needs serialization, adds network cost
TransactionsAn eviction can run before the commit, letting another thread re-cache old data. Use a transaction-aware cache manager (TransactionAwareCacheManagerProxy)
MutabilityCaffeine returns the same object: if a caller changes it, every reader sees the change. Cache immutable DTOs
Self-invocationAs with all proxies: no caching

Scheduling

@EnableScheduling registers ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, which finds @Scheduled methods and hands them to a TaskScheduler. These methods take no arguments and should return void.

@Component
class Jobs {
  @Scheduled(fixedRate = 60_000)                 // start every 60s, measured start to start
  void poll() { }

  @Scheduled(fixedDelay = 60, initialDelay = 10, timeUnit = TimeUnit.SECONDS)   // 60s after the previous END
  void sync() { }

  @Scheduled(cron = "0 15 2 * * MON-FRI", zone = "Asia/Kolkata")
  void nightly() { }

  @Scheduled(cron = "${jobs.cleanup.cron:-}")    // "-" disables it, so config can switch it off
  void cleanup() { }
}

Spring cron has six fields, with seconds first: second minute hour day-of-month month day-of-week. Linux cron has five. Also available: L (last), W (nearest weekday), # (nth weekday), and macros such as @daily.

BehaviourDetail
One thread by defaultBoot's scheduler pool size is 1 (spring.task.scheduling.pool.size). One slow job delays all others
OverlapA given task does not overlap itself on a pool; a fixedRate run that overruns delays the next one. Adding @Async removes that protection
ExceptionsLogged by the default error handler; later runs continue
Multiple instances⚠ Every instance runs every job. Use ShedLock (a lock row or key), Quartz clustering, or a Kubernetes CronJob

Async Execution

@EnableAsync registers AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor. Calling an @Async method through the proxy submits it to an executor and returns at once.

@Configuration @EnableAsync
class AsyncConfig implements AsyncConfigurer {
  @Bean ThreadPoolTaskExecutor mailExecutor() {
    var t = new ThreadPoolTaskExecutor();
    t.setCorePoolSize(4);
    t.setMaxPoolSize(16);
    t.setQueueCapacity(200);              // bounded, or max is never reached
    t.setThreadNamePrefix("mail-");
    t.setRejectedExecutionHandler(new ThreadPoolExecutor.CallerRunsPolicy());
    t.setTaskDecorator(r -> {             // copy MDC to the worker thread
      Map<String, String> mdc = MDC.getCopyOfContextMap();
      return () -> { if (mdc != null) MDC.setContextMap(mdc); try { r.run(); } finally { MDC.clear(); } };
    });
    t.setWaitForTasksToCompleteOnShutdown(true);
    t.setAwaitTerminationSeconds(20);
    return t;
  }
  @Override public AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler getAsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler() {
    return (ex, method, args) -> log.error("async {} failed", method.getName(), ex);
  }
}

@Service class Mailer {
  @Async("mailExecutor")
  public CompletableFuture<Receipt> send(Mail m) {
    return CompletableFuture.completedFuture(smtp.send(m));
  }
  @Async public void fireAndForget() { }           // exception goes to the uncaught handler
}
  • Return types: void, Future, or CompletableFuture. Anything else returns null to the caller.
  • Which executor: the qualifier in the annotation, else the unique TaskExecutor bean, else a bean named taskExecutor, else SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor, which starts a new thread per task with no limit. Boot supplies applicationTaskExecutor: 8 core threads, unbounded queue.
  • Pool order: a ThreadPoolExecutor fills core threads, then the queue, and adds threads up to max only when the queue is full. With an unbounded queue, maxPoolSize is never used. Many pools configured with "max 50" run with 8 threads forever.
  • Lost context: transaction, SecurityContext, request scope and MDC are ThreadLocal-based and do not carry over. Use a TaskDecorator, or DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor.
  • Exceptions: a void method's exception is invisible to the caller.
  • Self-invocation runs it synchronously.

Spring Data Overview

Spring Data removes repository boilerplate across stores: JPA, JDBC, R2DBC, MongoDB, Redis, Elasticsearch, Cassandra. At startup it scans for interfaces extending Repository and creates a JDK proxy for each via a RepositoryFactoryBean. For JPA, calls to standard methods go to SimpleJpaRepository; query methods go to an interceptor that was prepared at startup, so a bad method name fails early.

Repository                               // marker
 └ CrudRepository / ListCrudRepository   // save, findById, delete; the List variant returns List
    └ PagingAndSortingRepository / ListPagingAndSortingRepository   // since 3.0 these do NOT extend Crud
       └ JpaRepository                   // flush, saveAll, getReferenceById, batch deletes

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, JpaSpecificationExecutor<Order> {

  List<Order> findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThanOrderByCreatedAtDesc(Status s, BigDecimal min);   // derived
  Optional<Order> findFirstByCustomerIdOrderByCreatedAtDesc(long id);
  boolean existsByNumber(String number);
  long countByStatus(Status s);

  @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.id = :id")      // JPQL
  Optional<Order> findWithItems(@Param("id") long id);

  @Query(value = "select * from orders where created_at < ?1 limit 100", nativeQuery = true)
  List<Order> oldBatch(Instant before);

  @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true)                                    // a bulk update needs this
  @Transactional
  @Query("update Order o set o.status = 'EXPIRED' where o.createdAt < :t")
  int expire(@Param("t") Instant t);

  @EntityGraph(attributePaths = "items")                                   // fetch without JPQL
  Page<Order> findByCustomerId(long id, Pageable p);

  List<OrderSummary> findByStatus(Status s);                               // interface projection
}
public interface OrderSummary { Long getId(); BigDecimal getTotal(); }
  • Paging: Page runs an extra count query. Slice does not. Window with ScrollPosition gives keyset scrolling.
  • Transactions: SimpleJpaRepository is @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level, with write methods overriding it. Your derived query methods are not automatically transactional unless a service is. Each repository call outside a service runs in its own transaction.
  • save(): calls persist for a new entity and merge otherwise, judged by a null id or null @Version. An entity with an assigned id is treated as existing, triggering a SELECT first, unless it implements Persistable.
  • Auditing: @EnableJpaAuditing with @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedBy.
  • Custom logic: a fragment interface plus an ...Impl class is composed into the repository.

Retry and Concurrency Limits

Remote calls fail for short-lived reasons: a timeout, a 503, a dropped connection. A retry with exponential backoff and jitter handles these. Spring offers two options:

  • Spring Framework 7 core resilience: @Retryable and @ConcurrencyLimit in org.springframework.resilience.annotation, switched on with @EnableResilientMethods. There is also a programmatic RetryTemplate in org.springframework.core.retry. No extra dependency is needed.
  • Spring Retry (the separate spring-retry project, used on Framework 6 and earlier): @EnableRetry, @Retryable(retryFor = ..., maxAttempts = 3, backoff = @Backoff(delay = 200, multiplier = 2)), and @Recover for a fallback method. It is now in maintenance mode, and Framework 7's core support replaces it.

Both work through AOP proxies, so the usual proxy rules apply: self-invocation is not retried, and only beans managed by Spring are advised. For circuit breakers, bulkheads and rate limiters, use Resilience4j.

@Configuration
@EnableResilientMethods                       // Spring Framework 7
class ResilienceConfig { }

@Service
class RatesClient {
  @Retryable(includes = IOException.class, maxRetries = 4, delay = 200, multiplier = 2)
  public Rates fetch() { ... }                // only safe because the call is idempotent

  @ConcurrencyLimit(10)                       // at most 10 concurrent callers; useful with virtual threads
  public Report heavyReport() { ... }
}

// Spring Retry style (Framework 6 / Boot 3)
@Retryable(retryFor = TransientDataAccessException.class, maxAttempts = 3,
           backoff = @Backoff(delay = 100, multiplier = 2))
public void save(Order o) { ... }
@Recover
public void saveFallback(TransientDataAccessException e, Order o) { ... }

FactoryBean: Beans That Build Beans

A FactoryBean<T> is a bean whose job is to produce another object. When you inject or look up the bean by name, Spring calls getObject() and gives you the product, not the factory. Prefix the name with & (ctx.getBean("&myClient")) to get the factory itself. Frameworks use it to hide complex construction: Spring Data's JpaRepositoryFactoryBean, MyBatis' SqlSessionFactoryBean, and the proxies behind @HttpExchange clients. In application code, a @Bean method is almost always simpler. Spring Framework 7 also adds BeanRegistrar for programmatic, AOT-friendly registration of several beans in a loop or under conditions.

public class ClientFactoryBean implements FactoryBean<PaymentClient> {
  private String baseUrl;                                   // set from configuration
  @Override public PaymentClient getObject() { return PaymentClient.connect(baseUrl); }
  @Override public Class<?> getObjectType() { return PaymentClient.class; } // used for type matching
  @Override public boolean isSingleton() { return true; }
}

Controlling JSON with Jackson

For @RestController, MappingJackson2HttpMessageConverter (or its Jackson 3 version in Boot 4) turns objects into JSON. Interviewers often ask about the common annotations:

AnnotationEffect
@JsonProperty("full_name")Renames the field. With access = WRITE_ONLY, it can be read from requests but is never written to responses (for passwords)
@JsonIgnoreLeaves the field out in both directions
@JsonInclude(NON_NULL)Leaves out null values
@JsonFormat(pattern = "yyyy-MM-dd")Formats a date per field. A global ISO-8601 setting is usually better
@JsonIgnoreProperties(ignoreUnknown = true)Tolerates extra fields that the class does not have
@JsonTypeInfo / @JsonSubTypesPolymorphic payloads with a type discriminator
@JsonView(Views.Public.class)Returns a subset of fields per endpoint. Separate DTOs are usually clearer

Records work out of the box. The best defence against leaking fields is a dedicated response DTO, not annotations on JPA entities.

Interview Questions — Spring

What is IoC and DI?

IoC (Inversion of Control) is the principle: the framework controls object creation and lifecycle instead of your code. DI (Dependency Injection) is how Spring implements it: dependencies are given to an object rather than created by it. This gives loose coupling, easy testing with mocks, and swappable implementations.

Types of DI — which is recommended and why?
  • Constructor (recommended): dependencies can be final and immutable, they're guaranteed present, the class is easy to unit test without Spring, and circular dependencies show up early. With a single constructor, @Autowired isn't needed.
  • Setter: for optional dependencies.
  • Field (@Autowired on a field): hides dependencies, can't be final, and is hard to test. Avoid it.
BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext?

BeanFactory is the basic container. Beans are created lazily. ApplicationContext extends it and adds eager singleton creation, event publishing, i18n (MessageSource), AOP integration, environment and profiles, and automatic BeanPostProcessor registration. Always use ApplicationContext.

What are the bean scopes?
ScopeDescription
singleton (default)One instance per container
prototypeA new instance each time the bean is requested. Spring doesn't call its destroy callbacks
requestOne per HTTP request
sessionOne per HTTP session
applicationOne per ServletContext
websocketOne per WebSocket session

💡 If you inject a prototype into a singleton, you only get one prototype instance. Use ObjectProvider<T>, @Lookup or a scoped proxy instead.

@Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller?

All of them are picked up by component scanning. @Service and @Controller are stereotypes (semantics only). @Repository also enables exception translation (SQLException → DataAccessException). @Controller is handled by Spring MVC, and @RestController = @Controller + @ResponseBody.

@Autowired, @Qualifier, @Primary — how does Spring resolve beans?

Spring injects by type. If several beans match, @Primary marks the default, @Qualifier("name") picks a specific one, and as a fallback the parameter name is matched against the bean name. If nothing matches you get NoSuchBeanDefinitionException. If several match and none is chosen, you get NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException. Inject List<PaymentGateway> to receive all of them.

@Bean vs @Component?

@Component goes on your class and is found by scanning. @Bean goes on a method in a @Configuration class. Use it for third-party classes you can't annotate (RestTemplate, ObjectMapper) or for complex construction logic.

What is a circular dependency? How to fix it?

A → B → A. With constructor injection it fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException. Since Spring Boot 2.6, circular references are prohibited by default. Fixes: redesign (extract a third class; this is the best option), use setter injection (needs spring.main.allow-circular-references=true on Boot 2.6+), use @Lazy on one dependency, or use events.

Explain @Transactional — propagation & isolation.

Propagation (what happens when a transactional method calls another):

  • REQUIRED (default): join the existing transaction or start a new one.
  • REQUIRES_NEW: suspend the current transaction and always start a new one (e.g. audit logs that must be saved even if the outer transaction rolls back).
  • SUPPORTS, NOT_SUPPORTED, MANDATORY, NEVER, NESTED (savepoint).

Isolation: READ_UNCOMMITTED (dirty reads) → READ_COMMITTED → REPEATABLE_READ → SERIALIZABLE. The higher the level, the fewer anomalies (dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads) and the lower the concurrency.

Pitfalls: rollback happens only for unchecked exceptions by default (use rollbackFor for others). It works on non-private methods with class-based proxies since Spring 6.0 (public-only before that, and for interface proxies) called through the proxy, so self-invocation skips it. A try/catch that swallows the exception prevents the rollback. Use readOnly=true for queries.

What is AOP? Give real uses.

Aspect-Oriented Programming separates cross-cutting concerns (logging, transactions, security, caching, metrics, retries) from business code. Spring implements it with runtime proxies: JDK dynamic proxies for interfaces, CGLIB subclasses otherwise (the Boot default). @Transactional, @Cacheable, @Async and @PreAuthorize are all built on AOP.

@Controller vs @RestController; @RequestParam vs @PathVariable vs @RequestBody?
@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserController {
  @GetMapping("/{id}")                         // /api/users/5
  public UserDto get(@PathVariable Long id) {...}

  @GetMapping                                  // /api/users?page=0&size=10
  public Page<UserDto> list(@RequestParam(defaultValue = "0") int page,
                            @RequestParam(defaultValue = "10") int size) {...}

  @PostMapping
  public ResponseEntity<UserDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody UserDto dto) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.CREATED).body(service.save(dto));
  }
}

@PathVariable identifies a resource. @RequestParam is for filtering and paging. @RequestBody deserializes a JSON body. @RequestHeader reads headers.

How do you handle exceptions globally?
@RestControllerAdvice
public class GlobalHandler {
  @ExceptionHandler(ResourceNotFoundException.class)
  public ResponseEntity<ErrorDto> notFound(ResourceNotFoundException ex) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(404).body(new ErrorDto("NOT_FOUND", ex.getMessage()));
  }
  @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class)
  public ResponseEntity<Map<String,String>> invalid(MethodArgumentNotValidException ex) {
    Map<String,String> errors = new HashMap<>();
    ex.getBindingResult().getFieldErrors().forEach(e -> errors.put(e.getField(), e.getDefaultMessage()));
    return ResponseEntity.badRequest().body(errors);
  }
}

Spring 6 also supports ProblemDetail (RFC 9457, which replaced RFC 7807) responses.

How does Spring Security work? Explain JWT flow.

Spring Security is a chain of servlet filters (SecurityFilterChain). The flow is Authentication → AuthenticationManager → AuthenticationProvider → UserDetailsService + PasswordEncoder, and the result is stored in the SecurityContextHolder (a ThreadLocal). Authorization uses authorizeHttpRequests rules or @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')").

What is the difference between @RequestMapping and @GetMapping?

@GetMapping is shorthand for @RequestMapping(method = GET). There are also Post, Put, Delete and Patch variants. @RequestMapping on a class sets the base path.

What are Spring profiles?

Profiles let you have environment-specific beans and config. Annotate with @Profile("dev"), use application-dev.yml, and activate with spring.profiles.active=prod (an environment variable, JVM argument or property).

How do you do validation in Spring?

Bean Validation (spring-boot-starter-validation): put constraints like @NotNull, @NotBlank, @Size, @Email, @Min, @Pattern on DTO fields, then add @Valid to @RequestBody. Use @Validated on a class for method or group validation. For custom rules, write a @Constraint annotation with a ConstraintValidator.

What happens between new AnnotationConfigApplicationContext(...) and the first usable bean?

The context registers internal post-processors, then refresh() runs. ConfigurationClassPostProcessor parses configuration and creates bean definitions. All BeanPostProcessors are created. Non-lazy singletons are instantiated, populated and initialized, with proxies applied at the end. Finally ContextRefreshedEvent is published. Definitions always exist before instances, which is why a BeanFactoryPostProcessor can still change them.

BeanFactoryPostProcessor vs BeanPostProcessor?

A BeanFactoryPostProcessor edits definitions once, before beans exist: for example, resolving ${...} or parsing @Configuration. A BeanPostProcessor sees every instance around initialization and may replace it, as the AOP auto-proxy creator does. Both are detected automatically by ApplicationContext. Their @Bean methods should be static.

Why does a @Transactional method called in @PostConstruct run without a transaction?

@PostConstruct runs in postProcessBeforeInitialization, before the proxy is created in postProcessAfterInitialization. The call also uses this. So no interceptor is involved. Move the work to an ApplicationReadyEvent listener, or a SmartInitializingSingleton that calls another bean, or use TransactionTemplate.

Explain the three-level cache. Why not two levels?

singletonObjects holds finished beans, earlySingletonObjects holds early references already handed out, and singletonFactories holds lambdas that produce early references. Two levels would suffice if beans were never proxied. Because a bean in a cycle may need a proxy, the injected early reference must already be that proxy. The factory delays this decision until a cycle really needs it, so normal beans keep the usual "proxy at the end" flow. The second level ensures the factory result is created once and shared.

Output: A has a field @Autowired B and an @Async method; B has a field @Autowired A. What happens?

It depends on creation order. Tested with spring.main.allow-circular-references at plain Spring's default: registering A first fails with BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: "has been injected into other beans in its raw version". Registering B first succeeds. When A is created first, B receives raw A as the early reference, then the async post-processor wraps A, so B would hold the wrong object. Spring detects this and aborts. When B is first, A is fully proxied before B needs it.

Why can't constructor injection use the early-reference trick? What can it do instead?

The early reference is the object produced by the constructor. In a constructor cycle, neither constructor can finish, so no object exists to expose. Instead, mark one parameter @Lazy, which injects a CGLIB proxy that finds the real bean on first use, or inject ObjectProvider<T>. Tested: with LA(@Lazy LB b) and LB(LA a), the context starts, and b is a CGLIB class. The best fix is still removing the cycle.

Output: singleton Sing has @Autowired Proto p, ObjectProvider<Proto> op, and a @Lookup method. Are repeated accesses the same instance?

Tested: s.direct() == s.direct() is true, since the field was injected once. op.getObject() == op.getObject() is false. s.look() == s.look() is false, because @Lookup is overridden to call getBean each time.

Are Spring singletons the same as the GoF Singleton? Are they thread-safe?

No to both. GoF means one instance per class loader. Spring means one instance per bean definition per container: two @Bean methods can create two singletons of one class, and two contexts hold separate ones. Spring adds no synchronization, so mutable fields are shared by all threads. Safe creation at startup is guaranteed, but not safe use.

Output: a @Configuration class has @Bean Repo repo() and two @Bean Svc methods that call repo(). How many Repo objects? And with proxyBeanMethods=false?

Tested. Full mode: one ("Repo created" prints once), a.r == b.r is true, because the CGLIB subclass intercepts repo(). Lite mode: three, one for the bean and two from plain Java calls, and a.r == b.r is false. The two extra objects are unmanaged: no injection, no proxies, no destroy callback.

What is the difference between @Primary, @Fallback, and @Qualifier?

@Primary is declared on a bean: "pick me when several match". @Fallback (Framework 6.2) is the opposite: "pick me only if nothing else does", which suits library defaults. @Qualifier is on the injection point and narrows the candidates first, so it overrides @Primary.

@Autowired vs @Resource vs @Inject?

@Autowired is Spring's: by type, then qualifiers, supports required=false. @Inject (Jakarta) behaves the same, without required. @Resource (Jakarta) goes by name first, falling back to type, and works on fields and setters. It is handy when you have several beans of a type and want one by name.

What is the difference between ${...} and #{...}?

${app.x} is resolved from the Environment by the placeholder mechanism. #{...} is evaluated by the SpEL engine and can call beans, do arithmetic and access static methods. They combine: #{'${app.hosts}'.split(',')}: placeholders are resolved first, then SpEL runs.

How do you run code after startup? Compare the options.
OptionWhenNote
@PostConstructOne bean is initializedNo proxy; other beans may not be ready
SmartInitializingSingletonAll singletons existFine for internal wiring
ContextRefreshedEventContext refreshedMay fire multiple times, including from child contexts
CommandLineRunner (Boot)After start, before readyFailure stops the app
ApplicationReadyEvent (Boot)App is accepting trafficFor background tasks
Are application events synchronous? What happens if a listener throws?

Synchronous by default: publishEvent returns only when all listeners finish. The listener shares the caller's thread and transaction, so an exception propagates to the publisher, stops later listeners, and may roll back the transaction. Use @Async to detach, or @TransactionalEventListener to run after the commit. You can also set an executor on the multicaster, but that makes every listener async, including ones that assumed otherwise.

You publish an event in a method with no @Transactional and a @TransactionalEventListener does not fire. Why?

The listener registers a synchronization with the current transaction. No transaction means nothing to synchronize with, so the event is dropped and only a debug message is logged. Tested: the event from the non-transactional method never arrived. Set fallbackExecution = true, or fix the transaction boundary.

Output: one aspect with @Around, @Before, @After, @AfterReturning, @AfterThrowing; the method succeeds. What is the order?

Tested on 6.2: around-before, before, method, afterReturning, after, around-after. On an exception: around-before, before, method, afterThrowing, after, around-catch. Since 5.2.7, @After runs after @AfterReturning and @AfterThrowing in the same aspect. Do not write tests that depend on two same-type advices in one aspect, whose order is undefined.

Which proxy does Spring use, and why does Boot default to CGLIB?

Plain Spring uses a JDK proxy when the bean implements an interface, and CGLIB otherwise. Boot sets spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true, so always CGLIB. The reason is usability: with JDK proxies, injecting the concrete class fails, and a bean's type would change when someone adds @Transactional. CGLIB's limits are final classes and methods.

Output: a bean with a final method is proxied. What does the final method return?

Tested with a field String nf = "field": nonfin() returns field; fin() returns null with no advice run; reading bean.nf directly returns null. The final method cannot be overridden, so it runs on the proxy object, which was created by Objenesis without running constructors or initializers. Any injected field would be null too, giving an NPE.

Can Spring AOP advise private methods, static methods, or objects you created with new?

No. Proxies only exist for container-managed beans, and a subclass can only override non-private, non-static, non-final methods. For these cases use AspectJ weaving. @Configurable with AspectJ can inject into objects built by new.

How would you build a @RateLimited or @Timed annotation?
@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
public @interface RateLimited { int perSecond(); }

@Aspect @Component
class RateLimitAspect {
  private final Map<Method, Semaphore> limits = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();
  @Around("@annotation(cfg)")
  Object limit(ProceedingJoinPoint pjp, RateLimited cfg) throws Throwable {
    Method m = ((MethodSignature) pjp.getSignature()).getMethod();
    Semaphore s = limits.computeIfAbsent(m, k -> new Semaphore(cfg.perSecond()));
    if (!s.tryAcquire()) throw new TooManyRequests();
    try { return pjp.proceed(); } finally { s.release(); }
  }
}

The retention must be RUNTIME, the method must be reached through the proxy, and the semaphore here limits concurrency rather than rate; a real rate limiter uses a token bucket. An interviewer may also ask where to set @Order: this should wrap the transaction, not run inside it.

Walk through what @Transactional does at runtime, step by step.

The caller hits the proxy. TransactionInterceptor reads attributes. getTransaction applies propagation: for a new transaction it takes a connection, sets auto-commit off, sets isolation and read-only, and binds the connection to the thread. The target method runs; JdbcTemplate or the EntityManager uses the thread-bound resource. For JPA, commit triggers a flush. On an exception, rollback rules are evaluated.
