Finally the resource is unbound and the connection is released.

Output: outer @Transactional inserts, calls inner @Transactional (REQUIRED) that throws, and outer catches. What happens?

Tested. Outer prints "caught" and returns, then its commit fails with UnexpectedRollbackException: Transaction rolled back because it has been marked as rollback-only. No rows remain. The inner interceptor marked the shared transaction rollback-only. To tolerate the failure, use REQUIRES_NEW or NESTED on the inner method, or do not use a transaction there.

Output: outer inserts 'outer', calls inner REQUIRES_NEW which inserts 'new' and commits, then outer throws. What is left?

Only new (tested). The inner transaction committed on its own connection before the outer failed. In the opposite case, inner REQUIRES_NEW throws and outer catches: only outer remains, and no UnexpectedRollbackException, because the transactions are independent. NESTED gives that same result here, through a savepoint, but an outer rollback would also undo the nested work.

A method throws IOException from a @Transactional method. Does it roll back?

No. It is checked, so the transaction commits and the exception still reaches the caller. Tested: the row was present after the exception. Use rollbackFor = Exception.class, or wrap the exception in a runtime exception.

Is @Transactional still limited to public methods?

This older rule is outdated. Since Framework 6.0, protected and package-visible methods are transactional with class-based proxies; a test confirmed this for a package-private method on 6.2. JDK proxies still need interface methods, which are public, and private and final methods never work. Reactive transaction methods, and those in interface-based proxies, must still be public.

Should @Transactional go on the controller, service, or repository?

On the service: it defines the business unit of work, which may span several repositories. On a controller, it keeps a connection during serialization and external calls. On repositories alone, each call commits separately. Spring Data repositories have their own for single calls. Keep the transaction as short as possible, with no remote calls inside.

How do you write to a database and send a Kafka message atomically?

There is no shared transaction, and @Transactional covers only the database. Sending before the commit may publish something that gets rolled back; sending after the commit may lose the message on a crash. The standard answer is the transactional outbox: insert the message into an outbox table in the same transaction, and a relay or CDC tool such as Debezium publishes it. Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent.

How do you handle two data sources with transactions?

Define two DataSource beans, two EntityManagerFactory or JDBC setups, and two transaction managers, one @Primary. Select with @Transactional("reportingTm"). A method using one manager does not cover the other. A two-phase commit needs JTA and is usually avoided; use a saga or outbox. For read/write routing, use AbstractRoutingDataSource wrapped in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so that the read-only flag is known before a connection is chosen.

Production shows "Connection is not available, request timed out" under load. How do you diagnose it?

Connections are held too long or leaked. Check hikaricp.connections.active and pending; set leakDetectionThreshold; take a thread dump to see what holders do. Usual causes: remote calls inside a transaction, Open Session in View keeping the connection through rendering, REQUIRES_NEW pool deadlock, or slow queries. Fix the cause before increasing the pool.

Describe the request path through DispatcherServlet, including argument resolution.

Filters run, then doDispatch. The HandlerMapping returns handler plus interceptors. preHandle runs. RequestMappingHandlerAdapter asks resolvers for each argument, using message converters for bodies, and runs validation. The method runs. Return handlers write the body with a converter chosen by Accept, or a view is rendered. postHandle and afterCompletion follow. Any exception goes to the HandlerExceptionResolver chain.

How does Spring choose the HttpMessageConverter?

For reading: the first converter whose canRead accepts the parameter type and Content-Type. None gives 415. For writing: it intersects the Accept header with what the converters can produce for the return type and the mapping's produces, picks the most specific media type, then the first converter that can write it. None gives 406. Extending configureMessageConverters replaces the defaults; in Boot, declare an HttpMessageConverter bean to add one.

Filter vs Interceptor: which would you use for authentication, request logging, and tenant resolution?

Authentication: a filter, as Spring Security does, since it must also protect static resources and unmapped paths. Request body logging: a filter, because it can wrap the request. Tenant resolution that needs the handler's annotations: an interceptor. If a business rule needs arguments: an aspect.

Why doesn't @RestControllerAdvice catch exceptions from my servlet filter or for authentication failures?

It runs inside DispatcherServlet, and filters run outside it. Handle errors in the filter itself; in Spring Security use AuthenticationEntryPoint and AccessDeniedHandler. A filter can also delegate to a HandlerExceptionResolver bean named handlerExceptionResolver to reuse the same handlers.

@Valid vs @Validated? Why is my @Min on a @RequestParam ignored, or not?

@Valid is the standard and cascades to nested objects. @Validated is Spring's, adding groups and, on a class, method-level validation via a proxy. Before Framework 6.1, a constraint directly on a controller parameter needed @Validated on the class, and failed with ConstraintViolationException. Since 6.1, Spring does it natively and raises HandlerMethodValidationException. A missed @Valid on a nested field is the classic cause of "nested validation is ignored".

How would you upload a 2 GB file without running out of memory?

Do not buffer it. MultipartFile.getBytes() loads it all into the heap. Options: use the input stream and copy to storage; raise limits; or best, give the client a presigned object-storage URL so the file bypasses the app. Support resumable or chunked upload for flaky networks. Validate size and type, scan content, and generate the stored name yourself.

RestClient vs WebClient: which would you choose in a servlet app?

RestClient for ordinary calls: blocking, simple, shares the same message converters. WebClient pulls in WebFlux and reactive types, and earns that when you need concurrent fan-out or streaming. With virtual threads, you can even get concurrency with RestClient in simple tasks. Both need timeouts, and a shared configured builder.

What is backpressure, and what happens without it?

Backpressure lets a consumer signal how much it can accept, using request(n). Without it, a fast producer forces the consumer to buffer without bound, or drop data, until memory runs out. Reactor offers onBackpressureBuffer, onBackpressureDrop and limitRate. It works across the network only when the protocol supports it, for example via TCP flow control.

Output: what does this print? Mono.just("x").map(v -> (String) null).onErrorResume(e -> { print(e.getClass()); return Mono.just("y"); }).subscribe(print)

Tested: NullPointerException, then y. Reactive Streams forbids null elements, so a mapper returning null becomes an error signal. For "no value", use mapNotNull or return Mono.empty() from a flatMap. Similarly, Mono.empty().map(...) never runs the mapper, and .defaultIfEmpty("empty!") supplies the value.

subscribeOn vs publishOn?

subscribeOn sets the thread on which the subscription and source run, wherever it appears in the chain. The first one nearest the source wins. publishOn switches the thread for operators after it, and can appear several times. Use subscribeOn(Schedulers.boundedElastic()) to wrap blocking sources.

When would you not choose WebFlux?

When the app uses JDBC/JPA, has ordinary CRUD load, or the team has little reactive experience. Debugging and stack traces are harder, one blocking call does serious harm, and every dependency must be non-blocking. Virtual threads now meet most high-concurrency needs in the blocking model. It remains a good fit for gateways and streaming.

@Cacheable returned stale data after an update. What are the likely causes?
  • The update method lacks @CachePut or @CacheEvict, or uses a different key.
  • The evict is self-invoked, so it never ran.
  • Local cache on several instances: only one was evicted. Use Redis, or pub/sub invalidation.
  • The eviction ran before commit and a reader re-cached old data.
  • A @Query or another service wrote directly to the database.
Output: what does @Cacheable do with a null return? How do you avoid caching nulls?

By default, most providers store a null marker, and subsequent calls return null without running the method. This protects against penetration by repeated lookups of absent ids, but can hide newly added rows. Use unless = "#result == null". An Optional return is unwrapped automatically for this check.

fixedRate vs fixedDelay vs cron, and what if a job takes longer than its interval?

fixedRate measures start to start. fixedDelay measures end to next start. cron uses calendar times. An overrunning job does not overlap itself; the next run starts late. With the default single scheduler thread, other jobs wait as well. If @Async is added, runs can overlap.

Your app runs 5 replicas and a nightly @Scheduled job sends emails. What goes wrong and how do you fix it?

All five run it, so customers get five emails. Options: ShedLock with @SchedulerLock and a database or Redis lock, Quartz with a clustered job store, a dedicated Kubernetes CronJob, or a leader election. Make the job idempotent regardless, for example by marking rows as sent, since locks can expire during long runs.

Why might an @Async pool with core 5, max 50 and default queue never exceed 5 threads?

ThreadPoolExecutor adds non-core threads only when the queue rejects a task. ThreadPoolTaskExecutor's default queue capacity is Integer.MAX_VALUE, so it never fills. Tasks pile up, latency grows, and memory may run out. Set a bounded queue and a rejection policy such as CallerRunsPolicy for natural backpressure.

Why is SecurityContextHolder empty in my @Async method?

The context is in a ThreadLocal, and the task runs on another thread. Wrap the executor in DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor, or set a TaskDecorator. Spring's ContextPropagatingTaskDecorator with Micrometer context propagation handles observability data. The same applies to MDC and request attributes.

How does a Spring Data interface with no implementation work?

@EnableJpaRepositories (automatic in Boot) scans for repository interfaces and registers a JpaRepositoryFactoryBean for each, which builds a proxy. Inherited CRUD methods are delegated to SimpleJpaRepository. For query methods, QueryLookupStrategy at startup parses the name into a PartTree, or reads @Query, and prepares a query. A typo in a property name fails at startup.

What are the main changes in Spring Framework 6 and 7?

6.x: Java 17 baseline, Jakarta EE 9+ (jakarta.*), AOT and native image support, ProblemDetail, @HttpExchange, RestClient (6.1), virtual thread support (6.1), @Fallback and @MockitoBean (6.2). 7.0: still Java 17 minimum, Jakarta EE 11, null-safety through JSpecify annotations, first-class API versioning in MVC and WebFlux, BeanRegistrar, core retry and concurrency-limit resilience annotations, and @ImportHttpServices.

Design: an order must update stock, charge a card, and send email. How do you structure transactions in Spring?

Keep the database transaction small: validate, create the order in PENDING state, and reserve stock in one @Transactional method. Charge outside the transaction with an idempotency key and timeouts. Update the status in a second short transaction. Send the email from an AFTER_COMMIT listener or, for guarantees, via an outbox. On failure, a compensating action releases the stock. This avoids holding locks and connections during slow external calls.

FactoryBean vs BeanFactory?

BeanFactory is the container: the root interface that holds and creates beans. FactoryBean is one bean inside the container that produces another object. Asking for "client" gives you getObject()'s result, and "&client" gives you the factory. 💡 Mention a real example: each Spring Data repository is produced by a RepositoryFactoryBean.

How should @Retryable and @Transactional be combined?

The retry must sit outside the transaction. Each attempt then runs in a fresh transaction, after the failed one has rolled back. If the retry is inside, it retries against a transaction that is already marked rollback-only or holds a broken connection. The simplest way is to put @Retryable on a caller bean that calls the @Transactional service. You can also order the advisors so that retry has higher precedence. Retry only transient errors, such as deadlock, lock timeout or optimistic lock failure. Never retry validation errors.

Which operations are safe to retry automatically?

Only idempotent ones: GET, PUT, DELETE, or POST with an idempotency key. Retrying a non-idempotent "charge card" call after a timeout can charge the customer twice, because the first request may have succeeded. Also cap the attempts, use exponential backoff with jitter so that clients do not all retry together, and respect Retry-After. Never retry 4xx errors except 408, 425 and 429. Retries in several layers multiply: 3 retries in each of 3 layers make 27 calls.

ResponseEntity vs @ResponseStatus vs ResponseStatusException?

  • ResponseEntity<T>: full control of status, headers and body per call, for example ResponseEntity.created(uri).body(dto).
  • @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.CREATED) on a handler: a fixed status. On an exception class, it maps that exception to a status.
  • throw new ResponseStatusException(NOT_FOUND, "Order 7"): an ad-hoc error status without a custom exception class. It renders as ProblemDetail.
In larger codebases, prefer domain exceptions with one @RestControllerAdvice, so that the status mapping lives in one place.

How do you accept a password in a request but never return it?

The best approach is separate request and response DTOs: CreateUserRequest has the password, and UserResponse does not. If you must share one class, use @JsonProperty(access = JsonProperty.Access.WRITE_ONLY). @JsonIgnore would block it in both directions. Never serialize JPA entities directly. You risk leaking fields and lazy-loading errors, and every schema change becomes an API change.

Why are my LocalDateTime values serialized as arrays like [2025,1,31,10,0]?

Jackson's WRITE_DATES_AS_TIMESTAMPS feature is on, or the Java time module is missing, because the ObjectMapper was created with new ObjectMapper() rather than Spring Boot's auto-configured one. Boot registers the Java time module and turns off timestamps, so dates are written as ISO-8601 strings. Inject the Boot mapper, or customize it, instead of creating your own. For APIs, prefer Instant or OffsetDateTime, which keep the offset, over LocalDateTime, which does not.

Spring Boot Productivity

Opinionated Spring: auto-configuration, starters, embedded server, Actuator, externalized config.

Typical Layered Architecture

# application.yml
server:
  port: 8081
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:mysql://localhost:3306/shop
    username: ${DB_USER}
    password: ${DB_PASS}
  jpa:
    hibernate.ddl-auto: validate      # none | validate | update | create | create-drop
    show-sql: true
management:
  endpoints.web.exposure.include: health,info,metrics,prometheus
app:
  payment:
    timeout: 5s
    retries: 3
@ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.payment")
public record PaymentProps(Duration timeout, int retries) {}   // type-safe config, enable with @EnableConfigurationProperties / @ConfigurationPropertiesScan

Auto-Configuration Mechanism

A plain Spring app needs dozens of bean definitions for a data source, a transaction manager, Jackson and a web server. Auto-configuration ships those definitions as ordinary @Configuration classes, each guarded by conditions so it applies only when it makes sense and backs off when you define your own bean. There is no magic: it is @Import and @Conditional, both from core Spring.

@EnableAutoConfiguration
  = @AutoConfigurationPackage                         // records your package, used by @EntityScan and JPA repositories
  + @Import(AutoConfigurationImportSelector.class)
  1. AutoConfigurationImportSelector reads all META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports files on the class path through ImportCandidates.load. Each line is a class name. Before Boot 2.7 the list lived in spring.factories; that route was removed in 3.0.
  2. It removes anything in exclude or spring.autoconfigure.exclude.
  3. Fast filters (AutoConfigurationImportFilter) discard most candidates using pre-computed metadata, without loading the classes. An app may start with well over a hundred candidates and keep a small fraction.
  4. It is a DeferredImportSelector, so these classes are processed after all your configuration. This is the key fact: by the time @ConditionalOnMissingBean is evaluated, your beans are already registered, so "user beans win".
  5. Ordering among auto-configurations uses @AutoConfiguration(before = ..., after = ...) and @AutoConfigureOrder.
ConditionMatches when
@ConditionalOnClass / OnMissingClassA class is or is not on the class path. Safe even if the class is absent, since it is read from bytecode metadata
@ConditionalOnBean / OnMissingBeanA bean is or is not already registered. Order-sensitive: reliable only inside auto-configuration
@ConditionalOnSingleCandidateExactly one bean of a type, or one primary
@ConditionalOnPropertyA property has a value; matchIfMissing sets the default
@ConditionalOnResourceA resource exists
@ConditionalOnWebApplication / OnNotWebApplicationServlet or reactive web context, or not
@ConditionalOnExpressionA SpEL expression is true
@ConditionalOnJavaJava version range
@ConditionalOnCloudPlatformKubernetes, Cloud Foundry and so on
@ConditionalOnThreadingVirtual or platform threads active (Boot 3.2)

Debugging. Start with --debug, or set debug=true, to print the condition report with positive matches, negative matches and the reason for each. /actuator/conditions shows the same at runtime. To see which class created a bean, use /actuator/beans.

Gotcha: A class in your component scan that also appears in an imports file gets processed too early and its conditions misbehave. Keep auto-configurations out of scanned packages. Also, @ConditionalOnMissingBean in your own @Configuration depends on scan order, so it is not reliable there.

The Startup Sequence

Event, in orderState at that moment
ApplicationStartingEventOnly listeners are registered. No Environment, no context
ApplicationEnvironmentPreparedEventEnvironment is ready, no context yet
ApplicationContextInitializedEventContext created, initializers ran, no bean definitions
ApplicationPreparedEventDefinitions loaded, refresh not started
ContextRefreshedEvent, WebServerInitializedEventDuring and at the end of refresh
ApplicationStartedEventContext refreshed, runners not yet called
ApplicationReadyEventRunners done, ready for traffic
ApplicationFailedEventStartup threw an exception

Listeners for the first few events cannot be ordinary beans, because no beans exist yet. Register them with SpringApplication.addListeners(...) or in META-INF/spring.factories. Other early hooks are EnvironmentPostProcessor (adds property sources) and ApplicationContextInitializer.

public static void main(String[] args) {
  SpringApplication app = new SpringApplication(ShopApplication.class);
  app.setBannerMode(Banner.Mode.OFF);
  app.addListeners(new EarlyListener());
  app.setApplicationStartup(new BufferingApplicationStartup(2048));   // feeds /actuator/startup
  app.run(args);
}

To speed up startup: inspect with /actuator/startup, limit scanning, try spring.main.lazy-initialization=true (faster start, but errors move to first use and the first requests are slow), and consider CDS or AOT, described below.

Runners

CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner beans run after ApplicationStartedEvent, in the main thread, in @Order sequence. Three consequences follow. An exception in a runner aborts startup. A long runner delays readiness, which is useful for cache warm-up, since Kubernetes will not route traffic yet. And a runner in a @SpringBootTest also runs, unless you exclude it with a profile.

@Component @Order(1) @Profile("!test")
class WarmCache implements ApplicationRunner {
  @Override public void run(ApplicationArguments args) {
    boolean full = args.containsOption("full-warmup");     // --full-warmup
    List<String> plain = args.getNonOptionArgs();
    catalog.warm(full);
  }
}

For a batch-style app, set spring.main.web-application-type=none, and return an exit code with System.exit(SpringApplication.exit(ctx, () -> 2)) or an ExitCodeGenerator bean.

Starters and Dependency Management

A starter is a nearly empty JAR with a POM that pulls in a tested set of dependencies. Version alignment comes separately from the spring-boot-dependencies BOM, which spring-boot-starter-parent inherits. That is why you write no version numbers.

<properties>
  <java.version>21</java.version>
  <postgresql.version>42.7.4</postgresql.version>  <!-- override one managed version -->
</properties>

<!-- If your project already has a parent, import the BOM instead -->
<dependencyManagement><dependencies><dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-dependencies</artifactId>
  <version>${spring-boot.version}</version>
  <type>pom</type><scope>import</scope>
</dependency></dependencies></dependencyManagement>

The parent also sets the Java version, encoding, resource filtering with @...@ delimiters, and plugin defaults. With the BOM import alone you do not get those, and property-based version overrides do not work; re-declare the artifact in dependencyManagement first.

Version note: Boot 4 splits the large auto-configure JAR into focused modules, with matching starters. spring-boot-starter-webmvc takes over from spring-boot-starter-web, and tests get per-technology starters. Transitional spring-boot-starter-classic and spring-boot-starter-test-classic help during migration.

Building a Custom Starter

A company usually packages shared concerns such as audit logging or a standard HTTP client as a starter. The convention is two modules: acme-audit-spring-boot-autoconfigure with the code, and acme-audit-spring-boot-starter with only dependencies. Never name your own artifact spring-boot-starter-*; that prefix is reserved for official ones.

@ConfigurationProperties("acme.audit")
public record AuditProperties(@DefaultValue("true") boolean enabled,
                              @DefaultValue("https://audit.internal") URI endpoint,
                              @DefaultValue("5s") Duration timeout) { }

@AutoConfiguration(after = RestClientAutoConfiguration.class)
@ConditionalOnClass(RestClient.class)
@ConditionalOnProperty(prefix = "acme.audit", name = "enabled", matchIfMissing = true)
@EnableConfigurationProperties(AuditProperties.class)
public class AuditAutoConfiguration {

  @Bean
  @ConditionalOnMissingBean                  // lets the app replace it
  AuditClient auditClient(RestClient.Builder builder, AuditProperties props) {
    return new HttpAuditClient(builder.baseUrl(props.endpoint().toString()).build());
  }

  @Bean
  @ConditionalOnMissingBean
  AuditAspect auditAspect(AuditClient client) { return new AuditAspect(client); }
}
# src/main/resources/META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports
com.acme.audit.AuditAutoConfiguration
<!-- generates spring-configuration-metadata.json, for IDE completion of acme.audit.* -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-configuration-processor</artifactId>
  <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>
// Test the conditions without starting a whole app
class AuditAutoConfigurationTest {
  private final ApplicationContextRunner runner = new ApplicationContextRunner()
      .withConfiguration(AutoConfigurations.of(AuditAutoConfiguration.class, RestClientAutoConfiguration.class));

  @Test void createsClientByDefault() {
    runner.run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).hasSingleBean(AuditClient.class));
  }
  @Test void backsOffWhenDisabled() {
    runner.withPropertyValues("acme.audit.enabled=false")
          .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).doesNotHaveBean(AuditClient.class));
  }
  @Test void userBeanWins() {
    runner.withBean(AuditClient.class, () -> mock(AuditClient.class))
          .run(ctx -> assertThat(ctx).getBean(AuditClient.class).isNotInstanceOf(HttpAuditClient.class));
  }
}

Mark optional integrations as optional in the auto-configure POM, and guard them with @ConditionalOnClass, so applications that do not use them are not forced to include them.

Embedded Servers

Instead of deploying into a server, the server runs inside your JVM. During onRefresh, ServletWebServerApplicationContext looks up the single ServletWebServerFactory bean, and auto-configuration supplies one based on what is on the class path. It then registers DispatcherServlet and filters through ServletContextInitializers. Connectors begin accepting requests at the end of refresh.

ServerModelNote
TomcatServlet, thread per requestDefault for the servlet stack
JettyServletAlternative; good for many idle connections
UndertowServletSupported in Boot 3.x, dropped in Boot 4 since it lacks Servlet 6.1 support
Reactor NettyNon-blocking event loopDefault for WebFlux
server:
  port: 8080
  shutdown: graceful
  max-http-request-header-size: 8KB    # default
  forward-headers-strategy: framework  # behind a proxy: honour X-Forwarded-*
  compression:
    enabled: true
    min-response-size: 2KB
  http2.enabled: true
  ssl.bundle: web                      # SSL bundles, Boot 3.1+
  tomcat:
    threads:
      max: 200                         # default: max concurrent request threads
      min-spare: 10
    max-connections: 8192              # default: accepted connections
    accept-count: 100                  # default: OS queue once connections are full
@Bean WebServerFactoryCustomizer<TomcatServletWebServerFactory> tomcat() {
  return f -> f.addConnectorCustomizers(c -> c.setProperty("maxKeepAliveRequests", "200"));
}

If a port behind a load balancer sees the wrong scheme or client IP, the cause is usually missing forward-headers-strategy: redirects and Location headers will then point at http://.

Externalized Configuration: the Full Order

Boot adds property sources to the Environment in a fixed order, and the first one that defines a key wins. This lets the same artifact run in any environment. From highest precedence:

  1. Devtools global settings, when active.
  2. @TestPropertySource, then @DynamicPropertySource, then test properties attributes.
  3. Command-line arguments (--server.port=9000).
  4. SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON.
  5. ServletConfig and ServletContext init parameters; JNDI.
  6. Java system properties (-Dserver.port=9000).
  7. OS environment variables.
  8. random.* values.
  9. Config data files, in the order below.
  10. @PropertySource on configuration classes.
  11. Defaults set by SpringApplication.setDefaultProperties.

Config data files, highest first: profile-specific outside the JAR, non-profile outside the JAR, profile-specific inside the JAR, non-profile inside. So a profile file beats a plain file at the same level, and an external plain application.yml beats a packaged application-prod.yml.

Locations searched, later overriding earlier: class path root, class path /config, current directory, ./config/, and direct subdirectories of ./config/. If both .properties and .yml exist at one location, .properties wins. Keep to one format.

# application.yml: several documents in one file
spring:
  application.name: shop
  config:
    import:
      - optional:file:./secrets.yml               # ignored if missing
      - optional:configtree:/run/secrets/         # Kubernetes secrets mounted as files
---
spring:
  config.activate.on-profile: prod
server.port: 8443
---
spring:
  config.activate.on-profile: "dev | local"
logging.level.com.shop: DEBUG

Relaxed binding. spring.datasource.url maps from the environment variable SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: dots become underscores, dashes are removed, uppercase. So my.main-project.person is MY_MAINPROJECT_PERSON, and list element app.hosts[0] is APP_HOSTS_0. @ConfigurationProperties fully supports this; @Value only partly, so use the canonical kebab-case form there.

Secrets belong in environment variables, mounted files, or a vault, not in a repository. Placeholders like ${DB_PASS:default} are resolved against the whole Environment.

Profiles in Boot

java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod,eu
SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod java -jar app.jar

spring:
  profiles:
    default: local             # used when none is active
    group:
      prod: [db-postgres, metrics, eu]     # activating prod also activates these
    include: audit             # always added (only in non-profile documents)
Gotcha: Since Boot 2.4, spring.profiles.active, include and group are invalid inside a profile-specific document, and startup fails. When several profiles are active, the last one listed has the highest precedence. Prefer a few environment-level profiles over a combinatorial set, and keep real differences in external configuration.

@ConfigurationProperties in Depth

@ConfigurationProperties("app.payment")
@Validated
public record PaymentProperties(
    @NotNull URI url,
    @DefaultValue("5s") Duration timeout,        // 500ms, 5s, 2m are all accepted; plain 500 means ms
    @DefaultValue("10MB") DataSize maxPayload,
    @Min(0) @DefaultValue("3") int retries,
    @DefaultValue Retry retry,                   // an empty @DefaultValue builds it with its own defaults
    Map<String, Merchant> merchants,             // app.payment.merchants.amazon.key=...
    List<String> currencies) {

  public record Retry(@DefaultValue("200ms") Duration backoff) { }
  public record Merchant(String key) { }
}

@SpringBootApplication
@ConfigurationPropertiesScan                     // registers all in this package tree
public class ShopApplication { }

// For a third-party class: bind on a @Bean method
@Bean @ConfigurationProperties("app.pool")
HikariDataSource reportingDataSource() { return new HikariDataSource(); }
Feature@ConfigurationProperties@Value
Relaxed bindingFullLimited
ValidationYes, fails at startupNo
Nested objects, lists, mapsYesAwkward
IDE metadataYes, with the processorNo
SpELNoYes
ImmutabilityRecords and constructor bindingConstructor parameters only

Binding is done by the Binder class, called from ConfigurationPropertiesBindingPostProcessor for JavaBean-style classes, or at construction for records. If a class has a single parameterized constructor, constructor binding is used automatically; with several, mark one @ConstructorBinding. An unknown key does not fail by default.

Logging

Your code logs through SLF4J, a facade. Boot's default implementation is Logback, wired by spring-boot-starter-logging. Bridges send other logging APIs (JUL, Log4j API, Commons Logging) to the same place. By default, output goes to the console at INFO; files are off until you set logging.file.name.

logging:
  level:
    root: INFO
    com.shop: DEBUG
    web: DEBUG                         # a built-in group
    sql: DEBUG
  group:
    shop-core: com.shop.order, com.shop.payment
  file.name: logs/app.log
  logback.rollingpolicy:
    max-file-size: 10MB                # default
    max-history: 7                     # default
  structured.format.console: ecs       # Boot 3.4+: ecs, gelf, logstash
<!-- src/main/resources/logback-spring.xml, not logback.xml, which loads too early for these -->
<configuration>
  <include resource="org/springframework/boot/logging/logback/defaults.xml"/>
  <springProperty name="appName" source="spring.application.name"/>
  <appender name="CONSOLE" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
    <encoder><pattern>${CONSOLE_LOG_PATTERN}</pattern></encoder>
  </appender>
  <springProfile name="prod">
    <root level="WARN"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
  </springProfile>
  <springProfile name="!prod">
    <root level="INFO"><appender-ref ref="CONSOLE"/></root>
  </springProfile>
</configuration>
  • To Log4j2: exclude spring-boot-starter-logging, add spring-boot-starter-log4j2. Having two SLF4J bindings causes a warning and an arbitrary choice.
  • Correlation: put a request id in MDC, or rely on Micrometer Tracing, which adds traceId and spanId to log lines.
  • Parameterized logging: log.debug("order {}", id) avoids building the string when DEBUG is off.
  • In containers: log to stdout in structured JSON and let the platform collect it.
  • Never log passwords, tokens, or card numbers.

DevTools and Local Development

Restart is the main feature. DevTools uses two class loaders: a base loader for JARs that rarely change, and a restart loader for your classes. When a class file changes, it discards only the restart loader and rebuilds the context, which is much faster than a JVM restart. It is not hot swap: state is lost.

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-devtools</artifactId>
  <scope>runtime</scope>
  <optional>true</optional>
</dependency>

It also turns off template caching, starts a LiveReload server, and sets web logging to DEBUG. It disables itself when run from a fully packaged JAR, and by default is excluded from the repackaged archive. A library with a static cache of classes can break, because the same class loaded by two loaders gives a ClassCastException such as "X cannot be cast to X".

Related tools: spring-boot-docker-compose (Boot 3.1) starts services from compose.yaml and wires connection details automatically, and Testcontainers can do the same at development time through a test-scoped main class.

Packaging and the Executable JAR

Java cannot load a JAR nested in a JAR. The Boot Maven and Gradle plugins repackage the normal JAR and add a small loader that can.

app.jar
 ├ META-INF/MANIFEST.MF             Main-Class: org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher
 │                                  Start-Class: com.shop.ShopApplication
 ├ org/springframework/boot/loader/ the loader classes (not nested)
 └ BOOT-INF/
    ├ classes/                      your code and resources
    ├ lib/                          dependencies, as nested JARs
    ├ classpath.idx                 class path order
    └ layers.idx                    layer assignment

On start, JarLauncher creates a class loader that reads the nested JARs, finds Start-Class, and calls its main. The loader package moved in Boot 3.2, as shown. The original thin JAR is saved as app.jar.original.

Layered JARs

A Docker image is a stack of layers, and a layer is rebuilt when any file in it changes. A single fat JAR is one 80 MB layer, re-pushed on each one-line fix. Layers split the JAR by rate of change.

LayerContainsChanges
dependenciesRelease dependenciesRarely
spring-boot-loaderLoader classesOn Boot upgrade
snapshot-dependenciesSNAPSHOT dependenciesOften
applicationYour classes and resourcesEvery build

Docker Images

# Dockerfile, following the Boot reference layout for 3.3+
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre AS builder
WORKDIR /builder
ARG JAR_FILE=target/*.jar
COPY ${JAR_FILE} application.jar
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar application.jar extract --layers --destination extracted

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd --system app
USER app
WORKDIR /application
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /builder/extracted/application/ ./
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "application.jar"]

Older Boot versions use java -Djarmode=layertools -jar app.jar extract. The extracted form also starts faster than a fat JAR and enables class data sharing. Alternatives:

MethodCommandPros and cons
Dockerfiledocker build .Full control; you maintain the base image and flags
Cloud Native Buildpacksmvn spring-boot:build-imageNo Dockerfile; layers, memory calculator and non-root user are handled; needs Docker; less control
JibMaven or Gradle pluginBuilds without a Docker daemon; ideal for CI
Gotcha: Use the exec form of ENTRYPOINT so that Java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM; the shell form swallows it, breaking graceful shutdown. MaxRAMPercentage makes the heap follow the container limit. Heap is not total memory: metaspace, threads and direct buffers need the rest, so setting 100% gets the container killed with OOM.

Graceful Shutdown

Without it, a deployment cuts off in-flight requests. server.shutdown defaults to graceful since Boot 3.4 (immediate before that). On SIGTERM:

  1. The JVM shutdown hook closes the context. ContextClosedEvent is published, and readiness becomes REFUSING_TRAFFIC.
  2. SmartLifecycle beans stop in phases. The web server stops accepting, and waits for active requests.
  3. Each phase may use up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s). After that, remaining requests are aborted.
  4. Beans are destroyed: Hikari closes, and @PreDestroy runs.
spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase: 25s

# Kubernetes
terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 45        # must exceed the phase timeout, else SIGKILL
lifecycle:
  preStop:
    exec: { command: ["sleep", "10"] }   # wait for endpoint removal to reach proxies

The preStop sleep covers a race: Kubernetes sends SIGTERM and removes the pod from load balancing at about the same time, so a few requests still arrive after the server stops accepting. Note also that kill -9 and an out-of-memory kill run no hooks at all.

Exception Handling and ProblemDetail

An exception nobody handles goes to the servlet container, which forwards to /error. BasicErrorController serves that path, returning JSON or a Whitelabel HTML page based on Accept, using DefaultErrorAttributes. Details are hidden by default.

server.error:
  include-message: never           # default never: messages may leak internals
  include-stacktrace: never        # default
  include-binding-errors: never    # default
  whitelabel.enabled: false

Boot reports standard errors as RFC 9457 application/problem+json when spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true (or the WebFlux equivalent). That registers a ResponseEntityExceptionHandler subclass. RFC 9457 replaced RFC 7807 in 2023; the format is the same.

public class OutOfStock extends ErrorResponseException {       // carries its own ProblemDetail
  public OutOfStock(String sku) {
    super(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, asProblem(sku), null);
  }
  private static ProblemDetail asProblem(String sku) {
    ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "No stock for " + sku);
    p.setTitle("Out of stock");
    p.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.example/problems/out-of-stock"));
    p.setProperty("sku", sku);                                 // becomes a top-level JSON member
    return p;
  }
}

@RestControllerAdvice
class Errors extends ResponseEntityExceptionHandler {
  @Override protected ResponseEntity<Object> handleMethodArgumentNotValid(
      MethodArgumentNotValidException ex, HttpHeaders h, HttpStatusCode s, WebRequest r) {
    ProblemDetail p = ex.getBody();
    p.setProperty("errors", ex.getFieldErrors().stream()
        .map(e -> Map.of("field", e.getField(), "message", String.valueOf(e.getDefaultMessage())))
        .toList());
    return handleExceptionInternal(ex, p, h, s, r);
  }
  @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class)                           // last resort, no internals in the body
  ProblemDetail unexpected(Exception ex) {
    log.error("unhandled", ex);
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.INTERNAL_SERVER_ERROR, "Unexpected error");
  }
}
HTTP/1.1 409
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{ "type": "https://api.shop.example/problems/out-of-stock", "title": "Out of stock",
  "status": 409, "detail": "No stock for ABC-1234", "instance": "/orders", "sku": "ABC-1234" }

Virtual Threads in Boot

With Java 21 and Boot 3.2+, spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true runs Tomcat and Jetty request handling, applicationTaskExecutor and the scheduler on virtual threads. @Async then uses a SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor, and Kafka and RabbitMQ listeners follow too.

A virtual thread is scheduled by the JVM on a few carrier threads. When it blocks on I/O, it unmounts and the carrier serves another one. So blocking gets cheap, and the 200-thread limit disappears. CPU-bound work does not get faster.

Gotcha:
  • The bottleneck moves. With 10,000 concurrent requests and a pool of 20 connections, requests queue and time out. Limit concurrency to downstreams with a semaphore; spring.task.execution.simple.concurrency-limit caps task execution.
  • Pinning. On Java 21 to 23, blocking inside synchronized holds the carrier. JEP 491 fixed this in Java 24, so Java 25 LTS is better for this. On 21, use ReentrantLock in hot paths and check with -Djdk.tracePinnedThreads.
  • Do not pool them. Pooling defeats the purpose. Limit a resource with a semaphore rather than a pool size.
  • ThreadLocal caches no longer reuse anything, because each task gets a new thread.
  • JVM exit. Virtual threads are daemon threads. An app with only @Scheduled work needs spring.main.keep-alive=true to keep running.

GraalVM Native Image and AOT

native-image compiles the application ahead of time to a standalone executable. It performs a closed-world analysis: everything reachable must be known at build time, and the rest is removed. Result: startup in tens of milliseconds and much lower memory, in exchange for long builds and a lower peak throughput than a warmed-up JIT unless profile-guided optimization is used.

Spring is highly dynamic, which clashes with that. Boot's AOT engine (spring-boot:process-aot) therefore runs at build time. It starts the context up to the point of creating definitions, evaluates conditions, and generates Java source that registers beans directly, plus reachability hints for reflection, resources and proxies. CGLIB classes are generated at this stage.

./mvnw -Pnative native:compile           # local build with GraalVM
./mvnw -Pnative spring-boot:build-image  # build in a container, no local GraalVM needed

@RegisterReflectionForBinding(LegacyDto.class)      // hint: this class is used reflectively

class MyHints implements RuntimeHintsRegistrar {
  public void registerHints(RuntimeHints hints, ClassLoader cl) {
    hints.resources().registerPattern("templates/*.txt");
  }
}
@ImportRuntimeHints(MyHints.class) @Configuration class HintsConfig { }

Limits: the class path and bean set are fixed at build time. @Profile and @ConditionalOnProperty are decided at build time too, so a profile cannot change which beans exist at runtime. Property values can still change. Reflection in libraries needs hints.

OptionStartupPeak throughputCost
Normal JVMSecondsBest after warm-upNone
CDS / AOT cacheNoticeably fasterSameTraining run; matching JVM. -XX:AOTCache arrived with JEP 483 in Java 24
Spring AOT on the JVMFasterSameConditions fixed at build; start with -Dspring.aot.enabled=true
CRaCVery fast restoreSameA checkpoint; needs a supporting JDK and Linux
Native imageMillisecondsLower without PGOLong builds; closed world

Testing Pointers

The test section covers tools in detail. For Boot, the key idea is slices: load only the part of the context a test needs.

AnnotationLoads
@WebMvcTestMVC beans for named controllers; services must be mocked
@WebFluxTestWebFlux equivalent
@DataJpaTestJPA, repositories, transaction per test with rollback
@JdbcTest, @DataRedisTest, @DataMongoTestOther stores
@JsonTestJackson serialization only
@RestClientTestClient beans with a mock server
@SpringBootTestFull context; webEnvironment = RANDOM_PORT for a real server
@Testcontainers
@SpringBootTest(webEnvironment = SpringBootTest.WebEnvironment.RANDOM_PORT)
class OrderApiIT {
  @Container @ServiceConnection                       // Boot 3.1: sets the connection properties for you
  static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:17");

  @Autowired TestRestTemplate rest;

  @Test void placesOrder() {
    var res = rest.postForEntity("/orders", new CreateOrder("ABC-1234", 1), OrderDto.class);
    assertThat(res.getStatusCode()).isEqualTo(HttpStatus.CREATED);
  }
}

Boot caches contexts between test classes with identical configuration. Each new combination of @MockitoBean makes a new context, slowing the suite. @DirtiesContext has the same cost. @DataJpaTest rolls back, but its rollback hides flush errors; call flush() to expose them. A test transaction also keeps entities attached, hiding LazyInitializationException that production would hit.

Migrating to Boot 3 and Boot 4

AreaBoot 2 to 3Boot 3 to 4
Java17 minimum17 minimum; 25 is the current LTS
FrameworkSpring 6Spring 7
Platformjavax.* to jakarta.* (EE 9/10)Jakarta EE 11, Servlet 6.1
SecuritySpring Security 6: SecurityFilterChainSpring Security 7: non-lambda DSL and and() gone
JPAHibernate 6Hibernate 7
JSONJackson 2Jackson 3 by default (tools.jackson packages; annotations keep com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation)
StructureAutoConfiguration.importsModular auto-configuration and renamed starters
RemovedSleuth, Spring-factories auto-configurationUndertow; @MockBean and @SpyBean in favour of @MockitoBean, @MockitoSpyBean
TestingJUnit 5JUnit 6

A safe sequence:

  1. Move to the last minor of your current line, such as 2.7 or 3.5, and clear all deprecation warnings, since each release removes what the last one deprecated.
  2. Upgrade Java first if necessary, and fix third-party libraries that lack Jakarta versions.
  3. Add spring-boot-properties-migrator at runtime scope: it reports renamed properties at startup and temporarily maps them. Remove it afterwards.
  4. Let OpenRewrite recipes do mechanical changes, such as javax to jakarta imports and API renames.
  5. Read the official migration guide; check behavior changes rather than only compile errors. Examples: trailing-slash matching in Boot 3, Hibernate 6's changed ID sequences, changed metric names, and spring.mvc.problemdetails error shapes.
  6. Run the full integration test suite, and canary-deploy.

Serving an Angular SPA from Spring Boot

There are two deployment shapes. In the first, Angular is served separately (Nginx, a CDN, Firebase Hosting) and calls the API on another origin or through a reverse proxy. In the second, Boot serves the built files from classpath:/static, which gives one artifact and no CORS. In the second case:

  • Copy the Angular build output (dist/<app>/browser in Angular 17+) into src/main/resources/static. A build plugin such as frontend-maven-plugin can do this.
  • Deep links: refreshing /orders/7 asks the server for that path. Without a fallback it returns 404 or the Whitelabel page. Forward unknown non-API paths to index.html.
  • Caching: the hashed bundles (main-ABC123.js) can be cached for a year. index.html must be no-cache, or users keep loading an old version.
  • During development, use the Angular CLI proxy (proxy.conf.json), so that ng serve sends /api to localhost:8080 without CORS.
@Configuration
class SpaConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  @Override
  public void addResourceHandlers(ResourceHandlerRegistry registry) {
    registry.addResourceHandler("/**")
        .addResourceLocations("classpath:/static/")
        .resourceChain(true)
        .addResolver(new PathResourceResolver() {
          @Override
          protected Resource getResource(String path, Resource location) throws IOException {
            if (path.startsWith("api/")) return null;                 // unknown API path: real 404
            Resource r = location.createRelative(path);
            return r.exists() && r.isReadable() ? r : new ClassPathResource("/static/index.html");
          }
        });
  }
}
// @RestController mappings are checked before this resource handler, so the API still works.

Profile Groups and Activation Rules

A profile group gives one name to several profiles, so that --spring.profiles.active=prod can switch on proddb and prodmq at once. It replaced the older trick of using spring.profiles.include inside profile files.

spring:
  profiles:
    group:
      prod: [proddb, prodmq, json-logs]
      dev:  [localdb, devtools]
---
spring:
  config:
    activate:
      on-profile: proddb            # this document applies only when proddb is active
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://db:5432/app
  • Since Boot 2.4, spring.profiles.active and spring.profiles.include are not allowed in profile-specific documents. Boot fails at startup with an InvalidConfigDataPropertyException.
  • @Profile("!prod") negates a profile, and @Profile("cloud & !test") combines profiles.
  • spring.profiles.default applies only when no profile is active.

Everyday Web Settings

PropertyDefaultWhy you change it
spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size1MBUploads larger than this fail with MaxUploadSizeExceededException
spring.servlet.multipart.max-request-size10MBTotal size of a multipart request with several files
server.servlet.context-path/Run the app under /app. The base path in Angular's index.html must match
server.compression.enabledfalseGzip for JSON and text, if no proxy in front already compresses
server.forward-headers-strategynoneTrust X-Forwarded-* behind a load balancer, for correct redirects and links
server.error.include-stacktraceneverKeep it that way in production
spring.jackson.default-property-inclusionalwaysnon_null leaves nulls out of JSON
spring.jackson.time-zoneJVM zoneSet UTC for predictable java.util.Date output

Global Jackson Configuration

Boot auto-configures one ObjectMapper (in Boot 4, a Jackson 3 JsonMapper), which MVC, RestClient and WebClient all use. Its defaults differ from a plain new ObjectMapper(): FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES is off, Java time types are written as ISO strings, and all Module beans are registered. You can customize it with spring.jackson.* properties or a customizer bean. Defining your own ObjectMapper bean replaces Boot's and loses these defaults.

@Bean   // Boot 3 (Jackson 2). Boot 4 uses JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer for Jackson 3
Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer jsonCustomizer() {
  return b -> b.serializationInclusion(JsonInclude.Include.NON_NULL)
               .featuresToEnable(DeserializationFeature.FAIL_ON_NULL_FOR_PRIMITIVES);
}

Interview Questions — Spring Boot

Spring vs Spring Boot?
SpringSpring Boot
Lots of manual configuration (XML or Java)Auto-configuration with sensible defaults
Deploy a WAR to an external serverEmbedded Tomcat/Jetty/Undertow, executable fat JAR
Manage dependency versions yourselfStarters plus a managed BOM
No production toolingActuator: health, metrics

Boot is Spring. It just removes the boilerplate.

How does auto-configuration work?

@EnableAutoConfiguration loads the candidate classes listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (it was spring.factories before Boot 2.7). Each one is guarded by @Conditional* annotations. For example, DataSourceAutoConfiguration only runs if a JDBC driver is on the classpath and you haven't defined your own DataSource. Your beans always take priority. To exclude one: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class).

What are starters? Name a few.

Starters are dependency descriptors that bundle compatible libraries. Examples: spring-boot-starter-web (MVC, Tomcat, Jackson), -data-jpa (Hibernate, HikariCP), -security, -validation, -actuator, -test (JUnit 5, Mockito, AssertJ), -webflux, -cache, -amqp, and spring-kafka added directly (there is no Kafka starter before Boot 4).

@Value vs @ConfigurationProperties?

@Value("${app.x:default}") injects a single value and supports SpEL. @ConfigurationProperties binds a whole group of properties into a type-safe object. It supports relaxed binding, validation (@Validated) and IDE metadata. Use it for anything more than one or two values.

Property source precedence order?

From highest to lowest (simplified): command-line args → SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON → Java system properties → OS environment variables → application-{profile}.yml → application.yml → @PropertySource → defaults. Files outside the jar override the ones packaged inside it.

What is Spring Boot Actuator?

Production-ready endpoints under /actuator: health (with liveness and readiness probes for Kubernetes), info, metrics, prometheus, env, beans, mappings, loggers (change log levels at runtime), threaddump, heapdump. It uses Micrometer for metrics. Secure the sensitive endpoints.

How to change embedded server / port? How to deploy as WAR?

Port: server.port=9090 (use 0 for a random port). Server: exclude spring-boot-starter-tomcat and add -jetty or -undertow. WAR: set <packaging>war</packaging>, mark Tomcat as provided, and extend SpringBootServletInitializer.

CommandLineRunner vs ApplicationRunner?

Both run once after the context has started (seeding data, warm-up). CommandLineRunner.run(String... args) receives the raw args. ApplicationRunner.run(ApplicationArguments) receives parsed options. Control the order with @Order.

How do you test a Spring Boot app?
  • Unit: JUnit 5 + Mockito (@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class), @Mock, @InjectMocks). No Spring involved.
  • @WebMvcTest(UserController.class) + MockMvc + @MockitoBean (Boot 3.4+; previously @MockBean): web layer only.
  • @DataJpaTest: JPA slice with an embedded DB, rolled back after each test.
  • @SpringBootTest: the full context, for integration tests. Combine with Testcontainers for a real database or Kafka.
@WebMvcTest(UserController.class)
class UserControllerTest {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
  @MockitoBean UserService service;
  @Test void getUser() throws Exception {
    when(service.find(1L)).thenReturn(new UserDto(1L, "Ana"));
    mvc.perform(get("/api/users/1"))
       .andExpect(status().isOk())
       .andExpect(jsonPath("$.name").value("Ana"));
  }
}
What changed in Spring Boot 3?

Requires Java 17+ and Spring Framework 6. Moved from javax → jakarta packages. GraalVM native image support (AOT). Observability with Micrometer Tracing (Sleuth was removed). ProblemDetail errors. HTTP interface clients (@HttpExchange). Virtual thread support (spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Boot 3.2). RestClient (3.2).

What does spring-boot-devtools do?

Automatic restart when classpath files change, LiveReload, and dev-friendly defaults such as disabled template caching. It's turned off automatically in a packaged jar running in production.

How to create a custom starter / auto-configuration?

Write a @AutoConfiguration class with @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean beans and a @ConfigurationProperties class, and register it in META-INF/spring/…AutoConfiguration.imports. Package it as xyz-spring-boot-starter.

RestTemplate vs WebClient vs RestClient vs Feign?

RestTemplate: synchronous, in maintenance mode. WebClient: reactive and non-blocking (WebFlux). RestClient (Boot 3.2): a modern synchronous fluent API, the replacement for RestTemplate. OpenFeign: declarative interface clients, popular in microservices. There's also Spring's own @HttpExchange interfaces.

How do you enable caching / scheduling / async?

@EnableCaching + @Cacheable("users"), @CacheEvict, @CachePut (with Caffeine or Redis). @EnableScheduling + @Scheduled(cron = "0 0 * * * *") or fixedRate. @EnableAsync + @Async returning CompletableFuture. All three are proxy-based, so self-invocation doesn't work.

What exactly does @SpringBootApplication do, and why should it sit in a root package?

It combines @SpringBootConfiguration, @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan. Scanning and @AutoConfigurationPackage start from its package. Put it in a sub-package and sibling packages are not scanned, and JPA entities or repositories there are not found. You can move it with scanBasePackages, @EntityScan and @EnableJpaRepositories, but the root package is simpler.

Why are user beans able to override auto-configured beans?

Two facts combine. AutoConfigurationImportSelector is a DeferredImportSelector, so its classes are processed after all user configuration. And auto-configured beans carry @ConditionalOnMissingBean. So when the condition is evaluated, your bean is already registered, and the auto-configured one is skipped.

I added a DataSource dependency and the app fails with "Failed to configure a DataSource". Why? What are the options?

A starter brought JDBC classes onto the class path, so DataSourceAutoConfiguration activated, but no URL is configured, and no embedded database is available. Supply spring.datasource.url, add H2, or exclude it: @SpringBootApplication(exclude = DataSourceAutoConfiguration.class). The message comes from a FailureAnalyzer, which produces those readable startup errors.

How do you find out why a bean was not created?

Run with --debug and read the conditions report, or use /actuator/conditions. Each auto-configuration shows which condition failed: for example, "@ConditionalOnClass did not find required class". If your own component is missing, check the scan package, the @Profile, and any @Conditional.

What is the difference between spring.factories and AutoConfiguration.imports today?

Auto-configurations are listed only in the .imports file since Boot 3.0. spring.factories is still used for other extension points: ApplicationListener, EnvironmentPostProcessor, ApplicationContextInitializer, FailureAnalyzer. A library upgraded from Boot 2 with auto-configuration in spring.factories silently does nothing on Boot 3.

Describe the Spring Boot startup sequence.

The constructor deduces the application type and loads initializers and listeners. run() prepares the Environment, reading config files. It creates the context, applies initializers, and loads sources. refresh() processes configuration including auto-configuration, creates the web server in onRefresh, creates singletons, and starts accepting. Then ApplicationStartedEvent, runners, and ApplicationReadyEvent. Any failure triggers ApplicationFailedEvent, and failure analyzers print advice.

Output: precedence. application.yml has server.port=8080, env var SERVER_PORT=8081, JVM -Dserver.port=8082, and argument --server.port=8083. Which wins? Remove the argument?

8083: command-line arguments are higher. Without it, 8082: Java system properties beat OS environment variables. Without that, 8081, then 8080. Many answers put environment variables above system properties; the documented order is the reverse.

A value in application-prod.yml is ignored in production even though prod is active. Why?

Something of higher precedence defines it: an environment variable set by a chart, a system property, or an external config file, such as config/application.yml in the working directory, which outranks a packaged profile file. Check /actuator/env, which lists every source containing the key and which one wins. Also check for a typo in the profile activation.

Can you use YAML with @PropertySource?

Not directly: it supports .properties and XML. YAML needs a custom PropertySourceFactory. In Boot, the normal route is spring.config.import, which takes YAML and also participates correctly in precedence.

How do you bind a complex list or map from YAML, and override it with an environment variable?
app:
  hosts: [a.internal, b.internal]
  limits: { gold: 100, silver: 10 }

Use List<String> hosts and Map<String, Integer> limits in a properties record. Environment form: APP_HOSTS_0=x, APP_LIMITS_GOLD=200. Lists are replaced as a whole by a higher source, not merged element by element. Maps merge by key. Environment variable names lose case, so map keys become lowercase.

How do you validate configuration at startup?

Add @Validated and constraints to a @ConfigurationProperties type. Startup fails with a clear report if the value is missing or invalid, which is better than failing on the first request. It needs a Bean Validation implementation on the class path. Records with @DefaultValue avoid null defaults.

How can you refresh configuration without restarting?

Plain Boot binds once at startup, so no. Spring Cloud adds @RefreshScope and a /refresh endpoint that rebuilds marked beans. On Kubernetes, the usual pattern is immutable config plus a rolling restart. Log levels are an exception: /actuator/loggers changes them live.

How do you create a multi-module starter so that it does not force dependencies on users?

Put code in an auto-configure module, with integration dependencies marked optional. Guard each integration with @ConditionalOnClass. The starter module depends on the auto-configure module plus the common libraries. Test with ApplicationContextRunner, using FilteredClassLoader to simulate a missing class. Use @ConditionalOnMissingBean so that users can override.

Does the default Tomcat handle only 200 concurrent requests? What actually limits it?

Three numbers apply. max-connections (8192): accepted sockets. threads.max (200): requests actively being processed. accept-count (100): the OS backlog once connections are full. A 201st active request waits for a thread rather than failing. Beyond connections plus backlog, clients see refused or timed-out connections. In practice the database pool usually limits you first.

Why does a Boot JAR need a special loader? What is in BOOT-INF?

The JDK's URLClassLoader cannot read a JAR within a JAR. Copying classes together ("shading") causes clashes. So Boot keeps dependencies as nested JARs in BOOT-INF/lib, classes in BOOT-INF/classes, and JarLauncher in the top level, with a loader that reads nested entries. Consequently resource.getFile() fails for class-path entries.

Why are layered images better, and how do you customize layers?

Docker reuses unchanged layers, so a typical deployment pushes only a few MB of application classes rather than the whole fat JAR, and pulls are quick. You can define custom layers in the plugin configuration, for example a separate layer for company libraries. Copy order in the Dockerfile matters: least-changing first, because a change invalidates all layers above it.

Buildpacks vs Dockerfile vs Jib?

Buildpacks give a good secure image without a Dockerfile, and rebasing can patch the OS layer without rebuilding the app. A Dockerfile is the most flexible and familiar. Jib needs no daemon, so it works in restricted CI. For a platform team standardizing many services, Buildpacks or Jib reduce drift.

Users get 502 errors during every deployment. How do you fix it?

Verify graceful shutdown is on, and that Java is PID 1 with exec-form entrypoint, so SIGTERM arrives. Add a preStop sleep for endpoint propagation. Make terminationGracePeriodSeconds exceed the shutdown timeout. Add a readiness probe so new pods get traffic only when ready. Check that the load balancer's idle timeout exceeds the app's keep-alive timeout, a common cause of 502s even outside deployments.

Where should the warm-up go: @PostConstruct, CommandLineRunner, or ApplicationReadyEvent?

In a CommandLineRunner or ApplicationRunner, if traffic must wait: readiness turns true only after runners. ApplicationReadyEvent runs after readiness, so traffic is already flowing. @PostConstruct runs too early, and on a raw object. A failed runner stops startup, so catch errors if warm-up is optional.

How do you configure ProblemDetail globally, and how do you add custom fields?

Set spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true for framework exceptions. For your own, throw ErrorResponseException or a subclass, or return ProblemDetail from an @ExceptionHandler, and call setProperty("key", value) for extension members, which serialize at the top level. Extend ResponseEntityExceptionHandler to customize standard errors. Titles and details can be localized through MessageSource codes.

Why do I get a 401 or empty response instead of my error JSON with Spring Security?

The error forward to /error is a separate dispatch, and Spring Security 6 applies authorization to all dispatcher types. If /error is not permitted, an anonymous client gets 401 rather than the real 400 or 500 body. Permit /error, or map errors in @RestControllerAdvice so that no forward happens.

What does spring.threads.virtual.enabled change, and what can break?

The server's request threads, applicationTaskExecutor, and scheduling use virtual threads. What can break: exhausting the connection pool or overloading a downstream, as there is no longer a thread limit acting as a throttle; pinning on Java before 24 with synchronized around I/O; heavy thread-local caches; and apps exiting early without spring.main.keep-alive. Run a load test, and watch pool wait times.

Native image vs JVM for a service. How do you decide?

Native suits scale-to-zero, serverless, and CLI tools, where startup and memory dominate. A long-running high-throughput service generally benefits from the JIT and has simpler tooling: full heap dumps, agents, and normal profilers. Consider also that builds take minutes and use much memory, and dynamic libraries may need hints. CDS or the AOT cache gives part of the startup gain at low risk.

What does AOT processing generate?

Java source that registers bean definitions without reflection, class files for proxies, and JSON reachability hints under META-INF/native-image. It freezes the outcome of conditions and profiles at build time, so these cannot change at runtime. You can also use the output on a normal JVM.

@SpringBootTest vs @WebMvcTest: when does each make sense? Why is my suite slow?

@WebMvcTest verifies HTTP mapping, validation, and serialization with mocked services. @SpringBootTest verifies real wiring end to end. Slowness normally comes from many distinct contexts: differing @MockitoBean sets, properties, profiles, and @DirtiesContext. Share a base configuration and containers to maximize context reuse.

How do you upgrade a Boot 2.7 service to Boot 3 or 4?

Clear deprecations on 2.7. Raise Java to 17 or higher. Replace javax with jakarta, using OpenRewrite. Update libraries that are not Jakarta-ready. Convert security to SecurityFilterChain. Use the properties migrator. Handle Hibernate 6 changes and URL-matching changes. Go to the latest 3.x before 4, then address Spring 7, Jackson 3 and starter changes. Rely on integration tests and canary deployment.

What breaks when moving from Jackson 2 to Jackson 3 in Boot 4?

Packages change from com.fasterxml.jackson to tools.jackson, except that annotations stay in com.fasterxml.jackson.annotation. The main type is JsonMapper, which is immutable and built through a builder. Custom serializers and modules need updating, and certain defaults differ, so response formats may change. Contract tests catch this. Boot 4 retains a route for keeping Jackson 2 during migration.

Is it a good idea to make all beans lazy?

It speeds up startup, but moves errors to the first request, makes that request slow, and hides problems that a failed start would reveal. Spring's eager default provides fail-fast behavior. For a production service, prefer it; lazy mode can make sense in development. Use @Lazy(false) to exempt specific beans.

How do you run two HikariCP pools, one for writes, one for reports?
@Bean @Primary @ConfigurationProperties("app.db.main")
DataSourceProperties mainProps() { return new DataSourceProperties(); }

@Bean @Primary
HikariDataSource mainDs(DataSourceProperties mainProps) {
  return mainProps.initializeDataSourceBuilder().type(HikariDataSource.class).build();
}

@Bean @ConfigurationProperties("app.db.reports")
HikariDataSource reportsDs() { return new HikariDataSource(); }

Defining any DataSource disables the auto-configured one, so you now own the JPA and transaction setup for the second. Note that HikariDataSource binds jdbc-url, not url. Mark one as @Primary for the components that inject a single data source.

What happens if two auto-configurations define the same bean name?

Bean overriding is off, so the second registration raises BeanDefinitionOverrideException, unless it is guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean. Correct auto-configurations use ordering with after and the condition. Setting spring.main.allow-bean-definition-overriding=true hides the conflict.

Design: how would you standardize 50 microservices on Boot?

Publish an internal parent or BOM that aligns versions, an internal starter for logging, tracing, security and error format, plus a project template. Enforce rules with ArchUnit or build checks, and automate upgrades with Renovate and OpenRewrite. Provide a golden image or Buildpack configuration. Avoid putting business logic in shared starters; they should hold cross-cutting concerns only, and be versioned so that services can upgrade independently.

Refreshing an Angular route such as /orders/7 shows a 404 or the Whitelabel page. Why, and how do you fix it?

The Angular router uses HTML5 URLs, so on refresh the browser asks the server for /orders/7, and no controller or file matches it. Configure a fallback that serves index.html for unknown, non-API, non-file paths, using a PathResourceResolver or a forwarding controller. Then Angular's router takes over. Keep /api/** out of the fallback, so that a wrong API URL still returns a real 404 JSON response and not HTML.

Should Angular be bundled into the Boot JAR or deployed separately?

Bundled: one artifact and one origin, so no CORS. It suits internal apps and small teams. But a UI change needs a backend release, and static files are served by the JVM. Separate (CDN or Nginx): independent deployments, edge caching, and the API scales separately. You then need CORS, or a reverse proxy that puts both under one domain. That proxy setup also keeps cookie-based auth simple. For most production systems, separate deployment behind one domain is the cleanest choice.

Uploads over 1 MB fail with MaxUploadSizeExceededException. What do you do?

Raise spring.servlet.multipart.max-file-size and max-request-size to a deliberate limit, not to unlimited. Also check any proxy limit in front, such as Nginx client_max_body_size. Handle the exception in @RestControllerAdvice and return a 413 Payload Too Large ProblemDetail. Add a matching size check in Angular, so the user gets feedback before uploading. For very large files, use presigned object-storage URLs instead of streaming through the app.

What is a profile group? Can application-prod.yml activate another profile?

A group (spring.profiles.group.prod=proddb,prodmq) expands one active profile into several. A profile-specific file cannot set spring.profiles.active or include. Boot rejects this at startup, because a profile that activates other profiles made the old loading order unpredictable. Define the activation in a group in application.yml, or set it from outside with an environment variable or argument.

The API silently ignores a misspelled JSON field such as "emial". Why, and should it?

Boot's ObjectMapper turns off FAIL_ON_UNKNOWN_PROPERTIES, so unknown fields are dropped. This is the "tolerant reader" approach, which helps API evolution because older servers accept newer clients. The cost is that typos go unnoticed. Combine it with Bean Validation (@NotBlank email), so that a missing required field still fails. If you need strict input, set spring.jackson.deserialization.fail-on-unknown-properties=true. Then a typo returns 400, but every client must stop sending fields the server does not know.

I declared my own ObjectMapper bean and now dates and modules behave differently. Why?

Boot's JacksonAutoConfiguration backs off when you define an ObjectMapper bean, so its builder defaults no longer apply: the Java time module, ISO dates, the relaxed unknown-property setting, and the spring.jackson.* properties. Use a Jackson2ObjectMapperBuilderCustomizer (or JsonMapperBuilderCustomizer in Boot 4) or properties to tweak the mapper instead of replacing it. If you really need a second mapper, build it from the injected builder.

Spring Boot Actuator Production-ready

Built-in endpoints that let you monitor and manage a running Spring Boot app: health checks, metrics, info, log levels, environment and thread dumps. It's how ops tooling, Kubernetes and Prometheus see inside your service.

Setup & configuration

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-actuator</artifactId>
</dependency>
<!-- for /actuator/prometheus -->
<dependency>
  <groupId>io.micrometer</groupId>
  <artifactId>micrometer-registry-prometheus</artifactId>
</dependency>
# application.yml
management:
  server:
    port: 9090                       # optional: separate port, never exposed publicly
  endpoints:
    web:
      base-path: /actuator           # default
      exposure:
        include: health,info,metrics,prometheus,loggers
        exclude: env,beans
  endpoint:
    health:
      show-details: when-authorized  # never | always | when-authorized
      show-components: always
      probes:
        enabled: true                # /health/liveness and /health/readiness
      group:
        readiness:
          include: readinessState,db,redis
    shutdown:
      enabled: false                 # POST /actuator/shutdown - keep disabled
    env:
      show-values: when-authorized   # Boot 3: values masked by default
  info:
    env.enabled: true
    git.mode: simple
    java.enabled: true
    os.enabled: true
  metrics:
    tags:
      application: ${spring.application.name}   # common tag on every metric
    distribution:
      percentiles-histogram:
        http.server.requests: true
      percentiles:
        http.server.requests: 0.5,0.95,0.99
info:
  app:
    name: order-service
    version: '@project.version@'

Main endpoints

EndpointWhat it gives youExposed over web by default?
/healthUP, DOWN, OUT_OF_SERVICE or UNKNOWN, aggregated from all HealthIndicators✔ Yes (the only one)
/health/liveness, /readinessKubernetes probe groupsWith health, when probes are enabled (enabled automatically on K8s)
/infoApp name, version, git commit, build time, Java and OS info✘ (since Boot 2.5)
/metrics, /metrics/{name}Micrometer metric names and values, which you can drill into by tag✘
/prometheusEvery metric in Prometheus text format✘
/loggersRead and change log levels at runtime✘
/env, /configpropsResolved properties and their sources (values are masked)✘ (sensitive)
/beans, /conditionsEvery bean; the auto-configuration report (why a bean was or wasn't created)✘
/mappingsEvery @RequestMapping route✘
/threaddump, /heapdumpDiagnose deadlocks and memory leaks (heapdump downloads an .hprof file)✘ (very sensitive)
/httpexchangesThe last N HTTP requests (needs an HttpExchangeRepository bean). It was called httptrace before Boot 3✘
/scheduledtasks, /caches, /flyway, /liquibase, /sbomScheduled jobs, caches, DB migrations, software bill of materials✘
/shutdownGraceful shutdown (POST)✘ Disabled

Health checks in depth

// Custom health indicator: bean name "paymentApiHealthIndicator" → component "paymentApi"
@Component
public class PaymentApiHealthIndicator implements HealthIndicator {
  private final RestClient client;
  public PaymentApiHealthIndicator(RestClient.Builder b) { this.client = b.baseUrl("https://pay.example.com").build(); }

  @Override
  public Health health() {
    try {
      long t = System.currentTimeMillis();
      client.get().uri("/ping").retrieve().toBodilessEntity();
      return Health.up().withDetail("latencyMs", System.currentTimeMillis() - t).build();
    } catch (Exception e) {
      return Health.down(e).withDetail("url", "https://pay.example.com").build();
    }
  }
}

// GET /actuator/health  (show-details: always)
{
  "status": "UP",
  "components": {
    "db":         { "status": "UP", "details": { "database": "MySQL", "validationQuery": "isValid()" } },
    "diskSpace":  { "status": "UP", "details": { "total": 499963174912, "free": 91943821312, "threshold": 10485760 } },
    "paymentApi": { "status": "UP", "details": { "latencyMs": 42 } },
    "ping":       { "status": "UP" }
  }
}

Liveness vs Readiness (Kubernetes)

Liveness: "Is the app alive, or stuck?" If it fails, Kubernetes restarts the pod. Keep it simple and don't include external dependencies like the DB. If you do and the database goes down, every pod restarts in a loop.
Readiness: "Can the app serve traffic right now?" If it fails, the pod is removed from the Service load balancer but not restarted. It's fine to include critical dependencies here. Readiness is also OUT_OF_SERVICE while the app is starting up and during graceful shutdown.
# deployment.yaml
livenessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
  initialDelaySeconds: 30
  periodSeconds: 10
  failureThreshold: 3
readinessProbe:
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 9090 }
  periodSeconds: 5
startupProbe:                         # slow-starting apps: protects liveness during boot
  httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 9090 }
  failureThreshold: 30
  periodSeconds: 5

// Change availability from code (e.g. while warming a cache)
@Component
class Warmup {
  Warmup(ApplicationEventPublisher pub) {
    AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(pub, this, ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC);
    // ... warm up ...
    AvailabilityChangeEvent.publish(pub, this, ReadinessState.ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC);
  }
}

Metrics with Micrometer

Micrometer is a facade for metrics, the way SLF4J is a facade for logging. You instrument once and it exports to Prometheus, Datadog, New Relic, CloudWatch or others. Metrics are dimensional: a name plus tags (key/value pairs), e.g. http.server.requests{uri="/api/orders", method="POST", status="201"}.

MeterUse forExample
CounterA value that only goes uporders placed, payment failures
GaugeA current value that goes up and downqueue size, active sessions, cache size
TimerDuration and count of events (plus percentiles)method latency, external call time
DistributionSummaryDistribution of non-time valuespayload size, order amount
LongTaskTimerLong tasks that are still runningbatch jobs
@Service
public class OrderService {
  private final Counter placed;
  private final Timer paymentTimer;
  private final Queue<Order> pending = new ConcurrentLinkedQueue<>();

  public OrderService(MeterRegistry registry) {
    this.placed = Counter.builder("orders.placed").description("Orders placed")
                         .tag("channel", "web").register(registry);
    this.paymentTimer = Timer.builder("payment.call").publishPercentiles(0.95, 0.99).register(registry);
    Gauge.builder("orders.pending", pending, Queue::size).register(registry);
  }

  public Order place(OrderDto dto) {
    Order o = paymentTimer.record(() -> paymentClient.charge(dto));   // times the call
    placed.increment();
    return o;
  }
}

// Annotation style (needs TimedAspect bean / Observation support)
@Timed(value = "report.generate", percentiles = {0.95})
public Report generate() { ... }

// Boot 3 Observation API: one instrumentation → metrics + traces
Observation.createNotStarted("inventory.check", observationRegistry)
           .lowCardinalityKeyValue("warehouse", "chennai")
           .observe(() -> inventory.check(sku));
