GET /actuator/metrics                                  → list of names
GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests             → COUNT, TOTAL_TIME, MAX + available tags
GET /actuator/metrics/http.server.requests?tag=uri:/api/orders&tag=status:500
GET /actuator/metrics/jvm.memory.used?tag=area:heap
GET /actuator/metrics/hikaricp.connections.active

# Prometheus scrape (prometheus.yml)
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: order-service
    metrics_path: /actuator/prometheus
    static_configs: [{ targets: ['order-service:9090'] }]

# PromQL examples (Grafana)
rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m])                 # 5xx per second
histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))  # p95 latency
💡 Built-in metrics you get for free: http.server.requests, jvm.memory.*, jvm.gc.pause, jvm.threads.*, process.cpu.usage, system.cpu.usage, hikaricp.connections.*, tomcat.sessions.*, logback.events, spring.data.repository.invocations, cache hit/miss, Kafka consumer metrics. ⚠ Avoid high-cardinality tags such as userId or orderId: every distinct value creates a new time series and can exhaust memory.

Info, Loggers & custom endpoints

<!-- pom.xml: adds build info + git info to /actuator/info -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId><artifactId>spring-boot-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions><execution><goals><goal>build-info</goal></goals></execution></executions>
</plugin>
<plugin><groupId>io.github.git-commit-id</groupId><artifactId>git-commit-id-maven-plugin</artifactId></plugin>

// Custom info
@Component
class FeatureInfo implements InfoContributor {
  public void contribute(Info.Builder b) { b.withDetail("features", Map.of("newCheckout", true)); }
}

# Change log level at runtime - no restart!
curl http://localhost:9090/actuator/loggers/com.shop.order
curl -X POST http://localhost:9090/actuator/loggers/com.shop.order \
     -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}'

// Custom endpoint → /actuator/features
@Component
@Endpoint(id = "features")
public class FeaturesEndpoint {
  private final Map<String, Boolean> flags = new ConcurrentHashMap<>(Map.of("newCheckout", false));

  @ReadOperation   public Map<String, Boolean> all() { return flags; }                    // GET
  @ReadOperation   public Boolean one(@Selector String name) { return flags.get(name); }     // GET /features/{name}
  @WriteOperation  public void set(@Selector String name, boolean enabled) { flags.put(name, enabled); }  // POST
  @DeleteOperation public void remove(@Selector String name) { flags.remove(name); }        // DELETE
}
// @WebEndpoint = HTTP only, @JmxEndpoint = JMX only, @RestControllerEndpoint deprecated since Boot 3.3

Securing Actuator

@Bean
@Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain actuatorChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
  return http
    .securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
    .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
        .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to(HealthEndpoint.class, InfoEndpoint.class)).permitAll()
        .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("prometheus")).hasRole("MONITORING")
        .anyRequest().hasRole("ADMIN"))
    .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
    .build();
}
⚠ Security rules: never expose env, heapdump, threaddump, configprops or shutdown publicly. A heap dump contains passwords and tokens that are sitting in memory. Run management endpoints on a separate internal port, expose only what you need, and protect the rest with a role.

Endpoint Access Control (Boot 3.4+)

Boot 3.4 replaced the on/off enabled switch with an access level, which also allows an endpoint to be read-only. Enabled or disabled still differs from exposed: an endpoint needs access and exposure to be reachable.

management:
  endpoints:
    access:
      default: read-only             # none | read-only | unrestricted
      max-permitted: read-only       # a hard ceiling, for example set by a platform team
  endpoint:
    loggers:
      access: unrestricted           # allows POST
    heapdump:
      access: none

Before 3.4, use management.endpoint.<id>.enabled and management.endpoints.enabled-by-default, which are deprecated since then.

Probes When the Management Port Is Separate

A separate management.server.port is good for security, but it uses its own web stack. If the main connector is exhausted or broken, a probe on the management port can still report success, so Kubernetes keeps sending traffic to a dead pod. The fix is to serve the two probe groups on the main port too:

management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths: true
# liveness  is now also at  http://host:8080/livez
# readiness is now also at  http://host:8080/readyz

# Any health group can get an additional path
management.endpoint.health.group.custom.additional-path: "server:/healthz"

Point the Kubernetes probes at /livez and /readyz on the application port. These paths respond without opening the other actuator endpoints to the public. This also applies to the probe manifests earlier in this section, which target port 9090.

Readiness from runners, and failure behaviour

Boot sets readiness to ACCEPTING_TRAFFIC only after runners complete, so an ApplicationRunner is the simplest place to warm a cache; no event publishing is needed. If a runner throws, startup fails. To take a pod out of rotation temporarily, publish ReadinessState.REFUSING_TRAFFIC, then back. Avoid expensive checks in health indicators: a probe that calls a slow database each few seconds multiplies load across replicas. Cache the result, and watch slow-indicator warnings:

management.endpoint.health.logging.slow-indicator-threshold: 10s   # the default
management.endpoint.health.cache.time-to-live: 5s                  # cache read-only responses

Tracing and Observability

The three signals answer different questions. Metrics: is something wrong? Traces: where is it slow, across services? Logs: what exactly happened? Since Boot 3, the Micrometer Observation API is one instrumentation point that produces metrics and spans, and Micrometer Tracing bridges to OpenTelemetry or Brave. It replaces Spring Cloud Sleuth.

<dependency><groupId>io.micrometer</groupId><artifactId>micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel</artifactId></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.opentelemetry</groupId><artifactId>opentelemetry-exporter-otlp</artifactId></dependency>
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1               # the default: 10%, so most requests have no exported trace

With a tracer present, logs get traceId and spanId through the MDC, and the W3C traceparent header propagates across RestClient, WebClient and messaging, if those clients are built from the auto-configured builders. A client built with RestClient.create() does not take part. Boot 4 adds spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry, and groups the exporter configuration there.

Exemplars link a metric to a trace id, so a Grafana latency spike can jump straight to one slow trace.

Metric Details Worth Knowing

// Customize or limit metrics globally
@Bean MeterFilter denyNoisy() {
  return MeterFilter.denyNameStartsWith("tomcat.sessions");
}
@Bean MeterFilter maxUris() {
  return MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags("http.server.requests", "uri", 100, MeterFilter.deny());
}

// Bind metrics for a component, without touching business code
@Component
class QueueMetrics implements MeterBinder {
  private final OrderQueue queue;
  QueueMetrics(OrderQueue q) { this.queue = q; }
  @Override public void bindTo(MeterRegistry r) {
    Gauge.builder("orders.queue.size", queue, OrderQueue::size).register(r);
  }
}
management:
  observations:
    annotations:
      enabled: true                 # Boot 3.2+: @Timed, @Counted, @Observed via aspects
  metrics:
    distribution:
      slo:
        http.server.requests: 100ms,300ms,1s      # buckets at your target latencies
Gotcha:
  • Gauge holds a weak reference to the measured object. If nothing else references it, the object is collected, and the value becomes NaN. Queue fields on a bean are fine; a local variable is not.
  • publishPercentiles computes client-side percentiles per instance, and they cannot be averaged across instances. Use histograms and histogram_quantile for fleet-wide values.
  • The uri tag uses the mapping template (/orders/{id}), which keeps cardinality low. Building the URL by string in RestClient instead of using a URI template creates a new tag value per id.

Other Endpoints

EndpointPurpose
/startupStartup steps and their durations. Needs BufferingApplicationStartup. GET reads them; POST also drains the buffer
/logfileLog file contents, with HTTP Range, when a log file is configured
/auditeventsSecurity audit events; needs an AuditEventRepository bean
/sessionsLists and deletes Spring Session sessions
/quartzQuartz jobs and triggers
/integrationgraphSpring Integration flow graph

From Metrics to Alerts: Useful PromQL

Dashboards are for investigating; alerts should fire on symptoms that users feel. Alert on rate, errors and duration of http.server.requests, and on saturation signals such as pool waits and heap. Avoid alerting on raw CPU or on single-instance spikes. The queries below assume the Prometheus registry. Percentile queries also need management.metrics.distribution.percentiles-histogram.http.server.requests=true, so that histogram buckets are published.

# Error ratio over 5 minutes (5xx responses / all responses)
sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count{status=~"5.."}[5m]))
  / sum(rate(http_server_requests_seconds_count[5m]))

# p95 latency across all instances (aggregate buckets, then compute the quantile)
histogram_quantile(0.95,
  sum by (le, uri) (rate(http_server_requests_seconds_bucket[5m])))

# Threads waiting for a DB connection: an early sign of pool exhaustion
max(hikaricp_connections_pending) > 0

# Heap usage ratio
sum(jvm_memory_used_bytes{area="heap"}) / sum(jvm_memory_max_bytes{area="heap"})
  • Use a for: 5m clause in the alert rule, so that a short spike does not page anyone.
  • Tie alerts to an SLO ("99.5% of requests succeed in under 300 ms") and alert on the error budget burn rate, not on every threshold breach.
  • Exclude /actuator/** from latency SLOs, or the probe traffic dilutes the numbers.

Build and Git Info

/actuator/info is most useful when it shows which build is running. Generate META-INF/build-info.properties (the build-info goal of spring-boot-maven-plugin, or springBoot { buildInfo() } in Gradle) and git.properties (the git-commit-id plugin). Boot then exposes them, and also offers BuildProperties and GitProperties beans for your own code. Add custom data with an InfoContributor.

@Component
class FeatureFlagsInfo implements InfoContributor {
  private final FeatureFlags flags;
  FeatureFlagsInfo(FeatureFlags flags) { this.flags = flags; }
  @Override public void contribute(Info.Builder b) {
    b.withDetail("features", flags.enabledNames());       // appears under "features" in /actuator/info
  }
}
// management.info.env.enabled=true is needed for info.* properties (off by default since Boot 2.6)

Interview Questions — Actuator

What is Spring Boot Actuator and why use it?

A sub-project that adds production-ready features through HTTP or JMX endpoints: health checks, metrics, app info, log level management, environment and bean inspection, and thread and heap dumps. You get observability without writing any code, Kubernetes probes, Prometheus metrics for Grafana dashboards and alerts, and faster troubleshooting in production, such as switching a package to DEBUG without a restart.

Which endpoints are enabled and exposed by default? How do you expose more?

Almost every endpoint is enabled (shutdown isn't), but over HTTP only /health is exposed. Enabled and exposed are separate settings. To expose more: management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus, or * for everything (not in production). JMX exposure is separate (management.endpoints.jmx.exposure.include).

How does /health decide UP or DOWN? How to add a custom check?

Every HealthIndicator bean contributes a component status. The StatusAggregator combines them in severity order (DOWN > OUT_OF_SERVICE > UP > UNKNOWN), so the worst one wins. The HTTP status follows: DOWN and OUT_OF_SERVICE return 503, UP returns 200. For a custom check, implement HealthIndicator (or the reactive ReactiveHealthIndicator) and return Health.up()/down().withDetail(...). Disable one with management.health.redis.enabled=false. Use health groups to build custom aggregates like readiness.

Liveness vs readiness probes — what goes where?

Liveness answers whether the app is broken and needs a restart. Keep external dependencies out of it, or a database outage will cause a cascade of restarts. Readiness answers whether the pod can take traffic; if not, it's removed from the load balancer. It can include the DB and cache. Boot tracks LivenessState and ReadinessState automatically: readiness turns on after startup and off during graceful shutdown (server.shutdown=graceful). Add a startupProbe for apps that boot slowly.

What is Micrometer? Counter vs Gauge vs Timer?

Micrometer is a vendor-neutral metrics facade ("SLF4J for metrics") with dimensional, tagged metrics. You record through a MeterRegistry, and a registry implementation exports the data (Prometheus, Datadog, and so on). Counter: only increases (requests, errors). Gauge: a sampled current value (queue size). Timer: count, total time, max and optional percentiles or histograms (latency). DistributionSummary: a distribution of sizes or amounts.

How do you integrate Actuator with Prometheus and Grafana?

Add micrometer-registry-prometheus and expose the prometheus endpoint. Prometheus pulls (scrapes) /actuator/prometheus on an interval, and Grafana queries Prometheus with PromQL for dashboards (RPS, error rate, p95 latency, JVM heap, Hikari pool usage) and alerts. Enable percentiles-histogram for accurate latency quantiles across all instances. Add a common application tag so you can filter by service.

How do you change log levels at runtime?

Send POST /actuator/loggers/{logger.name} with {"configuredLevel":"DEBUG"}. Use null to reset it. It takes effect immediately with no restart. Secure this endpoint.

How do you create a custom actuator endpoint?

Annotate a bean with @Endpoint(id="x") and its methods with @ReadOperation (GET), @WriteOperation (POST) and @DeleteOperation (DELETE). Use @Selector for path segments. It's technology-agnostic, so the same endpoint works over HTTP and JMX. Then expose it with exposure.include.

How do you secure actuator endpoints?

Use a dedicated SecurityFilterChain with EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint(): permit health and info, and require a role for the rest. Run them on a separate management.server.port that isn't reachable from the internet. Keep the exposure list minimal and leave show-details: when-authorized. Boot 3 masks /env values by default (show-values). Never expose heapdump publicly.

What changed in Actuator with Spring Boot 3?

httptrace became httpexchanges. Env and configprops values are masked by default. Micrometer Observation API and Micrometer Tracing replace Spring Cloud Sleuth. @RestControllerEndpoint was deprecated in 3.3. Native-image support was added, along with an /sbom endpoint (3.3).

What is Spring Boot Admin?

A community project (codecentric) that provides a web UI on top of Actuator for many services. It shows health, metrics, logs, log levels, JVM details and notifications. Clients register directly or through service discovery.

How would you debug a production issue using Actuator?

Check /health to see which dependency is DOWN. Check /metrics for spikes in http.server.requests with status=5xx, saturation in hikaricp.connections.pending, and jvm.gc.pause. Switch the package logger to DEBUG through /loggers. Take a /threaddump to find blocked or deadlocked threads. Use /heapdump with Eclipse MAT for memory leaks. Use /info to confirm which build is deployed. Then correlate with traces and logs (traceId).

Enabled vs exposed vs access: what is the difference?

Access (or enabled before 3.4) decides whether the endpoint exists and what it permits. Exposure decides which technology publishes it, web or JMX. Both are needed. An endpoint with read-only access rejects write operations even if exposed.

Probes run on the management port, the app stopped accepting requests, but the pod still gets traffic. Why?

The management server has its own connector and thread pool, so it stays healthy while the main one is stuck. Enable management.endpoint.health.probes.add-additional-paths=true, and point probes at /livez and /readyz on the main port.

A gauge reports NaN after a while. Why?

Micrometer keeps a weak reference to the state object, so it does not stop garbage collection. If the object was local, it is collected, and the gauge returns NaN. Hold it in a long-lived field, or use the strong reference option Gauge.Builder.strongReference(true).

Why can you not average p95 across instances?

A percentile is not additive: two pods with p95 of 100 ms and 900 ms do not mean 500 ms overall, as it depends on request counts and distributions. Export histogram buckets, sum the buckets across pods, and compute the quantile from those in Prometheus.

How do traces connect across microservices?

The first service creates a trace id. Each HTTP or messaging client adds a traceparent header, and the next service continues that trace in a child span. Spans are exported to a backend such as Tempo, Jaeger or Zipkin. In Spring, this works when you use the auto-configured builders, and Micrometer Tracing is on the class path. @Async work needs context propagation.

Traces are missing for most requests. Is something broken?

Often no: the default sampling probability is 0.1, so 90% are not exported. Raise it in lower environments, or use tail-based sampling in an OpenTelemetry Collector, to keep all errors and slow traces while keeping cost under control.

Can a health check bring down production?

Yes. An expensive indicator hit by many probes adds load. A dependency included in liveness causes restart storms during an outage. A shared dependency in readiness can remove every pod at once, which turns a partial failure into a total one. Keep liveness internal, and include in readiness only what the instance cannot work without.

Which alerts would you set up for a Spring Boot REST service?

Use the RED signals from http.server.requests: the error rate (5xx ratio), latency (p95 or p99 from histogram buckets), and a traffic drop to near zero. Add saturation signals: hikaricp.connections.pending, heap usage after GC, thread pool queue size, and Kafka consumer lag where it applies. Finally, alert when the readiness probe fails or a pod restarts. Each alert should have a for duration and a runbook. Page only on user-facing symptoms, and send the rest to a ticket queue.

How do you see which version and commit is running in production?

Generate build-info.properties with the Boot build plugin and git.properties with the git-commit-id plugin. Expose the info endpoint. /actuator/info then shows the artifact version, build time, branch and commit id. Inject BuildProperties to log the version at startup, or to add it as a common metric tag. This makes it easy to compare metrics before and after a deployment.

Prometheus scraping vs pushing metrics with OTLP: what is the difference?

With pull (/actuator/prometheus), Prometheus discovers the targets and scrapes them. It is simple and shows target health ("up"), but it needs network access to every pod. With push (the OTLP registry), the app sends metrics to an OpenTelemetry Collector or a vendor backend. This works across network boundaries and for short-lived jobs, and it uses one protocol for metrics, traces and logs. Boot supports both through Micrometer registries. Choose according to your platform, and do not expose the scrape endpoint publicly.

Is Actuator available over JMX?

Yes, but JMX is off by default (spring.jmx.enabled=false since Boot 2.2). If you enable it, the endpoints exposed over JMX are set separately with management.endpoints.jmx.exposure.include. JMX helps with tools like JConsole or VisualVM, and in legacy environments. In containers, HTTP endpoints and Prometheus are the norm. If JMX is used remotely, it must be secured with authentication and TLS, because an open JMX port can allow remote code execution.

How do you monitor a @Scheduled or batch job?

Recent Spring versions record an observation for @Scheduled methods (tasks.scheduled.execution) when an ObservationRegistry is present. That gives duration and outcome. Add a LongTaskTimer to see jobs that are running now and how long they have run, and a gauge such as last_success_timestamp. Alert when time() - last_success_timestamp is too large, because a job that never runs produces no error metric at all.

Swagger / OpenAPI API Docs

Machine-readable API contracts, interactive documentation, and generated client and server code. In Spring Boot 3 this means springdoc-openapi.

TermMeaning
OpenAPI Specification (OAS)The standard (YAML or JSON) for describing REST APIs: paths, operations, parameters, schemas, security. Versions 3.0 and 3.1. It was originally called the "Swagger Specification" (2.0).
SwaggerThe tooling brand from SmartBear: Swagger UI (interactive docs), Swagger Editor, Swagger Codegen.
springdoc-openapiThe library that generates an OpenAPI 3 spec from Spring MVC or WebFlux code and bundles Swagger UI. Use 2.x for Boot 3.
SpringfoxThe old library (Swagger 2, @EnableSwagger2, @Api, @ApiOperation). Abandoned and doesn't work with Boot 3. Migrate to springdoc.

Setup

<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
  <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui</artifactId>   <!-- webflux-ui for WebFlux -->
  <version>2.8.x</version>
</dependency>
<!-- That's it: open http://localhost:8080/swagger-ui.html -->
springdoc:
  api-docs:
    path: /v3/api-docs
    enabled: true                 # set false in prod if docs must not be public
  swagger-ui:
    path: /swagger-ui.html
    operations-sorter: method
    tags-sorter: alpha
    try-it-out-enabled: true
    persist-authorization: true   # keep the JWT after a page refresh
  packages-to-scan: com.shop.order.api
  paths-to-match: /api/**
  default-produces-media-type: application/json

Global configuration: info, servers, JWT security

@Configuration
@SecurityScheme(name = "bearerAuth", type = SecuritySchemeType.HTTP, scheme = "bearer", bearerFormat = "JWT")
public class OpenApiConfig {

  @Bean
  OpenAPI shopOpenAPI() {
    return new OpenAPI()
      .info(new Info().title("Order Service API").version("v1")
            .description("Create, track and cancel orders")
            .contact(new Contact().name("Platform Team").email("platform@example.com"))
            .license(new License().name("Apache 2.0")))
      .servers(List.of(new Server().url("https://api.example.com").description("Prod"),
                       new Server().url("http://localhost:8080").description("Local")))
      .addSecurityItem(new SecurityRequirement().addList("bearerAuth"));   // lock icon on all ops
  }

  @Bean
  GroupedOpenApi publicApi() {           // dropdown "groups" in Swagger UI
    return GroupedOpenApi.builder().group("public").pathsToMatch("/api/v1/**").build();
  }
  @Bean
  GroupedOpenApi adminApi() {
    return GroupedOpenApi.builder().group("admin").pathsToMatch("/admin/**").build();
  }
}

Documenting controllers & models

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/v1/orders")
@Tag(name = "Orders", description = "Order lifecycle operations")
public class OrderController {

  @Operation(summary = "Get order by id", description = "Returns a single order with its items")
  @ApiResponses({
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", description = "Found",
        content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = OrderDto.class))),
    @ApiResponse(responseCode = "404", description = "Order not found",
        content = @Content(schema = @Schema(implementation = ProblemDetail.class)))
  })
  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  public OrderDto get(@Parameter(description = "Order id", example = "1001") @PathVariable Long id) { ... }

  @Operation(summary = "Search orders")
  @GetMapping
  public Page<OrderDto> search(
      @Parameter(description = "Filter by status") @RequestParam(required = false) OrderStatus status,
      @ParameterObject Pageable pageable) { ... }          // expands page, size, sort params

  @Operation(summary = "Place an order")
  @ApiResponse(responseCode = "201", description = "Created")
  @PostMapping
  public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest req) { ... }

  @Hidden                                      // exclude from docs
  @PostMapping("/internal/reindex")
  public void reindex() { ... }
}

@Schema(description = "Request to place an order")
public record CreateOrderRequest(
    @Schema(description = "Customer id", example = "42", requiredMode = Schema.RequiredMode.REQUIRED)
    @NotNull Long customerId,

    @ArraySchema(schema = @Schema(implementation = OrderItemRequest.class), minItems = 1)
    @NotEmpty List<@Valid OrderItemRequest> items,

    @Schema(description = "Optional coupon", example = "DIWALI10", maxLength = 20)
    @Size(max = 20) String coupon) {}

springdoc reads Bean Validation annotations automatically: @NotNull becomes required, @Size becomes minLength/maxLength, @Min/@Max become minimum/maximum, and @Pattern becomes pattern. Enums become an enum list, and Jackson's @JsonProperty names are respected.

What the generated spec looks like

openapi: 3.0.1
info: { title: Order Service API, version: v1 }
servers: [ { url: https://api.example.com, description: Prod } ]
security: [ { bearerAuth: [] } ]
paths:
  /api/v1/orders/{id}:
    get:
      tags: [Orders]
      summary: Get order by id
      operationId: get
      parameters:
        - { name: id, in: path, required: true, description: Order id, schema: { type: integer, format: int64 }, example: 1001 }
      responses:
        '200': { description: Found, content: { application/json: { schema: { $ref: '#/components/schemas/OrderDto' } } } }
        '404': { description: Order not found }
components:
  securitySchemes:
    bearerAuth: { type: http, scheme: bearer, bearerFormat: JWT }
  schemas:
    CreateOrderRequest:
      type: object
      required: [customerId, items]
      properties:
        customerId: { type: integer, format: int64, example: 42 }
        coupon:     { type: string, maxLength: 20, example: DIWALI10 }

Annotation cheat sheet (springdoc / swagger-annotations v3)

AnnotationWherePurposeSpringfox equivalent
@TagClassGroups operations in the UI@Api
@OperationMethodsummary, description, operationId, deprecated@ApiOperation
@ApiResponse(s)MethodStatus codes and their response schemas@ApiResponse
@ParameterParamDescription, example, required@ApiParam
@ParameterObjectParamExpands an object (e.g. Pageable) into query params-
@SchemaDTO / fieldDescription, example, format, requiredMode, allowableValues@ApiModel / @ApiModelProperty
@ArraySchemaFieldDescribes array items and their min/max-
@HiddenClass / method / paramExcludes it from the spec@ApiIgnore
@SecurityScheme / @SecurityRequirementConfig / methodDefines auth (bearer, OAuth2, API key) and applies itsecuritySchemes()

Spring Security + Swagger UI

.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
    .requestMatchers("/v3/api-docs/**", "/swagger-ui/**", "/swagger-ui.html").permitAll()  // or hasRole("DEV")
    .anyRequest().authenticated())
// In Swagger UI: click "Authorize" → paste the JWT (without the "Bearer " prefix) → every "Try it out" call sends it.

Contract-first with openapi-generator

<plugin>
  <groupId>org.openapitools</groupId>
  <artifactId>openapi-generator-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions><execution>
    <goals><goal>generate</goal></goals>
    <configuration>
      <inputSpec>${project.basedir}/src/main/resources/api/order-api.yaml</inputSpec>
      <generatorName>spring</generatorName>
      <apiPackage>com.shop.order.api</apiPackage>
      <modelPackage>com.shop.order.api.model</modelPackage>
      <configOptions>
        <interfaceOnly>true</interfaceOnly>          <!-- generate OrdersApi interface -->
        <useSpringBoot3>true</useSpringBoot3>
        <useTags>true</useTags>
      </configOptions>
    </configuration>
  </execution></executions>
</plugin>

// You implement the generated interface - the compiler enforces the contract
@RestController
class OrdersController implements OrdersApi {
  @Override public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> getOrder(Long id) { ... }
}

# Generate an Angular client for the front-end team
npx @openapitools/openapi-generator-cli generate -i http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs \
    -g typescript-angular -o src/app/api

Versions: springdoc and OpenAPI

Spring Bootspringdoc
2.x1.x (springdoc-openapi-ui), now end of life
3.x2.x (springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui)
4.x3.x, same artifact names

OpenAPI 3.1 aligns fully with JSON Schema 2020-12. The visible differences from 3.0: nullable: true is replaced by type: [string, "null"], example gives way to examples, and top-level webhooks can be described. Some generators and gateways lag behind 3.1, so check your tools, and set the version explicitly if necessary:

springdoc.api-docs.version: openapi_3_1     # or openapi_3_0

Polymorphism and Generics

Inheritance in a request or response must be explicit, or clients only see the base type.

@Schema(oneOf = {CardPayment.class, UpiPayment.class},
        discriminatorProperty = "type",
        discriminatorMapping = {
          @DiscriminatorMapping(value = "card", schema = CardPayment.class),
          @DiscriminatorMapping(value = "upi",  schema = UpiPayment.class) })
@JsonTypeInfo(use = JsonTypeInfo.Id.NAME, property = "type")
@JsonSubTypes({ @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = CardPayment.class, name = "card"),
                @JsonSubTypes.Type(value = UpiPayment.class,  name = "upi") })
public sealed interface Payment permits CardPayment, UpiPayment { }

Generic wrappers such as ApiResponse<OrderDto> are resolved from the method's return type, so ResponseEntity<ApiResponse<OrderDto>> works and yields a schema named ApiResponseOrderDto. A raw ResponseEntity<?> or Object gives an empty schema; fix it with @ApiResponse and @Schema(implementation = ...).

File Upload and Read-Only Fields

@Operation(summary = "Upload an invoice")
@PostMapping(path = "/invoices", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
public void upload(@RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file,
                   @RequestPart("meta") InvoiceMeta meta) { ... }

public record OrderDto(
    @Schema(accessMode = Schema.AccessMode.READ_ONLY) UUID id,       // not asked for in requests
    @Schema(accessMode = Schema.AccessMode.WRITE_ONLY) String pin,   // never shown in responses
    @Schema(deprecated = true) String legacyCode,
    @Schema(type = "string", format = "decimal", example = "19.99") BigDecimal total) { }

Using one DTO for reading and writing forces this kind of annotation. Separate request and response records usually document the API more honestly.

Customizers

// Modify the whole document: a common error response on every operation
@Bean OpenApiCustomizer problemResponses() {
  return api -> api.getPaths().values().forEach(path ->
      path.readOperations().forEach(op ->
          op.getResponses().addApiResponse("500", new ApiResponse().description("Unexpected error"))));
}

// Per operation: expose a custom annotation in the docs
@Bean OperationCustomizer rateLimitDocs() {
  return (operation, handler) -> {
    RateLimited r = handler.getMethodAnnotation(RateLimited.class);
    if (r != null) operation.addExtension("x-rate-limit", r.perSecond());
    return operation;
  };
}

Stable Specs for Generators

Client code quality depends on the spec. The usual problems:

  • operationId: derived from the method name. Two controllers with get() produce get and get_1, so generated method names change when code moves. Set @Operation(operationId = "getOrder").
  • Ordering: springdoc.writer-with-order-by-keys=true sorts output, so diffs in Git stay meaningful.
  • Schema names: two classes with one simple name collide. springdoc.use-fqn=true uses full names, or rename with @Schema(name = ...).
  • Page: serializing Spring's PageImpl exposes an unstable structure. Return your own page record, or PagedModel.
  • Lint: Spectral checks style rules on the document in CI.
<!-- Produce the spec at build time, so that CI can diff it -->
<plugin>
  <groupId>org.springdoc</groupId>
  <artifactId>springdoc-openapi-maven-plugin</artifactId>
  <executions><execution><phase>integration-test</phase><goals><goal>generate</goal></goals></execution></executions>
  <configuration>
    <apiDocsUrl>http://localhost:8080/v3/api-docs.yaml</apiDocsUrl>
    <outputFileName>openapi.yaml</outputFileName>
  </configuration>
</plugin>
<!-- This plugin needs the app running: start it with spring-boot-maven-plugin's start and stop goals -->

Behind a Gateway

Behind a proxy, generated servers URLs and "Try it out" can point to the internal host. Set server.forward-headers-strategy=framework, so that X-Forwarded-* headers are honoured, or define servers explicitly. With a path prefix, also set springdoc.swagger-ui.config-url, or the UI cannot find its spec. In microservices, one portal commonly aggregates documents: Swagger UI can list several with springdoc.swagger-ui.urls, each pointing to a service's /v3/api-docs through the gateway.

Gotcha: The permit list shown earlier covers /v3/api-docs/**, but /v3/api-docs.yaml is a different path, and is not matched by it. Add it to the list if you serve YAML.

Alternatives and Related Tools

ToolUse
Spring REST DocsDocumentation produced from passing tests, so it cannot drift; the tests take more work
Redoc, ScalarAlternative viewers for the same OpenAPI document
PrismMock server from a spec, and validating proxy
SchemathesisProperty-based API tests generated from a spec
openapi-diff, oasdiffDetect breaking changes between versions in CI

How Java Types Map to OpenAPI Schemas

Generated clients, such as the TypeScript client for Angular, depend on these mappings. Check them when a field arrives in the wrong type.

JavaOpenAPI type / formatNote
int, Integer / longinteger / int32 / int64JavaScript numbers lose precision above 2^53. Consider string ids
BigDecimalnumberA TS number is a double. Money is often sent as a string or as minor units
LocalDatestring / date2025-03-01
OffsetDateTime, Instantstring / date-timeHas an offset. Preferred for timestamps
LocalDateTimestring / date-timeDocumented as date-time, but sent without an offset: a common source of time-zone bugs
UUIDstring / uuid
enumstring + enum listAdding a value can break strict generated clients
List<T>, Set<T>array (uniqueItems for Set)
Map<String, V>object + additionalPropertiesFor dynamic keys
byte[]string / byte (Base64)Use binary and a file endpoint for large content
MultipartFile, Resourcestring / binaryFile upload and download
Optional<T>TUnwrapped, and not marked required

Documenting Event-Driven APIs: AsyncAPI

OpenAPI describes request and response over HTTP. For Kafka, RabbitMQ, WebSocket or MQTT messages, the equivalent standard is AsyncAPI. It uses a similar YAML structure: channels (topics), operations (send and receive), messages with headers, and payload schemas, often JSON Schema or Avro. In Spring, Springwolf can generate an AsyncAPI document from @KafkaListener and producer beans, and it has a UI similar to Swagger UI. Alternatively, keep the event contract in a Schema Registry (Avro or Protobuf) with compatibility rules. Event schemas also need versioning and compatibility checks, just as REST does.

asyncapi: 3.0.0
info: { title: Order Events, version: 1.0.0 }
channels:
  orderPlaced:
    address: orders.placed.v1
    messages:
      OrderPlaced:
        payload:
          type: object
          required: [orderId, total]
          properties:
            orderId: { type: string, format: uuid }
            total:   { type: string, description: decimal amount as string }

Interview Questions — Swagger / OpenAPI

What is the difference between Swagger and OpenAPI?

OpenAPI is the specification, governed by the OpenAPI Initiative under the Linux Foundation. Swagger is the original name, now the brand for SmartBear's tools (UI, Editor, Codegen). Swagger 2.0 was renamed OpenAPI 2.0, and today you write OpenAPI 3.x documents and view them in Swagger UI.

How do you add Swagger to a Spring Boot 3 project?

Add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui (2.x). No annotations are needed: the spec is at /v3/api-docs and the UI at /swagger-ui.html. Then enrich it with an OpenAPI bean (info, servers, security), @Tag/@Operation/@Schema, and permit those paths in Spring Security. Springfox doesn't work with Boot 3 because of the jakarta namespace and because it's no longer maintained.

How does springdoc generate the documentation?

At startup, or on the first request to /v3/api-docs, it inspects Spring's RequestMappingHandlerMapping to find every endpoint. It reads method signatures (@PathVariable, @RequestParam, @RequestBody, return types), uses Jackson to build schemas from DTOs, applies Bean Validation constraints, and merges in the Swagger annotations. The result is cached.

Code-first vs contract-first (API-first) — which is better?

Code-first (springdoc): fast, and the documentation always matches the code, but the API design happens implicitly. Contract-first: write api.yaml first, review it with consumers, and generate server interfaces and client SDKs with openapi-generator. Front-end and back-end teams can work in parallel against mocks (Prism), breaking changes show up in review, and the compiler enforces the contract. Contract-first is preferred for public or multi-team APIs.

How do you document JWT authentication in Swagger?

Define a security scheme: @SecurityScheme(name="bearerAuth", type=HTTP, scheme="bearer", bearerFormat="JWT"), or in the OpenAPI bean under components. Apply it globally with addSecurityItem or per operation with @SecurityRequirement(name="bearerAuth"). Swagger UI then shows an Authorize button. For OAuth2 you can configure the authorization code flow with PKCE so users can log in from the UI.

How do you hide endpoints or group APIs?

Hide them with @Hidden, or with the springdoc.paths-to-exclude or packages-to-scan settings. Group them with GroupedOpenApi beans (public, admin, internal), which appear as a dropdown in the UI with a separate spec URL each (/v3/api-docs/public).

Should Swagger UI be enabled in production?

Usually not for internal or private APIs: it reveals your attack surface. Options: springdoc.swagger-ui.enabled=false and api-docs.enabled=false in the prod profile, or keep it behind authentication or VPN-only access, or publish the spec to an internal developer portal instead. Public APIs often do publish their docs deliberately.

How do you show examples and error responses?

Use @Schema(example = "...") on fields, @ExampleObject inside @Content for full JSON examples, and @ApiResponse(responseCode="404", content=@Content(schema=@Schema(implementation=ProblemDetail.class))) for errors. You can also add global responses with an OperationCustomizer or OpenApiCustomizer bean.

How do you version APIs in OpenAPI docs?

Use one GroupedOpenApi per version (/api/v1/**, /api/v2/**), set info.version, and mark old operations with @Operation(deprecated = true), which Swagger UI shows struck through. Keep the spec files in Git and diff them in CI (openapi-diff) to catch breaking changes.

How can the Angular team use your OpenAPI spec?

Run openapi-generator with -g typescript-angular to get typed services and models (OrdersService.getOrder(id): Observable<OrderDto>), so nobody hand-writes HTTP calls or interfaces and type mismatches fail at compile time. Re-run it in CI whenever the spec changes.

Why does a generated client's method name keep changing?

The name comes from operationId, which springdoc derives from the Java method name, and de-duplicates with suffixes. Adding or moving a controller can shift those suffixes. Set an explicit @Operation(operationId = ...) on public operations.

How do you document a polymorphic request body?

Use @Schema(oneOf = {...}, discriminatorProperty = "type") with @DiscriminatorMapping, and matching Jackson @JsonTypeInfo and @JsonSubTypes so the runtime accepts what the document promises. Test both directions, since the annotations are independent.

How do you make sure the documented API matches the implementation?

Code-first generation stays close, but only reflects what is annotated: hand-written @ApiResponse values can be wrong. Add a contract test: validate real responses against the spec in integration tests, or run Schemathesis. For spec-first, generated interfaces let the compiler enforce signatures. Diff the spec in CI to catch accidental change.

What does OpenAPI 3.1 change? Why might you stay on 3.0?

3.1 is compatible with JSON Schema 2020-12, replaces nullable with type arrays, and adds webhooks. You might stay on 3.0 if generators, gateways or validators in your toolchain are not ready. springdoc can output either.

Swagger UI shows the wrong server URL or a CORS error in production. What do you check?

The spec's servers list usually holds the internal URL. Enable forwarded-header handling, or set servers explicitly. A CORS error comes from Try it out calling a different origin than the UI's, so align these, or allow that origin in the API's CORS configuration.

Swagger annotations vs REST Docs: how do you choose?

Annotations are quick, and give a live UI, but mix documentation with code and can drift. REST Docs is verified by tests, and can produce OpenAPI through a community extension, at the cost of writing those tests. Many teams prefer springdoc for internal APIs, and invest more in public ones.

How do you document an endpoint that returns a PDF or another file?

Declare the media type and a binary schema, so that Swagger UI shows a download link and generators produce a Blob return type:

@ApiResponse(responseCode = "200", content = @Content(mediaType = "application/pdf",
    schema = @Schema(type = "string", format = "binary")))
@GetMapping(value = "/invoices/{id}/pdf", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF_VALUE)
ResponseEntity<Resource> pdf(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }

Also document the Content-Disposition response header and the 404 response.

The Angular client receives wrong times or rounded amounts. What in the spec might cause it?

Common causes: LocalDateTime is sent without an offset, and the browser interprets it in local time. BigDecimal becomes a TypeScript number (a double), which loses precision. Large long ids exceed Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER. Fix the API types, not the client: use Instant or OffsetDateTime, send money as a decimal string or as integer minor units, and expose large ids as strings. Then document the format with @Schema(type = "string", format = "...") where needed.

How do you document Kafka or other message-based interfaces?

Use AsyncAPI, the messaging counterpart of OpenAPI. It describes channels or topics, message payloads and headers, and who publishes or subscribes. Generate it with a tool like Springwolf, or write it contract-first. Combine it with a Schema Registry (Avro or Protobuf) that enforces backward compatibility, so that producers cannot break consumers. Publish both the OpenAPI and AsyncAPI documents in the same developer portal.

How do you document a field with dynamic keys, such as a map of attributes?

A Map<String, V> becomes type: object with additionalProperties set to the schema of V. Generators turn this into { [key: string]: V } in TypeScript, or into a Map in Java. If the keys are actually a fixed set, model them as a real class with named properties instead. That gives type safety and documentation for each field.

Spring Security AuthN / AuthZ

The filter chain architecture, the authentication flow, password encoding, method security, OAuth2, CSRF and CORS.

@Configuration @EnableWebSecurity @EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain filterChain(HttpSecurity http, JwtAuthFilter jwtFilter) throws Exception {
    return http
      .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())                         // stateless REST API
      .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
      .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
      .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
          .requestMatchers("/auth/**", "/actuator/health").permitAll()
          .requestMatchers("/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
          .anyRequest().authenticated())
      .addFilterBefore(jwtFilter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
      .build();
  }
  @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }
  @Bean AuthenticationManager authManager(AuthenticationConfiguration cfg) throws Exception { return cfg.getAuthenticationManager(); }
}

@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #id == authentication.principal.id")
public UserDto getUser(Long id) { ... }

Filter Chain Architecture

Spring Security is built almost entirely from servlet filters, so it acts before any controller and also protects static files and unmapped URLs. The challenge is that the servlet container knows nothing about Spring beans, and filters are registered before beans exist. Three layers solve this.

  • DelegatingFilterProxy is a standard servlet filter registered with the container. It looks up the bean named springSecurityFilterChain lazily and delegates to it.
  • FilterChainProxy is that bean. It applies StrictHttpFirewall, which rejects suspicious URLs such as encoded slashes or path traversal. It picks the first matching SecurityFilterChain, runs its filters, and clears the SecurityContext at the end.
  • SecurityFilterChain is a matcher plus an ordered list of filters.

Default filter order

Filters exist based on the configuration, and FilterOrderRegistration fixes their relative order. The main ones in sequence:

FilterJob
DisableEncodeUrlFilterKeeps session ids out of URLs
WebAsyncManagerIntegrationFilterPropagates the context to Spring async request threads
SecurityContextHolderFilterLoads the context from the repository for the request
HeaderWriterFilterAdds security response headers
CorsFilterHandles preflights; must precede authentication
CsrfFilterVerifies the CSRF token on unsafe methods
LogoutFilterHandles the logout URL
OAuth2AuthorizationRequestRedirectFilterRedirects to the authorization server
OAuth2LoginAuthenticationFilterHandles the authorization code callback
UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilterHandles form login POSTs
BearerTokenAuthenticationFilterReads the Authorization: Bearer token
BasicAuthenticationFilterReads HTTP Basic credentials
RequestCacheAwareFilterResumes the request that was interrupted by login
SecurityContextHolderAwareRequestFilterImplements request.isUserInRole() and similar
AnonymousAuthenticationFilterSupplies an anonymous token if nobody logged in
SessionManagementFilterSession-related checks
ExceptionTranslationFilterCatches security exceptions from below and sends 401, 403, or a redirect
AuthorizationFilterApplies authorizeHttpRequests rules. Last in the chain

To see the chain, set logging.level.org.springframework.security=TRACE: it logs every filter per request. @EnableWebSecurity(debug = true) also prints requests, for local use only.

Several chains, and how rules are matched

@Bean @Order(1)
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
  return http.securityMatcher("/api/**")             // which requests this chain handles
      .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
          .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/api/products/**").permitAll()
          .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
          .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/api/orders").hasAuthority("order:write")
          .anyRequest().authenticated())
      .csrf(c -> c.disable())
      .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
      .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
      .build();
}

@Bean @Order(2)
SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {   // no securityMatcher: everything else
  return http
      .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
          .requestMatchers("/", "/login", "/css/**", "/error").permitAll()
          .anyRequest().authenticated())
      .formLogin(f -> f.loginPage("/login").defaultSuccessUrl("/home"))
      .logout(l -> l.logoutSuccessUrl("/"))
      .build();
}

securityMatcher selects the chain; requestMatchers selects a rule inside it. Rules are checked top to bottom and the first match wins, so specific rules go first. Boot's default is to require authentication for everything, with form and Basic login and a generated password in the log. Declaring your own SecurityFilterChain bean replaces that default.

Gotcha:
  • A custom filter annotated @Component is registered twice: Boot adds every Filter bean to the servlet container, and you add it to the chain. It then also runs for other chains. Either do not make it a bean, or disable the container registration with a FilterRegistrationBean where setEnabled(false).
  • Avoid WebSecurityCustomizer.ignoring(): ignored paths lose all headers and firewall protection. Use permitAll().
  • In Spring Security 6, authorization applies to all dispatch types, including FORWARD and ERROR. A 500 forwards to /error, which then gets 401 unless permitted. That is why a broken endpoint can look like an auth failure.
  • The first rule in the list above permits only GET. A rule without a method matches all methods, which is a common accidental opening.

Authentication Flow Objects

TypeRole
AuthenticationA request to log in, and also the result. Holds principal (who), credentials (password, erased after login), authorities, and authenticated
AuthenticationManagerOne method: authenticate(Authentication). Returns an authenticated token, throws AuthenticationException, or returns null if it cannot decide
ProviderManagerThe usual manager. Loops over providers until one accepts; has an optional parent manager for fallback
AuthenticationProviderDoes the actual check. supports(Class) says which token types it handles
DaoAuthenticationProviderUses UserDetailsService plus PasswordEncoder
AuthenticationEntryPointStarts authentication when there is none: redirect to login, or a 401 response
AccessDeniedHandlerHandles an authenticated user who lacks rights: 403

A form login step by step:

  1. UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter matches POST /login, and creates an unauthenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.
  2. ProviderManager finds DaoAuthenticationProvider, because supports is true for that token type.
  3. The provider loads the user, checks the account status (locked, disabled, expired), and compares the password using the encoder.
  4. It returns a new authenticated token with authorities. ProviderManager erases credentials and publishes AuthenticationSuccessEvent.
  5. The filter applies the session strategy (a new session id), stores the context with SecurityContextRepository, and calls AuthenticationSuccessHandler.
  6. On failure, it clears the context and calls AuthenticationFailureHandler.

When a user is not found, the provider still runs a dummy password check, so that attackers cannot find valid usernames by timing the response. It also reports BadCredentialsException rather than UsernameNotFoundException by default, for the same reason.

How 401 vs 403 is decided

AuthorizationFilter throws AccessDeniedException. ExceptionTranslationFilter, one step above it, catches it. If the current user is anonymous, the filter treats this as "not logged in": it stores the request and calls the entry point. If the user is authenticated, it calls AccessDeniedHandler. An AuthenticationException always goes to the entry point.

// A custom provider for an API key header
public class ApiKeyToken extends AbstractAuthenticationToken {
  private final String key;
  public ApiKeyToken(String key) { super(null); this.key = key; setAuthenticated(false); }
  public ApiKeyToken(String key, Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> auths) {
    super(auths); this.key = key; setAuthenticated(true);
  }
  @Override public Object getCredentials() { return key; }
  @Override public Object getPrincipal()   { return key; }
}

@Component
class ApiKeyProvider implements AuthenticationProvider {
  private final ApiKeyStore store;
  ApiKeyProvider(ApiKeyStore store) { this.store = store; }

  @Override public Authentication authenticate(Authentication a) {
    String key = (String) a.getCredentials();
    return store.find(key)
        .map(c -> new ApiKeyToken(key, c.authorities()))
        .orElseThrow(() -> new BadCredentialsException("invalid key"));
  }
  @Override public boolean supports(Class<?> type) { return ApiKeyToken.class.isAssignableFrom(type); }
}

A JSON login endpoint

For session-based SPAs you can replace the form with a controller. Since Security 6 the context is no longer saved automatically by SecurityContextHolderFilter, so you must save it yourself.

@RestController
class SessionLoginController {
  private final AuthenticationManager manager;
  private final SecurityContextRepository repo = new HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository();
  private final SecurityContextHolderStrategy holder = SecurityContextHolder.getContextHolderStrategy();
  SessionLoginController(AuthenticationManager m) { this.manager = m; }

  @PostMapping("/session")
  void login(@RequestBody LoginRequest r, HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res) {
    Authentication auth = manager.authenticate(
        UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(r.username(), r.password()));
    SecurityContext ctx = holder.createEmptyContext();      // new context, avoids a race on the old one
    ctx.setAuthentication(auth);
    holder.setContext(ctx);
    repo.saveContext(ctx, req, res);                        // without this, the login is lost
  }
}

UserDetailsService

UserDetailsService has one method, loadUserByUsername, which adapts your user storage to Spring Security. It knows nothing about passwords being correct. It only returns a UserDetails with the stored hash, and authorities and status flags.

@Service
class AppUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
  private final UserRepository users;
  AppUserDetailsService(UserRepository u) { this.users = u; }

  @Override @Transactional(readOnly = true)
  public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String email) {
    AppUser u = users.findWithRolesByEmail(email)
        .orElseThrow(() -> new UsernameNotFoundException("not found"));
    return User.withUsername(u.getEmail())
        .password(u.getPasswordHash())
        .authorities(u.getRoles().stream().map(r -> "ROLE_" + r.getName()).toArray(String[]::new))
        .accountLocked(u.isLocked())
        .disabled(!u.isActive())
        .build();
  }
}

Keep your JPA entity separate from UserDetails. If a detached entity sits in the session, you get LazyInitializationException, and the serialized session is exposed to entity changes. Return a small immutable object instead. Load roles eagerly in the query.

A UserDetailsService bean plus a PasswordEncoder bean is picked up automatically: Spring builds a DaoAuthenticationProvider for you. Do not call it per request in a JWT filter unless you need fresh data, because that adds a database query to each call.

PasswordEncoder

Passwords are never stored or decrypted; they are hashed with a slow function, and matches() hashes the input with the stored salt and compares. Speed is the enemy: an attacker with a stolen table tries billions of guesses, and a slow hash limits this.

EncoderTypeNote
Argon2PasswordEncoderMemory-hardOWASP's first choice (Argon2id); expensive on GPUs. Needs Bouncy Castle
BCryptPasswordEncoderCPU-hardDefault and very common. Strength 10 means 210 rounds; each increment doubles the time
SCryptPasswordEncoderMemory-hardGood alternative
Pbkdf2PasswordEncoderCPU-hardRequired in FIPS environments
NoOpPasswordEncoderNoneDeprecated, tests only
// Tested with spring-security-crypto 6.4
BCryptPasswordEncoder bc = new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
String h = bc.encode("secret");     // $2a$10$..., always 60 characters
h.equals(bc.encode("secret"));      // false: a fresh random salt each time
bc.matches("secret", h);            // true: the salt is stored inside the hash

// Format: $2a$10$ + 22-char salt + 31-char hash
//         version, cost

DelegatingPasswordEncoder adds an algorithm prefix so that several schemes coexist: {bcrypt}$2a$10$.... PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder() encodes with BCrypt and reads all the known formats. This lets you raise the cost later: implement UserDetailsPasswordService, and DaoAuthenticationProvider re-hashes on the next successful login when upgradeEncoding says the stored hash is outdated. A stored hash with no prefix makes matches() throw IllegalArgumentException, as tested, which is a common migration problem; fix it with setDefaultPasswordEncoderForMatches.

Gotcha: BCrypt only uses the first 72 bytes. On 6.4, tested, a 73-character password matched the hash of its 72-character prefix with no error. Validate the maximum length on input. Each hash is deliberately expensive, and the cost doubles with each strength step, so rate-limit the login endpoint to stop it becoming a denial-of-service target. CompromisedPasswordChecker (Security 6.3) can reject known leaked passwords.

SecurityContext and SecurityContextHolder

SecurityContextHolder → SecurityContext → Authentication. The holder stores the context in a ThreadLocal, so any code on the request thread can get the current user with no parameter passing.

  • Load: SecurityContextHolderFilter asks a SecurityContextRepository for the context. For a session app, that is HttpSessionSecurityContextRepository.
  • Clear: it is cleared in a finally, which is vital because pooled threads are reused. A leak would make one user's request see another user's identity.
  • Save: since 6.0 this must be explicit, as shown above. Stateless apps never save it.
StrategyBehaviour
MODE_THREADLOCALDefault: per thread
MODE_INHERITABLETHREADLOCALChild threads inherit it. Dangerous with pools, because a pooled thread keeps the identity of whoever created it
MODE_GLOBALOne context for the JVM, for desktop apps

For async work, use DelegatingSecurityContextRunnable, DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService or DelegatingSecurityContextAsyncTaskExecutor. WebFlux stores the context in the Reactor context, accessed by ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.

Method Security

URL rules are coarse. Method security protects the service itself, so a new controller or message listener cannot bypass it. @EnableMethodSecurity enables @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize by default. Each annotation has an AOP interceptor, such as AuthorizationManagerBeforeMethodInterceptor, which delegates to an AuthorizationManager.

@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled = true, jsr250Enabled = true)

@Service class OrderService {
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #customerId == authentication.name")
  public List<Order> listFor(String customerId) { ... }     // #customerId needs -parameters at compile

  @PostAuthorize("returnObject.ownerId == authentication.name")
  public Order get(long id) { ... }                         // method RUNS, then checks: no side effects here

  @PreFilter("filterObject.ownerId == authentication.name")
  public void updateAll(List<Order> orders) { ... }

  @PostFilter("hasRole('ADMIN') or filterObject.ownerId == authentication.name")
  public List<Order> all() { ... }                          // loads everything, then filters in memory

  @PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.canEdit(#id, authentication)") // delegate complex rules to a bean
  public void edit(long id) { ... }

  @Secured("ROLE_ADMIN") public void close() { }            // simple list, no SpEL
  @RolesAllowed("ADMIN") public void purge() { }            // Jakarta standard
}

@Component("orderAccess")
class OrderAccess {
  public boolean canEdit(long id, Authentication a) { return repo.isOwner(id, a.getName()); }
}

// A meta-annotation avoids repeating expressions
@Target(ElementType.METHOD) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('order:write')")
public @interface CanWriteOrders { }
AnnotationWhenSpELNote
@PreAuthorizeBeforeYesThe usual choice
@PostAuthorizeAfterYesFor decisions needing the result. The transaction may still commit unless the denial exception rolls it back
@PreFilter / @PostFilterFilters a collectionYesInefficient; prefer filtering in the query
@SecuredBeforeNoRequires exact names with ROLE_
@RolesAllowedBeforeNoJSR-250

Newer features: @AuthorizeReturnObject and @HandleAuthorizationDenied (Security 6.3) authorize at the field level and mask or replace denied results. A role hierarchy (RoleHierarchyImpl.fromHierarchy("ROLE_ADMIN > ROLE_USER")) lets ADMIN imply USER.

Gotcha: Method security is AOP, so self-invocation, private and final methods bypass it silently. Denial raises AuthorizationDeniedException, a subclass of AccessDeniedException. A catch-all @ExceptionHandler(Exception.class) in your advice catches it first, and the client gets 500 rather than 403; rethrow it, or add a specific handler.

Session Management

SessionCreationPolicyBehaviour
ALWAYSCreates a session if none exists
IF_REQUIRED (default)Creates one when needed, for example at login
NEVERDoes not create one, but uses an existing one
STATELESSNever creates or reads one, for tokens
http.sessionManagement(s -> s
    .sessionFixation(f -> f.changeSessionId())   // the default on servlet 3.1+
    .maximumSessions(1)                          // needs a HttpSessionEventPublisher bean
    .maxSessionsPreventsLogin(false)             // false: the oldest session expires
);
server.servlet.session:
  timeout: 30m              # default 30m
  cookie: { http-only: true, secure: true, same-site: lax, name: SID }

Session fixation: an attacker gets a session id, tricks a victim into using it, and after the victim logs in the attacker's id is authenticated. Changing the id at login defeats this. Spring does so by default.

Scaling: an in-memory session lives on one instance. Spring Session moves it to Redis or a database by replacing the HttpSession implementation through a filter, with no code changes; everything stored must be serializable. Use SessionRegistry with care: the default is in-memory, so concurrency limits across instances need a shared registry such as SpringSessionBackedSessionRegistry.

Remember-me: http.rememberMe(...) sets a long-lived cookie. The token-based form hashes the password in; the persistent form stores a series and token in the database, and detects theft.

CSRF in Depth

A browser attaches cookies to a request automatically, whichever site triggered it. If bank.com authenticates by cookie, a hidden form on evil.com posting to bank.com/transfer carries the victim's session. The server cannot tell it apart from a real click. The defence needs something that evil.com cannot supply: a secret the page reads and sends back, which another origin cannot read because of the same-origin policy.

  1. CsrfFilter skips safe methods: GET, HEAD, TRACE, OPTIONS. This is why GET must never change state.
  2. For others, it reads the expected token from a CsrfTokenRepository, and the actual token from the _csrf parameter or X-CSRF-TOKEN header.
  3. On a mismatch: 403.
SituationApproach
Server-rendered formsDefault: session token; Thymeleaf inserts the hidden field
SPA using a session cookieCookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse(): JavaScript reads the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and echoes it in X-XSRF-TOKEN. Angular's HttpClient does this out of the box for same-origin requests
API with Bearer tokens in headersDisable: nothing is attached automatically
JWT in a cookieStill needs CSRF protection, as it is a cookie
http.csrf(c -> c
    .csrfTokenRepository(CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse())
    .csrfTokenRequestHandler(new CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler())); // plain token for the header

Since 6.0 the token is loaded lazily, so it is not written until something reads it, and the default handler XOR-masks the token per response, which defends against the BREACH compression attack. A SPA reading the raw cookie needs the plain handler as above, and an endpoint or filter that touches the token so the cookie is issued. The SameSite=Lax cookie attribute blocks most cross-site POSTs and is good extra protection, but it is not a complete replacement.

CORS with Spring Security

The Same-Origin Policy stops a page reading responses from another origin (scheme, host and port). CORS lets a server relax that. For a simple request the browser does send it and just hides the response from JavaScript. So CORS does not stop a state-changing request reaching your server; CSRF protection does that. For other requests, the browser first sends a preflight: OPTIONS with Origin, Access-Control-Request-Method and Access-Control-Request-Headers.

@Bean CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
  CorsConfiguration c = new CorsConfiguration();
  c.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.shop.com"));
  c.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "PATCH", "DELETE"));
  c.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Authorization", "Content-Type", "X-XSRF-TOKEN"));
  c.setExposedHeaders(List.of("Location", "ETag"));
  c.setAllowCredentials(true);
  c.setMaxAge(3600L);
  UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource src = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
  src.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", c);
  return src;
}
// http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults()) finds this bean by its name

CorsFilter sits before the authentication filters, so preflights, which carry no credentials, succeed. Never reflect an arbitrary Origin with credentials: any site could then read authenticated data.

Form Login, HTTP Basic and Logout

http.formLogin(f -> f
        .loginPage("/login")                // your page; GET is yours, POST goes to the filter
        .loginProcessingUrl("/login")
        .defaultSuccessUrl("/dashboard")    // or the saved request, if there is one
        .failureUrl("/login?error"))
    .logout(l -> l
        .logoutUrl("/logout")               // POST when CSRF is on
        .deleteCookies("SID")
        .invalidateHttpSession(true))
    .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults());

Flow: an anonymous request for /orders reaches AuthorizationFilter, which denies it. ExceptionTranslationFilter saves the request in a RequestCache and redirects to /login. After login, the success handler redirects to the saved URL.

HTTP Basic sends Authorization: Basic base64(user:password) with each request. Base64 is not encryption, so TLS is essential. On failure, the entry point returns 401 with WWW-Authenticate: Basic, making browsers show a dialog. Since a BCrypt check runs on each request, it can dominate CPU; keep it to internal tools.

OAuth 2.0

Before OAuth, an app that wanted your photos asked for your password. OAuth 2.0 (RFC 6749) instead lets the user grant limited access: the app gets a token for specific scopes, for a limited time, and revocable, without ever seeing the password. It is about authorization.

GrantUsed byStatusHow it works
Authorization Code + PKCEWeb apps, SPAs, mobileStandardUser logs in at the server; client swaps a short code for tokens
Client CredentialsService to serviceStandardClient authenticates as itself; no user and no refresh token
Refresh TokenAny with a userStandardSwap a refresh token for a new access token
Device Authorization (RFC 8628)TVs, CLIsStandardDevice shows a code; user approves on a phone; device polls
Token Exchange (RFC 8693)MicroservicesExtensionSwap one token for another, for on-behalf-of calls
JWT Bearer (RFC 7523)Server to serverExtensionPresent a signed JWT as the grant
ImplicitFormerly SPAs⚠ Removed in OAuth 2.1Token in the URL fragment: leaks through history and referrers
Resource Owner PasswordLegacy first-party apps⚠ Removed in OAuth 2.1Client handles the password, undoing the point of OAuth

PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange, RFC 7636) protects against code interception, for example by a malicious app registered for the same mobile URL scheme. The client invents a random secret, the code_verifier, and sends only its hash in step 4: code_challenge = BASE64URL(SHA256(verifier)). In step 8 it reveals the verifier. The server hashes it and compares. An attacker with the code has no verifier. RFC 7636's example, checked with Node:

code_verifier:  dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk
code_challenge: E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM   (method S256)

Other protections: state is a random value that the client verifies on return, which stops CSRF on the callback. The authorization server must exactly match redirect_uri, or an open redirect leaks the code. Public clients such as SPAs cannot keep a secret, so PKCE is mandatory for them. OAuth 2.1 requires it for all.

For SPAs, the most secure current pattern is Backend for Frontend (BFF): a small server performs the OAuth flow as a confidential client, holds the tokens, and gives the browser only an HttpOnly session cookie.

Spring as OAuth2 client

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      client:
        registration:
          keycloak:
            client-id: shop-web
            client-secret: ${OIDC_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: authorization_code
            scope: openid,profile,email
          inventory:                                 # machine-to-machine
            provider: keycloak
            client-id: shop-svc
            client-secret: ${SVC_SECRET}
            authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
        provider:
          keycloak:
            issuer-uri: https://auth.shop.com/realms/shop
http.oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults());          // browser login

// RestClient that fetches, caches and renews the client-credentials token (Security 6.4+)
@Bean RestClient inventory(RestClient.Builder b, OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
  var interceptor = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);
  interceptor.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(request -> "inventory");
  return b.baseUrl("https://inventory.internal").requestInterceptor(interceptor).build();
}

OpenID Connect

An access token tells an API what may be done; it says nothing reliable about who the user is, or how they logged in. Using OAuth alone for login is a known mistake: a token stolen by another app could log in to yours. OIDC adds identity on top of OAuth 2.0.

  • Trigger: include the openid scope. Others include profile and email.
  • ID token: a signed JWT for the client, with iss, sub, aud (the client id), exp, iat, nonce, auth_time, and profile claims.
  • UserInfo endpoint: returns claims, using the access token.
  • Discovery: {issuer}/.well-known/openid-configuration publishes endpoints and the JWKS URL. That is how Spring configures itself from issuer-uri.
  • Nonce: a client-chosen random value echoed in the ID token, which prevents replay.
  • Logout: RP-Initiated Logout ends the session at the provider; Spring has OidcClientInitiatedLogoutSuccessHandler.
ID tokenAccess tokenRefresh token
AudienceThe clientThe APIThe authorization server
PurposeProve the loginCall the APIGet a new access token
FormatAlways JWTJWT or opaqueOpaque to the client
Send to API?NeverYesNever

With oauth2Login, the principal becomes an OidcUser: use @AuthenticationPrincipal OidcUser user. Default authorities are OIDC_USER and SCOPE_*. Map provider roles with a GrantedAuthoritiesMapper bean or a custom OidcUserService.

Resource Server

A resource server is your API. It does not log anyone in; it validates tokens. With oauth2ResourceServer().jwt(), BearerTokenAuthenticationFilter extracts the token, JwtAuthenticationProvider uses a JwtDecoder to verify the signature against the JWKS and validate exp, nbf and iss, and a converter turns the Jwt into a JwtAuthenticationToken.

spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt:
  issuer-uri: https://auth.shop.com/realms/shop       # discovers the JWKS at startup or first use
  audiences: shop-api                                 # not checked unless you configure it
  # jwk-set-uri: ...                                  # avoids the startup call to the issuer
// Keycloak places roles in realm_access.roles. Map them to ROLE_*
@Bean JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthenticationConverter() {
  JwtAuthenticationConverter conv = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
  conv.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(jwt -> {
    Map<String, Object> realm = jwt.getClaimAsMap("realm_access");
    if (realm == null) return List.of();
    @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<String> roles = (List<String>) realm.getOrDefault("roles", List.of());
    return roles.stream().map(r -> (GrantedAuthority) new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r)).toList();
  });
  conv.setPrincipalClaimName("preferred_username");
  return conv;
}

// In a controller
@GetMapping("/me") Map<String, Object> me(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
  return Map.of("sub", jwt.getSubject(), "email", jwt.getClaimAsString("email"));
}
JWT validationOpaque token + introspection (RFC 7662)
CheckLocal signature checkCalls the authorization server per request or with a cache
LatencyTinyA network hop
RevocationOnly at expiry unless extra is builtImmediate
Spring.jwt().opaqueToken()

Keys rotate with no downtime: NimbusJwtDecoder caches the JWKS and re-fetches on an unknown kid. The default clock skew allowance is 60 seconds. Testing: mvc.perform(get("/api/orders").with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")))), or @WithMockUser(roles = "ADMIN") for session-style checks.

Security Headers

HeaderDefault value in Spring SecurityProtects against
Cache-Control, Pragma, Expiresno-cache, no-store, max-age=0, must-revalidateSensitive pages kept by shared caches
X-Content-Type-OptionsnosniffMIME sniffing turning an upload into a script
Strict-Transport-Securitymax-age=31536000 ; includeSubDomains, on HTTPS onlyTLS downgrade
X-Frame-OptionsDENYClickjacking
X-XSS-Protection0Disables the old browser auditor, which itself caused holes
Content-Security-PolicyNot set: you must define itXSS, data injection
Referrer-PolicyNot setURLs leaking to other sites
Permissions-PolicyNot setUnwanted browser features
http.headers(h -> h
    .contentSecurityPolicy(c -> c.policyDirectives(
        "default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data:; object-src 'none'; frame-ancestors 'none'"))
    .referrerPolicy(r -> r.policy(ReferrerPolicyHeaderWriter.ReferrerPolicy.STRICT_ORIGIN_WHEN_CROSS_ORIGIN))
    .frameOptions(f -> f.sameOrigin())                   // needed for the H2 console in development
    .httpStrictTransportSecurity(s -> s.maxAgeInSeconds(31536000).includeSubDomains(true)));

OWASP Top 10 for Java Applications

This is the 2021 list, the one usually quoted in interviews.

RiskJava exampleDefence
A01 Broken Access ControlGET /orders/42 returns any user's order (IDOR); a missing check on an admin endpointDeny by default; check ownership in the service or query (findByIdAndOwner)
A02 Cryptographic FailuresMD5 passwords, secrets in Git, plain HTTP, Random for tokensBCrypt or Argon2, TLS, SecureRandom, AES-GCM, a vault
A03 Injection"select * from u where n='" + name + "'", JPQL concatenation, SpEL, LDAP, OS commands, XSSBind parameters, an allowlist for sort columns, output encoding
A04 Insecure DesignNo rate limit on password reset; predictable reset linksThreat modelling, abuse cases, limits
A05 Security MisconfigurationExposed /actuator/env, default passwords, stack traces in errors, XXE enabledHardened defaults, separate management port, reviews
A06 Vulnerable ComponentsLog4Shell (CVE-2021-44228), Spring4Shell (CVE-2022-22965)Dependabot or Renovate, OWASP Dependency-Check, an SBOM
A07 Identification and Auth FailuresNo lockout, weak session handling, sessions that survive logoutMFA, throttling, regenerated session ids, breached password checks
A08 Software and Data IntegrityJava deserialization of untrusted bytes; unsigned updates; unpinned CI actionsAvoid ObjectInputStream on input, use ObjectInputFilter, sign artifacts
A09 Logging and Monitoring FailuresNo audit of failed logins; tokens in logsLog security events, listen to AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent, alerting
A10 SSRFA "fetch this URL" feature reaches 169.254.169.254 cloud metadataAllowlist hosts, block private ranges, resolve then validate

The 2025 revision moves Security Misconfiguration to A02, adds Software Supply Chain Failures (broadening Vulnerable Components), folds SSRF into Broken Access Control, and adds Mishandling of Exceptional Conditions.

// SQL injection in JPA: an unsafe query
em.createQuery("select u from User u where u.name = '" + name + "'");                // vulnerable
em.createQuery("select u from User u where u.name = :n").setParameter("n", name);    // safe

// A sort parameter cannot be bound, so use an allowlist
private static final Set<String> SORTABLE = Set.of("createdAt", "total");
if (!SORTABLE.contains(sort)) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.BAD_REQUEST);

// XXE: disable DTDs on every XML parser that sees untrusted input
DocumentBuilderFactory f = DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance();
f.setFeature("http://apache.org/xml/features/disallow-doctype-decl", true);

// Mass assignment: bind a DTO, not an entity. This lets a client set "admin": true
@PostMapping("/users") User create(@RequestBody User u) { return repo.save(u); }

// Path traversal
Path p = base.resolve(userInput).normalize();
if (!p.startsWith(base)) throw new SecurityException();

Complete JWT-Based Configuration

Modern Spring Security can issue and validate JWTs without a third-party library or a custom filter, using Nimbus through spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server. This variant has the API sign its own tokens with an RSA key. The JWT section shows the hand-written filter alternative. If a real authorization server is available, drop the encoder and use only the decoder.

@Configuration
@EnableWebSecurity
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class SecurityConfig {

  @Value("${app.jwt.public-key}")  private RSAPublicKey publicKey;     // e.g. classpath:keys/app.pub
  @Value("${app.jwt.private-key}") private RSAPrivateKey privateKey;   // load from a secret store in prod

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())                                        // Bearer header, no cookies
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/auth/login", "/auth/refresh", "/error").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/actuator/health/**").permitAll()
            .requestMatchers("/api/admin/**").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(j -> j.jwtAuthenticationConverter(jwtAuthConverter())))
        .build();                       // the 401 and 403 responses come from the bearer token handlers
  }

  @Bean JwtDecoder jwtDecoder() {
    NimbusJwtDecoder d = NimbusJwtDecoder.withPublicKey(publicKey).build();
    d.setJwtValidator(JwtValidators.createDefaultWithIssuer("https://api.shop.com"));
    return d;
  }

  @Bean JwtEncoder jwtEncoder() {
    JWK jwk = new RSAKey.Builder(publicKey).privateKey(privateKey).keyID("key-2026-1").build();
    return new NimbusJwtEncoder(new ImmutableJWKSet<>(new JWKSet(jwk)));
  }
