  private JwtAuthenticationConverter jwtAuthConverter() {
    JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter roles = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    roles.setAuthoritiesClaimName("roles");
    roles.setAuthorityPrefix("ROLE_");
    JwtAuthenticationConverter c = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
    c.setJwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter(roles);
    return c;
  }

  @Bean PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
  }

  @Bean AuthenticationManager authenticationManager(AuthenticationConfiguration cfg) throws Exception {
    return cfg.getAuthenticationManager();                             // uses UserDetailsService + encoder
  }
}

@Service
class TokenService {
  private final JwtEncoder encoder;
  TokenService(JwtEncoder e) { this.encoder = e; }

  String issue(Authentication auth) {
    Instant now = Instant.now();
    List<String> roles = auth.getAuthorities().stream()
        .map(GrantedAuthority::getAuthority)
        .map(r -> r.replaceFirst("^ROLE_", ""))
        .toList();
    JwtClaimsSet claims = JwtClaimsSet.builder()
        .issuer("https://api.shop.com")
        .subject(auth.getName())
        .issuedAt(now)
        .expiresAt(now.plus(15, ChronoUnit.MINUTES))
        .id(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
        .claim("roles", roles)
        .build();
    return encoder.encode(JwtEncoderParameters.from(claims)).getTokenValue();  // RS256 by default
  }
}

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/auth")
class AuthController {
  private final AuthenticationManager manager;
  private final TokenService tokens;
  AuthController(AuthenticationManager m, TokenService t) { this.manager = m; this.tokens = t; }

  @PostMapping("/login")
  Map<String, Object> login(@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest r) {
    Authentication a = manager.authenticate(
        UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(r.username(), r.password()));
    return Map.of("accessToken", tokens.issue(a), "tokenType", "Bearer", "expiresIn", 900);
  }
}

public record LoginRequest(@NotBlank @Email String username, @NotBlank @Size(max = 72) String password) { }

A failed authenticate throws BadCredentialsException from the controller. With no handler, ExceptionTranslationFilter finds it in the cause chain of the escaping exception, and the entry point sends a 401 with an empty body. Add an @ExceptionHandler(AuthenticationException.class) that returns a ProblemDetail if clients need a JSON error.

Object-Level Authorization Mechanics

Role checks answer "may this user call this endpoint?". Most real bugs are about this record. Spring offers several tools:

  • A bean in SpEL: @PreAuthorize("@orderAuthz.canRead(#id, authentication)"). It is explicit, unit-testable, and the most common choice.
  • PermissionEvaluator: implement hasPermission(auth, targetId, targetType, permission) and write @PreAuthorize("hasPermission(#id, 'Order', 'read')"). It gives one central policy for many types. Spring Security ACL is the heavy version with ACL tables.
  • A custom AuthorizationManager for URL rules, for example checking the {orgId} path variable against the user's org claim with .requestMatchers("/orgs/{orgId}/**").access(...).
  • Query scoping: findByIdAndOwnerId(id, userId) or a Hibernate filter for the tenant. This is safest for lists and pagination.
@Component("orderAuthz")
class OrderAuthz {
  private final OrderRepository repo;
  OrderAuthz(OrderRepository repo) { this.repo = repo; }
  public boolean canRead(UUID orderId, Authentication auth) {
    String userId = auth.getName();
    return repo.existsByIdAndCustomerId(orderId, userId)
        || auth.getAuthorities().stream().anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("ROLE_SUPPORT"));
  }
}

@PreAuthorize("@orderAuthz.canRead(#id, authentication)")
@GetMapping("/orders/{id}")
OrderDto get(@PathVariable UUID id) { ... }   // needs -parameters (on by default in Boot builds) for #id

Multi-Tenant Resource Servers (Several Issuers)

A SaaS API may accept tokens from several identity providers or Keycloak realms, one per tenant. A single issuer-uri cannot express this. JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver reads the iss claim, checks it against an allow-list, and validates the token with that issuer's JWKS. Never trust an issuer just because it appears in a token, or anyone can mint tokens from their own server.

@Bean
SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
  var resolver = JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver.fromTrustedIssuers(
      "https://idp.example.com/realms/tenant-a",
      "https://idp.example.com/realms/tenant-b");
  http.authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a.anyRequest().authenticated())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.authenticationManagerResolver(resolver));
  return http.build();
}

Passkeys and One-Time-Token Login

Spring Security 6.4 added two passwordless options:

  • Passkeys (WebAuthn): the device creates a key pair per site. The server stores only the public key, and the browser signs a challenge after biometrics or a PIN. They are phishing-resistant, because the browser binds the credential to the origin (the relying-party id), so a fake domain cannot use it. They need the webauthn4j dependency and persistent storage for credentials.
  • One-time token (magic link): oneTimeTokenLogin() generates a short-lived, single-use token. You provide a OneTimeTokenGenerationSuccessHandler bean that sends it, for example by email. It is convenient, but only as secure as the user's mailbox.
http.formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
    .webAuthn(w -> w.rpName("My App")
                    .rpId("example.com")
                    .allowedOrigins("https://example.com"))
    .oneTimeTokenLogin(Customizer.withDefaults());

API Keys for Machine Clients

Partners and scripts sometimes cannot do OAuth. If you issue API keys:

  • Generate a long random key. Show it once. Store only a hash (SHA-256 is fine for high-entropy keys) plus a short prefix for lookup.
  • Read it from a header (X-API-Key or Authorization), never from the query string, because query strings end up in logs.
  • Write a filter that looks up the hash and puts an Authentication with scoped authorities into the context. Then reuse normal URL and method security.
  • Support rotation (two active keys), expiry, per-key rate limits, and audit logging.

Where possible, prefer OAuth2 Client Credentials: tokens are short-lived and scoped, and the identity provider handles revocation.

Interview Questions — Spring Security

Authentication vs Authorization?

Authentication answers "who are you?" (login: credentials, token, certificate). Authorization answers "what are you allowed to do?" (roles, authorities, ACLs). Authentication always comes first.

Explain Spring Security's internal flow.
  1. The request reaches DelegatingFilterProxy, which hands it to FilterChainProxy, which picks the matching SecurityFilterChain.
  2. An authentication filter extracts credentials into an Authentication token (unauthenticated).
  3. AuthenticationManager (ProviderManager) delegates to an AuthenticationProvider, which loads the user through UserDetailsService and checks the password with PasswordEncoder.
  4. On success, the authenticated token is stored in the SecurityContextHolder.
  5. AuthorizationFilter checks the access rules. ExceptionTranslationFilter turns failures into 401 or 403.
Role vs Authority?

Both are GrantedAuthority objects. A role is just an authority with the ROLE_ prefix: hasRole("ADMIN") checks ROLE_ADMIN, while hasAuthority("order:write") checks the exact string. Use roles for coarse-grained access and authorities or permissions for fine-grained access.

Why BCrypt? Why not MD5/SHA?

BCrypt is slow by design (with an adjustable cost factor) and salted automatically, which defends against rainbow tables and brute force. MD5 and SHA are fast, which makes brute force easy. Alternatives are Argon2 and SCrypt. DelegatingPasswordEncoder stores an {bcrypt} prefix so the algorithm can be migrated later.

What is CSRF? When can you disable it?

Cross-Site Request Forgery: a malicious site makes your browser send an authenticated request using your cookies. Spring defends against it with a synchronizer token. You can disable it for stateless APIs that use Bearer tokens in headers, because the browser doesn't attach those automatically. Keep it enabled for cookie or session-based apps.

Method-level security?

Enable it with @EnableMethodSecurity. Then use @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')") and @PostAuthorize("returnObject.owner == authentication.name"), which take SpEL expressions, plus @Secured("ROLE_ADMIN") and @RolesAllowed. It's AOP proxy-based.

OAuth2 vs OpenID Connect? Roles in OAuth2?

OAuth2 is for authorization (delegated access, access tokens). OIDC is a layer on top for authentication, adding an ID token (a JWT) and the userinfo endpoint. The OAuth2 roles are Resource Owner (the user), Client (the app), Authorization Server (Keycloak, Okta, Auth0), and Resource Server (your API). Grant types: Authorization Code + PKCE (web and SPA apps), Client Credentials (service to service), Refresh Token. Implicit and Password grants are deprecated.

How to configure a Resource Server in Spring Boot?
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://keycloak/realms/shop
http.oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()));

Spring fetches the JWKS public keys, validates the signature, expiry and issuer, and maps scopes to SCOPE_xxx authorities.

How do you get the current logged-in user?

SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication(), or in a controller use @AuthenticationPrincipal UserDetails user or a Principal parameter.

What changed in Spring Security 6?

WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter was removed, so you declare a SecurityFilterChain bean instead. authorizeRequests became authorizeHttpRequests, antMatchers became requestMatchers, and the lambda DSL is preferred (mandatory only from Security 7). @EnableGlobalMethodSecurity became @EnableMethodSecurity.

Why does Spring Security need DelegatingFilterProxy and FilterChainProxy, and not just one filter?

The container initializes filters before Spring is ready, and it cannot inject beans. DelegatingFilterProxy is a lightweight bridge that resolves a Spring bean lazily. FilterChainProxy gives one central place to apply the firewall, clear the context, and select among several chains, which plain URL-mapped servlet filters cannot do, as they cannot match on arbitrary request properties.

How do you add a custom filter, and where should a JWT filter go?

Use addFilterBefore(filter, UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class), addFilterAfter, or addFilterAt. A token filter belongs before AuthorizationFilter and normally before UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter, so the context is set for later filters. It must not be run twice, so extend OncePerRequestFilter, and watch out for automatic servlet registration of filter beans.

Who produces a 401, and who a 403?

ExceptionTranslationFilter catches AuthenticationException and AccessDeniedException from further down. AuthenticationException, or AccessDeniedException for an anonymous user, goes to AuthenticationEntryPoint: 401 or a login redirect. For an authenticated user, it goes to AccessDeniedHandler: 403. Customize these with http.exceptionHandling(...).

The API returns 403 on POST but GET works. Why?

The first suspect is CSRF: it is on by default and rejects unsafe methods without a token. For a stateless token API, disable it. Other causes: a role rule on POST, or a failed CORS preflight, which browsers show differently. TRACE logging for Spring Security shows which filter rejected it.

What is the difference between permitAll() and web.ignoring()?

permitAll() leaves the request in the chain: headers, firewall, and CSRF apply, and the context is available, but any user passes. ignoring() skips the chain entirely, so no protection applies, and the logs warn against it except for truly static content.

How do ProviderManager and multiple AuthenticationProviders interact?

It iterates over providers, calling those whose supports is true. The first non-null result wins. An AuthenticationException is remembered, and the next provider tried, except for account-status exceptions, which stop immediately. If all fail, the parent manager gets a turn. If none supports the token, it throws ProviderNotFoundException.

Why erase credentials after authentication?

The Authentication object lasts in the context, and possibly the session. Keeping a plaintext password there increases exposure, for example in a heap dump or a serialized session. ProviderManager calls eraseCredentials by default. A cached UserDetails shared between authentications may need care, because the same object may get erased.

What happens to the SecurityContext at the end of a request?

It is cleared from the ThreadLocal in a finally block. With a session, what was saved stays in the session under SPRING_SECURITY_CONTEXT. A failure to clear it in custom code is a critical bug, because the pooled thread would carry the identity into the next request.

Is it safe to use hasRole in a @PreAuthorize with a JWT from Keycloak?

Only after mapping. The default converter creates SCOPE_* from scope, and ignores Keycloak's realm_access.roles. So hasRole('ADMIN') will fail unless a converter maps it to ROLE_ADMIN. Scopes describe what the client may do; roles describe the user. Effective access should consider both.

Scopes vs roles?

A scope limits what a client application was delegated by the user: orders:read. A role or permission describes what the user can do. A token with an admin user but only orders:read scope should only read orders. In Spring, a scope appears as SCOPE_orders:read.

Is @PostAuthorize safe on a method that changes data?

Risky. The method has already run. If it is transactional and the interceptor is outside the transaction, the commit may have happened by the time access is denied. Use @PreAuthorize for writes. Reserve @PostAuthorize for reads, where the decision depends on the returned object.

How do you prevent one user reading another's order (IDOR)?

A role check is not enough: every customer has the same role. Scope the data: findByIdAndCustomerId(id, currentUserId), returning 404 when there is no match, or a bean-based @PreAuthorize("@orderAccess.isOwner(#id, authentication)"). Use non-sequential ids as hardening, not as the control. Write tests with a second user. This is the top item for both OWASP lists.

A stolen session cookie: how do you limit the damage?

Set HttpOnly, Secure, and SameSite. Use a short idle timeout and absolute lifetime. Change the id at login. Require re-authentication for sensitive actions, ask for MFA, and offer a "log out all devices" feature backed by a session store. Monitoring for sudden changes of IP or device adds detection.

Does disabling CSRF for a JWT API always make sense?

Only if the token travels in a header set by JavaScript. If the JWT is in a cookie, the browser attaches it automatically, so CSRF applies; keep protection on, or at least use SameSite plus a header check. The decision depends on how the credential is sent, not on whether it is a JWT.

Output: which requests are denied? .requestMatchers("/admin/**").authenticated() then .requestMatchers("/admin/users").hasRole("ADMIN")

Any logged-in user can reach /admin/users. Rules are evaluated in order, and the first match decides, so the broad rule hides the second. Put specific rules first. In fact, Spring Security detects a rule placed after anyRequest() and fails at startup, but it cannot detect this overlap.

Why is @AuthenticationPrincipal null, or of the wrong type?

The resolver casts the principal to the parameter type, and gives null if it does not match. The principal type depends on how the user logged in: UserDetails for form login, Jwt for a resource server, OidcUser for OIDC, and a String for anonymous. For stable code, use a CurrentUser abstraction or a @CurrentSecurityContext expression.

Authorization Code vs Client Credentials: when do you use each?

Authorization Code with PKCE is for a user acting through an application: consent is involved, and the token carries the user. Client Credentials is for a machine acting for itself: batch jobs, service-to-service. If an API needs the original user, use token relay or Token Exchange, not Client Credentials.

Explain PKCE. Does it replace the client secret?

The client creates a random verifier, sends its SHA-256 hash in the authorization request, and presents the verifier when redeeming the code. It proves that whoever redeems the code is who started the flow. It does not authenticate the client. A confidential client should keep its secret too. For a public client that has no secret, PKCE is the protection.

What does state protect against? And nonce?

state binds the callback to the browser session that began the flow, stopping an attacker from injecting their own code (login CSRF). nonce binds the ID token to the session, stopping replay of a captured ID token. Spring generates and verifies both.

Why should an access token not be used as proof of login?

An access token is meant for the API, and any app that received it could present it to yours, so it does not prove the user authenticated to your client. That is the "confused deputy" issue. The ID token has aud set to your client id, so verify it instead. That is why login uses OIDC, not bare OAuth.

How would you secure a SPA with Keycloak? Where do the tokens live?

Preferred: a BFF. Spring acts as an oauth2Login client, and the browser holds an HttpOnly session cookie with CSRF protection. Spring Cloud Gateway's TokenRelay filter can attach the access token to downstream calls, so tokens never reach JavaScript. The alternative, a public client with Authorization Code + PKCE in the browser with an in-memory token, is simpler but exposes tokens to XSS.

How does a service call another service while keeping the user's identity?

Token relay: forward the same access token, if the audience allows. Better is Token Exchange (RFC 8693), to get a token scoped to the downstream service. Service identity is added by Client Credentials or mTLS. Do not trust a plain X-User-Id header unless the network strictly guarantees that only the gateway can set it.

How does Spring verify JWT keys, and what happens when the authorization server rotates them?

From issuer-uri, it finds the jwks_uri, and fetches the public keys. The token's kid selects the key. An unknown kid triggers a refresh. So during rotation, the server should publish the new key before signing with it, and keep the old key until old tokens expire.

What is the difference between @EnableWebSecurity and @EnableMethodSecurity?

@EnableWebSecurity sets up HttpSecurity and filter chains; Boot applies it automatically when the starter is present. @EnableMethodSecurity registers the AOP interceptors for annotations. It is not automatic. Without it, @PreAuthorize is silently ignored, which is a serious and quiet failure. Test that denied calls really are denied.

What is a SecurityContextRepository, and why did Spring Security 6 change saving?

It loads and saves the context between requests. In 5.x, SecurityContextPersistenceFilter saved automatically at the end, requiring response wrapping and writing sessions even when unneeded. SecurityContextHolderFilter in 6 only loads. Authentication mechanisms save explicitly. The migration trap is that custom login code stops persisting login.

How would you implement account lockout after 5 failed logins?

Listen for AuthenticationFailureBadCredentialsEvent and increment a counter in Redis or the database, with expiry. At the threshold, set locked, which UserDetails reports and the provider enforces. Listen for AuthenticationSuccessEvent to reset it. Beware that a hard lockout allows an attacker to lock out a victim, so prefer exponential delays, and combine with IP-based rate limiting and MFA.

How do you test security rules?
@WebMvcTest(OrderController.class)
@Import(SecurityConfig.class)
class OrderSecurityTest {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

  @Test void anonymousGets401() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/api/orders")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
  }
  @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "USER") void userCannotDelete() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(delete("/api/admin/orders/1").with(csrf())).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
  }
  @Test void adminWithJwt() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/api/admin/stats").with(jwt().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN"))))
       .andExpect(status().isOk());
  }
}

@WebMvcTest does not load your config by default if it is a plain @Configuration, so import it. For method security, also test with a Spring context, since mocks bypass the proxy.

What is the Log4Shell vulnerability, and why did it matter to Spring apps?

CVE-2021-44228: Log4j 2 expanded ${jndi:ldap://...} in logged strings, loading remote code. Logging a user-supplied header was enough. Spring Boot's default is Logback, so most apps were not directly affected, unless they used Log4j2. The lesson is to know your dependency tree, keep an SBOM, and be able to patch quickly.

Why is Java serialization dangerous?

ObjectInputStream.readObject builds objects and runs their readObject methods before your code sees them. A crafted byte stream can chain library classes ("gadgets") into remote code execution. Never deserialize untrusted data; use JSON with explicit DTOs and turn off Jackson default typing. If unavoidable, use ObjectInputFilter, added in Java 9.

What changed in Spring Security 7?

It ships with Spring Boot 4 and Framework 7. Deprecated parts are gone: the non-lambda DSL and and(); AntPathRequestMatcher and MvcRequestMatcher in favour of PathPatternRequestMatcher; and the OAuth2 password grant. Clear deprecation warnings under the 6.5 line first, using the preparation guide.

Design: secure a public API, an admin UI, and internal services in one platform.
  • An identity provider (Keycloak, Okta) issues tokens; users log in with Authorization Code + PKCE and MFA for admins.
  • An API gateway terminates TLS, rate-limits, and validates tokens early.
  • Each service still validates the JWT as a resource server, including audience, for zero trust.
  • Fine-grained rules live in the services, in method security and ownership queries.
  • Internal calls use Client Credentials or mTLS through a mesh.
  • The admin UI uses a BFF with server sessions, short timeouts, and CSRF protection.
  • Secrets stay in a vault, and security events go to a central log with alerts.
Why is @PostFilter a poor choice for a list endpoint?

@PostFilter("filterObject.ownerId == authentication.name") runs after the method. The database returns every row, and the filtering happens in memory. That is slow, and it breaks pagination: page 1 might show 3 items instead of 20, and the total count is wrong. Put the restriction into the query (WHERE owner_id = ?, a Specification, or a Hibernate tenant filter) and keep @PostFilter for small, already-bounded collections.

How do you accept JWTs from several Keycloak realms or identity providers?

Use JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver.fromTrustedIssuers(...) with an explicit allow-list. It picks the decoder by the token's iss claim and fetches that issuer's keys, and it rejects unknown issuers. For a dynamic tenant list, implement the resolver against a tenant table. After authentication, check that the tenant in the token matches the tenant of the requested resource, or one tenant's admin may act on another tenant's data.

What are passkeys, and why are they considered phishing-resistant?

A passkey is a WebAuthn credential: a private key on the device or synced by the platform, with the public key registered at the server. Login is a signed challenge after the user unlocks with biometrics or a PIN, so no shared secret crosses the network. The browser binds the credential to the site's origin, so a look-alike phishing domain cannot obtain a valid signature. A database leak exposes only public keys. Spring Security 6.4+ supports passkeys with http.webAuthn(...).

How would you add multi-factor authentication to a Spring app?

The simplest robust option is to delegate MFA to the identity provider (Keycloak, Okta, Entra ID) and check the token's acr or amr claim for sensitive operations. In-app, the classic approach is two steps. After the password, the user gets a partial authentication with a limited authority, such as MFA_REQUIRED. Only after a valid TOTP code or passkey do they receive their full authorities. Spring Security 7 adds built-in multi-factor support that tracks which factors the user has completed. Protect the second step with rate limiting, and provide recovery codes.

How would you implement API-key authentication in Spring Security?

Add a OncePerRequestFilter (or an AuthenticationFilter with a custom converter and provider) before the authorization filter. It reads the key from a header, looks up the hashed key, and builds an authenticated token with the client's scopes as authorities. Then it sets the token into the SecurityContextHolder, or lets the provider do this. Return 401 through the AuthenticationEntryPoint on failure. Use a separate SecurityFilterChain with securityMatcher("/partner/**"), so that key-based access does not mix with user logins. Add rotation, expiry, rate limits and audit logging.

SAML vs OpenID Connect?

Both provide single sign-on. SAML 2.0 is older and XML-based, with signed assertions sent through browser redirects or POSTs. It is still common in enterprises and in identity providers such as ADFS. OIDC is built on OAuth 2.0, uses JSON and JWTs, and suits SPAs, mobile apps and APIs. Spring Security supports SAML through saml2Login() and OIDC through oauth2Login(). A common pattern is to let Keycloak broker the SAML connection to a customer and issue OIDC tokens to your apps, so the apps speak only OIDC.

What is Spring Authorization Server, and when would you run your own?

It is the Spring project for building an OAuth 2.1 and OpenID Connect provider, with endpoints such as authorize, token, JWKS, introspection and discovery. It replaced the old Spring Security OAuth server. Use it when you need deep customization or must embed the identity provider in your product. Otherwise, a ready-made server like Keycloak or a managed service usually costs less to operate: running an authorization server means owning key rotation, consent, MFA, and the security patches.

JWT Tokens

JSON Web Token: a compact, signed, self-contained token used for stateless authentication.

// jjwt 0.12.x
SecretKey key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(Decoders.BASE64.decode(secret));   // ≥ 256-bit

String token = Jwts.builder()
    .subject(user.getUsername())
    .claim("roles", roles)
    .issuedAt(new Date())
    .expiration(new Date(System.currentTimeMillis() + 15 * 60_000))
    .signWith(key)
    .compact();

Claims claims = Jwts.parser().verifyWith(key).build()
    .parseSignedClaims(token).getPayload();         // throws if signature invalid / expired

@Component
public class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String h = req.getHeader("Authorization");
    if (h != null && h.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
      String username = jwtService.extractUsername(h.substring(7));
      if (username != null && SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() == null) {
        UserDetails ud = userDetailsService.loadUserByUsername(username);
        if (jwtService.isValid(h.substring(7), ud)) {
          var auth = new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(ud, null, ud.getAuthorities());
          auth.setDetails(new WebAuthenticationDetailsSource().buildDetails(req));
          SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(auth);
        }
      }
    }
    chain.doFilter(req, res);
  }
}

Structure in Detail

A JWT (RFC 7519) is a set of JSON claims packed in a URL-safe string. The family of standards is called JOSE: JWS (RFC 7515) is the signed form, JWE (RFC 7516) the encrypted form, JWK (RFC 7517) describes keys, and JWA (RFC 7518) lists algorithms. When people say "JWT" they nearly always mean a JWS.

Each part is Base64URL encoded: standard Base64 with + and / replaced by - and _, and no = padding, so the token is safe in URLs and headers. The signature is computed over the exact ASCII string header.payload. Real token, generated and checked with Node, signed with HS256:

eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiIsInR5cCI6IkpXVCJ9                      {"alg":"HS256","typ":"JWT"}
.eyJzdWIiOiI0MiIsInJvbGVzIjpbIlVTRVIiXSwiaWF0IjoxNzMwMDAwMDAwLCJleHAiOjE3MzAwMDA5MDB9
                                                          {"sub":"42","roles":["USER"],"iat":1730000000,"exp":1730000900}
.6Eq6ChVoSidrUOiCz2O_b5bEXatOJMkNBcReSmhNw8A              HMAC-SHA256 of the two parts above

// Anyone can read a JWS, no key needed
JSON.parse(Buffer.from(token.split('.')[1], 'base64url'))   // Node
new String(Base64.getUrlDecoder().decode(token.split("\\.")[1]), UTF_8)   // Java
Header fieldMeaningRisk
algSigning algorithmAttacker-controlled; never let it choose how you verify
typMedia type, usually JWT. at+jwt marks an access token (RFC 9068)Helps avoid confusing token types
kidWhich key signed itTreat as untrusted input; only look it up in a fixed key set
jku, x5u, jwkWhere to find the key, or the key itselfIgnore them: otherwise the attacker supplies the verifying key

A JWT is larger than a session id, and is sent on each request. Avoid stuffing it with claims: many servers and proxies limit total header size (Tomcat's default is 8 KB).

Signing Algorithms

A signature proves two things: the token came from a key holder, and it was not changed. The important question is who needs the signing key.

AlgorithmTypeKeySignature sizeNote
HS256 / 384 / 512HMAC, symmetricShared secret, at least as long as the hash: 256 bits for HS25632 bytesFast. All verifiers can also forge tokens
RS256 / 384 / 512RSA PKCS#1 v1.52048-bit or more256 bytes at 2048-bitMost widely supported; fast to verify, slow to sign
PS256RSA-PSS2048-bit or more256 bytesA more modern padding than RS256
ES256 / 384ECDSAP-256 curve64 bytesSmall tokens and keys; requires a good random source
EdDSAEd2551932-byte key64 bytesFast and hard to misuse; library support varies
noneNo signatureNone0⚠ Must be rejected
HS256RS256 / ES256
Trust modelEveryone with the key can issue tokensOnly the issuer can sign; others just verify
Key distributionA secret must reach each servicePublic keys published through a JWKS URL
RotationCoordinated deploymentPublish new key, sign with it, retire old key
Third partiesImpossibleNatural
FitsA single application that both issues and verifiesMicroservices, SSO, external consumers

Key rotation with JWKS. The issuer publishes keys at, for example, /.well-known/jwks.json. Each token's kid header selects the key. The steps are: add the new public key, wait for caches to refresh, sign with the new key, and remove the old key once its last token has expired.

{ "keys": [ { "kty": "RSA", "use": "sig", "alg": "RS256", "kid": "2026-11", "n": "0vx7...", "e": "AQAB" } ] }

A SecretKey for HS256 must be random, not a password-like phrase. Generate with openssl rand -base64 32, and keep it in a secret manager.

Claims

Beyond the registered names, RFC 7519 distinguishes public claims (registered with IANA, such as email, or collision-resistant names like a URL) and private claims agreed between parties, such as tenant. Times are NumericDate: seconds since the epoch, not milliseconds. Putting milliseconds in exp gives a token that expires tens of thousands of years from now.

A correct verifier must check all of these:

  1. The algorithm is the expected one, from your configuration, not the token.
  2. The signature, using the right key.
  3. exp, and nbf if present, with a small clock skew (30 to 60 seconds).
  4. iss: the issuer you trust.
  5. aud: it was issued for this service. Otherwise a token for a low-value service works against a high-value one.
  6. Token type, so that a refresh token cannot be used as an access token.

What to put in it: a stable user id, and short lists of roles or scopes. What not to: passwords, secrets, or personal data, since the payload is readable and may end up in logs. Roles in a token are a snapshot: if an admin is demoted, the token stays valid until exp. High-risk operations should re-check the database.

Access and Refresh Tokens

A stateless token cannot be recalled, so its lifetime is the risk window. A short lifetime reduces risk but would force constant logins. The two-token design separates these needs.

Access tokenRefresh token
PurposeCall APIsGet new access tokens
Lifetime5 to 15 minutesDays or weeks, with an absolute limit
FormatJWT, verified locallyBest as an opaque random string
Server stateNoneStored (hashed) in a database or Redis
Sent toEvery APIOnly the token endpoint
RevocableHardEasy: delete or mark the row

This gives a useful property: state only on the rare path. APIs handle thousands of requests per second with no lookup, while the refresh endpoint, called every few minutes per user, checks the database. Revoking access means refusing the next refresh, so the worst-case delay equals the access token's lifetime.

Refresh Token Rotation and Reuse Detection

A long-lived refresh token in a browser is a valuable target. Rotation means each use returns a new refresh token and invalidates the old one. A stolen token then has limited life, and theft becomes detectable: if an already-used token is presented, either the attacker or the victim is replaying it, and the server cannot tell which, so it revokes the entire family.

Race condition: two tabs may refresh at once, or a response may be lost in a bad network. The second legitimate call looks like reuse, and logs the user out. Mitigations: allow a short grace period (say 10 seconds), during which the previous token's successor can be returned, and make the client serialize refresh calls with a single in-flight promise.

Revocation Strategies

StrategyHowLatency to take effectCost
Short expiry15-minute tokensUp to 15 minutesNone
Refresh revocationDelete the refresh rowUp to access lifetimeRead on refresh only
Denylist by jtiRedis key with TTL equal to the remaining lifetimeImmediateRedis lookup per request
Token versionver claim compared with the user's current versionImmediate, per userLookup per request, cacheable
iat cutoffReject tokens issued before the user's "logged out at"Immediate, per userLookup per request
IntrospectionAsk the auth server (opaque token)ImmediateNetwork hop
Key rotationRemove the signing keyImmediate for allEveryone is logged out
Interview: A per-request denylist looks like a return to server-side state, and it is. The honest answer is that immediate revocation always needs some shared state. The design trade-off is the size of that state: a small denylist of revoked tokens is cheaper than a session for every user. A denylist entry can also expire with the token.

Where to Store Tokens in a Browser

LocationXSS can steal it?CSRF risk?Survives reload?Note
localStorageYesNoYes, and it is never cleared by itselfSimple; a single XSS gives persistent theft
sessionStorageYesNoYes, in that tabA slightly shorter exposure
JavaScript memoryHarder; malicious script can still hook callsNoNo: use a refresh cookieGood for access tokens
HttpOnly cookieCannot be read; but a script can still send requestsYes; need SameSite and a CSRF tokenYesGood for refresh tokens
BFF server sessionNo token in the browser at allHandled as a normal sessionYesThe strongest; needs a backend

A common design: keep the access token in memory, and the refresh token in a cookie restricted to the refresh path.

ResponseCookie cookie = ResponseCookie.from("__Host-rt", refreshToken)
    .httpOnly(true)          // not readable by JavaScript
    .secure(true)            // HTTPS only
    .sameSite("Strict")      // not sent on cross-site requests
    .path("/")               // __Host- requires path=/ and no Domain
    .maxAge(Duration.ofDays(14))
    .build();
response.addHeader(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie.toString());

The __Host- prefix makes the browser enforce Secure, no Domain, and path=/. If you prefer to limit the cookie to /auth/refresh, drop that prefix, or use __Secure-. SameSite=Strict requires the SPA and API to be on the same site; if they are not, you need SameSite=None; Secure and proper CSRF protection, plus withCredentials on the client.

Gotcha: ⚠ "HttpOnly solves XSS" is a misconception. It stops the theft of the token, but a script on the page can still act as the user. Prevent XSS first: output encoding, Content Security Policy, and dependency hygiene.

Attacks and Defences

AttackHow it worksDefence
alg: noneChange the header to {"alg":"none"} (eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0), edit the payload, drop the signature. A naive library accepts itFix the allowed algorithm on the server
Key confusion (RS256 to HS256)The server uses RSA, and its public key is public. The attacker sets alg: HS256 and signs with the public key's bytes as the HMAC secret. A generic verify(token, key) does an HMAC with that key, and passesTie the key to one algorithm. Never read alg to choose the verification method
Weak secretOffline brute force on a captured token, with hashcat -m 16500. No server contact neededA 256-bit random secret, or asymmetric keys
Signature not checkedThe code decodes without verifying, such as calling a decode function instead of verifyUse one parser that verifies; review the code
kid injectionkid reaches a file path or SQL query: ../../dev/null gives an empty keyLook it up in a map of known keys
jku/x5u/jwk abuseHeader points to the attacker's key, or causes SSRFIgnore them; use a configured JWKS URL
Audience confusionA token for service A is replayed on service B with the same issuerCheck aud
Token theft by XSSA script reads localStorageCSP, encoding, memory or cookie storage
Leak via URL or logsTokens in query strings reach logs and referrersHeaders only; mask logs
ReplayA captured token is reused until expiryTLS, short lifetime, sender-constrained tokens: DPoP (RFC 9449) or mTLS (RFC 8705)
Library flaws"Psychic signatures", CVE-2022-21449: Java 15 to 18 accepted all-zero ECDSA signatures, so ES256 could be forgedPatch the JDK and libraries
// The confusion bug, as pseudo-code
String alg = header.get("alg");
Key key = publicKey;                       // "our verification key"
verifier = Signature.forAlg(alg);          // BUG: the attacker chooses the algorithm
verifier.verify(data, sig, key);

// Safe with JJWT: an RSA public key can only verify with RSA algorithms
Jwts.parser().verifyWith(rsaPublicKey).build().parseSignedClaims(token);

Complete Spring Implementation with a Custom Filter

This is the hand-rolled version with JJWT 0.12 and rotating refresh tokens. Use it to understand the mechanism, or where an external authorization server is not an option. The Security section shows the shorter variant built on Spring's resource server. The access token is an HS256 JWT. The refresh token is opaque, stored hashed, and rotated with reuse detection.

1. Dependencies and properties

<dependency><groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId><artifactId>jjwt-api</artifactId><version>0.12.6</version></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId><artifactId>jjwt-impl</artifactId><version>0.12.6</version><scope>runtime</scope></dependency>
<dependency><groupId>io.jsonwebtoken</groupId><artifactId>jjwt-jackson</artifactId><version>0.12.6</version><scope>runtime</scope></dependency>
app.jwt:
  secret: ${JWT_SECRET}              # base64, at least 32 random bytes
  issuer: https://api.shop.com
  audience: shop-api
  access-ttl: 15m
  refresh-ttl: 14d
@ConfigurationProperties("app.jwt")
public record JwtProperties(String secret, String issuer, String audience,
                            Duration accessTtl, Duration refreshTtl) { }

2. JwtService

@Service
public class JwtService {
  private final SecretKey key;
  private final JwtProperties props;
  private final JwtParser parser;

  public JwtService(JwtProperties props) {
    this.props = props;
    this.key = Keys.hmacShaKeyFor(Decoders.BASE64.decode(props.secret()));  // rejects too-short keys
    this.parser = Jwts.parser()
        .verifyWith(key)                  // the key decides the algorithm family, not the token
        .requireIssuer(props.issuer())
        .requireAudience(props.audience())
        .clockSkewSeconds(30)
        .build();
  }

  public String issueAccess(long userId, Collection<String> roles) {
    Instant now = Instant.now();
    return Jwts.builder()
        .id(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
        .issuer(props.issuer())
        .audience().add(props.audience()).and()
        .subject(Long.toString(userId))
        .claim("roles", roles)
        .issuedAt(Date.from(now))
        .expiration(Date.from(now.plus(props.accessTtl())))
        .signWith(key, Jwts.SIG.HS256)
        .compact();
  }

  public Claims parse(String token) {     // throws JwtException if invalid or expired
    return parser.parseSignedClaims(token).getPayload();
  }
}

3. The filter

The existing example in this section assumes the token parses. Here, a bad token must give a clean 401 rather than a 500, and public endpoints must keep working. It reads claims rather than hitting the database for each request.

public class JwtAuthFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {     // not a @Component, added to the chain by hand
  private static final String PREFIX = "Bearer ";
  private final JwtService jwt;
  private final AuthenticationEntryPoint entryPoint;

  public JwtAuthFilter(JwtService jwt, AuthenticationEntryPoint entryPoint) {
    this.jwt = jwt;
    this.entryPoint = entryPoint;
  }

  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String header = req.getHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);
    if (header == null || !header.startsWith(PREFIX)) {
      chain.doFilter(req, res);                               // anonymous; AuthorizationFilter decides
      return;
    }
    try {
      Claims c = jwt.parse(header.substring(PREFIX.length()));
      @SuppressWarnings("unchecked") List<String> roles = c.get("roles", List.class);
      var authorities = roles.stream().map(r -> new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_" + r)).toList();
      var auth = UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.authenticated(c.getSubject(), null, authorities);
      auth.setDetails(new WebAuthenticationDetailsSource().buildDetails(req));

      SecurityContext ctx = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
      ctx.setAuthentication(auth);
      SecurityContextHolder.setContext(ctx);
    } catch (JwtException | IllegalArgumentException e) {     // expired, tampered, malformed
      SecurityContextHolder.clearContext();
      entryPoint.commence(req, res, new BadCredentialsException("Invalid token", e));
      return;                                                 // do not continue the chain
    }
    chain.doFilter(req, res);
  }
}

4. Security configuration

@Configuration @EnableWebSecurity @EnableMethodSecurity
@EnableConfigurationProperties(JwtProperties.class)
class SecurityConfig {

  @Bean AuthenticationEntryPoint jsonEntryPoint(ObjectMapper mapper) {
    return (req, res, ex) -> {
      ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Missing or invalid token");
      res.setStatus(401);
      res.setHeader(HttpHeaders.WWW_AUTHENTICATE, "Bearer");
      res.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
      mapper.writeValue(res.getOutputStream(), p);
    };
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http, JwtService jwt, AuthenticationEntryPoint entryPoint) throws Exception {
    return http
        .csrf(c -> c.disable())                               // Bearer header; see the note on /auth/refresh
        .sessionManagement(s -> s.sessionCreationPolicy(SessionCreationPolicy.STATELESS))
        .exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(entryPoint))
        .authorizeHttpRequests(a -> a
            .requestMatchers("/auth/**", "/error").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .addFilterBefore(new JwtAuthFilter(jwt, entryPoint), UsernamePasswordAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .build();
  }

  @Bean PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(12); }

  @Bean AuthenticationManager manager(AuthenticationConfiguration c) throws Exception {
    return c.getAuthenticationManager();
  }
}
Gotcha: Disabling CSRF is correct for Bearer-header calls, but /auth/refresh and /auth/logout authenticate by cookie, so they need their own protection. Here that is SameSite=Strict on the cookie plus a required X-Requested-With header in step 6. A cross-site form cannot set a custom header, and a cross-origin script triggers a preflight that CORS refuses.

5. Refresh tokens with rotation

@Entity @Table(name = "refresh_token", indexes = @Index(columnList = "tokenHash", unique = true))
public class RefreshToken {
  @Id @GeneratedValue Long id;
  String tokenHash;              // SHA-256 of the raw token: a DB leak reveals nothing usable
  long userId;
  UUID familyId;                 // all tokens descended from one login
  Instant expiresAt;
  Instant usedAt;                // set on rotation
  boolean revoked;
}

public class RefreshReuseException extends RuntimeException { }

public record TokenPair(String access, String refresh) { }

@Service
public class RefreshService {
  private final RefreshTokenRepository repo;
  private final JwtService jwt;
  private final JwtProperties props;
  private final UserRepository users;
  private final SecureRandom random = new SecureRandom();

  // constructor omitted

  @Transactional
  public TokenPair login(AppUser u) { return mint(u, UUID.randomUUID()); }

  // noRollbackFor is essential: the family revocation must commit, although the method throws
  @Transactional(noRollbackFor = RefreshReuseException.class)
  public TokenPair rotate(String raw) {
    RefreshToken old = repo.findForUpdateByTokenHash(sha256(raw))   // pessimistic lock against races
        .orElseThrow(() -> new BadCredentialsException("unknown token"));

    if (old.usedAt != null || old.revoked) {
      repo.revokeFamily(old.familyId);
      throw new RefreshReuseException();
    }
    if (old.expiresAt.isBefore(Instant.now())) throw new BadCredentialsException("expired");

    old.usedAt = Instant.now();
    return mint(users.getReferenceById(old.userId), old.familyId);
  }

  @Transactional
  public void logout(String raw) {
    repo.findByTokenHash(sha256(raw)).ifPresent(t -> repo.revokeFamily(t.familyId));
  }

  private TokenPair mint(AppUser u, UUID family) {
    byte[] bytes = new byte[32];
    random.nextBytes(bytes);
    String raw = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString(bytes);

    RefreshToken t = new RefreshToken();
    t.tokenHash = sha256(raw);
    t.userId = u.getId();
    t.familyId = family;
    t.expiresAt = Instant.now().plus(props.refreshTtl());
    repo.save(t);
    return new TokenPair(jwt.issueAccess(u.getId(), u.roleNames()), raw);
  }

  private static String sha256(String s) {
    try {
      byte[] d = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256").digest(s.getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
      return HexFormat.of().formatHex(d);
    } catch (NoSuchAlgorithmException e) { throw new IllegalStateException(e); }
  }
}

A refresh token may be hashed with fast SHA-256 rather than BCrypt, because it is 256 bits of randomness and cannot be guessed. Slow hashing protects low-entropy human passwords.

6. The controller

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/auth")
class AuthController {
  private static final String COOKIE = "refresh_token";
  private final AuthenticationManager manager;
  private final RefreshService refresh;
  private final UserRepository users;

  // constructor omitted

  @PostMapping("/login")
  ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> login(@Valid @RequestBody LoginRequest r) {
    manager.authenticate(UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.unauthenticated(r.email(), r.password()));
    return respond(refresh.login(users.findByEmail(r.email()).orElseThrow()));
  }

  @PostMapping("/refresh")
  ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> refresh(@CookieValue(COOKIE) String raw,
                                             @RequestHeader("X-Requested-With") String csrfGuard) {
    return respond(refresh.rotate(raw));
  }

  @PostMapping("/logout")
  ResponseEntity<Void> logout(@CookieValue(name = COOKIE, required = false) String raw,
                              @RequestHeader("X-Requested-With") String csrfGuard) {
    if (raw != null) refresh.logout(raw);
    return ResponseEntity.noContent().header(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie("", Duration.ZERO).toString()).build();
  }

  private ResponseEntity<Map<String, Object>> respond(TokenPair p) {
    return ResponseEntity.ok()
        .header(HttpHeaders.SET_COOKIE, cookie(p.refresh(), Duration.ofDays(14)).toString())
        .header(HttpHeaders.CACHE_CONTROL, "no-store")
        .body(Map.of("accessToken", p.access(), "tokenType", "Bearer", "expiresIn", 900));
  }

  private ResponseCookie cookie(String v, Duration age) {
    return ResponseCookie.from(COOKIE, v).httpOnly(true).secure(true).sameSite("Strict")
        .path("/auth").maxAge(age).build();
  }

  @ExceptionHandler({AuthenticationException.class, RefreshReuseException.class})
  ProblemDetail denied(RuntimeException e) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED, "Authentication failed");
  }
}

The client flow: on a 401 from an API, call /auth/refresh once, store the new access token, and replay the failed request. Concurrent 401s must share one refresh call. If the refresh fails, redirect to login.

7. Testing

class JwtServiceTest {
  JwtProperties p = new JwtProperties(TEST_B64_SECRET, "iss", "aud", Duration.ofMinutes(15), Duration.ofDays(1));
  JwtService svc = new JwtService(p);

  @Test void roundTrip() {
    assertThat(svc.parse(svc.issueAccess(42, List.of("USER"))).getSubject()).isEqualTo("42");
  }
  @Test void tamperedPayloadRejected() {
    String[] parts = svc.issueAccess(42, List.of("USER")).split("\\.");
    String forged = parts[0] + "." + Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
        .encodeToString("{\"sub\":\"1\"}".getBytes(UTF_8)) + "." + parts[2];
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> svc.parse(forged)).isInstanceOf(SignatureException.class);
  }
  @Test void noneAlgRejected() {
    String header = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString("{\"alg\":\"none\"}".getBytes(UTF_8));
    String body   = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding().encodeToString("{\"sub\":\"1\"}".getBytes(UTF_8));
    assertThatThrownBy(() -> svc.parse(header + "." + body + ".")).isInstanceOf(JwtException.class);
  }
}

JWT for WebSockets and Server-Sent Events

The browser WebSocket and EventSource APIs cannot set an Authorization header. The options are:

  • A cookie on the handshake. This works if the API shares the site, but check the Origin header on the handshake, because WebSockets have no CORS protection (cross-site WebSocket hijacking).
  • A token in the STOMP CONNECT frame, validated in a ChannelInterceptor. It is the most common choice with Spring and SockJS/STOMP clients.
  • A short-lived, single-use ticket in the query string, obtained through an authenticated REST call. Never put the real access token in the URL, because URLs end up in proxy and server logs.

The socket lives longer than the token. Either close connections when exp passes and let the client reconnect with a fresh token, or ask the client to re-authenticate in-band.

@Configuration
@EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
class WsAuthConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {
  private final JwtDecoder decoder;
  private final JwtAuthenticationConverter converter = new JwtAuthenticationConverter();
  WsAuthConfig(JwtDecoder decoder) { this.decoder = decoder; }

  @Override
  public void configureClientInboundChannel(ChannelRegistration reg) {
    reg.interceptors(new ChannelInterceptor() {
      @Override
      public Message<?> preSend(Message<?> msg, MessageChannel ch) {
        var acc = MessageHeaderAccessor.getAccessor(msg, StompHeaderAccessor.class);
        if (acc != null && StompCommand.CONNECT.equals(acc.getCommand())) {
          String h = acc.getFirstNativeHeader("Authorization");
          if (h == null || !h.startsWith("Bearer ")) throw new BadCredentialsException("Missing token");
          Jwt jwt = decoder.decode(h.substring(7));          // checks signature, exp, iss, aud
          acc.setUser(converter.convert(jwt));                // later frames use this principal
        }
        return msg;
      }
    });
  }
}

Opaque Access Tokens, Introspection and the Phantom Token Pattern

An access token does not have to be a JWT. An opaque token is a random reference. The resource server asks the authorization server what it means, through token introspection (RFC 7662). This gives instant revocation and reveals nothing to the client, but every request needs a network call. Caching the result reduces the cost but delays revocation again.

spring:
  security:
    oauth2:
      resourceserver:
        opaquetoken:
          introspection-uri: https://idp.example.com/oauth2/introspect
          client-id: orders-api
          client-secret: ${INTROSPECTION_SECRET}
# and in the chain: .oauth2ResourceServer(o -> o.opaqueToken(Customizer.withDefaults()))

The phantom token pattern combines both. External clients get opaque tokens, so no claims leak to browsers or third parties. The API gateway introspects each one, usually with a cache, and forwards a JWT to internal services, which then validate it locally. In short: privacy and revocation at the edge, speed inside.

ID Token vs Access Token

ID token (OIDC)Access token (OAuth2)
PurposeTells the client who logged in and howLets the client call an API
Audience (aud)The client idThe API or resource server
FormatAlways a JWTA JWT or an opaque token
Validated byThe client, including nonceThe resource server, including aud and scopes
Send to APIs?NoYes, as a Bearer token

Interview Questions — JWT

What is JWT and what are its three parts?

A JWT is a compact, URL-safe token: Header (alg, typ) . Payload (claims) . Signature. The server verifies the signature, so it can trust the claims without a DB or session lookup. That's what makes it stateless.

Is JWT encrypted? Where is it stored?

A signed JWT (JWS) is only Base64URL-encoded, so anyone can read it. Don't put secrets in it. Use JWE if you need encryption. Storage: an HttpOnly + Secure + SameSite cookie protects against XSS (add CSRF protection). Memory or localStorage is simpler but exposed to XSS. A common pattern is the access token in memory and the refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie.

Registered claims?

iss (issuer), sub (subject or user id), aud (audience), exp (expiry), nbf (not before), iat (issued at), jti (unique token id, used for revocation lists). You can add custom claims such as roles or tenant.

How do you log out / revoke a JWT?

JWTs can't be "deleted", because they're valid until exp. Options: short expiry plus refresh tokens, a denylist of jti values in Redis until expiry, a per-user token version or "password changed at" claim, and rotating and revoking refresh tokens in the DB.

Session-based vs token-based authentication?
SessionJWT
Server stores the session; the client holds a JSESSIONID cookieServer stores nothing; the token carries the state
Easy to revokeHard to revoke
Scaling needs sticky sessions or a shared store (Redis)Scales horizontally; good for microservices and mobile
HS256 vs RS256?

HS256 is symmetric: the same secret signs and verifies, so every verifier has to know the secret. RS256 is asymmetric: the auth server signs with a private key, and services verify with the public key published at a JWKS endpoint. Prefer RS256 in microservices.

Common JWT security mistakes?

Accepting alg: none · weak secrets · not checking exp/aud/iss · long-lived access tokens · putting PII in the payload · sending tokens over plain HTTP · storing them in localStorage without XSS protection.

Why are JWTs Base64URL and not plain Base64?

Standard Base64 uses +, / and =, which have meanings in URLs and need escaping. Base64URL uses - and _, and removes padding, so a token can go in a URL, form or header unchanged. Encoding is reversible, and gives no confidentiality.

Can you change the payload of a JWT? What happens?

Anyone can decode, edit and re-encode it. But the signature covers the original bytes, so verification fails without the key. Even changing whitespace in the JSON invalidates it. So a JWT is tamper-evident, not tamper-proof, and it is secret only if encrypted.

JWS vs JWE: when would you use encryption?

JWS provides integrity; JWE provides confidentiality. Use JWE, or better, an opaque token, if claims must be hidden from the client or from intermediaries. A token can be nested: signed, then encrypted. JWE adds cost and complexity, so first ask whether that data needs to be in the token.

Which signing algorithm would you choose today, and why?

For one app that issues and verifies, HS256 with a strong random secret is adequate. For several services or third parties, use asymmetric: RS256 for compatibility, ES256 or EdDSA for smaller tokens, in a stack that supports them. The choice is about key distribution, more than about speed.

Is RS256 slower? Does it matter?

RSA signing is slow, on the order of milliseconds; RSA verification is fast, because the public exponent is small. HMAC is the fastest in both directions. ECDSA signing is fast, and its verifying is slower than RSA's. Tokens are signed rarely and verified often, so RS256 suits that pattern. In practice, for a typical API, this cost is small compared with I/O.

How does a resource server know which public key to use?

The token's header has a kid, and the server fetches the issuer's JWKS, usually found through OIDC discovery. It caches keys, and refreshes on an unknown kid. The JWKS URL must come from your configuration, not from the token.

Explain the algorithm confusion attack in detail.

The server signs with RS256. An attacker takes the public key, sets alg to HS256, and computes an HMAC using the bytes of that public key as the secret. A flawed verifier reads alg, and calls HMAC with its "verification key", which is that same public key, so the signature matches. The attacker can now forge any token. The fix is to pin the algorithm to the key, as modern libraries do with typed keys.

Why is the aud claim important?

All services trusting one issuer accept its signature. Without an audience check, a token for a weak service, even for a compromised one, is accepted by the payments service. The check binds a token to its intended recipient. Spring's resource server does not validate it unless you set audiences.

Why not just make the JWT long-lived?

A JWT cannot be recalled without extra state. A 30-day token that leaks is a 30-day breach, and its claims go stale, such as roles after a demotion. Short-lived access tokens with server-tracked refresh tokens keep the fast path stateless while preserving control.

Why make the refresh token opaque rather than a JWT?

A refresh token is checked against the database anyway, for revocation and rotation, so a self-contained format adds nothing. An opaque random value reveals no data, cannot be mistaken for an access token, and is simple. Store only its hash.

Explain refresh token rotation. What attack does it address?

Each refresh returns a new token and marks the old one used. It limits the value of a stolen token. If an old token reappears, both parties have the same chain, so the server revokes the family, forcing login. It addresses long-term undetected token theft, especially in public clients without a client secret.

In a rotation implementation, revokeFamily runs and then an exception is thrown. What can go wrong?

With a plain @Transactional, the runtime exception rolls back the transaction, undoing the revocation. The attacker's family stays valid. Use noRollbackFor, return a result rather than throwing, or do the revocation in a REQUIRES_NEW method on another bean.

Two browser tabs refresh at the same moment and the user is logged out. Why, and how do you fix it?

Both tabs send the same refresh cookie. The first rotates it; the second looks like reuse. Fix on the client with one shared in-flight refresh, or a cross-tab lock such as the Web Locks API. On the server, allow a short grace window, and lock the row. Log these so that you can distinguish them from real attacks.

How do you log out a user everywhere?

Revoke all the user's refresh token families. For access tokens, bump a tokenVersion on the user, or store a cutoff time, and reject older tokens; this needs a cached per-request lookup. If you accept up to 15 minutes of delay, revoking refresh tokens alone is enough.

How would you implement a jti denylist efficiently?

On logout, write SET denylist:{jti} 1 EX {remaining seconds} to Redis. The filter checks EXISTS after verifying the signature, not before, so that attackers cannot cause lookups cheaply. The TTL frees entries automatically. For scale, a Bloom filter or local cache can avoid some lookups. If Redis is down, you must decide whether to fail open or closed; for high-value APIs, fail closed.

localStorage or cookie for tokens?

There is no universally right answer; each has a risk. localStorage is exposed to XSS, with persistent theft. Cookies are exposed to CSRF, which is well understood and can be mitigated with SameSite and tokens. So: access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, or use a BFF with no tokens in the browser. State that XSS still lets an attacker act on the page.

Does putting a JWT in a cookie bring back CSRF?

Yes. CSRF depends on automatic sending, and cookies are sent automatically, whatever they hold. Use SameSite, plus an anti-CSRF token or custom header. Bearer-in-header JWTs are immune only because JavaScript must attach them explicitly.

Output: what does the first segment of eyJhbGciOiJub25lIiwidHlwIjoiSldUIn0.xxx. decode to, and what should a server do?

The first part decodes to {"alg":"none","typ":"JWT"}, which was checked with Node. That header indicates an unsigned token. A correct server rejects it, even if the payload looks fine and the third segment is empty. JJWT's parseSignedClaims throws, since there is no signature.

Why does an expired token produce a 500 in many hand-written filters?

JJWT throws ExpiredJwtException from the filter. Filters run outside DispatcherServlet, so @ControllerAdvice never sees it, and it is not an AuthenticationException, so ExceptionTranslationFilter rethrows it. The result is a 500. Catch JwtException in the filter and call the entry point.

Should the JWT filter load the user from the database on each request?

The trade-off is freshness against statelessness. Claims only: fast, no lookup, stale for up to the TTL. Loading the user: detects disabled accounts immediately, but adds a query to each request, and removes the main benefit. A middle path uses claims, with a small cached check for high-risk operations.

Clock differences between servers cause random 401s. What do you do?

Run NTP on all hosts, and allow a small leeway, as with clockSkewSeconds(30); Spring's default skew is 60 seconds. A large leeway extends the token's real lifetime, so keep it small.

Session cookie vs JWT for a typical company web application?

For one server-rendered or same-site app, a session is simpler and easier to revoke. Stateless JWTs help where tokens cross domains or services, for mobile clients, or with a separate identity provider. "JWT because it scales" is weak: Spring Session with Redis scales well, too. A stateful session is often right, and the question is about revocation and topology.

How would you make a stolen access token useless?

Bind it to the client: DPoP (RFC 9449) has the client sign each request with a private key, with the public key's thumbprint in the token. mTLS (RFC 8705) binds it to a client certificate. A thief with only the token cannot produce the proof. Without these, a bearer token is usable by whoever holds it.

What is the difference between JWT and PASETO?

PASETO is an alternative token format that fixes the algorithm by version, so there is no alg header to attack. It removes the classic confusion and none bugs, by design. JWT is the established standard, and needed for OIDC interoperability, and those bugs are solved by correct libraries.

Design: authentication for a web app, a mobile app, and 10 microservices.
  • Use an identity provider with OIDC, Authorization Code + PKCE for both clients.
  • Web: BFF with a cookie session. Mobile: refresh tokens in the Keychain or Keystore, with rotation.
  • Access tokens: JWT, 5 to 15 minutes, ES256 or RS256, with aud per API, and keys from JWKS.
  • A gateway validates and rate-limits; each service validates again.
  • Service-to-service uses client credentials or token exchange.
  • Logout revokes refresh tokens; critical operations re-check state in the database.
How do you authenticate a WebSocket connection with a JWT?

The browser WebSocket API cannot send an Authorization header. With STOMP, send Authorization: Bearer ... in the CONNECT frame headers. In a ChannelInterceptor on the inbound channel, decode it with the JwtDecoder and call accessor.setUser(...). Then message-level security (@EnableWebSocketSecurity) can authorize destinations. Alternatives are a same-site cookie with an Origin check on the handshake, or a short-lived one-time ticket in the URL. Handle token expiry on long-lived connections.

Opaque access tokens vs JWT access tokens?

JWT: verified locally with a cached public key, so it is fast and needs no network call. But it is hard to revoke before exp, and its claims are readable by anyone who holds it. Opaque: revocation is immediate, and nothing leaks. But every check is an introspection call, which adds latency and makes the authorization server a dependency on the request path. Big platforms often use both: opaque outside and JWT inside (the phantom token pattern).

Should the Angular app send the ID token or the access token to the API?

Always the access token. The ID token's audience is the client app. It is meant for the client to learn who logged in, and it carries no API scopes. An API that accepts ID tokens can be fed a token issued to any client of the same identity provider. The resource server must check that aud is the API. 💡 With the BFF pattern, the browser holds neither token, only a session cookie.

An admin removes a user's ADMIN role, but the user's JWT still says ADMIN. What do you do?

The token is a snapshot of the user's rights. The options are:

  • Short access-token lifetimes (5 to 15 minutes), so the change applies at the next refresh. Make the refresh endpoint re-read the roles from the database.
  • A token version or "roles changed at" value per user. Compare it with the token's iat in a cheap cached check, and reject older tokens.
  • Revoke the user's refresh tokens and add the current jti to a denylist.
  • For highly sensitive operations, check permissions in the database rather than trusting claims.
Why should a JWT never be put in a URL query parameter?

URLs are recorded in many places: web server and proxy access logs, browser history, bookmarks, analytics, and the Referer header sent to other sites. Anyone with access to those can replay the token until it expires. Use the Authorization header or a secure cookie. If a URL is unavoidable (a download link or WebSocket handshake), use a dedicated, short-lived, single-use, narrowly scoped ticket, not the access token.

In a microservice chain, should every service validate the JWT, or only the gateway?

Every service should validate it (zero trust). Local verification with cached JWKS keys costs microseconds. Trusting a header like X-User-Id from "inside the network" means any compromised pod, or a request that bypasses the gateway, can impersonate any user. The gateway handles coarse checks such as authentication, rate limits and routing. Each service checks iss, aud, exp and its own fine-grained authorization. For calls between services, forward the user token or exchange it for a down-scoped token. Do not invent your own headers.

REST API Design HTTP

Resources, HTTP methods, status codes, idempotency, versioning, pagination, HATEOAS, and documentation.

MethodUseIdempotentSafeTypical success code
GETRead a resource or collectionYesYes200
POSTCreate, or trigger an actionNoNo201 + Location
PUTReplace the whole resource (or upsert)YesNo200 / 204
PATCHPartial updateNot guaranteedNo200 / 204
DELETERemoveYesNo204
HEAD / OPTIONSHeaders only / supported methods (CORS preflight)YesYes200
Status familyCodes to know
2xx Success200 OK · 201 Created · 202 Accepted (async) · 204 No Content
3xx Redirect301 Moved Permanently · 302 Found · 304 Not Modified (ETag cache)
4xx Client error400 Bad Request · 401 Unauthorized (not authenticated) · 403 Forbidden (no permission) · 404 Not Found · 405 Method Not Allowed · 409 Conflict · 415 Unsupported Media Type · 422 Unprocessable · 429 Too Many Requests
5xx Server error500 Internal Server Error · 502 Bad Gateway · 503 Service Unavailable · 504 Gateway Timeout

REST Constraints in Depth

REST was defined by Roy Fielding in his 2000 dissertation as the architectural style behind the Web. It is a set of constraints, not a protocol or a standard, and strictly speaking is not tied to HTTP, although HTTP is where everyone uses it. Each constraint trades something away to gain a property.

ConstraintMeaningGainPractical consequence
Client-serverUI and data storage are separateIndependent evolutionThe Angular app and API deploy separately
StatelessEach request has all the needed context; no client session on the serverAny instance can serve any request; easy scalingAuthentication travels with each call. Resource state in a database is fine; conversation state is not
CacheableResponses state whether they may be cachedFewer round tripsCache-Control, ETag
Uniform interfaceOne generic way to interactGeneric tools work everywhereSame methods and status codes on all resources
Layered systemA client cannot tell whether it talks to the origin or an intermediaryGateways, CDNs, load balancersDo not rely on client IP without forwarded headers
Code on demand (optional)Server may send executable codeExtensible clientsJavaScript on the web

The uniform interface has four parts: identification of resources (URIs), manipulation through representations (you change a resource by sending JSON that describes it, not by touching it directly), self-descriptive messages (media types and headers tell how to process each message), and HATEOAS (responses link to what can happen next).

Interview: Most "REST APIs" are really JSON over HTTP, at Richardson level 2. Saying so, and explaining why that is fine for most internal APIs, is a stronger answer than claiming full REST compliance.

Richardson Maturity Model

Leonard Richardson's model grades how fully an API uses the web. Fielding himself says only the top level counts as REST.

LevelIdeaExample
0: The swamp of POXOne URI, one method; HTTP is only a tunnelPOST /api with {"action":"getOrder","id":7}. SOAP and many RPC APIs
1: ResourcesSeparate URIs, usually still one verbPOST /orders/7 with {"action":"cancel"}
2: HTTP verbsMethods and status codes used correctlyGET /orders/7, DELETE /orders/7, 201, 404, 409
3: HypermediaResponses contain links that drive the workflow"_links": {"cancel": {"href": "/orders/7/cancel"}}

HTTP Methods: Full Semantics

RFC 9110 defines the semantics. Safe means the client does not request a state change, so a crawler can follow it. Idempotent means N identical requests have the same effect on the server as one, so a client can retry after a timeout. Every safe method is idempotent.

MethodSafeIdempotentCacheableRequest bodyExample
GETYesYesYesNo defined meaning, avoidGET /orders/7
HEADYesYesYesAvoidLike GET with no body: size or existence check
OPTIONSYesYesNoRareCORS preflight, Allow header
TRACEYesYesNoNoEcho, generally disabled for security
PUTNoYesNoYesPUT /users/7/avatar: full replacement, or create at a client-known URI
DELETENoYesNoAvoidDELETE /orders/7
POSTNoNoOnly with explicit freshness; rareYesCreate under a collection; process something
PATCHNoNot by definitionRareYesPartial update
CONNECTNoNoNoNoTunnel through a proxy
  • Idempotent does not mean same response. The first DELETE /orders/7 returns 204; the second returns 404. The server state is the same, so it is idempotent.
  • Idempotent does not mean no side effects. A PUT may update a modifiedAt column, or write a log line. What counts is the state the client intended.
  • PATCH can be idempotent if it sets values ({"status":"PAID"}). It is not if it uses an instruction such as "add 5 to balance".
  • Safe is about intent. A GET that writes a metrics row is still safe. A GET /orders/7/delete violates the method, and a crawler or link prefetch could fire it.

PATCH formats. JSON Merge Patch (RFC 7396, application/merge-patch+json): send a partial object; null removes a field. It is simple but cannot set a value to null, or change one element in an array. JSON Patch (RFC 6902, application/json-patch+json): a list of operations, so it is more powerful and more complex.

PATCH /users/7                          PATCH /users/7
Content-Type: application/merge-patch+json   Content-Type: application/json-patch+json

{ "phone": null, "city": "Pune" }       [ { "op": "test", "path": "/ver", "value": 3 },
                                          { "op": "replace", "path": "/city", "value": "Pune" },
                                          { "op": "remove", "path": "/phone" } ]

Status Codes: the Complete Working Set

CodeNameUse it when
200OKSuccess with a body
201CreatedA resource was created. Add Location
202AcceptedQueued, not yet finished
204No ContentSuccess with no body: delete, or an update returning nothing
206Partial ContentAnswer to a Range request
207Multi-StatusWebDAV origin; used for bulk results that differ per item
301 / 308Moved Permanently / Permanent RedirectThe URL changed. 308 keeps the method; 301 may turn POST into GET
302 / 307Found / Temporary RedirectTemporary. 307 keeps the method
303See OtherAfter a POST, fetch the result here with GET
304Not ModifiedThe conditional GET matched; use the cached copy
400Bad RequestMalformed syntax, or validation failure
401UnauthorizedNot authenticated. Must include WWW-Authenticate
403ForbiddenAuthenticated, no permission
404Not FoundNo such resource. Can also hide existence from unauthorized callers
405Method Not AllowedResource exists, method does not. Must include Allow
406Not AcceptableCannot produce any format in Accept
408Request TimeoutThe client was too slow sending
409ConflictConflicts with current state: duplicate, invalid transition
410GoneRemoved on purpose, and permanently
412Precondition FailedIf-Match failed: a lost-update guard
413Content Too LargeBody over the limit
415Unsupported Media TypeCannot read the Content-Type
422Unprocessable ContentWell-formed but semantically invalid
428Precondition RequiredYou require If-Match, and it was missing
429Too Many RequestsRate limit. Add Retry-After
431Request Header Fields Too LargeHeaders over the limit: often a big cookie or JWT
500Internal Server ErrorA bug or unhandled failure
501Not ImplementedThe server does not support the method at all
502Bad GatewayA proxy got a bad response from upstream
503Service UnavailableOverloaded or down; add Retry-After
504Gateway TimeoutA proxy timed out waiting for upstream

Common judgement calls:

  • 400 vs 422: teams differ. A common rule is 400 for unparseable JSON, and 422 for valid JSON failing business validation. Spring's default for validation is 400. Consistency matters more than the choice.
  • Empty search result: 200 with [], not 404. The collection exists.
  • 409 vs 412: 409 for a state conflict; 412 when a precondition header failed.
  • 403 vs 404: returning 404 for a resource the user may not see avoids confirming that it exists.
  • 200 with an error body: avoid it. Intermediaries, retries and monitoring depend on the status.
  • A retry guide: 5xx and 429 may be retried with backoff; for 4xx, fix the request first. Retry 500 on non-idempotent methods only with an idempotency key.

URI and Representation Design

GET    /orders                     list
POST   /orders                     create
GET    /orders/42                  read one
GET    /orders/42/items            sub-collection
PUT    /orders/42/shipping-address singleton sub-resource
POST   /orders/42/cancellation     action modelled as a resource
GET    /users/me                   current user alias
POST   /orders/search              complex search with a body; treat like a safe read
  • Nesting: one level is usually enough. Prefer /items/9 to /customers/1/orders/42/items/9, as an item has its own identity.
  • Identifiers: sequential ids leak business volume and invite enumeration. UUIDs or ULIDs avoid this, but ownership checks are still required. UUIDv7 stays roughly time-ordered, which is kinder to database indexes.
  • Actions: try a state field or a noun first (POST /orders/42/cancellation, or PATCH with a status). If that is forced, POST /orders/42/cancel is acceptable.
  • Dates: ISO 8601 in UTC: 2026-11-04T10:15:30Z.
  • Money: never a float. Use a string "19.99" or integer minor units, plus a currency.
  • Enums: adding a value can break strict clients. Document that clients must tolerate unknown values.
  • Null vs absent: decide and document. It matters a lot for PATCH.
  • Field names: one convention, usually camelCase in JSON.
  • Never expose entities: a DTO decouples the API from the schema, prevents lazy-loading surprises, and stops mass assignment.

Versioning

First avoid the need. Additive changes do not break clients if they ignore unknown fields ("be liberal in what you accept"): new optional request fields, new response fields, new endpoints. Breaking changes include removing or renaming a field, changing a type or format, adding a required input, tightening validation, or changing semantics or default behaviour.

StrategyExampleProsCons
URI path/v2/ordersVisible, simple routing, easy to cache and test in a browserThe URI of a resource changes; coarse-grained
HeaderX-API-Version: 2Clean URIsHarder to test; caches need Vary
Media typeAccept: application/vnd.shop.v2+jsonThe most RESTful; per resourceUnfamiliar; harder tooling
Query?v=2EasyPollutes URLs; easy to forget
Date-basedApi-Version: 2026-11-01Fine-grained evolution, used by some public APIsNeeds a transformation layer on the server
// Before Framework 7: separate mappings
@GetMapping(path = "/orders/{id}", headers = "X-API-Version=2")
@GetMapping(path = "/orders/{id}", produces = "application/vnd.shop.v2+json")

// Spring Framework 7 / Boot 4: first-class API versioning
@Configuration
class ApiVersionConfig implements WebMvcConfigurer {
  @Override public void configureApiVersioning(ApiVersionConfigurer c) {
    c.useRequestHeader("X-API-Version");
  }
}
@GetMapping(path = "/orders/{id}", version = "1.1")  OrderV1 v1(@PathVariable long id) { ... }
