@GetMapping(path = "/orders/{id}", version = "2.0")  OrderV2 v2(@PathVariable long id) { ... }

// Announce retirement, with the Deprecation (RFC 9745) and Sunset (RFC 8594) headers
Deprecation: @1780272000
Sunset: Wed, 30 Jun 2027 23:59:59 GMT
Link: <https://api.shop.example/docs/migrate-v2>; rel="deprecation"

Internally, keep one service layer and map to version-specific DTOs at the controller. Track usage per version with a metric, to know when a version can be turned off.

Pagination

OffsetKeyset (seek)Opaque cursor
Request?page=500&size=20?afterId=10234&size=20?cursor=eyJpZCI6...
Deep pagesSlow: the database reads and discards all skipped rowsConstant with an indexConstant
Rows inserted during pagingSkips or repeats rowsStableStable
Jump to page 50YesNoNo
Total countCostly COUNT(*)Not neededNot needed
FitAdmin tablesInternal feedsPublic APIs: the server can change the format
-- Offset: reads 10,020 rows to return 20
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20 OFFSET 10000;

-- Keyset: the sort needs a unique tie-breaker, with an index on (created_at, id)
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:lastCreatedAt, :lastId)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC LIMIT 20;
// Cursor: encode the position so clients treat it as opaque. Fetch one extra to know whether more exist
@GetMapping
public PageResponse<OrderDto> list(@RequestParam(required = false) String cursor,
                                   @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Max(100) int size) {
  Position pos = cursor == null ? Position.START : Position.decode(cursor);
  List<Order> rows = repo.findPage(pos.createdAt(), pos.id(), PageRequest.of(0, size + 1));
  boolean more = rows.size() > size;
  List<Order> page = more ? rows.subList(0, size) : rows;
  String next = more ? Position.of(page.get(size - 1)).encode() : null;
  return new PageResponse<>(page.stream().map(mapper::toDto).toList(), next);
}

public record PageResponse<T>(List<T> data, String nextCursor) { }
Link: <https://api.shop.example/orders?cursor=abc>; rel="next"     # RFC 8288

Always cap size, and always use a deterministic sort. Without a unique tie-breaker, rows sharing a timestamp may repeat or disappear between pages. In Spring Data, Page runs a count query, Slice skips it, and Window with ScrollPosition.keyset() gives keyset scrolling.

Filtering, Sorting and Field Selection

GET /orders?status=PAID&status=SHIPPED              multiple values mean OR
GET /orders?minTotal=100&createdAfter=2026-01-01    explicit named ranges
GET /orders?sort=-createdAt,total                   minus for descending
GET /orders?fields=id,total,status                  sparse fieldset
GET /products?q=keyboard                            free-text search
public class OrderSpecs {
  public static Specification<Order> hasStatus(List<Status> s) {
    return (root, q, cb) -> s == null || s.isEmpty() ? null : root.get("status").in(s);
  }
  public static Specification<Order> minTotal(BigDecimal min) {
    return (root, q, cb) -> min == null ? null : cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(root.get("total"), min);
  }
}

@GetMapping
Page<OrderDto> search(OrderFilter f, @PageableDefault(sort = "createdAt", direction = Sort.Direction.DESC) Pageable p) {
  Specification<Order> spec = Specification.allOf(hasStatus(f.status()), minTotal(f.minTotal()));
  return repo.findAll(spec, p).map(mapper::toDto);
}
Gotcha: ⚠ Allowlist filterable and sortable fields. Passing a client's sort value into a query builds an injection or data-exposure hole, for example sort=password revealing hash order. Unindexed filters on a big table are a denial-of-service path too.

HATEOAS in Practice

Links let a client follow what the server says is possible, rather than copying business rules. If the order is already shipped, the response has no cancel link, so a UI can hide the button without knowing the rule.

{ "id": 7, "status": "PAID",
  "_links": {
    "self":   { "href": "https://api.shop.example/orders/7" },
    "ship":   { "href": "https://api.shop.example/orders/7/shipment" },
    "refund": { "href": "https://api.shop.example/orders/7/refund" } } }
@Component
class OrderAssembler implements RepresentationModelAssembler<Order, EntityModel<OrderDto>> {
  @Override public EntityModel<OrderDto> toModel(Order o) {
    EntityModel<OrderDto> m = EntityModel.of(OrderDto.from(o),
        linkTo(methodOn(OrderController.class).get(o.getId())).withSelfRel());
    if (o.isCancellable()) {
      m.add(linkTo(methodOn(OrderController.class).cancel(o.getId())).withRel("cancel"));
    }
    return m;
  }
}

In practice, few clients are truly link-driven, so the benefit is greatest for public, long-lived APIs and workflows. Formats: HAL (application/hal+json), and others like JSON:API. Spring HATEOAS needs correct forwarded headers behind a proxy to build proper absolute links.

Content Negotiation

One resource can have many representations. The client states preferences, and the server picks.

HeaderDirectionPurpose
Content-TypeBothThe format of this body
AcceptRequestFormats wanted: application/json, application/xml;q=0.5
Accept-LanguageRequestLanguage: hi-IN, en;q=0.8
Accept-EncodingRequestCompression: gzip, br
VaryResponseWhich request headers changed the response; caches key on them

The q value (0 to 1, default 1) ranks preferences. In Spring, consumes matches Content-Type and produces matches Accept. A request that matches neither gets 415 or 406.

@GetMapping(path = "/reports/{id}", produces = {MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE, "text/csv"})
ResponseEntity<?> report(@PathVariable long id, @RequestHeader(HttpHeaders.ACCEPT) String accept) { ... }

// XML: add jackson-dataformat-xml and Spring registers the converter
// Download with a chosen format
@GetMapping(path = "/orders/export", produces = "text/csv")
void csv(HttpServletResponse res) throws IOException { ... }

If a response varies by a header, set Vary so that a CDN does not serve JSON to a client that asked for CSV. Spring's CORS support adds Vary: Origin for you, but other variants are your responsibility.

HTTP Caching and Conditional Requests

HTTP caching has two steps. Freshness: can the stored copy be used with no network call? Validation: once stale, ask the server if the copy is still good, at the price of one small round trip.

DirectiveMeaning
max-age=60Fresh for 60 seconds
s-maxage=300The same, for shared caches like CDNs
public / privateMay be stored by shared caches / only by the browser
no-cacheMay store, but must revalidate before each use
no-storeDo not store at all: for sensitive data
must-revalidateDo not use a stale copy on error
stale-while-revalidate=30Serve stale and refresh in the background
immutableNever changes: fingerprinted assets
GET /products/9                     First request
HTTP/1.1 200 OK
ETag: "v42"
Cache-Control: private, max-age=60

GET /products/9                     After 60s
If-None-Match: "v42"
HTTP/1.1 304 Not Modified           No body

PUT /products/9                     Safe update
If-Match: "v42"
HTTP/1.1 412 Precondition Failed    Somebody changed it first

A strong ETag ("v42") means byte-identical. A weak one (W/"v42") means semantically equivalent, and is not valid for If-Match, or Range requests.

@GetMapping("/products/{id}")
ResponseEntity<ProductDto> get(@PathVariable long id, WebRequest request) {
  Product p = service.find(id);
  String etag = "\"" + p.getVersion() + "\"";            // @Version gives a cheap, accurate ETag
  if (request.checkNotModified(etag)) return null;       // Spring writes the 304
  return ResponseEntity.ok()
      .eTag(etag)
      .cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofSeconds(60)).cachePrivate())
      .body(mapper.toDto(p));
}

@PutMapping("/products/{id}")
ResponseEntity<ProductDto> update(@PathVariable long id,
                                  @RequestHeader(value = HttpHeaders.IF_MATCH, required = false) String ifMatch,
                                  @Valid @RequestBody ProductUpdate body) {
  if (ifMatch == null) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.PRECONDITION_REQUIRED);
  Product p = service.find(id);
  if (!ifMatch.equals("\"" + p.getVersion() + "\"")) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.PRECONDITION_FAILED);
  return ResponseEntity.ok(mapper.toDto(service.update(p, body)));   // @Version still guards the write race
}
Gotcha: ShallowEtagHeaderFilter saves bandwidth but not work: the server still builds the entire response, then hashes it. A version-based ETag can skip work. Authenticated responses must be marked private, or a CDN may serve one user's data to another. A response with no Cache-Control may still be cached heuristically. Spring Security's default is no-store style headers, which you must override per endpoint.

Idempotency Keys

Picture a payment POST whose response is lost to a network timeout. Did it run? Retrying may charge twice; not retrying may lose the order. An idempotency key, a unique value generated by the client per logical operation, lets the server recognize a retry and return the original result. This pattern is common in payment APIs, and an IETF draft standardizes an Idempotency-Key header.

  1. The client generates a UUID, and sends it with the request. It reuses that key on retries.
  2. The server tries to insert (tenant, key, request hash, status=IN_PROGRESS). A unique constraint is what guarantees safety under concurrency.
  3. If inserted: process the request, and store the status and body, ideally in the same transaction as the business change.
  4. If the key exists and is complete: return the stored response. Do not repeat the work.
  5. If the key exists and is in progress: return 409, and let the client retry later.
  6. If the key exists with a different request hash: return 422. That is a client bug.
  7. Expire keys after a while, such as 24 hours.
@Service
public class IdempotencyService {
  private final IdempotencyRepository repo;
  private final TransactionTemplate tx;
  // constructor omitted

  public StoredResponse execute(String key, String requestHash, Supplier<StoredResponse> action) {
    try {
      repo.saveAndFlush(new IdempotencyRecord(key, requestHash));     // the unique constraint decides the winner
    } catch (DataIntegrityViolationException e) {
      IdempotencyRecord r = repo.findById(key).orElseThrow();
      if (!r.getRequestHash().equals(requestHash)) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.UNPROCESSABLE_ENTITY);
      if (r.isInProgress()) throw new ResponseStatusException(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, "request in progress");
      return r.toResponse();                                           // a replay: same status and body
    }
    try {
      return tx.execute(s -> {
        StoredResponse res = action.get();
        repo.complete(key, res.status(), res.body());
        return res;
      });
    } catch (RuntimeException e) {
      repo.deleteById(key);                                            // a failure may be retried
      throw e;
    }
  }
}

Deduplication has to cover external effects, too: pass the key on to the payment provider, so a crash between the provider's charge and your commit does not double-charge. Natural keys, like a client-supplied order number with a unique constraint, also work and are simpler if the domain has one.

Error Format: RFC 9457

RFC 9457, "Problem Details for HTTP APIs", replaced RFC 7807 in 2023. It gives one JSON format with the media type application/problem+json.

MemberMeaning
typeA URI identifying the problem type, ideally with documentation. Default about:blank
titleShort summary of the type; the same for all occurrences
statusHTTP status, repeated for convenience
detailExplanation of this occurrence
instanceA URI for this occurrence
ExtensionsAny further fields, such as errors or traceId
HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://api.shop.example/problems/validation",
  "title": "Validation failed",
  "status": 400,
  "detail": "2 fields are invalid",
  "instance": "/orders",
  "traceId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736",
  "errors": [
    { "field": "items[0].quantity", "message": "must be at least 1" },
    { "field": "email", "message": "must be a valid address" }
  ]
}

Clients should branch on type or a stable code, not on detail text, which may be localized. Never include stack traces, SQL, class names or internal hostnames. Spring's ProblemDetail support is covered in the Boot section. For 5xx errors, return a traceId, and log the details under it.

Rate Limiting

Rate limits protect capacity, control cost, and block abuse such as credential stuffing.

AlgorithmHowProsCons
Fixed windowCounter per minuteSimple and cheapBursts at the edge: double the rate across a window boundary
Sliding logStores each timestampAccurateMemory per request
Sliding window counterWeights the previous windowAccurate enough and cheapAn approximation
Token bucketTokens refill at a steady rate; a request takes oneAllows controlled bursts; the usual choiceTwo parameters to tune
Leaky bucketA queue drains at a fixed rateA smooth outputBursts wait, or are dropped
// Bucket4j: 100 requests per minute, per client key
public class RateLimitFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  private final Map<String, Bucket> buckets = new ConcurrentHashMap<>();   // use Redis-backed buckets when clustered

  private Bucket newBucket() {
    return Bucket.builder()
        .addLimit(limit -> limit.capacity(100).refillGreedy(100, Duration.ofMinutes(1)))
        .build();
  }

  @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String key = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Api-Key")).orElse(req.getRemoteAddr());
    ConsumptionProbe probe = buckets.computeIfAbsent(key, k -> newBucket()).tryConsumeAndReturnRemaining(1);
    if (probe.isConsumed()) {
      res.setHeader("X-RateLimit-Remaining", String.valueOf(probe.getRemainingTokens()));
      chain.doFilter(req, res);
    } else {
      long seconds = TimeUnit.NANOSECONDS.toSeconds(probe.getNanosToWaitForRefill()) + 1;
      res.setStatus(429);
      res.setHeader(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, String.valueOf(seconds));
      res.setContentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PROBLEM_JSON_VALUE);
      res.getWriter().write("{\"title\":\"Too Many Requests\",\"status\":429}");
    }
  }
}
  • Where: at the gateway or edge for coarse protection (NGINX, Spring Cloud Gateway's Redis rate limiter), and in the service for tenant-aware business quotas.
  • Key: API key or user when known; IP only as a fallback, since many users share one IP behind NAT.
  • Distributed: per-instance counters multiply the limit by the replica count. Use Redis with an atomic Lua script.
  • Failure: decide what happens if Redis is down. Most fail open for general APIs, and closed for login.
  • Headers: Retry-After is standard. X-RateLimit-* is common, and an IETF draft defines RateLimit fields.
  • Clients: retry with exponential backoff and jitter, to prevent synchronized waves.
Gotcha: The filter above never removes buckets, so an attacker varying a key grows memory forever. Use a size-bounded Caffeine cache in real code. And getRemoteAddr() is the proxy's address behind a load balancer unless forwarded headers are handled.

Bulk Operations

A client with 500 updates should not need 500 calls, but a single batch raises hard questions: what if item 37 fails?

SemanticsBehaviourResponseFit
All or nothingOne transaction; any failure rolls back all200, or 400/422 with item errorsRelated items, such as lines of one order
Partial successEach item stands alone207 with per-item statusIndependent items, imports
AsyncJob accepted, status polled202Large or slow batches
POST /products/bulk
{ "items": [ { "clientRef": "a1", "sku": "ABC-1", "price": "10.00" },
             { "clientRef": "a2", "sku": "BAD",   "price": "-1" } ] }

HTTP/1.1 207 Multi-Status
{ "results": [
    { "clientRef": "a1", "status": 201, "id": 901 },
    { "clientRef": "a2", "status": 422, "error": { "title": "Invalid price" } } ] }

Rules: cap the batch size and return 413 beyond it; give each item a client reference so results can be matched; never let a 207 hide failures, because clients that only check for 2xx will miss them; and use JDBC batching (hibernate.jdbc.batch_size) on the server. With partial success, retries should be idempotent per item. Do not run each item in the same transaction, or one failure marks everything rollback-only.

Long-Running Operations

Holding an HTTP connection for minutes is fragile: proxies time out, and threads stay busy. Convert the operation into a resource.

@PostMapping("/reports")
ResponseEntity<JobDto> start(@Valid @RequestBody ReportRequest r) {
  Job job = jobs.submit(r);                                  // persist, then enqueue, ideally via an outbox
  return ResponseEntity.accepted()
      .location(URI.create("/jobs/" + job.getId()))
      .header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "5")
      .body(JobDto.from(job));
}

@GetMapping("/jobs/{id}")
ResponseEntity<JobDto> status(@PathVariable UUID id) {
  Job job = jobs.get(id);
  if (job.isDone()) {
    return ResponseEntity.status(HttpStatus.SEE_OTHER).location(job.resultUri()).build();
  }
  return ResponseEntity.ok().header(HttpHeaders.RETRY_AFTER, "5").body(JobDto.from(job));
}

Alternatives to polling: a webhook when it finishes, or server-sent events for progress. Support DELETE /jobs/55 for cancellation. Keep job state in a database, so that restarts do not lose it, and include failed states with a problem detail in the job body.

API Security Checklist

The Security and JWT sections cover mechanisms. The OWASP API Security Top 10 (2023) shows what fails in APIs specifically:

RiskExampleDefence
API1 Broken Object Level AuthorizationGET /orders/43 returns another customer's orderCheck ownership on every object
API2 Broken AuthenticationNo throttling on login, long-lived tokensStandards-based auth, MFA
API3 Broken Object Property Level AuthorizationA response exposes isAdmin; a request can set it (mass assignment)Separate request and response DTOs
API4 Unrestricted Resource Consumption?size=1000000, big uploadsSize limits, timeouts, rate limits
API5 Broken Function Level AuthorizationA user calls an admin endpointDeny by default; rules per function
API6 Unrestricted Access to Sensitive Business FlowsBots buying up stockBusiness-level limits and detection
API7 SSRFA webhook URL pointing to internal hostsURL allowlists
API8 Security MisconfigurationVerbose errors, permissive CORSHardening reviews
API9 Improper Inventory ManagementA forgotten v1 still liveAn API catalogue; retire old versions
API10 Unsafe Consumption of APIsTrusting data from a partner APIValidate third-party data as well

REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC

RESTGraphQLgRPC
ContractOpenAPI (optional)Schema (required).proto (required)
TransportHTTP/1.1, 2, 3Usually a single HTTP POST endpointHTTP/2
PayloadJSON, usuallyJSONProtobuf binary
Data shapeServer decidesClient selects fieldsFixed message types
Over-fetchingCommonSolvedFixed
CachingHTTP, CDN, built inHard: POSTs need client or persisted query cachingApplication level
StreamingSSE, chunkedSubscriptions, usually over WebSocketUnary, server, client, bidirectional
BrowserNativeNativeNeeds gRPC-Web or a proxy
ErrorsHTTP statusOften 200 with an errors arraygRPC status codes
Key riskMany round tripsN+1 resolvers; costly nested queriesHarder debugging; L4 load balancers pin long-lived connections
Best forPublic and CRUD APIs, broad compatibilityVaried front-ends and aggregating many sourcesLow-latency internal calls, polyglot services
// Protobuf: field numbers, not names, are on the wire, which enables safe evolution
service OrderService {
  rpc GetOrder (GetOrderRequest) returns (Order);
  rpc WatchOrders (WatchRequest) returns (stream OrderEvent);       // server streaming
}
message Order { int64 id = 1; string status = 2; reserved 3; }       // never reuse a removed number

# GraphQL: one request, exactly these fields
query { order(id: 7) { status items { sku qty } customer { name } } }

A common architecture combines them: REST or GraphQL at the edge, gRPC or messaging inside. In GraphQL, a resolver for customer on each of 100 orders creates N+1 calls unless a DataLoader batches them; Spring for GraphQL offers @BatchMapping. Also limit query depth and complexity, since a nested query can be a denial of service.

Webhooks

Polling wastes calls and adds delay. A webhook reverses direction: when an event happens, your server POSTs to a URL the consumer registered.

Sender responsibilities:

  • Sign each payload with an HMAC, using a per-subscriber secret, and include a timestamp to prevent replay.
  • Deliver asynchronously from a queue or outbox, not inside the business transaction.
  • Retry with exponential backoff for hours or days, then disable and alert.
  • Give each event a unique id. Delivery is at-least-once, and order is not guaranteed.
  • ⚠ Validate subscriber URLs against SSRF: block private ranges, and re-check after DNS resolution.
  • Offer a way to list and replay missed events.

Receiver responsibilities: verify the signature over the raw bytes in constant time, reject old timestamps, respond 2xx quickly, queue the work, and deduplicate by event id.

POST /hooks/shop HTTP/1.1
X-Shop-Event-Id: evt_01JC9...
X-Shop-Timestamp: 1793786400
X-Shop-Signature: sha256=8f4e...

{ "type": "order.paid", "data": { "orderId": 7 } }
@PostMapping("/hooks/shop")
ResponseEntity<Void> receive(@RequestBody byte[] raw,                         // raw bytes: re-serialized JSON differs
                             @RequestHeader("X-Shop-Timestamp") long ts,
                             @RequestHeader("X-Shop-Signature") String sig,
                             @RequestHeader("X-Shop-Event-Id") String eventId) throws Exception {
  if (Math.abs(Instant.now().getEpochSecond() - ts) > 300) return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();

  Mac mac = Mac.getInstance("HmacSHA256");
  mac.init(new SecretKeySpec(secret, "HmacSHA256"));
  mac.update((ts + ".").getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
  byte[] expected = mac.doFinal(raw);
  byte[] actual = HexFormat.of().parseHex(sig.substring("sha256=".length()));
  if (!MessageDigest.isEqual(expected, actual)) return ResponseEntity.status(401).build();  // constant time

  if (!seen.add(eventId)) return ResponseEntity.ok().build();                  // a duplicate: acknowledge only
  queue.publish(raw);                                                          // process elsewhere
  return ResponseEntity.ok().build();
}

Complete Controller Example

@RestController
@RequestMapping(path = "/api/v1/orders", produces = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
@Validated
public class OrderController {
  private final OrderService service;
  private final OrderMapper mapper;

  public OrderController(OrderService service, OrderMapper mapper) {
    this.service = service;
    this.mapper = mapper;
  }

  // Paged, filtered list. Clients get 200 with an empty list, never 404
  @GetMapping
  public PageResponse<OrderDto> list(@RequestParam(required = false) List<OrderStatus> status,
                                     @RequestParam(required = false) String cursor,
                                     @RequestParam(defaultValue = "20") @Min(1) @Max(100) int size,
                                     @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return service.list(jwt.getSubject(), status, cursor, size);
  }

  // Read one, with a conditional GET. Ownership is enforced in the service: 404 if not yours
  @GetMapping("/{id}")
  public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> get(@PathVariable UUID id, WebRequest request, @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    Order o = service.getOwned(id, jwt.getSubject());
    String etag = etag(o);
    if (request.checkNotModified(etag)) return null;
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(etag).cacheControl(CacheControl.noCache().cachePrivate()).body(mapper.toDto(o));
  }

  // Create. Idempotency key makes retries safe; 201 + Location + ETag
  @PostMapping(consumes = MediaType.APPLICATION_JSON_VALUE)
  public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> create(@RequestHeader("Idempotency-Key") @NotBlank String key,
                                         @Valid @RequestBody CreateOrderRequest body,
                                         @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    Order o = service.create(key, jwt.getSubject(), body);
    URI location = ServletUriComponentsBuilder.fromCurrentRequest()
        .path("/{id}").buildAndExpand(o.getId()).toUri();
    return ResponseEntity.created(location).eTag(etag(o)).body(mapper.toDto(o));
  }

  // Partial update with optimistic concurrency. If-Match is required: 428 if missing, 412 if stale
  @PatchMapping(path = "/{id}", consumes = "application/merge-patch+json")
  public ResponseEntity<OrderDto> patch(@PathVariable UUID id,
                                        @RequestHeader(HttpHeaders.IF_MATCH) String ifMatch,
                                        @Valid @RequestBody OrderPatch patch,
                                        @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    Order o = service.patch(id, jwt.getSubject(), ifMatch, patch);
    return ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(etag(o)).body(mapper.toDto(o));
  }

  // A business action. 409 if the current state does not allow it
  @PostMapping("/{id}/cancellation")
  @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
  public void cancel(@PathVariable UUID id, @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    service.cancel(id, jwt.getSubject());
  }

  // Delete. Idempotent in effect: 204, then 404
  @DeleteMapping("/{id}")
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")
  @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT)
  public void delete(@PathVariable UUID id) {
    service.delete(id);
  }

  private static String etag(Order o) { return "\"" + o.getVersion() + "\""; }
}

public record CreateOrderRequest(@NotEmpty List<@Valid OrderLine> items, @Size(max = 20) String coupon) { }
public record OrderLine(@NotBlank String sku, @Min(1) int quantity) { }
public record OrderDto(UUID id, OrderStatus status, BigDecimal total, Instant createdAt) { }

@RestControllerAdvice
class OrderErrors {
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
  ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFoundException e) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, "Order not found");
  }
  @ExceptionHandler(IllegalOrderStateException.class)
  ProblemDetail conflict(IllegalOrderStateException e) {
    ProblemDetail p = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.CONFLICT, e.getMessage());
    p.setType(URI.create("https://api.shop.example/problems/invalid-order-state"));
    p.setProperty("currentStatus", e.current());
    return p;
  }
  @ExceptionHandler(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class)
  ProblemDetail stale(ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException e) {
    return ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.PRECONDITION_FAILED, "Order was changed by someone else");
  }
}

File Upload and Download Endpoints

Files show up in nearly every real API, such as documents, reports and images.

  • Upload: POST multipart/form-data with the file plus a JSON part for the metadata. Return 201 Created with a Location header. Do not trust the client's Content-Type or filename. Check the size, detect the type from the content's magic bytes, store the file under a generated name, and scan it for malware where required.
  • Large files: give the client a presigned object-storage URL, or support resumable, chunked uploads. Do not stream gigabytes through the app.
  • Download: GET with the correct Content-Type and Content-Disposition: attachment; filename*=UTF-8''.... When a controller returns Resource, Spring MVC handles Range requests and answers 206 Partial Content, which gives resumable downloads and video seeking.
  • Prefer binary transfer over Base64 in JSON, which is about 33% larger and must be buffered in memory.
@PostMapping(path = "/documents", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
ResponseEntity<DocumentDto> upload(@RequestPart("file") MultipartFile file,
                                   @RequestPart("meta") @Valid DocumentMeta meta) {
  DocumentDto saved = service.store(file, meta);          // validates size and type, streams to storage
  return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/documents/" + saved.id())).body(saved);
}

@GetMapping("/documents/{id}/content")
ResponseEntity<Resource> download(@PathVariable UUID id) {
  StoredFile f = service.load(id);
  return ResponseEntity.ok()
      .contentType(MediaType.parseMediaType(f.contentType()))
      .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION,
              ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(f.name(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8).build().toString())
      .body(f.resource());                                  // Range / 206 supported automatically
}

Correlation and Request IDs

When a user reports "it failed at 10:42", you need one id that links the client, the gateway, every service, and the logs. Accept an incoming X-Request-Id (validate its length and characters), or generate one. Put it into the MDC so that every log line carries it, echo it in the response header, and include it in error bodies (a ProblemDetail property). In traced systems, the W3C traceparent header (via Micrometer Tracing) already does this across services. Then expose the trace id to clients rather than creating a second id.

@Component
class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  private static final Pattern SAFE = Pattern.compile("[A-Za-z0-9-]{8,64}");
  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String id = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Request-Id"))
        .filter(v -> SAFE.matcher(v).matches())               // never log untrusted raw input
        .orElseGet(() -> UUID.randomUUID().toString());
    MDC.put("requestId", id);
    res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", id);
    try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.remove("requestId"); }
  }
}

Interview Questions — REST

What is REST? What are its constraints?

REST (REpresentational State Transfer) is an architectural style built on HTTP. Its constraints: client–server, stateless (each request carries everything needed), cacheable, uniform interface (resources identified by URIs, manipulated through representations, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS), layered system, and optionally code-on-demand.

REST vs SOAP vs GraphQL vs gRPC?
RESTSOAPGraphQLgRPC
Style over HTTP; JSONProtocol; XML envelope, WSDLOne endpoint; the client picks its fieldsHTTP/2 + Protobuf, binary, streaming
Simple, cacheableWS-Security, strict contractsNo over- or under-fetchingVery fast service-to-service calls
What does idempotent mean? Is PUT idempotent? POST?

Idempotent means repeating the same request N times has the same effect as sending it once. GET, PUT, DELETE, HEAD and OPTIONS are idempotent. POST isn't: two POSTs create two orders. To make a POST safe to retry, have the client send an Idempotency-Key header and have the server store and deduplicate it.

PUT vs PATCH vs POST?

PUT replaces the entire resource at a known URI; fields you leave out are reset. PATCH changes only the fields you send (JSON Merge Patch or JSON Patch). POST creates a resource under a collection, where the server assigns the id, or runs a non-CRUD action.

401 vs 403?

401 Unauthorized: you aren't authenticated (the token is missing or invalid). Send credentials. 403 Forbidden: you're authenticated but don't have permission (wrong role).

Best practices for URI design?
  • Use nouns, plural, lowercase, hyphenated: /api/v1/order-items
  • Express hierarchy with paths: /customers/42/orders
  • Put filtering, sorting and paging in the query: ?status=PAID&sort=createdAt,desc&page=0&size=20
  • No verbs in URIs; the HTTP method is the verb. Use action sub-resources only for real actions: POST /orders/7/cancel
  • Return a consistent error body (RFC 9457 ProblemDetail).
How do you version an API?

URI versioning (/v1/users, the most common), a header (X-API-Version: 2), media type (Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json), or a query param (?version=2). Never break existing clients. Add fields compatibly and deprecate old versions with a sunset date.

How do you implement pagination?

Offset (page/size, Spring Pageable): simple, but slow for deep pages and unstable when rows are inserted. Cursor/keyset (?after=lastId, WHERE id > ? ORDER BY id LIMIT n): fast and stable, good for infinite scroll. Return metadata (totalElements, next link).

What is HATEOAS?

Hypermedia As The Engine Of Application State: responses include links to the actions available next (_links: { self, cancel, pay }), so the client discovers the flow instead of hard-coding URLs. Spring HATEOAS provides EntityModel and linkTo(methodOn(...)).

How do you secure a REST API?

HTTPS everywhere · authentication (OAuth2 / JWT / API keys) · role- or scope-based authorization · input validation · rate limiting (429) · proper CORS · don't leak stack traces · hash passwords with BCrypt · protect against injection (parameterized queries) · audit logging · short-lived tokens with refresh.

What is CORS?

Cross-Origin Resource Sharing: the browser hides the response of a JS call to a different origin (the simple request is still sent) unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Non-simple requests (PUT, custom headers, JSON) are preceded by an OPTIONS preflight. In Spring, use @CrossOrigin or a global CorsConfigurationSource plus http.cors().

How do you document APIs?

OpenAPI 3 / Swagger: add springdoc-openapi-starter-webmvc-ui and you get /swagger-ui.html and /v3/api-docs. Annotate with @Operation, @ApiResponse, @Schema. Contract-first teams generate code from the YAML spec instead.

How do you use HTTP caching in REST?

Use Cache-Control: max-age=60, ETag with If-None-Match (returns 304 if unchanged), and Last-Modified with If-Modified-Since. Spring offers ShallowEtagHeaderFilter and ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(..).

Is REST the same as HTTP? Can you have REST without HTTP?

No. REST is an architectural style, and HTTP is a protocol. Fielding's constraints do not mention HTTP, though it was designed alongside them, and is the only common implementation. Likewise, using HTTP does not make an API RESTful: a single POST endpoint uses HTTP but is at level 0.

What does stateless really mean? Does it forbid a database or login?

It means the server keeps no client session state between requests; each request supplies what is needed, such as a token. Resource state in a database is normal. A server-side session is a departure from the constraint, but a Redis-backed session still gives many of the scaling benefits. A login that issues a token fits well.

What is the Richardson Maturity Model? Where do most APIs sit?

Level 0 is one endpoint. Level 1 adds resources. Level 2 adds HTTP verbs and status codes. Level 3 adds hypermedia. Most production APIs are at level 2, because level 3's cost rarely pays off for internal clients. Fielding says only level 3 is truly REST.

Is DELETE idempotent if the second call returns 404?

Yes. Idempotency concerns the effect on server state, and not the response. After one or many calls, the resource is gone. Returning 204 on all calls is also valid. What matters is that a retried delete does no extra harm.

Is PATCH idempotent? Is POST ever idempotent?

PATCH is not guaranteed. It depends on the document: "set status" is, "append item" is not. POST is not by definition, but an idempotency key or natural unique key can make a specific endpoint behave idempotently.

Why are safe and idempotent methods important in practice?

Intermediaries and clients act on them. Browsers and proxies can retry a GET; HTTP clients automatically retry idempotent requests on connection failure; crawlers and link previewers fetch GET links. An unsafe action behind a GET, such as GET /logout, can be triggered accidentally, and enables CSRF.

PUT vs POST for creation: when does each apply?

POST to a collection when the server chooses the identifier. PUT when the client knows the URI, as with PUT /users/alice/settings, or a client-generated UUID, which makes creation naturally idempotent. PUT returns 201 on create, and 200 or 204 on replace.

What is the difference between 301, 302, 303, 307, and 308?

301 and 308 are permanent, and 302, 303 and 307 are temporary. 301 and 302 allow clients to change POST to GET, for historical reasons. 307 and 308 forbid that. 303 explicitly tells the client to GET another URI, which fits the Post/Redirect/Get pattern and finished async jobs.

A validation failure: 400 or 422? A duplicate email: 400 or 409?

Validation is either 400 or 422, chosen consistently; Spring's default is 400. A duplicate email is usually 409, since the request is valid but conflicts with existing state. Be aware that it confirms that the email exists; a registration flow may respond generically to prevent account enumeration.

502 vs 503 vs 504?

All usually come from a gateway. 502: the upstream sent an invalid response, or the connection dropped, as in a crash. 503: the service is unavailable, for example no healthy instances, or overload. 504: the upstream took too long. Diagnosis differs: crashed pods, capacity, or slow dependencies.

Should a client receive 404 or 403 for someone else's resource?

404 is generally better for object-level access, as 403 confirms existence, which helps enumeration. 403 suits role-based denial on a route everyone knows about. Be consistent, and log the real reason.

Offset vs keyset pagination: explain why OFFSET 1000000 is slow.

The database cannot jump to a row number; it must walk and discard the first million index entries or rows, so cost grows with depth. Keyset uses an indexed WHERE condition to seek directly, so cost is stable at any depth. It cannot jump to arbitrary pages, and needs a unique sort key.

Why use an opaque cursor rather than exposing lastId?

An opaque cursor hides the implementation, letting the server change the sort or storage without an API break, and it can hold several fields such as a timestamp and id. Clients cannot craft positions, particularly if the cursor is signed. It also tells clients not to do arithmetic on it.

What is the right way to return a paginated Spring Data Page?

Returning PageImpl directly serializes an internal structure that may change; Spring Data warns about this. Map it to your own response record, or use PagedModel, or @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO). A stable shape is part of your API contract.

How would you evolve a response field from a string to an object without breaking clients?

Do not change it in place. Add a new field, such as shippingAddress next to address, and keep the old one populated. Mark it deprecated in the OpenAPI document, track its usage, notify consumers, and remove it after a sunset date, or in a new version. Consumer-driven contract tests help detect dependants.

What is a breaking change? Is adding an enum value one?

It is any change that can fail a correct existing client: removing fields, changing types, adding required inputs, or stricter validation. Adding an enum value is technically additive, but breaks clients that deserialize strictly, which Jackson does by default. So document the rule, and have clients use READ_UNKNOWN_ENUM_VALUES_AS_NULL or a default.

no-cache vs no-store?

A common confusion. no-cache permits storing, but requires revalidation before use, so you get cheap 304s. no-store forbids storing anywhere, for sensitive data.

How do ETags prevent the lost update problem?

Two clients read version 3. Client A sends PUT with If-Match: "3", and it succeeds, making version 4. Client B sends If-Match: "3", and gets 412, so it must re-read and merge. This is optimistic concurrency over HTTP. On the server, combine it with JPA's @Version, which closes the small gap between check and write.

Walk through implementing an idempotency key. What are the race conditions?

Two concurrent duplicates must not both proceed, so a unique constraint on the key picks one winner; a check-then-insert is a race. The loser returns 409, or waits for the result. If the worker crashes after charging but before recording, the record remains in progress, so you need a timeout, plus a downstream call that also carries the key. Hash the request, to detect a key reused with different content.

Which errors should be stored against an idempotency key?

Store definitive outcomes, including business 4xx responses, so that a retry gets the same answer. Do not store transient failures such as 5xx or timeouts where nothing happened, so that the retry can really try again. Validation failures that happen before work begins need not be stored at all.

Why does RFC 9457 matter? How would you handle a mix of error types?

A standard shape lets gateways, libraries and clients handle errors generally, without a custom parser per API. Keep type stable, extend with fields like errors, and localize title and detail, if needed. Make filter-level errors such as 401 and 429 use the same format, or clients must handle two.

Implement a rate limit across 10 instances. What are the challenges?

A shared store is needed, usually Redis. The token-bucket check must be atomic, so use a Lua script, or Bucket4j's Redis integration. Each check adds latency, so a small local allocation can reduce that, at some accuracy cost. Clock differences are avoided by using Redis time. Define behaviour for when Redis fails, and use per-tenant keys, so one customer cannot exhaust others' capacity.

Client sends 10,000 items in one POST. How do you design this?

Set a limit and reject above it with 413. For large volumes, accept a file or stream, return 202 with a job, and process in chunks of committed batches. Report per-item results, and make it resumable through per-item idempotency. For medium sizes, use synchronous partial success with 207.

Long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket vs webhooks?
TechniqueDirectionFit
PollingClient asksSimple, infrequent
Long pollingServer holds the requestWorks anywhere; heavy
SSEServer to browser over HTTPNotifications, progress; reconnects automatically
WebSocketTwo-wayChat, collaboration
WebhooksServer to serverIntegrations
Why compute a webhook signature over raw bytes, and why compare in constant time?

Parsing and re-serializing JSON can change whitespace or key order, breaking the HMAC, so verify the exact bytes received. String.equals exits at the first differing byte, leaking timing information that may help forge a signature; MessageDigest.isEqual avoids that. A timestamp in the signed data stops replay of an old capture.

When is GraphQL a poor choice?

When an API is simple CRUD with stable consumers, when CDN caching is important, when file transfer dominates, or for service-to-service calls. Adopting it means handling query cost limits, N+1, authorization per field, and non-HTTP-based error monitoring. It pays off with many diverse clients on a rich data graph.

Why is gRPC faster than JSON over HTTP?

Protobuf is compact and parses quickly, without field names on the wire. HTTP/2 multiplexes many calls over one connection, with header compression. Generated stubs also save hand-written code. The gain is real for high-volume internal traffic, and modest when a slow database dominates. HTTP/2 support is possible for REST, too, so the protocol alone is not the difference.

How do you make a client resilient when calling your REST API?

Set connect and read timeouts. Retry only idempotent operations, or those with a key, with exponential backoff and jitter, and honour Retry-After. Add a circuit breaker such as Resilience4j. Limit concurrency with a bulkhead. Handle unknown fields and enum values gracefully, and propagate a deadline across calls where possible.

How do you ensure the API contract stays stable between teams?

Keep the OpenAPI document in version control, generate or verify from it, diff in CI to catch breaking changes, and add consumer-driven contract tests such as Pact or Spring Cloud Contract. Have a deprecation policy with sunset dates, and monitor who still uses old fields or versions.

Design: a REST API for a payment system.
  • Resources: /payments, /payments/{id}/refunds, with a state machine: CREATED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED, FAILED.
  • Idempotency: a mandatory key on POST, forwarded to the provider.
  • Amounts: integer minor units with an ISO 4217 currency.
  • Async: 202 for slow providers, plus a signed webhook for results.
  • Consistency: an outbox for events, a ledger with append-only entries, and If-Match on changes.
  • Security: OAuth2 scopes, per-object authorization, TLS, and no raw card data.
  • Errors: RFC 9457 with decline codes.
  • Operations: per-merchant rate limits, audit logs, and trace ids.
How do you design a file upload API safely?

Accept multipart/form-data, or a presigned URL flow for large files. Enforce size limits in both the proxy and the app. Detect the real type from the content rather than the extension or the client header, and keep an allow-list of types. Store the file under a generated name outside the web root, never under the user's path, to prevent path traversal. Scan for malware where required, and serve files back with Content-Disposition: attachment and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so that an uploaded HTML file cannot run as a page on your domain. Return 201 with the new resource's location, and 413 or 415 for files that are too big or of the wrong type.

How do you return a download with a non-ASCII file name, such as an invoice in Tamil or with accents?

Use the RFC 6266 / RFC 5987 form filename*=UTF-8''... (percent-encoded), which Spring's ContentDisposition.attachment().filename(name, StandardCharsets.UTF_8) produces. Building the header by string concatenation breaks on quotes and non-ASCII characters, and can allow header injection. On the Angular side, read the name from the header. With CORS, the server must list Content-Disposition in Access-Control-Expose-Headers, or the browser hides it from JavaScript.

Soft delete: what should GET return after a resource is deleted?

To the API client, a soft-deleted resource should look deleted. DELETE returns 204. A later GET returns 404, or 410 Gone if you want to say that it existed and was removed on purpose. List endpoints leave it out. If users can restore items, model that explicitly, for example POST /documents/7/restore or a /trash collection. Watch for unique constraints, such as a deleted user's email blocking a new signup. Also, soft delete alone does not satisfy "right to erasure" requirements for personal data.

What is a correlation id, and how is it different from a trace id?

A correlation or request id is a single value attached to every log line and response for one request, often X-Request-Id. A trace id (W3C traceparent) does the same job, and also carries span ids, so tracing tools can show the timing tree across services. With Micrometer Tracing, use the trace id as your correlation id: it is already in the MDC, so log it and return it to clients. A separate request id is useful mainly when there is no tracing, or for an id the client creates and controls.

The Angular screen makes 12 API calls to render one page. How do you fix a chatty API?

Options: embed related data on request (GET /orders/7?expand=customer,items, as Stripe does). Add a purpose-built read endpoint or a BFF (Backend for Frontend) that aggregates calls on the server, close to the data. Use field selection to keep payloads small. Use GraphQL if many different screens need flexible shapes. Also check that the calls run in parallel (forkJoin) rather than in sequence, and that HTTP/2 is enabled. Keep the core resources clean, and put the aggregation in the BFF layer.

Should a REST API reject unknown fields in a request body?

The usual rule is the tolerant reader: ignore unknown fields, which is Spring Boot's Jackson default. This lets clients and servers evolve independently. A newer client can send a field that an older server does not know yet, and nothing breaks. The trade-off is that typos are silently ignored, so validate required fields explicitly. Some teams reject unknown fields on PATCH or other critical commands, where a misspelled field would silently do nothing. In that case, document it, and return 400 with the name of the unknown field.

JPA & Spring Data JPA Persistence

The specification for ORM in Java. Entities, the persistence context, relationships, fetching, and querying.

Entity Lifecycle States

@Entity @Table(name = "orders")
public class Order {
  @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
  private Long id;

  @Column(nullable = false, length = 50)
  private String status;

  @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)           // owning side (has FK)
  @JoinColumn(name = "customer_id")
  private Customer customer;

  @OneToMany(mappedBy = "order", cascade = CascadeType.ALL, orphanRemoval = true)
  private List<OrderItem> items = new ArrayList<>();

  @Version private Integer version;            // optimistic locking

  public void addItem(OrderItem i) { items.add(i); i.setOrder(this); }  // keep both sides in sync
}

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
  List<Order> findByStatusAndCustomerNameContainingIgnoreCase(String status, String name);  // derived query

  @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.id = :id")      // JPQL + fetch join
  Optional<Order> findWithItems(@Param("id") Long id);

  @EntityGraph(attributePaths = {"customer"})
  Page<Order> findByStatus(String status, Pageable pageable);

  @Modifying @Query("update Order o set o.status = :s where o.id in :ids")
  int bulkUpdate(@Param("s") String s, @Param("ids") List<Long> ids);
}

The Object-Relational Mismatch

An ORM (object-relational mapper) converts between Java objects in memory and rows in tables. It exists because the two models disagree on basic things, and hand-written JDBC code spends most of its time bridging them. Knowing these mismatches explains why JPA has the features it has.

MismatchObjectsTablesJPA's answer
Identity== and equals()Primary key@Id; inside one persistence context, one row maps to one instance
GranularityMany small classes (Address, Money)One wide table@Embeddable
Inheritanceextends, polymorphismNothing equivalent@Inheritance strategies
AssociationsReferences, one-directional, collectionsForeign keys, naturally both directions; many-to-many needs a third tableRelationship annotations, owning side, mappedBy
NavigationWalk the graph: order.getCustomer().getCity()Join up front, in one statementLazy loading and fetch plans (and the N+1 problem they can cause)
Typesenum, Instant, value objectsSQL types@Enumerated, AttributeConverter
Change trackingPlain field writesExplicit UPDATE statementsDirty checking at flush
Interview: JPA does not remove SQL from the job. It writes SQL for you, and you are still responsible for it. A senior answer about any JPA problem describes the SQL that was actually sent.

Entity Mapping Annotations

An entity is a class whose instances map to rows. The spec requires @Entity, an @Id, a public or protected no-arg constructor, and a non-final class (a final class cannot be subclassed by a lazy proxy). Records cannot be entities, because they have no no-arg constructor and are immutable, but they work as embeddables (JPA 3.2) and as DTOs.

@Entity
@Table(name = "employee",
       uniqueConstraints = @UniqueConstraint(columnNames = {"tenant_id", "email"}),
       indexes = @Index(name = "idx_emp_dept", columnList = "department_id"))
public class Employee {
  @Id @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.SEQUENCE, generator = "emp_seq")
  @SequenceGenerator(name = "emp_seq", sequenceName = "emp_seq", allocationSize = 50)
  private Long id;

  @Column(name = "full_name", nullable = false, length = 120)
  private String name;

  @Column(updatable = false)                    // left out of UPDATE statements
  private Instant createdAt;

  @Enumerated(EnumType.STRING)                  // stores "ACTIVE", not 0
  @Column(length = 20)
  private Status status;

  @Convert(converter = MoneyConverter.class)    // custom type <-> column mapping
  private Money salary;

  @Lob
  private String biography;                     // CLOB / TEXT

  @Transient
  private int cachedScore;                      // not persisted at all

  protected Employee() { }                      // required by JPA, hidden from callers
}
AnnotationPurposeWhat to know
@TableTable name, schema, constraints, indexesConstraints and indexes only matter if the provider generates the schema; with Flyway they are documentation
@ColumnColumn name, nullability, length, precision, insertable, updatablenullable and length are mainly DDL hints, not input validation. Default string length is 255. Use Bean Validation for input checks
@EnumeratedEnum as ORDINAL (default) or STRINGORDINAL stores position, so inserting a constant in the middle silently changes the meaning of old rows. Use STRING
@Convert / AttributeConverter<X,Y>Custom type to column type@Converter(autoApply = true) applies it to every attribute of that type. Not allowed on @Id, @Version or @Enumerated attributes
@LobLarge text or binaryOften better in a separate table or object storage so normal reads stay small
@TransientExclude a fieldDifferent from the Java transient keyword, which is about serialization (though JPA also skips transient fields)
@TemporalLegacy, for Date/CalendarNot needed for java.time types. Deprecated in JPA 3.2
@Basic(fetch = LAZY)Lazy scalar fieldOnly a hint: Hibernate ignores it unless bytecode enhancement is on
@AccessField or property accessDefault follows the placement of @Id. Prefer field access: getters can then hold logic without interfering with loading
@SecondaryTableOne entity over two tablesRare; a real one-to-one is often clearer
@ElementCollectionCollection of basics or embeddables (no identity of their own)Stored in a separate table via @CollectionTable. A change to a List without an order column deletes and re-inserts all its rows
@OrderBy / @OrderColumnSort on load / persist the list position@OrderBy("createdAt DESC") adds ORDER BY to the loading SQL. @OrderColumn adds an index column and turns a bag into a real list
Gotcha: @Column(nullable = false) does not replace @NotNull. Input validation should fail with a 400 before any SQL, not with a DataIntegrityViolationException at flush.

ID Generation in Depth

The existing answer lists the strategies. What interviewers probe is what each one does to the order of SQL and to batching.

  • IDENTITY: the database assigns the id during INSERT. Hibernate needs the id to put the entity in the persistence context, which is keyed by id, so persist() runs the INSERT immediately rather than at flush. That is why JDBC batching of inserts is impossible with it.
  • SEQUENCE: Hibernate calls select nextval(...), gets the id without inserting, and delays the INSERT until flush, so inserts can be batched.
  • allocationSize makes sequences cheap. With the default pooled optimizer and allocationSize = 50, Hibernate hits the sequence once per 50 ids and hands out the rest from memory. The database sequence's INCREMENT BY must equal allocationSize, or ids can collide; Hibernate checks this at startup by default. Gaps are normal: a restart throws away unused values.
  • TABLE: a row in a table, locked per allocation. Portable, slow, and a contention point. Avoid.
  • AUTO (the default for a bare @GeneratedValue): Hibernate picks by id type and dialect. For numeric ids on a database with sequences it uses a sequence. On MySQL, which has no sequences, it emulates one with a table, which is the slow option. On MySQL state IDENTITY explicitly.
  • UUID: generated in the application, so no round trip. Random UUIDs (v4) scatter inserts across a B-tree index, which hurts write performance and cache locality, most of all on clustered primary keys like InnoDB's. Prefer time-ordered UUIDs, or a bigint PK plus a separate public UUID.
  • Assigned: no @GeneratedValue; you set the id yourself. Spring Data's save() then sees a non-null id and runs a SELECT plus merge(). Implement Persistable to avoid that.
// Hibernate 6 default when you write just GenerationType.SEQUENCE:
// a per-entity sequence named like employee_SEQ, allocation size 50.
// (Hibernate 5 used one shared hibernate_sequence; set
//  hibernate.id.db_structure_naming_strategy=legacy when migrating an old schema.)

create sequence emp_seq start with 1 increment by 50;   -- must match allocationSize

Embeddables and Composite Keys

An embeddable is a value object with no identity or table of its own. Its fields become columns in the owner's table. It solves the granularity mismatch: the table stays wide while the code gets a real Address type.

@Embeddable
public record Address(String street, String city, @Column(name = "zip") String zipCode) { }

@Entity
public class Customer {
  @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;

  @Embedded
  private Address billing;

  @Embedded
  @AttributeOverrides({                     // same type twice: rename the columns
    @AttributeOverride(name = "street",  column = @Column(name = "ship_street")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "city",    column = @Column(name = "ship_city")),
    @AttributeOverride(name = "zipCode", column = @Column(name = "ship_zip"))
  })
  private Address shipping;
}

// Composite primary key, option 1: an embedded id
@Embeddable
public class OrderItemId implements Serializable {
  private Long orderId;
  private Integer lineNo;
  // no-arg constructor, equals and hashCode required
}

@Entity
public class OrderItem {
  @EmbeddedId private OrderItemId id;

  @ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
  @MapsId("orderId")                        // this FK is also part of the PK
  @JoinColumn(name = "order_id")
  private Order order;
}

// Composite primary key, option 2: @IdClass keeps fields flat on the entity
@Entity @IdClass(EnrollmentId.class)
public class Enrollment {
  @Id private Long studentId;
  @Id private Long courseId;
}

Composite key classes must be Serializable, public, and implement equals/hashCode. @EmbeddedId reads as e.getId().getOrderId() in code and e.id.orderId in JPQL; @IdClass reads as e.studentId. If all fields of an embedded value are null, Hibernate loads the whole embedded object as null by default, so guard against that in calling code. Natural composite keys are also awkward as foreign keys for other tables, which is one more reason to prefer a surrogate key.

Relationships, One by One

Relational databases have one mechanism: a foreign key column. JPA needs to know which Java field controls that column. That field is the owning side. The other field, if any, is the inverse side and declares mappedBy. JPA reads only the owning side when writing. Changing just the inverse side is silently ignored; that is the most common relationship bug.

MappingOwnerDefault fetchTable shapeAdvice
@ManyToOneAlways this sideEAGERFK on this tableThe best-behaved mapping. Always set LAZY
@OneToMany(mappedBy) bidirectionalThe ManyToOneLAZYFK on childThe normal parent/child form. Use a helper to set both sides
@OneToMany unidirectional, no join columnThis sideLAZYExtra join tableAvoid: a table nobody wanted
@OneToMany @JoinColumn unidirectionalThis sideLAZYFK on childWorks, but inserts the child and then sends an extra UPDATE to set the FK
@OneToOneThe side with the FKEAGERFK with unique constraint, or shared PKPrefer a @MapsId shared key on the child
@ManyToManyThe side with @JoinTableLAZYJoin tableUse Set. Promote to an entity once the link needs columns
// One-to-one with a shared primary key: no separate FK column, no extra index,
// and the child can be found by the parent's id directly.
@Entity
public class UserProfile {
  @Id private Long id;

  @OneToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)
  @MapsId                                  // id column doubles as the FK to users.id
  @JoinColumn(name = "id")
  private User user;
}

// Many-to-many written properly
@Entity
public class Student {
  @ManyToMany(cascade = {CascadeType.PERSIST, CascadeType.MERGE})   // never REMOVE here
  @JoinTable(name = "student_course",
    joinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "student_id"),
    inverseJoinColumns = @JoinColumn(name = "course_id"))
  private Set<Course> courses = new HashSet<>();

  public void enroll(Course c)   { courses.add(c);    c.getStudents().add(this); }
  public void withdraw(Course c) { courses.remove(c); c.getStudents().remove(this); }
}

@Entity
public class Course {
  @ManyToMany(mappedBy = "courses")
  private Set<Student> students = new HashSet<>();
}

Cascade and orphanRemoval in detail

Cascade means "when this operation is applied to the parent, apply it to the associated entities too." It concerns entity state transitions and has nothing to do with the SQL ON DELETE CASCADE clause, which is enforced in the database. orphanRemoval is an additional rule for composition: a child with no parent has no meaning, so taking it out of the collection deletes it.

Action (mappedBy collection)No cascadecascade = REMOVEorphanRemoval = true
em.remove(parent)FK violation if children existChildren deletedChildren deleted
parent.getItems().remove(child)No SQL: the inverse side is ignoredNo SQL: nothing cascadesChild deleted at flush
parent.setItems(newList)No SQLNo SQLHibernate throws "A collection with orphan deletion was no longer referenced". Mutate the collection instead (clear() then addAll())

CascadeType.REMOVE loads each child and deletes it row by row. For large collections, delete with a bulk JPQL statement or use a database ON DELETE CASCADE foreign key (Hibernate's @OnDelete(action = OnDeleteAction.CASCADE) generates it) so the database does the work.

Inheritance Strategies Compared

Beyond the summary in the question below: pick a strategy by the queries you run, because the shape of the SQL is the real difference.

@Entity
@Inheritance(strategy = InheritanceType.SINGLE_TABLE)
@DiscriminatorColumn(name = "pay_type")
public abstract class Payment {
  @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;
  private BigDecimal amount;
}
@Entity @DiscriminatorValue("CARD")
public class CardPayment extends Payment { private String lastFour; }
@Entity @DiscriminatorValue("BANK")
public class BankPayment extends Payment { private String iban; }

// Polymorphic query, works under all three strategies:
List<Payment> all = em.createQuery("select p from Payment p", Payment.class).getResultList();
// Narrow with type() or treat():
//   select p from Payment p where type(p) = CardPayment
//   select p from Payment p where treat(p as CardPayment).lastFour = :l
SINGLE_TABLEJOINEDTABLE_PER_CLASS@MappedSuperclass
Tables1Base + one per subclassOne per concrete classOne per concrete class
Polymorphic readOne simple SELECTOuter joins to all subclassesUNION ALLNot possible: no shared entity type
Insert1 row2+ rows1 row1 row
NOT NULL on subclass columnsNo, must be nullableYesYesYes
Association to base typeYes, real FKYes, real FKYes, but no real FK possibleNo
Use whenFew subclass columns, polymorphic reads dominateIntegrity matters, subclasses differ a lotRarelyYou only share fields (audit, id)
Gotcha: TABLE_PER_CLASS cannot use IDENTITY ids, because ids must be unique across all the tables and each table would count on its own. Use a shared sequence.

The Persistence Context, the Heart of JPA

The persistence context (PC) is an in-memory map from (entity class, id) to the managed instance, plus a loaded-state snapshot of each one and a queue of pending SQL actions. Everything that seems magical in JPA comes from this one structure:

  • First-level cache: find() checks the map first. Two find() calls for one id in one transaction run one SELECT and return the same object, so == is true.
  • Identity guarantee: query results go through the map too. If a row's entity is already managed, the query returns the existing instance and ignores the fresh row data. This gives repeatable reads at the application level, even on READ COMMITTED, and also means stale data after bulk updates.
  • Dirty checking: at flush, each managed entity is compared field by field with its snapshot. Cost grows with the number of managed entities, which is why a huge PC is slow and why the snapshot roughly doubles memory per entity.
  • Write-behind: SQL is queued and sent at flush rather than at each call, which lets Hibernate batch and reorder it.

Flush modes and flush order

Flushing synchronises the PC to the database. JPA's FlushModeType.AUTO flushes before commit and before any query that may need pending changes. Hibernate's native Session API is smarter about what it can skip for JPQL, but does less for native SQL: Hibernate cannot parse which tables native SQL touches. Through EntityManager (what Spring uses), a native query flushes everything in AUTO mode; through the bare Session API it does not, unless you add synchronized tables.

Hibernate executes queued actions in a fixed order, not the order you called them: inserts, then updates, then collection removals and changes, then deletes. So if you remove a row and insert a new one with the same unique key in one transaction, the INSERT runs first and violates the constraint. Fix it by calling flush() after the remove, or better by updating the existing row.

EntityManager API

MethodWhat it doesWatch out for
persist(e)Transient to managedThrows for a detached entity. Mutates and keeps the same instance
find(cls, id)Looks in the PC, then L2 cache, then DB; returns entity or nullOverloads take a lock mode and hints
getReference(cls, id)Returns an uninitialized proxy, no SQLA wrong id fails only on first field access
merge(e)Copies state onto a managed instance, returns that instanceUse the return value. Runs a SELECT if the entity is not loaded. Null fields overwrite
remove(e)Managed to removedArgument must be managed: em.remove(em.merge(d)) for a detached one
refresh(e)Overwrites the entity from the DBDiscards unflushed changes
detach(e) / clear()Evicts one / all from the PCUnflushed changes are lost, so flush first
contains(e)Is it managed here?Handy in tests
flush()Sends pending SQLNeeds an active transaction
lock(e, mode)Applies a lock to a managed entitySee the locking section
createQuery / createNativeQuery / createNamedQueryQueriesPass a result class for type safety
unwrap(Session.class)Reaches the provider APICouples code to Hibernate
@Service
public class TransferService {
  @PersistenceContext
  private EntityManager em;       // a shared, thread-safe proxy, NOT a real EntityManager

  @Transactional
  public void rename(Long id, String name) {
    Employee e = em.find(Employee.class, id);
    if (e == null) throw new NotFoundException(id);
    e.setName(name);              // no save() call: dirty checking writes it at commit
  }
}

A real EntityManager is not thread-safe. Spring injects a proxy that, on each call, delegates to the one bound to the current transaction (held in a ThreadLocal by TransactionSynchronizationManager). That is why injecting it into a singleton is safe. In Spring Boot, plain constructor injection of EntityManager gives the same shared proxy.

JPQL, Criteria and Native Queries

JPQL

JPQL queries entities and fields, and Hibernate translates it into SQL for your dialect. Parameters are bound, never concatenated, which prevents SQL injection.

// Joins follow associations, so no ON clause is needed
select o from Order o join o.customer c where c.city = :city

// Fetch join: load the association in this query (fills the entity)
select distinct o from Order o left join fetch o.items where o.status = :s

// Aggregates, group by, having
select c.city, count(o), sum(o.total)
from Order o join o.customer c
group by c.city having count(o) > 10

// Subquery, case, coalesce, member of
select e from Employee e
where e.salary > (select avg(x.salary) from Employee x where x.dept = e.dept)

select p from Post p where :tag member of p.tags

// Constructor expression (DTO)
select new com.acme.OrderRow(o.id, c.name, o.total) from Order o join o.customer c
  • e.dept.name in a path is an implicit inner join, so rows with a null dept vanish. Write left join when that matters.
  • A plain join filters rows but does not initialize the association. Only join fetch does.
  • setMaxResults and setFirstResult replace LIMIT. HQL also has limit and offset.
  • getSingleResult() throws NoResultException on zero rows and NonUniqueResultException on several. JPA 3.2 adds getSingleResultOrNull().
  • Named queries (@NamedQuery) are parsed at startup, so typos fail fast. Spring Data @Query JPQL strings are validated at startup too.
  • Bulk update and delete statements skip the PC. See bulk operations below.

Criteria API

Criteria builds the same query as a Java object tree. It exists for queries assembled at runtime from optional filters, where string concatenation is error-prone. With the generated static metamodel (Employee_, produced by Hibernate's annotation processor) attribute names are compile-checked.

public List<Employee> search(String name, BigDecimal minSalary, Long deptId) {
  CriteriaBuilder cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
  CriteriaQuery<Employee> q = cb.createQuery(Employee.class);
  Root<Employee> e = q.from(Employee.class);

  List<Predicate> where = new ArrayList<>();
  if (name != null)      where.add(cb.like(cb.lower(e.get(Employee_.name)), "%" + name.toLowerCase() + "%"));
  if (minSalary != null) where.add(cb.ge(e.get(Employee_.salary), minSalary));
  if (deptId != null)    where.add(cb.equal(e.get(Employee_.dept).get(Department_.id), deptId));

  q.select(e).where(where.toArray(Predicate[]::new)).orderBy(cb.asc(e.get(Employee_.name)));
  return em.createQuery(q).setMaxResults(50).getResultList();
}

Native queries

Use native SQL for what JPQL cannot express: database hints, vendor functions, some recursive queries, or reporting SQL. Results come back as entities (if you select all columns), as scalar rows (Object[] or Tuple), or as DTOs through @SqlResultSetMapping with @ConstructorResult.

List<Employee> rows = em.createNativeQuery(
    "select * from employee where tsv @@ to_tsquery(:q)", Employee.class)
  .setParameter("q", query)
  .getResultList();
OptionBest forWeakness
Derived methodSimple lookups by one to three fieldsLong names; no joins beyond property paths
@Query JPQLStatic queries, fetch joins, DTOsFixed shape
Criteria / SpecificationDynamic search filtersVerbose, hard to read
Querydsl / jOOQComplex, type-safe queriesExtra dependency, code generation
Native SQLVendor features, heavy reportingNot portable; bypasses flush tracking in the plain Session API

Projections and DTOs

Loading entities means extra columns, snapshots, dirty checking, and risk of lazy loading. For read-only views, select only what you need. Interface projections, class DTOs and records all avoid the PC completely, except when an interface projection is "open".

// 1. Closed interface projection: Spring Data selects only these columns
public interface OrderSummary {
  Long getId();
  BigDecimal getTotal();
  CustomerView getCustomer();                // nested projection
  interface CustomerView { String getName(); }
}
List<OrderSummary> findByStatus(String status);

// 2. Open projection: SpEL, so Spring must load the whole entity
public interface FullName {
  @Value("#{target.first + ' ' + target.last}") String getFull();
}

// 3. Record DTO via constructor expression (needs the fully qualified name in JPQL)
public record OrderRow(Long id, String customer, BigDecimal total) { }

@Query("""
    select new com.acme.dto.OrderRow(o.id, c.name, o.total)
    from Order o join o.customer c
    where o.status = :s
    """)
List<OrderRow> rows(@Param("s") String s);

// 4. Dynamic projection: the caller picks the type
<T> List<T> findByCustomerId(Long id, Class<T> type);

Spring Data Repositories

At startup Spring Data creates a proxy for each repository interface. The proxy's target is SimpleJpaRepository, and for each custom method it parses the method name or @Query into a prepared query. Bad property names fail at startup, not at call time. SimpleJpaRepository is annotated @Transactional(readOnly = true) at class level with write methods overridden as @Transactional; that is why a repository call works without your own transaction. Each call then gets its own short transaction and PC, unless a service-level transaction wraps them.

Query derivation

The name is split at By. The left is the subject (find, read, get, count, exists, delete, plus Distinct, Top5, First). The right is property expressions joined by And and Or, then an optional OrderBy.

KeywordExampleSQL idea
And / OrfindByCityAndAgecity=? and age=?
BetweenfindByPriceBetweenbetween ? and ?
LessThan / GreaterThanEqualfindByAgeGreaterThanEqualage >= ?
IsNull / IsNotNullfindByManagerIsNullmanager_id is null
Like / StartingWith / ContainingfindByNameContaininglike %?% (Containing adds wildcards; Like does not)
In / NotInfindByStatusIn(List)in (...)
True / FalsefindByActiveTrueactive = true
IgnoreCasefindByEmailIgnoreCaseupper(email) = upper(?)
OrderByfindByCityOrderByNameDescorder by name desc
Top / FirstfindTop5ByOrderBySalaryDesclimit 5
Nested pathfindByCustomer_Cityjoin to customer; the underscore removes ambiguity

@Query, @Modifying and bulk operations

public interface EmployeeRepo extends JpaRepository<Employee, Long>,
                                      JpaSpecificationExecutor<Employee> {

  @Query(value = "select * from employee where dept_id = :d", nativeQuery = true)
  List<Employee> byDeptNative(@Param("d") Long dept);

  @Query(value = "select e from Employee e join fetch e.dept where e.active = true",
         countQuery = "select count(e) from Employee e where e.active = true")
  Page<Employee> activeWithDept(Pageable p);            // explicit count: fetch joins do not belong in it

  @Transactional
  @Modifying(flushAutomatically = true, clearAutomatically = true)
  @Query("update Employee e set e.salary = e.salary * :f where e.dept.id = :d")
  int raise(@Param("f") BigDecimal factor, @Param("d") Long dept);
}

A bulk JPQL statement runs directly in the database. It does not touch the PC, so it causes three problems, each with a fix:

  • Unflushed changes are not seen by the statement. flushAutomatically = true flushes first (under AUTO, Hibernate would usually flush affected tables anyway).
  • Managed entities become stale. clearAutomatically = true clears the PC. Any unflushed work would be lost, which is why the two are used together.
  • @Version, cascades, lifecycle callbacks and @LastModifiedDate do not run. Set the version yourself in the statement if you rely on it (e.version = e.version + 1), or HQL's update versioned.
Deletion styleSQLCascades, callbacks?
deleteById(id), delete(e)SELECT + DELETEYes
deleteByStatus(s) (derived)SELECT all, then one DELETE eachYes
deleteAll()SELECT all, then one DELETE eachYes
deleteAllInBatch(), deleteAllByIdInBatch(ids)One DELETENo
@Modifying @Query("delete ...")One DELETENo

Paging, sorting and scrolling

Pageable p = PageRequest.of(0, 20, Sort.by("createdAt").descending().and(Sort.by("id")));
Page<Order>  page  = repo.findByStatus("NEW", p);     // data + COUNT query
Slice<Order> slice = repo.findSliceByStatus("NEW", p); // fetches size + 1, no COUNT

// Keyset scrolling, Spring Data 3.1+: no OFFSET at all
Window<Order> w = repo.findFirst20ByStatusOrderByIdAsc("NEW", ScrollPosition.keyset());
if (w.hasNext()) {
  ScrollPosition next = w.positionAt(w.size() - 1);    // pass this to the next call
}

// REST controller: ?page=0&size=20&sort=createdAt,desc binds automatically
@GetMapping public Page<OrderDto> list(Pageable p) { return repo.findAll(p).map(mapper::toDto); }

OFFSET n makes the database produce and discard n rows, so deep pages get slower linearly. Keyset pagination (where id > :last order by id limit 20) uses the index and stays fast, but cannot jump to page 500. Always add a unique tie-breaker such as id to a sort, or rows can repeat or vanish between pages. Spring Data 3.3+ warns that the JSON of PageImpl is not a stable format; @EnableSpringDataWebSupport(pageSerializationMode = VIA_DTO) gives a stable one.

Specifications

A Specification<T> wraps one Criteria predicate as a composable object, so a search screen can combine optional filters without one method per combination.

public final class EmployeeSpecs {
  public static Specification<Employee> nameLike(String n) {
    return (root, query, cb) -> n == null ? null
        : cb.like(cb.lower(root.get("name")), "%" + n.toLowerCase() + "%");
  }
  public static Specification<Employee> inDept(Long id) {
    return (root, query, cb) -> id == null ? null
        : cb.equal(root.get("dept").get("id"), id);
  }
}

Page<Employee> result = repo.findAll(
    Specification.allOf(EmployeeSpecs.nameLike(name), EmployeeSpecs.inDept(dept)), pageable);

A null predicate means "no condition". A fetch inside a Specification breaks the count query that paging runs, so check query.getResultType() != Long.class before fetching.

@EntityGraph

An entity graph is a per-query fetch plan: which associations to load eagerly, without rewriting the query. It turns into LEFT OUTER JOINs.

@Entity
@NamedEntityGraph(name = "Order.detail",
  attributeNodes = { @NamedAttributeNode("customer"),
                     @NamedAttributeNode(value = "items", subgraph = "items") },
  subgraphs = @NamedSubgraph(name = "items", attributeNodes = @NamedAttributeNode("product")))
public class Order { ... }

@EntityGraph("Order.detail")                 // or attributePaths = {"customer", "items.product"}
Optional<Order> findDetailedById(Long id);

EntityGraphType.FETCH (the Spring Data default) treats unlisted attributes as lazy; LOAD keeps their mapped fetch type. The JPA spec states this for all attributes, but a basic field stays loaded with Hibernate unless bytecode enhancement is used.

Auditing

@Configuration
@EnableJpaAuditing(auditorAwareRef = "auditor")
class JpaConfig {
  @Bean AuditorAware<String> auditor() {
    return () -> Optional.ofNullable(SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication())
                         .map(Authentication::getName);
  }
}

@MappedSuperclass
@EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class)
public abstract class Audited {
  @CreatedDate      @Column(updatable = false) private Instant createdAt;
  @LastModifiedDate                            private Instant updatedAt;
  @CreatedBy        @Column(updatable = false) private String  createdBy;
  @LastModifiedBy                              private String  updatedBy;
}

The listener hooks JPA callbacks (@PrePersist, @PreUpdate), so it runs only for changes made through the PC. Bulk statements bypass it. For a history of every change, use Hibernate Envers, covered in the Hibernate section.

Locking and Concurrency

A lost update is the problem to solve: two users read version A, both edit, and the second save silently overwrites the first. Database transactions alone do not prevent it when the read and the write are in separate requests.

Optimistic locking with @Version

On each update of a versioned entity, Hibernate runs update ... set version = 6 where id = ? and version = 5. If zero rows were updated, someone else got there first, and Hibernate throws OptimisticLockException (Spring translates it to ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException). No locks are held between read and write, so this scales, and it works across HTTP requests if the client sends the version back.

// The version must travel through the client, or two requests each read a fresh one
public record UpdateOrder(String status, long version) { }
