@Transactional
public void update(Long id, UpdateOrder cmd) {
  Order o = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
  if (o.getVersion() != cmd.version())
    throw new ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException(Order.class, id);   // map to 409 Conflict
  o.setStatus(cmd.status());
}

// Retry belongs OUTSIDE the transaction (Spring Retry annotation shown): each attempt needs fresh data
@Retryable(retryFor = ObjectOptimisticLockingFailureException.class, maxAttempts = 3)
public void updateWithRetry(...) { txService.update(...); }

Version types: int/long and wrappers, short, and timestamps (less safe, because of clock precision). A version also increments when an owned collection changes. Do not set it by hand on a managed entity.

Lock modes

LockModeTypeSQL effectPurpose
NONENone. @Version still checked on updateDefault
OPTIMISTICVersion re-checked at commit, even if the entity was only read"This row I read must not have changed" (a reference value you depended on)
OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTVersion bumped even with no changeProtect an aggregate root when only a child changed
PESSIMISTIC_READFOR SHARE where supportedOthers can read, cannot write
PESSIMISTIC_WRITEFOR UPDATEExclusive; serialises a critical section
PESSIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENTFOR UPDATE + version bumpExclusive lock that optimistic readers also see
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "3000"))
@Query("select a from Account a where a.id = :id")
Optional<Account> lockById(@Param("id") Long id);

// Money transfer: always lock in id order, or two opposite transfers deadlock
@Transactional
public void transfer(long from, long to, BigDecimal amt) {
  long first = Math.min(from, to), second = Math.max(from, to);
  Account a = repo.lockById(first).orElseThrow();
  Account b = repo.lockById(second).orElseThrow();
  Account src = a.getId() == from ? a : b;
  Account dst = a.getId() == from ? b : a;
  src.debit(amt);
  dst.credit(amt);
}

// Job queue: workers skip rows locked by others (-2 is Hibernate's value for SKIP LOCKED)
@Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE)
@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "jakarta.persistence.lock.timeout", value = "-2"))
List<Job> findTop10ByStatusOrderByIdAsc(String status);
Gotcha: a pessimistic lock lasts until the transaction ends and needs a transaction to exist. Never hold one across an HTTP call or user think time. Under MySQL, FOR UPDATE on an unindexed column can lock far more rows than you meant.

N+1: Every Fix, and When Each One Fits

The N+1 question below shows the shape of the problem. The important part is that it can come from EAGER mappings too: a JPQL select o from Order o ignores @ManyToOne(EAGER) while building the SQL, and only afterwards, seeing the eager field, loads each customer one at a time. EAGER does not fix N+1; it makes it unavoidable.

FixSQL shapeGood forLimit
join fetch1 query with JOINTo-one, or one collectionRow explosion; collection plus paging breaks
@EntityGraph1 query with LEFT JOINSame, on repository methodsSame limits
hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size / @BatchSize1 + a few IN (...) queriesGlobal safety net; multiple collections; pagingSeveral queries, not one
@Fetch(SUBSELECT)1 + where parent_id in (original query)Loading all children of a whole resultRe-runs the first query; odd with paging
DTO projection1 query, chosen columnsRead screens and APIsNot modifiable
Two-step ids then fetchPage of ids, then fetch by id inPaging with collectionsTwo queries
Separate queries per collectionOne query per bagMultipleBagFetchExceptionMore round trips; relies on the PC merging results
L2 cacheCache hitsRead-mostly reference dataHides the problem; invalidation
// Paging over a parent with a collection, the safe way:
Page<Long> ids = repo.findIdsByStatus("NEW", pageable);                // select o.id ...
List<Order> orders = repo.findWithItemsByIdIn(ids.getContent());       // join fetch o.items
// (re-sort in memory or add the same order by, since IN does not preserve order)

// Test that fails if the query count changes, using Hibernate statistics
Statistics stats = sessionFactory.getStatistics();
stats.clear();
service.listOrders();
assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isLessThanOrEqualTo(2);

LazyInitializationException and Open-in-View

A lazy field holds a proxy or wrapper that remembers its session. Accessing it needs a live persistence context. With transaction-scoped contexts, the service returns, the context closes, and access in the controller throws LazyInitializationException.

Open Session in View (OSIV) is Spring's OpenEntityManagerInViewInterceptor, on by default in Boot (spring.jpa.open-in-view=true, and Boot logs a startup warning about it). It opens the context at the start of the web request and closes it at the end, so lazy loading works in controllers and during JSON serialization. The costs:

  • Lazy loads happen outside any service transaction, in auto-commit mode, each as its own statement. Business reads are spread into the serialization layer, invisible to the code reader.
  • Database work can run late in the request, after external calls, keeping connections busy for longer and increasing pool contention under load.
  • It hides N+1 problems until production volume, because code that should have failed instead runs quietly slowly.
  • Entities remain managed across service calls in one request, which causes surprising identity and flush behaviour.

The recommended setup is spring.jpa.open-in-view=false, then fix each exception properly: map to DTOs inside the transaction and fetch what the view needs. hibernate.enable_lazy_load_no_trans=true is a further anti-pattern: each lazy access opens a temporary session and connection.

Transactions with JPA

All writes need an active transaction: on Spring's shared EntityManager, persist, merge, remove and flush throw TransactionRequiredException without one. Under Spring, @Transactional on a public method of a Spring bean does this: the proxy gets a connection, sets auto-commit to false, binds an EntityManager to the thread, calls your method, flushes, commits (or rolls back on an unchecked exception), and closes the context.

RuleDetail
Self-invocationthis.other() bypasses the proxy, so its @Transactional does nothing
Rollback defaultRollback on RuntimeException and Error. Checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor says otherwise
After rollbackAll entities in the context become detached. Their in-memory state still shows the failed changes. Do not reuse them
After an exception inside JPAMost JPA exceptions mark the transaction rollback-only. Catching one and continuing gives UnexpectedRollbackException at commit
REQUIRES_NEWSuspends the outer transaction and opens a second connection and a new PC; entities from the outer one are not visible there. Can deadlock a small pool
readOnly = trueWith Hibernate: flush mode MANUAL and no snapshots, saving memory and CPU; also a connection hint usable for read-replica routing
Isolation@Transactional(isolation = ...) applies only when a new transaction starts; a joining call inherits the outer level
Extended context@PersistenceContext(type = EXTENDED) outlives a transaction. Only for stateful beans; rarely used in Spring apps
Event timing@TransactionalEventListener(phase = AFTER_COMMIT) sends emails and messages only after a real commit
Gotcha: do not make HTTP calls inside a @Transactional method. The DB connection stays checked out for the whole call, so a slow partner service can drain HikariCP and take down unrelated endpoints.

What changed in JPA 3.2 (Jakarta EE 11, Hibernate 7, Spring Boot 4)

  • EntityManagerFactory.runInTransaction() and callInTransaction() for simple programmatic transactions.
  • Type-safe find(...) options through FindOption (lock mode, timeout, cache mode).
  • getSingleResultOrNull() on queries.
  • JPQL additions: union, intersect, except, cast, left, right, replace, nulls first/last, and || for concatenation.
  • Records as embeddables, plus @EnumeratedValue to choose the stored value of an enum.
  • Deprecated: Date, Calendar and @Temporal. Use java.time.

Custom Repository Fragments

When a derived query, @Query or Specification is not enough (dynamic native SQL, bulk JDBC, a Criteria query with tuples), add a fragment: a plain interface plus an implementation whose class name is the interface name with the Impl postfix. Spring Data detects it by name, and the repository interface extends both JpaRepository and the fragment. Calls to fragment methods go to your class; everything else goes to SimpleJpaRepository.

  • The implementation is a normal Spring bean, so you can inject EntityManager, JdbcTemplate or other beans.
  • Fragment methods are not covered by the repository's default transactions: annotate them with @Transactional (or rely on the calling service).
  • A fragment can be reused across several repositories, and a fragment method with the same signature as a built-in one (for example save) overrides it.
public interface OrderSearch {
    List<OrderSummary> search(OrderFilter f);
}

class OrderSearchImpl implements OrderSearch {          // name = fragment + "Impl"
    private final EntityManager em;
    OrderSearchImpl(EntityManager em) { this.em = em; }

    @Override
    @Transactional(readOnly = true)
    public List<OrderSummary> search(OrderFilter f) {
        var cb = em.getCriteriaBuilder();
        var q  = cb.createQuery(OrderSummary.class);
        var o  = q.from(Order.class);
        var where = new ArrayList<Predicate>();
        if (f.status() != null) where.add(cb.equal(o.get("status"), f.status()));
        if (f.from() != null)   where.add(cb.greaterThanOrEqualTo(o.get("createdAt"), f.from()));
        q.select(cb.construct(OrderSummary.class, o.get("id"), o.get("total")))
         .where(where.toArray(Predicate[]::new));
        return em.createQuery(q).setMaxResults(100).getResultList();
    }
}

public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long>, OrderSearch { }

Multiple Data Sources and Read/Write Routing

Spring Boot auto-configures one DataSource, one EntityManagerFactory and one JpaTransactionManager. As soon as you define your own, the auto-configuration backs off and you must wire each persistence unit yourself.

  • Two different databases (for example a main DB and a legacy reporting DB): one @Configuration per database, each with its own DataSource, LocalContainerEntityManagerFactoryBean scanning its own entity package, its own transaction manager, and @EnableJpaRepositories(basePackages = ..., entityManagerFactoryRef = ..., transactionManagerRef = ...). Mark one set @Primary.
  • Same schema, primary + read replica: keep one EntityManagerFactory and put an AbstractRoutingDataSource in front of two pools, choosing by TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly(). Wrap it in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the connection is fetched after the read-only flag is set, not when the transaction begins.
  • A transaction spans one transaction manager. Writes to two databases in one method are not atomic unless you use XA/JTA, which most teams avoid in favour of an outbox or idempotent retries.
  • Replica lag means read-your-writes is not guaranteed: route reads that follow a write in the same user flow to the primary.
public class RoutingDataSource extends AbstractRoutingDataSource {
    @Override
    protected Object determineCurrentLookupKey() {
        return TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly() ? "replica" : "primary";
    }
}

@Bean @Primary
DataSource dataSource(@Qualifier("primaryPool") DataSource primaryPool,
                      @Qualifier("replicaPool") DataSource replicaPool) {
    var routing = new RoutingDataSource();
    routing.setTargetDataSources(Map.<Object, Object>of("primary", primaryPool, "replica", replicaPool));
    routing.setDefaultTargetDataSource(primaryPool);
    routing.afterPropertiesSet();
    return new LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy(routing);   // resolve the key at first statement
}

Testing the Persistence Layer

@DataJpaTest starts a slice: entities, repositories, EntityManager, TestEntityManager, Flyway/Liquibase, but no controllers or services. Each test runs in a transaction that rolls back. By default it replaces your DataSource with an embedded one; with Testcontainers you keep the real database engine.

  • Use @AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = Replace.NONE) plus a container annotated @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+), which sets the connection properties for you.
  • Call em.flush() and em.clear() before asserting, so the test really hits SQL and constraints instead of the first-level cache.
  • Guard against N+1 regressions by asserting the statement count (Hibernate Statistics, or a library wrapping the DataSource such as datasource-proxy).
  • Reuse a single container across test classes (a static container in a base class or Testcontainers reuse) to keep the suite fast.
@DataJpaTest
@AutoConfigureTestDatabase(replace = AutoConfigureTestDatabase.Replace.NONE)
@Testcontainers
class OrderRepositoryTest {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static PostgreSQLContainer<?> db = new PostgreSQLContainer<>("postgres:16-alpine");

    @Autowired OrderRepository repo;
    @Autowired TestEntityManager tem;

    @Test
    void loadsOrdersWithItemsInOneQuery() {
        tem.persist(TestData.orderWithItems(3));
        tem.flush();
        tem.clear();                                   // force a real SELECT

        var stats = tem.getEntityManager().getEntityManagerFactory()
                       .unwrap(SessionFactory.class).getStatistics();
        stats.setStatisticsEnabled(true);
        stats.clear();

        var orders = repo.findAllWithItems();
        orders.forEach(o -> o.getItems().size());
        assertThat(stats.getPrepareStatementCount()).isEqualTo(1);
    }
}

Interview Questions — JPA

JPA vs Hibernate vs Spring Data JPA?

JPA is the specification (jakarta.persistence): annotations plus the EntityManager API. Hibernate is the most popular implementation and adds its own features (caching, @BatchSize, filters). Spring Data JPA is an abstraction on top of JPA that writes repository implementations for you (derived queries, paging, auditing).

What is the persistence context / EntityManager?

The persistence context is the set of managed entity instances, effectively a first-level cache keyed by id. The EntityManager is the API to it: persist, find, merge, remove, createQuery, flush. In Spring, a transaction-scoped context lasts for the duration of the transaction. Inside it, each id maps to one instance, and changes are written at flush through dirty checking.

ID generation strategies?
  • IDENTITY: a DB auto-increment column (MySQL). Disables JDBC batch inserts.
  • SEQUENCE: a DB sequence (Postgres, Oracle). The best for performance, because allocationSize lets Hibernate pre-allocate ids.
  • TABLE: a separate table that simulates a sequence. Slow.
  • AUTO: the provider picks.
  • UUID: @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.UUID) (JPA 3.1).
Explain relationships and owning side / mappedBy.

The types are @OneToOne, @OneToMany, @ManyToOne, @ManyToMany. The owning side is the one that holds the foreign key (@JoinColumn). Only changes on the owning side are written to the DB. The inverse side declares mappedBy = "fieldName". In a bidirectional OneToMany/ManyToOne, the ManyToOne side is always the owner. ManyToMany uses @JoinTable. If the join table needs extra columns, model it as a separate entity.

Default fetch types? Lazy vs Eager?
MappingDefault
@ManyToOne, @OneToOneEAGER (change it to LAZY!)
@OneToMany, @ManyToManyLAZY

Best practice is to make everything LAZY and fetch what you need per use case with JOIN FETCH or @EntityGraph.

What is the N+1 select problem? How to fix?

Loading N parents and then touching a lazy association on each one fires 1 + N queries. Fixes: JOIN FETCH in JPQL, @EntityGraph, Hibernate @BatchSize(size=50) or hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size (uses IN queries), @Fetch(FetchMode.SUBSELECT), or DTO projections. Detect it by turning on SQL logging or using Hibernate statistics.

Cascade types and orphanRemoval?

The cascade types PERSIST, MERGE, REMOVE, REFRESH, DETACH, ALL pass the operation from the parent to its children. orphanRemoval=true deletes a child once it's removed from the parent's collection. Use these only for real parent-owns-child (composition) relationships. Never put CascadeType.REMOVE on ManyToOne or ManyToMany.

JPQL vs Native Query vs Criteria API vs Derived queries?
  • Derived: findByEmailAndActiveTrue. The query is generated from the method name.
  • JPQL: queries entities and fields rather than tables, and is DB-independent.
  • Native: @Query(value="…", nativeQuery=true) for DB-specific SQL.
  • Criteria API / Specifications: type-safe dynamic queries (search filters). JpaSpecificationExecutor, or Querydsl.
CrudRepository vs PagingAndSortingRepository vs JpaRepository?

CrudRepository gives basic CRUD. PagingAndSortingRepository adds findAll(Pageable/Sort) (since Spring Data 3 it no longer extends CrudRepository). JpaRepository adds JPA-specific methods (flush, saveAndFlush, deleteAllInBatch, getReferenceById) and returns List instead of Iterable.

Does save() do insert or update?

SimpleJpaRepository.save() calls persist() if the entity is new (a null wrapper @Version; with no version field or a primitive one, a null id or a primitive id of 0) and merge() otherwise. With assigned (manual) ids, this means an extra SELECT before the merge. Implement Persistable<ID> to control what counts as new.

Optimistic vs Pessimistic locking?

Optimistic: a @Version column. The UPDATE includes WHERE version=?, and if another transaction changed the row you get OptimisticLockException and retry. Good when conflicts are rare. Pessimistic: @Lock(LockModeType.PESSIMISTIC_WRITE) issues SELECT … FOR UPDATE, a DB lock. Good for heavy contention (inventory, wallets).

What causes LazyInitializationException? Fix?

Accessing a lazy association after the session or transaction has closed, for example in the controller or during JSON serialization. Fix: fetch what you need inside the transaction (JOIN FETCH or EntityGraph), map to DTOs inside the service, or use @Transactional on the service method. Avoid relying on Open-Session-In-View (spring.jpa.open-in-view=false is recommended) and don't use EAGER as a workaround.

Inheritance mapping strategies?
  • SINGLE_TABLE (default): one table with a discriminator column. The fastest, but child columns must be nullable.
  • JOINED: a table per class joined by PK. Normalized, but needs joins.
  • TABLE_PER_CLASS: a full table per concrete class. Polymorphic queries need UNIONs.
  • @MappedSuperclass: shares fields (id, audit columns) without being an entity.
What are projections? How to auditing (createdAt etc.)?

Projections fetch only the columns you need: interface-based (interface NameOnly { String getName(); }), class or record DTOs (select new com.x.Dto(o.id, o.total) …), or dynamic. Auditing: @EnableJpaAuditing plus @CreatedDate, @LastModifiedDate, @CreatedBy with @EntityListeners(AuditingEntityListener.class).

Why shouldn't you use Lombok @Data on entities?

Its generated equals/hashCode/toString include every field, including lazy associations. That triggers lazy loading, infinite recursion in bidirectional relationships, and broken behavior in Sets when the id changes after persist. Use @Getter @Setter instead, and write equals/hashCode based on the id or a business key.

What does this print, and how many SELECTs run? (first-level cache)
@Transactional
void demo() {
  Employee a = em.find(Employee.class, 1L);
  Employee b = em.find(Employee.class, 1L);
  Employee c = em.createQuery("select e from Employee e where e.id = 1", Employee.class).getSingleResult();
  System.out.println((a == b) + " " + (a == c));
}

It prints true true, with two SELECTs. The second find is answered from the persistence context. The JPQL query always goes to the database, because the cache is keyed by id and a query is not an id lookup. But the row that comes back is resolved through the context, which returns the existing instance.

A native UPDATE changes a row, then find() runs in the same transaction. Which value do you see?
Employee e = em.find(Employee.class, 1L);    // name = "old"
em.createNativeQuery("update employee set name = 'new' where id = 1").executeUpdate();
System.out.println(em.find(Employee.class, 1L).getName());

It prints old. find returns the managed instance and never reads the row. Worse, if a field of that entity is dirty, a later flush may write the old values back. Fix with em.refresh(e), em.clear(), or @Modifying(clearAutomatically = true).

Is an UPDATE sent here, and which name ends up in the DB?
@Transactional
void rename(Employee detached) {     // detached has id = 1
  Employee managed = em.merge(detached);
  detached.setName("A");
  managed.setName("B");
}

The DB gets B. merge copies the detached state into the managed copy and returns that copy. detached remains detached, so setting "A" on it has no effect. Dirty checking sees "B" on the managed copy. The classic bug is calling em.merge(x) and continuing to use x, ignoring the return value. Spring Data's save() has the same trap: use x = repo.save(x).

Does this code update the DB? There is no save() call.
@Transactional
public void activate(Long id) {
  Employee e = repo.findById(id).orElseThrow();
  e.setActive(true);
}

Yes, as long as activate is really running in a transaction, which requires a public method called through the Spring proxy. e is managed, so dirty checking generates the UPDATE at flush before commit. Calling repo.save(e) there is redundant. Remove @Transactional and nothing is written, because findById's own transaction has ended and e is detached.

Why is the foreign key null after this save?
Order o = new Order();
OrderItem i = new OrderItem();
o.getItems().add(i);          // inverse side only
repo.save(o);                 // cascade ALL

The item is inserted thanks to the cascade, but order_id is null (or the insert fails with NOT NULL), because OrderItem.order, the owning side, was never set. JPA ignores Order.items when writing the FK. Always use a helper that sets both sides: items.add(i); i.setOrder(this);.

Why does a persisted entity disappear from a HashSet? How should equals/hashCode be written?
Set<Bad> s = new HashSet<>();
Bad b = new Bad("x");          // hashCode = Objects.hash(id, name), id is null
s.add(b);
b.id = 1L;                     // what persist does with a generated id
System.out.println(s.contains(b) + " " + s.size());   // false 1
s.remove(b);
System.out.println(s.size());                         // 1

Once the id changes, hashCode changes, so the entry sits in a bucket nobody looks in, and it can be neither found nor removed. A generated id is assigned at persist or flush, so a new entity added to a Set before saving hits exactly this problem. The standard pattern is below: transient entities are equal only to themselves, and the hash is constant so it never changes.

@Override public boolean equals(Object o) {
  if (this == o) return true;
  if (!(o instanceof Employee other)) return false;   // instanceof, so a proxy subclass matches
  return id != null && id.equals(other.getId());      // getter: a proxy's field is not populated
}
@Override public int hashCode() { return Employee.class.hashCode(); }  // constant; not getClass(), a proxy would differ

Hibernate proxies are subclasses, so with proxies in play getClass() comparisons fail in equals. A constant hash costs nothing unless a single Set holds thousands of entities, which you should not load anyway. If there is a stable natural key (ISBN, email), base equals/hashCode on that instead.

orphanRemoval vs CascadeType.REMOVE?

REMOVE fires when the parent is removed. orphanRemoval does this too and additionally fires when a child is unlinked from the parent's collection. Use orphanRemoval only when the child cannot exist without this parent and is never moved between parents; moving a child to another parent may delete it, because it was removed from the old collection.

What is MultipleBagFetchException and how do you solve it?

A bag is a List mapped without an order column: an unordered collection that allows duplicates. Fetch-joining two bags in one query gives a Cartesian product of rows (10 items times 10 tags = 100 rows per order). Since bags allow duplicates, Hibernate cannot tell which rows are real and refuses at startup or query time.

  • Best: run two queries in one transaction, each fetching one collection. The persistence context merges them into the same parents.
  • Set hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size and fetch one collection or none.
  • Change to Set: this stops the exception but keeps the Cartesian product, so it often only hides the performance problem.
What happens when you use pagination with a collection JOIN FETCH?

A LIMIT applied to joined rows would cut through a parent's children, so Hibernate cannot apply it in SQL. It loads all matching rows and paginates in memory, logging a warning (HHH90003004 in Hibernate 6, HHH000104 earlier). That can load a full table per request. Set hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true to turn it into an exception. Fix with the two-step pattern (page ids, then fetch by ids) or batch fetching. ToOne fetch joins do not multiply rows and are safe with paging.

Why is the inverse side of @OneToOne eagerly loaded even with fetch = LAZY?

For a null reference, Java needs null; for a present one, it needs a proxy. On the owning side the FK column tells Hibernate which applies. On the inverse side (mappedBy) there is no column in this table, so to decide between null and proxy Hibernate must query the other table anyway, and so it just loads the entity. Fixes: map only the owning side with @MapsId and look it up by the same id; bytecode enhancement; or, if the relationship is optional only in theory, optional = false, which helps in some mappings.

Why use Set rather than List for @ManyToMany?

When one element is removed from a List bag, Hibernate does not know which join row to target, because a bag has no identity per row. It deletes all rows for that owner and re-inserts the remaining ones. With a Set it removes exactly one row.

Unique constraint violation when replacing a child in one transaction. Why?
Profile old = repo.findByUserId(1L);
repo.delete(old);
repo.save(new Profile(1L));      // same unique user_id

The flush order is fixed: inserts before deletes. The INSERT fails on the unique index because the DELETE has not run yet, regardless of the order in your code. Options: call repo.flush() after the delete, or update the existing row in place, which is simpler and uses fewer statements.

Why does a query trigger an UPDATE before it runs?

In AUTO flush mode, Hibernate flushes pending changes that could affect the query, so the query sees your own transaction's writes. This surprises people when validation queries inside a @Transactional method send half-finished entities to the database. If needed, a query can use setFlushMode(FlushModeType.COMMIT), but understand that it then may not see those changes.

What does @Transactional(readOnly = true) do with Hibernate?

Three things. Spring sets the Hibernate flush mode to MANUAL, so no accidental flush happens. Hibernate's session is set read-only, so entities loaded get no snapshot, which saves memory and dirty-check time. And connection.setReadOnly(true) gives the driver a hint, usable with routing to a read replica. It is not a security guarantee: a @Modifying query still runs unless the database rejects it. It also does nothing when joining an existing writable transaction.

findById vs getReferenceById?

findById runs a SELECT (or uses a cache) and returns an Optional. getReferenceById returns a lazy proxy without SQL, and throws EntityNotFoundException on first access if the row is absent. Use the reference when you only need a foreign key:

Comment c = new Comment(text);
c.setPost(postRepo.getReferenceById(postId));   // INSERT only, no SELECT of post
commentRepo.save(c);

Returning that proxy from a controller fails with a Jackson error mentioning ByteBuddyInterceptor or hibernateLazyInitializer. The real cure is not to serialize entities; return DTOs.

Why not expose entities directly in REST responses?
  • The API becomes coupled to the schema: renaming a column breaks clients.
  • Lazy fields fail or trigger N+1 during serialization.
  • Bidirectional links cause infinite recursion (@JsonIgnore and @JsonManagedReference are bandages).
  • Internal fields leak (password hash, flags).
  • Accepting entities as input allows mass assignment: a client can set role or version.

Map to request and response DTOs at the service boundary, by hand or with MapStruct.

Page vs Slice vs List vs Window? How do you page through millions of rows?

Page runs a COUNT and knows total pages. Slice fetches size + 1 and knows only whether a next page exists, which suits infinite scroll and avoids the costly COUNT. List with a Pageable has neither. Window with ScrollPosition is keyset scrolling. For millions of rows use keyset paging, because OFFSET degrades linearly. For a full export use a stream in a read-only transaction:

@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.fetchSize", value = "1000"))
@Query("select o from Order o")
Stream<Order> streamAll();

@Transactional(readOnly = true)
public void export(Writer out) {
  try (Stream<Order> s = repo.streamAll()) {       // must be closed
    s.forEach(o -> { write(out, o); em.detach(o); });   // keep the context small
  }
}

On MySQL, driver streaming needs a fetch size of Integer.MIN_VALUE or the useCursorFetch option; otherwise the driver buffers everything. On PostgreSQL it needs auto-commit off, which the transaction gives you.

Closed vs open interface projection, and why does it matter?

A closed projection exposes only getters that match entity properties, so Spring Data can select just those columns. An open projection uses @Value with SpEL, whose needs are unknown ahead of time, so the whole entity must be loaded and no query optimization is possible. Use a Java default method or a DTO instead when you want a computed field and fast queries.

How do you map a native query to a DTO?

Spring Data interface projections work with native queries when aliases match the getter names, which is the easiest route:

public interface CityTotal { String getCity(); BigDecimal getTotal(); }

@Query(value = """
    select c.city as city, sum(o.total) as total
    from orders o join customer c on c.id = o.customer_id
    group by c.city""", nativeQuery = true)
List<CityTotal> totals();

The standard JPA option is @SqlResultSetMapping with @ConstructorResult on an entity. select new works only in JPQL, never in native SQL.

@Modifying forgot clearAutomatically. What goes wrong? And why might it throw?

Without @Modifying at all, an update query throws, because Spring Data expects a SELECT. Without a transaction it throws TransactionRequiredException: custom repository methods are not covered by the default write transaction, so add @Transactional on the method or the calling service. Without clearAutomatically, managed entities keep old values, so a later findById in the same transaction returns stale data.

saveAll on 100,000 rows is slow. Why, and how do you fix it?

saveAll calls save in a loop. With IDENTITY, each row is one round trip and batching is disabled. With assigned ids, each row causes an extra SELECT through merge. All entities pile up in the context, so every flush checks more entities. Fixes:

  1. Use SEQUENCE with an allocation size matching the batch size, or JDBC directly for pure loads.
  2. Set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, hibernate.order_inserts=true, hibernate.order_updates=true.
  3. Process in chunks: flush() and clear() every 50, or one short transaction per chunk.
  4. Implement Persistable for assigned ids.
  5. For true bulk loads, use JdbcTemplate.batchUpdate or the database's COPY or LOAD command.
Explain the lock modes and when you would use OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT.

Scenario: Order has a cap on total value and items are separate rows. Two transactions each add an item. Neither changes the orders row, so its version does not change, and both commit, breaking the cap. Loading the order with OPTIMISTIC_FORCE_INCREMENT bumps the version even without a change, so the second transaction fails. This is how you make a whole aggregate behave as one consistency unit.

Optimistic or pessimistic locking for a seat booking or flash sale?

It depends on contention. On hot rows, optimistic locking causes a retry storm: nearly every transaction fails, wasting work. Pessimistic locking queues them, but holds connections and limits throughput to one row at a time. For a counter, the best solution is usually neither: a single atomic statement.

@Modifying
@Query("update Stock s set s.qty = s.qty - :n where s.sku = :sku and s.qty >= :n")
int reserve(@Param("sku") String sku, @Param("n") int n);    // 0 rows means sold out

The row lock lasts one statement, and a CHECK constraint can back it up. For extreme load, move reservation to Redis with a Lua script or a queue, then persist asynchronously.

Two users edit the same record in a web form. How do you stop the second silently overwriting the first?

Send version to the client with the form (or as an ETag). On submit, the client returns it. The service loads the entity, compares versions, and on mismatch returns 409 Conflict or 412 Precondition Failed with If-Match. Merging a detached DTO-built entity containing the old version also triggers OptimisticLockException. Without a client-held version, each request reads a new version and the check protects only the few milliseconds between read and write.

What does a deadlock look like with JPA, and how do you avoid it?

Transaction 1 locks account A then wants B, while transaction 2 locks B then wants A. The database detects the cycle and aborts one (Spring raises CannotAcquireLockException or DeadlockLoserDataAccessException depending on database and version). Prevention: lock rows in a fixed order (sorted ids), keep transactions short, add indexes so locks cover fewer rows, and use lock timeouts. Hibernate's own flush order helps by ordering updates when hibernate.order_updates=true. Retry the whole transaction when it happens; the failed one left no effect.

How do you implement soft delete?

Hibernate 6.4+ has @SoftDelete, which turns removes into updates of a flag column and filters reads. Earlier, or for a deleted-at timestamp, combine @SQLDelete(sql = "update emp set deleted_at = now() where id = ?") with @SQLRestriction("deleted_at is null") (Hibernate 6.3+, replacing @Where, which is removed in 7). Consider: unique constraints must allow reinserts (a partial unique index), native queries do not get the filter, foreign keys still point to soft-deleted rows, and tables grow, so old rows may need archiving.

What are JPA lifecycle callbacks and entity listeners? When would you avoid them?

Callbacks are annotated methods run at state transitions: @PrePersist, @PostPersist, @PreUpdate, @PostUpdate, @PreRemove, @PostRemove, @PostLoad. They go on the entity or a class named in @EntityListeners. Typical use: set timestamps, normalize data. @PreUpdate runs at flush only if the entity is dirty. Pre callbacks must not call the EntityManager or change relationships; the spec leaves that behaviour undefined. They do not run for bulk statements. Keep business logic out of them, as it is invisible to readers.

How do you map an enum safely when the DB value differs from the name?

Use an AttributeConverter, which stays stable when constants get renamed:

@Converter(autoApply = true)
public class StatusConverter implements AttributeConverter<Status, String> {
  public String convertToDatabaseColumn(Status s) { return s == null ? null : s.code(); }
  public Status convertToEntityAttribute(String c) { return c == null ? null : Status.fromCode(c); }
}

JPA 3.2 adds @EnumeratedValue, which marks an enum field as the stored value. Comparing in JPQL with a converted attribute uses the Java enum value as usual; converters apply to parameters too.

A @Transactional method calls a slow REST API. The app stalls under load. Walk through the diagnosis.

Symptoms: hikaricp.connections.pending rises and requests time out with SQLTransientConnectionException: Connection is not available, even though the DB is idle. Each request holds a connection for the full HTTP call. With a pool of 10 and a 2-second partner call, throughput caps at 5 requests per second. Fix: read in one short transaction, call the API outside any transaction, write in a second short transaction, and use a version check to detect changes in between. Disable OSIV, or it extends connection use. Add a connection pool timeout and a client timeout. If the steps must be consistent, the outbox pattern moves the call out of the transaction entirely.

How can REQUIRES_NEW deadlock the connection pool?

The outer transaction holds connection 1 and the inner needs connection 2. If every pool connection is held by an outer transaction, all threads wait for a second connection that will never be released: a pool deadlock, ended only by the timeout. Make the pool larger than the max concurrency of nested calls, or remove the nested transaction. Also remember the inner transaction does not see the outer's uncommitted rows, and a lock held by the outer can block the inner forever within the same thread.

Does persisting a parent with a detached child work?

With CascadeType.PERSIST, no: the cascade reaches the detached child and Hibernate throws "detached entity passed to persist" (in Hibernate 7 this can appear as EntityExistsException). It happens when a DTO-built child carries an id. Without cascade, a reference to a detached entity works for a ManyToOne because only its id is needed; better, use getReferenceById. Calling save() when the parent has an id uses merge, which cascades MERGE instead.

@EntityGraph vs JOIN FETCH?

Both load an association in the same query. join fetch is part of the query text and can combine with conditions on the fetched data. Filtering on a fetched collection is risky, however: join fetch o.items i where i.qty > 1 gives you an entity with a partial collection, which looks complete, and could cause bad writes. @EntityGraph is declared separately, can be applied on derived queries and findAll, and always uses LEFT JOIN. Use the graph for reuse on simple queries, and fetch join for full control.

Does Spring Data's CrudRepository.findAll() on a mapped EAGER relation use one query?

No. findAll runs JPQL. EAGER mapping does not change JPQL's SQL, so eager ManyToOnes are then loaded with one extra query per distinct associated id. em.find by id, by contrast, uses a join for EAGER associations. That difference is why EAGER seems fine in a demo with findById and collapses on list pages.

How would you implement a search API with 8 optional filters?

Not with 256 repository methods, nor with (:name is null or e.name = :name) in one query, which can produce poor plans on some databases. Use Specifications, Querydsl or Criteria: build a list of predicates for only the filters provided. Add paging, a whitelist of sortable fields (a raw sort parameter can reference anything), a max page size, and indexes for the common filter combinations. Fetch to-one associations with an entity graph and project to a DTO. Query by Example (Example.of(probe)) is an alternative for equality-only filters.

Why does a @Transactional test hide bugs?

A test-level @Transactional keeps one persistence context open for the whole test and rolls back at the end. So lazy loading works where it would fail in production, the first-level cache answers reads so mappings are not really tested, flush may never happen, so constraints do not fire, and AFTER_COMMIT listeners never run. Call em.flush(); em.clear(); before assertions, or run without test transactions and clean up. Use Testcontainers with the real database rather than H2, since dialect differences hide real problems.

How does Spring Data decide the transaction for a derived query, and do two repo calls share a context?

Without a service-level transaction, each call opens its own transaction and context. Two findById(1L) calls then run two SELECTs and return two different instances (with OSIV on, the context is shared across the request, so they would be the same instance). Inside a service @Transactional, repository calls join it and share one context.

You see StaleObjectStateException in logs without any concurrent users. What might cause it?

Common causes beyond real concurrency: the same entity saved twice via different detached copies, a merge with an entity whose id was built by hand, the client re-sending an old version, a retry reusing a stale object, or a database trigger or bulk statement changing the version outside Hibernate. An update of a row that no longer exists gives the same failure, since zero rows matched. Log the id and both versions, and check for double submits.

How do you call a stored procedure with Spring Data JPA?

Use @Procedure on a repository method: @Procedure(procedureName = "apply_discount") void applyDiscount(Long orderId, BigDecimal pct);. Parameters map by position (or by name with @Param), and a single OUT parameter becomes the return value. For several OUT parameters or a result set, declare @NamedStoredProcedureQuery on the entity, or call em.createStoredProcedureQuery(...) in a custom fragment. Keep business logic in Java where possible; procedures are hard to test, version and port.

When would you use @ElementCollection, and what are its pitfalls?

For a collection of values with no identity of their own: tags, phone numbers, or embeddable addresses, stored in a child table via @CollectionTable. Pitfalls:

  • A List without @OrderColumn is a bag: changing one element deletes all rows for the owner and re-inserts them.
  • Elements cannot be queried, referenced or loaded on their own, and are always owned by the parent's lifecycle.
  • Lazy by default, so the same N+1 and LazyInitializationException rules apply.
Prefer a Set (with proper equals/hashCode on the embeddable) or @OrderColumn; once the element needs its own id, audit columns or queries, promote it to an entity with @OneToMany.

save() of a duplicate email did not throw, but the transaction failed later. Why, and how should you handle unique-constraint violations?

save() usually only schedules the INSERT; the SQL runs at flush, typically at commit, after your try/catch has exited. The exception then surfaces as DataIntegrityViolationException from the transaction proxy. Options: call saveAndFlush() inside the try block when you need to react immediately; or let it propagate and map it to 409 Conflict in a @RestControllerAdvice. A pre-check with existsByEmail is good for a friendly message but is not enough on its own because of the race between check and insert; the unique index is the real guarantee. After the exception, the persistence context is unusable, so do not keep working in the same transaction.

You have two DataSources. Why does @Transactional on a method not roll back writes to the second one?

@Transactional uses one transaction manager, the @Primary one unless you name another with @Transactional("reportingTxManager"). Writes through the second EntityManagerFactory run in their own (or no) transaction, so they commit independently. Spring has no safe built-in way to make both atomic: ChainedTransactionManager is deprecated because a failure between the two commits still leaves them inconsistent. Use JTA/XA if you truly need it, or redesign with an outbox, idempotent consumers and compensation.

Spring Boot with virtual threads enabled: does JPA get faster?

Throughput for blocking I/O can improve because request threads are no longer scarce, but the connection pool becomes the limit: thousands of virtual threads will queue on a pool of 10 to 50 Hikari connections, and connectionTimeout errors appear instead of thread exhaustion. Keep transactions short, never hold a transaction across a remote call, and size the pool for what the database can handle, not for the number of threads. On JDKs before 24, synchronized blocks in older JDBC drivers or libraries could pin virtual threads to carriers; use current drivers and JDK 24+ where possible.

How do you route read-only queries to a read replica, and what is the catch?

Put an AbstractRoutingDataSource in front of the primary and replica pools, choose the key from TransactionSynchronizationManager.isCurrentTransactionReadOnly(), and wrap it in LazyConnectionDataSourceProxy so the connection is picked after Spring has set the read-only flag. Then @Transactional(readOnly = true) services read from the replica. The catch is replication lag: a user who just saved something may not see it. Send reads that follow a write in the same flow to the primary, or route by a short "recent writer" window.

Hibernate ORM

The JPA provider in depth: Session API, caching levels, dirty checking, and the classic API questions.

Caching Levels

Architecture and Bootstrap

Hibernate is a JPA provider with a richer native API. In a Spring Boot app you rarely see its classes, because EntityManagerFactory is a SessionFactory and EntityManager is a Session: SessionFactory extends EntityManagerFactory, and Session extends EntityManager. Reach the native API with em.unwrap(Session.class).

Startup is expensive because Hibernate reads every mapping, builds a metamodel, compiles entity persisters (the prepared SQL and metadata per entity), prepares bytecode proxies, and checks the schema if asked. That result is the immutable SessionFactory, built once. A Session is cheap: it borrows a connection only when it needs one.

// Native bootstrap, without Spring. Spring Boot does the equivalent for you.
StandardServiceRegistry registry = new StandardServiceRegistryBuilder()
    .configure()                                    // reads hibernate.cfg.xml
    .build();
Metadata metadata = new MetadataSources(registry)
    .addAnnotatedClass(Employee.class)
    .buildMetadata();
SessionFactory factory = metadata.buildSessionFactory();

factory.inTransaction(session -> {                  // opens, commits or rolls back, closes
  session.persist(new Employee("Ann"));
});
Inside a SessionWhat it holds
Persistence contextMap of EntityKey (class + id) to entity, plus loaded-state snapshots, collection entries, and proxies
ActionQueuePending inserts, updates, deletes and collection actions, sorted at flush
JDBC coordinatorAcquires and releases the connection, batches statements
Event systemEach operation fires an event; default listeners do the work (persist fires a PersistEvent, handled by DefaultPersistEventListener)

Since every operation is an event, you can extend behaviour by registering your own listener, which is how Envers and Bean Validation integrate.

Session API: States and Operations in Hibernate 6 and 7

The legacy Hibernate methods existed before JPA. They were deprecated in 6.0 and removed in 7.0, so old tutorials no longer compile on Spring Boot 4 (Hibernate 7.1). Session.get remains but is deprecated in favor of find.

Old callStatus in 7.0Use insteadKey difference
save(e)Removedpersist(e)persist returns void; read the id from the entity
update(e)Removedmerge(e)update reattached the same object; merge copies and returns a managed one
saveOrUpdate(e)Removedpersist if transient, merge if detachedYour code now says which case it is
delete(e)Removedremove(e)Same effect
load(cls, id)RemovedgetReference(cls, id)Same semantics
get(cls, id)Deprecatedfind(cls, id)Same semantics
// What merge(detached) does, step by step:
// 1. Look for the id in the persistence context.
// 2. If absent, SELECT the row (L2 cache first). Row missing: treat as new.
// 3. Copy every field from the argument onto the managed instance.
// 4. Compare versions, and throw if the detached copy is older.
// 5. Cascade MERGE. Return the managed instance.
// At flush, dirty checking writes only what actually differs.

Employee managed = session.merge(detachedEmployee);   // use this reference from here on

Other useful native loading APIs are listed here because interviewers like them:

// Load many by id in one query, using the persistence context first
List<Employee> list = session.byMultipleIds(Employee.class).multiLoad(1L, 2L, 3L);

// Business key lookup, with an optional cache of natural id to primary key
Employee e = session.bySimpleNaturalId(Employee.class).load("ann@acme.com");

Dirty Checking Internals

By default, at flush Hibernate walks every managed entity and compares each attribute to the snapshot taken at load time. No proxy intercepts your setter, which is why direct field writes are still detected. The cost is proportional to the number of managed entities times attributes, on every flush, even if nothing changed.

The ways to reduce that cost:

  • Read-only loading: @Transactional(readOnly = true), or query hint org.hibernate.readOnly, stores no snapshot.
  • Bytecode enhancement with dirty tracking: the build plugin rewrites entity classes so that setters record which fields changed, and flush needs no comparison.
  • @Immutable entities are never checked.
  • Keeping sessions small: flush and clear in batch work.

By default the UPDATE lists all columns, not just changed ones. It looks wasteful but means one statement per entity that can be prepared once and reused. @DynamicUpdate sends only changed columns, at the cost of generating SQL each time. It is useful for wide tables, or when two transactions update different columns of the same row. With versionless optimistic locking (@OptimisticLocking(type = DIRTY)) it is required.

Second-Level Cache in Depth

The L2 cache sits at the SessionFactory level so several sessions can share loaded data and skip the DB. It stores a disassembled copy of the entity state (an array of field values) rather than the entity object, which is why two sessions never share one instance. On a hit, Hibernate builds a new entity in the session from that array.

Region typeStoresNotes
EntityField values by idUsed by find and lazy to-one, not by JPQL queries
CollectionIds of the elementsEnable with @Cache on the collection. Child entities must be cached too, or each id becomes a SELECT
Natural idNatural id to primary key@NaturalIdCache
QueryQuery + params to idsSeparate switch, see below
Update timestampsLast change time per tableUsed to validate query results
# application.yml: L2 cache through JCache with Caffeine
# dependencies: hibernate-jcache, caffeine's jcache module
spring:
  jpa:
    properties:
      hibernate:
        cache:
          use_second_level_cache: true
          use_query_cache: true
          region.factory_class: jcache
        javax.cache.provider: com.github.benmanes.caffeine.jcache.spi.CaffeineCachingProvider
        generate_statistics: true
    # ENABLE_SELECTIVE is the default: only @Cacheable entities are cached

@Entity
@Cacheable
@Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE, region = "country")
public class Country {
  @Id private String code;
  private String name;

  @OneToMany(mappedBy = "country")
  @Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE)     // caches the id list
  private Set<City> cities = new HashSet<>();
}
StrategyHow it stays consistentUse for
READ_ONLYNever updated; modifying throwsImmutable reference data. Fastest
NONSTRICT_READ_WRITENo locks; entry invalidated after commit, with a short stale windowRare updates, where brief staleness is fine
READ_WRITEA soft lock replaces the entry during the write; readers go to the DB until commitNormal default for data that changes
TRANSACTIONALEnlisted in the JTA transaction; needs a provider that supports itStrong consistency with Infinispan under JTA
ProviderTypeFit
Caffeine, via JCacheLocal to the JVMSingle node, or data that can be stale per node
Ehcache 3, via JCacheLocal; clustered with TerracottaSame, plus off-heap and disk tiers
InfinispanLocal, replicated or invalidation clusterClusters, transactional caching
HazelcastDistributedClusters
Redisson (Redis)RemoteTeams already on Redis. Each hit is a network call

Cache behaviour per operation: CacheMode is NORMAL (read and write), GET (read only), PUT (write only), REFRESH (write, forcing overwrite), IGNORE (neither). Use IGNORE in batch jobs that would otherwise flood the cache. In standard JPA these map to the hints jakarta.persistence.cache.retrieveMode and storeMode.

Gotcha: L2 cache does not suit every entity. Good candidates are read often, changed rarely, and tolerant of some staleness: countries, products, config. Bad candidates are frequently updated or changed outside Hibernate, because other apps, SQL scripts and triggers do not invalidate it. Multiple app instances with a local cache also go out of sync unless the provider handles it.

Query cache mechanism

@QueryHints(@QueryHint(name = "org.hibernate.cacheable", value = "true"))
List<Country> findByContinent(String continent);

// Programmatic eviction
sessionFactory.getCache().evictEntityData(Country.class, "NL");
sessionFactory.getCache().evictAllRegions();
entityManagerFactory.getCache().evict(Country.class);    // JPA equivalent

Batching

Two unrelated features share the word "batch", and mixing them up is a common interview slip.

JDBC write batchingBatch fetching
Settinghibernate.jdbc.batch_size@BatchSize, hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size
PurposeSend many INSERT or UPDATE statements in one round tripLoad many lazy associations with one IN query
SolvesSlow writesN+1 reads
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_inserts=true       # group by entity so batches do not break
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.order_updates=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_versioned_data=true
# Driver side rewriting into multi-row form:
# MySQL:      jdbc:mysql://host/db?rewriteBatchedStatements=true
# PostgreSQL: jdbc:postgresql://host/db?reWriteBatchedInserts=true
@Transactional
public void importAll(List<Row> rows) {
  int i = 0;
  for (Row r : rows) {
    em.persist(toEntity(r));
    if (++i % 50 == 0) {       // same as batch_size
      em.flush();              // send this batch
      em.clear();              // release memory and dirty-check cost
    }
  }
}

// StatelessSession: no persistence context, no dirty checking, no cascades
try (StatelessSession s = sessionFactory.openStatelessSession()) {
  Transaction tx = s.beginTransaction();
  rows.forEach(r -> s.insert(toEntity(r)));   // runs right away
  tx.commit();
}

Without ordering, a batch is sent each time the statement text changes, so inserts alternating between parent and child form batches of one. StatelessSession has no first-level cache, no lazy loading, no cascades, and ignores interceptors and some events. In 7.0, it uses the L2 cache by default, and hibernate.jdbc.batch_size no longer applies to it, so check the batch setup when upgrading.

For reading huge results with a bounded memory footprint, use session.createQuery(...).scroll(ScrollMode.FORWARD_ONLY) (ScrollableResults) or getResultStream() with a fetch size, evicting as you go.

Fetch Type vs Fetch Mode

FetchType (JPA) answers when to load: EAGER or LAZY. FetchMode (Hibernate) answers how: which SQL to use.

@Fetch(...)SQLNote
SELECTSeparate query per ownerDefault for collections. Combine with @BatchSize
JOINOuter join in the same queryImplies eager. Applies to find, and is ignored by JPQL/HQL, which then uses separate selects
SUBSELECTwhere owner_id in (select ... original query)Collections only. Loads the collection of all owners in the previous result at once
@Entity
public class Author {
  @OneToMany(mappedBy = "author")
  @BatchSize(size = 25)                     // first access loads up to 25 collections with IN
  private List<Book> books = new ArrayList<>();
}

// Loading 100 authors, then touching books on each one:
//   1 query for authors + 4 queries for books (100 / 25) instead of 100
// Also usable on the entity class: @BatchSize on Book batches proxy loading for ManyToOne.

Hibernate-Specific Mapping Features

@Formula, @Generated and friends

@Entity
public class Post {
  @Formula("(select count(*) from comment c where c.post_id = id)")   // raw SQL, part of each SELECT
  private int commentCount;                                           // read-only

  @Column(insertable = false, updatable = false)
  @Generated                                       // re-read after the database generates it
  private String searchVector;

  @CreationTimestamp private Instant createdAt;    // set by Hibernate on insert
  @UpdateTimestamp   private Instant updatedAt;    // set on every update

  @ColumnTransformer(read = "pgp_sym_decrypt(ssn, 'key')",
                     write = "pgp_sym_encrypt(?, 'key')")
  private String ssn;                              // SQL applied in each read and write
}

@Formula is plain SQL and runs for every load of the entity, so a correlated subquery there adds its cost to each row, including list pages. The value is not refreshed after a change in the session. Other useful annotations:

AnnotationEffect
@NaturalIdMarks a business key, immutable by default, with a generated unique constraint
@ImmutableNo dirty checks, no UPDATE. In 7.0, HQL updates and deletes of it throw by default
@SubselectMaps an entity to a read-only SQL query, like a view in code
@DynamicInsert / @DynamicUpdateOmit null or unchanged columns
@SQLRestriction (6.3+)Always-on WHERE fragment; replaces @Where, removed in 7
@SQLOrder (6.3+)SQL order for a collection; replaces Hibernate's @OrderBy, removed in 7
@SQLDelete / @SQLInsert / @SQLUpdateCustom CRUD SQL
@SoftDelete (6.4+)Remove becomes an update of a flag
@TenantId (6.0+)Discriminator-based multi-tenancy
@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)Stores a Java object as a JSON column
@OnDeleteGenerates ON DELETE CASCADE in the DDL
@Entity
public class Product {
  @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)          // jsonb on PostgreSQL, json on MySQL
  private Map<String, Object> attributes;
}

@Filter

A filter is a named, parameterized WHERE fragment that can be switched on per session. @SQLRestriction is always on; a filter is optional. Typical uses: tenant visibility, "active only", date windows.

@Entity
@FilterDef(name = "activeOnly", parameters = @ParamDef(name = "active", type = Boolean.class))
@Filter(name = "activeOnly", condition = "active = :active")
public class Account { ... }

Session session = em.unwrap(Session.class);
session.enableFilter("activeOnly").setParameter("active", true);
// Now applies to HQL, Criteria and lazy collections for this session
Gotcha: filters are not applied to native SQL, and historically did not apply to find() by id. 6.5 added applyToLoadByKey on @FilterDef for that. Do not rely on a filter alone for tenant isolation unless tests cover each access path.

Naming Strategies

Mapping a Java name to a column happens in two steps.

  1. Implicit naming (ImplicitNamingStrategy): decides a logical name when you did not give one, for example the name of a join column or join table.
  2. Physical naming (PhysicalNamingStrategy): rewrites every logical name, including ones you wrote in @Column, into the real identifier. Good for prefixes and for snake case.

Spring Boot's default physical strategy turns firstName and even @Column(name = "firstName") into first_name, which surprises people porting a schema. In Boot 3 the class is CamelCaseToUnderscoresNamingStrategy. To keep names exactly as written:

spring.jpa.hibernate.naming.physical-strategy=org.hibernate.boot.model.naming.PhysicalNamingStrategyStandardImpl

// Or write a custom strategy
public class PrefixStrategy extends PhysicalNamingStrategyStandardImpl {
  @Override public Identifier toPhysicalTableName(Identifier name, JdbcEnvironment env) {
    return Identifier.toIdentifier("app_" + name.getText(), name.isQuoted());
  }
}

Interceptors, Events and Auditing History

MechanismLevelGood for
JPA callbacks, @PrePersistOne entitySimple normalisation, timestamps
InterceptorSession or factory; sees all entitiesCross-cutting checks, changing state before save
Event listenersFactory; low level, full accessAudit and integrations, can do extra SQL through the event source
StatementInspectorEvery SQL stringLogging, comments, tracing, count assertions
EnversModuleFull version history of entities
// Log and tag SQL
public class TagInspector implements StatementInspector {
  @Override public String inspect(String sql) {
    return "/* app=orders */ " + sql;
  }
}

// Register with Spring Boot
@Bean
HibernatePropertiesCustomizer hibernateCustomizer() {
  return props -> props.put(AvailableSettings.STATEMENT_INSPECTOR, new TagInspector());
}

// An event listener, added at startup
public class AuditListener implements PostUpdateEventListener {
  @Override public void onPostUpdate(PostUpdateEvent e) {
    String[] names = e.getPersister().getPropertyNames();
    for (int i : e.getDirtyProperties()) {
      log.info("{}#{} {} changed", e.getEntity().getClass().getSimpleName(), e.getId(), names[i]);
    }
  }
  @Override public boolean requiresPostCommitHandling(EntityPersister p) { return false; }
}

@Component
class ListenerSetup {
  ListenerSetup(EntityManagerFactory emf) {
    SessionFactoryImpl sf = emf.unwrap(SessionFactoryImpl.class);
    sf.getServiceRegistry().getService(EventListenerRegistry.class)
      .appendListeners(EventType.POST_UPDATE, new AuditListener());
  }
}

Envers (hibernate-envers) adds @Audited on an entity: each commit writes to a *_AUD table with a revision number, and AuditReader queries past state.

Dialects

A dialect tells Hibernate how to speak a particular database: SQL syntax for paging, sequences and locks; function names; and the mapping from Java types to column types. Since Hibernate 6, it detects the database and version from JDBC metadata, so hibernate.dialect usually should not be set. A single class such as MySQLDialect or PostgreSQLDialect adapts to the version; version-suffixed classes like MySQL8Dialect are deprecated. Rarer databases are in hibernate-community-dialects. You still set it when no connection is available at startup.

Hibernate 6 and 7: What Changed

Version (Spring Boot)ChangeEffect on your code
6.0 (Boot 3.0 ships 6.1)Jakarta namespacejavax.persistence becomes jakarta.persistence
6.0New query engine, SQM (Semantic Query Model) for HQL and Criteria; results read by column positionStricter HQL; faster; fewer generated aliases
6.0Automatic deduplication of root entities in join fetch queriesdistinct no longer needed for that purpose
6.0New type system: @JdbcTypeCode, @JavaType, generic UserType<T>Custom types need rewriting; @TypeDef gone
6.0Default sequence per entity, <name>_SEQOld hibernate_sequence schemas need migrating or the legacy setting
6.0HQL gains window functions, set operations (union), limit; ResultTransformer replaced by TupleTransformer and ResultListTransformerLess need for native SQL
6.x@TenantId, @SoftDelete, @SQLRestriction, JSON and array mapping, records as embeddablesLess custom code
6.6Jakarta Data repositories via the annotation processorAn alternative to Spring Data repositories
7.0 (Boot 4.0 ships 7.1)Jakarta Persistence 3.2; Java 17 baseline; license moves to Apache 2.0Upgrade path; see JPA 3.2 in the JPA section
7.0save/update/saveOrUpdate/delete/load removed; @Proxy, @Where, @LazyToOne, Hibernate @OrderBy removed; Hibernate's @Cascade deprecatedOld code fails to compile
7.0Refreshing or locking a detached entity is an error; native queries return java.time types; stricter annotation validation, so invalid combinations fail at bootTests may reveal hidden bugs
7.0cascade = PERSIST no longer implied on @Id or @MapsId associationsDeclare it explicitly if you relied on it

Schema Management: ddl-auto vs Flyway and Liquibase

ddl-auto compares mappings with a database at startup. It is fine for tests and prototypes, but it cannot rename a column (it sees a new one), transform data, control ordering, review changes, or roll out across environments the same way. Production schemas belong in versioned migrations.

Value of spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-autoAt startupUse
noneNothingProduction, with migrations
validateFails on mismatch; changes nothingProduction: catches mapping drift at boot
updateAdds missing items; never drops or renamesLocal experiments only
createDrops, then createsLocal or test data sets
create-dropSame, also drops at shutdownBoot default for an embedded DB with no migration tool
src/main/resources/db/migration/
  V1__create_orders.sql
  V2__add_customer_email.sql
  R__refresh_reporting_view.sql      -- repeatable: re-run when its checksum changes

# application.properties
spring.flyway.enabled=true
spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=validate
FlywayLiquibase
MigrationsNumbered SQL (or Java) filesChangelogs in XML, YAML, JSON or SQL
History tableflyway_schema_historydatabasechangelog, plus a lock table
StyleSimple; you write the SQLDatabase-neutral change types, contexts, preconditions
RollbackForward-fix is the norm; undo is a paid featureRollback blocks in open source

Spring Boot runs the migration before the EntityManagerFactory starts, so validate checks the migrated schema. In Boot 4, modular auto-configuration means you add spring-boot-starter-flyway rather than only flyway-core. Never edit an applied migration: the checksum check will fail at startup on any environment that has run it.

Performance Tuning and Statistics

Measure first. Turn on visibility, find the query pattern, then fix it. Work from cheapest fix to most invasive.

# Visibility
logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=debug
logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=trace                 # parameter values, Hibernate 6+
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.generate_statistics=true
logging.level.org.hibernate.stat=debug
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.log_slow_query=200              # ms, Hibernate 6.2+

# Safety rails
spring.jpa.open-in-view=false
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.query.fail_on_pagination_over_collection_fetch=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.default_batch_fetch_size=50

# Throughput
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.jdbc.fetch_size=100
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.query.in_clause_parameter_padding=true
spring.jpa.properties.hibernate.connection.provider_disables_autocommit=true   # with Hikari auto-commit=false
Statistics s = sessionFactory.getStatistics();
s.setStatisticsEnabled(true);
long sql     = s.getPrepareStatementCount();
long flushes = s.getFlushCount();
long hits    = s.getSecondLevelCacheHitCount();
long misses  = s.getSecondLevelCacheMissCount();
String slow  = s.getQueryExecutionMaxTimeQueryString();
QueryStatistics q = s.getQueryStatistics("select o from Order o");   // per-query count and times
SymptomLikely causeFix
Query count grows with rowsN+1Fetch plan, batch fetching, DTO
One query returns far more rows than expectedCartesian product of fetched collectionsSeparate queries
High CPU at flushThousands of managed entitiesRead-only, DTOs, chunks
High heap in batch jobsSession never clearedflush + clear, StatelessSession
Connection pool waitsLong transactions, OSIV, remote calls in a transactionShorten; disable OSIV
Inserts slowIDENTITY, no batchingSEQUENCE + batch_size
Heap dominated by query plansMany different IN list sizesParameter padding; smaller plan_cache_max_size
Everything slow, one tableMissing indexRead the EXPLAIN plan; ORM settings cannot fix it

In production, publish statistics through Micrometer (hibernate-micrometer; Boot binds it when statistics are enabled), and use datasource-proxy or p6spy to see final SQL with values and timing. Enabling statistics has a small overhead, so many teams keep it in tests and turn it on in production as needed.

Custom Types in Hibernate 6: Converter, JavaType/JdbcType, UserType

Hibernate 6 replaced @TypeDef and the old Type hierarchy with a split model: a JavaType describes the Java side, a JdbcType the SQL side. Pick the simplest tool that works:

NeedToolNotes
Map a value object to one column (Money to DECIMAL, enum code to CHAR)JPA AttributeConverterPortable, simplest; cannot be used on @Id or @Version
Change only the SQL type of a standard Java type (JSON, UUID as BINARY, arrays)@JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON), @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.ARRAY)No code; Hibernate uses Jackson or JSON-B for JSON if on the classpath
Teach Hibernate a new Java type with its own equality, mutability and literal rendering@JavaType + a JavaType<T> implementationRare; used for libraries of types
Full control over reading/writing, including several columnsUserType<T> / CompositeUserType<T> via @TypeMost code; also handles dirty checking via deepCopy and equals
@Entity
public class Product {
    @Id @GeneratedValue private Long id;

    @Convert(converter = MoneyConverter.class)     // value object, one column
    private Money price;

    @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON)                   // jsonb in PostgreSQL, JSON in MySQL
    private Map<String, Object> attributes;

    @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.ARRAY)                  // text[] in PostgreSQL
    private String[] tags;
}

@Converter
class MoneyConverter implements AttributeConverter<Money, BigDecimal> {
    public BigDecimal convertToDatabaseColumn(Money m) { return m == null ? null : m.amount(); }
    public Money convertToEntityAttribute(BigDecimal v) { return v == null ? null : new Money(v); }
}

Gotcha: a mutable value such as a JSON Map is dirty-checked by comparing a snapshot, so changing a nested key is detected, but it costs a deep copy per load. Mapping JSON to an immutable record is cheaper and safer.

Working with Proxies: the Hibernate Utility Class

  • Hibernate.isInitialized(entity.getItems()): has the proxy or collection been loaded? Use it before serializing or logging to avoid triggering lazy loading.
  • Hibernate.initialize(proxy): force loading while the session is open (one query per call, so not a fix for N+1).
  • Hibernate.unproxy(obj): return the real entity instance, loading it if needed.
  • Hibernate.getClass(obj): the real entity class, not the generated proxy subclass. Never compare getClass() in equals on entities; proxies break it.
  • Hibernate.isPropertyInitialized(entity, "field"): for attributes made lazy by bytecode enhancement.

Serializing an entity graph with Jackson after the session closes either throws LazyInitializationException or, inside OSIV, silently fires queries. The jackson-datatype-hibernate module can render uninitialized proxies as null or as id-only, but the real fix is to return DTOs.

Interview Questions — Hibernate

What is Hibernate and why use it over JDBC?

An ORM framework that maps Java objects to tables. Compared with JDBC: no boilerplate (connections, ResultSet mapping), DB-independent HQL and dialects, automatic dirty checking, caching, lazy loading, relationship mapping, transaction integration, and translation of exceptions into unchecked ones. Downsides: a learning curve, and hidden performance problems such as N+1.

SessionFactory vs Session?

SessionFactory: immutable, thread-safe, expensive to build, one per database, owns the L2 cache. Session: short-lived, not thread-safe, one per unit of work or request, owns the L1 cache, wraps a JDBC connection.

get() vs load() (and JPA find vs getReference)?
get() / find()load() / getReference()
Hits the DB immediately (unless cached)Returns a proxy; the DB is hit on first access
Returns null if not foundThrows ObjectNotFoundException / EntityNotFoundException on access
Use when you need the dataUse to set an FK without loading the row: order.setCustomer(em.getReference(Customer.class, 5L))
save() vs persist() vs saveOrUpdate() vs merge() vs update()?
  • persist() (JPA): makes a transient entity managed. Returns void, and the INSERT may be delayed until flush.
  • save() (Hibernate, deprecated in 6, removed in 7): returns the generated id right away.
  • update(): reattaches a detached instance. Throws if the session already holds an instance with the same id.
  • saveOrUpdate(): chooses save or update. Deprecated in 6, removed in 7, along with update().
  • merge() (JPA): copies the detached object's state onto a managed instance and returns that managed copy. The argument itself stays detached.
What is dirty checking?

When an entity is loaded, Hibernate keeps a snapshot of its state. At flush time it compares the managed entity with the snapshot and generates UPDATEs for changed fields automatically, so no save() call is needed inside a transaction. @DynamicUpdate limits the UPDATE to the changed columns.

First-level vs second-level cache vs query cache?

L1: scoped to the Session, enabled by default, can't be disabled; use clear() or evict() to empty it. L2: scoped to the SessionFactory and shared across sessions. You enable it (hibernate.cache.use_second_level_cache, a provider, and @Cacheable + @Cache(usage = CacheConcurrencyStrategy.READ_WRITE) on entities). Concurrency strategies: READ_ONLY, NONSTRICT_READ_WRITE, READ_WRITE, TRANSACTIONAL. Query cache: caches query result ids; best for data that's read often and rarely changes.

What is HQL? How is it different from SQL?

HQL (Hibernate Query Language), a superset of JPQL, is object-oriented: you query entity names and fields, not tables and columns. It supports polymorphism, associations through dots and joins, named parameters, and pagination with setFirstResult/setMaxResults. Example: from Employee e where e.dept.name = :d order by e.salary desc.

How does lazy loading work internally?

Hibernate puts a proxy (a ByteBuddy subclass) in place of a lazy ToOne field, and a PersistentBag/PersistentSet wrapper in place of collections. The first access to them triggers a SELECT, which needs an open session. Hibernate.initialize(obj) forces loading. Calling getId() on a proxy doesn't hit the DB.

What is flush? Flush modes?

Flush writes the pending changes from the persistence context to the DB (SQL is executed, but not committed). FlushMode.AUTO (default) flushes before commit and before queries that touch affected tables. COMMIT flushes only at commit. MANUAL flushes only when you call flush(), which is useful for read-only work.

openSession() vs getCurrentSession()?

openSession() always creates a new session, and you must close it. getCurrentSession() returns the session bound to the current context (thread or JTA, or Spring's transaction). It's closed automatically at commit. Spring code uses the injected EntityManager instead.

How to do batch inserts efficiently?

Set hibernate.jdbc.batch_size=50, order_inserts=true and order_updates=true. Use SEQUENCE ids, because IDENTITY disables batching. Call flush() and clear() every N entities to bound the L1 cache. For huge loads, use StatelessSession or JDBC batch directly.

Hibernate entity requirements?

The class needs @Entity, an @Id, and a no-arg constructor (protected or public). It must not be final if you want proxies, and neither should its methods. Consistent equals/hashCode is recommended, and collections should be initialized. Field and property access is chosen based on where @Id is placed.

What is the hibernate.ddl-auto / hbm2ddl.auto setting?

none (production) · validate (checks the schema matches) · update (adds columns, never drops them; risky) · create (drops and creates at startup) · create-drop (also drops at shutdown; for tests). In production, manage schemas with Flyway or Liquibase.

In what order do these SQL statements run?
@Transactional
void demo() {
  Author a = new Author("A");          // @GeneratedValue(IDENTITY)
  em.persist(a);
  System.out.println("after persist");
  a.setName("B");
  em.flush();
  System.out.println("after flush");
}

INSERT, then after persist, then UPDATE, then after flush. IDENTITY forces the INSERT during persist, because Hibernate needs the id. The rename is seen by dirty checking. With SEQUENCE the order is: a nextval call, after persist, then at flush a single INSERT that already contains "B" with no UPDATE, as the queued insert reads the entity's current state.

Why does entity instanceof Sub fail for an entity obtained through a lazy ManyToOne?

A lazy reference to the base type Payment is a proxy subclass of Payment, since Hibernate does not know the real type without reading the row. So instanceof CardPayment is false and a cast throws ClassCastException, even when the row is a card payment. Fixes: Hibernate.unproxy(payment) gives the real object; or put the behaviour in a polymorphic method, which the proxy forwards to the target; or fetch the association in the query. Hibernate.getClass(obj) tells you the real class.

What is NonUniqueObjectException, and how does merge avoid it?

A persistence context holds one instance per id. The old update(detached) reattached the given object, so if the session had already loaded the same id, the two instances conflicted and it threw. merge copies state into the existing managed instance, so no conflict arises. In Hibernate 7 the problem goes away with update itself. An equivalent can still happen with lock or with cascaded persist, so a detached instance should not be mixed with a loaded one of the same id.

Is find() served by L2 cache when the entity is already in L1? And a JPQL query?

find checks L1, then L2, then the database. Queries are different: without the query cache, JPQL and Criteria always hit the DB. Rows are then matched to L1, and L1 wins. A query does not read entity state from L2, though it may populate it. So enabling L2 alone does not speed up list pages built on JPQL.

How can the query cache make performance worse?

Three ways. (1) If the result's entity is not in L2, or was evicted, each id triggers a separate SELECT, giving N+1. Cache those entities too, with a similar or longer TTL. (2) Any write on a used table invalidates all query results for it, so on write-heavy tables, you pay for storing entries you never reuse. (3) Queries with varied parameters create many entries with a low hit rate. Check getQueryCacheHitCount before deciding. A well-placed application-level @Cacheable on a DTO is often better.

What happens to the L2 cache after a bulk update or native SQL?

HQL bulk statements know the target entity, so Hibernate invalidates that entity's region and timestamps. A native query has unknown effects, so Hibernate invalidates all regions conservatively. Narrow it via query.unwrap(NativeQuery.class).addSynchronizedEntityClass(Order.class). A change made outside the app (another service, a DBA script, a trigger) is not seen at all, and stale data lives until TTL expiry. This is the main reason to keep TTLs reasonable.

Two app nodes each use local Caffeine as L2. What goes wrong?

Node A updates a row, and invalidates only its own cache. Node B serves stale data until its entry expires. Worse, an entity with @Version read stale on B then fails an update with an optimistic lock error. Options: restrict L2 to data where a short TTL is acceptable, or use a cluster-aware provider (Infinispan invalidation mode, Hazelcast, Redisson), or skip L2 and cache at the service layer with explicit eviction via events.

What does @BatchSize do, in numbers? Is it the same as jdbc.batch_size?

No, as covered above. With 100 authors and @BatchSize(size = 25) on books, touching the first author's books loads books for up to 25 authors with where author_id in (...). Total: 1 + 4 queries.
