It is a read optimisation. jdbc.batch_size groups writes. default_batch_fetch_size applies batch fetching globally and is usually a good default to set in new projects.

You set batch_size=50 yet inserts run one by one. What is your checklist?
  1. IDENTITY ids disable insert batching. Switch to SEQUENCE.
  2. Is the property really active? The Spring key has the prefix spring.jpa.properties.
  3. Mixed entities without order_inserts=true break batches.
  4. Is the code flushing after each row, for example through saveAndFlush?
  5. In logs, the plain SQL log shows one line per row even when batched. Verify with statistics, datasource-proxy, or the server.
  6. MySQL needs rewriteBatchedStatements=true for real gain.
  7. @DynamicInsert or differing SQL strings prevent grouping.
Why is FetchMode.JOIN ignored by my JPQL query?

JPQL states exactly which joins to run. Hibernate honours your query and treats @Fetch(JOIN) as a mapping default only for fetches it plans itself, such as find. The association, being eager, then loads through additional selects after the query. To join in JPQL, write join fetch or use an entity graph.

@Formula vs a @Transient getter vs a generated column?

A @Transient getter computes in Java from loaded fields: no SQL cost, but cannot be queried, and it needs the data loaded. @Formula computes in SQL, can reference other tables, can be used in HQL conditions, and costs extra on every load. A database generated column is computed by the database and can be indexed, so it is best when a value is filtered or sorted often. If only some screens need the value, use a DTO query.

@Filter vs @SQLRestriction?

@SQLRestriction is static, always applied, with no parameters, and is suited to soft delete. @Filter is named, has parameters, and is enabled per session, which suits tenants and "as of" dates. Both are raw SQL conditions and both are skipped by native queries, so neither is a security boundary on its own.

Explain multi-tenancy strategies in Hibernate.
StrategyIsolationCostMechanism
Discriminator columnLowest; a bug can leak dataCheapest, thousands of tenants@TenantId field, added to all queries automatically
Separate schemaMediumModerate; migrations for each schemaMultiTenantConnectionProvider switches schema
Separate databaseHighest; per-tenant backup and scaleHighest; a pool per tenantConnection provider picks a data source

All need CurrentTenantIdentifierResolver, usually reading a request-scoped value from the JWT. Beware of asynchronous threads, where that context is missing.

A column annotated @Column(name="userName") is mapped to user_name. Why?

Boot's default physical naming strategy applies to every identifier, explicit ones included. Set the physical strategy to PhysicalNamingStrategyStandardImpl to keep the name as written.

Interceptor vs event listener vs @PrePersist vs Envers: which and when?

Use @PrePersist for logic about one entity. Use an Interceptor for a cross-entity rule, such as stamping a tenant field. Use event listeners for fine-grained, global behaviour such as publishing change events. Use Envers when the requirement is "show me the record as of last March". Note that all of these see only changes that pass through Hibernate. To capture all data changes regardless of source, use database triggers or CDC.

What does upgrading from Spring Boot 2.x (Hibernate 5) to 3.x (Hibernate 6) break?
  • javax to jakarta imports (the OpenRewrite recipe automates most of it).
  • Sequences: ids restart or fail because of new default names. Use hibernate.id.db_structure_naming_strategy=legacy or rename.
  • Custom UserTypes and @Type usage need rewriting.
  • HQL that was tolerated now fails, for example comparing mismatched types.
  • Time zone handling for OffsetDateTime and Instant changed.
  • Spring's SpringPhysicalNamingStrategy class is gone, replaced by Hibernate's equivalent.

The safe route is to go to the latest 2.7 first, fix deprecations, then step to 3.x, and run the full integration tests against a real database.

Why was DISTINCT needed for join fetch in Hibernate 5, and what about 6?

A collection fetch returns one row per child, so in Hibernate 5 the same parent appeared several times in the result list. distinct removed duplicates in memory, but was also sent to the database, where it is useless and slows sorting. The hint hibernate.query.passDistinctThrough=false stopped that. Hibernate 6 removes duplicates from entity results automatically and the hint is gone. Writing distinct is harmless in 6 but no longer required for that purpose.

Why not use ddl-auto=update in production?

It never drops or renames: renaming a field leaves the old column and creates an empty new one, so data seems to vanish. It does not migrate data, cannot make changes reviewable, may lock large tables at app startup, can race between instances, and diverges across environments. The app's DB user would need DDL rights, which violates least privilege. Use migrations plus validate.

Flyway fails at startup with a checksum mismatch. What happened, and what do you do?

Someone edited an already-applied migration file, so its stored checksum differs. Do not edit history. Restore the file and add a new version. If the change was only cosmetic (comments), flyway repair updates stored checksums. For a failed migration on a database without transactional DDL (such as MySQL), fix the partial state manually, then run repair. Version collisions between feature branches are a common related problem: use timestamps for versions, or enforce ordering in CI.

How do you rename a column with zero downtime?

During a rolling deploy, old and new code run together, so a single-step rename breaks one of them. Use expand, migrate, contract:

  1. Expand: add the new column (nullable). No old code changes.
  2. Release: write to both, read from old.
  3. Backfill old rows in small batches.
  4. Release: read from new, still write to both.
  5. Release: write only to new.
  6. Contract: drop the old column in a later release.
What is bytecode enhancement? When is it worth it?

A build-time plugin (hibernate-enhance-maven-plugin, or Gradle equivalent) rewrites entity bytecode. It offers lazy loading of basic attributes, lazy loading of the inverse @OneToOne, in-line dirty tracking, and automatic sync of bidirectional links. It is worthwhile for entities with huge columns that you do not want to move, or for avoiding snapshot comparisons in large sessions. The cost is a more complex build. In most apps, DTO projections reach the same goal more simply.

When is @DynamicUpdate worth using?

Use it for wide tables with few changed columns, when you want to reduce log volume for replication or CDC, or to avoid overwriting columns changed by concurrent writers (it narrows lost-update risk at column level; without @Version, this does not remove it). Hibernate must build the statement per flush, which costs a little CPU and loses the shared prepared statement, so do not apply it to everything.

Is it safe to use a Session in parallelStream() or @Async?

No. A Session and its persistence context are not thread-safe. With Spring, the transaction and the EntityManager are bound to a ThreadLocal. Worker threads in parallelStream or @Async do not see them. So those threads run outside your transaction, and passing a managed entity to them can corrupt the session or throw LazyInitializationException. Pass ids or DTOs to other threads, and let each use its own transaction. The same applies to virtual threads and to CompletableFuture.

A long-running Hibernate batch job slows down over time, then runs out of memory. Why?

The session retains every loaded entity. Memory grows, and each flush re-checks all of them, so the time per chunk rises steadily: quadratic total cost. Fix by working in chunks with flush() and clear(), with one short transaction per chunk so failures can restart from a checkpoint; or use StatelessSession. Spring Batch's chunk-oriented steps do this for you. Set CacheMode.IGNORE to avoid flooding L2. Keyset-read the input, because OFFSET also slows down over time.

What is @NaturalId, and why use it next to a surrogate key?

A natural id is a real-world unique value such as ISBN or email. Keep a numeric PK for joins and mark the natural one @NaturalId. You gain a generated unique constraint, an API (bySimpleNaturalId) that checks the session first, and optional caching. Hibernate resolves natural id to PK in the session, so repeat lookups avoid SQL, which plain findByEmail queries do not.

Hibernate vs Spring Data JDBC vs MyBatis vs jOOQ?
ToolModelChoose it for
Hibernate / JPAFull ORM: managed state, lazy loadingRich write models, CRUD-heavy domains
Spring Data JDBCSimple aggregates; no lazy loading or dirty checkingDDD aggregates, predictable SQL
MyBatisSQL mapper; you write the SQLSQL-centric teams, legacy schemas
jOOQType-safe SQL built from the schemaComplex queries and reporting

They combine well: Hibernate for writes, and jOOQ or plain SQL for reads.

What is the query plan cache?

Parsing HQL into an SQL plan is costly, so Hibernate caches plans by query string (size set by hibernate.query.plan_cache_max_size). It is separate from the query result cache and always on. Concatenating literal values into a query string creates a new entry per value, wasting this cache and allowing SQL injection. IN lists of varying length have the same effect, and in_clause_parameter_padding=true rounds their sizes up to powers of two.

@CreationTimestamp vs Spring Data @CreatedDate vs a DB default?

@CreationTimestamp is Hibernate-only, needs no configuration, and sets the value in the JVM at insert. @CreatedDate works with any Spring Data store, and with @CreatedBy gives you users too, but requires @EnableJpaAuditing. A database default (DEFAULT now()) also covers rows written outside the app. All clocks differ a bit across nodes; a database clock gives a single source of truth when ordering matters.

How would you diagnose a page that went from 200ms to 8s after new data was added?
  1. Enable SQL logs or a tracing agent for that request and count statements. A jump in count suggests N+1.
  2. If count is low, find the slow statement and run EXPLAIN ANALYZE: look for a sequential scan or a wrong join order, then add an index.
  3. Check row counts: a collection fetch may be producing a Cartesian product.
  4. Check Hikari pending counts and lock waits.
  5. Check flush time in statistics. A big context makes flush slow.
  6. Fix, then add a test that asserts the query count so it cannot regress.
How do you log the SQL Hibernate runs, including bind parameters? Why not show_sql?

spring.jpa.show-sql=true prints to stdout, bypassing the logging framework, without parameters or timestamps. Use loggers instead: logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG for statements and logging.level.org.hibernate.orm.jdbc.bind=TRACE for parameter values (Hibernate 6; Hibernate 5 used org.hibernate.type.descriptor.sql). Add hibernate.format_sql for readability and hibernate.session.events.log.LOG_QUERIES_SLOWER_THAN_MS for slow queries. In production avoid bind logging because it leaks personal data; prefer a DataSource proxy or database-side slow query logs.

How should you store timestamps with Hibernate so time zones do not shift values?

Store instants in UTC and map them as Instant (or OffsetDateTime) to a column type that holds an instant, such as PostgreSQL timestamptz. Set hibernate.jdbc.time_zone=UTC so the JDBC driver does not convert using the JVM's default zone, and run servers in UTC. In Hibernate 6.2+, hibernate.timezone.default_storage controls whether the offset is normalized to UTC or stored in a separate column. Use LocalDate/LocalDateTime only for values that are not instants (a birthday, a clinic's opening time).

Does Hibernate validate Bean Validation annotations, and when?

Yes. With Hibernate Validator on the classpath (the default with spring-boot-starter-validation), Hibernate validates entities on pre-persist and pre-update and throws ConstraintViolationException at flush. It also uses @NotNull and @Size to add NOT NULL and column lengths when it generates DDL. This is a safety net, not input validation: validate DTOs in the controller with @Valid so clients get a 400 before any SQL. Control it with jakarta.persistence.validation.mode (auto, callback, none).

Jackson throws "No serializer found for class ...HibernateProxy" or ByteBuddyInterceptor. What is happening?

You are serializing a lazy @ManyToOne that is still a proxy. Jackson sees the generated subclass and its internal handler field. Fixes in order of preference: return a DTO or projection; fetch the association in the query; register Hibernate6Module (jackson-datatype-hibernate) to write uninitialized proxies as null or id-only. Annotating with @JsonIgnoreProperties({"hibernateLazyInitializer", "handler"}) hides the symptom but still triggers lazy loading during serialization.

What is Jakarta Data and how does it compare with Spring Data JPA?

Jakarta Data (part of Jakarta EE 11) is a standard repository API: you declare interfaces with @Repository, @Find, @Query, @Insert and so on. Hibernate implements it (6.6+) with an annotation processor that generates the implementation at compile time on top of a StatelessSession, so query errors fail the build, not startup, and there is no persistence context or dirty checking. Spring Data JPA builds proxies at runtime over a stateful EntityManager and has a much larger ecosystem (Specifications, auditing, projections). In a Spring Boot project Spring Data remains the default; Jakarta Data matters more for Jakarta EE and Quarkus users.

How do you map a PostgreSQL jsonb column and query inside it?

Map it with @JdbcTypeCode(SqlTypes.JSON) to a Map, a record or a POJO; Hibernate 6 serializes it with Jackson. Standard JPQL has no JSON operators (recent Hibernate versions add JSON functions to HQL), so filtering inside the document usually uses a native query, for example where attributes ->> 'color' = :color, backed by a GIN or expression index. If you filter on a field often, promote it to a real column: JSON is good for flexible attributes, not for core relational data.

MongoDB NoSQL documents

MongoDB is a document database that stores flexible, JSON-like BSON documents in collections. It shines for evolving schemas, hierarchical data and horizontal scaling, and integrates with Spring Boot through Spring Data MongoDB.

// mongosh – insert, query, index, aggregate
db.orders.insertOne({
  customerId: ObjectId("665f1c2e9b1e8a3d4c2b1a00"),
  status: "PAID",
  items: [ { sku: "BK-101", qty: 2, price: 450 }, { sku: "PN-7", qty: 1, price: 120 } ],
  total: 1020,
  createdAt: new Date()
});

db.orders.find({ status: "PAID", total: { $gte: 500 } }, { items: 0 })
         .sort({ createdAt: -1 }).limit(10);

db.orders.createIndex({ status: 1, createdAt: -1 });

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "PAID" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", revenue: { $sum: "$total" }, orders: { $sum: 1 } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 5 }
]);

Documents, Collections & BSON

A document is a set of field/value pairs, comparable to a row but able to hold nested objects and arrays. Documents live in collections (like tables) inside a database. Documents in one collection don't need identical fields, though you can enforce structure with JSON Schema validation. Every document has a unique _id, by default an ObjectId (12 bytes: timestamp, random value, counter), so it is roughly time-ordered.

Data is stored as BSON (Binary JSON), which adds types JSON lacks: ObjectId, Date, Decimal128 (use for money), Int32/Int64, binary data. Maximum document size is 16 MB; larger files go to GridFS or object storage.

SQL vs NoSQL – When to Choose Which

  • Relational (MySQL, PostgreSQL): fixed schema, normalised tables, joins, strong ACID transactions across many tables, mature reporting. Best for highly relational data with complex queries and integrity constraints – banking ledgers, billing, ERP, most classic business systems.
  • Document (MongoDB): flexible schema, data stored the way the application reads it (aggregates), easy horizontal scaling via sharding, high write throughput. Best for catalogs with varying attributes, content management, user profiles, event/IoT data, rapid prototyping.

Terminology: table → collection, row → document, column → field, join → $lookup or embedding, primary key → _id. MongoDB now supports multi-document ACID transactions, and relational DBs support JSON columns, so the choice is about the access patterns and data shape, not "NoSQL can't do transactions".

CRUD & Query Operators

db.users.insertMany([{ name: "Asha", age: 28, tags: ["admin"] }, { name: "Ravi", age: 34 }]);

db.users.find({ age: { $gt: 25, $lte: 40 } });           // comparison
db.users.find({ $or: [{ city: "Chennai" }, { age: { $lt: 18 } }] });
db.users.find({ tags: { $in: ["admin", "editor"] } });   // array contains any
db.users.find({ email: { $exists: false } });
db.users.find({ name: { $regex: "^As", $options: "i" } });
db.orders.find({ items: { $elemMatch: { sku: "BK-101", qty: { $gte: 2 } } } });
db.orders.find({ "address.city": "Pune" });              // dot notation for nested fields

db.users.updateOne({ name: "Ravi" }, { $set: { city: "Pune" }, $inc: { loginCount: 1 } });
db.users.updateMany({}, { $unset: { legacyFlag: "" } });
db.users.updateOne({ name: "Asha" }, { $push: { tags: "editor" } });
db.users.updateOne({ email: "x@y.com" }, { $set: { name: "X" } }, { upsert: true });
db.users.deleteOne({ name: "Ravi" });

Operators: comparison ($eq $ne $gt $gte $lt $lte $in $nin), logical ($and $or $not $nor), element ($exists $type), array ($all $elemMatch $size), update ($set $unset $inc $push $addToSet $pull). Single-document writes are always atomic.

Projection, Sort, Limit & Pagination

The second argument of find is a projection: { name: 1, email: 1, _id: 0 } includes fields, { password: 0 } excludes them (don't mix include and exclude except for _id). sort({ createdAt: -1 }) sorts descending, limit(n) caps results, skip(n) offsets. Large skip values are slow because the server still walks skipped documents; for deep pagination use range/keyset pagination: find({ _id: { $lt: lastSeenId } }).sort({ _id: -1 }).limit(20).

Indexes & explain()

Without an index MongoDB performs a collection scan (COLLSCAN). Indexes are B-trees:

  • Single field: createIndex({ email: 1 }, { unique: true }).
  • Compound: { status: 1, createdAt: -1 }. Follow the ESR rule – Equality fields first, then Sort, then Range. A compound index also serves queries on its prefix (status alone).
  • Multikey: automatic when indexing an array field.
  • Text: createIndex({ title: "text", body: "text" }), queried with $text: { $search: "spring boot" }. Atlas Search (Lucene) is more powerful.
  • TTL: createIndex({ createdAt: 1 }, { expireAfterSeconds: 3600 }) auto-deletes documents – great for sessions, OTPs, logs.
  • Also: partial, sparse, hashed (for sharding), geospatial (2dsphere), wildcard.
db.orders.find({ status: "PAID" }).sort({ createdAt: -1 }).explain("executionStats");
// Check: winningPlan.stage = IXSCAN (good) vs COLLSCAN (bad),
// totalKeysExamined / totalDocsExamined close to nReturned, no in-memory SORT stage

Indexes speed reads but cost RAM and slow writes, so index for real query patterns. A covered query is answered entirely from the index when all filtered and projected fields are in it.

Aggregation Pipeline

The aggregation pipeline passes documents through stages, each transforming the stream – MongoDB's equivalent of GROUP BY, joins and reporting queries. Put $match (and $sort) early so indexes are used and fewer documents flow downstream.

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { createdAt: { $gte: ISODate("2025-01-01") } } },
  { $unwind: "$items" },                                   // one doc per array element
  { $group: { _id: "$items.sku",
              unitsSold: { $sum: "$items.qty" },
              revenue: { $sum: { $multiply: ["$items.qty", "$items.price"] } } } },
  { $lookup: { from: "products", localField: "_id",        // left outer join
               foreignField: "sku", as: "product" } },
  { $unwind: "$product" },
  { $project: { _id: 0, sku: "$_id", name: "$product.name", unitsSold: 1, revenue: 1 } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } },
  { $limit: 10 }
]);

Other useful stages: $addFields/$set, $count, $facet (multiple sub-pipelines, e.g. results + total count), $bucket, $out/$merge (write results to a collection). Each stage has a 100 MB memory limit unless spilling to disk is allowed (allowDiskUse, on by default since 6.0).

Schema Design: Embed vs Reference

Design for how the application reads data: "data that is accessed together should be stored together."

  • Embed when the child belongs to the parent and is read with it, the relationship is one-to-one or one-to-few, and the array is bounded (order line items, addresses). Benefits: one read, atomic single-document updates.
  • Reference (store the other document's _id) when the related data is large, shared by many parents, updated independently, or unbounded (a product's reviews, a user's audit events). Join with $lookup or a second query.
  • Avoid unbounded arrays (hits 16 MB and degrades performance). Patterns: subset (embed the latest 10 reviews, reference the rest), extended reference (copy a few frequently read fields like customer name), bucket (group time-series readings per hour), computed (store precomputed totals).

Transactions, Replica Sets & Sharding

Transactions: single-document operations are atomic. Since 4.0 (replica sets) and 4.2 (sharded clusters), MongoDB supports multi-document ACID transactions, but they add overhead and have a default 60-second limit; a good schema minimises the need for them. Write durability is tuned with write concern (w: "majority" is the default) and read consistency with read concern.

Replica set: one primary accepting writes and several secondaries replicating its oplog. If the primary fails, members elect a new primary automatically (usually within seconds). Read preference can route reads to secondaries (possibly stale). Transactions require a replica set.

Sharding: horizontal partitioning of a collection across shards (each a replica set) by a shard key; mongos routers direct queries, config servers hold metadata. Choose a key with high cardinality, even distribution and that appears in most queries – a monotonically increasing key (like a timestamp) creates a hot shard unless hashed. Queries without the shard key become scatter-gather across all shards.

Spring Data MongoDB

// application.yml: spring.data.mongodb.uri=mongodb://localhost:27017/shop
@Document(collection = "orders")
@CompoundIndex(def = "{'status': 1, 'createdAt': -1}")
public class Order {
    @Id private String id;                       // maps to ObjectId _id
    @Indexed private String customerId;
    private OrderStatus status;
    private List<OrderItem> items;               // embedded documents
    @Field("total") private BigDecimal total;
    @CreatedDate private Instant createdAt;
    @Version private Long version;               // optimistic locking
}

public interface OrderRepository extends MongoRepository<Order, String> {
    List<Order> findByStatusAndTotalGreaterThan(OrderStatus status, BigDecimal min);
    Page<Order> findByCustomerId(String customerId, Pageable pageable);
    @Query(value = "{ 'items.sku': ?0 }", fields = "{ 'items': 0 }")
    List<Order> findContainingSku(String sku);
}

@Service @RequiredArgsConstructor
public class OrderStatsService {
    private final MongoTemplate mongo;

    public void markShipped(String id) {
        mongo.updateFirst(Query.query(Criteria.where("_id").is(id)),
                          new Update().set("status", OrderStatus.SHIPPED), Order.class);
    }

    public List<Document> revenueByCustomer() {
        Aggregation agg = Aggregation.newAggregation(
            Aggregation.match(Criteria.where("status").is("PAID")),
            Aggregation.group("customerId").sum("total").as("revenue"),
            Aggregation.sort(Sort.Direction.DESC, "revenue"));
        return mongo.aggregate(agg, "orders", Document.class).getMappedResults();
    }
}

Use MongoRepository for standard CRUD and derived queries; use MongoTemplate for partial updates, dynamic criteria, upserts, bulk ops and aggregations. Note: @Indexed annotations only create indexes when spring.data.mongodb.auto-index-creation=true (off by default); in production manage indexes explicitly. Enable @EnableMongoAuditing for @CreatedDate, and use @Transactional with a MongoTransactionManager bean for multi-document transactions.

Updating Arrays and Atomic Read-Modify-Write

A single-document update is atomic, so many "transactions" in SQL become one update in MongoDB. Array updates have their own operators:

  • $: the first array element matched by the query filter.
  • $[]: every element.
  • $[id] with arrayFilters: every element matching a named condition.
  • $pull removes matching elements; $addToSet adds only if absent; $push with $each, $sort and $slice keeps a capped, sorted array (for example "last 10 events").
  • findOneAndUpdate (Spring: findAndModify) updates and returns the document in one atomic step, which is how you implement counters, sequence numbers, or "claim the next job".
// Set qty on the line item for sku BK-101 only
db.orders.updateOne(
  { _id: orderId, "items.sku": "BK-101" },
  { $set: { "items.$.qty": 3 } });

// Mark every unpaid item as cancelled
db.orders.updateOne(
  { _id: orderId },
  { $set: { "items.$[i].status": "CANCELLED" } },
  { arrayFilters: [ { "i.status": "UNPAID" } ] });

// Keep only the 10 most recent events
db.devices.updateOne({ _id: id },
  { $push: { events: { $each: [evt], $sort: { at: -1 }, $slice: 10 } } });
// Spring Data: atomic counter / claim a job
Query q = Query.query(Criteria.where("status").is("PENDING")).with(Sort.by("createdAt"));
Update u = new Update().set("status", "RUNNING").set("worker", workerId).currentDate("startedAt");
Job job = mongoTemplate.findAndModify(q, u,
        FindAndModifyOptions.options().returnNew(true), Job.class);   // null if nothing pending

Concurrency and Transactions in Spring Data MongoDB

  • Optimistic locking: add @Version Long version to the document. save() then updates with {_id: ..., version: n} in the filter and throws OptimisticLockingFailureException if another writer got there first.
  • Prefer targeted updates ($set, $inc) over load-modify-save(); save() replaces the whole document and can overwrite fields another request just changed.
  • Multi-document transactions need a replica set (or sharded cluster). Register a MongoTransactionManager bean; then @Transactional works. Keep them short (default lifetime limit is 60 seconds) and retry on TransientTransactionError.
  • Auditing: @EnableMongoAuditing with @CreatedDate/@LastModifiedDate; it decides "new" by a null id or null version.
@Configuration
class MongoTxConfig {
    @Bean
    MongoTransactionManager transactionManager(MongoDatabaseFactory f) {
        return new MongoTransactionManager(f);
    }
}

@Document("accounts")
public class Account {
    @Id private String id;
    @Version private Long version;
    private BigDecimal balance;            // stored as Decimal128 with a converter or @Field(targetType = DECIMAL128)
}

Change Streams

A change stream is a subscription to inserts, updates, replaces and deletes on a collection, database or whole deployment, built on the replica-set oplog (so it needs a replica set, which Atlas always is). Each event carries a resume token: store it after processing and pass it as resumeAfter on restart to continue without gaps, as long as the oplog still holds that point. Use cases: cache invalidation, pushing updates to WebSocket clients, syncing to a search index, or a simple outbox relay. For large-scale fan-out or long retention, stream changes into Kafka (the MongoDB Kafka connector or Debezium) instead.

// Node.js driver (a ChangeStream is an async iterable)
const cs = db.orders.watch(
  [ { $match: { operationType: { $in: ["insert", "update"] } } } ],
  { fullDocument: "updateLookup", resumeAfter: savedToken });
for await (const change of cs) {
  handle(change.fullDocument);
  saveToken(change._id);                 // the resume token
}

Interview Questions — MongoDB

What is MongoDB and how does it differ from a relational database?

MongoDB is a document-oriented NoSQL database storing BSON documents in collections with a flexible schema. Relational databases store rows in tables with a fixed schema, normalise data and use joins. MongoDB typically embeds related data in one document, scales horizontally with sharding, and models data around application access patterns, while relational DBs excel at complex joins and strict relational integrity.

When would you choose MongoDB over MySQL, and vice versa?

Choose MongoDB for varying or evolving attributes (product catalogs, CMS, profiles), hierarchical aggregates read as a whole, high write volume, or when horizontal scaling is a priority. Choose MySQL/PostgreSQL for highly relational data, complex ad-hoc reporting with joins, strict constraints and foreign keys, and multi-entity transactions as the norm (finance, billing). Many systems use both (polyglot persistence).

What is BSON and what is an ObjectId?

BSON is a binary encoding of JSON-like documents that is fast to traverse and supports extra types such as Date, ObjectId, Decimal128, 32/64-bit integers and binary data. An ObjectId is a 12-byte default _id: a 4-byte timestamp, a 5-byte random value and a 3-byte counter, so it's unique without coordination and roughly sortable by creation time (getTimestamp()).

Embed or reference – how do you decide?

Embed when data is owned by the parent, read together, and bounded in size (one-to-few) – you get one read and atomic updates. Reference when the related data is large, unbounded, shared among many documents, or updated independently (many-to-many, one-to-many with thousands of children). Hybrid patterns like subset or extended reference embed only the frequently needed part.

💡 Watch the 16 MB document limit and never let an array grow without bound.

Explain the aggregation pipeline with an example.

It is a sequence of stages where each stage transforms the stream of documents: $match filters, $group aggregates, $project reshapes, $sort/$limit order and trim, $unwind flattens arrays and $lookup joins another collection. Example – top customers by revenue:

db.orders.aggregate([
  { $match: { status: "PAID" } },
  { $group: { _id: "$customerId", revenue: { $sum: "$total" } } },
  { $sort: { revenue: -1 } }, { $limit: 5 }
]);
What does $unwind do and when is $lookup used?

$unwind deconstructs an array field, outputting one document per element – useful before grouping by array items (e.g. sales per SKU from order line items). $lookup performs a left outer join with another collection in the same database, adding matching documents as an array field; it can also run a sub-pipeline. Heavy reliance on $lookup may indicate the schema should embed more.

What types of indexes does MongoDB support?

Single-field, compound, multikey (arrays), text, geospatial (2dsphere), hashed (sharding), wildcard, plus options like unique, partial, sparse and TTL. A TTL index on a date field deletes documents after expireAfterSeconds via a background task that runs about every 60 seconds – useful for sessions, OTPs and temporary tokens.

How do you design a compound index? What is the ESR rule?

Order fields by Equality (exact matches) first, then Sort fields, then Range filters ($gt, $lt, $in on large sets). For find({status:"PAID", total:{$gt:500}}).sort({createdAt:-1}) the index is {status:1, createdAt:-1, total:1}. The index also serves queries on its leftmost prefix, so avoid redundant indexes.

How do you analyse a slow query?

Run .explain("executionStats") and check whether the winning plan is IXSCAN or COLLSCAN, compare totalDocsExamined to nReturned, and look for in-memory SORT stages. Use the database profiler or slow-query log (and Atlas Performance Advisor) to find slow operations, then add or adjust indexes, add projections and limit result size.

Does MongoDB support transactions?

Yes. Every single-document operation is atomic, including updates of nested arrays. Multi-document ACID transactions are supported on replica sets (4.0+) and sharded clusters (4.2+) with snapshot isolation. They have performance cost and a default 60-second lifetime, so prefer schema designs where a business operation touches one document. In Spring, use @Transactional with a configured MongoTransactionManager.

What is a replica set and how does failover work?

A replica set is a group of mongod nodes holding the same data: one primary for writes and secondaries that replicate the primary's oplog. If the primary becomes unreachable, the remaining members hold an election and promote a secondary, typically within seconds; drivers with retryable writes reconnect automatically. Use an odd number of voting members (e.g. 3) to keep a majority.

What is sharding and how do you pick a shard key?

Sharding distributes a collection's data across multiple shards for horizontal scale, with mongos routing queries using the shard key. A good key has high cardinality, distributes writes evenly, and is included in most queries so they target one shard. Avoid monotonically increasing keys (timestamps, ObjectIds) with ranged sharding because all inserts hit one shard – use a hashed or compound key instead.

What are write concern and read preference?

Write concern sets how many nodes must acknowledge a write: w:1 (primary only) or w:"majority" (default, survives failover), optionally with journaling. Read preference chooses which members serve reads: primary (default, consistent), primaryPreferred, secondary, nearest. Reading from secondaries scales reads but may return stale data. Read concern controls the consistency level (local, majority, snapshot).

MongoRepository vs MongoTemplate?

MongoRepository provides CRUD, paging and derived query methods (findByStatusOrderByCreatedAtDesc) plus @Query JSON queries – minimal code for common cases. MongoTemplate gives full control: dynamic Criteria, partial updates with Update ($set, $inc), upserts, findAndModify, bulk operations and aggregations. Many services use both – repositories for basics, a custom repository with the template for complex queries.

How do you implement pagination efficiently?

skip/limit (Spring's Pageable) is simple but gets slower with deep pages because skipped documents are still scanned, and a total count adds another query. For large data sets or infinite scroll use keyset pagination: sort on an indexed unique field and query { _id: { $lt: lastId } } with limit. Spring Data supports this with Window/ScrollPosition.

How do you store money and dates correctly in MongoDB?

Use Decimal128 (Java BigDecimal, mapped with a converter or @Field(targetType = FieldType.DECIMAL128)) for currency to avoid floating-point errors, or store integer minor units (paise/cents). Store timestamps as BSON Date (UTC, Java Instant), not strings, so range queries, sorting and TTL indexes work.

How do you enforce some structure on a schemaless collection?

Use schema validation with $jsonSchema on the collection (required fields, types, enums), with validationLevel and validationAction (error or warn). In the application, rely on typed domain classes (Spring Data @Document), Bean Validation, unique indexes, and a schemaVersion field to migrate documents gradually (tools like Mongock help).

How do you update one element inside an array, or all elements matching a condition?

Use the positional operator $ to update the first element matched by the query ({"items.sku": "A"} then $set: {"items.$.qty": 3}), $[] for all elements, and the filtered positional operator $[name] with arrayFilters for all elements matching a condition. All of these are atomic within the document. In Spring Data, Update.set("items.$[i].status", ...) combined with update.filterArray(Criteria.where("i.status").is("UNPAID")) does the same.

How do you prevent lost updates in MongoDB with Spring Data?

Two complementary techniques. First, avoid read-modify-write: send atomic operators ($inc, $set, $push) with updateFirst or findAndModify, optionally with a condition in the filter (for example stock >= qty) so the update only applies when the rule holds. Second, when you must load and save a whole document, add @Version: the save includes the version in the filter and throws OptimisticLockingFailureException on a conflict, which you retry or report as 409.

@DBRef vs @DocumentReference vs storing the id yourself?

@DBRef stores a {$ref, $id} object; it is resolved with one extra query per reference (N+1) and $lookup handles it awkwardly. @DocumentReference (Spring Data MongoDB 3.3+) stores just the id (or a custom key) and can resolve lazily, which is leaner. Storing a plain id field and loading related data explicitly, or with $lookup in an aggregation, is the most transparent and usually the recommended choice. If you find yourself needing many references per read, revisit the schema: embed or duplicate the fields you read together (the extended reference pattern).

What are change streams and how do you make a consumer survive restarts?

Change streams let an application subscribe to data changes (built on the oplog, so a replica set is required). Each event has a resume token in _id; persist it after you process the event and reopen the stream with resumeAfter or startAfter. Processing should be idempotent because a crash between handling and saving the token replays the event. If the token has fallen off the oplog window, the stream cannot resume and you need a full resync, so size the oplog for your longest expected outage. In Spring, use MongoTemplate with a MessageListenerContainer or ReactiveMongoTemplate.changeStream(...).

How do you test Spring Data MongoDB code?

Use the @DataMongoTest slice, which configures MongoTemplate and repositories only, with a real MongoDB from Testcontainers: @Container @ServiceConnection static MongoDBContainer mongo = new MongoDBContainer("mongo:7");. The Testcontainers MongoDB module starts a single-node replica set, so transactions and change streams also work. Avoid embedded or in-memory fakes: index behaviour, aggregation stages and transactions differ. Create indexes in tests the same way as in production (migration tool or explicit ensureIndex), since auto-index-creation is off by default.

How do you insert or update a million documents efficiently?

Use bulk writes: insertMany or bulkWrite in the shell, BulkOperations in Spring (mongoTemplate.bulkOps(BulkMode.UNORDERED, Order.class)), in batches of a few thousand. Unordered mode lets the server continue after an error and parallelize; ordered stops at the first error. Use upserts (updateOne with upsert: true) for idempotent re-runs. For a one-off load, consider creating secondary indexes after the import, and use write concern majority if the data must survive a failover.

What are read concern and causal consistency?

Read concern controls how durable the data you read is: local (default, may later be rolled back after a failover), majority (acknowledged by a majority, will not roll back), linearizable (most recent majority write, single document, slow), and snapshot inside transactions. Combined with write concern majority, it gives durable reads. Causally consistent sessions guarantee read-your-own-writes and monotonic reads even when reads go to secondaries: the driver passes the operation time of your last write so a secondary waits until it has caught up.

MongoDB or PostgreSQL with jsonb?

PostgreSQL jsonb gives flexible documents with GIN indexes alongside relational tables, joins, constraints and mature transactions, which suits mostly relational data with some variable attributes. MongoDB is stronger when the document is the main model: rich update operators on nested arrays, an aggregation pipeline, built-in horizontal scaling with sharding, change streams, and integrated search in Atlas. Pick by data shape and team skills; many teams avoid running both unless there is a clear reason.

What are time-series collections and when would you use them?

A time-series collection (MongoDB 5.0+) is created with timeField, an optional metaField (for example a device id) and a granularity. MongoDB stores measurements internally in compressed buckets (the bucket pattern done for you), which cuts storage and speeds time-range queries. Use it for metrics, IoT readings, vitals or audit-style events, usually with a TTL via expireAfterSeconds. Updates and deletes are more limited than in normal collections, so it fits append-mostly data.

Can MongoDB do vector search for AI features?

Yes, on Atlas (and in recent self-managed editions): you store embeddings as an array field, define a vector search index, and query with the $vectorSearch aggregation stage to find the nearest neighbours, optionally pre-filtered by metadata. This lets a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) feature keep documents, metadata and embeddings in one store. Spring AI has a MongoDB Atlas vector store integration. Atlas Search ($search) covers full-text relevance search, and both can be combined in hybrid search.

Firebase BaaS

Firebase is Google's Backend-as-a-Service: authentication, real-time NoSQL databases, file storage, hosting, serverless functions and push notifications that client apps use directly through SDKs, secured by security rules. A Spring Boot backend can sit alongside it, verifying Firebase ID tokens with the Admin SDK.

// Angular (AngularFire, standalone) – app.config.ts
export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideFirebaseApp(() => initializeApp(environment.firebase)),
    provideAuth(() => getAuth()),
    provideFirestore(() => getFirestore()),
  ],
};

// tasks.service.ts – real-time query of the signed-in user's tasks
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class TasksService {
  private db = inject(Firestore);
  private auth = inject(Auth);

  myOpenTasks(): Observable<Task[]> {
    const uid = this.auth.currentUser!.uid;
    const q = query(collection(this.db, 'tasks'),
                    where('ownerId', '==', uid), where('done', '==', false),
                    orderBy('dueDate'), limit(20));
    return collectionData(q, { idField: 'id' }) as Observable<Task[]>;
  }

  add(title: string) {
    return addDoc(collection(this.db, 'tasks'),
      { title, done: false, ownerId: this.auth.currentUser!.uid, createdAt: serverTimestamp() });
  }
}

What Firebase Offers

  • Build: Authentication, Cloud Firestore, Realtime Database, Cloud Storage, Hosting / App Hosting, Cloud Functions, Remote Config, App Check, Data Connect (PostgreSQL), Firebase AI Logic.
  • Run & engage: Cloud Messaging (FCM), Crashlytics, Performance Monitoring, Analytics, A/B Testing, App Distribution.

A Firebase project is a Google Cloud project, so Firestore, Storage and Functions also appear in the GCP console and can be used with IAM, Cloud Logging and other GCP services. Clients talk to Firebase directly, which removes much backend code but moves authorisation into security rules. The local Emulator Suite (firebase emulators:start) runs Auth, Firestore, Functions, Storage and more for development and rules testing.

Firebase Authentication

Firebase Auth handles sign-up/sign-in with email/password, email link, phone (SMS OTP), anonymous accounts, and federated providers (Google, Apple, Microsoft, Facebook, GitHub); upgrading to Identity Platform adds SAML/OIDC, MFA and multi-tenancy. After sign-in the SDK holds a short-lived ID token (a JWT, valid one hour) and a refresh token, refreshing automatically. The ID token contains the uid, email and any custom claims (e.g. role: "admin") set from the Admin SDK.

// AngularFire
await signInWithEmailAndPassword(this.auth, email, password);
await signInWithPopup(this.auth, new GoogleAuthProvider());
user(this.auth).subscribe(u => this.currentUser.set(u));     // auth state stream
const idToken = await this.auth.currentUser?.getIdToken();   // send to your API

Cloud Firestore vs Realtime Database

Realtime Database (RTDB) is the original product: one large JSON tree, synced in real time over a persistent connection. Queries are limited (sort/filter on one property at a time), data must be denormalised and kept shallow, and it scales by adding database instances (shards). It has very low latency and is billed mainly by bandwidth and storage.

Cloud Firestore is the recommended choice for new apps: documents (up to 1 MiB, with fields, maps, arrays) organised in collections and subcollections. It supports compound queries, ordering, range filters, in/array-contains, or queries, aggregations (count, sum, average), transactions and batched writes, offline persistence, automatic scaling and multi-region replication. Billing is per document read, write and delete plus storage. Queries are always backed by indexes (single-field automatic; composite indexes defined in firestore.indexes.json) so query time depends on result size, not collection size.

// Firestore modular SDK (v9+)
const ref = doc(db, 'users', uid);
await setDoc(ref, { name: 'Asha', plan: 'free' }, { merge: true });
await updateDoc(ref, { loginCount: increment(1), tags: arrayUnion('beta') });
const snap = await getDoc(ref);

// Real-time listener (returns an unsubscribe function)
const unsub = onSnapshot(query(collection(db, 'rooms', roomId, 'messages'),
                               orderBy('sentAt', 'desc'), limit(50)),
                         s => this.messages = s.docs.map(d => ({ id: d.id, ...d.data() })));

// Realtime Database equivalent
onValue(ref(rtdb, `rooms/${roomId}/messages`), s => console.log(s.val()));

Always unsubscribe listeners (e.g. in ngOnDestroy or via takeUntilDestroyed) – every live listener keeps a connection and incurs reads on changes.

Security Rules

Because clients access the database directly, security rules are the authorisation layer for Firestore, RTDB and Storage. Rules match paths, check request.auth (the verified user), request.resource.data (incoming data) and resource.data (existing data), and can validate fields. Rules are not filters: a query is rejected unless the rules allow every possible result, so queries must include the same constraints (e.g. where('ownerId','==',uid)). The Admin SDK bypasses rules entirely.

rules_version = '2';
service cloud.firestore {
  match /databases/{database}/documents {
    match /tasks/{taskId} {
      allow read, update, delete: if request.auth != null
                                  && resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid;
      allow create: if request.auth != null
                    && request.resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid
                    && request.resource.data.title is string
                    && request.resource.data.title.size() < 200;
    }
    match /admin/{doc=**} {
      allow read, write: if request.auth.token.role == 'admin';   // custom claim
    }
  }
}

Never ship "test mode" rules (allow read, write: if true) to production; test rules with the emulator and @firebase/rules-unit-testing. App Check adds attestation that requests come from your genuine app.

Cloud Storage, Hosting & Cloud Functions

Cloud Storage for Firebase stores user files (images, PDFs) in a Google Cloud Storage bucket, with client SDK uploads (resumable, with progress) and Storage security rules, e.g. users may only write to /users/{uid}/... and files must be under 5 MB and image/*.

const fileRef = ref(storage, `users/${uid}/avatar.jpg`);
await uploadBytes(fileRef, file, { contentType: file.type });
const url = await getDownloadURL(fileRef);

Firebase Hosting serves static sites and SPAs (Angular, Ionic PWA) over a global CDN with free SSL, custom domains, preview channels per pull request and rewrites (SPA fallback to index.html, or routing /api/** to Cloud Functions or Cloud Run). App Hosting targets server-rendered frameworks (Angular SSR, Next.js). Deploy with firebase deploy --only hosting.

Cloud Functions for Firebase run server-side Node.js (or Python) code on events: HTTPS requests, callable functions (auto-verified auth), Firestore/RTDB/Storage triggers, Auth events, Pub/Sub and scheduled jobs. 2nd gen functions run on Cloud Run with higher concurrency. Use them for trusted logic: sending emails, payments, aggregating counters, setting custom claims. Event triggers deliver at least once, so handlers must be idempotent.

// functions/src/index.ts
export const onOrderCreated = onDocumentCreated('orders/{orderId}', async (event) => {
  const order = event.data?.data();
  await getFirestore().doc(`stats/${order?.shopId}`)
    .set({ orderCount: FieldValue.increment(1) }, { merge: true });
});

FCM Push Notifications

Firebase Cloud Messaging delivers notifications and data messages to Android, iOS (via APNs) and web (via service worker) for free. The client obtains a registration token and sends it to your backend, which stores it per user. The server sends via the HTTP v1 API (OAuth2 service-account auth; the legacy server-key API was shut down in 2024) or the Admin SDK, targeting a token, a topic (/topics/news) or a condition. Notification messages are shown automatically by the OS when the app is in the background; data messages are handled by app code. Remove tokens when FCM returns "unregistered".

// Spring Boot (firebase-admin) – send to a device
Message msg = Message.builder()
    .setToken(deviceToken)
    .setNotification(Notification.builder().setTitle("Order shipped").setBody("Arriving tomorrow").build())
    .putData("orderId", orderId)
    .build();
String messageId = FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().send(msg);

Firebase with Angular, Ionic & a Spring Boot Backend

AngularFire (@angular/fire) is the official Angular library: providers in app.config.ts, injectable Auth/Firestore/Storage and RxJS streams (collectionData, docData, user, authState) that work with the async pipe or toSignal. Route guards can use AuthGuard with redirectUnauthorizedTo. In Ionic (Angular + Capacitor) the web SDK works in the WebView, but native features – Google/Apple sign-in, push notifications, Crashlytics – usually use Capacitor plugins such as @capacitor-firebase/authentication and @capacitor-firebase/messaging (or @capacitor/push-notifications), with google-services.json / GoogleService-Info.plist added to the native projects.

When you have your own API, the client sends the Firebase ID token as Authorization: Bearer <token> and the Spring Boot backend verifies it with the Firebase Admin SDK (signature, issuer, audience, expiry). Alternatively configure Spring Security as an OAuth2 resource server with issuer https://securetoken.google.com/PROJECT_ID.

@Configuration
public class FirebaseConfig {
    @Bean
    FirebaseApp firebaseApp() throws IOException {
        // On GCP uses the attached service account; locally GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS
        FirebaseOptions options = FirebaseOptions.builder()
            .setCredentials(GoogleCredentials.getApplicationDefault()).build();
        return FirebaseApp.initializeApp(options);
    }
}

@Component @RequiredArgsConstructor
public class FirebaseTokenFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    private final FirebaseApp app;

    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String header = req.getHeader(HttpHeaders.AUTHORIZATION);
        if (header != null && header.startsWith("Bearer ")) {
            try {
                FirebaseToken token = FirebaseAuth.getInstance(app)
                    .verifyIdToken(header.substring(7), true);   // true = check revoked
                var authorities = "admin".equals(token.getClaims().get("role"))
                    ? List.of(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("ROLE_ADMIN")) : List.<GrantedAuthority>of();
                SecurityContextHolder.getContext().setAuthentication(
                    new UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken(token.getUid(), null, authorities));
            } catch (FirebaseAuthException e) {
                res.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_UNAUTHORIZED, "Invalid Firebase token");
                return;
            }
        }
        chain.doFilter(req, res);
    }
}

// Set a custom claim (picked up after the client refreshes its token)
FirebaseAuth.getInstance().setCustomUserClaims(uid, Map.of("role", "admin"));

Pricing, Limits & Caveats

  • Plans: Spark (free, no-cost quotas) and Blaze (pay as you go, includes the free tier). Cloud Functions and some features require Blaze. Set budget alerts – budgets alert but do not cap spending.
  • Firestore bills per document read/write/delete: listeners on large collections, unpaginated queries, and loops of reads in the client can create large bills. Denormalise and paginate (limit, startAfter), and use aggregation queries instead of reading all docs to count.
  • Firestore limits: 1 MiB per document, a sustained write rate of about 1 write/second per single document (use distributed counters), batched writes and transactions limited by request size (formerly 500 operations), composite indexes needed for many compound queries, limited server-side joins and no full-text search (use Algolia/Typesense/Elastic or vector search extensions).
  • Vendor lock-in and data export: migration away requires rewriting data access; schedule managed exports for backups (or enable point-in-time recovery).
  • Cold starts and regions for Functions; choose the database location carefully, since it cannot be changed later.
  • Firebase config in the client (apiKey) is not a secret – security comes from rules, App Check and API key restrictions, never from hiding the config.

Querying Firestore: What You Can and Cannot Do

  • Every query is index-backed, so query cost scales with the result size, not the collection size. Single-field indexes are automatic; queries combining filters with an orderBy on another field need a composite index. The error message contains a console link that creates it; commit the result to firestore.indexes.json so all environments match.
  • Operators: ==, !=, <, <=, >, >=, in, not-in, array-contains, array-contains-any, plus or()/and() composite filters. Range filters on several fields are now supported, but each extra range field adds index and cost considerations.
  • Collection group queries search every subcollection with the same id (for example all comments under any post). They need a collection-group index and a rules match on /{path=**}/comments/{id}.
  • Pagination uses cursors (startAfter(lastDoc)), not offsets. An offset still reads, and bills, the skipped documents.
  • Aggregations: count(), sum() and average() run on the server and bill roughly one read per batch of index entries, much cheaper than downloading documents. For dashboards that refresh constantly, maintain counters with Cloud Functions instead.
  • Not available: joins, full-text search (use Algolia, Typesense or Elastic via an extension or function), and "field does not exist" queries.
import { collection, query, where, orderBy, limit, startAfter,
         getDocs, getCountFromServer, collectionGroup } from 'firebase/firestore';

// Page 1 of a user's open tasks, newest first (needs composite index: ownerId, status, createdAt desc)
const base = query(collection(db, 'tasks'),
  where('ownerId', '==', uid), where('status', '==', 'open'),
  orderBy('createdAt', 'desc'), limit(20));
const page1 = await getDocs(base);

// Next page: continue after the last snapshot
const last = page1.docs[page1.docs.length - 1];
const page2 = await getDocs(query(base, startAfter(last)));

// Server-side count, without downloading documents
const total = (await getCountFromServer(base)).data().count;

// All comments by this user across every post
const mine = await getDocs(query(collectionGroup(db, 'comments'), where('authorId', '==', uid)));

Environments, Emulators and CI

  • One Firebase project per environment (dev, staging, prod), not one project with prefixed collections. Rules, auth users, quotas and billing are per project. Map aliases in .firebaserc with firebase use --add and deploy with firebase deploy --project staging.
  • Everything as code: firestore.rules, firestore.indexes.json, storage.rules and functions live in the repo and deploy from CI, never edited only in the console.
  • Emulator Suite for local development and tests; in Angular, call connectFirestoreEmulator/connectAuthEmulator when an environment flag is set. Emulators are free and can be seeded with --import.
  • Rules unit tests with @firebase/rules-unit-testing in CI (firebase emulators:exec "npm test"), covering allowed and denied cases.
  • Hosting preview channels (firebase hosting:channel:deploy pr-42) give each pull request a temporary URL.
  • Authenticate CI with a service account or Workload Identity Federation instead of the deprecated firebase login:ci token.
// rules.test.ts (runs against the Firestore emulator)
import { initializeTestEnvironment, assertSucceeds, assertFails } from '@firebase/rules-unit-testing';
import { readFileSync } from 'node:fs';
import { doc, getDoc } from 'firebase/firestore';

const env = await initializeTestEnvironment({
  projectId: 'demo-test',
  firestore: { rules: readFileSync('firestore.rules', 'utf8') },
});

test('a user can read only their own profile', async () => {
  const alice = env.authenticatedContext('alice').firestore();
  await assertSucceeds(getDoc(doc(alice, 'users/alice')));
  await assertFails(getDoc(doc(alice, 'users/bob')));
});

Interview Questions — Firebase

What is Firebase and when would you use it?

Firebase is a Backend-as-a-Service on Google Cloud providing auth, real-time NoSQL databases, file storage, hosting, serverless functions, push messaging and app quality tools via client SDKs. It suits MVPs, mobile/web apps needing real-time sync or offline support, chat and collaboration features, and small teams wanting less backend infrastructure. For complex relational data, heavy reporting or strict backend control, a traditional API with a SQL database may be better – or a hybrid.

Firestore vs Realtime Database?

Realtime Database is a single JSON tree with very low-latency sync, simple queries (one sort/filter key) and bandwidth-based pricing. Firestore uses documents and collections, supports richer compound queries, aggregations, transactions, offline support, automatic scaling and multi-region replication, billed per operation. Firestore is the default for new projects; RTDB still fits presence systems or many tiny, frequent updates.

How does Firebase Authentication work end to end?

The client signs in with a provider through the Firebase SDK and receives an ID token (JWT, one-hour expiry) plus a refresh token that the SDK uses to renew it. Firebase services read the token automatically and expose it as request.auth in security rules. Your own backend receives the token in the Authorization header and verifies it with the Admin SDK, getting the uid and custom claims.

How do you verify a Firebase ID token in a Spring Boot backend?

Initialise FirebaseApp with Application Default Credentials, then in a Spring Security filter extract the Bearer token and call FirebaseAuth.getInstance().verifyIdToken(token) (pass true to also check revocation). On success build an Authentication from the uid and custom claims; on FirebaseAuthException return 401. Alternatively use spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server with the issuer https://securetoken.google.com/<projectId>, since the tokens are standard JWTs.

What are custom claims and how do you implement roles?

Custom claims are extra key/values (max 1000 bytes) embedded in a user's ID token, set only from a trusted environment with the Admin SDK: setCustomUserClaims(uid, Map.of("role","admin")). They appear in request.auth.token in rules and in the verified token on your backend. The client must refresh its token (getIdToken(true)) to see new claims.

What are security rules and why are they critical?

Since web and mobile clients access Firestore, RTDB and Storage directly, rules are the only server-side gate on who can read or write which data and in what shape. They check authentication, ownership, roles via claims, and validate incoming fields. Misconfigured rules (e.g. open test-mode rules) are a common cause of data leaks; test them with the emulator and unit tests before deploying.

"Rules are not filters" – what does that mean?

Firestore doesn't silently drop documents a user can't read; it evaluates whether the query could return any forbidden document and rejects the whole query if so. Therefore if rules require resource.data.ownerId == request.auth.uid, the client query must include where('ownerId', '==', uid), otherwise it fails with permission-denied.

How do real-time listeners work and what should you watch out for?

onSnapshot (or AngularFire's collectionData) opens a listener that delivers the initial result and then every change, including local pending writes for latency compensation. Each document returned and each change counts as a read. Always unsubscribe when the component is destroyed, limit and paginate listened queries, and avoid listening to large collections.

How do you model data in Firestore?

Model for your queries: documents in top-level collections or subcollections (e.g. rooms/{id}/messages), denormalise frequently displayed fields since there are no joins, and keep documents small (1 MiB limit). Use subcollections or separate collections for unbounded lists rather than huge arrays. Use transactions or batched writes to keep duplicated data consistent, or Cloud Functions triggers to fan out updates.

Transactions vs batched writes in Firestore?

A transaction reads documents and then writes based on those values; it retries automatically if data changed concurrently (e.g. decrement stock only if available). A batched write groups multiple writes (set/update/delete) that succeed or fail atomically without reads. Both are atomic; batched writes can be queued while offline, but transactions require a connection.

What are Cloud Functions used for in a Firebase app?

Trusted server-side logic that shouldn't run in the client: sending emails or FCM messages, processing payments with secret keys, maintaining counters and denormalised data on Firestore triggers, resizing uploaded images on Storage triggers, setting custom claims on user creation, and scheduled cleanup. Handlers must be idempotent because event delivery is at least once.

How do push notifications with FCM work?

The app requests notification permission and gets an FCM registration token, which it sends to the backend to store per user/device. The backend sends messages via the FCM HTTP v1 API or Admin SDK to a token, topic or condition; FCM routes them through APNs on iOS and the service worker on web. Notification payloads display automatically in the background, data payloads are handled by app code; clean up tokens that return unregistered errors.

How do you use Firebase in an Ionic app?

The Firebase JS SDK / AngularFire works inside the Capacitor WebView for Firestore and most Auth flows. For native-only capabilities – Google/Apple native sign-in, push notifications, Crashlytics, Analytics – use Capacitor plugins (e.g. @capacitor-firebase/authentication, @capacitor-firebase/messaging) and add google-services.json and GoogleService-Info.plist to the Android and iOS projects. Popup/redirect web sign-in is unreliable in WebViews, which is why native plugins are preferred.

Is it a problem that the Firebase apiKey is visible in the front-end code?

No – the Firebase config including apiKey only identifies the project; it does not grant access to data. Protection comes from security rules, Firebase Auth, App Check and API key restrictions in the Google Cloud console. Service account keys and Admin SDK credentials, by contrast, are real secrets and must never be in client code.

What are common Firebase pricing pitfalls?

Firestore charges per document read, so unbounded listeners, reading whole collections to count, and N+1 read patterns in the UI inflate costs; use limit, pagination, aggregation queries and caching. Cloud Functions in loops (a trigger writing to the collection that triggers it) can run away. Use Blaze plan budget alerts and monitor usage dashboards, remembering that budgets alert but do not stop billing.

What are Firestore's main limits?

Documents max 1 MiB; about one sustained write per second to the same document (use distributed counters for hot counters); queries need indexes and some combinations need composite indexes; no native full-text search or server-side joins; and the database location is fixed at creation. Large analytics are better exported to BigQuery.

When would you combine Firebase with your own Spring Boot backend?

When you want Firebase's auth, real-time sync or FCM but also need complex business logic, relational data in MySQL/PostgreSQL, third-party integrations with secrets, or reporting. The front end authenticates with Firebase and calls the Spring Boot API with the ID token; the backend verifies it, applies authorisation, and uses the Admin SDK to write to Firestore or send FCM messages where needed.

💡 Keep one source of truth per piece of data to avoid sync problems between Firestore and SQL.

How do you sign a user out of all devices, or block a disabled user immediately?

ID tokens are self-contained JWTs valid for about one hour, so disabling a user does not invalidate tokens already issued. Call admin.auth().revokeRefreshTokens(uid) (or FirebaseAuth.revokeRefreshTokens in Java), which stops refreshes and records a revocation time. To reject already-issued ID tokens before they expire, verify with verifyIdToken(token, true) on your backend, and in security rules compare request.auth.token.auth_time with a revocation timestamp you store per user. Checking revocation costs an extra lookup, so do it on sensitive endpoints.

ID token or session cookie for a server-rendered app?

The client SDK keeps the ID token in the browser and refreshes it automatically, which suits SPAs calling APIs with a Bearer header. For server-side rendering (Angular SSR, a traditional web app), exchange the fresh ID token once for a session cookie with createSessionCookie(idToken, {expiresIn}), valid from 5 minutes to 2 weeks, set it as HttpOnly; Secure; SameSite, and verify it on each request with verifySessionCookie(cookie, true). Because it is a cookie, add CSRF protection.

What is anonymous authentication, and how do you keep the user's data when they sign up later?

Anonymous auth gives a visitor a real uid without credentials, so security rules and per-user data (a cart, a draft) work immediately. When they register, call linkWithCredential (or linkWithPopup) on the current user: the anonymous account is upgraded and keeps the same uid, so no data migration is needed. If the credential already belongs to another account, linking fails with credential-already-in-use and you must merge data yourself. Clean up abandoned anonymous accounts periodically; Identity Platform can delete them automatically.

Why can sequential document ids or timestamp fields limit Firestore write throughput?

Firestore splits data by key ranges. Monotonically increasing document ids, or an indexed field like createdAt written at a high rate, send every write to the same end of the range, creating a hotspot. Use the auto-generated random ids, and for very high write rates on a collection with an increasing indexed field, exempt that field from indexing or spread writes (for example a shard prefix). Ramp up traffic gradually (the "500/50/5" guideline: start at 500 writes per second and grow by 50% every 5 minutes) so Firestore can split ranges. Separately, a single document sustains only about one write per second; use distributed counters for hot documents.

How do you evolve the data model in Firestore without a schema migration tool?

Old and new document shapes coexist, so code must handle both. Common approach: add a schemaVersion field; make readers tolerate missing fields with defaults; write new fields from the new version of the app; then backfill existing documents with a one-off Admin SDK script using BulkWriter (batched, rate-limited, retrying). Remove old fields only after every client version still in use (mobile apps update slowly) no longer reads them, and tighten security rules last. For heavier changes, a Cloud Function can migrate documents lazily on write.

Why does a collection group query fail with permission-denied even though the user can read each document?

Rules written as match /posts/{postId}/comments/{commentId} apply to that path only. A collection group query is evaluated against a recursive wildcard, so you need a rule such as match /{path=**}/comments/{commentId} { allow read: if resource.data.visibility == 'public'; }. Remember that rules are not filters: the query's own where clauses must guarantee every possible result passes the rule. A collection-group index is also required.

How do you back up Firestore and recover from a bad deployment that corrupted data?

Enable point-in-time recovery (PITR), which keeps versions for up to 7 days so you can read data as of an earlier time and write it back, and schedule managed exports (or scheduled backups) to Cloud Storage for long-term retention; exports can be imported into another project or loaded into BigQuery. Exports are not atomic snapshots across a busy database, so use PITR for precise restores. Test the restore process, and protect against the main cause of corruption with rules tests, staged rollouts and validation in Cloud Functions.

How do you protect a Cloud Function from abuse?

For onCall functions, check request.auth (and custom claims) at the start and throw HttpsError('unauthenticated') or 'permission-denied'; enable enforceAppCheck: true so only your genuine app can call it. For onRequest HTTP functions, verify the ID token yourself, restrict CORS, and keep public endpoints idempotent. Validate inputs, set maxInstances to cap cost from traffic spikes, and add budget alerts, because a loop or attack on a pay-per-use function shows up on the bill.

Microservices Architecture

Service decomposition, gateway, discovery, config, resilience, communication, data consistency, observability, deployment.

Monolith vs Microservices: the Real Trade-off

A microservice is a small, independently deployable service that owns one business capability and its data. The main benefit is organisational: teams release without coordinating. The main cost is that every in-process method call becomes a network call, which can fail, time out, or arrive twice.

MonolithModular monolithMicroservices
Deploy unitOneOneMany
Module boundariesConventionEnforced (packages, Spring Modulith, ArchUnit)Network
TransactionsACID across everythingACIDLocal only; sagas between services
ScalingAll togetherAll togetherPer service
Failure modeWhole appWhole appPartial, cascading if unprotected
Ops costLowLowHigh: CI/CD, tracing, platform team
FitsSmall team, early productMost productsMany teams, uneven scale, long life
Gotcha: the distributed monolith is the worst outcome: services that must deploy together, share a database, or call each other synchronously in long chains. You pay all the costs and gain no independence. The test is simple: can one team deploy its service today without telling anyone?

Decomposition with Domain-Driven Design

The hard problem is where to draw the lines. Wrong boundaries mean chatty services and cross-service transactions, and they are expensive to move later. Domain-Driven Design (DDD) gives vocabulary for this.

  • Ubiquitous language: the shared terms of the business and the code.
  • Bounded context: a boundary inside which each term has one meaning. "Product" in Catalog has images and descriptions; in Shipping it has weight and dimensions. These are two models and should not be merged into one shared class.
  • Aggregate: a cluster of objects changed together as a unit, with one root (Order with its lines). One transaction changes one aggregate. Aggregates refer to each other by id, not by object reference. A service generally holds one or more aggregates.
  • Domain event: a fact in past tense, such as OrderPlaced. Events connect contexts.
  • Context map: how contexts relate. An anti-corruption layer (ACL) translates a foreign or legacy model at the boundary, so it cannot leak into yours.
  • Event storming: a workshop that puts domain events on a wall in time order. Clusters reveal contexts.

Practical checks for a boundary: it changes for one business reason, it has one owner team, it needs few synchronous calls to do its job, and data that must be consistent together stays within it. If two services always change together, they are one service.

Strangler fig migration

A big-bang rewrite is high risk because nothing ships until everything ships. The strangler fig pattern, named after a vine that gradually replaces its host tree, moves one capability at a time behind a routing layer.

  1. Put a routing facade (gateway) in front of the monolith. Nothing changes yet.
  2. Pick a capability with few dependencies and clear value.
  3. Build the new service, and add an ACL for monolith calls.
  4. Copy data and keep it synced. Run read traffic in shadow mode and compare results.
  5. Route a small share of traffic, then all of it. Keep rollback open.
  6. Delete the old code and tables. Skipping this step leaves two systems forever.

Inter-Service Communication

REST / HTTPgRPCMessaging (Kafka, RabbitMQ)
StyleRequest/responseRequest/response and streamingFire and forget, pub/sub
FormatJSON, human-readableProtobuf binary, schema firstAvro, Protobuf, JSON
TransportHTTP/1.1 or 2HTTP/2 multiplexedBroker protocol
Coupling in timeBoth must be upBoth must be upDecoupled; broker buffers
Browser supportNativeNeeds gRPC-Web or a proxyNone directly
Best forPublic APIs, simple callsInternal, low-latency, polyglotEvents, workflows, load levelling

Synchronous clients in Spring

// Declarative HTTP interface (Spring Framework 6+), the modern alternative to Feign.
// Spring Cloud OpenFeign is in maintenance mode.
@HttpExchange("/api/stock")
public interface InventoryClient {
  @GetExchange("/{sku}")
  StockDto stock(@PathVariable String sku);
}

@Configuration
class ClientConfig {
  @Bean @LoadBalanced                       // resolves logical service names
  RestClient.Builder restClientBuilder() { return RestClient.builder(); }

  @Bean
  InventoryClient inventoryClient(RestClient.Builder b) {
    var factory = new SimpleClientHttpRequestFactory();
    factory.setConnectTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(1));
    factory.setReadTimeout(Duration.ofSeconds(2));            // never run without timeouts
    RestClient rc = b.baseUrl("http://inventory-service").requestFactory(factory).build();
    return HttpServiceProxyFactory.builderFor(RestClientAdapter.create(rc)).build()
                                  .createClient(InventoryClient.class);
  }
}

gRPC

You define the contract in a .proto file and generate client and server stubs. Field numbers, not names, identify data on the wire, which is why schema evolution rules are strict: never reuse a number, and add new optional fields only.

syntax = "proto3";
service Inventory {
  rpc Reserve (ReserveRequest) returns (ReserveReply);              // unary
  rpc WatchStock (StockQuery) returns (stream StockEvent);          // server streaming
  rpc Upload (stream Line) returns (UploadSummary);                 // client streaming
  rpc Sync (stream Delta) returns (stream Delta);                   // bidirectional
}
message ReserveRequest { string sku = 1; int32 qty = 2; }
message ReserveReply   { bool ok = 1; string reservation_id = 2; }

gRPC deadlines carry the remaining time budget across hops, so a downstream service stops work the caller has abandoned. Plain L4 load balancing distributes badly here: HTTP/2 keeps one long connection, so all calls from a client can pin to a single pod. Use client-side balancing through a headless Kubernetes Service, or a service mesh.

Asynchronous messaging

Events reduce coupling: OrderService publishes OrderPlaced and does not know who listens. Distinguish three message kinds: a command (do this, one handler), an event (this happened, zero or more handlers), and a query. Event payloads come in two styles: thin events carry ids, so consumers call back and couple again; event-carried state transfer includes the data, so consumers keep a local copy. See the Kafka section for delivery details.

Service Discovery and Load Balancing

Beyond the summary below, the mechanism of Eureka is often probed. Each instance registers itself at startup and sends a heartbeat every 30 seconds. The server evicts an instance after 90 seconds without heartbeats. Clients cache the registry and refresh it every 30 seconds, so a dead instance can get traffic for a while, which is why client retries matter. If too many heartbeats vanish at once, Eureka enters self-preservation: it assumes the network is at fault and stops evicting. Eureka prefers availability over consistency (AP in CAP terms); Consul and ZooKeeper use a consensus protocol and favour consistency.

Load balancingWhereExampleNotes
Client-sideIn the callerSpring Cloud LoadBalancerNo extra hop; each language needs a library
Server-side L4Proxy on TCPKubernetes Service, NLBFast; sees connections rather than requests
Server-side L7Proxy on HTTPNGINX, Envoy, ALB, IngressRoutes by path or header; TLS termination
SidecarProxy next to each podIstio, LinkerdLanguage-neutral; adds latency and ops work

Algorithms: round robin (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer's default), random, weighted, least connections, and consistent hashing (the same key goes to the same instance, useful for caches or sticky state).

API Gateway and Config

Spring Cloud Gateway comes in two flavours: Server WebFlux (reactive, the original) and Server WebMVC (servlet stack, works with virtual threads). A route combines predicates (does this request match?) and filters (change the request or response), and a target URI. lb:// means "resolve through discovery".

@Bean
RouteLocator routes(RouteLocatorBuilder b, KeyResolver userKey) {
  return b.routes()
    .route("orders", r -> r.path("/api/orders/**")
      .filters(f -> f
        .stripPrefix(1)                                 // /api/orders/1 -> /orders/1
        .requestRateLimiter(c -> c.setRateLimiter(new RedisRateLimiter(10, 20))  // refill, burst
                                  .setKeyResolver(userKey))
        .circuitBreaker(c -> c.setName("orders").setFallbackUri("forward:/fallback/orders"))
        .retry(c -> c.setRetries(2).setMethods(HttpMethod.GET)))
      .uri("lb://order-service"))
    .build();
}

BFF (Backend for Frontend) is a gateway variant: one tailored API per client type, so mobile does not need the same payload as web. Keep gateways free of business logic: otherwise they become a new monolith that every team must change.

Config details. A client declares spring.config.import=optional:configserver:http://config:8888. Config Server serves files by {application}/{profile}/{label}, where label is usually a Git branch. Boot's bootstrap.yml stage is legacy.
