Live refresh: POST /actuator/refresh rebinds @RefreshScope beans and @ConfigurationProperties on one instance, and /actuator/busrefresh broadcasts through Spring Cloud Bus. Secrets go to Vault, or use {cipher} values. Under Kubernetes, use ConfigMaps and restart pods with a rolling update, which is simpler and easier to audit.

Resilience with Resilience4j

In a chain of synchronous calls, one slow dependency uses up threads in its callers, and the failure spreads backwards. That is a cascading failure. Slow is worse than down, since an instant error frees a thread but a hanging call holds one. Resilience patterns bound the damage.

resilience4j:
  circuitbreaker:
    instances:
      payment:
        sliding-window-type: COUNT_BASED
        sliding-window-size: 20                  # last 20 calls
        minimum-number-of-calls: 10              # no decision before this
        failure-rate-threshold: 50               # percent
        slow-call-duration-threshold: 2s
        slow-call-rate-threshold: 80             # slow calls count too
        wait-duration-in-open-state: 30s
        permitted-number-of-calls-in-half-open-state: 5
        ignore-exceptions: [com.acme.ValidationException]   # business errors do not trip it
  retry:
    instances:
      payment:
        max-attempts: 3                          # includes the first call
        wait-duration: 200ms
        enable-exponential-backoff: true
        exponential-backoff-multiplier: 2
        enable-randomized-wait: true             # jitter
        retry-exceptions: [java.io.IOException]
  bulkhead:
    instances:
      payment: { max-concurrent-calls: 20, max-wait-duration: 0 }
  ratelimiter:
    instances:
      payment: { limit-for-period: 100, limit-refresh-period: 1s, timeout-duration: 0 }
  timelimiter:
    instances:
      payment: { timeout-duration: 2s }
PatternProblem solvedHowPitfall
TimeoutHung threadsUpper limit on a callToo long is useless; must be shorter than the caller's
RetryBrief faultsTry again, with backoff and jitterDuplicates a non-idempotent call; amplifies load
Circuit breakerHammering a failing serviceStop calling, let it recoverFallback must be real, not a hidden lie
BulkheadOne dependency eating all threadsCap on concurrent callsSize from load tests
Rate limiterOverload; protecting yourself or a partner quotaCap on calls per periodPer-instance limit; shared limits need Redis
FallbackUser impactDefault, cached value, or a queued taskShould not call yet another fragile service

Circuit breaker states. CLOSED counts outcomes in a sliding window, count-based or time-based. When the failure rate or slow rate passes the threshold (after minimum calls), it moves to OPEN: calls fail immediately with CallNotPermittedException. After the wait, it goes to HALF_OPEN and allows a few trial calls. If they do well it closes; if they fail it re-opens. There are also administrative states: DISABLED, FORCED_OPEN, and METRICS_ONLY. The aspect-mode @TimeLimiter and @Bulkhead(type = THREADPOOL) need a CompletableFuture return type.

Retry amplification: three layers that each try 3 times can turn one failing call into 27 at the bottom, just when that service is weakest. Retry at one layer only, and consider a retry budget. Jitter stops all clients retrying in the same instant. Timeout budget: if the gateway allows 3s, inner calls must total less. Pass the remaining deadline along when you can. Capacity follows Little's Law: concurrency = throughput × latency, so 100 requests per second at 200 ms needs about 20 concurrent slots, a sensible starting point for bulkhead size.

Rate limiting algorithms

AlgorithmIdeaCharacter
Fixed windowCount per minuteSimple; allows double bursts at a boundary
Sliding windowRolling log or weighted countersAccurate; more memory
Token bucketTokens refill at a fixed rate, one is spent per requestAllows bursts up to bucket size; common
Leaky bucketA queue drains at a fixed rateSmooth output; adds delay

Distributed Transactions

Why 2PC is usually avoided

Two-phase commit (2PC) has a coordinator. In prepare, each participant durably records its work, holds locks, and votes yes or no. In commit, if all voted yes, the coordinator tells all to commit; otherwise to abort. If the coordinator dies after prepare, participants are blocked, holding locks with no way to decide alone. It also requires all resources to support XA, which brokers and many cloud services do not, and it couples availability: the system is up only if all participants are.

Saga: orchestration vs choreography

ChoreographyOrchestration
ControlEach service reacts to eventsA central coordinator sends commands
CouplingLoose, but event chains are hiddenParticipants depend on the orchestrator only
VisibilityHard: no single view of progressState is stored in one place
Cycles and complexityGrows badly with stepsHandles branches, timeouts, retries
Best for2 to 4 simple stepsLonger business workflows
// A minimal orchestrator: state is persisted, so a crash can resume from it
public enum SagaState { STARTED, PAYMENT_DONE, STOCK_RESERVED, COMPLETED, COMPENSATING, FAILED }

@Service
class CheckoutSaga {
  @Transactional
  public void on(PaymentCaptured e) {
    Saga s = sagas.findByOrderId(e.orderId()).orElseThrow();
    if (s.getState() != SagaState.STARTED) return;      // duplicate delivery: ignore
    s.setState(SagaState.PAYMENT_DONE);
    outbox.publish(new ReserveStock(e.orderId(), s.getItems()));
  }

  @Transactional
  public void on(StockRejected e) {
    Saga s = sagas.findByOrderId(e.orderId()).orElseThrow();
    if (s.getState() != SagaState.PAYMENT_DONE) return;
    s.setState(SagaState.COMPENSATING);
    outbox.publish(new RefundPayment(e.orderId()));     // undo the earlier step
  }
}

Step types matter. Compensatable steps can be undone (reserve stock, charge a card). A pivot step is the point of no return. Retryable steps come after the pivot and must eventually succeed. Put steps that are easy to undo first and irreversible ones (sending an email, shipping) last.

A saga gives ACD without Isolation: others can see intermediate state. Countermeasures: semantic lock (status PENDING, so others know to wait or reject), commutative updates, re-reading a value before acting, and version checks. Compensation is a business action, not a rollback: a refund is a new transaction, and the customer may have seen the charge.

TCC (Try, Confirm, Cancel) is a related pattern: Try reserves a resource with a timeout, Confirm uses the reservation, and Cancel releases it. It suits reservations such as seats, and needs extra API endpoints.

Outbox and CDC

The dual-write problem: updating the database and publishing to a broker are two systems, with no shared transaction. A crash between them loses the event, or sends one for a change that rolled back. The outbox solves this by writing both to one database.

@Transactional
public Order place(PlaceOrder cmd) {
  Order o = orders.save(Order.from(cmd));
  outbox.save(new OutboxEvent(UUID.randomUUID(), "Order", o.getId().toString(),
                              "OrderPlaced", json(o)));    // same transaction
  return o;
}

// Polling relay, the simplest version. Safe with several instances thanks to SKIP LOCKED.
@Scheduled(fixedDelay = 500)
@Transactional
public void relay() {
  for (OutboxEvent e : outbox.lockNextBatch(100)) {     // ... order by id limit 100 for update skip locked
    kafka.send("orders", e.getAggregateId(), e.getPayload()).join();
    outbox.delete(e);
  }
}
Polling publisherLog-based CDC (Debezium)
MechanismQuery the outbox tableRead the database's WAL or binlog
LatencyPolling intervalLow
Load on DBRepeated queriesSmall
SetupCode onlyKafka Connect, log access
FailureDuplicate on crash after sendDuplicate on restart

Publishing raw table changes through CDC, with no outbox, makes your schema a public contract. The outbox lets you publish stable domain events. Debezium has an outbox event router for this purpose. The mirror on the consumer side is the inbox: record the message id in the same transaction as the side effect, as shown under idempotency below.

CQRS and Event Sourcing

The two ideas are independent and are often combined. CQRS says read and write have different shapes, so give them different models. The write side enforces rules on normalised tables. The read side serves denormalised views, perhaps in Elasticsearch or Redis, built from events. The cost is that reads lag behind writes, so the UI must cope, for example by returning the new data from the command response, or by waiting for a version.

Event sourcing stores events as the source of truth. The current state is a fold of events.

// Rebuild an account from its events
public static Account replay(List<AccountEvent> events) {
  Account a = new Account();
  for (AccountEvent e : events) a = a.apply(e);
  return a;
}

Account apply(AccountEvent e) {
  return switch (e) {
    case Deposited d -> withBalance(balance.add(d.amount()));
    case Withdrawn w -> withBalance(balance.subtract(w.amount()));
  };
}

// Append with an optimistic check: UNIQUE (aggregate_id, version) rejects concurrent writers
// insert into events (aggregate_id, version, type, payload) values (?, ?, ?, ?)

Practical concerns: snapshots avoid replaying millions of events. Event schemas evolve, and old events live forever, so use upcasters to read old versions. Deleting personal data under GDPR conflicts with an immutable log; a common answer is crypto-shredding: encrypt with a per-user key and delete the key. Use it where history is the domain (ledgers, audits), and not as a general default.

Idempotency and Consistency

An operation is idempotent if repeating it has the same effect as doing it once. Networks make this compulsory. A timeout does not tell the caller whether the work happened, so it retries. Retries, broker redelivery and double-clicks all produce duplicates.

// HTTP: client sends Idempotency-Key: 6f1c... with a POST
@Transactional
public PaymentResult charge(String key, ChargeRequest req) {
  var existing = idempotency.findById(key);
  if (existing.isPresent()) return existing.get().result();       // replay the stored answer
  // Unique PK on key: two racing requests cannot both insert
  idempotency.saveAndFlush(new IdempotencyRecord(key, hash(req)));
  PaymentResult r = gateway.charge(req, key);                      // pass the key downstream too
  idempotency.storeResult(key, r);
  return r;
}

// Consumer: dedupe table written with the business change
@Transactional
public void handle(OrderPlaced e) {
  int inserted = jdbc.update(
      "insert into processed_event(id) values (?) on conflict do nothing", e.eventId());
  if (inserted == 0) return;      // already done
  invoices.createFor(e);
}

Other ways to get idempotency: natural upserts, conditional updates (where status = 'PENDING'), and version checks. Verify that a repeated key has the same request hash, and return 422 if it differs. Keep records for longer than the longest retry window.

CAP and PACELC

CAP: when a network partition happens, a replicated system must choose between Consistency (every read sees the latest write, or errors) and Availability (every node answers). Partitions are not optional, so the theorem is not "pick any two". PACELC extends it: if Partition, A or C; Else, choose Latency or Consistency. It captures the everyday trade-off: waiting for replicas is slower.

SystemPACELC classMeaning
Single-leader relational DB, synchronous replicaPC/ECRefuses or stalls instead of serving wrong data
Cassandra, DynamoDB (default settings)PA/ELAlways answers, may be stale; tunable per request
Spanner, CockroachDBPC/ECStrong consistency with consensus, paying latency

Consistency is a spectrum: linearizable (acts like one copy), sequential, causal, read-your-writes, monotonic reads, eventual. Most microservice systems use eventual consistency between services and strong consistency inside one. With replicas, R + W > N gives overlapping quorums, so reads see the latest write.

Observability

Monitoring tells you that something broke; observability helps you find out why, without shipping new code. The three pillars answer different questions.

PillarQuestionStackWatch out for
MetricsIs it healthy? How much?Micrometer, Prometheus, GrafanaHigh-cardinality labels (user id) blow up storage
LogsWhat exactly happened here?JSON logs, ELK, Loki, SplunkPersonal data; volume and cost
TracesWhere did the time go across services?OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Jaeger, ZipkinSampling loses rare events

Useful metric sets. RED for services: Rate, Errors, Duration. USE for resources: Utilization, Saturation, Errors. The four golden signals: latency, traffic, errors, saturation. Use percentiles (p95, p99) rather than averages, which hide tail latency. Alert on SLOs (service level objectives), like "99.9% of requests under 300ms over 30 days". An error budget is the 0.1% you may spend on risk.

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for telemetry: APIs, SDKs, the OTLP protocol, and a Collector that receives, processes and forwards data. A trace is a tree of spans; each span has a name, a start and end, attributes, and a parent. Context travels in the W3C traceparent header across HTTP and in message headers across Kafka.

# Spring Boot 3: spring-boot-starter-actuator, micrometer-tracing-bridge-otel,
# opentelemetry-exporter-otlp. (Boot 4 also offers spring-boot-starter-opentelemetry.)
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 0.1              # default; 1.0 in dev
  otlp:
    tracing:
      endpoint: http://otel-collector:4318/v1/traces
  endpoints:
    web:
      exposure:
        include: health,info,prometheus
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs                  # JSON logs, Boot 3.4+
@Service
class PaymentService {
  private final ObservationRegistry registry;
  private final Counter failures;

  PaymentService(ObservationRegistry r, MeterRegistry m) {
    registry = r;
    failures = Counter.builder("payment.failures").tag("provider", "acme").register(m);
  }

  PaymentResult pay(Order o) {
    return Observation.createNotStarted("payment.charge", registry)
        .lowCardinalityKeyValue("currency", o.currency())     // a metric tag and a span attribute
        .observe(() -> gateway.charge(o));                    // one timer, one span, log correlation
  }
}

Sampling. Head sampling decides at the start of a trace, cheaply, but rare errors can be dropped. Tail sampling decides in the Collector after the trace is complete, so it can keep all errors and slow traces, at a higher cost.

Interview: trace context does not cross a thread pool or @Async on its own. Use a context-propagating executor. Without it the trace breaks and the MDC is empty.

Microservice Security in Depth

Three separate questions: who is the end user, which service is calling, and may they do this?

  • Edge: the gateway terminates TLS, runs the OAuth2 login or validates JWTs, removes spoofable headers, and rate limits.
  • User identity: each service is a resource server that also validates the token. Do not trust "it came from inside". TokenRelay filter in Spring Cloud Gateway forwards the user's token.
  • Service identity: mTLS (both sides present certificates) proves which workload is calling, and encrypts traffic. A service mesh automates certificate issue and rotation, typically with SPIFFE identities. The client-credentials grant gives a service its own token.
  • Authorization: coarse checks at the gateway (scope), and fine ones (does this user own this order?) in the service, where the data is.
  • Token scope: use audience claims, so a token for service A cannot be replayed on B. Token exchange (RFC 8693) narrows a token per hop.
  • Network: Kubernetes NetworkPolicies default-deny between namespaces. Only the gateway is exposed.
  • Secrets: Vault or a cloud secret manager, with rotation. Kubernetes Secrets are only base64 unless encryption at rest is enabled.
  • Supply chain: scan images and dependencies, sign images, run as non-root.
# Resource server: Spring Security reads the JWKS from the issuer to verify signatures
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri: https://keycloak.acme.com/realms/shop
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences: order-service

Docker for Java Services

A container is an isolated process that shares the host kernel, using namespaces and cgroups. An image is a stack of read-only layers, so layers that do not change are cached and shared. That is why dependencies should sit in a lower layer than your code.

# Multi-stage build: build tools stay out of the final image
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN ./mvnw -q -DskipTests package
RUN java -Djarmode=tools -jar target/app.jar extract --layers --destination /layers

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd -r app
USER app
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=build /layers/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /layers/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=build /layers/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=build /layers/application/ ./
ENV JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
  • The JVM is container-aware and reads cgroup limits. Use MaxRAMPercentage instead of a fixed -Xmx. The heap is not the whole process: metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers need the rest, or the kernel kills the container (exit code 137, OOMKilled).
  • Use the exec form of ENTRYPOINT, so Java is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM.
  • Alternatives without a Dockerfile: mvn spring-boot:build-image (Buildpacks) or Jib.
  • Docker Compose is for local multi-service runs. Boot's spring-boot-docker-compose can start them for you.

Kubernetes for Deployment

Kubernetes keeps actual state matching declared state: controllers constantly reconcile. You state "3 replicas of this image" and it replaces failed pods.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: order-service } }
  strategy:
    type: RollingUpdate
    rollingUpdate: { maxSurge: 1, maxUnavailable: 0 }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: order-service } }
    spec:
      terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 40
      containers:
        - name: app
          image: registry.acme.com/order-service:1.4.2     # never :latest
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          envFrom: [{ configMapRef: { name: order-config } }]
          resources:
            requests: { cpu: "500m", memory: "768Mi" }     # used for scheduling
            limits:   { memory: "768Mi" }                  # exceeding it gets the pod killed
          startupProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
            failureThreshold: 30
            periodSeconds: 5
          livenessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness, port: 8080 }
          readinessProbe:
            httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 }
          lifecycle:
            preStop: { sleep: { seconds: 5 } }             # let endpoints update first
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata: { name: order-service }
spec:
  selector: { app: order-service }
  ports: [{ port: 80, targetPort: 8080 }]
ObjectRole
PodSmallest unit: one or more containers sharing a network. Disposable
DeploymentManages ReplicaSets for stateless apps, rolling updates, rollback
StatefulSetStable identity and storage: databases, Kafka
ServiceStable virtual IP and DNS name. Types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer
Ingress / Gateway APIHTTP routing from outside
ConfigMap / SecretConfiguration as env vars or files
HPAScales replicas on CPU or custom metrics
PodDisruptionBudgetKeeps a minimum running during node maintenance
Job / CronJobRun to completion, or on a schedule
Namespace, NetworkPolicyIsolation and traffic rules
ProbeQuestionOn failureRule
StartupHas it finished booting?Restart after thresholdCovers slow JVM starts; other probes wait for it
LivenessIs the process wedged?Pod restartedDo not check the DB: a DB outage would restart all pods
ReadinessCan it take traffic now?Removed from the Service, not restartedMay check essential dependencies

Graceful shutdown: on deletion, Kubernetes removes the pod from endpoints and sends SIGTERM at about the same time, so traffic can still arrive briefly. A short preStop delay covers it. Boot then finishes in-flight requests (graceful shutdown is the default from Boot 3.4), up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase. Set terminationGracePeriodSeconds above that sum, or the pod is killed with SIGKILL.

Deployment Strategies Compared

StrategyHowRollbackCostRisk
RecreateStop old, start newRedeployLowestDowntime
RollingReplace pods graduallyRoll back; takes minutesSlight extra capacityTwo versions live together
Blue/greenFull copy ready, switch trafficInstant switch backDoubleShared DB needs compatibility; a big-bang user impact
Canary1%, 10%, 50%, 100% with metrics gatesFastSmallNeeds good metrics and traffic split (mesh, Argo Rollouts, Flagger)
ShadowMirror traffic to new, discard responsesNo effect on usersDouble loadSide effects must be disabled
Feature flagsDeploy dark, enable by codeToggleFlag debtSeparates deploy from release

Data: Database per Service and Caching

Database per service means a service's tables are private; other services use its API or events. It may be a separate schema with separate credentials on a shared server, as long as access is enforced. It enables independent schema changes and technology choice. The losses: cross-service joins, foreign keys, and ACID transactions.

NeedSolution
Show data from several servicesAPI composition in a BFF; beware fan-out latency
Search or report across themCQRS read model or data warehouse fed by events
Validate a referenceLocal replica from events, or a synchronous call
Consistent multi-service changeSaga
Global unique idsUUIDv7, or Snowflake-style ids (time + machine + sequence)

Caching patterns with Redis

PatternReadWriteTrade-off
Cache-asideApp checks cache, on miss loads DB and fillsApp writes DB, then deletes the keyMost common; first read is slow
Read-throughCache loads from DB itselfSimpler app code; needs a loader
Write-throughWrite to cache and DB synchronouslyFresh cache; slower writes
Write-behindWrite to cache, DB later in batchesFast; risk of data loss
@Cacheable(cacheNames = "product", key = "#id", sync = true)   // sync: one loader per key on this node
public ProductDto get(Long id) { return mapper.toDto(repo.findById(id).orElseThrow()); }

@CacheEvict(cacheNames = "product", key = "#cmd.id")
@Transactional
public void update(UpdateProduct cmd) { ... }

// Distributed lock: SET key token NX PX 10000. Release with a Lua check-and-delete:
// if redis.call('get', KEYS[1]) == ARGV[1] then return redis.call('del', KEYS[1]) else return 0 end
FailureMeaningDefence
Stampede (dogpile)A hot key expires and thousands of requests hit the DBSingle-flight lock, early refresh
AvalancheMany keys expire at once, or the cache diesTTL jitter, replicas, circuit breaker around the DB
PenetrationRequests for keys that do not exist always missCache "not found" briefly, Bloom filter
Hot keyOne key overloads one Redis nodeLocal near-cache, key splitting
Stale after writeDelete race with a concurrent reader refilling old dataShort TTL, delete after commit, versioned keys

Delete rather than update on write: two concurrent updates can write the cache in the opposite order to the DB. Evict after commit, or a reader may refill the old value before commit. A Redis lock is good for efficiency (avoiding duplicate work), not for safety, because a paused holder can outlive its lease. For safety, use a fencing token checked by the resource, or a database constraint. Redlock is debated for this reason.

Calling Other Services with the Right Token

A service calling another service has two choices: forward the user's token (the downstream service needs to know who the user is and apply their permissions) or use its own token from the client-credentials grant (background jobs, Kafka consumers, or calls where the user identity does not matter). Spring Security's OAuth2 client support fetches, caches and refreshes client-credentials tokens for you.

# application.yml: register the service as an OAuth2 client
spring.security.oauth2.client:
  registration.inventory:
    provider: keycloak
    client-id: order-service
    client-secret: ${INVENTORY_CLIENT_SECRET}
    authorization-grant-type: client_credentials
    scope: inventory.read
  provider.keycloak.issuer-uri: https://idp.example.com/realms/shop
@Bean
RestClient inventoryClient(RestClient.Builder b, OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
    var oauth = new OAuth2ClientHttpRequestInterceptor(manager);   // Spring Security 6.4+
    oauth.setClientRegistrationIdResolver(req -> "inventory");
    return b.baseUrl("http://inventory").requestInterceptor(oauth).build();
}

// Forwarding the current user's token instead (resource server side)
ClientHttpRequestInterceptor relayUserToken() {
    return (req, body, exec) -> {
        if (SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication() instanceof JwtAuthenticationToken jwt) {
            req.getHeaders().setBearerAuth(jwt.getToken().getTokenValue());
        }
        return exec.execute(req, body);
    };
}

Gotcha: the security context is thread-bound. In @Async methods, CompletableFuture pools or Kafka listeners there is no user token; wrap executors with DelegatingSecurityContextExecutor or use client credentials.

Interview Questions — Microservices

Monolith vs Microservices — pros and cons?
MonolithMicroservices
Simple to build, test and deploy at firstIndependent deployment and scaling of each service
One tech stackA different stack per service is possible
One failure can take down the whole appFault isolation
Gets slow to change as it growsDistributed complexity: network, consistency, tracing, DevOps cost

💡 Start with a well-modularized monolith and split it when team size or scaling actually needs it.

How do you decompose a system into microservices?

Split by business capability or DDD bounded context (Orders, Payments, Inventory). Aim for high cohesion and loose coupling, a database per service, and one owning team. For legacy systems, use the Strangler Fig pattern to carve services out gradually.

Synchronous vs asynchronous communication?

Sync (REST with Feign or WebClient, gRPC): simple request/response, but it creates temporal coupling and cascading failures. Async (Kafka, RabbitMQ events): decoupled, resilient, scalable, but eventually consistent and harder to debug. Use sync for queries that need an immediate answer and async for state changes and notifications.

What is service discovery?

Service instances are dynamic (they autoscale and their IPs change), so they register with a registry (Eureka, Consul). Client-side discovery: the client looks up instances and load-balances itself (Spring Cloud LoadBalancer + lb://order-service). Server-side discovery: a load balancer or Kubernetes Service does it, with DNS order-service.default.svc. In Kubernetes you usually don't need Eureka.

What does an API Gateway do?

It's the single entry point. It handles routing, authentication and token validation, rate limiting, SSL termination, CORS, request aggregation (BFF), and logging and metrics. Tools: Spring Cloud Gateway (reactive), Kong, NGINX, AWS API Gateway.

How is centralized configuration handled?

Spring Cloud Config Server backed by Git. Clients load it with spring.config.import=configserver: and refresh with @RefreshScope or Spring Cloud Bus. In Kubernetes, use ConfigMaps and Secrets, or Vault for secrets.

Explain fault-tolerance patterns.
  • Circuit breaker: stop calling a failing service and return a fallback.
  • Retry with exponential backoff and jitter (only for idempotent calls).
  • Timeout: always set connect and read timeouts.
  • Bulkhead: isolate thread pools so one slow dependency can't use them all up.
  • Rate limiter.
@CircuitBreaker(name = "payment", fallbackMethod = "payFallback")
@Retry(name = "payment")
public PaymentResponse pay(Order o) { return paymentClient.pay(o); }
public PaymentResponse payFallback(Order o, Throwable t) { return PaymentResponse.pending(); }
How do you handle distributed transactions?

Avoid 2PC/XA: it's slow and blocking. Use the Saga pattern: a sequence of local transactions, each publishing an event, with compensating actions when something fails. Choreography means services react to each other's events (decentralized). Orchestration means a central orchestrator directs the steps (Camunda, Temporal, a custom orchestrator). Combine it with the Transactional Outbox pattern so the DB write and the event publish are atomic.

What is the Outbox pattern?

In the same DB transaction as the business change, write the event to an outbox table. A relay process (a poller or Debezium CDC) reads the outbox and publishes to Kafka. This avoids the "DB committed but the message was lost" dual-write problem. Consumers must be idempotent because delivery is at-least-once.

What are CQRS and Event Sourcing?

CQRS: separate write models (commands) from read models (queries), each optimized and scaled independently, with read views often built from events. Event Sourcing: store the sequence of events instead of the current state, and rebuild state by replaying them. You get a full audit trail and time travel, at the cost of more complexity.

Database per service — how to query across services?

Use API composition (an aggregator or BFF calls several services), CQRS read models (materialized views built from events), or data replication through events. Never share a DB between services, because that couples their schemas.

How do you do distributed tracing and logging?

A trace id (one per request across all services) plus a span id per hop, propagated in headers (W3C traceparent). In Boot 3, use Micrometer Tracing with a Brave or OpenTelemetry bridge, exported to Zipkin, Jaeger or Tempo. Write logs as JSON with the traceId in MDC, and centralize them in ELK, Splunk or Loki.

How do you secure microservices?

Do authentication at the gateway with OAuth2/OIDC (Keycloak). Pass the JWT downstream, and have each service validate it as a resource server. For service-to-service calls, use the client-credentials grant or mTLS (a service mesh like Istio). Keep secrets in Vault or Kubernetes Secrets. Apply zero trust.

Docker & Kubernetes basics for microservices?

Docker: package each service as an image (a Dockerfile, or mvn spring-boot:build-image). Kubernetes objects: Pod, Deployment (replicas, rolling updates), Service (stable DNS and load balancing), Ingress, ConfigMap/Secret, HPA (autoscaling), and liveness/readiness probes, which map to Actuator /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness.

What is the 12-factor app?

Codebase · Dependencies · Config in the environment · Backing services as attached resources · Build/release/run · Stateless processes · Port binding · Concurrency · Disposability · Dev/prod parity · Logs as event streams · Admin processes.

Feign client example?
@FeignClient(name = "inventory-service")      // resolved via discovery / LB
public interface InventoryClient {
  @GetMapping("/api/stock/{sku}")
  StockDto stock(@PathVariable String sku);
}
// enable with @EnableFeignClients
Deployment strategies?

Rolling (the Kubernetes default) · Blue-Green (switch traffic between two full environments) · Canary (send a small percentage of traffic first) · feature flags. All of them need backward-compatible APIs and DB migrations (expand → migrate → contract).

When should you NOT use microservices?

When the team is small, the domain is still being discovered (boundaries will move), there is no automation for deployment and monitoring, or the load is uniform. A modular monolith gives clean boundaries without network failures, and you can extract a module later with evidence. Common valid reasons to split are: team autonomy at scale, very different scaling or compliance needs, or a component with a separate release cycle. "Everyone does it" is not a reason.

How big should a microservice be?

Lines of code is the wrong measure. A service should cover one bounded context, be owned by one team (two-pizza size), be deployable alone, and be able to do its core work with few sync calls. Signs that it is too small: every feature touches several services, or chatty calls. Too big: several teams collide in it, or parts have very different load.

Choreography or orchestration for a 6-step order flow with timeouts?

Orchestration. Six steps with compensations and timeouts need one place that holds the state and answers "where is order 123?". Event chains would hide this across six services, and a change in order needs edits in several. Use a workflow engine (Temporal, Camunda) or a persisted state machine, with the engine owning retries and timers. Participants remain simple command handlers and must be idempotent. Keep the orchestrator free of business logic other than sequencing.

What happens if a compensation fails?

Compensations must be retryable and idempotent: keep retrying with backoff from a persisted state, since the system cannot roll back the rollback. After a retry limit, move the saga to a FAILED state with an alert and a human process (a refund queue). Design so compensations cannot fail for business reasons: a refund should not depend on the order still being valid. Record each step so operators can see and repair.

Outbox: why not publish to Kafka first, then write the DB? Or use @TransactionalEventListener?

Publishing first can emit an event for a change that then rolls back. Using @TransactionalEventListener(AFTER_COMMIT) avoids that, but a crash between commit and publish loses the event: the listener's work is only in memory. The outbox makes the intent durable in the same commit. Kafka transactions do not span your database, and XA is rarely available. The accepted cost is at-least-once delivery, so consumers deduplicate. Also, event order per aggregate must be preserved: key messages by aggregate id, and relay sequentially.

What is CDC, and how does Debezium work?

Change Data Capture reads committed changes from the database's transaction log (MySQL binlog, PostgreSQL WAL through logical replication) and emits them as events. Debezium runs as a Kafka Connect source connector. It does an initial snapshot, then tails the log, storing its position in Kafka offsets so it can resume. It misses nothing that committed, needs no triggers, and adds little load. Watch out: an idle connector on PostgreSQL makes the replication slot retain WAL, filling the disk, so monitor slots.

Explain exactly-once in microservices.

Exactly-once delivery over an unreliable network is impossible in the general case, as a sender cannot know if a lost ack means lost work. What you build is at-least-once delivery + idempotent processing = effectively once. Kafka transactions give exactly-once within Kafka, but side effects such as emails and payments need your own dedupe. If an interviewer pushes, describe the failure point: crash after the side effect and before the ack.

Which HTTP methods are idempotent, and how do you make POST safe?

By definition GET, HEAD, PUT, DELETE and OPTIONS are idempotent; POST and PATCH are not. "Idempotent" concerns server state, not the response: a second DELETE may return 404 but changes nothing more. Make POST safe with a client-generated Idempotency-Key, stored with a unique constraint and the result. For retries at the gateway, only auto-retry idempotent methods by default.

What does the circuit breaker do differently from a retry, and how do they combine?

A retry assumes the fault is short and tries again. A breaker assumes that it is not and stops trying for a while. Combined, the retry goes outside: each attempt is recorded by the breaker, and once open, the retry gets CallNotPermittedException. Configure that as non-retryable, so it does not spin. Ignore 4xx business errors in both, since they will not recover and do not mean the service is unhealthy.

Fallback method is not called. Why might that be?
  • The signature must match the original parameters plus one trailing exception parameter, and the same return type.
  • Self-invocation bypasses the Spring AOP proxy, so annotations on inner calls do nothing.
  • Fallback selection picks the method with the most specific exception type, so another overload may have been chosen.
  • The Spring AOP starter or the Resilience4j Spring Boot starter is missing, so no aspect runs.
Thread pool bulkhead vs semaphore bulkhead?

A semaphore limits concurrent calls on the caller's thread: cheap, but it cannot abandon a blocked call. A thread pool runs calls on a separate pool: stronger isolation and timeouts can abandon waiting, at the cost of context switches and context propagation. With virtual threads, threads stop being the scarce resource, but downstream capacity still is, so semaphores remain the natural limiter.

One downstream service is slow, and now your whole system is timing out. Walk through it.

Diagnose: traces show where the time went; thread and pool metrics show saturation; find the first service whose latency rose. Stop the bleeding: shed load, open the breaker manually, disable the feature with a flag, scale, or roll back. Prevent: shorter timeouts, bulkhead per dependency, a breaker that counts slow calls, fallback, and moving non-critical calls to async. Set load shedding, so a busy service returns 503 quickly instead of queueing until everyone times out.

How does an event-driven system handle ordering and duplicates?

Order: partition by aggregate id, so one aggregate's events stay in sequence, and avoid expecting order across aggregates. Include a version or sequence number so a consumer can detect gaps and ignore old events: apply only if event.version > stored.version. Duplicates: dedupe by event id. Late events: decide per case whether to buffer, drop, or use last-write-wins. A retry topic can reorder events; for keys needing strict order, block the partition or park all later events for that key.

How do you version APIs and events without breaking consumers?

Follow tolerant reader: ignore unknown fields. Make only additive changes: new optional fields, never renames or type changes. For a breaking change, add /v2 or a new event type, run both, track who uses old ones, then retire it. For events, use Schema Registry with compatibility rules. Consumer-driven contract tests (Pact, Spring Cloud Contract) fail the provider's build if it breaks a consumer's expectation, removing most need for end-to-end test suites.

How do you test microservices?
LayerPurposeTools
UnitLogicJUnit, Mockito
IntegrationReal DB and brokerTestcontainers
ComponentOne service, other services stubbedWireMock, MockMvc
ContractAPI compatibilityPact, Spring Cloud Contract
End-to-endA few critical flowsSmall suite only; slow and flaky
ResilienceBehaviour under failureChaos Monkey, Toxiproxy, load tests
Why not use a shared library for domain models across services?

A shared library of DTOs couples release cycles: one change forces all services to upgrade, and it brings back the coupling you split to avoid. Each context should have its own model, even when it duplicates fields. Sharing is fine for technical concerns such as logging and security starters, kept stable. For contracts, generate clients from OpenAPI or protobuf files.

What is a service mesh, and do you need one?

A mesh (Istio, Linkerd) puts a proxy beside each pod, or a node-level one, which handles mTLS, retries, timeouts, traffic split and metrics, with no code changes. A control plane configures them. It suits polyglot fleets of many services. For a few Spring services it adds latency, resources and operational burden, and libraries are simpler. Avoid doubling retries in both mesh and code.

How does Spring Cloud Gateway's RequestRateLimiter work?

It uses a token bucket in Redis, updated by a Lua script so the read-modify-write is atomic. replenishRate is tokens per second and burstCapacity is the bucket size. A KeyResolver chooses what is limited: user, API key, or IP. An exhausted bucket gets HTTP 429 with X-RateLimit-* headers. Decide what happens if Redis fails: failing open keeps traffic flowing but with no limit.

Why must liveness probes not depend on the database?

If the DB has a blip, every pod's liveness fails at once and Kubernetes restarts all of them. That turns a short database issue into a full outage, with a thundering herd of JVM starts and connection storms hitting the recovering DB. Liveness should only say "this process is stuck and a restart would help". Readiness may reflect dependencies, because it merely stops traffic.

Why do Java pods get OOMKilled with a healthy heap?

The container limit covers the whole process: heap, metaspace, code cache, thread stacks, GC overhead and direct buffers. With MaxRAMPercentage=90 on a small limit, the non-heap part overflows, and the kernel kills it (exit 137) without any Java exception. Keep 25 to 30% for non-heap, use Native Memory Tracking (-XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary) to measure, and set memory request equal to the limit for predictability. CPU limits cause a separate issue: throttling during GC and startup, seen as latency spikes.

How do you scale a Kubernetes service on queue lag instead of CPU?

CPU misses I/O-bound consumers, which can be idle while falling behind. Use KEDA, or HPA with custom metrics, based on Kafka consumer lag. Do not exceed the partition count, since extra consumers sit idle. Allow for rebalancing during scale-up, and add a stabilisation window so replicas do not flap.

How do you run a DB migration with blue/green or rolling deployments?

Old and new versions share the database during the rollout, and rollback must still work. So schema changes must be backward compatible: expand (add nullable), deploy code that handles both, backfill, then contract in a later release. Run migrations as a separate job or init step, and avoid long table locks (use online schema tools, or concurrent index builds). Never combine a destructive change with the release that stops using the data.

Canary shows no errors but revenue fell. What did you miss?

Canary gates usually watch technical signals (5xx, latency). Add business metrics: checkout conversion, payment success rate. A 1% canary may also lack enough traffic for rare flows, or may not include some regions. Sticky assignment keeps a user on one version across requests. Use a longer soak, or A/B analysis for subtle effects.

Cache-aside: why delete the key after a DB write, not before?

If you delete first, a concurrent reader misses, reads the old row, and refills the cache with old data before your write lands. If you delete after commit, the window shrinks: a reader must have read old data just before your commit and written it just after your delete. A TTL bounds that remaining risk. For a stricter approach, drive eviction from CDC events or use versioned keys.

How do you make distributed locks safe?

First ask if you need one. A unique constraint, conditional update, or a single Kafka partition consumer often suffices. If you do, use a lease with a TTL and a random owner token, and release only if the token matches. A process pause (GC) can outlive the lease, so two holders can exist. Fix with a fencing token: a rising number issued with the lock, and the resource rejects older tokens. For strong guarantees use a consensus system (etcd, ZooKeeper), or a database row lock.

What are SLI, SLO and SLA?

An SLI is a measured indicator, such as the percentage of requests under 300ms. An SLO is an internal target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is a contract with penalties, and should be looser than the SLO. 99.9% allows about 43 minutes of downtime per 30 days. When the error budget runs out, teams slow feature work and fix reliability. For a chain of dependent services availability multiplies: three services at 99.9% give about 99.7%.

A request is slow only sometimes. How do you find out why?

Look at p99, not the average. Filter traces by duration and compare slow with fast ones to see which span grows. Exemplars link a metric spike to specific traces. Group by instance (one bad pod or node), by endpoint, and by tenant or payload size. Common causes: GC pauses, pool waits, a cold cache, retries (the trace shows repeats), a lock, or noisy neighbours. Ensure sampling keeps slow traces.

Design: an e-commerce checkout across Order, Payment and Inventory.
  1. Entry: POST /orders with an idempotency key, through the gateway. Order service writes status PENDING and an outbox event in one transaction, then returns 202 with the order id.
  2. Saga: an orchestrator drives reserve stock (with expiry), then capture payment (the pivot), then confirm.
  3. Failures: payment declined releases stock and cancels. A saga timeout cancels and compensates. A payment timeout needs a status query to the provider, never a blind retry. Use the key at the provider.
  4. Order of steps: reserving before charging means rare, cheap compensation.
  5. Reads: the client polls or gets a WebSocket update; a read model serves "my orders".
  6. Non-critical: emails and analytics consume events and cannot block checkout.
  7. Observability: trace id through events, saga state dashboard, alerts on stuck sagas.
Design: flash sale for 10,000 items and 1 million users.

Protect the core: CDN for static pages, a gateway rate limit, and a queue or token system at the door. Pre-load stock into Redis and decrement with an atomic Lua script, so only winners go further. Publish reservations to Kafka and let order service consume at a rate the DB can take; the client polls for status. Reservations expire and return stock. Prevent oversell with a DB guard: update ... where qty >= :n, or a CHECK constraint. Stop bots and duplicates with a per-user limit in Redis. Pre-scale before the sale, as autoscaling reacts too slowly, and load test in advance.

Design: a notification service for email, SMS and push.

Other services publish domain events. The service consumes them, looks up templates and preferences, and writes a notification row. Separate topics or queues per channel and priority, so a marketing blast cannot delay password resets. Per-provider workers use rate limiters, retries with backoff, a DLT, and provider failover through a circuit breaker. Dedupe with (user, event, channel). Track status from provider webhooks. Respect quiet hours and unsubscribes.

A customer was charged twice. How could it happen and how do you prevent it?

Likely path: the payment call timed out after the provider had processed it, then the client, gateway or a retry layer sent it again; or a message was redelivered after a crash before commit; or the user double-clicked. Prevent with a stable idempotency key per payment attempt, generated once and stored before calling, and passed to the provider. Disable automatic retries on non-idempotent POSTs. Apply dedupe at the consumer. Reconcile daily against provider reports, because every money system needs a detective control as well as a preventive one.

You must split a large shared database owned by a monolith. What is the sequence?
  1. Map tables to contexts, finding which code reads and writes each.
  2. Stop cross-module access inside the monolith first: replace joins with calls through a module API.
  3. Move tables to a separate schema with separate credentials while still in one process.
  4. Extract the service, with the monolith calling it.
  5. Copy data with CDC, verify counts and checksums, cut over writes, then remove old tables.

Decide who is the source of truth at each stage, and keep exactly one writer per table. Dual writes without an outbox will drift.

How do you do multi-region deployments?

Active-passive is simpler: one region serves writes, and another is a warm standby with async replication, so failover risks some data loss (RPO) and takes time (RTO). Active-active reduces latency and offers better availability, but concurrent writes conflict. Avoid conflicts by giving each user a home region, or use consensus databases at higher write latency, or CRDTs and last-write-wins for tolerant data. Keep clocks out of correctness logic, and test failover regularly.

What is the sidecar pattern, and what other deployment patterns matter?

A sidecar is a helper container in the same pod that adds a cross-cutting feature, such as a mesh proxy or log forwarder. An ambassador proxies outbound calls. An adapter normalises output, such as metrics. An init container runs setup before the app starts, for example waiting for a dependency.

Is Eureka still needed on Kubernetes? What about Config Server?

Usually not. Services and DNS replace Eureka, and ConfigMaps and Secrets replace most of Config Server. Keep Spring Cloud parts if you run outside Kubernetes too, need client-side balancing logic, or need Git-backed, audited config with dynamic refresh. Avoid running two discovery systems at once, since they can disagree.

Long synchronous chains: A calls B calls C calls D. How would you fix the design?

Availability multiplies and latency adds, and each hop needs its own timeout. Options: replicate the needed data locally from events, so A does not need C at request time; merge services that are always called together; convert the flow to async with a 202 and later status; or have one aggregator call them in parallel rather than as a chain. Ask if the data has to be fresh to the millisecond, since often it does not.

What is Conway's Law and why does it matter for microservices?

Conway's Law says a system's structure mirrors the communication structure of the organization that builds it. If three teams share one service, it becomes a coordination bottleneck; if one team owns ten tightly coupled services, they behave like a monolith with network calls. The inverse Conway manoeuvre shapes teams around the bounded contexts you want, each team owning its services end to end (code, database, deployment, on-call). In interviews, tie service boundaries to both the domain and team ownership, not to technical layers.

How do you recognize a distributed monolith, and how do you fix it?

Symptoms: services must be released together; a change to one feature touches many repositories; services share a database or a domain-model library; long synchronous call chains where one slow service takes everything down; and an end-to-end test environment that is the only place anything can be verified. Fixes: redraw boundaries around business capabilities and merge services that always change together; give each its own data; replace synchronous chains with events and local copies of the data each service needs; version contracts with consumer-driven contract tests so services deploy independently. Sometimes the right answer is a modular monolith.

The UI saves an order, then immediately reloads the list from a read model, and the new order is missing. How do you handle read-your-writes with eventual consistency?

The command side committed, but the projection or replica has not caught up. Options:

  • Return the created resource (or its id and version) from the command and show it directly, merging it into the list on the client (optimistic UI).
  • Have the read side expose the last applied version or offset; the client passes the version it expects and the query waits briefly or falls back to the source of truth.
  • Route reads for a user who just wrote to the primary or owning service for a short window.
  • Push updates to the client via WebSocket or SSE when the projection is updated.
Tell the product owner where data can be briefly stale; not every screen needs strong consistency.

Two services update the same customer, and events arrive out of order. Why not just compare timestamps?

Clocks on different machines drift, NTP can move them backward, and two events can share a millisecond, so "last timestamp wins" silently loses updates. Use a value that the owner of the data increments: an aggregate version or sequence number. Consumers store the last version applied per entity and ignore events with a lower or equal version (or park them if a gap appears). Kafka keying by entity id keeps one entity's events in order within a partition. Where multiple writers are unavoidable, consider logical clocks or a merge rule specific to the domain.

WebFlux or Spring MVC with virtual threads for a new microservice?

With Java 21+ and spring.threads.virtual.enabled=true, Spring MVC handles large numbers of concurrent blocking calls (JDBC, RestClient) with simple imperative code, readable stack traces and normal ThreadLocal-based tooling, which fits most CRUD and integration services. WebFlux still makes sense for streaming (SSE, WebSocket fan-out), backpressure-aware pipelines, or an already reactive stack (R2DBC, reactive gateway). Either way the real limit becomes downstream capacity: connection pools, rate limits and bulkheads still matter.

A Kafka consumer in your service calls another service that requires a JWT. Which token do you use?

There is no user request on a consumer thread, so there is no user token to relay, and storing users' tokens in events is a bad idea because they expire and leak. Use the service's own client-credentials token with a narrow scope. If the downstream decision depends on the user, put the user id (and tenant) in the event and let the downstream service authorize on that, trusting the calling service through its service identity (scope, audience or mTLS).

Apache Kafka Event Streaming

A distributed, partitioned, replicated commit log for high-throughput event streaming.

// Spring Kafka
@Service
public class OrderEvents {
  private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreated> kafka;
  public void publish(OrderCreated e) {
    kafka.send("orders", e.orderId(), e);          // key = orderId → ordering per order
  }
}

@KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing", concurrency = "3")
public void onOrder(OrderCreated e, Acknowledgment ack) {
  billingService.process(e);                        // make idempotent!
  ack.acknowledge();                                // manual commit after success
}

# application.yml
spring.kafka:
  bootstrap-servers: localhost:9092
  producer: { acks: all, properties: { enable.idempotence: true } }
  consumer: { group-id: billing, auto-offset-reset: earliest, enable-auto-commit: false }
  listener: { ack-mode: manual }

Cluster Roles and the Path of a Message

Kafka looks like a message queue but is built as a distributed log. A log is an append-only file: writes go to the end, and readers keep their own position. Most of Kafka's behaviour follows from that one design choice: reading does not delete anything, so many consumers can read independently and replay history.

RoleJob
BrokerStores partition replicas and serves produce and fetch requests
ControllerManages metadata: topics, leaders, ISR, broker liveness. In KRaft mode, a quorum of controllers
Partition leaderThe replica that takes all writes (and, by default, reads) for one partition
FollowerA replica that fetches from the leader, exactly like a consumer does
Group coordinatorA broker that manages one consumer group and its committed offsets
Transaction coordinatorA broker that manages transaction state for a producer
  1. The client connects to any address in bootstrap.servers and fetches metadata: which broker leads each partition. Those are only entry points; list a few so startup survives one being down.
  2. The producer serialises the record, picks a partition, and batches it.
  3. The batch goes straight to the partition's leader.
  4. The leader appends to its log. Followers fetch it and append to theirs.
  5. Once all in-sync replicas have it, the high watermark advances and the leader acknowledges (with acks=all).
  6. Consumers fetch from the leader, up to the high watermark, and commit their positions.
Gotcha: clients connect to the addresses brokers advertise in metadata. A wrong advertised.listeners gives the classic symptom in Docker: bootstrap works, then the client tries to reach an internal hostname and fails.

Replication: ISR, Leader and High Watermark

Each partition has a replication factor (RF) of copies, on different brokers (and racks, if broker.rack is set). The ISR (in-sync replica set) is the leader plus followers that have caught up within replica.lag.time.max.ms (default 30 seconds). A follower that falls behind leaves the ISR, and rejoins once it has caught up. It is lag in time that counts, rather than in message count.

When a leader dies, the controller picks a new leader from the ISR, and all its acknowledged data is there by definition. Records above the high watermark may be truncated on replicas after the new leader takes over; they were never acknowledged with acks=all, so the producer will retry them. Leader epochs, a number that goes up with each new leader, let replicas find exactly where their log diverged, which avoids silent data loss in edge cases.

RF / min.insync.replicas / acksBrokers downResult
3 / 2 / all0 or 1Writes work. No acknowledged data lost. Recommended
3 / 2 / all2Writes fail with NotEnoughReplicas; reads of existing data continue
3 / 1 / all (default min ISR)2Writes work with a single copy; if that disk dies, data is gone
3 / 3 / all1Writes stop. One node's maintenance halts the topic
2 / 2 / all1Writes stop. So RF=2 gives either weak durability or weak availability
3 / any / 1LeaderRecords acknowledged by the leader alone can be lost

unclean.leader.election.enable=false (the default) means that if all ISR members are gone, the partition stays offline rather than electing an out-of-sync replica, which would lose data. Set it to true only where availability beats accuracy, such as a metrics topic. Followers can also serve consumers, through replica.selector.class and the client's client.rack (follower fetching), which reduces cross-zone traffic.

KRaft vs ZooKeeper

Older Kafka stored metadata in a separate ZooKeeper ensemble, with one broker acting as controller. Metadata lived in two systems, a failover meant reloading all state into the new controller, and partition counts were limited. KRaft (Kafka Raft) puts metadata into Kafka itself, as a replicated log: the internal __cluster_metadata topic, which a quorum of controllers replicates with a Raft-based protocol.

ZooKeeper modeKRaft mode
Systems to operateKafka + ZooKeeperKafka only
Metadata storeZnodesAn event log, with snapshots
FailoverNew controller reloads stateStandby controllers already have it, so failover is fast
Metadata updatesController pushes RPCsBrokers fetch the log incrementally
StatusRemoved in Kafka 4.0Production-ready since 3.3; the only mode from 4.0

A node's role is set with process.roles=broker, controller, or both (combined mode, for dev only). Run 3 or 5 controllers: a quorum needs a majority, so 3 tolerate 1 failure and 5 tolerate 2. Migrating a ZooKeeper cluster must happen on a 3.x bridge release before moving to 4.x.

Log Storage: Segments, Retention and Compaction

On disk, a partition is a directory, and the log is split into segments. Only the newest, the active segment, takes writes. Splitting matters because deletion and compaction work on whole closed segments, so deleting old data is removing a file, not rewriting one.

Setting (topic-level)Broker defaultMeaning
segment.bytes1 GiBRoll a new segment at this size
segment.ms7 daysOr after this long, even if not full
retention.ms7 daysDelete closed segments whose newest record is older. -1 keeps forever
retention.bytes-1 (no limit)Size limit per partition, not per topic
cleanup.policydeletedelete, compact, or both
min.cleanable.dirty.ratio0.5Compaction starts when this share of the log is uncompacted
delete.retention.ms1 dayHow long tombstones stay visible

Retention is not exact. An expired record lives on until its whole segment expires, and the active segment is never deleted. On a quiet topic, data lives until segment.ms rolls the segment and retention passes on top of that. To delete data quickly, set segment.ms low too.

Log compaction mechanism

A compacted topic keeps at least the latest record for each key. Background cleaner threads copy closed segments, skipping any record whose key appears again later. Offsets do not change, so the log simply has gaps. Order is preserved. The newest records in the active segment are not compacted, so duplicates may exist until cleaning runs. A compacted topic is therefore "at least the last value", not "exactly one per key". A record with a null value is a tombstone, which deletes the key after delete.retention.ms; consumers that have been away for longer than that may miss the deletion.

__consumer_offsets is itself a compacted topic. So are Kafka Streams changelogs and Kafka Connect's config topics. Tiered storage (production-ready since Kafka 3.9) moves old closed segments to object storage such as S3, which allows long retention without large broker disks.

Producer Internals

ConfigDefaultEffect
acksall (since 3.0)Durability, see the question below
enable.idempotencetrue (since 3.0)No duplicates from retries
batch.size16 KBMax bytes per batch, per partition
linger.ms5 (0 before Kafka 4.0)How long to wait for a batch to fill
compression.typenonegzip, snappy, lz4, zstd; applied per batch
buffer.memory32 MBTotal buffer. When full, send() blocks
max.block.ms60 sMax block in send(), then TimeoutException
delivery.timeout.ms120 sOverall limit for a record, retries included
request.timeout.ms30 sLimit for one request
retriesInteger.MAX_VALUEEffectively limited by delivery.timeout.ms
max.in.flight.requests.per.connection5Unacknowledged requests per broker
max.request.size1 MBMust fit broker message.max.bytes

Batching is a throughput lever. A larger batch means fewer requests and a better compression ratio, at the cost of some latency. linger.ms controls that trade-off. A batch stays compressed through the broker and is decompressed by the consumer, so compression saves network and disk, end to end.

Partitioning

  • Explicit partition in the ProducerRecord: used as given.
  • Key present: murmur2(keyBytes) % numPartitions. The same key maps to the same partition as long as the count is unchanged.
  • No key: a sticky partitioner fills one batch for a partition, then moves on, which gives bigger batches than round robin. Since 3.3, this is built into the default behaviour and is adaptive: it sends less to slower brokers.
  • Custom Partitioner class for special routing.

Hot partitions arise from skewed keys: one big customer sends half the traffic to one partition, and adding partitions does not help. Use a composite key if per-entity order allows it.

Idempotent producer

Without idempotence, an ack lost on the way back causes a retry and a duplicate. With it, the broker gives each producer a producer id (PID), and the producer numbers each batch per partition. The broker tracks the last sequences for each PID and partition, and it discards a repeat, returning success. A gap raises an error, so order is protected even with 5 in-flight requests and retries. This covers one producer session only: after a restart without a transactional.id, a new PID means that no deduplication against earlier sends is possible.

Transactions

Transactions make writes across multiple partitions, plus the consumer offset commit, all succeed or all fail. This is what makes consume-transform-produce exactly-once.

  1. initTransactions(): finds the transaction coordinator using transactional.id, and receives a PID and an epoch. A higher epoch fences an older zombie instance with the same id, so its writes are rejected.
  2. beginTransaction(), then send(): the coordinator records each partition touched in __transaction_state.
  3. sendOffsetsToTransaction(): includes the consumer's offsets.
  4. commitTransaction(): the coordinator writes PREPARE_COMMIT, then places a control marker into each partition, then writes COMPLETE. That is a two-phase commit inside Kafka.
  5. A read_committed consumer reads only up to the last stable offset (LSO), the point before the first open transaction, and skips aborted records. An open transaction therefore delays consumers, up to transaction.timeout.ms (default 60 s).
producer.initTransactions();
while (running) {
  ConsumerRecords<String, Order> records = consumer.poll(Duration.ofMillis(500));
  if (records.isEmpty()) continue;
  producer.beginTransaction();
  try {
    for (var r : records) producer.send(new ProducerRecord<>("invoices", r.key(), toInvoice(r.value())));
    producer.sendOffsetsToTransaction(nextOffsets(records), consumer.groupMetadata());
    producer.commitTransaction();
  } catch (ProducerFencedException e) {
    producer.close();                   // a newer instance took over: stop
    throw e;
  } catch (KafkaException e) {
    producer.abortTransaction();
    rewindTo(consumer, records);        // seek back and reprocess
  }
}

Consumer Groups and Rebalancing

A consumer is a poll loop: it calls poll(), processes what it receives, commits, and repeats. The KafkaConsumer is not thread-safe (the producer is). Two liveness signals exist: a background thread sends heartbeats, within session.timeout.ms (default 45 s), which detects a crashed process. And the poll loop must call poll() within max.poll.interval.ms (default 5 minutes), which detects stuck processing. Exceed the second and the consumer leaves the group even though it is alive, so its partitions move, and its later commit fails with CommitFailedException.

Consumer configDefaultMeaning
group.idnoneGroup membership
auto.offset.resetlatestWhere to begin with no valid committed offset: earliest, latest, none
enable.auto.committrueCommit in the background every auto.commit.interval.ms (5 s). Spring Kafka sets it false by default
max.poll.records500Max records returned per poll
fetch.min.bytes1Broker waits for this much data
fetch.max.wait.ms500...or for this long
isolation.levelread_uncommittedread_committed hides aborted and open transactions
heartbeat.interval.ms3 sKeep at about a third of the session timeout

The rebalance protocol

In the classic protocol, a member sends JoinGroup to the coordinator. One member is the group leader, and it computes the assignment on the client side with the configured assignor. It then sends the plan in SyncGroup, and each member receives its partitions. Each rebalance has a generation number, and commits from an old generation are rejected, which prevents zombie writes.

AssignorBehaviourRebalance type
RangeAssignorPer topic, ranges of partitions. Co-partitioned topics align, which suits joins. Uneven across many topicsEager
RoundRobinAssignorEven across all partitionsEager
StickyAssignorEven, and moves as few as possibleEager
CooperativeStickyAssignorSame, but only the moved partitions stopIncremental

In an eager rebalance everyone gives up all partitions, so the whole group stops. In a cooperative rebalance, members keep what they retain, and a second round moves the rest. The default partition.assignment.strategy is [RangeAssignor, CooperativeStickyAssignor], which uses range but allows a rolling upgrade to cooperative.

New consumer protocol (KIP-848): generally available in Kafka 4.0, enabled on clients with group.protocol=consumer. The broker computes assignments, and reconciliation is incremental, with no global stop. It speeds up rebalances in large groups. The default on clients remains classic.

Static membership: set group.instance.id to a stable name, such as the pod name. A restart within the session timeout does not cause a rebalance, as the member returns to its old partitions. This is valuable for rolling deploys and stateful consumers.

Offsets

A committed offset means "the next offset to read" for a group and partition, stored in the compacted __consumer_offsets topic (50 partitions by default). Commits for a group with no active members expire after offsets.retention.minutes (7 days). A long outage can thus reset a group to auto.offset.reset.

# Inspect and reset. The group must be inactive to reset.
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server k:9092 --group billing --describe
kafka-consumer-groups.sh --bootstrap-server k:9092 --group billing --topic orders \
  --reset-offsets --to-datetime 2026-11-01T00:00:00.000 --execute

# Create and describe a topic
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server k:9092 --create --topic orders \
  --partitions 12 --replication-factor 3 --config min.insync.replicas=2
kafka-topics.sh --bootstrap-server k:9092 --describe --topic orders

Delivery Semantics, Ordering and Retries in Depth

Delivery has three links, and each can fail: producer to broker, broker durability, broker to consumer. The guarantee of the whole is that of the weakest link.

FailureWhat happensProtection
Ack lost, producer retriesDuplicate in logIdempotent producer
send() callback ignoredLost record, unnoticedCheck the future; alert on failures
Leader dies with acks=1Lost recordacks=all, min.insync.replicas=2
Consumer crash after processing, before commitReprocessedIdempotent handler
Commit before processing, then crashSkippedCommit after processing
App crash with records in the producer bufferLostFlush on shutdown, or wait for ack before commit

Kafka's exactly-once only covers Kafka: read from a topic, write to a topic, commit offsets, atomically. A database or HTTP write is not part of the transaction. For those, use at-least-once plus an idempotent write, or store the offset in the same database transaction as the result, and seek() to it at startup.

Retry strategies on the consumer

ApproachBehaviourTrade-off
Blocking retry (DefaultErrorHandler)Re-seeks and retries the record in place, with backoffKeeps order; blocks the partition
Non-blocking (@RetryableTopic)Moves the record to retry topics with delay; the main partition continuesGood throughput; breaks order for that key
Dead letter topicAfter final failure, park it with error headersNeeds monitoring and a replay tool
Parking per keyOn failure, store later records for that key until repairedKeeps order per key; more code

Split errors into two types. Transient (a timeout, a database down): retry, and if a dependency is down, pause the listener. Permanent (bad data, a failed validation): retrying is pointless, so send straight to the DLT. A DLT that no one reads is data loss with extra steps, so alert on it and have a way to replay.

Spring Kafka in Depth

@Configuration
class KafkaConfig {
  @Bean
  NewTopic ordersTopic() {                // created at startup if absent, by KafkaAdmin
    return TopicBuilder.name("orders").partitions(12).replicas(3)
        .config(TopicConfig.MIN_IN_SYNC_REPLICAS_CONFIG, "2").build();
  }

  @Bean
  DefaultErrorHandler errorHandler(KafkaTemplate<Object, Object> template) {
    var recoverer = new DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer(template);   // sends to orders.DLT, same partition
    var backOff = new ExponentialBackOffWithMaxRetries(4);
    backOff.setInitialInterval(1_000);
    backOff.setMultiplier(2.0);
    var handler = new DefaultErrorHandler(recoverer, backOff);
    handler.addNotRetryableExceptions(ValidationException.class);  // straight to the DLT
    return handler;                       // Boot wires a single CommonErrorHandler bean into the factory
  }
}

@Service
class OrderPublisher {
  private final KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreated> kafka;
  OrderPublisher(KafkaTemplate<String, OrderCreated> kafka) { this.kafka = kafka; }

  public CompletableFuture<SendResult<String, OrderCreated>> publish(OrderCreated e) {
    var record = new ProducerRecord<>("orders", e.orderId(), e);
    record.headers().add("event-type", "OrderCreated".getBytes(StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
    return kafka.send(record).whenComplete((res, ex) -> {          // CompletableFuture since 3.0
      if (ex != null) log.error("publish failed for {}", e.orderId(), ex);
      else log.debug("sent to {}", res.getRecordMetadata());
    });
  }
}

@Component
class OrderListener {
  @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "billing", concurrency = "3")
  public void onOrder(ConsumerRecord<String, OrderCreated> rec) {
    billing.process(rec.value());                                  // exception goes to the error handler
  }

  @KafkaListener(topics = "orders.DLT", groupId = "billing-dlt")
  public void onDead(ConsumerRecord<String, OrderCreated> rec) {
    Header reason = rec.headers().lastHeader(KafkaHeaders.DLT_EXCEPTION_MESSAGE);
    alerts.raise(rec.value(), new String(reason.value(), StandardCharsets.UTF_8));
  }
}

// Non-blocking retries: Spring creates the retry topics and a -dlt topic (3.x syntax)
@RetryableTopic(attempts = "4", backoff = @Backoff(delay = 1000, multiplier = 2))
@KafkaListener(topics = "payments", groupId = "ledger")
public void onPayment(Payment p) { ledger.post(p); }

@DltHandler
public void paymentDlt(Payment p) { log.error("dead payment {}", p.id()); }

// Batch listener
@KafkaListener(topics = "metrics", batch = "true")
public void onBatch(List<Metric> batch) { repo.saveAll(batch); }
spring:
  kafka:
    bootstrap-servers: k1:9092,k2:9092,k3:9092
    producer:
      key-serializer: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringSerializer
      value-serializer: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroSerializer
      properties: { linger.ms: 20, compression.type: zstd }
    consumer:
      group-id: billing
      auto-offset-reset: earliest
      # Bad bytes would otherwise fail inside poll(), in an endless loop:
      key-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      value-deserializer: org.springframework.kafka.support.serializer.ErrorHandlingDeserializer
      properties:
        spring.deserializer.key.delegate.class: org.apache.kafka.common.serialization.StringDeserializer
        spring.deserializer.value.delegate.class: io.confluent.kafka.serializers.KafkaAvroDeserializer
    listener:
      ack-mode: record
      concurrency: 3
AckModeCommits when
BATCH (default)All records from a poll were processed
RECORDEach record; safest and slowest
TIME / COUNT / COUNT_TIMEBy time, by count, or both
MANUALYour ack.acknowledge(); queued and committed with the batch
MANUAL_IMMEDIATEYour ack; commits at once

concurrency = "3" creates three consumers in the same group, each with its own thread and Kafka consumer. The real parallelism is min(concurrency × instances, partitions). DefaultErrorHandler with no custom backoff retries 9 times with no delay (10 attempts in all), then logs and skips. Keep total retry time below max.poll.interval.ms; the handler seeks and re-polls between attempts for this reason. For tests use @EmbeddedKafka or Testcontainers.

Schema Registry and Message Evolution

Producers and consumers deploy separately and logs retain old data, so schemas need rules. Schema Registry is a separate service that stores versioned Avro, Protobuf or JSON schemas per subject (by default <topic>-value). A serializer registers or looks up the schema and prefixes each message with a magic byte and a 4-byte schema id, so the payload does not repeat field names.

CompatibilityGuaranteeAllowedUpgrade first
BACKWARD (default)New schema reads old dataDelete fields; add optional fieldsConsumers
FORWARDOld schema reads new dataAdd fields; delete optional fieldsProducers
FULLBothAdd or delete optional fields onlyEither
*_TRANSITIVEAgainst all earlier versions, not only the lastSame, stricterSame
NONENo checkAnythingRisky
{ "type": "record", "name": "OrderCreated", "namespace": "com.acme",
  "fields": [
    { "name": "orderId", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "total",   "type": { "type": "bytes", "logicalType": "decimal", "precision": 12, "scale": 2 } },
    { "name": "coupon",  "type": ["null", "string"], "default": null }   // optional: union + default
  ] }

Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect

Kafka Streams is a library, not a cluster: your app contains the processing, and scales by starting more instances, which share the work through a consumer group. A KStream is a stream of events. A KTable is a changelog view: the latest value per key. State lives in local RocksDB stores, backed up to compacted changelog topics so a moved task can rebuild it. Set processing.guarantee=exactly_once_v2 for EOS.

StreamsBuilder b = new StreamsBuilder();
KStream<String, Order> orders = b.stream("orders");

orders.filter((id, o) -> o.total().signum() > 0)
      .groupBy((id, o) -> o.customerId())
      .windowedBy(TimeWindows.ofSizeWithNoGrace(Duration.ofMinutes(5)))
      .count(Materialized.as("orders-per-customer"))
      .toStream()
      .map((win, n) -> KeyValue.pair(win.key(), n))
      .to("customer-order-counts");

Key concepts: event time vs processing time, windows (tumbling, hopping, session), grace periods for late events, and co-partitioning for joins: both inputs need the same partition count and key. A change of key triggers a repartition topic. Alternatives are Apache Flink, for large stateful jobs, and ksqlDB.

Kafka Connect moves data with configuration rather than code. Workers run connectors, split into tasks. Source connectors read into Kafka; sink connectors write out. In distributed mode, workers form a group and rebalance tasks. Single Message Transforms (SMTs) do light per-record changes. Converters handle formats, and a DLQ can be set for sink errors.

POST /connectors
{ "name": "orders-cdc",
  "config": {
    "connector.class": "io.debezium.connector.postgresql.PostgresConnector",
    "database.hostname": "db", "database.port": "5432",
    "database.user": "cdc", "database.password": "${file:/secrets/db.properties:password}",
    "database.dbname": "shop", "topic.prefix": "shop",
    "table.include.list": "public.outbox" } }

Why Kafka Is Fast

  • Sequential I/O: appending to a log avoids disk seeks. Sequential disk throughput is far higher than random disk throughput.
  • Page cache: Kafka writes into the OS page cache and leaves flushing to the OS, instead of fsyncing each message. Durability comes from replication, not fsync. Recent data is served from memory; a large part of RAM should be left to the OS, not the JVM heap. A cold consumer reading old data pushes that cache around, which can hurt tail latency for others.
  • Zero-copy: Java's FileChannel.transferTo uses the OS sendfile call to move bytes from page cache to socket with no copy through user space. It works because the on-disk format equals the wire format. TLS disables it, as bytes must be encrypted in the JVM.
  • Batching and compression at every step: producer, broker and consumer all work on batches.
  • Simple broker: no per-message tracking, as consumers hold their own position, so many consumers cost little.
  • Partitioning: parallelism scales out with brokers.

Tuning by goal

GoalProducerConsumerTopic and broker
ThroughputLarger batch.size, linger.ms 10 to 100, lz4 or zstdHigher fetch.min.bytes, batch listenersMore partitions
LatencyLow linger.msfetch.min.bytes=1Fewer partitions per broker, fast disks
Durabilityacks=all, idempotenceCommit after processingRF 3, min ISR 2, unclean election off
Availabilityacks=1 if loss is acceptableStatic membership, cooperative rebalancingRF 3, min ISR 1 or 2, rack awareness

Sizing a Cluster

A worked example: 50,000 messages per second at 2 KB each, kept for 7 days, RF 3.

  • Ingress: 50,000 × 2 KB = 100 MB/s. After compression at about 2:1 this is 50 MB/s.
  • Disk: 50 MB/s × 604,800 s ≈ 30 TB per copy, × 3 = 91 TB, plus about 35% headroom: roughly 120 TB.
  • Network: inbound 50 MB/s, replication out 100 MB/s, consumers (3 groups) 150 MB/s: about 300 MB/s in total across the cluster.
