  • Brokers: with 20 TB usable disk per broker, 6 or 7 brokers. Leave room for one to fail without saturating disks or network.
  • Partitions: max(target throughput / per-producer rate, target / per-consumer rate). If one consumer handles 5 MB/s of decompressed work, 100 MB/s needs 20 partitions. Round up, leaving room for growth: 24 to 30.
  • Memory: broker heap around 4 to 6 GB; the rest goes to page cache.

Monitor: UnderReplicatedPartitions and UnderMinIsrPartitionCount (should be 0), OfflinePartitionsCount (0), ActiveControllerCount (exactly 1), request latency, disk use, and consumer lag per group.

Security: TLS for encryption, SASL (SCRAM, OAUTHBEARER, GSSAPI) or mTLS for authentication, and ACLs (per principal, per topic or group) for authorization.

Kafka vs RabbitMQ in Depth

AspectKafkaRabbitMQ
Core modelPartitioned log; "dumb broker, smart consumer"Exchanges route to queues; "smart broker, dumb consumer"
After consumptionStays until retentionRemoved after ack (RabbitMQ Streams add log-style queues)
ReplayBuilt inNot with classic or quorum queues
RoutingTopic and key; logic is in consumersDirect, topic, fanout, headers exchanges
Per-message featuresNone natively: no TTL per message, priority, or delayTTL, priority, dead-letter exchanges, delayed delivery plugin
Ack granularityOffset per partition (share groups add per-record acks)Per message, with redelivery
Scale of consumersLimited by partitions in classic groupsCompeting consumers, any number
ThroughputVery high, disk-based retentionHigh, lower than Kafka; best with short queues
FitsEvent streams, CDC, analytics, event sourcingTask queues, RPC, complex routing

Queues for Kafka (KIP-932): share groups let several consumers read the same partition, each acknowledging records individually, with delivery counts. This removes the "one consumer per partition" limit for task-queue workloads. It arrived as early access in Kafka 4.0 and was declared production-ready in 4.2. Ordering per partition is not preserved in a share group.

Testing Kafka Code

  • Unit tests: keep listener methods thin and test the handler they call with plain JUnit. For Kafka Streams topologies use TopologyTestDriver, which runs without a broker.
  • @EmbeddedKafka (spring-kafka-test): an in-JVM broker, fast to start, good for Spring wiring tests. It is not your production broker version or configuration.
  • Testcontainers with @ServiceConnection (Boot 3.1+): a real Kafka (KRaft) container, closer to production, and the place to test serializers, Schema Registry, transactions and error handling.
  • Consumption is asynchronous, so assert with Awaitility instead of Thread.sleep. Use unique topic or group names per test, set auto.offset.reset=earliest in tests, and test the failure paths too: a poison message should end up in the DLT.
@SpringBootTest
@Testcontainers
class OrderEventsIT {

    @Container @ServiceConnection
    static KafkaContainer kafka = new KafkaContainer("apache/kafka-native:3.8.0");

    @Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, OrderPlaced> template;
    @Autowired ShipmentRepository shipments;

    @Test
    void createsShipmentForOrder() {
        template.send("orders", "o-1", new OrderPlaced("o-1", BigDecimal.TEN));

        await().atMost(Duration.ofSeconds(10))
               .untilAsserted(() -> assertThat(shipments.findByOrderId("o-1")).isPresent());
    }

    @Test
    void poisonMessageGoesToDlt(@Autowired KafkaTemplate<String, String> raw) {
        raw.send("orders", "bad", "{not json");
        // consume from "orders-dlt" (or "orders.DLT" with DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer) and assert it arrived
    }
}

Tracing and Observability with Spring Kafka

Kafka breaks the HTTP call chain, so trace context must travel in record headers. With Micrometer Tracing on the classpath, enable observation on both sides: the template writes a W3C traceparent header and the listener container continues the trace, so one trace shows the HTTP request, the produce, and the consume with its database work.

spring.kafka.template.observation-enabled=true
spring.kafka.listener.observation-enabled=true
management.tracing.sampling.probability=0.1
  • Producer metrics to watch: record-error-rate, request-latency-avg, buffer-available-bytes (near zero means send() will block).
  • Consumer metrics: lag per partition (records-lag-max), time since last poll, rebalance rate, and listener processing time from the observation timer.
  • Add business ids (order id) to logs via MDC inside the listener, and alert on DLT topics receiving anything.

Interview Questions — Kafka

What is Kafka? Core terms?

A distributed event streaming platform. Topic: a named stream of events. Partition: an ordered, append-only log and the unit of parallelism. Offset: a record's position in a partition. Broker: a server. Producer/Consumer. Consumer group: a set of consumers sharing the work. Replication factor: number of copies of each partition. Leader/follower, ISR (in-sync replicas). Cluster metadata is managed by KRaft; ZooKeeper is gone as of Kafka 4.0.

Kafka vs RabbitMQ?
KafkaRabbitMQ
A log: messages are retained (by time or size) and can be replayedA queue: messages are removed once acknowledged
Very high throughput, streaming, event sourcingComplex routing (exchanges), per-message priority, RPC
Consumers pull and track their own offsetsThe broker pushes to consumers
Ordered per partitionOrdered per queue
How does Kafka guarantee ordering?

Only within a partition. Send related events with the same key (e.g. orderId) so they land in the same partition. To keep that order under retries, enable idempotence (enable.idempotence=true, which permits max.in.flight ≤ 5).

Delivery semantics: at-most-once, at-least-once, exactly-once?
  • At-most-once: commit the offset before processing. Messages can be lost.
  • At-least-once (most common): process, then commit. Messages can be duplicated, so make consumers idempotent (a dedupe table or upserts).
  • Exactly-once: idempotent producer + transactions (transactional.id) + isolation.level=read_committed. Only end-to-end within Kafka (consume-transform-produce).
What does acks=0/1/all mean?

acks=0: don't wait at all (fastest, can lose data). acks=1: wait for the leader only (lost if the leader dies before replicating). acks=all: wait for all ISRs, combined with min.insync.replicas=2 (the most durable; the default since Kafka 3.0).

What is consumer rebalancing?

When consumers join or leave or partitions change, the group coordinator reassigns partitions. During an eager rebalance consumption pauses. Cooperative (incremental) rebalancing, static membership (group.instance.id), and keeping max.poll.interval.ms larger than your processing time all reduce the disruption. Partitions can't be shared within a group, so consumers beyond the partition count sit idle.

What is consumer lag? How to handle slow consumers?

Lag is the latest offset minus the committed offset. Monitor it with Burrow, Prometheus or kafka-consumer-groups.sh --describe. Fixes: add partitions and consumers, increase concurrency, batch processing, tune max.poll.records, do heavy work asynchronously.

How do you handle failed messages (poison pills)?

Use Spring Kafka's DefaultErrorHandler with a FixedBackOff or ExponentialBackOff and send failures to a Dead Letter Topic through DeadLetterPublishingRecoverer, or use @RetryableTopic for non-blocking retry topics. Use ErrorHandlingDeserializer for bad payloads.

Retention and log compaction?

retention.ms / retention.bytes delete old segments. cleanup.policy=compact keeps only the latest value per key, which suits changelogs and state such as a user's latest profile. A null value (tombstone) deletes the key.

How many partitions should a topic have?

Base it on the target throughput divided by per-consumer throughput, plus room to grow. More partitions mean more parallelism, but also more file handles and longer leader elections. You can increase partitions but never decrease them, and increasing them changes where keys map.

What are Kafka Streams and Kafka Connect?

Kafka Streams: a Java library for stateful stream processing (map, filter, join, windowed aggregations, KTable). Kafka Connect: a framework for moving data in and out (source and sink connectors: JDBC, Debezium CDC, Elasticsearch, S3) without writing code. Schema Registry: Avro or Protobuf schemas with compatibility rules.

A topic has 3 partitions. A group has 4 consumers. What happens? What about 2 consumers?

With 4 consumers, three get one partition each, and the fourth is idle (a hot standby). With 2, one gets two partitions and the other one. Within a group, one partition goes to one consumer in the classic protocol. A second group with any size receives all messages independently.

RangeAssignor with 2 topics of 3 partitions each and 2 consumers. How many partitions does each get?

Range works per topic. For each topic, C1 gets 2 and C2 gets 1, as sorted order favours C1 both times. So C1 has 4, and C2 has 2. With many topics this skew grows. Round-robin or sticky gives 3 and 3. Range remains useful when you need partition N of two topics on one consumer, for joins.

RF=3, min.insync.replicas=2, acks=all. Two brokers die. What about reads and writes?

Partitions that have a live replica which was in the ISR stay readable through the survivor, which becomes leader if needed. Producers get NotEnoughReplicasException, as the ISR is 1 and fewer than 2. That is deliberate: it prefers refusing writes to accepting ones with only one copy. If the survivor was not in the ISR, the partition is offline unless unclean election is on.

A new consumer group joins an existing topic with default settings, and reads nothing. Why?

auto.offset.reset defaults to latest, so with no committed offset, it starts at the end and sees new messages only. Set earliest to read history. This setting applies only when there is no valid committed offset. Changing it on a running group does nothing. Also note the trap: if offsets expire or a retention delete passes the committed offset, a reset occurs, either skipping data (latest) or reprocessing (earliest).

What happens with auto-commit if the consumer crashes?

Auto-commit runs inside poll(), committing the offsets returned by the previous poll, on an interval. So in a simple synchronous loop it is at-least-once: a crash reprocesses the records since the last commit. But if you hand records to another thread, a commit may run before they finish, and a crash loses them. That is why async processing needs manual commits.

Consumers keep rebalancing, and the same messages are processed repeatedly. Why?

Classic cause: processing a batch takes longer than max.poll.interval.ms. The consumer is kicked out, its commit fails with CommitFailedException, its partitions are reassigned, and the new owner starts again from the last commit, repeating the cycle. Fix: reduce max.poll.records, raise the interval, speed up the handler, or commit per record. Other causes: GC pauses over the session timeout, frequent pod restarts (use static membership), or a retry loop inside the listener.

session.timeout.ms vs max.poll.interval.ms vs heartbeat.interval.ms?

Heartbeats run on a background thread, and tell the coordinator the process is alive; if none arrive within session.timeout.ms the member is removed. max.poll.interval.ms measures gaps between poll() calls, and detects a live process whose processing is stuck. The separation lets a slow handler run for minutes without failing liveness, while crashes are detected in seconds.

Does max.in.flight=5 risk reordering?

With idempotence off and retries on, yes: batch 1 fails, batch 2 succeeds, and batch 1's retry lands after it. The old fix was max.in.flight=1, at a throughput cost. With idempotence on, sequence numbers let the broker reject out-of-order batches, so the client retries in order, and order holds for up to 5 in flight. Setting a value above 5 with idempotence enabled is a config error.

Is send() synchronous? How do you know a record was written?

It is asynchronous: it serialises, buffers, and returns a future. It may still block, up to max.block.ms, for metadata or buffer space, which can stall a web thread when the cluster is down. Check the result through whenComplete or .get(timeout). A fire-and-forget kafka.send() in Spring silently drops failures. Calling .get() per message kills batching, so call flush() or collect futures instead.

What is the relationship between linger.ms, batch.size and delivery.timeout.ms?

A batch is sent when it reaches batch.size or has waited linger.ms, whichever comes first. It is also sent sooner if buffer memory is under pressure. delivery.timeout.ms covers the entire time from send() to final result: lingering, queuing, retries, and in-flight time. It must be at least linger.ms + request.timeout.ms. After it passes, the callback receives a timeout, and the outcome is unknown: the record may have been written.

How does adding partitions affect a running system?

It triggers a rebalance. New keys may hash to different partitions, so per-key order breaks across the change: old events for key K are in partition 2, and new ones in partition 7, read concurrently. Compacted topics and Streams state also rely on stable partitioning. If order matters, drain and move to a new topic, or over-provision at the start. Partitions cannot be reduced. To reduce, create a new topic and migrate.

How would you preserve ordering with parallel processing in one consumer?

Spring concurrency keeps order per partition, since each partition has one thread. If you need more parallelism than partitions, hash each record's key to one of N single-threaded workers, so one key always maps to one worker. Commit only offsets for which all earlier records are finished, tracking them per partition, and pause fetching when queues fill. Confluent's Parallel Consumer library implements this.

What does a poison pill do without ErrorHandlingDeserializer?

The failure occurs inside poll() before the listener sees the record. The container cannot move past it, so the consumer fails repeatedly on the same offset, flooding logs, while the partition stops. ErrorHandlingDeserializer catches the failure and passes the error to the handler, which can route the raw bytes to a DLT. The DLT publisher needs a byte array serializer to send the original unchanged.

DefaultErrorHandler vs @RetryableTopic: when do you pick each?

Use the blocking handler when order per key matters, or when retries are short. A long outage holds the partition, which is sometimes what you want: a failing dependency will fail all messages anyway. Use @RetryableTopic when records are independent and one bad record should not hold up the rest. It requires extra topics, and is at odds with batch listeners and transactions. A retry-topic consumer must wait until a record's delay has passed, and does so by pausing its partitions.

Does Kafka exactly-once include my database write?

No. Transactions cover Kafka partitions and offset commits only. In a listener that writes to a database and then commits, a crash between them repeats the record. Choices: an idempotent write keyed on a business id or (topic, partition, offset); storing the offset in the same DB transaction and seeking on start; or the outbox on the producing side. In Spring, a transaction-synchronised listener can commit the DB first, then Kafka, which narrows but does not remove the window, so dedupe is still required.

What is a zombie producer, and how is it fenced?

An instance that paused (long GC, partition) and was replaced, then resumes and writes. Both believe they are active, so an exactly-once pipeline would duplicate work. With a stable transactional.id, each initTransactions() increases the epoch. The broker rejects lower epochs with ProducerFencedException. For consumers, the generation in offset commits gives similar protection. In Spring, transaction-id-prefix builds ids per producer.

Consumer lag keeps growing. Walk through it.
  1. Is it all partitions or just one? One suggests a hot key or a poison record.
  2. Is producer rate up, or consumer rate down? Compare records-consumed-rate with incoming rate.
  3. Are there rebalances? Stop-the-world cycles look like lag.
  4. Is downstream (DB, API) slow? Time the handler. Most lag is a slow dependency.
  5. Fix: batch writes, scale consumers up to the partition count, and add partitions only if already at that limit.
  6. Recovery: temporarily add consumers. If the data is stale and disposable, skip forward with an offset reset.
Lag is measured as 0, but the data is old. How can that be?

Offset lag compares offsets, not time. A producer may be delayed: outbox stuck, CDC stopped, or stuck in linger or buffers. Under read_committed, an open transaction holds the LSO, so a consumer reads nothing new. Measure end-to-end latency by comparing a record's timestamp with processing time, not just offset lag.

Offsets in a compacted or transactional topic: why can't you assume offset + 1 is the next record?

Compaction leaves gaps, as removed records keep their offset numbers unused. Transactional topics hold control markers that occupy offsets and are never delivered. So do not compute lag as a record count and do not require contiguous offsets. Always commit lastProcessed.offset() + 1 as the next position, and let the consumer jump gaps.

Can Kafka lose acknowledged messages?

With RF 3, min ISR 2, acks=all, and unclean election off, loss needs all ISR copies to fail before the data is on disk. Since Kafka does not fsync each message, a simultaneous power loss of all ISR nodes could lose recent data, which is why replicas belong in different racks or zones. Risky setups lose data more easily: acks=1, min ISR 1 (the default), and unclean election. Loss is also caused by retention deleting unread data, or by ignored send failures.

What is the maximum message size, and how should you handle large payloads?

The default is about 1 MB. Changing it means raising producer max.request.size, broker or topic message.max.bytes, replica.fetch.max.bytes, and consumer fetch limits. Large messages hurt memory and throughput. The usual pattern is the claim check: put the file in object storage, and publish a reference. Compression helps with repetitive payloads.

How do you delete a single user's data from Kafka for GDPR?

You cannot edit a log. On a compacted topic keyed by user, write a tombstone. On a retained topic, keep retention short enough to satisfy the deadline, or use crypto-shredding: encrypt sensitive fields with a per-user key held elsewhere, and delete the key to make the data unreadable. Best of all, keep personal data out of events and send a reference.

How do you implement delayed messages in Kafka?

Kafka has no native per-message delay. Common approaches: tiered delay topics (delay-1m, delay-1h), where a consumer pauses until each record is due; a database scheduler that publishes when the time arrives; or Spring's retry topics for retries. If delays are core to the workload, a broker with delay support or a scheduler service may be a better fit.

How do you replicate across data centres?

MirrorMaker 2, built on Connect, copies topics, configs and consumer offsets between clusters, with topic names prefixed by the source. It is asynchronous, so failover may lose recent records, and offsets differ between clusters, requiring offset translation. For zero data loss across nearby zones, use a stretch cluster with synchronous replication, at a latency cost. Active-active needs loop prevention and conflict handling.

What is the difference between a Kafka Streams KStream, KTable and GlobalKTable?

A KStream treats every record as an independent event: two records for a key both count. A KTable treats a later record as an update to the key, partitioned across instances. A GlobalKTable holds the full table on each instance, which allows lookups by a non-partition key without repartitioning, and suits small reference data. Stream-table join enriches each event with the current table value.

Kafka Streams vs Flink vs a plain @KafkaListener?

Use a plain listener for per-record work and side effects. Use Kafka Streams for joins, windows and aggregations in a Java service, with Kafka as both source and sink. Use Flink when jobs need their own cluster, complex event time handling, multiple sources, or very large state. Streams needs no new infrastructure, but its state must be restored when tasks move, so use num.standby.replicas to shorten that.

BACKWARD compatibility: can you add a required field? Which side deploys first?

No: a new reader needs a value for old records, so a new field must have a default. Deleting a field is allowed. Consumers upgrade first, since they can then read both old and new data. Registry rejects incompatible schemas when a producer tries to register them, ideally checked in CI using the Maven plugin rather than at runtime.

Why was enable.auto.commit=false not enough to make my consumer safe?

That only moves commits to Spring. With AckMode BATCH, a poll's records commit together after all succeed. With an error handler that recovers (skips) a record after retries, its offset is committed, so anything other than a DLT means loss. Calling ack.acknowledge() in a finally block, or catching all exceptions in the listener, silently acknowledges failures. Handing work to an executor and returning acknowledges work that is not done. Safety comes from commit after a durable result.

Why is Kafka fast if it writes everything to disk?

Writes land in the page cache and are appended sequentially, so "writing to disk" does not mean a synchronous seek per message. Reads of recent data are served from memory. Batching lowers per-message overhead, compression reduces bytes, and zero-copy avoids copying between kernel and user space. The broker keeps no per-consumer per-message state. See the performance section above for detail.

How would you design an order event pipeline for 100,000 events per second?
  1. Topic design: orders.v1, keyed by order id, 48 or more partitions, RF 3, min ISR 2, with Avro and registry.
  2. Producers: outbox or CDC for correctness, lz4 or zstd, linger.ms 10 to 50.
  3. Consumers: separate groups by purpose (billing, search, analytics), idempotent, batch writes.
  4. Failures: retry, DLT, replay tool, alerts on lag and DLT rate.
  5. Evolution: compatibility set to BACKWARD or FULL, contract checks in CI.
  6. Capacity: compute disk, network and partitions as in the sizing section, then load test.
  7. Downstream: tiered storage or a sink to S3 for long-term analytics.
When should you NOT use Kafka?

When volume is small and a database table or RabbitMQ would do, because Kafka adds real operational cost. For low-latency request/reply, per-message priority or delay, or complex broker-side routing. For queries: it is not a database, and keyed lookups need a store built from the stream. For many small topics or very large payloads, too.

Spring for Apache Kafka or Spring Cloud Stream?

Spring for Apache Kafka (KafkaTemplate, @KafkaListener) exposes Kafka directly: partitions, offsets, transactions, error handlers, seeking. Spring Cloud Stream is a higher-level binder abstraction: you write Supplier/Function/Consumer beans and bind them to destinations in configuration, and the same code can run on Kafka or RabbitMQ. It is quick for simple pipelines but hides Kafka-specific behaviour and adds another layer of configuration to debug. Most teams that are committed to Kafka use Spring Kafka directly.

Can you do request-reply over Kafka?

Yes, with ReplyingKafkaTemplate: it sends a record with REPLY_TOPIC and CORRELATION_ID headers and returns a future that completes when a reply with that correlation id arrives; the server side is a @KafkaListener with @SendTo. Each requesting instance needs its own reply partition or topic (or must filter by correlation id), and you must set timeouts. It is usually a smell: if the caller waits synchronously, HTTP or gRPC is simpler. Use it when the work must go through Kafka anyway, for example for buffering or audit.

How do you connect a Spring Boot app to a secured Kafka cluster?

Set the security protocol and SASL mechanism, with credentials from a secret store, not the repository:

spring.kafka.bootstrap-servers=broker1:9093,broker2:9093
spring.kafka.security.protocol=SASL_SSL
spring.kafka.properties.sasl.mechanism=SCRAM-SHA-512
spring.kafka.properties.sasl.jaas.config=org.apache.kafka.common.security.scram.ScramLoginModule required username="${KAFKA_USER}" password="${KAFKA_PASSWORD}";
spring.kafka.ssl.trust-store-location=file:/etc/kafka/truststore.p12

Managed services often use OAUTHBEARER or IAM-based mechanisms instead. The principal also needs ACLs: WRITE on topics it produces to, READ on topics and its consumer group, and IDEMPOTENT_WRITE/transactional id permissions where used.

What do you put in record headers vs the payload?

The payload holds the business event. Headers hold metadata needed to route or process it without deserializing: event type and schema version, a unique event id for deduplication, correlation and trace ids (traceparent), source service, and tenant id. Spring Kafka uses headers for type information (__TypeId__), retry and DLT metadata (original topic, exception message). Do not put secrets or large data in headers, and treat them as part of the contract.

How do you document and standardize events so other teams can consume them?

Schemas (Avro, Protobuf or JSON Schema) in a Schema Registry define the payload and enforce compatibility. AsyncAPI is the event equivalent of OpenAPI: it describes channels (topics), messages, keys and headers, and can generate docs and code. CloudEvents is a CNCF spec for common event metadata (id, source, type, time, subject), with a Kafka binding that maps them to headers. Also document ownership, the partition key, ordering guarantees and retention for each topic.

Why can a test with @EmbeddedKafka pass while production fails?

The embedded broker usually runs one node with replication factor 1, default configs, and maybe a different version, so it cannot reveal problems with min.insync.replicas, ACLs, TLS, topic configs created by a platform team, message size limits, or Schema Registry compatibility. Tests often also auto-create topics that production forbids. Run integration tests against a Testcontainers broker configured like production, and keep a smoke test in a real staging cluster.

Angular Front-end

Components, data binding, DI, RxJS, routing, forms, change detection, signals, and performance.

// Standalone component with signals + new control flow (Angular 17+)
@Component({
  selector: 'app-user-list',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [CurrencyPipe, RouterLink],
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  template: `
    <input [value]="query()" (input)="query.set($any($event.target).value)" placeholder="Search">
    @if (loading()) { <p>Loading…</p> }
    @for (u of filtered(); track u.id) {
      <a [routerLink]="['/users', u.id]">{{ u.name }} – {{ u.salary | currency:'INR' }}</a>
    } @empty { <p>No users</p> }
  `
})
export class UserListComponent {
  private api = inject(UserService);
  query = signal('');
  users = toSignal(this.api.getUsers(), { initialValue: [] });
  loading = computed(() => this.users().length === 0);
  filtered = computed(() => this.users().filter(u => u.name.toLowerCase().includes(this.query().toLowerCase())));
}

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class UserService {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);
  getUsers() { return this.http.get<User[]>('/api/users').pipe(retry(2), catchError(() => of([]))); }
}

// Functional interceptor: attach JWT
export const authInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const token = inject(AuthService).token();
  return next(token ? req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }) : req);
};

// Routes with lazy loading + guard
export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: 'users', loadComponent: () => import('./users/user-list.component').then(m => m.UserListComponent) },
  { path: 'admin', canActivate: [() => inject(AuthService).isAdmin()], loadChildren: () => import('./admin/routes') },
  { path: '**', redirectTo: '' }
];

Which Angular feature arrived when

Angular releases a major version about every six months, and interviewers often probe whether you know the modern API. This table reflects the stable status of each feature.

FeatureIntroducedStable or default
Standalone componentsv14 previewStable v15; ng new generates them from v17; standalone: true is the implicit default from v19
signal, computedv16 previewStable v17
@if, @for, @switch, @deferv17 previewStable v18. *ngIf, *ngFor and *ngSwitch are deprecated from v20
input(), output(), model(), signal queriesv17.xStable v19
effect, linkedSignal, toSignal, toObservablev16 to v19Stable v20
Zoneless change detectionv18 experimental (provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection)Stable v20.2 as provideZonelessChangeDetection; default for new apps from v21
Full-app hydrationv16 previewStable v17. Incremental hydration stable v20
resource, rxResource, httpResourcev19 experimentalCheck your version: their API has changed across releases
Signal Formsv21 experimentalCheck your version

Architecture: how an Angular app starts

  1. main.ts calls bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig).
  2. Angular creates the root environment injector from appConfig.providers.
  3. It finds the root selector (such as app-root) in index.html and creates the root component and its view.
  4. Change detection renders the template. The router activates the initial route and fills <router-outlet>.
// main.ts
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, appConfig).catch(console.error);

// app.config.ts
export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [
    provideRouter(routes, withComponentInputBinding(), withPreloading(PreloadAllModules)),
    provideHttpClient(withFetch(), withInterceptors([authInterceptor, errorInterceptor])),
    provideZonelessChangeDetection(),     // v20.2+ (a default from v21)
    provideClientHydration(withEventReplay()),
  ],
};

Ivy is the compiler and runtime used since v9. The Angular compiler turns each template into TypeScript instructions, stored as a static ɵcmp definition on the class. It compiles each component on its own, which gives smaller bundles because unused parts are tree-shaken and rebuilds are faster.

Standalone components vs NgModules

NgModuleStandalone
Where dependencies are declaredIn the module (declarations, imports, exports); the component does not show themIn the component's own imports
Unit of lazy loadingModule (loadChildren)loadComponent, or a route array with loadChildren
Providersproviders, forRoot(), forChild()provideX() functions, route providers
Tree-shakingCoarser: a shared module pulls more inFiner: only what each component imports
StatusSupported, common in older codeRecommended for new code

The two interoperate. A standalone component can import an NgModule, and a module can import a standalone component. To migrate, run ng generate @angular/core:standalone. Keep third-party modules working with importProvidersFrom(SomeModule).

Components, templates and data binding in depth

@Component({
  selector: 'app-order-card',
  imports: [DatePipe, CurrencyPipe, HighlightDirective],
  changeDetection: ChangeDetectionStrategy.OnPush,
  encapsulation: ViewEncapsulation.Emulated,     // default
  host: { class: 'card', '[class.urgent]': 'urgent()', '(click)': 'select()' },
  templateUrl: './order-card.component.html',
  styleUrl: './order-card.component.css',
})
export class OrderCardComponent {
  order = input.required<Order>();
  urgent = input(false, { transform: booleanAttribute });   // <app-order-card urgent />
  selected = output<Order>();
  select() { this.selected.emit(this.order()); }
}
SyntaxBinds toExample
{{ expr }}Text, converted to string{{ user.name }}
[prop]DOM property or component input[disabled]="saving"
[attr.x]HTML attribute; use where no property exists[attr.aria-label]="label"
[class.x], [style.x]One class or style[style.width.px]="w"
(event)Event or output; $event holds the payload(keyup.enter)="save()"
[(x)]Sugar for [x] and (xChange)[(value)]="name"
#refTemplate variable<input #q /> {{ q.value }}
@let (v18.1+)Local read-only template variable@let total = price() * qty();

Template expressions are a safe subset of JS. There is no assignment in bindings, no new, and no window access. They should be fast and free of side effects, because they run on every check. In development, Angular evaluates them twice per check. If the value changed between the two, you get ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError.

View encapsulation: Emulated (default) adds unique attributes to scope CSS. ShadowDom uses a real shadow root. None makes the styles global.

Directives in depth

// Attribute directive with a signal input
@Directive({
  selector: '[appHighlight]',
  host: { '(mouseenter)': 'on(true)', '(mouseleave)': 'on(false)' },
})
export class HighlightDirective {
  color = input('yellow', { alias: 'appHighlight' });
  private el = inject(ElementRef<HTMLElement>);
  private r = inject(Renderer2);
  on(active: boolean) { this.r.setStyle(this.el.nativeElement, 'background', active ? this.color() : ''); }
}

// Structural directive: controls a template
@Directive({ selector: '[appHasRole]' })
export class HasRoleDirective {
  private tpl = inject(TemplateRef<unknown>);
  private vcr = inject(ViewContainerRef);
  private auth = inject(AuthService);
  appHasRole = input.required<string>();
  constructor() {
    effect(() => {
      this.vcr.clear();
      if (this.auth.roles().includes(this.appHasRole())) this.vcr.createEmbeddedView(this.tpl);
    });
  }
}
// <button *appHasRole="'ADMIN'">Delete</button> desugars to
// <ng-template [appHasRole]="'ADMIN'"><button>Delete</button></ng-template>

Directive composition (v15+) applies directives to a component through hostDirectives: [{ directive: Tooltip, inputs: ['text'] }], giving reuse without inheritance. Prefer the host metadata or Renderer2 over direct DOM access, since those also work under SSR.

Built-in control flow

@if (user(); as u) {
  <p>{{ u.name }}</p>
} @else if (loading()) {
  <app-spinner />
} @else {
  <p>Please log in</p>
}

@for (o of orders(); track o.id; let i = $index, last = $last) {
  <app-order-card [order]="o" [class.last]="last" />
} @empty {
  <p>No orders</p>
}

@switch (status()) {
  @case ('PAID') { <span>Paid</span> }
  @default { <span>Pending</span> }
}

@defer (on viewport; prefetch on idle) {
  <app-heavy-chart [data]="data()" />
} @placeholder (minimum 300ms) {
  <div>Chart preview</div>
} @loading (after 100ms; minimum 500ms) {
  <app-spinner />
} @error {
  <p>Could not load the chart</p>
}

@for variables are $index, $first, $last, $even, $odd, $count. track is mandatory, and it tells Angular which item is which so DOM nodes are moved rather than recreated. Use a stable id. track $index is only acceptable for static lists, because it reuses DOM nodes by position, so inputs and focus can stick to the wrong row after a reorder.

@defer triggerLoads when
on idle (default)The browser is idle
on viewportThe placeholder enters the viewport
on interaction, on hoverThe user interacts with or hovers over the placeholder
on immediate, on timer(2s)Straight after render, or after a delay
when cond()A condition becomes true, once

Components inside @defer must be standalone and not referenced elsewhere in the same file's class, or the compiler cannot move them to a separate chunk. On the server, deferred blocks render their @placeholder, unless incremental hydration is used.

Pipes

@Pipe({ name: 'truncate' })                      // pure by default
export class TruncatePipe implements PipeTransform {
  transform(value: string, max = 20, tail = '…'): string {
    return value.length > max ? value.slice(0, max) + tail : value;
  }
}
// {{ title | truncate:30 }}   {{ price | currency:'INR':'symbol':'1.2-2' }}
// {{ when | date:'dd MMM yyyy' }}   {{ data$ | async | json }}   {{ user?.name ?? 'Guest' }}

A pure pipe is run only when the input reference changes, or a primitive's value does. So pushing to an array does not re-run a pure filter pipe: replace the array instead. Each pure pipe's result is cached per use in a template. An impure pipe gets its own instance per use and runs on every check. A computed() signal often replaces a custom pipe when the logic belongs to one component.

Lifecycle hooks: exact behaviour

HookRunsUse forWatch out
constructorAt creationDI, field setup, effect()Signal inputs have no value yet (reading a required one throws); no DOM
ngOnChangesBefore init and when a decorator @Input changesReacting to input changesNot called for mutations; not called for signal inputs
ngOnInitOnce, after first inputs are setStart-up work, loading dataRuns on the server in SSR as well
ngDoCheckEvery check of the parentRare custom change detectionVery hot
ngAfterContentInit, CheckedAfter projected content is readyReading @ContentChild
ngAfterViewInit, CheckedAfter the view and children renderReading @ViewChild; DOM librariesChanging bound state here triggers ExpressionChanged errors
afterNextRender, afterEveryRenderAfter the browser DOM is updated; never on the serverThird-party DOM libraries, measuringafterEveryRender was called afterRender before v20
ngOnDestroy or DestroyRef.onDestroyBefore removalCleanupNot called when the browser tab closes

Parents run ngOnInit before children. ngAfterViewInit runs on children before parents, since a parent's view is complete only when its children are.

// Modern equivalents
const destroyRef = inject(DestroyRef);
destroyRef.onDestroy(() => chart.dispose());
afterNextRender(() => chart = new Chart(this.canvas().nativeElement));   // call in injection context

Inputs and outputs: decorators vs signal APIs

DecoratorSignal API
Input@Input() name = ''name = input('')
Required@Input({ required: true })input.required<string>()
Transform@Input({ transform: numberAttribute })input(0, { transform: numberAttribute })
Alias@Input('alias')input(0, { alias: 'alias' })
React to changengOnChanges or a settercomputed() or effect()
Readthis.namethis.name(), read-only
Output@Output() x = new EventEmitter<T>()x = output<T>()
Two-way@Input() v plus @Output() vChangev = model(0)
Query@ViewChild(Ref)ref = viewChild(Ref), a signal

input() gives a read-only signal, so a child cannot overwrite it, and computed values derive from it automatically. output() is not an RxJS Subject: it has emit and a subscribe that cleans up with the component. Convert one with outputToObservable if you need operators.

Signals in depth

A signal is a wrapper around a value that tracks who reads it. When computed or a template reads a signal, Angular records a dependency edge in a reactive graph, using an active-consumer variable. When a signal is written, it marks dependents as possibly dirty (a push of notification), but nothing is recomputed until someone reads (a pull). That gives lazy evaluation and glitch-free values: a consumer never sees a half-updated state.

const count = signal(0);
const double = computed(() => count() * 2);     // lazy, memoized, read-only
count.set(1);
count.update(c => c + 1);
const ro = count.asReadonly();                  // expose this from a service

// Dependencies are dynamic: only signals read in the last run count
const label = computed(() => showName() ? name() : 'hidden');
// While showName() is false, changes to name() do not recompute

// Custom equality: skip updates when nothing meaningful changed
const user = signal<User>(u, { equal: (a, b) => a.id === b.id });

// effect: side effects only. Runs at least once, then after dependencies change
effect((onCleanup) => {
  const id = setTimeout(() => save(form()), 500);
  onCleanup(() => clearTimeout(id));
});

// Read without creating a dependency
effect(() => log(`query ${query()} by ${untracked(user).name}`));

// linkedSignal: writable, but resets when the source changes
const options = input.required<Option[]>();
const selected = linkedSignal(() => options()[0]);
const picked = linkedSignal({
  source: options,
  computation: (opts, prev) => opts.find(o => o.id === prev?.value.id) ?? opts[0],
});
selected.set(other);                             // user override, until options change

// resource: async data as signals (see the version table)
const userRes = resource({
  params: () => ({ id: userId() }),
  loader: ({ params, abortSignal }) => fetch(`/api/users/${params.id}`, { signal: abortSignal }).then(r => r.json()),
});
// userRes.value()  userRes.isLoading()  userRes.error()  userRes.reload()
NeedUse
Local statesignal
Value derived from other valuescomputed, never an effect that writes another signal
Derived, but the user can override itlinkedSignal
Sync to something outside the graph: logging, localStorage, a chart, focuseffect
Async data for a keyresource, or RxJS with toSignal
Event streams, debouncing, cancellation, retriesRxJS
Gotcha: signals compare with Object.is. Mutating an object in place (list().push(x)) changes nothing as far as Angular can see. Use update(l => [...l, x]). Effects need an injection context; outside one, pass { injector }. toSignal subscribes immediately and has undefined as its first value unless you give initialValue or requireSync. computed must have no side effects.

Dependency injection in depth

DI means a class asks for what it needs instead of creating it. Angular keeps injectors, which map a token to a provider, the recipe for creating the value. Each injector builds a token once and caches it, so within that injector the value is a singleton.

// Tokens for non-class values
export const API_URL = new InjectionToken<string>('API_URL', {
  providedIn: 'root',
  factory: () => '/api',          // tree-shakable default
});

providers: [
  OrderService,                                       // same as below
  { provide: OrderService, useClass: OrderService },
  { provide: Logger, useClass: environment.production ? RemoteLogger : ConsoleLogger },
  { provide: API_URL, useValue: 'https://api.example.com' },
  { provide: Storage, useFactory: () => isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID)) ? localStorage : memoryStorage() },
  { provide: OldApi, useExisting: NewApi },           // alias: one instance, two tokens
  { provide: PLUGINS, useValue: pluginA, multi: true },   // multi: inject gets an array
  { provide: PLUGINS, useValue: pluginB, multi: true },
]

// inject() options (replace @Optional, @Self, @SkipSelf, @Host)
private log = inject(Logger, { optional: true });     // null instead of an error
private here = inject(Theme, { self: true });         // only this element's injector
private up = inject(Tree, { skipSelf: true });        // start from the parent
private host = inject(Theme, { host: true });         // stop at the host component

// App start-up work (provideAppInitializer is v19+; it replaces APP_INITIALIZER)
provideAppInitializer(() => inject(ConfigService).load());
Where you provideInstance shared byTree-shakable?
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })The whole appYes
bootstrapApplication providersThe whole appNo
Route providers: [...]That route and its children, created onceNo
Component providersThat component instance, its view and projected contentNo
Component viewProvidersThat component and its view, but not projected contentNo

inject() and the injection context

inject() works only in an injection context: field initialisers, constructors, provider factories, functional guards, resolvers and interceptors. Calling it after an await or in a setTimeout throws NG0203. To use it elsewhere, capture EnvironmentInjector and call runInInjectionContext(injector, fn). Compared with constructor parameters, inject() makes inheritance easier (no super(...) chain), and it enables functional guards and reusable injectX() helpers.

Interview: a classic trap is a service that is meant to be a singleton but is also listed in a lazy route's or component's providers. Each injector then has its own instance, and state appears to vanish between screens. Fix it by providing the service once, usually with providedIn: 'root'.

Services and state in a service

A service is a class for logic and data that does not belong to one view: API calls, caching, shared state. A simple signal store in a service is enough for many apps.

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CartService {
  private readonly _items = signal<CartItem[]>([]);
  readonly items = this._items.asReadonly();
  readonly total = computed(() => this._items().reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0));

  add(item: CartItem) { this._items.update(l => [...l, item]); }
  remove(id: number)  { this._items.update(l => l.filter(i => i.id !== id)); }
}

Routing in depth

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: '', pathMatch: 'full', redirectTo: 'orders' },
  {
    path: 'orders',
    title: 'Orders',
    canActivate: [authGuard],
    providers: [OrderStore],                     // route-scoped service
    children: [
      { path: '', loadComponent: () => import('./order-list').then(m => m.OrderList) },
      {
        path: ':id',
        loadComponent: () => import('./order-detail').then(m => m.OrderDetail),
        resolve: { order: orderResolver },
        canDeactivate: [unsavedGuard],
      },
    ],
  },
  { path: 'admin', canMatch: [adminGuard], loadChildren: () => import('./admin/admin.routes') },
  { path: '**', component: NotFound },           // keep last: first match wins
];

export const authGuard: CanActivateFn = (route, state) => {
  const auth = inject(AuthService), router = inject(Router);
  return auth.isLoggedIn() || router.createUrlTree(['/login'], { queryParams: { returnUrl: state.url } });
};

export const orderResolver: ResolveFn<Order> = route =>
  inject(OrderApi).get(route.paramMap.get('id')!);

export const unsavedGuard: CanDeactivateFn<OrderDetail> = c =>
  !c.form.dirty || confirm('Discard your changes?');

// With withComponentInputBinding(), params, query params and resolved data arrive as inputs
export class OrderDetail {
  id = input.required<string>();    // from :id
  order = input.required<Order>();  // from the resolver
}
GuardQuestion it answersRuns
canMatchShould this route config be considered at all? If not, the router tries the next route. Blocks lazy code downloadDuring route matching
canActivateChildCan any child activate?Before each child activation
canActivateCan this route activate?After matching; a lazy chunk may already be loaded
canDeactivateCan the user leave?First among the guard checks, starting at the deepest route
resolveNot a guard: fetches data before activationAfter all guards pass

A guard returns boolean, UrlTree (redirect) or RedirectCommand, or an Observable or Promise of these. A client-side guard is a user-experience feature, not security: the code can be bypassed, so the Spring backend must authorise every request.

Navigation lifecycle

Router events run in this order: NavigationStart, RoutesRecognized, GuardsCheckStart, GuardsCheckEnd, ResolveStart, ResolveEnd, NavigationEnd, with NavigationCancel or NavigationError on failure. A new navigation cancels the current one (the router uses switchMap internally). Filter these events to show a global progress bar.

  • Preloading: withPreloading(PreloadAllModules) loads lazy chunks in the background after start-up.
  • Reuse: going from /orders/1 to /orders/2 reuses the component, so ngOnInit does not run again. Subscribe to paramMap, or use signal inputs, which update on each navigation.
  • Snapshot trap: route.snapshot.paramMap is only the value at creation time.
  • Deployment: with HTML5 URLs, a refresh on /orders/1 asks the server for that path, so the server must fall back to index.html.

Forms in depth

// Typed reactive form
interface AddressForm { city: FormControl<string>; pin: FormControl<string>; }

export class SignupComponent {
  private fb = inject(NonNullableFormBuilder);

  form = this.fb.group({
    email: ['', {
      validators: [Validators.required, Validators.email],
      asyncValidators: [emailFreeValidator(inject(UserApi))],
      updateOn: 'blur',                      // run on blur, not on each keystroke
    }],
    password: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(8)]],
    confirm: ['', Validators.required],
    address: this.fb.group<AddressForm>({
      city: this.fb.control('', Validators.required),
      pin: this.fb.control('', Validators.pattern(/^\d{6}$/)),
    }),
    phones: this.fb.array([this.fb.control('')]),
  }, { validators: [matchFields('password', 'confirm')] });

  addPhone() { this.form.controls.phones.push(this.fb.control('')); }

  submit() {
    if (this.form.invalid) { this.form.markAllAsTouched(); return; }
    const value = this.form.getRawValue();   // includes disabled controls
  }
}

// Custom synchronous, cross-field validator
export const matchFields = (a: string, b: string): ValidatorFn => (group: AbstractControl) =>
  group.get(a)?.value === group.get(b)?.value ? null : { mismatch: true };

// Custom async validator
export const emailFreeValidator = (api: UserApi): AsyncValidatorFn => control =>
  timer(300).pipe(
    switchMap(() => api.emailExists(control.value)),
    map(taken => (taken ? { emailTaken: true } : null)),
    catchError(() => of(null)),
  );
<form [formGroup]="form" (ngSubmit)="submit()">
  <input formControlName="email" />
  @if (form.controls.email.touched && form.controls.email.hasError('required')) {
    <small>Email is required</small>
  }
  <div formGroupName="address"><input formControlName="city" /></div>
  <div formArrayName="phones">
    @for (c of form.controls.phones.controls; track $index) {
      <input [formControlName]="$index" />
    }
  </div>
  <button [disabled]="form.pending">Save</button>
</form>
APIBehaviour
setValueMust supply every control, otherwise throws
patchValueUpdates the supplied ones
resetClears state. Controls set to nullable reset to null unless built with nonNullable
value vs getRawValue()value leaves out disabled controls, so its fields are typed as optional
valueChanges, statusChangesObservables. Combine with debounceTime for auto-save
StatusVALID, INVALID, PENDING, DISABLED
Interaction flagsdirty/pristine (value changed by the user), touched/untouched (blurred)
FormRecordA group with dynamic keys of the same type

Async validators run only after all sync validators pass. ControlValueAccessor makes your own component work with formControlName and ngModel: implement writeValue, registerOnChange, registerOnTouched, and optionally setDisabledState, then register with { provide: NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR, useExisting: forwardRef(() => StarRating), multi: true }. Map Spring's validation errors back to the form with control.setErrors({ server: message }).

HttpClient and interceptors in depth

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class OrderApi {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);
  private base = inject(API_URL);

  search(q: string, page = 0) {
    const params = new HttpParams().set('q', q).set('page', page);
    return this.http.get<Page<Order>>(`${this.base}/orders`, { params });
  }
  create(order: NewOrder) {
    return this.http.post<Order>(`${this.base}/orders`, order, { observe: 'response' });  // full HttpResponse
  }
  upload(file: File) {
    const body = new FormData(); body.append('file', file);
    return this.http.post('/api/files', body, { reportProgress: true, observe: 'events' });
  }
  download(id: number) {
    return this.http.get(`/api/reports/${id}`, { responseType: 'blob' });
  }
}

// Error and token-refresh interceptor
export const errorInterceptor: HttpInterceptorFn = (req, next) => {
  const auth = inject(AuthService), router = inject(Router);
  return next(req).pipe(
    catchError((err: HttpErrorResponse) => {
      if (err.status === 401 && !req.url.endsWith('/auth/refresh')) {
        return auth.refresh().pipe(                // a shared, single refresh call
          switchMap(token => next(req.clone({ setHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } }))),
          catchError(e => { router.navigate(['/login']); return throwError(() => e); }),
        );
      }
      return throwError(() => err);
    }),
  );
};

// Per-request flags use HttpContext
export const SKIP_SPINNER = new HttpContextToken<boolean>(() => false);
http.get(url, { context: new HttpContext().set(SKIP_SPINNER, true) });
  • Requests are immutable, so an interceptor must clone.
  • withInterceptors([a, b]) runs requests in order a then b, and responses in reverse, like a chain of servlet filters.
  • Class-based interceptors (HttpInterceptor) need withInterceptorsFromDi().
  • HttpClient is cold: nothing is sent until you subscribe, and each subscribe sends a new request.
  • withFetch() uses the fetch API, which is recommended under SSR. Upload progress events need XHR.
  • When an interceptor refreshes a token, several 401s can arrive at once. Share one refresh with shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) or a BehaviorSubject gate, or the refresh token gets used several times.
  • Under SSR, provideClientHydration() caches GET responses in the page, so the browser does not repeat them during hydration.

RxJS in depth

An Observable is a function that, when subscribed, connects an observer to a producer. The contract is next*(error|complete)?: any number of values, then at most one terminal event. The subscription holds the teardown. Operators are functions from observable to observable. Each one subscribes to the one before, so pipe builds a chain that does nothing until the final subscribe.

const tick$ = new Observable<number>(subscriber => {
  let n = 0;
  const id = setInterval(() => subscriber.next(n++), 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);        // teardown: unsubscribe, error or complete
});

// A custom operator is just a function
const onlyOk = <T extends { ok: boolean }>() => (src: Observable<T>) => src.pipe(filter(x => x.ok));
GroupOperators
Createof, from, fromEvent, interval, timer, defer, EMPTY, NEVER, throwError
Transformmap, scan, reduce, pairwise, buffer, bufferTime, toArray, groupBy
Filterfilter, take, takeWhile, takeUntil, skip, first, last, distinctUntilChanged, debounceTime, throttleTime, auditTime
FlattenswitchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, exhaustMap
CombinecombineLatest, forkJoin, zip, merge, concat, race, withLatestFrom, startWith
ErrorscatchError, retry, timeout, finalize
Multicastshare, shareReplay
Utilitytap, delay, observeOn
OperatorWhen a new value arrives during an inner streamUseDo not use for
switchMapCancel the running inner, start the newSearch, route params, latest winsWrites: a cancelled POST may still reach the server
mergeMapRun bothIndependent parallel work; pass a concurrency limit as its second argumentAnything where order matters
concatMapQueue the newOrdered writes, sequential savesFast sources with slow inners: the queue grows
exhaustMapIgnore the newLogin or submit buttons, refresh pullCases where the last value must be processed

Unsubscribing: the options in order of preference

  1. async pipe or toSignal: no manual subscription, cleaned up with the view.
  2. takeUntilDestroyed(destroyRef?): place it last in the pipe. Without an argument it needs an injection context.
  3. take(1) or first(): for a single value.
  4. Manual Subscription, unsubscribed in ngOnDestroy.
Gotcha: takeUntil belongs last in the pipe. An operator after it, such as switchMap, keeps its inner subscription alive once the notifier fires. Also avoid nested subscribes: a subscribe inside subscribe cannot be cancelled in one place and loses error handling. Use a flattening operator.

A Subject is both an observable and an observer. Keep it private and expose subject.asObservable(), so that outsiders cannot call next. Marble tests use TestScheduler to run timing logic with virtual time.

Change detection in depth

Change detection (CD) is how Angular keeps the DOM in sync with data. Each component instance has a view (LView) with its template bindings. A check walks the views from the root, re-evaluates bindings, compares each with the previous value, and updates only the DOM nodes that differ. There is no virtual DOM.

Zone.js mode

Zone.js monkey-patches async browser APIs (setTimeout, addEventListener, promises, XHR) so Angular knows when a task has ended. NgZone then calls ApplicationRef.tick(), which checks the tree. It does not know what changed, so it checks all Default components.

OnPush

An OnPush component is skipped, with its subtree, unless it has been marked dirty. Marking happens when:

  1. An @Input receives a new reference (compared with Object.is).
  2. An event listener in its template fires.
  3. markForCheck() is called; the async pipe does this for you.
  4. A signal read in its template changes.

Marking goes from the component up to the root, so the path is walked during the next tick. A setTimeout that changes a plain field in an OnPush component runs CD but skips this component, so the screen does not update. That is the most common OnPush bug.

ChangeDetectorRef

MethodEffect
markForCheck()Marks this view and its ancestors for the next tick; does not run CD
detectChanges()Runs CD immediately on this view and its children
detach(), reattach()Remove from or return to the CD tree, for manual control
checkNoChanges()Dev-mode check: throws if values changed

Signals and zoneless

When a signal read by a template changes, the view is marked, and a tick is scheduled. Zoneless mode removes zone.js: instead of patching the browser, Angular schedules CD when it is told something changed: a signal update, markForCheck(), a template listener, the async pipe, or a component being attached. So a plain field set in a setTimeout will not update the view in any way. The benefits are a smaller bundle, simpler stack traces, and no CD triggered by unrelated async tasks. Migrating means using signals or markForCheck, and replacing code that depends on NgZone.onStable.

// In zone mode: stop a chatty listener triggering CD for the whole app
inject(NgZone).runOutsideAngular(() => {
  window.addEventListener('mousemove', this.onMove);
});
Gotcha: ExpressionChangedAfterItHasBeenCheckedError is a development-only check that a binding's value differs from one read to the next within a tick, usually because a child updates parent state in ngAfterViewInit, or a getter returns a new value each time. It reveals a real one-way-flow problem. Fix the data flow, for instance by computing the value earlier or using a signal. Wrapping in setTimeout only hides it.

State management: NgRx and SignalStore

// NgRx classic Store
export const OrderActions = createActionGroup({
  source: 'Orders',
  events: {
    load: emptyProps(),
    loadSuccess: props<{ orders: Order[] }>(),
    loadFailure: props<{ error: string }>(),
  },
});
export const ordersFeature = createFeature({
  name: 'orders',
  reducer: createReducer(
    { orders: [] as Order[], loading: false, error: null as string | null },
    on(OrderActions.load, s => ({ ...s, loading: true })),
    on(OrderActions.loadSuccess, (s, { orders }) => ({ ...s, orders, loading: false })),
    on(OrderActions.loadFailure, (s, { error }) => ({ ...s, error, loading: false })),
  ),
});
export const loadOrders = createEffect((actions$ = inject(Actions), api = inject(OrderApi)) =>
  actions$.pipe(
    ofType(OrderActions.load),
    switchMap(() => api.list().pipe(
      map(orders => OrderActions.loadSuccess({ orders })),
      catchError(e => of(OrderActions.loadFailure({ error: e.message }))),   // inner, so the effect survives
    )),
  ), { functional: true });
// In a component
orders = inject(Store).selectSignal(ordersFeature.selectOrders);

// NgRx SignalStore: lighter, built on signals
export const OrderStore = signalStore(
  { providedIn: 'root' },
  withState({ orders: [] as Order[], loading: false }),
  withComputed(({ orders }) => ({ count: computed(() => orders().length) })),
  withMethods((store, api = inject(OrderApi)) => ({
    load: rxMethod<void>(pipe(
      tap(() => patchState(store, { loading: true })),
      switchMap(() => api.list()),
      tap(orders => patchState(store, { orders, loading: false })),
    )),
  })),
);
OptionGood forCost
Component signalsState used by one componentNone
Service with signals or BehaviorSubjectFeature or shared state in small and medium appsYour own conventions
NgRx SignalStoreStructured feature stores, little boilerplateA dependency
NgRx StoreLarge apps, many teams, event-driven flows, DevTools time travelMost boilerplate

Content projection, queries and dynamic components

// card.component.html: multi-slot projection
<header><ng-content select="[card-title]">Default title</ng-content></header>  <!-- fallback: v18+ -->
<section><ng-content /></section>
<footer><ng-content select="app-card-actions" /></footer>

// usage
<app-card>
  <h2 card-title>Order 42</h2>
  <p>Body text</p>
  <app-card-actions />
</app-card>

// Template passing: the parent supplies how a row is drawn
<app-table [rows]="rows" [rowTpl]="row"></app-table>
<ng-template #row let-item let-i="index">{{ i }}: {{ item.name }}</ng-template>
// inside app-table
<ng-container *ngTemplateOutlet="rowTpl(); context: { $implicit: r, index: $index }" />

// Queries
input = viewChild.required<ElementRef<HTMLInputElement>>('search');     // own template
rows = viewChildren(RowComponent);                                     // signal of a list
tabs = contentChildren(TabComponent, { descendants: true });           // projected
focus() { this.input().nativeElement.focus(); }

// Dynamic components
@Component({ template: `<ng-container #host />` })
export class Dialogs {
  private host = viewChild.required('host', { read: ViewContainerRef });
  async open() {
    const { ConfirmDialog } = await import('./confirm-dialog');        // lazy
    const ref = this.host().createComponent(ConfirmDialog);
    ref.setInput('message', 'Delete this order?');
    ref.instance.closed.subscribe(() => ref.destroy());
  }
}
// Declarative version
<ng-container *ngComponentOutlet="widget(); inputs: { data: data() }" />

Projected content is created by the parent, and it lives in the parent's change-detection context, even if the child hides it with @if. Projected content is always instantiated. To render lazily, take a TemplateRef instead of using ng-content. Decorator queries: @ViewChild(x, { static: true }) resolves before ngOnInit but cannot see content inside @if. Use ref.setInput() and not instance.x = y, because setInput marks OnPush components dirty and works with signal inputs.
