CSRIn the browserApps behind a login
SSROn the server per requestPublic pages with changing data, SEO
SSG / prerenderAt build timeMarketing pages, docs

ng add @angular/ssr adds a Node server, and route-level modes are set in server.routes.ts with RenderMode.Server, RenderMode.Prerender and RenderMode.Client. Hydration means Angular reuses the server's DOM rather than destroying and recreating it, attaching listeners and state, which avoids a flash and a layout shift. withEventReplay() records clicks made before the code is ready and replays them. Incremental hydration (withIncrementalHydration()) leaves @defer (hydrate on viewport) blocks dehydrated until needed, which also delays their JS.

  • The server has no window, document or localStorage. Guard browser-only code with isPlatformBrowser(inject(PLATFORM_ID)), or put it in afterNextRender.
  • The DOM must match on both sides. Direct DOM manipulation or invalid HTML (a <div> in a <p>) causes hydration mismatch errors (NG0500 and related). Use ngSkipHydration as a last resort for a component.
  • Timers or an open observable keep the app unstable, delaying server rendering. Use afterNextRender for those.

Testing

describe('OrderList', () => {
  let fixture: ComponentFixture<OrderList>;
  let http: HttpTestingController;

  beforeEach(async () => {
    await TestBed.configureTestingModule({
      imports: [OrderList],                     // standalone component goes in imports
      providers: [provideHttpClient(), provideHttpClientTesting(), provideRouter([])],
    }).compileComponents();
    fixture = TestBed.createComponent(OrderList);
    http = TestBed.inject(HttpTestingController);
  });

  it('renders rows returned by the API', async () => {
    fixture.detectChanges();
    http.expectOne('/api/orders').flush([{ id: 1, name: 'Pen' }]);
    await fixture.whenStable();
    const rows = fixture.nativeElement.querySelectorAll('li');
    expect(rows.length).toBe(1);
  });

  afterEach(() => http.verify());               // fails on unexpected requests
});

// Signal inputs in a test
fixture.componentRef.setInput('order', { id: 1 });

// Replace a dependency
TestBed.overrideProvider(OrderApi, { useValue: { list: () => of([]) } });

// Time control in zone-based tests
it('debounces', fakeAsync(() => {
  component.query.set('a');
  tick(300);
  expect(api.search).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
}));

// Marble test
const scheduler = new TestScheduler((a, e) => expect(a).toEqual(e));
scheduler.run(({ cold, expectObservable }) => {
  const src = cold('a-b-c|');
  expectObservable(src.pipe(map(v => v.toUpperCase()))).toBe('A-B-C|');
});

Layers: pure unit tests for services and pipes, component tests with TestBed, and end-to-end tests with Playwright or Cypress. Karma with Jasmine was the historic default; Karma is deprecated, and Vitest is the default runner for new projects from v21. Query the DOM as a user does, or use CDK component harnesses so tests do not depend on Material's internal markup. RouterTestingHarness tests routed components. Test behaviour and rendered output rather than private methods.

Build, configuration and deployment

  • Builder: the application builder uses esbuild and Vite, and has been the default since v17. It replaced the webpack builder for new projects.
  • Configuration: angular.json holds per-environment options: fileReplacements swaps environment.ts. Budgets fail a build that grows too large. These values are compiled in, so for one build to run in many environments, load a config.json at start-up with provideAppInitializer.
  • Dev proxy: ng serve --proxy-config proxy.conf.json forwards /api to Spring Boot on port 8080, avoiding CORS in development.
  • Output: ng build writes hashed files to dist/. Cache hashed files for a long time, and never cache index.html.
  • Upgrades: ng update @angular/core @angular/cli applies code migrations, one major version at a time.
  • Strictness: keep strict and strictTemplates on, so that template errors are compile errors.
  • i18n: mark text with i18n attributes or $localize, run ng extract-i18n. The build produces one bundle per locale.
# nginx: serve the SPA and proxy the API
location / {
  root /usr/share/nginx/html;
  try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html;         # deep links fall back to Angular
}
location /api/ { proxy_pass http://order-service:8080; }
// Or served from Spring Boot: copy dist/ into src/main/resources/static at build time,
// then forward unknown non-file paths to index.html so deep links work.
@Controller
class SpaController {
  @GetMapping("/{path:[^.]*}")            // single-segment, no dot
  String forward() { return "forward:/index.html"; }
}

Global error handling and error reporting

Angular sends every uncaught error (template errors, errors thrown in event handlers, unhandled promise rejections inside the zone) to a single ErrorHandler. Its default just calls console.error. In a real app you replace it to log to a monitoring tool (Sentry, a Spring Boot log endpoint) and show a friendly message. HTTP errors are best handled separately in an interceptor, because the interceptor knows the status code and can decide to retry, redirect to login (401), or show a toast.

  • ErrorHandler: last-resort catch for code bugs. Do not try to recover there, just report.
  • HTTP interceptor: expected failures such as 401, 403, 409, 422 and 5xx. Map a Spring ProblemDetail body to a user message.
  • Component level: catchError in the stream that needs a fallback value, so one failed widget does not blank the page.
  • Zoneless apps: errors from code outside Angular's callbacks are not always routed to ErrorHandler. Newer versions offer provideBrowserGlobalErrorListeners() to hook window error events; check your version.
@Injectable()
export class AppErrorHandler implements ErrorHandler {
  private toast = inject(ToastService);
  private log = inject(LogService);

  handleError(error: unknown): void {
    const err = error instanceof Error ? error : new Error(String(error));
    this.log.report({ message: err.message, stack: err.stack, url: location.href });
    this.toast.error('Something went wrong. Please try again.');
  }
}

// app.config.ts
export const appConfig: ApplicationConfig = {
  providers: [{ provide: ErrorHandler, useClass: AppErrorHandler }]
};

Accessibility (a11y) in Angular

Interviewers increasingly ask how you make an SPA accessible, especially in healthcare and government work where WCAG 2.1/2.2 AA is often a requirement. The main SPA-specific problems are focus and announcements: a route change replaces content without a page load, so a screen reader user may not know anything happened.

  • Use native elements (<button>, <a routerLink>, <label for>) before ARIA. A clickable <div> is not keyboard accessible.
  • Bind ARIA with attribute binding: [attr.aria-expanded]="open()", [attr.aria-invalid]="ctrl.invalid".
  • Angular CDK a11y: cdkTrapFocus for dialogs, LiveAnnouncer to announce messages such as "3 results found", FocusMonitor to know if focus came from keyboard or mouse, ListKeyManager for arrow-key navigation in custom lists.
  • On navigation: set a unique page title (a title on each route or a custom TitleStrategy) and move focus to the main heading.
  • Show form errors in text linked with aria-describedby, not only by colour.
  • Test with keyboard only, a screen reader, Lighthouse/axe, and lint rules from @angular-eslint template accessibility rules.
// Announce search results and move focus after navigation
private announcer = inject(LiveAnnouncer);
results = computed(() => this.store.results());
constructor() {
  effect(() => this.announcer.announce(`${this.results().length} results found`, 'polite'));
}

// Route config with titles
{ path: 'patients', title: 'Patients', loadComponent: () => import('./patients.component') }

Micro-frontends and Angular Elements

Large organisations sometimes split one front end into several apps owned by different teams. Know the options and their costs, because the honest interview answer is often "only if team boundaries demand it".

ApproachHow it worksTrade-off
Module Federation (webpack) / Native Federation (esbuild, ES modules + import maps)A shell app loads remote apps' bundles at runtime and shares Angular and RxJS as singletonsIndependent deploys; version alignment of shared libraries is the hard part
Angular Elements (createCustomElement)Wraps a component as a standard Custom Element (<order-widget>) usable in any page, including a JSP or React pageFramework-agnostic; each element bundle may carry its own Angular runtime
iframesFully isolated pagesStrong isolation; poor UX, hard communication, accessibility issues
Monorepo (Nx) with librariesOne build, code split into libs with enforced boundariesSimplest; no independent deployment
// Angular Elements: expose a component to non-Angular pages
const app = await createApplication({ providers: [provideHttpClient()] });
const el = createCustomElement(OrderWidgetComponent, { injector: app.injector });
customElements.define('order-widget', el);
// usage in a legacy page:  <order-widget order-id="42"></order-widget>

Interview Questions — Angular

AngularJS vs Angular?

AngularJS (1.x) is JavaScript, MVC with $scope, two-way digest cycles, and is end-of-life. Angular (2+) is TypeScript, component-based, has hierarchical DI, AOT compilation, RxJS, a CLI, and is much faster.

What are standalone components? NgModule vs standalone?

Since v14 (ng new generates them from v17; standalone: true is the default from v19), components can declare their own dependencies with imports: [] instead of being declared in an NgModule. You bootstrap with bootstrapApplication(App, { providers: [provideRouter(routes), provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([...]))] }). This means less boilerplate and better tree-shaking.

Types of data binding?

Interpolation {{ }} and property binding [ ] go from component to view. Event binding ( ) goes from view to component. Two-way binding [( )] is the "banana in a box", e.g. [(ngModel)], or model() signals in v17+.

Directives: component vs structural vs attribute?

Component: a directive with a template. Structural: changes the DOM layout (*ngIf, *ngFor, *ngSwitch, now the built-in @if / @for / @switch control flow). Attribute: changes appearance or behavior (ngClass, ngStyle, or custom ones using @HostListener and @HostBinding).

Pure vs impure pipes?

A pure pipe (the default) re-runs only when its input reference changes, so it's fast. An impure pipe (pure: false) runs on every change detection cycle; async is impure. Built-in pipes: date, currency, uppercase, json, async, slice, percent.

How does Dependency Injection work in Angular?

DI is hierarchical: the environment injector (root or route) sits above element injectors (component providers). providedIn: 'root' creates a tree-shakable singleton. Providers at component level give a new instance for that subtree. Inject with the constructor or inject(). Provider types: useClass, useValue, useFactory, useExisting. Use InjectionToken for non-class values.

How do components communicate?
  • Parent → child: @Input() / input() signal
  • Child → parent: @Output() EventEmitter / output()
  • Parent reads child: @ViewChild / viewChild()
  • Unrelated components: a shared service holding a BehaviorSubject or signal
  • App-wide state: NgRx / Signal Store
  • Through the router: params and query params
Observable vs Promise?
Observable (RxJS)Promise
Can emit many values over timeResolves once
Lazy: nothing happens until subscribedEager: starts immediately
Cancellable (unsubscribe)Can't be cancelled
Rich operators (map, filter, debounce, retry)then/catch only
Subject vs BehaviorSubject vs ReplaySubject vs AsyncSubject?

Subject: no initial value; late subscribers miss earlier emissions. BehaviorSubject: needs an initial value and gives the latest value to new subscribers (good for state). ReplaySubject(n): replays the last n values. AsyncSubject: emits only the last value, on complete.

switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap?
  • switchMap: cancels the previous inner observable (search typeahead).
  • mergeMap: runs all of them in parallel (independent saves).
  • concatMap: runs them one at a time, in order (queued writes).
  • exhaustMap: ignores new values while one is running (a login button clicked repeatedly).
this.search.valueChanges.pipe(
  debounceTime(300), distinctUntilChanged(),
  switchMap(q => this.api.search(q))
).subscribe(r => this.results = r);
How do you avoid memory leaks with subscriptions?

Use the async pipe (it unsubscribes automatically) · takeUntilDestroyed() (v16+) · toSignal() · take(1) · or call unsubscribe() in ngOnDestroy. HttpClient observables complete by themselves.

What are Signals? Signals vs RxJS?

Signals (v16+) are reactive values: signal() is writable, computed() is derived and memoized, and effect() runs side effects. They're synchronous and always have a current value, and they let Angular update only what changed, which opens the way to zoneless change detection. Use signals for UI state. Keep RxJS for async event streams (HTTP, websockets, debouncing). toSignal and toObservable bridge the two.

How does change detection work? What is OnPush?

Zone.js patches async APIs (events, timers, XHR), and after each one Angular checks the component tree from the top down. With OnPush, a component is checked only when an @Input reference changes, an event fires inside it, the async pipe emits, a signal it reads changes, or you call markForCheck(). Use immutable data with OnPush. Zoneless started as experimental in v18 (provideExperimentalZonelessChangeDetection()) and became stable in v20.2 as provideZonelessChangeDetection().

Template-driven vs Reactive forms?
Template-drivenReactive
Logic in the template (ngModel)Model defined in the class (FormGroup, FormControl, FormBuilder)
Asynchronous, simple formsSynchronous, scalable, easy to test, supports dynamic forms (FormArray)
Validation through directivesValidator functions (sync and async), typed forms (v14+)
form = this.fb.nonNullable.group({
  email: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.email]],
  password: ['', [Validators.required, Validators.minLength(8)]]
});
Routing: guards, resolvers, lazy loading?

Guards (functional since v15): canActivate, canActivateChild, canDeactivate (unsaved changes), canMatch (choose between routes). A resolver fetches data before the route activates. Lazy loading with loadComponent / loadChildren splits bundles and shrinks the initial load. @defer blocks (v17) lazy-load parts of a template.

What is an HTTP Interceptor? Uses?

Middleware that sits around every HttpClient request and response. Uses: attaching the JWT, global error handling (401 → redirect to login or refresh the token), a loading spinner, logging, caching, retries.

AOT vs JIT?

AOT (the default) compiles templates at build time: a smaller bundle, faster rendering, template errors caught early, and better security. JIT compiles in the browser at runtime; it was the old dev mode.

ViewChild vs ContentChild; ng-content?

@ViewChild queries elements in the component's own template (available in ngAfterViewInit). @ContentChild queries projected content passed between the component's tags with <ng-content> (available in ngAfterContentInit). <ng-content select=".header"> enables multi-slot projection.

How do you optimize Angular performance?

OnPush or signals · track in @for (trackBy) · lazy routes and @defer · pure pipes instead of methods in templates · virtual scrolling (CDK) · unsubscribing · SSR and hydration (@angular/ssr) · image optimization (NgOptimizedImage) · bundle budgets · esbuild builder.

ng-template vs ng-container vs ng-content?

<ng-template>: a template that isn't rendered until it's used (via ngTemplateOutlet or else blocks). <ng-container>: a grouping element that adds no DOM node. <ng-content>: the slot for content projection.

RxJS output: cold vs hot
const { Observable, share } = require('rxjs');
let runs = 0;
const cold = new Observable(sub => { runs++; sub.next('run ' + runs); sub.complete(); });
cold.subscribe(v => console.log('A', v));
cold.subscribe(v => console.log('B', v));
console.log('producer executions:', runs);

runs = 0;
const hot = new Observable(sub => { runs++; const t = setTimeout(() => { sub.next('run ' + runs); sub.complete(); }, 0); return () => clearTimeout(t); }).pipe(share());
hot.subscribe(v => console.log('C', v));
hot.subscribe(v => console.log('D', v));
console.log('producer executions with share:', runs);

Output (executed):

A run 1
B run 2
producer executions: 2
producer executions with share: 1
C run 1
D run 1

A cold observable creates its producer per subscriber, so two subscribers mean two executions. That is why subscribing twice to http.get() sends two requests. share() makes it hot: one execution is multicast to all subscribers.

RxJS output: the four Subject types with a late subscriber
const { Subject, BehaviorSubject, ReplaySubject, AsyncSubject } = require('rxjs');
function demo(name, s) {
  const seen = { early: [], late: [] };
  s.subscribe(v => seen.early.push(v));
  s.next(1); s.next(2);
  s.subscribe(v => seen.late.push(v));
  s.next(3);
  s.complete();
  console.log(name, JSON.stringify(seen));
}
demo('Subject        ', new Subject());
demo('BehaviorSubject', new BehaviorSubject(0));
demo('ReplaySubject2 ', new ReplaySubject(2));
demo('AsyncSubject   ', new AsyncSubject());

Output (executed):

Subject         {"early":[1,2,3],"late":[3]}
BehaviorSubject {"early":[0,1,2,3],"late":[2,3]}
ReplaySubject2  {"early":[1,2,3],"late":[1,2,3]}
AsyncSubject    {"early":[3],"late":[3]}

The late subscriber joins after 2. Subject gives only later values. BehaviorSubject gives the current value first, and the early subscriber also received the initial 0. ReplaySubject(2) replays the last two. AsyncSubject gives only the final value, on completion.

RxJS output: switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap
const { from, concatMap, mergeMap, switchMap, exhaustMap, timer, map, of, delay } = require('rxjs');
// Three clicks 10 ms apart; each starts a "request" of 40 ms
const clicks = () => from([1, 2, 3]).pipe(concatMap((v, i) => of(v).pipe(delay(i === 0 ? 0 : 10))));
const req = v => timer(40).pipe(map(() => v));
const run = (name, op) => new Promise(done => {
  const out = [];
  clicks().pipe(op(req)).subscribe({ next: v => out.push(v), complete() { console.log(name, out); done(); } });
});
(async () => {
  await run('mergeMap  ', mergeMap);
  await run('concatMap ', concatMap);
  await run('switchMap ', switchMap);
  await run('exhaustMap', exhaustMap);
})();

Output (executed):

mergeMap   [ 1, 2, 3 ]
concatMap  [ 1, 2, 3 ]
switchMap  [ 3 ]
exhaustMap [ 1 ]

mergeMap runs all three in parallel, and results arrive as they finish. concatMap queues them, so order is kept and all run. switchMap unsubscribes from the older request on each click, so only the last survives. exhaustMap ignores clicks while one is running, so only the first survives. Remember which values are lost: oldest with switchMap, newest with exhaustMap, none with the other two.

RxJS output: catchError position decides whether the stream survives
const { from, of, throwError, map, catchError, concatMap } = require('rxjs');
const api = n => n === 2 ? throwError(() => new Error('bad ' + n)) : of('ok ' + n);

from([1, 2, 3]).pipe(
  concatMap(api),
  catchError(e => of('outer: ' + e.message))
).subscribe({ next: v => console.log('A', v), complete: () => console.log('A complete') });

from([1, 2, 3]).pipe(
  concatMap(n => api(n).pipe(catchError(e => of('inner: ' + e.message))))
).subscribe({ next: v => console.log('B', v), complete: () => console.log('B complete') });

Output (executed):

A ok 1
A outer: bad 2
A complete
B ok 1
B inner: bad 2
B ok 3
B complete

An error terminates a stream. In A, catchError on the outer stream replaces the whole remainder, so 3 is never handled. A search box built this way stops working after one failed request. In B, the error is caught on the inner observable and the outer one keeps going. Put catchError inside the flattening operator for long-lived streams.

RxJS output: forkJoin vs combineLatest vs zip vs withLatestFrom
const { Subject, forkJoin, combineLatest, zip, withLatestFrom, of, EMPTY } = require('rxjs');
function setup() { return { a: new Subject(), b: new Subject() }; }
function drive(a, b) { a.next('a1'); b.next('b1'); a.next('a2'); b.next('b2'); a.next('a3'); a.complete(); b.complete(); }

let s = setup(); const log = n => v => console.log(n, v.join('+'));
combineLatest([s.a, s.b]).subscribe(log('combineLatest')); drive(s.a, s.b);
s = setup(); zip(s.a, s.b).subscribe(log('zip')); drive(s.a, s.b);
s = setup(); s.a.pipe(withLatestFrom(s.b)).subscribe(log('withLatestFrom')); drive(s.a, s.b);
s = setup(); forkJoin([s.a, s.b]).subscribe(log('forkJoin')); drive(s.a, s.b);
forkJoin([of(1), EMPTY]).subscribe({ next: () => console.log('forkJoin next'), complete: () => console.log('forkJoin with EMPTY: completes with no value') });

Output (executed):

combineLatest a1+b1
combineLatest a2+b1
combineLatest a2+b2
combineLatest a3+b2
zip a1+b1
zip a2+b2
withLatestFrom a2+b1
withLatestFrom a3+b2
forkJoin a3+b2
forkJoin with EMPTY: completes with no value

combineLatest emits on any source once all have emitted. zip pairs by position. withLatestFrom emits only when the primary source emits. forkJoin waits for completion and emits the last values, like Promise.all. If any source completes without a value, forkJoin completes with no emission, a common cause of a silently missing result. If a source never completes, it never emits.

RxJS output: shareReplay and refCount
const { Observable, shareReplay, Subject, takeUntil, interval, take } = require('rxjs');
let subs = 0;
const src = new Observable(s => { subs++; console.log('connect', subs); const t = setInterval(() => s.next(1), 5); return () => { clearInterval(t); console.log('teardown'); }; });
const leaky = src.pipe(shareReplay(1));
const a = leaky.subscribe();
a.unsubscribe();
console.log('after unsubscribe: no teardown printed for shareReplay(1)');
setTimeout(() => {
  const safe = src.pipe(shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }));
  const b = safe.subscribe();
  b.unsubscribe();
  console.log('refCount:true tore down');
  process.exit(0);
}, 10);

Output (executed):

connect 1
after unsubscribe: no teardown printed for shareReplay(1)
connect 2
teardown
refCount:true tore down

shareReplay(1) defaults to refCount: false, so if the source never completes, it stays subscribed forever after the last subscriber leaves, which is a leak. Use shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) unless the source completes on its own (as HTTP does) and you want a permanent cache.

RxJS output: synchronous emission, take, first and firstValueFrom
const { of, EMPTY, first, take, firstValueFrom, Subject, lastValueFrom } = require('rxjs');
console.log('before');
of(1, 2, 3).pipe(take(2)).subscribe({ next: v => console.log(v), complete: () => console.log('complete') });
console.log('after');
EMPTY.pipe(take(1)).subscribe({ complete: () => console.log('take(1) on empty: completes quietly') });
EMPTY.pipe(first()).subscribe({ error: e => console.log('first() on empty:', e.name) });
firstValueFrom(EMPTY, { defaultValue: 'fallback' }).then(console.log);
const s = new Subject();
s.next('lost');
s.subscribe(v => console.log('got', v));
s.next('seen');

Output (executed):

before
1
2
complete
after
take(1) on empty: completes quietly
first() on empty: EmptyError
got seen
fallback

Observables are not inherently async: of emits synchronously during subscribe. A Subject has no memory, so a value emitted before anyone subscribes is lost. first() throws EmptyError when nothing arrives, while take(1) simply completes. firstValueFrom replaces the deprecated toPromise().

RxJS output: debounceTime vs throttleTime vs auditTime
const { Subject, debounceTime, throttleTime, auditTime, sampleTime } = require('rxjs');
const schedule = [[0, 'a'], [10, 'b'], [20, 'c'], [80, 'd']];
const run = (name, op) => new Promise(done => {
  const s = new Subject(), out = [];
  s.pipe(op).subscribe(v => out.push(v));
  schedule.forEach(([t, v]) => setTimeout(() => s.next(v), t));
  setTimeout(() => { console.log(name, out); s.complete(); done(); }, 160);
});
(async () => {
  await run('debounceTime(40)', debounceTime(40));
  await run('throttleTime(40)', throttleTime(40));
  await run('auditTime(40)   ', auditTime(40));
})();

Output (executed):

debounceTime(40) [ 'c', 'd' ]
throttleTime(40) [ 'a', 'd' ]
auditTime(40)    [ 'c', 'd' ]

debounceTime emits the last value after a quiet period. throttleTime emits the first value and then ignores others for the window. auditTime waits for the window and then emits the latest. sampleTime emits the latest on a fixed clock. Typeahead uses debounce, a double-click guard uses throttle, and scroll position usually uses audit.

RxJS output: retry, finalize and teardown order
const { defer, of, throwError, retry, tap, finalize, map, catchError, Observable, timer } = require('rxjs');
let attempts = 0;
defer(() => { attempts++; console.log('attempt', attempts); return attempts < 3 ? throwError(() => new Error('fail')) : of('data'); }).pipe(
  retry({ count: 2, delay: () => timer(1) }),
  finalize(() => console.log('finalize')),
).subscribe({ next: console.log, complete: () => console.log('complete') });

Output (executed):

attempt 1
attempt 2
attempt 3
data
complete
finalize

retry re-subscribes to the source, so a cold HTTP observable sends a new request each time. The object form accepts a delay function for backoff. count: 2 means two retries, three attempts in all. finalize runs on completion, error or unsubscribe, after complete, making it the right place to stop a loading spinner.

RxJS output: scan, reduce, distinctUntilChanged with objects
const { of, scan, reduce, distinctUntilChanged, map, startWith, pairwise } = require('rxjs');
const out = [];
of(1, 2, 3).pipe(scan((a, b) => a + b, 0)).subscribe(v => out.push(v));
console.log('scan', out);
of(1, 2, 3).pipe(reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)).subscribe(v => console.log('reduce', v));
const objs = [];
of({ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }).pipe(distinctUntilChanged()).subscribe(v => objs.push(v.id));
console.log('by reference', objs);
const byId = [];
of({ id: 1 }, { id: 1 }, { id: 2 }).pipe(distinctUntilChanged((a, b) => a.id === b.id)).subscribe(v => byId.push(v.id));
console.log('by id', byId);
const pairs = [];
of(1, 2, 3).pipe(startWith(0), pairwise()).subscribe(p => pairs.push(p.join('>')));
console.log(pairs);

Output (executed):

scan [ 1, 3, 6 ]
reduce 6
by reference [ 1, 1, 2 ]
by id [ 1, 2 ]
[ '0>1', '1>2', '2>3' ]

scan emits every intermediate accumulation, which makes it a tiny state store: actions$.pipe(scan(reducer, init)). reduce emits once on completion, so it never emits on an endless stream. distinctUntilChanged compares by reference, so new objects always pass unless you give a comparator.

Walk through what happens when a user clicks a button in a zone-based Default app.
  1. The browser dispatches the event, and zone.js's patched listener runs inside the Angular zone.
  2. Your handler runs and updates state.
  3. When the task's stack empties, NgZone.onMicrotaskEmpty fires, and ApplicationRef.tick() runs.
  4. Angular walks the tree from the root, re-evaluates bindings, and writes changed values to the DOM.
  5. In dev mode, a second pass verifies that no binding changed.
A child with OnPush doesn't refresh after the parent does this.user.name = 'New'. Why? What are the fixes?

The reference held by [user] is unchanged, so Object.is reports no change and the child stays clean. Fixes, best first: hold the data in a signal and update it with a new object; or assign a new object with this.user = { ...this.user, name: 'New' }. Calling markForCheck() in the child works but hides the mutation.

markForCheck() vs detectChanges()?

markForCheck() flags this view and all ancestors so the next tick visits them. It does not run anything itself, and it is what you use with OnPush after a change arrives from outside, such as a WebSocket callback. detectChanges() runs a check right now on this view and its children, and can be used when the view is detached. Calling it from a parent's hook during a check can throw or cause extra work.

What happens to zone-based code after moving to zoneless?

Anything that updated a plain field in a setTimeout, promise or third-party callback and relied on a global tick stops refreshing the view. Components must notify Angular through signals, markForCheck (or the async pipe), or template events. Also remove zone.js from the polyfills build option, and replace code using NgZone.onMicrotaskEmpty or onStable with afterNextRender. Tests that use fakeAsync depend on zone.js, so need to be changed. Converting components to OnPush first is the usual migration path, as OnPush code is close to zoneless-ready.

computed vs effect vs linkedSignal: which would you use to reset a selection when a list changes?

linkedSignal. The selection is writable by the user but must reset or re-derive when the source changes. A computed is read-only, so the user could not change it. An effect that calls selected.set(...) works but runs later than the render that needs the value, which causes an extra pass and a moment of inconsistent state. Treat "effect that writes a signal" as a warning sign.

Why might an effect not re-run? Why might it loop?

It tracks only signals read synchronously in its last run. If a read sits after an await or inside a setTimeout, or an early return skipped it, there is no dependency. It also does not re-run when a signal is set to an equal value. It loops when it reads and writes the same signal. Fix by wrapping the read in untracked(), or preferably by replacing the effect with computed.

Signals vs RxJS: when would you still pick RxJS?

A signal holds a current value; an observable describes values over time. Signals drop intermediate writes: setting a signal twice in one task means a template or effect sees only the last. So they cannot model events you must not miss. Use RxJS for debouncing, retry, cancellation, combining streams, and WebSockets. A common pattern is RxJS for the async pipeline, and toSignal at the end, so that the template reads a signal.

providers vs viewProviders?

Both create an instance per component. providers are visible to the component, its view children and to content projected into it. viewProviders are hidden from projected content. So content passed in through ng-content gets the outer value, which prevents a library component's internals from leaking into its consumers' content.

useClass vs useExisting vs useValue vs useFactory; what is a multi provider?

useClass creates a new instance of the class. useExisting is an alias pointing to an already provided token, so there is one instance under two tokens. Getting this wrong by using useClass makes two instances. useValue supplies a ready object. useFactory runs a function, which may call inject(). With multi: true, many providers contribute to one token and injection gives an array. Validators (NG_VALIDATORS) and value accessors work this way.

What does NullInjectorError: No provider for X mean, and how do you debug it?

The lookup went through every injector and none had the token. Typical causes: the service has no @Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' }); provideHttpClient() is missing from the app config; a component is looking for a token provided only in a sibling route; or a test has not provided a dependency. The error shows the chain, such as R3InjectorError(Standalone[App])[A -> B -> C], whose last item is what is missing.

What is forwardRef?

JS classes are not hoisted, so a decorator that refers to a class declared later in the file sees it in its TDZ. forwardRef(() => MyClass) delays the read until it is needed. It is common in NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR providers, since the provider is in the class's own decorator.

canActivate vs canMatch: which stops a lazy bundle from downloading?

canMatch. It runs while matching, before the lazy code is loaded. If it returns false, the router moves on to the next matching route, so you can have two path: 'dashboard' entries for admin and user. canActivate runs after matching. Remember that hiding a bundle is not security, since all JS is public.

Resolver vs loading in the component: which is better?

A resolver delays navigation until data arrives, so the page shows complete data, but the user sees nothing happen while waiting, and a failed resolve cancels navigation. Loading in the component navigates immediately and shows a skeleton, which feels faster and lets you handle errors in place. Most modern apps prefer the second approach, keeping resolvers for data that the page cannot render without.

Why does the same component not re-initialise on /orders/1 to /orders/2?

The router's default RouteReuseStrategy reuses a component when the route config is the same. So constructor and ngOnInit do not run again. Read the id reactively: route.paramMap.pipe(switchMap(...)), or a signal input with withComponentInputBinding(), feeding a resource or computed.

value vs getRawValue(); setValue vs patchValue; typed form pitfalls?

value omits disabled controls, and so in typed forms each field's type includes undefined. getRawValue() includes them. setValue demands every key and patchValue takes a subset. Without nonNullable, reset() sets null, so each control's type is T | null. Using NonNullableFormBuilder or fb.nonNullable removes the null. Type inference needs an initial value, so declare an interface for an initially empty FormArray.

How do you build a custom form control?

Implement ControlValueAccessor: writeValue receives a value from the model, registerOnChange(fn) saves the callback that you call when the user changes the value, registerOnTouched(fn) saves the one you call on blur, and setDisabledState handles disabling. Register with NG_VALUE_ACCESSOR using multi: true. For OnPush controls, writeValue is called outside of inputs, so update a signal or call markForCheck. Implementing Validator and registering NG_VALIDATORS adds built-in validation.

Does cancelling HTTP with switchMap stop the backend?

No. Unsubscribing aborts the browser's request, so the response is ignored, but the server may already be processing it. Spring does not normally notice a client disconnect until it writes the response. That is why switchMap suits reads, not writes. For writes use concatMap or exhaustMap, and make the endpoint idempotent, such as with an idempotency key.

Implement a typeahead with error handling and a loading flag.
export class Search {
  private api = inject(SearchApi);
  query = new FormControl('', { nonNullable: true });
  loading = signal(false);

  results = toSignal(this.query.valueChanges.pipe(
    map(q => q.trim()),
    debounceTime(300),
    distinctUntilChanged(),
    tap(() => this.loading.set(true)),
    switchMap(q => (q ? this.api.search(q) : of([])).pipe(
      catchError(() => of([])),                 // inner: the stream survives
      finalize(() => this.loading.set(false)),
    )),
  ), { initialValue: [] });
}

Each operator has a job: debounceTime limits requests, distinctUntilChanged skips identical terms, switchMap drops stale responses, the inner catchError keeps the stream alive, and toSignal handles unsubscribing.

How would you cache an HTTP result and share one request across components?
@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class CountryApi {
  private http = inject(HttpClient);
  readonly countries$ = this.http.get<Country[]>('/api/countries').pipe(shareReplay(1));
}

The first subscriber triggers the request. The rest get the replayed value. Since HTTP completes, the plain shareReplay(1) is safe here. A failure is not cached, because shareReplay resets on error. For invalidation, start from a refresh trigger: refresh$.pipe(startWith(undefined), switchMap(() => http.get(...)), shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true })). For time-based expiry, keep a timestamp, or use an interceptor-level cache.

Why is calling a method in a template bad? When is it fine?

A method in a binding runs on every check of that view, so an expensive one (sorting, filtering) can run many times per second. Prefer a computed or a pure pipe. Calling a signal is also a function call, but it is a cheap read of a memoized value, so {{ total() }} is fine when total is a signal. With OnPush, or for trivial getters, the cost is usually unimportant.

trackBy/track: what happens without it, and with track $index?

With identity tracking and fresh objects from an API, every item looks new, so the DOM is destroyed and rebuilt, which is slow and loses focus and input state. With track item.id, nodes are kept and reordered. With track $index the node at position n stays and only its bindings change, so stateful content (an input's typed value, an open dropdown) ends up attached to a different item when items are removed or reordered.

ng-container and ngTemplateOutlet: build a reusable table whose cell layout is supplied by the parent.

Accept a template with rowTpl = input.required<TemplateRef<{ $implicit: Row }>>() or find it with contentChild(TemplateRef). Render it with <ng-container *ngTemplateOutlet="rowTpl(); context: { $implicit: r }" />. The parent writes <ng-template let-row>...</ng-template>. Unlike ng-content, this renders the template once per row, and passes data from child to parent's template. A static ngTemplateContextGuard on a directive can give strict typing for let- variables.

ElementRef vs Renderer2: when do you touch the DOM directly?

Bindings come first. When you need imperative work, Renderer2 abstracts the DOM and works under SSR. ElementRef.nativeElement gives the raw element, for example to call focus() or to give a canvas to a chart library, which should sit in afterNextRender. Setting innerHTML directly bypasses Angular's sanitiser, which is an XSS risk. Use the [innerHTML] binding, which sanitises.

How does Angular protect against XSS? What does bypassSecurityTrustHtml do?

Angular treats every bound value as untrusted. Interpolation escapes text. [innerHTML], [href] and [style] pass through contextual sanitising, which removes scripts and javascript: URLs. AOT also means template text is not built from user strings. DomSanitizer.bypassSecurityTrust* tells Angular to trust a value, so only use it with content you control. Never build templates from user input. HttpClient also supports CSRF: it reads the XSRF-TOKEN cookie and sends the X-XSRF-TOKEN header on same-origin mutating requests.

Explain NgRx in an interview in under a minute. When would you avoid it?

The store holds one state tree. Components dispatch actions that describe events. Pure reducers compute the next state. Selectors read memoized slices. Effects listen for actions, make API calls, and dispatch results. You get predictable flows, time-travel debugging and easy testing. Avoid it for small apps, form state, or data that only one screen uses, because the boilerplate outweighs the benefit. A service with signals, or SignalStore, is often enough.

Why must a reducer be pure? Why are selectors memoized?

A pure reducer takes state and action and returns a new state, with no I/O or mutation. Purity means the same action log always reproduces the same state, which enables time travel and simple tests, and new references let OnPush detect changes by reference. createSelector remembers its last inputs and returns the cached result if those references are unchanged, so derived data is not recomputed and subscribers do not get a new array on every state change.

Scenario: an effect stops working after the first API failure.

The catchError is on the outer actions$ stream, so the error completes the effect's stream. Move catchError inside switchMap, on the API call, and return a failure action. NgRx does resubscribe effects a limited number of times by default, but you should not depend on that.

What is hydration, and what breaks it?

Hydration reuses server-rendered DOM on the client: Angular walks the existing nodes rather than creating new ones, then attaches listeners. It breaks when the client's DOM would differ from the server's: direct DOM manipulation, third-party scripts that alter the markup, invalid HTML that the browser's parser repairs, or a render that depends on Date.now() or Math.random() in the template. CDN settings that strip comment nodes also break it, since Angular relies on them. Check the console for NG05xx messages.

Why might SSR hang or time out?

The server waits until the app is stable, meaning no pending tasks. A setInterval, an open WebSocket, or a long-lived observable keeps it unstable. Move those into afterNextRender, which only runs in the browser, or guard them with isPlatformBrowser. Pending HTTP calls count too, so a slow API delays the response. Give them timeouts.

fakeAsync vs waitForAsync vs real async tests?

fakeAsync runs the test in a fake zone, with virtual time moved by tick() and flush(), so tests of timers and debounce are fast. It cannot deal with real XHR, and it needs zone.js. waitForAsync waits for pending tasks in the zone. Plain async/await with fixture.whenStable() works for both zone and zoneless tests. A runner's fake timers, such as those in Vitest or Jest, are the zoneless replacement for tick.

How do you test a service that uses HttpClient?
TestBed.configureTestingModule({ providers: [provideHttpClient(), provideHttpClientTesting()] });
const api = TestBed.inject(OrderApi);
const ctrl = TestBed.inject(HttpTestingController);

let result: Order[] | undefined;
api.list().subscribe(r => result = r);

const req = ctrl.expectOne('/api/orders');
expect(req.request.method).toBe('GET');
req.flush([{ id: 1 }]);
expect(result?.length).toBe(1);
ctrl.verify();

To test failures, use req.flush('fail', { status: 500, statusText: 'Server Error' }). Order matters: provideHttpClient() comes before provideHttpClientTesting().

Scenario: a big list of 20,000 rows lags on every keystroke in a filter box. How do you diagnose and fix it?
  1. Profile with Angular DevTools to see which components re-run, and the Performance panel to separate script time from layout.
  2. Debounce the input.
  3. Render fewer DOM nodes with CDK virtual scroll or server-side pagination.
  4. Use OnPush rows with a stable track.
  5. Compute the filter in a computed, so it runs once per change, and remove function calls from row templates.
  6. If the filter itself is slow, run it in a Web Worker, or on the server.
Scenario: design the front end of an order dashboard for a large team.

Standalone feature folders with lazy route arrays, one per domain. Each feature has route-scoped stores (SignalStore or signal services) and generated API clients from the Spring OpenAPI document. Shared UI lives in a library, with Storybook if the team needs one. OnPush everywhere, signals for state, RxJS for streams such as live updates over SSE or WebSocket. Interceptors for auth, correlation IDs and error toasts. Budgets and lint rules enforcing boundaries, such as an Nx workspace with module boundaries. Tests: unit for logic, harness-based component tests, a thin Playwright suite for critical flows. Deploy static files behind nginx or a CDN, with runtime config loaded at start-up.

How do you deal with a Spring Boot backend and Angular on different origins in development and production?

In development, use the Angular dev-server proxy so the browser sees one origin, and CORS does not arise. In production, either serve both under one domain (nginx routes /api to Spring), or enable CORS in Spring with an explicit origin list. If cookies are used across sites, you need SameSite=None; Secure and withCredentials: true in HttpClient. Angular's automatic XSRF header is added only to same-origin relative URLs, so a cross-origin API needs its own solution.

What is @defer doing at compile time?

The compiler sees which standalone components, directives and pipes are used only inside a @defer block, and moves them out of the eager imports into dynamic import() calls, creating a separate chunk. At run time, the trigger loads that chunk and then renders the block. If a dependency is referenced by a viewChild query or elsewhere in the same template outside the block, it stays eager, and @defer silently saves nothing.

EventEmitter vs Subject; can a service use output()?

EventEmitter extends Subject, and it is meant for @Output; using it for service messaging works but is discouraged. output() is only valid in components and directives, since it is tied to their lifetime. In a service, use a private Subject with asObservable(), or a signal.

ErrorHandler vs an HTTP error interceptor: which handles what?

An interceptor handles expected HTTP failures: it sees the status code, can retry idempotent calls, refresh a token on 401, redirect on 403, and convert a Spring ProblemDetail into a message. ErrorHandler is the last resort for unexpected bugs, such as a TypeError in a template; it should report and notify, not recover. If an HTTP error is not caught anywhere, it eventually reaches ErrorHandler too. 💡 Avoid showing two toasts for one failure by deciding where each kind of error is displayed.

How do you use httpResource / resource, and when would you still use HttpClient with RxJS?

httpResource(() => `/api/patients/${id()}`) creates a request that re-runs whenever the signals it reads change, and exposes value(), isLoading(), error() and reload() as signals. A previous request is cancelled when the inputs change, so it behaves like switchMap. It suits reads driven by component state. Use HttpClient directly for writes (POST/PUT/DELETE), and RxJS for complex flows such as debounce plus retry plus polling. These APIs were experimental when introduced, so check the version before relying on details.

PathLocationStrategy vs HashLocationStrategy: which do you use and what does the server need?

The default path strategy gives clean URLs (/patients/42), but a refresh sends that path to the server, so the server must return index.html for unknown non-API paths (nginx try_files or a Spring forward controller). The hash strategy (provideRouter(routes, withHashLocation())) gives /#/patients/42; the server only ever sees /, so no rewrite is needed. Hash URLs are uglier and do not work with SSR, so use them only when you cannot configure the server.

How do you set page titles per route, and why does it matter?

Add title: 'Patients' to a route, or a resolver function for dynamic titles. For a common suffix such as "Patients | MyApp", provide a custom TitleStrategy that overrides updateTitle(). Titles help users with many tabs open, help screen reader users know the page changed, and help SEO when combined with SSR. The Meta service sets description and Open Graph tags.

Should production builds ship source maps?

Source maps let error monitoring tools turn minified stack traces into real file and line numbers. A common approach is to generate them ("sourceMap": { "scripts": true, "hidden": true } in angular.json), upload them to the monitoring tool during CI, and not deploy them publicly. "Hidden" source maps are generated without the sourceMappingURL comment, so browsers do not fetch them. Shipping them publicly exposes readable source code, which is usually not a disaster since front-end code is public anyway, but it should be a deliberate choice.

How does Angular work with a Content Security Policy (CSP)?

A strict CSP blocks inline scripts and inline styles unless they carry a nonce. Angular inserts component styles at runtime, so you give it the nonce: add ngCspNonce="{{random}}" on the root element (filled in by the server per request) or provide the CSP_NONCE token. The server sets the same value in Content-Security-Policy: script-src 'self' 'nonce-…'; style-src 'self' 'nonce-…'. Do not use eval-style code, and note that AOT means Angular itself does not need unsafe-eval.

When would you NOT split an Angular app into micro-frontends?

When one team, or a few teams with a shared release cycle, own the app. Micro-frontends add runtime loading, shared dependency version management, duplicated styles, cross-app routing and harder end-to-end testing. A monorepo with lazy-loaded feature libraries and enforced module boundaries (for example Nx tags) gives most of the code-ownership benefit with one build. Choose micro-frontends when teams truly need independent deployment or must combine different frameworks.

How do you make a custom dropdown or modal accessible?

Prefer native elements (<select>, <dialog>) or a tested library such as Angular Material or CDK. If you build one: give it the right role (role="listbox", role="dialog" with aria-modal="true" and aria-labelledby), support keyboard (Escape closes, arrow keys move, Enter selects), trap focus inside a modal with cdkTrapFocus, and return focus to the trigger button on close. Reflect state with [attr.aria-expanded] and aria-activedescendant.

JavaScript Language

Scope, hoisting, closures, this, prototypes, the event loop, promises and async/await, ES6+ features.

console.log('1');
setTimeout(() => console.log('2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('3'));
console.log('4');
// Output: 1 4 3 2   (sync → microtasks → macrotasks)

Types and coercion rules

JavaScript has eight types: seven primitives (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and object. Coercion is the automatic conversion of a value to another type when an operator needs it. The language has three core conversions, and every odd result comes from them.

ValueToNumberToStringToBoolean
undefinedNaN'undefined'false
null0'null'false
true / false1 / 0'true' / 'false'itself
'' and ' '0itself'' false, ' ' true
'12', '12px'12, NaNitselftrue
[], [5], [1,2]0, 5, NaN'', '5', '1,2'true
{}NaN'[object Object]'true
SymbolTypeErrorTypeError if implicit; String(sym) workstrue
BigInt 1nNumber(1n) is 1; unary +1n is a TypeError'1'0n false, others true

How an object becomes a primitive

  1. If it has Symbol.toPrimitive, call it with a hint: 'number', 'string' or 'default'.
  2. Otherwise, for the hints number and default, try valueOf(), then toString(). For hint string, try toString() first.
  3. Use the first result that is a primitive. If there is none, throw a TypeError.

For a plain object or array, valueOf() returns the object itself, which is not a primitive, so toString() decides.

The == algorithm (loose equality)

  1. Same type: compare like ===. Objects compare by reference.
  2. null and undefined equal each other and nothing else.
  3. Number vs string: convert the string to a number.
  4. A boolean on either side: convert the boolean to a number and restart.
  5. Object vs primitive: apply ToPrimitive to the object and restart.
  6. BigInt vs number or string: compare the mathematical values.
Tip: the one accepted use of == is x == null, which checks for both null and undefined. Everywhere else use ===. To compare objects, you need your own deep comparison.

Operators worth knowing

OperatorBehaviourTrap
a ?? bb only if a is null or undefinedCannot be mixed with || or && without parentheses (SyntaxError)
a?.b, a?.[k], a?.()Stops and gives undefined if a is nullishNot valid on the left side of an assignment
||=, &&=, ??=Assign only if the condition holdsThe right side is not evaluated otherwise
**Exponent, right-associative-2 ** 2 is a SyntaxError; write (-2) ** 2
%Remainder, sign follows the dividend-7 % 3 is -1, as in Java
& | ^ ~ << >> >>>Work on 32-bit integersValues above 2³¹ wrap, so x | 0 truncates to 32 bits
inIs the key on the object or its prototypes?'length' in [] is true
instanceofIs C.prototype on the chain?Fails for arrays from another iframe; use Array.isArray
deleteRemoves an own propertyDoes nothing to variables; a hole in arrays
void xEvaluates x, gives undefinedMostly seen in minified code
,Evaluates both, gives the lastLoses this in (0, o.f)()

Destructuring, rest and spread

// Rename, default, nested, computed key
const { id: userId, role = 'USER', address: { city } = {}, [key]: dynamic } = user;

// Function parameters: the shape is the documentation
function createUser({ name, email, active = true } = {}) { /* ... */ }

// Immutable updates, the pattern Angular OnPush and NgRx rely on
const next = { ...state, user: { ...state.user, name: 'Asha' } };
const added = [...list, item];
const removed = list.filter(x => x.id !== id);
const replaced = list.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, done: true } : x);

// Remove a key without mutating
const { password, ...safeUser } = user;

// Merge order: later keys win, so put defaults first
const cfg = { ...defaults, ...overrides };

Rest collects (it appears on the left, or in parameters) and spread expands (on the right, or in a call). Array destructuring works with any iterable, and object destructuring reads properties. Destructuring a null or undefined value throws a TypeError, so give a default such as = {}. A statement that starts with { is a block, so destructuring assignment needs parentheses: ({ a } = obj);.

Copy a rangeslice(start, end)NoNew array

Copying forms (ES2023)toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with(i, v)NoNew array

sort has been stable since ES2019: equal items keep their relative order. For numbers, use (a, b) => a - b. For human-language strings use a.localeCompare(b) or an Intl.Collator.

Object utilities and property descriptors

Every property has a descriptor: value, writable, enumerable, configurable, or get and set for accessors. Object.defineProperty defaults them all to false. Three levels of lock exist, and all are shallow.

Add propsDelete propsChange values
Object.preventExtensionsNoYesYes

Gotcha: these are one-way. In the earlier Object.freeze snippet, the later Object.defineProperty(o, 'id', ...) line would throw TypeError: Cannot define property id, object is not extensible if run on the same object. Read those lines as separate examples.

Classes: everything beyond the basics

class Account {
  static #created = 0;                       // private static
  static MIN = 100;                          // public static
  static { Account.MIN = Number(process.env.MIN ?? 100); }   // static block (ES2022)

  #balance = 0;                              // private instance field, set per instance
  owner;                                     // public field, on the instance

  constructor(owner) { this.owner = owner; Account.#created++; }

  get balance() { return this.#balance; }    // accessor on the prototype
  set balance(v) { throw new Error('use deposit'); }

  deposit(n) { this.#check(n); this.#balance += n; return this; }   // return this: chaining
  #check(n) { if (n <= 0) throw new RangeError('amount'); }         // private method

  static of(owner) { return new this(owner); }   // `this` is the class, so subclasses work
  toString() { return `${this.owner}: ${this.#balance}`; }
  [Symbol.iterator]() { return [this.owner, this.#balance][Symbol.iterator](); }
}

class Savings extends Account {
  deposit(n) { return super.deposit(n * 1.01); }   // super.method
}

// Mixin: a function from a class to a class
const Timestamped = Base => class extends Base { at = Date.now(); };
class Order extends Timestamped(Object) {}
FeatureJavaScript classJava class
InheritancePrototype chain, single extends, any expression allowedClass-based, single extends, interfaces
Privacy#x is enforced at run timeprivate is enforced by the compiler and JVM, and reflection may bypass it
OverloadingNone; the last definition wins. Check arguments insteadBy signature
InterfacesNone at run time (TypeScript adds them at compile time)Yes
HoistingTDZ, like letNot applicable
MethodsNon-enumerable, on the prototype, can be detached (lose this)Always bound to the receiver

const m = new Map([['a', 1]]);
m.set('b', 2).set('c', 3);                // chainable
for (const [k, v] of m) console.log(k, v);
Object.fromEntries(m);                    // Map → object
new Map(Object.entries(obj));             // object → Map

const s = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]);
[...s];                                   // [1, 2, 3], the standard dedupe
const ids = new Set(list.map(x => x.id));
ids.has(5);                               // O(1) on average, versus includes which is O(n)

// ES2025 Set methods (modern browsers, Node 22+)
// a.union(b)  a.intersection(b)  a.difference(b)  a.symmetricDifference(b)
// a.isSubsetOf(b)  a.isSupersetOf(b)  a.isDisjointFrom(b)

Modules: forms you will be asked about

export const a = 1;                 // named
export default class Foo {}         // default, at most one per module
export { x as y };                  // renamed
export * from './other.js';         // re-export all named (not default)
export { default as Foo } from './foo.js';   // barrel files

import Foo, { a, y as z } from './m.js';
import * as ns from './m.js';       // namespace object, read-only
import './side-effect.js';          // run for its side effects only
import.meta.url;                    // URL of this module
const mod = await import('./lazy.js');       // dynamic import, returns a promise

A module's top-level code runs once, however many times it is imported. Module instances are cached by resolved URL. Circular imports are allowed, and ES module live bindings make them work in many cases, but reading a const from a module that has not finished evaluating throws a ReferenceError (the TDZ). Barrel files (index.ts re-exporting everything) are convenient, but they can pull in more code than needed and make bundles and test start-up heavier.

Error handling

Built-in errorThrown when
ReferenceErrorAn unknown name, or a TDZ access
TypeErrorWrong type: calling a non-function, reading a property of null, assigning to a const
RangeErrorValue out of range, such as stack overflow or new Array(-1)
SyntaxErrorBad code, or JSON.parse on bad input
URIErrordecodeURIComponent('%')
AggregateErrorPromise.any when everything fails; holds .errors
DOMExceptionBrowser APIs, such as AbortError, QuotaExceededError
class ValidationError extends Error {
  constructor(field, options) { super(`Invalid ${field}`, options); this.name = 'ValidationError'; this.field = field; }
}
try {
  await save(order);
} catch (err) {
  if (err instanceof ValidationError) showFieldError(err.field);
  else throw new Error('Could not save order', { cause: err });   // wrap, keep the original (ES2022)
}
// Catch-all reporting
window.addEventListener('error', e => report(e.error));           // uncaught sync errors
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', e => report(e.reason));

Only catch what you can handle, and rethrow the rest. try/catch does not see errors thrown later in a callback, because that callback runs on a fresh stack. In async code, await inside try does catch rejections. Unlike Java there are no checked exceptions and only one catch per try, so branch with instanceof.

Regular expressions

SyntaxMeaning
g i m s u y d vFlags: global, ignore case, multi-line anchors, dot matches newline, Unicode, sticky, match indices, Unicode sets
\d \w \s . \bDigit, word char, whitespace, any char, word boundary. Capitals negate
* + ? {n,m}Greedy quantifiers; append ? for lazy
( ) (?: ) (?<name> )Capturing, non-capturing, named group
\1 \k<name>Back-reference
(?= ) (?! ) (?<= ) (?<! )Lookahead, negative lookahead, lookbehind, negative lookbehind
\p{L} \p{Lu}Unicode property escapes; needs the u or v flag
MethodReturnsUse
re.test(s)BooleanYes or no check
re.exec(s)Match with groups, or nullManual loop
s.match(re)Match, or all strings with gWith g, groups are lost
s.matchAll(re)Iterator of matchesAll matches with groups; requires g
s.replace(re, x)New stringx can use $1, $<name>, or be a function
s.split(re)ArraySplit on a pattern
Gotcha: nested quantifiers such as (a+)+$ backtrack exponentially on inputs that nearly match. This is ReDoS (regular expression denial of service). JS regexes run on the main thread, so a bad pattern on user input freezes the page or a Node server. Keep patterns simple and limit input length.

Date, time zones and Intl

A Date holds one number: milliseconds since 1 January 1970 UTC. It has no time zone. The zone appears only when you format it, or use the local getters such as getHours(). Pass instants between a Java backend and the browser as ISO-8601 strings with an offset (2026-11-04T10:30:00Z), which map to Instant or OffsetDateTime in Java. A date without a time, such as a birth date, should stay as 'YYYY-MM-DD' (Java LocalDate), since converting it to an instant can shift the day. The newer Temporal API addresses the design problems of Date, with separate types for instants and plain dates. Check current browser support before relying on it, or use a library such as date-fns or Luxon.

new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { style: 'currency', currency: 'INR' }).format(1234567.5);  // ₹12,34,567.50
new Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', { notation: 'compact' }).format(1234567);                  // 12L
new Intl.DateTimeFormat('en-GB', { dateStyle: 'medium', timeStyle: 'short', timeZone: 'Asia/Kolkata' })
  .format(new Date(0));                                                                   // 1 Jan 1970, 05:30
new Intl.RelativeTimeFormat('en', { numeric: 'auto' }).format(-1, 'day');                 // yesterday
new Intl.ListFormat('en', { type: 'conjunction' }).format(['a', 'b', 'c']);               // a, b, and c
new Intl.PluralRules('en', { type: 'ordinal' }).select(22);                               // 'two' (for 22nd)
['ä', 'a', 'z'].sort(new Intl.Collator('de').compare);                                    // a ä z

Create an Intl formatter once and reuse it, since constructing one is expensive. toLocaleString() builds one internally on each call.

DOM events in detail

el.addEventListener('click', handler, {
  capture: false,      // listen during the capture phase?
  once: true,          // remove automatically after the first call
  passive: true,       // promises not to call preventDefault, so scrolling stays smooth
  signal: ctrl.signal  // remove on abort
});

// Custom events: bubbles must be set explicitly
el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('cart:add', { detail: { id: 7 }, bubbles: true }));

// Delegation that survives nested elements inside the button
list.addEventListener('click', e => {
  const btn = e.target.closest('button[data-id]');
  if (btn && list.contains(btn)) remove(btn.dataset.id);
});
MemberMeaning
e.targetThe element where the event started; can be a nested child
e.currentTargetThe element whose listener is running; null after the handler returns, so read it before any await
e.stopPropagation()Stops moving to other elements; other listeners on this element still run
e.stopImmediatePropagation()Also stops the remaining listeners on this element
e.preventDefault()Cancels the default action, if e.cancelable is true
e.composedPath()The full path, including inside open shadow roots
e.isTrustedfalse for events made by script

Most events bubble. Exceptions include focus, blur, mouseenter, mouseleave, load and scroll on elements. Use focusin, focusout, mouseover and mouseout for delegation. input fires on each change, change on commit (usually blur). Use e.key, since keyCode is deprecated. Prefer pointerdown and related events when you need to support mouse, touch and pen with a single code path.

// Web Storage holds strings only, so serialise, and handle errors
try {

} catch (e) { /* QuotaExceededError, or storage blocked */ }
const prefs2 = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem('prefs') ?? '{}');

window.addEventListener('storage', e => { if (e.key === 'logout') location.assign('/login'); });

// Server sets a secure session cookie
// Set-Cookie: SESSION=abc; Path=/; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Max-Age=3600
Cookie attributeEffect

Debounce vs throttle, visually

Polyfills and transpilers

A polyfill adds a missing runtime API using existing features, for example defining Array.prototype.at where it does not exist. A transpiler rewrites syntax the runtime cannot parse, for example turning ?. into conditional checks, since you cannot polyfill syntax. core-js is the common polyfill library, Babel, TypeScript and esbuild handle transpiling, and a browserslist configuration sets the targets. A polyfill must check first (if (!Array.prototype.at)) and define the method with Object.defineProperty as non-enumerable, otherwise it appears in for...in loops.

Observer APIs: IntersectionObserver, ResizeObserver, MutationObserver

These browser APIs replace expensive polling and scroll/resize listeners. The browser calls you back asynchronously and in batches, so they do not block scrolling.

APITells you whenTypical use
IntersectionObserverAn element enters or leaves the viewport (or another root)Infinite scroll, lazy-loading images, "seen" analytics, sticky header state
ResizeObserverAn element's size changes (not just the window)Responsive components, charts that redraw to fit their container
MutationObserverDOM children, attributes or text changeReacting to third-party widgets that change the DOM
// Infinite scroll: load the next page when a sentinel at the bottom becomes visible
const sentinel = document.querySelector('#sentinel');
const io = new IntersectionObserver(async ([entry]) => {
  if (!entry.isIntersecting || loading) return;
  loading = true;
  appendRows(await fetchPage(++page));
  loading = false;
}, { rootMargin: '200px' });          // start loading 200px before it is visible
io.observe(sentinel);
// later: io.disconnect();            // always disconnect to avoid leaks

const ro = new ResizeObserver(entries => {
  for (const e of entries) chart.resize(e.contentRect.width);
});
ro.observe(document.querySelector('#chart'));

Web Components: Custom Elements, Shadow DOM and templates

Web Components are browser-native components that work in any framework or none. Ionic's UI and Angular Elements are built on them.

  • Custom Elements: customElements.define('user-card', class extends HTMLElement {…}). Lifecycle callbacks: connectedCallback, disconnectedCallback, attributeChangedCallback (for names listed in static observedAttributes).
  • Shadow DOM: this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }) gives the element its own DOM tree whose styles do not leak in or out. Outside CSS can style it only through CSS custom properties and ::part().
  • <template> and <slot>: inert markup to clone, and placeholders where the user's child content is shown (like Angular's ng-content).
  • Element names must contain a hyphen. Attributes are strings; pass objects through properties.
class UserCard extends HTMLElement {
  static observedAttributes = ['name'];
  constructor() {
    super();
    this.attachShadow({ mode: 'open' }).innerHTML =
      `<style>p { color: var(--card-color, navy); }</style>
       <p part="label"></p><slot></slot>`;
  }
  attributeChangedCallback(attr, oldV, newV) {
    this.shadowRoot.querySelector('p').textContent = newV;   // textContent: no XSS
  }
}
customElements.define('user-card', UserCard);
// <user-card name="Asha"><small>Admin</small></user-card>

Newer additions worth knowing (ES2024 and ES2025)

  • Promise.withResolvers() returns { promise, resolve, reject }, so you can resolve a promise from outside without the constructor wrapper pattern.
  • Map.groupBy(items, fn) groups into a Map; use it when the keys are not strings (Object.groupBy returns a plain object).
  • Iterator helpers: iterators gain .map(), .filter(), .take(), .drop(), .toArray(); these are lazy, unlike array methods. Iterator.from(x) wraps any iterable.
  • Array.fromAsync(asyncIterable) collects an async iterable into an array.
  • RegExp v flag, String.prototype.isWellFormed(), resizable ArrayBuffer, and Atomics.waitAsync are less often asked.
  • Check browser support (or your transpiler and core-js target) before relying on the newest features in production.
// Promise.withResolvers: wrap a one-time event
function waitForMessage(ws) {
  const { promise, resolve, reject } = Promise.withResolvers();
  ws.addEventListener('message', e => resolve(JSON.parse(e.data)), { once: true });
  ws.addEventListener('error', reject, { once: true });
  return promise;
}

// Lazy iterator helpers: only the first 3 matching items are computed
function* ids() { let i = 0; while (true) yield i++; }
const firstEvens = ids().filter(n => n % 2 === 0).take(3).toArray();  // [0, 2, 4]

Interview Questions — JavaScript

var vs let vs const?
varletconst
ScopeFunctionBlockBlock
HoistingHoisted and initialized to undefinedHoisted but in the TDZ (ReferenceError)TDZ
Re-declareYesNoNo
ReassignYesYesNo (the object can still be mutated)
What is hoisting?

Declarations are moved to the top of their scope during compilation. Function declarations are fully hoisted, so you can call them before they're defined. var is hoisted as undefined. let, const and class are hoisted but sit in the Temporal Dead Zone until their declaration runs. Function expressions and arrow functions follow the rules of the variable they're assigned to.

What is a closure? Give a use case.

A function that remembers variables from its outer lexical scope even after that outer function has returned. Uses: data privacy, factories, memoization, debounce, currying.

function counter() {
  let count = 0;                       // private
  return { inc: () => ++count, get: () => count };
}
const c = counter(); c.inc(); c.inc(); c.get(); // 2

// classic loop bug
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 3 3 3
for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i)); // 0 1 2
How does this work? Arrow vs normal functions?

this depends on how a function is called: as a method it's the object · as a plain call it's undefined in strict mode (or window otherwise) · with new it's the new instance · with call/apply/bind it's whatever you pass · in event handlers it's the element. Arrow functions have no this of their own; they inherit it from the enclosing scope (lexical this). They also have no arguments and can't be used with new.

call vs apply vs bind?

fn.call(obj, a, b) invokes now with arguments listed out · fn.apply(obj, [a, b]) invokes now with an array · fn.bind(obj, a) returns a new function with this fixed, to call later.

== vs ===? Truthy/falsy?

== converts types before comparing ('5' == 5 is true, null == undefined is true). === is strict: no conversion. Always use ===. The falsy values: false, 0, -0, 0n, "", null, undefined, NaN. Everything else is truthy, including [] and {}.

null vs undefined?

undefined: declared but not assigned, a missing property, or no return value. null: explicitly set to "no value". typeof null === 'object' is a historical bug. Use ?? (nullish coalescing) and ?. (optional chaining).

Explain prototypes and prototypal inheritance.

Every object has a hidden [[Prototype]] link. When a property isn't found on the object, JS walks up the prototype chain. class is syntactic sugar over this.

class Animal { speak() { return 'generic'; } }
class Dog extends Animal { speak() { return 'woof ' + super.speak(); } }
Object.getPrototypeOf(new Dog()) === Dog.prototype; // true
Promises and async/await — and Promise combinators?

A Promise is pending, then either fulfilled or rejected. async functions always return a promise, and await pauses until it settles (use try/catch for errors).

async function load() {
  try {
    const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([api.user(), api.orders()]); // parallel
    return { user, orders };
  } catch (e) { console.error(e); }
}

Promise.all fails if any one fails · allSettled waits for all and returns each result · race settles with the first to settle · any resolves with the first to fulfill.

Explain the event loop (microtasks vs macrotasks).

JS runs on one thread. Async work is handed to Web or Node APIs, and their callbacks are queued. When the call stack is empty, the loop runs all microtasks (promises) first, then one macrotask (setTimeout, I/O), renders, and repeats. See the diagram above.

Debounce vs Throttle (implement debounce)?

Debounce: run once after the calls have stopped for N ms (search input). Throttle: run at most once every N ms (scroll, resize).

function debounce(fn, ms) {
  let t;
  return (...args) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...args), ms); };
}
Important ES6+ features?

let/const · arrow functions · template literals · destructuring · default, rest and spread parameters · classes · modules (import/export) · Promises · Map/Set/WeakMap · Symbol · iterators and generators · async/await (ES2017) · optional chaining ?. and nullish ?? (ES2020) · Array.prototype.at, Object.hasOwn · structuredClone (HTML standard, not ECMAScript) · Array.prototype.toSorted/toReversed (ES2023) · Object.groupBy (ES2024).

map vs forEach vs filter vs reduce?
const nums = [1, 2, 3, 4];
nums.map(n => n * 2);              // [2,4,6,8]  new array
nums.filter(n => n % 2 === 0);     // [2,4]
nums.reduce((acc, n) => acc + n, 0); // 10
nums.forEach(n => console.log(n)); // returns undefined (side-effects only)
Shallow copy vs deep copy?

A shallow copy ({...obj}, Object.assign, [...arr]) copies only the top level, so nested objects are still shared. A deep copy uses structuredClone(obj) (modern) or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), which loses Dates, functions and undefined, and fails on cycles.

Event bubbling, capturing and delegation?

Events travel in three phases: capture (window down to the target), target, then bubble (back up). addEventListener(type, fn, true) listens in the capture phase. stopPropagation() stops the travel and preventDefault() cancels the default action. Delegation: put one listener on a parent and check e.target, which is efficient and also works for elements added later.

What is currying? Pure functions? Higher-order functions?

Currying: f(a,b,c) → f(a)(b)(c). A pure function returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects. A higher-order function takes or returns functions (map, filter, debounce).

localStorage vs sessionStorage vs cookies?
localStoragesessionStorageCookie
About 5–10 MB, kept until clearedLasts only as long as the tabAbout 4 KB, has an expiry
Readable by JS (XSS risk)Readable by JSSent with every request; can be HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite
What is TypeScript and why use it (Angular)?

A typed superset of JS that compiles to JS. It gives static types, interfaces, generics, enums, access modifiers and decorators. Errors are caught at compile time, and IDE support and refactoring are better. Know interface vs type, union and intersection types, unknown vs any, generics, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record, Readonly).

Output: coercion with + and other operators
console.log(1 + '2', '3' - 1, '3' * '4', true + true, [] + [], [] + {}, 1 + null, 1 + undefined);
console.log('5' + + '2', '5' - - '2', +[], +{}, +'', +null, +undefined, +true, +'12px', +' 12 ');
console.log(1 < 2 < 3, 3 > 2 > 1, 'b' > 'a', '10' < '9', 10 < '9');

Output (executed):

12 2 12 2  [object Object] 1 NaN
52 7 0 NaN 0 0 NaN 1 NaN 12
true false true true false

+ concatenates if either side is a string after ToPrimitive; other arithmetic operators always convert to numbers. [] becomes '' and {} becomes '[object Object]'. 3 > 2 > 1 is true > 1, which is 1 > 1. Two strings compare by UTF-16 code units, so '10' < '9' is true; with a number on one side, both become numbers.

Output: the == table
console.log([] == false, [] == ![], '' == 0, '0' == false, null == 0, null >= 0, undefined == 0);
console.log(null == undefined, NaN == NaN, [1] == 1, [1, 2] == '1,2', ({}) == '[object Object]');
console.log(new String('a') == 'a', new String('a') == new String('a'), new String('a') === 'a');

Output (executed):

true true true true false true false
true false true true true
true false false

[] == ![]: ![] is false, then both sides reach 0. null == 0 is false because null equals only undefined under ==, yet null >= 0 is true because relational operators convert null to 0. Two objects compare by reference, so conversion never happens.

Output: typeof, parseInt and numbers
console.log(typeof NaN, typeof null, typeof [], typeof function () {}, typeof class {}, typeof 1n, typeof Symbol());
console.log(parseInt('12px'), parseInt('px12'), Number('12px'), parseInt('0x1f'), parseInt('101', 2), parseFloat('1.5.5'));
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt));
console.log(0.1 + 0.2, (0.1 + 0.2).toFixed(2), 1.005.toFixed(2), 2 ** 53 + 1, 1 / 0, -1 / 0, 0 / 0, 0 === -0);
console.log(Math.max(), Math.min(), Math.max(1, 'a'), Math.max(...[1, 5, 3]), Number.isNaN('a'), isNaN('a'));

Output (executed):

number object object function function bigint symbol
12 NaN NaN 31 5 1.5
[ 1, NaN, NaN ]
0.30000000000000004 0.30 1.00 9007199254740992 Infinity -Infinity NaN true
-Infinity Infinity NaN 5 false true

map passes (value, index, array), so parseInt('2', 1) and parseInt('3', 2) are NaN (radix 1 is invalid and 3 is not a binary digit). 1.005 is stored slightly below 1.005, so it rounds down. 2**53 + 1 is not representable. Math.max() with no arguments is -Infinity, the identity for max. isNaN coerces; Number.isNaN does not.

Output: object keys are strings or symbols
const a = {}, b = { k: 1 }, c = { k: 2 };
a[b] = 'first';
a[c] = 'second';
console.log(a[b], Object.keys(a));
const o = { 1: 'x', b: 'y', 2: 'z', a: 'w' };
console.log(Object.keys(o), o['1'] === o[1]);
const m = new Map([[b, 'first'], [c, 'second']]);
console.log(m.get(b), m.get({ k: 1 }), new Map([[NaN, 1]]).get(NaN), new Map([[0, 1]]).get(-0));
console.log(new Set([1, '1', 1, NaN, NaN, {}, {}]).size);

Output (executed):

second [ '[object Object]' ]
[ '1', '2', 'b', 'a' ] true
first undefined 1 1
5

Both object keys stringify to '[object Object]'. Key order is: integer-like keys ascending, then strings in insertion order, then symbols. A Map keeps object identity and uses SameValueZero, so NaN equals NaN and -0 equals 0.

Output: array quirks
const arr = [1, 2, 3];
arr.length = 1; arr[3] = 9;
console.log(arr, arr.length);
console.log([, , ].length, new Array(3), new Array(3).length, new Array('3'), Array.of(3));
console.log(new Array(2).map(() => 1), Array.from({ length: 2 }, (_, i) => i * 2), [...Array(2).keys()]);

console.log(d, d.length, 1 in d);

console.log([1, 2, 3].includes('2'), [NaN].includes(NaN), [NaN].indexOf(NaN), [1, 2, 3].at(-1), [3, 4].findLast(n => n > 0));

[ 1, <2 empty items>, 9 ] 4
2 [ <3 empty items> ] 3 [ '3' ] [ 3 ]
[ <2 empty items> ] [ 0, 2 ] [ 0, 1 ]
[ 1, <1 empty item>, 3 ] 3 false
[ 1, 10, 9 ] [ 1, 9, 10 ] [ 'a', 'b' ]

Writing past the end leaves holes. map skips holes, so filling with Array.from or .fill() is needed. delete on an array makes a hole and keeps the length. The default sort compares strings, so 10 comes before 9. reverse and sort mutate; toSorted and toReversed return copies.

Output: destructuring, defaults and spread
const { a = 1, b = 2, c = 3 } = { a: null, b: undefined };
console.log(a, b, c);
const { x: { y = 5 } = {}, ...rest } = { p: 1, q: 2 };
console.log(y, rest);
let m = 1, n = 2; [m, n] = [n, m];
console.log(m, n);
const [first, , third = 'd', ...others] = 'hello';
console.log(first, third, others);
const orig = { n: 1, nested: { v: 1 }, get g() { return 'computed'; } };
const copy = { ...orig, n: 2 };
copy.nested.v = 99;
console.log(orig.n, orig.nested.v, Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(copy, 'g').value);
