function f({ id, name = 'anon' } = {}, ...args) { return [id, name, args.length]; }
console.log(f(), f({ id: 1 }, 2, 3));

Output (executed):

null 2 3
5 { p: 1, q: 2 }
2 1
h l [ 'l', 'o' ]
1 99 computed
{ '0': 7, '1': 'i' } [ 'a', 'b', 1 ]
[ undefined, 'anon', 0 ] [ 1, 'anon', 2 ]

A default applies only for undefined, never for null. Spread makes a shallow copy and runs getters, so the copy holds a plain value. Spreading null or undefined in an object is allowed, but in an array or call it throws because they are not iterable.

Output: logical operators and short-circuit
console.log(0 || 'a', 0 ?? 'a', '' || 'b', '' ?? 'b', null ?? 'c', undefined || null);
console.log(1 && 2, 0 && 2, null?.x, null?.x.y.z, ({}).a?.(), void 0);
let v = 0; v ||= 5; let w = 0; w ??= 5; let u = 1; u &&= 7;
console.log(v, w, u);
console.log(!!'false', !!'0', !!0, !![], !!{}, !!NaN, !!-1, !!0n);
let i = 0;
const r = i++ + ++i;
console.log(r, i, typeof (1, 'x'));

Output (executed):

a 0 b  c null
2 0 undefined undefined undefined undefined
5 0 7
true true false true true false true false
2 2 string

|| and && return one of their operands, not a boolean. || falls through on any falsy value and ?? only on null or undefined. Optional chaining short-circuits the whole rest of the chain. i++ yields 0 and leaves i at 1; then ++i makes it 2.

Output: ToPrimitive, valueOf, toString and Symbol.toPrimitive
const money = {
  amount: 5,
  valueOf() { return this.amount; },
  toString() { return 'INR ' + this.amount; }
};
console.log(money + 1, `${money}`, String(money), money * 2, money + '');
const hinted = { [Symbol.toPrimitive](hint) { return hint === 'number' ? 42 : hint === 'string' ? 'str' : 'default'; } };
console.log(+hinted, `${hinted}`, hinted + '');
console.log(`${[1, [2, 3]]}`, `${{}}`, String(null), String([null]), String([undefined, 1]), [] + null);
console.log(new Date(0) + 1 === new Date(0).toString() + '1', new Date(5) - 1);

Output (executed):

6 INR 5 INR 5 10 5
42 str default
1,2,3 [object Object] null  ,1 null
true 4

ToPrimitive takes a hint. For number and default it tries valueOf first, for string it tries toString first, and Symbol.toPrimitive overrides both. Date is the exception: its default hint is string, so date + 1 concatenates. Subtraction always hints number.

Output: strings, template literals and tagged templates
const s = 'abc';
s[0] = 'z';
console.log(s, s.length, s.at(-1), 'a-b-c'.replaceAll('-', '+'), 'a-b-c'.replace('-', '+'), 'x'.padStart(3, '0'));
console.log('😀'.length, [...'😀'].length, 'abc'.slice(-2), 'abc'.substring(2, 0), 'abc'.substr?.(1, 1));
function tag(strings, ...vals) { return strings.raw.join('|') + ' / ' + vals.join(','); }
console.log(tag`a${1}b\n${2}c`);
console.log(`line1
line2`.split('\n').length, 'ab'.repeat(2), ' x '.trim().length, 'a,b,,c'.split(','), 'abc'.split(''));

Output (executed):

abc 3 c a+b+c a+b-c 00x
2 1 bc ab b
a|b\n|c / 1,2
2 abab 1 [ 'a', 'b', '', 'c' ] [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]

Strings are immutable, and the assignment is silently ignored in sloppy mode. .length counts UTF-16 code units, so an emoji is 2, while spread iterates code points. substring swaps its arguments if needed. A tag function receives the literal parts and the values separately, which is how libraries implement safe SQL and HTML templates.

A derived class's fields are set up right after super() returns. During the parent's construction, the overridden init already runs but bField does not exist yet. Java has the same trap with overridden methods called from constructors. Static members inherit through the class's own prototype chain, so B.count reads A.count.

Write a polyfill: Array.prototype.myMap, myFilter and myReduce
Array.prototype.myMap = function (fn, thisArg) {
  const out = new Array(this.length);
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    if (i in this) out[i] = fn.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this);   // skip holes like the native one
  }
  return out;
};
Array.prototype.myFilter = function (fn, thisArg) {
  const out = [];
  for (let i = 0; i < this.length; i++) {
    if (i in this && fn.call(thisArg, this[i], i, this)) out.push(this[i]);
  }
  return out;
};
Array.prototype.myReduce = function (fn, ...init) {
  let i = 0, acc;
  if (init.length) acc = init[0];
  else {
    while (i < this.length && !(i in this)) i++;
    if (i >= this.length) throw new TypeError('Reduce of empty array with no initial value');
    acc = this[i++];
  }
  for (; i < this.length; i++) if (i in this) acc = fn(acc, this[i], i, this);
  return acc;
};
console.log([1, , 3].myMap(x => x * 2), [1, 2, 3].myFilter(x => x > 1));
console.log([1, 2, 3].myReduce((a, b) => a + b), [1, 2].myReduce((a, b) => a + b, 10));
try { [].myReduce((a, b) => a + b); } catch (e) { console.log(e.message); }

Output (executed):

[ 2, <1 empty item>, 6 ] [ 2, 3 ]
6 13
Reduce of empty array with no initial value

Interviewers look for four details: this usage (so no arrow function), thisArg, skipping holes with i in this, and reduce without an initial value. Using a rest parameter tells "no initial value" apart from an explicit undefined. In real polyfills, define these with Object.defineProperty so they are non-enumerable.

Write polyfills: call, apply, bind, and new
Function.prototype.myCall = function (ctx, ...args) {
  ctx = ctx == null ? globalThis : Object(ctx);
  const key = Symbol();                 // avoids clobbering an existing property
  ctx[key] = this;
  try { return ctx[key](...args); } finally { delete ctx[key]; }
};
Function.prototype.myApply = function (ctx, args = []) { return this.myCall(ctx, ...args); };
Function.prototype.myBind = function (ctx, ...bound) {
  const target = this;
  function wrapped(...args) {
    const isNew = this instanceof wrapped;
    return target.apply(isNew ? this : ctx, [...bound, ...args]);
  }
  wrapped.prototype = Object.create(target.prototype);
  return wrapped;
};
function myNew(Ctor, ...args) {
  const obj = Object.create(Ctor.prototype);
  const r = Ctor.apply(obj, args);
  return (typeof r === 'object' && r !== null) || typeof r === 'function' ? r : obj;
}
function greet(g, p) { return `${g} ${this.name}${p}`; }
const u = { name: 'Asha' };
console.log(greet.myCall(u, 'Hi', '!'), greet.myApply(u, ['Hey', '?']), greet.myBind(u, 'Yo')('.'));
function Pt(x) { this.x = x; }
const BP = Pt.myBind({ x: 'ignored' }, 7);
console.log(new BP().x, new BP() instanceof Pt, myNew(Pt, 3).x, myNew(Pt, 3) instanceof Pt);

Output (executed):

Hi Asha! Hey Asha? Yo Asha.
7 true 3 true

The trick behind call is to make the function a temporary method, so that implicit binding sets this. bind must detect a new call so the instance wins over the bound object. new returns the constructor's result only if that is an object.

Write polyfills: Promise.all, allSettled, race and a retry helper
Promise.myAll = iterable => new Promise((resolve, reject) => {
  const items = [...iterable], out = new Array(items.length);
  let left = items.length;
  if (!left) return resolve(out);
  items.forEach((p, i) => Promise.resolve(p).then(v => {
    out[i] = v;
    if (--left === 0) resolve(out);
  }, reject));
});
Promise.myAllSettled = iterable => Promise.myAll([...iterable].map(p =>
  Promise.resolve(p).then(value => ({ status: 'fulfilled', value }), reason => ({ status: 'rejected', reason }))));
Promise.myRace = iterable => new Promise((res, rej) => {
  for (const p of iterable) Promise.resolve(p).then(res, rej);
});
async function retry(fn, { times = 3, delayMs = 10 } = {}) {
  for (let attempt = 1; ; attempt++) {
    try { return await fn(attempt); }
    catch (e) {
      if (attempt >= times) throw e;
      await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r, delayMs * 2 ** (attempt - 1)));  // exponential backoff
    }
  }
}
const later = (v, ms) => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
(async () => {
  console.log(await Promise.myAll([later('slow', 20), later('fast', 1), 3]));
  console.log(await Promise.myAll([]), await Promise.myRace([later('a', 20), later('b', 1)]));
  console.log(await Promise.myAllSettled([1, Promise.reject('no')]));
  console.log(await retry(n => { if (n < 3) throw new Error('fail ' + n); return 'ok on attempt ' + n; }));
})();

Output (executed):

[ 'slow', 'fast', 3 ]
[] b
[
  { status: 'fulfilled', value: 1 },
  { status: 'rejected', reason: 'no' }
]
ok on attempt 3

Common mistakes: pushing results in completion order rather than by index, counting with the array's length (it is preset, and holes fool it), forgetting the empty-input case, and not wrapping plain values with Promise.resolve.

Write utilities: debounce with cancel, throttle, once, memoize, curry
function debounce(fn, ms, { leading = false } = {}) {
  let t;
  function d(...args) {
    const callNow = leading && t === undefined;
    clearTimeout(t);
    t = setTimeout(() => { t = undefined; if (!leading) fn.apply(this, args); }, ms);
    if (callNow) fn.apply(this, args);
  }
  d.cancel = () => { clearTimeout(t); t = undefined; };
  return d;
}
function throttle(fn, ms) {
  let last = -Infinity, timer, lastArgs;
  return function (...args) {
    const wait = ms - (Date.now() - last);
    lastArgs = args;
    if (wait <= 0) { last = Date.now(); fn.apply(this, args); }
    else if (!timer) timer = setTimeout(() => {       // trailing call with the latest args
      timer = null; last = Date.now(); fn.apply(this, lastArgs);
    }, wait);
  };
}
const once = fn => { let done = false, r; return (...a) => done ? r : (done = true, r = fn(...a)); };
const memoize = (fn, key = (...a) => JSON.stringify(a)) => {
  const cache = new Map();
  return (...a) => { const k = key(...a); if (!cache.has(k)) cache.set(k, fn(...a)); return cache.get(k); };
};
const curry = fn => function c(...a) { return a.length >= fn.length ? fn(...a) : (...b) => c(...a, ...b); };

const log = [];
const db = debounce(x => log.push('debounced ' + x), 20);
db(1); db(2); db(3);
const th = throttle(x => log.push('throttled ' + x), 20);
th(1); th(2); th(3);
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log(log);
  let calls = 0;
  const sq = memoize(n => { calls++; return n * n; });
  sq(4); sq(4);
  const init = once(() => 'initialised');
  console.log(calls, init(), init(), curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1)(2)(3), curry((a, b, c) => a + b + c)(1, 2)(3));
}, 60);

Output (executed):

[ 'throttled 1', 'debounced 3', 'throttled 3' ]
1 initialised initialised 6 6

Debounce waits for silence, so it suits search boxes. Throttle guarantees a steady maximum rate, so it suits scroll and resize. Keep the trailing call in throttle, otherwise the final position is lost. The fn.apply(this, args) preserves this when these wrap methods. Note that with memoize, a JSON.stringify key fails on cycles and treats undefined and missing fields the same, so accept a custom key function.

Coding: deep clone, deep equal, flatten, groupBy
function deepClone(v, seen = new WeakMap()) {
  if (v === null || typeof v !== 'object') return v;
  if (seen.has(v)) return seen.get(v);                 // handles cycles
  if (v instanceof Date) return new Date(v);
  if (v instanceof RegExp) return new RegExp(v);
  if (v instanceof Map) { const m = new Map(); seen.set(v, m); v.forEach((x, k) => m.set(deepClone(k, seen), deepClone(x, seen))); return m; }
  if (v instanceof Set) { const s = new Set(); seen.set(v, s); v.forEach(x => s.add(deepClone(x, seen))); return s; }
  const out = Array.isArray(v) ? [] : Object.create(Object.getPrototypeOf(v));
  seen.set(v, out);
  for (const k of Reflect.ownKeys(v)) out[k] = deepClone(v[k], seen);
  return out;
}
function deepEqual(a, b) {
  if (Object.is(a, b)) return true;
  if (typeof a !== 'object' || typeof b !== 'object' || !a || !b) return false;
  if (Object.getPrototypeOf(a) !== Object.getPrototypeOf(b)) return false;
  if (a instanceof Date) return a.getTime() === b.getTime();
  const ka = Reflect.ownKeys(a), kb = Reflect.ownKeys(b);
  return ka.length === kb.length && ka.every(k => deepEqual(a[k], b[k]));
}
const flatten = (a, d = Infinity) => a.reduce((o, x) => o.concat(Array.isArray(x) && d > 0 ? flatten(x, d - 1) : [x]), []);
const groupBy = (xs, f) => xs.reduce((g, x) => { (g[f(x)] ??= []).push(x); return g; }, {});

const src = { d: new Date(0), list: [1, { a: 1 }], m: new Map([['k', 1]]) };
src.self = src;
const c = deepClone(src);
console.log(c.self === c, c.d instanceof Date, c.list[1] !== src.list[1], c.m.get('k'));
console.log(deepEqual({ a: [1, { b: NaN }] }, { a: [1, { b: NaN }] }), deepEqual({ a: 1 }, { a: 1, b: undefined }), deepEqual([], {}));
console.log(flatten([1, [2, [3, [4]]]]), flatten([1, [2, [3]]], 1));
console.log(groupBy(['apple', 'bob', 'avocado'], s => s[0]));

Output (executed):

true true true 1
true false false
[ 1, 2, 3, 4 ] [ 1, 2, [ 3 ] ]
{ a: [ 'apple', 'avocado' ], b: [ 'bob' ] }

Mention structuredClone first, and write this version when asked. The WeakMap handles cycles and shared references. Note that deepEqual is not cycle-safe here; a thorough version tracks visited pairs. The built-in Object.groupBy (ES2024, Node 21+) does the same job and returns a null-prototype object.

Coding: EventEmitter, LRU cache, async task queue with a concurrency limit
class Emitter {
  #h = new Map();
  on(e, fn) { (this.#h.get(e) ?? this.#h.set(e, new Set()).get(e)).add(fn); return () => this.off(e, fn); }
  off(e, fn) { this.#h.get(e)?.delete(fn); }
  once(e, fn) { const off = this.on(e, (...a) => { off(); fn(...a); }); return off; }
  emit(e, ...a) { [...(this.#h.get(e) ?? [])].forEach(fn => fn(...a)); }
}
class LRU {
  #m = new Map();
  constructor(cap) { this.cap = cap; }
  get(k) {
    if (!this.#m.has(k)) return undefined;
    const v = this.#m.get(k);
    this.#m.delete(k); this.#m.set(k, v);       // Map keeps insertion order, so re-insert = most recent
    return v;
  }
  set(k, v) {
    this.#m.delete(k); this.#m.set(k, v);
    if (this.#m.size > this.cap) this.#m.delete(this.#m.keys().next().value);
  }
  keys() { return [...this.#m.keys()]; }
}
async function pool(tasks, limit) {
  const out = []; let next = 0, running = 0, peak = 0;
  async function worker() {
    while (next < tasks.length) {
      const i = next++;
      peak = Math.max(peak, ++running);
      out[i] = await tasks[i]();
      running--;
    }
  }
  await Promise.all(Array.from({ length: limit }, worker));
  return { out, peak };
}
const em = new Emitter(); const seen = [];
em.once('a', v => seen.push('once ' + v)); const off = em.on('a', v => seen.push('on ' + v));
em.emit('a', 1); off(); em.emit('a', 2);
console.log(seen);
const lru = new LRU(2); lru.set('a', 1); lru.set('b', 2); lru.get('a'); lru.set('c', 3);
console.log(lru.keys());
const job = (v, ms) => () => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
pool([job(1, 15), job(2, 5), job(3, 5), job(4, 5)], 2).then(console.log);

Output (executed):

[ 'once 1', 'on 1' ]
[ 'a', 'c' ]
{ out: [ 1, 2, 3, 4 ], peak: 2 }

The emit copies the handler set so a handler can remove itself during iteration. The LRU relies on Map's insertion order, which gives O(1) get and set. The pool runs limit workers that pull the next index, and the single-threaded model makes next++ safe.

Coding: common string, array and interval questions
const isAnagram = (a, b) => [...a].sort().join('') === [...b].sort().join('');
const isPalindrome = s => { const t = s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, ''); return t === [...t].reverse().join(''); };
const firstUnique = s => { const c = new Map(); for (const ch of s) c.set(ch, (c.get(ch) ?? 0) + 1); return [...c].find(([, n]) => n === 1)?.[0]; };
const twoSum = (a, t) => { const m = new Map(); for (let i = 0; i < a.length; i++) { if (m.has(t - a[i])) return [m.get(t - a[i]), i]; m.set(a[i], i); } };
const dedupe = a => [...new Set(a)];
const chunk = (a, n) => a.length ? [a.slice(0, n), ...chunk(a.slice(n), n)] : [];
const capitalize = s => s.replace(/\b\w/g, c => c.toUpperCase());
const fib = n => { let [a, b] = [0, 1]; while (n--) [a, b] = [b, a + b]; return a; };
const maxSub = a => a.reduce(([best, cur], x) => { cur = Math.max(x, cur + x); return [Math.max(best, cur), cur]; }, [-Infinity, 0])[0];
const merge = iv => [...iv].sort((a, b) => a[0] - b[0]).reduce((o, [s, e]) => {
  const last = o.at(-1);
  if (last && s <= last[1]) last[1] = Math.max(last[1], e); else o.push([s, e]);
  return o;
}, []);
console.log(isAnagram('listen', 'silent'), isPalindrome('A man, a plan, a canal: Panama'), firstUnique('swiss'));
console.log(twoSum([2, 7, 11, 15], 9), dedupe([1, 1, 2]), chunk([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], 2), capitalize('hello big world'));
console.log(fib(10), maxSub([-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4]), merge([[1, 3], [2, 6], [8, 10], [15, 18]]));

Output (executed):

true true w
[ 0, 1 ] [ 1, 2 ] [ [ 1, 2 ], [ 3, 4 ], [ 5 ] ] Hello Big World
55 6 [ [ 1, 6 ], [ 8, 10 ], [ 15, 18 ] ]

Say the complexity. twoSum with a Map is O(n) time and O(n) space; isAnagram by sorting is O(n log n), and a count map makes it O(n). maxSub is Kadane's algorithm. merge is O(n log n) because of the sort.

Why can a Java long ID arrive wrong in the browser? How do you fix it?

JSON numbers are parsed into IEEE-754 doubles, which are exact only up to 2⁵³−1. JSON.parse('{"id":9007199254740993}').id gives 9007199254740992, with no error. Snowflake-style IDs and many database keys exceed this limit. The fix is on the server: send such IDs as strings, for example with @JsonSerialize(using = ToStringSerializer.class) or a global Jackson module. Treat them as opaque strings in TypeScript. BigInt is not a solution by itself, because JSON.parse has already lost the digits and JSON.stringify throws on BigInt.

for...in vs for...of vs forEach vs a classic for?
Iteratesbreakawait inside works?
forWhatever you codeYesYes
for...ofValues of any iterableYesYes
for...inEnumerable string keys, inherited tooYesYes
forEachArray items, skipping holesNo; only a throw exitsNo; the promises are ignored

Do not use for...in on arrays. Keys are strings and it may include extra properties. Use arr.some or for...of if you need to stop early.

slice vs splice?

slice(start, end) copies a range and leaves the original unchanged. splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) changes the original in place and returns the removed items. The modern non-mutating version of splice is toSpliced. With Angular OnPush, you need the non-mutating forms, because a new reference is what triggers an update.

How is a class different from a constructor function?
  • A class must be called with new.
  • Class bodies are always strict.
  • Methods are non-enumerable and have no prototype, so they cannot be used with new.
  • Classes sit in the TDZ until declared.
  • In a derived class, this does not exist until super() returns, because the base constructor allocates the object. That is also why extending Array or Error works with classes.
  • Only classes offer #private, fields, and static blocks.
#private vs TypeScript private vs closure privacy?

TypeScript private exists only at compile time, so at run time the field is an ordinary property. #field is enforced by the engine, and access from outside is a SyntaxError. It also cannot be seen by Object.keys or Proxy: a method using #x called on a Proxy wrapper throws a TypeError. Closure variables are private too, but they cost one function per instance, and other instances cannot reach them. #x can be read on any instance of the same class, like Java's private.

How do you make an object iterable?

Objects are not iterable by default, so for (const x of {}) throws a TypeError. Add a [Symbol.iterator] method that returns an object with next(), usually by writing it as a generator: *[Symbol.iterator]() { yield* Object.entries(this); }. Iterables are consumed by for...of, spread, array destructuring, Array.from, new Map, new Set and Promise.all. A generator object is its own iterator, so it can only be consumed once.

target vs currentTarget; stopPropagation vs stopImmediatePropagation vs preventDefault?

target is where the event began and currentTarget is where the listener sits, which is exactly the difference that matters in delegation. stopPropagation stops the event from reaching further elements, stopImmediatePropagation also blocks later listeners on the same element, and preventDefault cancels the browser's action and does not affect propagation. Avoid stopPropagation in app code, since it silently breaks delegated handlers and analytics higher up the tree.

What does a passive event listener do?

For touchstart and wheel, the browser must normally wait for your handler in case it calls preventDefault to stop the scroll. { passive: true } tells it you will not, so the compositor can scroll at once, without waiting for the main thread. Browsers treat these listeners as passive by default on window, document and body. Calling preventDefault in a passive listener is ignored and logs a console warning.

Where should a JWT or session token live in the browser?

Each option has a trade-off.

  • localStorage: simple, but any XSS can read and steal the token.
  • HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie: script cannot read it, which limits the damage of XSS, but the browser sends it automatically, so you need CSRF protection (SameSite and a CSRF token).
  • Short-lived access token in memory, refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie: a common compromise; a page reload silently gets a new access token.

No storage choice saves you from XSS completely, since a script on your page can make authenticated calls. So also apply a Content Security Policy and output encoding.

How do you keep tabs in sync?

Writing to localStorage fires a storage event in the other tabs of the same origin, not in the tab that wrote. A cleaner API is BroadcastChannel: const c = new BroadcastChannel('auth'); c.postMessage('logout'); c.onmessage = ..., which sends structured data and also works in workers. Use cases are logging out everywhere and keeping a cart in sync.

When would you use IndexedDB instead of localStorage?

Use IndexedDB when the data is large, needs indexes or range queries, consists of objects or Blobs, or must be read from a worker or service worker. Examples are offline PWA data and client-side caches of many records. localStorage is synchronous, so each read blocks the main thread, and it is limited to a few MB of strings, which suits small preferences. The IndexedDB API is event-based and verbose, so wrappers such as idb or Dexie are common.

What is XSS in plain JavaScript, and which APIs are dangerous?

XSS happens when untrusted text is treated as code. Dangerous sinks are innerHTML, outerHTML, insertAdjacentHTML, document.write, eval, new Function, setTimeout with a string, and href set to a javascript: URL. Safe alternatives are textContent, setAttribute for known attributes, and createElement. Where HTML is required, sanitise with a library such as DOMPurify. Add a Content Security Policy as a second layer. Angular sanitises template bindings automatically, unless you bypass it with DomSanitizer.

Number vs BigInt: what are the rules?

Number is a 64-bit double, safe up to ±(2⁵³−1) as integers. BigInt is arbitrary precision, written 10n or BigInt('10'). You cannot mix them in arithmetic: 1n + 1 is a TypeError. Comparison does work (1n == 1 is true, 1n === 1 is false). Math functions do not accept BigInt, division truncates (7n / 2n is 3n), and JSON.stringify throws. It is also slower, so use it only when you need the range.

How does JS compare object contents, and what is the cost of each way?

There is no built-in deep comparison. JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b) depends on key order and loses undefined, Dates and so on. A recursive compare (see the deepEqual question) or a library such as lodash.isEqual is reliable. For frameworks, the usual approach is immutable updates, so that one reference check, a === b, can stand in for a deep comparison at O(1). That is the thinking behind OnPush and NgRx.

TypeScript: any vs unknown vs never; interface vs type?

any turns off checking. unknown accepts anything, but you must narrow it before use, so it is the safe choice for external data. never is the type with no values: the return type of a function that always throws, and the result of an exhaustive switch, which gives a compile error if a case is missing. interface describes object shapes, can be extended and merged across declarations. type can also name unions, tuples, mapped and conditional types. All TypeScript types are erased at compile time, so a type does not validate a JSON response at run time. For that, use a schema validator, such as Zod.

Scenario: a user types fast and results flicker with old data. Fix it in plain JS.
let ctrl;
const onInput = debounce(async q => {
  ctrl?.abort();                              // cancel the previous request
  ctrl = new AbortController();
  try {
    const res = await fetch(`/api/search?q=${encodeURIComponent(q)}`, { signal: ctrl.signal });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error(res.status);
    render(await res.json());
  } catch (e) {
    if (e.name !== 'AbortError') showError(e);
  }
}, 300);

Debouncing reduces the number of requests, and aborting removes the race where a slow old response overwrites a newer one. encodeURIComponent stops characters like & breaking the query. In Angular, debounceTime with switchMap does the same.

How do you lazy-load images or build infinite scroll without a scroll listener?

For images, use the native loading="lazy" attribute first. For custom behaviour, use IntersectionObserver: observe a sentinel element or each image, and act when entry.isIntersecting is true. It runs off the main scroll path and is batched, unlike a scroll handler that fires many times per second and often forces layout by calling getBoundingClientRect(). Use rootMargin to start loading early, and call unobserve or disconnect when done.

What is Shadow DOM and how does it differ from Angular's emulated encapsulation?

Shadow DOM is a browser-enforced separate DOM tree: outside CSS selectors cannot reach inside, and inside styles do not leak out. Angular's default ViewEncapsulation.Emulated only simulates this by adding generated attributes (like _ngcontent-abc) to elements and rewriting selectors; global styles can still affect the component. ViewEncapsulation.ShadowDom uses real Shadow DOM. To theme a shadow component from outside, use CSS custom properties (they inherit through the boundary) and ::part().

How does client-side routing work in plain JavaScript (History API)?

history.pushState(state, '', '/orders/42') changes the URL and adds a history entry without a request; your code then renders the matching view. Back and forward buttons fire a popstate event, which you handle to re-render. replaceState changes the current entry without adding one. Because the URL is real, the server must return index.html for those paths on refresh. Frameworks such as Angular's router wrap exactly this. The newer Navigation API (navigation.addEventListener('navigate', …)) is a cleaner replacement where supported.

Why does [10, 1, 2].sort() give [1, 10, 2]? How do you sort correctly?

Without a comparator, sort converts elements to strings and compares UTF-16 code units, so "10" comes before "2". Pass a comparator: arr.sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers, a.name.localeCompare(b.name) for text (or an Intl.Collator for large lists). sort mutates the array and is stable since ES2019; use toSorted() for a copy. 💡 Sorting objects by date: (a, b) => new Date(a.at) - new Date(b.at).

What is the difference between an attribute and a property on a DOM element?

An attribute is what is written in the HTML (getAttribute('value')), always a string. A property is the live JavaScript value on the DOM object (input.value), which can be any type. Some are linked: changing id updates both. Others are not: value and checked attributes hold the initial value, while the properties hold the current one. Angular's [value] binds a property; [attr.aria-label] binds an attribute.

How do you copy text to the clipboard, and why can it fail?

Use await navigator.clipboard.writeText(text). It returns a promise and works only in a secure context (HTTPS or localhost), usually only after a user gesture such as a click, and may need permission when reading with readText(). Wrap it in try/catch and show a fallback message. The old document.execCommand('copy') is deprecated.

JavaScript Deep Dive Internals

How JavaScript actually runs: the engine, execution contexts, the scope chain, closures, this, prototypes, promises, modules, memory, and the browser rendering pipeline.

1. How the engine runs your code (V8)

💡 Performance insight: the JIT optimizes for stable shapes (hidden classes). Objects created with the same properties in the same order share a shape. Adding or deleting properties on the fly, or mixing types in an array, causes deoptimization.

2. Execution Context & Call Stack

3. Scope chain & lexical scope

Scope types: global, function (var), block (let, const, class inside {}), and module (each ES module has its own top-level scope). Assigning to an undeclared variable in sloppy mode creates an accidental global. "use strict", which is automatic in modules and classes, makes that a ReferenceError instead.

4. Closures in depth

function createBankAccount(initial) {
  let balance = initial;                       // private: not reachable from outside
  return {
    deposit(amt) { balance += amt; return balance; },
    withdraw(amt) {
      if (amt > balance) throw new Error('Insufficient funds');
      balance -= amt; return balance;
    },
    get balance() { return balance; }
  };
}
const acc = createBankAccount(100);
acc.deposit(50);   // 150
acc.balance;       // 150   - but acc.balance = 0 does nothing; `balance` itself is unreachable

A closure is a function bundled with a reference to the lexical environment it was created in. As long as the inner function is reachable, the variables it closes over stay alive and aren't garbage-collected. Uses: data privacy and the module pattern, factories, partial application and currying, memoization caches, keeping state in event handlers, debounce and throttle, React hooks. Pitfalls: stale closures (a callback that captured an old value), and memory held longer than expected when a closure captures a large object.

5. The this keyword: four binding rules, plus arrows

PriorityHow the function is calledthis isExample
1 (highest)new bindingthe newly created objectnew User()
2Explicit: call, apply, bindthe object you passfn.call(obj)
3Implicit: method callthe object to the left of the dotobj.fn()
4Default: plain callundefined (strict) or globalThisfn()
-Arrow functioninherited from the enclosing scope (lexical); none of the rules above apply() => this
-DOM event handler (regular function)the element (e.currentTarget)btn.onclick = function(){ this }
class Timer {
  seconds = 0;
  startBroken() { setInterval(function () { this.seconds++; }, 1000); }   // this = window (browser) or the Timeout object (Node): no error, but seconds is never updated
  startArrow()  { setInterval(() => { this.seconds++; }, 1000); }        // ✔ lexical this
  startBind()   { setInterval(function () { this.seconds++; }.bind(this), 1000); }   // ✔
}
const { startArrow } = new Timer();   // destructuring a method loses its `this` (implicit binding lost)

6. Prototypes & inheritance

class Animal { constructor(name) { this.name = name; } eat() { return `${this.name} eats`; } }
class Dog extends Animal { bark() { return 'Woof'; } }
const rex = new Dog('Rex');

Object.getPrototypeOf(rex) === Dog.prototype;            // true
Object.getPrototypeOf(Dog.prototype) === Animal.prototype; // true
rex instanceof Animal;                                    // true (walks the chain)
rex.hasOwnProperty('name'); rex.hasOwnProperty('eat');    // true, false

// What `class` desugars to (roughly):
function AnimalFn(name) { this.name = name; }
AnimalFn.prototype.eat = function () { return this.name + ' eats'; };
function DogFn(name) { AnimalFn.call(this, name); }
DogFn.prototype = Object.create(AnimalFn.prototype);
DogFn.prototype.constructor = DogFn;

// What `new` does:
// 1. creates {}  2. links its [[Prototype]] to Fn.prototype  3. calls Fn with this = {}
// 4. returns the object (unless Fn returns its own object)

prototype is a property of functions: the object that instances will link to. __proto__ (or Object.getPrototypeOf) is the actual link that every object has. Methods live on the prototype, so they're shared by all instances and memory-efficient. Class fields (seconds = 0) and #private fields live on each instance.

7. Promises, async/await & error flow

// Callback hell → Promise chain → async/await (same logic)
getUser(id, (err, u) => { getOrders(u, (err, o) => { getItems(o[0], (err, i) => { /* … */ }); }); });

getUser(id).then(u => getOrders(u)).then(o => getItems(o[0])).catch(handle);

async function load(id) {
  try {
    const u = await getUser(id);
    const o = await getOrders(u);
    return await getItems(o[0]);
  } catch (e) {
    handle(e);
  } finally {
    hideSpinner();
  }
}

// ⚠ Sequential when it could be parallel:
const a = await fetchA(); const b = await fetchB();             // slow: A then B
const [a2, b2] = await Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()]);       // fast: both at once

// ⚠ forEach does not await:
items.forEach(async i => await save(i));                        // fires all, doesn't wait
for (const i of items) await save(i);                           // sequential, awaited
await Promise.all(items.map(save));                             // parallel, awaited

// Global safety nets
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection', e => log(e.reason));
process.on('unhandledRejection', r => log(r));                  // Node

async/await under the hood: an async function always returns a Promise. Each await pauses the function, schedules the rest as a microtask once the awaited promise settles, and returns control to the event loop, so the thread isn't blocked. It works like a generator combined with promises.

8. Iterators, generators & Symbols

// Any object with [Symbol.iterator]() is iterable (for...of, spread, destructuring)
class Range {
  constructor(from, to) { this.from = from; this.to = to; }
  *[Symbol.iterator]() { for (let i = this.from; i <= this.to; i++) yield i; }
}
[...new Range(1, 5)];   // [1,2,3,4,5]

// Generators: pausable functions
function* idGen() { let id = 1; while (true) { const reset = yield id++; if (reset) id = 1; } }
const g = idGen(); g.next().value; g.next().value; g.next(true).value;   // 1, 2, 1

// Async iteration (streams, paginated APIs)
async function* pages(url) {
  while (url) { const r = await (await fetch(url)).json(); yield r.items; url = r.next; }
}
for await (const items of pages('/api/orders?page=0')) render(items);

9. ES Modules vs CommonJS

ES Modules (import/export)CommonJS (require/module.exports)
LoadingStatic: analysed before running; asynchronousDynamic, synchronous, at runtime
BindingsLive read-only bindingsA copy of the exported value
Tree-shaking✔ Bundlers can remove unused exports✘ Hard to do
Top-level await✔✘
this at the top levelundefined (strict by default)module.exports
WhereBrowsers (<script type="module">), modern Node, Angular, ViteLegacy Node, older npm packages
// math.js
export const PI = 3.14;
export default function area(r) { return PI * r * r; }
// app.js
import area, { PI } from './math.js';
const { heavy } = await import('./heavy.js');    // dynamic import → code-splitting / lazy loading

10. Memory management & garbage collection

JS uses mark-and-sweep: starting from the roots (globals, the current call stack, closures in use), the GC marks everything reachable and frees the rest. V8's collector is generational: a young generation (Scavenger, fast and frequent) and an old generation (Mark-Compact, run incrementally and concurrently). Circular references are fine because reachability is what counts.

Common leakFix
Accidental globalsUse strict mode and let/const
Timers and intervals that are never clearedclearInterval on component destroy
Event listeners that are never removedremoveEventListener, or { signal } with an AbortController
Detached DOM nodes still referenced from JSDrop the references and null out caches
Caches or Maps that keep growingWeakMap/WeakSet (keys held weakly), or an LRU limit
Closures capturing large objectsCapture only what you need
Unsubscribed Observables (Angular)async pipe, takeUntilDestroyed

To diagnose, use Chrome DevTools: the Memory tab (heap snapshots, comparing snapshots, allocation timeline) and the Performance monitor.

11. Objects: copying, freezing, Proxy & Reflect

const o = { a: 1, nested: { b: 2 } };
Object.freeze(o);      // no add/remove/change (shallow!)  o.nested.b = 3 still works
Object.seal(o);        // no add/remove, but can change existing
Object.defineProperty(o2, 'id', { value: 7, writable: false, enumerable: false, configurable: false }); // o2 = any non-frozen object; on a frozen one this throws TypeError

// Proxy: intercept operations (Vue 3 reactivity, validation, logging)
const user = new Proxy({}, {
  set(target, key, value) {
    if (key === 'age' && (!Number.isInteger(value) || value < 0)) throw new TypeError('Invalid age');
    return Reflect.set(target, key, value);
  },
  get(target, key) { return key in target ? Reflect.get(target, key) : `no ${String(key)}`; }
});

// Equality algorithms
NaN === NaN;          // false
Object.is(NaN, NaN);  // true
Object.is(0, -0);     // false (=== says true)
[NaN].includes(NaN);  // true  (SameValueZero)
[NaN].indexOf(NaN);   // -1    (===)

12. Data types & how values are passed

Primitive (immutable, compared by value)typeof
string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, symbol'string', 'number', 'bigint', 'boolean', 'undefined', 'symbol'
null'object' (a historical bug)
Object (mutable, compared by reference): plain objects, arrays, functions, Date, Map, Set…'object' / 'function'

JavaScript is pass-by-value. For objects, the value passed is a reference (sometimes called "call by sharing"): mutating the object is visible to the caller, but reassigning the parameter isn't. Numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, so 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3. Use integers in paise or cents for money, and Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER is 2⁵³−1 (use BigInt beyond that).

13. The browser: rendering pipeline, DOM & script loading

  • Reflow (layout) is expensive. It's triggered by changing size or position, adding nodes, or reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect() right after a write ("layout thrashing"). Batch your reads and writes, use transform and opacity for animations, and use requestAnimationFrame.
  • Event propagation runs capture (window → target), then target, then bubble (target → window). Delegation means one listener on a parent that uses e.target.closest('.item').
  • DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed and deferred scripts have run. load fires when images, CSS and iframes have also loaded.
  • Use DocumentFragment or build the markup first to insert many nodes with a single reflow.

14. The event loop, step by step

The event loop is the host's scheduler (the browser's or Node's, not the JS engine's). A task (also called a macrotask) is one unit of work that starts from an empty call stack: running a script, a timer callback, a click handler, a network callback. A microtask is a callback that must run as soon as the current JS finishes, before anything else happens. Microtasks exist so that a promise's reaction runs promptly and in order, without giving the page a chance to render half-updated state.

QueueFilled byDrained
Task queues (several, browser picks)setTimeout, setInterval, UI events, MessageChannel, postMessage, network callbacksOne task per turn
Microtask queuethen/catch/finally, continuation after await, queueMicrotask, MutationObserverCompletely, after each task and each callback, including microtasks added meanwhile
Animation frame callbacksrequestAnimationFrameOnce per rendered frame, before style and layout. Callbacks added during this step wait for the next frame
Idle callbacksrequestIdleCallbackWhen the browser has spare time. Not supported everywhere, and may not run for a long time unless you pass a timeout

Timers are minimums, not schedules

  • The delay means "not sooner than". The callback waits for the stack to empty and for its turn in the queue. A 5-second sync loop delays a setTimeout(fn, 0) by 5 seconds.
  • Browsers clamp nested timers: after five levels of nesting, the minimum delay is 4 ms (from the HTML spec).
  • Background tabs throttle timers heavily, often to once a second or less. Never compute elapsed time by counting ticks; compare performance.now() values.
  • setInterval does not queue a backlog of calls. If the callback runs longer than the interval, ticks are dropped or run back to back. A setTimeout that reschedules itself at the end gives a fixed gap between runs.

The Node.js loop is different

Node runs on libuv, whose loop goes through fixed phases. There is no rendering step. Between each callback, Node runs the process.nextTick queue and then the promise microtask queue.

PhaseRuns
timersExpired setTimeout and setInterval callbacks
pending callbacksSome deferred system callbacks, such as TCP errors
idle, prepareInternal
pollFetches new I/O events and runs their callbacks; may block here if nothing else is due
checksetImmediate callbacks
close callbackssocket.on('close') and similar
Gotcha: "Node's thread pool handles all I/O" is a common misconception. Sockets use the operating system's non-blocking APIs (epoll, kqueue, IOCP) from the main loop thread. The libuv pool (4 threads by default, set by UV_THREADPOOL_SIZE) serves file system calls, dns.lookup, and CPU-heavy crypto and zlib work. Timers are handled by the loop itself.

15. Inside V8: tiers, hidden classes and inline caches

V8 has more tiers than the classic "interpreter plus TurboFan" picture. Ignition interprets bytecode and collects type feedback. Sparkplug is a very fast baseline compiler with no optimisation. Maglev is a mid-tier optimising compiler. TurboFan is the top tier, producing the most optimised code at the highest compile cost. Code climbs the tiers as it gets hotter, and falls back (deoptimises) if a speculation fails.

A hidden class (V8 calls it a Map) records an object's layout: which properties it has and at which offset. Objects built in the same order share one. An inline cache sits at a property-access site and remembers "for this hidden class, the value is at offset N", which skips the dictionary lookup. A site that sees one shape is monomorphic (fastest), a few shapes polymorphic, and many shapes megamorphic (falls back to a slower generic lookup).

function P(x, y) { this.x = x; this.y = y; }     // same order → same hidden class
const a = new P(1, 2), b = new P(3, 4);

const c = { x: 1, y: 2 }, d = { y: 2, x: 1 };   // different order → different hidden classes
delete a.y;                                     // a usually switches to slow dictionary mode

const nums = [1, 2, 3];                         // compact small-integer array
nums.push(1.5);                                 // transitions to a double array
nums.push('x');                                 // transitions to a generic array (no way back)
const holes = new Array(1000);                  // "holey" array; lookups may check the prototype chain

Treat these as explanations for hot loops, not rules for everyday code. Measure before optimising.

16. this in the less obvious places

WhereValue of this
Top level of a classic scriptwindow (globalThis)
Top level of an ES moduleundefined
Top level of a CommonJS filemodule.exports
Class field initialiser, including arrow fieldsThe instance
static method or static blockThe class itself
Getter or setterThe object the property was read from, even if defined on a prototype
setTimeout(function () {...}) callbackwindow in browsers and a Timeout object in Node, even in strict code, because the host supplies this. It is not undefined
Array callback, forEach(fn, thisArg)thisArg, else undefined (strict) or the global object (sloppy)
Sloppy function called with a primitive: fn.call(5)A boxed Number object. In strict mode, the primitive 5
Listener added with addEventListener (regular function)The element the listener is on (currentTarget)
Arrow listenerThe enclosing this; use e.currentTarget for the element
Gotcha: the earlier Timer.startBroken() example does not throw a TypeError. In a browser this is window, so this.seconds++ quietly creates window.seconds with the value NaN. In Node it writes to the Timeout object. The bug is still real, and it is harder to spot because nothing fails. The instance's seconds simply never changes.

17. Hoisting and the TDZ, by declaration type

"Hoisting" does not physically move code. It describes the fact that the engine registers every declaration of a scope when it enters that scope, before running any statement.

DeclarationScopeOn scope entryRead before declarationCreates a global object property (classic script)
varFunction or globalCreated, set to undefinedundefinedYes
functionFunction; block in strict modeCreated and set to the functionWorksYes
let, constBlockCreated, uninitialisedReferenceErrorNo
classBlockCreated, uninitialisedReferenceErrorNo
importModuleLinked before the module body runsWorks unless a cycle means the exporter has not run yetNo

The TDZ is about time, not position. A function declared above a let can read it, provided it is called after the let has run. In a switch, all cases share one block, so let in one case is in scope, and possibly in its TDZ, in the others. Wrap a case in braces to avoid that.

18. Memory leaks in practice

A leak in a garbage-collected language is memory that is still reachable but that you will never use again. So the question is always "who is still holding a reference?". DevTools calls this holder the retainer. Two numbers appear in heap snapshots: shallow size is the object's own memory, and retained size is what would be freed if the object were collected, including everything only it keeps alive.

Closures in one scope share a context

V8 stores the captured variables of a scope in one context object, shared by all closures created in that scope. If any closure captures a variable, every sibling closure keeps that variable alive, even a sibling that never mentions it.

let keep = null;
function replace() {
  const prev = keep;
  const unused = () => prev;       // puts prev in the shared context
  keep = { big: new Array(1e6).fill('x'), method() { return 1; } };
}                                  // method's context holds prev, so every old `big` stays alive
for (let i = 0; i < 40; i++) replace();
// node --expose-gc, measured after gc(): about 320 MB retained.
// With the `unused` line removed: about 11 MB, one array.

Cleaning up with AbortController

class Widget {
  #ac = new AbortController();
  mount(el) {
    const { signal } = this.#ac;
    window.addEventListener('resize', this.onResize, { signal });  // removed on abort
    el.addEventListener('click', this.onClick, { signal });
    fetch('/api/data', { signal }).then(this.render).catch(() => {});
  }
  unmount() { this.#ac.abort(); }                                  // one call cleans up everything
}

WeakMap, WeakRef and FinalizationRegistry

ToolWhat it doesUse
WeakMap, WeakSetThe key is held weakly. A value lives as long as its key doesMetadata for objects you do not own, such as DOM nodes
WeakRef (ES2021)A weak pointer. deref() returns the object or undefinedCaches of expensive objects
FinalizationRegistry (ES2021)Calls back at some point after an object is collectedReleasing an associated resource as a safety net. It may never run, so it cannot replace explicit cleanup

The heap-snapshot workflow

  1. Open the suspect page and take a baseline heap snapshot in the DevTools Memory tab (it forces a GC).
  2. Perform the action several times, such as opening and closing a dialog.
  3. Take a second snapshot and switch to the Comparison view. Sort by # Delta and look for object counts that grew with each repetition.
  4. Filter for Detached to find DOM nodes that left the document but are still referenced.
  5. Select one instance and read the Retainers panel from the bottom up to find the root reference.

In Node, watch process.memoryUsage(), start with --inspect to attach DevTools, and write snapshots with v8.writeHeapSnapshot(). The old-space limit is set by --max-old-space-size (in MB).

19. Web Workers in depth

async code does not make CPU work faster or move it off the main thread. It only stops the thread from waiting. A JSON.parse of a huge string blocks input and rendering whether or not it is inside an async function. A worker is a real OS-level thread with its own event loop and its own JS heap, so heavy work there leaves the page responsive.

// main.js
const worker = new Worker(new URL('./parse.worker.js', import.meta.url), { type: 'module' });
worker.onmessage = e => render(e.data);
worker.onerror = e => console.error(e.message);
const buffer = await file.arrayBuffer();
worker.postMessage({ buffer }, [buffer]);   // transfer: no copy, buffer becomes unusable here
// worker.terminate() stops it immediately

// parse.worker.js
self.onmessage = ({ data }) => {
  const text = new TextDecoder().decode(data.buffer);
  const rows = text.split('\n').map(l => l.split(','));
  self.postMessage({ count: rows.length });
};
  • No shared memory by default. postMessage uses the structured clone algorithm, which copies Maps, Sets, Dates, typed arrays and cycles. It cannot copy functions or DOM nodes, and it loses class prototypes. Copying a large object takes time on both ends.
  • Transferables (ArrayBuffer, MessagePort, ImageBitmap, OffscreenCanvas) move ownership in near-constant time. The sender's ArrayBuffer is detached and has length 0.
  • Available in a worker: fetch, timers, IndexedDB, WebSocket, crypto. Not available: the DOM, window, localStorage.
  • SharedArrayBuffer is real shared memory, coordinated with Atomics (add, compareExchange, wait, notify). Browsers require cross-origin isolation, meaning the headers Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, as a Spectre mitigation. Atomics.wait is not allowed on the browser's main thread.
Dedicated WorkerShared WorkerService WorkerWorklet
PurposeBackground CPU work for one pageOne worker shared by same-origin tabsNetwork proxy, offline, pushHooks into the render or audio pipeline
LifetimeUntil the page closes or terminate()Until its last client closesEvent-driven; the browser stops it when idleTied to the pipeline
CommunicationpostMessageMessagePortpostMessage, fetch eventsLimited

In Node the equivalent is worker_threads. Use it for CPU work only, since Node's async I/O already does not block. In Angular, ng generate web-worker scaffolds a worker and wires up the build.

Interview: a worker costs start-up time and memory, and copying data has a cost. For small tasks, it can be slower than running them on the main thread. Workers pay off for sustained CPU work; many small jobs are better served by chunking with scheduler.yield() or setTimeout.

Service Workers in depth: lifecycle and caching strategies

A Service Worker is a script that runs in the background, separate from the page, and acts as a programmable network proxy for its origin. It powers offline support, PWA installability, and push notifications. It needs HTTPS (localhost is allowed) and cannot touch the DOM.

  1. Register: navigator.serviceWorker.register('/sw.js'). Its scope is the folder it is served from.
  2. install: pre-cache the app shell. If any file fails, installation fails.
  3. waiting: a new version waits until all tabs using the old one are closed, unless it calls self.skipWaiting().
  4. activate: delete old caches; clients.claim() takes control of open pages immediately.
  5. fetch: intercept every request in scope and decide how to answer it.
StrategyBehaviourGood for
Cache firstServe from cache; go to network only on a missHashed JS/CSS bundles, fonts, icons
Network firstTry network; fall back to cache when offlineAPI data that should be fresh, HTML pages
Stale-while-revalidateServe cache immediately, update the cache in the backgroundAvatars, non-critical lists, config
Network only / cache onlyNo fallbackPOST requests and payments / pre-cached offline page
// sw.js: stale-while-revalidate for GET requests
self.addEventListener('fetch', event => {
  if (event.request.method !== 'GET') return;          // never cache writes
  event.respondWith((async () => {
    const cache = await caches.open('runtime-v1');
    const cached = await cache.match(event.request);
    const network = fetch(event.request).then(res => {
      if (res.ok) cache.put(event.request, res.clone());
      return res;
    });
    return cached ?? network;
  })());
});

In Angular, ng add @angular/pwa generates ngsw-config.json, where asset groups and data groups (with freshness or performance strategies) are configured instead of hand-written code. Workbox does the same for other projects.

Measuring performance: Core Web Vitals and Performance APIs

Google's Core Web Vitals measure user experience from real users and affect search ranking.

MetricMeasures"Good" targetCommon fixes
LCP Largest Contentful PaintWhen the main content (hero image, heading) appears2.5 s or lessFaster server/CDN, preload the hero image, avoid render-blocking CSS/JS, SSR
INP Interaction to Next Paint (replaced FID in 2024)Delay from a click or keypress until the screen updates, worst case across the visit200 ms or lessBreak long tasks, debounce, move work to a Worker, smaller change detection
CLS Cumulative Layout ShiftHow much visible content jumps around0.1 or lessSet image width/height or aspect-ratio, reserve space for ads and banners, font-display

Lab tools (Lighthouse, DevTools Performance panel) test one simulated load; field data (CrUX, the web-vitals library sending to your backend) shows what real users get. Interviewers like candidates who know the difference.

// Custom timings with the User Timing API
performance.mark('search-start');
await runSearch();
performance.mark('search-end');
performance.measure('search', 'search-start', 'search-end');

// Observe long tasks and LCP from real users
new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  for (const e of list.getEntries()) report(e.entryType, e.startTime, e.duration);
}).observe({ type: 'longtask', buffered: true });
new PerformanceObserver(list => {
  const last = list.getEntries().at(-1);
  report('LCP', last.startTime);
}).observe({ type: 'largest-contentful-paint', buffered: true });

Bundling, tree shaking, code splitting and resource hints

What the browser downloads is decided at build time. Know what the bundler (esbuild/Vite in Angular 17+, webpack in older projects) does for you:

  • Tree shaking: removes exports that are never imported. It needs static ES module import/export and code without side effects at import time. CommonJS require and libraries that patch globals defeat it; "sideEffects": false in a library's package.json helps.
  • Code splitting: every dynamic import() (lazy routes, @defer) becomes its own chunk loaded on demand.
  • Minification and content hashing (main.3f9a1c.js) so files can be cached for a year with Cache-Control: immutable, while index.html is never cached long.
  • Source maps map minified code back to the source for debugging and error tracking.
HintMeaning
rel="preconnect"Open the DNS + TCP + TLS connection early to an origin you will use soon (API, CDN)
rel="preload"Fetch a resource needed for this page now, at high priority (hero image, key font)
rel="modulepreload"Preload an ES module and its parsing, for a chunk you know will be imported
rel="prefetch"Low-priority fetch of something the next page will probably need
fetchpriority="high"Raise or lower priority of a specific image or fetch

Interview Questions — JavaScript Deep Dive

Is JavaScript single-threaded? Then how does it do async work?

The JS engine runs your code on one main thread with one call stack. The host (browser or Node) does async work in the background: network, timers and I/O run on browser threads or, in Node, through libuv (sockets use the OS's non-blocking APIs, timers run in the event loop, and the libuv thread pool handles file I/O, DNS lookups and some crypto). When that work finishes, its callback is queued, and the event loop pushes it onto the stack once the stack is empty: all microtasks first, then one macrotask, then rendering. For real parallel JS, use Web Workers or Node worker_threads, which communicate through message passing or SharedArrayBuffer.

Explain execution context and hoisting at the engine level.

Before running a script or function body, the engine creates an execution context in two phases. In the creation phase it sets up the environment record: var gets undefined, function declarations are stored in full, let, const and class are registered but uninitialized (the TDZ), this is bound, and the outer environment reference is linked. In the execution phase the code runs line by line. "Hoisting" is just the visible effect of the creation phase.

What exactly is a closure? Give a real-world use and a pitfall.

A closure is a function plus a reference to the environment it was defined in. That lets it read and update those variables after the outer function has returned. Use: private state (counters, a bank account, the module pattern), configured callbacks (makeLogger('AUTH')), memoization and debouncing. Pitfall: stale values (a setInterval callback that captured old state), and memory retention, because large objects stay alive as long as the closure does.

How is this determined? What's the priority order?

It depends on the call site. The priority is new > explicit (call, apply, bind) > implicit (obj.method()) > default (undefined in strict mode). Arrow functions skip all of these and take this lexically. A bound function can't be re-bound with call or apply, but new still overrides bind.

prototype vs __proto__ vs Object.create?

Fn.prototype is the object that instances made with new Fn() will inherit from. obj.__proto__ (properly, Object.getPrototypeOf(obj)) is the object's actual internal [[Prototype]] link. Object.create(proto) makes a new object whose [[Prototype]] is proto, without calling a constructor. Object.create(null) gives a "dictionary" object with no inherited keys.

Microtask vs macrotask — can microtasks starve rendering?

Yes. The loop drains the entire microtask queue before it renders or takes the next macrotask. A promise chain that keeps queueing microtasks would freeze the page. Long synchronous work blocks too, so split it into chunks with setTimeout or scheduler.yield(), or move it to a Worker. requestAnimationFrame callbacks run just before the next paint.

What does new do step by step?
  1. Creates an empty object.
  2. Sets its [[Prototype]] to Constructor.prototype.
  3. Calls the constructor with this set to the new object.
  4. Returns that object, unless the constructor explicitly returns a different object.
ES Modules vs CommonJS?

ESM is static (imports are resolved before the code runs), which enables tree-shaking. It loads asynchronously, has live bindings, is strict by default, and supports top-level await. CJS's require runs synchronously at runtime and copies values. In Node, ESM is used when the file is .mjs or "type":"module". Dynamic import() works in both and returns a promise. Angular and modern bundlers are ESM-first.

How does garbage collection work in JS? How do you find a memory leak?

Mark-and-sweep based on reachability from the roots, with V8 splitting the heap into a young generation (scavenged frequently) and an old generation (mark-compact). Leaks are objects that are unintentionally still reachable: forgotten timers and listeners, detached DOM nodes, global caches, closures. To find one, take heap snapshots before and after an action in DevTools, compare them, and follow the "Retainers" path to see what's holding the object.

Map vs Object; WeakMap vs Map?

Map accepts any key type (objects too), preserves insertion order, has size, is directly iterable, is faster for frequent add and delete, and has no prototype keys that could collide. Object keys are only strings or symbols, and it's what JSON works with. A WeakMap requires object keys and holds them weakly: when the key is garbage-collected, the entry disappears. It isn't iterable. Use it for private data or metadata attached to DOM nodes and objects without causing leaks.

What is the Temporal Dead Zone?

The time between entering a scope and reaching the let, const or class declaration. Accessing the variable during that time throws a ReferenceError. It catches use-before-declare bugs that var's undefined would hide. typeof x also throws inside the TDZ.

Explain event delegation and why it's efficient.

Because events bubble, you can attach one listener to a common ancestor and identify the real source with e.target.closest(selector). Fewer listeners means less memory and faster setup. It also works for elements added later, which is why jQuery's .on('click', '.row', fn) exists. focus and blur don't bubble, so use focusin and focusout.

async vs defer on script tags?

Both download without blocking HTML parsing. async runs as soon as it has downloaded (interrupting the parser), in no guaranteed order, which suits independent scripts like analytics. defer runs after parsing finishes, in document order, before DOMContentLoaded, which suits app scripts that need the DOM. Module scripts are deferred by default.

What is strict mode and what does it change?

Turn it on with "use strict" (it's automatic in modules and classes). It throws on assignment to undeclared variables, sets this to undefined in plain calls, forbids duplicate parameter names and with, throws on writes to read-only properties, and stops eval from leaking variables. You get safer code and more room for engine optimizations.

Why is 0.1 + 0.2 !== 0.3? How do you handle money?

Numbers are IEEE-754 binary floating point, and 0.1 can't be represented exactly in binary, so the sum is 0.30000000000000004. Compare with an epsilon (Math.abs(a-b) < Number.EPSILON). For money, store integer minor units (paise) or use a decimal library, and format with Intl.NumberFormat('en-IN', {style:'currency', currency:'INR'}).

What are Web Workers / Service Workers?

A Web Worker runs JS on a background thread, with no DOM access, and communicates through postMessage. Use it for CPU-heavy work like parsing or image processing. A Service Worker is a programmable network proxy between the page and the network, used for offline caching (PWAs), push notifications and background sync. It requires HTTPS.

Output: Promise executor, then, and setTimeout
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
new Promise(res => {
  console.log('C');
  res();
  console.log('D');
}).then(() => console.log('E'));
console.log('F');

Output (executed):

A
C
D
F
E
B

The executor passed to new Promise runs synchronously, and calling res() does not stop it, so C and D print during the sync phase. The .then callback is a microtask and the timer a macrotask.

Output: code around await in an async function
async function f() {
  console.log('1');
  await null;
  console.log('2');
}
console.log('3');
f();
console.log('4');

Output (executed):

3
1
4
2

An async function runs synchronously up to its first await. Everything after the await is a continuation, scheduled as a microtask, even when the awaited value is not a promise.

Output: a microtask queued inside a macrotask, and a macrotask queued inside a microtask
setTimeout(() => {
  console.log('t1');
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('m1'));
}, 0);
setTimeout(() => console.log('t2'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => {
  console.log('m2');
  setTimeout(() => console.log('t3'), 0);
});

Output (executed):

m2
t1
m1
t2
t3

After the sync script, microtasks drain (m2, which adds t3 at the back of the timer queue). Then t1 runs. The microtask queue is drained after each macrotask, so m1 runs before t2. Browsers and Node 11+ both behave this way. t3 was queued last, so it runs last.

Output: two promise chains interleaving
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(1)).then(() => console.log(2));
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log(3)).then(() => console.log(4));

Output (executed):

1
3
2
4

Chains do not run to completion. Each .then queues the next one only when its own callback finishes, so the two chains take turns: first-level callbacks 1 and 3, then second-level 2 and 4.

Output: returning a promise from then (the classic extra-ticks puzzle)
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => { console.log(0); return Promise.resolve(4); })
  .then(console.log);
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log(1))
  .then(() => console.log(2))
  .then(() => console.log(3))
  .then(() => console.log(5))
  .then(() => console.log(6));

Output (executed):

0
1
2
3
4
5
6

Returning a plain value would print 4 right after 1. Returning a promise costs extra ticks: the spec queues a NewPromiseResolveThenableJob (one tick), which calls .then on the returned promise, and that callback is another microtask (a second tick) before the outer promise resolves and its handler can be queued. So the second chain gets ahead by two steps.

Output: async function returning a value vs returning a promise
async function a() { return 'a'; }
async function b() { return Promise.resolve('b'); }
async function c() { return await Promise.resolve('c'); }
b().then(console.log);
c().then(console.log);
a().then(console.log);
Promise.resolve()
  .then(() => console.log('tick 1'))
  .then(() => console.log('tick 2'))
  .then(() => console.log('tick 3'))
  .then(() => console.log('tick 4'));

Output (executed):

a
tick 1
c
tick 2
b
tick 3
tick 4

a resolves immediately, so its handler joins the queue during the sync phase. c awaits a native promise, which takes one tick, then resolves. b resolves its implicit promise with another promise, which costs the thenable job described in the previous question, so it comes last. That is why return await is not slower than return promise in modern engines.

Output: async callback inside forEach
async function run() {
  [1, 2, 3].forEach(async n => {
    await null;
    console.log(n);
  });
  console.log('done');
}
run();

Output (executed):

done
1
2
3

forEach ignores the promise each callback returns, so run continues straight to 'done'. Use for...of with await for sequential work, or await Promise.all(arr.map(fn)) for parallel work.

Output: return vs return await inside try/catch
async function f() {
  try {
    return Promise.reject(new Error('boom'));
  } catch (e) {
    return 'f caught';
  }
}
async function g() {
  try {
    return await Promise.reject(new Error('boom'));
  } catch (e) {
    return 'g caught';
  }
}
f().then(console.log, e => console.log('f rejected:', e.message));
g().then(console.log, e => console.log('g rejected:', e.message));

Output (executed):

g caught
f rejected: boom

return promise leaves the try block before the rejection is observed, so the local catch never sees it. return await waits inside the try. Use return await whenever a surrounding try must handle the failure.

Output: resolve, reject and throw in the same executor
new Promise((res, rej) => {
  res('first');
  rej('second');
  console.log('still running');
  throw new Error('third');
}).then(v => console.log('ok', v), e => console.log('err', e));

Output (executed):

still running
ok first

A promise settles once. Later resolve, reject and even throw calls in the executor are ignored, but the code still runs. An exception in the executor becomes a rejection only if the promise is still pending.

Output: then with a non-function, catch recovery, and finally pass-through
Promise.resolve(1).then(2).then(v => console.log('a', v));
Promise.reject(1)
  .catch(v => v + 1)
  .then(v => { console.log('b', v); return v * 10; })
  .finally(() => 99)
  .then(v => console.log('c', v));
Promise.resolve('x').finally(() => { throw new Error('from finally'); })
  .catch(e => console.log('d', e.message));

Output (executed):

a 1
b 2
d from finally
c 20

A non-function argument to then is ignored and the value passes through. catch returns a fulfilled promise, so the chain recovers. finally ignores its callback's return value (99 is dropped), but a throw inside it replaces the outcome.

Output: Promise combinators
const ok = (v, ms) => new Promise(r => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
const no = (v, ms) => new Promise((_, r) => setTimeout(() => r(v), ms));
(async () => {
  console.log('all', await Promise.all([ok('a', 30), ok('b', 10), 'c']));
  console.log('race', await Promise.race([ok('slow', 30), no('fast-fail', 10)]).catch(e => 'rejected ' + e));
  console.log('any', await Promise.any([no('x', 5), ok('y', 20)]));
  console.log('settled', await Promise.allSettled([ok(1, 1), no(2, 1)]));
  await Promise.any([no('p', 1), no('q', 1)]).catch(e => console.log(e.name, e.errors));
  console.log('empty', await Promise.all([]), await Promise.allSettled([]));
})();

Output (executed):

all [ 'a', 'b', 'c' ]
race rejected fast-fail
any y
settled [
  { status: 'fulfilled', value: 1 },
  { status: 'rejected', reason: 2 }
]
AggregateError [ 'p', 'q' ]
empty [] []

all keeps input order, not completion order, and accepts plain values. race takes the first to settle, success or failure. any takes the first success and rejects with an AggregateError if all fail. An edge case worth saying aloud: a rejected Promise.all does not cancel the other operations; they keep running.

Output: microtasks starving a timer
let n = 0;
setTimeout(() => console.log('timer ran after n =', n), 0);
function loop() {
  if (++n < 100000) queueMicrotask(loop);
}
loop();

Output (executed):

timer ran after n = 100000

The timer cannot run until the microtask queue is empty, and each microtask adds another. A browser would not paint during that time either, and with no bound on n the tab freezes. Yielding through a macrotask (setTimeout, scheduler.yield()) lets the loop render and handle input.

Output (Node): nextTick, promise, setImmediate and a timer inside an I/O callback
const fs = require('fs');
fs.readFile(__filename, () => {
  setTimeout(() => console.log('timeout'), 0);
  setImmediate(() => console.log('immediate'));
  process.nextTick(() => console.log('nextTick'));
  Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('promise'));
  console.log('sync');
});

Output (executed):

sync
nextTick
promise
immediate
timeout

In Node, the process.nextTick queue runs before the promise microtask queue. Inside an I/O callback the loop is in the poll phase, so the next phase is check (setImmediate), before timers come round again. From the main module, the order of setTimeout(0) and setImmediate is not deterministic, because it depends on how long process start-up took.

Output: awaiting a thenable, and a throw in an async function
const thenable = { then(res) { console.log('then called'); res(42); } };
(async () => {
  console.log('before');
  console.log(await thenable);
})();
console.log('after');
async function boom() { throw new Error('x'); }
const p = boom();
console.log(p instanceof Promise);
p.catch(e => console.log('caught', e.message));

Output (executed):

before
after
true
then called
caught x
42

await calls then on any object that has one, and it does so in a microtask, so 'after' prints before 'then called'. An async function never throws synchronously: a throw becomes a rejected promise.

Output: this with method extraction, arrows and nested functions (strict mode)
'use strict';
const o = {
  name: 'o',
  regular() { return this?.name; },
  arrow: () => typeof this,
  nestedArrow() { return (() => this.name)(); },
  nestedFn() { return (function () { return this; })(); }
};
const detached = o.regular;
console.log(o.regular());
console.log(detached());
console.log(o.arrow());
console.log(o.nestedArrow());
console.log(o.nestedFn());

Output (executed):

o
undefined
object
o
undefined

this comes from the call, so detached() is a plain call and gets undefined in strict mode. An object literal does not create a scope for this, so arrow takes it from the enclosing code. In a CommonJS file that is module.exports (hence 'object'); in an ES module it would print 'undefined'. An arrow inside a method inherits the method's this; a regular nested function does not.

Output: the parenthesis and comma traps
'use strict';
const o = { f() { return this === o; } };
console.log(o.f());
console.log((o.f)());
console.log((0, o.f)());
let g;
console.log((g = o.f)());
console.log([o.f][0]());

Output (executed):

true
true
false
false
false

(o.f)() keeps the reference, so this stays o. The comma and assignment operators return the function value, which loses the object. [o.f][0]() is a method call on the array, so this is the array.

Output: bind twice, call on an arrow, and new on a bound function
'use strict';
function who() { return this?.id; }
const a = { id: 'a' }, b = { id: 'b' };
console.log(who.bind(a).bind(b)());
console.log(who.bind(a).call(b));
const arrow = () => this;
console.log(arrow.call(a) === a);
function P(id) { this.id = id; }
const BoundP = P.bind({ id: 'ignored' });
console.log(new BoundP('from new').id);
try { new arrow(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }

Output (executed):

a
a
false
from new
TypeError: arrow is not a constructor

The first bind wins, because a bound function stores its target and ignores later this values. call on an arrow has no effect. new beats bind, so the instance is created normally. Arrows have no [[Construct]] and no prototype.

Output: constructor return values
function A() { this.x = 1; return { x: 2 }; }
function B() { this.x = 1; return 2; }
function C() { this.x = 1; return null; }
console.log(new A().x, new B().x, new C().x);
class D { constructor() { return [1]; } }
console.log(new D() instanceof D, Array.isArray(new D()));
class F {}
try { F(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }

Output (executed):

2 1 1
false true
TypeError: Class constructor F cannot be invoked without 'new'

If a constructor returns an object, that object replaces the new instance. Primitives, including null, are ignored. Classes must be called with new.

Output: this through the prototype chain, callbacks and class fields
const base = { greet() { return 'hi ' + this.name; }, get upper() { return this.name.toUpperCase(); } };
const child = Object.create(base);
child.name = 'child';
console.log(child.greet(), child.upper);
const ctx = { factor: 3 };
console.log([1, 2].map(function (n) { return n * this.factor; }, ctx));
console.log([1, 2].map(n => n * (this.factor ?? 10), ctx));
class Counter {
  n = 0;
  incArrow = () => ++this.n;
  incMethod() { return ++this.n; }
}
const c = new Counter();
const { incArrow, incMethod } = c;
console.log(incArrow());
try { incMethod(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }
console.log(Object.keys(c), Object.getOwnPropertyNames(Counter.prototype));

Output (executed):

hi child CHILD
[ 3, 6 ]
[ 10, 20 ]
1
TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'n')
[ 'n', 'incArrow' ] [ 'constructor', 'incMethod' ]

this stays the object the method was called on, even when the method is found on a prototype. The second argument of map sets this for regular functions but does nothing for arrows. An arrow class field survives detaching, but it is a separate closure on every instance, while a method is one shared function on the prototype. Class bodies are strict, so a detached method has this === undefined.

Output: var shadowing an outer variable
var x = 1;
function f() {
  console.log(x);
  var x = 2;
  console.log(x);
}
f();
console.log(x);

Output (executed):

undefined
2
1

The inner var x is created at function entry, so the first read sees the local undefined, not the outer 1.

Output: function declaration and var with the same name
console.log(typeof foo);
var foo = 1;
function foo() {}
console.log(typeof foo);
var bar;
function bar() {}
console.log(typeof bar);

Output (executed):

function
number
function

During the creation phase the function declaration initialises the binding, and var foo does not reset it. The assignment foo = 1 happens at run time. var bar; has no assignment, so bar stays a function.

Output: TDZ in an inner block, and typeof
let a = 1;
{
  try { console.log(a); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }
  let a = 2;
  console.log(a);
}
console.log(typeof neverDeclared);
try { console.log(typeof later); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }
let later = 1;

Output (executed):

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'a' before initialization
2
undefined
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'later' before initialization

The inner let a is hoisted to the top of its block and shadows the outer one from the first line of the block, which is the evidence that let is hoisted. typeof is safe for undeclared names but not for names in their TDZ.

Output: TDZ in default parameters
function f(a = b, b = 1) { return [a, b]; }
try { f(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }
console.log(f(5));
function g(a, b = a * 2, c = () => a) { a = 10; return [a, b, c()]; }
console.log(g(1));
function h(a, c = () => a) { var a; a = 10; return [a, c()]; }
console.log(h(1));

Output (executed):

ReferenceError: Cannot access 'b' before initialization
[ 5, 1 ]
[ 10, 2, 10 ]
[ 10, 1 ]

Parameters initialise left to right, so a = b reads b in its TDZ. Parameter defaults have their own scope. In g, assigning to a updates the parameter, which the closure sees. In h, the var a creates a separate body variable initialised from the parameter, so the closure keeps seeing the parameter's 1.

Output: function declared in a block (sloppy vs strict)
console.log(typeof g);
{
  console.log(typeof g);
  function g() {}
}
console.log(typeof g);
(function () {
  'use strict';
  { function h() {} }
  console.log(typeof h);
})();

Output (executed):

undefined
function
function
undefined

In sloppy mode (Annex B of the spec) a block-level function is fully hoisted inside its block and also creates a var-like binding outside, which is undefined until the block runs. In strict mode it is simply block-scoped.

Output: named function expressions, and classes before declaration
const f = function g() { return typeof g; };
console.log(f(), typeof g);
const h = function inner() { inner = 1; return typeof inner; };
console.log(h());
try { new C(); } catch (e) { console.log(e.name + ': ' + e.message); }
class C {}
console.log(typeof hoisted, typeof exprVar);
function hoisted() {}
var exprVar = function () {};

Output (executed):

function undefined
function
ReferenceError: Cannot access 'C' before initialization
function undefined

A named function expression's name exists only inside the function, and in sloppy mode assigning to it fails silently. Classes are in the TDZ like let. Function expressions follow the rules of the variable that holds them.

Output: per-iteration let bindings and accidental globals
const fs = [];
for (let i = 0; i < 4; i++) {
  fs.push(() => i);
  i++;
}
console.log(fs.map(f => f()));
function leak() { var a = b = 1; }
leak();
console.log(typeof a, typeof b);

Output (executed):

[ 1, 3 ]
undefined number

let in a for head creates a fresh binding per iteration, copied forward before the increment. The first closure's i saw the body's i++ and stayed at 1; the second ended at 3. var a = b = 1 means b = 1; var a = b;, so b becomes an accidental global.

Output: arguments aliasing and function length
function sloppy(a) { arguments[0] = 99; return a; }
