function strict(a) { 'use strict'; arguments[0] = 99; return a; }
function withDefault(a, b = 2) { arguments[0] = 99; return a; }
console.log(sloppy(1), strict(1), withDefault(1));
console.log(sloppy.length, ((a, b = 2, c) => 0).length, ((...r) => 0).length);
const arrowArgs = function () { return (() => arguments[0])(); };
console.log(arrowArgs('outer'));

Output (executed):

99 1 1
1 1 0
outer

Only sloppy functions with simple parameters alias arguments to named parameters. A function's length counts the parameters before the first default or rest. Arrows have no arguments of their own, so they read the enclosing function's.

Why might setTimeout(fn, 0) run after 50 ms or more?

0 is a minimum, not a promise. The callback must wait for the current task to finish, for every microtask to drain, and for its turn among other tasks. A render may also come first. Nested timers are clamped to 4 ms after five levels, and background tabs are throttled further. To measure time accurately, use performance.now() and do not count ticks.

requestAnimationFrame vs setTimeout for animation?

requestAnimationFrame runs just before the browser paints, is aligned with the display refresh, and pauses in background tabs. A timer is not synchronised with frames, so it can run twice in one frame (wasted work) or miss a frame (jank). Inside rAF, use the timestamp argument to advance the animation by elapsed time, so it runs at the same speed on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens. Only CSS transform and opacity animations avoid main-thread layout altogether.

What is a long task, and how do you break one up?

A long task is any task over 50 ms. During it the page cannot respond, which hurts INP (Interaction to Next Paint, a Core Web Vital). Options:

  1. Split the work into chunks and yield between them with await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r)), or await scheduler.yield() where supported.
  2. Move sustained CPU work into a Web Worker.
  3. Use requestIdleCallback for low-priority work.

Do not yield using a promise: await Promise.resolve() only queues a microtask, so the browser still cannot render.

Is Node.js single-threaded?

Your JS runs on one thread per isolate, but the process has more. libuv's pool runs file system calls, dns.lookup and some crypto and zlib work (4 threads by default). Network sockets are non-blocking OS calls made from the main thread. V8 also has GC and compiler helper threads. For parallel JS, use worker_threads, or the cluster module to fork multiple processes that share a port.

What are hidden classes and inline caches, and what can you do to help them?

A hidden class describes an object's layout. An inline cache stores, per access site, the offset of a property for the shapes seen so far. Help them by initialising all properties in the constructor in the same order, avoiding delete on hot objects, and passing same-shaped objects through hot functions. Keep arrays to one element type and avoid holes. Treat this as tuning for hot paths, guided by a profiler.

Why does JSON.parse sometimes beat an object literal, and what is lazy parsing?

V8 uses lazy parsing: it pre-parses inner functions only enough to find syntax errors and captured variables, and fully compiles a function on its first call. For large data, JSON's grammar is much simpler than JS, so JSON.parse('...') can be faster than the same data as a JS literal. A practical consequence is that shipping less JS improves start-up more than micro-optimising it.

Scenario: an Angular or React SPA's memory grows on every route change. How do you investigate?
  1. Reproduce with a repeatable cycle, such as route A to B and back, ten times.
  2. Compare heap snapshots before and after, and filter for Detached nodes and growing component classes.
  3. Read the retainer path. The usual holders are subscriptions never unsubscribed, listeners on window or document, intervals, a third-party chart or map that was never destroyed, a singleton service holding an array of components, and caches without limits.
  4. Fix with the framework's teardown (takeUntilDestroyed, ngOnDestroy) or AbortSignal, then repeat the measurement to confirm.

Memory that grows then falls after a GC is normal. A rising baseline after forced GCs is the sign of a leak.

WeakRef vs WeakMap, and why is relying on GC timing dangerous?

A WeakMap ties a value's life to a key, and you cannot observe when it goes away. A WeakRef lets you test whether an object is still alive, through deref(). GC timing is unspecified and varies across engines and runs, and an object may never be collected before the program ends. So program logic must not depend on it, and a FinalizationRegistry callback is only an extra safety net.

What can't structured clone copy? How is it different from JSON?

It throws DataCloneError on functions and DOM nodes. It keeps Dates, Maps, Sets, RegExps, typed arrays, BigInt, undefined, and circular references, all of which JSON loses or fails on. It drops prototypes (a class instance arrives as a plain object), getters (only the value is copied), and property descriptors. It is defined by the HTML standard, not ECMAScript, and is exposed as structuredClone().

Scenario: a 200 MB CSV must be parsed and displayed in the browser without freezing it. Design it.
  1. Do not read it all into a string. Use file.stream() and read it in chunks with a TextDecoderStream.
  2. Parse inside a Web Worker, so the main thread stays responsive.
  3. Post rows to the page in small batches, using transferable typed arrays where possible, or keep rows in the worker or IndexedDB and send only the requested page.
  4. Render with a virtual scroller so that only the visible rows exist in the DOM.
  5. Show progress and support cancelling with worker.terminate().

If only summaries are needed, consider uploading the file and processing it on the server.

Why does SharedArrayBuffer need special headers?

Shared memory lets a thread build a very precise timer, by incrementing a counter in a loop while another thread reads it. That timer makes Spectre-style side-channel attacks practical. Browsers therefore enable SharedArrayBuffer only for cross-origin isolated pages, which guarantees no cross-origin data shares the process. Set Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin and Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp, then check self.crossOriginIsolated.

How do you cancel async work in JavaScript?

A promise itself cannot be cancelled, so cancellation is a convention built on AbortController. Pass controller.signal to fetch, addEventListener and your own functions. Your function checks signal.aborted or listens for the abort event, and rejects with signal.reason. signal.throwIfAborted() makes this short. AbortSignal.timeout(ms) aborts by time, and AbortSignal.any([a, b]) combines signals. Remember the distinction in the error name: a manual abort gives AbortError and a timeout gives TimeoutError.

What is a closure's cost compared with a class method?

A closure-based object creates new function objects per instance, while class methods are one function on the prototype. For a million objects that is a real memory difference. Use prototype methods for many instances, and closures for small numbers of objects or for callbacks.

A user still sees the old version of a PWA after a deploy. Why, and how do you fix it?

The browser downloads the new service worker, but it stays in the waiting state while any tab controlled by the old one is open, and the old one keeps serving cached files. Fixes: listen for the new worker (registration.onupdatefound, or Angular's SwUpdate.versionUpdates) and show "A new version is available, reload", then call skipWaiting() and reload. Also make sure sw.js / ngsw.json are served with Cache-Control: no-cache so the update check is not itself cached.

What is the difference between a Service Worker and a Web Worker?

A Web Worker belongs to one page, lives as long as that page, and exists to run heavy computation off the main thread; the page talks to it with postMessage. A Service Worker belongs to an origin and scope, is shared by all tabs, can run when no page is open (push, background sync), and is mainly a network proxy. Neither can access the DOM. The browser can stop an idle service worker at any time, so it must not keep state in global variables; use IndexedDB or the Cache API.

Lighthouse gives 95 but real users complain the page is slow. How can both be true?

Lighthouse is a lab test: one load, one device profile, often with an empty or warm cache, and no logged-in data or slow third-party scripts. Real users have older phones, bad networks, bigger accounts, and they interact, which affects INP and is barely measured by a page-load test. Collect field data with the web-vitals library or a RUM tool, segment by device and page, then reproduce the slow cases in the DevTools Performance panel with CPU throttling.

Why might tree shaking not remove an unused library function?

Common reasons: the library is published as CommonJS; you imported the whole namespace in a way the bundler cannot analyse (import _ from 'lodash' instead of lodash-es named imports); the module has top-level side effects, so the bundler must keep it; or something references it dynamically, for example by string key. Use a bundle analyser (source-map-explorer, esbuild metafile) to see what is actually included.

What causes "Maximum call stack size exceeded"? Does JavaScript have tail call optimisation?

Each function call pushes a frame on the call stack; deep or infinite recursion exceeds the engine's limit (often around ten thousand frames, depending on frame size). ES2015 specified proper tail calls, but only Safari implements them, so you cannot rely on TCO in Chrome or Node. Fixes: convert recursion to a loop with an explicit stack array, use a trampoline, or process in chunks. Another common cause is accidental recursion, such as a setter that assigns to itself or an Angular effect that writes a signal it reads.

preload vs prefetch: what happens if you use them wrongly?

preload is high priority for the current page; preloading things that are not used soon wastes bandwidth and competes with critical resources, and Chrome warns in the console when a preloaded resource is not used within a few seconds. prefetch is idle-time, low priority for a future navigation; using it for something the current page needs makes that resource arrive late. Preloading fonts also needs the crossorigin attribute, or the font is downloaded twice.

AJAX Async HTTP

Asynchronous JavaScript And XML: exchanging data with the server in the background and updating part of the page without reloading it. Today the data is almost always JSON, but the name stuck.

XMLHttpRequest (the original API)

readyStateConstantMeaning
0UNSENTCreated; open() not called yet
1OPENEDopen() called
2HEADERS_RECEIVEDsend() called; status and headers available
3LOADINGDownloading the body; responseText is partial
4DONEFinished, successfully or not. Check status
function getUsers() {
  const xhr = new XMLHttpRequest();
  xhr.open('GET', '/api/users?page=0', true);          // true = async (sync XHR is deprecated)
  xhr.setRequestHeader('Accept', 'application/json');
  xhr.setRequestHeader('Authorization', 'Bearer ' + token);
  xhr.responseType = 'json';
  xhr.timeout = 5000;

  xhr.onload = function () {                            // fires at readyState 4
    if (xhr.status >= 200 && xhr.status < 300) render(xhr.response);
    else showError('HTTP ' + xhr.status);
  };
  xhr.onerror   = () => showError('Network error');     // DNS, CORS, offline
  xhr.ontimeout = () => showError('Timed out');
  xhr.upload.onprogress = e => { if (e.lengthComputable) bar.value = e.loaded / e.total; };  // upload progress
  xhr.send();
}

// Old-school style you may see in legacy code
xhr.onreadystatechange = function () {
  if (xhr.readyState === 4 && xhr.status === 200) { const data = JSON.parse(xhr.responseText); }
};

// POST JSON
xhr.open('POST', '/api/users');
xhr.setRequestHeader('Content-Type', 'application/json');
xhr.send(JSON.stringify({ name: 'Arun', email: 'arun@x.com' }));
// xhr.abort() cancels

Fetch API (the modern standard)

// GET
async function loadUsers() {
  const res = await fetch('/api/users?page=0', {
    headers: { Accept: 'application/json', Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }
  });
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);   // ⚠ fetch does NOT reject on 404/500!
  return res.json();
}

// POST JSON
const res = await fetch('/api/users', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json' },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Arun', email: 'arun@x.com' }),
  credentials: 'include'                // send cookies cross-origin (default 'same-origin')
});

// File upload with FormData (browser sets multipart boundary - don't set Content-Type yourself)
const fd = new FormData(document.querySelector('#uploadForm'));
fd.append('file', fileInput.files[0]);
await fetch('/api/files', { method: 'POST', body: fd });

// Timeout + cancellation
const ctrl = new AbortController();
const timer = setTimeout(() => ctrl.abort(), 5000);
try { await fetch('/api/slow', { signal: ctrl.signal }); }
catch (e) { if (e.name === 'AbortError') showError('Cancelled / timed out'); }
finally { clearTimeout(timer); }
// or: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })

// Reusable wrapper with JSON + error handling
async function api(path, { method = 'GET', body, ...opts } = {}) {
  const res = await fetch(`/api${path}`, {
    method,
    headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', ...(token && { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` }) },
    body: body ? JSON.stringify(body) : undefined,
    ...opts
  });
  const data = res.status === 204 ? null : await res.json().catch(() => null);
  if (!res.ok) throw Object.assign(new Error(data?.detail || res.statusText), { status: res.status, data });
  return data;
}

Spring Boot backend for those calls

@RestController
@RequestMapping("/api/users")
public class UserApi {
  @GetMapping                       public Page<UserDto> list(Pageable p) { return service.list(p); }
  @PostMapping                      public ResponseEntity<UserDto> create(@Valid @RequestBody UserDto dto) {
    UserDto saved = service.create(dto);
    return ResponseEntity.created(URI.create("/api/users/" + saved.id())).body(saved);
  }
  @PostMapping(path = "/avatar", consumes = MediaType.MULTIPART_FORM_DATA_VALUE)
  public void upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file) { storage.save(file); }
}

// CORS when the front end is on another origin (e.g. Angular dev server :4200)
@Bean
CorsConfigurationSource cors() {
  var c = new CorsConfiguration();
  c.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("http://localhost:4200"));
  c.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST", "PUT", "DELETE", "OPTIONS"));
  c.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("*"));
  c.setAllowCredentials(true);
  var src = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
  src.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", c);
  return src;
}

es.addEventListener('order', e => showToast(JSON.parse(e.data)));

// SSE server
@GetMapping(path = "/stream", produces = MediaType.TEXT_EVENT_STREAM_VALUE)
public SseEmitter stream() {
  SseEmitter emitter = new SseEmitter(0L);              // no timeout
  emitters.add(emitter);
  emitter.onCompletion(() -> emitters.remove(emitter));
  return emitter;
}
// elsewhere: emitter.send(SseEmitter.event().name("order").data(orderDto));

Fetch options and the Response object

OptionValuesNote
modecors (default), same-origin, no-corsno-cors gives an opaque response: JS cannot read its status or body, so it does not "fix" CORS
credentialssame-origin (default), include, omitWhether cookies and HTTP auth are sent
cachedefault, no-store, no-cache, reload, force-cache, only-if-cachedControls the HTTP cache for this request
redirectfollow (default), error, manualRedirects are followed invisibly. res.redirected and res.url tell you it happened
keepalivetrueThe request may outlive the page, for analytics at unload. Body size is limited to 64 KB

referrerPolicy, integrity, priorityReferrer control, sub-resource integrity, a hint for fetch priority
const res = await fetch(url);
res.ok;  res.status;  res.statusText;  res.headers.get('content-type');  res.url;

// The body is a one-time stream
await res.json();
await res.json();                      // TypeError: Body is unusable, already read
const copy = res.clone();              // clone BEFORE reading if two readers need it

// Read a large or streamed response piece by piece
const reader = res.body.pipeThrough(new TextDecoderStream()).getReader();
for (;;) {
  const { value, done } = await reader.read();
  if (done) break;
  appendToScreen(value);               // LLM output, NDJSON feeds, progress bars
}

// Query strings: never build them by hand
const qs = new URLSearchParams({ q: 'a b&c', page: 1 });   // q=a+b%26c&page=1
fetch(`/api/search?${qs}`);
Gotcha: AbortSignal.timeout() rejects with a TimeoutError, not an AbortError, so the earlier check e.name === 'AbortError' misses it. Check both names when you combine timeouts with manual cancellation, for example via AbortSignal.any([ctrl.signal, AbortSignal.timeout(5000)]). Also note that the earlier api() wrapper sends Content-Type: application/json on GETs too, which turns every cross-origin GET into a preflighted request. Set the header only when a body is present.

CORS in detail: simple vs preflighted requests

A request is simple (no preflight) when the method is GET, HEAD or POST; headers are limited to safelisted ones; and Content-Type is text/plain, multipart/form-data or application/x-www-form-urlencoded. Everything else needs a preflight. Access-Control-Max-Age lets the browser reuse a preflight result, which saves a round trip. Only a small set of response headers are readable by default; to read Location or a custom header, the server must send Access-Control-Expose-Headers.

In Spring Security, enable CORS in the filter chain with http.cors(withDefaults()). Otherwise the security filter rejects the unauthenticated OPTIONS with a 401 or 403 before MVC's CORS handling can run. That is the usual reason a preflight fails when @CrossOrigin looks correct.

Caching AJAX responses

HeaderEffect
Cache-Control: max-age=60The browser reuses the response for 60 s with no request
Cache-Control: no-cacheMay store, but must revalidate each time
Cache-Control: no-storeNever store; use it for sensitive data
Cache-Control: privateBrowser only, not shared caches. Use it for user data
ETag with If-None-MatchThe server answers 304 with no body if unchanged
Vary: Origin, Accept-EncodingStops a cached response being reused for a different origin or encoding

With a 304, fetch handles revalidation for you: JS sees a normal 200 with the cached body. In Spring, ResponseEntity.ok().eTag(version).cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(Duration.ofMinutes(1))).body(dto) sets these, and ShallowEtagHeaderFilter adds ETags by hashing the output. Old IE cached GET AJAX aggressively, which is why legacy code adds ?_=timestamp (jQuery's cache: false).

Patterns used in real front ends

// Retry with exponential backoff and jitter: only idempotent requests
async function fetchRetry(url, opts = {}, tries = 3) {
  for (let i = 0; ; i++) {
    try {
      const res = await fetch(url, opts);
      if (res.status < 500 && res.status !== 429) return res;      // do not retry other 4xx
      if (i >= tries - 1) return res;
      const after = Number(res.headers.get('Retry-After'));
      await sleep(after ? after * 1000 : 2 ** i * 200 + Math.random() * 100);
    } catch (e) {
      if (e.name === 'AbortError' || i >= tries - 1) throw e;
      await sleep(2 ** i * 200);
    }
  }
}

// Download a file from an authenticated endpoint
const res = await fetch('/api/reports/7', { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
const url = URL.createObjectURL(await res.blob());
const a = Object.assign(document.createElement('a'), { href: url, download: 'report.pdf' });
a.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);                                             // avoid a leak

// Optimistic update: change the UI first, undo on failure
const before = item.liked;
render({ ...item, liked: !before });
try { await api(`/items/${item.id}/like`, { method: 'POST' }); }
catch { render({ ...item, liked: before }); toast('Could not save'); }

// Infinite scroll with IntersectionObserver instead of a scroll listener
new IntersectionObserver(([e]) => { if (e.isIntersecting) loadNextPage(); })
  .observe(document.querySelector('#sentinel'));

// Send analytics while the page closes
navigator.sendBeacon('/api/events', JSON.stringify({ page: location.pathname }));

Downloading files (PDF, Excel) from a Spring Boot API

A plain link works for public files, but when the API needs an Authorization header you must download with AJAX and hand the bytes to the browser. The server should send Content-Disposition with the file name, and if the front end is on another origin, CORS must expose that header or JavaScript cannot read it.

// Spring Boot
@GetMapping("/api/reports/{id}/pdf")
public ResponseEntity<byte[]> pdf(@PathVariable long id) {
  byte[] bytes = reportService.render(id);
  return ResponseEntity.ok()
      .contentType(MediaType.APPLICATION_PDF)
      .header(HttpHeaders.CONTENT_DISPOSITION,
              ContentDisposition.attachment().filename("report-" + id + ".pdf").build().toString())
      .body(bytes);
}
// CORS config: .exposedHeaders("Content-Disposition")

// Browser
const res = await fetch(`/api/reports/${id}/pdf`, { headers: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` } });
if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
const name = /filename="?([^";]+)"?/.exec(res.headers.get('Content-Disposition') ?? '')?.[1] ?? 'download.pdf';
const url = URL.createObjectURL(await res.blob());
const a = Object.assign(document.createElement('a'), { href: url, download: name });
a.click();
URL.revokeObjectURL(url);                       // free the memory

For very large files, prefer a short-lived signed URL (or a one-time download token in the query string) and let the browser download directly, because res.blob() holds the whole file in memory. In Angular, use http.get(url, { responseType: 'blob', observe: 'response' }) to get both the blob and the headers.

WebSocket with STOMP and Spring Boot

Raw WebSocket only sends frames; STOMP adds destinations, subscriptions and headers on top, and Spring's message broker routes them. This is the usual stack for chat, live dashboards and notifications to a specific user.

// Spring Boot
@Configuration @EnableWebSocketMessageBroker
public class WsConfig implements WebSocketMessageBrokerConfigurer {
  public void registerStompEndpoints(StompEndpointRegistry r) {
    r.addEndpoint("/ws").setAllowedOriginPatterns("https://app.example.com");
  }
  public void configureMessageBroker(MessageBrokerRegistry r) {
    r.enableSimpleBroker("/topic", "/queue");   // or a relay to RabbitMQ for many instances
    r.setApplicationDestinationPrefixes("/app");
  }
}
@Controller
class ChatController {
  @MessageMapping("/chat")                         // client sends to /app/chat
  @SendTo("/topic/messages")                      // broadcast to all subscribers
  ChatMessage send(ChatMessage msg) { return msg; }
}
// server push to one user: messagingTemplate.convertAndSendToUser(user, "/queue/alerts", alert);

// Browser (@stomp/stompjs)
const client = new Client({ brokerURL: 'wss://api.example.com/ws',
                            connectHeaders: { Authorization: `Bearer ${token}` },
                            reconnectDelay: 5000 });
client.onConnect = () => client.subscribe('/topic/messages', m => show(JSON.parse(m.body)));
client.activate();
client.publish({ destination: '/app/chat', body: JSON.stringify({ text: 'hi' }) });
  • The simple broker lives in one JVM; with several instances behind a load balancer, use a broker relay (RabbitMQ, ActiveMQ) so every instance sees every message.
  • Authenticate in the STOMP CONNECT frame with a ChannelInterceptor, because browsers cannot set custom headers on the WebSocket handshake.

Consistent API errors: ProblemDetail (RFC 9457)

Spring Boot 3 supports the standard application/problem+json format (RFC 7807, updated by RFC 9457). Using one error shape everywhere lets the front end write a single error handler.

// Spring Boot: spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true, plus custom handlers
@RestControllerAdvice
class ApiErrors {
  @ExceptionHandler(OrderNotFoundException.class)
  ProblemDetail notFound(OrderNotFoundException ex) {
    ProblemDetail pd = ProblemDetail.forStatusAndDetail(HttpStatus.NOT_FOUND, ex.getMessage());
    pd.setTitle("Order not found");
    pd.setProperty("orderId", ex.getId());
    return pd;
  }
}
// Response: {"type":"about:blank","title":"Order not found","status":404,"detail":"...","orderId":42}

// Front end: one parser for every call
async function api(url, opts) {
  const res = await fetch(url, opts);
  if (res.ok) return res.status === 204 ? null : res.json();
  const isProblem = res.headers.get('Content-Type')?.includes('problem+json');
  const body = isProblem ? await res.json() : { title: res.statusText, status: res.status };
  throw Object.assign(new Error(body.detail ?? body.title), { problem: body });
}

Interview Questions — AJAX

What is AJAX and what problem does it solve?

AJAX is a technique, not a library: JavaScript sends HTTP requests in the background (XHR or fetch), gets data (JSON, XML, HTML fragments), and updates part of the DOM. It avoids full page reloads, which makes the app faster and more responsive, keeps UI state (scroll position, form input), and uses less bandwidth. It's what makes SPAs, autocomplete, infinite scroll and live validation possible.

Explain readyState and status in XMLHttpRequest.

readyState tracks the request lifecycle: 0 UNSENT, 1 OPENED, 2 HEADERS_RECEIVED, 3 LOADING, 4 DONE. status is the HTTP result (200, 404, 500…), meaningful from state 2 onwards. Success means readyState === 4 and a 2xx status. status === 0 means a network error, a CORS block, or an aborted request.

fetch vs XMLHttpRequest — key differences and gotchas?

fetch is promise-based and cleaner, supports streaming bodies, works with Service Workers, and uses Request/Response objects. Gotchas: it doesn't reject on HTTP errors (only on network failures), so always check res.ok. Cookies aren't sent cross-origin unless you set credentials:'include'. There's no built-in timeout (use AbortSignal.timeout()), and no upload progress events. XHR still wins for upload progress.

What is the Same-Origin Policy and how does CORS relax it?

The browser stops JS on origin A (scheme + host + port) from reading responses from origin B. CORS is the server opting in through response headers: Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers, -Credentials. "Non-simple" requests (PUT or DELETE, Content-Type: application/json, custom headers like Authorization) trigger an OPTIONS preflight first. CORS is enforced by the browser only: Postman and server-to-server calls ignore it. With credentials, the allowed origin can't be *.

How do you send the CSRF token with AJAX to Spring Security?

For cookie or session-based apps, Spring expects the token in a header such as X-CSRF-TOKEN or X-XSRF-TOKEN. Option 1: render <meta name="_csrf" content="${_csrf.token}"> and copy it into every request ($.ajaxSetup or a fetch wrapper). Option 2: CookieCsrfTokenRepository.withHttpOnlyFalse() writes an XSRF-TOKEN cookie, which JS reads and sends back as X-XSRF-TOKEN. Angular's HttpClient does this automatically. Stateless JWT APIs usually disable CSRF.

What data formats can AJAX use? Why JSON over XML?

JSON, XML, HTML fragments, plain text, binary (Blob or ArrayBuffer), and FormData/multipart. JSON won because it maps directly onto JS objects (JSON.parse), is lighter than XML, easy to read, and supported everywhere (Jackson on the Spring side). JSONP was an old hack for cross-domain GETs using a script tag. It's insecure, so use CORS instead.

How do you avoid race conditions with AJAX (e.g. a search box)?

Responses can arrive out of order, so a slow reply for "an" can overwrite the result for "ang". Fixes: abort the previous request (AbortController, jqXHR.abort()), or ignore stale responses using a request counter. In Angular, switchMap does this automatically. Add debounce so you don't send a request on every keystroke.

How do you handle errors, loading state and retries in AJAX?

Show a spinner and disable the button while the request is in flight, and hide it in finally. Separate network errors (offline, CORS, timeout) from HTTP errors (4xx means show a validation message, 401 means redirect to login, 5xx means show a "try again" message). Retry only idempotent requests, with exponential backoff. Show the server's error details, such as a ProblemDetail detail field, to the user.

Is AJAX bad for SEO / browser history? How do SPAs fix it?

Content loaded by JS might not be indexed, and AJAX navigation doesn't change the URL, so Back and bookmarks break. Fixes: the History API (pushState, popstate) or a router (Angular Router) for real URLs, plus SSR or pre-rendering (Angular SSR, hydration) so crawlers see the content.

Polling vs long polling vs SSE vs WebSocket — which one when?

Polling is the simplest but wasteful. Long polling is a fallback. SSE is server-to-client only, uses plain HTTP, reconnects automatically, and is ideal for notifications and progress. WebSocket is bidirectional and low-latency, for chat and collaboration, but needs stateful connections and more infrastructure work (sticky sessions or a message broker for scaling).

Does a failed CORS check stop the request from reaching the server?

It depends. For a preflighted request, a failed preflight means the real request is never sent. For a simple request, such as a form-encoded POST, the server receives and executes it, and the browser merely stops JS reading the response. So CORS is not a server-side protection and must not be used in place of authentication or CSRF defences.

I see "CORS error" in the console, but Postman works. Walk through the fix.
  1. Look in the Network tab for the OPTIONS request and its status.
  2. A 401 or 403 on OPTIONS: Spring Security is blocking it. Use http.cors(...).
  3. A 200 with no Access-Control-Allow-Origin: the origin in the config does not match exactly (scheme, host and port all count).
  4. A wildcard with credentials: set an explicit origin, and allowCredentials(true).
  5. A proxy or gateway may strip the headers, or add them twice; a duplicate header value also fails.
  6. A 500 on the actual request often shows as a CORS error, since error responses may lack the headers.

Postman ignores CORS, so it only proves the API works.

What is res.ok for a 304, 301 or 404?

res.ok is true only for status 200 to 299. A 404 resolves with ok === false. A 301 is followed automatically, so you see the final response, with res.redirected === true. A revalidated 304 is turned into a 200 from cache. fetch rejects only when no HTTP response was obtained: DNS failure, refused connection, CORS block or abort.

What do you do if two parts of the code need to read the same fetch Response?

The body is a stream and can be consumed once, so a second read throws a TypeError. Call res.clone() before reading. A service worker's cache-and-return flow is the classic case: cache.put(req, res.clone()); return res;. Cloning a large streamed response buffers data in memory, so read once and pass the parsed value around if you can.

How do you show upload progress and download progress?

Upload: use XHR's xhr.upload.onprogress, since standard fetch has no upload progress event. In Angular, use reportProgress: true with the XHR backend. Download: fetch can do it by reading res.body chunks and comparing the bytes read with Content-Length. That header is missing when compressed or chunked, so show an indeterminate spinner in that case.

Which methods are safe to retry automatically?

GET, HEAD, PUT and DELETE are idempotent by definition, so they can be retried on a network failure or 503. POST is not, as a lost response does not tell you whether the server acted, and a retry could create a duplicate order. Make POST safe by sending an Idempotency-Key header that the server stores with the result. Do not retry 4xx, except for 408 and 429, and honour Retry-After. Add jitter to avoid many clients retrying at the same moment.

What is JSONP, exactly, and why was it dangerous?

A <script> tag is not restricted by the Same-Origin Policy. JSONP loads /api?callback=cb, and the server responds with JavaScript: cb({"a":1}), which then runs. It supports only GET, has no proper error handling, and gives the remote server full script execution in your page. Spring removed its JSONP support. CORS replaced it.

Offset vs cursor pagination for an infinite scroll?

With offset (?page=3, LIMIT 20 OFFSET 60), the database still scans skipped rows, so deep pages are slow, and rows inserted during scrolling produce duplicates or gaps. With a cursor (?after=lastId, WHERE id > ?), each page uses the index, so it is fast at any depth and stable under inserts, but you cannot jump to page 50. Use a cursor for feeds and offset for admin tables with page numbers.

How do you avoid request waterfalls and duplicate calls on a page?

Send independent requests in parallel with Promise.all or forkJoin. Share an in-flight request: keep a Map of URL to promise, return the same promise while it is pending, and remove it when settled. Cache results with a short lifetime. On the API side, an aggregate endpoint or a Backend-for-Frontend replaces many calls with one. HTTP/2 allows many parallel streams over one connection, while HTTP/1.1 browsers limit each origin to about six connections.

Scenario: you get 401 on a call, refresh the token, and repeat. What can go wrong?

Several requests fail together and each one starts its own refresh. With rotating refresh tokens, the second refresh uses a token that has already been consumed, and the user is logged out. Keep a single shared refresh promise: the first 401 starts it, and the others await it, then retry once. Exclude the refresh endpoint from this logic, otherwise a failure loops forever. Limit each request to one retry. If the refresh fails, clear state and go to login.

Is it safe to insert an AJAX response with innerHTML?

Not when it holds user-supplied data. Stored values such as a name of <img src=x onerror=...> become script execution, which is stored XSS. Use textContent or a framework's binding, or sanitise with DOMPurify if HTML is required. Encode values placed in URLs with encodeURIComponent. On the server, send correct Content-Type headers, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so JSON is never interpreted as HTML.

What's a CSRF risk with AJAX if the API uses cookies?

The browser sends cookies with cross-site requests in some cases, so another site can trigger a state-changing call even though it cannot read the response. A JSON content type gives some protection through preflight, but that is not a design you should rely on. Use SameSite=Lax or Strict cookies, plus a CSRF token, and check the Origin header. A fetch with Authorization: Bearer from memory is not CSRF-prone, since browsers do not attach that automatically.

The file downloads but is named "download" or the header is null. Why?

On a cross-origin call, JavaScript can only read a small list of "CORS-safelisted" response headers (such as Content-Type). Content-Disposition is not on it, so res.headers.get('Content-Disposition') returns null until the server adds Access-Control-Expose-Headers: Content-Disposition (in Spring: exposedHeaders("Content-Disposition")). The same applies to custom headers like X-Total-Count used for pagination.

How do you send a JWT with EventSource (SSE)?

You cannot: EventSource does not allow custom headers. Options: use cookie authentication (same-site, with withCredentials: true for cross-origin), pass a short-lived, single-use token in the query string (never the main access token, since URLs end up in logs), or use fetch with a streaming res.body reader and parse the SSE format yourself, which supports headers and POST bodies. The fetch approach loses automatic reconnection, so you add that yourself.

Why do WebSocket messages reach only some users when the app runs on two servers?

Each WebSocket connection is pinned to one server instance. With Spring's in-memory simple broker, a message published on instance A is delivered only to clients connected to A. Fix it with a broker relay (enableStompBrokerRelay to RabbitMQ or ActiveMQ) or a pub/sub layer such as Redis that fans messages out to all instances. Sticky sessions on the load balancer keep a client on one instance but do not solve fan-out.

REST vs GraphQL from the front-end point of view?

REST: one URL per resource, HTTP caching and status codes work naturally, simple to secure and monitor; but a screen may need several calls (under-fetching) or get fields it does not use (over-fetching). GraphQL: one endpoint, the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one round trip, with a typed schema; but HTTP caching is harder (usually POST), errors often come back with status 200 in an errors array, and the server must guard against expensive queries. Spring supports it via Spring for GraphQL. Choose GraphQL when many different clients need different shapes of the same data.

What does a 204 No Content mean for your fetch code?

res.ok is true, but there is no body, so await res.json() throws a SyntaxError. Check res.status === 204 (or the Content-Length) before parsing. Spring returns 204 from ResponseEntity.noContent().build() or a void method annotated @ResponseStatus(HttpStatus.NO_CONTENT), which is common for DELETE.

How do you send an array or a list of IDs to a Spring @RequestParam?

Spring binds repeated parameters or a comma list to List<Long> ids: ?ids=1&ids=2 or ?ids=1,2. Build it with URLSearchParams: ids.forEach(id => params.append('ids', id)). Avoid the bracket style ids[]=1 that some libraries produce by default (jQuery without traditional: true, some Axios serializers). For long lists, use a POST with a JSON body to stay under URL length limits.

jQuery DOM & AJAX library

"Write less, do more." A small library that wraps DOM selection, traversal, manipulation, events, animation and AJAX behind one chainable API. It's still common in legacy JSP and Thymeleaf apps and admin panels, so expect questions about it in maintenance-heavy projects.

Core API by category

<script src="https://code.jquery.com/jquery-3.7.1.min.js"></script>

// ---- Document ready (DOM parsed; doesn't wait for images) ----
$(function () { init(); });                    // shorthand for $(document).ready(fn)

// ---- Selectors (CSS + jQuery extensions) ----
$('#id'); $('.cls'); $('div p'); $('ul > li'); $('input[type="email"]');
$('li:first'); $('tr:even'); $('input:checked'); $(':input'); $('p:contains("Java")');

// ---- Traversal ----
$('#row').parent(); $('#row').closest('table'); $('#row').children('td');
$('#row').find('.price'); $('#row').siblings(); $('#row').next(); $('li').eq(2); $('li').first();

// ---- Manipulation ----
$('#title').text('Orders');                  // safe (escapes HTML)
$('#box').html('<b>Hi</b>');                // ⚠ XSS if content is user input
$('#name').val();  $('#name').val('Arun');    // form values
$('#link').attr('href', '/home');            // HTML attribute
$('#chk').prop('checked', true);             // live DOM property
$('#card').addClass('active').removeClass('hidden').toggleClass('open');
$('#card').css({ color: 'red', 'font-size': '14px' });
$('#list').append('<li>New</li>').prepend('<li>First</li>');
$('<div/>', { class: 'toast', text: 'Saved' }).appendTo('body');
$('.temp').remove();   $('#list').empty();   const $d = $('#panel').detach();   // keeps data/events
$('#row').data('id');                         // reads data-id="42"

// ---- Events ----
$('#save').on('click', function (e) { e.preventDefault(); $(this).prop('disabled', true); });
$('#table').on('click', '.delete-btn', function () {           // ✔ delegated: works for future rows
  const id = $(this).closest('tr').data('id');
  deleteRow(id);
});
$('#search').on('input', debounce(function () { search($(this).val()); }, 300));
$('#modal').one('shown', fn);                 // runs once
$(document).on('keydown', e => { if (e.key === 'Escape') closeModal(); });
$('#save').off('click');                      // remove handlers
$('#form').trigger('submit');

// ---- Effects ----
$('#msg').hide().fadeIn(300).delay(2000).fadeOut(300);
$('#panel').slideToggle(200);
$('#box').animate({ opacity: 0.5, left: '+=50' }, 400);

// ---- Utilities ----
$.each([1, 2, 3], (i, v) => console.log(i, v));
const merged = $.extend(true, {}, defaults, options);   // deep merge
$.isArray(x); $.trim(s); $.map(arr, fn);                  // (prefer native today)

jQuery AJAX in depth

// Global setup: JSON + CSRF header for Spring Security + JWT
$.ajaxSetup({
  contentType: 'application/json',
  headers: {
    'X-CSRF-TOKEN': $('meta[name="_csrf"]').attr('content'),
    Authorization: 'Bearer ' + localStorage.getItem('token')
  }
});

// Full form
$.ajax({
  url: '/api/users',
  type: 'POST',                          // or method
  data: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Arun', email: 'arun@x.com' }),
  dataType: 'json',                      // expected response type
  timeout: 5000,
  beforeSend() { $('#spinner').show(); }
})
.done((user, textStatus, jqXHR) => {
  $('#users').append(`<tr data-id="${user.id}"><td>${escapeHtml(user.name)}</td></tr>`);
})
.fail((jqXHR, textStatus, err) => {
  if (jqXHR.status === 400) showErrors(jqXHR.responseJSON);
  else if (jqXHR.status === 401) location.href = '/login';
  else alertBox('Error: ' + (jqXHR.responseJSON?.detail || err));
})
.always(() => $('#spinner').hide());

// Shorthands
$.get('/api/users', { page: 0 }, data => render(data));
$.getJSON('/api/users/1').done(render);
$.post('/api/login', $('#loginForm').serialize());        // form-urlencoded: name=..&pwd=..
$('#result').load('/fragments/table.html #rows');          // inject an HTML fragment

// Parallel requests with Deferred
$.when($.getJSON('/api/user/1'), $.getJSON('/api/orders?user=1'))
 .done((userRes, ordersRes) => render(userRes[0], ordersRes[0]));

// jqXHR is "thenable" → works with async/await
const user = await $.getJSON('/api/users/1');

// Global AJAX events (e.g. one spinner for all calls)
$(document).ajaxStart(() => $('#spinner').show()).ajaxStop(() => $('#spinner').hide());

Mini CRUD example: a JSP/Thymeleaf page with jQuery and a Spring REST API

<form id="empForm">
  <input name="name" required> <input name="salary" type="number" required>
  <button>Add</button>
</form>
<table id="empTable"><tbody></tbody></table>

<script>
$(function () {
  const $tbody = $('#empTable tbody');                    // cache the selector
  const row = e => $('<tr>').attr('data-id', e.id)
      .append($('<td>').text(e.name), $('<td>').text(e.salary),
              $('<td>').html('<button class="del">Delete</button>'));

  $.getJSON('/api/employees').done(list => $tbody.append(list.map(row)));   // one DOM insert

  $('#empForm').on('submit', function (e) {
    e.preventDefault();
    const body = Object.fromEntries(new FormData(this));
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/employees', method: 'POST', contentType: 'application/json',
             data: JSON.stringify(body) })
     .done(emp => { $tbody.append(row(emp)); this.reset(); });
  });

  $tbody.on('click', '.del', function () {                // delegation
    const $tr = $(this).closest('tr');
    $.ajax({ url: '/api/employees/' + $tr.data('id'), method: 'DELETE' })
     .done(() => $tr.fadeOut(200, () => $tr.remove()));
  });
});
</script>

Writing a jQuery plugin

(function ($) {
  $.fn.highlight = function (options) {
    const settings = $.extend({ color: 'yellow', duration: 800 }, options);
    return this.each(function () {                        // keep chainability
      const $el = $(this), orig = $el.css('background-color');
      $el.css('background-color', settings.color)
         .delay(settings.duration)
         .queue(next => { $el.css('background-color', orig); next(); });
    });
  };
})(jQuery);

$('.new-row').highlight({ color: '#dff0d8' }).addClass('seen');

jQuery vs Vanilla JS

TaskjQueryVanilla JS (modern)
Select$('.item')document.querySelectorAll('.item')
Ready$(fn)document.addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', fn) or defer
Class.addClass('a')el.classList.add('a')
Event delegation.on('click', '.btn', fn)parent.addEventListener('click', e => e.target.closest('.btn') && fn(e))
Text / HTML.text() / .html()el.textContent / el.innerHTML
Closest.closest('tr')el.closest('tr')
AJAX$.getJSON(url)fetch(url).then(r => r.json())
Animation.fadeIn()CSS transitions, el.animate() (Web Animations API)
Each$.each / .eachforEach, for...of
💡 Where jQuery stands today: the cross-browser problems it solved are gone (old IE is dead, and querySelectorAll, classList, fetch and closest exist natively), and frameworks like Angular manage the DOM declaratively. Don't mix jQuery DOM manipulation into Angular components, because it bypasses change detection. It's still fine for small server-rendered pages and for maintaining legacy apps. Recent versions are 3.7.x, plus the 4.0 line, which drops old browsers.

The $() function and filtering methods

CallDoes
$('.a'), $('.a', ctx)Selects, optionally within a context (same as $(ctx).find('.a'))
$(domEl), $(array)Wraps existing elements
$('<div>')Creates elements when the string looks like HTML
$(fn)Runs at DOM ready
$($x)Returns a new jQuery object for the same elements
Gotcha: because a string may be read as HTML, $(userInput) can execute script. Classic DOM XSS: $(location.hash). Use $('#' + CSS.escape(id)) or document.getElementById.
$('li').get(0);          // raw DOM element ($('li')[0] is the same)
$('li').eq(0);           // jQuery object wrapping element 0
$('li').toArray();
$('li').length;
$('li').index(el);

$('li').filter('.on');   // narrow this set
$('li').not('.on');      // remove from this set
$('li').has('a');        // keep elements with a matching DESCENDANT
$('li').is('.on');       // boolean: does any match?
$('li').add('.extra');   // grow the set
$('li').find('a').addBack();   // the links plus the li elements
$('li').find('a').end();       // back to the li set

// .each: `return false` breaks, `return true` continues
$('li').each(function (i, el) { if (i === 2) return false; });

// .map: returns a jQuery object, so call .get() for a real array
const ids = $('tr').map((i, el) => $(el).data('id')).get();

$('#a').clone(true);          // true copies data and events; beware of duplicate ids
$('p').wrap('<div class="w"></div>');  $('p').unwrap();
$('#old').replaceWith('<p>new</p>');
$('.item').before('<hr>').after('<hr>');

.data(), dimensions and positions

.data('id') reads a data-id attribute once, converts the type ("42" becomes the number 42, "true" a boolean, and JSON strings are parsed), and stores it in jQuery's internal cache. .data('id', 7) writes only to this cache and does not touch the attribute. So a later .attr('data-id') or a CSS selector like [data-id="7"] still sees the old value. A long numeric ID such as "00123" or a large number keeps its string form, since it would not round-trip as a number.

MethodIncludes
.width()Content only
.innerWidth()Content and padding
.outerWidth()Content, padding, border
.outerWidth(true)Also margin
.offset()Position relative to the document; can be set
.position()Position relative to the offset parent; read-only
.scrollTop()Scroll position; pair with .animate({ scrollTop })

Events: custom events, namespaces and the event object

// Namespaces: remove only your handlers
$(window).on('resize.gallery', layout);
$(window).off('.gallery');

// Custom events are a light pub-sub on the DOM
$('#cart').on('cart:updated', (e, total) => $('#badge').text(total));
$('#cart').trigger('cart:updated', [3]);      // extra args follow the event

$('#x').trigger('click');          // runs handlers, bubbles, and runs the default action
$('#x').triggerHandler('click');   // first element only, no bubbling, no default action, returns the value

// Handler data, several events at once
$('#a').on('click', { id: 5 }, e => console.log(e.data.id));
$('#a').on({ mouseenter: on, mouseleave: off });
$('#a').on('click', function (e) { e.stopImmediatePropagation(); });

jQuery wraps the native event in a normalised jQuery.Event; use e.originalEvent for the native one, for instance for e.originalEvent.clipboardData. Shortcut methods such as .click(fn) are deprecated from 3.3, so prefer .on().

Gotcha: .trigger('cart:updated') reaches only handlers bound through jQuery. It does not dispatch a native event, so addEventListener('cart:updated', ...) never fires. Use el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent(...)) when native code must hear it.

Effects queue

Animations on an element run through a queue named fx, one after the other. Rapid hovers can stack many animations, so the element keeps moving after the mouse has left. Call .stop(true, true) first, which clears the queue and jumps to the end. .finish() ends everything at once. .delay() works only for queued operations, so .delay(1000).addClass('x') does not delay the class change. Use .queue() or a callback. $('#a').promise().done(fn) runs when all animations for that set have finished. $.fx.off = true disables animations, which helps in tests.

$.ajax options not covered above

$.ajax({
  url: '/api/report',
  data: { ids: [1, 2] },        // ids[]=1&ids[]=2 by default
  traditional: true,            // ids=1&ids=2, which suits Spring's List<Long> @RequestParam
  cache: false,                 // appends ?_=timestamp to GETs
  statusCode: { 404: showMissing, 403: showDenied },
  xhrFields: { withCredentials: true },       // send cookies cross-origin
  processData: false,           // needed with FormData
  contentType: false,           // lets the browser set the multipart boundary
  dataFilter: (raw, type) => raw,             // pre-process the raw response
});

// Run before every request, a cleaner place for headers than $.ajaxSetup
$.ajaxPrefilter((options, original, jqXHR) => {
  if (!options.crossDomain) jqXHR.setRequestHeader('X-CSRF-TOKEN', token);
});

// Upload with progress
$.ajax({
  url: '/api/files', method: 'POST', data: fd, processData: false, contentType: false,
  xhr() {
    const x = new XMLHttpRequest();
    x.upload.addEventListener('progress', e => $('#bar').val(e.loaded / e.total));
    return x;
  },
});

Gotchas: $.ajaxSetup changes defaults for all code on the page, including plugins, and the jQuery docs advise against it. For instance, the earlier global contentType: 'application/json' also applies to $.post() with .serialize(), so the server receives a form-encoded body labelled as JSON. success, error, and complete callbacks in the options still work; only the older jqXHR.success() and friends were removed in 3.0, replaced by .done(), .fail(), .always().

Security and versions

  • jQuery 3.5.0 fixed two XSS issues in HTML parsing (CVE-2020-11022 and CVE-2020-11023), where passing even "sanitised" HTML to .html() and similar could run code. If a legacy app is on an older version, this is the first thing to upgrade.
  • $.parseHTML(html, null, false) parses without running scripts, but event-handler attributes can still fire when inserted. It is not a sanitiser.
  • $.getScript and dataType: 'script' execute a remote response. For cross-domain URLs, jQuery 3 stopped evaluating script automatically unless dataType says so.
  • jQuery Migrate restores removed APIs and logs warnings during an upgrade.
  • The slim build omits AJAX and effects, for smaller pages that need only DOM work.
  • jQuery 4.0 drops older browsers and removes long-deprecated helpers, including $.isArray, $.trim, $.parseJSON, $.type, $.now and $.isFunction. So the earlier $.isArray and $.trim lines need native Array.isArray and String.prototype.trim there.

Plugins you meet in legacy Spring apps

// DataTables with Spring Data Pageable (server-side processing)
$('#orders').DataTable({
  serverSide: true,
  ajax: (d, callback) => {
    const page = d.start / d.length, sort = `${d.columns[d.order[0].column].data},${d.order[0].dir}`;
    $.getJSON('/api/orders', { page, size: d.length, sort }).done(p => callback({
      draw: d.draw, recordsTotal: p.totalElements, recordsFiltered: p.totalElements, data: p.content
    }));
  },
  columns: [{ data: 'id' }, { data: 'customer' }, { data: 'amount' }],
});

// jQuery Validation
$('#form').validate({
  rules: { email: { required: true, email: true, remote: '/api/email-free' } },
  submitHandler(form) { /* AJAX submit */ },
});

Global AJAX events and session expiry in legacy Spring apps

jQuery fires global events on document for every $.ajax call (unless global: false): ajaxStart/ajaxStop when the first request starts and the last one finishes, and ajaxSend, ajaxSuccess, ajaxError, ajaxComplete per request. They are the jQuery equivalent of an Angular interceptor and are ideal for a global spinner and central error handling.

A classic bug: when the server session expires, Spring Security redirects an AJAX call to the login page; the browser follows the redirect silently and your success callback receives login-page HTML with status 200. Fix it on the server by returning 401 for AJAX requests, then handle it once on the client.

// One spinner for all calls
$(document)
  .on('ajaxStart', () => $('#spinner').show())
  .on('ajaxStop',  () => $('#spinner').hide())
  .on('ajaxError', (e, xhr) => {
    if (xhr.status === 401) location.href = '/login?expired';
    else if (xhr.status >= 500) showToast('Server error, please try again');
  });

// Spring Security 6: answer 401 instead of redirecting for API/AJAX calls
http.exceptionHandling(ex -> ex.defaultAuthenticationEntryPointFor(
    new HttpStatusEntryPoint(HttpStatus.UNAUTHORIZED),
    new RequestHeaderRequestMatcher("X-Requested-With", "XMLHttpRequest")));

jQuery adds the X-Requested-With: XMLHttpRequest header automatically to same-origin requests, which is why this matcher works. Native fetch does not add it.

Interview Questions — jQuery

What is jQuery and why was it so popular?

A fast, small JS library (about 30 KB gzipped) that gave one consistent API across browsers at a time when IE6–8, Firefox and Safari all behaved differently. Its strengths: CSS-selector DOM queries, implicit iteration and chaining, easy event handling, a simple AJAX API, animations, and a huge plugin ecosystem (DataTables, Select2, jQuery Validation).

$(document).ready() vs window.onload?

ready fires when the DOM is parsed (DOMContentLoaded), before images and stylesheets finish loading. You can register many handlers, and they still run if registered after the event has fired. window.onload waits for everything (images, CSS, iframes), and assigning it directly allows only one handler (each assignment overwrites the last). Use ready for DOM setup and load when you need image dimensions.

What does $ mean? What is jQuery.noConflict()?

$ is just an alias for the jQuery function. If another library (Prototype, an old MooTools) also uses $, call jQuery.noConflict() to release it, then use jQuery(...) or wrap your code: (function($){ ... })(jQuery);.

.attr() vs .prop()?

.attr() reads and writes the HTML attribute, which is the initial value in the markup. .prop() reads and writes the live DOM property, which is the current state. For checkboxes, .attr('checked') keeps returning the original attribute after the user clicks, while .prop('checked') returns true or false. Use prop for checked, selected, disabled and value-like state, and attr for things like href, data-* and aria-*.

.text() vs .html() vs .val()?

.text() gets or sets text content and escapes HTML, so it's XSS-safe. .html() gets or sets inner HTML and parses markup, so it's dangerous with user input. .val() gets or sets the value of form controls (input, select, textarea).

.on() vs .click() vs .bind()/.live()/.delegate()?

.on() (since 1.7) is the single unified API. .click(fn) is shorthand for .on('click', fn). .bind() and .delegate() are deprecated and .live() was removed, all in favour of .on(). With a selector argument, .on('click', '.row', fn) does delegation: the handler sits on the parent and matches descendants, including ones added later. Remove handlers with .off(), and use namespaces ('click.myPlugin') so you can remove only your own.

event.preventDefault() vs event.stopPropagation() vs return false?

preventDefault() cancels the browser's default action (following a link, submitting a form). stopPropagation() stops the event bubbling up to ancestors. return false in a jQuery handler does both. In a native addEventListener handler it does neither, and in an inline onclick attribute it only prevents the default. Be explicit and call the methods you mean.

.remove() vs .detach() vs .empty()?

.empty() removes the children but keeps the element. .remove() removes the element and its jQuery data and event handlers. .detach() removes the element but keeps its data and events, so you can re-insert it later (useful for heavy DOM manipulation off-screen).

this vs $(this) inside a handler?

this is the raw DOM element, so you use native APIs like this.value and this.id. $(this) wraps it in a jQuery object so you can use .closest(), .data() and so on. In arrow functions this isn't the element, so use e.currentTarget. Cache wrappers you use repeatedly: const $btn = $(this);.

What is a Deferred / Promise in jQuery? $.when?

$.Deferred() is jQuery's promise implementation. You resolve or reject it, and consumers chain .done(), .fail(), .always() and .then(). Every $.ajax call returns a jqXHR, which is a Deferred, so $.when(a, b).done(...) waits for several requests in parallel, like Promise.all. Since jQuery 3, Deferreds follow Promises/A+ and work with await.

What does .serialize() do? How do you send JSON instead?

$('form').serialize() produces a URL-encoded string (name=Arun&age=30), which Spring binds with @ModelAttribute or @RequestParam. .serializeArray() gives [{name, value}]. For a @RequestBody JSON endpoint, build an object and send JSON.stringify(obj) with contentType: 'application/json'.

How do you improve jQuery performance?

Cache selectors (const $list = $('#list')). Start from an ID and use .find() rather than broad selectors. Build HTML in memory and insert it once instead of appending in a loop. Use event delegation instead of thousands of handlers. Detach elements before heavy changes. Avoid jQuery-only pseudo-selectors (:visible, :first) in hot paths, and prefer CSS animations. Or replace jQuery with native APIs.

.closest() vs .parents() vs .parent()?

.parent() goes up exactly one level. .parents(sel) returns all matching ancestors up to the document. .closest(sel) starts with the element itself and returns the first match going up (zero or one element), which makes it the standard choice for finding the row from a clicked button.

Should you use jQuery with Angular?

Generally no. Angular owns the DOM through templates and change detection, and jQuery changes are invisible to it, which causes inconsistent state, memory leaks and SSR problems. Use bindings, directives, Renderer2, or ElementRef sparingly. If a legacy jQuery plugin is unavoidable, wrap it in a directive: initialize it in ngAfterViewInit, destroy it in ngOnDestroy, and run it outside the Angular zone if it's noisy.

What does .data('id', 5) do to the DOM attribute?

Nothing. It writes to jQuery's internal cache only. .data('id') returns 5, but .attr('data-id') gives the old value, and a selector [data-id="5"] does not match. To keep them in sync, use .attr('data-id', 5). Note that after .data() has cached the value, later .attr() changes are not seen by .data().

Why does $('#a').map(...) not behave like an array, and how do you fix it?

jQuery's .map returns a jQuery object, with an argument order of (index, element), the reverse of Array.prototype.map. Call .get() or .toArray() for a real array. $.map(array, (value, index) => ...) is different again: the order is (value, index), and returned arrays are flattened, while null results are removed.

Why is a delegated handler sometimes not firing?
  • An inner handler calls stopPropagation(), so the event never reaches the delegating ancestor.
  • The ancestor itself was replaced, for instance by .html() on the parent, which removes the listener.
  • The event does not bubble natively. jQuery maps focus and blur to bubbling versions for delegation.
  • The selector does not match at click time. It is evaluated against the element and its ancestors up to the delegate.
$(el).remove() vs el.remove(): why does it matter for memory?

jQuery stores handlers and data in its own internal structure, linked to the element. $(el).remove(), .empty() and .html('...') clean up that data for the removed subtree. Native el.remove() or el.innerHTML = '' leaves the entries behind, so handler closures stay referenced, a slow leak. In a page that mixes both, always remove through jQuery.

.prop('disabled') vs .attr('disabled') vs .is(':disabled'); how do you read a checkbox?

.prop('checked') returns a boolean for the current state, and .is(':checked') gives the same result as a readable test. .attr('checked') reflects the markup, returning 'checked' or undefined, and does not follow clicks. For all checked values in a group: $('input[name=role]:checked').map((i, e) => e.value).get(). .val() on a checkbox gives its value attribute, not whether it is checked.

What's the cost of :visible, :first and other jQuery extensions?

jQuery first tries the fast native querySelectorAll. Pseudo-selectors that are not CSS, such as :first, :eq(), :visible and :has() (in older browsers), make it fall back to the slower Sizzle engine in JavaScript. :visible also reads layout, forcing a reflow per element. Use .filter(':visible') on a small set, and .first() instead of :first.

Why is async: false a bad idea? What does it do to the page?

It makes a synchronous XHR, freezing the main thread, so that clicks, scroll and animation all stop until the response arrives. Synchronous XHR on the main thread is deprecated, and browsers log a warning. It also cannot be used with dataType: 'jsonp'. Developers use it to "return" a value from a function. The fix is to return the jqXHR or a promise and to continue in .done() or with await.

What's the output order? $(fn) vs inline code, and .then on a resolved Deferred in jQuery 3.
const d = $.Deferred().resolve('v');
d.done(v => console.log('done', v));
d.then(v => console.log('then', v));
console.log('sync');
// Prints: done v, sync, then v

.done is the old jQuery API, and it runs synchronously on a resolved Deferred. .then follows Promises/A+ from jQuery 3, so it is always asynchronous. Since 3.0, $(fn) is also asynchronous, even if the document is already ready, so a handler registered after the DOM is ready still runs after the current script.

How do you migrate a jQuery page to modern code step by step?
  1. Upgrade to the latest 3.x with jQuery Migrate, and fix its warnings.
  2. Put tests around key flows with Playwright or Cypress.
  3. Replace helpers with native equivalents (fetch, classList, closest), starting with new code.
  4. Replace plugins one at a time. DataTables and Select2 have non-jQuery options.
  5. Rewrite heavy screens as Angular components or web components, mounted inside the old page, and move routes over gradually (the strangler pattern).
  6. Remove jQuery when no code uses it. Some plugins keep it alive for a long time, so track these.
How would you write a plugin with destroy and per-element state?
(function ($) {
  class Counter {
    constructor(el, opts) {
      this.$el = $(el); this.n = opts.start;
      this.$el.on('click.counter', () => this.$el.text(++this.n));
    }
    destroy() { this.$el.off('.counter').removeData('counter'); }
  }
  $.fn.counter = function (arg) {
    return this.each(function () {
      const inst = $.data(this, 'counter');
      if (typeof arg === 'string') inst?.[arg]();                     // $('.x').counter('destroy')
      else if (!inst) $.data(this, 'counter', new Counter(this, $.extend({ start: 0 }, arg)));
    });
  };
})(jQuery);

Key points are: an IIFE to protect $, returning this.each to keep chaining, one instance per element stored with $.data, namespaced events, and a destroy that undoes everything.

$.extend shallow vs deep; how is it different from spread?

$.extend({}, a, b) copies top-level properties, like { ...a, ...b }. $.extend(true, {}, a, b) merges recursively into plain objects and arrays. Two differences from spread: $.extend skips undefined values, while spread copies them; and it also copies inherited enumerable properties. Calling it without a target object as first argument modifies the first object, a frequent bug when defaults gets changed for all calls.

How do you prevent a form from being submitted twice with jQuery?

Disable the submit button when the request starts and re-enable it in .always(), so it is restored on success and failure. Check a flag at the start of the handler for fast double-clicks. The server should still be safe against duplicates (an idempotency key or a unique constraint), because the client can never fully guarantee it.

$('#orderForm').on('submit', function (e) {
  e.preventDefault();
  const $btn = $(this).find('[type=submit]');
  if ($btn.prop('disabled')) return;
  $btn.prop('disabled', true);
  $.post('/api/orders', $(this).serialize())
    .done(showSuccess)
    .always(() => $btn.prop('disabled', false));
});
How do you upload a file with jQuery AJAX to a Spring MultipartFile endpoint?

Build a FormData from the form (or append the file) and set processData: false so jQuery does not try to turn it into a query string, and contentType: false so the browser sets multipart/form-data with the correct boundary. Setting the content type manually breaks the boundary and Spring cannot parse the parts.

const fd = new FormData();
fd.append('file', $('#file')[0].files[0]);
$.ajax({ url: '/api/upload', type: 'POST', data: fd, processData: false, contentType: false });
// Spring: @PostMapping("/api/upload") void upload(@RequestParam("file") MultipartFile file)
Why does Spring not bind an array sent with $.ajax data: { ids: [1, 2] }?

By default $.param serializes arrays in PHP style as ids[]=1&ids[]=2, and Spring's @RequestParam List<Long> ids expects ids=1&ids=2. Pass traditional: true in the $.ajax options (or set it in $.ajaxSetup), or send JSON with contentType: 'application/json' and JSON.stringify to a @RequestBody.

$.each vs .each: what is the difference?

$('li').each(fn) iterates over a jQuery collection of DOM elements; inside, this is the raw element. $.each(obj, fn) is a general utility that iterates over any array or object; the callback gets (index, value) or (key, value). In both, returning false stops the loop early, which native forEach cannot do. Note the argument order is the reverse of native forEach(value, index).

What changed in jQuery 4, and what breaks when upgrading?

jQuery 4 drops support for old browsers such as IE 10 and earlier, removes long-deprecated utilities (for example $.isArray, $.trim, $.type, $.isFunction, $.now; use native equivalents), and changes some focus event ordering and JSONP auto-promotion behaviour. The safe path is: upgrade to the latest 3.x, add jQuery Migrate to log every deprecated call, fix the warnings, then move to 4 and remove Migrate. Check that plugins such as DataTables or Select2 support the target version.

HTML & CSS SCSS · Bootstrap

Semantic, accessible HTML gives a page its structure and meaning; CSS (often written in SCSS and combined with Bootstrap 5) handles layout, responsiveness and visual design.

<main class="container">
  <form class="row g-3" novalidate>
    <div class="col-12 col-md-6">
      <label for="email" class="form-label">Email</label>
      <input id="email" type="email" class="form-control" required autocomplete="email">
    </div>
    <div class="col-12">
      <button type="submit" class="btn btn-primary">Save</button>
    </div>
  </form>
</main>

/* styles.scss */
@use "sass:math";
$gap: 1rem;
.card-grid {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: repeat(auto-fill, minmax(16rem, 1fr));
  gap: $gap;
  &__item { padding: math.div($gap, 2); }
}

Semantic HTML5 & Accessibility

Use elements for their meaning: <header>, <nav>, <main>, <aside>, <footer> are landmarks screen readers can jump between; <article> and <section> group content; headings h1–h6 should form a logical outline. Use <button> for actions and <a href> for navigation — never a clickable <div>.

  • Every image needs alt; decorative images use alt="".
  • Every input needs a <label for> (or aria-label when no visible label exists).
  • First rule of ARIA: prefer native elements; add ARIA (aria-expanded, aria-live, role="dialog") only when HTML has no equivalent.
  • Keep keyboard focus visible, ensure logical tab order and adequate colour contrast (WCAG AA: 4.5:1 for normal text).

Forms & Validation

HTML5 offers built-in constraint validation: required, type="email|number|url|date", min/max, minlength/maxlength, pattern. The CSS pseudo-classes :valid, :invalid and :user-invalid style state. Frameworks like Angular add novalidate and handle validation in reactive forms, but client-side validation is only UX — always validate again on the server (e.g. Bean Validation in Spring Boot).

<input id="pin" name="pin" inputmode="numeric" pattern="[0-9]{6}"
       required aria-describedby="pin-help">
<small id="pin-help">6 digits</small>

Box Model, Specificity & the Cascade

Every element is a box: content → padding → border → margin. With the default box-sizing: content-box, width applies only to content, so padding and border add to the rendered size. border-box makes width include padding and border, which is far easier to reason about — Bootstrap's reboot sets it globally. Vertical margins between block elements can collapse (the larger one wins); this does not happen inside flex or grid containers.

*, *::before, *::after { box-sizing: border-box; }

Specificity & the cascade: when rules conflict, the browser considers: origin and !important → cascade layers (@layer) → specificity → source order. Specificity is counted as (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements): #nav .item a = (1,1,1). Inline styles beat selectors; !important beats both and should be a last resort. :where() has zero specificity, :is()/:not() take the specificity of their most specific argument. Some properties (colour, font) inherit; others (margin, border) do not.

Flexbox & CSS Grid

Flexbox is one-dimensional (row or column) and content-driven — ideal for toolbars, nav bars, centring and aligning items. Key properties: justify-content (main axis), align-items (cross axis), flex-wrap, gap, and on children flex: grow shrink basis. Grid is two-dimensional (rows and columns) and layout-driven — ideal for page layouts and card galleries.

.toolbar { display: flex; align-items: center; justify-content: space-between; gap: .5rem; }
.toolbar .search { flex: 1 1 auto; }

.layout {
  display: grid;
  grid-template-columns: 240px 1fr;
  grid-template-areas: "side main";
}
@media (max-width: 767.98px) {
  .layout { grid-template-columns: 1fr; grid-template-areas: "main" "side"; }
}

Positioning, Stacking Context & z-index

position: static (default), relative (offset from normal spot, still occupies space), absolute (removed from flow, positioned against nearest positioned ancestor), fixed (against viewport), sticky (relative until a scroll threshold, then sticks). z-index only orders elements within the same stacking context. A new stacking context is created by e.g. a positioned element with a z-index, opacity < 1, transform, filter, isolation: isolate. That is why a modal with z-index: 9999 can still appear behind something — its parent's context is lower.

Responsive Design, Units & Custom Properties

Mobile-first: write base styles for small screens, then add min-width media queries to enhance. Always include <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">. Use fluid layouts, max-width: 100% on images, srcset/<picture> for responsive images, and container queries (@container) for component-level responsiveness.

  • px — absolute; rem — relative to root font size (best for spacing/type, respects user settings); em — relative to the element's own font size (compounds when nested); % — relative to parent; vw/vh — 1% of viewport (dvh handles mobile browser bars); clamp(min, preferred, max) for fluid type.
  • Custom properties (--brand: #0d6efd; color: var(--brand, blue);) are runtime, inherit through the DOM and can be changed with JS or per theme — unlike Sass variables, which are compiled away.
:root { --space: 1rem; --text: #222; }
[data-theme="dark"] { --text: #eee; }
h1 { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 2.5rem); color: var(--text); }
@media (min-width: 768px) { .grid { grid-template-columns: repeat(2, 1fr); } }

Transitions, Animations & Performance

transition animates a property change between two states; @keyframes + animation define multi-step, looping animations. For smooth 60fps, animate only transform and opacity, which the browser can composite on the GPU; animating width, top or margin triggers layout (reflow) and paint every frame. Use will-change sparingly and respect @media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce).

.card { transition: transform .2s ease, opacity .2s ease; }
.card:hover { transform: translateY(-4px); }
@media (prefers-reduced-motion: reduce) { .card { transition: none; } }

SCSS / Sass

Sass is a CSS preprocessor; SCSS is its CSS-compatible syntax. Features: variables ($primary), nesting with & for parent reference (great for BEM), partials (_buttons.scss, not compiled alone), mixins (@mixin/@include, reusable blocks with arguments), @extend (share selectors), functions (@function, plus built-in modules like sass:math, sass:color), and control flow (@if, @each). The modern module system uses @use and @forward; @import is deprecated because it pollutes the global namespace and duplicates CSS.

// _mixins.scss
@mixin respond($bp) {
  @if $bp == md { @media (min-width: 768px) { @content; } }
}
@function rem($px) { @return math.div($px, 16) * 1rem; }

// card.scss
@use "sass:math";
@use "mixins" as m;
.card {
  padding: m.rem(12);
  &:hover { box-shadow: 0 2px 8px rgba(0,0,0,.15); }
  @include m.respond(md) { padding: m.rem(24); }
}

Bootstrap 5

Bootstrap 5 is a mobile-first CSS framework (no jQuery dependency since v5). The grid is flexbox-based: .container → .row → .col-* with 12 columns and breakpoints sm (576px), md (768px), lg (992px), xl (1200px), xxl (1400px). .col-12 .col-md-6 means full width on mobile, half from md up. Utilities (d-flex, justify-content-between, mt-3, p-2, text-center, d-none d-md-block) cover most one-off styling. Components: navbar, card, modal, dropdown, toast, accordion, forms with .form-control and .is-invalid. 5.3 adds colour modes via data-bs-theme="dark" and exposes CSS variables.

// custom.scss — override variables BEFORE importing Bootstrap
$primary: #6f42c1;
$border-radius: .5rem;
$enable-shadows: true;
@import "bootstrap/scss/bootstrap";   // Bootstrap 5 still uses @import internally

// Or at runtime with CSS variables (5.3):
// .btn-primary { --bs-btn-bg: #6f42c1; }

Modern CSS: :has(), container queries, nesting and cascade layers

These are supported in all current major browsers and are now common interview topics because they replace JavaScript or preprocessor tricks.

  • :has(), the "parent selector": style an element based on what it contains. .card:has(img), label:has(+ input:invalid), form:has(:user-invalid) button { opacity: .5 }.
  • Container queries: a component responds to the width of its container, not the viewport, so the same card works in a sidebar and a main column. Declare container-type: inline-size on the parent, then use @container. Units cqi/cqw are relative to the container.
  • Native nesting: .card { &:hover { … } .title { … } } works without Sass.
  • @layer: declare layer order once (@layer reset, base, components, utilities;). A later layer always wins over an earlier one regardless of specificity, and unlayered styles beat all layers. This tames third-party CSS such as Bootstrap.
  • :is() vs :where(): both match any selector in the list; :where() has zero specificity, ideal for easily overridden defaults.
  • @supports: feature detection, for example @supports (container-type: inline-size) { … }.
.sidebar, .main { container-type: inline-size; }

.product-card { display: grid; gap: 1rem; }
@container (min-width: 480px) {
  .product-card { grid-template-columns: 160px 1fr; }   /* side-by-side only when there is room */
}

@layer vendor, app;
@import url('bootstrap.css') layer(vendor);
@layer app { .btn { border-radius: 999px; } }            /* wins even against .btn.btn-primary */

Tailwind CSS: utility-first styling

Tailwind provides small single-purpose classes (flex, p-4, text-sm, md:grid-cols-2, hover:bg-blue-600, dark:bg-gray-900) that you compose in markup. A build step scans your templates and generates only the classes you use, so the final CSS is small.

BootstrapTailwind
ApproachReady-made components (.btn, .modal, .navbar) plus some utilitiesUtilities only; you build the components
LookRecognisable default look unless themedNo default look; fully custom design
JSIncludes JS for dropdowns, modals, tooltipsNone; use Angular, Headless UI or your own code
CustomiseSass variables / CSS variablesTheme config (design tokens) in tailwind.config.js, or CSS @theme in v4
Best forAdmin panels and fast standard UIsCustom-designed products and design systems
  • Responsive prefixes are mobile-first: md: applies from the md breakpoint up.
  • Class names must appear as full strings in source; building them dynamically ('bg-' + color) is not detected by the scanner.
  • Repeated combinations are extracted into components (Angular components) rather than overused @apply.
  • Tailwind 3 runs as a PostCSS plugin with a content list in the config; Tailwind 4 moved configuration into CSS and detects sources automatically.
<button class="rounded-lg bg-blue-600 px-4 py-2 text-white hover:bg-blue-700
               focus-visible:outline focus-visible:outline-2 disabled:opacity-50
               md:px-6 dark:bg-blue-500">
  Save
</button>

Images, fonts and layout stability (LCP and CLS)

Most real-world speed problems in HTML/CSS come from images and fonts. The rules below directly improve Largest Contentful Paint and Cumulative Layout Shift.

  • Always give images width and height attributes (or CSS aspect-ratio) so the browser reserves space before the image loads; this prevents layout shift.
  • loading="lazy" for images below the fold; never lazy-load the hero/LCP image. Give it fetchpriority="high" instead.
  • srcset + sizes: let the browser pick a resolution for the screen. <picture> with <source>: choose a different format (AVIF, WebP) or a different crop (art direction).
  • object-fit: cover fills a box without distortion.
  • Fonts: font-display: swap shows fallback text immediately; preload the main font file; use WOFF2 and a subset.
  • Angular's NgOptimizedImage (ngSrc) enforces most of these automatically.
<picture>
  <source type="image/avif" srcset="hero-800.avif 800w, hero-1600.avif 1600w">
  <img srcset="hero-800.jpg 800w, hero-1600.jpg 1600w"
