       sizes="(max-width: 768px) 100vw, 50vw"
       width="1600" height="900" alt="Clinic reception desk"
       fetchpriority="high">
</picture>

.avatar { width: 48px; aspect-ratio: 1; object-fit: cover; border-radius: 50%; }

Display, visibility and the block formatting context

TechniqueTakes space?Clickable?Read by screen readers?Animatable?
display: noneNoNoNoNot by default
visibility: hiddenYesNoNoYes (discrete)
opacity: 0YesYesYesYes (smooth)
Visually hidden class (clip, 1px size)No visible spaceNoYesNo
hidden attributeSame as display: noneNoNoNo
  • block: starts on a new line, takes full width, accepts width/height. inline: flows in text, ignores width/height and vertical margins. inline-block: flows inline but accepts width, height and all margins.
  • A block formatting context (BFC) is an isolated layout region: floats inside it are contained, and its margins do not collapse with its children's. Created by display: flow-root (the clean way), overflow other than visible, flex/grid items, absolute positioning, and others. It is the modern replacement for the "clearfix" hack.

Document essentials: doctype, head, SEO and native elements

<!DOCTYPE html>                                   <!-- standards mode; without it, quirks mode -->
<html lang="en">                                  <!-- language for screen readers and translation -->
<head>
  <meta charset="utf-8">
  <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1">
  <title>Patients | Clinic Portal</title>
  <meta name="description" content="Manage patient records and appointments.">
  <meta property="og:title" content="Clinic Portal">       <!-- link previews in chat apps -->
  <meta name="theme-color" content="#0f766e">
</head>
  • <dialog>: a native modal. dialog.showModal() gives a backdrop, focus handling, Escape to close and top-layer rendering (no z-index fights). Style the backdrop with ::backdrop.
  • <details>/<summary>: accessible accordion with no JavaScript.
  • <template>: inert markup cloned by JavaScript. data-* attributes: custom data read with el.dataset.
  • Dark mode: define colours as custom properties and redefine them in @media (prefers-color-scheme: dark); add color-scheme: light dark so form controls and scrollbars match.

Interview Questions — HTML & CSS

What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?

Semantic HTML uses elements that describe their meaning — <nav>, <main>, <article>, <button> — rather than generic <div>s. It improves accessibility (screen readers expose landmarks and roles), SEO (search engines understand structure) and maintainability. Native elements also come with built-in keyboard behaviour; a <button> is focusable and activates on Enter/Space for free.

When should you use ARIA attributes?

Only when native HTML cannot express the semantics — e.g. custom widgets like tabs (role="tablist", aria-selected), expandable panels (aria-expanded), live regions for async messages (aria-live="polite") or icon-only buttons (aria-label). ARIA changes only what assistive tech announces; it does not add behaviour, so you must also handle keyboard interaction. Incorrect ARIA is worse than none. 💡 Prefer <button> over <div role="button" tabindex="0">.

Explain the CSS box model and box-sizing.

Each element is content surrounded by padding, border and margin. With content-box (default), width: 200px plus padding: 20px and a 1px border renders 242px wide. With border-box, the total stays 200px and the content shrinks. Most projects (and Bootstrap) apply border-box to all elements for predictable sizing.

How is CSS specificity calculated?

As a tuple (IDs, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, elements/pseudo-elements), compared left to right. #main .btn:hover = (1,2,0) beats .nav .btn.primary = (0,3,0). Inline styles beat any selector, !important overrides normal declarations, and if specificity is equal the later rule wins. 💡 Keep specificity low and flat (single classes, BEM) so overrides stay easy.

Flexbox vs Grid — when do you use each?

Flexbox is one-dimensional and content-out: great for aligning items in a row or column, like a navbar or button group. Grid is two-dimensional and layout-in: you define rows and columns and place items, ideal for page layouts and card galleries. They combine well — a grid page layout whose cells use flex to align their contents.

How do you centre a div horizontally and vertically?

The modern way is flex or grid on the parent:

.parent { display: grid; place-items: center; }
/* or */
.parent { display: flex; justify-content: center; align-items: center; }

For an absolutely positioned element: top: 50%; left: 50%; transform: translate(-50%, -50%);. Horizontal-only centring of a block: margin-inline: auto with a set width.

Difference between position relative, absolute, fixed and sticky?

relative offsets the element from its normal position but keeps its space in the flow. absolute removes it from flow and positions it relative to the nearest positioned ancestor (or the initial containing block). fixed positions relative to the viewport and stays during scroll. sticky behaves like relative until a scroll offset is reached, then sticks within its parent — commonly used for table headers.

Why does my z-index not work?

Usually because of stacking contexts. z-index only compares siblings within the same stacking context, and properties like transform, opacity < 1, filter or a positioned parent with a z-index create a new one. A child can never escape above its parent's context. Also, z-index has no effect on position: static elements (except flex/grid items). 💡 Render modals and overlays at the end of body (Angular CDK overlay does this).

What is mobile-first design?

You write base CSS for the smallest screens and add min-width media queries to progressively enhance for larger screens. It keeps mobile CSS lean, forces content prioritisation and matches how Bootstrap's breakpoints work (.col-md-6 applies from md upward). The opposite, desktop-first, uses max-width queries to undo styles.

rem vs em vs px vs %?

px is fixed. rem is relative to the root (html) font size — consistent and respects the user's browser font setting, so it is preferred for font sizes and spacing. em is relative to the current element's font size and compounds when nested, useful for padding that should scale with a button's text. % is relative to the parent's corresponding dimension; vw/vh to the viewport.

CSS custom properties vs Sass variables?

Sass variables ($brand) are resolved at compile time and disappear from the output — they cannot change at runtime. CSS custom properties (--brand) live in the browser, cascade and inherit, can be scoped to a selector or media query and updated from JavaScript. Use Sass variables for build-time configuration and custom properties for theming such as dark mode.

Which CSS properties should you animate for performance and why?

transform and opacity. The rendering pipeline is style → layout → paint → composite; these two can be handled in the composite step on the GPU, while properties like width, height, top or margin force layout recalculation and repaint every frame, causing jank. Use translate instead of left, and scale instead of changing width.

What are mixins, partials and @use in SCSS?

A partial is a file prefixed with _ that is only meant to be included, not compiled alone. A mixin is a reusable block of declarations, optionally with parameters and @content, inserted with @include. @use loads a module once with a namespace (@use "mixins" as m; then m.respond(md)), replacing the deprecated @import which caused global name collisions and duplicated output.

Mixin vs @extend vs function in Sass?

A mixin copies its declarations into every place it is included and accepts arguments. @extend makes a selector share another selector's rules by grouping selectors in the output — smaller CSS, but can produce surprising selector chains and does not work across media queries. A function returns a value (e.g. converting px to rem) rather than declarations. Prefer mixins for parameterised styles and functions for calculations.

Explain the Bootstrap 5 grid system.

It is a 12-column flexbox grid: .container (or .container-fluid) holds .rows, and rows hold .cols. Column classes are mobile-first: .col-12 .col-md-6 .col-lg-4 means full width on phones, half from 768px, a third from 992px. Gutters are set with .g-*, .gx-*, .gy-*; .col without a number shares space equally, and .offset-* / .order-* adjust placement.

How do you customise Bootstrap's theme?

Install Bootstrap via npm and import its Sass source instead of the compiled CSS. Override variables such as $primary, $font-family-base or $grid-breakpoints before the import, and optionally import only the parts you need to reduce bundle size. In Bootstrap 5.3 you can also override CSS variables at runtime (--bs-primary, component-level --bs-btn-bg) and use data-bs-theme="dark" for colour modes. 💡 Avoid editing files inside node_modules.

What is margin collapsing?

When vertical margins of adjacent block elements (or a parent and its first/last child with no padding/border between) touch, they combine into a single margin equal to the larger value rather than their sum. It only happens vertically and in normal block flow — not in flex or grid containers, or with floated/absolutely positioned elements. Adding padding, a border or using display: flow-root on the parent prevents it.

display: none vs visibility: hidden vs opacity: 0?

display: none removes the element from layout and from the accessibility tree. visibility: hidden keeps its space but hides it from view, clicks and screen readers. opacity: 0 keeps space and it is still clickable and announced, which can trap keyboard users on invisible buttons. To hide text visually but keep it for screen readers, use a "visually hidden" utility class (Bootstrap's .visually-hidden, Tailwind's sr-only).

Pseudo-class vs pseudo-element?

A pseudo-class (single colon) selects an existing element in a particular state: :hover, :focus-visible, :nth-child(2n), :checked, :has(). A pseudo-element (double colon) styles a part of an element or inserts generated content: ::before, ::after, ::placeholder, ::first-line, ::selection. ::before and ::after need a content property to render.

Media queries vs container queries: when do you use each?

Use media queries for page-level layout decisions based on the viewport or user preferences (number of columns in the page grid, prefers-reduced-motion, prefers-color-scheme, print). Use container queries for reusable components that may be placed in containers of different widths, such as a card shown in a sidebar and in a main area. They work well together: media queries for the page shell, container queries inside components.

Tailwind vs Bootstrap: which would you choose?

Bootstrap gives ready-made, accessible-ish components and JavaScript behaviour, so it is fastest for internal tools and admin UIs where a standard look is fine. Tailwind gives a design-token system of utilities and no default look, which suits custom designs and design systems, and produces small CSS because unused classes are never generated. Common criticisms of Tailwind are long class lists in markup, solved by extracting components. Mixing both in one project usually causes conflicting resets and should be avoided.

How do you stop the page jumping while images and ads load (CLS)?

Reserve the space up front: set width and height on every <img> and <video> (the browser derives the aspect ratio), use aspect-ratio or a min-height for embeds, ads and skeleton loaders, and never insert banners above existing content unless the user asked. Use font-display: swap with a fallback font of similar metrics, and animate with transform instead of changing top or height.

What is :focus-visible and why not just remove outlines?

:focus-visible matches when the browser decides a focus ring should be shown, which is typically keyboard navigation and not mouse clicks. Writing outline: none on :focus makes the site unusable for keyboard users and fails WCAG. Instead, style :focus-visible with a clear ring and leave mouse clicks quiet. Also add a skip link ("Skip to main content") as the first focusable element so keyboard users can bypass the navigation.

What is a BFC and when have you needed one?

A block formatting context is an independent layout box. Creating one on a parent makes it contain its floats (so its height includes floated children), stops margin collapsing between it and its children, and stops it overlapping a neighbouring float. The clean way is display: flow-root; older code used overflow: hidden or a clearfix. With flexbox and grid it is needed less often, but it explains many "why is my container height zero" bugs.

What happens if you leave out the DOCTYPE or the viewport meta tag?

Without <!DOCTYPE html>, browsers render in quirks mode, which emulates old browser bugs (for example a different box model for some elements and odd table sizing), so layouts break unpredictably. Without the viewport meta tag, mobile browsers render the page at a desktop width of about 980px and zoom out, so your media queries for small screens never match and text is tiny.

Why use the native <dialog> element instead of a div modal?

showModal() renders the dialog in the browser's top layer above everything, so no z-index or stacking-context problems; it makes the rest of the page inert, closes on Escape, moves focus into the dialog and returns it on close, and exposes the right role to screen readers. A div modal needs all of that coded by hand. Use <form method="dialog"> inside it to close with a button value.

TypeScript Typed JavaScript

TypeScript is a statically typed superset of JavaScript that compiles to plain JS; it catches errors at compile time, powers rich IDE tooling and is the language Angular is built with.

interface Patient {
  readonly id: number;
  name: string;
  email?: string;
}

type ApiResult<T> =
  | { status: 'ok'; data: T }
  | { status: 'error'; message: string };

function handle<T>(res: ApiResult<T>): T | null {
  switch (res.status) {
    case 'ok':    return res.data;          // narrowed: data exists
    case 'error': console.error(res.message); return null;
  }
}

type PatientUpdate = Partial<Omit<Patient, 'id'>>;

Why TypeScript & Type Inference

TS adds a compile-time type system on top of JavaScript: types are erased at build time and do not exist at runtime. Benefits: errors caught before running, safe refactoring, autocomplete, self-documenting APIs and better teamwork on large codebases. It uses structural typing ("duck typing") — two types are compatible if their shapes match, regardless of name, unlike Java's nominal typing.

You annotate where it adds value (function parameters, public APIs) and let inference handle the rest: let count = 0 is inferred as number; const role = 'admin' is the literal type 'admin'. as const makes an object or array deeply readonly with literal types. The satisfies operator (TS 4.9+) checks a value against a type without widening it.

let ids: number[] = [1, 2];
function add(a: number, b: number): number { return a + b; }
const routes = { home: '/', admin: '/admin' } as const;   // readonly literal values
const config = { port: 8080 } satisfies Record<string, number>;

Interfaces vs Type Aliases

Both describe object shapes. Interfaces can be extended, implemented by classes and support declaration merging (re-declaring adds members — used to augment library types). Type aliases can name any type: unions, intersections, tuples, primitives, mapped and conditional types. Common convention: interface for object/DTO shapes and public contracts, type for unions and compositions.

interface Person { name: string }
interface Employee extends Person { empId: number }

type Id = string | number;
type Point = [x: number, y: number];
type Admin = Employee & { permissions: string[] };

Unions, Intersections & Narrowing

A union A | B is "either"; an intersection A & B is "both". With a union you can only use members common to all parts until you narrow:

  • typeof x === 'string' — primitives
  • x instanceof Date — classes
  • 'email' in x — property existence
  • Truthiness / equality checks (if (x != null))
  • Discriminated unions — a shared literal property (kind, status) that switch narrows on
  • Custom type guards: function isCat(a: Animal): a is Cat
type Shape = { kind: 'circle'; r: number } | { kind: 'rect'; w: number; h: number };
function area(s: Shape): number {
  switch (s.kind) {
    case 'circle': return Math.PI * s.r ** 2;
    case 'rect':   return s.w * s.h;
    default: const _exhaustive: never = s; return _exhaustive;  // compile error if a case is missing
  }
}

Generics & Constraints

Generics let functions, classes and interfaces work with many types while preserving type information — like Java generics, but erased differently (no runtime types at all). Constrain them with extends, and use keyof to relate parameters. Angular uses generics everywhere: Observable<T>, HttpClient.get<T>(), signal<T>(), FormControl<T>.

function getProp<T, K extends keyof T>(obj: T, key: K): T[K] {
  return obj[key];
}
interface Page<T> { content: T[]; totalElements: number; }   // matches a Spring Page response

this.http.get<Page<Patient>>('/api/patients?page=0');

Utility Types

  • Partial<T> — all properties optional (PATCH payloads)
  • Required<T> — all properties required
  • Readonly<T> — all properties readonly (shallow)
  • Pick<T, 'a' | 'b'> / Omit<T, 'id'> — select or remove keys
  • Record<K, V> — object with keys K and values V (lookup maps)
  • ReturnType<typeof fn>, Parameters<typeof fn>, Awaited<P>
  • NonNullable<T>, Exclude<U, X>, Extract<U, X>
type CreatePatientDto = Omit<Patient, 'id'>;
const labels: Record<'ACTIVE' | 'INACTIVE', string> = { ACTIVE: 'Active', INACTIVE: 'Inactive' };
// Under the hood, a mapped type:
type MyPartial<T> = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };

Enums vs Union Literals; any vs unknown vs never

Enums (enum Role { Admin = 'ADMIN' }) generate a runtime object; numeric enums are reverse-mapped and loosely typed. String literal unions (type Role = 'ADMIN' | 'USER') have zero runtime cost, work naturally with JSON from a backend and are often preferred; pair with an as const array when you need the values at runtime. const enum is inlined but problematic with isolated module builds.

  • any — turns off type checking; spreads unsafety. Avoid.
  • unknown — the safe top type: anything can be assigned, but you must narrow before using it (ideal for parsed JSON, catch (e)).
  • never — the bottom type: a value that never occurs (function that always throws, exhaustive check).
  • void — function returns nothing useful.

Classes & Access Modifiers

TS classes add public (default), private, protected and readonly, abstract classes and implements. TS private is compile-time only; JavaScript's #field is truly private at runtime. Parameter properties declare and assign a field in the constructor signature. In Angular 14+ you can also use the inject() function instead of constructor injection.

@Injectable({ providedIn: 'root' })
export class PatientService {
  private readonly http = inject(HttpClient);
  #cache = new Map<number, Patient>();          // runtime-private
  constructor(private readonly logger: Logger) {} // parameter property
  findAll(): Observable<Patient[]> { return this.http.get<Patient[]>('/api/patients'); }
}

Decorators (Angular)

Decorators are functions applied with @ to classes, members or parameters to attach metadata or change behaviour. Angular relies on them: @Component, @Injectable, @Directive, @Pipe, @NgModule, and member decorators @Input, @Output, @HostListener, @ViewChild. Angular historically uses the legacy experimentalDecorators implementation; TS 5.0 added standard ECMAScript decorators (which do not support parameter decorators). Modern Angular (17+) increasingly replaces member decorators with functions: input(), output(), viewChild(), inject().

@Component({ selector: 'app-card', standalone: true, template: '<h3>{{ title() }}</h3>' })
export class CardComponent {
  title = input.required<string>();   // signal input (replaces @Input)
  @Output() selected = new EventEmitter<number>();
}

tsconfig, Strict Mode & Modules

"strict": true enables a family of checks: strictNullChecks (null/undefined are separate types), noImplicitAny, strictPropertyInitialization (class fields must be initialised — use ! only when you are sure), strictFunctionTypes, useUnknownInCatchVariables. Other useful flags: noUncheckedIndexedAccess, noImplicitReturns, target, module, moduleResolution: "bundler", paths for import aliases. Angular adds strictTemplates in angularCompilerOptions.

TS uses ES modules: every file with a top-level import/export is a module with its own scope. Prefer named exports; use import type { X } for type-only imports (erased from output). Third-party JS libraries get types from .d.ts declaration files, often via @types/* packages.

// tsconfig.json (excerpt)
{
  "compilerOptions": {
    "strict": true,
    "noImplicitReturns": true,
    "target": "ES2022",
    "moduleResolution": "bundler",
    "paths": { "@core/*": ["src/app/core/*"] }
  },
  "angularCompilerOptions": { "strictTemplates": true }
}

Mapped, conditional and template literal types

These are how utility types such as Partial and ReturnType are built, and senior interviews often ask you to write one.

  • Mapped type: loop over keys. { [K in keyof T]: … }. Modifiers: readonly, ?, and removing them with -readonly and -?. Key remapping with as.
  • Conditional type: T extends U ? X : Y. When T is a bare type parameter and receives a union, it distributes over each member.
  • infer: capture part of a type inside a conditional type.
  • Template literal types: build string types, for example event names or API paths.
// Mapped types: how Partial and Readonly are written, plus key remapping
type MyPartial<T>  = { [K in keyof T]?: T[K] };
type Mutable<T>    = { -readonly [K in keyof T]: T[K] };
type Getters<T>    = { [K in keyof T as `get${Capitalize<string & K>}`]: () => T[K] };
// Getters<{ name: string }>  →  { getName: () => string }

// Conditional + infer
type ElementOf<T> = T extends readonly (infer E)[] ? E : never;
type Unwrap<T>    = T extends Promise<infer V> ? Unwrap<V> : T;   // like Awaited
type A = ElementOf<string[]>;                 // string

// Distribution over unions
type NonNull<T> = T extends null | undefined ? never : T;
type B = NonNull<string | null>;              // string

// Template literal types
type Entity = 'patient' | 'order';
type EventName = `${Entity}:${'created' | 'deleted'}`;   // 'patient:created' | 'patient:deleted' | ...

Type guards, assertion functions and exhaustive checks

Built-in narrowing (typeof, instanceof, in, equality, discriminant checks) covers most cases. When the check is in a separate function, you must tell the compiler what it proves.

interface ApiError { status: number; detail: string }

// User-defined type guard: returns boolean, narrows in the caller
function isApiError(x: unknown): x is ApiError {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'status' in x && 'detail' in x;
}

// Assertion function: throws if false, narrows everything after the call
function assertDefined<T>(v: T, msg = 'missing value'): asserts v is NonNullable<T> {
  if (v == null) throw new Error(msg);
}

// Exhaustive switch: adding a new status becomes a compile error here
type Status = 'ACTIVE' | 'SUSPENDED' | 'CLOSED';
function label(s: Status): string {
  switch (s) {
    case 'ACTIVE': return 'Active';
    case 'SUSPENDED': return 'On hold';
    case 'CLOSED': return 'Closed';
    default: { const never: never = s; throw new Error(`Unhandled ${never}`); }
  }
}

A type guard is only as correct as its body: TypeScript trusts x is ApiError without verifying it. Since TS 5.5, simple arrow functions such as arr.filter(x => x !== null) infer the type predicate automatically.

Functions: overloads, tuples and generic defaults

// Overloads: several call signatures, one implementation
function parse(v: string): number;
function parse(v: string[]): number[];
function parse(v: string | string[]): number | number[] {
  return Array.isArray(v) ? v.map(Number) : Number(v);
}
const n = parse('5');        // number
const ns = parse(['1', '2']); // number[]

// Tuples: fixed length and position types, optional labels
type Range = [start: number, end: number];
function useToggle(): readonly [boolean, () => void] { /* ... */ return [true, () => {}]; }

// Variadic tuple and generic default
type Prepend<T extends unknown[], H> = [H, ...T];
interface Page<T = unknown> { content: T[]; totalElements: number; number: number }

// const type parameter (TS 5.0): infer literal types without "as const" at the call site
function route<const T extends readonly string[]>(paths: T) { return paths; }
const r = route(['home', 'orders']);       // readonly ['home', 'orders']

Prefer a union parameter or generics over overloads when the return type does not depend on the input type; overloads are best when it does.

Types disappear at runtime: validation and branded types

All types are erased when compiled. http.get<User>() is a promise to the compiler, not a check: if the Spring API renames a field, the code compiles and fails at runtime. For data crossing a trust boundary (API responses, localStorage, URL params, messages) validate at runtime.

  • Schema libraries (Zod, Valibot, io-ts) define a schema once and infer the static type from it, so the two cannot drift.
  • Generate types from the backend's OpenAPI spec (springdoc-openapi plus an OpenAPI TypeScript generator) so DTO changes break the front-end build instead of production.
  • Branded types stop mixing up values with the same primitive type, such as a PatientId and an OrderId that are both numbers.
import { z } from 'zod';
const PatientSchema = z.object({ id: z.number(), name: z.string(), dob: z.string().date() });
type Patient = z.infer<typeof PatientSchema>;          // type derived from the schema
const patient = PatientSchema.parse(await res.json());  // throws if the shape is wrong

// Branded types
type PatientId = number & { readonly __brand: 'PatientId' };
type OrderId   = number & { readonly __brand: 'OrderId' };
const toPatientId = (n: number) => n as PatientId;
function loadPatient(id: PatientId) { /* ... */ }
// loadPatient(orderId);   // compile error: OrderId is not PatientId

Interview Questions — TypeScript

What is TypeScript and why use it over JavaScript?

TypeScript is a superset of JavaScript that adds static types and compiles (transpiles) to plain JS. It catches type errors at compile time, enables reliable refactoring and IDE autocomplete, and documents intent in code. Types are erased at runtime, so it adds no runtime overhead — but also no runtime validation, so data from APIs still needs checking where it matters.

Interface vs type alias — what is the difference?

Both can describe object shapes and both can be extended (extends vs &). Only interfaces support declaration merging and are slightly clearer in error messages for objects. Only type aliases can represent unions, tuples, primitives, mapped and conditional types. 💡 A common rule: interfaces for object contracts/DTOs, types for unions and compositions — and be consistent.

What is the difference between any, unknown and never?

any disables type checking — you can do anything with it, and it silently spreads. unknown accepts any value but forces you to narrow (typeof, type guard) before using it, so it is the safe choice for untrusted data. never represents values that cannot exist: a function that always throws, or the leftover type in an exhaustive switch.

What is type narrowing? Give examples.

Narrowing is how TS refines a broad type (like a union) to a more specific one based on control flow. Techniques: typeof for primitives, instanceof for classes, in for property checks, equality/truthiness checks, discriminated unions and user-defined type guards:

function isPatient(x: unknown): x is Patient {
  return typeof x === 'object' && x !== null && 'name' in x;
}
What is a discriminated union?

A union of object types that share a common literal property (the discriminant), such as status: 'loading' | 'success' | 'error'. Switching on that property narrows to the exact member, so TS knows which fields exist. Adding a never default case gives an exhaustiveness check — the compiler errors if a new variant is added but not handled. It is ideal for modelling UI or request state.

Explain generics and generic constraints.

Generics parameterise types so code is reusable yet type-safe: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined returns the element type of whatever array you pass. Constraints restrict what T can be: <T extends { id: number }> guarantees T has an id; <K extends keyof T> guarantees a valid key. Unlike Java there is no type at runtime at all, so you cannot do new T() or instanceof T.

Name some utility types and when you'd use them.

Partial<T> for update/PATCH payloads or form values; Omit<T, 'id'> for create DTOs; Pick<T, K> for list-view projections; Readonly<T> for immutable state; Record<K, V> for lookup maps; ReturnType<typeof fn> to derive types from functions; NonNullable<T> to strip null/undefined. They are built on mapped and conditional types.

Enum vs string literal union — which do you prefer?

A literal union (type Status = 'ACTIVE' | 'INACTIVE') has no runtime footprint, matches JSON from a Spring backend directly and gives the same autocomplete and safety. Enums create a runtime object, which is useful when you need to iterate values or want a namespace, but numeric enums accept any number and add bundle weight. Many teams prefer unions plus const STATUSES = ['ACTIVE', 'INACTIVE'] as const when runtime values are needed.

What does strict mode enable, and why is strictNullChecks important?

"strict": true turns on noImplicitAny, strictNullChecks, strictPropertyInitialization, strictFunctionTypes, strictBindCallApply, alwaysStrict and useUnknownInCatchVariables. With strictNullChecks, null and undefined are not assignable to other types, so you must handle them explicitly — eliminating most "cannot read property of undefined" bugs. 💡 New Angular projects enable strict mode by default; keep it on.

What are the optional chaining, nullish coalescing and non-null assertion operators?

user?.address?.city short-circuits to undefined if any part is null/undefined. value ?? 'default' uses the default only for null/undefined (unlike ||, which also replaces 0 and ''). value! tells the compiler "trust me, not null" — it does nothing at runtime, so overusing it hides bugs.

What are decorators and how does Angular use them?

Decorators are functions applied with @ that annotate classes or members with metadata or wrap behaviour. Angular's compiler reads @Component, @Injectable, @Directive, @Pipe metadata to generate code, and member decorators like @Input, @Output, @ViewChild, @HostListener wire up bindings. In Angular 17+ many member decorators have signal-based function equivalents (input(), output(), viewChild()) and DI can use inject().

Is TypeScript's private really private?

No — private and protected are enforced only by the compiler; after compilation the field is a normal JS property accessible via obj['field']. JavaScript's native #field syntax is enforced at runtime. For Angular templates, note that private members cannot be used in the template; use protected for template-only members.

What is structural typing?

TS checks compatibility by shape, not by declared name. If an object has all required properties of an interface, it is assignable to it even if it never "implements" it. This differs from Java's nominal typing. One nuance: object literals passed directly get excess property checks, so extra unknown properties are flagged.

What does keyof and typeof do in a type position?

keyof T produces a union of T's property names (keyof Patient → 'id' | 'name' | 'email'). typeof value in a type position extracts the type of a variable, so you can derive types from runtime constants: type Route = typeof routes[keyof typeof routes]. Combined with indexed access types (T[K]) they enable type-safe helpers.

How do you type an HTTP response from a Spring Boot API in Angular?

Define an interface matching the JSON DTO and pass it as the generic to HttpClient:

interface PatientDto { id: number; name: string; dob: string; }
getAll(): Observable<PatientDto[]> {
  return this.http.get<PatientDto[]>('/api/patients');
}

The generic is only a compile-time assertion — nothing is validated at runtime — so keep DTO interfaces in sync with the backend (or generate them from an OpenAPI spec). Dates arrive as strings in JSON.

What are declaration files (.d.ts)?

They contain only type information (no implementation) describing the shape of JavaScript code, so TS can type-check usage of plain JS libraries. Many libraries ship their own; others have community types in @types/* (e.g. @types/node). You can also write declare module 'x' or augment existing types via declaration merging.

Type annotation vs "as" assertion vs "satisfies": what is the difference?

An annotation (const c: Config = {…}) checks the value and then the variable has the wider declared type, losing literal details. An assertion ({…} as Config) tells the compiler "trust me"; it skips most checks and can hide bugs, such as a missing property. satisfies ({…} satisfies Config) checks the value against the type but keeps the inferred, narrower type, so you get both validation and precise autocomplete. Prefer annotations or satisfies; keep as for cases where you know more than the compiler, such as DOM element types.

Write a type that makes every property of a nested object readonly.

Use a recursive mapped type with a conditional to stop at functions and primitives:

type DeepReadonly<T> = T extends (...args: any[]) => any ? T
  : T extends object ? { readonly [K in keyof T]: DeepReadonly<T[K]> }
  : T;

The built-in Readonly<T> is shallow. This is a type-level guarantee only; use Object.freeze if you also need runtime protection.

What is a type predicate (x is T) and what is the risk?

A function returning x is T tells the compiler that when it returns true, the argument has type T. It lets you narrow unknown data such as a parsed JSON body or a caught error. The risk is that TypeScript does not verify the body: a guard that only checks one property will happily "prove" a wrong type. Keep guards small and tested, or use a schema library for complex shapes.

Does http.get<Patient[]>() validate the response? How do you keep front-end and Spring DTOs in sync?

No. The generic only casts the parsed JSON; nothing is checked at runtime. To catch drift: generate TypeScript models from the Spring Boot OpenAPI document in CI, so a renamed field breaks the build; validate critical responses with a schema (Zod) and report mismatches; and remember that Java LocalDate/Instant arrive as strings, and large long IDs can lose precision as JavaScript numbers, so type them as string when needed.

Abstract class vs interface in TypeScript?

An interface is compile-time only: it describes a shape, produces no JavaScript, and a class can implement many. An abstract class exists at runtime, can hold shared implementation, constructors and fields, and declares abstract members that subclasses must implement; a class can extend only one. In Angular, an abstract class is also useful as a DI token ({ provide: PaymentGateway, useClass: StripeGateway }), because interfaces vanish at runtime and cannot be tokens.

Index signature vs Record vs Map: which do you use for a lookup table?

{ [key: string]: number } and Record<string, number> are equivalent for open string keys; Record<'A' | 'B', number> requires exactly those keys, which is great for exhaustive lookups. Note that by default obj[key] on an open index signature is typed as number, not number | undefined; enable noUncheckedIndexedAccess to be honest about missing keys. Use a Map when keys are not strings, when entries are added and removed often, or when insertion order and size matter.

What does distributive conditional type mean? Give an example where it surprises people.

When a conditional type checks a bare type parameter, a union argument is split and each member is checked separately: type ToArray<T> = T extends any ? T[] : never turns string | number into string[] | number[], not (string | number)[]. To prevent distribution, wrap both sides in a tuple: [T] extends [any] ? T[] : never. This is also why Exclude and Extract work on unions.

Ionic Framework Hybrid mobile

Ionic is an open-source UI toolkit of mobile-optimised web components that, combined with Angular and Capacitor, lets you ship one web codebase as an Android app, an iOS app and a Progressive Web App.

// home.page.ts — Ionic 8 + Angular standalone + Capacitor
import { Component } from '@angular/core';
import { IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent, IonButton } from '@ionic/angular/standalone';
import { Camera, CameraResultType } from '@capacitor/camera';

@Component({
  selector: 'app-home',
  standalone: true,
  imports: [IonHeader, IonToolbar, IonTitle, IonContent, IonButton],
  template: `
    <ion-header><ion-toolbar><ion-title>Home</ion-title></ion-toolbar></ion-header>
    <ion-content class="ion-padding">
      <ion-button expand="block" (click)="takePhoto()">Take photo</ion-button>
    </ion-content>`
})
export class HomePage {
  async takePhoto() {
    const photo = await Camera.getPhoto({ quality: 80, resultType: CameraResultType.Uri });
    console.log(photo.webPath);
  }
}

What Ionic Is

Ionic provides a library of UI web components (built with Stencil) that look and behave like native iOS and Android controls — buttons, lists, tabs, modals, gestures and page transitions. The app itself runs as HTML/CSS/JS inside a native WebView; that is what "hybrid" means. Ionic is framework-agnostic with official bindings for Angular, React and Vue, and the native layer is provided by Capacitor. Compared to React Native or Flutter, Ionic reuses web skills and code (including an existing Angular codebase) at the cost of not rendering truly native widgets.

Ionic + Angular

An Ionic Angular app is a normal Angular app plus @ionic/angular. Since Ionic 7.5, the recommended approach is standalone components imported from @ionic/angular/standalone (tree-shakable, lazy-loaded per component), bootstrapped with provideIonicAngular(). Everything Angular offers — services, DI, RxJS, signals, reactive forms, HttpClient, interceptors calling a Spring Boot REST API — works unchanged. The Ionic CLI (ionic start, ionic serve) wraps the Angular CLI.

// main.ts
bootstrapApplication(AppComponent, {
  providers: [
    provideIonicAngular({ mode: 'md' }),           // optional: force Material style
    provideRouter(routes, withPreloading(PreloadAllModules)),
    provideHttpClient(withInterceptors([authInterceptor]))
  ]
});

Capacitor vs Cordova

Capacitor (by the Ionic team) is the modern native runtime and the default for Ionic 7/8. Cordova is the older Apache project. Key differences:

  • Capacitor treats native projects (android/, ios/) as source artefacts you commit and open in Android Studio/Xcode; Cordova regenerates them at build time.
  • Capacitor has a modern Promise-based plugin API, first-class TypeScript types and easy custom plugins in Swift/Kotlin.
  • Capacitor plugins also run on the web (PWA) where possible; it supports most Cordova plugins for backwards compatibility.
  • Cordova is in maintenance mode for many plugins; new projects should use Capacitor.

UI Components & Platform Styling

Core components: ion-app, ion-header/ion-toolbar/ion-title, ion-content (scroll container), ion-list/ion-item, ion-button, ion-input, ion-select, ion-card, ion-tabs, ion-menu, ion-modal, ion-refresher, ion-infinite-scroll, and overlay controllers (AlertController, ToastController, LoadingController). Ionic automatically applies platform modes: ios style on iPhone and md (Material Design) elsewhere.

Theming uses CSS custom properties (--ion-color-primary, --background), and since components use Shadow DOM, you style internals via documented CSS variables and ::part(). Use .ios/.md classes on html, or Platform.is('ios') in code, for platform-specific tweaks. Safe-area insets (notches) are exposed as --ion-safe-area-*.

:root { --ion-color-primary: #3880ff; }
.ios ion-toolbar { --background: #f8f8f8; }
ion-button::part(native) { text-transform: none; }

Navigation & Routing

Ionic Angular uses the standard Angular Router, but renders pages in <ion-router-outlet> instead of <router-outlet>. Ionic's outlet maintains a navigation stack: pages stay in the DOM when you navigate forward, enabling native-style animated transitions and swipe-back on iOS. Consequently Angular's ngOnInit fires only once per page instance, so use Ionic lifecycle hooks ionViewWillEnter, ionViewDidEnter, ionViewWillLeave, ionViewDidLeave to refresh data each time a page is shown. Tabs use nested child routes under ion-tabs; NavController offers navigateForward/navigateBack/navigateRoot with correct animation direction.

export const routes: Routes = [
  { path: 'patients', loadComponent: () => import('./patients.page').then(m => m.PatientsPage) },
  { path: 'patients/:id', loadComponent: () => import('./patient-detail.page').then(m => m.PatientDetailPage) },
  { path: '', redirectTo: 'patients', pathMatch: 'full' }
];

ionViewWillEnter() { this.load(); }   // runs every time the page becomes active

Native APIs via Capacitor Plugins

Capacitor exposes device features through plugins installed from npm: @capacitor/camera, @capacitor/geolocation, @capacitor/preferences (key-value storage), @capacitor/filesystem, @capacitor/push-notifications, @capacitor/network, @capacitor/haptics, @capacitor/app (back button, app state). Each plugin has a JS API that bridges to native Swift/Kotlin code. Permissions must be declared in AndroidManifest.xml and Info.plist, and requested at runtime. You can write custom plugins when no existing one fits.

import { Geolocation } from '@capacitor/geolocation';
import { Capacitor } from '@capacitor/core';

if (Capacitor.isNativePlatform()) {
  const pos = await Geolocation.getCurrentPosition();
  console.log(pos.coords.latitude, pos.coords.longitude);
}

Build & Run on Android / iOS

The workflow: build the web app, copy it into the native projects, then build natively. capacitor.config.ts holds appId, appName and webDir (the Angular output folder). Android requires Android Studio + SDK; iOS requires a Mac with Xcode. Live reload on a device is possible with -l --external.

npm install @capacitor/android @capacitor/ios
npx cap add android
npx cap add ios
ionic build                 # ng build → www/ (or dist/)
npx cap sync                # copy web assets + update native plugins
npx cap open android        # build/sign/run in Android Studio
npx cap run ios -l --external   # run on device with live reload

Performance Tips & PWA

  • Lazy-load pages (loadComponent) and use standalone Ionic imports so only used components are bundled.
  • Use trackBy / @for (...; track item.id) in lists; for very long lists use virtual scrolling (Angular CDK cdk-virtual-scroll-viewport) or ion-infinite-scroll with paginated API calls.
  • Prefer OnPush change detection and signals; avoid heavy work on the main thread.
  • Animate with transform/opacity; optimise and lazy-load images (ion-img loads when visible).
  • Cache API data locally (Preferences, SQLite, IndexedDB) for offline use; minimise bridge calls to native plugins in tight loops.

Because Ionic apps are web apps, the same build can be a PWA: add a service worker and web manifest with ng add @angular/pwa, giving installability, offline caching and fast repeat loads. PWAs have limited native access compared with Capacitor builds (especially on iOS), so many teams ship both from one codebase.

Push notifications with Capacitor, FCM and a Spring Boot backend

Push uses the platform services: Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) on Android and APNs on iOS (FCM can forward to APNs so the backend uses one API). The flow:

  1. The app asks for permission and registers with @capacitor/push-notifications.
  2. The OS returns a device token; the app sends it to your Spring Boot API, which stores it against the logged-in user.
  3. The backend sends a message to that token with the Firebase Admin SDK.
  4. The app handles pushNotificationReceived (app in foreground: show your own in-app banner) and pushNotificationActionPerformed (user tapped the notification: navigate to the right page).
import { PushNotifications } from '@capacitor/push-notifications';

async initPush() {
  if (!Capacitor.isNativePlatform()) return;              // web uses the Push API / FCM web SDK instead
  let perm = await PushNotifications.checkPermissions();
  if (perm.receive === 'prompt') perm = await PushNotifications.requestPermissions();
  if (perm.receive !== 'granted') return;

  await PushNotifications.addListener('registration', t =>
    this.http.post('/api/devices', { token: t.value, platform: Capacitor.getPlatform() }).subscribe());
  await PushNotifications.addListener('pushNotificationActionPerformed', a =>
    this.zone.run(() => this.router.navigateByUrl(a.notification.data.route)));
  await PushNotifications.register();
}

// Spring Boot (Firebase Admin SDK)
Message msg = Message.builder().setToken(deviceToken)
    .setNotification(Notification.builder().setTitle("Appointment").setBody("Tomorrow at 10:00").build())
    .putData("route", "/appointments/42").build();
FirebaseMessaging.getInstance().send(msg);

Tokens change (reinstall, restore), so update them on every app start and delete tokens the send API reports as invalid. Do not put sensitive data such as health details in the visible notification text, because it appears on the lock screen.

Deep links and app links

A deep link opens a specific page of the app from an email, SMS or web page. Custom schemes (myapp://orders/42) are easy but any app can claim the same scheme. Verified links use a normal https URL: Android App Links (a assetlinks.json file on your domain under /.well-known/) and iOS Universal Links (an apple-app-site-association file plus the Associated Domains entitlement). If the app is not installed, the same URL opens the website.

import { App } from '@capacitor/app';

App.addListener('appUrlOpen', ({ url }) => {
  this.zone.run(() => {
    const path = new URL(url).pathname;          // https://app.example.com/orders/42 → /orders/42
    this.router.navigateByUrl(path);
  });
});

Run navigation inside NgZone.run in zone-based apps, because Capacitor callbacks come from native code outside Angular's zone and the view would otherwise not update.

Authentication and secure storage on mobile

  • OAuth / OpenID Connect: use the Authorization Code flow with PKCE in the system browser (Custom Tabs on Android, ASWebAuthenticationSession on iOS), then return to the app with a deep link. Do not show the login page in an embedded WebView: the app could read the password, and identity providers such as Google block it.
  • Where to keep tokens: @capacitor/preferences and localStorage are not encrypted. Store refresh tokens in the iOS Keychain or Android Keystore-backed storage through a secure storage plugin, and keep the access token in memory.
  • Biometrics (fingerprint, Face ID) via a plugin can unlock the stored refresh token; biometrics alone is a local check, not authentication to the server.
  • Sessions: short-lived access tokens, refresh on resume, and clear secure storage on logout.

App lifecycle, overlays and device UI

NeedAPI
App goes to background / returnsApp.addListener('appStateChange', ({ isActive }) => …), also pause/resume: refresh data or tokens on resume, pause timers and sockets
Modals, alerts, toasts, loading, action sheetsControllers (ModalController.create(), AlertController…) or inline <ion-modal [isOpen]="open()">; modal.onDidDismiss() returns data to the caller
On-screen keyboard covering inputs@capacitor/keyboard (resize mode, keyboardWillShow events), Ionic scrolls focused inputs into view
Status bar colour and style, splash screen@capacitor/status-bar, @capacitor/splash-screen (hide it when the first page is ready)
Notches and home indicatorIonic applies env(safe-area-inset-*) via --ion-safe-area-* variables
Network on/off@capacitor/network networkStatusChange to show offline mode and sync later

Live updates and app store releases

  • A Capacitor app has two parts: the native shell (plugins, permissions, icons) and the web bundle. Changes to the web bundle alone can be shipped over the air with live update services (Ionic Appflow, Capgo, or self-hosted) without a store review.
  • Store rules allow OTA updates of interpreted code only if they do not change the app's primary purpose; anything touching native code or new permissions needs a new store build.
  • Release checklist: bump versionCode/versionName (Android) and build number/version (iOS); build a signed AAB (keep the upload key safe, use Play App Signing) and an archive in Xcode; test through internal testing / TestFlight; complete privacy declarations (Data safety on Play, privacy manifest and App Privacy on iOS).
  • Automate with Fastlane or a CI service; run ng build then npx cap sync before every native build.

Interview Questions — Ionic Framework

What is Ionic and how does a hybrid app work?

Ionic is a UI toolkit of mobile-styled web components for building cross-platform apps with web technologies. A hybrid app is a web app (HTML/CSS/JS) packaged inside a native shell that renders it in a WebView; a native runtime (Capacitor) provides a bridge so JavaScript can call device APIs like the camera or GPS. One codebase targets Android, iOS and the web.

What is the difference between Capacitor and Cordova?

Both bridge web code to native APIs. Capacitor is the modern successor: native projects are committed source you open in Android Studio/Xcode, plugins use a Promise-based typed API, plugins can also work on the web, and writing custom native code is straightforward. Cordova regenerates native platforms from config and relies on an older plugin model. Capacitor can run most Cordova plugins, so migration is incremental. 💡 New Ionic projects use Capacitor by default.

Ionic vs React Native vs Flutter?

Ionic renders web components in a WebView, so it reuses web/Angular skills and code and also deploys as a PWA. React Native renders real native widgets driven by JavaScript; Flutter draws its own widgets with the Skia/Impeller engine using Dart. Ionic is fastest to adopt for web teams and great for business/form-driven apps; RN and Flutter can feel more native for heavy animation or graphics-intensive apps.

Why use ion-router-outlet instead of router-outlet?

ion-router-outlet keeps previously visited pages in a navigation stack instead of destroying them, enabling native page transition animations, swipe-to-go-back on iOS and preserved scroll position. It still uses Angular Router configuration underneath. The trade-off is that component lifecycle differs, so you rely on Ionic page lifecycle events.

What are Ionic page lifecycle hooks and why are they needed?

ionViewWillEnter, ionViewDidEnter, ionViewWillLeave and ionViewDidLeave. Because Ionic caches pages in the stack, ngOnInit runs only once when a page is first created and ngOnDestroy only when it is popped. To refresh data each time a user returns to a page (e.g. after editing a record on a detail page), load it in ionViewWillEnter.

How do you access native device features?

Install the relevant Capacitor plugin, run npx cap sync, declare permissions in the Android manifest / iOS Info.plist, and call its TypeScript API:

import { Camera, CameraResultType } from '@capacitor/camera';
const img = await Camera.getPhoto({ resultType: CameraResultType.Base64 });

Wrap plugin calls in an Angular service so components stay testable and you can provide a web fallback.

What does npx cap sync do?

It runs cap copy (copies the built web assets from webDir into the native Android and iOS projects) and cap update (installs/updates native dependencies for Capacitor plugins, e.g. Gradle and CocoaPods/SPM). Run it after every web build you want to test natively and after adding or upgrading plugins.

How do you build and publish an Ionic app for Android and iOS?

Run ionic build (production Angular build), npx cap sync, then npx cap open android / ios. In Android Studio generate a signed AAB for Google Play; in Xcode configure signing with an Apple developer account and archive to upload to App Store Connect. iOS builds require macOS (or a cloud build service). Set the bundle ID via appId in capacitor.config.ts.

How does Ionic handle platform-specific styling?

Ionic applies a mode automatically — ios on Apple devices and md (Material) elsewhere — so the same component renders with platform-appropriate look and behaviour. You can force a mode globally via provideIonicAngular({ mode: 'ios' }) or per component with the mode attribute, target .ios/.md classes in CSS, and use the Platform service (platform.is('android')) in code.

How do you theme Ionic components?

Through CSS custom properties: global colours such as --ion-color-primary (with shade/tint/contrast variants) in variables.scss, and component-level variables like --background or --color. Because many components use Shadow DOM, normal selectors cannot reach internals — use the documented variables or ::part(). Ionic 8 ships dark mode palettes you can enable via class or system preference.

How do you store data locally in an Ionic app?

For small key-value settings use @capacitor/preferences (backed by SharedPreferences / UserDefaults). For larger structured or offline data use SQLite (via a community Capacitor SQLite plugin) or IndexedDB-based libraries such as Ionic Storage. Avoid relying on localStorage for important data on iOS, as the OS can clear WebView storage. Never store secrets like raw passwords; use secure storage plugins for tokens where required.

How do you call a Spring Boot backend from an Ionic app?

Exactly as in Angular — HttpClient in a service with interceptors for JWT headers and error handling. Points specific to mobile: the device cannot reach localhost, so use the machine's LAN IP or a deployed URL; configure CORS on the backend for the app's origin (capacitor://localhost on iOS, http://localhost on Android); and use HTTPS, since Android blocks cleartext by default. Capacitor's CapacitorHttp can route requests natively to bypass CORS.

How do you improve performance of long lists in Ionic?

Paginate on the server and load more with ion-infinite-scroll, render only visible rows using Angular CDK virtual scroll, and use track in @for so DOM nodes are reused. Combine with OnPush/signals, lazy-loaded images and pull-to-refresh (ion-refresher) rather than auto-reloading everything.

How do you handle the Android hardware back button?

Ionic handles it by default for navigation, overlays and menus. For custom behaviour (e.g. confirm before exit), subscribe to platform.backButton.subscribeWithPriority(10, () => ...) or use App.addListener('backButton', ...) from @capacitor/app, and call App.exitApp() when appropriate.

Can an Ionic app be a PWA? What are the limitations?

Yes. Add @angular/pwa for a service worker and manifest, deploy to an HTTPS host, and users can install it from the browser with offline support. Limitations: restricted native API access (Bluetooth, some background tasks and full push support vary by platform, especially iOS Safari), no app store presence by default, and storage that the browser may evict. Capacitor builds fill these gaps from the same code.

How do you debug an Ionic app on a device?

For Android, open chrome://inspect in Chrome on the desktop to attach DevTools to the WebView; for iOS, enable Web Inspector on the device and use Safari's Develop menu. Native logs appear in Android Studio Logcat and the Xcode console. Use ionic serve in the browser for fast UI iteration and live reload (npx cap run android -l --external) on real devices.

Why do API calls work in the browser but fail with CORS errors on the device?

In the native app, the web code is served from a local origin: capacitor://localhost on iOS and https://localhost (Capacitor 6+ default; older versions used http://localhost) on Android. To the Spring Boot API these are cross-origin, so add them to allowedOrigins. Alternatively, enable CapacitorHttp, which patches fetch/XHR to make requests from native code, so CORS does not apply; cookies and some interceptors behave differently with it, so test carefully.

How do you write a custom Capacitor plugin?

Generate one with npm init @capacitor/plugin. You define a TypeScript interface, implement it in Kotlin/Java (a class extending Plugin with @CapacitorPlugin and methods annotated @PluginMethod that call call.resolve(...)) and in Swift, plus an optional web implementation. In the app, registerPlugin<MyPlugin>('MyPlugin') returns a typed proxy, and every call is an async promise across the bridge. For a quick app-only plugin you can put the native class directly in the app's Android/iOS project.

How do you test an Ionic Angular app?

Unit tests for components and services work exactly as in Angular (Jasmine/Karma or Jest/Vitest). Mock Capacitor plugins, because they do not run in a test browser: wrap them in your own Angular service and provide a fake. End-to-end tests of the web build run with Cypress or Playwright in a mobile viewport. For real device behaviour (permissions, camera, push), use Appium or manual testing on devices and emulators, plus internal test tracks and TestFlight before release.

How would you make an Ionic app work offline and sync later?

Cache the app shell (it is already bundled locally in a native app; a service worker does this for a PWA). Store data locally in SQLite (a Capacitor SQLite plugin) or IndexedDB rather than Preferences, which is for small key-value settings. Queue writes made offline in a local outbox table with a client-generated ID, and replay them when @capacitor/network reports a connection. The Spring Boot API should treat that ID as an idempotency key and detect conflicts, for example with a version number, so replays do not create duplicates.

How do you handle runtime permissions (camera, location) properly?

Ask just in time, when the user taps the feature, not at startup, and explain why first. Call checkPermissions(), then requestPermissions() if the state is prompt. If it is denied, the OS will not show the dialog again, so show a message with a button that opens the app settings. Declare permissions in AndroidManifest.xml and the usage description strings in iOS Info.plist; a missing iOS description crashes the app when the permission is requested.

What security measures matter for a hybrid app that shows sensitive data?

Everything in the web bundle can be extracted from the APK/IPA, so never ship secrets (API keys with write access, client secrets). Use PKCE login in the system browser, keep tokens in Keychain/Keystore, enforce HTTPS, and consider certificate pinning for high-risk apps. Turn off WebView debugging in release builds, enable code shrinking/obfuscation for native code, and optionally detect rooted or jailbroken devices. Hide sensitive screens in the app switcher snapshot and avoid sensitive text in push notifications. The server must still enforce all authorisation.

When would you not choose Ionic for a mobile app?

When the app is dominated by heavy graphics or animation (games, AR, complex real-time video), needs deep integration with many platform features that have no maintained plugins, or must feel exactly like each platform's latest native UI at all times. In those cases native (Kotlin/Swift), Flutter or React Native fit better. Ionic is strong when a team already knows Angular, the app is mostly forms, lists and API calls, and sharing one codebase across Android, iOS and the web matters.

Jenkins & CI/CD DevOps

Continuous integration and delivery: pipelines, the Jenkinsfile, agents, triggers, credentials, and how deployment fits in.

// Jenkinsfile (Declarative)
pipeline {
  agent any
  tools { maven 'Maven-3.9'; jdk 'JDK-21' }
  environment {
    IMAGE = "registry.example.com/order-service:${env.BUILD_NUMBER}"
    SONAR = credentials('sonar-token')
  }
  triggers { pollSCM('H/5 * * * *') }          // or GitHub webhook
  options { timeout(time: 30, unit: 'MINUTES'); buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '20')) }
  stages {
    stage('Checkout') { steps { checkout scm } }
    stage('Build & Test') {
      steps { sh 'mvn -B clean verify' }
      post { always { junit 'target/surefire-reports/*.xml' } }
    }
    stage('Sonar') { steps { withSonarQubeEnv('sonar') { sh 'mvn sonar:sonar' } } }
    stage('Docker') {
      steps {
        withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'docker-creds', usernameVariable: 'U', passwordVariable: 'P')]) {
          sh 'echo $P | docker login registry.example.com -u $U --password-stdin'
          sh 'docker build -t $IMAGE . && docker push $IMAGE'
        }
      }
    }
    stage('Deploy to Prod') {
      when { branch 'main' }
      input { message 'Deploy to production?' }
      steps { sh 'helm upgrade --install order ./chart --set image.tag=$BUILD_NUMBER' }
    }
  }
  post {
    success { echo 'Done' }
    failure { mail to: 'team@example.com', subject: "Build failed: ${env.JOB_NAME}", body: "${env.BUILD_URL}" }
  }
}

CI vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment

Continuous IntegrationContinuous DeliveryContinuous Deployment
What it automatesMerge, build, unit tests on every changeEverything up to a production-ready artifact, deployed to stagingEverything, including production
Production releaseNot addressedA person presses the buttonAutomatic if all checks pass
RequiresSmall, frequent merges and fast testsReliable automated tests, versioned artifacts, repeatable deploymentsAll of that plus feature flags, canary releases, automatic rollback and strong monitoring

The key rule is build once, deploy many. The same image, tagged with a Git SHA or build number, moves through dev, test and production. Only configuration differs. Rebuilding for each environment means production runs something that was never tested.

Architecture: controller, agents, executors

TermMeaning
ControllerThe central server: UI, config, scheduling, build records. Formerly called "master"
NodeAny machine that can run builds, including the controller
AgentA process on a node that connects to the controller and runs work. Formerly "slave"
ExecutorOne slot for one build or Pipeline node block. Usually about one per CPU core at most
LabelA tag on agents, used for selecting them: agent { label 'linux && docker' }
WorkspaceA directory on the agent for one job
JENKINS_HOMEThe controller's directory holding all state. Back this up
Gotcha: run with 0 executors on the controller. A build on the controller has access to Jenkins's files, including secrets, and heavy builds starve the UI. Recent LTS lines require Java 17 or newer to run the controller and agents. The JDK used to build your project is separate, set through tools or a Docker image.

Job types: freestyle vs Pipeline

FreestylePipelineMultibranch Pipeline
Configured inWeb UIJenkinsfile (or inline)Jenkinsfile per branch
Version controlNo (XML on the controller)YesYes
Stages, parallel, approvalNeeds chaining of jobsBuilt inBuilt in
Survives controller restartNoYes (durable steps)Yes
Use todaySmall utility jobs, legacyOne fixed branch or ops jobApplication repositories

Declarative vs Scripted: mechanics

Both run on the same Pipeline engine. The Groovy you write is transformed in CPS (continuation-passing style), so the engine can save the state of the program to disk after each step. That is why a Pipeline survives a controller restart, and it is the source of its strange limits.

DeclarativeScripted
Top-level blockpipeline { }node { }
Syntax checkValidated before running; a typo fails at onceFails at run time, possibly late in the build
StructureFixed sectionsFree Groovy: loops, try/catch
Restart from a stageYes, from the UINo
post, when, optionsBuilt-inHand-written
Dynamic stagesLimited (matrix, script block)Natural
// Scripted equivalent of a small pipeline
node('docker') {
  try {
    stage('Checkout') { checkout scm }
    stage('Test')     { sh 'mvn -B verify' }
    def services = ['order', 'payment']
    def branches = services.collectEntries { s -> [(s): { sh "./deploy.sh ${s}" }] }
    stage('Deploy')   { parallel branches }
  } catch (e) {
    currentBuild.result = 'FAILURE'
    throw e
  } finally {
    junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: '**/surefire-reports/*.xml'
  }
}

CPS pitfalls

  • Variables held across a step must be serializable. A non-serializable object such as Matcher causes NotSerializableException. Keep it in a method annotated @NonCPS, or drop the reference before the next step.
  • @NonCPS methods cannot call Pipeline steps such as sh.
  • Keep logic in shell scripts or Maven. Heavy Groovy runs on the controller and loads it. A single large method can exceed the JVM's method size limit, giving Method code too large.
  • Scripts run in the Groovy sandbox unless trusted, and unapproved method calls fail with RejectedAccessException until an admin approves them.

Complete Jenkinsfile: Java and Angular app

This pipeline builds a Spring Boot API and an Angular UI in one repository, tests them in parallel, runs SonarQube, builds images, deploys to staging automatically and to production after approval. Each piece is explained after the code.

@Library('company-pipeline@v2') _             // shared library, pinned to a tag

pipeline {
  agent none                                  // no executor held at top level

  parameters {
    choice(name: 'TARGET', choices: ['staging', 'production'], description: 'Deploy target')
    booleanParam(name: 'SKIP_E2E', defaultValue: false, description: 'Skip end-to-end tests')
    string(name: 'VERSION_OVERRIDE', defaultValue: '', description: 'Optional version')
  }

  options {
    timeout(time: 45, unit: 'MINUTES')
    timestamps()                              // Timestamper plugin
    disableConcurrentBuilds(abortPrevious: true)   // a newer push cancels the older build
    buildDiscarder(logRotator(numToKeepStr: '30', artifactNumToKeepStr: '5'))
    skipDefaultCheckout()
  }


  environment {
    REGISTRY  = 'registry.example.com/shop'
    IMAGE_TAG = "build-${env.BUILD_NUMBER}"
  }

  stages {
    stage('Build and test') {
      parallel {
        stage('Backend') {
          agent { docker { image 'maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21'; args '-v $HOME/.m2:/root/.m2' } }
          steps {
            checkout scm
            sh 'mvn -B -Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=true verify'
            stash name: 'api-jar', includes: 'api/target/*.jar'
          }
          post {
            always {
              junit 'api/target/surefire-reports/*.xml, api/target/failsafe-reports/*.xml'
              archiveArtifacts artifacts: 'api/target/*.jar', onlyIfSuccessful: true
            }
          }
        }
        stage('Frontend') {
          agent { docker { image 'node:22-alpine' } }
          steps {
            checkout scm
            dir('ui') {
              sh 'npm ci'
              sh 'npx ng lint'
              sh 'npx ng test --watch=false'
              sh 'npx ng build --configuration production'
            }
            stash name: 'ui-dist', includes: 'ui/dist/**'
          }
        }
      }
    }

    stage('Code quality') {
      agent { docker { image 'maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21' } }
      steps {
        checkout scm
        withSonarQubeEnv('sonar') {
          sh 'mvn -B sonar:sonar -Dsonar.projectKey=shop'
        }
        timeout(time: 5, unit: 'MINUTES') {
          waitForQualityGate abortPipeline: true      // needs a webhook from SonarQube to Jenkins
        }
      }
    }

    stage('Images') {
      agent { label 'docker' }
      when { anyOf { branch 'main'; buildingTag() } }
      steps {
        checkout scm
        unstash 'api-jar'
        unstash 'ui-dist'
        withCredentials([usernamePassword(credentialsId: 'registry',
                         usernameVariable: 'REG_USER', passwordVariable: 'REG_PASS')]) {
          sh '''
            echo "$REG_PASS" | docker login registry.example.com -u "$REG_USER" --password-stdin
            docker build -t $REGISTRY/api:$IMAGE_TAG api
            docker build -t $REGISTRY/ui:$IMAGE_TAG ui
            docker push $REGISTRY/api:$IMAGE_TAG
            docker push $REGISTRY/ui:$IMAGE_TAG
          '''
        }
      }
      post { always { sh 'docker logout registry.example.com || true' } }
    }

    stage('Deploy to staging') {
      agent { label 'deploy' }
      when { branch 'main' }
      steps {
        checkout scm
        withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'kubeconfig-staging', variable: 'KUBECONFIG')]) {
          sh 'helm upgrade --install shop ./chart -n staging --set image.tag=$IMAGE_TAG --wait --timeout 5m'
        }
      }
    }

    stage('End-to-end') {
      agent { docker { image 'mcr.microsoft.com/playwright:v1.49.0-jammy' } }
      when { allOf { branch 'main'; not { expression { params.SKIP_E2E } } } }
      steps {
        checkout scm
        dir('e2e') { sh 'npm ci && npx playwright test' }
      }
    }

    stage('Approve production') {
      agent none                                 // waiting holds no executor
      when { allOf { branch 'main'; expression { params.TARGET == 'production' } } }
      steps {
        milestone(ordinal: 1, label: 'approval')
        timeout(time: 2, unit: 'HOURS') {
          input message: "Deploy ${env.IMAGE_TAG} to production?", ok: 'Deploy', submitter: 'release-managers'
        }
        milestone(ordinal: 2, label: 'approved')  // older builds cannot overtake this one
      }
    }

    stage('Deploy to production') {
      agent { label 'deploy' }
      when { allOf { branch 'main'; expression { params.TARGET == 'production' } } }
      options { lock(resource: 'production-env') }     // Lockable Resources plugin
      steps {
        checkout scm
        withCredentials([file(credentialsId: 'kubeconfig-prod', variable: 'KUBECONFIG')]) {
          sh 'helm upgrade --install shop ./chart -n prod --set image.tag=$IMAGE_TAG --wait --timeout 10m --atomic'
        }
      }
    }
  }

  post {
    fixed     { slackSend channel: '#builds', color: 'good',   message: "Fixed: ${env.JOB_NAME} #${env.BUILD_NUMBER}" }
    failure   { slackSend channel: '#builds', color: 'danger', message: "Failed: ${env.BUILD_URL}" }
    unstable  { slackSend channel: '#builds', color: 'warning', message: "Tests failed: ${env.BUILD_URL}" }
  }
}
DirectiveWhy it is used here
agent none at topEach stage picks its own agent, and the approval step does not hold an executor for hours
-Dmaven.test.failure.ignore=trueMaven finishes even if tests fail, so junit can publish results. The junit step then marks the build UNSTABLE
parallelRuns both stages at once, each with its own agent and workspace
stash, unstashCopy files between agents through the controller. Fine for small artifacts; use a repository such as Nexus for large ones
whenSkips a stage on conditions; a skipped stage does not fail the build
sh '''...'''Single quotes, so the shell expands variables, not Groovy. This keeps secrets out of the logged command and out of process arguments
milestoneIf a newer build passes the same point, older ones are aborted, which stops an old build deploying over a newer one
lockOnly one build touches production at a time
--atomicHelm rolls back on a failed release
SectionOptions
agentany, none, label, node { label; customWorkspace }, docker, dockerfile, kubernetes { yaml }
whenbranch, tag, buildingTag, changeRequest, changeset, environment, expression, triggeredBy, not, allOf, anyOf, beforeAgent true
parametersstring, text, booleanParam, choice, password
postalways, changed, fixed, regression, aborted, failure, success, unstable, unsuccessful, cleanup
Credential kindsSecret text, username and password, SSH key, secret file, certificate

With environment { X = credentials('id') }, a username-password credential creates three variables: X (user:pass), X_USR and X_PSW. Put beforeAgent true in a when to skip a stage without first allocating an agent. matrix { axes { ... } } runs a set of stages over combinations, such as JDK 17 and 21 on Linux and Windows.

Shared libraries

A shared library is a Git repository of reusable Pipeline code, registered under Manage Jenkins, System, Global Pipeline Libraries. It stops many Jenkinsfiles drifting apart.

company-pipeline/
├── vars/                 # global steps, callable as functions
│   ├── mavenBuild.groovy
│   └── standardPipeline.groovy
├── src/com/acme/         # regular Groovy classes
│   └── Version.groovy
└── resources/            # non-Groovy files, read with libraryResource
    └── settings.xml

// vars/mavenBuild.groovy
def call(Map cfg = [:]) {
  def goals = cfg.goals ?: 'clean verify'
  sh "mvn -B ${goals}"
  junit allowEmptyResults: true, testResults: '**/surefire-reports/*.xml'
}

// vars/standardPipeline.groovy: a whole pipeline as one step
def call(Map cfg) {
  pipeline {
    agent { label 'docker' }
    stages {
      stage('Build') { steps { mavenBuild(goals: cfg.goals) } }
      stage('Image') { steps { sh "docker build -t ${cfg.image}:${env.BUILD_NUMBER} ." } }
    }
  }
}

// Jenkinsfile in a service
@Library('company-pipeline@v2') _
standardPipeline(goals: 'verify', image: 'registry.example.com/order-service')

Pin a version (tag) so a library change cannot break every build at once. Test the library's steps with the JenkinsPipelineUnit framework. Libraries configured globally are trusted and run outside the sandbox, so restrict who can push to that repository.

Multibranch pipelines and webhooks

  1. A Multibranch job (or an Organization Folder, one level higher) has a branch source such as GitHub.
  2. Branch indexing scans the repository, and creates one child job per branch or PR with a Jenkinsfile, and removes them when the branch goes.
  3. A webhook from GitHub (POST to https://jenkins.example.com/github-webhook/) triggers a scan of what changed. A low-frequency periodic scan catches missed hooks.
  4. Jenkins reports build status back to the PR as a commit status or check. Branch protection can then demand it before merge.
TriggerBehaviourTrade-off
WebhookThe SCM pushes an event to JenkinsImmediate and cheap, but Jenkins must be reachable from the SCM
pollSCM('H/5 * * * *')Jenkins asks the SCM on a scheduleWorks behind a firewall, wasteful and slower
cron('H 2 * * *')Builds on schedule, changed or notNightly builds
upstreamWhen another job finishesChains jobs

H in cron syntax stands for a hash of the job name. It spreads jobs across the period, so that they do not all start at the same minute.

Plugins

Almost every Jenkins feature, including Pipeline itself, is a plugin. This power is also its main weakness: plugins depend on each other, and updates can conflict. Keep the set small, track the versions, upgrade on a test controller first, and install from a plugins.txt using the plugin installation manager in a custom Docker image. Blue Ocean no longer gets feature updates; the Pipeline Graph View plugin is the suggested replacement for visualising runs.

AreaPlugins
Core pipelinePipeline, Multibranch, Git, GitHub Branch Source, Pipeline Stage View
AgentsSSH Build Agents, Kubernetes, Docker Pipeline
SecurityCredentials Binding, Matrix Authorization, Role-based Authorization, LDAP, OIDC or SAML login
Quality and reportsJUnit, Coverage, SonarQube Scanner, Warnings Next Generation
AdminConfiguration as Code (JCasC), Job DSL, Timestamper, Workspace Cleanup, Lockable Resources

Security

  • Authentication and authorisation: connect to SSO or LDAP, disable anonymous access, and use matrix or role-based permissions per folder.
  • Controller isolation: no builds on the controller, and a Jenkinsfile from a PR must not reach production credentials. Scope credentials to a folder, so only the right jobs can see them.
  • PRs from forks: treat as untrusted. A malicious PR could change the Jenkinsfile to print secrets. The GitHub Branch Source's default "trust" settings handle this; do not loosen them on public repositories.
  • Secret handling: masking only hides exact matches in logs, so a Base64-encoded secret would be printed. Never use Groovy interpolation for secrets: sh "curl -u $PASS" passes the secret through the Groovy layer and the process list, and Jenkins warns about it. Use sh 'curl -u "$PASS"'.
  • Script Console: Manage Jenkins, Script Console runs arbitrary Groovy as the Jenkins user, and it is root-equivalent for that server. Limit Administer permission strictly.
  • Patching: Jenkins publishes frequent security advisories for core and plugins. Use the LTS line, patch quickly, and do not expose it publicly without an authenticating proxy.
  • External secrets: use the HashiCorp Vault plugin or a cloud secret manager, with short-lived credentials where possible.
  • Configuration as code: JCasC (YAML for system configuration) and Job DSL (jobs as code) let a controller be rebuilt from Git.

Troubleshooting

SymptomLikely causeWhat to do
Build stuck "Waiting for next available executor"No online agent has that label, or all executors are busyCheck the label expression and node status; add agents or autoscale
Passes locally, fails in JenkinsDifferent JDK, env, or missing toolBuild in a pinned Docker image; print java -version and env; use mvn -B
Disk full on an agentOld workspaces and Docker layerscleanWs(), docker system prune on a schedule, ephemeral agents
Agent goes offlineNetwork, Java mismatch, low disk (monitored by node health)Read the agent log under Manage Nodes
NotSerializableExceptionA non-serializable object held across a stepMove it to @NonCPS
RejectedAccessExceptionSandbox blocked a methodMove it to a trusted library, or get an approval in In-process Script Approval
Controller slow or crashingHeap too small, many old builds, plugin bugs, Groovy loadThread dump and GC logs; buildDiscarder; -Xmx tuning; fewer plugins
Webhook does not fireUnreachable URL, missing trailing slash, secret mismatchSee delivery status in GitHub; check the log under GitHub Hook Log
docker: not found in a stageThe image for this agent has no Docker CLIRun Docker steps on a labelled host agent, or use a builder such as Kaniko or Buildah in Kubernetes
Stage cannot find files from an earlier stageDifferent agent or workspaceUse stash, or one agent for the whole pipeline

Use Replay to re-run a Pipeline with an edited script without committing, and Restart from Stage for declarative pipelines. The Pipeline syntax generator at /pipeline-syntax shows the steps your installed plugins offer. A Jenkinsfile can be linted through /pipeline-model-converter/validate.

Jenkins vs GitHub Actions

JenkinsGitHub Actions
HostingYou run the controller and agentsSaaS; GitHub-hosted or self-hosted runners
DefinitionGroovy JenkinsfileYAML in .github/workflows/
Unit of reusePlugins, shared librariesMarketplace actions, reusable workflows
ExecutionLong-lived or Kubernetes agentsFresh VM per job
SecretsCredentials store, VaultEncrypted secrets, OIDC to cloud providers
Parallelparallel, matrixJobs run parallel by default, matrix, needs for order
