Approvalinput stepEnvironments with required reviewers
SCM supportAnyGitHub
CostsServers and admin timePer-minute for hosted runners on private repositories
Pick whenOn-premises networks, complex custom needs, multiple SCMs, existing investmentCode on GitHub, a small team, no CI admin
# .github/workflows/ci.yml: the same idea as the first stages above
name: ci
on:
  push: { branches: [main] }
  pull_request:
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '21', cache: maven }
      - run: mvn -B verify
  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 22, cache: npm, cache-dependency-path: ui/package-lock.json }
      - run: npm ci && npx ng test --watch=false && npx ng build
        working-directory: ui

DevSecOps: Security Stages in the Pipeline

"Shift left" means catching security problems in CI, not in production. A typical Java + Angular pipeline adds these gates:

CheckWhat it findsTypical tools
Secret scanningKeys, passwords committed to GitGitleaks, GitHub secret scanning
SCA (dependency scan)Known CVEs in Maven/npm librariesOWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, npm audit, Dependabot
SASTInsecure code patterns (SQL injection, XSS)SonarQube security rules, Semgrep, CodeQL
Image scanCVEs in the base image and OS packagesTrivy, Grype, Docker Scout
SBOM + signingInventory of components; proof the image came from CICycloneDX/Syft for SBOM, Cosign for signatures
DASTRuntime issues against a deployed test environmentOWASP ZAP baseline scan
stage('Security') {
  parallel {
    stage('Deps')  { steps { sh 'mvn -B org.owasp:dependency-check-maven:check -DfailBuildOnCVSS=7' } }
    stage('Image') { steps { sh "trivy image --exit-code 1 --severity HIGH,CRITICAL myapp:${GIT_COMMIT}" } }
  }
}

Fail the build on HIGH/CRITICAL only, keep a reviewed suppression file for false positives, and run the slow scans (DAST, full SCA) nightly if they slow down every PR.

Artifact Versioning and Database Migrations

  • SNAPSHOT vs release: Maven 1.4.0-SNAPSHOT is mutable and is for development; a release 1.4.0 is immutable and is published once to Nexus/Artifactory.
  • Version scheme: SemVer (MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH) for humans, plus the Git SHA or build number for traceability, e.g. image tag 1.4.0-a1b2c3d. Never deploy latest.
  • Release build: usually triggered by a Git tag (buildingTag() in a when block) so the tag, artifact and image all match.
  • DB migrations: run Flyway/Liquibase as a pipeline step (or a Kubernetes Job) before the new version rolls out, rather than having every replica race to migrate on startup. Migrations must be backward compatible (expand → migrate → contract) so the old version keeps working during a rolling or blue-green deployment.

Interview Questions — Jenkins

What is CI/CD? CI vs Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment?

CI: every commit is built and tested automatically, so problems are found early. Continuous Delivery: every build is releasable, and production deploys need a manual approval. Continuous Deployment: every passing build goes to production automatically.

What is Jenkins? Controller–agent architecture?

An open-source automation server with more than 1800 plugins. The controller (formerly "master") hosts the UI, configuration and scheduling. Agents (nodes) run the builds and connect over SSH or JNLP, or run as Docker or Kubernetes pods. Executors are the build slots on each agent.

Declarative vs Scripted pipeline?

Declarative (pipeline { }): a structured, opinionated syntax with built-in post, when, options and validation. This is the recommended style. Scripted (node { }): full Groovy, more flexible but harder to maintain. Declarative can embed script { } blocks.

What is a Jenkinsfile and why keep it in Git?

Pipeline-as-code. It's versioned and reviewed alongside the app, gives each branch its own pipeline (Multibranch Pipeline), and is reproducible and auditable.

How are builds triggered?

SCM webhooks (GitHub or Bitbucket push, PR) · pollSCM · cron (scheduled builds) · upstream or downstream jobs · manual runs or parameters · the remote API.

How do you manage secrets/credentials?

Use the Credentials plugin (username/password, secret text, SSH key, certificate), accessed through credentials() or withCredentials. Jenkins masks them in logs. Never hard-code secrets. You can integrate with Vault.

What is a Multibranch Pipeline / Shared Library?

Multibranch: Jenkins scans the repo and creates a pipeline automatically for every branch or PR that has a Jenkinsfile. Shared Library: reusable Groovy steps (vars/, src/) kept in a separate repo and loaded with @Library('my-lib') _, so pipelines stay DRY across many services.

post conditions in a pipeline?

always, success, failure, unstable (for example, failing tests), changed, fixed, regression, aborted, cleanup. Used for notifications, publishing test reports, and workspace cleanup.

How do you run stages in parallel?
stage('Tests') {
  parallel {
    stage('Unit')        { steps { sh 'mvn test' } }
    stage('Integration') { steps { sh 'mvn verify -Pit' } }
  }
}
Common plugins you've used?

Git, Pipeline, Blue Ocean, Credentials Binding, Docker Pipeline, Kubernetes, SonarQube Scanner, JUnit, JaCoCo, Slack Notification, Role-based Authorization, Artifactory or Nexus, Email Extension.

Jenkins vs GitHub Actions vs GitLab CI?

Jenkins is self-hosted, highly customizable through plugins, and heavier to maintain. GitHub Actions and GitLab CI are SaaS-native, configured in YAML, and tightly integrated with their repositories. They're increasingly common in newer projects.

Why is it recommended to have 0 executors on the controller?

Security first: a build on the controller runs as the Jenkins user with access to JENKINS_HOME, including encrypted credentials and their keys, so a malicious or buggy build can read all of them. Second, stability: builds compete for CPU and memory with the UI and the scheduler, and a runaway build can bring down the service. Use separate agents, ideally ephemeral containers.

What runs on the agent and what runs on the controller in a Pipeline?

Steps such as sh, bat and checkout run on the agent. The Groovy logic that surrounds them runs on the controller, in the CPS engine. So new File('x').text in a Jenkinsfile reads the file on the controller, not the workspace. Use readFile, fileExists and writeFile, which are steps and do run on the agent. It also explains why heavy Groovy loops slow Jenkins for everyone.

Why does a Pipeline survive a controller restart? What does that require?

The engine saves the program's position after each step, and steps such as sh run as separate durable processes on the agent, tracked through log files. After a restart, the build resumes where it stopped. This requires serializable local variables, which is why NotSerializableException occurs. Durability settings (MAX_SURVIVABILITY, SURVIVABLE_NONATOMIC, PERFORMANCE_OPTIMIZED) trade this safety against disk writes. Freestyle jobs do not resume.

SUCCESS vs UNSTABLE vs FAILURE vs ABORTED?

SUCCESS: all fine. UNSTABLE: the build ran, but a quality step reported problems, typically junit found test failures. FAILURE: a step failed, such as a non-zero sh exit. ABORTED: stopped by a user, a timeout or a newer build. By default, later stages still run after UNSTABLE, so gate deployment with when { expression { currentBuild.currentResult == 'SUCCESS' } }, or use junit and fail the build deliberately. To record a stage failure and continue, use catchError(buildResult: 'SUCCESS', stageResult: 'FAILURE') { ... }.

What's the difference between environment, withEnv, withCredentials and params?

environment defines variables for the pipeline or a stage, set before steps run. withEnv(['A=1']) { } does the same for a block, and is useful in scripted code. withCredentials binds secrets for a block, and they are masked in logs. params.X reads a build parameter. Note that params values are typed (a boolean parameter is a real boolean), while environment variables are always strings, so env.FLAG == 'true' is needed.

What does sh 'echo $BUILD_NUMBER ${env.BUILD_NUMBER}' do?

Single-quoted Groovy strings are not interpolated, so the text goes to the shell unchanged. The shell expands $BUILD_NUMBER correctly, but ${env.BUILD_NUMBER} is not valid shell, so it fails with a "bad substitution" error. In double quotes, Groovy expands both before the shell sees them. Rule: use single quotes with shell variables, double quotes for Groovy variables, and escape with \$ to pass one through to the shell.

How do you avoid rebuilding the same image for each environment?

Build once in CI, tag the image with the Git SHA or build number, and push. Later stages only re-deploy that tag with a different configuration (Helm values, Kubernetes ConfigMaps and Secrets, environment variables). Spring profiles or external config handle backend differences. For Angular, load a config.json at start-up, since build-time environment.ts values would force a rebuild per environment. Promote by digest for a tamper-proof reference.

How do you speed up a slow pipeline?
  1. Find the slow stage using stage view timings.
  2. Cache dependencies: a shared .m2, a registry cache, npm ci with a cache.
  3. Run tests in parallel: parallel stages, Surefire forkCount, the Parallel Test Executor plugin.
  4. Do not repeat work: build once and stash.
  5. Run expensive checks only where needed, using changeset or path filters in a monorepo.
  6. Use layer caching in Docker, and put COPY pom.xml before the sources.
  7. Use a shallow clone in checkout.
How do you scale Jenkins?

The controller scales mostly by being kept light, and agents scale horizontally. Use the Kubernetes plugin for ephemeral pod agents that are created per build. For many teams, split into several controllers per organisation or department rather than one huge instance, since one controller is a single point of failure and open-source Jenkins has no built-in active-active mode. Keep build logs small, discard old builds, and store artifacts in Nexus or S3.

How do you back up and restore Jenkins?

Back up JENKINS_HOME, in particular config.xml, jobs/, users/, plugins/ and secrets/. Without secrets/, stored credentials cannot be decrypted, so store that directory securely. Workspaces and caches can be skipped. The modern method is to rebuild, not restore: Jenkins in a Docker image with pinned plugins, JCasC for configuration, Job DSL or Organization Folders for jobs. Then only build history and secrets need backing up.

stash vs archiveArtifacts?

stash keeps files for reuse later in the same build on another agent, and they are removed at the end of the build. archiveArtifacts stores files with the build record on the controller, downloadable afterwards. Neither is designed for huge files: for real release artifacts, publish to Nexus, Artifactory or S3.

How do you implement a rollback?

With immutable versioned images, a rollback is a redeployment of the last good tag. helm rollback shop reverts the release, and helm upgrade --atomic does so automatically on failure. A parameterised job can take a version as input. Database changes make this harder. Use backward-compatible migrations (expand, migrate, contract) with Flyway, so that old code still works against the new schema. A rollback is safest when a deployment is decoupled from a release through feature flags.

Blue-green vs canary vs rolling deployment?
StrategyHow it worksTrade-off
RollingReplace instances a few at a time. Kubernetes defaultNo extra cost, but two versions run together
Blue-greenRun a full new environment, then switch traffic at onceInstant rollback, double resources
CanarySend a small share of traffic to the new version and increase it while watching metricsLowest risk, needs traffic control and good monitoring
How would you run integration tests that need MySQL and Kafka?

Use Testcontainers in the Maven verify phase, which starts real containers from test code. The agent needs access to a Docker daemon, which can be the host's socket, or a Docker-in-Docker sidecar in Kubernetes. Mounting the host socket gives the build root-equivalent access to the host, so only do this on dedicated, trusted agents. Alternatives are docker compose up in a stage with teardown in post { always { } }, or a sidecar container in a Kubernetes agent pod.

How does the SonarQube quality gate work in a Pipeline?

withSonarQubeEnv injects the server URL and token. The scanner uploads the analysis, and SonarQube processes it asynchronously in a background task. Then waitForQualityGate pauses the pipeline. It needs a webhook configured in SonarQube pointing to https://jenkins.example.com/sonarqube-webhook/. Without it, the step waits until the timeout. The gate typically checks new code for coverage, duplication, and no new critical issues. With abortPipeline: true, a failed gate fails the build.

What are Docker agents vs Kubernetes agents vs static agents?

Static agents are always-on machines. They are simple and allow caches, but drift over time and cost money when idle. Docker agents (agent { docker { } }) run the stage inside a container on a host, giving a pinned toolchain. Kubernetes agents are pods created per build, possibly with several containers (maven, node, docker) and a container('maven') { } block choosing where a step runs. They scale well and leave no state, but need external caching.

Scenario: two pipelines deploy at once and overwrite each other. Fix it.

Add disableConcurrentBuilds() within a job. Across jobs, use a lock(resource: 'env-name') from the Lockable Resources plugin. Add milestone steps so that an older build cannot deploy after a newer one has passed that point. On the target side, Helm refuses a concurrent release while another operation is in progress, and Kubernetes rollouts are idempotent, which adds a further safety net.

Scenario: a secret appears in the build log. What do you do?
  1. Treat it as compromised and rotate it first; deleting logs does not undo exposure.
  2. Delete the affected build logs, and check anyone who could see them.
  3. Find the cause: often set -x, a Groovy-interpolated string, or an encoded or transformed value that the mask cannot match.
  4. Fix the script, and use short-lived credentials where possible.
  5. Add secret scanning, such as Gitleaks, to the pipeline.
Scenario: design CI/CD for 30 microservices.

Give each service its own repository or a monorepo with path filters, and an Organization Folder to discover them. Keep a one-line Jenkinsfile that calls a versioned shared-library pipeline, so a change to the process is made in one place. Stages: build, unit test, contract tests (Pact or Spring Cloud Contract), SonarQube, image build, image scan (Trivy), push. For deployment, use a GitOps tool such as Argo CD, which watches a config repository that CI updates with the new tag. Progress from dev to staging to production with automated checks and canary analysis. Use Kubernetes agents, a central dashboard, and DORA metrics (deployment frequency, lead time, change failure rate, time to restore).

What's a Dockerfile layout for fast, small Spring Boot and Angular images?
# Spring Boot: multi-stage, layered
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -B -q dependency:go-offline      # cached unless pom.xml changes
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -B -q -DskipTests package
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
RUN useradd -r app
USER app
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /app.jar
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "/app.jar"]

# Angular: build with Node, serve with nginx
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY package*.json .
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npx ng build --configuration production
FROM nginx:alpine
COPY --from=build /src/dist/ui/browser /usr/share/nginx/html
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf

Copying dependency files before the source keeps layer caching useful. The runtime stage holds no build tools. Run as non-root. The exact Angular output folder depends on the project name in angular.json.

How do you test a Jenkinsfile change safely?

Push to a branch, as Multibranch runs that branch's own Jenkinsfile. Use Replay to try an edit without a commit. Lint it through the declarative validator endpoint or a CLI. For shared libraries, write unit tests with JenkinsPipelineUnit and load a branch of the library with @Library('lib@feature-x'). Guard deployment stages with when { branch 'main' }, so that test branches cannot reach production.

What is pipeline-as-code's benefit over clicking in the UI?

The process lives next to the code it builds, so it is reviewed in PRs, versioned, and consistent with the code at any commit. A branch can change its own build. An old release can be rebuilt with its original pipeline. Disaster recovery is easier, because no knowledge lives only in a controller's XML files. Audit is simpler, since Git shows who changed what.

What is the difference between input as a stage directive and as a step?

The directive (stage { input { message '...' } steps { } }) is evaluated before the stage enters its agent, so a stage-level agent is not held while waiting. It also applies before when, unless you set beforeInput true in the when. The step (input message: '...' in steps) runs wherever it is, so inside an agent stage it occupies an executor for the whole wait. Either way, wrap it with a timeout, so an unanswered build does not stay open indefinitely. A top-level agent any also holds an executor, which is why long approvals call for agent none.

How do you handle a flaky test or a flaky network step?

For network calls, wrap the step in retry(3) { sh '...' }, or use options { retry(2) } on a stage. In Kubernetes agents, retry(count: 2, conditions: [kubernetesAgent(), nonresumable()]) re-runs only on agent loss. For tests, retrying only hides bugs, so report them: Surefire's rerunFailingTestsCount labels flaky tests, and then you can track and fix them. Never let a retry hide a real failure in a deployment stage, since a repeated deployment may not be idempotent.

How do you run the same stages over JDK 17 and JDK 21?
stage('Compatibility') {
  matrix {
    axes {
      axis { name 'JDK';  values '17', '21' }
      axis { name 'DB';   values 'mysql', 'postgres' }
    }
    excludes {
      exclude {
        axis { name 'JDK'; values '17' }
        axis { name 'DB';  values 'postgres' }
      }
    }
    agent { docker { image "maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-${JDK}" } }
    stages {
      stage('Test') { steps { sh 'mvn -B verify -Pdb-$DB' } }
    }
  }
}

matrix creates one parallel branch per combination, here three. Each axis value is available as an environment variable.

How can a Jenkins job be triggered from a script?

Call the REST API with a user's API token: curl -X POST -u user:token "https://jenkins.example.com/job/deploy/buildWithParameters?TARGET=staging". API tokens do not need the CSRF crumb that session-based requests do. The response's Location header gives the queue item, which you can poll for the build number. Add /api/json to most Jenkins URLs for JSON data. The jenkins-cli.jar client is an alternative.

How do you trigger another job from a Pipeline and pass parameters?

Use the build step: build job: 'deploy-orders', parameters: [string(name: 'TAG', value: env.GIT_COMMIT)], wait: true, propagate: true. With wait: false it fires and forgets; propagate: false lets the caller continue even if the downstream job fails (you can inspect the returned build's result). The declarative triggers { upstream('build-orders') } does the reverse — start this job when another finishes. 💡 Prefer one pipeline with stages over long chains of jobs; chains are hard to trace.

In a monorepo, how do you build only what changed?

Use when { changeset 'backend/**' } on a stage so it runs only if files under that path changed, or compute changed paths with git diff --name-only origin/main...HEAD. Build tools help too: Maven -pl module -am builds one module and its dependencies, and Nx/Turborepo do affected-only builds for Angular. Always run the full build on main or nightly as a safety net, because path filters can miss shared-library changes.

What is CPS in Jenkins Pipeline and when do you need @NonCPS?

Pipeline Groovy is transformed into Continuation-Passing Style so that the program state can be serialised to disk — that is how a build survives a controller restart. The side effect is that some Groovy/Java features behave oddly (closures in each, non-serialisable objects like Matcher held across steps cause NotSerializableException). @NonCPS marks a helper method to run as plain Groovy; it must be fast, must not call pipeline steps such as sh or echo, and its locals are not persisted. 💡 Best fix: keep logic in shell scripts or a shared library, and keep the Jenkinsfile thin.

Which security checks would you add to a CI pipeline?

Secret scanning (Gitleaks), dependency/SCA scanning (OWASP Dependency-Check, Snyk, npm audit), SAST (SonarQube security rules, CodeQL), container image scanning (Trivy), and optionally SBOM generation and image signing (Syft/CycloneDX + Cosign). DAST with OWASP ZAP runs against a deployed test environment. Gate on severity (fail on HIGH/CRITICAL), track suppressions in Git with a reason, and run heavy scans nightly to keep PR feedback fast.

Where should Flyway/Liquibase migrations run in CI/CD?

Run them once per deployment as a dedicated step or job (pipeline stage, Kubernetes Job, Helm pre-upgrade hook) before the new pods roll out, using a DB user with DDL rights that the app itself does not need. Running on application startup works for small apps (Flyway takes a lock), but with many replicas it slows startup and couples migration failures to pod crashes. Write migrations backward compatible so a rollback of the code does not require a rollback of the schema. In CI, validate migrations against a throwaway database (Testcontainers) on every PR.

How do you version build artifacts and Docker images?

Use SemVer for releases and attach the Git SHA (or build number) for traceability: orders:1.4.0-a1b2c3d. SNAPSHOT versions are for development only; release artifacts are immutable and published once. Release builds are usually triggered by a Git tag so code, artifact and image line up. Never deploy latest — you cannot tell what is running or roll back reliably; pin by tag or, better, by image digest.

Splunk Logging / Monitoring

Collecting, indexing and searching machine data (logs). SPL queries, dashboards and alerts for production support.

# Errors in order-service in the last 24h, by exception type
index=prod sourcetype=app_logs service=order-service level=ERROR earliest=-24h
| rex field=_raw "(?<exception>[a-zA-Z.]+Exception)"
| stats count by exception
| sort -count

# Trace a single request across microservices
index=prod traceId="4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736" | sort _time | table _time service level message

# 95th percentile response time per endpoint, 5-minute buckets
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs | timechart span=5m perc95(response_time) by uri_path

# HTTP 5xx rate
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs status>=500 | timechart span=1m count as errors

# Top 10 slowest APIs
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs | stats avg(response_time) as avg_ms, count by uri_path | sort -avg_ms | head 10

Architecture in depth

Splunk splits work into three tiers: collect (forwarders), store and index (indexers), and search (search heads). A search head does not read files itself. It distributes a search to every indexer, each runs its part on its own data (the map step), and the search head merges results (the reduce step). That is why adding indexers makes both ingest and search faster.

ComponentJobKey config or note
Universal Forwarder (UF)A small agent that tails files and ships raw data in 64 KB blocks. Does not parse events, except for structured file formatsinputs.conf, outputs.conf
Heavy Forwarder (HF)A full Splunk instance: can parse, route, mask, and filter before indexingUses more resources; useful for HEC tiers and routing
IndexerParses events, writes them to indexes, answers searchesindexes.conf, props.conf, transforms.conf
Search Head (SH)UI, SPL parsing, knowledge objects, result mergingSearch-time props.conf, lookups, saved searches
Deployment ServerPushes apps and config to forwarders that phone homeserverclass.conf
Cluster ManagerRuns an indexer cluster. Formerly "Cluster Master"Replication factor, search factor
SH Cluster DeployerPushes apps to a search head cluster, which elects a captainSeparate from the deployment server
License ManagerTracks daily ingestGoing over the limit triggers warnings
Monitoring ConsoleDashboards about Splunk's own healthFirst stop for platform problems
# UF: inputs.conf: which files
[monitor:///var/log/order-service/*.log]
index = prod
sourcetype = order_app
disabled = false

# UF: outputs.conf: where to send, with automatic load balancing between indexers
[tcpout:prod_indexers]
server = idx1.example.com:9997, idx2.example.com:9997
useACK = true

Forwarders send to port 9997 by default. Load balancing rotates between indexers. useACK makes the forwarder keep data until the indexer confirms it. HEC listens on 8088, and the web UI on 8000, the management port is 8089.

Clustering

Indexer clustering keeps copies of each bucket. The replication factor (RF) is the number of copies of raw data, and the search factor (SF) is how many of those are searchable (with index files). With RF=3 and SF=2, losing two indexers loses no data. Search head clustering replicates knowledge objects and gives high availability on the search tier. SmartStore keeps warm data in object storage such as S3, with indexers acting as a cache, so storage and compute scale apart.

What happens to an event: the data pipeline

Getting event boundaries and timestamps right at ingest is the most important step in Splunk administration, since neither can be changed afterwards without re-indexing.

# props.conf for a Java app whose stack traces span many lines
[order_app]
SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false
LINE_BREAKER = ([\r\n]+)(?=\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}T)      # a new event starts at a timestamp
TIME_PREFIX = ^
TIME_FORMAT = %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%z
MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD = 30
TRUNCATE = 20000                                    # default is 10000 bytes
KV_MODE = none

# For JSON logs: search-time extraction, automatic
[order_json]
KV_MODE = json
TIME_PREFIX = "@timestamp":"
TIME_FORMAT = %Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%z

# Mask card numbers at index time
[access_logs]
SEDCMD-mask_card = s/\b\d{12}(\d{4})\b/XXXXXXXXXXXX\1/g

Indexes and buckets

An index is a directory of buckets, and each bucket covers a time range. A bucket holds two main things: rawdata, the compressed original events, and .tsidx time-series index files, which map terms to event locations. There is also a bloom filter, which quickly rules out buckets that cannot contain a term.

StateMeaningSearchableMoves on when
HotOpen for writingYesIt reaches max size or age, or the indexer restarts
WarmRead-only, on fast storageYesmaxWarmDBCount is exceeded
ColdRead-only, on cheaper storageYesRetention or size limit reached
FrozenDeleted by default, or archived to coldToFrozenDirNoManual restore
ThawedRestored from an archiveYesRemoved by hand
# indexes.conf
[prod]
homePath   = $SPLUNK_DB/prod/db
coldPath   = $SPLUNK_DB/prod/colddb
thawedPath = $SPLUNK_DB/prod/thaweddb
frozenTimePeriodInSecs = 7776000     # 90 days (the default is about 6 years)
maxTotalDataSizeMB = 500000          # data freezes at whichever limit is hit first

A bucket freezes only when its newest event passes the retention age. So one bad event with a far-future timestamp can keep a whole bucket alive. Warm bucket directories are named db_<newestTime>_<oldestTime>_<id>, which lets Splunk skip buckets outside a search's time range. That is why narrowing time is the strongest speed-up.

Fields, sourcetypes and extraction

Each event has default fields: _time, _raw, host, source, sourcetype, index, _indextime. The sourcetype names the format of the data, and it selects the parsing rules in props.conf. Other fields are usually extracted at search time ("schema on read"): only the raw event is stored, and rules are applied when you search.

MethodWhenUse
KV_MODE=json, autoSearch timeJSON and key=value logs are extracted automatically
INDEXED_EXTRACTIONS=jsonIndex time, on the forwarderStructured files; larger index, and do not combine with KV_MODE=json or fields double
rexIn a queryOne-off extraction
EXTRACT-name in props.confSearch timeA permanent regex for a sourcetype
REPORT-name and transforms.confSearch timeA reusable or multi-field extraction
Field Extractor UISearch timeGenerates the regex for you
FIELDALIAS, EVAL-nameSearch timeStandard names, computed fields

Prefer search-time extraction, since it can be changed at any moment and does not enlarge the index. Index-time fields are for special cases, such as a field used in nearly every tstats query.

SPL in depth

SPL is a pipeline: each | takes the table of results from the previous command. The implied search at the start reads from indexes. Filter as early as possible, because streaming commands such as eval and rex run on the indexers, while transforming commands such as stats reduce the data, and everything after them runs on the search head.

search and time

index=prod sourcetype=order_app level=ERROR (service=order OR service=payment) NOT "health check" earliest=-15m@m latest=now
index=prod uri="/api/orders/*" status>=500
index=prod earliest=-1d@d latest=@d          # all of yesterday, snapped to midnight
index=prod earliest=-7d@w1 latest=@w1        # last full week, Monday to Monday

@ snaps to a unit: -1h@h is the previous hour start. A wildcard at the end of a term (order*) is cheap; a leading one (*order) must scan and is slow. field=value matches a whole field, and it is case-insensitive for the value but case-sensitive for the field name.

stats and its relatives

| stats count, dc(user) as users, avg(ms) as avg_ms, perc95(ms) as p95, max(ms) as max_ms,
        values(status) as statuses, latest(message) as last_msg, sum(amount) as revenue by service, host
| stats count(eval(status>=500)) as errors, count as total by uri | eval rate=round(errors/total*100,2)
| eventstats avg(ms) as svc_avg by service | where ms > 3*svc_avg       # compare each event to its group
| streamstats count as n window=5 avg(ms) as moving_avg by service       # running calculation
| chart count over service by status                                     # 2-dimensional table
| top limit=5 uri  |  rare user

eval

| eval seconds = ms/1000
| eval severity = case(status>=500,"server", status>=400,"client", true(),"ok")
| eval tier = if(amount > 10000, "gold", "normal")
| eval user = coalesce(userId, user_id, "anonymous")
| eval slow = if(like(uri, "/api/report%") AND ms>2000, 1, 0)
| eval day = strftime(_time, "%Y-%m-%d"), hour = tonumber(strftime(_time, "%H"))
| eval parsed = strptime(orderDate, "%Y-%m-%d")
| eval ageMin = round((now() - _time)/60, 1)
| eval domain = lower(mvindex(split(email, "@"), 1))
| eval clean = replace(uri, "/\d+", "/{id}")
| where isnotnull(traceId) AND match(uri, "^/api/v\d+/")

In eval and where, field names are bare and strings use double quotes. In a search command, quotes mark a literal term. where uses eval expressions, while the search command uses keyword matching with wildcards. A null in an eval arithmetic expression gives null, so use coalesce or fillnull.

rex

| rex field=_raw "userId=(?<userId>\d+)\s+took=(?<ms>\d+)ms"
| rex field=message "(?<exception>[\w.]+Exception):\s(?<reason>.*)"
| rex max_match=0 field=_raw "orderId=(?<orderId>\w+)"      # all matches: a multivalue field
| rex mode=sed field=uri "s/\d+/{id}/g"                       # rewrite with sed syntax
| spath path=payment.status output=payStatus                  # JSON or XML, without regex
| spath path=items{}.sku output=sku | mvexpand sku             # array to one row per value

timechart, bin and table

| timechart span=5m count by status limit=10 useother=f
| timechart span=1m perc95(ms) as p95, avg(ms) as avg
| eval c=1 | timechart span=1m per_second(c) as rps
| bin _time span=10m | stats count by _time, service
| timewrap 1week                                 # overlay this week on previous weeks
| table _time service level message              # choose and order columns
| fields - _raw, punct                           # remove fields, faster than table
| rename cs_uri as uri, "resp time" as ms
| sort - count | head 20
| dedup traceId sortby -_time                    # keep the most recent per traceId

timechart is stats by _time buckets, plus filling gaps with 0. stats by _time without bin gives a row for every distinct timestamp. sort has a default limit of 10,000 results, so use sort 0 -field for no limit.

transaction

| transaction traceId maxspan=5m maxpause=1m startswith="Received order" endswith="Order saved"
| where duration > 2 | table traceId duration eventcount closed_txn
# The same with stats: faster, and works across indexers
| stats min(_time) as start, max(_time) as end, count as events, values(service) as services by traceId
| eval duration=end-start | where duration>2

transaction adds duration, eventcount and closed_txn. It is memory-heavy, runs on the search head and may evict partial groups. Use it only when you need start and end conditions, IDs that are reused over time, or the raw events merged together. If there is a unique ID, use stats.

lookup

# CSV file uploaded as a lookup definition: error_codes
| lookup error_codes code OUTPUT description, team
| lookup users.csv userId AS user OUTPUTNEW department     # OUTPUTNEW: only fill empty fields
| inputlookup vip_customers.csv | search tier=gold
index=prod [ | inputlookup vip_customers.csv | fields customerId ]   # subsearch filter
| stats count by host | outputlookup hosts_seen.csv                 # write results to a lookup

A lookup enriches events from a CSV, a KV store collection, or an external script. An automatic lookup set on a sourcetype applies itself. Keep very large or frequently changing reference data in the KV store.

join, subsearch and alternatives

index=orders status=FAILED
| join type=left traceId [ search index=payments earliest=-1h | fields traceId gateway error ]

# Preferred: fetch both datasets, group with stats
(index=orders status=FAILED) OR index=payments earliest=-1h
| stats values(status) as status, values(gateway) as gateway, values(error) as error by traceId
| where isnotnull(status)

A subsearch in [ ] runs first, and its result is inserted into the outer search. Subsearches have limits: by default 60 seconds, and 10,000 results for a normal subsearch or 50,000 for join. Past the limit, results are silently cut off, which is why a join can give wrong counts without any error. append adds results as rows, and appendcols adds them as columns.

tstats and acceleration

| tstats count where index=prod by sourcetype, host                 # reads tsidx only: very fast
| tstats count where index=prod by _time span=1h, host
| metadata type=sourcetypes index=prod                              # list what data exists
| eventcount summarize=false index=* | dedup index | table index

tstats searches index-time metadata rather than raw events, so it can be hundreds of times faster, but works only on indexed fields or accelerated data models. Report acceleration and summary indexing (using collect) pre-compute results for heavy dashboards.

Search modeBehaviour
FastExtracts only fields you name; no event details for transforming searches
Smart (default)Field discovery unless the search is transforming
VerboseAll fields and all events; slowest

Writing fast searches

  1. Always set index, sourcetype and the narrowest time range.
  2. Filter on terms in the base search, rather than with a later where.
  3. Use fields early to drop what you do not need.
  4. Prefer stats to transaction, join and dedup on large data.
  5. Avoid leading wildcards, and NOT when a positive filter will do.
  6. Use tstats for counts on indexed fields.
  7. Check the Job Inspector (Job, Inspect Job) to see where time went, such as command.search.rawdata versus dispatch.stream.remote.

Dashboards

Splunk offers Dashboard Studio (JSON definition, absolute layouts, modern visuals) and Classic dashboards (Simple XML). Good dashboards share one base search so that a page with ten panels does not run ten searches. Inputs such as time pickers and dropdowns set tokens, which panels read as $service$. A drilldown sends a click to another dashboard or search, carrying the clicked value. Schedule the heavy searches and show the saved results.

# Panel query using tokens from a dropdown and a time picker (time applied by the input)
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs service=$service$ uri=$uri_filter$
| timechart span=$span$ perc95(ms) as p95, count(eval(status>=500)) as errors

A typical operations dashboard follows the RED method: Rate (requests per second), Errors (5xx rate), Duration (p50, p95, p99), each by service and endpoint, with a panel of top exceptions and a deployment-marker annotation.

Alerts

SettingOptionsAdvice
TypeScheduled (cron) or real-timePrefer scheduled. A real-time search stays running and holds resources on the search head and indexers
Time windowe.g. earliest=-6m@m latest=-1m@mEnd a minute in the past to allow for indexing lag
Trigger conditionResult count, custom conditionDo the logic in SPL and alert when results > 0
TriggerOnce, or for each resultPer-result can flood the channel
ThrottleSuppress for N minutes, by fieldPrevents repeat paging
ActionsEmail, webhook, log event, PagerDuty and Slack appsInclude a link and a runbook
# Alert: 5xx rate above 5% with at least 50 requests, in the last 5 minutes
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-6m@m latest=-1m@m
| stats count as total, count(eval(status>=500)) as errors by service
| eval pct=round(errors/total*100,2)
| where total>=50 AND pct>5

# Alert: a service has stopped logging
| tstats latest(_time) as last where index=prod by host
| eval silentMin=round((now()-last)/60) | where silentMin>10

# Alert: abnormal volume compared with the same time last week
index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-15m@m latest=@m | stats count as now_count
| appendcols [ search index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-7d-15m@m latest=-7d@m | stats count as last_week ]
| where now_count > 3*last_week AND now_count > 20

Java application logging to Splunk

RouteHowTrade-off
File plus Universal ForwarderThe app writes to a rolling file; the UF tails itReliable, buffers during outages, keeps the app simple
stdout in KubernetesA node-level collector (Splunk OpenTelemetry Collector) reads container logs and sends to HECThe standard for containers
Direct to HEC from the appA logging appender makes HTTP callsNo agent, but logs can be lost in outages, and the app takes on the network load
// Spring Boot 3.4+: structured JSON with no extra libraries
// application.yml
logging:
  structured:
    format:
      console: ecs        # also: logstash, gelf
management:
  tracing:
    sampling:
      probability: 1.0    # traceId and spanId go in MDC with Micrometer Tracing

// Older versions: logback-spring.xml with logstash-logback-encoder
<appender name="JSON" class="ch.qos.logback.core.ConsoleAppender">
  <encoder class="net.logstash.logback.encoder.LogstashEncoder">
    <customFields>{"service":"order-service","env":"prod"}</customFields>
  </encoder>
</appender>

// Direct to HEC with splunk-library-javalogging
<appender name="SPLUNK" class="com.splunk.logging.HttpEventCollectorLogbackAppender">
  <url>https://splunk.example.com:8088</url>
  <token>${SPLUNK_HEC_TOKEN}</token>
  <index>prod</index>
  <sourcetype>_json</sourcetype>
  <batch_size_count>100</batch_size_count>
  <batch_interval>1000</batch_interval>
  <layout class="ch.qos.logback.classic.PatternLayout"><pattern>%msg</pattern></layout>
</appender>

// Wrap it in AsyncAppender, so logging never blocks a request thread

// Add business context with MDC
@Component
class CorrelationFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  @Override protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    MDC.put("userId", currentUserId(req));
    try { chain.doFilter(req, res); }
    finally { MDC.clear(); }            // threads are pooled: always clear
  }
}
log.info("order placed orderId={} amount={} ms={}", id, amount, elapsed);
log.error("payment failed orderId={}", id, exception);   // last arg = exception, full stack trace
Gotcha: MDC is thread-local. It does not cross @Async, CompletableFuture or reactive boundaries by itself. Use a TaskDecorator, or Micrometer's context propagation. With JSON, a stack trace stays inside one field of one event, avoiding the classic problem of each line being split into its own event.

HTTP Event Collector (HEC)

HEC is an HTTP endpoint on port 8088 that accepts events with a token, with no forwarder involved. Each token has a default index and sourcetype, and a list of allowed indexes.

curl https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector/event \
  -H "Authorization: Splunk 12345678-1234-1234-1234-123456789012" \
  -d '{"time":1793793600,"host":"app-1","source":"order-service","sourcetype":"_json","index":"prod",
       "event":{"level":"ERROR","message":"payment timeout","orderId":"A-42"},
       "fields":{"env":"prod"}}'
# {"text":"Success","code":0}

# Raw text endpoint, parsed with sourcetype rules
curl ".../services/collector/raw?sourcetype=order_app" -H "Authorization: Splunk $TOKEN" -d 'plain log line'

# Health check
curl https://splunk.example.com:8088/services/collector/health

Send batches: several JSON event objects can be concatenated in one body. With indexer acknowledgement on, you send an X-Splunk-Request-Channel header, get an ackId, then poll /services/collector/ack to confirm that data was indexed, which gives at-least-once delivery. A 200 without acknowledgement means only that the event was received. Common errors are 401/403 (bad or disabled token), 400 (invalid data format) and 503 (server busy, queues full). Put a load balancer in front of a HEC tier.

Production troubleshooting queries

# 1. What broke, and when did it start? Error volume by service
index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-4h | timechart span=5m count by service

# 2. Top exceptions, with a sample message
index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-1h
| rex "(?<exception>[\w.]+(?:Exception|Error))"
| stats count, latest(message) as sample, dc(host) as hosts by service, exception | sort -count

# 3. Did a deployment cause it? New errors today that were not seen yesterday
index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-1h | rex "(?<exception>[\w.]+Exception)" | stats count by exception
| join type=left exception [ search index=prod level=ERROR earliest=-25h latest=-24h
    | rex "(?<exception>[\w.]+Exception)" | stats count as yesterday by exception ]
| where isnull(yesterday)

# 4. Is one host misbehaving?
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs status>=500 earliest=-30m | stats count by host | sort -count

# 5. Follow a request end to end
index=prod traceId=4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736
| sort 0 _time | table _time service host level message

# 6. Latency by endpoint, normalising IDs in the URL
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-1h
| eval path=replace(uri_path, "/\d+", "/{id}")
| stats count, perc50(ms) as p50, perc95(ms) as p95, perc99(ms) as p99 by path
| where count>20 | sort -p95

# 7. Slow requests that a backing call explains (DB, downstream)
index=prod "HikariPool" OR "Connection is not available" OR "SQLTimeoutException" earliest=-1h
| timechart span=1m count by host

# 8. Memory and GC trouble
index=prod ("OutOfMemoryError" OR "GC overhead limit exceeded") earliest=-24h
| stats count, earliest(_time) as first, latest(_time) as last by host
| convert ctime(first) ctime(last)

# 9. Restarts: how often did each pod start?
index=prod "Started OrderApplication" earliest=-24h | timechart span=1h count by host

# 10. Kafka consumer lag or DLT messages
index=prod ("Sending to DLT" OR "rebalance" OR "lag") service=order-consumer earliest=-1h
| timechart span=5m count by service

# 11. Failed logins from one IP (possible attack)
index=security action=login result=failure earliest=-15m
| stats count, dc(user) as users by src_ip | where count>20 | sort -count

# 12. Top API clients, a noisy neighbour
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-1h | top limit=10 client_id

# 13. Is data arriving? Indexing lag per sourcetype
index=prod earliest=-15m | eval lag=_indextime-_time
| stats avg(lag) as avg_lag, max(lag) as max_lag, count by sourcetype, host | sort -max_lag

# 14. Splunk's own errors: parsing, timestamps, truncation
index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd (log_level=ERROR OR log_level=WARN)
  (component=DateParserVerbose OR component=LineBreakingProcessor OR component=AggregatorMiningProcessor)
| stats count by component, data_sourcetype

# 15. Licence usage per day and index
index=_internal source=*license_usage.log type=Usage earliest=-7d@d
| eval GB=b/1024/1024/1024 | timechart span=1d sum(GB) by idx

Access Control, Apps and Add-ons

  • Roles (authorize.conf) grant capabilities and, importantly, which indexes a user may search (srchIndexesAllowed, srchIndexesDefault). Separate sensitive data into its own index — index is the unit of access control and retention, not sourcetype.
  • Search filters on a role can further restrict events (for example env=prod), and roles can cap search concurrency and time range to protect the cluster.
  • Users usually authenticate via SAML/LDAP with groups mapped to Splunk roles.
  • App: a package of dashboards, saved searches and knowledge objects for users. Add-on (TA): no UI, just inputs, parsing (props/transforms) and field extractions for a data source; deployed to forwarders, indexers and search heads as needed.

Data Models, CIM and Baseline Detection

The Common Information Model (CIM) is a shared set of field names (src, dest, user, action, status) so that searches work across different vendors' logs. A data model is a structured, hierarchical view of events that can be accelerated (pre-built summaries), which is what lets tstats query millions of events in seconds.

Static thresholds ("alert if errors > 100") misfire with traffic patterns. A simple baseline compares now to normal:

index=app sourcetype=orders level=ERROR earliest=-7d
| bin _time span=5m
| stats count by _time
| eventstats avg(count) as avg stdev(count) as sd
| eval upper = avg + 3*sd
| where count > upper AND _time >= relative_time(now(), "-15m")

Splunk also offers predict (forecasting), anomalydetection, and the Machine Learning Toolkit for more advanced cases.

Interview Questions — Splunk

What is Splunk and how did you use it?

A platform for collecting, indexing, searching and visualizing machine data: logs, metrics, events. In a project you use it for production debugging (searching by traceId or error), dashboards (error rate, latency), alerts (for example, more than 50 5xx responses in 5 minutes triggers PagerDuty or Slack), and audit and security analysis. 💡 Have a real incident story ready: "we found the root cause by searching by traceId…"

Main Splunk components?

Universal Forwarder: a lightweight agent that ships logs. Heavy Forwarder: can parse and filter before sending. Indexer: parses, indexes and stores data. Search Head: the UI and the search engine. Deployment Server: manages forwarder configs. Cluster Manager (formerly Cluster Master): manages indexer clustering and replication. HEC: an HTTP Event Collector that accepts events directly from apps.

Common SPL commands?

search, stats (count, avg, sum, dc, perc95), timechart, chart, table, fields, rex (regex field extraction), eval (computed fields), where, sort, head/tail, dedup, top/rare, transaction, join, lookup, spath (JSON).

stats vs eventstats vs streamstats vs transaction?

stats aggregates and returns only the summary rows. eventstats adds the aggregate as a field to every event. streamstats computes running aggregates in event order. transaction groups related events into one (by id, startswith or endswith). It's slower, so prefer stats where you can.

Index vs sourcetype vs source vs host?

index: the logical store, with its own retention and access control (prod, dev). sourcetype: the data format, which determines parsing (access_combined, json). source: the file path or input. host: the machine the data came from. Always filter by index and time first, for performance.

How should applications log for Splunk?

Use structured JSON logs (Logback or Log4j2 JSON encoder) with timestamp, level, service, traceId, spanId and userId. Don't log secrets or PII. Use the right log levels. Put correlation ids in MDC. Send to stdout in Kubernetes, picked up by a forwarder or the Splunk OTel collector, or send directly to HEC.

How do you create alerts and dashboards?

Save a search, then choose Save As → Alert. Pick scheduled or real-time, set a trigger condition (number of results greater than N) and an action (email, webhook, Slack, PagerDuty), and add throttling. For dashboards, use Dashboard Studio panels built from saved searches, with time pickers and drilldowns.

Splunk vs ELK stack?

Splunk is commercial (licensed by ingest volume), enterprise-ready and easy to use, with powerful SPL. ELK (Elasticsearch + Logstash/Beats + Kibana) is open source and cheaper but takes more operational effort. Alternatives: Grafana Loki, Datadog, New Relic.

Explain what happens from a line being written to it showing up in a search.
  1. The app writes a log line to a file.
  2. The Universal Forwarder notices it, tags it with host, source and sourcetype, and sends blocks over TCP 9997.
  3. The indexer's pipeline breaks the stream into events, finds the timestamp (_time), and applies masking and routing rules.
  4. The event goes into the hot bucket: compressed into rawdata, with its terms in the tsidx file.
  5. A search head sends the search to the indexers. Each checks bucket time ranges, bloom filters, and tsidx, reads matching raw events, extracts fields, and returns results.

The usual delay is seconds. A larger gap between _indextime and _time shows a forwarder or queue problem.

Index-time vs search-time processing?

Index time covers what is stored: event breaking, timestamp, default fields, masking, routing, and any indexed fields. Changing it only affects new data. Search time covers what you see: field extraction, aliases, calculated fields, lookups, tags, event types. These apply to all data right away. Splunk is designed as schema on read, so you put as much as possible at search time.

Universal Forwarder vs Heavy Forwarder: when do you need the heavy one?

Use the UF by default, since it is light and does minimal processing. Use an HF when you need to parse or filter before the indexers, for instance routing events to different indexes or clusters, dropping noise to save licence, masking at the edge, or running add-ons that pull data from APIs. The HF is a full Splunk instance, so it costs more resources and parsing work happens there.

Multi-line stack traces appear as separate events. How do you fix this?

Set line breaking in props.conf for the sourcetype, on the first full instance (indexer or HF): SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false and a LINE_BREAKER with a lookahead for the timestamp. This is faster than leaving line merging enabled with BREAK_ONLY_BEFORE. A better long-term fix is JSON logging, so the stack trace is one field. New settings only affect new data. Long traces may also hit TRUNCATE.

Events show the wrong time. What are the likely causes?

Splunk found the wrong timestamp or the wrong zone. Set TIME_PREFIX, TIME_FORMAT and MAX_TIMESTAMP_LOOKAHEAD. Set TZ for the sourcetype or host if logs have no offset. Check for events far in the future or past, since these land in odd buckets and retention behaves strangely. Search with index=x | eval lag=_indextime-_time to see the problem, and check DateParserVerbose messages in _internal. Fixing old events requires re-indexing.

stats vs chart vs timechart?

stats gives a table, grouped by any number of fields. chart gives a two-dimensional table: over one field, by a second. timechart is chart with _time as the x-axis, automatic bucketing, and zeros for empty buckets. A top-level timechart ... by field keeps the top 10 series and groups the rest as OTHER, unless you set limit=0 or useother=f.

join vs stats vs lookup for combining data?

Use stats ... by key over a combined base search whenever possible. It is distributed, has no subsearch limits and handles large data. Use lookup when the other side is reference data. Use join only for small subsearches, and be aware of the limits on rows and time: truncation is silent, so counts may be wrong. Default join is an inner join, and it keeps only the first match on the right side unless you set max=0.

dedup vs stats latest(); what's the trap in dedup?

dedup field keeps the first event per value, in search order (normally newest first), and drops the rest. It also drops events that do not have the field, unless you add keepempty=true. stats latest(x) by key does a similar job in a distributed way and is usually faster. Only use dedup when you need the whole event.

where vs search in the pipeline?

search matches terms and fields with wildcards, and the values have search semantics. where takes an eval expression, so you can compare two fields (where a > b), which search cannot do, and call functions (where match(uri, "regex")). With where, a bare word means a field, so a string needs double quotes. A common bug is where status=ERROR, which compares to a field named ERROR.

What are multivalue fields?

A field holding several values in one event, created by values(), rex max_match=0, split or JSON arrays. Functions: mvcount, mvindex, mvfilter, mvjoin, mvzip. mvexpand field creates one row per value, which you need before counting by that value. mvexpand is memory-limited, so filter first.

How do you find the slowest 1% of requests per endpoint?
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-1h
| eval path=replace(uri_path, "/\d+", "/{id}")
| eventstats perc99(ms) as p99 by path
| where ms >= p99
| table _time path ms traceId host | sort -ms

eventstats keeps the raw rows and adds the group value. So each event can be compared with its own group, and you keep the traceId for follow-up. stats would lose the events.

Find users who started checkout but did not finish.
index=prod (event=checkout_started OR event=checkout_completed) earliest=-1h
| stats values(event) as steps, min(_time) as started by sessionId
| where mvcount(steps)=1 AND steps="checkout_started"
| eval waiting=round((now()-started)/60,1) | sort -waiting

This is the pattern for detecting a missing event. transaction ... keepevicted=true and looking for closed_txn=0 works too, but costs more.

How do you calculate an error rate and compare it to last week?
index=prod sourcetype=access_logs earliest=-7d@h latest=@h
| timechart span=1h count(eval(status>=500)) as errors, count as total
| eval rate=round(errors/total*100,2)
| fields _time rate
| timewrap 1day series=short

Or compare two windows with appendcols. Dividing by a count of 0 gives null, which is fine for charts, but test it in alerts.

A dashboard is slow. How do you fix it?
  1. Open the Job Inspector for the slowest panel and see which phase costs the most.
  2. Tighten time and add index and sourcetype.
  3. Use one base search with post-process searches, rather than many similar ones.
  4. Replace join or transaction with stats.
  5. Use tstats on an accelerated data model, or schedule the search and load the cached result with loadjob or a saved report.
  6. Check that panels do not all refresh at once.
Why was my alert missed or fired late?

Common causes: the scheduled search was skipped because the search head hit its concurrency limit (check index=_internal sourcetype=scheduler status=skipped); the search window ends at now, so late-arriving events are missed; the schedule and window do not line up, leaving gaps; throttling suppressed it; or the mail action failed (check python.log). Use windows offset by a minute or more, and overlap them only if a throttle handles duplicates.

How would you reduce Splunk licence use?

Licence (in the common ingest model) counts raw data indexed per day. Find the biggest sources from license_usage.log. Turn off DEBUG logs in production, and stop logging full request bodies. Filter noise before indexing by sending it to nullQueue with props.conf and transforms.conf on an indexer or HF. Shorten JSON keys. Note that retention does not change licence use, as it counts ingest, but retention does affect storage costs.

# props.conf
[access_logs]
TRANSFORMS-drop = drop_health
# transforms.conf
[drop_health]
REGEX = GET /actuator/health
DEST_KEY = queue
FORMAT = nullQueue
How do you mask sensitive data?

Best: do not log it, by redacting in the app's logging layer. As a safety net at index time, use SEDCMD in props.conf, or a transforms.conf rule that rewrites _raw, on the first parsing tier. Search-time masking only hides data from view, and it stays on disk. Once stored unmasked, the data must be deleted and re-ingested. Restrict access to sensitive indexes by role, and audit it with index=_audit.

What's a knowledge object? Name some.

A user-defined item that adds meaning to data at search time: field extractions, calculated fields, field aliases, lookups, event types (a saved search as a label), tags, macros (a reusable SPL fragment, invoked with backticks), data models, workflow actions. They live in apps and have sharing permissions (private, app, global). A macro keeps long common filters in one place.

What's in the internal indexes?

_internal holds Splunk's own logs (splunkd, metrics, scheduler, license usage). _audit records user activity and searches. _introspection records resource use. _configtracker tracks changes to configuration files on recent versions. They are used for checking whether a forwarder is sending, why searches are skipped, and who ran what. For example, index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd component=Metrics group=tcpin_connections shows connected forwarders.

A forwarder's logs aren't appearing. How do you debug it?
  1. Check the data is not just in another index or time range: search index=* host=theHost earliest=-1d.
  2. On the host: splunk list monitor and splunk list forward-server, and is the process running?
  3. Read $SPLUNK_HOME/var/log/splunk/splunkd.log for connection errors and for TailReader messages.
  4. Check file permissions for the user running the UF.
  5. Check the path pattern in inputs.conf with splunk btool inputs list --debug.
  6. Look for blocked queues on the indexers, and network access to 9997.
  7. A file rotated with identical header bytes can be skipped, since the CRC of its start matches a seen file; crcSalt or initCrcLength addresses this.
What is btool? How are config files merged?

Splunk merges all .conf files by precedence across system/local, apps/*/local, apps/*/default and system/default. Never edit default. splunk btool props list order_app --debug shows the effective setting and which file set it. It is the key tool when a setting seems ignored.

What's an indexer cluster's RF and SF, and what happens when a peer fails?

RF is how many raw-data copies exist, SF how many are immediately searchable. When a peer fails, the cluster manager reassigns primaries, and tells other peers to make new copies to restore RF and SF. Searches continue while the cluster is "search factor met". Data forwarded to the failed peer is handled by automatic load balancing to the others. A multi-site cluster keeps copies per data centre.

Scenario: production latency jumped at 14:05. Walk through your investigation.
  1. Confirm scope: timechart span=1m perc95(ms) by service, to find the first affected service.
  2. Check it by host and endpoint, to see whether it is one instance, one path or everything.
  3. Check changes: deployment logs, restarts ("Started OrderApplication"), config changes.
  4. Check error patterns from 14:00 to 14:10: timeouts, HikariPool exhaustion, GC, Kafka rebalance.
  5. Take one slow traceId, follow it across services and find the slow gap between timestamps.
  6. Correlate with metrics (database, CPU) in Grafana or Splunk Observability.
  7. Write down the timeline, save the searches as an alert so that recurrence is caught sooner.
Scenario: design logging for 50 microservices in Kubernetes.

Standardise a JSON log format with timestamp, level, service, version, env, traceId, spanId, message. Log to stdout. Run the Splunk OpenTelemetry Collector as a DaemonSet to send to a HEC tier behind a load balancer. Use one index per environment or data sensitivity, since permissions and retention are per index. Use a sourcetype per format, not per service. Pick a retention per index. Use a shared logging library so teams get MDC and redaction by default. Budget ingest by team, with dashboards and alerts. Keep metrics and traces in their own tools, and link them by traceId.

What's a good log line? What should not be logged?

A good line is machine-parsable and answers who, what, outcome and how long: {"level":"WARN","service":"order","traceId":"...","event":"payment_retry","orderId":"A-42","attempt":2,"ms":840}. Use stable event names and fields rather than free text, as dashboards depend on them. Do not log passwords, tokens, card numbers, personal data or full payloads. Avoid logging an exception at every layer, as it inflates error counts. Choose levels with care: ERROR means a person should look, WARN a recoverable oddity, INFO a business event, DEBUG off in production.

How do you restrict which teams can see which logs in Splunk?

Put data with different sensitivity in different indexes, then give each role access only to the indexes it needs via srchIndexesAllowed in authorize.conf (or the Roles UI). Map SAML/LDAP groups to those roles. Role search filters can narrow further, and knowledge objects have private/app/global sharing permissions. 💡 Index is the boundary for both access and retention, so design indexes around those two needs, not around applications alone.

What is the CIM and why do data models matter?

The Common Information Model normalises field names across sources (for example user, src, action) so one search or dashboard works for logs from many vendors. Data models define a structured view on top of CIM-compliant data, and when accelerated they store summaries that tstats can query very fast. Security tools like Splunk Enterprise Security rely on CIM data models heavily.

App vs add-on (TA) in Splunk?

An app delivers a user experience: dashboards, saved searches, reports and navigation. A technology add-on has no UI; it contains inputs, line-breaking/timestamp rules and field extractions for a specific data source (for example a TA for Linux or AWS logs). Install the TA where its settings apply: inputs on forwarders, index-time parsing on indexers or heavy forwarders, search-time extractions on search heads.

How would you alert on an abnormal error spike instead of a fixed threshold?

Build a baseline: bucket counts with bin/timechart, compute avg and stdev over the last week with eventstats, and alert when the current bucket exceeds, say, avg + 3*stdev. Better still, compare the same hour last week (timewrap) to handle daily seasonality, or alert on the error rate rather than the raw count so traffic growth doesn't fire it. Add throttling so one incident creates one alert.

Splunk vs Prometheus/Grafana — do you need both?

They solve different problems. Splunk indexes logs/events and is great for searching arbitrary text, investigations and audit. Prometheus stores numeric time-series metrics scraped from endpoints such as Spring Boot's /actuator/prometheus; it is cheap and fast for dashboards and alerting on rates, latencies and saturation. Many teams use metrics for "is something wrong?" and logs for "why?", with a shared trace ID to jump between them. Splunk can store metrics too (metrics indexes, mstats), but cost usually favours a metrics system for high-volume numbers.

Git, GitHub & SVN Version control

Git is a distributed version control system where every clone holds the full history; GitHub adds hosting, pull requests and CI, while SVN is the older centralised model still found in many enterprises.

# Typical feature-branch workflow
git switch main && git pull --rebase
git switch -c feature/patient-search
# ...edit files...
git add -p                         # stage hunks interactively
git commit -m "feat: add patient search endpoint"
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main             # replay my commits on latest main
git push -u origin feature/patient-search
# open a Pull Request on GitHub → review → CI green → squash & merge

The Git Model

Git stores snapshots, not diffs. Three areas matter: the working tree (files on disk), the index / staging area (what the next commit will contain) and the repository (.git, the object database). A commit is an immutable object identified by a SHA hash, pointing to a tree snapshot, its parent commit(s), author and message. A branch is just a movable pointer (a file containing a commit hash) that advances when you commit; HEAD points to the current branch (or directly to a commit in "detached HEAD" state). Because branches are cheap pointers, creating and switching branches is instant.

working tree --git add--> index --git commit--> local repo --git push--> remote
     <---------- git restore / git switch / git checkout ----------
                                        local repo <--git fetch-- remote

Common Commands

  • git init / git clone <url> — create or copy a repository
  • git status, git diff (unstaged), git diff --staged
  • git add <file>, git add -p, git commit -m, git commit --amend (rewrite the last local commit)
  • git switch -c <branch> / git branch -d; git restore <file> discards working-tree changes
  • git fetch (download, no merge) vs git pull (fetch + merge or rebase)
  • git push -u origin <branch>, git push --force-with-lease (safe force after rebase)
  • git log --oneline --graph --all, git show, git blame, git reflog (history of HEAD — your safety net)
  • git bisect — binary search to find the commit that introduced a bug

Merge vs Rebase & Resolving Conflicts

Merge combines branches by creating a merge commit with two parents (or a fast-forward if no divergence). It preserves true history and is safe on shared branches, but history can get noisy. Rebase replays your commits on top of another base, producing new commits with new hashes and a linear history. Golden rule: never rebase commits others have already pulled (shared/public branches); rebase your own local or feature branch to keep it current. Interactive rebase (git rebase -i) lets you squash, reorder and reword commits before opening a PR.

A conflict occurs when both sides changed the same lines. Git marks the file; you edit it to the correct result, then git add and continue (git merge --continue or git rebase --continue), or abort with --abort.

<<<<<<< HEAD
    return repo.findByName(name);
=======
    return repo.findByNameIgnoreCase(name);
>>>>>>> feature/search

git add PatientService.java
git rebase --continue      # or: git merge --continue

Cherry-pick, Revert, Reset & Stash

git cherry-pick <sha> applies one specific commit onto the current branch as a new commit — typical for back-porting a hotfix to a release branch. git revert <sha> creates a new commit that undoes a previous one; it is safe on shared branches because history is not rewritten. git reset moves the current branch pointer backwards and rewrites history — use only on local, unpushed work:

  • --soft — move HEAD; keep changes staged (useful to re-squash commits)
  • --mixed (default) — move HEAD; keep changes in the working tree but unstaged
  • --hard — move HEAD and discard all changes in index and working tree (recover via git reflog if needed)

git stash shelves uncommitted changes so you can switch context; git stash pop reapplies and removes, git stash apply keeps the stash, git stash list shows them; -u includes untracked files.

git reset --soft HEAD~3        # undo last 3 commits, keep changes staged
git revert a1b2c3d             # safe undo on main
git stash push -m "wip search" && git switch hotfix/login
git cherry-pick 9f8e7d6

Tags & .gitignore

Tags mark specific commits, usually releases (v1.4.0, semantic versioning). Annotated tags (git tag -a v1.4.0 -m "Release 1.4.0") store author, date and message and are recommended for releases; lightweight tags are just names for a commit. Tags are not pushed by default: git push origin v1.4.0 or --tags. CI pipelines often trigger release builds on tags.

.gitignore lists patterns Git should not track: build outputs, dependencies and secrets. It does not affect files already tracked — run git rm --cached <file> first. Never commit credentials; if one leaks, rotate it, because it remains in history.

# .gitignore for Spring Boot + Angular
target/
build/
.gradle/
node_modules/
dist/
.angular/
*.log
.env
.idea/
application-local.properties

Branching Strategies

  • Feature branches (GitHub Flow): short-lived branch per feature/bug off main, merged via PR; main is always deployable. Simple and popular.
  • Git Flow: long-lived main (production) and develop (integration), plus feature/*, release/* and hotfix/* branches. Suits scheduled, versioned releases but adds overhead and merge pain.
  • Trunk-based development: everyone integrates small changes into main at least daily, with very short-lived branches and feature flags for unfinished work. Requires strong automated tests and CI; enables continuous delivery.

Use conventional commit messages (feat:, fix:, refactor:) and branch naming (feature/JIRA-123-search) to keep history readable.

Pull Requests & Code Review

A pull request (merge request in GitLab) proposes merging a branch, showing the diff, discussion and CI status. Good PRs are small and focused, with a clear description, linked ticket and tests. Repositories use branch protection rules: required reviews, passing status checks, no direct pushes to main, and CODEOWNERS for automatic reviewer assignment. Merge options: merge commit (keeps all commits), squash and merge (one clean commit per PR), rebase and merge (linear history of individual commits). Reviewers check correctness, readability, tests, security and performance — commenting on code, not people.

GitHub Actions Basics

GitHub Actions is GitHub's built-in CI/CD. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/, triggered by events (push, pull_request, workflow_dispatch, schedule, tags). A workflow has jobs that run on runners (GitHub-hosted or self-hosted) and jobs contain steps that run shell commands or reusable actions (actions/checkout, actions/setup-java). Jobs run in parallel unless linked with needs. Secrets are stored in repository settings and accessed as ${{ secrets.NAME }}.

name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-java@v4
        with: { distribution: temurin, java-version: '21', cache: maven }
      - run: mvn -B verify
  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v4
        with: { node-version: 20, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci && npm run build && npm test -- --watch=false

SVN Concepts & Git vs SVN

Apache Subversion (SVN) is a centralised VCS: one central server holds the repository and history; clients have a working copy of one revision. Conventional layout is /trunk (main line), /branches and /tags — branches and tags are cheap server-side directory copies. Revisions are global incrementing numbers (r1024) rather than hashes. Key commands: svn checkout (get a working copy), svn update (pull latest), svn add, svn commit (sends directly to the server — no local commits), svn status, svn diff, svn log, svn revert, svn merge, svn copy (branch/tag). SVN supports file locking for binary assets and partial checkouts of subdirectories.

  • Git: distributed, full history locally, works offline, fast cheap branching, commits are local until pushed, powerful merging/rebasing; huge ecosystem (GitHub, GitLab, Actions).
  • SVN: centralised, needs server for most operations, simpler mental model, path-based access control, file locking, good with large binaries and partial checkout.
  • Migration: git svn clone or tools like svn2git convert history including trunk/branches/tags.
svn checkout https://svn.example.com/repo/trunk myproject
svn update
svn add src/NewFile.java
svn commit -m "Add NewFile"
svn copy ^/trunk ^/branches/release-2.0 -m "Create release branch"

Git Internals: Blobs, Trees, Commits

Git is a content-addressed object store. A blob holds file contents, a tree maps names to blobs and sub-trees (a directory), and a commit points to one root tree, its parent commit(s), author and message. Each object is identified by the hash of its content (SHA-1, with SHA-256 repositories supported in newer versions). Branches and tags are just refs pointing to commit hashes, which is why identical files are stored once and why changing any old commit changes every hash after it (rewriting history).

Rewriting and Recovering History

# fix the last commit (message or forgotten file) - only if not pushed
git add Forgotten.java && git commit --amend --no-edit

# clean up a feature branch before a PR
git commit --fixup=a1b2c3d          # mark a fix for an earlier commit
git rebase -i --autosquash origin/main   # pick / squash / reword / drop

# recover "lost" work after a bad reset or rebase
git reflog                           # HEAD@{3}: commit: add payment API
git reset --hard HEAD@{3}            # or: git branch rescue HEAD@{3}

# find the commit that introduced a bug
git bisect start; git bisect bad; git bisect good v1.4.0
git bisect run mvn -q test -Dtest=PaymentTest   # automatic binary search
git bisect reset

Rule: rewrite only commits that nobody else has based work on; after rewriting a pushed feature branch, use git push --force-with-lease.

Hooks, Forks and Repository Hygiene

  • Hooks are scripts in .git/hooks (pre-commit, commit-msg, pre-push). They are not committed, so teams share them with Husky + lint-staged (Angular/Node) or the pre-commit framework. Use them for formatting, linting and Conventional Commit checks; keep real enforcement in CI because hooks can be skipped with --no-verify.
  • Fork workflow: origin = your fork, upstream = the original repo. git fetch upstream && git rebase upstream/main keeps your fork current; PRs go from fork branch to upstream.
  • Line endings: Windows uses CRLF, Linux LF. Add .gitattributes with * text=auto and *.sh text eol=lf so scripts don't break in Docker/Linux CI.
  • Submodules pin another repo at a commit; they are easy to get wrong (forgotten --recurse-submodules). Alternatives: publish shared code as a versioned package (Maven/npm) or use a monorepo.
  • Large files: binaries bloat history forever; use Git LFS or an artifact store.

Interview Questions — Git, GitHub & SVN

What is the difference between Git and GitHub?

Git is the distributed version control tool that runs locally and tracks history. GitHub is a hosting platform for Git repositories that adds collaboration features: pull requests, code review, issues, branch protection, Actions CI/CD, packages and security scanning. GitLab and Bitbucket are alternatives offering similar features.

Explain the working tree, staging area and repository.

The working tree is your files on disk; the staging area (index) is the snapshot you are preparing for the next commit; the repository (.git) stores committed history. git add moves changes into the index and git commit records the index as a commit. Staging lets you commit only part of your changes (git add -p), keeping commits focused.

What is a branch in Git, really?

A lightweight, movable pointer to a commit — literally a file under .git/refs/heads containing a SHA. When you commit on a branch, the pointer moves to the new commit. HEAD is a pointer to the current branch. That is why branching is instant and cheap in Git, unlike SVN where a branch is a directory copy on the server.

git fetch vs git pull?

git fetch downloads new commits and updates remote-tracking branches like origin/main without touching your working branch. git pull is fetch followed by a merge (or a rebase with --rebase / pull.rebase=true) into the current branch. 💡 Fetching first lets you inspect incoming changes with git log HEAD..origin/main before integrating.

Merge vs rebase — when do you use each?

Merge preserves history exactly and adds a merge commit; it is safe for shared branches. Rebase rewrites your commits onto a new base for a linear history, ideal for updating a personal feature branch with the latest main before a PR. Never rebase commits that others have based work on, because it rewrites hashes; after rebasing a pushed feature branch, push with --force-with-lease.

How do you resolve a merge conflict?

Run git status to see conflicted files, open each and edit the region between <<<<<<<, ======= and >>>>>>> to the correct combined code, removing the markers. Then git add the file and run git merge --continue (or git rebase --continue). Build and run tests before pushing. Use an IDE merge tool for complex cases, and --abort to start over. 💡 Pulling main frequently keeps conflicts small.

git reset vs git revert?

git revert adds a new commit that inverts an earlier commit — history is preserved, so it is the right way to undo something already pushed to a shared branch. git reset moves the branch pointer backwards, effectively removing commits from the branch's history; it is for local, unpushed work. Resetting pushed commits forces everyone else to reconcile rewritten history.

Explain git reset --soft, --mixed and --hard.

All three move HEAD/the branch to the target commit. --soft leaves the undone changes staged; --mixed (the default) leaves them in the working tree but unstaged; --hard discards them from both index and working tree. Example: git reset --soft HEAD~1 undoes the last commit but keeps the work ready to recommit. Lost commits after --hard can usually be recovered with git reflog.

What is git cherry-pick and when is it useful?

It applies the changes of one or more specific commits onto the current branch as new commits. Typical uses: back-porting a bug fix from main to a release or hotfix branch, or rescuing a commit made on the wrong branch. Overusing it duplicates commits across branches, which can confuse later merges; -x records the original commit hash in the message.

What is git stash?

It saves uncommitted changes (staged and unstaged) onto a stack and cleans the working tree, so you can switch branches for an urgent fix. git stash pop reapplies the latest and removes it; apply keeps it; git stash list and git stash drop manage the stack; -u includes untracked files. For longer interruptions, a WIP commit on a branch is often safer.

Compare Git Flow, GitHub Flow and trunk-based development.

Git Flow uses main + develop plus feature, release and hotfix branches — structured, suits versioned scheduled releases, but heavyweight.
