GitHub Flow uses short-lived feature branches off an always-deployable main merged via PRs. Trunk-based integrates small changes into main at least daily with feature flags hiding incomplete work, requiring strong CI and tests; it best supports continuous delivery. Choice depends on release cadence and team size.

What makes a good pull request and code review?

A good PR is small, single-purpose, has a descriptive title and summary (what and why), links the ticket, includes tests and passes CI. Reviewers look for correctness, edge cases, readability, naming, test coverage, security (input validation, secrets) and performance, giving specific, respectful comments and distinguishing blockers from suggestions. Branch protection enforces required approvals and green checks before merge.

Squash and merge vs rebase and merge vs merge commit?

Merge commit keeps all branch commits plus a merge commit — full history. Squash and merge combines the PR into a single commit on main — clean, one commit per feature, easy to revert, but loses granular commits. Rebase and merge replays each commit onto main linearly without a merge commit. Many teams use squash for feature PRs.

What is GitHub Actions? Describe a workflow.

GitHub's CI/CD platform. A workflow is a YAML file in .github/workflows triggered by events like push or pull_request; it contains jobs that run on runners, and each job has steps that run commands or reusable actions. For a Java + Angular project, a workflow would check out code, set up JDK and Node with caching, run mvn verify and npm ci && npm run build, then optionally build a Docker image and deploy on merge to main. Secrets are injected from repository/environment settings.

A file is in .gitignore but Git still tracks it — why?

.gitignore only prevents untracked files from being added; files already committed stay tracked. Remove it from the index while keeping it on disk with git rm --cached path/to/file, commit, and it will be ignored from then on. If it contained secrets, rotate them — they remain in history unless it is rewritten.

What is the difference between Git and SVN?

Git is distributed: every clone has full history, so commits, branches, log and diff work offline and are fast; you commit locally and push later. SVN is centralised: the server holds history, svn commit goes straight to the server, and revisions are sequential numbers. Branching in Git is a cheap pointer, while SVN branches are directory copies under /branches. SVN offers file locking, path-level permissions and partial checkouts, which some teams with large binary assets prefer.

Explain SVN trunk, branches and tags, and the basic workflow.

By convention /trunk is the main development line, /branches holds feature or release lines and /tags holds read-only release snapshots — all created with svn copy. The daily workflow is svn checkout once, then svn update to get others' changes, edit, svn status/svn diff to review, and svn commit -m to publish. Conflicts are resolved during update and marked with svn resolve.

How do you undo a commit that was already pushed to main?

Use git revert <sha> (for a merge commit, git revert -m 1 <sha>) and push the new commit — this keeps shared history intact. Avoid git reset + force push on shared branches, since it breaks teammates' clones and is usually blocked by branch protection. 💡 If the change was a deployment issue, a revert PR goes through the normal CI pipeline, giving a traceable rollback.

You ran git reset --hard and lost commits. Can you get them back?

Yes, usually. git reflog records every position HEAD has been in, including commits no longer on any branch. Find the entry before the reset and run git reset --hard HEAD@{n} or create a branch at it. Reflog entries are local and expire (by default around 90 days for reachable, 30 for unreachable), and uncommitted changes discarded by --hard are not recoverable — commit or stash first.

How does git bisect work?

It binary-searches history between a known good and a known bad commit. You mark commits good or bad and Git checks out the midpoint each time, so 1,000 commits need about 10 steps. git bisect run <script> automates it: the script exits 0 for good and non-zero for bad (a failing test). Finish with git bisect reset.

How do you squash or edit commits before opening a PR?

Use interactive rebase: git rebase -i origin/main, then change pick to squash/fixup (combine), reword (edit message), edit (amend content) or drop. git commit --fixup=<sha> plus git rebase -i --autosquash automates the ordering. Only do this on your own branch, then git push --force-with-lease. For just the last commit, git commit --amend is enough.

A password was committed and pushed. What do you do?

First rotate/revoke the secret — assume it is compromised the moment it was pushed, because clones, forks and caches may already have it. Then remove it from history with git filter-repo (or BFG), force-push, and ask collaborators to re-clone; on GitHub, contact support to purge cached views if needed. Finally prevent a repeat: move the value to a secret manager or environment variable, add the file to .gitignore, and enable secret scanning or a pre-commit hook such as Gitleaks. 💡 A git revert alone is not enough — the secret is still in history.

What are Git hooks and how do you share them with a team?

Hooks are scripts Git runs at points like pre-commit, commit-msg and pre-push. The .git/hooks folder is not versioned, so teams use Husky (with lint-staged to lint only staged files) for Angular projects, or the pre-commit framework / a Maven plugin for Java. Typical checks: Prettier/ESLint, Spotless/Checkstyle, commit message format, quick unit tests. Hooks are a convenience; CI is the real gate because --no-verify skips them.

How do you keep a fork in sync with the original repository?

Add the original as a second remote: git remote add upstream <url>. Then git fetch upstream and either git rebase upstream/main (clean history on your feature branch) or merge it, and push to your fork (origin). Open PRs from your fork's branch to upstream's main. GitHub's "Sync fork" button does the same for the default branch.

Why do shell scripts fail in Docker after being committed from Windows?

They were checked out or committed with CRLF line endings, so Linux sees /bin/sh^M and fails with "bad interpreter" or "not found". Fix with a .gitattributes file (* text=auto, *.sh text eol=lf) and renormalise with git add --renormalize .. core.autocrlf is a per-machine setting, so .gitattributes is the reliable, versioned fix.

How does Git store data internally?

As immutable objects addressed by the hash of their content: blobs (file contents), trees (directories), commits (tree + parents + metadata) and annotated tags. Branches are refs — small files holding a commit hash — and HEAD points to the current branch. Because a commit hash covers its parent, changing any commit changes all descendants, which is why rebasing creates new commits and why pushed history should not be rewritten. Objects are compressed into packfiles to save space.

What is a signed commit and why would a team require it?

A signed commit carries a GPG, SSH or S/MIME signature (git commit -S) proving it was made by the holder of that key, since the author name and email in a commit can be set to anything. GitHub shows a "Verified" badge and branch protection can require signed commits. It is part of software supply-chain security alongside protected branches, required reviews and CODEOWNERS.

Docker & Containers Images · Compose

Docker packages an application with its runtime, libraries and config into an immutable image that runs the same way on a laptop, CI server or cloud. For a Java full stack developer it is the standard way to ship Spring Boot services and Angular front ends.

# Multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot app
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
RUN mvn -q dependency:go-offline
COPY src ./src
RUN mvn -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
RUN addgroup -S app && adduser -S app -G app
COPY --from=build /app/target/*.jar app.jar
USER app
EXPOSE 8080
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75"
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]

Containers vs Virtual Machines

A virtual machine virtualises hardware: each VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor, so it is heavy (GBs, boots in minutes). A container virtualises the OS: it is just an isolated process on the host kernel, using Linux namespaces (isolation of PIDs, network, mounts, users) and cgroups (CPU/memory limits). Containers start in milliseconds to seconds and are MBs in size, but share the host kernel, so isolation is weaker than a VM.

  • Image – read-only template (layers + metadata).
  • Container – a running (or stopped) instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top.
  • Registry – stores and distributes images (Docker Hub, GCP Artifact Registry, AWS ECR, GitHub GHCR).

Images, Layers & Caching

Each filesystem-changing instruction (RUN, COPY, ADD) creates a new layer. Layers are content-addressed and shared between images, so pulling a second image built on the same base is fast. During a build Docker reuses a cached layer if the instruction and its inputs are unchanged; once a layer changes, every layer after it is rebuilt.

So order instructions from least to most frequently changing: copy pom.xml / package.json first and install dependencies, then copy source code. A code change then reuses the dependency layer. Use a .dockerignore (exclude target/, node_modules/, .git, secrets) to keep the build context small and avoid cache busting.

Dockerfile Instructions

  • FROM – base image; every stage starts with it. Pin versions (eclipse-temurin:21-jre), never rely on latest.
  • WORKDIR – sets (and creates) the working directory for following instructions.
  • COPY – copies files from the build context (or --from=stage). ADD also extracts tar files and fetches URLs; prefer COPY.
  • RUN – executes a command at build time and commits the result as a layer. Chain and clean up in the same RUN to keep layers small.
  • ENV – environment variable available at build and run time. ARG is build-time only.
  • EXPOSE – documentation of the port the app listens on; it does not publish it (that is -p 8080:8080).
  • USER – switch to a non-root user for the following instructions and at runtime.
  • CMD vs ENTRYPOINT – ENTRYPOINT is the executable that always runs; CMD supplies default arguments (or the default command) and is replaced by arguments given to docker run.
  • HEALTHCHECK – command Docker runs periodically to mark the container healthy/unhealthy.
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]
CMD ["--spring.profiles.active=prod"]
# docker run myapp --spring.profiles.active=dev   -> overrides only CMD

Multi-stage Builds (Spring Boot & Angular)

A multi-stage build uses a heavy build image (JDK + Maven, or Node) and copies only the artifact into a slim runtime image. The final image has no compiler, no source and no build cache, so it is smaller and has a smaller attack surface. Spring Boot also supports layered jars (java -Djarmode=tools -jar app.jar extract --layers) to put dependencies and application classes in separate layers, and mvn spring-boot:build-image builds an OCI image with Cloud Native Buildpacks without a Dockerfile.

# Angular app served by nginx
FROM node:22-alpine AS build
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build -- --configuration production

FROM nginx:1.27-alpine
COPY nginx.conf /etc/nginx/conf.d/default.conf
COPY --from=build /app/dist/my-app/browser /usr/share/nginx/html
EXPOSE 80

# nginx.conf: SPA fallback so deep links work
# location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html; }

Volumes, Bind Mounts & Networks

A container's writable layer disappears when the container is removed. For persistent data use:

  • Named volumes (-v mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql) – managed by Docker, best for database data.
  • Bind mounts (-v $(pwd)/src:/app/src) – map a host directory; great for local dev hot-reload and config files.
  • tmpfs – in-memory, for scratch or sensitive temp data.

Networks: the default bridge network gives containers private IPs. On a user-defined bridge network (which Compose creates automatically) containers resolve each other by service name through Docker's embedded DNS, e.g. jdbc:mysql://db:3306/app. host network shares the host's network stack; none disables networking.

Docker Compose

Compose describes a multi-container app in compose.yaml and starts it with docker compose up -d. Use depends_on with condition: service_healthy so the app waits until the DB is actually ready.

services:
  app:
    build: .
    ports: ["8080:8080"]
    environment:
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL: jdbc:mysql://db:3306/appdb
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_USERNAME: app
      SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      SPRING_KAFKA_BOOTSTRAP_SERVERS: kafka:9092
    depends_on:
      db:    { condition: service_healthy }
      kafka: { condition: service_started }

  db:
    image: mysql:8.4
    environment:
      MYSQL_DATABASE: appdb
      MYSQL_USER: app
      MYSQL_PASSWORD: ${DB_PASSWORD}
      MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: ${DB_ROOT_PASSWORD}
    volumes: [mysql-data:/var/lib/mysql]
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "mysqladmin", "ping", "-h", "localhost"]
      interval: 10s
      retries: 5

  kafka:
    image: apache/kafka:3.8.0      # KRaft mode, no ZooKeeper
    ports: ["9092:9092"]

volumes:
  mysql-data:

Variables like ${DB_PASSWORD} are read from a .env file next to the compose file (keep it out of Git). Common commands: docker compose up -d --build, down -v, logs -f app, ps, exec db mysql -u app -p.

Environment Variables, Secrets & Health Checks

Follow 12-factor config: the same image runs in every environment and differences come from env vars (Spring Boot maps SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL to spring.datasource.url automatically). Never bake passwords into an image with ENV or COPY – they are visible in docker history and layers. For build-time secrets use BuildKit RUN --mount=type=secret,id=npmrc ...; at runtime use Docker/Compose secrets (mounted at /run/secrets/...), Kubernetes Secrets, or a cloud secret manager.

Health checks let the orchestrator restart or stop routing to unhealthy containers. With Spring Boot Actuator, expose /actuator/health and, on Kubernetes, the /actuator/health/liveness and /readiness groups.

Logs, Exec & Debugging

docker ps -a                          # running and stopped containers
docker logs -f --tail 100 app         # stream stdout/stderr
docker exec -it app sh                # shell inside a running container
docker inspect app                    # config, IP, mounts, health status
docker stats                          # live CPU / memory usage
docker run --rm -it --entrypoint sh myimg   # debug an image that crashes on start
docker image history myimg            # layers and their sizes
docker system prune                   # remove unused data

Applications should log to stdout/stderr, not files; Docker and the platform collect it. Exit code 137 usually means the container was OOM-killed (SIGKILL) – check memory limits and JVM heap settings. Modern JVMs are container-aware; size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage rather than a fixed -Xmx.

Image Size, Security & Kubernetes Basics

  • Use slim bases: *-jre-alpine, distroless (gcr.io/distroless/java21) or a custom jlink runtime.
  • Run as a non-root user, pin base image versions/digests, scan images (Docker Scout, Trivy), rebuild regularly for patches.
  • One process per container; keep secrets out of images; use read-only root filesystems where possible.
  • Tag images with immutable versions (git SHA or semver) and push: docker tag app europe-docker.pkg.dev/proj/repo/app:1.4.2 then docker push ....

Kubernetes orchestrates containers across a cluster. A Pod is the smallest unit (one or more containers sharing network and storage). A Deployment declares the desired number of pod replicas and handles rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service gives a stable DNS name and load-balances across pods (ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer). An Ingress routes external HTTP traffic; ConfigMaps and Secrets inject config; liveness/readiness probes drive restarts and traffic routing.

apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata: { name: orders }
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: orders } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: orders } }
    spec:
      containers:
        - name: orders
          image: europe-docker.pkg.dev/proj/repo/orders:1.4.2
          ports: [{ containerPort: 8080 }]
          readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }

Networks, Restart Policies and Lifecycle

Network driverBehaviourUse
bridge (default)Private network on one host; user-defined bridges give DNS by container nameLocal apps, Compose
hostShares the host's network stack; no port mappingMax network performance (Linux only)
noneNo networkingIsolated batch jobs
overlaySpans several hostsSwarm; Kubernetes uses CNI plugins instead

Restart policies: no (default), on-failure[:N], always, unless-stopped. Lifecycle: created → running → paused/stopped → removed. docker stop sends SIGTERM, waits (10 s by default) then SIGKILL; docker kill sends SIGKILL immediately. Exit codes: 0 normal, 1 app error, 137 = 128 + 9 (SIGKILL, often OOM-killed — check docker inspect --format '{{.State.OOMKilled}}'), 143 = 128 + 15 (SIGTERM).

Faster Builds: BuildKit, Multi-arch, Jib

# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
FROM maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY pom.xml .
COPY src ./src
# cache ~/.m2 between builds without baking it into a layer
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 mvn -B -q package -DskipTests

FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre
COPY --from=build /src/target/*.jar /app/app.jar
USER 1000
ENTRYPOINT ["java","-jar","/app/app.jar"]
  • Multi-arch: docker buildx build --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 -t repo/app:1.0 --push . builds one tag that works on Intel servers and Apple Silicon / ARM cloud machines.
  • Jib (Maven/Gradle plugin) builds an optimised, layered Java image with no Dockerfile and no Docker daemon; Cloud Native Buildpacks (spring-boot:build-image) do similar. Good for standardising images across many services.
  • Ecosystem: images follow the OCI spec; Docker Engine uses containerd + runc underneath; Kubernetes talks to containerd/CRI-O directly; Podman is a daemonless, rootless-friendly Docker-compatible CLI.

Kubernetes Essentials Beyond Pods

resources:
  requests: { cpu: "250m", memory: "512Mi" }   # used for scheduling
  limits:   { memory: "768Mi" }                # exceed it -> OOMKilled
readinessProbe: { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/readiness, port: 8080 } }
livenessProbe:  { httpGet: { path: /actuator/health/liveness,  port: 8080 } }
  • Requests reserve capacity for scheduling; limits cap usage (memory over the limit is killed, CPU over the limit is throttled). Set JVM heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 so heap + metaspace + threads fit inside the memory limit.
  • HPA scales replicas on CPU/memory or custom metrics; rolling update (maxSurge, maxUnavailable) replaces pods gradually and kubectl rollout undo rolls back.
  • ConfigMap = non-secret config, Secret = base64-encoded (not encrypted by default) sensitive values; StatefulSet for databases needing stable identity and storage; Job/CronJob for batch work.

Interview Questions — Docker & Containers

What is the difference between a container and a virtual machine?

A VM runs a full guest OS on a hypervisor and virtualises hardware, so it is heavy and slow to boot but strongly isolated. A container is an isolated process sharing the host kernel, using namespaces for isolation and cgroups for resource limits. Containers are lightweight, start in seconds and pack densely, but isolation is weaker because the kernel is shared.

What is the difference between an image and a container?

An image is an immutable, layered template containing the filesystem and metadata (entrypoint, env, ports). A container is a running instance of an image with its own writable layer, network and process space. You can start many containers from one image; changes inside a container are lost when it is removed unless stored in a volume.

CMD vs ENTRYPOINT?

ENTRYPOINT defines the executable that always runs; CMD provides default arguments (or a default command if no entrypoint). Arguments passed to docker run image args replace CMD but are appended to ENTRYPOINT; you override the entrypoint only with --entrypoint. Use the exec (JSON array) form so the process is PID 1 and receives SIGTERM for graceful shutdown.

💡 Shell form (CMD java -jar app.jar) wraps the process in /bin/sh -c, which may not forward signals.

COPY vs ADD? RUN vs CMD?

COPY just copies files from the build context; ADD additionally auto-extracts local tar archives and can download URLs, so prefer COPY for predictability. RUN executes at build time and creates a layer (e.g. installing packages); CMD is the default command executed at container start.

How does Docker layer caching work and how do you optimise it?

Each instruction produces a layer; if the instruction and its inputs (files copied, command text) are unchanged, the cached layer is reused, but a change invalidates all subsequent layers. Copy dependency manifests first (pom.xml, package*.json), install dependencies, then copy source code. Add a .dockerignore and combine related RUN commands with cleanup in one step.

What is a multi-stage build and why use it?

A Dockerfile with several FROM stages: earlier stages build the artifact using a full toolchain (Maven + JDK, Node), and the final stage copies only the result (COPY --from=build) onto a slim runtime image. The result is a much smaller image without compilers or source code, which is faster to pull and has fewer vulnerabilities.

How would you containerise an Angular application?

Use a Node stage to run npm ci and ng build, then copy the dist output into an nginx:alpine image. Configure nginx with try_files $uri $uri/ /index.html so client-side routes work on refresh, and add caching headers for hashed assets. Runtime API URLs can be injected via a config JSON loaded at startup or env substitution in nginx templates, since the build output is static.

Volume vs bind mount?

A named volume is managed by Docker under its own storage area, portable across hosts and ideal for database data. A bind mount maps a specific host path into the container; it depends on the host's directory structure and is mainly used in development (live source code, config files). Both survive container removal; data in the container's writable layer does not.

How do containers in Docker Compose talk to each other?

Compose creates a user-defined bridge network for the project, and each service is reachable by its service name via Docker's internal DNS. So the Spring Boot app connects to jdbc:mysql://db:3306/appdb, not localhost – inside a container localhost is the container itself. Port publishing (ports:) is only needed for access from the host.

depends_on doesn't wait for MySQL to be ready. How do you fix it?

Plain depends_on only controls start order. Add a healthcheck to the DB service (e.g. mysqladmin ping) and use depends_on: db: condition: service_healthy. The application should still retry connections (HikariCP/Spring retries, or a startup retry) because in production dependencies can restart at any time.

How do you handle secrets with Docker?

Never put secrets in the Dockerfile via ENV, ARG or copied files – they persist in image layers and history. Inject them at runtime: env vars from an untracked .env for local dev, Docker/Compose secrets mounted under /run/secrets, Kubernetes Secrets, or a cloud secret manager. For build-time credentials (private npm/Maven repos) use BuildKit --mount=type=secret.

A container keeps restarting. How do you debug it?

Check docker ps -a for the exit code and docker logs for the stack trace. docker inspect shows the health status, env and mounts; exit code 137 points to OOM kill, 1 to an application error. Start the image with --entrypoint sh to inspect files and config interactively, or docker exec into it if it stays up long enough.

How do you reduce image size and improve security?

Use multi-stage builds and minimal bases (JRE-only, alpine or distroless), clean package caches in the same RUN, and use .dockerignore. For security: run as non-root with USER, pin image versions, scan with Trivy or Docker Scout, avoid secrets in layers, drop Linux capabilities and use read-only filesystems where possible, and rebuild regularly to pick up base-image patches.

How does the JVM behave inside a container?

Since JDK 10 (backported to 8u191) the JVM is container-aware: it reads cgroup memory and CPU limits rather than host values. By default the max heap is 25% of the container limit, so set -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75 or similar. Leave headroom for metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers, otherwise the kernel OOM-kills the container (exit 137).

What does EXPOSE do? Is it required to publish a port?

EXPOSE is documentation/metadata of the port the application listens on; it does not open anything on the host. Publishing is done at run time with -p hostPort:containerPort (or -P to publish all exposed ports to random host ports). Containers on the same network can reach each other's ports regardless of EXPOSE.

Explain Pod, Deployment and Service in Kubernetes.

A Pod is one or more tightly coupled containers sharing an IP and volumes – the unit Kubernetes schedules. A Deployment manages a ReplicaSet to keep N identical pods running and performs rolling updates and rollbacks. A Service provides a stable virtual IP and DNS name that load-balances across pods selected by labels, since pod IPs change as pods are recreated.

Docker Compose vs Kubernetes?

Compose runs a multi-container app on a single host and is ideal for local development, testing and small deployments. Kubernetes is a cluster orchestrator offering self-healing, horizontal scaling, rolling deployments, service discovery, config/secret management and multi-node scheduling. Many teams use Compose (or Testcontainers) locally and Kubernetes (e.g. GKE) or a serverless container platform (Cloud Run) in production.

How do you tag and push an image to a registry?

Build with a meaningful tag, authenticate, then push:

docker build -t orders:1.4.2 .
docker tag orders:1.4.2 europe-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/orders:1.4.2
gcloud auth configure-docker europe-docker.pkg.dev
docker push europe-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/orders:1.4.2

💡 Use immutable tags (version or git SHA) for deployments; latest makes rollbacks and auditing unreliable.

A container exits with code 137. What does it mean?

137 = 128 + 9, so the process received SIGKILL. The most common cause is the out-of-memory killer: the container exceeded its memory limit (docker inspect shows OOMKilled: true; Kubernetes shows reason OOMKilled). For a JVM, check that heap (MaxRAMPercentage) plus metaspace, thread stacks and direct buffers fit the limit. Another cause is docker stop timing out because the app ignored SIGTERM — 143 means it exited on SIGTERM.

docker stop vs docker kill? How do you get graceful shutdown in Spring Boot?

stop sends SIGTERM and, after a grace period (10 s default, -t to change), SIGKILL; kill sends SIGKILL at once. For graceful shutdown the Java process must be PID 1 or receive the signal (exec-form ENTRYPOINT, or --init/tini), and Spring Boot should finish in-flight requests: server.shutdown=graceful with spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase. In Kubernetes, make the grace period (terminationGracePeriodSeconds) longer than the Spring timeout.

What Docker network drivers exist, and how do containers find each other?

bridge (default, single host), host (share the host's network), none, overlay (multi-host) and macvlan. On a user-defined bridge network — which Compose creates automatically — Docker's embedded DNS resolves container/service names, so the app connects to jdbc:mysql://db:3306. The default bridge network has no name resolution. Inside a container, localhost is the container itself, not the host.

What restart policies does Docker support?

no (default), on-failure[:max-retries] (restart only on non-zero exit), always (also restarts when the daemon starts, even after a manual stop) and unless-stopped (like always, but respects a manual stop). In Compose: restart: unless-stopped. In Kubernetes, restarts are handled by the pod's restartPolicy and the controller, with CrashLoopBackOff delays.

How do you use Docker in integration tests for a Spring Boot app?

Use Testcontainers: the test starts real MySQL, Kafka or Redis containers, and Spring Boot 3.1+ wires them with @ServiceConnection, so no manual URL properties are needed. Containers are thrown away after the run, so tests are repeatable and match production engines better than H2. In CI the agent needs Docker access; reuse containers across test classes (a shared static container) to keep runs fast.

@Testcontainers @SpringBootTest
class OrderRepoIT {
  @Container @ServiceConnection
  static MySQLContainer<?> db = new MySQLContainer<>("mysql:8.4");
}
Docker vs containerd vs Podman vs OCI?

OCI is the open standard for image format and runtime, so any compliant tool can run any compliant image. containerd is the runtime daemon that manages containers (with runc doing the low-level work); Docker Engine is built on it, and Kubernetes uses containerd or CRI-O directly (dockershim was removed in 1.24). Podman is a daemonless, rootless-friendly CLI compatible with most docker commands. An image built with Docker runs fine on all of them.

How do you build images for both x86 and ARM?

Use docker buildx with --platform linux/amd64,linux/arm64 and push; the registry stores a multi-platform manifest list and each machine pulls the matching variant. Base images must exist for both architectures (official Temurin, Node and nginx images do). Emulation (QEMU) makes cross-builds slow, so CI often uses native ARM runners. This matters for developers on Apple Silicon and for cheaper ARM cloud instances.

Kubernetes requests vs limits — and why does it matter for Java?

Requests are what the scheduler reserves on a node; limits are the maximum. Exceeding the memory limit kills the pod (OOMKilled); exceeding the CPU limit throttles it, which can slow JVM startup and GC. For Java, set memory request = limit for predictability, size the heap with -XX:MaxRAMPercentage (around 70–75%) to leave room for non-heap memory, and be careful with tight CPU limits on latency-sensitive services.

What is Jib and when would you use it instead of a Dockerfile?

Jib is a Maven/Gradle plugin from Google that builds an OCI image directly from the build, without a Dockerfile or Docker daemon. It separates dependencies, resources and classes into layers automatically, so code changes rebuild only a small layer, and builds are reproducible. Use it to standardise images across many Java services or in CI agents without Docker; use a Dockerfile when you need OS packages or custom setup. Spring Boot's build-image (Buildpacks) is a similar no-Dockerfile option.

Google Cloud (GCP) Deploy & run

Google Cloud Platform provides managed compute, databases, storage and DevOps tooling. For a full stack developer the key path is: build a Docker image, push it to Artifact Registry, run it on Cloud Run or a VM, and connect it to Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage and Secret Manager with a least-privilege service account.

# Build, push and deploy a Dockerized Spring Boot app to Cloud Run
gcloud config set project my-project
gcloud artifacts repositories create apps --repository-format=docker --location=asia-south1

gcloud builds submit --tag asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/apps/orders:1.0.0

gcloud run deploy orders \
  --image asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-project/apps/orders:1.0.0 \
  --region asia-south1 \
  --service-account orders-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com \
  --add-cloudsql-instances my-project:asia-south1:orders-db \
  --set-env-vars SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  --set-secrets DB_PASSWORD=orders-db-password:latest \
  --min-instances 0 --max-instances 10 --memory 1Gi \
  --allow-unauthenticated

Projects, Regions & Zones

Everything in GCP lives in a project – the unit of billing, IAM, APIs and quotas – identified by a globally unique project ID. Projects can be grouped into folders under an organization. Resources are global (VPC networks, global load balancers), regional (Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, regional buckets, e.g. asia-south1 Mumbai) or zonal (Compute Engine VMs, persistent disks, e.g. asia-south1-a). Spread across zones for high availability and across regions for disaster recovery; pick regions close to users and for data-residency rules. APIs must be enabled per project: gcloud services enable run.googleapis.com sqladmin.googleapis.com.

IAM & Service Accounts

IAM answers who (principal: user, group, service account) can do what (role = collection of permissions) on which resource. Roles are basic (Owner/Editor/Viewer – too broad for production), predefined (e.g. roles/cloudsql.client, roles/storage.objectViewer) or custom. Policies are inherited down the hierarchy (org → folder → project → resource).

A service account is an identity for workloads. Give each service its own SA with only the roles it needs (least privilege). Code running on GCP uses Application Default Credentials to get tokens from the metadata server, so you never ship a JSON key. Avoid downloadable SA keys; for CI outside GCP (e.g. GitHub Actions) use Workload Identity Federation.

gcloud iam service-accounts create orders-sa --display-name="Orders service"
gcloud projects add-iam-policy-binding my-project \
  --member="serviceAccount:orders-sa@my-project.iam.gserviceaccount.com" \
  --role="roles/cloudsql.client"

Compute Options: Compute Engine, Cloud Run, GKE, App Engine

  • Compute Engine – IaaS virtual machines. Full OS control; you manage patching, scaling (Managed Instance Groups + autoscaler) and deployment. Good for legacy apps, a classic LAMP/PHP stack, or software needing a specific OS setup. Supports Spot VMs for cheap interruptible workloads.
  • Cloud Run – serverless containers. Deploy any stateless container that listens on $PORT; Google handles HTTPS, autoscaling (including to zero) and load balancing. Billed per use. Usually the first choice for Spring Boot APIs and PHP apps in containers. Cloud Run jobs run batch tasks to completion.
  • GKE – managed Kubernetes. Autopilot mode manages nodes for you; Standard gives full node control. Choose it for many microservices, complex networking, or when the team already uses Kubernetes.
  • App Engine – older PaaS: Standard (language runtimes, scale to zero) and Flexible (containers on VMs). Still supported, but Google now steers new workloads toward Cloud Run.
  • Cloud Run functions (formerly Cloud Functions) – event-driven single-purpose functions.

Cloud SQL, Cloud Storage & Artifact Registry

Cloud SQL is managed MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQL Server: automated backups, point-in-time recovery, patching, read replicas and a high-availability option with a standby in another zone. Connect securely using the Cloud SQL Auth Proxy / language connectors (IAM-authorised, encrypted, no IP allow-listing) or via private IP in your VPC.

# Spring Boot with the Cloud SQL Java connector (MySQL)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:mysql:///ordersdb?cloudSqlInstance=my-project:asia-south1:orders-db&socketFactory=com.google.cloud.sql.mysql.SocketFactory
spring.datasource.username=orders
spring.datasource.password=${DB_PASSWORD}

Cloud Storage holds objects (files) in buckets with globally unique names. Storage classes: Standard, Nearline (≈monthly access), Coldline (≈quarterly), Archive (≈yearly); lifecycle rules move or delete objects automatically. Use uniform bucket-level access with IAM and signed URLs to let browsers upload/download privately without exposing credentials.

Artifact Registry stores Docker images and Maven, npm and other packages (it replaced Container Registry). Image paths look like REGION-docker.pkg.dev/PROJECT/REPO/IMAGE:TAG.

Cloud Build & CI/CD

Cloud Build runs build steps in containers, triggered manually or by pushes to GitHub/GitLab/Bitbucket. A cloudbuild.yaml lists steps; each step is a container image. A typical pipeline: run tests, build the image, push to Artifact Registry, deploy to Cloud Run. Cloud Deploy adds promotion across dev/staging/prod.

# cloudbuild.yaml
steps:
  - name: maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21
    entrypoint: mvn
    args: ["-q", "verify"]
  - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker
    args: ["build", "-t", "asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/apps/orders:$SHORT_SHA", "."]
  - name: gcr.io/cloud-builders/docker
    args: ["push", "asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/apps/orders:$SHORT_SHA"]
  - name: gcr.io/google.com/cloudsdktool/cloud-sdk
    entrypoint: gcloud
    args: ["run", "deploy", "orders", "--region=asia-south1",
           "--image=asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/$PROJECT_ID/apps/orders:$SHORT_SHA"]

Networking & Firewall Basics

A VPC network is global; its subnets are regional with their own IP ranges. Firewall rules (or newer firewall policies) are stateful and apply to VMs by network tag or service account; by default ingress is denied and egress allowed (the default network adds some permissive rules you should review). Expose web apps through a Cloud Load Balancer (global HTTPS LB with managed certificates, Cloud CDN and Cloud Armor WAF). VMs without external IPs reach the internet through Cloud NAT. Cloud Run reaches private resources (private-IP Cloud SQL, Memorystore) via Direct VPC egress or a Serverless VPC Access connector.

gcloud compute firewall-rules create allow-http \
  --network=default --allow=tcp:80,tcp:443 \
  --target-tags=web --source-ranges=0.0.0.0/0

Cloud Logging, Monitoring & Secret Manager

Cloud Logging automatically captures stdout/stderr from Cloud Run, GKE and App Engine (VMs need the Ops Agent). Write structured JSON logs (fields like severity, message, logging.googleapis.com/trace) so you can filter in Logs Explorer and correlate with traces. Logs can be routed by sinks to BigQuery, Cloud Storage or Pub/Sub, and log-based metrics can drive alerts.

Cloud Monitoring provides metrics dashboards (CPU, latency, request count, instance count), uptime checks and alerting policies (email, Slack, PagerDuty). Cloud Trace and Error Reporting complement it.

Secret Manager stores versioned secrets (DB passwords, API keys) with IAM-controlled access (roles/secretmanager.secretAccessor) and audit logs. Cloud Run can mount a secret as an env var or file; Spring Cloud GCP can read ${sm@secret-name} directly.

echo -n "s3cr3t" | gcloud secrets create orders-db-password --data-file=-
gcloud logging read 'resource.type="cloud_run_revision" AND severity>=ERROR' --limit=20

Deploying Spring Boot or PHP, Scaling & Cost

Spring Boot on Cloud Run: make the app listen on server.port=${PORT:8080}, build the image (Dockerfile, Jib or Buildpacks), push to Artifact Registry, deploy with a dedicated service account, Cloud SQL connection and secrets. Since instances can start on demand, reduce cold starts with --min-instances 1, startup CPU boost, lazy initialisation, or AOT/GraalVM native images. Keep the service stateless – store sessions and files in a database, Memorystore or Cloud Storage.

PHP app: either containerise it (php-fpm + nginx, or php:8.3-apache) and deploy to Cloud Run, or run a classic LAMP stack on a Compute Engine VM with a firewall rule for 80/443 and Cloud SQL for MySQL.

Scaling: Cloud Run scales on concurrent requests (default concurrency up to 80 per instance, configurable) between min and max instances; MIGs scale VMs on CPU or load; GKE uses HPA and cluster autoscaler. Cost basics: use the pricing calculator, set budgets and alerts, scale to zero for low-traffic services, right-size VMs and SQL instances, use committed-use or sustained-use discounts, Spot VMs for batch, lifecycle rules for storage, and watch egress charges and idle resources.

Pub/Sub and Background Work

Pub/Sub is GCP's managed messaging service: publishers send to a topic, each subscription gets its own copy (fan-out), and subscribers receive messages by pull or push (HTTP POST to e.g. a Cloud Run URL). Delivery is at-least-once, so consumers must be idempotent; it supports ordering keys, dead-letter topics, retry policies and (optionally) exactly-once delivery for pull subscriptions.

NeedService
Decouple services, fan-out eventsPub/Sub
Run a task at a fixed time (cron)Cloud Scheduler → HTTP endpoint, Pub/Sub or a Cloud Run job
Queue individual HTTP tasks with rate limits and retriesCloud Tasks
Run a container to completion (batch, migration, report)Cloud Run jobs
React to events (file uploaded to GCS, audit log entry)Eventarc → Cloud Run / Cloud Run functions

Choosing a Database on GCP

ServiceTypePick it for
Cloud SQLManaged MySQL / PostgreSQL / SQL ServerTypical Spring Boot / PHP app, regional, up to large single-instance sizes
AlloyDBPostgreSQL-compatible, high performanceHeavier Postgres workloads and analytics on operational data
SpannerDistributed SQL, strong consistencyGlobal scale, horizontal writes, very high availability
FirestoreServerless document NoSQLMobile/web apps, real-time sync, flexible schema
BigtableWide-column NoSQLHuge time-series / IoT throughput
BigQueryServerless data warehouseAnalytics and reporting with SQL, not OLTP
MemorystoreManaged Redis / Valkey / MemcachedCaching, sessions, rate limiting

Cloud SQL reliability: enable HA (a standby in another zone with automatic failover), automated backups + point-in-time recovery, and read replicas for read scaling. Connect over private IP or the Cloud SQL connectors / Auth Proxy.

Resource Hierarchy and Infrastructure as Code

  • Organization → Folders → Projects → Resources. IAM policies are inherited downward (a role granted on a folder applies to every project in it); Organization Policies set guardrails such as allowed regions or "no service-account keys".
  • Typical layout: one project per environment per system (app-dev, app-prod) for isolation of IAM, quotas and billing.
  • Terraform (with the Google provider; state in a GCS bucket) is the common way to create projects, networks, Cloud SQL, Cloud Run services and IAM bindings reproducibly and reviewed in PRs. Avoid manual console changes in production — they cause drift.
resource "google_cloud_run_v2_service" "api" {
  name     = "orders-api"
  location = "asia-south1"
  template {
    service_account = google_service_account.api.email
    containers { image = "asia-south1-docker.pkg.dev/my-proj/apps/orders:1.4.0" }
  }
}

Interview Questions — Google Cloud (GCP)

What is the difference between a region and a zone?

A region is a geographic location (e.g. asia-south1) containing several isolated zones (asia-south1-a/b/c), each an independent failure domain. Zonal resources such as VMs fail with their zone, so for HA you spread instances across zones (regional MIGs, Cloud SQL HA). Regional services like Cloud Run are already replicated across zones.

What is a service account and how should an app authenticate to GCP services?

A service account is a non-human identity for applications. Attach a dedicated SA to the Cloud Run service, VM or GKE workload (via Workload Identity) and grant it only needed roles. Client libraries use Application Default Credentials, fetching short-lived tokens from the metadata server – no key files in code or images. Use Workload Identity Federation for external CI instead of exported JSON keys.

Basic vs predefined vs custom IAM roles?

Basic roles (Owner, Editor, Viewer) apply across all services and are too broad for production. Predefined roles are curated per service by Google, e.g. roles/run.invoker or roles/cloudsql.client. Custom roles bundle exactly the permissions you choose when predefined roles are too wide. Follow least privilege and grant roles to groups or SAs, not individuals.

Cloud Run vs Compute Engine vs GKE vs App Engine – when to choose which?

Cloud Run: stateless containerised HTTP services or jobs, minimal ops, scale to zero – the default for most APIs. GKE: many services needing Kubernetes features (custom networking, sidecars, stateful sets, fine-grained control). Compute Engine: full OS control, legacy or stateful software, special hardware (GPUs). App Engine: legacy PaaS apps; new projects generally use Cloud Run.

What are Cloud Run's requirements and limitations?

The container must listen on the port given by the PORT env var (default 8080), be stateless, and handle requests within the configured timeout (up to 60 minutes). The filesystem is in-memory and ephemeral, instances can be stopped anytime, and with request-based billing CPU is only guaranteed while handling requests (instance-based billing keeps it allocated for background work). Cold starts matter for JVM apps.

💡 Use --min-instances and startup CPU boost for latency-sensitive Spring Boot services.

How do you connect a Cloud Run Spring Boot service to Cloud SQL securely?

Grant the service account roles/cloudsql.client, add the instance with --add-cloudsql-instances and use the Cloud SQL Java connector (socket factory) or Unix socket, which authenticate via IAM and encrypt traffic. Alternatively, use private IP with Direct VPC egress. Store the DB password in Secret Manager or use IAM database authentication to avoid passwords entirely.

How do you store secrets on GCP?

Use Secret Manager: secrets are versioned, encrypted, access-controlled with IAM and audited. Inject them into Cloud Run as env vars or mounted files (--set-secrets), read them with client libraries, or via Spring Cloud GCP. Avoid plain env vars in deploy scripts, secrets in Git, or secrets baked into images.

What is Artifact Registry and how does it relate to Container Registry?

Artifact Registry is GCP's managed repository for container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, etc.) with regional repos, IAM and vulnerability scanning. It is the successor to Container Registry (gcr.io), which has been deprecated. Authenticate Docker with gcloud auth configure-docker REGION-docker.pkg.dev.

Explain Cloud Storage classes and how to give users temporary access to a private file.

Standard for frequently accessed data; Nearline, Coldline and Archive for data accessed roughly monthly, quarterly or yearly – cheaper storage but retrieval fees and minimum durations. Lifecycle rules can transition or delete objects. For temporary private access generate a signed URL from the backend with an expiry, so the browser uploads/downloads directly without credentials or making the bucket public.

How would you set up CI/CD for a Spring Boot app on GCP?

Create a Cloud Build trigger on pushes to main that runs tests, builds the image tagged with the commit SHA, pushes it to Artifact Registry and runs gcloud run deploy. Use a dedicated build service account with minimal roles. For multiple environments use Cloud Deploy or separate triggers, and Cloud Run traffic splitting for canary releases and fast rollback to a previous revision.

How do firewall rules work in a GCP VPC?

Firewall rules are defined at the VPC level, are stateful (return traffic allowed automatically), and target instances by network tag, service account or all instances. Implied rules deny all ingress and allow all egress; you add allow rules such as tcp:443 from 0.0.0.0/0 for web tags, and restrict SSH to IAP's range (35.235.240.0/20) instead of the whole internet.

How do you view logs and set up alerts for a Cloud Run service?

Stdout/stderr go to Cloud Logging automatically; filter in Logs Explorer by resource.type="cloud_run_revision" and severity, ideally using structured JSON logs. In Cloud Monitoring create alerting policies on metrics like 5xx rate, request latency or instance count, or on log-based metrics, and route notifications to email/Slack. Uptime checks catch full outages.

How does Cloud Run scale?

Cloud Run adds instances based on incoming concurrent requests and CPU, up to --max-instances, and scales down to --min-instances (zero by default). Each instance handles up to the configured concurrency (default 80, max 1000). Set max instances to protect downstream resources like the Cloud SQL connection limit, and size the HikariCP pool accordingly.

How would you deploy a PHP application on GCP?

The modern route is to containerise it (e.g. php:8.3-apache or nginx + php-fpm), push to Artifact Registry and deploy on Cloud Run, using Cloud SQL for MySQL and Cloud Storage for uploads since the container filesystem is ephemeral. Alternatively run a LAMP stack on a Compute Engine VM with firewall rules for HTTP/HTTPS and manage patching yourself. App Engine Standard also supports PHP runtimes.

How do you control GCP costs?

Set billing budgets with alerts, label resources by team/environment, and review billing reports (or export to BigQuery). Use scale-to-zero services, right-size VMs and databases (Recommender suggestions), committed-use discounts for steady workloads, Spot VMs for batch, storage lifecycle rules, and delete idle disks, IPs and snapshots. Watch network egress, which is often an overlooked cost.

Give some common gcloud commands.
gcloud auth login
gcloud config set project my-project
gcloud compute instances list
gcloud compute ssh my-vm --zone asia-south1-a --tunnel-through-iap
gcloud run services list --region asia-south1
gcloud run services logs read orders --region asia-south1
gcloud sql connect orders-db --user=root
gcloud storage cp report.pdf gs://my-bucket/reports/

💡 gcloud storage is the newer, faster replacement for gsutil.

What is Pub/Sub and how does it compare to Kafka?

Pub/Sub is a fully managed, serverless messaging service: topics, subscriptions (each gets every message), pull or push delivery, at-least-once by default, with dead-letter topics and ordering keys. Kafka is a distributed log you run (or buy managed) with partitions, consumer groups, long retention and replay by offset. Pub/Sub needs no capacity planning and suits event-driven GCP apps; Kafka gives more control over ordering, retention and stream processing. GCP also offers Managed Service for Apache Kafka if you need Kafka APIs.

How do you run scheduled or background jobs on GCP?

For cron, Cloud Scheduler calls an HTTP endpoint, publishes to Pub/Sub or starts a Cloud Run job (a container that runs to completion, with retries and parallel tasks). For per-item async work with rate limiting, enqueue tasks in Cloud Tasks. For reacting to events like a file landing in Cloud Storage, use Eventarc to trigger a Cloud Run service. Avoid long work inside a normal Cloud Run request — requests have a timeout and CPU may be throttled outside requests unless "CPU always allocated" is set.

Cloud SQL vs Firestore vs Spanner vs BigQuery — how do you choose?

Relational, transactional, regional app with JPA → Cloud SQL. Global scale with horizontal writes and strong consistency → Spanner. Document data, mobile/web clients, real-time listeners → Firestore. Analytics over large datasets with SQL → BigQuery (not for OLTP). Add Memorystore for caching. 💡 Start with Cloud SQL for most Spring Boot apps; justify anything else by a specific requirement.

How do you make Cloud SQL highly available and recoverable?

Enable the HA configuration: a synchronous standby in another zone with automatic failover (a short outage of seconds to a minute; apps need connection retry, which HikariCP plus retries handles). Turn on automated backups and point-in-time recovery (binary logs / WAL), test restores regularly, and add read replicas (also cross-region) for read scaling or disaster recovery. Use maintenance windows and deny periods to control upgrades.

How does Cloud Run handle deployments and rollbacks?

Each deploy creates an immutable revision. Traffic can be split between revisions by percentage, so you can canary (--no-traffic deploy, then gcloud run services update-traffic --to-revisions=rev2=10), use tagged revision URLs for testing, and roll back instantly by sending 100% back to the previous revision. Revisions also capture env vars, secrets and scaling settings, so config changes are versioned too.

Explain the GCP resource hierarchy and IAM inheritance.

Organization → folders → projects → resources. IAM policies set at a higher level are inherited by everything below and the effective policy is the union, so a broad grant at the folder level cannot be removed at the project level (deny policies are the exception). Organization Policies add constraints like allowed locations or disabling service-account key creation. Billing is linked at the project level, and projects are the main boundary for isolation between environments.

Why use Terraform for GCP instead of the console or gcloud scripts?

Terraform is declarative: you describe the desired state and it computes a plan of changes, which can be reviewed in a PR and applied by CI. State (stored remotely in a GCS bucket with locking) lets it detect drift and manage dependencies between resources. It makes environments reproducible (dev and prod from the same modules) and auditable. Console clicks are fine for exploration, but not for production infrastructure.

How does a GitHub Actions or Jenkins pipeline deploy to GCP without a service-account key file?

Use Workload Identity Federation: GCP trusts the CI system's OIDC token (for example GitHub's), exchanges it for short-lived credentials, and lets the pipeline impersonate a deploy service account with only the roles it needs (Artifact Registry Writer, Cloud Run Developer, Service Account User). No long-lived JSON key exists to leak or rotate. On GKE, Workload Identity does the same for pods.

Sentry & Error Monitoring Observability

Sentry captures exceptions and performance traces from back ends and front ends, groups them into issues with stack traces, breadcrumbs and user context, and alerts the team. It is one piece of observability alongside logs (e.g. Splunk, ELK, Cloud Logging) and metrics.

# Spring Boot 3 – pom.xml: io.sentry:sentry-spring-boot-starter-jakarta
# application.yml
sentry:
  dsn: ${SENTRY_DSN}
  environment: ${APP_ENV:dev}
  release: orders-service@1.4.2
  traces-sample-rate: 0.1          # 10% of transactions traced
  send-default-pii: false

// Manual capture with extra context
try {
    paymentClient.charge(order);
} catch (PaymentException ex) {
    Sentry.withScope(scope -> {
        scope.setTag("payment.provider", "stripe");
        scope.setContexts("order", Map.of("id", order.getId(), "amount", order.getTotal()));
        Sentry.captureException(ex);
    });
    throw ex;
}

What Sentry Does

  • Error monitoring – captures unhandled (and manually reported) exceptions with stack trace, local context, request data, device/browser info and the events leading up to the error.
  • Issue grouping – similar events are fingerprinted into one issue, showing count, affected users, first/last seen, and regression status.
  • Performance / tracing – records transactions and spans (HTTP requests, DB queries, external calls) for latency analysis and distributed traces across services.
  • Releases – ties errors to a deployed version and commits, showing which release introduced or resolved an issue ("suspect commits").
  • Extras: Session Replay for front ends, profiling, cron monitoring, uptime checks, user feedback widget.

Sentry is available as SaaS (sentry.io) or self-hosted.

DSN & SDK Setup (Java, Angular, PHP)

The DSN (Data Source Name) is a per-project URL telling the SDK where to send events, e.g. https://publicKey@o123.ingest.sentry.io/456. It only allows sending events, so it is not a secret in the browser, but keep it in config/env vars rather than hard-coding. Spring Boot's starter auto-registers an exception resolver and integrates with Logback/Log4j2 so ERROR logs become events.

// Angular (standalone) – main.ts with @sentry/angular
import * as Sentry from "@sentry/angular";

Sentry.init({
  dsn: environment.sentryDsn,
  environment: environment.name,
  release: "web-app@1.4.2",
  integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration(), Sentry.replayIntegration()],
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  tracePropagationTargets: ["localhost", /^https:\/\/api\.example\.com/],
  replaysSessionSampleRate: 0.0,
  replaysOnErrorSampleRate: 1.0,
});

// app.config.ts providers
{ provide: ErrorHandler, useValue: Sentry.createErrorHandler() },
{ provide: Sentry.TraceService, deps: [Router] },
// PHP (composer require sentry/sentry) – Laravel/Symfony have dedicated packages
\Sentry\init([
    'dsn' => getenv('SENTRY_DSN'),
    'environment' => 'production',
    'release' => 'portal@2.3.0',
    'traces_sample_rate' => 0.1,
]);
try { $service->run(); } catch (\Throwable $e) { \Sentry\captureException($e); }

Breadcrumbs, Context, Tags & User

Breadcrumbs are a trail of events before the error: HTTP calls, navigation, console logs, clicks, log statements. SDKs record many automatically; add your own for business steps. Tags are indexed key/value pairs you can search and filter on (tenant, payment.provider). Contexts/extra data are structured, non-indexed details. The user (id, email, ip) shows how many users an issue affects. Scopes hold this data; in Spring the request scope is isolated per request.

Sentry.addBreadcrumb("Checkout started for cart " + cartId, "checkout");
Sentry.setTag("tenant", tenantId);
User user = new User();
user.setId(String.valueOf(currentUser.getId()));   // prefer an ID over email
Sentry.setUser(user);

Environments, Releases & Source Maps

Set environment (dev, staging, production) so you can filter and route alerts. Set release to a version or git SHA and create the release in CI with sentry-cli, associating commits and marking deploys; Sentry then flags regressions (a resolved issue that reappears in a new release).

Production Angular bundles are minified, so stack traces are unreadable without source maps. Generate them in the build ("sourceMap": true in angular.json for production, or hidden source maps), upload them to Sentry for the same release, and do not deploy the .map files publicly. Java needs no source maps, though ProGuard/R8-obfuscated Android builds need mapping files.

npx @sentry/wizard@latest -i sourcemaps          # one-time setup
sentry-cli releases new web-app@1.4.2
sentry-cli sourcemaps inject ./dist/web-app/browser
sentry-cli sourcemaps upload --release=web-app@1.4.2 ./dist/web-app/browser
sentry-cli releases finalize web-app@1.4.2

Sampling, Quotas & Noise Control

Errors are usually sent at 100% (sampleRate), while performance transactions are sampled (tracesSampleRate: 0.05–0.2 in production) because they are high volume and count against quota. tracesSampler lets you sample dynamically, e.g. drop health checks and keep 100% of checkout. Reduce noise with ignoreErrors/ignoreExceptions, beforeSend filtering, inbound filters (browser extensions, legacy browsers), and spike protection / rate limits on the project.

Alerts & Issue Grouping

Sentry groups events by a fingerprint computed mainly from the stack trace (in-app frames), falling back to exception type and message. Bad grouping happens when messages contain dynamic values or stack traces differ; fix it with custom fingerprints in the SDK or server-side fingerprint/stack-trace rules, and merge duplicate issues in the UI.

  • Issue alerts – trigger on a new issue, a regression, or an issue seen more than N times / by N users in a time window.
  • Metric alerts – trigger on aggregates such as error rate, p95 latency, failure rate or Apdex crossing a threshold.
  • Route to email, Slack, Teams, PagerDuty or Jira; assign owners via ownership rules / code owners.
Sentry.init({ /* ... */,
  beforeSend(event, hint) {
    if (hint.originalException instanceof HttpErrorResponse && hint.originalException.status === 401) return null;
    event.fingerprint = ["{{ default }}", event.tags?.["tenant"] ?? "none"];
    return event;
  }
});

PII Scrubbing & Privacy

Error events can contain request bodies, headers, cookies, query strings and user data. Keep sendDefaultPii off unless needed, avoid putting personal or health data into messages, tags or breadcrumbs, and scrub in beforeSend/beforeBreadcrumb. On the server, enable Data Scrubbing (default scrubbing of passwords, tokens, credit cards) and Advanced Data Scrubbing rules, plus "prevent storing IP addresses". Session Replay masks all text and inputs by default. For regulated data (GDPR, HIPAA) consider data residency (EU region), retention settings, a data processing agreement, or self-hosting.

Observability: Logs, Metrics, Traces & Correlation IDs

The three pillars of observability:

  • Logs – timestamped records of discrete events; rich detail, best for "what exactly happened" (Splunk, ELK/OpenSearch, Loki, Cloud Logging).
  • Metrics – numeric time series (request rate, error rate, latency percentiles, JVM heap); cheap to store, ideal for dashboards and alerts (Prometheus + Grafana, Micrometer, Cloud Monitoring).
  • Traces – the path of one request across services as a tree of spans with timings; best for finding where latency or failures happen (OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Zipkin, Sentry, Datadog).

Sentry vs Splunk vs APM: Sentry is developer-focused – exceptions with code context, grouping, releases, plus lightweight tracing. Splunk is a log search and analytics platform (SIEM, operational and security logs, SPL queries) – broader and better for compliance and ad-hoc investigation, but not focused on deduplicated errors. APM tools (Datadog, New Relic, Dynatrace, Elastic APM) focus on full-stack performance metrics, infrastructure and service maps. Teams often combine them.

A correlation ID (or trace ID) is generated at the edge and passed through every service (headers like W3C traceparent, X-Request-Id), logged in every log line via MDC, and attached to Sentry events, so one ID links logs, traces and errors for a single request. Micrometer Tracing in Spring Boot 3 propagates trace IDs and puts traceId/spanId in the MDC automatically.

@Component
public class CorrelationIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
    @Override
    protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest req, HttpServletResponse res, FilterChain chain)
            throws ServletException, IOException {
        String id = Optional.ofNullable(req.getHeader("X-Request-Id")).orElse(UUID.randomUUID().toString());
        MDC.put("requestId", id);
        Sentry.setTag("request_id", id);
        res.setHeader("X-Request-Id", id);
        try { chain.doFilter(req, res); } finally { MDC.remove("requestId"); }
    }
}
# logback pattern: %d %-5level [%X{requestId}] [%X{traceId}] %logger - %msg%n

SLIs, SLOs and Error Budgets

  • SLI (indicator): a measured ratio, e.g. "share of /api/orders requests that return non-5xx in under 500 ms".
  • SLO (objective): the target for the SLI over a window, e.g. 99.9% over 30 days. SLA is the contractual promise to customers, usually looser than the SLO, with penalties.
  • Error budget = 100% − SLO. At 99.9% over 30 days that is about 43 minutes of "bad" time. If the budget is being burned fast, slow down releases and fix reliability; if there is plenty left, ship faster.
  • Alert on burn rate (how fast the budget is being consumed) rather than on every single error — it cuts noise and catches real user impact.

Issue Triage Workflow and Alert Fatigue

  • Assign new issues automatically with ownership rules / code owners (by path, URL or tag), so every issue has an owner.
  • Resolve → "in next release" or "in commit": if the error reappears in a later release, Sentry reopens it as a regression.
  • Archive / ignore until a condition ("until it affects 100 users", "for 7 days") for known noise; use ignoreErrors / beforeSend or inbound filters for errors you never want (browser extensions, bots, legacy browsers).
  • Alert on new issues, regressions and spikes in users affected — not every event. Route to the owning team's channel; page only for production, high-impact alerts.
  • Review the top issues each sprint and link them to tickets; a dashboard of unresolved high-volume issues per team keeps quality visible.

Tracing Across Angular and Spring Boot

When the Angular SDK has tracing enabled, it adds sentry-trace and baggage headers (and can emit W3C traceparent) to outgoing requests that match tracePropagationTargets. The Spring Boot SDK continues the same trace, so one view shows the click, the HTTP call, the controller, the SQL queries and any error. Restrict targets to your own API domains — leaking trace headers to third parties can break their CORS.

Sentry.init({
  dsn: environment.sentryDsn,
  integrations: [Sentry.browserTracingIntegration()],
  tracesSampleRate: 0.1,
  tracePropagationTargets: [/^https:\/\/api\.example\.com/],
});

The backend's CORS config must allow the sentry-trace and baggage request headers.

Interview Questions — Sentry & Error Monitoring

What is Sentry and why use it instead of just logs?

Sentry is an error and performance monitoring platform. Instead of searching raw logs, it captures exceptions with full stack traces, request/user context and breadcrumbs, deduplicates them into issues, shows frequency and affected users, links them to releases and commits, and alerts the team. Logs are still needed for general event history; Sentry makes errors actionable.

What is a DSN? Is it safe to expose it in a front-end app?

The DSN is the project-specific endpoint and public key the SDK uses to send events. It only permits submitting events, not reading data, so it is acceptable in browser bundles – Sentry's own guidance treats it as public for client SDKs. Abuse (spam events) is mitigated with allowed domains, rate limits and inbound filters. Still keep it in environment config, not hard-coded.

How do you integrate Sentry with Spring Boot?

Add sentry-spring-boot-starter-jakarta (Spring Boot 3) and set sentry.dsn, environment, release and traces-sample-rate. It auto-captures unhandled exceptions from controllers, adds request data, and with the Logback integration turns ERROR logs into events and lower levels into breadcrumbs. Exceptions handled by your own @ControllerAdvice may need an explicit Sentry.captureException if you still want them reported.

How do you integrate Sentry with Angular?

Install @sentry/angular, call Sentry.init() in main.ts before bootstrapping, and provide Sentry.createErrorHandler() as Angular's ErrorHandler. Add browserTracingIntegration() and TraceService for route-change performance, and set tracePropagationTargets so trace headers flow to your API for distributed tracing. Upload source maps in CI so stack traces map back to TypeScript.

What are breadcrumbs?

Breadcrumbs are a chronological trail of events leading up to an error – navigation, clicks, XHR/fetch calls, console messages, log statements, DB queries. They are buffered in memory and only sent with an event, so they help reproduce what the user or service did before failing. You can add custom ones (Sentry.addBreadcrumb) and filter sensitive ones in beforeBreadcrumb.

Tags vs context vs extra data?

Tags are indexed and searchable key/value strings, used for filtering, grouping in the UI and alert conditions (keep cardinality reasonable). Contexts are structured objects shown on the event (order details, device info) but not indexed. User is a special context to count affected users. Use tags for things you'll filter by, context for detail you'll read.

Why are source maps important and how do you handle them securely?

Minified production JavaScript produces stack traces like main.3f2a.js:1:48213. Uploading source maps for the matching release lets Sentry de-minify traces to the original TypeScript file and line. Generate maps in CI, upload with sentry-cli or the bundler plugin, and remove them from the deployed assets (or use hidden source maps) so your source isn't publicly downloadable.

What are releases and environments used for?

environment separates dev/staging/prod events for filtering and alert routing. release tags events with the deployed version, enabling "first seen in release", regression detection, suspect commits, release health (crash-free sessions) and matching source maps. Set both from CI so they are consistent across back end and front end.

What is sampling and how do you choose rates?

Sampling sends only a fraction of events to control volume and cost. Errors are typically kept at 100%, while transactions are sampled (e.g. 5–20% in production, 100% in dev). Use tracesSampler to drop noise like health checks and keep critical flows at higher rates. Sampling decisions propagate in distributed traces so a trace is either complete or dropped.

How does Sentry group errors, and what if grouping is wrong?

Sentry fingerprints events primarily from in-app stack frames, otherwise from exception type and normalised message, and events with the same fingerprint form one issue. If unrelated errors merge or one error splits into many (e.g. dynamic IDs in messages), set a custom fingerprint in the SDK, add server-side fingerprint/stack-trace rules, or merge issues manually.

What kinds of alerts would you configure?

Issue alerts for new issues and regressions in production, and frequency alerts (e.g. more than 100 events or 50 users in an hour). Metric alerts on error rate, p95 transaction duration or failure rate of key endpoints. Route critical alerts to on-call (PagerDuty/Slack) and the rest to a channel or Jira, with ownership rules assigning issues to teams to avoid alert fatigue.

How do you prevent sensitive data (PII) from reaching Sentry?

Keep sendDefaultPii false, set only a user ID rather than email/name, and never put personal or medical data in exception messages or tags. Scrub fields in beforeSend and beforeBreadcrumb, enable server-side data scrubbing and advanced scrubbing rules, disable IP storage, and keep Session Replay masking on. For strict compliance, choose data residency, shorter retention, or self-hosted Sentry.

Sentry vs Splunk vs an APM tool like Datadog or New Relic?

Sentry is developer-centric error tracking with code-level context, grouping and release tracking plus tracing. Splunk is a log ingestion and search platform used for operations, security (SIEM) and analytics across all log data. APM tools cover performance metrics, infrastructure, service maps and traces at scale. They overlap but complement each other – e.g. Sentry for exceptions, Splunk for logs/audit, Prometheus/Grafana or an APM for metrics.

What are the three pillars of observability?

Logs (detailed discrete events), metrics (aggregated numeric time series for dashboards and alerts), and traces (end-to-end request paths across services as spans). Monitoring tells you that something is wrong; observability lets you ask why by correlating the three. OpenTelemetry is the vendor-neutral standard for producing all three.

What is a correlation ID and how do you implement it in Spring Boot?

A unique ID per request, created at the entry point (gateway or first service) or taken from an incoming header, propagated to downstream calls and included in every log line, so you can trace one request across services. Implement with a servlet filter that sets it in the MDC and response header, and forward it in RestClient/WebClient/Feign interceptors and Kafka headers. In Spring Boot 3, Micrometer Tracing does this automatically with W3C traceparent and traceId in MDC.

💡 Also attach the ID as a Sentry tag so a support ticket's request ID leads straight to the error.

How do you capture handled exceptions or messages manually?

Call Sentry.captureException(ex) for caught exceptions you still want visibility on, or Sentry.captureMessage("Payment retry exhausted", SentryLevel.WARNING) for notable conditions without an exception. Use Sentry.withScope (Java) or Sentry.withScope(scope => ...) (JS) to add tags/context only to that event. Don't report expected business validation errors – they create noise.

What are SLI, SLO, SLA and an error budget?

An SLI is a measurement of good events over total events (successful, fast requests). An SLO is the internal target for it, such as 99.9% over 30 days. An SLA is the external contract, usually looser, with consequences if missed. The error budget (100% − SLO) is how much unreliability you can afford; teams use it to balance shipping features against reliability work, and alert on how fast it is being burned.

Your team ignores Sentry because it has thousands of issues. How do you fix it?
  • Filter noise at the source: inbound filters, ignoreErrors, denyUrls for extensions, and beforeSend for known harmless errors.
  • Fix grouping with fingerprints so one bug is one issue.
  • Assign ownership rules so every issue lands with a team.
  • Alert only on new issues, regressions and user-impact spikes, routed per team.
  • Triage the top issues weekly, resolve them "in next release", and archive the rest with conditions.

💡 The goal is that every alert is actionable.

How does a trace connect the Angular front end with the Spring Boot back end?

The browser SDK starts a transaction for a page load or navigation and attaches sentry-trace and baggage headers to requests whose URLs match tracePropagationTargets. The Java SDK reads these headers and continues the same trace ID, adding spans for the controller, JDBC and outgoing HTTP calls. The backend must allow those headers in CORS. The same idea works with OpenTelemetry's W3C traceparent header.

Breadcrumbs, tags or MDC values go missing for code run in @Async or a thread pool. Why?

Sentry's scope and SLF4J's MDC are stored per thread (thread-local). When work moves to another thread — @Async, CompletableFuture.supplyAsync, an executor — that context is not copied by default. Fix it by wrapping tasks to copy the context: a Spring TaskDecorator that copies MDC.getCopyOfContextMap() and forks the Sentry scope, or Micrometer context-propagation for Reactor. The same caution applies to virtual threads created by a custom executor.

Ad blockers stop Sentry events from the browser. What can you do?

Use the SDK's tunnel option: the browser sends events to an endpoint on your own domain (for example /monitoring), and your backend forwards them to Sentry. Because the request goes to your domain, blockers don't filter it. Validate that the forwarded DSN/project is yours so the endpoint can't be abused as an open proxy, and rate-limit it.

How do you monitor scheduled jobs (for example a nightly @Scheduled task)?

Errors alone don't tell you a job didn't run. Use cron/heartbeat monitoring: the job sends a check-in when it starts and when it finishes (Sentry Cron Monitors, or a heartbeat to an uptime tool), and an alert fires if a check-in is missed or the job runs too long or fails. Also emit a metric for duration and records processed, and log a clear summary line per run.

What does "resolve in next release" do, and what is a regression?

Marking an issue resolved in the next release tells Sentry the fix will ship in the next release it sees (based on the release value set in the SDK and created in CI). Events from older releases don't reopen it, but if the same error happens in the fixed release or later, Sentry reopens it as a regression and can alert. That only works if every deployment sets a correct release (for example the Git SHA or version).

PHP 8 & Twig Server-side

Modern PHP (8.x) is a typed, object-oriented language with Composer packages, PSR standards and a shared-nothing request model. Twig is the template engine that keeps HTML apart from PHP logic and escapes output by default.

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

namespace App\Patient;

enum Status: string {
    case Active   = 'active';
    case Inactive = 'inactive';
}

final class Patient
{
    public function __construct(
        public readonly int $id,
        public readonly string $name,
        private Status $status = Status::Active,
        private ?Address $address = null,
    ) {}

    public function city(): ?string
    {
        return $this->address?->city;          // nullsafe operator
    }

    public function label(): string
    {
        return match ($this->status) {
            Status::Active   => "{$this->name} (active)",
            Status::Inactive => "{$this->name} (inactive)",
        };
    }
}

$p = new Patient(id: 42, name: 'Asha');       // named arguments
echo $p->label();

Request Lifecycle (php-fpm / Apache)

PHP uses a shared-nothing model: every HTTP request starts with a clean state, runs the script, sends the response and throws away all objects and variables. Nothing stays in memory between requests unless you put it in a session, a cache (Redis, APCu) or the database.

  • Nginx + php-fpm: the web server forwards .php requests over FastCGI to a pool of PHP worker processes (FPM = FastCGI Process Manager). Pool size is set with pm.max_children.
  • Apache + mod_php: PHP runs inside the Apache process. Apache can also hand requests to php-fpm through proxy_fcgi.
  • OPcache stores the compiled opcodes in shared memory so scripts are not parsed again on every request. Turn it on in production.
  • Steps: web server → FPM worker → autoload / bootstrap → router / front controller → controller → template → response → state is cleared.

Java works differently. A Spring Boot app is one long-running JVM with singletons and connection pools that live across requests. In PHP, "application startup" runs on every request.

Variables, Types, strict_types & Arrays

Variables start with $ and are dynamically typed. You can add scalar types (int, float, string, bool) and array, object, mixed, iterable, callable, nullable ?T, union types int|string (8.0), intersection types A&B (8.1), never (8.1), and DNF types (A&B)|null (8.2).

By default PHP coerces scalars, so "5" passed to an int parameter becomes 5. Putting declare(strict_types=1); as the first statement of a file turns off coercion for calls made from that file, and a wrong type throws TypeError. Compare with === (checks type and value) rather than == (loose comparison).

<?php
declare(strict_types=1);

function dose(int $mg): string { return "$mg mg"; }

dose(5);      // "5 mg"
dose("5");    // TypeError under strict_types (would coerce without it)

var_dump(0 == "a");   // false in PHP 8 (was true in PHP 7)
var_dump("1" === 1);  // false

Arrays & key functions. The PHP array is an ordered hash map. One type covers lists (indexed, integer keys) and maps (associative, string keys). Arrays are passed by value with copy-on-write. Objects are passed by handle.

$ids   = [10, 20, 30];                         // indexed
$vital = ['bp' => '120/80', 'pulse' => 72];   // associative

$vital['temp'] = 98.6;
foreach ($vital as $key => $value) { echo "$key: $value\n"; }

$doubled = array_map(fn($n) => $n * 2, $ids);
$big     = array_filter($ids, fn($n) => $n > 15);
$sum     = array_reduce($ids, fn($c, $n) => $c + $n, 0);
$names   = array_column($rows, 'name', 'id');  // id => name map
[$first, $second] = $ids;                      // destructuring
$merged  = [...$ids, 40];                      // spread
$found   = array_find($ids, fn($n) => $n > 15); // PHP 8.4
